Future conservation actions will include field surveys of the known ranges of all four subspecies with the objective of identifying two or more sites within each range that could be developed as protected areas. The above-mentioned activities will then be launched in nearby communities, and people will also be trained in protected area administration and management, nature guiding and interpretation, small business management and other vocations that help to promote the sustainable use of their protected area under the supervision of the government’s Department of Wildlife Conservation. Efforts to mitigate human-monkey conflicts with active participation of local communities will also be an important component of future conservation actions.Active participation of local communities in managing and deriving sustainable benefits from natural habitats is a new concept in Sri Lanka. It was presented and discussed during two workshops where it received favourable responses from government authorities and non-governmental organizations. Therefore, this idea has been incorporated into a Conservation Action Plan for all Sri Lankan monkey species that is currently being developed according to IUCN guidelines. When this Action Plan is completed it will be submitted to the Sri Lankan government and the IUCN for approval.While a sensible conservation action plan has been developed its implementation will depend a great deal on political will, financial support and many unknowns about people and their environment. Therefore, even with unfettered financial and political support it may take several years to bring this action plan to fruition. However, a start has been made with the hope that the threat of endangerment and extinction of the Purple-faced Langur will be eliminated as soon as possible.

rationale: Although the population trend is increasing, the species is listed as Critically Endangered as currently there are fewer than 50 mature individuals remaining. The entire population exists on Cat Ba Island, where it has a small range that is prone to habitat impacts from threats of fires, tourism and development.
habitat: This species is associated with forests on limestone (karst) hills. The caves found in this habitat are thought to offer protection from predators and temperature extremes but, if accessible to people, this habitat is also where human hunters capture or kill sleeping Langurs (Nadler et al., 2003). It is arboreal and terrestrial, and diurnal and mildly crepuscular. Like other Langurs, this species is mainly folivorous, with leaves making up between 75-87% of its diet; the rest is composed of fruit, flowers, and stems (Hendershott et al., in prep.). Forty-two families of plants with 98 plant species have been reported to constitute their diet. Social composition is unimale-multifemale groups with and, despite the small number of animals remaining, bachelor bands composed of several males have been identified (Luu Tuong Bach and Le Van Dung, 2013). Home range is estimated to be ca 30–50 ha. Group size ranges from solitary animals up to 21-23 animals with no “undisturbed” groups from which to evaluate natural group size.Breeding happens through the year with winter months showing a large increase in frequency of births.  February and April are the months with the most births.  Given the approximately 6-month gestation period this indicates that the peak conception month is August, near the end of the rainy season.
threats: Poaching, primarily for traditional "medicine" with secondary hunting for sport has been recognized as the most severe historical threat to Cat Ba Langurs, and the reason for the precipitous decline in their population over the past decades (Nadler and Long, 2000). Reproductively valuable males were often the most common victims due to their behavior (Stenke and Chu Xuan Canh, 2004). This is highly questionable, however, as their behaviour is not enormously different and, if anything, females would be easier to hunt as they are often grouped together and there are more of them per group (Leonard Neahga in litt., 31 October 2019).Hunting for meat seems to have happened rarely due to the reputed poor taste of langur meat.Habitat disturbance and fragmentation resulting from the growing human population on Cat Ba Island (due in large part to the country's designation of the island as a new tourism center for northern Viet Nam), and rampant fires due to honey collectors (Nadler and Long, 2000) are also threats.Poorly regulated tourism in the inadequately managed Cat Ba National Park has direct effects on langur natural history, such as the disturbance to habitat in the karst archipelago where these monkeys live. The small size and fragmented nature of the remaining Cat Ba Langur population means that the species is at risk of inbreeding effects (or intrinsic effects to avoid inbreeding by not breeding at all), extremely limited mate-choice due to the small number of available females, and the chance of a natural or human disaster causing total or effective extinction. However, according to Leonard Neahga (in litt., 31 October 2019) the population would have been very small even at its peak, and would have been small for the last 12,000 years when the langurs were confined to Cat Ba as a result of rising sea levels. It is unlikely that the population was ever above 4-5,000 individuals at any point over the last 12,000 years. This suggests that major inbreeding effects would have already happened in the deep past and, potentially, been weeded out. The threat of disease remains a major concern.The presence of a group of non-native macaques on a nearby tourist island that have extensive daily contact with humans is a cause for concern due to the potential of escape and disease transmission.
population: The confirmed population of Trachypithecus poliocephalus in June 2016 was 51-54 individuals (30-35 mature individuals), a sharp drop from was 64-70 as of November 2015 (CBLCP unpublished information). As of this update the reason for this drop appears to have been poaching by people from the neighbouring province (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019). Previously published population numbers contain errors and a reevaluation of observation records indicates that in 2000 the population totalled between 40 and 53 animals. Records indicate that in 2003 the count was 40 confirmed animals, reaching 48 by 2010, and 56 by early 2014 (Leonard et al. 2015). Exact counts are difficult as some groups remain in inaccessible areas and are rarely seen.Previous population counts were not given at a regular time on the year, resulting in the appearance of a much greater fluctuation in population than is actually the case.  A January 01 population count from 2001-2019 based on CBLCP records removes some variation in previous population counts: 2000 47; 2001 47; 2002 40; 2003 40; 2004 40; 2005 43; 2006 46; 2007 47; 2008 48; 2009 49; 2010 48; 2011 50; 2012 49; 2013 53; 2014 56; 2015 59; 2016 53; 2017 55; 2018 57; 2019 60 (CBLCP unpublished information). The years prior to 2003 do not have reliable population counts. The total population as of October 2019 is 67 individuals (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019).Population numbers taken at the middle of the year often report higher numbers than the year-end/year-beginning counts due to them being taken after the majority of birth have taken place, but before infant mortality due to infanticide during the latter half of the year (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019).In 2015 there were three isolated subpopulations, down from a reported seven subpopulations in 2004. Movement observations in 2014 and 2015 indicate that at least two of the previously recorded seven subpopulations should be considered as a single subpopulation.Despite the decline in the number of subpopulations the over-all population numbers are on the rise, with a brief down-turn in 2015. Group size averages 5.9 to 6.5 animals, based on the October 2019 population of 67 individuals in 10-11 groups. Within each subpopulation some groups are single sex and there are several cases of solitary animals, usually male.  Average population growth is 2-3% per year with year-by-year variation from -10% to +8% (CBLCP unpublished information).The population declined to an estimated 500-600 langurs in 1970-1986 from an estimated 2,400-2,700 langurs that appears to have thrived in the ‘optimal’ karst habitat (Nadler and Long 2000). The population declined further in 1999-2000 by 50% or more from 104-135 individuals to 40-53 individuals.Phan et al. (2014) reported a population of 50-60 individuals on Cat Ba Island, in 12 groups of 4.67 individuals and through simulation studies predict an increase to 86 individuals in 2050. A more recent PVA (Lees et al., 2014) indicates a best guess increase in population to 200-300 individuals by 2050. The October 2019 population of 67 individuals is divided into 10-11 groups, including solitary animals and a bachelor male group, with an average group size of 5.9-6.5 individuals. Attempted male take-overs resulting in group fragmentation and reforming accounts for the variability in group number and size (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019).The 2014 PVA (Lees et al.) calculated extinction risks in two sites across the island and one off the island: The Sanctuary, Cua Dong, and the captive population at the Cuc Phuong National Park. The analyses showed a moderate extinction risk for the first population i.e. the Sanctuary with a 10.6% risk of extinction in the worst case scenario or ‘pessimistic’ case over 100 years. The Cua Dong population was most at risk with a 40.5% risk of extinction at the worst case scenario over 100 years. The low reproductive rate and low carrying capacity of the site increase the probability of extinction. The captive population ran a very high extinction risk of 100% in the worst case and 95% in the best case (or ‘optimistic’) over 50 years, owing to the susceptibility of the population to inbreeding and due to small population size.Births per year have been steadily increasing, with approximately 30% of the reproductively active females giving birth per year from 2014 until present (2019) except for 2016. A concurrent increase in infant mortality has been recorded, the majority of which have been linked with infanticide during male take-over attempts.  This combined with the current lack of predators on Cat Ba indicates that the primary cause of infant deaths is likely to be infanticide (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019).From 2014 to October 2019 infant mortality has averaged 22%, but is highly variable on a year-by-year level, ranging from 13% to 36%.  Infant mortality averaged over the years the CBLCP has been active, 2000-present (2019) is 16% with a variation ranging from 0% to 36% on individual years (Neahga Leonard in litt., 31 October 2019).
range: This species is known only from northern Viet Nam. Trachypithecus poliocephalus is confined to Cat Ba Island, in Ha Long Bay off the northeastern coast of Viet Nam. There it is further restricted to an area of occupancy of less than a 22 km². The entire population resides within Cat Ba National Park after the 2006 expansion of the park borders to include langur habitat (Decision No. 2355/QD-UBND). The Langurs are regularly seen at sea level and collar data from two translocated individuals indicates a preference for habitat ranging from sea level to 130 m elevation (CBLCP unpublished information).
useTrade: Earlier, the species was poached primarily for traditional "medicine" with secondary hunting for sport. Now, it is protected and rarely utilized.
conservationActions: This species is currently listed in CITES Appendix II. Classified as Critically Endangered and listed as a Top 25 Endangered Primate since 2000.Since November 2000, T. poliocephalus and its habitat on Cat Ba have been the subject of the Cat Ba Langur Conservation Project (implemented by the Münster Zoo and the Zoological Society for the Conservation of Species and Populations, ZGAP, currently administered by Zoo Leipzig), which has been focused on the improvement of protection status for the species and its habitat, and has initiated two important programs. The first is a langur sanctuary located inside Cat Ba National Park and a "buffer zone" of the World Heritage Site "Halong Bay". Fifty-eight percent of the remaining population lives in the sanctuary. The second is a Langur-guarding program that is meant to protect 42% of the population that exists elsewhere in the national park. This program puts the subpopulations and their ranges under joint control of the national park and local people who patrol the ranges and offer community conservation education. The most important steps in the recovery of this subspecies now are continued protection from encroachment, a reduction in the habitat fragmentation and subpopulation isolation, and an increase in reproductive output and genetic health of the entire population, suggesting the need for translocation and meta-population management, including the ex-situ population. Poaching of the Langurs specifically appears to have completely stopped on Cat Ba with the last confirmed incident in 2001, although the threat remains and the drop in population in early 2016 raises the possibility that poaching by non-local people is experiencing a revival.A few T. poliocephalus are held in the collection of the Endangered Primate Rescue Center, Cuc Phuong National Park, Viet Nam (Nadler 1999), numbering five individuals at time of writing, coming from only two founders.Some of the recommended interventions are connecting populations across sites and designing management plans for the small captive population (Lees et al. 2014).

rationale: Considering the extensive habitat loss from forest fires and clearance for oil palm plantations and hunting for pet trade that has taken place within the range of the species, there has been a suspected decline probably at a rate of more than 30% over the past three generations (approximately 36 years), thus qualifying if for listing as Vulnerable under criterion A2cd. Given the continuing rate of decline in habitat as per the World Forest Status report in the habitat and increased hunting, the species is expected to decline at the same rate in the future thus also qualifying for criterion A3cd.
habitat: Most of what is known of this species is from Peninsular Malaysia, which is a small portion of the range for the species. In Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo it is known mostly from riparian and mangrove forest (V. Nijman pers. comm.), while in Sumatra it is found in a variety of primary and secondary forest types, including riverine, mangrove, swamp, montane and coastal (Furuya 1961, MacKinnon and MacKinnon 1987). It is occasionally found in plantations. This species is mainly folivorous, with leaves comprising 60 to 80% of the diet (Nadler et al. 2003). However, it will also feed on fruit, seeds, flowers, and young shoots (Bernstein 1968, Furuya 1961). They are not seasonal breeders and the average gestation period is 194.6 days and ovarian cycle of ca 24 days. Allomothering is common in this species.
threats: Disappearance of suitable lowland habitat due to land clearance (especially for oil palm plantations) and forest fires is a major threat to this species, especially in Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo. The species is hunted in Sarawak, while in Sumatra it is heavily traded and is a popular pet.Trachypithecus c. vigilance has a very restricted distribution on Serasan Island (62 km²), and it is threatened by land clearance and forest fires. Trachypithecus c. cristatus is hunted for meat and captured as pets.
population: Very little is known about this species, and most of what is known is from Peninsular Malaysia. It is reported to be rare in Borneo.
range: This species occurs in Brunei, Indonesia (Bangka, Belitung, Kalimantan Borneo, the Natuna Islands, Lingga, Bintang, Sugi, Jombol, and Bakang in the Riau Archipelago, and Sumatra), and Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak Borneo, and a strip along the western coast of the Peninsula). It might occur on Batam in the Riau Archipelago as well (Groves 2001).Trachypithecus cristatus cristatus: occurs in Brunei, Indonesia (Bangka, Belitung, Kalimantan Borneo, Lingga, Bintang, Sugi, Jombol, and Bakang in the Riau Archipelago, and Sumatra), and Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak Borneo, and a strip along the western coast of the Peninsula). May occur on Batam in the Riau Archipelago as well (Groves 2001).Trachypithecus cristatus vigilans: occurs on Sirhassen (Serasen), in the Natuna Islands, Indonesia (Groves 2001).
useTrade: The species is hunted in Sarawak, while in Sumatra it is heavily traded and is a popular pet.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. It is known to occur in at least four protected areas: Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park and Gunung Leuser National Park in Indonesia, and Bako National Park and Taman Negara National Park in Malaysia; is may occur as well in Tanjung Puting National Park, Indonesia (M. Richardson pers. comm.). There is a small worldwide captive population.

rationale: Trachypithecus barbei is assessed as Vulnerable. It is known from three locations with an extent of occurrence of 6,811 km². There is a suspected continuing decline in number of mature individuals due to hunting, and decline in habitat quality due to human activities.
habitat: This species is found in moist subtropical evergreen forests in the border area between Myanmar and Thailand.
threats: Hunting of unclear intensity occurs in China and Thailand. In addition, there is a suspected continuing decline of the population due to a decline in habitat quality due to human activities.
population: There is no information about the population size. No recent information about population trends. However, it is suspected to be undergoing continuing decline due to hunting, and decline in habitat quality due to human activities.
range: There exists only little information about the distribution of the species. One infant was recorded in June 2013 from Tanintharyi Nature Reserve, Myanmar (1,700 km²) (Kolleck et al. 2013). On the Thailand side of the border, interview results confirm the occurrence from Sai Yok Yai National Park (500 km²) and in Thong Pha Phum National Park (1,120 km²) where three groups were recorded with 15–25 individuals (Nadler, pers. comm.).
useTrade: It is hunted for food and 'medicine'.
conservationActions: One infant was recorded in June 2013 from Tanintharyi Nature Reserve, Myanmar (Kolleck et al. 2013), and the species is known to occur in Sai Yok Yai National Park and in Thong Pha Phum National Park in Thailand (Nadler, pers. comm). Three animals are known from captive facilities in Thailand (Dusit and Pata Zoos, Bangkok and Krabok Koo Wildlife Breeding Center) (Nadler, pers. comm.). No conservation actions are known to be in place for this species.

rationale: Even though the species appears to be widespread with the extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated at ~120,000km2 (DWNP 2010), forest loss probably exceeded 70% over 3 generations (36 years) has led to a suspected decline in population of over 50% in that time from hunting, habitat loss, fragmentation, habitat conversion to agriculture, and pet trade.
habitat: This species prefers closed primary forests, but is also found in old-growth secondary and disturbed forests, plantations, urban areas, and parks, suggesting a fairly high adaptive capability when compared with most colobine species. It is diurnal, primarily arboreal, and folivorous, although the diet is relatively varied and the animals will also consume fruit, flowers and other items. Individuals are able to take advantage of unripe fruit, which have chemical defenses, by the same means that they break down toxins in plant leaves, using the bacteria found in their digestive system (MacKinnon and MacKinnon 1980). Populations living in commensalism with humans frequently consume domesticated fruits and vegetables, and processed foods. This species is found in unimale-multifemale or multimale-multifemale groups, with a group size of 10-20 individuals. Home range approximates 33 ha and daily movement of 950 m/day. They are not seasonal breeders, and have a gestation period of 150 days (Groves et al. 2013). In certain places, they are sympatric with T. selangorensis, P. femoralis, and P. siamensis.
threats: Hunting for food is a major threat, as is fragmentation, habitat loss and degradation due to expanding oil palm plantations, agriculture, urbanization, and touristic development (Groves et al. 2013). In Peninsular Malaysia the langurs are frequent victims of road-kill (Boonratana 2003).
population: On the mainland, at five sites surveyed (Kuala Lompat, Pasoh, Sungai Kenyam, Ulu Sebol, and Lesong), the density was estimated at 1.8-7.3 groups/km2, with an average group size of 14 individuals. The population status of several of the insular forms (Penang, Langkawi, Dayang Bunting, Tarutao, East Perhentian, Pennan) is unclear. Some small isolated mainland populations outside protected areas are likely extirpated (e.g. in Kuala Berang, Malaysia) or suffer from genetic erosion (e.g. in Bukit Pelindung, Malaysia).
range: This species occurs in Malaysia (throughout the Malay Peninsula along with a few small adjacent islands), southern Myanmar (including the Mergui Archipelago), and southwestern Thailand (including adjacent islands). It is found north to 15°10'N in Myanmar and Thailand (Groves 2001, Roos et al. 2014). T. o. obscurus: Found on Peninsular Malaysia, north to about Perlis State. T. o. carbo: Found off the western coast of the Thai-Malay Peninsula, specifically on Tarutao Island (Thailand), and on Dayang Bunting Islands and Langkawi Island (Malaysia). T. o. flavicauda: Found in northern Peninsular Malaysia, from Perlis north to the northern border of the species' range; southern Myanmar (S of c.15°10’N including James, Kisseraing, and King Islands in the Mergui Archipelago) and southwestern Thailand (including Koh Lak Island). T. o. halonifer: Restricted to Penang Island, off Peninsular Malaysia. T. o. sanctorum: Restricted to Zadetkyi Kyun (St. Matthew Island) in the Mergui Archipelago, off western Myanmar. T. o. seimundi: Occurs on Ko Phangan Island (Pennan Island), Thailand; may possibly occur in adjacent eastern coast of the Thai-Malay Peninsula. T. o. styx: Occurs on East Perhentian Island, and probably also on the adjacent eastern coast of the Thai-Malay Peninsula.
useTrade: The species is hunted for food throughout its range.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. It is known to occur in a number of protected areas, including: Krau Wildlife Reserve, Penang Botanical Gardens, Taman Negara National Park (Malaysia); Kaeng Krachan, Khao Sam Roi Yot, Khao Sok, Phangan, Tarutao, and Thale Ban National Parks (Thailand) (Groves et al. 2013). Outside the protected areas, an isolated population at Khao Lommuak receives protection by virtue of being located within an air force base. Though population estimates are not available it is believed to be stable or showing ‘slow decline’. The insular forms are restricted and need more research and survey to understand the conservation status of these subspecies. It is relatively common in captivity.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered as there is reason to believe the population has declined by at least 50% over the past three generations (36 years) due primarily to hunting and habitat loss. The species is hunted for food and traditional “medicine,” sometimes as illegal exports to China. Habitat loss from agriculture and wood extraction is a major threat. A large length of the Chindwin (where the species was discovered) and its adjacent plains are scheduled to be inundated by the Tazone hydro-electric power dam (currently on hold). As well as direct loss of habitat through inundation this will result in massive increases in hunting as the construction labourers will be expected to live off the land, and the reservoir formed will greatly increase accessibility to a huge area of foothill forest; without specific, directed, management, hunters will no doubt take advantage of this. Habitat loss is severe habitats below 900 m in Myanmar, where degradation and fragmentation are ongoing. Hence, the species is suspected to decline at the same rate in the future also unless measures are taken to halt the trend.
habitat: This species occurs primarily in evergreen and semi-evergreen forests. It is largely arboreal, sometimes terrestrial, and folivorous. Records with known altitudes range from 200 to 2,500 m (Pocock, 1939) but it is possible that the species does not have viable populations in the upper 600-1,200 m of this range: collecting expeditions very rarely encountered it in the highlands, compared with its evident abundance in the Chindwin lowlands. It does not occur in the lower Chindwin, below the change from largely evergreen forest to largely deciduous.
threats: These animals are hunted for food and traditional “medicine,” sometimes as illegal exports to China. Habitat loss for agriculture and wood extraction is also a major threat. A large length of the Chindwin (where the species was discovered) and its adjacent plains are scheduled to be inundated by the Tazone hydro-electric power dam. As well as direct loss of habitat through inundation this will result in massive increases in hunting as the construction labourers will be expected to live off the land, and the reservoir formed will greatly increase accessibility to a huge area of foothill forest; without specific, directed, management, hunters will no doubt take advantage of this. A very large area of suitable habitat falls within the proposed Hukaung Tiger Reserve, but it is unclear whether this area supports morphologically typical animals. If they do not occur in Hukaung, habitat loss is a sever threat to the species, because most other protected areas in the Myanmar part of its range are highland, and habitat below 900 m is heavily degraded and fragmented, and such processes are ongoing.
population: Numbers are not known for this species, but the populaiton is believed to be declining rapidly owing to loss of habitat and hunting. The total population must be small, given the species’ restricted geographical range.
range: This species occurs in southwestern China (Dulongjiang Valley, northwestern Yunnan) and northeastern Myanmar. In Myanmar, south of the Hukaung valley, it is found only east of the Chindwin River, with allied Trachypithecus pileatus to the west (Pocock, 1939). The situation in the Chindwin headwaters (Hukawng valley) is unclear, because animals show morphological variation suggesting the possibility of inter-gradation with T. pileatus and/or undescribed variation within T. shortridgei (Duckworth and Tizard pers. comm). Morphologically typical animals also occur east of the Hukaung (Pidaung) and north almost to Hkakaborazi (Pocock, 1939). It also occurs along the Dulong River in Gongshan District, Yunnan (Groves 2001).
useTrade: The species is hunted for meat.
conservationActions: This species is listed in CITES Appendix I. In Myanmar it is a protected species under the Wildlife Protection Law and occurs in at least two protected areas: Hukaung Tiger Reserve where taxonomic status is unresolved, Hponkanrazi Wildlife Sanctuary and Hkakaborazi National Park. In China it is a protected species and occurs in one protected area, Gaoligongshan Nature Reserve (L. Yongcheng pers. comm.).

rationale: Rungwecebus kipunji is sparsely distributed (Davenport et al. 2006, 2008; Bracebridge et al. 2011, 2012). The small areas of habitat where it occurs (42.4 km² in Rungwe-Kitulo and ~25 km² in Ndundulu), and the species' patchy distribution in Rungwe-Kitulo give grounds for considerable conservation concern. Totalling 68 km², its area of occupancy (AOO) is below the 500 km² upper threshold for an Endangered listing under criterion B2. At 3,518 km², the taxon’s extent of occurrence (EOO) also meets the threshold for criterion B1. In addition, the habitat is fragmented and remote sensing analyses of forest loss in Rungwe-Kitulo indicate a decline over the last 30 years, which although now slowing, is continuing. The management of Mt Rungwe is currently dependent on funds from the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS). Forest loss has been reduced but continues in key areas. Persistent hunting of these monkeys across Rungwe-Kitulo (and possibly Ndundulu) – especially individuals which raid crops – as well as the precarious nature of the small population in Ndundulu, where logging, charcoal making and unmanaged resource extraction are commonplace, lead us to project a continuing decline in AOO, area, extent and quality of habitat, and the number of mature individuals remaining. As a consequence, the species is here listed as EN B1ab+2ab.
habitat: Habitat ranges from degraded montane and upper montane forest from 1,700–2,150 m in Rungwe-Kitulo (Davenport et al. 2006, 2008, Bracebridge et al. 2011, 2012) to submontane forest in Ndundulu (Davenport and Jones 2005, Jones et al. 2005). In Rungwe-Kitulo, the canopy is often broken and between 10 and 30 m with emergents reaching 35 m. Kipunji prefers steep-sided gullies and valley edges and is rarely found far from streams (Davenport 2013). Ridges and open areas are generally avoided and the animals are not territorial (De Luca et al. 2010). The forest was much reduced by logging from 1960s to 1980s (Lovett 1986, McKone and Walzem 1994, Machaga et al. 2004, Davenport 2005, 2006). Thick undergrowth is typical, with the tree fern Cyathea manniana, wild banana Ensete ventricosum, and large stands of bamboo Sinarundinaria alpina common in the south and southeast of Mt Rungwe and the northwest of Livingstone. The upper limits of this distribution are likely due to the floristic changes at around 2,000–2,200m asl, where bamboo Sinarundinaria alpina, often interspersed with Hagenia abyssinica or Podocarpus latifolius, dominate (Bracebridge et al. 2011). The species rarely frequents the bamboo and leaves the forest only to raid nearby crops, especially maize. In southern Mt Rungwe, annual rainfall ranges from ca 185–280 cm and there is an indistinct and short dry season from June to October. In Ndundulu, the Parinari excelsa-dominant forest is undisturbed and the canopy is unbroken, reaching heights of 40–50 m. When comparing predictions from an interpolation analysis for a habitat suitability model with the EOO, the vast majority of the most suitable areas in Rungwe-Kitulo were already occupied by Kipunji (Bracebridge et al. 2011). The best forest for Kipunji would be at mid to lower altitude with a closed canopy. However, as much of Rungwe-Kitulo contains heterogeneous forest, reflecting a history of disturbance (Davenport et al. 2006, Davenport, 2009), forest is often fragmented and contains a mix of primary, secondary and regenerating forest. This suggests that while not optimal, Kipunji can tolerate disturbed habitat reasonably well (Bracebridge et al. 2011).
threats: The Rungwe-Kitulo forests are degraded. Logging, charcoal making, illegal hunting and unmanaged resource extraction have long been commonplace (Machaga et al. 2004, Davenport 2005, 2006). The narrow Bujingijila corridor linking Mt Rungwe Nature Reserve to Livingstone Forest in Kitulo National Park, and the corridors joining the northern and southern sections of Livingstone, are encroached by farmers and degraded (Davenport 2005, Mwakilema and Davenport 2005). Subpopulations are therefore fragmented even within the same forest protected area. Kipunji is hunted with log traps and with also with dogs (Davenport 2005, 2006), mainly as retribution for the crop-raiding of maize (and the leaves of beans and potatoes) and primarily from January to April. However, the monkey is also occasionally hunted for food. Although Ndundulu Forest is in good condition and largely undisturbed, the species is present there in low numbers (Davenport et al. 2008) and the reasons for this are unclear (Marshall et al. 2015). Both Kilombero and Mt Rungwe Nature Reserves lack management resources.
population: Surveys totalling 2,864 hours and covering 3,456 km of transect were undertaken by Davenport et al. (2008) to determine distribution and group numbers. In addition, 772 hours of simultaneous multi-group observational follows in Rungwe-Kitulo and Ndundulu forests enabled 209 total counts to be carried out. Davenport et al. (2008) estimated some 1,042 individuals in Rungwe-Kitulo, ranging from 25 to 39 individuals per group (µ = 30.65; SE = 0.62; n = 34), and 75 individuals in Ndundulu, ranging from 15 to 25 individuals per group (µ = 18.75; SE = 2.39; n = 4). The total Kipunji population was thus estimated to be 1,117 animals in 38 groups (µ = 29.39; SE = 0.85; n = 38). The Ndundulu population is restricted and the Rungwe-Kitulo population is highly fragmented with isolated subpopulations remaining in degraded habitat (Davenport et al. 2008). Kipunji densities appear to be over three times greater in the secondary forests of Rungwe-Kitulo than in the primary forests of the Udzungwa population (Davenport et al. 2008), which is likely an effect of forest quality, but also perhaps competition with other diurnal primates not present in Rungwe-Livingstone (Bracebridge et al. 2011).
range: A Tanzanian endemic known from two populations separated by ca 350 km of non-forested, agricultural land. One population is at 1,750–2,450 m asl in 12.4 km² of Rungwe-Kitulo Forest (Davenport et al. 2008) in the Southern Highlands of south-western Tanzania (09.12º-09.18ºS, 33.67º-33.92ºE). The Rungwe-Kitulo Forest includes Mt Rungwe Nature Reserve (150 km²) and the Livingstone Forest (191 km²), which lies within the 412 km² Kitulo National Park (Davenport 2002, Davenport and Bytebier 2004, Davenport et al. 2005, 2006, 2008). Mt Rungwe and Livingstone Forest (in Kitulo) are connected by the Bujingijila Corridor, a 2-km wide degraded forest connection (Davenport 2005, 2006, Mwakilema and Davenport 2005). The Kipunji inhabits the wetter forest of south Mt Rungwe and isolated groups are scattered in the north and south of Livingstone Forest (Davenport et al. 2006, 2008, Bracebridge et al. 2011).  The other population of R. kipunji is found at 1,300–1,750 m asl in the Vikongwa Valley, Ndundulu Forest (07.67º-07.85ºS, 35.17º-36.83ºE; ca 180 km of closed forest), in the Kilombero Nature Reserve in the Udzungwa Mountains, south-central Tanzania (Jones et al. 2015). The area known to be occupied by the species in the Ndundulu Forest is approximately 25 km² (Davenport pers obs. in Marshall et al. 2015) and Kipunji density is low. Research indicates that the animal is absent from the contiguous Udzungwa Mountains National Park (Davenport et al. 2008, Marshall et al. 2015). The species' area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be 42.4 km² in Rungwe-Kitulo (Bracebridge et al. 2011) and ~25 km² in Ndundulu (Davenport pers. obs. in Marshall et al. 2015), with a combined total AOO of only 67.5 km².
useTrade: Occasionally hunted for food. More often hunted as retribution for crop-raiding using log traps or dogs (Davenport 2005, 2006). Hunting of Kipunji is illegal.
conservationActions: Rungwecebus kipunji is listed on Appendix II of CITES. Kipunji occurs entirely in protected areas, 48.4% in Kitulo National Park, 44.9% in Mt Rungwe Nature Reserve and 6.7% in the Kilombero Nature Reserve (Davenport et al. 2008). However, only the national park has independent management activities and resources, and they remain limited, especially in the forest. The focus of current Kipunji conservation work is the protection and restoration of the montane habitats of Mt Rungwe, especially the forest connections, such as the (2.1 km²) Bujingijila corridor (Davenport 2006, Bracebridge et al. 2011). Protecting corridors is of the highest priority for the conservation of this genus/species and Bujingijila could provide habitat for an additional 88 Kipunji (8% population increase), using density estimates from the 2008 census (Bracebridge et al. 2013). It also has the benefit of reconnecting the Mt Rungwe and Kitulo kipunji subpopulations. Furthermore, conservation management, while focusing on promoting old growth forest, should also consider populations of some important pioneer tree species such as Macaranga capensis, both in the forest and in reforestation schemes outside the species’ current Area of Occupancy (Bracebridge et al. 2012).Kipunji is being used as a 'flagship species' by WCS's long-term Southern Highlands Conservation Program in and around Rungwe-Kitulo, especially in education and awareness raising activities, and as part of a long-term monitoring programme. A habituated group is monitored daily for research, and a new group is being habituated for tourism.

rationale: Sciurocheirus gabonensis is assessed as Least Concern as the species is relatively widespread and there are no current major threats believed to be resulting in a range-wide population decline.
habitat: This species lives in the lower levels of mature tropical moist forest, and in secondary and logged forest, up to an altitude of 800 m. In mature forest it forages on the ground in areas with a clear floor and numerous lianas and tree trunks (Ambrose 2013). Diet is predominantly fruit, along with insects, snails and frogs (Charles-Dominique 1977). At Makokou the ranges of males (30-60 ha) were 3-5 times greater than those of females (8–10 ha) (Charles-Dominique 1977). Adult females are inferred to give birth once each year, usually to a singleton, but occasionally to twins (Charles-Dominique 1977).
threats: Habitat loss is the main threat to populations of this species, because it is not targeted by human hunters (although it may occasionally be caught in snares set for other mammals). Both small-scale forest clearance for subsistence farming and industrial logging contribute to forest loss within the range of S. gabonensis, with industrial logging being the most significant factor in Gabon (Tyukavina et al. 2018). The spread of industrial agriculture in the African moist-forest zone, particularly oil-palm cultivation, is a growing threat (Arcus Foundation 2014). FAO (2015) reports that annual forest loss in 2010-2015 was 1.1% in Cameroon, 0.9% in Gabon, and 0.1% in Republic of Congo. Selective logging of mature forest and rotational small-scale farming are not major threats to this species because of its ability to utilize secondary forest, but it will not persist where there is large-scale conversion of forest to cropland (such as monoculture oil-palm plantation).
population: This species has not been carefully studied across most of its range. Ambrose (2003) found it to occur in relatively low densities in primary forest in Cameroon, with the highest densities in logged littoral forest. In a primary and secondary forest mosaic at Makokou in Gabon, Charles-Dominique (1977) reports a density of 15-20 individuals per sq. km.
range: This species occurs from the Sanaga River in Cameroon, south through mainland Equatorial Guinea (Rio Muni) to the Ogooué River in Gabon and east through the southern Central African Republic and the Republic of the Congo,  probably to the Congo and Ubangui Rivers. The related species S. makandensis has been described from the Fôret des Abeilles in Gabon (Ambrose 2013), but it is presently uncertain whether populations of Sciurocheirus occurring in forests in Gabon south of the Ogooué River (outside the Fôret des Abeilles) and into the western part of the Congo Republic belong to this species, to S. makandensis, or to an as yet undescribed form; Ambrose (2003) mapped the populations in these forests as of “unknown” affinity.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It occurs in a number of protected areas in parts of its range.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as this species is widespread and common in many parts of its range and is not declining fast enough to place it in the Near Threatened category.
habitat: Euoticus elegantulus lives in primary and secondary lowland and mid-altitude moist forests. This nocturnal, arboreal species primarily feeds on gums and resins from trees and lianas, supplemented by invertebrates. Foraging individuals follow a regular route in the forest canopy, visiting gum-producing sites in sequence, and making an average of 100 gum-collections each hour (Charles-Dominique 1977, Ambrose 1999). Individuals forage alone but sleep communally. Females give birth to a single offspring annually (Charles-Dominique 1977).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to E. elegantulus. This species is not hunted and, in much of its range, human population density is relatively low. It is probably locally threatened through a loss of forest habitat, particularly as a result of increasing industrial-scale oil-palm cultivation (Arcus Foundation 2015).
population: Euoticus elegantulus is a locally common species with a large geographic range. Reported to be most abundant in secondary forest where gum and resin-producing food trees are more common. In the 1970s, its population in Makokou, Gabon, was 15–20 individuals/km² (Charles-Dominique 1977).
range: Euoticus elegantulus occurs between the Sanaga River in Cameroon and the Congo and Ubangui Rivers in Republic of the Congo. Present in Cameroon, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea (Rio Muni), Republic of Congo,  Angola (Cabinda enclave), and Democratic Republic of Congo (Kongo Central Province, north of the Congo River) (Ambrose 2013).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. Known to occur, or likely occurs, in many major protected areas in the region, including Boumba-Bek, Campo Ma’an and Lobéké National Parks and the Dja Biosphere Reserve in Cameroon; Dzanga-Ndoki National Park in Central African Republic; Monte Alen National Park in Equatorial Guinea (Rio Muni); the 12 terrestrial national parks of Gabon; Conkouati-Douli, Odzala-Koukoua and Nouabalé-Ndoki National Parks in Republic of Congo; andMaiombe National Park, Angola (Cabinda).

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered as it is has an area of occupancy (AOO) less than 500 km² (AOO is 356 km²) triggering criterion B2. Paragalago rondoensis is known from eight highly threatened forest patches (surveys have not recorded this species in two additional forest patches, where it was last recorded in 1992). The population severely fragmented and there is continuing decline in AOO; area and quality of habitat; and number of locations where the taxon occurs.There are two population clusters, 400 km apart: a northern meta-population in the coastal forests close to Dar es Salaam city and further north in Sadaani National path, and a southern meta-population as close as 22 km east/northeast of the coastal town of Lindi. The known range is under severe threat, as there is continuing loss and degradation of the species' habitat.
habitat: This species is found in patches of the East African coastal dry forest mosaic, usually in moist evergreen forest patches, often on east facing slopes and escarpments. It is presumed to give birth to one or two young per year.
threats: The main threats to this species are from ongoing habitat degradation of the Tanzanian coastal mosaic of forest, coastal woodland and thicket, mainly from logging, charcoal manufacture and agricultural expansion (Green et al. 2010). Paragalago rondoensis prefers high canopy evergreen forests of which there is very little left as a proportion of the coastal forest ecosystem (Burgess and Clarke 2000). This is despite the fact that all the sites where they occur are officially fall within legally designated protected areas. Deforestation rates between 1990–2000 for Tanzanian coastal forests are estimated at 0.6 %.y-1 (Tabor et al. 2010). The levels of threat vary from site to site. Forests closer to Dar es Salaam the capital city have suffered high demand for timber and charcoal (Ahrends 2005, Ahrends et. al. 2010) which has severely affected four sites where P. rondoensis occurs.This species is known from eight patches of forest which are under different management authorities and structures which intern impacts on the effective habitat protection on the ground (see Table 1 in the Supplementary Material). National Parks have the highest management capacity and resource levels, followed by Nature Reserves, Village Forest Reserves, National Forest Reserves, and Local Government Forest Reserves. Paragalago rondoensis is therefore most secure in Zaraninge forest protected in Sadaani National Park, Rondo Nature Reserve and Noto Forest Village Forest reserves cluster. All other localities are under severe pressure.
population: This is an uncommon species. Four individuals were recorded in a 0.5-ha plot in 2008 (A. Perkin unpubl. data 2008).
range: This species is known from eight isolated forest patches in Tanzania: Zaraninge forest (in Sadaani NP), Pande Game Reserve, Pugu/Kazimzumbwe, Ruvu South, Litipo, Ruawa, Chitoa, Noto forest reserves and Rondo Nature Reserve. It was previously recorded in Litipo and Ziwani forest reserves, but its presence is doubtful since there have been no records since 1992, despite considerable geographically widespread effort. It typically occurs at elevations of 200–900 m, but has been recorded as low as 100 m asl in Ziwani and Litipo forests. The known distribution encompasses 87.4 km² of coastal forest (area of occupation 356 km²). The type population on the Newala Plateau, 50–90 km south of the nearest extant population on the Rondo plateau, was extirpated by forest clearance for cashew plantations in the 1960s–1970s.
useTrade: This species is not hunted.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES.All currently known sites are officially within some sort of legally protected area, and all require improved management, especially the sites designated as Forest Reserves.International donor- and NGO-supported projects at a national level and at site level positively benefit P. rondoensis conservation. In the recent past NGO projects have helped to arrest some threats and have had one site (Noto) declared a protected area as a Village Forest Reserve. However, without external support many of these PAs are poorly resourced.Additional surveys in the intervening areas to determine whether the species is present or not are urgently required. Population monitoring is needed. Further genetic studies are important in understanding the phylogenetics of the northern and southern meta populations.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread and common, present in a number of protected areas throughout the range, and there are no major threats.
habitat: Demidoff's Dwarf Galago mainly occurs in primary and secondary tropical moist forests, but is also present in savanna woodlands, riverine, deciduous, littoral and gallery forests (Ambrose & Butynski 2013, Bersacola et al. 2015). This species is commonly associated with the understorey of secondary forest and forest edges, such as road sides, beside water courses and tree-fall zones (Ambrose & Butynski 2013). It prefers vegetation below 5 m, particularly dense undergrowth with fine branches (±1 cm) where it scurries, rather than leaping (Ambrose & Butynski 2013; Bersacola et al. 2015). It sleeps in small groups of up to 10 individuals, huddling in dense vegetation or in rounded leaf nests (Bearder et al. 2003). This galago has an insectivore-frugivore diet, consisting mainly of invertebrates (such as beetles and moths) and snails, but also fruits, gum, leaves and buds (Nekaris 2013). It gives birth to one or two young per year. The vocal profile is available on: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galagoides/demidovii/
threats: This species is locally threatened by habitat loss through deforestation for timber and conversion to agricultural land.
population: This species is common and widespread. Encounter rates range from 0.3 animals/km in semi-arid savanna woodland in western Angola, and 0.6 animals/km on Bioko Island (Croce 2009), to 6.8 animals/km in the northern part of the Angolan Escarpment (Bersacola et al. 2015).
range: This species has been recorded from southern Senegal and Guinea-Bissau in the west, through the Guinean forests of West Africa and into the Congo Basin. In the east it ranges as far as the River Nile north of Lake Victoria in Uganda and southwards along the Albertine Rift region, including northern Tanzania. In the south, it is found in the Cuanza Sul province of Angola, and possibly as far south as the Lukuga River (DRC) in the east. Widely sympatric with G. thomasi, but G. demidoff is thought to be absent from the Dahomey Gap: Ghana, Togo and Benin (Dowsett-Lemaire & Dowsett 2011).
conservationActions: Galago demidoff is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Paragalago granti is widespread over southeastern Africa and locally common. There is no indication that P. granti is currently undergoing a significant range-wide decline.
habitat: Paragalago granti is a nocturnal and arboreal species that occupies dry coastal forest, gallery forest, lowland evergreen and semi-evergreen forest and species-rich woodlands, including hilly miombo woodlands (e.g., Mahenge foothills) (Butynski et al. 2006, Honess et al. 2013). In ‘sand forest’ and dense woodland in northeastern South Africa (Génin et al. 2015, Yokwana et al. 2015).This species uses tree holes and is presumed to give birth to one or two young per year. Twinning appears to be common in South Africa (Génin et al. 2015).Paragalago granti is omnivorous, eating invertebrates, fruits, gums, flowers, and occasionally small birds (Honess 1996b, Lumsden and Masters 2001, Honess et al. 2013, Génin et al. 2015).A vocal profile of P. granti is available at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galagoides/mozambique-dwarf-galago-galagoides-granti/
threats: Paragalago granti is able to survive in habitats marginally affected by humans (Honess et al. 2013, Génin et al. 2015). There appear to be no major threats resulting in a range-wide population decline. Local declines are taking place due to habitat loss from clear-cutting and intensive agriculture related to fast-growing human populations.
population: Paragalago granti is locally common and abundant in evergreen and semi-evergreen forest and thicket, although its optimal habitat remains unknown (Honess et al. 2013, Génin et al. 2015). In southern Tanzania, most common in Namatimbili, Mtopwa, Ruawa, Ndimba, Matumbi Hills, Noto, Chitoa Forest and Rondo Nature Reserve (Honess 1996b, A. Perkin pers. obs. 2016). Is a common and widespread species.
range: Paragalago granti occurs from the Kilombero-Rufiji River and Udzungwa Mountains of southeastern Tanzania, southwards through eastern Mozambique, southern Malawi, and eastern Zimbabwe to Tshanini Nature Reserve in extreme northeastern South Africa (Smithers and Lobão Tello 1976, Smithers 1983, Jenkins 1987, Honess 1996b, Wallace 2005, Butynski et al. 2006, Bearder and Karlsson 2009, Perkin et al. 2011, Honess et al. 2013, Génin et al. 2015, Yokwana et al. 2015). Foley et al. (2014) report presence in Mahale National Park and Sitebe Mountains in southeastern Tanzania, but validation is required (Butynski et al. 2006). Validation also needed for a record from Mount Namuli in Mozambique. Recorded to at least 1,800 m asl (Butynski et al. 2006).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It is present in the East Ngorima Reserve and Chimanimani National Park of Zimbabwe.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread and relatively common, and there are no major threats believed to be resulting in a major range-wide decline.
habitat: G. thomasi are found in savanna and open woodland areas (e.g. Miombo), littoral and riparian forests, marshland, and at the margins of montane forest from at sea level up to 2,690 m above sea level. This species also occupies farmland and plantations (Ambrose & Butynski 2013), but avoids areas of grassland. They have been found in forests where no other galagos are present. G. thomasi are found in all strata although when sympatric with G. demidoff they tend to occupy the upper strata (10-20 m above ground; Bearder et al. 2003). G. thomasi tends to use broader support and leaps more frequently than G. demidoff. They build nests in thorn trees or nest in dense tangles of vegetation (Bearder et al. 2003, Kingdon 2015). Group size is normally 1-5, although in Uganda groups of up to 12 individuals were observed to nest together (Ambrose & Butynski 2013). They forage separately at night. Their diet consists mainly of insects, but also gum, fruits and seeds. This species gives birth to one or two young annually and births take place throughout the year (Ambrose & Butynski 2013).The vocal profile of G. thomasi is available on: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galagoides/thomass-dwarf-galago-galagoides-thomasi/
threats: This species is locally threatened by habitat loss through deforestation for timber and conversion to agricultural land, but there are no major threats to the species as a whole.
population: This is a widespread, adaptable and often common species. Highest densities have been observed in old secondary and mountain forests. No density estimates are available but encounter rates range from 0.2 animals/hr on Bioko Island (Ambrose & Perkin 2000) to 3 animals/hr in Okomu National Park, Nigeria (Bearder & Oates 2009).
range: Galagoides thomasi is found in West and Central Africa, although the distribution limits are uncertain. Animals currently assigned to this species have been recorded as museum specimens or in the wild from Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea (Bioko), Gabon, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Republic of Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia. The species may also occur in Angola, Guinea, Guinea Bissau, Central African Republic, Burundi and South Sudan, but this remains to be confirmed.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, Paragalago cocos is fairly widespread, locally abundant, and able to persist in secondary and/or highly fragmented vegetation. Although it is affected by habitat loss in some parts of its geographic range, there are no major threats to the species.
habitat: Paragalago cocos typically occupies the middle storey of dry, mixed, coastal lowland moist forest, riverine forest and secondary growth such as cultivated mosaic habitat (Bearder et al. 2003, Butynski et al. 2006, Harcourt and Perkin 2013). It has been found in Acacia woodland in some places where Galago senegalensis is absent (e.g. Bodhei on the north coast of Kenya; de Jong and Butynski 2011). G. cocos is also present in mixed cultivation, which includes coconut palm (Cocos nucifera), mango (Mangifera indica), cashew nut (Anacardium occi), and neem (Azadirachta indica). G. cocos sleeps in tree holes (de Jong and Butynski 2011; Harcourt and Perkin 2013). Paragalago cocos is omnivorous, feeding on both invertebrates and fruit. Females give birth to singletons (rarely twins) twice a year (Harcourt and Perkin 2013).Paragalago cocos is sympatric with Galago senegalensis and Otolemur garnettii, and is parapatric with G. z. udzungwensis or, perhaps, narrowly sympatric at a few sites on coastal north Tanzania. It is also probably parapatric with Galago gallarum near the coast in southeast Kenya (Butynski and de Jong 2004, Butynski et al. 2006).The vocal profile of P. cocos is available at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galagoides/cocos/ and a photographic map at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/photography/photomap/
threats: Paragalago cocos is locally threatened over much of its range by conversion of habitat to farm land, including plantations of pineapple and sisal. Persist in high density, however, in secondary growth, gardens and farms where a good tree cover occurs (Harcourt and Perkin 2013).
population: Paragalago cocos is the most abundant and widespread galago in the coastal forests of Kenya. Densities of ca 170–180 individuals/km² have been reported at both Gedi and Diani, Kenya (Harcourt and Nash 1986).
range: Paragalago cocos is endemic to the coastal region of Kenya and northern Tanzania (Butynski et al. 2006). From the north coast of Kenya to the northern coast of Tanzania (Mgambo Forest Reserve and Kilulu Hill Forest Reserve). Paragalago cocos might occur on the south coast of Somalia as far north as the Juba River or Shabeelle River (Butynski et al. 2006). A locality record from Nairobi (see Butynski et al. 2006, Harcourt and Perkin 2013) appears unfounded (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2014). At altitudes from sea level to at least 210 m asl on coastal of Kenya, and to at least 350 m asl in the foothills of the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania (Butynski et al. 2006).
conservationActions: Paragalago cocos is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It is present in the Arabuko-Sokoke National Park, Shimba Hills National Reserve, Tana River Primate National Reserve, Kipini Conservancy, Dodori National Reserve and probably Boni National Reserve, Kenya (Butynski et al. 2006, de Jong and Butynski 2011, Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2011). There is a need to better determine the geographic range, especially in Somalia (Butynski et al. 2006).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Widespread species which is sometimes locally common. There are no major threats that would lead to a significant range-wide population decline.
habitat: Galago gallarum is a nocturnal, arboreal species which lives in semi-arid thorn scrub and thorn scrub/woodlands. Occupies all strata within Acacia-Commiphora deciduous bushland and thicket (Butynski and de Jong 2004, 2013). Occupies woodland (including Acacia spp, Newtonia hildebrandtii, Melia volkensii) bordering swamp and Acacia-Commiphora bushland. Survives in severely degraded habitats (de Jong and Butynski 2010). Lives in drier and thornier habitats than any other African primate (Butynski and de Jong 2004, 2013).  G. gallarum is either solitary or exists in small groups. There is no information on reproduction, but it is likely that a single infant is born.G. gallarum produces a distinctive loud ‘quack’ call (Butynski and de Jong 2004). Their vocal profile can be found at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galago/gallarum/ and photographs at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/photography/
threats: A number of subpopulations throughout the range may be threatened by habitat degradation, fragmentation and loss. However, the semi-arid areas these galagos occupy are of little value for crop production. Present in over-grazed and over-browsed, degraded habitats (Butynski and de Jong 2004, 2013).
population: Galago gallarum is patchily distributed and locally common. Absent from large areas of unsuitable habitat throughout its range. Density over much of the range is <1 animal/ha, but much higher at some sites (e.g., >4 animals/ha in Meru National Park; Butynski and de Jong 2004).
range: Galago gallarum is endemic to the semi-arid thorn scrub and thorn scrub/woodlands of central and eastern Kenya, southern Somalia, and extreme south and extreme central east Ethiopia (Butynski and de Jong 2004, 2013). Distribution may extend into southeast Sudan but no records as yet. Present between the Webi Shebeli River Valley, Somalia, in the northeast and Tana River, Kenya, in the southwest. Towards Lake Turkana (at least as far west as South Horr) in Kenya and the Rift Valley in Ethiopia in the northwest. Not known to occur west of the Eastern Rift Valley. Distribution limits in the Ogaden area, south Ethiopia, and east and north of the Webi Shebeli River not known. Found in oases dominated by acacia and doum palm Hyphaene thebaica in the southeast Chalbi Desert, northern Kenya. Found from sea level to 1,250 m asl (Butynski and de Jong 2013).Narrowly sympatric with Galago senegalensis in Meru National Park, Kenya (Butynski and de Jong 2004) and near the Ndoto Mountains, Samburu County, Kenya (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong unpubl. data).
conservationActions: Galago gallarum is listed on Appendix II of CITES. In Kenya, present in Meru National Park, Shaba National Reserve, Arawale National Reserve and Dodori National Reserve (Butynski and de Jong 2004; de Jong and Butynski 2011). Further studies on the biogeography, taxonomy and ecology of this species are needed.

rationale: Galago matschiei is listed as Least Concern. The species is widespread, in some areas common, and present in several well protected sites. The geographic range is declining. This is mainly due to habit degradation, fragmentation and loss caused by rapidly expanding human populations. Overall, however, this species is not threatened range-wide.
habitat: Galago matschiei is an arboreal, nocturnal primate which occupies all strata within both primary and secondary lowland, mid-altitude, montane and bamboo forest; especially where Parinari excelsa is the dominant tree (Kingdon 2015, Ambrose 2006, Butynski and de Jong 2013). G. matschiei is omnivorous. They presumably feed on insects, fruits, flowers and gums. Their diet, however, is poorly known (Kingdon 2015, Ambrose 2006, Butynski and de Jong 2013). G. matschiei produces a distinctive loud call called ‘churr’ (Zimmerman 1990, Bearder et al. 1995, Ambrose 2002, 2006). Their vocal profile can be found at http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galago/matschiei/ and a photographic map at http://www.wildsolutions.nl/photography/
threats: Galago matschiei is locally threatened by deforestation, degradation and fragmentation mainly due to a fast growing human population in their geographical range, the conversion of forest into agricultural land and pasture, and the expansion of human settlements (Butynski and de Jong 2013).
population: Galago matschiei is relatively common in some sites, such as Kibale National Park, Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Zika Forest Reserve and Mpanga Forest Reserve (Ambrose 2002, 2006; Butynski & de Jong 2013). Encounter rates in Uganda vary between 0.08 and 1.71 individuals/hour and 0.00 to 0.57 calls per hour (Ambrose 2002, 2006).
range: Galago matschiei is found primarily in the forests of the Albertine Rift. Out-lying populations occur north of Lake Victoria and in the Bondo-Bili area of DR Congo. In forests from near Lake Albert (including Budongo), southwards along the flanks of the Albertine Rift to the southern end of the Itombwe Massif, DRC (Omari et al. 1999, Butynski and de Jong 2013). There is a narrow eastward range extension to just west of the Nile River, where in forest such as Mabira and Mpanga (Ambrose 2002). There is also a record from Moroto in northeast Uganda (Nash et al. 1989).  Galago matschiei occurs at 670–2,500 m asl (Dowsett and Dowsett-Lemaire 1990, Butynski and de Jong 2013).
conservationActions: Galago matschiei is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It lives in a number of protected areas, including Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (Uganda), Kibale National Park, and several forest reserves in southwest Uganda, Kahuzi-Biega National Park in DRC, Nyungwe National Park in Rwanda, and Kibira Natinal Park in Burundi. Additional surveys on population numbers and range are required, and taxonomic work is needed to elucidate the status of the Itombwe population.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, the Northern Lesser Galago is widespread and locally abundant. Although it is affected by habitat loss in some parts of its geographical range there are no major range-wide threats to the species.
habitat: Galago senegalensis is found in savanna woodland (e.g. miombo), in dense to open bushland, (e.g. Laikipia Plateau, Tsavo Region, Kenya), in montane forest (e.g. Mau Forest, Kenya, Otzi Mountains and Agoro-Agu Forest Reserve in the Imatong Mountains, northern Uganda, Harenna Forest, Ethiopia), riverine woodland (Tana River Primate National Reserve, coastal Kenya), and in secondary and/or highly fragmented forest and woodland, including cultivated areas [e.g. Isiolo, central Kenya (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016) and Jinack Island, The Gambia (Svensson and Bearder 2013)]. G. senegalensis avoids areas of grassland, and is sometimes found in close-canopy montane forest when no other species of galago is present (e.g. Mau Forest Complex, Kenya), otherwise, it is not a forest species (Nash et al. 2013).  In woodlands and riverine forest at low altitude, Galago senegalensis is sometimes sympatric with Paragalago cocos, Otolemur garnettii and O. crassicaudatus, and narrowly sympatric with Galago gallarum (e.g., lower Tana River forest) and, perhaps, Galago moholi and Perodicticus potto (Butynski and de Jong 2004, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016).  Galago senegalensis occurs from sea level to 2,400 m asl (G. s. senegalensis, Mau Forest Complex, Kenya; T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016).  Galago senegalensis is nocturnal, arboreal and omnivorous. It feeds mainly on gum, invertebrates and fruit (Nash et al. 2013), and builds nests in dense thorn trees or in tree holes (Bearder et al. 2003, Nash et al. 2013, Svensson and Bearder 2013, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016). Group size is 2–5, although they forage separately. They are presumed to give birth to one or two young annually (Nash 1983). Vocal profile of G. senegalensis is available at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/galago/senegalensis/ and a photographic map at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/photography/photomap/.
threats: Galago senegalensis is able to survive in habitats marginally affected by humans and near human settlements. There are no major threats resulting in a range-wide population decline. Local declines are taking place due to habitat loss from clear-cutting and intensive agriculture related to fast-growing human populations in its geographic range.
population: Galago senegalensis is locally common throughout its range. Typically G. s. braccatus exists in densities <1 individual/ha in scrubby habitats and in closed canopy forest at higher altitudes (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016). Higher densities (2.4 individuals/ha) occur in yellow fever tree (Acacia xanthophloea) woodland (Off et al. 2008, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016). On the Laikipia Plateau, central Kenya, can reach 300–500 individuals/km² in whistling thorn (Acacia drepanolobium) and yellow fever tree woodland (Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2016). Encounter rates have been recorded as 0.1 individuals/km (1.0 individuals/h) by vehicle in Ol Pejeta Conservancy, Laikipia Plateau (1,800–1,900 m asl), 1.1 individuals/h by foot in Makindu (960 m asl), 1.2 individuals/km (1.4 individuals/h) by foot in Kajiado, south Kenya (1,500 m asl), and 1.1 individuals/km (3.4 indiduals/h) by vehicle in Kora National Park, central Kenya (500 m asl) (Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2016) In Tanzania, encounter rates with G. s. braccatus were 0.1 individuals/km (2.4 individuals/h) by vehicle in Tanga (10 m asl), 0.9 individuals/h by foot in Meia Meia (1,330 m asl), 4.1 individuals/km (3.5 individuals/h) by foot near Mikumi National Park (470 m asl), and 4.0 individuals/h by foot at Mto wa Mbu, Lake Manyara National Park (970 m asl; T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2008).Galago s. sotikae encountered at the rate of 2.5 individuals/km (7.1 individuals/h; 1,480 m) in Grumeti Game Reserve, western Serengeti, Tanzania, 0.9 individuals/hr by foot in Meia Meia (1,330 m asl), 4.1 individuals/km (3.5 individuals/h) by foot near Mikumi National Park (470 m asl), and 4.0 individuals/h by foot at Mto wa Mbu, Lake Manyara National Park, Tanzania (970 m asl; T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016).
range: Galago senegalensis is endemic to tropical Africa and has a large geographical range. It occurs from Senegal in the west to Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia in the east, southwards through Kenya to south Tanzania. The limits of the distribution remain poorly understood. It is sympatric with Galago gallarum in central Kenya (e.g., Meru National Park), and potentially sympatric with with Galago moholi in Tanzania. Four subspecies are recognised (Grubb et al. 2003, Nash et al. 2013): Galago s. senegalensis (Senegal Lesser Galago). Ranges from Senegal and the Gambia in the west through to Sudan, Uganda (including Otzi Mountains, Imatong Mountains, and Kidepo Valley National Park) into western Kenya (west of the Great Rift Valley). Sites include Mt. Elgon National Park, Saiwa Swamp National Park, Mau Forest Complex and Cherangani Hills (Nash et al. 2013; de Jong and Butynski 2014a,b; Butynski and de Jong in press). Galago s. braccatus (Kenya Lesser Galago). Known from a number of districts in Kenya (east of the Eastern Rift Valley, including the Central Highlands, coastal forests, Nairobi, Meru – Kora Region and Tsavo Region), southwards to northeast and north-central Tanzania (Nash et al. 2013, Butynski and de Jong 2004, de Jong and Butynski 2009). The southern and northern extent of the range is poorly understood. Galago s. dunni (Ethiopia Lesser Galago). Somalia and the Ogaden region of Ethiopia. Limits of range unknown (Nash et al. 2013). Galago s. sotikae (Uganda Lesser Galago). Ankole (south Uganda) to Mwanza (south of Lake Victoria, Tanzania) to the Telek River (Mara Ecosystem, southern Kenya), southwards to northern and central Tanzania (including Lake Manyara National Park, Mikumi National Park, Serengeti-Grumeti Region, north of Dodoma, Selous Game Reserve; Nash et al. 2013, T. Butynski, Y. de Jong and A. Perkin pers. obs. 2016). The southern limit of G. s. sotikae is probably in far southern Tanzania near Lake Rukwa (A. Perkin pers. obs. 2016).
conservationActions: Galago senegalensis is listed on Appendix II of CITES. Occurs in a large number of protected areas throughout the range including Tsavo West National Park, Tsavo East National Park, Mt. Kenya National Park, Meru National Park, Kora National Park, Samburu National Reserve, Shaba National Reserve, Buffalo Springs National Reserve in Kenya. In Tanzania, in Grumeti Game Reserve, Serengeti National Park, Lake Manyara National Park, Tarangire National Park and Mikumi National Park (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016). In Uganda, in Kidepo Valley National Park, Otzi Forest Reserve, Agoro-Agu National Reserve (Butynski and de Jong 2014). In the Gambia, in Niumi National Park (Svensson and Bearder 2013).

rationale: Otolemur crassicaudatus is listed as Least Concern as the species is relatively widespread and common, present in a number of well-managed protected areas, and there are no major threats, other than bushmeat hunting. Population monitoring is recommended, because fragmentation is increasing dramatically among forests along the east coast of South Africa owing to expansion of sugar cane and forestry plantations.
habitat: This species is mostly found in coastal forest, woodland and riparian forest. In the southern parts of the range (e.g. KwaZulu-Natal and the Limpopo Province), the species is found in riparian and coastal forest, whereas in the northern parts of the range it extends into bushland and open woodland (Skinner & Chimimba 2005). This species may possibly be found in timber plantations, and in western Swaziland have adapted to living in wattle forests. It is not uncommon in urban gardens and farmland where there is sufficient tree growth to afford them shelter and where there are orchards of tropical and semi-tropical fruits to provide food. Sleeps alone or in groups of 2-6 and generally disperses solitarily or in small groups at night to forage. It gives birth to between one and three infants per year (Skinner & Chimimba 2005). O. c. monteiri is known from Brachystegia woodlands and riparian forests. It extends over a wide range using corridors of vegetation along rivers and streams. On the other hand, O. c. kirkii is mostly found in coastal forest, woodland and riparian bushland and, in the northern parts of the range, it extends into bushland and open woodland. It is not uncommon in urban gardens and farmland where there is sufficient tree growth to afford them shelter and where there are orchards of tropical and semi-tropical fruits to provide food.
threats: There are no known major threats other than habitat destruction. However, it may be locally threatened in parts of its range through the loss of suitable forest habitat. For example, although O. c. monteiri was once common around Lake Victoria, it has now almost completely disappeared together with the woodlands, due to cultivation. Similarly, huge swathes of previously available forest have been replaced by avocado and fruit orchards in Mpumalanga Province, and areas that once resounded with galago calls are now silent.
population: This is a relatively common species, but populations are isolated form one another by virtue of the fragmented distribution of the forests in which they are found.
range: This species ranges from the KwaZulu-Natal Province in eastern South Africa, and northwards into Swaziland and Mpumalanga and Limpopo Provinces, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and southern Malawi (Chikwawa), Zambia, Angola, south-eastern Republic of Congo, Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania and southern Kenya. Up to 1,800 m in the highlands of eastern Zimbabwe. Three or four subspecies are recognized: O. c. crassicaudatus is known from the South African provinces of KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo; O. c. kirkii ranges from Massangena, Mozambique, in the south to Zimbabwe and southern Malawi in the north; and O. c. monteiri is found in the Brachystegia miombo woodland zone from Angola in the west, to Zambia, Malawi and northern Mozambique in the east and from here north to Rwanda and western and south-eastern Kenya. Some taxonomic authorities state that O. c. monteiri can be split into two groups with a monteiri group present from Angola, through the southern Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia, Zimbabwe, northern Mozambique, Malawi and southern Tanzania (Tabora). The distribution of the argentatus grouping is unclear, but it has been recorded from Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It occurs in several protected areas. Taxonomic and survey work is needed to determine the relationship of the subspecies O. c. monteiri.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Otolemur garnettii is widespread and locally common. Major threats include habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation. The species is not thought to be threatened range-wide.
habitat: The nocturnal and arboreal O. garnettii has a wide geographical range. In submontane and montane forest, dry coastal forest, riverine gallery forest and forest-agriculture mosaics (Harcourt and Perkin 2013). It is able to persist in secondary and/or highly fragmented forest and in cultivated areas, urban suburbs and neem forest (de Jong and Butynski 2009, 2011; Harcourt & Perkin 2013). Otolemur garnettii is omnivorous, with a diet consisting of 50% animal matter (mainly invertebrates such as beetles, orthopterans and centipedes) and 50% fruits (Harcourt and Perkin 2013). They sleep in dense tangles or clumps of trees. They are not reported to make nests or sleep in tree holes (Bearder et al. 2003). Females give birth to one or two young annually. The vocal profile of O. garnettii is available at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/vocal-profiles/otolemur/garnettii/ and a photographic map at: http://www.wildsolutions.nl/photography/photomap/.
threats: Major threats for O. garnettii are habitat loss and fragmentation. As a result, O. garnettii is locally threatened by the conversion of habitat to agricultural land, fuel wood collection, expansion of human settlements and tourism. Otolemur garnettii is killed as a presumed agricultural pest and a symbol of bad luck (Harcourt and Perkin 2013). Hunted in southwest Tanzania (Makonde tribal area) for bushmeat (Harcourt and Perkin 2013). In Zanzibar, they are trapped for dog food (A. Perkin pers. obs. 2012). Live individuals have been observed for sale as pets in Kenya and Tanzania, and recorded in international pet trade for sale in United Arab Emirates (Svensson et al. 2016).
population: Otolemur garnettii is a widespread and locally abundant species (e.g., on the Kenyan Highlands and on the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba). It is, however, patchily distributed and conspicuously absent from some forests (e.g., Matundu Forest Reserve, Tanzania). At Diani and Gedi, Kenya, it is found at densities of ca 31-38 individuals/km² (Nash & Harcourt 1986).Foot and vehicle surveys at more than 20 sites in Kenya and Tanzania yielded encounter rates of between 1 and 5 individuals per hour. In Kenya, it is most abundant at the Tana River Primate National Reserve, Ngaia Forest Reserve, Meru Forest Reserve and Diani (de Jong and Butynski 2004, 2009). In Tanzania, this was the primate most often encountered in Ngezi-Vumawimbi Nature Forest Reserve (Pemba Island), Zanzibar Island, Arusha, Zaraninge Forest and Lake Manyara National Park (Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2011).
range: Otolemur garnettii is endemic to eastern East Africa and extreme northern Mozambique. Patchily distributed from near Mogadishu in southern Somalia southwards through Kenya and Tanzania to extreme northern Mozambique (just south of the Ruvuma River; Olson 1979, Harcourt & Perkin 2013). It is also found in Milo Forest, the only known site in the Southern Highlands of Tanzania, on the northern end of Lake Malawi (Honess 1996, A. Perkin and T. Davenport pers. obs. 2010 cited in Harcourt & Perkin 2013). O. garnettii is present on Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia Islands (Tanzania) and Manda Island (Kenya). A population occurs in the Central Kenya Highlands, east of the Eastern Rift Valley (Harcourt and Perkin 2013) and in Tsavo. There are no records for Malawi (Ansell and Dowsett 1988). Otolemur garnettii ranges from sea level to about 2,000 m asl, occasionally up to 2,400 m (Olson 1979, Harcourt and Perkin 2013). It is sympatric with Paragalago zanzibaricus, Paragalago cocos, Galago senegalensis, Paragalago granti and (narrowly) with Otolemur crassicaudatus (T. Butynski & Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2016).  Four subspecies are recognised: Otolemur g. garnettii (Zanzibar Small-eared Galago). Endemic to Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia Islands, Tanzania. Otolemur g. panganiensis (Pangani Small-eared Galago). Ranges from the Loita Hills and Taveta in Kenya to Lake Manyara, Mount Meru, Mount Kilimanjaro and Tanga, southwards to the south bank of the Ruvumu River in northern Mozambique (Olsen 1979, Butynski and de Jong 2012, Harcourt & Perkin 2013). Otolemur g. lasiotis (White-tailed Small-eared Galago). From the Juba River in southern Somalia, southwards along the Kenya coast to Tanga, northern Tanzania. In Taita Hills and Kibwezi area, Kenya (north of Mount Kilimanjaro; de Jong & Butynski 2009, Harcourt & Perkin 2013). Otolemur g. kikuyuensis (Kikuyu Small-eared Galago). Endemic to the Central Kenya Highlands east of the Eastern Rift Valley (e.g., Nairobi, Ngong Hills, Aberdares Range, Masinga area, Nyambeni Range, Mount Kenya; de Jong and Butynski 2004, Harcourt and Perkin 2013, T. Butynski & Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2014).
conservationActions: Otolemur garnettii is listed on Appendix II of CITES.
