population: Considering that the area of occupancy estimated for Callicebus coimbrai covers approximately 22,500 ha, Jerusalinsky (2013) calculated a total remnant population of approximately 4,500 individuals. This estimate was based on an extrapolation of the medium population density established for the species (0.20 individuals/ha; Chagas and Ferrari 2011; Rocha 2011), on known group sizes and group densities (4 individuals per group and 5 groups/km²; Bicca-Marques and Heymann 2013) and on direct observations (Jerusalinsky 2013). In a more conservative estimation, Jerusalinsky (2013) considered only the effectively recorded groups and a medium group size of four individuals to calculate a population estimate of app. 650 individuals. Despite this wide variation, the number of mature individuals should be more than 250 and less than 2,500 individuals, which are the threshold values for the category Endangered under the criterion C. Furthermore, as the largest fragment occupied by the species measures app. 3,000 ha, Jerusalinsky (2013) concluded that no subpopulation contains more than 250 mature individuals. A population decline is suspected.
range: Kobayashi and Langguth (1999) described Callicebus coimbrai from three sites in the state of Sergipe, northeastern Brazil, and proposed the range of the species to be limited to the coastal rainforest of this region, extending from the right (south) bank of the Rio São Francisco, in Sergipe, to the left (north) bank of the Rio Itapicuru, in northern Bahia. In the following years, some new localities were reported from inside this range (Sousa 2000, 2003). While searching for the distributional limits of Callicebus barbarabrownae, Printes (2005) recorded C. coimbrai at Lamarão do Passé, Bahia, extending the species’ range 200 km further south of that proposed by Kobayashi and Langguth (1999). Subsequently, several surveys have substantially increased the knowledge about the species’ distribution and conservation status (Jerusalinsky et al. 2006; Printes 2007; Sousa et al. 2008; Ferrari et al. 2013; Marques et al. 2013; Hilário 2013; Jerusalinsky 2013). The taxon is now confirmed for 125 sites in the states of Bahia and Sergipe, which encompass an estimated total area of occupancy of 22,500 ha (225 km²), representing less than 1% of its original extent of occurrence of about 30,000 km² (Jerusalinsky 2013). These sparsely occupied fragments vary in size from 5 ha or less (for example Lamerão/Minas d’Água, Bahia, and Fazenda Riacho Seco, Sergipe, both with 4 ha) to 1,000 ha. The largest fragment with about 3,000 ha is located in the southernmost part of its current distribution at São Francisco do Paraguaçu in Bahia (Sousa et al. 2008; Hilário 2013; Jerusalinsky 2013). To the north the species’ distribution is limited by the São Francisco River, since no records or reports of Callicebus were obtained from the left bank of this river which was systematically searched by several primates surveys recently conducted in the region (Jerusalinsky 2013, Fialho et al. 2014). To the East, a small forest belt along the Atlantic Ocean coast separates the species from reaching the coast since it seems the species is completely absent from certain vegetation (forest) types growing along the coast such as mangroves and restingas (Jerusalinsky 2013). To the South, the lower Paraguaçu River forms the limit between the geographic ranges of C. coimbrai, restricted to the left (or north) bank, and C. melanochir, found on the right (or south) bank (Printes et al. 2013; Jerusalinsky 2013). Further west, in the region of Feira de Santana, both banks of the Paraguaçu River are inhabited by C. barbarabrownae (Printes 2007; Printes et al. 2011, 2013). Without a physical barrier between the eastern distributional limit of C. barbarabrownae and the western limit of C. coimbrai, these two species appear to be delimited by an ecological barrier of about 50 km, that is the drier forests associated with the Caatinga biome to the West (C. barbarabrownae) and the more humid habitats associated with the Atlantic Forest to the East (C. coimbrai; Jerusalinsky 2013; Printes et al. 2013; Ferrari et al. 2013). Complementary surveys and genetic studies are required to fully understand the preterit and current patterns of distribution of these two species.
useTrade: Although cases of hunting and live capture were reported for C. coimbrai (Jerusalinsky et al. 2006; Sousa et al. 2008; Jerusalinsky 2013), they do not represent the major threats for the species (Jerusalinsky 2013). Nevertheless, hunting may have an increasing impact on C. coimbrai as its population becomes gradually more exposed to hunting due to a reduction and fragmentation of forest patches, thus facilitating easy access for hunters (Jerusalinsky 2013). The few reported cases in which C. coimbrai was maintained as a pet, resulted from sporadic encounters of individuals dispersing through a fragmented landscape. Informants consistently report this species as non-adequate to be kept in captivity (Jerusalinsky 2013). There are no reported cases on the commercialization of this species for the pet trade (or other utilizations).
conservationActions: In 2011, the National Center for Research and Conservation of Brazilian Primates (CPB/ICMBio/MMA) coordinated the elaboration of the National Action Plan for the Conservation of Northeastern Primates, setting the conservation strategies for five species, including C. coimbrai (Brazil/ICMBio 2011). This plan established goals to protect the remaining habitats of the species and to work on establishing the connectivity between populations. The Action Plan initiated several studies to better understand the risks and the use of space by the species in a severely fragmented landscape. Although first scientific results (see Ferrari et al., 2013; Hilário 2013; Jerusalinsky 2013; Marques et al. 2013; Souza-Alves 2013) were transferred into conservation action, there is still more to do to effectively reduce the risks of extinction. The ‘Refúgio de Vida Silvestre Mata do Junco’ (Mata do Junco Wildlife Refuge), decreed in December 2007 by the Sergipe State government, remains the only strictly protected area containing populations of Callicebus coimbrai. Measuring app. 900 ha, this protected area was particularly created to protect this species. Besides that, a dozen of small, privately owned reserves and a handful of non-federal and state protected areas also provide some protection to the few remaining habitat patches. Aiming to reduce pressure on remnant populations, some restrictions and mitigating measures were adopted at both the federal and the state level, for the establishment of new rural settlements and in environmental licensing processes (such as gas pipelines). At both state and municipal levels, less specific initiatives have already been implemented. The species is listed in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Plecturocebus modestus is assessed as Endangered due to a suspected population decline that will likely be greater than 50% over the next three generations (26.4 years). It is suspected that populations will rapidly decline due to: 1) the continued human population increases (projected at ca 38% over 27 years into the future based on historical rates of increase) which will lead to increased rates of hunting; 2) continued forest loss (of at least 13% over 27 years based on historical Global Forest Watch forest loss rates for the Jose Ballivian Region; Global Forest Watch 2020); and 3) rapid habitat fragmentation and degradation after the road is paved between Rurrenabaque and Santa Rosa (which will further exacerbate habitat loss, fragmentation and hunting through increase human incursion in to the area; Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013). This road passes directly through the species’ range.Based on recent information, P. modestus occurs in a restricted range of 9,073 km² (WCS unpublished data), representing a slight increase compared to previous data (8,966.4 km²; Wallace et al. 2013) due to the use of better-quality satellite imagery. Around 40% of the range of P. modestus is forest that is naturally fragmented in a savanna-forest matrix (Wallace et al. 2013). However, the occurrence of P. modestus is not uniform in the forested areas. Though the distribution area is above the extent of occurrence (EOO) threshold for the species to be considered Endangered, much of the habitat may not be suitable for the species and thus its area of occupancy may be relatively small.The region is highly sensitive to increases in forest loss and fragmentation caused principally by accidents during grassland burning applied in pasture management for cattle ranching (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013, Siles et al. 2019). A 2016 study in Bolivia found that rapid frontier expansion for cattle ranching and agriculture, as well as extreme dry conditions (which may occur in the future due to climate change) could result in increased fire risk of 1.8 times higher than in 2010 in high-risk areas (Devisscher et al. 2016). Moreover, the current paving of the North Corridor, a major road passing through the range of P. modestus, represents a significant risk of habitat loss due to potential expansion of human settlements, as well as changes in land use (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013). This situation will be exacerbated by recent changes in the Land Use Plan for the Beni Department which openly encourage and facilitate mechanized agriculture in the region.It is suspected that populations will rapidly decline due to habitat reduction related to the above risks. Additional evidence of threats in the region include forest loss of at least 13% over 27 years based on historical Global Forest Watch forest loss rates for the Jose Ballivian Region (Global Forest Watch 2020), and continued human population increases (projected at c. 38% over 27 years into the future based on historical rates of increase) which may increase hunting rates.A marginal portion of the distribution of P. modestus occurs within the Biosphere Reserve Estación Biológica del Beni, a national protected area. The species is mainly found in two municipal protected areas, Pampas del Yacuma and Rhukanrhuka, which are currently working to consolidate their management.
habitat: This taxon occurs in relatively dry forest patches within a forest-savanna mosaic (Felton et al. 2006, Wallace et al. 2013). Although P. olallae is found in the same savannah ecosystem, the forests where P. modestus occurs are drier, as they are not associated to permanent water courses (Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010). Martinez and Wallace (2007) and Lopez-Strauss (2008) detail average group sizes of 3 and 2.64 individuals, respectively.A recent behavioural ecology study estimated the home range for P. modestus as 9.69 ha (Martinez 2014). Diet of this species was mainly frugivorous, also consuming flowers and invertebrates (Arnez 2012, Morrison 2014, WCS unpublished data). Only groups of two adults with no young individuals were found in the small forest patches (Martinez 2014). Considering the dry forest habitat and observed diet, it is probable that this species could be facing important pressures regarding habitat quality, thereby conditioning group size.
threats: There is forest loss and habitat fragmentation within the range of P. modestus, related to cattle ranching, the principal economic activity in the region, that manages grasslands as pastures using annual burning techniques (Wallace et al. 2013). Indeed, observations confirmed that a group of P. olallae left its territory due to heavy smoke from grassland burning (Martinez and Wallace 2011). This was not documented for P. modestus, but both species live in the same region with similar land uses. The coming major improvement to a regional road, The Northern Corridor that passes across the distributional range of P. modestus, represents a critical threat of high deforestation pressure promoted by a potential increase of new human settlements (Felton et al. 2006; Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010; Wallace et al. 2013). If not planned properly, this improved road could promote increases on cattle ranching grasslands area and is likely to increase hunting pressure too. The rescue of a specimen individual held as a pet in a rural community (Martinez et al. 2013), as well an individual at the Senda Verde wildlife rescue centre, provides evidence of the risks of the pet trade for P. modestus. Finally, the observations of small group sizes of P. modestus in more fragmented forests, in combination with inbreeding rates as compared to P. olallae (Barreta et al. 2019), suggest potential limitations in habitat suitability of the dry forests inhabited by this species, which will need to be assessed in relation to climatic change.
population: In 2002, Felton et al. (2006) conducted titi monkey surveys and interviewed local residents at four localities: Puerto Santa Cruz on the Rio Yacuma; La Laguna; Petaca; and Naranjal. Titis were relatively abundant in Naranjal, not encountered at all in Petaca (although local residents claim they occur there), and are no longer present in La Laguna (probably exterminated through hunting). Examination of the holotypes indicates that the Rio Yacuma groups were P. olallae, while two of three groups found in Naranjal were P.  modestus (the third appeared to combine characters from both species).Lopez-Strauss (2008) estimated density for both P. olallae and P. modestus based on territorial calling behaviour and an adapted point-count methodology. From this assessment, P. modestus presented an average density of 4.93 (DS±4.58) groups per km² (Lopez-Strauss and Wallace 2015). These assessments assumed a ubiquitous presence of P. modestus in the forested areas across its range, but according to recent observations on P. olallae in the same region (Martinez and Wallace in press), the presence of this species may be restricted to just some forest types. Given habitat degradation risks and potential increases in hunting pressures in the region, it is suspected that the population could suffer a decline of 50% over the next three generations (ca 26.4 years).
range: This species is endemic to Bolivia, with a restricted range estimated at 9,073 km² (Wallace et al. 2013, WCS unpublished data) between the Beni and Maniqui rivers, in the southwestern Beni Department. It is estimated that only 40% of the area is forest in the savannah-forest matrix and not all the forest may be suitable for P. modestus (Wallace et al. 2013). The distribution of this primate is split in two zones of fragmented forests with similar dry conditions on both sides of the Yacuma River, where P. olallae is found (Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010; Wallace et al. 2013). The area inhabited by P. modestus corresponds to a drier forest habitat than the area of P. olallae, and there is a seasonally flooding grassland where no titi monkeys are present apparently serving as an effective migration barrier between these two primate species (Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010; Wallace et al. 2013). Found below 200 m asl.It is suspected that the extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO), and habitat quality for this species will continue to decline at rates faster than historically seen, due to the paving of a road that runs directly through the species’ range. The paving of this road will exacerbate habitat degradation, which was already taking place at high rates primarily due to uncontrolled fires from agriculture. The recent approval of the Land Use Plan for the Beni Department (PLUS Beni), also promotes large-scale mechanized agriculture in the Llanos de Moxos representing a particular threat in areas with improved transport networks.
useTrade: One individual of P. modestus is currently (April 2017) in a rescue centre (Senda Verde) after being confiscated from a wildlife trader. The increase of human population in the region promoted by the ongoing paving of the road (North Corridor) could promote increased wildlife hunting, as well as the illegal pet trade, including for P. modestus.
conservationActions: A very small part of the range of this species is included within the Biosphere Reserve Estación Biológica del Beni (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013), a national protected area. Most of the range of P. modestus is found in two municipal protected areas: Pampas del Yacuma and Rhukanrhuka (in Santa Rosa del Yacuma and Reyes municipalities, respectively). In both cases, P. modestus is recognized as a conservation priority and conservation actions are stated as urgently required. Recently the Pampas del Yacuma protected area developed its management plan which will help the conservation of this endemic primate. A recent work added information about vulnerable zones for P. modestus regarding excessive flooding, uncontrolled fires, and deforestation, representing a good start point for further conservation actions to conserve forest habitats in the region (Siles et al. 2019).Conservation programs in the region include the Greater Madidi Landscape Conservation Program of the Wildlife Conservation Society in northern La Paz and south-western Beni Departments, which has led research efforts on both Bolivian endemics since 2002 and provided technical and financial support for the development of the management plan for the Pampas del Yacuma protected area. In addition, WCS currently supports the development of distinct management tools for the recently created Rhukanrhuka municipal protected area.Plecturocebus modestus is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its relatively large range in a pristine region of the Amazon, and because there are no known major threats believed to be resulting in a decline sufficient to qualify it for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: There are no data available on the ecology of this species. Titi monkeys are known to occur in a wide range of habitats, although some species exhibit habitat preferences, for example Cheracebus lucifer is reported to prefer white-sand forests (E. Heymann pers. comm. 2008), and Plecturocebus donacophilus drier forests (Ferrari et al. 2000; R. Wallace pers. comm.). Species of the Plecturocebus genus are considered tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activity or seasonal flooding (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The diet of titis comprises mainly fruit pulp, leaves, insects and seeds. They form small, pair-bonded, territorial groups and are considered monogamous. They have small home (1.5-30 km²) and day ranges (0.5-1.5 km²).
threats: This species occurs in a remote part of the Amazon, and there are currently no known major threats.
population: There is no information available on the population status of this species.
range: Central Amazonia, Amazonas state, Brazil, south of the Rio Solimões in the interfluve delineated by the lower Rios Purús, Solimões and Madeira, south as far as the Rio Ipixuna (or Paranapixuna). Hershkovitz (1990) considered the species sympatric with Plecturocebus dubius, P. brunneus, and P. cupreus, based on, in his view, mislabeled specimens collected by the Olalla brothers in Boca Río Inuya, Iquitos, Río Orosa, Río Tapiche and Sarayacu, Rio Ucayali, in the department of Loreto, Peru. Voss and Emmons (1996) note that Hershkovitz' report on the sympatry of two members of the moloch Group (P. cupreus and P. caligatus) was an error caused by "inadvertently listing both original and revised identifications of the same series from Orosa among the specimens examined". The correct identification for the monkeys is Plecturocebus (cupreus) cupreus. Specimens collected by Peres (1993) along both banks of the Rio Juruá and deposited in the Muséu Goeldi, Belém, all were identified as Plecturocebus (cupreus) cupreus (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The geographic distribution for P. caligatus described above contradicts that given by Hershkovitz (1990), who fills in its actual distribution with P. dubius. Four specimens of P. caligatus were caught in July 2001 by locals along the north bank of Lago Jarí at the mouth of Igarapé Bacaba and released at the same place after being measured and photographed, and a complete skeleton with some hair found on the forest floor was collected (private collection no. MGMR55) on the north bank of Rio Ipixuna near its mouth, a few kilometers south of the town of Tapauá.Byrne et al. (2016) proposed that Plecturocebus dubius is a junior synonym of P. caligatus, and that thus the distribution of P. caligatus should include that of P. dubius. Therefore, this species’ distribution would be Central Amazonia, south of the Rio Solimões in the interfluve delineated by the Rios Purús, and Madeira, possibly as far south as the Rio Ituxi (a right bank tributary of the Purus), where it would be limited by the presence of the newly reinstated species P. toppini. (Vermeer and Tello-Alvarado, 2015). However, this taxonomic change is still under debate, and we will regard both taxa as valid until further evidence has been published.
conservationActions: The species is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to having a relatively large range in a region that is still secure from anthropogenic impact, and there is no evidence of any major threats resulting in a decline that would qualify the species for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Monção et al. (2008) mentioned Plecturocebus bernhardi occurring in secondary growth forest. Titi monkeys (Plecturocebus spp.) are known to occur in a wide range of habitats, although some species exhibit habitat preferences, for example Cheracebus lucifer is reported to prefer white-sand forests (E. Heymann pers. comm. 2008), and P. donacophilus drier forests (Ferrari et al. 2000; R. Wallace pers. comm.). Members of the P. moloch and P. cupreus groups are considered tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activity or seasonal flooding (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The diet of titis comprises mainly fruit pulp, leaves, insects and seeds. They form small, pair-bonded, territorial groups and are considered monogamous. They have small home (1.5-30 km²) and day ranges (0.5-1.5 km²).
threats: This species occurs in a remote region still relatively isolated from anthropogenic impact, and there are currently no known major threats.
population: Two sighting rates with an average of 0.19 / 10 Km were recorded in Ipixuna Indigenous Land (Cardozo & Vale Junior-2012).
range: Prince Bernhard's Titi monkey is endemic to Brazil, it is present in the states of Amazonas and Rondônia as a resident and native and Mato Grosso as native and uncertain presence (Veiga 2008b).Occurs between the Madeira and Aripuana rivers, with its northern boundary given by this confluence, the eastern boundary is defined by Madeira and Jiparaná rivers in the states of Amazonas and Rondônia. Although (Van Roosmalen et al. 2002) have inferred distribution also between the rivers Aripuanã and Roosevelt, the recent description of Plecturocebus miltoni (Dalponte, Ennes e Silva Jr. 2014) excludes it from that region. The distribution can be expanded to the southwest, south of Ji-Parana river near the headwaters, in the municipality of Alto Alegre dos Parecis, Rondônia, as noted by Monção et al. (2008).There is a possible sighting of the taxon in a 50 ha reserve in Alta Floresta (Mato Grosso) (Stepp 2003), which needs confirmation. The geographical distribution of Plecturocebus bernhardi, Plecturocebus cinerascens and Plecturocebus hoffmannsi, can overlap in the area of ​​the headwaters of the Juruena river, Aripuanã and Roosevelt (Veiga 2008b).
conservationActions: Thought to occur in Alta Floresta Reserve in Mato Grosso State in Brazil (Stepp 2003). There are Plecturocebus bernhardi records in the Sustainable Development Reserve of Juma (van Roosmalen et al. 2002) and Indigenous Land Ipixuna (215,000 ha) (Cardoso & Vale Junior 2012), both in the Amazon. It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Although occurring over a relatively wide range, surviving even in small forest fragments, and showing some tolerance to disturbed habitats, Callicebus nigrifrons is listed as Near Threatened as it is reasonable to assume that the species has undergone a decline of more than 20% over the past 24 years (three generations) due to extensive habitat loss and fragmentation in the remnants of Atlantic forest in southeastern Brazil. Almost qualifies as threatened under criterion A2c.
habitat: Callicebus nigrifrons inhabits the Atlantic forest, including transitional ecosystems to the Cerrado biome (Melo et al. 2015). The species occurs in both mature rain forest and disturbed fragments, and is able to inhabit isolated forest fragments (Ferrari 2013; Melo et al. 2015). These titis are invariably highly frugivorous (43-74% of the diet), but they also eat relatively large quantities of leaves (5-33%) and flowers (11-24%), and also consumes arthropods in small quantities (0-10%) (Souza et al. 1996, Neri 1997, Franco 2006, Trevelin et al. 2007, Caselli and Setz 2011). This species is monogamous and territorial, living in small family groups (2 to 6 individuals) (Torres de Assumpção 1983, Stallings and Robinson 1991, Neri 1997, Cäsar et al. 2008). Callicebus nigrifrons is relatively active compared to other titi species, with only 29-35% of their time spent resting, while foraging and feeding accounted for 26-40%, moving 24-33%, and engaging in social behaviour less than 6% (Souza et al. 1996, Caselli and Setz 2011). The recorded home range size for the species varies from 21 ha to 48 ha and is the largest ever recorded for the genus (Torres de Assumpção 1983, Neri 1997). Daily movements recorded for a C. nigrifrons group were also largest compared to any other titi, varying from 740 m to 2,697 m, with a mean of 1,270 m per day (Neri 1997).
threats: This species inhabits the most developed and populous region of Brazil, and has suffered extensive habitat loss and fragmentation. Although the species is widespread, the conversion of forest areas into extensive cattle ranches and agriculture, logging practices and urbanization, have led to extreme fragmentation of the forests within its range, resulting in small isolated populations. In many places, they have been locally or regionally extirpated, even where forests patches remain. Hunting pressure and captures for the pet trade do not seem to be major threats for the species, or even specifically directed to it, due to its small body size and shy behavior. Nevertheless, these threats may have increasing impacts on C. nigrifrons as its populations become gradually more exposed due to the reduction and fragmentation of forest patches, where other preferentially hunted species are already locally extinct. Electrocution, road kills and predation by domestic dogs are increasingly becoming a risk as development programs advance and human populations become larger and denser across the species’ range.
population: The total remnant population is unknown, but it is inferred to be larger than 10,000 individuals based on the extent of the areas occupied by the species, especially those in protected areas (Melo et al. 2015). The highest population density of C. nigrifrons was recorded in a 50-ha forest fragment, estimated to be 80–100 individuals per km² (Soares 2006), which is six times higher than that of C. personatus (a similar-sized species living in the same habitat). Estimates from other studies found lower values: 3,5 individuals/km² at São José Farm, São Paulo (Bernardo and Galetti 2004); 4,51 individuals/km² in Viçosa, Minas Gerais (Santana et al. 2008); 7-10 individuals/km² (Torres de Assumpção 1983); 15.67 ± 6.51 individuals/km² (Chiarello and Melo 2001); 23,9 individuals/km² at Pouso Alegre Municipal Park, Minas Gerais (Costa et al. 2009).Although occurring over a relatively wide range, surviving even in small forest fragments, and showing some tolerance to disturbed habitats, it is reasonable to assume that the species has undergone a decline of more than 20% over the past 24 years (three generations) due to extensive habitat loss and fragmentation in the remnants of Atlantic forest in southeastern Brazil.
range: Callicebus nigrifrons is endemic to Brazil and distributed over a relatively wide area in the south-eastern region of the country, having the most ample distribution of any personatus-group species (van Roosmalen et al. 2002, Printes et al. 2013, Melo et al. 2015). Its range includes the northern part of São Paulo, the southern and central part of Minas Gerais, the entire Rio de Janeiro and the extreme south of Espírito Santo States (Printes et al. 2013, Melo et al. 2015). It is found north of the Tietê and east of the Paraná and Parnaíba Rivers, and on both banks of the upper Rio São Francisco. To the north, the species’ range may be limited by ecological factors inherent to the Cerrado savannas of the central Brazilian Plateau, given that titis are absent from much of this biome (Ferrari, 2013).  To the east and northeast, the species extends to the Mantiqueira and Espinhaço Ranges, where it meets the distribution of C. personatus (Printes et al. 2013, Melo et al. 2015), although it remains unclear to what extent their distributions are in contact or intergrade with one another (Printes et al. 2013, Melo et al. 2015). The Serra do Mar coastal range in São Paulo is the southernmost limit of the geographic distribution of the genus, and the highest latitude at which titis occur in the wild (Ferrari 2013). There are indications (inferences, suspicion) that the current distribution of the taxon is reduced in relation to its historical extent of occurrence, which is currently estimated as less than 500,000 km² (Melo et al. 2015).There is extensive habitat loss and fragmentation in the remnants of Atlantic forest in southeastern Brazil where this species occurs.
useTrade: Captures for the pet trade do not seem to be major threats for the species due to its small body size and shy behavior.
conservationActions: Occurs in several protected areas, including: the Serra do Mar Reserve complex and the Cantareira State Park, in São Paulo; Rio Doce State Park, Serra do Brigadeiro State Park, Serra da Canastra National Park, Serra do Gandarela National Park, and private reserves such as Mata do Sossego and Santuário do Caraça, in Minas Gerais; Itatiaia National Park at the border of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais; and Caparaó National Park at the border of Espírito Santo and Minas Gerais (Melo et al. 2015). The extensive fragmentation of remaining habitat throughout its range may necessitate a program to restore connectivity of these protected populations, or even a meta-population management strategy in the future (Printes et al. 2013). It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable based on a suspected ongoing population reduction of more than 30% over three generations (27 years) and a suspected reduction at similar rates in the future, owing to high levels of deforestation inside its relatively restricted range.
habitat: Plecturocebus brunneus was observed in the terra-firme forest in northern Rondônia but absent in the savannah habitat in the south (Ferrari et al. 2000). No further information on the ecology and behaviour of P. brunneus exists. Members of the P. moloch and P. cupreus groups are considered tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activity or seasonal flooding (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The diet of titis comprises mainly fruit pulp, leaves, insects and seeds. They form small, pair-bonded, territorial groups and are considered monogamous. They have small home (1.5-30 km) and day ranges (0.5-1.5 km).
threats: The state of Rondônia has suffered intense human colonisation and deforestation over the past thirty-five years, more than 50% has been affected by unsustainable deforestation and habitat fragmentation. Fortunately most immigrants come from southern Brazil, and they do not normally hunt primates.The principal threats for the species are rural settlements, agriculture, urban expansion, deforestation, extension of the energy network, increased road construction, reduction of habitat and hunting. Strong threats such as continuation of deforestation, construction of hydropower plants and small hydroelectric power plants, transmission lines and rural settlements affect approximately of 50% of the habitat in the distribution range of the taxon. There is hunting in indigenous lands, but the impact on the population is unknown.
population: Considering the high rates of deforestation within its relatively small distribution range, the population of P. brunneus is suspected to have decreased considerably in the recent past, with the decline still ongoing and reaching more than 30% reduction over three generations (27 years). This is due to a number of threats, including forest loss. There are high levels of deforestation inside the species' relatively restricted range (22% forest loss from 2000 to 2018 across the whole state of Rondônia, Global Forest Watch 2020).
range: This species has a restricted range, found in the state of Rondônia (between the Mamoré, Madeira and Jiparaná rivers); possibly limited to the south in Brazil by the Serra dos Pacaás (Ferrari et al. 2000).There are high levels of deforestation inside the species' relatively restricted range (22% forest loss from 2000 to 2018 across the whole state of Rondônia, Global Forest Watch 2020).
useTrade: There is hunting in indigenous lands, but the impact on the population is unknown.
conservationActions: Protected in the PARNA Pacaás Novos (708,664 ha), REBIO Guaporé (615,771 ha), REBIO Jaru (346,861 ha), ESEC Samuel (71,061 ha) (Rylands & Bernardes 1989), PE Guajará-Mirim (200,071 ha) (Ferrari et al. 1995), FLONA Jamari (222,114 ha) (Messias et al. 2012), RESEX Rio Ouro Preto (204,631 ha), REBIO Estadual do Rio Ouro Preto (56,581 ha) (Messias 2002), PARNA Serra da Cutia (283,501 ha) (Messias 2004).It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Although this species has a restricted range, it is listed as Least Concern. There is no indication of any anthropogenic threats for the time being and no suggestion that the species is currently undergoing a significant decline.
habitat: There are no data available on the ecology of this species. Titi monkeys  are known to occur in a wide range of habitats, although some species exhibit habitat preferences, for example Cheracebus lucifer is reported to prefer white-sand forests (E. Heymann pers. comm.) and Plecturocebus donacophilus dry forest (Ferrari et al. 2000; R. Wallace pers. comm.). Species of the Plecturocebus genus are considered to be tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activities or seasonal flooding (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The diet of titis comprises mainly fruit pulp, leaves, insects and seeds. They form small, pair-bonded, territorial groups and are considered monogamous. They have small home- (1.5-30 km²) and day ranges (0.5-1.5 km).
threats: Although this species has a small geographic range, it is relatively well protected by isolation from areas of human colonisation. Currently, there are no major threats.
population: There is no information available on the population status of this species.
range: According to van Roosmalen et al. (2002), Plecturocebus baptista has a disjunct distribution. It occurs in central Brazilian Amazonia, south of the Rio Amazonas, east of the Rio Madeira in the state of Amazonas (reaching almost as far as the state of Pará), and north of the Paraná do Canumã, Paraná do Urariá, and Paraná do Ramos (van Roosmalen et al. 2002). It was first seen in the wild on the west (left) bank of the Rio Uíra-Curupá, and is believed to have crossed over the Paraná do Ramos west of the town of Parintins forming an enclave population in the lower Rio Uíra-Curupá-Andirá interfluve. Further surveys are required in this area to establish the exact range.
conservationActions: A small part of the species' range is within the Andira Marau Amerindian Reserve.It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Plecturocebus ornatus is listed as Vulnerable in light of a continued decline inferred from more than a 30% loss of habitat in the past three generations (24 years), which is expected to continue at the same rate for the next three generations, due to a decline in area of occupancy and habitat quality as a consequence of deforestation caused by African palm oil expansion, petrol exploration and exploitation, illicit crops and expanding human settlements (Carretero-Pinzón 2013).
habitat: Titi monkeys are known to occur in a wide range of habitats, although some species exhibit habitat preferences, for example Cheracebus lucifer is reported to prefer white-sand forests (Heymann pers. comm., 2008) and Plecturocebus donacophilus drier forests (Ferrari et al. 2000, Wallace pers. comm.). Members of the Plecturocebus moloch and Plecturocebus cupreus groups are considered tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activity or seasonal flooding (Roosmalen et al. 2002). Plecturocebus ornatus typically occurs in lowland tropical forests (canopy 15-20 m) (Defler 2010) and disturbed habitats (Mason 1968). A recent research in San Martin area, in 100 forest fragments, found P. ornatus groups in fragments of gallery forest, lowland rainforest and Mauritia flexuosa swamps (Carretero-Pinzón and Defler, in prep).The ecology of this species has been studied in the department of Meta by Mason (1965, 1966, 1966, 1968, and 1971) and Robinson (1977, 1979, 1979, 1981, and 1982). Polanco (1992) and Porras (2000) studied a population near the Duda River.
threats: This species occurs in an area subject to intense human colonization that has been subject to widespread habitat destruction and fragmentation. As mentioned by Carretero-Pinzón (2013) a reduction of 35% of their distribution area has occurred in the last decade. This habitat loss and fragmentation has been produced by cattle ranching, palm oil plantation extensions and petrol exploration and exploitation (Wagner et al. 2009, Carretero-Pinzón 2013).
population: Robinson (1977) recorded a population density of five individuals/ km². Wagner et al. (2009) found higher densities (192.2 ind/ km2) in small fragments, while Carretero-Pinzón (2013) found lower densities (57.94 ind/ km2 and 1.073 ind/ km2) for range of fragments between 16 ha and 1,050 ha.Carretero-Pinzón (2013) reported a 35% reduction of distribution area for this species between 2003 and 2013 caused by habitat loss and fragmentation. Habitat loss is continuing. As a result, it is suspected that the population has suffered a reduction of at least 30% over the last 24 years (three generations), and that this reduction is likely to continue over the next 24 years.
range: This species occurs in eastern Colombia, in the department of Cundinamarca (Medina) north as far as the lower Río Upía/ Río Meta, south into the department of Meta, along the base of the Cordillera Oriental and the Sierra de la Macarena to the Río Guayabero/ upper Río Guaviare. It is the only member of the cupreus and moloch group occurring north of the Rios Amazonas/ Solimões/ Napo axis, in the upper Río Orinoco basin and is separated from the nearest other member of the cupreus group (Plecturocebus discolor) in the south by at least 350 km (Roosmalen et al. 2002). Eastern limits are poorly known but probably extend beyond Metica River (Defler 2010).
conservationActions: This species occurs in La Macarena National Park and Tinigua National Park. Although some populations are found within protected areas, guerilla activity makes it difficult to monitor these areas (T. Defler pers comm.).It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Callicebus melanochir occurs in the Atlantic Forest in the south of the state of Bahia, and extreme north of the state Espírito Santo and northeast Minas Gerais. It is suspected that the population is declining at a rate of at least 30% over three generations (24 years), spanning a period between 2010 and 2034, through conversion of its forests for agriculture and cattle-ranching. As such it is classified as Vulnerable (VU A4c).
habitat: An inhabitant of Brazil's Atlantic forest, where it occurs also in areas of degraded habitat and has been observed in cabruca (cacao plantations shaded by native trees) in the regions of Ilhéus and Itabuna. There are very few studies on the ecology and behaviour of members of the personatus group. However, Callicebus melanochir has been the subject of a few studies in Bahia. They live in small family groups, with a home range of 22–24 ha (Müller 1996, Heiduck 2002) and a mean day range of approximately 1 km (Müller 1996). The diet comprises mainly fleshy fruit parts, seeds and young leaves (Heiduck 1997). A group in Serra do Teimoso Reserve, Jussari, was highly frugivorous, with 90% of their diet composed of fruit, complemented by leaves, flowers and other items (Cardoso and Santos 2005).
threats: This species inhabits the most developed and populous region of Brazil, in a region that has suffered from extensive habitat loss and fragmentation and where there is now very little remaining forest cover (estimated from between 5 to 10%). The reduction of available habitat for the eastern Brazilian titis is ongoing, mainly due to pressures for cattle ranching and agriculture. Hunting pressure is probably negligible to moderate in most cases, given their small body size.
population: There is no information on the population status of this species. The population is highly fragmented. The species is suffering an ongoing population decline suspected to be greater than 30% over three generations (24 years), spanning a period between 2010 and 2034, due to conversion of its forests for agriculture and cattle-ranching.
range: According to Hershkovitz (1990), Callicebus melanochir is found in Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil between the right margin of the Rio Paraguaçú in the state of Bahia (C. barbarabrownae occurs north from the right bank of the Rio Paraguacú), and the left bank of the Rio Mucuri in northern Espírito Santo (see also Oliver and Santos 1991, Flesher 1999). Van Roosmalen et al. (2002) claimed that the species may overlap with C. personatus in the Itaúnas and Mucuri river valleys, in the north of Espírito Santo (see also Canale 2008). Cerrado (savanna), liana forest, and dry deciduous forest limit its range in the west, and it is likely that C. melanochir ranges no further west into Minas Gerais than Montes Claros (Printes 2005). It may formerly have occurred in the Pardo-Jequitinhonha interfluvium, but the forests of this region have now been replaced by cattle pasture and recent surveys found no Callicebus there. This species may reach as far south as the Rio Doce (300 km to the south). South of the Rio Jequitinhonha, C. melanochir is restricted to the humid coastal forest. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated at 124,798 km² (minimum convex polygon) and its area of occupation is larger than 2.000 km².There is ongoing conversion of forests across the species range for agriculture and cattle-ranching.
useTrade: Hunting pressure is probably negligible to moderate in most cases, given their small body size.
conservationActions: Protected areas:Bahia: Una Biological Reserve (18,715 ha) (Santos et al. 1987, de Vleeschouwer et al. 2004, Printes 2007, Canale 2008), Lemos Maia Experimental Station (170 ha), Djalma Bahia Experimental Station (145 ha), Experimental Station Canavieiras (500 ha) (Pinto 1994), Pau Brasil National Park (18,934 ha) (Printes 2007), Monte Pascoal National Park (22.332 ha).Espírito Santo: Córrego Grande Biological Reserve (1.489 ha), Córrego do Veado Biological Reserve (2.383 ha) 7300 ha), Rio Preto National Forest (2.831 ha) (Canale 2008).Listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its relatively large range in a pristine region of the Amazon, and because there are no known major threats believed to be resulting in a decline sufficient to qualify it for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Rohe and Silva Jr. (2009) observed P. dubius occupying areas of ‘Campinarana’ and ‘terra-firme’ open canopy forests covered by palms. They also reported several individuals during an intraspecific agonistic interaction on an unpaved road that crosses the Rio Mucuim. The animals were on the right bank of the Rio Mucuim, close to the wooden bridge that crosses this river. This observation could imply a possible range expansion of P. dubius into the distributional range of P. stephennashi. The average group size observed in this study was approximately 3 individuals.Titi monkeys are known to occur in a wide range of habitats, although some species exhibit habitat preferences, for example Cheracebus lucifer is reported to prefer white-sand forests (E. Heymann pers. comm. 2008), and Plecturocebus donacophilus drier forests (Ferrari et al. 2000; R. Wallace pers. comm.). Members of the P. moloch group are considered tolerant of habitat disturbance caused by human activity or seasonal flooding (van Roosmalen et al. 2002).The diet of titis comprises mainly fruit pulp, leaves, insects and seeds. They form small, pair-bonded, territorial groups and are considered monogamous. They have small home (1.5-30 km) and day ranges (0.5-1.5 km).
threats: This species occurs in a remote isolated region of the Amazon, and is not considered to be under any immediate threat.
population: There is no information on the population status of this species.
range: According to Veiga (2008e) Plecturocebus dubius has a relatively large, but poorly known, range that includes parts of northern Bolivia, south-eastern Peru and three Brazilian states. It occurs between the Madeira and Purus rivers. In the northern boundary, it occurs on both banks of the river Mucuim (Rohe and Silva Jr. 2009) (but a better investigation is required between the Ipixuna and Mucuim rivers to verify co-occurrence with Plecturocebus stephennashi), and both right (east) bank tributaries of the Rio Purús.  The southern limit is unknown. Van Roosmalen et al. (2002) placed P. dubius in northern Bolivia, but Rowe and Martinez (2003) found no evidence to support this supposition, and P. brunneus is the species in the Pando, north and south of the Río Madre de Dios (R. Wallace pers. comm.)
conservationActions: This species is present in the following Reserves. Amazonas State: REBIO Abufari (233,864 ha) (Rylands and Bernardes 1989), Parque Nacional do Mapinguari (Rohe and Silva Jr 2009), TI Caititu (Veiga 2008e).Rondônia State: ESEC Estadual Antônio Mujica Nava (18,281 ha) (Messias et al. 2001), ESEC Cuniã (186,743 ha) (M.R. Messias personal communication).Rondônia e Amazonas: TI Kaxarari (Veiga 2008e).It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Plecturocebus oenanthe is assessed as Critically Endangered as it is estimated that a population reduction of ≥80% has occurred over the last 25 years due to massive deforestation of this species' preferred habitat as a result of increased human population pressure and intensification of agricultural activities.
habitat: This species is known to occur in low secondary forests and remnant forest and has been seen in bamboo stands, viney thickets, fruit crops and palm-dominated semi-flooded forests (“aguajales” and “renacales”) (DeLuycker 2006, 2007a).  Mark (2003) noted that occurrence records (both sightings and calls) were frequently located near rivers and streams.  Bóveda-Penalba et al. (2009), also found the species in forests located far away from rivers and claim that the species does not seem to be bound to a specific habitat, and confirmed their presence in inundated areas with aguajales (Mauritia flexuosa) and renacales (Ficus trigona), but also drier zones with ojés (Ficus anthelmintica), tangaranas (Triplaris sp.), zapotes (Ponteria mimosa), and ceticos (Cecropia sp.). These Titi Monkeys appear to be able to survive (at least in the short term in the absence of hunting) in forest fragments and relatively large groups have been registered in fragments of forest.  The titi monkey occupies the valleys to the south-east of the distribution of Lagothrix flavicauda and Aotus miconax. Although L. flavicauda is generally present above 1,500 m (DeLuycker, 2007c, Shanee 2011), at some localities possible sympatry is possible with both species, as recent surveys have reported these species as low as 1,100 m (Shanee et al. 2015, Allgas et al. 2015). Titi Monkeys are known to be monogamous and live in small family groups. In the first long-term study of P. oenanthe (undertaken in an isolated fragment), a group of five monkeys (an adult male and female and their three offspring) used an area of 2.5 ha (DeLuycker 2007a). This group’s diet consisted mainly of fruits (54%), insects (22%), though young seeds, flowers and non-reproductive plant parts such as leaves, shoots and tendrils and new meristem were also eaten (DeLuycker 2012). Liana species were particularly important in the diet, as were fruits from stem-parasitic plants from the mistletoe family, and the group spent a considerable amount of time foraging for insects (DeLuycker 2006). In contrast with Titi Monkeys at other sites, the group used only three sleeping sites during the entire study. They shared the fragment with saddleback tamarins (Leontocebus leucogenys) (DeLuycker 2006). Titi monkeys are often encountered in association with saddleback tamarins, but also share their habitat with Aotus sp., Alouatta sp. Sapajus macrocephalus and Saimiri boliviensis peruviensis (Shanee et al. 2013a, Proyecto Mono Tocón, unpubl. data)Variation in pelage colouration has been reported (Mark 2003, DeLuycker 2006). The extensive surveys of Proyecto Mono Tocón suggest a high phenotypical variation within P. oenanthe.  Animals in the northern part of San Martin (the Alto Mayo Valley) are mostly brownish with a white mask, while in the south many animals lack the white mask and have an orange to dark brown body. Mixed pairs with offspring have also been observed (Proyecto Mono Tocón, unpublished data).
threats: The main threats to this species are habitat loss and fragmentation, and hunting pressure. The region has suffered intense human colonization over the last 30 years because of a major agrarian programme, which has attracted huge numbers of immigrants. Agricultural activities include the cultivation of rice and coffee; cattle ranching and selective timber extraction also occur. The region is characterized by rapid rates of deforestation (estimates vary from 40,000 to 100,000 ha per year) and fragmentation, and has lost at least 40% of its forest cover, mainly from the low-altitude river basins (the preferred habitat of this species) over the last 20 years (Mark 2003, DeLuycker 2006, Shanee et al. 2011). The construction of a two-lane all-weather road, which was asphalted in 2003 - La Carretera Marginal, Via Marginal, or Carretera Fernando Belaunde Terry - which runs all the way to the coast (Chiclayo) and past Tarapoto has contributed to the influx of immigrants and a change from subsistence to small-scale farming. It has also altered the spatial distribution of human settlers, who now follow the highway far into the valley and high forests, and the lack of planning or state-regulated land occupation and use puts protected areas and remaining forests at risk (DeLuycker 2006).The species is only found at the borders of large protected areas of San Martin. Recent studies (Bóveda-Penalba et al. 2009; Shanee et al. 2011) determined that an estimated 60% of the species original range has already been lost, and its current range comprises mostly small fragments of secondary forest. Most groups encountered live in small highly degraded remnants of forest, isolated from other populations. The species is being hunted for its meat, both the Aguarunas and recent immigrants hunt this species (Mark 2003, DeLuycker 2006, Bóveda-Penalba et al. 2009). While Titi Monkeys may not be a particularly lucrative source of protein, hunting pressure is likely to increase as preferred game become scarce and fragmentation facilitates access. These Titi Monkeys are used as pets (Shanee  2012, Mark 2003, DeLuycker 2006, Bóveda-Penalba et al. 2009) and have been found for sale at markets (Rowe and Martinez 2003, Mark 2003, Shanee 2012, Jan Vermeer pers. observations) and encountered along with Aotus miconax at tourist centres in the upper Mayo valley (Mark 2003).
population: A few short surveys were undertaken by Rowe and Martinez (2003), Mark (2003) and DeLuycker (2006), while long-term extensive surveys have been conducted by Proyecto Mono Tocón (Bóveda-Penalba et al. 2009, Proyecto Mono Tocón unpublished data). Aldrich (2006) undertook a song-based survey of a population at Tarangue (a 74 ha private reserve near Moyobamba) and estimated a population density of 1.4 individuals per ha. Group sizes were unusually large for Titi Monkeys, with 20% of groups containing six to eight individuals. Rowe and Martinez (2003) carried out a four-day survey, and although they did not observe the species in the wild, they heard several groups of Titi Monkeys (presumed to be P. oenanthe) vocalizing in a forest remnant at 925 m. They photographed a family being sold at a local market that had been captured near Rioja. Mark (2003) carried out surveys at five sites and observed monkeys in fragments as small as 2 ha (804 m asl). Density studies at and around Pucunucho and Mangapaquina (a 23.5 ha private conservation area near Juanjui) resulted in an estimated population density of 0.36 groups and 1.27 individuals per ha (N. Allgas, pers comm.). Other studies in larger protected areas gave densities of only 0.19 to 0.33 individuals per hectare, with higher densities on the borders of the protected areas (Proyecto Mono Tocón, unpublished data). It is probable that the higher densities in the smaller study areas reflect the critical situation of the species, with animals finding their last refuge in small forest fragments surrounded by pasture, leading to unsustainable overcrowding of the last remaining habitat. Differences in habitat types may also lead to differences in densities.It is estimated that a population reduction of ≥80% has occurred over the last 25 years due to massive deforestation of this species' preferred habitat as a result of increased human population pressure and intensification of agricultural activities.
range: Until 2007, this species was thought to be endemic to the upper Rio Mayo valley or Alto Mayo (Hershkovitz 1990). However, a study by Bóveda-Penalba et al. 2009, undertaken over six months at 96 localities, revealed that its distribution extends much further to the south of the Department of San Martin, extending into the Bajo Mayo and Huallaga Central, reaching the lowland area on the right bank of the Rio Huayabamba. This area is heavily deforested, and to date only a few areas were found where a viable population might live, although further research is needed to confirm this. Mark (2003) and DeLuycker (2006) suggested that the species’ altitudinal range may be restricted to below 1,000 m. The study undertaken by Bóveda-Penalba et al. (2009) registered the species between 252 and 1,053 metres asl, but later studies confirmed that the species might live in areas of up to 1,400 metres asl (Proyecto Mono Tocón, unpublished data; Shanee et al 2013 a,b), with low densities in the higher altitudes (Proyecto Mono Tocón, unpublished data; S. Shanee pers. comm).  Analyses show an estimated original range of 14,686 km², but that more than more of 55% of its original habitat has disappeared (Shanee et al. 2013c). Of the remaining habitat, only 1,930 km² is rated as “good” (Shanee et al. 2013c) and climate change could further aggravate the situation. There is an urgent need for additional surveys of all potential habitats in San Martin, and larger tracts of forest. The species lives in certain areas in sympatry with Plecturocebus discolor (Vermeer et al. 2011).There has been significant deforestation of this species' preferred habitat as a result of increased human population pressure and intensification of agricultural activities.
useTrade: It is locally hunted for food, and animals are taken as pets.
conservationActions: Very little attention has been given to forest conservation in this region. This species’ range include the borders and buffer zone of the Bosque de Protección de Alto Mayo, which extends from the town of Rioja north along the border between the departments of San Martín and Amazonas, however protection in this area is poor. During short surveys of the Reserve, no titis were detected in the high-altitude areas which make up most of the reserve. Other protected areas in this species’ range include small to medium-sized conservation areas, often managed by local communities with support of NGOs. The total surface of the protected habitat does not exceed 15,000 hectares. Mark (2003) and DeLuycker (2006) have emphasized the potential importance of both privately owned reserves and Amerindian reservations for the long-term conservation of this species. There are 14 indigenous Aguaruna communities located throughout the Alto Mayo region. The large tracts of forested land allocated to these well-organized communities could play a key role in conservation initiatives (Mark 2003). However, collaboration with these communities has proven to be very difficult, and there seems to be little interest in nature conservation. Proyecto Mono Tocón, started in 2007 as an initiative of Le Conservatoire pour la Protection des Primates, a French foundation created by the French zoo La Vallée des Singes. The main objective of this project is the conservation of San Martin Titi Monkey (P. oenanthe) and its habitat. It has three well-defined lines of work: Conservation, Research and Environmental Education. The Proyecto Mono Tocón works directly with local people, local governments and other NGOs in establishing community conservation areas. Other local NGOs active for the conservation of Plecturocebus oenanthe include the Asociación Amazónicos por la Amazonía (AMPA) and Neotropical Primate Conservation (NPC).  It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered due to a suspected population decline that will be greater than 80% for three generations in to the future (27 years). It is suspected that populations will rapidly decline due to: 1) the continued human population increases (projected at ca 38% over 27 years into the future based on historical rates of increase) which will lead to increased rates of hunting; 2) continued forest loss (of at least 13% over 27 years based on historical Global Forest Watch forest loss rates for the Jose Ballivian Region; Global Forest Watch 2020); and 3) rapid habitat fragmentation and degradation after the road is paved between Rurrenabaque and Santa Rosa (which will further exacerbate habitat loss, fragmentation and hunting through increase human incursion in to the area; Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013).The species has a restricted range (383.4 km²), making it even more vulnerable to rapid population declines due to ongoing and increased threats listed above. Though this is above the threshold for the species to be considered Critically Endangered on the basis of its extent of occurrence (EOO), it should be emphasized that only one-third of this area is forested (Wallace et al. 2013). The region is highly sensitive to forest loss and fragmentation caused principally by accidents during grassland burning applied in pasture management for cattle ranching (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013, Siles et al. 2019). A 2016 study in Bolivia have found that rapid frontier expansion (such as found here) and extreme dry conditions (which may occur in the future due to climate change) could result in increased fire risk of 1.8 times higher than in 2010 in high-risk areas (Devisscher et al. 2016).The species is found in two municipal protected areas, Pampas del Yacuma and Rhukanrhuka, which are currently attempting to consolidate their management. Nevertheless, P. olallae, is not found in any national protected areas.
habitat: This taxon occurs within a forest-savanna mosaic, and is restricted to gallery and riverine forest of the Yacuma River (Felton et al. 2006, Wallace et al. 2013). Although P. modestus is found in the same savannah ecosystem, P. olallae occurs in more humid forest associated with the Yacuma River and its seasonal flooding regime (Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010). Martinez and Wallace (2007) and Lopez-Strauss (2008) details average group sizes of 2.7 and 2 individuals, respectively. The most recent assessment reports an average group size of 2.4 individuals (Martinez and Wallace in press).A recent behavioural ecology study estimated the home range for P. olallae as 7.16 ha (Martinez 2014). The diet was mainly frugivorous, with leaves as the second most consumed item (López 2011, WCS unpublished data). In heavily fragmented forests, terrestrial group movements corresponded to 7% of total group movements (Martinez and Wallace 2011). Similar terrestrial movements were observed when groups of P. olallae lost territories due to anthropogenic causes (smoke from grassland burning) and spatial competition with other primates (Saimiri boliviensis and Aotus spp.) (Martinez and Wallace 2011).
threats: There is forest loss and habitat fragmentation within the range of P. olallae, related to the main economic activity in the region, cattle ranching, that manages grasslands as pastures using annual burning techniques (Wallace et al. 2013). Significant forest fragmentation was suggested as promoting terrestrial movements of P. olallae, increasing exposure to predation risks (Martinez and Wallace 2011). Uncontrolled fire during grassland burning to promote pasture regrowth can affect forest coverage, reducing habitat availability for P. olallae (Martinez and Wallace in press). Indirect effects of fire represent a threat for this species, as was observed in one group leaving its territory due to heavy smoke, when the grassland next to its forest patch was burned (Martinez and Wallace 2011). Critically, the ongoing major improvement to a regional road, The Northern Corridor, that passes close to the distributional range of P. olallae, implies high deforestation pressures related to potential new human settlements (Felton et al. 2006; Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010; Wallace et al. 2013). The improved road could promote increases in cattle ranching and may increase hunting pressure too.The disappearance of the species from the type locality—La Laguna—(Felton et al. 2006), and the rescue of a hunted specimen (Martinez et al. 2013) indicates that they may be threatened locally by hunting as they are used as bait for fishing. Spatial competition with sympatric primates such as Saimiri boliviensis and Aotus spp. may also be a threat to P. olallae (Martinez and Wallace 2011).
population: The species was formerly only known from the type locality: La Laguna, 5 km from Santa Rosa, [upper río] Beni, Bolivia, altitude about 200 m (Tarifa 1996, Anderson 1997). In 2002, Felton et al. (2006) conducted titi monkey surveys and interviewed local residents at four locations: Puerto Santa Cruz on the Río Yacuma; the type locality of La Laguna; Petaca; and Naranjal. Titis were relatively abundant in Naranjal, not encountered in Petaca (although local residents claim they occur there), and are no longer present in La Laguna (probably exterminated through hunting). Examination of holotypes indicates that groups encountered in Rio Yacuma were P. olallae, while two of three groups found in Naranjal were P. modestus (the third appeared to combine characters from both species).Lopez-Strauss (2008) estimated density for both P. olallae and P. modestus using territorial calling behaviour and an adapted point-count methodology. From this assessment, the average density estimated for P. olallae was 5.94 (DS±3.50) groups per km² (Lopez-Strauss and Wallace 2015).According to the most recent assessment (Martinez and Wallace in press), the total estimated population size is a maximum of 2,855 individuals. This estimate assumes ubiquitous distribution in forests, however, for areas where more precise data is available the distribution of titi monkey groups is not ubiquitous (WCS unpublished data). Given restrictions in suitable habitat, and conservation threats such as habitat degradation (due to human activities and climatic change) and increasing hunting, it is suspected that the population could suffer a decline of 80% over the next three generations (ca 27 years).
range: This species is endemic to Bolivia with a very restricted range; its extent of occurrence (EOO; based on the distribution map) is estimated to be around 677 km², of which available and suitable forest habitat might be less than one-third (Wallace et al. 2013, Martinez and Wallace in press). This area is located in the forests associated with the Yacuma River, in southwestern Beni Department (Martinez and Wallace 2007, 2010; Wallace et al. 2013, Martinez and Wallace in press).According to a recent assessment (Martinez and Wallace in press), Plecturocebus olallae has a restricted range (383.4 km²) in which forest coverage is around 54%. Not all the forest coverage identifiable from satellite imagery corresponds to tree-forest as there are shrub-forests not suitable for this species. Although forest types are not identifiable from satellite imagery, shrub-forests were found to be more than 60% of some forested areas. Population density estimations vary from 3 to 12 groups per square kilometres, with the lower values found in the larger forest areas where this species does not occur in taller forests. This shows that apart from the fragmented nature of forests immersed in a savannah matrix, not all the already scarce forest coverage is suitable habitat for Olalla’s titi monkey. Though the distributional area is above the threshold for the species to be considered Critically Endangered on the basis of its extent of occurrence (EOO), it should be emphasized that according to the most recent data even previous considerations that one-third of the range of P. olallae represents suitable habitat (Wallace et al. 2013) may represent an overestimation.It is suspected that its area of occupancy (AOO) and habitat quality of the species will continue to decline at rates faster than historically seen, due to the paving of a road that lies adjacent to its small range. The paving of this road will exacerbate habitat degradation, which was already taking place at high rates primarily due to uncontrolled fires from agriculture. The recent approval of the Land Use Plan for the Beni Department (PLUS Beni), also promotes large-scale mechanized agriculture in the Llanos de Moxos representing a particular threat in areas with improved transport networks.The region is highly sensitive to increases in forest loss and fragmentation caused principally by accidents during grassland burning applied in pasture management for cattle ranching (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013, Siles et al. 2019). A 2016 study in Bolivia found that rapid frontier expansion for cattle ranching and agriculture, as well as extreme dry conditions (which may occur in the future due to climate change) could result in increased fire risk of 1.8 times higher than in 2010 in high-risk areas (Devisscher et al. 2016). Moreover, the current paving of the North Corridor, a major road passing immediately adjacent to the range of P. olallae, represents a significant risk of habitat loss due to potential expansion of human settlements as well as changes in land use (Martinez and Wallace 2010, Wallace et al. 2013). This situation will be exacerbated by recent changes in the Land Use Plan for the Beni Department which openly encourage and facilitate mechanized agriculture in the region.
useTrade: Martinez et al. (2013) indicates that they may be threatened locally by occasional hunting, as they can be used as bait for fishing. It is suspected that hunting rates will increase due to the increasing human population of the region promoted by the ongoing paving of the road (North Corridor) which is adjacent to the small P. olallae range.
conservationActions: The species does not occur in any national protected areas, but is present in two municipal protected areas: Pampas del Yacuma and Rhukanrhuka, in Santa Rosa del Yacuma and Reyes municipalities, respectively. In both cases, P. olallae is recognized as a conservation priority, but conservation actions are urgently needed. Recently the Pampas del Yacuma protected area developed a management plan which will help in the conservation of this endemic primate. A recent work added information about vulnerable zones for P. olallae regarding excessive flooding, uncontrolled fires and deforestation, representing a good starting point for further conservation actions for forest habitats in the region (Siles et al. 2019). Also, a recent assessment updated information on distribution and abundance, as well as conservation threats for P. olallae (Martinez and Wallace in press).Conservation programs in the region include the Greater Madidi Landscape Conservation Program of the Wildlife Conservation Society in northern La Paz and southwestern Beni Departments, who led research on the species and worked with the Santa Rosa Municipality in the development of the Pampas del Yacuma protected area management plan. In addition, WCS currently supports the development of distinct management tools for the recently created Rhukanrhuka municipal protected area.Plecturocebus olallae is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Although hunted by locals, its range is within one of the most pristine and preserved parts of the Amazon where human population densities are low and no development projects are planned for the near future, hence assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: No information on the habitat preference or ecology of this species is currently available.
threats: Little information on the threats facing this species is currently available.
population: No population information is currently available.
range: If confirmed that C. israelita deserves full species status and does not represent a junior synonym of C. chiropotes, the boundary separating these two taxa is the Rio Orinoco (Amazonas State, Venezuela), with the former being restricted to the left bank and the latter to the right bank.  In Brazil, C. israelita is restricted to the Rio Branco – Rio Marauia interfluvial area (left bank of the Rio Negro in Amazonas and Roraima States).

rationale: Chiropotes utahickae is considered Vulnerable (VU A4cd), as a population reduction of 30% or more is suspected over the course of 30 years or three generations—the current (2019-2028) and two subsequent generations (2029-2048). This is based upon Global Forest Watch data for the Brazilian states of Para and Mata Grosso. The data suggests that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has impacted the previous generation (2009-2018), 25% or more of this species’ suitable habitat is likely to be lost by the year 2048. Combined with continued evidence of subsistence hunting, these threats place Chirpotes utahickae well above the threshold for Vulnerable status.
habitat: Uta Hick's bearded saki is endemic to the fluvial plain of Amazonia, where it occurs in tall terra firme humid forests at low altitudes. It was also recorded in disturbed forests.This species is highly frugivorous, with the diet comprised of seeds (53%), fruit pulp (26%), flowers (18%) and small quantities of insects, leaves and other plant parts (Santos 2002; Vieira 2005). In a study of a group on an island (129 ha), over 150 plant species were consumed. Important species include Alexa grandiflora (Fabaceae), Annona tenuipes (Annonaceae), Inga alba (Mimosaceae), Eschweilera sp. (Lecythidaceae) and Attalea speciosa (Arecaceae). Home range sizes between 60 and 100 ha, and average daily movement distances of 2.5 km were recorded by Vieira (2005). Recent studies have demonstrated that eastern Amazonian bearded sakis are more tolerant of anthropogenic habitat disturbance than previously assumed, with groups often able to survive in isolated fragments (<50 ha), some of which have been isolated for over 20 years (Ferrari et al. 2002; Santos 2002; Vieira 2005).
threats: The key threats to the species’ future survival are habitat loss and forest fragmentation. The establishment of several large infrastructure projects (such as the Transamazonian highway BR-230), which bisects the interfluvium from east to west, the Carajás Mineral Complex and the Tucuruí hydroelectric dam, led to considerable habitat loss. In the north of the species’ range, the habitat is under pressure from both, small-holder and large-scale farming activities as well as cattle ranching. The Uta Hick’s bearded saki is also hunted for its meat and fur, and hunting pressure is likely to increase due to habitat fragmentation.
population: Using standardized line transects, population densities and sighting rates have been calculated for a number of areas (see Table 1 in the Supplementary Information). Without hunting pressure this species can occur at high densities in altered habitats and small forest fragments than in areas of continuous forest (Bobadilla and Ferrari 1998, Ferrari et al. 1999).A population reduction of 30% or more is suspected over the course of 30 years or three generations—the current (2019-2028) and two subsequent generations (2029-2048).  This is due to habitat degradation and subsistence hunting.
range: Endemic to Brazil, the species inhabits the Amazon lowlands. The geographical distribution limited to the West is the Xingu River, the northern boundary is delimited by the Amazon River and to the East by the Tocantins-Araguaia River. (Hershkovitz 1985, Ferrari and Lopes 1996, Rylands 1994b, Silva Jr. and Figueiredo 2002). The southern boundary is unknown, although there is a sample in the National Museum in Rio de Janeiro, which indicates the Tapirapé River in north-eastern Mato Grosso as the collection locality (J. Silva Jr. pers. comm.). A survey of the central Cerrado in Brazil would be necessary to assess the species’ distribution in areas of contact with the Amazon forest where the species may also, although unlikely, occur (Lopes et al. 2008).Global Forest Watch data for the Brazilian states of Para and Mata Grosso suggests that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has impacted the previous generation (2009-2018), 25% or more of this species’ suitable habitat is likely to be lost by the year 2048.
useTrade: This species is threatened by subsistence hunting.
conservationActions: The following federal reserves occur within the Uta Hick’s bearded saki’s range:Pará State: REBIO de Tapirapé (103,000 ha)FLONA Carajás (411,949 ha)FLONA Caxiuanã (324,060 ha) FLONA Itacaiúna (141,400 ha) FLONA Tapirapé-Aquiri (190,000 ha) APA Igarapé Gelado (21,600 ha) RESEX Ipaú-Anilzinho (55,816 ha) RDS Itapuã-Baquiá (64,735 ha) State reserves in Pará include: the Parque Estadual da Serra dos Martírios/Andorinhas (24,897 ha) APA Lago de Tucuruí – margem esquerda (568,667 ha) APA São Geraldo do Araguaia (29,655 ha), RDS Alcobaça (36,128 ha) RDS Pucuruí-Ararão (29,049 ha) (Lopes et al. in press). Surveys are needed south of the rio Tapirapé in northern Mato Grosso to confirm range limits.The Primate Protection Centre (Centro de Proteção de Primatas Brasileiros; ICM/CPB), of the Federal Environmental Protection Institute (Instituto Chico Mendes), supports and coordinates primate conservation programmes throughout the country. An international committee to discuss and define actions for the conservation of Amazonian primate taxa (Comitê Internacional para Conservação e Manejo dos Primatas Amazônicos) was established by the CPB and the Instituto Chico Mendes (ICM), and together with the members of the Pitheciine Action Group (PAG) a Conservation Action Plan was developed for the Conservation of Endemic Species and Endangered Fauna of the Lower and Middle Xingu Region where the Uta Hick’s Bearded Saki occurs.It is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Over the last 20 years (approximately three generations), at least 30% of this species' habitat has been lost. It is suspected that the population has also declined by at least 30% as a result of this habitat loss, therefore the species is assessed as Vulnerable. It is likely that the species will continue declining at a similar rate over the next 20 years if habitat loss continues. In addition, levels of exploitation can be regionally high for the pet trade, yet impacts at the population level are unknown. Further research is needed (taxonomic, threat and ecological) in order to further assess this species.
habitat: This species can live in both primary and secondary forest, as well as along the coasts or on the edge of plantations (Niemitz 1979). This is often described as a lowland species, most common below 100 m elevation; however, there is at least one record from 1,200 m from the Bukit Baka-Bukit Raya National Park in western Kalimantan (Gorog and Sinaga 2008).The species is 100% carnivorous, eating mainly insects (including beetles, grasshoppers, cockroaches, butterflies, moths, praying mantis, ants, phasmids, and cicadas), but also small vertebrates (including bats, snakes, and birds) (Niemitz 1979). These animals are nocturnal and exhibit adaptations for vertical clinging and leaping modes of locomotion and prey capture (Roberts 1994). They spend a majority of their time below 2 m off the ground and only 5% above 3 m (Niemitz 1979, 1984; Crompton and Andau 1986, 1987).
threats: The principle threat to the species is habitat loss due to forest conversion, especially due to expanding oil palm plantations, fires and logging. The species is collected for the illegal pet trade, particularly, it is thought, in the vicinity of Lampung and Way Kambas National Park. It is wrongly considered a pest to agricultural crops, and can suffer, directly and indirectly, from contamination from agricultural pesticides.
population: Density has been variously calculated at 80 animals/km² in Sarawak (Niemitz 1979, 1984), 15–20 individuals/km² in Sabah (Crompton and Andau 1986, 1987), and 19–20 individuals/km² in Belitung (I. Yustian pers. comm.). Based on satellite studies of the extent of available habitat on Belitung Island, Yustian (2006) estimated a total population for Cephalopachus bancanus saltator of 29,440 (Yustian unpubl. data).
range: This species is found in Brunei, Indonesia (Bangka, Belitung, Karimata, southeastern Sumatra, Serasen in the South Natuna Islands, and Kalimantan Borneo), and Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak) (Groves 2005). The distribution in Sumatra is unknown but is thought to be delimited by the Musi River.Cephalopachus bancanus saltator is restricted to the island of Belitung (Billiton), Indonesia. Cephalopachus bancanus natunensis is confined to Serasan (Sirhassen) in the South Natuna Islands, and possibly nearby Subi Island, Indonesia. Cephalopachus bancanus borneanus occurs in Brunei, Indonesia (Kalimantan Borneo and Karimata Islands) and Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak Borneo) and on the island of Karimata (Indonesia). Cephalopachus bancanus bancanus occurs in southeastern Sumatra and the island of Bangka, Indonesia.
useTrade: The species is captured live for the pet trade.
