conservationActions: The species is protected by law in Indonesia and in Malaysia, and is listed in CITES Appendix II.Cephalopachus bancanus bancanus occurs in a few protected areas, such as Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park, Kerinci Seblat National Park, Way Kambas National Park (Indonesia) (M. Richardson pers. comm.); C. b. borneanus occurs in several protected areas, including Tasek Merimbun Sanctuary (Brunei); Bukit Baka Bukit Raya National Park, Kayan Mentarang National Park (Indonesia); Bako National Park, Gunung Malu National Park, Kinabalu National Park, Sapagaya Forest Reserve, Semengo Forest Reserve, Sepilok Forest Reserve (Malaysia) (M. Richardson pers. comm.); whileC. b. saltator and C. b. natunensis do not occur in any protected areas.

rationale: Tarsius tumpara is listed as Critically Endangered because there has been an estimated and continuing reduction in population size of at least 80% over the past three generations, based on actual levels of exploitation and on the direct observations by local people living in proximity to the tarsiers, along with declines in the area of occupancy (perhaps as little as 19.4 km²) and quality of habitat.
habitat: Tarsius tumpara has not been the subject of systematic study, but it has been surveyed in the wild by a team led by M. Shekelle (Shekelle et al. 2008), and Siau Island was surveyed by Riley (2002). By analogy with other wild Tarsier populations it is expected that this taxon is found in primary (although no tracts of primary forest have been found on Siau Island), secondary and mangrove forests, forest gardens, and a variety of other habitats of varying degrees of human disturbance that provide adequate shrubby cover. Shekelle and Salim (2009b) reported that their surveys found evidence of T. tumpara in only two places; on the shores of a small freshwater pond at the extreme southern end of the island, and on a steep cliff face along the east coast road where it runs next to the ocean. Numerous other sites that appeared promising turned up no evidence of the presence of tarsiers. There are reports that they can still be found high on the flanks of Mt Karengetang, near the caldera.Tarsius tumpara is phylogenetically linked to other Eastern Tarsiers, from the Sulawesi biogeographic region. All the species in this clade live in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 26. Anecdotal observations of T. tumpara, and those of its likely sister taxon, T. sangirensis, indicate that these species might sleep in dispersed social groups, particularly in disturbed habitat, and that this might be a response to predation, particularly by humans and human commensals, such as feral cats and dogs. Merker (2006) studied home range size in T. dentatus and found it to vary, depending on the degree of human disturbance, with home range size increasing with the degree of disturbance. Its diet is mostly large-bodied arthropods, with some small vertebrates.
threats: The primary threat to this taxon is that its range is restricted to one small, volcanic island. The volcano, Mt. Karengentang, is active and dominates more than 50% of its geographical range. This threat is exacerbated by a relatively large human population (311 people/km²) that has converted virtually all of the primary habitat to some form of human use (Shekelle and Salim 2009a, 2009b). In these ways, Tarsius tumpara faces a set of threats similar to those faced by T. sangirensis, but the threats are more acute for T. tumpara: a smaller island, a more active volcano, and higher human population density. Most troubling, however, are numerous credible reports that the local human population regularly eats tarsiers, up to 5 to10 animals at a sitting, and that tarsiers have been extirpated from areas where they were common as recently as 10 years ago. The population is likely scattered and reported heavily disturbed land on the southern end of the island and the land set apart for conversion. The tarsiers are found in two remote sites of the island where they are hunted and consumed as food. Might be found in Mount Tamata which is deemed ‘unofficially protected’. Tarsius tumpara is considered to be one of the world’s 25 most endangered primates by the IUCN Species Survival Commission Primate Specialist Group (Shekelle and Salim 2007, 2009b).Predation by feral cats and dogs are associated threats of habitat destruction due to human encroachment.
population: Shekelle and Salim (2009a) used remote sensing of remaining habitat and population density estimates from studies of other tarsier taxa to estimate the remaining populations being 1,358–12,470 individuals. The large range is a result of a large number of unknown pixels (obscured by clouds) in the GIS data set. Field surveys indicate no remaining primary habitat, however. Local people reported considerable declines of numbers since the late 1990s (Shekelle and Salim 2009b).
range: The species is found only on Siau Island (Indonesia), although it is conceivable that they are also present on some very small islands that are in proximity to Siau and separated only by shallow ocean. The Sangir and Siau islands are separated by ca 60 km of ocean with depths >1,000 m with zero gene flow between Tarsius sangirensis and T. tumpara.
useTrade: This species is locally hunted for food.
conservationActions: A local conservation organization, Celebes Bio, has begun surveys on the island.  A nascent tourism industry is forming slowly. Government proposals for expansion, including an airport, could threaten key habitat.

rationale: Tarsius sangirensis is listed as Endangered because it is known only from Sangihe Island which has a total area of 547 km². Its range is severely fragmented, and there is ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to clearing for agriculture.
habitat: This population has not been studied systematically in the wild, but was surveyed by Shekelle and associates (Shekelle et al. 1997, Shekelle 2003) and Riley (2002). Riley remarked that Tarsius sangirensis has a preference for primary forest, but may also occur in secondary habitats including sago swamps, scrub, nutmeg plantations, coconut plantations, and secondary forest growth. These results are similar to those of Shekelle and associates, except that Shekelle did not encounter any in primary forest, and Shekelle and Salim (2009) indicate that it is very unlikely that any primary forest now remains on the island. A study of Tarsius dentatus on Sulawesi by Merker et al. (2005; also Merker and Yustian 2008) showed that they were able to occupy agricultural land as long there were remnant patches of forest or dense shrubbery, although group sizes were smaller and population densities were considerably lower (less than half) than was found for virtually undisturbed old growth forest (estimated densities 268 individuals/km² versus 45 individuals/km²). Like other Eastern Tarsier species from the Sulawesi biogeographic region, this species lives in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 2–6. It might sleep in dispersed social groups, particularly in disturbed habitat, and that this might be a response to predation, particularly by humans and human commensals, such as feral cats and dogs. Unlike all other tarsiers, individuals are known to sleep on exposed bamboos, on top of palm leaves and trees and this behaviour is seen to reflect on the poor habitat availability. Great Sangihe Tarsiers are known to prefer typical sleeping sites as the other eastern tarsiers. Merker (2006) studied home range size in T. dentatus and found it to vary, depending on the degree of human disturbance, with home range size increasing with the degree of disturbance. Its diet is mostly large arthropods and some small vertebrates.
threats: Shekelle and Salim (2009) argue that the chief threat to tarsiers on Sangihe Island is habitat loss. One major driver of habitat loss is the clearing of forests and forest gardens for more intensive agriculture where underbrush is cleared, such as coconut monocrop, coconut/cocoa, nutmeg, and others (M. Shekelle pers. comm. 2010). Riley (2002), however, did not think that habitat loss was a major threat, given their presence in a variety of secondary habitats. This discrepancy emphasizes the need to determine the suitability of secondary habitats for sustainable tarsier populations. The volcano on Sangihe Island, Mt Awu, is active and one of the deadliest in Indonesia, and the human population density on the island is very high (260 people km²) (Shekelle and Salim 2009). There is practically no primary forest left and there are no protected areas in its range (Shekelle and Salim 2009).The tarsiers today survive in primary and late succession secondary forest, as the real habitat is now either fragmented, degraded or completely destroyed. The primary and secondary forest is now limited a 940 ha in Mt. Sahendaruman. This patch, though just a ‘green belt’ is locally known as hutun lindung or protected forest but is a ‘deceptive’ travesty of anything close to protection. The species requires immediate status reassessment as when designated as Endangered it was believed to be present on another island namely Siau. But later, the species in Siau was identified as a distinct taxon, Tarsius tumpara.
population: Shekelle and Salim (2009) used remote sensing to estimate the total population to be between 1,505 and 52,734 individuals, the very wide range being a result of uncertainty in the suitability of "brush" habitat for sustainable tarsier populations. Without including "brush", the population estimate is only 1,505–2,795 individuals. Riley (2002) estimated total population as 9,000–15,600, but those numbers drop to 300–500 if secondary habitat is excluded. Riley did not address the issue that, while tarsiers are recorded in secondary habitats, these might not support sustainable populations. Thus, the conclusions of both studies are similar; the viable population might be very small indeed, unless populations in suboptimal habitats are "sources" and not "sinks".
range: Currently this species is recorded as occurring only on Sangihe island, north of Sulawesi, Indonesia (Riley 2002), but it might occur in the other tiny islands of Sangihe chain.
useTrade: This species is locally hunted for food.
conservationActions: The taxon has been protected by national law since 1931, and is listed in CITES Appendix II. Two conservation initiatives begun in 2002 are serving to establish management systems on this archipelago and to educate its people on the environmental and conservation problems that the islands face, including those resulting from forest management and hunting (Riley 2002) (see Whitten 2006).

rationale: This species is considered Endangered as it is known to occur only on Peleng island, where it occurs in a number of fragmented populations, and a there is believed to be a continued decline in extent and quality of its habitat. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is smaller than 5,000 km².
habitat: This species is believed to inhabit primary and secondary lowland and mangrove forest (to 520 m) (M. Indrawan and Y. Masala pers. comm.). Like all tarsiers, it shows extreme adaptations for vertical clinging and leaping (VCL) in the understory of suitable tropical habitats, often two meters or less from the ground. Nocturnal, social primates, they are likely to live in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 2–6. Their diet is 100% live animal prey, mostly insects such as moths and crickets with some small vertebrates such as frogs and lizards.
threats: Geographic Information System (GIS) estimates indicate that only 211 km² of “good” habitat remains on Peleng Island (2,339 km²). This implies that perhaps as little as 9% of the original habitat of the island remains in good condition. Therefore, it seems likely that, while we know little about this species, habitat loss through slash and burn activities is a major threat. On the other hand, it is not clear that “good” habitat is also compatible with the needs of tarsier conservation. All tarsier species that have been studied in the wild are recorded in a number of non-forest habitats, but it remains an open question whether these habitats are suitable for sustainably reproducing populations. GIS data also provide an estimate of 1,474 km² of “fair” habitat remaining on Pulau Peleng. Together with “good” habitat, this yields a total of 1,685 km² of habitat that is potentially suitable for tarsier conservation, a figure that represents slightly more than 72% of the island’s total area. In other words, the estimate of the percentage of the original tarsier habitat that still remains on Pulau Peleng varies from 9 to 72%, depending on whether “fair” habitat is included in the model. This example illustrates the need for field surveys to determine the suitability of “fair” habitat for sustainable tarsier populations. In the meantime, we use a most conservative estimate that includes good habitat only. First-hand reports of conditions on Pulau Peleng are scant, but by analogy with other areas of Sulawesi, it should likely expect a continuing pattern of encroachment into tarsier habitat, leading to a decrease in the area of occupancy, quality of habitat, number of tarsier populations and mature individuals (M. Shekelle pers. comm.). Other threats may include illegal logging, agricultural pesticides, and predation by domestic animals (dogs and cats). Less than 10% area of the island is suitable for the tarsier and therefore their conservation status demands reassessment.
population: This taxon has not been studied in the wild. By analogy with other taxa of eastern tarsiers, we can estimate that densities in good habitat might be 156 individuals/km² (Gursky 1997), or, as for Tarsius dentatus (Merker 2003) up to 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 190 individuals/km² for slightly disturbed habitat, 130 individuals/km² for moderate disturbance, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitat.
range: This species is found on Peleng Island (Sody 1949), off the coast of the eastern peninsula of Sulawesi. There are unconfirmed reports that tarsiers might be present on other islands of the nearby Banggai Archipelago, and if these reports are accurate, then this would extend the range of Tarsius pelengensis.
useTrade: Use in this species is not known.
conservationActions: There are no decreed protection areas on Pulau Peleng. The species is listed in CITES Appendix II. Area of occupancy (AOO) for this species is considerably smaller than its overall area of distribution or cover, which is 1,925 km². Less than 10% area of the island is suitable for the tarsier and therefore their conservation status demands reassessment

rationale: Tarsius wallacei is assessed as Vulnerable based upon an extent of occurrence less than 9,000-10,000 km², severe fragmentation of the population, and continuing decline in area of occupancy and quality of habitat.
habitat: The species occurs in primary, secondary, and degraded forest habitats. Found in recently cleared agricultural lands, agroforestry lands and secondary forests, in Tinomba, on Isthmus of Palu, west of Tomini to ca 120°30’E, Isthmas of Palu coastlines to the East, Ampibabo village to west, and Marantale to South. (0°30’) Northern population lives mostly in degraded and mountainous habitat with an estimated distribution of 3,150 km². Southern population has a very small distribution of 50 km², west to the south west of Palu, around Uwamanje which is also the type locality (0°58’ S,119° 50’). Nocturnal and arboreal.So far, little is known on the ecology of Tarsius wallacei. Given the morphological and ecological similarity of the species to other Sulawesi lowland tarsiers, this nocturnal primate is expected to feed on live animal prey with insects as the main component of its prey and to spend daylight hours in holes or crevices of strangling figs (Ficus spp.).
threats: As with other tarsier species, Tarsius wallacei faces habitat loss and degradation effected by conversion of rainforest to cash crop plantations. In light of a very small range of the Uwemanje form, local policymaking in one or a few villages may be of high impact on this stock.
population: The isolated southern population of Tarsius wallacei occurs in a very small area of probably no more than 5x10 km (Merker et al. 2010). Satellite images suggest an even much smaller area of occupancy in this region and thus, although population estimates are still lacking, a critical status of this stock is conceivable.
range: This species occupies a discontinuous range in the province of Central Sulawesi. Northern and southern populations are isolated from each other by the Palu Bay, the city of Palu, and the southern parts of the Isthmus of Palu, an area now inhabited by the parapatric species Tarsius dentatus. The current evidence indicates that the northern population occurs within the following geographic limits: an unknown line just west of the village of Tomini to the northeast (about 120º30'E), the coastlines of the Isthmus of Palu to the east and to the west, and an unknown line between the village of Ampibabo and Marantale to the south (about 0º30'S). Along its northern border, this population borders the “Sejoli form” sensu Shekelle et al. (1997). At its southern limit, this population borders T. dentatus (Merker et al. 2010). The southern population occurs southwest to west of Palu, it is definitely known from the type locality Uwemanje only and probably occurs in a very small area from Uwemanje to the west. Approximately 9 km to the south T. dentatus is found, and 24 km to the northwest, T. lariang (Merker et al. 2010). The two populations are distinguished as T. wallacei Tinombo form (northern) and T. wallacei Uwemanje form (southern).
conservationActions: The species is included in CITES Appendix II. Classified Data Deficient on IUCN Red List. The range of the northern population of T. wallacei includes Gunung Sojol. More conservation research required to clarify status of Wallace’s tarsier.

rationale: This species is considered Vulnerable based on the continued loss of suitable habitat on Sulawesi, and the combined threats from habitat loss, conversion, degradation, pet trade, attacks by feral dogs and cats, and persecution. These threats are suspected to have contributed to a population decline of over 30% over the last 22.5 years (three generations). It is suspected that the population will continue to decline at the same rate into the future.
habitat: This species has been studied in the field (Tremble et al. 1993, Merker 2006, Merker et al. 2005, Merker 2003, Merker and Mühlenberg 2000, Gursky 1998). It occurs in primary, secondary and mangrove forests, forest gardens, and a variety of other habitats of varying degrees of human disturbance that provide adequate shrubby cover. Lore Lindu National Park: 70% of the park is hilly and montane at 1,000–1,500 m above sea level with 3,100 mm  annual rainfall. They feed mainly on insects such as moths and crickets, small vertebrates such as frog and lizards. The diet is 100% live animal prey, mostly insects with some small vertebrates.Like all tarsiers it shows extreme adaptations for vertical clinging and leaping (VCL) in the understory of suitable tropical habitats, often 0 m or less from the ground.Nocturnal and arboreal social primates, they likely live in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 2–7 individuals (Merker 2003), sharing their home range with more than one adult of the same sex. Prefers dense vegetation and tree cavities for sleeping. Normally one sleeping site and two or three alternative sites are used. Nocturnal as they are, their activity period commences a little after sundown and ends a bit before dawn, when they are known to travel fastest at a speed of 100 m/15 minutes to get to their sleeping sites. Activity during night is characterized by periods of inactivity and foraging. A little before dawn, these animals sing their ‘territorial duet’ before getting back to their sleeping sites.Home range sizes have been recorded as 1.0–1.8 ha depending on habitat type. Male home ranges as studied in Lori Lindu National Park were a little higher (1.8 ha) than female home ranges (1.6 ha). Home range of these tarsiers are largest in habitats where disturbances are well pronounced than in those that are little disturbed. Heavily disturbed habitats were further affected by herbicide that affected insect abundance, main source of tarsier food and natural supporters that facilitated tarsier locomotion. Home ranges of mated individuals overlap extensively but that is not so in the case of individuals outside the group. Nightly distances 600–1,260 m, varied with habitat, and distances increased with habitat disturbance. Dian’s tarsier can live in lowland and secondary forest but it is scarcer at higher elevations but a large part of its distribution in Sulawesi is in montane region.These tarsiers can survive and adapt to small scale agro-forestry and selective logging and disturbed forests are still a good survival bet for these tarsiers (Estrada et al. 2012).
threats: The primary threat to this species is loss of habitat loss due to illegal logging. Other threats include agricultural pesticides and predation by domestic animals (dogs and cats). In addition, some animals enter the pet trade. There has been extensive loss of lowland forest habitat. This species has some tolerance to forest conversion, although population densities decrease drastically with the level of habitat degradation and loss—from 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat to 45 individuals/km² in degraded habitats (Merker 2003).A crucial unknown variable in determining how critical the threats to this species is its elevational distribution. Geographic Information System (GIS) data indicate that large areas of quality forested habitat remain at higher elevations, but the vertical range of this species is believed to stop somewhere between 1,100–1,500 m, thus rendering a large portion of the best remaining habitat outside the range.The continued loss of suitable habitat on Sulawesi in the last 22.5 years (three generations), in addition to the combination of other threats is suspected to have contributed to the decline in the population by over 30%, and it is suspected that loss will continue in the future at this rate or higher.Although Tarsius dentatus has a large extent of occurrence (>20,000 km²) it is threatened with habitat degradation, local ethnic conflicts and other political unrest. Even protected areas in its range experience habitat loss and degradation, such slash-burn agriculturists in Morawali, who turn large areas of forest to alang-alang grass, while Lore Lindu has been affected by illegal loggers, and refugees fleeing conflict (Gursky et al. 2008).Major threats include: illegal logging that results in habitat loss, agricultural pesticides, predation by domestic dogs, cats and pet trade. Occurs in two protected areas: Lore Lindu National Park and Morowali Nature Reserve each threatened with illegal hunting and forest loss. Refugee invasion and settlements inside the Lore Lindu National Park threaten the habitat. Rattan harvesting, logging and burning to clear the forest for coffee and cacao plantations. In Morowali Nature Reserve, these tarsiers are hunted and dogs are used to catch and locate tarsiers and blow guns are used in the process too. Slash- and- burn agriculture and dry rice farming demand clearing and burning of forest and threaten the habitat.
population: Merker (2003) estimated population densities in a variety of pristine and human disturbed habitats. The values he calculated were 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 190 individuals/km² for slightly disturbed habitat, 130 individuals/km² for moderately disturbed habitat, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitat (Merker 2003). Population surveys in Lore Lindu found densities of 129 individuals/km². Higher in secondary forest (250 individuals/km²) than in primary forest (22 individuals/km²). In habitats with a ‘variety of human disturbance’, especially Kamarora, on the edge of Lore Lindu National Park, recorded densities were 268 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 187 individuals/km² in slightly disturbed habitat, 129 individuals/km² in moderately disturbed habitats, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitats. The species is scarce in high elevation forests.The density of these tarsiers in plantations of cacao and gliricidia (Gliricidia sepium), mixed in with shrubs of bamboo (Bambusa spp), and lang alang (Imperata cylindrica) and corn was 45 individuals/km² while it was 268 individuals/km² in undisturbed forests (Estrada et al. 2012).
range: This species occurs in the central and eastern portions of the central core of Sulawesi. The northern boundary is the Isthmus of Palu similar, but perhaps not identical, to the boundary between Macaca hecki and M. tonkeana. Along the eastern coast of the isthmus, the northern lies between the villages of Marantale (Shekelle et al. 1997) and Ampibabo (Stefan Merker unpubl. data). The boundary on the western coast of the isthmus is not known, but is assumed to be similar to the boundary between M. hecki and M. tonkeana. To the east, Tarsius dentatus is found in Ampana and Luwuk (Burton and Nietsch, 2010), and is assumed to extend to the end of the eastern peninsula (J. Burton unpubl. data). The western boundary appears to coincide with the Palu-Koru fault (Merker et al. 2010). The southern boundary from Lore Lindu National Park to the eastern coast of Sulawesi is unknown, but is inferred to be similar to the boundary between M. hecki and M. ochreata.
useTrade: Some of these animals have been recorded in pet trade in the recent past.
conservationActions: The species is listed in CITES Appendix II. Tarsiers are protected by national law and international treaties, including CITES Appendix II. Many portions of the range of this taxon are protected and indeed it occurs in at least two national parks (Lore Lindu and Morowali); however, there needs to be improved management of the currently protected areas to ensure the ongoing survival of the species. Public education to overcome the misconception that tarsiers are crop pests would be a step forward in improving conservation measures for the species. In fact the species might actually be beneficial to crops, as they eat, and may even have a dietary preference for, some real crop pests such as large grasshoppers.

rationale: Tarsius pumulus is assessed as Endangered because it has a small area of occupancy (175 km²) and that the species is known from only two isolated locations. In addition, the species is likely undergoing a decline in quality of habitat from localised, small scale exploitation of the habitat due to expanding human settlements.
habitat: Tarsius pumilus is among the least known primates in existence. It has only recently (August 2008) been rediscovered in the wild, captured, radio collared, photographed, and filmed. Morphological analysis of museum specimens indicates adaptations for life in colder, montane cloud forests (Musser and Dagosto 1987). Moss forests are characteristic of the presumed habitat.Hilly and mountainous regions in elevations between 1,800–2,200 m with trees covered in liverworts and mosses. Feeds on live animal prey as insects and lizards. Nocturnal and arboreal in habit.
threats: Its distribution is in all likelihood restricted to isolated mountain tops; it is known to occur in only two isolated locations. One threat to these habitats is the encroachment of human populations into montane regions to satisfy the needs of a growing human population. The destruction of montane forests in more densely populated south Sulawesi indicates that this fate may well be in store for Central Sulawesi's montane forests as the human population expands. Some areas of Central Sulawesi near known Tarsius pumilus sites are conflict zones, where factional fighting has seen the dislocation of large human populations that are then resettled in refugee camps. One such site lies along the main route to the Rorekatimbu capture locality.
population: The species is thought to live in extremely low densities due to low trapping rate.
range: This species occurs in southern and central Sulawesi, Indonesia and is currently only known to be present in two locations: Mt. Nokilalaki and Mt. Rantemario. The first specimen of Tarsius pumilus was collected in 1916 at 1,800 m from Rano Rano, in the mountains between Palu and Poso and the Latimojong Mts The second specimen, collected in 1930, came from 2,200 m on Mount Rantemario in South Sulawesi. A third specimen, which was found dead in a rat trap in May 2000, came from 2,200 m on the flank of Mount Rorekatimbu. The first live sighting was in 2008 and the first nearly after 80 years, when scientists captured and released three individuals and observed one other individual high up in the canopy. It is important to find other locations of presence in its presumed distribution to inform its conservation status assessment. The extent of occurrence is estimated at 5,231 km².
useTrade: Use of this species is not known.
conservationActions: It is listed on CITES Appendix II. The species is known to occur in at least one protected area (Lore Lindu National Park), although the form likely receives some protection on Mount Rantemario (M. Shekelle pers. comm.). Protected in Lore Lindu National Park and somewhat protected in Mount RanteMario.

rationale: Based on habitat loss alone, this species is considered Vulnerable in that at least 30% of the habitat has been converted in the past 20 years (approximately three generations). From 1990 to 2000, about 15.26% of the forest habitat on the island was converted to agriculture (A. Salim pers. comm.), and since that time at least an additional 10% has been lost. This listing is further justified by the fact that the taxon will be subdivided in the future and that some populations will have much greater threats than others. Tarsius tarsier, sensu lato, has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 91,781 km². Within this are 1,782 km² of old growth forest and 33,980 km² of good habitat, yielding an estimate of 35,852 km² of tarsier habitat that is considered good or better. Additionally, there are 27,528 km² of fair habitat. This produces an estimate of 63,380 km² of potentially usable tarsier habitat. Assessed in the broad sense, T. tarsier is easily the least endangered tarsier found in Wallacea. On the other hand, T. tarsier, sensu stricto is sympatric with Macaca maura, and by analogy is likely to be highly threatened. Thus, under the current taxonomy T. tarsier should be considered to have a conservation status of no greater than Vulnerable and possibly as little as Least Concern, but in the more restricted sense it would likely be a candidate for Critically Endangered. This example illustrates the urgent need for more taxonomic work on Sulawesian tarsiers. The problem is not trivial, since at least 17 potentially new taxa have been discovered within the population of tarsiers that Niemitz (1984) classified as a single subspecies. This is particularly true since, owing to the conservation threats to some smaller populations with restricted ranges, there is the possibility that they may go extinct before they have even been named. This is turn argues in favor of the most conservative conservation estimate that can be justified for T. tarsier.
habitat: Tarsius tarsier sensu stricto has not been the subject of systematic study, but by analogy with wild tarsier populations studied at Tangkoko and with T. dentatus at Lore Lindu National Park, it is expected that this taxon is found in primary, secondary and mangrove forests, forest gardens, and a variety of other habitats of varying degrees of human disturbance that provide adequate shrubby cover. It shows extreme adaptations for vertical clinging and leaping (VCL) in the understory of suitable tropical habitats, often two meters or less from the ground. Nocturnal social primates, they likely live in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 26. The home range is believed to be less than one hectare. Its diet is 100% live animal prey, mostly insects with some small vertebrates.Found in hills with bedrocks made of uplifted corals climbing to sparse vegetation and poor soil. Found mainly to occur in degraded forests, secondary growth patches and farmland scrubs. No information is available on their breeding except that a family captures in late September had two juveniles weighing 73g and 75g indicating that they were born just a few months ago. One such trapped family was found to include one adult female, an adult male, sub-adult female, and two juveniles. Monogamous or polygamous family structure with similar home ranges to lowland tarsiers.
threats: Major threats include habitat loss due to agriculture, illegal logging, mining of limestone for cement manufacture, agricultural pesticides, and predation by domestic animals (dogs and cats). Some animals are entering the pet trade (particularly from North Sulawesi, around Tankoko). Although there has been extensive loss of habitat, this species, however, has demonstrated some tolerance to forest conversion. Although seemingly among the least threatened of tarsiers owing to its relatively wide distribution, the possible existence of undescribed cryptic species makes it likely that some populations are more threatened than others. This species should be reassessed upon further taxonomic revision.The Selayar Island is proposed for a large oil refinery. Most of the forested region has already been altered and forests reduced or degraded. There are no protected areas either. This situation really calls for an up-gradation of their protected status to Critically Endangered.
population: Within Tarsius tarsier, sensu lato, the best studied population comes from Tangkoko, which is at the extreme northeast peninsula of Sulawesi, whereas Makassar, the type locality of T. tarsier sensu stricto, is at the extreme southwestern peninsula, and has not been the subject of systematic study. Population density estimates at Tangkoko are 70 individuals/km² (MacKinnon and MacKinnon 1980) and 156 individuals/km² (Gursky 1997). Merker (2003) estimated population densities for T. dentatus in a variety of pristine and human disturbed habitats near Kamarora, on the edge of Lore Lindu National Park. The values he calculated were 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 190 individuals/km² in slightly disturbed habitat, 130 individuals/km² in moderate disturbance, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitat.
range: By definition, Tarsius tarsier is the rump taxon of tarsiers that remain in the Sulawesi biogeographic region, after excluding the other named taxa, i.e. T. fuscus, T.  sangirensis, T. pumilus, T. dentatus, T. pelengensis, T. lariang, T. tumpara, T. wallacei, T. spectrumgurskyae, T. supriatnai, and T. niemitzi. This leaves T. tarsier, sensu lato, with an unlikely distribution that includes Selayar Island, Southeast Sulawesi, and the islands of Buton, Muna, and Kabaena, below 1,800 m (with an actual vertical distribution that likely stops somewhere between 1,100–1,500 m). As discussed by Brandon Jones et al. (2004), this is distribution is improbably disjunct. It is more likely that this population is subdivided into numerous insular and parapatric species, as hypothesized by Shekelle and Leksono (2004) and Brandon Jones et al. (2004), as the populations from the northern arm and from the Togian Islands were recently described.Area of occupancy for this species on Selayer Island is ca 820 km², and it will likely be classified as Endangered, when the alpha taxonomy of the genus Tarsius has been settled.
useTrade: The species is caught for the pet trade in parts of its range.
conservationActions: Tarsiers are protected by international treaties, including CITES Appendix II, as well as by national law. Categorized as Vulnerable by IUCN. Earlier IUCN assessments considered all Sulawesi  tarsiers as of this species but now the Selayar Tarsier is considered to be a distinct taxon endemic to Selayar Island.Many portions of the range of this taxon are within conservation areas, but there needs to be improved management of these areas to ensure the continued survival of the species. Public education to overcome the misconception that tarsiers are crop pests would be a step forward in improving conservation measures. Indeed, the species might actually be beneficial to crops, as they eat, and may even have a dietary preference for, some real crop pests such as large grasshoppers.

rationale: The Philippine Tarsier is assessed as Near Threatened based on an estimated significant decline over the last three generations (approximately 20 years) of less than, but approaching, 30%. This reduction is based habitat loss (the species occurs at higher densities in less disturbed forest habitats) and because of harvesting for the pet trade. The speies almost qualifies as threatened under criterion A2d.
habitat: The species occurs in both secondary and primary forest (although it is most abundant in the latter), from sea level up to 750 m. It is found at lower densities in edge habitats and secondary growth with many pole-sized trees and low-stature vegetation, as well as in gardens and other degraded habitats including agricultural areas and plantations. It feeds on small lizards, frogs, and insects.
threats: There are several contributing factors that make this species susceptible to extinction (Wright et al. 2003): infant mortality rates, both in the wild and in captivity, are very high; highly specialized diet; relatively limited geographical range; high population density and extensive habitat destruction. Although it is clearly adaptable to anthropogenic habitats that contain bushes or trees, it occurs at higher densities in less disturbed habitats, especially in primary forest (very little of which remains within its range) (I. Arboleda pers. comm.). It is also heavily harvested as food and especially for the pet trade. This is illegal, but there are recent anecdotal reports that the pet markets in Manila are being flooded with tarsiers retailing at less than PhP 500 per individual (I. Arboleda pers. comm.).
population: It is locally common and widespread, largely because of its tolerance of second growth habitat (Dagosto and Gebo 1995). However, it clearly occurs at higher densities in less disturbed habitats (I. Arboleda pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to the southeastern Philippines. It is restricted to the greater Mindanao faunal region, where it is found on Bohol, Dinagat, Leyte, Mindanao (Davao del Norte, Davao del Sur, Misamis Occidental, Misamis Oriental, South Cotabato, and Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga del Sur provinces), and Samar (Heaney et al. 1998). It is also reported from Basilan (Lawrence 1939), Biliran, Maripipi (Rickart et al. 1993), and Mindanao in Bukidnon province (Sanborn 1953).
useTrade: The species is hunted for food and captured for the pet trade.
conservationActions: The species is included in Appendix II of CITES and is protected under government law in the Philippines. Surveys of population status, particularly to determine its ability to persist in non-forest areas in the long-term, as well as taxonomic research, are needed. The species would also benefit from tighter controls on harvest and trade.This species occurs in a number of protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
habitat: Leontocebus nigrifrons occurs in Amazonian lowland forests, both primary and secondary, mainly on tierra firma but also in seasonally flooded forest, and can persist close to human settlements. Home-range size varies from 25 to 80 ha and home ranges overlap to a varying degree between neighbouring groups (Lledo Ferrer et al. 2011). The diet is composed of fruit pulps, exudates, nectar, invertebrates and small vertebrates (Garber 1988a, 1988b; Heymann et al. 2000; Knogge & Heymann 2003; Nickle and Heymann 1996). Groups generally include 3-8 individuals (Soini and Coppula 1981), and usually live in association with groups of Saguinus mystax (Heymann and Buchanan-Smith 2000). The mating system includes monogamy, polygyny, polyandry and polygynandry (Lledo Ferrer et al. 2011).Adult females are slightly larger than adult males. Mean body mass: females 376 g, males 354 g; mean head-body length: females: 214 mm, males: 205 mm (Soini and Coppula 1981)
threats: Leontocebus nigrifrons is common. No specific threats are currently identified.
population: Populations are suspected to be stable. Population densities of 22-38 individuals/km² have been recorded (Puertas and Bodmer 1993).
range: The range of Leontocebus nigrifrons lies between the Río Amazonas in the north, the ríos Ucayali and Tapiche in the west, Yavarí in the east, and Blanco in the south. It is endemic to Peru.
useTrade: Occasionally kept as a pet.
conservationActions: Leontocebus nigrifrons is found in the Area de Conservación Regional-Comunal Tamshiyacu-Tahuayo. So far, Saguinus fuscicollis was listed on CITES Appendix II; Leontocebus nigrifrons should be listed in the same appendix.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern since the species is unlikely to face any major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
habitat: They are diurnal primates, which live in groups of less than 12 individuals. Sampaio et al. (2015) reports on 13 groups, including 90 individuals, that were seen in terra firme forest and only one group was found in inundated forest (várzea or white-water inundated forest). Sampaio et al. (2015) also reported that L. crulimai could inhabit patches of dense bamboo (Guadua sp., locally known as tabocal). The formation of mixed groups with redcap moustached tamarins (Saguinus mystax pileatus) were very common (Sampaio et al. 2015).
threats: This species is not a target of hunting by local people or wildlife trade. Despite this species occurs at the border of the "deforestation arc" in South of Amazonas State, a great portion of the forests of the left bank of the Purus river are Protected Areas (PA) and the deforestation outside these PAs is relatively low since there are no unpaved or paved great roads on area. Ilegal logging on area is present.
population: In Rio Inauini L. cruzlimai was reported to have a relative abundance of 6.08 individuals/10 km. This makes the species one of the most abundant primate in the region (Sampaio et al. 2015). It is suspected that the population is stable, in the absence of significant threats from habitat degradation and hunting.
range: Leontocebus cruzlimai occurs in terra firme forests in the interfluvium of the Purus and Juruá Rivers, on the left bank of the middle Purus River, in the municipalities of Pauini and Boca do Acre, and in the south of the Amazonas State in Brazil. Its range extends between the Teuini and Inauini Rivers and south of the Inauini River on the left (west and north) bank of the Purus River. To the North it is probably restricted by the Pauini River (a left bank afluente of the Purus River) and similarly Hershkovitz (1977) described L. fuscicollis primitivus to occur on the left (northern) bank of the Pauini River. However, the exact limits of the species’ distribution remain unclear.
useTrade: This species is locally not hunted.
conservationActions: There are no current conservation programs concerning this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
habitat: Leontocebus leucogenys has not been studied in any detail in the wild. Some opportunistic observations have been made at Panguana Biological Station (Podloucky 1978, M. Göbel pers. comm.), where it is found in primary and secondary forest and close to plantations. During surveys, it was found in very forest fragments <3 ha in size (Shanee et al. 2013). Being distributed along the Andean foothills, it perhaps reaches higher altitudes (900-1000 m) than most other tamarins. Inferring from the closely related Leontocebus fuscicollis fuscicollis and Leontocebus illigeri, L. leucogenys feeds on fruit pulp, exudate, nectar, invertebrates and small vertebrates (Soini 1987, Terborgh 1983). Groups observed at Panguana ranged in size from 2 to 8 individuals (M. Göbel pers. comm.).
threats: This species is widespread and common, and it is not facing any significant threats.
population: The species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
range: Leontocebus leucogenys is distributed south of the Rio Marañón, from the Department San Martín through departments Huánuco and Pasco to the Río Perené, west of Rio Huallaga and the upper Rio Ucayali. It is endemic to Peru.
useTrade: This species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline. In Ecuador, the species is considered Near Threatened (NT), mainly due to the high rates of deforestation and fragmentation of the Amazonian forests. The species is hunted for the pet trade, posing another potential threat to the survival of the species (Tirira 2011).
habitat: Leontocebus lagonotus occurs in Amazonian lowland forests, both in tierra firme forest and in seasonally flooded forest, and can persist close to human settlements. The species has not been studied in any detail in the wild. Inferring from closely related species like L. illigeri, the diet is composed of fruit pulps, exudates, nectar, invertebrates and small vertebrates (Soini 1987). Groups of 4-9 individuals have been observed (Aquino et al. 2014; de la Torre in prep.).
threats: Leontocebus lagonotus is common. There are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline. In Ecuador, the species is considered Near Threatened (NT), mainly due to the high rates of deforestation and fragmentation of the Amazonian forests. The species is hunted for the pet trade, posing another potential threat to the survival of the species (Tirira 2011).
population: Population densities of 10.5 individuals/km² (Rio Itaya, Peru), 11.4 individuals/km² (Rio Pucacuro, Peru), 14.8 (Rio Itaya, Peru) and 34.8 (Rio Curaray) have been reported for Peru (Aquino et al. 2014; SERNANP 2013). In Ecuador population density has been estimated at 30 individuals/km² (Selva Viva Reserve, Napo and Arajuno Rivers) and 26 individuals/km² in the Yanacocha Reserve (Puyo, Pastaza) (de la Torre in prep.).The species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
range: Leontocebus lagonotus is distributed in Ecuador and Peru between the rivers Napo and Curaray in the North, Marañón in the South, and Amazon in the East. The western/south-western limits are not well known. The distribution of L. lagonotus in Ecuador appears to be restricted to the southern bank of the Napo River, along the Andean slopes (to an altitude of app. 1000 m asl) forming its western boundary. The eastern boundary seems to vary with latitude. In the north, close to the Napo River, the limit may be the confluence of the Shiripuno and Cononaco Rivers, whereas from the south bank of the Curaray River, the eastern limits expand to the Ecuador-Peru border (de la Torre in prep.).In Ecuador, the species is considered Near Threatened (NT), mainly due to the high rates of deforestation and fragmentation of the Amazonian forests.
useTrade: The species is hunted for the pet trade, posing a potential threat to the survival of the species (Tirira 2011).
conservationActions: Leontocebus lagonotus is found in the Parque Nacional Yasuní, Parque Nacional Sumaco-Napo Galeras and in three private reserves (Jatun Sacha, Selva Viva, Yanacocha) in Ecuador and in the Reserva Nacional Pucaruo in Peru. So far, Saguinus fuscicollis was listed on CITES Appendix II; Leontocebus lagonotus should be listed in the same appendix.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
habitat: L. fuscus is found in primary and secondary lowland forest and prefers dense vegetation in secondary forest (Rylands and Mittermeier 2013). Tamarin eats small fruits, nectar, gums and small animal prey. Group size varied between 4.5 and 5.5 individuals in surveys carried out in three indigenous reserves of the lower Río Caquetá in Colombia (Palacios 2003) and between 4 and 10 individuals in four different sites at Río Puré National Park (Palacios, unpublished data).
threats: It is a widespread and common species. Although in some areas is hunted for food and for pets, it is not threatened (Rylands & Mittermeier, 2013).
population: Densities between 7.1–26.5 individuals/km2 have been recorded in Río Puré National Park (Palacios, unpublished data) and between 3.4-14.2 individuals/km2 in indigenous reserves in the lower Río Caquetá in Colombia (Palacios et al. 2003). The species is widespread, common, and there are no major threats resulting in any significant population decline.
range: L. fuscus is found in southeastern Colombia and northwestern Brazil (in Amazonas state), north of the Rio Solimões between the rios Japurá-Caquetá and Iça-Putumayo. It is also found west of the Río Yarí to the north of the Río Caquetá, through the basin of the Río Caguán, and lower parts of the Río Orteguaza, west to the Andean foothills to 500m asl.
useTrade: Although in some areas is hunted for food and for pets, it is not threatened (Rylands & Mittermeier, 2013).
conservationActions: CITES Appendix II.In Brazil in the Amazonas state: ESEC Juamí-Japurá (831.524.72ha) (Rylands and Bernardes 1989, Rylands et al. 1993 and IBAMA 2005), RDS Mamirauá (1.124.000ha) (Rylands and Bernardes 1989, Rylands et al. 1993).In Colombia it is present in  Parque Nacional Natural La Paya (422.000ha) (Defler 1994), Parque Nacional Natural Cahuinarí (575.000ha) and Río Puré National Park (999.980ha) (Palacios, unpublished data).

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened as, although currently it is common, it is suspected to be undergoing a decline of around 20% over three generations (18 years), approaching the A4cd criterion, due to identified threats, including habitat loss and hunting for the pet trade.
habitat: Leontocebus illigeri occurs in Amazonian lowland forest, both in tierra firme forest and in seasonally flooded forest. Home-range size is around 16 ha (Soini 1987). The diet is composed of fruit pulps, exudates, nectar, invertebrates and small vertebrates (Soini 1987). Groups generally include 2-10 individuals (Soini 1987). Mean adult body mass is 293 g, mean head-body length 203 mm (Soini and Coppula 1981).
threats: Leontocebus illigeri is common. Although widespread, deforestation in north-eastern Peru is significantly reducing its habitat in certain areas. Hunting for the pet trade is also reducing some populations of this species.
population: Population densities: 18 individuals/km² have been recorded by Soini (1987).Deforestation rates in north-eastern Peru as well as offtake for the pet trade are suspected to have increased since the last assessment, so that the suspected ongoing population reduction is now reaching 20% over three generations (18 years).
range: Leontocebus illigeri is distributed between the rivers Huallaga in the West, Marañón in the North, and Ucayali in the East. It is also found between the Ucayali and the lower Tapiche Rivers. It is endemic to Peru.There is a suspected decrease in the Extent of Occurrence, Area of Occupancy, and habitat quality due to habitat degradation and loss.
useTrade: Commonly traded as pet animals (with pet trade increasing).
conservationActions: Leontocebus illigeri is found in the Reserva Nacional Pacaya-Samiria. So far, Saguinus fuscicollis was listed on CITES Appendix II; Leontocebus illigeri should be listed in the same appendix.

rationale: Cebus brunneus is considered Endangered (EN A4cd), as a population reduction of 50% or more can be inferred over the course of 48 years or three generations – the current (2019–2035) and two subsequent generations (2035–2066). This is based on Global Forest Watch data for the northern coastal states of Venezuela in which this species occurs. The data suggest that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has impacted the previous generation (2009–2034), 30% or more of this species’ suitable habitat could be lost by the year 2066.  Combined with hunting for the pet trade and in retaliation for crop-raiding, these threats place Cebus brunneus above the threshold for Endangered status.
habitat: Cordero-Rodríguez and Boher-Bentti (1988) conducted a study on the ontogeny and body size of a group of Cebus brunneus from Barlovento. Rivas and Salcedo (2011) reported this primate species from El Ávila National Park, and García et al. (2011) from Yurubí National Park. Bisbal and Naveda-Rodríguez (2010) indicated the presence of C. brunneus in the upper Guárico River.Cebus brunneus can be found in cloud forests, secondary forests, lowland rainforests, gallery forests, semi-deciduous forests. Venezuelan brown capuchins are tolerant to habitats modified by humans.
threats: The distribution of this species matches the location of the major urban areas of Venezuela such as the central cities of Caracas, Maracay, and Valencia (INE 2013). The largest concentration of human settlements in Venezuela lies within the states of Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, as well as the city of Caracas (INE 2013). These states are located right in the middle of the distribution of this endemic species. In addition, Caracas and the states of Miranda, Aragua and Carabobo are among the top five areas for human migration within the country (INE 2013). In central Venezuela, the transformation of forest is determined by the expansion of urban and industrial areas, such as the major industrial axis of the country located between Maracay and Valencia. Evergreen forests in the protected areas of northern Venezuela are classified as Least Concern (e.g. Macarao N.P., Henri Pittier N.P., and Pico Codazzi N.M.), while the semi-deciduous forests located below 1,000 m asl are classified as Vulnerable (Portillo-Quintero et al. 2010). Dry and deciduous forests of northern South America (below 600 m asl) that overlap with the distribution of C. brunneus are classified as Critically Endangered, and are virtually not covered by any protected area in north-central Venezuela (Portillo-Quintero C. and Sanchez-Azofeifa 2010). The authors further concluded that this region of endemism in South America is at very serious risk. For this region, they also reported an expected 84% forest loss within the next 20 years. Changes in the landscape also include deforestation and habitat conversion due to agricultural activities and cattle ranching, particularly in the western and eastern parts of the species’ range. In some areas, Venezuelan brown capuchins are alleged to crop damage, disclosing this species as a target for hunters. C. brunneus is also commonly used as a pet.
population: Cordero-Rodríguez and Boher (1988) reported mean group sizes of eight individuals, ranging from 2 to 20 individuals. The population is experiencing an observed ongoing decline that is estimated to be greater than 50% over three generations (48 years).
range: Cebus brunneus is restricted to the northern parts of Venezuela, occurring from the West at San Luis Mountain Range, Aroa Mountain Range, and Churuguara Mountain Range, along north-central Venezuela (Bachiller Mountain Range, Barlovento Plains, and Clarines Heights) to the East at the mountains of the Araya and Paria Peninsulas (Bodini 1989, Bodini and Pérez-Hernández 1987, Linares 1998, Urbani pers. comm.).Global Forest Watch data for the northern coastal states of Venezuela in which this species occurs, suggest that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has impacted the previous generation (2009–2034), 30% or more of this species’ suitable habitat could be lost by the year 2066 (Global Forest Watch 2020).
useTrade: Cebus brunneus and C. olivaceus (or C. brunneus x C. olivaceus) are of the most common primates found in Venezuelan zoos. Venezuelan brown capuchins are among the most illegally traded primates of Venezuela.
conservationActions: Basic and applied ecological studies are required for the Venezuelan brown capuchins. Hunting and illegal trading must be strictly forbidden. In addition, conservation programs must be implemented. Finally, it is urgent to fully control habitat fragmentation as well as logging. This species occurs in a number of protected areas, including:El Avila National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Henri Pittier National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Guatopo National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Macarao National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)San Esteban National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Morrocoy National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Sierra San Luis National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Yurubí National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Cueva Quebrada del Toro National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Mochima National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)Paria National Park (Venezuela, INPARQUES 1982)This species is listed in Appendix II of CITES (as Cebus olivaceus).

rationale: Macaca ochreata is considered Vulnerable due to an ongoing reduction in population size suspected to be more than 30% over the course of 33 years (three generations) in the past and future. This decline is based on rate of habitat loss and a projected increase in oil palm, cacao and cotton plantations, commercial timber harvest, and human settlement.
habitat: Macaca ochreata is found in mangrove and coastal forests, savanna habitat (Rawa Aopa National Park) and steep upland tropical forest at elevations up to 800 m (Faruhumpenai Nature Reserve). Booted Macaques are diurnal, arboreal, terrestrial. This subspecies is known to raid cacao plantations (Riley et al. 2007, Peterson et al. 2015). Little is known about the behavioural ecology of the Booted Macaque.
threats: The main threat to the species is forest loss. Although the southeastern province has 3,657 km² of protected area forest (Forestry Statistics of Indonesia, 2011), approximately 12,650 km² of remaining forest has been designated for commercial timber harvest or conversion to other uses by the Indonesian government. Resource collecting (e.g., rattan) within protected areas is also a threat (Lee et al. 2001).
population: The group density at two sites—Matano and Kasintuwu in Faruhumpenai Nature Reserve—was 0.97–1.56/km² and 1.45–2.00/km², respectively (Riley et al. 2007). Mixed tonkeana/ochreata groups occur in Faruhumpenai Nature Reserve (Riley et al. 2007). Group size ranged from eight individuals at Batikolo Wildlife Reserve to 22 individuals at Mangolo Recreation Forest. The minimum population size 15 years ago was estimated to be 180,000 individuals (WCS, unpublished data 2001). Miettinen et al. (2011) estimated a deforestation rate for the island of Sulawesi of 1.1% between 2000-2010. Over the course of 33 years, this rate would produce slightly greater than 30% forest loss (~30.6%). Thus, lacking other evidence, we assume that habitat loss between 1983–2016 was >30%, and we suspect the population size reduced by the same proportion. It is our observation that logging and forest degradation, both legal and illegal, continue in Indonesia, almost completely unchecked by laws and the dictates of sustainability. Therefore, we further infer that deforestation rate will continue into the foreseeable future at approximately the same pace. We do not find evidence in the published literature showing forest loss within the range of this taxon, and an island-wide GIS study of forest loss within each region of primate endemism in Sulawesi would be highly valuable, as it is virtually certain that forest loss rates in some areas are much higher than the average loss found by Miettinen et al. (2011).
range: Macaca ochreata is found throughout the southeastern peninsula, extending east to the eastern region of the central province where it borders with M. tonkeana at the La River, north of the lakes region to Faruhumpenai Nature Reserve (Riley et al. 2007), and west along the coast, across the Karaena River in its lower course, but does not reach into the uplands further inland (Groves 2001).
useTrade: The species is not utilised.
conservationActions: The taxon is listed in CITES Appendix II. Population estimates need to be updated, particularly given that forest loss has resulted in agroforest mosaics that make dispersal across forest habitat difficult (WCS 2001, unpublished report). Macaca ochreata ochreata is known to occur in at least five protected areas: Tanjung Batikolo Wildlife Reserve, Tanjung Peropa Game Reserve, Rawa Aopa Watomahai National Park, Padang Mata Osu, and Faruhumpenai Nature Reserve. Conservation measures should focus on these established protected areas in southeast Sulawesi, with priority given to Rawa Aopa National Park and Tanjung Peropa Wildlife Reserve. At present, data on the ecology and behaviour of the Booted Macaque is lacking. Population surveys and ecological studies should be carried out immediately in order to elucidate habitat requirement, minimum areas for conservation, and conservation status of this subspecies that will contribute ultimately to better protected area management plan and species action plan. There is also a need to develop mitigation efforts to help curb crop raiding and farmer retaliation, and to discourage local communities from keeping Booted Macaques as pets.

rationale: Macaca brunnescens is considered Vulnerable due to a continued decline suspected to be more than 30% over the course of 33 years (three generations) in the past and future, as a result of estimated habitat loss, and a projected increase in legal and illegal logging, mining, agricultural expansion and human settlement. In addition, its extent of occurrence is smaller than 20,000 km², is severely fragmented, and continues to decline.
habitat: Altitude varies from 0 to 200 m asl in coastal areas to approximately 400 m asl along the islands’ central areas with peaks reaching up to 1,000 m. Buton and Muna experience tropical climate with a June-September dry season and a November-April wet season with an annual rainfall 1,500-2,000 mm. Operation Wallacea have been collecting data on the Buton macaque over the past 15 years. Priston (2005) reports group size ranging between 20 and 40 individuals (mean = 32), but other surveys found group size to be relatively small  (4.1–11.7 individuals, with a mean of 7.5; Operation Wallacea 2005, 2006). Larger groups of Buton Macaques have been observed breaking up into smaller subgroups. Adult sex ratio (females to males) is two. Mean home range size for Buton macaques is 62 ha. Systematic feeding data come from short-term studies on M. o. brunnescens: 66% fruit (including crops), 20% stems and flowers, 12% leaves, and 2% invertebrates. Wild fruit consumed include Ficus spp. and kapok (Ceiba petandra). Buton macaques are considered one of the top three culprits of crop raiding (Operation Wallacea 2006; Priston et al., 2012). Cultivated crops (e.g., cacao, sweet potato, bananas, maize) comprised 24% of food items ingested.  The most common cultivated crop raided is sweet potato. Buton macaques spend almost equal amounts of time arboreally and terrestrially. Level of terrestriality depends on habitat type (i.e., more terrestrial in anthropogenically disturbed areas). Majority of its time travelling (43%) between feeding sites, foraging and feeding (21%), followed by resting (17%) and grooming (10.5%). Crop raiding groups spend more time grooming and resting than forest-based groups which spend more time travelling. Those that do crop raid spend approximately 32–38% of their day engaged in this activity.
threats: Both Muna and Buton islands have undergone extensive deforestation in recent years, due to legal and illegal logging, mining, and farming, and these macaques are consequently under threat. Muna has lost the majority of its forest, and the largest population of macaques survives on Buton. The Kakenauwe Nature Reserve and Lambusango Wildlife Reserve (total 615 km²) and perhaps in blocks of Protection Forest, Limited Protection and standard Production Forest (363.6 km²) in central Buton island represent a substantial remaining stand of forest and may support the largest remaining population of this endemic taxon. However, Whitten et al. (1987) predicted that only 8% of its total population occurs in protected areas, although a few new protected areas have been created in southeast Sulawesi since this estimate was made.
population: It is suspected that the population of the species has declined and is continuing to decline. Miettinen et al. (2011) estimated an annual deforestation rate for the island of Sulawesi of 1.1% between 2000 and 2010. Over the course of three generations (33 years), this rate would produce slightly greater than 30% forest loss (~30.6%). Thus, lacking other evidence, we assume that habitat loss between 1983 and 2016 was >30%, and we suspect that the population size reduced by the same proportion. It is our observation that logging and forest degradation, both legal and illegal, continue in Indonesia, almost completely unchecked by laws and the dictates of sustainability. Therefore, we infer that the deforestation rate will continue into the foreseeable future at approximately the same pace, and it is virtually certain that forest loss rates in some areas are much higher than the average loss found by Miettinen et al. (2011).Operation Wallacea, which has run a long-term service learning site on Buton island, conducted a survey in 2006 but wasn't able to generate a robust estimate because of a small sample size, however using several assumptions they generated a density of group of 2.6–7.7 km² leading to an overall population estimate of Lambusango of 6,221–18,435 individuals (Wheeler and Dwiyahreni 2007). More recent estimates of overall population size are lacking.
range: The Buton Macaque (Macaca brunnescens) inhabits the islands of Buton and Muna. In the past, the taxon is assumed to have ranged over both islands, but with habitat loss, habitat degradation, and hunting, it is now assumed that they remain only in isolated pockets inside and outside protected areas (Whitten et al. 1987).
useTrade: The taxon is not utilised.
conservationActions: This species is known to occur only on the islands of Buton and Muna in an undetermined area of forest surrounded by agricultural areas. At present, there is a lack of sound data on on the size, and ecology and behaviour of the Buton macaque. Population surveys and ecological studies should be carried out immediately in order to elucidate habitat requirement, minimum areas for conservation, and conservation status of this subspecies that will contribute ultimately to better protected areas management plan and species action plan.

rationale: The habitat in which Presbytis mitrata lives is experiencing conversion to agriculture and the species is targeted for illegal collecting for the pet trade. Although forest loss has almost certainly exceeded 70% over the last three generations (approximately 30 years) in the well-known area where this species occurs, it is suspected that at least 30% of the population has declined in the past. Due to ongoing threats the population is expected to continue to decline in the near future.
habitat: This species could be found in disturbed forest, primarily in understory, of primary, secondary forest, rubber plantations. It is considered tolerant of habitat conversion and to survive well in primary and secondary forest. They eat young leaves, mature leaves, unripe raw fruit, and seeds. It is a diurnal and arboreal species, with a home range of 14-29.5 ha. Daily distance travelled is around 300-1,360 m.
threats: There has been extensive loss of habitat, especially for oil palm plantations, and this is a serious threat. However, the species has some tolerance to forest conversion, but not to complete replacement of forests. Trapping of the species for the illegal pet trade is a threat across their range, with some incidental hunting for food.Patchy occurrence in disturbed forest though believed to cope well in such degraded habitat: habitat conversion and habitat degradation for Palm Oil Plantation. The pet trade is another threat and the current scenario of hunting and trapping is described as ‘heavy’. Field research necessary to understand distribution and intra-specific geographic variations.
population: The population is suspected to have declined by more than 30% in 30-35 years due to extensive habitat loss from conversion to agriculture. The species is targeted for illegal collecting for the pet trade.
range: South eastern Sumatra, from Batang Hari River, south-west to the upper Musi River drainage, eastern Barisan range, south of Lampung Province. Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park, Way Kambas National Park in Sumatra are two protected (Ami and Baker 1992, 1996) areas sheltering the species (Meyer et al. 2011).
useTrade: This species is illegally collected for the pet trade.
conservationActions: The species is included in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: The habitat in which Presbytis sumatranus lives is experiencing conversion to agriculture and the species is targeted for illegal collecting for the pet trade. Although forest loss has probably exceeded 70% over 30 years, the population is suspected to have declined by 50% in three generations (30 years approximately) and is continuing to decline.
habitat: This species inhabits secondary growth forests, lowland and hill rainforests, and old growth forest. As for Presbytis bicolour, this langur feeds on raw, unripe fruit, young leaves, mature leaves, seeds and flowers. No studies in the wild on these langurs but presumed to live in one male (multi female?) groups, defending ‘exclusive’ territories.
threats: The main threats to this langur are illegal pet trade, extensive degradation in the habitat range (more than 50% of forest loss over the past 30 years).
population: The species is suspected to be declining at a rapid rate due to massive ongoing habitat loss from conversion to agriculture and illegal collecting for the pet trade.
range: Presbytis sumatranus occurs in Western and North Central Sumatra (Northern Islands and the western coasts, south of Simpang Kiri River, North of Gunung Talamay, E coast of Wampu River, Barumun River, South East Rokan River and Batu Islands). It occurs in the Batang Gadis National Park (Meyer et al. 2011).
useTrade: It is illegally caught for the pet trade.
conservationActions: The species is included in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: This species is considered Endangered due to a past and continued population decline, estimated at more than 50% over the past 40 years (three generations) due to hunting and loss of habitat (Whittaker 2006). In 1986, Presbytis potenziani was listed as “Indeterminate,” and then evaluated as “Endangered” in 1988. Its status was downgraded to “Vulnerable” in 1996 (IUCN 2004) and then upgraded again to “Endangered” (IUCN 2008)  under criteria A2cd, which state that the species is facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild due to “(A) a reduction in population size based on […] (2) an observed, estimated, inferred, or suspected population size reduction of ≥50% over the last 10 years or three generations, whichever is the longer, where the reduction or its causes may not have ceased OR may not be understood OR may not be reversible, based on […] (c) a decline in area of occupancy, extent of occurrence and/or quality of habitat and (d) actual or potential levels of exploitation.” All these assessments were at the species-level, consequently including the former subspecies P. p. potenziani (now: P. potenziani) and P. p. siberu from Siberut (now: P. siberu). The latter was initially assessed “Vulnerable” (2000) and then upgraded to “Endangered” in 2008 due to a past and continued population decline, estimated at more than 50% over the past 40 years (3 generations) due to hunting and loss of habitat (Whittaker 2006). Although Whittaker’s evaluation suggests a rather substantial population decline, even on Siberut (where much more suitable habitat is still available compared to the southern islands), newer survey data from the National Park indicates, that the Siberut Langur is the most abundant of the four Siberut primates within the protected area, estimating a total population of 17,384 (11,014-27,439) individuals within the National Park alone (Quinten et al. 2015). Thus, the total population on Siberut is likely substantially higher than the 1,600–9,500 individuals Whittaker previously assumed (given that the circumstances/threats faced by the species have not actually changed, it is unlikely that the species has recuperated in between assessments). Nevertheless, at the same time, P. siberu is still the second most hunted primate on Siberut Island and annual off-take rates appear to be at least 17% if not much higher (see Quinten et al. 2014). None of the other primates on Siberut faces a higher off-take, when based on estimated population size.
habitat: Presbytis siberu is a diurnal and arboreal primate inhabiting the ever-wet rainforests of Siberut Island (rainfall of up to 4000 mm), where it is sympatric with Macaca siberu, Simias concolor, and Hylobates klossii. It has been found to live in primary and secondary lowland rainforests (Watanabe 1981), but—to a much lesser extent—it also uses swamp forests as well as mangroves, and sometimes ventures into the forest gardens of the Mentawai people (Quinten, 2010; Stirling and Quinten, 2013). The species was assumed to occur throughout its range in permanent “one female – one male” social groups (WWF 1980), together with their offspring (group size: 2–5; Watanabe, 1981), however, Hadi et al. (2012) report investigating two langur groups, the larger one consisting of eight individuals, including one adult male and three adult females. Home ranges of Presbytis siberu are recorded to comprise between 15 and 30 hectares (Tilson and Tenaza 1976; Hadi 2012). They may overlap with the ranges of neighbouring groups (but do not have to, c.f. Hadi 2012). Where they do overlap, certain core areas have been observed which are used more or less exclusively by one family group (Tilson and Tenaza 1976; Watanabe 1981); intrusion into these areas by others is habitually followed by aggressive behaviour incl. vocalization (Tilson and Tenaza 1976). Siberut Langurs exhibit a large repertoire of vocalizations, e.g. alarm calls, duetting, distraction display calls, contact calls etc. For the purpose of sleeping, the animal generally retreats to specific trees (often tall emergents) which are located in the species’ core area (Tilson and Tenaza 1976).Siberut Langurs feed predominantly on fruit, followed by leaves, and – to a much lesser extent – on flowers and other items (Hadi 2012); for a colobine, their diet is unusually frugivorous. Individuals spend the majority of their day resting (ca. half) or feeding, and—to a much lesser degree—travelling and foraging; very little of their time is used for social activities (Hadi 2012). Once every other year, between July and August, the female gives birth to a single offspring (Tilson and Tenaza 1976).
threats: Like all Siberut primates, this species is threatened mainly by hunting and commercial logging, as well as by conversion of forests into oil palm plantations, forest clearing and product extraction by local people (Whittaker 2006). Hunting pressure has increased in recent years as a result of improved access to remote areas due to logging roads and tracks, as well as the replacement of bows and arrows with air rifles (Whittaker 2006). Furthermore, local rituals and taboos that formerly regulated hunting have been progressively eroded due to missionary and state influences (Whittaker 2006; Quinten et al. 2014). Interview surveys in 50 villages on Siberut revealed that 24 % of the respondents were ‘active hunters’ and 68% of those respondents target Presbytis siberu. The average number hunted per three months was 2.3 per hunter, leading to off-take estimates of 1,679–3,385 animals per year (Quinten et al. 2014).
population: In the early eighties, the population of the Siberut Langur (then as P. potenziani) was estimated at between 46,000 and 47,000 individuals by two independent studies, based on home range size and population density (13.5 individuals/km²) of observed groups (WWF 1980; Watanabe 1981)—the most abundant primate species in Siberut at that time. More recent surveys in formally and informally protected areas on Siberut report lower densities:  In the Peleonan Forest in northern Siberut (protected by agreements with local landowners up until 2014), estimates range from 2.7 (1.3–5.3) in peat swamp habitat (Quinten et al. 2010) to 8.2 (4.8–14.1) in adjacent lowland rainforest on mineral soil (Waltert et al. 2008). Surveys within the island’s National Park yielded a density of 10.4 (6.6–16.5) individuals/km². On this basis, a total population of 17,384 (11,014–27,439) individuals was estimated for Siberut National Park alone, an area that covers >40 % of Siberut Island.Previous estimates of population decline for this species on Siberut (then as P. potenziani siberu; Whittaker, 2006) were based on density estimates for P. potenziani from the Pagai Islands (only 1–4 individuals/km²; Paciulli 2004), and most likely overestimated the actual decline. There is an urgent need for population surveys in unprotected habitat to properly assess the current status of this primate.
range: This species is endemic to Siberut, the northernmost of the Mentawai Islands off the west coast of Sumatra (Indonesia).
useTrade: This species is hunted rampantly for meat.
conservationActions: Due to its very recent elevation to species level, no CITES or previous Red List information is available for this species. As P. potenziani ssp. siberu it was protected under Indonesian law, classified as ‘Endangered’ and listed on CITES Appendix I. The following conservation actions were suggested by Whittaker (2006): "1) increased protection for Siberut National Park, which currently lacks enforcement, 2) formal protection of the Peleonan forest in North Siberut, which is home to unusually high primate populations and is easily accessible, 3) conservation education, especially regarding hunting, and 4) the development of alternative economic models for the local people to reduce the likelihood of selling off their lands to logging companies." Quinten et al.
