The tail lacks a terminal tuft. Each hind foot has three digits, with the middle one being the longest (Nowak 1991). Generation length is estimated to be two to three years based on data from Macdonald (2004).
threats: The drying of water sources and droughts threaten this species, although it remains unclear if these represent natural environmental changes or are driven by anthropogenic activity (Clark et al. 2006). Habitat degradation may also be resulting, through grazing by increasing numbers of livestock (Clark et al. 2006).
population: Current population data for this species are unavailable. It is most likely to be declining.
range: This species occurs in Mongolia and may also be present in China (G. Shenbrot pers. comm.). In Mongolia, it is known from the Dzungarian Gobi Desert, including Great Gobi Section B Strictly Protected Area (Sokolov and Shenbrot 1987, Sokolov et al. 1998). Its distribution in relation to Stylodipus andrewsi and S. telum requires further review (Holden and Musser 2005).
conservationActions: Approximately 41% of the species’ range in Mongolia occurs within protected areas (Clark et al. 2006). As this species occurs within protected areas, it is conserved under Mongolian Protected Area Laws; however, no conservation measures specifically aimed at this species have been established to date. It is recommended that further ecological research and the monitoring of population trends, to establish conservation measures should be undertaken. Research should also be conducted in the areas of distribution, threats, taxonomy, and habitat status. This species has been regionally Red Listed in Mongolia as Endangered A3c (Clark et al. 2006).

rationale: This species has a large range (well above the extent of occurrence threshold for criterion B). The population size has not been quantified, but it is not believed to approach the thresholds for the population size criterion of the IUCN Red List (i.e. less than 10,000 mature individuals in conjunction with appropriate decline rates and subpopulation qualifiers), as the species is described as abundant in at least parts of its range. Although there have been some population declines since the 1960s, it is not believed to approach the threshold for the population decline criterion of the IUCN Red List (i.e. declining more than 30% in ten years or three generations). For these reasons, it is evaluated as Least Concern. However, population trends need to be monitored.
habitat: Inhabits deserts and desertified steppes. In Europe it is usually distributed in hilly sands in river valleys, and arid areas, often with trees. Active at dusk and night. Enters hibernation with first frost. Lives in complex burrows, often occupies jird burrows. Feeds on seeds and partly on insects. Reproduction is once a year with litter size of 3-6 young.
threats: Habitat loss due to ploughing and overgrazing and pesticides affect some populations.
population: A widespread species that is relatively common in at least parts of its range. The Ukrainian subspecies S. t. falz-feini is naturally rare. It has a restricted range (extent of occurrence c.8,000 km2), and its area of occupancy is fragmented and declining as a result of habitat loss and degradation. The other European subspecies S. t. turovi is relatively common, and despite population decline since the 1960s it remains abundant in some parts of the area, e.g. Tsimlyansk.
range: This species occurs in steppes and desertified steppes in E Ukraine, N Caucasus, W Turkmenistan, W Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan; E to N Xinjiang, China (Shenbrot et al. 1995, Wilson and Reeder 2005). The range is fragmented: besides the major part of the range from the Caspian Sea to China there are several isolated populations. The two isolated populations in the European part of the range are represented by two different subspecies, S. t. falz-feini and S. t. turovi.
conservationActions: S. t. falz-feini is listed in the Red Data Book of Ukraine under category II (abundant species with rapidly declining population). S. t. turovi is listed in the local Red Data Book in Russia (Rostov District) as Data Deficient. The species is found in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because although it has a small range compared to other members of its genus, its extent of occurrence (EOO) and population size are nevertheless well above the thresholds for criteria B and C, respectively. Also, it is found in a number of protected areas. There are no recent data on population trend.
habitat: In the western part of its geogrpahical range it inhabits clay, often saline areas along low banks of drying river beds and lakes. Habitat here is covered with only Anabasis, Atriplex, Camophoroma, Climacoptera, Kochia, and Salsola vegetation. The highest density of animals is in areas with rich succulent vegetation. There have been sightings from other habitat types (clay or rubbly areas in sandy deserts, agricultural fields), though these are likely to be due to dispersal of young on their way to more suitable habitats (Shenbrot et al. 1995).It feeds mostly on the green parts of plants, and mainly on the succulent Climacoptera brachiata. The percentage of seeds in the diet increases from mid-summer onwards. It has obligate hibernations, which usually start at the end of October. If the year is very warm, it can be active until the beginning of November. Hibernation ends in mid-March, plus or minus two weeks depending on the temperature. It has three types of burrows: permanent, wintering and shelters. Permanent burrows have several passages and nest. Shelters are simple, with only one passage. Reproduction starts right after hibernation. The second reproduction cycle always starts at the same time, at the end of June. Gestation is 25–27 days, litter size is 3–8 (usually 4–5) young. The age at maturity for spring-born individuals is about four months, and for autumn-born individuals is about seven months.
threats: The main threat to this species is habitat loss due to climate change (higher precipitation level) resulting in steppe expansion.
population: Total number is relatively small due to small range, however, local abundance could be high. In spring it could be up to 20–30 individuals per ha, in autumn 50–60 individuals per ha (Mazin 1977). In the western part of the range population size was stable, while in the eastern part of the range the population experienced a sharp decline in the 1960s after several rainy years that resulted in steppe expansion (Vorontsov et al. 1969). Whilst more recent data on the population trend are not available, during studies in 2016, none were found in the western part of its geographic range (SW shore of Balkhash Lake and adjacent areas), where this species was quite common about 30 years ago (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2018). At the same time, the species was found to be common in the eastern part of its geographic range, between Alakol’ and Koshkarakol’ lakes (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2018).
range: This species is endemic to southeast Kazakhstan, occurring in the Lake Balkhash area. The geographic range is three large isolates (the first one at the west shore of Balkash lake and in south part of Ili River hollw, the second arounr the east shores of Balkash Lake and in Alakul’ Lake hollow, the third one in the NW foothills of Dzungarian Alatau mountains) and several small isolates in the North East foothills of Zailiyskiy Alatau, N foothills of Dzungarian Alatau and to the north of Balkash Lake.
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Alakol’ Nature Reserve (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2020).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occupies shrub-steppe or meadow habitats in mountainous regions, at high elevations (Smith and Xie 2008). It is sometimes found in spruce forests (Smith and Xie 2008). The preferred habitat seems to be alongside streams in cool forest areas (Nowak 1991). It was also recorded in dense shrubland resulting from deforestation (Giraudoux et al. 1998). Its diet "primarily consists of green plants" (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: A study conducted in southern Gansu in 1996 recorded this species as occurring in previously unknown habitat (dense shrubland), where it was characterized as not so rare (Giraudoux et al. 1998). Giraudoux et al. (1998) also indicate that this species is often recorded by Chinese surveys conducted in forests within its range.
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Yunnan provinces. E. s. setchuanus occurs in western Sichuan, northwestern Yunnan, and southwestern Qinghai, while E. s. vicinus occurs in southern Gansu, eastern Qinghai, southern Shaanxi, and Ningxia (Smith and Xie 2008). The species occurs at elevations ranging from 3,000 to 4,000 m asl (Holden and Musser 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Jiuzhaigou (Liu et al. 2005), Liupanshan, Taibaishan, Wanglang, and Wolong Nature Reserves (CSIS 2008), and is presumed to occur in other protected areas. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Vulnerable A1c (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, because it has an extremely large extent of occurrence of apporximately 2,084,447 km2 where it is found in several different habitats and there are no significant threats.
habitat: Inhabits desert and steppe habitats, preferentially in sand dunes overgrown with tamarisk, saxaul, and saltwort vegetation. Solitary, nocturnal, sometimes also active in dusk. When chased try to bury in the sand. Has simple temporary and complex permanent burrows. Permanent burrows can be up to 3 m long with several passages, part of which do not reach surface. Exits sealed with sand plugs. Feed on insects (mainly acridoids), arachnids and plant parts (mainly seeds). Spring reproduction starts in April - May, summer reproduction starts in May-June. Litter size is 2-5 young.
threats: Drying of water sources and droughts also threaten this species, although it remains unclear if these represent natural environmental changes or are driven by anthropogenic activity. Preyed upon by owls, red foxes, alpine weasels and marbled polecats. In Kazakhstan major threats include overgrazing. Also, burrow destruction and roadkills are significant.
population: Spatial distribution is very erratic, and number significantly fluctuates. In different subpopulations number can differ 1,7-14,5 times. According to some authors up to 13 individuals per 10 km tracking is considered high density (Scherbakov and Kochenev 1982). However, Gromov and Erbaeva (1995) wrote that in summer in Zaysan basin population density can be up to 60 individuals per 10 km of tracking.
range: Distributed in Kazakhstan, China, Mongolia. In Kazakhstan from northern Aral sea basin to Balkhash Lake and Zaysan basin. In Mongolia found in Great Lakes Depression, Valley of the Lakes, Dzungarian Govi Desert, Trans-Altai Govi Desert, Alashani Govi Desert, Northern Govi, and Eastern Govi (Sokolov et al. 1996). In the northern part the major factor that limits dispersal is deep freezing of soil during winter.
conservationActions: Listed as Rare in the 1987 and 1997 Mongolian Red Books (Shagdarsuren et al. 1987, MNE 1997). In the Red List of Kazakhstan is listed under category III (rare, small in number and limited range species). Occurs in protected areas along whole range (approximately 19% of the species’ range in Mongolia).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in protected areas, absence of known threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits desert and semi-desert habitats. It feeds on roots, tubers, insects and larvae. It exhibits nocturnal behaviour (Smith and Xie 2008). It may produce two litters per year, reproduction possibly occurring in May, with a litter size of 1-3 (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species occurs in China and Mongolia (Smith and Xie 2008). In China, it is known from the Balikun region of Xinjiang. In Mongolia, it is known from the Trans Altai Gobi Desert, Alashani Gobi Desert, and eastern parts of Eastern Gobi. It is parapatric in southern Mongolia with A. bullata (Holden and Musser 2005).
conservationActions: This species may be present in protected areas in China. Approximately 43% of the species’ range in Mongolia occurs within protected areas (Clark et al. 2006). In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004). In Mongolia, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Clark et al. 2006).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to it having a widespread distribution, including recent records in Iran and Lebanon. While there is evidence to suggest the population is declining, limited population data from recent years means that it cannot be ascertained the extent and rate to which this decline is occurring. There are threats within its range, primarily due to agricultural expansion, as well as other threats.  The species is experiencing local extinctions in some parts of its range and is sensitive to habitat changes - it cannot tolerate desert habitat. Further survey work to refine its distribution and establish the rate of declines across its range should be prioritised.
habitat: The species occurs in steppe and semi-desert habitats. There are some records from cultivated plains (Misonne 1957). Like all Allactaga species, this species is not found in loose sands. Primarily, jerboas are nocturnal rodents spending most of the daylight hours in underground burrows emerging at night to forage. Most species have a vegetarian diet. Females may give birth to up to nine young. March to July is the breeding season in Turkey, February to May in Iraq (Harrison and Bates 1991). There may be more than three litters per year (Çolak and Yigit 1998).
threats: The major threat to the species is agricultural expansion in Jordan and Syria. In Jordan, the species declined by approximately 50% from 1985 to 2005 owing to agricultural expansion; its population there continues to decline (Z. Amr pers. comm. 2005). The species' range is threatened by irrigation for cotton in Turkey. It is considered edible by several tribes of Bedouin in Jordan (Qumsiyeh 1996). Also, the species is hunted in some areas of Turkey. In Syria, there is massive capture (using spotlights at night) of the species which is sold to falconers for food (Serra pers. comm.).
population: When found together with Jaculus jaculus, A. euphratica is always less common (Qumsiyeh 1996). Amr (2000) reported this species to be common in Jordan, although in 2005 the species was described as relatively rare in Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Lebanon, and Turkey (SW Asia Workshop 2005). The populations in Iraq are unknown, as there have been no recent studies, while it has recently been recorded from Ilan province in western Iran (Darvish et al. 2012). In Jordan surveys have shown a decline in the species, in 2005 the species was very infrequently encountered in areas where it was previously considered common; the situation in Syria is similar with surveys from 2000-2003 showing a marked decrease in the population (Z. Amr pers. comm. 2006). Recent surveys in Saudi Arabia found the species at low density within its range (Paray and Al-Sadoon 2018).
range: Allactaga euphratica is recorded from Turkey, Syria, and eastern Jordan and Lebanon, through northern Saudi Arabia and Iraq to Kuwait and Iran. The southern and eastern limits of the range are poorly defined. The species has been recorded at elevations up to 2,660 m in Lebanon (Abi Said 2004).
useTrade: This species is captured in Syria and sold for falcon food (G. Serra in prep.).
conservationActions: The species occurs in at least several protected areas in Jordan. While there are protected areas within the species’ suitable habitat in Iran, its presence has not been confirmed within them (Farashi and Shariati 2017).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a fairly large extent of occurrence of approximately 272,318 km². However, it occupies specific habitat types and its area of occupancy may be quite small. It is rapidly declining due to ploughing of previously uncultivated land (but population trend has not been quantified), therefore it may qualify for a threatened category under criterion A once more information is available.
habitat: This species is a stenobiont, which inhabits incult areas of piedmont semidesert with light vegetation (wormwood, ephemeras, and saltworts). It prefers clay and argil sand grounds and avoids rubbly areas. In mountains it is found up to 1,000–1,390 m asl (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2020). It is an omnivore, which in spring feeds on green sprouts, in summer mainly feeds on seeds, then in second part of summer when there are drought conditions its diet changes to underground plant parts. Animals are present in the diet, but never as a main part (Yanushevich et al. 1975, Shenbrot et al. 1995).In the eastern part of its range hibernation may last from the beginning of October until the end of February (Chuya valley), or from the end of October to mid-March (Karatau). In the western part of its range (Nuratau) hibernation occurs from the second half of October until mid-February or beginning of March (Pavlenko and Gubaidulina 1970). It uses three types of burrows: permanent summer, wintering and temporary shelters. Permanent summer burrows are simple, with a main passage that leads to a nest, with two or three passages which bifurcate from the main path and lead to the surface, but do not end with an exit. Nests are 7–15 cm in diameter. Wintering burrows do not have additional exits and are deeper underground (61-89 cm). Passage length is between 161 and 178 cm (Shenbrot 1995).This is a nocturnal species which is most probably obligatory solitary. Reproduction occurs twice per season, in March-June and August–September. Litter size is 1 to 6 (usually 3–5) young.
threats: Vinogradov's Jerboa is a rare species. Its population is rapidly declining due to ploughing of previously uncultivated areas.
population: This is considered to be a rare species, in Talass valley, Kyrgyzstan, where it used to be common the population is rapidly declining due to ploughing uncultivated areas. Population density differs in different part of the range: in Chuya valley density is estimated to be between 0.5–16 individuals per ha (Yanushevich et al. 1972); in the Talass valley between 4–5 individuals per km of walking calculation (Shenbrot et al. 1995); and in Nuratau 0.5–0.6 individuals per ha (Pavlenko and Gubaidulina 1970). During an intensive search events in 2016–2019 in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in the areas where it was recorded previously, the species was not found (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2020).
range: This species is found in semi-desert piedmonts in South Kazakhstan, North West Kyrgyzstan and South Uzbekistan. Its range consists of two relatively large and two small isolated areas, which in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan the area is about 42,340 km² and in Uzbekistan it is about 10,028 km² (Shebrot pers. comm. 2020).
conservationActions: This species may occur in some protected areas. Two protected areas (Nuratau Nature Reserve, Uzbekistan and Karatau Nature Reserve, Kazakhstan) formally are within the species’ geographic range, but there are no direct evidences of occurring the species inside of these protected areas (G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2020).

rationale: This species has an extent of occurrence of approximately 13,189 km2. At present it is only known from a small number of sites and there is concern that the habitat is slowly shrinking. However, there are no known major threats and its range falls within a protected area, therefore it has been assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: Inhabits subalpine meadows and pastures, forest glades, and river banks with tall and dense grass or herbaceous understory (from 1,500 m asl) of southern slope of the Great Caucasus Mts. Solitary, active in dusk. Hibernates during winter. Feed on invertebrates and seeds. Reproduces once a year in summer.
threats: The species occurs in Teberda State reserve. No major threats, however, the species is naturally rare with small area of occupancy. Habitats are endangered by the increased exploitation (overgrazing, road and summer resort constructions etc.) as well as by the recent explosion in winter sport and tourism developments. This species is not threatened at the currently accepted level. Its distribution area includes several protected sites, and as Cserkész et al. (2016) demonstrated, it is not rare, even it could be considered common to suitable habitats. However, these habitats are slowly and continually shrinking so regular monitoring is required. Enormous development of recreation and sport tourism centres may have a strong effect on the birch mouse and other wildlife populations in this region. Ski slopes and their service areas are constructed on the subalpine meadows and roads leading there run along the streamside and these places are also important birch mouse habitats.
population: Shenbrot et al. (1995) suggested that it is fairly common in high mountain biotopes such as the Teberda river basin. Cserkész et al. (2016) found densities to be 2.6 specimens/100 trap-night in an Intensively grazed subalpine meadow (with Juniperus), nitrophilous weedy patches (Urtica, etc.) at 2,240 m asl and 13 specimens/100 trap-night in mesophilous broadleaf grassland at Teberda (1,985 m asl) and 2.1 specimens/10 tn in mesophilous pasture used as hayfield in the Kizgich-valley (Arkhyz, 1,500 m asl).
range: This species is found only in the northwestern Caucasus in the upper reaches of the North Klukhor River (Sokolov et al. 1987). The western limit of the Kluchor Birch Mouse distribution is the right bank of the Kizgich River, a tributary of the Great Zelenchuk (Holden-Musser et al. 2016), and the eastern limit verified by karyotype is in the Baksan ravine, Azau river valley near Mt. Elbrus.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: The majority of the range occurs within Teberda State Reserve.

rationale: This species is classified as Critically Endangered, as its extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both smaller than 4 km². It is known from a single location and there is a continued decline in quality of habitat.
habitat: The species occurs in subalpine meadows with tall grass on the higher forest border.
threats: Overgrazing due to clearing of tall grasses is a major threat to this species. Loss of tall grass from grass cutting for agriculture is also a threat in some areas. Habitat outside protected areas is projected to continue declining.
population: The species is currently only known from Sevan Pass, because searches in other areas such as the type locality were unable to find the species in 2012 and 2015 (M. Rusin pers. comm. 2016).
range: This species is known only from several localities close to terra typica in north-central Armenia, namely Lesser Caucasus, Pambakskiy Range, Marmarik River (Razdan River basin). Sites are summarized by Baskevich for Biodiversity Center [in Russian]. In the last 30 years Sicstica armenica has only been found twice: the first in Hancavan (type locality) and in 2015 on Sevan Pass (Rusin et al. 2017).
conservationActions: The Armenian Birch Mouse is listed as Vulnerable in the Red List of Armenia. It was recommended to protect the area where Sicista armenica was found, however, the project is still under revision by authorities.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened, because whilst it has an extent of occurrence of approximately 7,373 km²,  the range is not severely fragmented and there is no evidence for a continued decline in the habitat quantity or quality. Currently, it is only known from a small number of locations, probably due to a lack of research. In the future the species could qualify for a threatened category if the quantity and quality of the habitat declines.
habitat: The species occurs mainly in subalpine meadows in usually slightly disturbed, slightly nitrophilous montane-subalpine tall-herb communities at 1400 to 2,000 m. Optimal habitats occur at 1,500 m; rarely found in forests; active only 3-3.5 months/year; peak activity June-July. In captivity, the species feeds on insects, seeds and berries; litter size 4-6. It is a hibernating species.
threats: Overgrazing is a major threat. Loss of tall grass from grass cutting for agriculture is also a threat in some areas. Areas of suitable habitat outside protected areas are projected to decline further (GMA SW Asia workshop, 2005). Development of recreation and sport tourism centres may have a strong effect on the birch mouse in the Great Caucasus, with ski slopes and their service areas constructed on the subalpine meadows and roads running along streamsides (T. Cserkész pers. comm.).
population: The species can represent up to 25% of small mammal captures at 1,500 m above sea level, with 1-24 individuals per 100 pitfall traps. It is found at lower densities in Georgia (A. Bukhnikashvili pers. comm). Cserkész et al. (2016) captured it in 4.2-42.6 specimens / 100 trap-night relative frequency. It appears that the species is much more common in the western Caucasus than previously assumed; in its preferred habitat Sicista caucasica could be rated as a frequent species. The highest frequency was detected in non-grazed and non-mowed habitats.
range: This species is found in the western Caucasus. It is known from several localities in Russia (both in the south of Krasnodarsky Kray, at Teberda and Kavkazsky State Reserves (Sokolov et al. 1987, Shenbrot et al. 1995, Baskevich et al. 2004 Cserkész et al. 2016). Also occurs in Georgia (Shenbrot et al. 1995, Bukhnikashvili 2004). It is difficult to determine the distribution of this species, because the species can only be determined by karyotype or genotype. The species occurs at 1,400 to 2,000 m asl.
conservationActions: This species has been recorded from protected areas in the Western Caucasus, as well as outside of the protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, lack of current threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species has been collected at Alter do Chao, Santarem, within white sand grassland and gallery forest (J. Patton pers. comm.). This species is arboreal, probably nocturnal, and herbivorous. It is believed to live in lowland mature and secondary rainforests, although it readily enters the rafters of wooden structures. It is known to nests in tree holes (Patton 2015).
threats: The main threat to L. emiliae is deforestation (J. Patton pers. comm.).
population: This species is poorly studied and rarely seen. It has yet to be studied in the field. Locally common despite limited geographic range (Patton 2015).
range: This species is known from the lower reaches of the Rio Madeira, Rio Tapajós, and Rio Xingu; all south of the Amazon river in eastern Brazil (Fabre 2016; Patton 2015). The species has also been reported from Peru, however J. Patton (pers. comm.) considers the Peruvian report as invalid identification of the species.
conservationActions: There are several protected areas within its range, although it presence has not been reported from any of these.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution in Panama, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rat is found in evergreen and deciduous forest, mangroves, plantations, and second growth. It is nocturnal and strictly arboreal and has not been trapped on the ground. It moves slowly and may remain motionless for long periods, but climbs swiftly if pursued. During the day, adult pairs or lone individuals sleep in holes in trees. If disturbed, they stick their heads out. This behaviour is well known to rural residents, who report them occupying trees near water and always being in pairs. Pairs may travel and forage together at night. The diet probably includes fruit and young leaves. Its litter size is 1 to 2 young and breeding may occur year-round (Emmons et al. 2015).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown.
population: The population status of this species is largely unknown, but it is probably not uncommon. It is locally common on Isla del Rey (Reid 2009).
range: This species is found from central Panama (including the Isla San Miguel in the Gulf of Panama), south along the Pacific coast of Colombia and into northwestern Ecuador (Fabre 2016, Emmons et al. 2015). Two subspecies exist, with both occurring in Panama. One is the insular nominotypical form and the other is darlingi Thomas. There has been no evaluation of variation in populations from Colombia or Ecuador (Emmons et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in protected areas in Panama. Further surveys are needed into its distribution, threats, status, and ecological requirements.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in open areas of the Cerrado biome, which is known to demonstrate a wide structural complexity of habitats (Bezerra and Bonvicino 2015). It is a semi fossorial, colonial species with diurnal activity confined to savannah areas and their edges (Emerson pers. comm.). In Brazil, three females with single embryos were caught during the period June to December (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). Individuals of this species are predators and dispersers of seeds of the palms Attalea geraensis and Syagrus petraea. Breeding may be seasonal. (Bezerra and Bonvicino 2015).
threats: There are no major threats; however, habitat destruction through conversion to agriculture may affect the species in the southern part of the range (Vieira pers. comm.).
population: This species is patchy distributed but locally abundant (Filho pers. comm.).
range: This species is known from the Cerrado domain of central Brazil, extending south to Sáo Paulo state and the Chaco of Paraguay (Fabre 2016, Bezerra and Bonvicino 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas throughout its range (Vieira pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is locally threatened in specific sites, but not at the species scale.
habitat: This species is often found living alone or in pairs. They exhibit paternal care of young and delayed juvenile dispersal. Members of the same sex have exclusive home ranges, but the ranges of males and females often overlap. These characteristics suggest social monogamy (Emmons et al. 2015). Stallings et al. (1994) conducted surveys in the Biological Reserve of Poço das Antas, Rio de Janeiro State, southeastern Brazil and determined a home range can reach up to 1,000 m², with densities up to 1.47 per km². This is an arboreal species that primarily inhabits Atlantic coastal forest, inland rainforest, wet gallery forest, and bamboo patches. They are often found in bamboo thickets at watersheds, and dense thickets without bamboo in swamps. This species feeds on young shoots and leaves of bamboo and other plants (Emmons et al. 2015).
threats: This rodent is locally threatened by habitat destruction in Minas Gerais State, Brazil. Other threats include deforestation, fire, hunting pressure, and the presence of livestock and domestic dogs (Aguiar da Silva et al. 2012).
population: This species is naturally very rare. The ecological density is about 4.28 individuals per km² in Rio Grande do Sul State, southern Brazil (Silva 2005).
range: This species occurs along the Atlantic coast of Brazil into Uruguay, and inland to northeastern Argentina and eastern Paraguay (Fabre 2016, Emmons et al. 2015)
conservationActions: It occurs in some protected areas. Ongoing studies are being conducted by Emerson Vieira and Sergio Lucena.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is present in disturbed areas and continues to thrive.
habitat: This species occurs in moist grasslands of the southern cerrado and pampas habitats of Minas Gerais state, Brazil (Lacher and Alho 2001). It is also found in forest, at forest edges and in introduced grasslands in Atlantic Forest from Espirito Santo south to Argentina and Paraguay (A. Christof pers. comm.). This is a semifossorial species with features adapted for burrowing. It is an herbivore, and is active at night. It can be harmful to Pinus plantations. This species is primarily found under riparian vegetation in dense forests, but is a habitat generalist. It can also inhabit areas of altered vegetation communities (Bonviciono and Bezerra 2015).
threats: There are no known threats to this species.
population: There is no information on the population status of this species.
range: This species occurs in southwestern Brazil, northeastern Argentina, and southern Paraguay. More specifically, it can be found in southern Brazil from the states of Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, and Minas Gerais to Rio Grande do Sul, southern Paraguay in La Cordillera and Guaira departments and in the Misiones province of northeastern Argentina. This species has also been reported in the Cerrado at Serra das Araras Ecological Station, Porto Estrela, Mato Grosso state, Brazil, and has an unconfirmed report of their presence in northern Corrientes, Argentina (Fabre 2016, Bonvicino and Bezerra 2015). It has been recorded in Rio de Janeiro and Rio Grande do Sul States and one record for Espirito Santo State (A. Christoff pers. comm.).
conservationActions: The species occurs in Caparao National Park. Surveys are required to determine whether the species is synonymous with E. subspinosus and to determine necessary conservation measures.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a protected area, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species occurs in gallery forest and open vegetation, cerrado and rocky outcrops (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.). In the central Caatinga bioregion this species is found at elevations from 260 m to 1030 m; common in granite or sandstone outcrops, locally called lajeiros or lajedos, which provide crevices for temporary and secure shelter. Rocky habitats provide a cool refuge during the heat of the day, and warmth from radiation during cold nights. Nests, placed in crevices or tree cavities, are constructed of cotton, straw, or dry leaves. Individuals have been captured at the mouths of caves (Fabre 2016).
threats: This rodent is hunted and may be affected by fire in rupestrian fields (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).
population: This species is common throughout its range (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in central Brazil from central Bahia north to central Tocantins states (Fabre 2016, Pessoa et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in a protected area within its range (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Thrichomys apereoides inhabits xeric and rocky environments in caatinga and cerrado including human modified habitats in which the species can be an important agricultural pest (Fabre 2016, Mares and Ojeda 1982, Mares et al. 1985, Moojen 1952, Streilein 1982a).  Individuals may occupy caves and human dwellings. In Exu, Brazil, T. apereoides is associated primarily with granitic outcroppings (Streilein 1982d). In Bolivia, T. apereoides inhabits flat and arid shrub-dominated habitat devoid of large rocks (Anderson 1997). It is a crepuscular species (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). In Brazil, its reproduction occurs throughout the year with two or three litters of one to six young (average 3.1) produced after a gestation period of 89 days (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). Sexual maturity is reached between seven and nine months (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
threats: It is hunted for food although the species is not considered to have any major threats in operation throughout its range (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).
population: This species is very common throughout the range (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).
range: This species is found in Bahia and Minas Gerais states in east-central Brazil (Fabre 2016; Pessoa et al. 2015). T. apereoides is closely associated with a diagonal belt of open vegetation that stretches in a northeast to southwest direction between the Amazonian and Atlantic forests (Alho 1982, Mares and Ojeda 1982).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas within its range (Bonvicino and Geise pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species inhabits in open vegetation in cerrado and transition areas, forest edge and grassland (Lacher pers. comm.). Individuals occur in dry forest patches, including among aggregations of Attaleya phalerata palms. In the seasonally wet Pantanal devoid of rocky areas, animals have been caught in traps set in trees placed 1.5 m above the ground during the rainy season (Fabre 2016).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time.
population: This rodent is common and abundant throughout the range (C. Bonvicino pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in central and western Brazil in Tocantins, Goiás, and Mato Grosso states, through Paraguay and Bolivia (Pessoa et al. 2015). Their elevational range is mostly between 750 m and 1190 m, however, some reach a low of 130 m in the northern extreme of the range.
conservationActions: This species occurs in a number of protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, likely tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little is known of the biology of this species; it is probably adaptable to secondary habitats including gardens, anywhere there is a closed canopy; also found along stream edges (J. Patton pers. comm.). It is typically found in lowland rainforest, in seasonally inundated floodplains of whitewater or blackwater rivers. It is an arboreal species (Emmons and Patton 2015). During a survey three of the four specimens of this species captured were taken in the tree canopy. The digestive system physiology suggests it feeds on leaves (Geise et al. 2001). In the same survey, a single adult female was found to be pregnant with a single embryo. Pregnant females have been collected during the months of June and September (Emmons and Patton 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: The results of a study were unable to ascertain the true abundance of this species, it was unclear whether the trapping program failed or whether Makalata macrura is rare throughout the Rio Jurua (Geise et al. 2001). Emmons and Feer (1997) suggested that the species is locally common.
range: This species occurs throughout the western Amazon Basin, including southern Colombia and Venezuela, eastern Ecuador, and north-central Peru. Its range extends east through Western Brazil to the left bank of the lower Rio Negro and at least to the lower Rio Madeira. The geographic boundaries are poorly understood in the eastern and southern parts of its range (Fabre 2016, Emmons and Patton 2015).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species prefers lowland seasonally flooded tropical evergreen forest (Eisenberg and Redford 1999) and is common in secondary forest and gardens (J. Patton pers. comm.). It is strictly nocturnal, nests in hollow trees and feeds on seeds (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). This species is nocturnal, arboreal, and solitary. They feed primarily on fruit, unripe seeds, and leaves. They probably have a crepuscular activity period (Emmons and Patton 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time.
population: This species is generally restricted to riverine forests, but has been trapped in gardens surrounding Amerindian houses (Emmons and Patton 2015).
range: This species occurs throughout the Guianan region, including the islands of Trinidad and Tobago, from northern Venezuela, Guyana, Surinam, French Guiana, to eastern Amazonia generally east of the Rio Negro and Rio Madeira, to Maranhão and Ceará, and southwest to northwestern Bolivia (Fabre 2016, Emmons and Patton 2015).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas, including Madidi National Park in Bolivia.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category (Reid 2009, Adler 2011).
habitat: This species is usually found near creeks or streams in lowland evergreen forest, or in low-lying areas. It is nocturnal and terrestrial. During the day it occupies burrows, usually located on steep banks near water. Burrows are roughly horizontal and extend about 2 m to a nest chamber lined with shredded vegetation (Buchanan and Howell 1965). This large rat can be easily detected at night as it has good eyeshine, and, when disturbed, it usually runs swiftly to a burrow. It may remain at the burrow entrance, where it can be closely observed or even captured by hand. The diet includes fruit, insects (beetles and orthopteran remains have been found in its burrows), and some green plant matter. Litter size is one to three; young are precocious at birth and have soft fur. Spines develop after one month (Reid 2009). In areas with large expanses of wet habitats, such as along the Pacific slope in Colombia, it has been suggested that this species might reach higher densities and be polygynous or promiscuous (Adler 2011).
threats: There are no known major threats (Reid 2009).
population: It is uncommon to locally abundant in evergreen, lowland forest (Reid 2009).
range: This species occurs from northern Honduras (Fabre 2016, Patton and Emmons 2015) to northwestern Ecuador. Found at elevations ranging from lowlands to 800 m (Reid 2009). It occupies the aseasonal pluvial forests on the Pacific slope of Colombia and northern Ecuador (Adler 2011).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is nocturnal and arboreal in nature. Two young are born (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). It is present in primary forest.
threats: The species is affected by deforestation, although this is not considered a major threat at this time.
population: Its population is not well known but it is not thought to be particularly common (F. Catzeflis and J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs is known from the eastern Amazon Basin and Guianan region of Brazil, Guyana, Suriname, and French Guinana, east of the Rio Negro and north of the Rio Solimões and east of the Rio Xingu south of the Rio Solimões (Fabre 2016, Emmons et al. 2015)
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in many protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. There are rapid rates of habitat conversion, so this species may become threatened in the near future.
habitat: This species is a common inhabitant of dry tropical rainforest but also occurs in mid-savannah and grassland habitat near shaded areas such as trees or shrubs. It is present both in primary and secondary habitats, and has been reported to den in termite mounds as well as armadillo burrows (Fabre 2016). There is little information in the way of habitats and ecology, but the species was the most common rodent in some dry forests where the population remained stable for 10 years. It also bred in mid-savanna grassland habitats and denned in holes in termite mounds and armadillo burrows (Patton and Leite 2015).
threats: In Bolivia, there do not appear to be any major threats to this species. The dry forest in Bolivia, Paraguay, and Brazil is rapidly declining due to forest conversion for agriculture, and a pipeline from Brazil will increase this threat (J. Patton pers. comm.).
population: This is a common species in Bolivia.
range: This species occurs in eastern Bolivia, northern Paraguay, and central Brazil (Patton and Leite 2015). It occurs below from 50 - 1,000 m asl (Fabre 2016).
conservationActions: It is probably present in several protected areas in Bolivia. Further research is needed into the distribution and taxonomy of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, and because a large portion of its range occurs in protected areas and it is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species is found in non-flooded, or terra firme, lowland evergreen rainforest, and along the margins of both flooded vàrzea and igapó forest (Fabre 2016). Pregnant females have been recorded in May and October (Patton et al., 2000). Nothing else is known about the habitat or ecology of this species (J. Patton pers. comm.). This species is primarily terrestrial and nocturnal (Fabre 2016).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: This species is uncommon where it has been collected. This is the least represented member of the genus in scientific collections (J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in west central Amazonas state, Brazil, west of the Rio Madeira and on both sides of the Rio Solimoes; possibly extending into Colombia in the upper Rio Negro drainage and northeastern Peru (Patton and Leite 2015). Its altitudinal range reaches 300 m asl.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Jau National Park (Patton et al., 2000), and Amana and Mamiraua protected areas as well (A. Percequillo and J. Patton pers. comm.). Surveys to the west of its present range (to Iquitos, Peru) would be very helpful.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, and although it is relatively rare it occurs in many protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occupies seasonally flooded forest (both várzea and igapó) during dry season and margins of upland forest during the wet season (Fabre 2016) and it may also be locally common in terra firme forest (Pattons and Leite 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time (J. Ochoa pers. comm.).
population: In Ecuador this species is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.) and in Venezuela it is rare when sympatric with P. guyannensis (J. Ochoa pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in northern Peru, eastern Ecuador, southern Colombia, southern Venezuela, and northern Brazil (Patton and Leite 2015), largely north of the Río Marañón–Rio Solimões axis to the left bank of the Rio Negro at Manaus (Fabre 2016).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species at this time.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in well-drained forests, Cerrado gallery forests (Bonvicino et al. 2002), sometimes in creek-side and gallery forest but more commonly in primary forest where it may be sympatric with Cuvier Spiny-rat (P. cuvieri). Some have suggested that this species favours microhabitats with abundant babacu palms. Sympatry with Goeldi’s Spiny-rat (P. goeldii) has been documented along the southern margins of the Rio Amazonas and also with the Long-tailed Spiny-rat (P. longicaudatus) in the dry forests of the Cerrado in central Brazil (Fabre 2016).
threats: The southern and southeastern portion of its range in Cerrado is under significant threat due to agricultural expansion. The species is also facing additional threat due to the Trans-Amazon highway (J. Patton pers. comm.) and also logging and fire in Tocantins (P. Costa pers. comm.). The species is less threatened in the northern (Amazonian) portion of the range.
population: This species is locally abundant throughout its distribution and occurs only in unaltered vegetation (Bonvicino et al. 2002).
range: This species occurs in the Amazonian lowlands of eastern Brazil south of the Rio Amazonas, extending south to the Cerrado biome in eastern central Brazil, primarily in the Rio Tapajós, Rio Xingu, and Rio Tocantins-Araguaia fluvial systems of Pará, Maranhão, Tocantins, Minas Gerais, Goiás, and Mato Grosso states (Fabre 2016, Patton and Leite 2015). Its altitudinal range reaches 1,000 m asl.
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in Chapada dos Veadeiros National Park (Bonvicino et al. 2002) and National Park of Brasilia, Distrito Federal.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining anywhere near the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species mainly inhabits upland, non-seasonally flooded or terra firme forests including undisturbed rainforest and secondary or disturbed forests and garden plots. It extends upward to above 2,000 m giving it the broadest elevational range of any species of Proechimys (Patton and Leite 2015). In Rio Juruá (west Brazil), the pregnant and lactating females were collected throughout most of the year, suggesting that breeding is continuous. The mean litter size was two (range 1–3). Both males and females reached sexual maturity after they were fully grown and had moulted into their adult pelage (Fabre 2016).
threats: There are no major threats known at this time (J. Patton pers. comm.).
population: During a survey, P. simonsi was found to be common along the length of the Rio Jurua and well represented in the fauna of all four regional areas (Patton et al. 2000). This species is common and easily recognizable (J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the western Amazon Basin from southern Colombia (Caqueta and Florencia) through eastern Ecuador, eastern Peru, northern Bolivia, and into western Brazil (Patton and Leite. 2015). This species has the highest altitude for this genus from 50 to 2,000 m (Fabre 2016, Patton et al. 2000)
conservationActions: There are several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: They prefer seasonally flooded white-water or black-water forests, and in secondary or disturbed forests where water is nearby, gardens, and riverine or margins of flooded grasslands within the forest (Patton and Leite 2015). This species is a specialist of varzea habitat in areas subject to seasonal flooding within the lowland Amazon (Patton et al. 2000). Along the Rio Jurua, Brazil, P. steerei exhibits reproductive characteristics as might be expected for a species inhabiting seasonal habitats with early maturity, large litter sizes and a large percentage of young animals breeding (Patton et al. 2000). Litter size is twice as large as other species of this genus and it breeds at a much earlier age than others of the genus (J. Patton pers. comm.).
threats: There are no major threats at this time. The only future threat would be if the rivers were all dammed, destroying the varzea habitat (J. Patton pers. comm.).
population: This rodent is common throughout its range (J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in eastern and southern Peru, northwestern Bolivia, and western Brazil (Patton and Leite 2015). In the Amazon Basin it occurs largely south of the Rio Marañón–Rio Solimões axis in eastern Peru, northwestern Bolivia, and western Brazil east to the Rio Purus, but extending north of the Rio Solimões in the Imerí region west of the lower Rio Negro (Fabre 2016). Its altidudinal range is from 50 - 400 m (Fabre 2016).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas throughout its range (J. Patton pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, and because it is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is known only from upland, non-seasonally flooded (terra firme) rainforest where it may be found in undisturbed forest as well as in disturbed areas dominated by bamboo (Fabre in press). All specimens in Rio Jurua and Peru were collected from undisturbed terra firme forests (Patton and Leite 2015). The average litter is two. Further detailed information is not yet known. Data are inadequate to judge seasonality of reproduction, but breeding in the dry season has been confirmed (Patton and Leite 2015).
threats: There are no major threats known at this time; the isolated population is away from core development areas.
population: This species is uncommon. It is known only from a few specimens from five localities, although there have not been further studies within intermediate areas (J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species is known only from two localities in Rio Juruá  in western Amazonian Brazil and adjacent parts of eastern and southern Peru (Patton and Leite 2015). This species is replaced by P. gardneri to the east (J. Patton pers. comm.).
conservationActions: Some protected areas exist within its range, and the species has been collected from a National Park in Peru (J. Patton pers. comm.). More surveys are needed to determine its conservation status.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it does not appear to be under threat and it is unlikely to be declining anywhere near the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category (Reid 2009, M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
habitat: This large rat is found in lowland evergreen forest primary and second growth. Also occurs in deciduous forest, where it favours riparian corridors and low-lying areas. Nocturnal, mainly terrestrial and solitary. It travels along fallen logs or old walls but does not climb trees. At night it is often seen sitting quietly near buttress roots or logs. It walks slowly and sometimes freezes in a spotlight. This rat may use burrows during the day but often occupies shallow depressions under roosts and hollow logs, or in dense vegetation. The diet consists mainly of fruit and seeds, with lesser amounts of plant material, insects, and fungi. Palm nuts and other large seeds are carried to a sheltered spot to be eaten. They play significant roles in seed dispersal (Carvajal and Adler 2008) This species is used widely as a food source, and has the potential to be a significant protein source (Asprilla-Perea et al. 2012). Females give birth to one to five precocious young and may breed four times a year (Reid 2009). Maximum life spans are at least three years for both male and female (Oaks et al. 2008). In central Panama males have larger home ranges than females, but mating systems and territoriality probably depend on population density (Alder 2011).
threats: Deforestation is a threat in some parts of its range, although this species is thought to be tolerant to a degree of habitat destruction or alteration (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
population: This species is common and abundant throughout its geographic range (Oaks et al. 2008). There have been extensive studies on Panama populations, but very little of those in South American (Patton and Leite 2015).
range: This species occurs from eastern Honduras to southwestern Ecuador (Fabre 2016). It favours lowlands but can be found up to 800 m (Reid 2009).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in the dry tropical rainforest (Patton and Leite 2015) and in the forest edge. This rat is nocturnal, terrestrial and solitary. It feeds on seeds, fruit, fungi, and a few leaves and insects. It is tolerant of habitat degradation.
threats: There are no major threats to this species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
population: It is an abundant species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in northwest Venezuela and north central Colombia, around the foothills of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (Aguilera 1979, Woods and Kilpatrick 2005). It is a lowland species; it is found from sea level to 300 m asl. This species occurs in Sierra de Perijá and Sierra de Santa Marta in northeastern Colombia and northwestern Venezuela (Fabre 2016, Patton and Leite 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rat has been recorded in terra firme forest, including naturally disturbed forest with either high density of bamboo or in second growth. It is found in upland, nonseasonally inundated lowland rainforest, in disturbed, undisturbed, and second growth forests (Fabre 2016). It can often be found in garden plots where individuals feed on yucca and plantains (Patton and Leite 2015). It is less frequently found in forest that floods occasionally, not seasonally. This rodent has not been found in varzea forest (J. Patton pers. comm.). The modal litter size was 2 (range one to four). It is not known whether reproduction is seasonal or largely aseasonal in Brazil (Patton et al. 2000). Data suggest that breeding commences by the end of the dry season. Males occupy larger home ranges than females, and females maintain exclusive-use home ranges. This suggests a polygynous mating system. Low population densities have been reported (Patton and Leite 2015).
threats: There are no major threats at this time. This species does well in second growth and garden plots (J. Patton pers. comm.).
population: This rodent is common everywhere; there have been no population studies (J. Patton and M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.). However, low population densities have been reported (Patton and Leite 2015).
range: This species occurs in the western Amazonia from southern Colombia, eastern Ecuador, eastern Peru, northernwestern Bolivia, and the headwaters Region of the Río Jurua, west Brazil (Patton and Leite 2015, Woods and Kilpatrick 2005). Its range also extends up to southern Colombia to the Río Caqueta, including the Amazon at Iquitos, Colombia (Patton 1987, Patton and Leite 2015). This species reaches is found from 200 m - 1,800 m (Fabre 2016).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas including indigenous areas throughout its range (J. Patton pers. comm.). This rodent is eaten locally by indigenous people but only for subsistence (J. Patton pers. comm.). No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because it is probably in decline (but probably at a rate of less than 30% over ten years) and approximately only 20% of its habitat remains and it is vulnerable to habitat fragmentation in its current range, particularly in the south, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2c.
habitat: This rat is nocturnal, terrestrial and solitary. It occurs in dry lowland forest and tropical semi-deciduous forest (C. Boada pers. comm, Emmons et al. 2015).
threats: The major threat to this species is deforestation especially in the southern part of its range; introduced goats are causing destruction of low vegetation leading to erosion. Probably 20% of its habitat remains (C. Boada pers. comm.).
population: In Ecuador this species is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.), there is no information on its abundance in Peru.
range: This species is known only from the tropical dry forests of southwestern Ecuador and adjacent northwestern Peru (Patton and Leite 2015). It has an altitudinal range of sea level to 800 m asl. (Fabre 2016).
conservationActions: This species occurs in three protected areas in the north of its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: In western and central Amazonian Brazil and French Guiana the species inhabits upland, or terra firme rainforest, but it might be found equally in locally inundated forest or secondary upland forest and abandoned gardens (Patton and Leite 2015; Fabre in press). In French Guiana females maintain exclusive home ranges, males home ranges overlap with either sex; male home ranges are more than twice the surface area of those of females (Adler 2011).During a survey of the Jurua River, Brazil, many specimens were trapped in terra firme forests (28 of 57), they were also collected in locally inundated forest, secondary upland forest and abandoned gardens and were especially common in the latter (Patton et al. 2000). In the same survey, out of sampling months August to March, pregnant females were collected only in February and March. All litters comprised two young. Data are too limited to determine whether breeding is largely confined to the wet season or also extends through the dry period. Voss et al. (2001) also presents capture data for three different habitat plots in French Guiana, where the species is found equally in both secondary and primary forest (Voss et al. 2001).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time.
population: This rodent is abundant in primary forest but absent in secondary forest in French Guiana (F. Catzeflis pers. comm.). It is found in secondary forest in Rio Jurua in western Amazonia (Patton et al. 2000). It is a very abundant species in Tumucumaque National Parque (C. Silva pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs throughout the Amazon Basin in eastern Ecuador, Peru, eastern Brazil, Venezuela, and the Guianas (Patton and Leite 2015). This species occurs in scattered localities in eastern Amazonia, from the Guianan region of eastern Venezuela and French Guiana to the Carajas region of Pará State south of the Rio Amazonas, Montanhas de Tumucumaque National Park in Amapa State, and the left (east) bank of the Rio Negro near Manaus in central Amazonia, Amazonas State (Patton et al. 2000); also in Peru (Pacheco et al. 1995). Its elevation range is below 500 m asl. altitude (J. Patton pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Tumucumaque National Park (C. Silva pers. comm.) and several other protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in several protected areas, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in well-drained lowland forests, sometimes in gallery forest in otherwise more open areas. It is more common in primary forests but ranges into secondary forest and other human disturbed communities. It might occur sympatrically with Cuvier Spiny-rat (Fabre 2016). This rodent is nocturnal and mainly frugivorous but it also eats seeds and fungi (Eisenberg and Redford, 1999). This species can survive in agricultural landscape if there is some forest cover; its reproduction is seasonal in French Guiana (F. Catzeflis pers. comm.). This species is reportedly a seasonal breeder but little information is known (Fabre 2016). In French Guiana the species was caught mostly in well-drained forest but also occasionally in creekside forest, and also in primary forest (Patton and Leite 2015).
threats: In the past clear cutting was a threat in the Guianas; mining may have threatened the species in the Brazilian portion of its range.
population: This rodent is common in natural and degraded habitats (F. Catzeflis pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the Amazon Basin of northeastern Brazil (east of Rio Negro and north of Rio Amazonas) and southern Venezuela and Guyanan subregion of eastern Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana (Fabre in press). It is known only from lowlands up to 500 m asl.
conservationActions: This species is found in several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. However, the subspecies P. g. poliopus may be threatened due to the extent and quality of habitat degradation.
habitat: This species is abundant in primary and secondary dry tropical forests and extends into human agricultural croplands. Individuals have been trapped amidst the roots of wild pineapple in the arid forests of the northeastern slope of Lake Maracaibo (Fabre 2016). No dietary data are available, but this species, as with other Proechimys, probably feeds on seeds, fruits, and other plant parts (Fabre 2016).
threats: The eastern part of its range is undergoing habitat degradation, but overall there are no major threats. P. g. poliopus was previously listed as VU B1ab(iii), however it has since been grouped with P. guairae. Although P. g. poliopus is relatively abundant within its restricted range, the extent of this range (< 20,000 km2), the species is known from fewer than ten localities, and both the extent and quality of its habitat is apparently declining, even within protected areas, which are extractive preserves (Fabre 2016).
population: This species is considered common (M. Aguilera pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in northern and western Venezuela in the foothills of both sides of the Andes and upper Llanos north of the upper Rio Orinoco, including around Lake Maracaibo and the eastern slopes of the Sierra de Perija, and into adjacent northeastern Colombia (Patton and Leite 2015). It is possible that the species occurs in Colombia. It is found from sea level to 800 m asl.
conservationActions: It occurs in a number of protected areas especially in the west (M. Aguilera pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits seasonally flooded blackwater (igapó) and whitewater (várzea) rainforest, both primary and secondary, and typically along river margins (Fabre 2016).  It has also been collected in gardens and secondary and primary forest (P. Costa pers. comm.). Most of the localities where it has been reported to occur are along margins of rivers, though this may be an artefact of collection methods.
threats: The eastern Pará is currently under threat from deforestation and mining for iron and aluminium; other areas are experiencing expansion of soybean agriculture; the Cuiaba-Santarem highway also passes through part of the range. Its range is contracting from the south and south-east (A. Percequillo pers. comm.).Extrapolating deforestation rates (from Asner et al. 2005) for Pará and the northern 58% of the Mato Grosso (which roughly matches the distribution map for P. goeldii) for a three year period to ten years, the percent of habitat loss to the species’ is approximately 14%. However, Ewers et al. (2008) show that Amazonian deforestation rates vary greatly over time and a three year period would probably be too short on which to base a ten year projection, but even with a more grim average yearly loss the species is unlikely to lose 20% of its habitat in a ten year period. In any case, even 14% is an extraordinary rate of habitat loss over such a large area, but it should be noted that habitat loss is unlikely to translate directly to population decline in this species because it is probably able to tolerate some degree of habitat disturbance.
population: It is expected to be abundant (J. Patton pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in in the eastern Amazonian Brazil along both banks of the Rio Amazonas, largely east of the Rio Madeira, in the states of Amazonas and Para and south along the Tapajos, Xingu, and Tocantins-Araguaia rivers and their tributaries, reaching the cerrado biome in Mato Grosso state (Patton and Leite 2015). Its altitudinal range ranges from near sea level to 300 m.
conservationActions: This species is found in Xingu indigenous area and Cristalino State Ecological Reserve. Studies would be useful to determine whether the retraction of the range will adversely affect the species (J. Patton pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed stable population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This nocturnal and arboreal species is strongly associated with multistratal tropical evergreen forest (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). Habitat generally includes bamboo and cane thickets on the margins of seasonally inundated and upland rainforest. In Ecuador specifically, this species can be found in the canopy of tall forests. (Emmons et al. 2015). It is social and forages in bamboo clumps in family groups (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). Its home ranges reach up to 0.43 ha (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). It is a varzea specialist and is rarely seen but can be heard because of its very distinctive call. Little is known on the reproductive biology of this species, but pregnant females have been reported at the end of the rainy season in June in the central Amazon (Emmons et al. 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time.
population: This rodent is not common.
range: This species is distributed in the Amazon Basin from eastern Colombia south through eastern Ecuador, northern and central Peru to northeastern Bolivia and east along the Amazon River to its mouth in Brazil, extending north to the Río Orinico in Venezuela and south into the eastern Cerrado of Brazil (Fabre 2016, Emmons et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Habitat for this species includes bamboo and cane thickets typically along river margins. It has special adaptations for arboreal browsing, and produces staccato vocalizations (Emmons et al. 2015). In Bolivia, the species is found in Yungas forest areas where it is specifically restricted to disjunct patches of bamboo habitat. It can also be found in bamboo stands in disturbed areas, such as alongside rivers in urban areas. All localities are within tropical or subtropical areas.
threats: Although the species is restricted to bamboo habitats it is adaptable to habitat change, as long as some bamboo stands remain.
population: It is relatively common within suitable bamboo habitat.
range: This species occurs in the southwestern margins of the Amazon Basin, from central Peru south to central Bolivia, and east to Rio Juruá in Brazil. This range coincides with the large range of bamboo dominated forests in the western Amazon. This species generally occurs at higher elevations than D. dactylinus, or is restricted to the headwaters in river basins where the two species co-occur. (Fabre 2016, Emmons et al. 2015). This species occurs up to about 1,000 m.
conservationActions: This species is present in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because it is known from two remaining locations and its area of occupancy is likely less than 500 km2. Additionally, there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat with ongoing fragmentation of habitat.
habitat: The original specimen was found in a cave near Lagoa Santa, Minas Gerais (Emmons et al. 2002). This species inhabits the area between semideciduous forest and Cerrado, between 500 and 800 m (Leite and Loss 2015).
threats: The forest habitat where it occurs is highly reduced and fragmented (Emmons et al. 2002), and habitat destruction is ongoing in the Cerrado (Y. Leite pers. comm.).
population: This rodent is uncommon; it is known from only four specimens (Y. Leite pers. comm.).
range: This species originally occurred in Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais States, Brazil (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). It is now highly restricted to Minas Gerais and no longer in Rio de Janeiro (Y. Leite pers. comm.). It is known only from the Lagoa Santa region and Fazenda Santa Cruz in the Minas Gerais state of Brazil. They have been found in the valleys of Paraopeba and das Velhas rivers (Fabre 2016, Leite and Loss 2015).
conservationActions: This species has not been found in any protected areas (Y. Leite pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution (although it is recognized that it is patchily distributed and its area of occupancy may be less than 20,000 km²), the fact that it is common where it occurs, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is nocturnal and is probably folivorous (Leite 2003). It is strongly arboreal, and some species construct leaf nests in tree cavities (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). This species occupies fragmented habitats throughout northwestern Brazil, primarily in isolated areas of semidecidous forests (Leite and Loss 2015).
threats: The forest habitat where it occurs is highly reduced and fragmented (Emmons et al. 2002).
population: This rodent may be locally common although it occurs in fragmented and patchy habitat (Y. Leite pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the inland region of northeastern Brazil, from the southern portion of Ceará to the northernmost part of Minas Gerais. This range potentially extends to the coast in Alagoas and Pernambuco states (Fabre 2016, Leite and Loss 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in Araripe National Forest (Leite 2003). The species would benefit from habitat protection measures. Further studies on the ecology and life history of this species are required (Y. Leite pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is present in more intact sections of Atlantic Forest in Sao Paulo state.
habitat: This rodent is found mainly along coast in areas of broadleaf evergreen forest, but extends to west into Araucaria forests in the state of Parana. Northern range records are from above 1,000 m elevation, southern records are from lower elevations suggesting preference for cooler climates (Leite and Loss 2015, Leite 2003, Emmons et al. 2002).
threats: The forest habitat where it occurs is highly reduced and fragmented (Emmons et al. 2002).
population: This species is known from 15 specimens; it is known from wide range and may be locally common (Leite 2003).
