rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because that habitat is now a protected area (Ruiz 2017).  Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is larger than 20,000 km².
habitat: This species occurs in tropical montane cloud forests (Almendra et al. 2014). It favors cool, wet, highland forest, often near water, but sometimes enters wet field or brush (Reid 1997). It is nocturnal and terrestrial (Reid 1997).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to degredation and deforestation (Almendra et al. 2014). In Mexico, it is considered to be near threatened.
population: This species is uncommon (Reid 1997). In Mexico it has only been reported for 4 localities (Ceballos and Oliva 2005).
range: This species occurs in cloud forest elevations from Chiapas, México, through Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, to north central Nicaragua (Musser and Carleton 2005). This species occurs east of the Isthums of Tehuantepex and highlands of Chiapas and Central America (Almendra et al. 2014). It is found at elevations of 750 to 2,500 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: This species occurs in some protected areas, including Sierra de las Minas in Guatemala.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern since, although its extent of occurrence is less than 20,000 km², it occurs in an area of extensive, suitable habitat which does not appear to be under threat, has a presumed large population, and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: H. intectus is apparently terrestrial and nocturnal. It is known to inhabit both primary cloud forest and adjacent secondary growth, usually in cool and very humid environments (Gómez-Laverde et al. 2015).
threats: In the northern part of its range deforestation is prevalent (C. Delgado pers. comm.).
population: This species appear to be abundant (or at least easily trapped) at most places where it has been found to date (Voss et al. 2002).
range: This species is restricted to Cordillera Central of the central Andes of Columbia between 1,700 m and 2,800 m elevation. It is known in the departments of Antioquia, Quindío, and Risaralda (Gómez-Laverde et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This species is found in several reserves, but not national parks.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is poorly known. The area in which it is found is characterized by coastal lowland forest.
threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
population: This species is not considered to be rare.
range: This species occurs in low to intermediate elevations of western México, from south Sinaloa to southwest Oaxaca (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species' range falls within several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable given that it is known from three locations which are subject to distinctive threats, its area of occupancy is estimated to be less than 2,000 km², and the area and quality of habitat are declining due to deforestation. Additionally, the taxonomy of this species is unclear and it may be split into two distinct species, which would potentially impact the conservation status of the species.
habitat: This species occurs in humid mountain forests (Almendra et al. 2014). It has been known to tolerate anthropogenic disturbance (Ceballos and Oliva 2005). This species is poorly known.
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation of its cloud forest habitat. Its conservation status should be re-evaluted to account for a reduction of its distribution range for two lineages (Almendra et al. 2014).
population: This population represents two independent evolutionary lineages that are restricted to different mountains (Almendra et al. 2014).
range: This species is known from cloud forest elevations in the Sierra Madre Oriental (from Tamaulipas to Veracruz), the Sistema Montañosa (north Oaxaca), and the Sierra Madre del Sur (south Oaxaca), México (Ceballos and Oliva 2005, Almendra et al. 2014). This species is found at 1,500 -2,500 m asl.
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is not declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category and it occurs in protected areas.
habitat: It has been recorded from undisturbed Yungas and Tucumano Bolivian subtropical forest habitat; it is not known if occurs in secondary habitat.
threats: There are no major threats to the species, however, numerous populations are threatened. Various populations are threatened by loss of habitat through conversion to agricultural use (crops). The habitat of this species in the Argentinian part of the range is severely threatened, where the species is largely restricted to protected areas. In Bolivia, more habitats are available.
population: It is a reasonably common species.
range: This species occurs on the eastern slopes of the Andes of south-central Bolivia and northwest Argentina (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found at elevations of 500 to 2,100 m.
conservationActions: It is present in Tariquia Natural Reserve, Bolivia. It is present in two protected areas in Argentina. Further research is needed into the distribution, habitat and ecology of the species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent occurs in open areas, grasslands, forest borders, and in cerrado enclaves within the Amazon. It is a diurnal and nocturnal species. It feeds on insects and fruits.
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: This species is abundant to very common.
range: This species is known from central Brazil south of the Amazon River, extreme southeast Peru (as per Pacheco et al. 1995), and northeast Argentina (see Galliari et al. 1996); limits uncertain (Musser and Carleton, 2005). It also occurs in Paraguay and Bolivia.
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is well above criterion B1 thresholds and the species is not experiencing severe fragmentation. The only evidence that could possibly qualify the species under a threatened category is the fact that the species occurs in two disjoint areas both of which have a subspecies (Necromys obscurus and Necromys scagliarium). Both subspecies are known from less than 10 localities and occur in severely impacted areas (pers. comm. Guillermo D'Elía).
habitat: This species exhibits some fossorial tendency (Fornes and Massoia 1965). It is commonly captured at the borders of cultivated fields, moist areas near lagoons and streams along the coast, and among rocks in hilly environments (Reig 1964; E. M. González and Martínez Lanfranco 2010). This species occurs at the edge of marshes and meadows (Gonzalez 2001).
threats: Habitat loss is the major threat to this species. The natural grasslands and moist areas of the Pampean region have been continuously replaced by agricultural fields, pastures and urbanized areas. The little available information about its habitats and ecology show that it is very restricted to specific habitat conditions (like moist areas and natural grasslands) and may present reduced mobility due to its fossorial tendency.
population: There is no information on population parameters for this species. Only fossil records of this species from the Late Holocene in Buenos Aires province indicate a wider distribution than at present and that partially connected Argentinean and Uruguayan populations (Pardiñas and Tonni 2000, Pardiñas 1999b). The populations are very fragmented and restricted, however, where they occur they could be considered common.
range: The species has a disjunct distribution, in southern Uruguay and east-central Argentina (see localities in Pardiñas et al. 2015). Their range varies according to subspecies and is approximately 13,500 km² for N. o. scagliarum; and approximately 2,600 km² for N. o. obscurus.
conservationActions: This species occurs in at least one protected area.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 500 km², all individuals are in fewer than five locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, number of mature individuals and a reduction in locations. However, no specimens have been recorded since the late 1990s and there is an urgent need to catalogue this species. Considering some of its habitat has already been converted into urban landscapes this species may qualify for Critically Endangered listing with updated population and distribution information.
habitat: This species is poorly known. It is regarded as terrestrial (Marcelo Weksler pers comm). The region of Mindo, where this species occurs, is generally covered by montane rain forest (cloud forest), except in river valleys in which the forest is similar to late successional lowland rain forest, since these valleys were deforested some decades ago. The canopy is of moderate height (15 to 20 m), and the trees are covered by abundant epiphytes as well by a thin moss layer. The most common emergents are palms and giant bamboo. The understory is dense and formed by woody dicots (mainly Piperaceae and Melastomataceae), Musaceae, Zingiberaceae, Cuclanthacae, small Arecacae and a giant Equisetum, this last commonly along riverbeds. The litter layer is formed by logs, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits, and covers a thin humus layer. The small rivers in the Mindo region are shallow and sluggish, with muddy or sandy bottoms, while larger rivers are deeper and faster, with sandy, gravel, or cobble-bottomed. During July, mid winter, minimum and maximum daily air temperatures average 14 and 22°C, respectively (Percequillo 2015).
threats: One of the known localities of this species has been completely converted to an urban area. Approximately 40% of its habitat may have been destroyed (Tirira et al. 2008). Because this species was not recorded recently, (it was last recorded in 1996) other populations may also have been severely diminished. Survey work is urgently needed to confidently access the status of the species.
population: This species is rare. The last known record was from 1996 and this record was the first in 13 years. It is only known from 17 specimens total: one collected in 1996 (2), one collected in 1980 (3), 12 collected in 1934 (4), one collected in 1929 (Weksler et al. 2006), and two collected in 1913 (4).
range: This species is endemic to Ecuador, where it is known from only three localities. Two of these are in the vicinity of Mindo on the western slope (elevation 1,260 to 1,330 m ), in the Ecuadorean Andes: Esmeraldas, 2 km south of Alto Tambo (2); and Pichincha, Mindo, northwest of Quito (Percequillo 2015). One locality (Concepción, about 50 km northeast of Tena) is in the Amazonian lowlands (elevation 300 to 500 m) (Weksler et al. 2006, Percequillo 2015).
conservationActions: This species is not known from any protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm). There is a general need to protect the habitat of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened since its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 20,000 km², and its total area of occupancy is less than 300 km², but there are no major threats currently facing this species at this time. All relictual populations occur in protected areas. It is known only from three isolated populations, and although these populations are all protected there is an increasing potential threat from the effects of isolation and small populations due to its rarity. Further research is necessary on this species.
habitat: This is an arboreal species; it occurs in high altitude forest (Geise pers. comm).
threats: There are no known major threats at this time (Bonvicino pers. comm.), however the species has a very limited range and is currently occurring only in a few remaining protected areas. The species was likely more widespread and the remaining populations need protection. There is increasing threat of effects of isolation and small populations due to its rarity.
population: This is a very rare species; it is known only from three specimens collected in one year during over eight years of surveys. It is possible that the lack of collection in most years may be due to inappropriate survey methods (Geise pers. comm).
range: This species is restricted to adjacent areas of Rio de Janero, Minas Gerais and Sao Paulo States, Brazil (Bonvicino pers. comm). The species is known from three disjunct locations, and occurrence between these sites is unknown.
conservationActions: The species occurs mainly in national parks.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is a diurnal, fossorial, gregarious vole, living in groups of up to 20 individuals. It inhabits alpine meadows and dense vegetation growing at the edges of rhododendron and coniferous forest. It lives under rocks, bushes or leaf litter on the forest floor. It rarely ventures out in the open and is mostly found in tunnels (Molur et al. 2005, Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: In South Asia, habitat loss and degradation due to small-scale logging, invasive alien species, and to some extent predation by domestic dogs and cats pose as threats to this species (Molur et al. 2005).
population: Little is known about the abundance of this species.
range: This species is present in northern South Asia and southwestern China. In South Asia, this species has been recorded in Bhutan, India (West Bengal and Sikkim) and Nepal (Central, Eastern and Western Nepal) at altitudes above 2,500 m asl (Molur et al. 2005). In China, it is present in southern Xizang (Smith and Xie 2008) at 2,100 to 3,700 m asl.
conservationActions: The species is not protected under any legislation in South Asia. It has been recorded from Lang Tang National Park and Kanchanjunga National Park in Nepal. Surveys, ecological studies, population monitoring and habitat management are recommended for the species in South Asia (Molur et al. 2005).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in alpine meadows and shrubby mountainsides (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to this widespread species.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the provinces of Qinghai, Gansu, Sichuan, Xizang, and Yunnan (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies high mountains within its range (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Qinghaihuniaodao, Wanglang, Wolong, Changshanerhai, Nujiang (CSIS 2008), and Jiuzhaigou National Nature Reserves (Liu et al. 2005), and is likely to occur in Sanjiangyuan Nature Reserve and may be present in other protected areas. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is widespread, its population is not thought to be declining and there are no major threats.
habitat: It occurs in Arctic tundra, but no further details of its ecology are known.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is apparently secure.
range: This species occurs on the Seward Peninsula and south to Kuskokwin Bay, in south-central Alaska, United States.
conservationActions: The range of this species includes a few protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is very widespread, although it is only known from a few occurrences, there are no major threats to the species' habitat and its population is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The species' habitat includes rocky alpine tundra south of the High Arctic tundra zone (Musser and Carleton in Wilson and Reeder 2005). This lemming has been collected at the base of a glacial cirque (Youngman 1967). Little else known about this species.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: The current population status of this species is unknown. It is estimated that there are only a small number of occurrences (NatureServe).
range: This lemming is known from the Ogilvie Mountains, north-central Yukon Territory, Canada (Musser and Carleton, in Wilson and Reeder, 1993, 2005). It probably represents a relict population that became isolated above valley glaciers well over 10,000 years ago (Youngman 1967).
conservationActions: The range of this species includes a few protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required
habitat: This species primarily occurs in highlands and cloud forest (Musser and Carlton 2005). This species is poorly known, but is thought to consume arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and may be important spore dispersers (Mangan and Adler 2000). This species is most common in wt highland forest and elfin forest. (Reid 2009). In addition, this species is most abundant along small streams borders by bamboo, with dense growth of ferns and epiphytes (Timm et al. 1989).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. However, deforestation is a threat to some populations.
population: It is common in wet highland forest.
range: This species occurs in highlands of Costa Rica and westernmost Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: In Costa Rica, it is found in several protected areas, including Amistad and Talamanca.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed wide distribution and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category and the known range is well protected by National Parks.
habitat: This species is found in primary cloud forest. It is terrestrial, nocturnal, and omnivorous (M. Aguilera and B. Rivas pers. comm.). This species has been found in humid evergreen and cloud forests with subcanopies of fern, vines, and abundant moss and epiphytes (Handley 1976).
threats: There are no current threats because the habitat of this species is well protected by national parks.
population: This species is abundant (M. Aguilera pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to the Venezuelan Cordillera de la Costa and Sierra de San Luis in Northern venezuela (Franger 2012). In addition, its distribution across the Cordillera de la Coasta occurs in the Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Distrito Federal. Most records of its occurrence are in the northern slope and only a few in the southern slope with elevation ranges from 1,050 to 2,300 m (Patton et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas, specifically four National Parks.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is a terrestrial species found in primary and secondary Yungas humid forest. It is not present in cultivated areas.
threats: The habitat of this species is being lost through deforestation and conversion of land to agricultural use and is becoming fragmented, which could effect some populations - however, there are no major threats to the species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in the eastern Andes from southeastern Peru to central Bolivia. It occurs between 1,000 to 2,600 m, with most of the records from 1,200 to 1,500 m (Percequillo in prep.).
conservationActions: It is present in one protected area in Peru and at least four in Bolivia. There is a general need to protect the habitat of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because there are no declines in habitat or population due to the fact that it is well protected by national parks.
habitat: This is a poorly known species, that "inhabits the dense, cold, forested areas of the Páramo de Tamá, on the Venezuelan/Colombian border, where specimens have been taken in ground litter and under logs and roots" (from Percequillo et al. 2015). According to prior information on IUCN, it is a cloud forest specialist, nocturnal and omnivorous (Aguilera and Rivas pers. com.), and a "bioindicator of cloud forest conditions". It is terrestrial and solitary.
threats: There are no current threats because the habitat of this species is well protected by national parks.
population: There is no information on populational parameters for this species.
range: According to Percequillo et al. (2015), this species occurs on the forested slopes from northeastern Cordillera Oriental of Colombia in Boyacá department, through the Páramo de Tamá on the Colombian-Venezuelan border, to the northern portion of the Sierra de Mérida, in Trujillo state, Venezuela, and over an elevation range from 1,100 to 4,000 m. See Anderson and Raza (2010), who modeled the species’ climatic niche and potential distribution.
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed wide distribution and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The few specimens of N. auriventer are from “paramo or temperate plants,” “subtropical vegetation” (G. H. H. Tate notes cited in Musser et al. 1998:103), cultivated lands, second growth forest, and primary forest (Rageot and Albuja 1994).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown.
population: In Ecuador this species is uncommon (Tirira in prep.). In Peru it is known from one locality in the Apurímac drainage in the Cordillera Oriental (Patton et al. 2015). There is no information on population parameters for this species.
range: According to Percequillo et al. (2015), Nephelomys auriventer is known from three localities in the upper Río Pastaza drainage at the Cordillera Oriental of Ecuador and from one locality in the Apurímac drainage in the Cordillera Oriental of Peru, at elevations ranging from 1,140 m (Mera) to 1,660 m (Huanhuachayo).
conservationActions: It occurs in Llanganates National Park, Ecuador, possibly two others (D. Tirira pers. comm.). Geographic range study is required for Peru.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is not declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This rodent inhabits primary and secondary cloud forest (Voss et al. 2004, Anderson 1997). It is not present in cultivated areas.
threats: The habitat of this species is being lost through deforestation and conversion of land to agricultural use, therefore it is becoming fragmented.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in southeast Peru through to west central Bolivia (Anderson 1997). This species is found at elevations of 1800 to 3200 m.
conservationActions: It is present in three protected areas in Bolivia. Further research is needed into the ecology of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rat is most common in forested lowland, in areas of dense undergrowth and around fallen logs. This species adapts well to secondary vegetation and plantations (Emmons and Feer 1997), and it is tolerant to habitat disturbance.This species is nocturnal, terrestrial, and solitary. It feeds on seeds, fruit, and insects. It runs about actively on the ground or on fallen logs; if frightened, it may bounce away with a series of high jumps. After the initial activity of the night, it may climb onto a branch at 1 to 2 m and rest motionless, head propped on the incisors against the branch. Breeding occurs year-round; litter size is 2 to 5 young, averaging 3.9 (Fleming 1971).
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species (R. Anderson pers. comm.).
population: It is common throughout its range.
range: This species occurs from Costa Rica, through Panama, to west and north central Colombia, west Ecuador, and north Venezuela (Musser et al. 1998; Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of sea level to 1,525 m.
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is found in lowland evergreen to lower montane cloud forest (Musser and Carleton 2005). Sometimes it is trapped up to 1.5 m above ground, but usually it is found on the ground, either under logs, around the roots of large trees, or among rocks along streams (Reid 1997).
threats: The species is threatened by deforestation, especially in the west of Colombia and Ecuador.
population: This species is uncommon to rare (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs from east Honduras, through east Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama, to west Colombia and west central Ecuador. It has an altitudinal range from sea level to 1,500 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: This species occurs in many protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is usually caught among boulders and along stone walls; it can be in association with the viscacha (Lagidium). The species is found in also in dry shrubland. The Chinchillula is nocturnal and herbivorous; stomachs usually contain leaves, seeds, and a few insects.
threats: There are no major threats to this species. It was historically trapped, around fifty years ago, for its skin; this is not a current threat to the species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in the Altiplano region of southern Peru, western Bolivia, and northern Chile (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 3,500 to 4,800 m.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas in Peru and Bolivia. No further conservation measures are needed.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is terrestrial and is found in sandy areas with mesquite vegetation. It is not found in disturbed areas.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: It is a rare species.
range: This species is known from Sechura Desert, northwest Peru (Musser and Carleton, 2005). It has been recorded from around 50 m.
conservationActions: It is present in the Santuario Historico Bosque de Pomac, a protected area. Further research in general is needed into this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This speciesd occurs from premontane to higher altitude humid habitats and has been reported from mountain fields, mountain scrub, primary and secondary forest (Bonvicino et al. 2002). It is a widespread species inhabiting conserved and altered vegetation but appears to have a restricted habitat use. The species is not limited in distribution by vegetation or elevation in Caparao National Park. It is a semi-fossorial insectivore, and typically a lowland species except for the Bahian range where it is found at higher altitudes (Leite pers. comm.). It probably breeds between Aprile and May.
threats: No major threats for this species are known.
population: This species is considered rare (not easy to capture) and not abundant (not caught in numbers) (Bonvicino et al. 2002). Their population varies according to geographic range but generally uncommon.
range: This species occurs in southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul states), in Argentina (it found in Misiones Province) and the eastern Paraguay (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Caparaó National Park (Bonvicino et al. 2002), Itatiaia National Park, Estação Biológica de Boracéia, Serra dos Órgãos National Park, Augusto Ruschi Biological Reserve, and several other protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is a diurnal and fossorial vole that inhabits temperate forests, and high altitude grassy habitats, especially along watercourses. It prefers high rocky mountains with scattered patches of grassland completely covered in snow part of the year. It lives in colonies, and digs deep burrows, especially in the banks of streams and lakes. It has also been recorded living among rocky crevices (Molur et al. 2005, Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to this species as a whole. In South Asia it is locally threatened by loss of habitat (Molur et al. 2005).
population: There is no information available on the population abundance of this species.
range: This species is present in northern South Asia, and much of western China. In South Asia, it is present in India (Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir) and Nepal (Western and Eastern Nepal) at altitudes above 4,500 m asl (Molur et al. 2005). In China, it is found on the Tibetan Plateau of Xinjiang, Xizang and Qinghai (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: The species has not been recorded from any protected areas. Additional studies are needed into the distribution, abundance and general ecology of this species.

rationale: Although this species is known mainly from two isolated locations (four records) from a large area, it is listed as Least Concern as it is likely to range more widely as there is a lot of available habitat for the species, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. More information is needed to confirm the conservation status and range of this poorly known species.
habitat: The habitat around Tapecua is a mixture of cloud forest vegetation, patches of columnar cacti and leguminous trees in open areas and broadleaf canopy trees and thick brush on hillsides and in ravines. This type of habitat extends for many kilometers to the south and north, and Tapecomys is likely to occur throughout. It is possible that this species is partially arboreal (Anderson and Yates 2000). In Argentina it was collected in similar habitat to the type locality. It is not known if it occurs in modified habitats.
threats: The threats to this poorly known species are not known.
population: It is known only from four specimens (two in Bolivia and two in Argentina). Attempts to collect additional specimens in May 1993 at the type locality were unsuccessful. It is not known whether this is indicative of a general rarity of this species, a low population level at that time, or a poor understanding of the habitat and habits of this species (Anderson and Yates 2000).
range: This species is known only from the type locality: southeast Bolivia, Tarija Department, Tapecua (21°26'S, 63°55'W), at 1,500 m (Anderson and Yates 2000), and from 24°04'S at approximately 63°55'W at 1,200 m in Jujuy Province, Argentina (Ferro et al. 2005).
conservationActions: It has not been recorded from any protected areas. Further research is needed into the range, habitat, ecology and threats to this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern. Although it is restricted to middle and high altitudinal ranges, it occurs mainly in protected areas and has a presumed large population. Through karyotyping studies, its extent of occurrence may well prove to be larger than is presently known. Furthermore, it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in middle to upper elevations (1,000-2,700 m), in disjunct mountain ranges (Musser and Carleton 2005). The species has a similar habitat requirements and ecology to D. dorsalis and D. sublineatus.
threats: The main threat to the species is habitat destruction within its range, it is also affected by fires which are common to the grasslands which it inhabits (L. Geise pers. comm.).
population: This rodent is known from three point localities (Caparao, Itatiaia, and Serra dos Orgãos); it is difficult to find in the field but its population is assumed to be large as it is thought to have a range which extends as far as other species in the same genus (L. Geise pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in east Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo and Rio de Janeiro States, southeastern Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in three protected areas: Caparao, Itatiaia, and Serra dos Orgãos National Parks.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category; also it occurs in several protected areas and is locally common.
habitat: This rodent is found in forest around 500 m elevation, inland from the coastline in the North and along the coast in the South (Geise and Costa pers. comm.).
threats: The major threats are habitat destruction and fragmentation.
population: This species is locally common (Voss 1993).
range: This species occurs along the Atlantic coast (Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo to Santa Catarina States), of southeast Brazil (Eisenberg and Redford 1999, Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered, because its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 500 km², its known from fewer than five locations, and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species occurs in wet grassland, grass and shrubs (Patton and Emmons 2015). It can be found in transition zones between sylvan and pastoral environments of the cerrado, which includes wet and mixed grassland, shrub and low trees. This species has a long tail and moderately long feet, making it presumably adapted to both sylvan and more pastoral habitats (Paresque and Hanson 2015).
threats: This species is threatened by its restricted distribution (Patton and Emmons 2015). Its habitat has been heavily degraded within its small extant of occurrence, and remaining potential habitat is severely fragmented.
population: Populations of this species are poorly known. There have not been any efforts to trap this species recently (E. Vieira pers. comm). It is restricted to two sites in where it occurs (Patton and Emmons 2015). The restricted distribution, combined with the low incidence of capture despite frequent collection efforts over the years, suggests that M. transitorius is a rare species (Paresque and Hanson 2015).
range: This rodent was known only from the type locality: Brazil, Federal District, Parque Nacional de Brasília, ca 20 km NW Brasília, 1,100 m (Eisenberg and Redford 1999, Paresque and Hanson 2015). A second individual was collected in 2003 outside the park, from the Federal District. The species has a relatively narrow distribution area.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Brasilia National Park.

rationale: This species has a wide distribution. There are no data regarding population size and trend, nor about threats, but here it is listed as Least Concern in view of the protected areas within its range.
habitat: This species has been found in dry shrublands/Espinal.
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: The abundance and population size of this species are not known.
range: This species occurs in northeastern Argentina in Entrerios, Corrientes, Chaco and Santa Fe.
conservationActions: It occurs in two national parks in Argentina.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in yungas habitat.
threats: No major threats are known for this species. It is often treated as a pest species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in yungas areas on the eastern slopes of the Andes in western Bolivia, from 600 to 2,700 m. The species has not been recorded from Peru, but occurs close to the Peruvian border in Bolivia and may occur further north. In Argentina it is found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucuman provinces.
conservationActions: No direct conservation measures are currently needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found on the borders of gallery forest, Cerrado (Bonvicino et al. 2003). Fagundes et al. (2000) found the species in transitional areas between Amazonian rain forest and Cerrado. No information available on the reproductive activity (Bonvicino pers. comm.).
threats: Habitat destruction is occurring throughout its range (except in protected areas) (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.).
population: No information is available on this species, although other species in the genus are common (Bonvicino et al. 2003). Although the species has been collected only from three localities, this is due to limited sampling (Bonvicino pers. comm.).
range: This species is known from Goias, Mato Grosso and Tocantins States, central Brazil (Bonvicino et al. 2003).
conservationActions: The species occurs in Araguaia National Park (Bonvincino et al. 2003).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in yungas and Tucumano boliviano forest (a dryer forest in the south of Bolivia). They are often more common in disturbed areas.
threats: This species does not have major threats at this time. The species is often treated as a pest species, but it is a minor threat.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species is found in the yungas of Chuquisaca, Tarija, and Southern Santa Cruz, Bolivia. It has an altitudinal range of 600 to 2,700 m.
conservationActions: No direct conservation measures are currently needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Further research is needed to define the true distribution of the species.
habitat: It prefers dry shrublands and grasslands (Espinal). Populations fluctuate.
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: This is an abundant species.
range: It occurs in west-central Argentina (Cordoba); the limits to the distribution of this species are poorly known (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because it has a restricted extent of occurrence (EOO) and is known from only three localities and two locations. Its known area of occupancy (AOO) in Peru is only 573 km² and potentially only two locations, within the Endangered threshold, however nothing is known about any aspect of trends or fluctuations in area of numbers. Further surveys are needed to determine the range and threats to this species.
habitat: This species occurs in the more humid eastern Cordillera bordering the Altiplano. Specimens from 8 mi SSW Limbani were captured “in barren, broken rock areas and . . . were near fleshy-leaved, pungent Senecio plants or piles of Senecio cuttings” (Pearson 1957:4). The recent specimen from Bolivia (Salazar-Bravo et al. 2011) was trapped at the entrance of a small, shallow cave fronted by the perennial shrub Cajophora horrida (Loasaceae) (Patton 2015). It can be found in areas that have some traditional pastoral use.
threats: The habitat in Peru currently has no protection status. There is an increasing threat of human encroachment (Doyle and Zahler 2003). The high elevation sites are also threatened over the longer term with climate change.
population: This is a very rare species. It has not been collected since 1970, although there have been no recent searches in this area.
range: This species is known from only three adjacent sites in the vicinity of Abra Aricoma and the head of the Limbani Valley, all above 4,500 m in the Cordillera Carabaya (of the Cordillera Oriental) in southern Peru, and one locality at 4,770 m in eastern La Paz department, Bolivia (Patton 2015). The specimen at this latter site was collected in 1987 and cannot reliably be assigned to either Punomys kofordi nor P. lemminus (Salazar-Bravo et al. 2011). It is therefore not included in this assessment. All P. kofordi have been recorded between 4,500 and 4,800 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known from any protected areas. Further research into the habitat, ecology, threats and range is needed for this poorly known species.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable because it has a very restricted area of occupancy and is known from only four locations. Its known area of occupancy in Peru is only 3,000 km²; further surveys are needed to determine the range and threats to this species. This species may also be threatened by wetland drainage and the future effects of climatic change.
habitat: This rodent shelters in rock crevices. It is diurnal and forages on the Senecio and Werneria plants within treeless wet puna habitat. The species is believed to persist in secondary puna habitats. Females have been recorded with only two embryos (Pearson 1951, 1957). This species has been observed feeding on various vegetation, mainly the fleshy leaved tola shrub and low, ground-pine-like herb. It occurs near rocks and surface water (Patton 2015).
threats: This montane species may be threatened by drainage of suitable wet habitat, although this needs to be confirmed. It has a restricted elevational range which is considered to be threatened by climatic changes.
population: It is a rare species, known from only a few specimens. It has not been recorded recently, but this may be because of low sampling effort.
range: This species occurs in the Cordillera Occidental of southern Peru. It is known only from four isolated locations. It has an elevational range of 4,400 to 4,900 m. (Patton 2015).
conservationActions: It is not present in any protected areas. Further studies are needed into the range, habitat, ecology of and threats to this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is poorly known. It is restricted to moist humid cloud forest and co-occurs with the larger Thomasomys hylophilus, which it resembles (Aagaard 1982). It is terrestrial, omnivorous, and nocturnal.
threats: No major threats, although deforestation is affecting the species in some parts of its range.
population: In Ecuador this rodent is uncommon (Tirira in prep.). In Venezuela it is rare (Linares 1998).
range: This species occurs in the north Andes, from central Ecuador (Musser et al. 1998), through central and north Colombia, to west Venezuela (Handley 1976, Linares 1998, Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 1,100 to 3,700 m.
conservationActions: This species occurs in a number of protected areas throughout its range. Further research is needed to determinate its taxonomic status.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Despite forest fragmentation, there are still areas of significant forest cover and point localities are widespread. This species is a poorly known, since it has only been described from a few localities, and there is still very little information on its extent of occurrence, status, threats and ecological requirements.
habitat: This rodent has been recorded in bamboo and secondary forest habitat (Percequillo pers. comm.). Specimens have also been collected from lowland rainforest.
threats: The major threats are deforestation, habitat destruction and wood extraction (Percequillo pers. comm.). As an Atlantic Forest inhabitant, habitat loss is the major threat to the species' conservation.
population: There is no information on population parameters for this species. However, in the last few years (from 2008 to 2015) new records of the species had been published, extending species distribution (see Maestri et al. 2015 for a review).
range: This species is known from type locality, Espirito Santo, southeastern Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005), and it has been collected more recently in a few more localities in Misiones province (Argentina) and others close to Rio de Janeiro and Santa Catarina. The known distribution is from Espirito Santo State, Brazil south along coast and inland to Misiones province in Argentina (Musser and Carleton 1993, Eisenberg and Redford 1999, Stallings et al. 1998, Percequillo and Paglia pers. comm.). Recently, three new individuals were discovered in Chapacó, Santa Catarina, extending the distribution of this species (Maestri et al. 2015). There is a distributional gap on the state of São Paulo, although Vivo et al. (2011) have reported the presence of the species in this state.
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in Parque Rio Doce, Minas Gerais State (Stallings et al. 1998), and in Bananal Ecological Station in Sao Paulo State (Percequillo pers. comm.). It is found in Iguazu National Park (Argentina).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion D2 because it has a very restricted population with only one remaining location, which is potentially threatened by the possibility of exotic species being introduced to the island. Currently the species is not in decline, however, the only other population was extirpated from a neighbouring island due to exotic species introductions. Thus this species is highly susceptible to rapid extinction in future should invasive species be introduced to its remaining distribution area.
habitat: Its ecology and natural history are poorly known. It is terrestrial and solitary.
threats: The history of the decline and likely extinction of the population on San Cristobal Island, with the increase and spread of introduced species has been well documented (Dowler et al. 2000). The introduction of exotic rats (Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus) to Santa Fe Island remains the main threat to the species. History suggests that the species could easily become extinct due to invasive predators and competitor species and this should be a conservation priority.
population: This species includes two populations: Aegialomys galapagoensis galapagoensis occured on San Cristobal Island, but this population is now extinct (Dowler et al. 2000, Tirira 2001); and A. g. bauri occurs in Santa Fe Island, where it is common (Dowler et al. 2000, Tirira 2001).
range: This species is endemic to the Galápagos Islands. It occurs only on Sante Fe (Barrington) Island, and previously occurred on San Cristobal (Chatham) Island (Percequillo 2015). Aegialomys galapagoensis was first described from specimens collected from Santa Cruz Island by Charles Darwin in 1835. Later studies suggested that A. bauri from Santa Fe, and A. galapagoensis were so similar that they may be considered conspecific (Patton and Hafner 1983).
conservationActions: Control exotic species and access to the island, and enact a program to prevent the introduction of common rats.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its wide range and occurrence in several protected areas and the fact that this species does not require a specialized habitat, and it is not currently declining fast enough to warrant a threatened listing.
habitat: This species occurs in small streams bordered by cloud forests (Patton and Emmons 2015). It is semiaquatic and riparian; it feed on aquatic insects. This water mouse has been captured near clear streams in rainforest (Emmons and Feer 1997). This genus has the least specialized habitat of its tribe. It is predated by foxes (C. Delgado pers. comm.).
threats: The major threat is habitat disturbance due to deforestation. This species is also threatened by its restricted occurrence (Patton and Emmons 2015).
population: This species is rare in areas that are not moist (Patton and Emmons 2015).
range: This species occurs in the Andes of west Colombia and north Ecuador (Musser and Carleton 2005; Patton and Emmons 2015). In Colombia it occurs in the Cordilleras Central and Occidental (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.). It has an altitudinal range of 1,800 to 3,750 m.
conservationActions: It occurs in three protected areas, two in Ecuador (D. Tirira pers. comm.), and one in Colombia, Paramillo National Park (C. Delgado pers. comm.). It may be present in other protected areas throughout its range (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion D2 because of its restricted number of populations (only five known) and a population decline (of unknown scale). The species is a habitat specialist (dependent on clear streams), is known from only from five widely separated localities in Venezuela and Guyana, and is estimated to be declining rapidly due to over-exploitation, shrinkage in distribution, and habitat destruction and degradation.
habitat: Specimens of this species have been trapped along small streams bordered by evergreen lowland rainforest, semi deciduous forest, or montane vegetation. This species is known to feed on insect and small, aquatic animals (Voss 2015). This rodent is semiaquatic.
threats: There is strong intensive habitat destruction and aquatic contamination due to deforestation, mines and agriculture (J. Ochoa pers. comm.) occurring within the range of the species which is inferred to be causing a population decline.
population: This species is uncommon and patchily distributed. It is known only from five locations within its broad distribution.
range: This species is known from only five localities in Venezuela and Guyana. It is known to occur at elevations ranging from near sea level to 1,400 m (Voss 2015).
conservationActions: It is found in Canaima National Park in Venezuela, and it may be present in Mochima National Park (J. Ochoa pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern since it occurs in an area of extensive, suitable habitat which appears not to be under threat, it has a presumed large population, and it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The Balta specimen was trapped in a small stream, and the Pakitza specimen was trapped at least 200 m from water. The surrounding habitat of both specimens was primary evergreen lowland forest (Voss 2015). The species feeds on aquatic insects and perhaps crabs. It is not present in modified areas.
threats: The area and habitat where this species has been recorded from are undisturbed, and there appear to be no immediate threats to this species.
population: It is rare or difficult to capture (Emmons and Feer 1997). No recent population data are available. The species is only known from specimens at two localities and does not seem to be easily captured.
range: This species is known from only two localities in the Amazonian lowlands of southeastern Peru. Madre de Dios, Pakitza (Pacheco and Vivar 1996) and Ucayali, Balta (Musser and Gardner 1974, Voss 2015). It has been recorded at elevations of 200 to 400 m (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
conservationActions: It is present in the Manu National Park and Alto Purus Reserve. General research into the habitat, ecology and distribution of this species is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 19,000 km², it is known from only two localities, and there is a continuing decline in its quality of habitat.
habitat: The two known specimens were captured in a stream bordered by semi-deciduous forest (Voss 2015). It is a semiaquatic species that feeds on aquatic invertebrates.
threats: There is strong pressure on this species from habitat destruction including deforestation, dams, and agriculture (J. Ochoa pers. comm).
population: This species is rare (J. Ochoa pers. comm). No recent population data are available. Only two specimens have been recorded (Voss 2015).
range: This species is known originally from the type locality of Paso Hondo, Rio Potosí, 14 km southeast Pregonero, Táchira, western Venezuela at 1,050 m elevation (Voss 2015). There is a new record of the species near La Azulita (08°43'N, 71°27'W, 1,200 m) (J. Ochoa and P. Soriano pers. comm).
conservationActions: This species is yet to be found in any protected areas (J. Ochoa pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It lives in open areas and is commonly found on boulder-strewn slopes with sparse vegetation, rock slides, and stone walls, as well as in Ctenomys burrows and viscacha colonies. It is also found in boggy areas. It is diurnal and has a varied diet. In Peru females have three to four embryos. In captivity females will produce three litters a year with three to five young per litter (Pearson 1951, Pine et al. 1979, Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in the Altiplano from south Peru (Arequipa Department) to extreme northeast Chile and west central Bolivia (3,450 to 4,770 m) (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is present in many protected areas. No direct conservation measures are currently needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its large distribution and occurrence in protected areas.
habitat: Abrothrix illutea is mainly associated with the "Bosque Montano", the upper elevational belt of the Yungas forest, where "aliso" (Alnus acuminata) and "pino del cerro" (Podocarpus parlatorei) are the dominant tree species. However, a few records of A. illutea are known from the "Selva Montana" between 700 and 1000 m. At its upper elevational limit they inhabit tall grass and brushy habitats along streams (Teta et al. 2011).
threats: The main threats to the species are wood extraction, intentional fires, and cattle activities.
population: There is no information available on the population and/or abundance of this species.
range: This species occurs in northwestern Argentina, in Tucumán and Catamarca Provinces between 700 and 2,500 m (Teta et al. 2011).
conservationActions: The range of the species is included in at least one national park and one reserve.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is basically nocturnal but also exhibits some diurnal activity (Feijoo et al. 2010). It occurs in forests and shrublands in southern Patagonia; it has been found in coastal localities with well-developed soils and dense vegetation cover of Junielia tridens, although very close to the Fuegian forest (Feijoo et al. 2010). A. lanosus basically occurs in open-habitats, mainly shrublands or shrubland-grassland steppes, associated with, or very close, to forest, but not actually inside it (Feijoo et al. 2010).
threats: There are no major threats for this species.
population: This is not a commom species.
range: This species occurs south through Última Esperanza and Magallanes, in southern Chile, to Tierra del Fuego, Argentina, as far north as northwestern Santa Cruz Province, Argentina (Galliari and Pardiñas 1999, Feijoo et al. 2010, Sandoval 2010).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas in Argentina and Chile.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because its known extent of occurrence is not much greater than 20,000 km² (EOO is around 24,800 km²), and populations are in decline because of loss of habitat due to increasing timber exploitation. The population is not known to be severely fragmented, and number of locations is not known, therefore currently it does not qualify for a threatened category. However, it almost qualifies as threatened under criterion B1.
habitat: This mouse is known from coastal rainforest (Valdivian forest) up to around 800 m. It is not found on any inshore islands (B. Patterson pers. comm). The species is found in dense Nothofagus forests.
threats: Threats include deforestation of the coastal forest for timber activities.
population: There is information on a decrease in collected specimens (Murua et al. 2003). There is evidence of decreasing of population in some localities (G. D'elia pers. comm).
range: This species occurs in the southern half of Chiloé Island and adjoining continental areas in southern Chile (D'Elía et al. 2015). It has been noted at Parque Nacional Nahuel Huapí in Argentina but never confirmed (Cabrera 1961, Galliari et al. 1996).
conservationActions: There are several protected areas within the range of the species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in shrub and herbaceous steppe habitats as well as in humid plains and Northofagus forests (Pearson 1995). Inhabits steppe habitat in northern Patagonia (Pearson and Smith 1999).
threats: No major threats for this species.
population: It is an abundant species in many places including forests and shrubs.
range: This species occurs in northern to central Chile, and borders along westernmost Argentina, to Patagonian region of S Chile and Argentina, including Tierra del Fuego (Musser and Carleton 2005). Distribution now includes A. hershkovitzi.
conservationActions: It is included in several protected areas along Chile and Argentina coastal areas and Patagonia.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is present in open grassland, rocky areas, shrub land, cultivated areas and rural houses.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is a very common species. It can have population fluctuations, with many animals found during the harvest season.
range: This species occurs in the Altiplano of central Peru (Arana-Cardó and Ascorra 1994) to western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina (Jayat et al. 2013). Recently it has been found in the region of Arica and Parinacota, Chile (Faúndez et al. 2015). It has an elevational range of about 2,200 to 5,000 m (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is present in many protected areas, at least 13 in Peru.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its area of occupancy is less than 500 km², all individuals are in fewer than five locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat from deforestation due to timber extraction and agriculture.
habitat: This species is found in cloud forests of conifers and oaks, associated with the volcanic peaks in western Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt and typically occupies wet environments associated with rocky slopes, ravines and gullies (Ceballos 2014, Wilson et al. 2017). It may be restricted to these fragmented and isolated regions due to its likely strong association with the formation of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018). Most known specimens have been caught on the ground, frequently under rocks with mosses (Ceballos 2014). León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018 observed some individuals feeding upon lichens and oak seeds. It appears to be a habitat specialist, but he details of its diet, behavior and ecology are unknown (Ceballos 2014). León-Tapia et al. 2018 describes the anatomy of the stomach and made an analysis of taxonomic relation between Nelsonia and Neotomodon (Alvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.)
threats: This species is currently threatened by habitat loss from deforestation due to timber extraction and agriculture throughout its restricted range (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm). Volcanic eruptions, climate change, pollution, the introduction of exotic species, forest fires, pests and diseases also pose potential threats to this species (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm., Arriola-Padilla et al. 2014, Aguado-Bautista et al. 2015, León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018).
population: The first specimens of this species were trapped in 1903 at the Tancítaro and Patambán mountains in the western region of the state of Michoacán (Merriam 1903). Specimens of this species have been described as rare, uncommon, and strongly associated with highland microhabitats in Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018). Ecological niche modeling efforts by León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018 found a restricted and isolated pattern of habitat suitability for this species. Taken with the geologic history of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, it is likely that there is some degree of genetic isolation or historical reduction of gene flow between areas with low or lack of environmental connectivity (León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018). There is a poor amount of population information available for this species and it is quite rare (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm., Ceballos 2014).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and inhabits several isolated localities in the high-elevation regions of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, from the eastern state of México to Colima (Ceballos 2014). It has been recorded in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Michoacán and México (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas, including El Nevado de Colima National Park, Pico de Tancítaro Flora and Fauna Protection Area and Sierra Chincua Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve (D. Tirira pers. comm., León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018). The preferred habitats of this rat are similar to those used by monarch butterflies in winter (Glendinning 1992) and efforts to preserve the butterfly's sanctuaries in Michoacán could indirectly benefit this species (Ceballos 2014). However, León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018 observed areas near El Nevado de Colima disturbed by livestock, farming, plums, hawthorn and corn orchards. They suggest microhabitat conservation across the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt to be the most appropriate conservation measure to take for this species as it is likely that these disturbances could affect the presence of the populations of N. goldmani because it needs a habitat with particular environmental characteristics and to be left undisturbed (León-Tapia and Cervantes 2018). This species in the Official Mexican Standard and it is regarded as of Special Protection (SEMARNAT 2010).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it does not currently meet the thresholds for a threatened category. More information is needed on its area of occupancy, as it could potentially be listed in a threatened category or as Near Threatened in the near future because its distribution is severely fragmented, and the extent and quality of its habitat are probably declining, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B2ab(iii).
habitat: This species is associated with relatively wet environments and often extremely cold and freezing habitats found in forests of conifers (Pinus and Abies), poplar (Populus), and oak (Quercus) in the Sierra Madre Occidental at elevations above 2,000 m (Wilson et al. 2017) Although its distribution is relatively large, it is restricted to rugged montane slopes and ravines with climax vegetation and is considered a high-elevation forest specialist (Ceballos 2014, Wilson et al. 2017). The natural history and ecology of this species are poorly known.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to timber extraction throughout its range.
population: There is currently no information the population estimates for this species, although is reported to be uncommon and locally scarce (Baker and Greer 1962, Matson and Baker 1986, Glendinning 1992).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and is known from the Sierra Madre Occidental from southern Durango to northern Jalisco and Aguascalientes (Musser and Carleton 2005, Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: Nelsonia neotomodon is protected and included in the category of Special Protection and endemic species (SEMARNAT 2010). It occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is locally common, occurs in protected areas, and is not known to be declining at a rate that would merit a threatened status. However, habitat fragmentation is occurring within their home range and could pose a threat to the species in the future.
habitat: Specimens have been captured in seasonally flooded semi-deciduous forests (Percequillo et al. 2008) and in periodically flooded grasslands along streams in the Cerrado (Bonvicino 2003). Pregnant females were captured in both dry and rainy seasons, suggesting that breeding takes place throughout the year; embryo counts range from two to four (Percequillo 2015).
threats: The major threats to this species are agriculture expansion, cattle and the growing soybean agroindustry.
population: This species is locally common (Bonvicino pers. comm).
range: This species is known from only two localities in Brazil: Fazenda Sertão do Formoso (formerly known as Fazenda Jucurutu) at 775 m in the municipality of Jaborandi, Bahia, Brazil and Parque Nacional Grande Sertão Veredas, Minas Gerais, Brazil (Percequillo 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Parque Nacional Grande Sertão Veredas, Minas Gerais, Brazil (Percequillo 2015) .

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is tolerant to habitat modification including agricultural areas (Langguth and Bonvicino 2002). A sample—previously attributed to C. andersoni now a synonym—was collected in a transitional mosaic between dense and high savanna, with open forest. Ground cover was a mixture of dead leaves and 30-40% of grass cover.
threats: Threats to some populations include agricultural expansion, cattle, and soybeans.
population: This species is very common (Langguth and Bonvicino 2002).
range: This species occurs in Cerrado of Matto Grosso do Sul to Goiás and west Minas Gerais, central Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay (Langguth and Bonvicino 2002).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas in its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is confined to gallery forest (including disturbed gallery forest) (Langguth and Bonvicino 2002). Other members of this group are tolerant of habitat modification.
threats: The major threat to some populations is agricultural expansion.
population: This species is uncommon (Langguth and Bonvicino 2002).
range: This species is known only from the type locality, south Brazil (Matto Grosso do Sul State, Municipality Maracaju, Fazenda da Mata) (Musser and Carleton 2005). Langguth and Bonvicino (2002) believe that this rodent also occurs in Bolivia and eastern Paraguay.
conservationActions: This species potentially occurs in several protected areas in its range in Paraguay and Brazil, but records are not known from those areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in marsh environments, favouring edges of wetlands, flood grasslands, and places with reed and straw vegetation, usually without trees (Gonzales and Massoia 2002, Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002). The species has been found in gallery forest in Buenos Aires province, Argentina (Bianchini and Delupi 1994). It feeds on insects and plants and is itself preyed upon by barn owls.
threats: Part of its range is under severe threat by rice plantations in Brazil and Uruguay which destroy its wetland habitat, however, the species is abundant to the north and south of this area. Another important threat is urbanization in northern habitat range.
population: It is an abundant species in Uruguay but less common in Argentina. The status of Brazilian populations has not been assessed (Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002), but it is locally abundant. The species is very rare in some localities in Argentina whilst in others it is common (Teta et al. 2007); it accounts for around 10% of the small mammal prey of the barn owl in the Delta del Paraná, whereas on the Islas de Ibicuy, Entre Rios Province, it was the third most common prey of the barn owl, approximately 20% of 2,367 individuals taken.
range: This species occurs along the Atlantic Coast of South America, from northeast Buenos Aires and south Entre Rios Provinces, Argentina, through Uruguay to Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil (Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002).
conservationActions: In Argentina D. kempi is protected at the Reserva Provincial Punta Lara and the Reserva Natural Estricta Otamendi in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina (Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002). In Uruguay, populations of D. k. langguthi are protected at Parque Lecocq in the Department of Montevideo and at Area Protegida Laguna de Castillos in the Department of Rocha (Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002). The status of Brazilian populations has not been assessed (Gonzalez and Pardinas 2002).

rationale: Florida Mouse is listed as Near Threatened because, while its area of occupancy (AOO) meets the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion B2, and there is continuing decline in the area and quality suitable habitat, it is not severely fragmented and the number of locations is likely more than 10. Therefore the species almost qualifies as Vulnerable under B2. Much of its habitat has been lost due to development, agriculture, and fire suppression and declines in gopher tortoise populations also affect habitat quality for this species. Therefore, this species may qualify for a Vulnerable listing under the B2 criterion in the future if the population becomes severely fragmented.
habitat: The major habitats for this species include scrub and sandhill associations, with scrub being the primary habitat. Populations tend to be larger in sand pine scrub than they are in longleaf pine-turkey oak habitats (Layne 1978), apparently due to the greater acorn production in the former (Layne 1992). Habitats that support good populations of the Florida scrub jay indicate high quality Podomys habitat (Layne 1992). Home ranges for this species are about one acre or less on average (Layne 1992). This species is omnivorous, diet includes seeds, nuts, fungi, insects, and other invertebrates; acorns are an important food source. Predation by various snakes, owls, and Carnivora probably is the major mortality factor (Layne 1992). This mouse probably breeds throughout the year, but mainly in fall and early winter (Layne 1992). Females probably seldom produce more than two litters each breeding season (Layne 1992). In the wild, only a small percentage of the population lives longer than one year, though longevity of several years is not uncommon in captives. When inactive, it occupies underground burrows, often made within those of gopher tortoises. In south-central Florida, burrows were exclusively within gopher tortoise burrows (both active and inactive) (Layne and Jackson 1994). Young are born in nests in underground burrows.
threats: Podomys floridanus depends on fire-maintained, xeric uplands occurring on deep, well-drained soils, especially scrub and sandhill (FWC 2013). Because of this habitat specificity, the major threat to the species is loss and degradation of habitat caused by conversion to other uses (e.g., development and agricultural use) and insufficient management (e.g., fire suppression) (FWC 2013). In addition to habitat loss and degradation, communities are also becoming increasingly fragmented and isolated (FWC 2013).  Dependence of the species on gopher tortoise burrows as sites for their own burrows (Jones and Layne 1993) leaves the species vulnerable to the decline of gopher tortoises in some habitats (FWC 2013). Red imported fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) may be a predatory threat to the Florida mouse (FWC 2013). Free-ranging domestic cats (Felis catus) may be another introduced predator (Loss et al. 2013).Impacts from climate change may produce further challenges for the conservation of the Florida mouse. At this time, potential impacts from climate change are not well understood; therefore, identification of appropriate management strategies is not readily possible (FWC 2013). The vulnerability of Florida mouse populations to climate change will depend on the degree to which the Florida mouse is likely to experience harm from stressors produced by changes in large-scale climatic drivers (FWC 2013). Vulnerability will be a result of multiple variables including the intensity and duration of the climate changes, the innate sensitivities of the Florida mouse to those changes, and, ultimately, the capacity of the Florida mouse to adapt to the changes that occur (FWC 2013).
population: The population size is unknown, but it is presumed that there are more than 10,000 mature individuals (FWC 2011). Population size and the number of subpopulations have both declined; populations have been extirpated or greatly reduced in much of its former range (Layne 1978). This species is known from several dozen collection sites (Jones and Layne 1993), but populations currently are not extant at all of these locations. Undoubtedly the species is continuing to decline due to habitat loss (Layne 1992). The species has disappeared from the Miami area and the Pinellas peninsula.
range: The species' occurs only in a narrow range of dry, natural communities in the northern 2/3 of peninsular Florida (FWC 2013). Historically, an isolated Florida mouse population occurred near Carrabelle in Franklin County (Layne 1992, Jones and Layne 1993). Although the Florida mouse probably no longer occurs on the coast of Pinellas County, a single specimen was captured in 1984 near Clearwater (Layne 1992).
conservationActions: While there have been a limited number of conservation actions taken specifically for the Florida mouse, the species has also benefited greatly from conservation actions taken for the benefit of the Gopher Tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) (FWC 2013). The Florida Mouse is a commensal of the Gopher Tortoise, and management efforts to maintain viable tortoise populations have benefited the Florida Mouse. Conservation actions taken for Threatened and Endangered species such as the Florida Scrub-jay (Aphelocoma coerulescens) and Red-cockaded Woodpecker (Picoides borealis) have also contributed to the conservation of the Florida Mouse (FWC 2013). Management to increase the quality of suitable habitats has been the recommended focus for conservation of viable Florida Mouse populations (FWC 2013). On many sites occupied by Florida mice, the quality of the habitat has become degraded by a lack of effective management, as well as by disturbance and fragmentation (FWC 2013). To help address management problems, the Florida mouse has been identified as a focal species in FWC’s Conservation, Prioritization and Recovery program (WCPR). Through the WCPR, management strategies designed to improve habitat quality for the Florida mouse are provided to managers of conservation lands with potentially suitable habitat (FWC 2013).
