This species occurs in many protected areas, including Archbold Biological Station, Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, Katharine Ordway Preserve, Lyonia Preserve, Ocala National Forest, Highlands Hammock State Park, Jonathan Dickinson State Park, San Felasco Hammock State Park, Tiger Creek Preserve, Withlacoochee State Forest, and Camp Blanding Training Site (FWC 2013). This species was recently removed from Florida's Endangered and Threatened Species List since its conservation status remains the same or has improved (FWC 2016).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, although the species is not abundant and is patchy within its wide distribution, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This rodent occurs in open grasslands areas, in campo cerrado transition zones (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.). Its distribution is patchy.
threats: Some populations are threatened by habitat destruction and fragmentation (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.).
population: The species is very difficult to capture in surveys, although it is commonly found in owl pellets (Bonvicino and Marinho-Filho pers. comm.). The species is rare relative to other species in the genus (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.).
range: This species is confined to the cerrado of central Brazil (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
conservationActions: This species occurs in three National Parks within its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in a wide range of habitat, including open grasslands, cerrado, and wet grasslands (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.).
threats: Although habitat destruction is occurring, it is not considered a major threat to this species (Marinho-Filho pers. comm.).
population: The species is common (Bonvicino pers. comm.).
range: This species is confined to the cerrado of central Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in at least three national parks.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view it has a wide distribution and does not qualify for any threat categories at present. However, the habitat that this species is restricted to in Peru is considerably declining and the species may be considered to be threatened in the future.
habitat: This species is associated with streams and wetlands with dense cover, in the Altiplano grasslands and shrubby steppe. It is not present in disturbed or cultivated areas. Embryo counts from Peruvian specimens ranged from one to two (Pearson 1951, Bárquez 1983, Eisenberg and Redford 1999). It is a herbivorous species. It is very associated to particular wetland areas.
threats: It is threatened in parts of its range through modification of the species' wetland habitat, for example through extraction of water for irrigation purposes.
population: It is an uncommon species.
range: This montane species ranges from central Peru (Junín Department), south through northernmost Chile and west Bolivia, to northwest Argentina (Sanborn 1947, Bárquez 1983, Anderson 1997, Pardiñas and Ortiz 2001, Musser and Carleton 2005). It is mostly found between 2,500 to 4,600 m.
conservationActions: It is known from several protected areas in Peru and two in Bolivia. Further general research into this species is needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The species is fossorial and is found in open steppe habitat with loose soil not sand. It has been recoded from cultivated fields though it can live in shallow mountainside soils, where it burrows, feeding on the underground parts of plants. It does not hibernate but may become inactive in the summer. The reproductive period is short. Females produces three embryos.
threats: There are no major threats to this species as a whole. In southern Turkmenistan, the habitat is being degraded in some areas by agriculture. In South Asia it is threatened by natural calamities such as drought, wildfires, avalanches and landslides and interspecific competitors (Molur et al. 2005).
population: The species is common in suitable habitats. It is uncommon in Turkmenistan.
range: This widespread species ranges from eastern Iran, through Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, east to Pakistan (Habibi 2003, Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005). It ranges from 300-400 m to 2400 m.
conservationActions: This species is present in many protected areas. No direct conservation measures as a whole are currently needed for this species.

rationale: This is a common species with no known major threats. It is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: It is mostly abundant in mountain grasslands and steppes from 700 to 2500 m. Also found in sandy semi-deserts in piedmonts. Ecology is similar to that of Ellobius talpinus. The species is colonial and subterranean; it appears on the ground only when it moves soil from the burrows. It feeds mostly on underground parts of plants (Gromov and Erbaeva 1995).
threats: No major threats are known to this species (GMA Turkey 2005).
population: In Turkey the density of this species is 240 individuals/ha. It is common in Iran and Armenia.
range: It occurs from south Transcaucasia through east Turkey and northwest Iran.
conservationActions: There are no records in protected areas in Turkey. It is found in protected areas in Armenia (GMA Turkey 2005).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species inhabits dry deciduous and scrub forest of caatinga and cerrado vegetation, it is an able climber and constructs nests in trees. It feeds on grains and sometimes insects. In captivity females mature at 83 days and give birth on average every forty days with a mean litter size of 3.8 (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
threats: Habitat destruction occurs within the range, though it is currently not a major threat to this species.
population: This species is locally abundant.
range: This species occurs in southeast Brazil, from Ceará to Rio Grande do Sul (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: The Chiapan Climbing Rat (Tylomys bullaris) is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because it is only known from 10 specimens, with the last one being over 40 years ago. The species occurs in just one location and it is likely to be experiencing a severe population decline caused by the complete conversion of native habitat due to urbanization and agriculture and introduced, invasive species. It is likely that there are now fewer than 50 mature individuals in the population.
habitat: Very little is known about the natural history of this species (Ceballos 2014). Other species in the genus Tylomys are arboreal or terrestrial, nocturnal and solitary (Emmons and Feer 1997). They have been found in hollow trees, lianas and rocks in well preserved forest (Ceballos 2014) and will feed on fruit, sprouts and bark (Álvarez del Toro 1977). It is associated with undisturbed, tropical deciduous forest, around the area of Tuxtla Gutierrez (Ceballos 2014).
threats: The area where this species is found has been modified by urbanization and conversion to agricultural land. It is likely that the native vegetation will disappear completely from this area and it is unlikely it will be able to be restored (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm). This species is threatened by introduced rats, cats and dogs (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm).
population: Fewer than 10 specimens of this species are known, with the last being collected more than 40 years ago, and all were collected from the type locality.
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and is only known from the type locality in Tuxtla Gutierrez, Chiapas, Mexico (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This rodent is considered threatened by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). It is an AZE trigger species for the Tuxtla Gutiérrez site (AZE 2018). It could potentially occur in one state park and one national park, Cañón del Sumidero (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is apparently arboreal in wet forest (M. Gómez-Laverde and R.P. Anderson pers. comm.). Like other climbing rats, this species inhabits cloud forest and tropical evergreen forest, in dense forest with tall trees (up to 30 m) and a dense shrub layer, where the crowns harbor great masses of vines and creepers with much parasitic and epiphytic growth. Most records state specimens were taken either on the ground, in shrubs, or in trees, in areas often associated with rock outcrops or cliffs. Climbing rats move very quickly through the branches, stems, and vines (Álvarez-Castañeda 2015).
threats: Major threats are deforestation and habitat loss; they are also hunted for food by local communities and sold locally, but this is not an important threat (M. Gómez-Laverde and D. Tirira pers. comm.).
population: It is apparently uncommon (Emmons and Feer 1997). It is not commonly collected as it is arboreal and difficult to capture (M. Gómez-Laverde and R.P. Anderson pers. comm.).
range: This species is known from few available specimens from the tropical forest on the lower slopes of the Andean cordilleras of Colombia and Ecuador south along through the Pacific lowlands to northwestern Ecuador. It occurs over an elevational range of 200 to 1,300 m (Álvarez-Castañeda 2015).
conservationActions: It probably occurs in several parks throughout the range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in mature evergreen and semideciduous forest, and dense, viney second growth, usually near rocks, caves, or cliffs (Reid 1997). It is nocturnal and semiarboreal. Though its movements are usually slow and deliberate, this large rat can travel with great speed and agility on vines and branches. Little is known of its diet; the stomach of an animal from Veracruz contained vegetation resembling lichen or bark (Hall and Dalquest 1963 in Reid 1997). Its gestation is about 40 days, and litter size averages 2.5 young (Herlm 1975 in Reid 1997).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species.
population: This rat is uncommon (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs from central Guerrero and central Veracruz, Mexico, south to southern Nicaragua, excluding the northern Peninsula (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from lowlands to 2,300 m.
conservationActions: Occurs in protected areas throughout its range. More research is needed on its distribution.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species favors mid-elevation evergreen forest on the Caribbean Slope, but it is also found in humid lowland forest, and in highland oak forest (Reid 1997). Sometimes considered house pest. This species requires some degree of canopy connectivity.
threats: There are no known major threats to this species.
population: It can be extremely abundant.
range: This species occurs in Costa Rica and west Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from lowlands to 2,700 m (Reid and Langtimm 1993 in Reid 1997).
conservationActions: Large populations of this species occur within protected areas.

rationale: This rodent is species assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because it has not been collected in at least 40 years. The species is only known from one location (the type locality), with a small extent of occurrence (EOO is estimated to be no more than 93 km²), and if it is still extant it is likely to be experiencing a severe population decline from complete conversion of native habitat due to urbanization and agriculture.
habitat: There are no accurate data available on the natural history of T. tumbalensis (Ceballos 2014). The species of this genus are nocturnal, arboreal and terrestrial (Ceballos 2014). They are solitary and frequently found between rocks, fallen logs and in caves and they depend on undisturbed and dense forests (Ceballos 2014). The area where the species is known from was originally tropical forest and none of the original forest currently exists (A. Cuaron pers. comm. 2018). Its diet possibly consisted of green plants (Emmons and Freer 1997).
threats: The area where the type locality for this species is located has now been completely deforested with no original vegetation left due to land use change to agriculture (A. Cuaron pers. comm. 2018).
population: This species is known from only one specimen collected from the type locality (Ceballos 2014). Searches for the species in 2015 and 2017 resulted in no new specimens; it has not been collected in at least 40 years (S. Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm. 2018).
range: This species is known only from the type locality in Tumbalá, Central Highlands of Chiapas, Mexico (Hall 1981).
conservationActions: This species is protected by the Mexican government (NOM-059_ECOL_2001) and is considered rare (SEMARNAT 2010). It does not occur in any protected areas, but the area where it is found is designated as an AZE (Alliance for Zero Extinction) site. This species is considered a good candidate for captive breeding efforts and there is a strong motive to bring it into captivity if any individuals are captured (S. Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: This mouse is listed as Near Threatened because, although it is considered common within its small range, the extent and quality of its habitat declining and its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 27,745 km²  which is close to the threshold for Vulnerable under B1. Continuing declines in its habitat and EOO are occurring which could list this species as Vulnerable under criterion B1 in the future.
habitat: This species inhabits rocky places at about 400 m elevation in a range of hills north of Bahía Blanca, in Buenos Aires department. There are no published data on ecology or behaviour of this species (Steppan and Ramirez 2015).
threats: The habitat of this species is threatened by overgrazing for horses.
population: It is an abundant species found in a wide variety of habitats, but restricted mainly to rocky outcrops (Robles et al. 2014).
range: This species is restricted to the Sierra de la Ventana in Buenos Aires province, eastern Argentina (Steppan and Ramirez 2015). The altitudinal range is from 500 m to 2,200 m, the maximum height of the Sierra de la Ventana.
conservationActions: The species is included in one protected area (Parque Provincial Ernesto Tornquist).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is present in primary and secondary Puna and dry forest and scrubland. It can be found in cultivated areas and pastureland. It is often found amongst rocks.
threats: There are no major threats to this species. The dry forest habitat of this species is susceptible to anthropogenic changes.
population: It is a common species in Bolivia, however in Argentina it is considered rare.
range: This species occurs on the upper slopes of eastern Andes, from south central Bolivia to northernmost Argentina (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an elevational range of about 2,100 to 4,500 m. In Argentina it is only found in Jujuy and Salta.
conservationActions: It is present in the Cuesta de Sama and Tariquia National Reserves in Bolivia. Further studies are needed into this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species occurs in habitats associated with Chilean matorral - semiarid and Mediterranean scrubland (Steppan 1998).
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: It is considered abundant.
range: This species occurs along coastal west-central Chile (Musser and Carleton 2005), from sea level to 2,000 m asl (Steppan 1998).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas.

rationale: This listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, has a tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This is a mouse of the high Andean bunchgrass and rocky areas, though it can occur at lower elevations in a few localities. It is strictly crepuscular. It is present in primary, secondary and cultivated areas and particularly in foggy grasslands.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: It is a common species. In Peru it was found at a density of 1.47 per hectare (Pearson and Ralph, 1978).
range: This species occurs in the upper Andean slopes, from south central Peru (Cuzco Department), to west Bolivia. This species is found from 1,700 to 4,900 m in Bolivia (Musser and Carleton 2005). The species has not been recorded in Chile. Jayat et al. (2016) proposed that specimens from Argentina are no longer P. osilae but P. nogalaris, recognizing it as a valid species.
conservationActions: It is present in four protected areas in Peru, many in Bolivia and several in Chile.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in a wide variety of habitats, including wetlands, Polylepis forest, altiplano, grasslands, shrublands, rocky areas and cultivated areas.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in the west central Peru, in and along the Andes to Santa Cruz Province, south Argentina, and adjacent Magallanes Province, south Chile; latitudinal (15-51°S) and altitudinal ranges (sea level-5,600 m) exceptional as currently defined (Kramer et al. 1999, Musser and Carleton 2005). In Peru and Bolivia it ranges between 2,000 and 4,500 m.
conservationActions: It is present in many protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be less than 500 km², all individuals are in fewer than five locations, and there is continuing decline in its extent of occurrence (EOO), AOO and the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species inhabits the brushy zone on the western Andean slopes (Steppan and Ramirez 2015). It is present in dry shrublands and rocky areas, but it is not present in open areas. It can be found at the edges of cultivated areas, but not in the areas themselves. No other data on reproduction, behaviour, or ecology has been published (Steppan and Ramirez 2015).
threats: The species is threatened by clearance of shrub habitat for pastoral grazing. It has a narrow distribution and is becoming increasingly fragmented in patches of remaining habitat. Habitat loss may have reduced population sizes for this species (Steppan and Ramirez 2015).
population: It is a rare species.
range: This species is restricted to the upper slopes of the western Andes in Ancash department, Peru. The four known localities range in elevation from 2,590 to 3,800 m (Steppan and Ramirez 2015).
conservationActions: It is present in the Huascaran National Park. Further research into this species is needed.

rationale: This species has a wide distribution. There are no data regarding population size and trend, neither about threats, but here it is listed as Least Concern in view of the protected areas within its range.
habitat: It inhabits rocky parts of mountain steppe habitats, associated with juniper and alpine meadows. This species feeds on green parts of plants, storing hay as a winter food source.
threats: There are no data available about threats to this species.
population: No data are available about population trend and status at present.
range: The species occurs in the Altai Mountains and Tuva region, north Khubsugul Lake Valley, south Bailkal Lake Valley, and nearby regions in northwest Mongolia.In Mongolia it is present in north-western Mongol Altai Mountain Range, northern Great Lakes Depression, Hövsgöl Mountain Range, and northern Hangai Mountain Range (Litvinov and Bazardorj 1992).
conservationActions: In Russia and Mongolia (approximately 40% of the species’ range) occurs within protected areas. Conservation measures required. Further research is recommended.

rationale: Although there is little information on distribution, population size and trends, or potential threats, this species has a fairly large range and presumably a large population. It also occurs in protected habitats, therefore it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species inhabits mountain-steppe habitats, associated with juniper, honey suckle, currant, cornel, gooseberry, dog-rose, willow and wormwood bushes. It lives between the roots of bushes. It is herbivorous. A female captured in June was lactating and had six placental scars.
threats: There are no data regarding threats to this species.
population: No population data are available at present.
range: It occurs at low to middle altitudes throughout the Gobi and Mongol Altai of S Mongolia and the Tuva region of Russia. One record from E Tian Shan, Xinjiang. Occurs at elevations of 900 to 2,500 m.In Mongolia it occurs in Mongol Altai Mountain Range, Trans Altai Govi Desert, Govi Altai Mountain Range and parts of Dzungarian Govi Desert (Bannikov 1954).
conservationActions: Approximately 20% of the species’ range in Mongolia occurs within protected areas. In the China Red List it is listed as Not Applicable; in the Russia Red List it is listed as Least Concern. Further research is recommended.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a well preserved protected area, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in tropical lowland rainforest. It is nocturnal and terrestrial (Weksler and Lóss 2015).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: This species is uncommon (Tirira in prep.).
range: This species occurs in the southeast Ecuador (Musser and Carleton 2005) and in Peru (Pacheco et al. 2009). It has an altitudinal range of 400 to 1,200 m (Weksler and Lóss 2015).
conservationActions: The species occurs in one protected area (Tirira in prep).

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because it has not been seen despite extensive searches over the last 50 years. Its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be less than 10 km², it has a single location and there is continuing decline in the area and quality of the species' habitat. The very specific habitat that the species was recorded from is considered to be almost entirely converted.
habitat: It is known only from the distinct Coastal Lomas ecosystem (with desert or dryland habitat) (Musser and Carlton 2005) and it has not been recorded from modified habitats. It is terrestrial and probably nocturnal.
threats: The area that the species is known from has been heavily disturbed through pastoral (goats) grazing and mining activities. The very specific habitat that the species was recorded from is considered to be almost entirely converted.
population: This species has not been recorded since 1949 despite intense searches throughout its restricted range (Zeballos and Vivar pers. comm.). The population is believed to have significantly declined, and the species (if it is still extant) is considered to be still declining because of extensive habitat loss within its small range (Zeballos and Vivar pers. comm.).
range: This species is known only from the Lomas de Atocongo, a group of low lying hills close to Lima in the west central Peru (Musser and Carleton 2005). It was recorded between 600 to 800 m.
conservationActions: This species has not been recorded from any protected areas. Further field studies are needed to try to determine whether this species still persists in the wild.

rationale: A widespread, common, and widely introduced species with no major threats, hence listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Muskrats are found in brackish and fresh-water lakes, ponds, streams, rivers, and marshes. Depending on the location, they will either dig burrows into waterside banks, or construct houses of vegetation. Houses are built so that the main chambers are above water level, but can only be entered through underwater tunnels. Separate structures are constructed for feeding and nesting (Feldhamer, 1999 in Wilson and Ruff, 1999). Muskrats exhibit many morphological adaptations for aquatic life, including lips that close behind incisors to allow gnawing under water, partially webbed hindfeet, and the ability to stay submerged for up to 20 minutes. Muskrats are primarily herbivorous, feeding on aquatic vegetation such as cattails and horsetails. During periods of food scarcity, individuals will also consume animal matter such as mussels, turtles, mice, birds, frogs and fish (Wilner et al. 1980)
threats: The majority of muskrat mortality is caused by humans. Muskrats are extensively trapped for their pelts, which are of increasing economic value around the world. High population densities of muskrats often result in destruction of local habitat, including damage to river banks caused by burrowing, and the reduction of aquatic vegetation due to over consumption for food and building materials. As a result, muskrats are often treated as a pest species and are trapped, hunted or poisoned to control population levels.
population: The muskrat is common to abundant in suitable habitats, with average densities of 40 individuals per hectare (Feldhamer, 1999 in Wilson and Ruff, 1999).
range: This species occurs in North America, from northern Canada and Alaska south through the United States, except the arid regions of the southwest and Texas, and the Florida peninsula. Introduced to Czech Republic in 1905 in order to establish fur farms, it is now present throughout the Palaearctic, Mongolia, China, northeast Korea, and Honshu Island, Japan. Also introduced in Argentina (Musser and Carleton 2005, Skyriene and Paulauskas 2012).
conservationActions: There are no measures currently in place to protect O. zibethicus. Common and considered "secure" (S5) or "apparently secure" (S3) throughout entire US range. One subspecies of concern: O. Z. ripensis (S2 in Texas). Status in Mexico needs to be assessed.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because although its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 20,000 km², it occurs in several protected areas and the extent and quality of its habitat may be declining only in parts of its range. This species is restricted to mature forest and it appears to no longer occur in one previously known locality. This makes it close to qualifying for Vulnerable under the B1 criterion; if it becomes severely fragmented or restricted to less than 10 locations the species will reassessed in one of the threatened categories.
habitat: This species occurs in montane cloud forests from 900-1,500 m (Middleton et al. 2007). Its biology is poorly known; it is nocturnal and terrestrial (Reid 1997).
threats: This species is threatened by increased deforestation and human development (Middleton et al. 2007).
population: This species is common on the southern slope of Volcan de Chiriqui in Panama from elevations of 1,000 m-1,500 m (Middleton et al. 2007). It may no longer occur in the Azuero Peninsula, where it has been looked for recently without success (Reid pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in western Panama Cerro Colorado and Volcan de Chiriqui (Middleton et al. 2007). It is known from 1,000 to 1,500 m (Carleton 1989). The species is known from two disjunct populations, which are being looked at taxonomically (Timm pers. comm).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: Although this species has a relatively small extent of occurrence, it is listed as Least Concern because the majority of its range is in a protected area, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in montane cloud forests from 900-1,500 m (Middleton et al. 2007).
threats: This species is threatened by an increase in deforestation and human development (Middleton et al. 2007).
population: This species is common where it occurs (Middleton et al. 2007).
range: This species occurs in the easternmost Panama and Serranía del Darién, and extreme northwest Colombia (Alberico et al. 2000, Musser and Carleton 2005, Middleton et al. 2007). In Colombia the species has been found between 100 to 500 m (Alberico et al. 2000).
conservationActions: The majority of the species' range is in a protected area.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 20,000 km², it is known from fewer than ten locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: Specimens have been collected in Valdivian temperate forest that has a habitat characterized by a majority of evergreen and a few deciduous trees, high annual rainfall (1,500–3,000 mm), wet and frost-free winters, and short dry summers. It has also been trapped in forest plantations with native vegetation under the canopy and deep soils (D’Elía 2015).
threats: In the region, forests are highly fragmented and under increasing pressure from logging activities.
population: This species is apparently scarce. According to Murúa et al. (2005), it was trapped just seven times during a 20 year trapping effort with nearly 213,000 trap nights at Fundo San Martín, where most specimens have been taken (D’Elía 2015).
range: This species is known from only five localities in a small portion of the Coastal Cordillera of southern Chile. The type locality occurs at an elevation of 100 m. (D’Elía 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is endemic to boreal habitats of the transvolcanic belt of central Mexico, and is restricted to "sacaton" grass and open pine forest (Williams et al. 1985).
threats: This species is threatened by urbanization and deforestation due to timber extraction, agricultural activities, grazing, and human recreational activities.
population: This species is common in suitable habitat, however, it is sensitive to changes in habitat.
range: This species is endemic to the Cordillera Transvolcanica, México. It occurs from west central Michoacán eastwards to central Veracruz (Musser and Carleton 2005), at an altitudinal range of approximately 2,500 to 4,300 m (Davis and Follansbee 1945 in Williams et al. 1985).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas within its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its has a maximum estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is 885 km², an estimated area of occupancy (AOO) of around 80 km², its habitat is severely fragmented, and there is a continuing decline in EOO, AOO, and quality of habitat. This species has lost 16-20% of its habitat over the past 10 years.
habitat: The habitat of the species has been described as humid Upper Austral Zone, dense oak forest, montane pine-oak forest, evergreen cloud-forest, and evergreen broadleaf rainforest; the habitat where it occurs is humid, with dense oak forest and cleared pastures (Frey and Cervantes 1997). This species is associated with mesic, well-drained soil (Getz 1985 in Frey and Cervantes 1997). It lives in burrows and in long subterranean tunnels (Bailey 1990 in Frey and Cervantes 1997).
threats: The habitat of this species is undergoing fragmentation from deforestation across its range. It is estimated to have lost 16-20% of its population based on habitat change over the past 10 years (Carton de Granmont and Cuaron pers. comm).
population: This is a relict species with a limited distribution (Frey and Cervantes 1997). No population information could be found.
range: This species occurs in Cerro Zempoaltépec (1,800 to 3,000 m), north central Oaxaca, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). Its distribution is restricted to the area south-east of Rio Cajones, Mixe District, Oaxaca in the two municipalities of Totontepec and Santa Maria Jalapa.The total area of occupancy (AOO) for this vole is estimated to be 80 km² (Frey and Cervantes 1997).
conservationActions: This species is listed on the Mexican Red List as subject to special protection, "sujeta a proteccion especial".

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is abundant in suitable habitat and tolerant of a wide range of habitats.
habitat: The species occurs in mixed forests, shrubland and forest clearings as well as in alpine pastures. The species prefers forest clearings and does well in degraded habitats. It also occurs in bogs. Females reproduce at the age of one year; this species produces 2 litters per season, each of 2-4 embryos.
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: The species is common over its distribution.
range: It occurs in northwest Turkey (humid forest along southern shore of Black Sea east of type locality), north Caucasus (Russia), south Caucasus (Georgia, Armenia, and west Azerbaijan), and northwest Iran. The western range limit are undefined; there are records further west based on morphology that have not been karyotyped. The southern and western range limits are not well defined (Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005). Elevation ranges from 500 to 1,400 m, rarely 2,100 m.
conservationActions: It occurs in protected areas. No specific conservation measures are in place or needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is very widespread, common, adaptable and there are no major threats.
habitat: Montane voles are found in alpine meadows in the south and mountain valleys in the north. They are found in wet meadows, cropland, especially fields and pastures of grass and legumes along fence rows; grassy areas by streams and lakes. They occupy shallow burrows and surface runways.Montane voles breed April-October. Females usually have two to three litters per year. Average litter size is about six; litter size peaked at three to four year intervals in northwestern Wyoming (Pinter 1986). Females of early cohorts begin breeding at four to five weeks in favourable years. Drought greatly reduced/delayed growth and attainment of sexual maturity in northwestern Wyoming (Negus et al. 1992).Diet includes grasses and sedges; leaves, stems, and roots of a wide variety of forbs. Predators include hawks, owls, foxes, badgers and coyotes. Montane voles are active throughout the year.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is considered secure within its range (NatureServe). Peak population density was 375-560 per hectare in Utah (Negus et al. 1986). Populations may fluctuate dramatically. Populations peaked at three to four year intervals in northwestern Wyoming (Pinter 1986).
range: This species is known from montane and intermontane areas of western United States from the Rocky Mountains northward into south-central British Columbia, Canada, west to the eastern slopes of the Cascade and Sierra Nevada ranges, south into northern New Mexico, and east along the Colorado-New Mexico border. The southernmost population is isolated in the White and Blue mountains of Arizona and New Mexico. Other southern subspecies also occur as isolated populations.
conservationActions: This species is not of conservation concern and its range includes many protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its has an maximum estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of only 510 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species can be found in evergreen rainforest; it also has been recorded in dense cloud forest and disturbed vegetation consisting of various grasses and wild strawberry (Fragaria sp.) within cloud forest, pine forest (Pinus sp.), and an ecotone of cloud and pine forest (Frey and Cervantes 1997). Captive specimens ate grasses but preferred the stems and leaves of wild strawberry (Frey and Cervantes 1997). A female taken in February was lactating. Litter size may be limited to a single young (Frey and Cervantes 1997).
threats: This species is losing habitat to deforestation in parts of its range. It is estimated to have lost 1-5% of its population based upon habitat change over the past 10 years (Carton de Granmont and Cuaron pers. comm).
population: There is no information available about population status for this species.
range: This species is found in north central Oaxaca, Mexico, on the eastern slopes of the Sierra de Juárez (1,500 to 2,500 m), including Vista Hermosa, Santiago Comaltepec, La Esperanza (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is not known to be present in any protected areas. The species is included on the Mexican Red List of 2001.

rationale: This is a widespread and common species with no major threats, and it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The preferred habitats are short grass meadows and agricultural grasslands and arable fields.
threats: This species is not under any specific threat.
population: This species is common throughout its range, and the trend is suspected to be stable.
range: The range of the Altai Vole extends from eastern Ukraine, central and southern European Russia to southern Asiatic Russia, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, eastern Türkiye, northwestern Iran, northern and eastern Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, northwest Mongolia and northwest China, from lowland areas up to 3,000 m (Zima 1993, Tougard et al. 2013, Pardinas et al. 2017, Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022, ASM 2024).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: No conservation measures are required for this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, although its extent of occurrence is less than 20,000 km², it is common within its limited range and well-adapted to agricultural lands (Wolff et al. 1997).
habitat: This species occurs in grass seed and grain fields, pastures, uncultivated field borders and wild regions (Steiner et al. 2007). Grey-tailed voles are associated almost exclusively with agricultural lands, especially grasses grown for seed, small grains, and permanent pastures of legumes and grasses. Also along grassy highway and railroad rights-of-way. They construct intricate runway and burrow systems. Nests are built underground or above ground under boards, bales, and debris scattered in fields (Verts and Carraway 1987). Breeding probably takes place throughout the year. Gestation is 21-23 days. Litter size averages about five young. In the laboratory, females as young as 18 days of age are capable of mating and subsequently producing viable offspring (Verts and Carraway 1987). Owls, hawks, foxes, skunks, and domestic and feral cats are common predators. Grey-tailed voles feed on succulent stems and leaves of a wide variety of green plants, including forbs, sedges, and grasses. Clover, wild onion, and false dandelion are also common food items (Verts and Carraway 1987).
threats: This species is threatened by agriculture in once abundant grasslands (Steiner et al. 2007).
population: This species is apparently secure within its range (NatureServe). Population densities fluctuate markedly, but few quantitative data are available. Within enclosures, densities comparable to 600 per hectare have been attained.
range: This species occurs in the Pacific Northwest, USA (Steiner et al. 2007). It is found in the lower elevations of Willamette Valley, Oregon, and at least two localities north of the Columbia River in adjacent Clark County, Washington in the United States. Specimens reported from east of the Cascade Mountains represent other species (Verts and Carraway 1987).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures required at present for this adaptable species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it has a very wide range, there are no major threats, and its populations are not in decline.
habitat: Taiga voles prefer early successional stage forests, especially black spruce in riparian habitats. They require rhizomes for winter food and good burrowing conditions such as occur where there is heavy moss cover. Because the preferred habitat may be limited in duration, populations are ephemeral and patchy in distribution. They make burrows with large dirt piles at the entrances. They also make runways through sphagnum. Young are born in underground burrows. In Alaska, litter size averages 8.8 (range 6-13). Females will produce one or two litters per year. The young of year do not breed (Wolff and Lidicker 1980). Grasses, horsetails, and lichens are important in the diet of these voles, they also eats blueberries (Whitaker 1980).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is considered secure (NatureServe). Populations undergo major fluctuations.
range: This species occurs in east-central Alaska in the United States, and central Yukon, and southern Mackenzie south to central Alberta and the western coast of Hudson Bay in Canada.
conservationActions: This species is not of conservation concern and its range includes several protected areas.

rationale: This species is poorly known and endemic to only one island where recent infrastructure development may be a threat. However, it has a reasonably large extent of occurrence of approximately 89,611 km² and is found in a number of protected areas, therefore is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Microtus sachalinensis lives in colonies. It inhabits open landscapes or places with small number of trees. It is also found in peatmoss bogs in mountain larch forests and tundra light forest. In dry places it digs burrows, in wet areas it uses small burrows in hillocks. In winter nests above ground were found. The species can swim. It feeds on marsh and meadow herbs and shrubs, and also consumes molluscs and bird eggs. It stores up to 10 kg of supplies. Reproduction occurs during the warm time of the year. It usually has one or two litters with 4-7 young in each.
threats: The threats to this species are unknown, but recent oil-related infrastructure development may influence the area of occupancy.
population: There is nothing known about the population of this species.
range: Endemic to Sakhalin Island. Found only in northern and central parts of the island.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: This species occurs in some protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because based on current evidence the species has a large extent of occurrence (74,466 km²), is found across a wide elevational range and there is no reason to consider that the species is declining, however, deforestation rates and the effects of this on the species are yet to be determined.
habitat: The species is found in humid subtropical forest of piedmont and lower mountain zone (600 - 1,000 m), and prefers forest clearings in early successional stage. The species has not been recorded outside of forest, and is likely to be dependent on forest. In Talysh found only in beech and hornbeam forests, with Parrotia persica and Quercus castanefolia. Inhabit steep slopes and deep ravines covered with shrubs, ferns and mosses. Leads semi-subterranean life. In contrast to many other vole species doesn't make passes between exits of the burrows. Feeds on underground plant parts. Most probably lives in family groups. Family area is small, limited to a single burrow with several exits (2 to 6). Reproduction starts in the end of March, litter size is 1-4 young.
threats: There is deforestation in this area.
population: Population size is slightly declining due to forest clearance, overgrazing.
range: This species is found only in forest zone of mountains bordering the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, in Lenkorani Lowland and North Talysh Mountains in Azerbaijan and the South Talysh Mountains and Alborz Mountains in northern Iran, where it is found between approximately 100-1,500 m asl (Nadachowski 2007).
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: The species has been found in one reserve in Azerbaijan (Zuvandinskiy Nature Sanctuary), and has several other protected areas in its range.

rationale: The species is listed as Least Concern because it has a relatively wide distribution with an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 327,434 km2, is found across a wide elevational gradient, and there there is no reason to suspect that the species is declining.
habitat: This species occurs in dry montane steppe habitats. In Turkmenia, it is found along river valleys, at moist areas with trees and shrubs (poplar, willow, elm, and dewberry). It feeds on green parts of different plants. It is colonial with a family area of 3-5 m square with 2-5 exits (Malygin, 1983). Pregnant females were found starting from April. It is possible that there is summer break in reproduction. Overwintered females give 2-3 litters per year. Average number of embryos is 6 (Marinina 1981).
threats: There are no known threats to this species. Range reductions could occur due to further climate aridification.
population: There are no data available for this species.
range: This species is found on mountains in Kopet-Dag Mountains in SW Turkmenistan and Iran (Khorassan Province) and the Hindu Kush of northern Afghanistan, at elevations from 300 to 2,000 m asl.
conservationActions: It occurs in many protected areas.

rationale: Although this species has a relatively restricted range, it tolerates some artificial habitats (e.g. arable land and fruit and vegetable gardens) and is not known to face any major threat, hence is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: This species inhabits xerophytic steppes and meadow-steppes at altitudes 1400-1700 m. It is also found in agricultural fields and fruit and vegetable gardens in that altitude range. Their burrows are simple.
threats: There are no major threats (GMA Turkey 2005).
population: The current status of the population is unknown (GMA Turkey 2005).
range: This species occurs in northeast to central Armenia, extending north into extreme south central Georgia and west into Turkey. It is separated in altitude from Microtus socialis and is found at higher elevations (above 1,400 m). The distribution map shows the approximate distribution of the species, but this needs verification.
conservationActions: No specific measures are known (GMA Turkey 2005).

rationale: Although the species is only known from a few areas, it faces no major threats, therefore, it is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species is found in open, dry habitats including farmlands.
threats: There are no known major threats. Although there are agricultural areas within its range, the species persists in these areas.
population: Little is known about the species' population abundance, however, the species is not very common. It can be a pest locally.
range: The species is restricted to central Turkey. The species' range limits are poorly known, and further work is needed to determine the species' distribution. Found from 200 to 800 m.
conservationActions: Part of the eastern edge of the range falls within Tuz Lake Special Protected Area (declared in the year 2000), which is not well managed for nature protection and has declined over the past 5 years. The species' natural history, ecology, and distribution need research.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable because it is now only known from only one island (historically it was known from two other neighbouring islands), it has an intrinsic tendency to undergo wide population fluctuations, and although there are no threats currently identified, the species' habitat is not protected and so there is the potential for detrimental human impacts on the habitat in the future. Introduction of invasive, predator species, such as feral cats, could plausibly drive this species to Critically Endangered or Extinct in a very short time.
habitat: The principal habitat for these voles are meadows dominated by beach grass (Ammophilia breviligulata) and poison ivy (Rhus radicans) (Hafner et al. 1998). They burrow in coarse loose sand, also on loose soil under or near any shelter (e.g., driftwood). Young are born in nests in underground burrows or under other cover. They breed from spring to fall. Gestation lasts about one month. Individual females produce up to several litters of four to five young per year. Most live probably less than one year.Home range is less than one acre. Cats, short-eared owl, northern harrier, and common garter snake are predators. Beach voles feed on beach grass stalks. They may also utilize seeds, and leaves of various plants and some insects. They are probably chiefly diurnal.
threats: There are no known threats to the species at present, but its very restricted range makes it vulnerable to threatening processes. Potential threats include introduced predators, habitat disruption by humans, and island erosion.
population: This species occurs only on one island. The population reportedly fluctuates between about 3,000 and 10,000 individuals but evidently does not exhibit regular long-term (3-4 year) cycles (Tamarin 1977). Density is about 12 per acre in low years, 37 per acre in peak years (density varied 5.8 fold over five years in another study).
range: This species' range is limited to Muskeget Island, off the west coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, United States (Tamarin and Kunz 1974). Historically this vole also occurred on nearby Adams and South Point islands, which can be regarded as part of Muskeget Island in the broad sense. Muskeget Island has changed shape, size, and position over time; it has moved more than 1,000 feet eastward since the 1800s (Surfrider Foundation, State of the Beach 2005; www.surfrider.org).
conservationActions: No conservation measures are known to be in place for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It inhabits grasslands and wet meadows at low elevations. It also present in coastal wetlands and open oak savanna with good ground cover.
threats: No major threats are known to the species as a whole. However, 4 subspecies (2 disjunct populations previously mentioned, one in northern Baja California, and one in the Los Angeles area) are of conservation concern.
population: Populations tend to be stable in coastal areas (around 200 individuals/ha), but in more strongly seasonal habitats densities vary dramatically over 2 to 5-year cycles, ranging from virtual absence to typical peaks of 450 individuals/ha.
range: It occurs from southwestern Oregon through central and western California (United States), and south into northern Baja California (Mexico). There are two disjunct populations in the Mohave Desert and White Mountain/Panamint ranges (California, USA).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. However, there are several protected areas within its range.M. c. scirpensis is a federally Endangered species in the United States, with an extant recovery plan. In California, there are several subspecies of conservation concern: M. c. mohavensis, M. c. sanpabloensis, M. c. scirpensis, M. c. stephensi, and M. m. vallicola.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, because whilst the species is only found on high elevations in the mountains of Taiwan and therefore has a fairly restricted extent of occurrence of approximately 5,333 km², there are no threats to the species habitat at present and it is found in a number of protected areas.
habitat: It occurs in highland forests (Smith and Xie 2008), with bushy bamboo understory (Yu 1993) including in coniferous, broadleaf, and mixed forests (Wu et al. 2012). The species can also be found in alpine meadows, feeding predominantly on Yushan cane (Yushania nittakayamesis) (Yeh et al. 2012), and also in scrub (Wu et al. 2012).
threats: In the past there was some deforestation in the highlands of Taiwan, however that has now mostly ceased and there are no longer any known threats to this species.
population: Currently there are no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to Taiwan, Province of China (Smith and Xie 2008). Its distribution is restricted to high mountain tops at elevations higher than 2,000 m asl (Wu et al. 2012).
useTrade: No use and trade information is available for this species.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Yushan National Park (Yu 1994), and in Taroko National Park (Wu et al. 2012). Further studies are needed into the abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, as although it is restricted to only two islands these are not inhabited and are both totally under protection so there are no known threats to the populations at present, and the populations although fluctuating, are thought to be stable.
habitat: This species occurs in rocky and willow patches of tundra (Weksler et al. 2010). On St. Matthew Island, this vole is most abundant in moist lowlands and on lower slopes; also in the Elymus community along beach ridges and the driftwood zone; it has been found up to about 240 m asl in moist, well-drained areas as well as around ponds and seepages. Burrows are in well vegetated rocky outcroppings. The species is not found in dry lowlands or in areas with much standing water (Rausch and Rausch 1968).On Hall Island, limited data indicate a mean litter size of seven, with most females producing only one litter (Rausch and Rausch 1968). Diet on St. Matthew Island includes Deschampsia, Artemesia, Rumex, Salix, Sedum, and Saxifraga. Insular Voles are important prey for such predators as Long-tailed Jaeger, Snowy Owl, Glaucous Gull, and Arctic Fox, they are occasionally preyed on by Polar Bears.
threats: No immediate threats are known, but the restricted range of this species increases its vulnerability to outside threats. This species lives in a very specific habitat that should be protected (Weksler et al. 2010).Fay noted that previously occupied habitat was destroyed by Reindeer introduced in 1944 on St. Matthew Island (Rausch and Rausch 1968). Reindeer population numbers increased to approximately 6,000 in 1963, but by the summer of 1966 only 42 remained and by the 1980s the population had completely died out.According to Rausch, predation by Arctic Fox, native to St. Matthew, appears to take place during years of high vole populations rather than when vole numbers are low; however, additional studies are needed to verify this pattern (Rausch and Rausch 1968). Predation by Long-tailed Jaegers and Snowy Owls occasionally occurs (Rausch and Rausch 1968). In any event, such predation is unlikely to pose a significant threat to the long-term viability of the vole population.
population: This species is restricted to where it occurs but has shown signs of dispersion of population (Weksler et al. 2010). This species is represented by two occurrences or subpopulations on different islands. Populations fluctuate widely. Beals found the voles "abundant everywhere" in 1944 (Rausch and Rausch 1968). The population was apparently at near maximum density in 1954 but was "very low" in 1957 (Klein 1959). The numbers were also low, and concentrations dispersed, in 1963 (Rausch and Rausch 1968). On the mainland, Batzli and Henttonen (1990) reported moderate tundra vole densities of 4-50 per hectare. The total area of St. Matthew Island is approximately 31,475 hectares (this area includes Pinnacle Island) and the total area of Hall Island is 1,443 hectares (Brewer 1996). The estimated population based on these densities would be between 131,672 - 1,645,900 individuals.The long-term population trend is unknown but appears to be stable. On a short-term basis, populations fluctuate from very low to very high (Rausch and Rausch 1968), but no predictable trend has been documented.
range: This species occurs in Continental Alaska and St. Matthew archipelago (Weksler et al. 2010). This species is known from Hall Island (subspecies abbreviatus) and St. Matthew Island (subspecies fisheri), in the Bering Sea, Alaska, United States.
conservationActions: Surveys are recommended to determine the nature and extent of any threats to the population of M. abbreviatus (Hafner et al. 1998). Populations on both islands are fully protected. Both St. Matthew Island and Hall Island are included in the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge.The population is not currently being monitored. Factors affecting population size and distribution are unknown. Current research needs include: 1) population size and trend estimates 2) habitat preferences 3) reproductive capacity 4) long-term population viability assessment 5) further assessment of taxonomic status.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because its area of occupancy (AOO) is probably not much greater than 2,000 km², and the extent and quality of its habitat are probably declining, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B2.
habitat: This rodent can be found in montane forest and pasture. It favors low-lying, damp areas in pine-oak forest and small clearings (Reid 1997). It is possibly diurnal or crepuscular, and it is terrestrial. Unlike most voles, which travel on runways through grassy areas, this species can be found in deep forest and does not appear to use runways. It probably eats plant material, although details of the diet have not been reported. A pregnant female, caught in January, had one embryo (Smith and Jones 1967, Reid 1997).
threats: This species is experiencing threates due to habitat modification in the Laguna Magdalena protected area in Guatemala, mainly due to overgrazing by sheep. Deforestation is also a threat to this species.
population: This species is considered uncommon to locally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in highland meadows of central Chiapas, México, and central Guatemala (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from 2,600 to 3,100 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the western portion of the Sierra de la Pinas National Park, which has a much higher level of protection than Laguna Magdalena National Park.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, likely occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in forest, forest-steppe and scrub meadow (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This is a widespread species, occurring in northwest China (Xinjiang province), Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It may be present in protected areas. Further studies are needed into the abundance of this species. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it has been found to have a wide distribution and there is no reason to suspect that the species is declining.
habitat: The species was found in cultivated fields such as alfalfa, clover, wheat, and in meadows in the foothills of valleys (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm). The species appears to prefer to occupy the lower elevations compared to M. socialis, especially when these two species exist sympatrically in the same region (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm).
threats: Although its distribution is still unclear, this species is probably adaptable. Human activities and drying out of its habitat over times could restrict its range to the suitable places in the west of Iran (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm).
population: It is said to be locally common or abundant within its range.
range: The type locality for this species was in northwestern Iran: Bu’in-Zahra (49º58′E, 35º39′N), 65 km south of Qazvin City, Qazvin Province. The species was more recently found at a number of other sites further west (Mahmoudi et al. 2015) and has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 81,497 km². It is found at elevations of 1,775-2,056 m asl and possibly has a wider range across Iran, possibly including in the east of the country (M. Mahmoudi pers. comm).
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: It is not known whether or not this species occurs in any protected areas.

rationale: This species has a moderately large range and may be locally abundant in suitable habitat. Although declines have been reported in some areas, it is not thought to be declining overall at nearly the rate required for listing in a threatened or Near Threatened category. It is here listed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species inhabits cereal and herb steppes in middle and higher mountain belts (1000-2500 m), often found at areas with trees and shrubs. In lower semi-desert belt (300-1000 m) it has been found only along rivers and moist ravines with clay and rubbly soils. It is abundant in fruit gardens and lucerne fields. In spring and summer it is active in dusk and down; in winter and early spring also diurnal. In winter it is active under snow. Burrows are shallow, however, sometimes up to 70 cm deep. The burrow system is complex with several exits. Exits are connected by paths on the ground. One colony can cover 5-12 m2. They feed on green parts of plants, roots, bulbs an seeds. Often feed on cultivated plants, wheat, barley, oats, corn and cotton. The species stores food, supplies that could be up to 3.5 kg. Reproductive period goes from February to October, litter size is 5-7 young. Gestation is 20-22 days (Zorenko, Golenistchev, Biodiversity Conservation center).
threats: There are no major threats to this species, however, in Turkmenistan the population is declining due to climate change (increased aridity) and overgrazing. This species does not adapt easily to new conditions.
population: The species is locally abundant in suitable habitat, and the population fluctuates (GMA Turkey2005). In Turkmenian the population is declining due to climate aridification and overgrazing. This species does not adapt easily to new conditions and that results in range shrinkage.
range: The species is found in Central and southwest Kopetdag (Turkmenistan) and northeast Iran. In central Kopetdag it is found in Chuli, Hailenau, Firuza River basin, Hermab, and Dushak Mt. In west Kopetdag along Sumbara and Chandyr rivers (Zorenko, Golenistchev, Biodiversity Conservation centre).
conservationActions: The species has been found in protected areas (GMA Turkey 2005).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it has a wide distribution and it occurs in protected areas, further research is needed about population current status and abundance, and threats.
habitat: It inhabits moist meadows in high mountain grasslands (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: The threats to this species are not known. Poisoning of voles and other small mammals on the Tibetan Plateau may have reduced the density of this species but new surveys are required to confirm this.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the southern region of Qinghai province (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies elevations ranging from 3,700-4,800 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species is present in Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve. Surveys are needed, as poisoning of small mammals on the Tibetan Plateau may have negatively impacted populations of this species. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Highland meadows/"vegas" in the high southern Andes region (Barquez et al. 2006).
threats: There are no major threats for this species.
population: There is no information available on the population and abundance of this species. It is considered to be an uncommon species.
range: This species occurs in west-central Argentina (Mendoza, Rio Negro and Neuquén Provinces) and adjacent regions of Chile (Santiago, Bío-Bío, and Araucanía Provinces), apparently at higher elevations (1,740-3,000 m); range limits unknown (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas in Chile and Argentina.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, presumed occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species prefers dense humid forest. It is a nocturnal rodent and occurs in lowland areas where it feeds on seeds, insects and fruit (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). The litter size ranges from two to four (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: No information available.
range: This species occurs in south-eastern Venezuela, Guyane, and Suriname (Weksler and Bonvicino 2015).
conservationActions: This species is presumably found in protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed stable population, occurrence in at least two protected areas, probable tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The majority of specimens were obtained in terra firme forest during survey of the Rio Jurua, some were also collected from seasonally flooded varzea forest (Patton et al. 2000). Pregnant females have been observed during August, September, October, November, May, and June, in both the wet and dry seasons suggesting that reproduction occurs throughout the year (Patton et al. 2000). It is thought that sexual maturity is reached at an early age (Patton et al. 2000).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: This rodent is known from a few specimens (total = 32) from 7 localities (Patton et al. 2000). It is thought to be reasonably abundant (Patton pers. comm.).
range: So far known from the central and lower drainage of the Rio Juruá, western Brazil; range limits require amplification (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This rodent is known from several indigenous reserves (Patton pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large and stable population.
habitat: The habitat of the species is upper tropical forest (Patton et al. 2000). Specimens collected from southeastern Peru in July during the dry season were all adults but none were in reproductive condition, the specimen from Brazil taken during the rainy season was pregnant with two near term embryos (Patton et al. 2000).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: There is no information on population or abundance.
range: So far known from the headwaters of the Rio Juruá, southeastern Peru and extreme west Brazil; range limits require amplification (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in the Manu Biosphere Reserve, Peru (Patton et al. 2000).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is widely distributed in lowland areas. It occurs in secondary and primary forest (Voss et al. 2001).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: There is no information on population or abundance.
range: This species occurs in southeast Suriname, French Guiana, and Amapá, Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed stable population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species in this nocturnal genus occur in lowland areas where they feed on seeds, insects and fruit (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). The litter size ranges from two to four (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: Populations in this genus undergo great fluctuations in abundance throughout the annual cycle (Eisenberg and Redford 1999).
range: This species occurs in southeast Venezuela, through Guyana, Suriname, and French Guiana, to Amapá, Brazil, and southwards to Amazonas and Pará, Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern since there are not major threats to this species. Additional research is need to better understand status and abundance of populations and to properly list the species.
habitat: It is a nocturnal, crepuscular, herbivorous and gregarious vole. It is associated with Himalayan moist temperate forest, is highly fossorial, and is colonial in habitat.
threats: This species is threatened in parts of its range by habitat loss and degradation due to expansion of intensive farming, planting of apple orchards and potato crops. It is also threatened by increasing human settlement in the region (Roberts 1997).
population: There is no information available on the population abundance of this species.
range: This endemic species occurs in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu, and Kashmir, India (Sharma et al. 2013) and to Murree hills in Punjab and five locations in North Western Frontier Province, Pakistan (Roberts 1997) at elevations of 1,800 to 3,000 m asl (Molur et al. 2005). It is estimated to have a very wide distribution in the region (Molur et al. 2005).
conservationActions: This species has been recorded within Ayubia National Park, Pakistan (Afza 2016). Additional studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, general ecology and threats to this little-known species.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its area of occupancy is less than 500 km2, its habitat is severely fragmented, it has fewer than five locations, and extensive continuing deforestation and habitat loss.
habitat: This species has nocturnal habits and its diet is based on seeds. The reproductive period extends from March to November, suggesting it is polyestric (Ceballos 2014). The litter comprises two to three offspring. This species is found in cloud and pine-oak forest (Ceballos 2014). it is an important species because it participates in the dispersal of seeds and fungal spores and in the removal of forest soil (Ceballos 2014).
threats: This species has a very restricted distribution and it is threatened by deforestation (Sanchez et al. 2005) and habitat destruction (Ceballos 2014).
population: There is no information on the population.
range: This species is known from eastern slopes of Sierra Madre Oriental (2,000-3,500 m), from south-eastern Hidalgo to central Veracruz, México (Musser and Carleton 2005, Vallejo and Gonzalez 2011, Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This species is listed as threatened under Mexican law and is not found in any protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is likely less than 5,000 km², it occurs in fewer than five locations, its population is severely fragmented, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to deforestation from timber extraction within its range.
habitat: This species is only known from cloud forests, pine forests, oak forests, and pine-oak forests with thickly vegetated areas and dense understories of vines and shrubs, at elevations of 3,000-3,500 meters (Ceballos 2014, Wilson et al. 2017). It is nocturnal, feeds on seeds and when threatened will climb trees (Ceballos 2014).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to deforestation from timber extraction within its range (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm). There is currently narcotics activity and social conflict in the area where this species is found; making it difficult to try to reverse the effects of this threat (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm).
population: Megadontomys thomasi is considered rare, but its population is currently thought to be stable (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm). This species is threatened by continuing habitat loss and fragmentation due to deforestation from timber extraction throughout its range and it is likely that most individuals are in small and relatively isolated subpopulations in remaining habitat fragments (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm).
range: This species is known only from the type locality and surrounding regions in the high Sierra Madre del Sur of central Guerrero, México, at 3,000-3,500 m (Musser and Carleton 2005, Wilson et al. 2017).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in some protected areas (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.) is considered under Special Protection (SEMARNAT 2010). This species is also an Alliance for Zero Extinction (AZE) trigger species for the Sierra Madre del Sur AZE site (AZE 2018).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 390 km², all individuals occur in fewer than five locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species is found in highland cloud and pine-oak forests, between 2,400-3,500 m. It generally observed in leaf litter and humus on the forest floor. Apparently, its diet consists of berries (Nowak 1999).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to deforestation, primarily from timber extraction.
population: This species is not common.
range: This species occurs in the Sierra Madre Oriental (Vallejo and Gonzalez 2011). It is found between 2,400 and 3,500 m.
conservationActions: This species is considered endangered by Mexican government (NOM-059-ECOL-2001).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is not declining in habitat or population, and it occurs in some well protected areas.
habitat: The Olive Montane Mouse (Aepeomys lugens) is reported in primary cloud forest and rarely in secondary habitats (Díaz de Pascual 1993, Aguilera et al. 2000), and also in seasonal forests and paramos (Soriano et al. 1999, Aguilera et al. 2000). Microhabitat preferences include beside logs and at the base of trees and tree ferns, among boulders covered with moss and lichen, in thick cover of herbs and ferns on the ground, and on logs (Handley 1976); usually in damp habitats and rarely in dry places (Ewel and Madriz 1968). This species is nocturnal and solitary, and may be semiarboreal (O. J. Linares 1998) or strictly terrestrial (Aagaard 1982). It is largely insectivorous, eating primarily arthropods, larvae, and worms (Díaz de Pascual 1993). Individuals can breed year-round but with a preference on the rainy season. Litter size is usually two, but it has been found to have up to seven young.
threats: Habitat loss could become a threat in the future (Ochoa et al. 2008). However, habitat loss is not currently a threat.
population: This species is locally common (Aguilera et al. 2000, J. Ochoa and M. Aguilera pers. comm.)
range: This species is found in the Mérida Andes of Venezuela (states of Táchira and Mérida), between 1,990 and 3,500 m (Pacheco 2015, Voss et. al 2002).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas in Venezuela. More collections are required.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because it has a small extent of occurrence (EOO is around 13,016 km²), it is known from less than 10 locations, and there is continuing decline in area and quality of habitat.
habitat: The species is almost entirely terrestrial and nocturnal. It is presumably omnivorous, but has some preference to insects (J. Ochoa pers. comm). Aepeomys reigi inhabits primary cloud forest and small patches of paramo (Handley 1976; Ochoa et al. 2001). Specimens have been found on the ground in densely forested areas (beside logs, at the base of trees and tree ferns, in rocky places, along trails, or near small streams) or in open areas (close to the ecotone between paramo and forest) covered by shrubs and herbaceous vegetation (Ochoa et al. 2001).
threats: The major threats are lost habitat in the Lara and Trujillo States close to the protected areas (Ochoa et al. 2008.).
