population: This species is locally common within remaining undisturbed habitat within its restricted distribution (J. Ochoa pers. comm).
range: This species is known from the Venezuelan Andes (Lara and Trujillo States), 1,600 to 3,230 m, western Venezuela (Pacheco 2015, Musser and Carleton, 2005). The type locality is Venezuela, Lara State, Parque Nacional Yacambu, 9 km SE Sanare, El Blanquito, 1,600 m; 09°40'N, 69°37'W (Ochoa et al. 2001).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Guaramacal and Yacambu National Parks. The species would benefit from a reduction in habitat loss close to protected areas (Ochoa et al., 2001)

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable because its area of occupancy is smaller than 2,000 km², it occurs in 10 locations, and it occupies forest fragments which are continuing to decline due to deforestation and habitat destruction. It was thought to be extinct, but now it has been found in ten localities, although it is still uncommon.
habitat: This species occurs in the Atlantic Forest habitat, around second growth semidecidous tropical forest and transitional formations of coastal vegetaion (Patton et al. 2015). Almost nothing is known about its natural history or ecology (Percequillo pers. comm).
threats: The major threats are habitat destruction and fragmentation (Percequillo pers. comm).
population: This rodent was considered extinct since no individuals had been found for more than 100 years (Pinheiro et al. 2004). It can now be found in ten localities, but it is still not common (Passamani et al. 2011).Steiner-Souza et al. 2008 trapped individuals using traps that were arboreal and baitless, and doubled the number of known specimens. The authors speculate that this species might not be as rare as originally thought, due to sampling bias in previous studies. However, this hypothesis is only based on a few field surveys.
range: This species endemic to the Atlantic Forest and is known from only nine localities in Espírtu Santo, São Paolo, Santa Catarina, Minas Gerais states, and part of Rio de Janeiro state in Brazil (Passamani et al. 2011, Patton et al 2015). The type locality is Rio de Janeiro State, but there are no records from this area since 1848 (Bergallo pers. comm). "The new occurrences documented in the present work in addition to existing data on R. rufescens identified the southernmost occurrence of the species within the Atlantic forest around Indaial, Santa Catarina (27°02’S, 49°08’W), and the northernmost in the surroundings of Santa Teresa, Espírito Santo State (19º58`S e 40º35`W), localities which are separated by at least 1,173 km" (Steiner-Souza et al. 2008).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Pincinguaba State Park in Sao Paolo state.

rationale: Although this species is known mainly from isolated records from a large area, it is listed as Least Concern in view of its tolerance of a range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This is believed to be an arboreal species; it has been collected at 2 m above ground and in pitfall traps. It has been found in a variety of habitats from dry cane fields in lowland areas close to rivers, to humid montane forest. It has been collected in disturbed forest.
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: It is known only from four specimens. This is likely to be a reflection of low sampling effort and inadequate methods.
range: This poorly known species is known from three localities. Two of these are in the Alto Madre de Dios river basin in Peru (Cuzco and Madre de Dios Departments), the third locality is at Bajo Hornuni, in Bolivia. It has been recorded between 450-2,100 m (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It has been collected in Cotapata National Park in Bolivia, and from Manu Biosphere Reserve in Peru. Further research is generally needed into this poorly known species.

rationale: Although its extent of occurrence is probably less than 10,000 km2, this species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is found along clear, cold streams in wet, highland forest (Reid 1997). One individual was caught alive on the bank of Rio Poasita, Costa Rica. It was observed swimming in captivity; only its head and tip of the tail were held above the water. This mouse ate sardines and rejected plant food (Starrett and Fisler 1970). In the wild it eats aquatic invertebrates; the stomachs of two individuals contained larvae of stoneflies, caddisflies, and mayflies (Hooper 1968, Reid 1997).
threats: Degraded water quality and streams are a potential major threat.
population: It is rare and local (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in the highlands of central Costa Rica and western Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found from 1,500 to 2,000 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It occurs in many protected areas in the Costa Rican cloud forest, including the Amistad National Park.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is found along fast-flowing, rocky-bottomed streams through cool, highland forest (Reid 2009), and occupies burrows with entrances above the waterline on the banks of streams. One burrow extended for at least 2 m (Reid 2009). This species may be slightly less aquatic in habits that other Rheomys species, but is always found closely associated with streams. This species is active both by day and by night. It is strong swimmer, capable of moving rapidly against the water current. Stomachs of two individuals contained caddisfly larvae, beetles, and spiders (Hooper 1968, Reid 2009). A captive mouse was highly vocal and made loud, low-frequency clicking calls by snapping the tongue against the roof of the mouth (Reid 1997, 2009).
threats: Stream quality degradation, water pollution, and deforestation are threats to this species.
population: This species of mouse is considered rare and local (Reid 2009).
range: This species is known from isolated segments in highlands of central Costa Rica and Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005; Reid 2009). It is found from 1,300 to 1,600 m (Reid 1997, 2009). In 2011, an individual was collected in Veragua rainforest, Limón (Rodríguez-Herrera et al. 2014).
conservationActions: It occurs in high-elevation protected areas in Costa Rica.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in riverine habitats in primary and secondary dry forest. Animals have additionally been recorded from wet natural grasslands. It can be found in agricultural areas. Little is known of the behaviour of this species, but it is probably similar to other members of the genus (Alvarez et al. 1984). It feeds on green plant material, fungi, some seeds, and insects. Its nests are usually built under cover of logs, rocks, or dense clumps of grass.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species, however it appears to be displaced by introduced murid rodents.
population: It is an uncommon species.
range: This species occurs in the Pacific coastal plain and contiguous Andean foothills of west Ecuador and northwest Peru (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found from sea level to 1,600 m.
conservationActions: It occurs in some protected areas (e.g. Arenillas Ecological Reserve in Ecuador, and Cerros de Amotape National Park and Coto de Caza El Angolo - part of the Biosphere Reserve of the Noroeste, in Peru). In general, further research into this species is needed.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This cotton rat is found in a variety of grass and grass-shrub habitats, and Pinon Juniper forest. Gestation is about 35 days and litters usually number 4 or 6 young. Young are raised in nests woven out of grasses; these can often be found by following a runway system. The young leave the nest when they are about one week old and begin to breed when they are about 6 weeks old (Wilson and Ruff 1999).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is locally common.One subspecies, S. f. goldmani, is considered to be extinct - this subspecies was located at the edge of the distribution in New Mexico.
range: This species occurs in southeast Arizona, west central New Mexico, and southwest Texas (United States), south through interior México to Guanajuato and northwest Michoacán (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. However, there are several protected areas within its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is restricted to grassy habitats, including edges of ponds, along drainages, in riparian habitats, adjoining agricultural fields, and in arid grassy patches.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is locally common.At least one subspecies, S. a. arizonae, is extinct.
range: The main range of this species is from southern Arizona southward through Sinaloa, Mexico. There is a disjunct population along the Colorado River in extreme western Arizona, extending marginally into adjoining California (and previously into Nevada where it is now considered extirpated).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. However, there are several protected areas within its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This stricly montane species is associated chiefly with mesic pine-oak habitat. In these areas, the species seems best adapted to mixed grass and shrub cover on shallow, rocky soils, even though they also have been caught in grassy meadows. This species is known to construct nests, burrows, and runways. However, in areas of sparse vegetation with low shrubs for cover, runway systems are obscure or absent. In fact, little or no sign of this species may be present, making its presence difficult to detect (Shump and Baker 1978). The gestation period for this species is about 35 days (Baker 1969 in Shump and Baker 1978).
threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
population: This species is common in suitable habitat within its range.
range: This species occurs in interior México, from southwestern Chihuahua and southern Nuevo Leon to central Oaxaca (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: A number of protected areas occurs within its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because it has a very restricted range: it is known from fewer than five locations within its extent of occurrence (EOO is 15,447 km²). This species is also in decline due to habitat conversion to agriculture and deforestation, however, not currently at a rate to qualify for a population reduction category, but could in the future if rates of change continue. If more locations are found this species should be re-evaluated.
habitat: Little is known of the behaviour of this species, but it is probably similar to other members of the genus. All known specimens were trapped in treeless vegetation between 3,500 and 3,800 m. Individuals have been captured on well drained slopes as well as near water (Voss 2015). It also occurs in dense reed mat forming a quaking bog in the middle of a shallow lake (Barnet 1999). Similar habitat preferences and run-making behaviour has been reported for other Sigmodon species (i.e., Voss 1992). One female specimen had four embryos (Barnet 1999).
threats: The major threats to this species are deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture, all of which are accelerating across its range.
population: This species is rare, known from less than 10 specimens (D. Tirira pers. comm).
range: This species is currently known from just two localities in the high Andes of Ecuador (Voss 2015). It has an altitudinal range of 3,500 to 4,000 m (D. Tirira pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in two protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 12,559 km², there are fewer than 10 locations, and the extent of its habitat is declining due to conversion to urban landscapes.
habitat: Trapping data for this species suggests a nocturnal activity pattern and presence in habitats near water bodies or flooded areas covered by dense grass and hydrophilic vegetation. Bibimys torresi is a secondary prey item of the Barn Owl in the Delta del Paraná, Argentina. Half of the six localities this species is noted from are known only from the dissection of owl pellets (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
threats: Populations of this species are declining due to conversion of habitat to urban landscapes.
population: This species appears to be uncommon. Long term trapping efforts produced few specimens (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
range: The distribution of Bibimys torresi is restricted to the islands and margins of Delta del Paraná in northern Buenos Aires and southernmost Entre Ríos provinces of Argentina. Fossil records indicate a previously larger range (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It is included in one Reserve (Protected Area).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is known to inhabit perisylvan grasslands, including severely disturbed habitats, from humid Chaco to northern Campos ecoregions. One specimen was captured in a small patch of marsh grasses in savannah. Field notes suggest that some Paraguayan specimens were trapped in small patches of humid grassland near or within remnants of evergreen forest. Most Argentinian records for this species are known from owl pellets (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
threats: There are no major threats for this species.
population: It is an abundant species.
range: This species occurs in a narrow band from eastern Chaco province, Argentina, through eastern Paraguay to southern Misiones and northwestern Corrientes provinces, Agrentina (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in at least 5 protected areas in Misiones province (Argentina) and Paraguay.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it is common to rare within its large range, it occurs in many protected areas, and its population is not declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Round-tailed Muskrats are a semi-aquatic species, preferring heavily vegetated freshwater habitats and restricted to permanent water bodies free of freezing (Hafner et al. 1998). Typically they occur in shallow grassy salt/freshwater marshes. In Florida, dense stands of Maidencane (Panicum hemitomon) and Pickerelweed (Pontederia lanceolata) provide preferred habitat (Layne 1978); other habitats include salt marshes on Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge and on Cape Sable (status in salt marshes on the northern Gulf coast needs further study). Pocosins and Carolina bays with a history of fire (i.e., not succeeding toward dense shrub bog) provide ideal habitat (Bergstrom et al. 2000). At Grand Bay, Georgia, Round-tailed Muskrats inhabit floating mats of bog like vegetation surrounded by open-water emergent marsh dominated by sedges such as Carex and Eleocharis spp.; these finer sedges are preferred house-building materials, whereas the coarser grass Panicum is preferred in Florida. The species is most abundant in areas with water 6-18 inches deep and a sandy, peaty, or soft substrate deep enough to allow burrowing to water during dry periods (Birkenholz 1972, Porter 1953).Dome-shaped houses, used for shelter and rearing young, are built among emergent vegetation; most house repair and new construction occurs in spring. In south-central Georgia, houses are attached to the surfaces of floating mats of Sphagnum and organic muck or to the bases of shrubs or small trees (Harper 1927, Birkenholtz 1963, Bergstrom et al. 2000). In sugarcane fields, houses, if present, are smaller and more rudimentary. Round-tailed Muskrats also build extensive tunnel systems in drained muck soils of sugarcane fields and agricultural areas. These muskrats construct floating feeding stands near house sites. In Georgia, denuded areas usually close to the edge of the mat were used as feeding stations. Round-tailed Muskrats are able to disperse between areas of suitable habitat across roads and small expanses of upland habitat and via ditches (Birkenholz 1963).This species breeds year-round, with a peak in late fall. May-November live-trapping in sugarcane fields yielded the largest number of juveniles and subadults in May (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). Gestation lasts 26-29 days. Litter size is 1-4 (average two); 4-6 litters per year. The young are sexually mature in 90-100 days. Reproductive potential is relatively low.Round-tailed Muskrats are apparently colonial in both marshes and muck fields. There is an average of about two houses for each individual, and generally no more than one adult uses each house. Burrow systems are occupied usually by single adults, a pair, a female and young, or one to two subadults (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). Home range is less than 2.5 acres. They are vulnerable to various reptilian, avian, and mammalian predators.They eat roots and stems of aquatic and semi aquatic vegetation; major food plants include arrowheads, pickerelweed, Nymphaea water lilies, maidencane, cut-grass, sedges, and grasses (Panicum, Sporobolus, and Echinochloa). In sugarcane fields, diet apparently is dominated by the sprouts, stalks, and roots of sugarcane, and by sedges and grasses (see Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). They are primarily nocturnal.
threats: The statewide population in Florida probably has declined as a result of wetland loss (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). Land fills, marsh drainage, and salt water intrusion have reduced the available habitat and further isolated some colonies (Layne 1978). Isolated populations are very vulnerable to extirpation caused by natural fluctuations in water levels (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992); these receive inadequate protection.
population: In Florida, this species is locally common on St. Johns marsh in Brevard County, near Hawthorne in Putnam County, and in the Lake Okeechobee region. Highest densities reported are for sugar cane fields in south Florida. In the sugarcane-growing region of Florida, the species is most common in western and northeastern Palm Beach County. It is apparently rare to absent and of spotty occurrence along the upper west Gulf Coast of Florida (Taylor and Suwannee counties south to Hillsborough County), in west-central Florida (Hillsborough, Polk, Manatee, Sarasota, and DeSoto counties), and in northeastern Florida (Nassau and Duval counties, and portions of Baker, Clay, and St. Johns counties); populations may be limited in certain formerly occupied coastal marshes where canals and reduced flows have allowed salt water intrusion (Layne 1978). Porter (1953) found Neofiber to be nearly or completely absent from many areas throughout Florida that previously supported dense populations. See Lefebvre and Tilmant (1992) for further details on the distribution in Florida. The total adult population size is unknown but certainly is at least many thousands. This species is represented by many occurrences or subpopulations throughout much of its former range. Wetland destruction has slowed in Florida but still occurs. With improved wetland protection, the rate of decline is probably much less than 30% over 10 years or three generations. Area of occupancy, number of subpopulations, and population size probably have declined (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992), but the extent of decline is uncertain.Average density is 50 individuals per acre, although peak densities can reach 100-120 per acre (Birkenholz 1972). On smaller natural marshes in central Florida, it may reach maximal densities of 250-300/ha, whereas on larger marshes (>1,000 ha) maximal densities are reported as 50/ha (Birkenholz 1963). Ecological densities in Georgi (1-3/ha) are much lower than the maximal densities reported for Florida (Bergstrom et al. 2000). Average home-range sizes for 23 radio-tracked Round-tailed Muskrats ranged from 1.263-2,071 m2 in isolated wetlands in south Florida (Schooley and Branch 2006), with individuals using 10-15 different rest sites within each home range. Muskrats typically used lodges for diurnal rest sites when their marsh habitat was inundated with water but switched largely to burrows when marshes dried up. Local populations often fluctuate tremendously, probably in response to water-level fluctuations and changes in habitat conditions (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). May wander or disperse a few or several hundred metres from permanent water. In the dry prairie region of south Florida (on and around Avon Park Air Force Range), Round-tailed Muskrats occupied 35.7% of 457 isolated wetlands in either one or both years of a survey. Local extinction (within a wetland patch) and recolonization occurred in many cases. Patch occupancy increased as patch size, spatial connectivity, and habitat quality increased (Schooley and Branch 2007). Cattle grazing can reduce habitat quality by removing key food and house-building plants such as Panicum sp. Dry prairie habitat of high quality—as the matrix surrounding isolated wetland habitats of Round-tailed Muskrat—was judged to facilitate recolonization of patches, whereas pine plantations were barriers to recolonization (Branch and Schooley 2005).
range: The Round-tailed Muskrat occurs in Florida and south-central and southeastern Georgia, ranging west to at least the Choctawhatchee River in Walton County, Florida (Lefebvre and Tilmant 1992). It is apparently most common in the Everglades region of Florida and the Okefenokee Swamp of Georgia.Bergstrom et al. (2000) concluded that the range is fairly continuous within suitable habitat from north-central Florida into south-central Georgia. There seems to be a gap of about 80 km between the Grand Bay population in south-central Georgia and the Okefenokee population to the east, though apparently suitable habitat is present in the gap (Bergstrom et al. 2000). The apparent gaps at the northern range limit may be the result of a combination of the fragmented, isolated distribution of palustrine wetlands and the generally low population densities causing localized extinction (Bergstrom et al. 2000). Habitats in Georgia may be peripheral dispersal sinks, occupied only following periods of exceptionally high densities in more central populations (Bergstrom et al. 2000). New localities in south-central Georgia (mainly the Grand Bay population) are closer to being contiguous to the previously described range of subspecies apalachicolae to the southwest in north Florida than to the range of subspecies exoristus, known from the eastern Okefenokee Swamp in Georgia (Hall 1981). The possibility exists that a large and viable population survives in the 30,000 ha of wet prairies and islands of the Okefenokee Swamp (only a fraction of which is actually suitable habitat); Harper (1927) estimated the population at 10,000, but Porter (1953) found very few signs of active houses and recent observations by T. Hon conform with Porter's findings. Georgia colonies that were reported in years past from southern Thomas County (W. Baker pers. comm.) and southwestern Lowndes County (T. Hon pers. comm.) were not found in recent aerial surveys (Bergstrom et al. 2000). Harper (1920) documented Neofiber in "prairie" habitats on the eastern side of the Okenfenokee Swamp. Schantz and Jenkins (1950) reported Neofiber skulls in barn owl pellets near Woodbine, Camden County (on the Satilla River, about 20 miles from the Atlantic Coast).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas, including Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, Georgia; Everglades National Park, Florida; Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary (National Audubon Society), Florida; Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park, Florida; and other Florida managed areas. It is protected from trapping and hunting in Florida and Georgia.The precise distribution of all occurrences needs to be determined. Representative subpopulations should be monitored. Occupied marsh habitats, including appropriate upland buffers and incoming drainage systems, are in need of further protection.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is abundant in grassland, clearings, marshy areas, second growth, and agricultural areas (Martino and Aguilera 1993).This species is nocturnal and terrestrial. Its diet includes seeds, fruit, and green plant material. This species makes short burrows in banks or under tree roots, leadings to nests made of grasses and plant down (Reid 1997). In Venezuela, breeding occurs year-round and litter size averages 4.1 (O’Connell 1982).
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: This rat is common, often abundant. It sometimes is a pest in agricultural areas (M. Aguilera pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the savannas from southeastern Costa Rica through Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, and the Guianas, to Brazil north of the Amazon River; including Trinidad and Tobago and smaller continental shelf islands adjacent to Panama and Venezuela (Musser and Carleton 2005). Occurs in the llanos of Venezuela.
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas (M. Aguillera pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its moderately wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining.
habitat: It occurs in grassland, clearings, marshy areas, second growth, and agricultural areas (Martino and Aguilera 1993). This species is nocturnal and terrestrial. The diet includes seeds, fruit, and green plant material. It makes short burrows in banks or under tree roots, leading to nests made of grasses and plant down.
threats: There do not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: This species occurs in an area that has not been recently well studied (R. P. Anderson pers. comm.) although it is likely to be common (as Z. brevicauda), often abundant (Martino and Aguilera 1993).
range: This species occurs in the intermontane valleys of north Colombia, 350 to 1,300 m (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs along small hills; reproduces between spring and mid-autumn producing 2-4 young per litter (Gonzalez 2001).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is locally common.
range: This species occurs in east-central Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul state) (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is present in dry coastal and semi arid biomes, shrubland, inter-Andean valleys and inundated areas. It can be found in secondary or disturbed habitat, but it is not present in cultivated areas.
threats: It is threatened by displacement in its habitat by introduced murids (such as Rattus). There is some habitat loss in the south of the species range.
population: It is uncommon. The species has seasonal population fluctuations, influence by El Niño effect.
range: This species ranges in western Peru. It is also present in the high northern Peruvian inter-Andean valleys near Chachapoyas, Amazonas Department. It has an elevational range from 400 to 2,850 m.
conservationActions: It is present in at least eight small protected areas. Further research is needed into the taxonomy of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, likely occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent has been taken from cerrado habitat and gallery forest in Terezina de Goias (Bonvicino et al. 2002). It has been collected in moderately disturbed areas (Weksler and Bonvicino pers. comm.).
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: This species is common.
range: This species occurs in cerrado (Goiás and Minas Gerais States) and caatinga (Paraíba and Pernambuco States) formations of northeast and central Brazil (Bonvicino and Weksler 1998).
conservationActions: This species has not been collected in any protected areas but it is likely to occur in some that are in its range.

rationale: Although its extent of occurrence is probably less than 20,000 km2, this species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, presence in protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in lower montane and montane wet forests (Musser and Carleton 2005); it occurs in second growth, brush, and cloud forest openings (Reid 1997). This species is found largely in edge habitat. It has been found at several localities with O. fulvescens (Reid 2009).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This mouse is common (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in central Costa Rica and western Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005, Reid 2009). It is found from 840 to 3,000 m (Reid 1997, 2009).
conservationActions: The Costa Rican population is mainly found in protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is adaptable to agricultural advances (Weksler and Bonvicino 2005). This is one of the least specialized species in diet and microhabitat requirements in a study of seasonal niche dynamics of coexisting rodent species of the cerrado habitat. During the dry season, the species preferred open areas with apparent soil and absent or rare herbs, shrubs and trees, the latter never more than 10%, it also occurred in grassy areas with dense, continuous herbaceous cover with up to 30% arboreal cover, or partially continuous herbaceous cover with up to 10% arboreal cover. The species is vegetarian. In Uruguay, this nocturnal, primarily herbivorous species occurs in mesic subtropical forest with closed canopy with sparsely vegetated understory and in drier thorn woodlands, where it breeds in late summer and autumn producing two to four embryos.
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: This species is very common. For additional information see Weksler and Bonvicino (2005).
range: This species occurs in east Paraguay, north Argentina, and Atlantic Forest region, central and southeast Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul to Paraíba, interior to Goías and Distrito Federal; also Ilha Grande) (Bonvicino and Weksler 1998, Andrades-Miranda et al. 2001) and Uruguay (Weksler and Bonvicino 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits subantarctic forest.
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: This is an abundant species.
range: This species occurs in the southern Patagonian regions of Chile and Argentina, including Tierra del Fuego (Musser and Carleton 2005) and neighbouring islands.
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is terrestrial and occurs in high montane forest and paramo (Linares 1998).
threats: There do not appear to be any major threats to this species; however, deforestation and habitat loss affect its area of occupancy.
population: It is locally common (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in Táchira, Andes of extreme west Venezuela, and Cordillera Oriental of east Colombia (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Although this species is poorly known, its distribution was observed to be restricted to areas of rock or accumulated brush in primarily arroyo forest (Ceballos 1990). It is found in tropical deciduous forest, xerophilius shrub, grasslands, oak-pine forest, and riparian vegetation. It can tolerate anthropogenic disturbance (Ceballos and Oliva 2005).The species builds burrows between rock or construct nests under accumulations of litter on the forest floor and in hollows of trees (Ceballos and Miranda 1990).Reproduction likely occurs year-round (Arroyo-Cabrales 2005).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss from deforestation and agriculture.
population: A study in Jalisco by Ceballos (1990) showed O. banderanus to be common in arroyo forest (semideciduous) with densities ranging from 1.6 to 8 individuals/ha, and scarce in deciduous forest (<1 individual/ha).
range: This species occurs from the coastal plain of south Nayarit to south Guerrero and in the interior of Michoacán and Guerrero along the basin of the Río Balsas, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found from sea level to 1,400 m asl (Ceballos and Oliva 2005).
conservationActions: There are no specific conservation measures in place for this species. Several protected areas are located within its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in primary and secondary moist forest along the eastern slopes of the Andes where a lot of leaf litter is present. The species does not occur in cultivated areas.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. It is locally threatened by temporary slash and burn agriculture (including coca) growing, although it can successfully colonize these areas once they have been abandoned and secondary growth has occurred.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs on the eastern slopes of the Andes, in southeast Peru and west central Bolivia (La Paz Department) (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of about 1,100 to 2,500 m (N. Bernal pers. comm.).
conservationActions: It is present in two protected areas in Bolivia, Madidi and Apolobamba National Parks, and Bahuaja-Sonene National Park in Peru. No direct conservation measures for this species are currently needed.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because, although it can be common in suitable habitat within its range, it has a relatively small distribution (its extent of occurrence estimated to be is 5,691 km²) and habitat within its range is being degraded. The species does occur in secondary habitat and is present in protected areas, however, if its population should begin to decline or become severely fragmented, it would likely qualify for a threatened category under criterion B1.
habitat: This mouse can be found in mature cloud forest, and is most common along steep banks of streams and in low-lying areas with numerous tree ferns and mosses (Reid 2009). It is also known from secondary habitats. It is usually terrestrial, occasionally on low logs or fallen trees. One female was pregnant with two embryos in December. The stomach contents of one captured individual contained green plant matter only (Reid 2009).
threats: There are no known major immediate threats to this species. It does, however, have a relatively small range, in which suitable habitat is decreasing due to forest loss.
population: The population is regarded as stable. It is described as very local but fairly common in its preferred habitat (Reid 2009).
range: This species is occurs in Central Guatemala only, specifically between Purulhá and Tucuru, Alta and Baja Verapaz; and Sierra de las Minas, Zacapa. It is found at elevations of 1,500 to 2,200 m (Reid 2009).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Sierra de las Minas biosphere reserve in Guatemala. Further taxonomic research is needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: P. eva is generally associated with patches of succulent vegetation and stony areas. It has been found in natural arid tropical scrub containing matorral sarcocaule such as cholla (Cilindro opuntia), palo Adan (Fouquieria diguetii), lomboy (Jatropha cinerea), viejito (Mammilaria), cardon (Pachicereus pringlei), and pitaya agria (Stenocereus gummosus). This rodent has also been collected in fields of chilli, corn, oranges, palms, sugarcane, and tamarind, and in areas with secondary vegetation. Pregnant females were captured during February, March, June, and July; and lactation was observed mainly in February, April, and July. Breeding was observed in July. The number of embryos averaged three (Alvarez-Castañeda and Cortes-Calva 2003).
threats: There are no major threats known to this species. However, the population on Carmen Island may be threatened by population decline from introduced species and predation by feral cats.
population: The population of Peromyscus eva increases more during the cooler months October to February than other species of rodents. On the slopes of the Sierra de la Laguna, the relative abundance of P. eva is closely related to elevation and vegetation (Alvarez-Castañeda and Cortes-Calva 2003).
range: This species is widely distributed throughout Baja California Sur and Carmen Island, México (Alvarez-Castañeda and Cortes-Calva 2003).
conservationActions: There are several protected areas within this species' range. The population of this species on Carmen Island is protected by Mexican law (NOM-059-ECOL-2001).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be in decline.
habitat: This species is ecologically diverse, with its 57 subspecies divided into two ecotypes: long-tailed, large-eared forest inhabitants and short-tailed, small-eared inhabitants of open country. Altogether, it is found in virtually every habitat within its range (tundra, taiga, temperate and boreal forests, swamps and bogs, prairies, deserts, and scrublands).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is extremely abundant in some habitats, varying both seasonally and annually.
range: This is the most widespread North American rodent. It is found throughout southern Canada, the United States, and north and central Mexico, including Baja California. It is absent from the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coastal plains of the United States, but its range does extend to the coast in east Texas.
conservationActions: It occurs in a number of protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 893 km², its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 500 km², all individuals occur in fewer than five locations, and there is a continuing decline in the number of locations and number of mature individuals.
habitat: This species is present in several habitats, but mainly in tropical deciduous forest. Often, this species has been found in the interior highlands, near dry riverbeds, and on the surrounding hillsides. This mouse lives under logs, projecting roots, rocks, and small ledges. Pregnant and lactating females and juveniles of both sexes were found in March (Alvarez-Castañeda and Mendez 2005).
threats: This species may be threatened due to competition for resources with introduced fauna (including Capra hircus, Odocoileus virginianus, and Rattus rattus) (Wilson 1991, Alvarez-Castañeda and Mendez 2005). There is a federal prison on María Madre, and the island houses more than 5,000 people, as well as cattle, horses, goats, sheep, donkeys, rabbits, poultry, and cats (Lopez-Forment et al. 1996). The population of P. madrensis on this island is likely the most threatened by introduced fauna.
population: This mouse is abundant in all habitats on María Cleofás Island, the least disturbed island in the chain. On other islands, this species is rare. No individuals were collected in 1991 on María Magdalena Island (Alvarez-Castañeda and Mendez 2005); this species may be extirpated from this island. This species was once the most common rodent in the Islas Marias (Alvarez and Mendez 2005).
range: This species occurs in the Islas Marías group: San Juanito, María Madre, María Magdalena, and María Cleofás, located off the central western coast of México (Alvarez-Castañeda and Mendez 2005).
conservationActions: This species is protected in Mexico (NOM-059-ECOL-2001). The range of this species is within Islas Marias Biosphere Reserve.

rationale: Tthis species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species of mouse is terrestrial and nocturnal. It is found in humid forests of the mountains, in cloud forests and forests of oak, at elevations of 1,300 to 3,000 m. It is sensitive to habitat modification and is only found in well preserved forests. In El Triunfo, Chiapas, most pregnant females were caught in the beginning of the rainy season (Horváth 2014). It is rare or absent from highly disturbed or logged areas (Reid 1997).
threats: There are no major threats to this species, although some of the parks that comprise the core area of the species are not adequately protected from habitat loss. Habitat modification would threaten this species.
population: Locally, this species can be relatively abundant. A large part of its distribution area coincides with the El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve, which suggests the long term survival and stability of these populations (Horváth 2014).
range: The Guatemalan Deermouse is found from the Sierra Madre mountains in southern Chiapas, to central and southeastern Guatemala (Horváth 2014). It occurs from 1,300 to 3,000 m (seldom below 2,000 m) (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It occurs in protected areas in Mexico and Guatemala. Taxonomic research is needed as there is confusion with P. mexicanus and other Peromyscus species. This species is abundant locally. An important part of its distribution lies within El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve, ensuring protection of its habitat (Horváth 2014).

rationale: Perote Deer Mouse (Peromyscus bullatus) is assessed as Critically Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 100 km², all individuals are in a single location, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species is poorly known. It inhabits plains and dunes of fine sand in xeric scrublands. It has only been caught at an elevation of 2,377 m (Martinez 2014). Dominant vegetation associations include grasslands and arid scrub in bottom lands and coniferous forests at higher elevations. This species is restricted to flat bottoms with areas of fine sandy soil that support grasses and a few trees (Juniperus dippeana) and Yucca. It has not been collected in rocky areas (Gonzalez-Ruiz et al. 2005). Females showed no signs of reproductive activity in March, June, September, or October (Gonzalez-Ruiz et al. 2005).
threats: A restricted range, a highly discriminating choice of habitat, low densities, and habitat deterioration may pose serious threats this species (Gonzales-Ruiz et al. 2005). It is threatened by the replacement of native thorny vegetation with crops in its highly restricted area of distribution (Martinez 2014).
population: Prior to 1950, this rodent was known from only seven specimens. This species was considered rare because only one specimen was collected by Hall and Dalquest (1963). Peromyscus bullatus exhibits very specific and strong habitat selection, and its preferred habitat is uncommon and restricted (Gonzalez-Ruiz et al. 2005). Its population is most likely declining due to replacement of native vegetation by crops in its distribution range (Martinez 2014).
range: This species is endemic to Veracruz, Mexico,where it is only known from its type locality in Perote (Musser and Carleton 2005) and El Limon (Martinez 2014). It is known from 2,250 to 2,500 m elevation (Gonzalez-Ruiz et al. 2005).
conservationActions: This species is protected in Mexico (NOM-059-ECOL-2001).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in chaparral, coniferous and oak woodlands, coastal sage scrub, and laurel and redwood forests. The species finds cover in natural holes and crevices and uses burrows of other animals. It often lives in stick nests built by wood rats. Young are born in complex nests of grasses, weeds and sticks located under logs or other debris.
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: It can be locally common.It has low but stable densities, with populations up to 104 individuals/ha depending on habitat and season. The species appears to associate with Neotoma fuscipes, with densities possibly correlating with abundance of Neotoma dens.
range: The species is restricted to southern California (United States) and northern Baja California (Mexico). It is found from sea level to 2,440 m.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The Transvolcanic Deermouse inhabits forests of oak, pine-oak, pine, and fir, and cloud forests at middle and upper elevations of the Eje Volcanico Transversal in Mexico. It has occasionally been found in places with little vegetation cover such as lava fields. It is a terrestrial and mainly nocturnal species. It feeds mostly on grasses and seeds, but supplements its diet with insects. Reproduction occurs in the rainy season from August to October, and in the dry, hot season (May) (Cruzado and Ceballos 2014).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation, particularly in the conifer forests.
population: This species is relatively abundant in some environments. Its stable population presents no problems of conservation (Cruzado and Ceballos 2014).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and is distributed along the Eje Volcanico Transversal, form Colima to Mexico City at elevations from 2,300 m to 2,600 m (Cruzado and Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: There are no specific conservation measures in place for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse is found in temperate montane regions. It favours edges and secondary growth of wet highland forest (Reid 1997). It can live in disturbed habitat of coffee and sugar cane plantations (Ceballos and Oliva 2005).It is largely insectivorous and includes ants, weevils, crickets, and beetles in the diet; a few seeds (Solanum sp. and others), and green plant material are also eaten (Alvarez et al. 1984, in Reid 1997).
threats: There are no known major threats. However, deforestation could pose a threat in the future.
population: It is locally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species has a disjunct range, occurring in humid montane and cloud forests in central Veracruz, central Guerrero, through Oaxaca and east Chiapas, México, to Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador (Musser and Carleton 2005). It can be found from 500 to 3,200 m (Carleton 1979, in Reid 1997).
conservationActions: There are no specific conservation measures in place for this species. It occurs in protected areas.

rationale: This rodent is listed as Critically Endangered because it has an extent of occurrence of less than 100 km², all individuals are known from a single location (San Esteban Island), and the species is likely to experience extreme fluctuations in population due to stochastic events and is threatened by introduced domestic cats and black rats.
habitat: The preferred habitats for this species are rocky areas or slopes in xeric scrublands (Ceballos 2014). Its diet includes seeds, green parts of plants, flowers, fruits and insects (Ceballos 2014).
threats: Given that this species is restricted to a very small island (<42 km²), it is likely to experience extreme fluctuations in population due to stochastic threats. This species is also threatened by the presence of domestic cats (Felis catus) and black rats (Rattus rattus) (Ceballos 2014). Black rats have been reported on the island since the 1930s and it can be assumed that somehow P. stephani has adapted to their presence (Ceballos 2014).
population: The population of this species is considered relatively large (Ceballos 2014).
range: This species is known only from San Esteban Island in the Gulf of California (Mexico) (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: No conservation measures are known to be in place for this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 16,400 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, there is continuing decline in population and in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species inhabits lowland tropical deciduous forest of the arid upper tropical zone west of the Sierra Madre Occidental. It most frequently occurs in primary deciduous forest, coastal scrub, flood plains, and lower river valleys, and is absent from drier hillsides. Mangroves swamps, palm groves, arroyos, and Acacia thickets have provided numerous captures (Roberts et al. 2001).Pregnant females were caught in February and September. Juveniles were caught in May (Carleton et al. 1982 in Roberts et al. 2001).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to agriculture throughout its range and the application of rodenticides. It is also threatened by deforestation (Sanchez et al. 2005).
population: This species is frequent in suitable habitat but is restricted to the areas in which it currently occurs (Roberts et al. 2001, Alvarez 2001).
range: This species occurs from west-central Sinaloa through west Nayarit, México, from sea level to 250 m (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures known to be in place for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, high tolerance to habitat modification and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse occurs in deciduous and semideciduous forest and second growth (Reid 1997). It is mainly terrestrial and can be trapped on the ground or on logs and low branches.Breeding occurs year-round, but reproductive activity is greatest in the wet season. Litter size is 1 to 4, mean 2.8 (Reid 1997).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is common (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in the Yucatán Peninsula, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). There have been recent observations reported from Guatemala (Zarza et al. 2003). It occurs at lowland elevations (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: There are no specific conservation measures for this species. There are several protected areas within its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 3,940 km², all individuals occur in fewer than five locations, and there is a likely continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species can be found in pine-oak forest, in Baccharis, rocks and fallen trees and in trees with thick foliage (Alvarez 2005). In these areas, trees have thick mats of mosses and lichens and many epiphytes, including large bromeliads and orchids. Various herbs and saplings, rocks, and fallen trees (Carleton 1977, Duellman 1965 and Alvarez-Castaneda 2005) form the understory. Other species collected with this species are Peromyscus boylii and Reithrodontomys fulvescens (Alvarez-Castañeda 2005).
threats: The area in which this species is found is used for timber extraction (Alvarez-Castaneda 2005, Sanchez et al. 2005).
population: This species is not very common. It is restricted to the wetter west of the Sierra Madre Occidental (Alvarez-Castaneda 2005).
range: This species occurs in isolated localities in the Sierra de Coalcomán, Michoacán, and in the Sierra Madre del Sur, Guerrero, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). Its range is restricted to the wetter areas on the west side of these mountain ranges (Alvarez-Castañeda 2005).
conservationActions: This species is under special protection by the Mexican government (Alvarez-Castañeda 2005).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a degree of habitat disturbance, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse is restricted to dry or semiarid rocky hills and valleys in dry, deciduous forest, brush, and thorn scrub (Reid 1997). Its biology is poorly known. It is terrestrial and always is trapped near rocks or boulders. In Nicaragua, a female with 3 embryos was caught in April (Jones and Yates 1983). Females were nonreproductive in December and January in Guatemala (Reid 1997).
threats: There are no major threats to this species (its rocky habitat is not farmed and it is found on rock walls). It is adaptable to habitat modification.
population: It is local and usually uncommon; however, it is occasionally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species is intermittently found in dry to semiarid lowlands of southeast Guatemala, southeast El Salvador, Honduras, and west Nicaragua (Musser and Carleton 2005). It can be found at 200 to 1,000 m (Huckaby 1980). A sub-fossil record from 2,000 - 3,000 years ago from Guanacaste province, Costa Rica, was found in 1988, so its range may extend into northwestern Costa Rica (Woodman 1988).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. It occurs largely outside of protected areas (R. Timm, N. Woodman, J. O. Cajas pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 10,908 km², its population is inferred to be severely fragmented based on its severely fragmented habitat, and there is continuing habitat loss from deforestation within its range.
habitat: This species occurs in cloud and pine forests (Lorenzo et al. 2006). It can be found in mature forest, second growth, and brushy, cutover areas. Below 2,200 m it is restricted to tall forest (Reid 1997). Its biology is poorly known. It is terrestrial and is usually trapped on the ground near large trees. Mean litter size is 2.0 (Reid 1997).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and fragmentation from logging for timber, and by habitat conversion for agriculture. The remaining habitat is severely fragmented. This species has lost more than 50% of its habitat over the past 30 years (Sanchez-Cordero 2005).
population: This habitat for this rodent is (Lorenzo et al. 2006). It is locally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in middle to high elevation cloud and pine-oak forest in central and southeast Chiapas, México (Musser and Carleton 2005, Lorenzo et al. 2006). It occurs from 1,400 to 2,900 m (Ceballos and Oliva 2005). Specimens have been found in Guatemala that are probably Peromyscus zarhynchus, but these have not been confirmed (S. Perez pers. comm).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. It is not found in protected areas.

rationale: This rodent is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct), but it may actually now be extinct. This species is only known from two specimens, the last of which was recorded over 60 years ago. It is inferred this species has less than 50 mature individuals. Based on its known locations, the extent of occurrence is likely severely fragmented, and the area is experiencing severe habitat loss due to agricultural activities in the region.
habitat: This species is poorly known. This species occurs in rocky landscapes and arid environments (Castaneda et al. 2014). This species is thought be specific to one vegetation type.
threats: The area where the species is found is experiencing loss of native vegetation due to agricultural conversion. This species is also threatened by dramatic climatic fluctuations (Castaneda et al. 2014).
population: No population information could be found. Only two specimens are known. The last specimen was seen 60 years ago.
range: This species occurs in south-east Puebla, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). This species is only known from two specimens: the type locality of Ciudad Serdan and a single skin from Tehuacan at 1,700 m (Hall 1981).
conservationActions: No conservation measures are known to be in place for this species.

rationale: Peromyscus mayensis is assessed as Critically Endangered because it has a small extent of occurrence (EOO is 89 km²), it occurs in a single location, and there is continuing decline in extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, and the extent and quality of its habitat due to intensive logging throughout its range.
habitat: This mouse can be found in mature, highland forest, where it seems to be restricted to cold, wet oak forest with scattered pines, abundant epiphytes and fallen trees, and a deep layer of leaf litter (Reid 1997). This species occurs in heavy leaf and moss area and feeds on insects (Matson et al. 2012). Its biology is poorly known. It is terrestrial, and burrows through the leaf litter under and along decaying logs and tree roots. The species appears to require a deep layer of litter, as it was not found in similar forest without deep litter at a slightly lower elevation (2,800 m). At 2,900 m, nightly frost slows decomposition of litter, while at 2,800 the litter layer is shallower due to warmer conditions (Reid 1997). Pregnant females were taken in May, with 1 to 3 embryos (mean of 1.8) (Carleton and Huckaby 1975). All individuals caught in December were non-reproductive (Reid 1997).
threats: This mouse is highly threatened due to intensive logging in its small range. Fire is also a potential threat because of the small size of its extent of occurrence. Climate change and/or a strong El Niño year, either of which could dry out the area, are other potential threats as the species requires wet leaf litter.
population: This species is common where it occurs (Matson et al. 2012).
range: This species occurs in Cerro Bobi, Guatemala (Matson et al. 2012). It is known only from the type locality and nearby vicinity (2,950 m) in the Huehuetenango Department, Guatemala, about 7 km northwest of Santa Eulalia, Yaiquich (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found from 2,900 to 3,000 m.
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Sierra de Cuchumatanes National Park, however, this park is rapidly being cut down and is not well protected. The species would benefit from an increased level of protection of its forest habitat.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 5,000 km², its habitat is severely fragmented, it has 4-5 locations and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: The biology, habitat and ecology of this species is poorly known  (Ceballos 2014). It has been found in pine-oak forests in the highest parts of its distribution and tropical subdeciduous forests in lower elevations (Baker and Womochel 1966).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss, primarily due to agriculture (Sanchez et al. 2005).These threats are currently increasing (Álvarez-Castañeda and Vázquez pers. comm.).
population: No population information is available for this species (Álvarez-Castañeda and Vázquez pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and occurs in the Pacific slopes of the Sierra Madre del Sur of Oaxaca, México (Musser and Carleton 2005, Sanchez et al. 2005, Ceballos 2014). It has an elevational range of between 700 and 1,900 m (Huckaby 1980).
conservationActions: There are currently no conservation measures in place for this species (Álvarez-Castañeda and Vázquez pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse occurs in semideciduous, secondary forest along streams. It is also found in rocky thorn scrub, evergreen and highland forest, coffee groves, and brush (Reid 1997). It climbs well but is largely terrestrial in habits. It does not swim and is reluctant to enter water. It is shy and secretive and is seldom seen at night, even where abundant. Stomachs of 27 individuals from Chiapas, Mexico contained 67% arthropods (primarily spiders, ants, crickets, and beetles), 23% seeds (Solanaceae and Compositae), and 10% green plant material (Alvarez et al. 1984). Caches of coffee beans and others seeds were found under rocks, logs, and near burrows in San Luis Potosi, Mexico (Dalquest 1953). Its burrows are located among the roots of trees, under logs, or in open areas of the forest floor. Breeding can take place year-round, although populations in seasonally dry areas are usually nonreproductive early in the dry season. Litter size is usually 2 to 3 young, mean 2.5 (Reid 1997).
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: It is widespread and often common or abundant (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs in México, along the Atlantic coast from south San Luis Potosí to the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and along the Pacific coast, from the Guerrero-Oaxaca border to central Chiapas; the upper foothills and middle elevation mountains in Guatemala, through El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua, to the highlands of Costa Rica and west Panamá (Chiriquí region) (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from lowlands to 3,000 m (usually 600 to 1,500 m) (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It is found in protected areas in Mexico and parts of Central America. Further research into its taxonomy is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 37 km² and its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 10 km², all individuals occur in only two locations, and there is a continuing decline in the number of mature individuals. This species is very close to qualifying as Critically Endangered; were it to be eliminated from either island or shown to have severely fragmented populations it would be reassessed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species occurs along canyons with ground vegetation and cacti of several varieties, including cardon (Pachycereus pringlei) and cholla (Cholla sp). Specimens collected on San Diego Island were caught on a rocky hillside with very little vegetation, only a few patches of bush, and some bush grass among rocks. Most rodents on Santa Cruz Island were collected in the bottom of canyons; very few were found in slopes and hills (Alvarez-Castañeda 2001). The dominant vegetation on San Diego Island includes banderita (Bouteloua radicosa), chaparro amargoso (Castela peninsularis), Euphorbia magdalenae, zacate (Heteropogon contortus), matacora (Jatropha cuneata), and cholla (Opuntia cholla). The vegetation on Santa Cruz Island includes torote (Bursera microphylla), campanilla (Jacquemontia abutiloides), matacora (Jatropha cuneata), and tacote (Viguiera deltoidea).
threats: Feral cats (Felis catus) are present on Santa Cruz Island (Alvarez-Castañeda 2001), but are not yet present on San Diego Island.
population: This species is restricted to only two small islands and the population is sparse (Walker 2006, Alvarez 2001).
range: This species occurs on two small islands of the coast of Baja California, Isla Santa Cruz, and Isla Santa Cruz, Mexico (Walker 2006).
conservationActions: This species is listed as threatened in Mexico (NOM-059-ECOL-2001).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found primarily in subtropical deciduous forest, riparian forest, and agricultural areas.
threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
population: This species is relatively common in suitable habitat.
range: This species occurs in the coastal lowlands of Jalisco and Colima, along Río Balsas to interior Michoacán, and in northernmost Guerrero, México (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: Part of this species' range occurs in protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in thorn scrub, forest edge, and clearings; it favours rocky areas with brush and scattered trees. It is found in stands of conifers but rarely enters mature broadleaf forest (Reid 1997). This species is nocturnal. Its preference for relatively open areas makes it easier to observe at night than related species. Stomachs of 11 individuals caught in Chiapas contained 91% athropods, 6% seeds, and 3% green plant material (Alvarez et al. 1984). Breeding can take place year-round; mean litter size is 2.3 young in Oaxaca, Mexico (Millar 1989).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is widespread and common (as Peromyscus levipes in Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs at higher elevations from south-east Hildalgo, central Veracruz, and central Guerrero to Oaxaca and Chiapas, México, south through the highlands of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras (Houseal et al. 1987, Schmidly et al. 1988, Bradley et al. 2000, Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are several protected areas within its range. There are no known conservation measures specific to this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be less than 500 km², it is only known from one location (the type locality) and it is threatened by deforestation within its range. Additionally, this species is not found in any protected areas. Lack of recent records and new localities of occurrence suggest the population is declining.
habitat: This species apparently occurs in montane forests. The type specimen was trapped in wet brush (Thomas and St. Leger 1926).
threats: The major threats are deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: It is rare, known only from one record (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is known only from its type locality in northern Peru: Goncha, Amazonas, at 2,591 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species does not occur in any protected area, but it could be present in Zona Protegida Alto Mayo (V. Pacheco pers. comm). Further surveys are needed into ecology, habitat requirements and conservation.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its tolerance of habitat modification, presumed large population, because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category and because it occurs in protected areas.
habitat: This species lives in montane forest and páramo habitats, in forest- dwelling form, but also in subtropical, temperate, and adjacent páramo vegetation (Anthony 1924, Tirira 2007).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: It is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Ecuador. It spans from Bolívar province in the south to Napo and Pichincha provinces in the north, at elevations from 1,800 to 4,500 m (Pacheco 2015). T. silvestris is a species with a very short range in distribution but is very common rodent in his distribution. The specimens from the Napo province in Ecuador are very old and could be confused regarding this locality, because the distribution of this species is only in the western slopes in the Andes (P. Moreno Cárdenas pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species occurs in one protected area (Antisana Ecological Reserve).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its tolerance of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits montane forests and páramo habitats, mainly in primary, secondary, and recently disturbed forests; habitats with moist mossy ground cover, fallen logs, and proximity to stands of Chusquea bamboo, in subalpine rainforest, in Polylepis thickets in the páramo, and in the shrubby páramo/forest ecotone (Barnett 1999; Voss 2003). It is mainly terrestrial, and uses microhabitat such as moss, banks of small streams, wet leaf litter under shrubs and branches, under clumps of grass, and low, moss- covered trees (Voss 2003). Nests have been found under root masses and among dead leaves of Espeletia shrubs, at heights between 15 cm and 1.5 m. A female with an embryo was captured at the end of June (Brito et al. 2012).
threats: Some populations are affected by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: It is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.). In northern Ecuador populations are common (Brito et al. 2015).
range: This species is endemic of the northern Andes; it occurs from southern Colombia (Nariño department) to central Ecuador (Azuay, Bolívar, Carchi, Mantufar, Chimborazo, Napo, and Pichincha departments), north of the Huancabamba Deflection (Voss 2003). Altitudinal distribution is between 2,000 and 4,300 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in serveral protected areas (D. Tirira and M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because it has a small extent of occurrence (8,933 km²), it is found in 8-10 locations and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to deforestation for illicit crops, and agriculture and potential burning of paramo habitats at higher elevations.
habitat: The species dwells in montane forest and paramos. Individuals had been found in a tropical cloud (wet) forest remnant over steep hillsides, surrounded by open pasture or planted to eucalyptus and Caribbean pine (A.L. Gardner pers. comm). There is no other information available on the ecology, population biology, or behaviour of this species (Pacheco 2015).
threats: Deforestation for illicit crops (e.g., coca), and agriculture is an important threat to this species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm). Burning of paramo habitats at higher elevations could also be a potential threat.
population: Little is known about this species. It was collected only in small numbers although potential habitat has not been adequately surveyed (M. Gómez-Laverde and V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is endemic to Colombia; it occurs only in and around the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, in extreme northern Colombia, from 2,000 to 3,600 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park although this is not effectively protected (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm). Further surveys are required on the ecology and population status of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable, because its extent of occurrence is less than 20,000 km², number of localities less than 10, and the its habitat is continuing to decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat.
habitat: The species’ habitat includes dense forests on the upper slopes of the páramo, cloud forest, and evergreen forest within the Lower Montane very humid forest. Individuals were found living among galleries naturally formed under mossy roots, logs, and debris, at the bases of trees and among tree roots, often in bamboo thickets, in thick growths of shrubs and tree ferns, on mossy tree limbs, in litter on stream banks, near streams, also in clearings used for pasture and crops (Osgood 1912, Handley 1976). Individuals are nocturnal, terrestrial to scansorial, solitary, and omnivorous. They feed on seeds and fruits (Linares 1998). A large list of ectoparasites is known.
threats: Although the species occurs in a national park, the area is threatened by deforestation, and agriculture.
population: The species is rare.
range: This species occurs in the Paramo de Tama in the extreme north of Cordillera Oriental, east Colombia, and the extreme south of Cordillera de Mérida, west Venezuela (Pacheco 2015). It occurs above 2,000 m.
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: The extent of occurrence for the species is greater than 20,000 km2, it is locally common and no major threats exists. Listed as Least Concern.
habitat: The habitats of this species are dense humid forests, and páramo vegetation. Specimens had been found under rocks in grassland or scrub vegetation, in fragmented or continuous forest, near streams, on riverine vegetation or on sandy banks (Thomas 1927, Leo and Romo 1992).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is locally common to rare (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs on the eastern slope of the Andes mountains in central and northern Peru, from Junín to San Martín departments. Its elevation range extents from 2,430 to 3,850 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species has been recorded in Yanachala Chemillén National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The habitat of this species include montane forests with low or high canopies, where trees reach 15 to 20 m and are covered with orchids, bromeliads, tree ferns, lichens, and mosses. Specimens have been collected on the ground in pristine humid montane forests and in disturbed forests near crops (V. Pacheco, unpubl. Data, Beltrán and Salinas 2010, C. Jiménez, pers. comm.).
threats: The major threats are deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is locally common (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Peru. It occurs in the eastern slope of the Andes in northern and central Peru. Its distribution range includes the departments of Amazonas, San Martín, and Huánuco, from the elevations of 2,280 to 3,350 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs close to (but has not been recorded in) the Zona Reservada Cordillera Colán, a protected area (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
