rationale: The species is listed as Least Concern because there is no continuing decline, no known fragmentation, no extreme fluctuations, and the number of locations has not been verified. This species is also locally common and protected in Otishi National Park in Peru.
habitat: This species lives in Elfin forest patches dominated by Polylepis (Rosaceae), Weinmannia (Cunoniaceae), and Chusquea bamboos (Poaceae) in places with deep moss (Ruelas and Britos 2017).
threats: No major threats currently exist because the species is protected in the Otishi National Park, but agriculture and deforestation could present a potential, future threat.
population: This species is locally common (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is only known from its type locality in southern Peru, Junin, Cordillera Vilcabamba, at 3,350 m (Pacheco 2015). Known in this location in Southern Peru. This needs to be verified by the Ecuadorian records from Tapichalaca Biological Reserve (Ruelas and Brito 2017).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Otishi National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, occurrence in one protected area, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species lives in humid upper montane forest, in pristine forests and in disturbed forests near crops.  Forests where trees are slender, reach heights of 10 to 15 m, and are densely covered by orchids, bromeliads, ferns, lichens, and mosses, and stands of Chusquea bamboo, and near crops at high relative abundance (Pacheco et al. 2007, Beltrán and Salinas 2010). It was collected on the ground and in tree branches (V. Pacheco, unpubl. data; Salas et al. 2013). It was described as a generalist species, since its diet included a high frequency of plant material (intact seeds), arthropods and mycorrhizal spores (Noblecilla and Pacheco 2012, Sahley et al. 2015).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: It is locally frequent (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Peru. It dwells montane forests in the Andes of central Peru from the departments of Huánuco south to Ayacucho. the altitudinal distribution is restricted from 2,050 to 3,673 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in one protected area, Yanachaga Chemillén National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern since it occurs in an area of extensive, suitable habitat which does not appear to be under threat, has a presumed large population, and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The habitat of this species correspond to humid montane forests (or Yungas) of northern Peru. Specimens have been found on the ground among dense shrubs and on the forest floor. Individuals with reproductive traits were registered from late July and August (dry season) (Pacheco 2015). This species is terrestrial and nocturnal.
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is locally common to frequent (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is restricted to northwestern Peru, west of the Río Marañón, in the departments of Piura, Cajamarca, La Libertad and Lambayeque, with an elevation range of 1,198 to 3,100 m (Pacheco 2015). This species occurs in the northwest Peru (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species is possibly occurs in Santuario Tabaconas-Namballe, however, this is currently unconfirmed (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because its area of occupancy (AOO) is suspected to be around 2,000 km² as it occupies a narrow band of high elevation habitats currently being deforested for lumber and agriculture. There is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat and number of locations. Almost qualifies as threatened under criterion B2. Although it occurs in several protected areas, these are only a portion of the former range.
habitat: This rodent has been trapped along streams with dense scrubby undergrowth broken by montane meadows (Eisenberg and Redford, 1999). The habitat described in the field notes of J. L. Patton (MVZ archives) correspond to elfin forest patches, specifically very wet bunch grass on gently sloping ground, steep slopes dominated by melastome shrubs and ferns, with a dense understory of grasses, elfin forest patches composed of bamboo thickets and large, moss and epiphyte covered trees. All of the specimens were found on the ground. Post-lactating females were captured after the local rainy season. It is possibly arboreal (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is locally frequent (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to the montane forest or Yungas of southeastern Peru, in Cusco department. It lives from 2,774 to 4,270 m of elevational range (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Otishi and Manu National Parks (V. Pacheco pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little is known of the behaviour of this species, but it is probably similar to other members of the genus. This species lives in cloud forests, in disturbed secondary forest sections of primary/secondary cloud forest mosaics, in shrubby paramo/forest ecotone, in subalpine rainforest, in primarily alpine grassland with patches of Polylepis forests, and secondary and riparian forests (Barnett 1999, Lee et al. 2011). Individuals have been captured most commonly on the ground, along the wet margins of small streams, in narrow trails, under mossy logs, or in holes under the roots of trees, and on mossy branches of small trees (Voss 2003). It prefers areas with abundant shrubby vegetation and little arborescent canopy development (Barnett 1999). Its diet includes seeds and insects (Jarrín- V. 2001). Females with embryos (3) and lactating were captured during the local dry season (Lee et al. 2011, Barnett 1999). The species was considered common in Ecuador (Tirira 2007) but rare in Colombia (Gómez- Laverde et al. 2008). It is terrestrial, and is frequent along the wet margins of small streams, also occurs near narrow trails through mossy debris and damp leaf litter (Voss 2003).
threats: We consider the species is threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture (V. Pacheco and C. Barriga pers. comm).
population: This species is frequent and sometimes common in moist habitats at high altitudes in Ecuador (D. Tirira pers. comm.). In Colombia it may be rare (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
range: This species can be found in the northern Andes through Colombia (from Antioquia in the north), Ecuador, and the north of the Huancabamba Deflection in northern Peru (Voss 2003, Pacheco 2003). It inhabits Andean forests and paramos from 1,300 to 3,800 m of elevation (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas in Ecuador (Tirira in prep.).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened, while its extent of occurrence (EOO) is larger than 20,000 km², the species has specific habitat requirements and its area of occupancy (AOO) is likely much smaller than the current estimated EOO. Additionally, the species does not occur in any protected areas, is known from less than 10 locations, and its habitat is threatened by deforestation and fragmentation. Further survey work is needed to properly assess this species extinction risk.
habitat: The habitats of this species include páramo thickets, the edge of the timberline in the dry forests of the Río Marañón valley, and dense and tall shrub habitats on rocky substrates, near rivers or streams (Thomas 1900; Osgood 1914; Pacheco 2015). Thomasomys praetor is nocturnal, terrestrial and perhaps arboreal.
threats: Some populations of this species are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is considered rare (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is endemic to Peru. It inhabits the western watershed and inter- Andean valleys of the northern Andes of Peru, between the Huancabamba Deflection and the Marañón River, from 2,050 to 4,000 m. It is distributed along Ancash, Cajamarca and La Libertad departments of Peru (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species does not occur in any protected area (V. Pacheco pers. comm). Further surveys are needed on ecology, habitat requirements and conservation.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in primary and secondary forests, preferring forested areas such as dense grass and reeds, shrubs, and trees (Barnett 1999) in subalpine rainforest (Voss 2003), temperate forest, or paramo (Tirira 2007). In Venezuela, specimens were caught in a tree near a stream in cloud forest and in the lower montane very humid forest (Handley 1976). In Ecuador, it was trapped in well- worn paths through mats of moss and liverworts on horizontal tree limbs, and on the ground at the edge of a stream, among tall grass in a clearing, and in a runway through dense mats of moss (Voss 2003). In Peru, it has been collected only in continuous and dense forest (Leo and Romo 1992, Patton 1987, Salas et al. 2013, V. Pacheco unpubl. data). Barnett (1999), Eisenberg and Redford (1999), Jarrín- V. (2001), Brito et al. (2012), and Salas et al. (2013) reported arboreality with nests built in trees at heights up to 6-7 m. The diet of this species consists on fruits, seeds, other plant material, and insects (Eisenberg and Redford 1999), with a preference for Passiflora fruits (Passifloraceae; Barnett 1999). It appears to be specialized on fruits. Sahley et al. (2015) found a high frequency of intact seeds on their faeces. Reproductive characteristics were noted in males in September (Barnett 1999), and embryo counts have been reported of two to three (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). The species may be either rare or difficult to capture (Barnett 1999).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, agriculture, and fragmentation which occurs across its distribution range (Pacheco and Gómez-Laverde 2008).
population: It is not as abundant as other species in the genus. Its population is declining (Pacheco and Gómez-Laverde 2008). In Ecuador it is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.).
range: This species is widely distributed along the Andean forests, from western Venezuela (Linares 1998), through Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, to west-central Bolivia (Musser and Carleton 2005), from 1,460 to 3,850 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 19,400 km², there is a lack of new records and new localities, and its habitat is threatened. This species is known from just one location in an area where illicit crops (e.g., coca) are a threat to its natural habitats. More information is needed on its range, occurrence in protected areas, and the effects of agricultural activities on this species.
habitat: This species is found in moist montane habitats including forest and paramo (Delgado et al. 2008). Nothing else is known regarding its habitat and ecology.
threats: The spread of illicit crops across the known range is a potential threat, but the effects on the species are unknown (Delgado et al. 2008).
population: Nothing is known of populations of this species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm).
range: This species occurs in the northern part of the western Andes in Colombia, in the departments of Antioquia and Risaralda (Pacheco 2015). It is known only from three localities with an elevation range from 2,800 m to 3,800 m (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
conservationActions: There are two protected areas within the potential range of this species but its presence there has not been confirmed. Further studies are required on the habitat, ecology and distribution of this species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 17,340 km², it is known to occur in fewer than 10 locations, and the extent of its habitat is decreasing. Currently it is known from only a single location that is threatened by conversion of habitat to agriculture.
habitat: This species’ habitats are grassy paramo, shrubby páramo/forest ecotone, grassy glades surrounded by forest, and deep inside subalpine rainforest. Individuals had been captured on the ground, along rabbit trails or runways through dense grass or low herbs, in runways through moss or damp litter, under mossy debris, at the bases of mossy trees, or along the wet margins of small streams (Voss 2003).
threats: The major threats are deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is frequently captured but only at a single location (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is known only from the Cordillera Oriental in the Ecuadorean provinces of Carchi, Pichincha, and Napo, around the altitude of 3,380 and 3,800 m (Voss 2003, Arcos et al. 2007). This species is very likely present in Colombia (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs close to two ecological protected areas: Antisana and Cayambe-Coca Ecological Reserves (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: Thomasomys macrotis is assessed as Least Concern because it occurs in a national park and there is no evidence of major threats affecting this species.
habitat: This species co-occurs with Thomasomys apeco (Gardner and Romo 1993). It inhabits upper montane elfin forest, in rocky areas or in grasslands near fragmented forests (Leo and Romo 1992).
threats: No major threats currently exist because the species is protected in the Rio Abiseo National Park.
population: This species is rare (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is restricted to the north-central Peruvian Andes, around Parque Nacional Río Abiseo in San Martín department, from 3,250 to 3,380 m (Pacheco 2015).  PERU: San Martín, 24 km NE of Pataz, Pampa del Cuy, Parque Nacional Río Abiseo (USNM 567243), Puerta del Monte, ca. 30 km NE of Los Alisos (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Rio Abiseo National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm).

rationale: The species is only known from one highly restricted location (Wilson et al. 2017). Although the EOO is less than 20,000 km2 and there is one location, this species does not meet another condition indicating that there is some sort of decline or extreme fluctuating populations. There are no statistics on population size. Therefore the species is assessed as Least concern.
habitat: This species inhabits upper montane forests and paramo-like habitats, near forest borders. Microhabitats include logs, streams in isolated patch of elfin forest, in  runways in wet pampa habitat, the surrounding of small shallow streams, and continuous forest. Individuals may be terrestrial or arboreal, and seem to breed in the dry season (Leo and Gardner 1993).
threats: No major threats currently exist because the species is protected in the Rio Abiseo National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
population: This species is apparently rare (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: It is known only from the type locality and the immediately surrounding area, in north central Peru, San Martín department, near Pataz, from 3,200 to 3,380 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits subalpine rainforest, paramo, minimally disturbed quenoa forests, elfin forest, bogs, and swampy cloud forest. Individuals have been trapped on the ground, among mossy boulders in an old lava flow, in areas with dense canopy and little groundcover but deep moss, and in dense and isolated clumps of composite bushes on exposed slopes covered with tussock grass (Barnett 1999, Voss 2003, Lee et al. 2011). Reproduction evidence was found in August, during the dry season (Barnett 1999). It is terrestrial. Five individuals were taken in Papallacta area in 1978; three were trapped among mossy boulders in an old lava flow that impounds the Rio Tambo to form a lake and two were taken on the ground in Subalpine Rain Forest in the valley of the Rio Papallacta (Voss 2003).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation and habitat fragmentation.
population: It is rare to uncommon. The Thomasomys cinnameus reported in 1988 was the first report since the original description based on a single specimen collected at 2,438 m near Hacienda San Francisco, Provincia Tunguragua, Ecuador (Voss 2003).
range: The distribution of this species comprises the Colombian and Ecuadorean Andes, in paramo and montane forests, from Antioquia in Colombia until Azuay in Ecuador. Altitude ranges from about 2,400 to 3,800 m (Pacheco 2015). It also occurs in Carchi province (D. Tirira pers. comm.) and southern Colombia, Nariño Department, Galeras Volcano (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
conservationActions: In Ecuador, this species occurs in two protected areas and close to other two (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable due to lack of recent records and new localities of occurrence which suggest the population is declining. Additionally, this population is only known from the type locality and may be subject to a future threat that could drive the species toward extinction. It does not occur in any protected areas.
habitat: Its habitat corresponds to the upper limit of forest, including rolling grassy meadows with scrub trees on some of the ridges and with thickets of brush on some of the slopes (Anthony 1923).
threats: Deforestation, and fragmentation are among the major threats that this species is facing (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
population: This is a rare species (D. Tirira pers. comm).
range: This species is known only from southern Ecuador, in Bestión, Azuay (Pacheco 2015) at 3,078 m.
conservationActions: No conservation measures are known to be in place for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its tolerance of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is poorly known. It occurs in high elevation elfin forest (Luna and Pachero 2002). Specimens have been captured along small mountain streams, in a valley with thick shrubbery and low stunted trees, and in open paramo with an abundance of low shrubbery and no trees (Anthony 1923). This species is considered terrestrial and nocturnal. It feeds on seeds and insects (Jarrín- V. 2001).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture. The forests of the Cordillera de Chilla (type locality) have suffered considerable fragmentation, large amounts of forests have been replaced by pastures and pine plantations (Brito in prep.)
population: It is uncommon.
range: This species is distributed from central Ecuador to northern Peru, in montane forest and paramo habitats of the western slope of the Andes Mts., from 2,750 to 3,350 m (Pacheco 2015, Brito in prep.).
conservationActions: It occurs in two protected areas, Santuario de Vida Silvestre Tabaconas-Lavaye in Peru and Bosque Protector Cashca Totaras in Ecuador (V. Pacheco and D. Tirira pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its abundance within its restricted distribution, its presumed large population, and because its habitat is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits subalpine rainforest and upper montane rainforest. Individuals have been captured in dense secondary vegetation, on the ground, in runways through wet leaf litter and mossy debris, beneath mossy logs, branches, or roots, and inside the trunk of a hollow tree (Voss 2003). In the vicinity of Papallacta, 17 specimens of Thomasomys erro were collected. Of these, 11 were taken in dense secondary vegetation, five in Subalpine Rain Forest, and one in Upper Montane Rain Forest. All recorded captures were on the ground (Voss 2003). Seven individuals has been collected in the Cordillera de la Virgen Negra, but their identification needs to be confirmed (Boada 2008).
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: It is rare. The Thomasomys erro reported in 1980 was the first report since the original description in the 1920s (Voss 2003).
range: This species is endemic to Ecuador, restricted to the Cordillera Oriental of north- central Ecuador, in Napo department. It distribution ranges across the elevations of 1,900 and 3,600 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Sumaco National Park and close to other two protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because, although a large part of its range occurs within protected areas, it has a moderately small extent of occurrence (EOO =  25,971 km², it is known from no more than 10 locations, and from areas where habitat availability and quality have declined. Therefore, it meets some, but not all, conditions for criterion B. Given its small distribution, it may be particularly vulnerable to threats of deforestation, and further research of threats and its population status is needed.
habitat: This species inhabits moist habitats and cloud forest habitats, such as the lower montane very humid forest (Eisenberg and Redford 1999; Handley 1976). Individuals have been found under a mossy log on damp ground and on a log over a small stream (Handley 1976). This mouse is nocturnal, terrestrial to arboreal, solitary, and omnivorous. Its diet consists of small fruits, plant material, and insects (Linares 1998).
threats: Habitat loss is likely a threat for this species. In the Mérida Andes, high-elevation habitat is increasingly taken over by agriculture, and mining may pose a future risk (Chacón-Moreno et al. 2021). Deforestation for pasture and cultivation has also been recorded in Sierra Nevada National Park where this species occurs (Gómez and Molina 2008). The type locality is now an urban area (B. Rivas pers. comm.).
population: Thomasomys vestitus is said to be a rare species (J. Ochoa pers. comm.), but little else is known about its population.
range: This species is endemic to the Mérida Andes in western Venezuela, at elevations between 1,600 and 2,500 m asl (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in Sierra Nevada National Park; it is likely to occur in other protected areas. Further surveys on distribution and ecology are required.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its relatively wide distribution. Now that Thomasomys vulcani includes T. rhoadsi, the extent of occurrence and number of locations have increased.
habitat: This species inhabits páramo, montane forests, and both subtropical and temperate forest (Castro and Román 2000, Tirira 2007, Brito et al. 2015). They prefer habitats in montane wet forest (P. Moreno- Cardenas pers. comm.). Specimens have been captured on rocky wooded slopes, with burrows below the surface of the soil and debris (Stone 1914), in disturbed plant fences, and more abundant in undisturbed forests (Pozo- R. et al. 2006). T. vulcani is terrestrial.
threats: The major threats are deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is uncommon (D. Tirira pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Ecuador. It is found in the north-central Andes, in Napo and Pichincha provinces, from 1,400 to 4,500 m (Pacheco 2015). However, the record in the Napo province could be wrong and belong to a T. fumeus; therefore the distribution of this species is only in the western slopes of the Andes in northern Ecuador (P. Moreno-Cárdenas pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species does not occur in any protected area (V. Pacheco pers. comm.). Further surveys are needed on ecology, habitat requirements and conservation.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in shrubs, in Chilean matorral.
threats: There are no major threats for this species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in central Chile; limits unknown (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in grasslands and is herbivorous.
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: It is a common species.
range: It is recorded in south Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul), north Argentina (Provincia de Entrerios) and Uruguay.
conservationActions: It occurs in several proteced areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: In Salta province, Argentina, this species is limited to transitional forest, occurring on very low mountains in the central part of the province, but it also may occur in drier portions of the subtropical forest. It was trapped in thick grass along road cuts and from areas of second growth (Mares et al. 1981). Anderson (1997), states that in general the limited data available for Bolivia fits with the habitats described in Argentina by Mares et al. (1981). In Bolivia, it is also known from pre-Puna grassland and Tucumano Boliviano forest habitats.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: It is an uncommon species, however, it can be locally common (i.e. in portions of Bolivia).
range: This species occurs on the eastern slopes of Andes in south-central Bolivia and northwest Argentina (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 600 to 3,700 m.
conservationActions: It is present in at least three protected areas in Bolivia and at least one national park in Argentina.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in wet Chaco, shrubby areas.
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: It is an abundant species.
range: This species occurs in south-central Bolivia, western Paraguay, and nearby Brazil, south through western Argentina to northern Santa Cruz Province (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is found in several protected areas in Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution including several protected areas, its presumed large population, and because its population is not believed to be in decline at present.
habitat: This is a nocturnal species found in a wide variety of habitats including forest, semi-desert, dry and moist savanna or woodland. It is often found in rocky areas. It is unclear as to whether the species has a single or two to three young in a litter.
threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
population: It is an uncommon species.
range: This species is known from fragmented localities across eastern Africa in Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. It occurs from sea level to 3,300 m asl.
conservationActions: Further research in to the ecological requirements of the species is needed. Its range includes several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because within its relatively large range its area of occupancy (AOO) is suspected to be less than 500 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and the extent of its forest habitat is declining. Ongoing fragmentation and deforestation threaten the species habitat. Deforested land is being reforested with non-native species, prohibiting the return of Wilfredomys oenax. There is no information about their population size. Also the species is recognized as naturally rare although the effort of capture has increased in the last ten years. The natural habitat has been  decreasing in the last  few years.
habitat: In Uruguay the species is restricted to patches of subtropical woodland with dense vegetation; they have also been caught in trees at night. This species is a lowland forest species, particularly susceptible to deforestation. In Brazil no information has been produced about habitat and ecology of this species (Vieira pers. comm.).
threats: The major threats are deforestation across the entire distributional range, which is currently highly fragmented. Timber extraction for the tobacco industry and replanting with exotic species monocultures (acacia, eucalyptus, pine) contributes to this issue. The deforestation of gallery forest on southern of distribution has enlarged the threats over the species (Vieira pers. comm).
population: This species is considered rare in Rio Grande do Sul, known from very few specimens, with two new records in Brazil for last 40 years. The populations status was never assessed (Vieira pers. comm).
range: This species occurs from south Brazil to north and central Uruguay (Musser and Carleton 2005). Recently, the species was rediscovered in south of Brazil with one specimen found dead, probably hit by a car, near the type locality, São Lourenço do Sul, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil (−31.347° −52.063°), and another collected at Parque Estadual do Espinilho (−30.185° −57.533°) (Machado et al. 2015). The species has two old records in southeastern Brazil, one from Curitiba (Ávila-Pires 1960) and other from Ubatuba, São Paulo (Brandão 2015) without new records for more than 50 years. In Uruguay the species was registered on the north and northeast, mainly associated with gallery and canyon forest (González et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It is found in some protected areas. Further efforts are need on the taxonomy and range of this species.

rationale: Although this species is known mainly from isolated records from a large area, it is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species is found in lower montane forest, and has only been recorded from primary forest on the eastern Andean slopes. It is nocturnal. It has been sometimes recorded in human dwellings adjacent to forest (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
threats: There do not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: The species is rare, perhaps due to its arboreal habits (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the east slopes of Peruvian Andes; its limits are unresolved (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 1,500 to 2,000 m (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas, including Manu National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be in decline.
habitat: This arboreal species is present in tropical rainforests (Musser and Carleton 2005), including terra firme and varzea forest (Eisenberg and Redford 1999). Its nests are located near the ground (Hershkovitz 1960) and its litter size ranges from two to four young.
threats: There are no major threats known.
population: This rodent apparently is uncommon, but widely distributed in Rio Jurua (Patton et al. 2000). In Central America it is uncommon (Reid 1997), and in Venezuela it is rare (Lord 1999).
range: This species occurs in tropical rainforests from south-western Costa Rica to central Brazil, including Guianas, Trinidad and Tobago; east Andean slopes of west-central Colombia to south-central Peru and into Bolivia (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas throughout the range. This species needs further taxonomic research.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This mouse is arboreal, solitary and has nocturnal activity. It is found in mature and secondary rainforest, dry forest, savannah, scrub, gardens and plantations. It feeds on fruit and green seeds and uses all levels of the forest, including occasionally the ground. It is most numerous in dense viny vegetation. It nests in tree holes, in dense masses of vines or epiphytes, and among palm leaves. It often invades houses in the forest and seems particularly fond of thatched roofs (Emmons and Feer 1997).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is often common (Emmons and Feer 1997).
range: This species is widespread through much of Bolivia, northern Paraguay, and west central Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 200 to 2,100 m.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is nocturnal, arboreal and occurs in tropical and subtropical rainforest and dry forest. This rodent eats on seeds and green fruits (Linares 1998).
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: It may be rare but is widespread in many localities (Linares 1998).
range: This species occurs in lowland Coastal Range and slopes of Cordillera de Mérida of north and west Venezuela (see Linares 1998), west to Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta of northeast Colombia, perhaps including the slopes of Cordillera Oriental (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 600 to 1,800 m in Venezuela (Linares 1998).
conservationActions: The species probably occurs in several protected areas in Venezuela.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it does not currently meet the thresholds for a threatened category. It could be listed in a threatened category or as Near Threatened in future assessments because although it is relatively widespread, it is rare and has experienced extensive habitat loss due to expanding agriculture, and its range is highly fragmented making it close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B. More accurate estimates of its extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, and population trends are needed.
habitat: Neotoma phenax has only been found in desert scrub and pine-oak forest habitats (Ceballos 2014). It burrows in the shrubs and short trees along rivers (Burt 1938). Within the state of Sinaloa it will nest in shrubs, on the ground, and in columnar cacti and thorn trees (Birney and Jones 1972). Persimmon fruits are considered an important part of their diet (Burt 1938).
threats: It is estimated that 60% to 70% of this species' range has been converted to agriculture (primarily for tomato and onion crops). This species' distribution is restricted and is being threatened by deforestation (G. Ceballos, pers. comm.).
population: This species is rare.
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and ranges extends down the Pacific coast from Guaymas, Sonora, to El Dorado located in the central region of Sinaloa (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm) and is considered as of Special Protection (SEMARNAT 2010).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 17,510 km², all individuals are known to occur in fewer than ten locations, and there is likely a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to flooding as a result of a recently constructed dam.
habitat: This woodrat is poorly known. It is found in the valley bottoms, in tropical deciduous forest. The species resides in riparian vegetation and along sandbanks and rocky environments. In addition, it also inhabits xeric scrubland, and has been recorded from 938 m to 1,904 m (Matson and Baker 1986).
threats: In 2007, a very large dam (El Cajon) was built downstream from this woodrat's primary range. It is expected that inundation of the rivers caused by this dam will result in extensive habitat loss for this species. This species has restricted distribution and scarce sightings (Ceballos 2014).
population: This species is not common.
range: This species is only know to occur in a small area of the west-central Mexican Altiplane. It has been recorded to occur in the states of Jasico and Zacatecas (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures underway.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Habitat preferences are similar to other members of the Neotoma group, preferring areas with dense vegetative cover, including chaparral, coastal scrub, and woodlands (Carraway and Verts 1991). Like other woodrats, N. macrotis builds large houses of sticks, bark, leaves and man-made objects discovered while foraging. Found on the ground, in trees and on hill slopes. Houses average one meter in diameter by one meter tall and consist of several chambers for food storage and nesting. These stick houses are typically inhabited by a single adult or female with pups.
threats: As a specialist in areas of dense vegetative cover, the Big-eared Woodrat is especially susceptible to habitat clearing caused by fire and livestock grazing.
population: Population densities are known from descriptions of N. fuscipes which is significantly more abundant in areas of dense vegetative cover, with estimates of 35 individuals per hectare, compared to 5 individuals/ha in open areas (Cranford 1999).
range: It is found from central and eastern California (United States) south into northwestern Baja California, Mexico (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: No conservation actions are known to this species. It probably occurs in a number of protected areas within its range.

rationale: This species is endemic to the United States of America, where it has a large range. However, it is a microhabitat specialist, dependent on rocky areas, and it has experienced declines in many parts of its range with a significant percentage of its historical range no longer occupied. Although quantitative data supporting the contention that this species has declined 30% over a 10 year period are not available, it is easy to argue by inference of the shrinking of its overall distribution and the loss of important populations throughout its range that it is very probable that this level of decline has occurred.The species has undergone precipitous range wide declines, being extirpated from New York state and with entire populations lost in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Maryland, and Indiana (Wilson and Ruff 1999). It is a specialist of talus and boulder field habitats and is largely distributed in metapopulations. These declines have serious implications for the maintenance of gene flow and dispersal.Numerous technical documents since the 1999 publication show continued declines in range and abundance. The state of West Virginia State Wildlife Action Plan (2015 West Virginia State Wildlife Action Plan; wvdnr.gov) lists Neotoma magister as a Priority 1 Species in Greatest Need of Concern. The NatureServe codes list the species as S3 (subnational Vulnerable) and G3/G4 (globally Vulnerable to Apparently Secure).The website of the Pennsylvania Game Commission focused on this species (Allegheny Woodrat; pa.gov - accessed 11/03/2024) lists it as threatened in Pennsylvania, due to loss of habitat, resources (chestnut and oaks), and disease (Raccoon roundworm parasite). There has also been loss of its preferred habitat resulting in increased fragmentation of metapopulations.The state of Virginia has similar concerns, listing it as a Species of Concern with a Moderate Conservation Level and placing it in its listing of Mammals of Greatest Conservation Need (Wildlife Action Plan | Virginia DWR - accessed 11/03/2024).This indicates declines and losses of populations throughout the range of the species. This species is listed as Near Threatened. Although it has a large range, it has experienced declines in many parts of its range with a significant percentage of its historical range no longer occupied. A reduction of close to 30% over the last ten years is suspected, making it close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2c. It is recommended that this species be assessed again within the next 3–4 years.
habitat: Typical habitat is rocky cliffs and talus slopes. These woodrats make midden mounds and stick piles among rocks, but secluded nest sites generally are not within stick houses (see Hayes and Harrison 1992).Throughout its range, this species is associated with extensive rocky areas such as outcrops, cliffs, talus slopes with boulders and crevices, and caves. It occasionally uses abandoned buildings but generally avoids humans. It generally occurs at higher elevations (to about 1,000 m) and is rarely found in lowlands or open areas. Because it is a habitat specialist, geographic range portrayals grossly exaggerate its true distribution. For example, the global range map shows approximately 40% of the land surface of Pennsylvania as included in Allegheny woodrat distribution, when in fact the Pennsylvania surface rock habitat currently occupied by woodrats covers less than one percent (0.77%) of the state (Hassinger pers. comm.).In southern New York, New Jersey, and adjacent Pennsylvania, woodrat habitat "consists of extensive boulder fields at the base of ridges with rock outcrops. These talus slopes consist of large boulders (10-20 ft. [3-6 m] across) piled in several layers. Neotoma lives among the cave like spaces formed by the piled boulders" (Sciascia 1990). Referring to the mountainous area of Pennsylvania, Merritt (1987) wrote, "limestone caves, rocky cliffs and accumulations of residual sandstone boulders marked by deep crevices with underground galleries represent favored habitat." Hall (1985) pointed out that good habitat is found "specifically at water gaps where cliff faces and boulder piles are usually abundant." Unpublished data from Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventories (eastern and western offices) make frequent references to woodrat occurrences in sandstone, limestone, or shale outcrops and cliffs, usually with crevices or abundant boulders; also solution caves and abandoned limestone quarries and mines. Associated forest is varied, including cove hardwoods, hemlock-birch, oak-pine, and various combinations of oaks, maples, hickories, beech, and yellow poplar (tulip-tree). Grape, mountain laurel, rhododendron and ferns are frequently mentioned. In West Virginia, woodrats are common in caves, rock shelters, outcrops with deep crevices, and riverbanks with an abundance of sandstone rocks and boulders. "In Maryland, this species is found predominately in cliffs, caves and rocky areas in the three western-most counties, and along cliffs of the Potomac River to the vicinity of Washington, D.C." (Feldhammer et al. 1984). In western Maryland "Pottsville Sandstone outcrops [provide] massive, blocky boulders and extensive cliffs with numerous crevices and miniature cave-like situations" (Thompson 1984). In Indiana, extant populations are restricted primarily to south-facing limestone bluffs on the Ohio River, where there are den sites in the rock and dense red-cedar (Cudmore 1983, Scott Johnson pers. comm.).In Kentucky, "cliffs with deep crevices, caves, or large boulders piled in such a way as to form numerous retreats and shelters are favored" (Barbour and Davis 1974). In Tennessee, "rocky cliffs, caves and fissures or tumbled boulders on the sides of mountains are the preferred habitat" (Hamilton 1943), and in North Carolina it is "rocky places and abandoned buildings at elevations above 3,000 ft (900 m)" (Adams 1987). Castleberry et al. (2001) suggest that forest clearcutting has minimal impact on woodrat movements, home range, and habitat use, as long as sufficient intact forest is retained adjacent to colonies. They mention, however, that harvesting methods that selectively remove important mast-producing tree species may represent the greatest threat from forest management.A large house of sticks, leaves, and miscellaneous debris is built, usually within a cave, crevice, or other well-protected place. This may be a mound like a muskrat house (typical construction in the range of other subspecies), but is more often open, giving the impression of a large bird's nest (Poole 1940). Outside diameter is about 35-60 cm (Patterson 1933) and the inner cavity is about 12 cm across (Poole 1940). The nest is lined with shredded bark of grape, red cedar, hemlock, or basswood, grass, fur, rootlets, and sometimes feathers (Poole 1940, Merritt 1987).Woodrats are basically solitary and unsociable, frequently fighting one another. Each lives alone in its house, except when breeding and raising young. Poole (1949) found "a great deal of individuality" in temperament, behaviour, food preferences, etc., among his captive Allegheny woodrats. When upset, woodrats may chatter their teeth or stomp their hind feet (Wiley 1980). Near the nests are found piles of sticks and trash called middens. Part of the materials found in woodrat houses and middens appears to be cached food in the form of nuts, seeds, berries, cuttings of vegetation, and mushrooms. But there may also be miscellaneous bits of trash, including rags, bits of metal, bones, pieces of glass, paper, etc. Newcombe (1930) and Poole (1940) compiled lists of such materials. The function of this compulsive collecting is unknown. Though solitary and territorial, woodrats most often occur in clusters due to patchiness of the rock outcrop, talus, and cave habitat, and conform to the concept of a metapopulation (Hassinger et al. 1996). Home ranges are small, 0.26-0.6 ha (Wright and Hall 1996); usually less than about 90 m across (Burt and Grossenheider 1976). Poole (1940) reported movements of 183 m and 92 m by two woodrats in Pennsylvania. Foraging movements, while often focused within rock habitat, may extend beyond the protection of rocks up to 160 m from the den site (Wright and Hall 1996). Den shifts tend be less than 100 m with a median of 40 m (Wright 1998), and woodrats, particularly females, often live their entire lives in the same outcrop (Feller, pers. obs., 1998). There are reports of large unidirectional movements of displaced woodrats, e.g., 1 km and 4 km (McGowan 1993), as well as naturally dispersing individuals, 0.3-1 km (McGowan 1993), 1 km (Feller, pers. obs., 1995), and up to 6 km (Wright pers. comm., 1998). While woodrats can travel long distances between patches, as distances increase, the chance of successful emigration between patches is likely to decrease, particularly in the absence of protective rock crevices. Barriers to dispersal are not clearly known, as woodrats have been documented to traverse seemingly inhospitable terrain, including roads, small streams, and small fields, though movements are largely within rock habitat (Feller, pers. obs.; Mengak pers. comm., 1998; Wright pers. comm., 1998). However, woodrats display unwary behaviour when crossing roads (Feller, pers. obs.), and road kills have been documented (Feller pers. obs.,1993; McGowan 1993). Predators include owls, skunks, weasels, foxes, raccoons, bobcats and large snakes. Humans have been killing woodrats for thousands of years - first for food, and much later out of prejudice, because of a resemblance to European rats. White-footed mice compete with woodrats for food (Rainey 1956), and in Indiana, opossums, raccoons and turkey vultures may compete for den sites (Cudmore 1983). Woodrats support many ecto- and endoparasites, including fleas, ticks, mites, chiggers, botflies, nematodes, and tapeworms (Cudmore 1985). Bubonic plague (Schwartz and Schwartz 1959) and rabies (Dowda et al. 1981) have been reported in wild woodrats. Woodrats are primarily vegetarian, and food preferences vary widely among individuals. Leaves, twigs, fruits, and seeds of many plants are eaten. They are primarily nocturnal.
threats: Possibly widespread deforestation and habitat fragmentation contributed to the initial decline of the species, isolating populations and eliminating dispersal and travel corridors (Sciascia pers. comm., 1994). Deforestation and associated reduction/elimination of food resources currently may be a threat to some local woodrat populations. Causes of the continuing decline are not yet fully understood, but some hypotheses have been offered. Probably the explanation lies in a combination of these and other factors that may differ locally in importance (Linzey 1990).Parasitism by the raccoon roundworm (Baylisascaris procyonis) has been identified as a significant cause of mortality and a probable major factor in the decline in several states (McGowan 1993; Hicks pers. comm., 1994; Johnson et al. 1997; LoGiudice 2000, 2006; Smyser et al. 2012b). Although rarely fatal to raccoons, infestation may cause cerebrospinal nematodiasis in other species and has caused declines in some populations (Kazacos 1983). New York released and monitored woodrats in formerly occupied areas and all the animals died (50 total, including the released adults and their progeny); 11 of the 13 recovered carcasses were infected by the roundworms (McGowan 1993; Hicks pers. comm., 1994). Stone observed that woodrat decline in New York coincided with a marked increase in raccoon numbers (Linzey 1990). Hayes (unpublished research proposal) suggested that woodrats may be especially vulnerable for two reasons: 1) among other novel items, woodrats are known to carry back to their nests the faeces of other animals, which might include raccoon scats contaminated with B. procyonis eggs, and 2) a "relatively long generation time increases the probability that individuals will become infested prior to reproduction." Both of these reasons recently have been documented (McGowan pers. comm., 1994). Additionally, McGowan (pers. comm., 1994) found that woodrats may colonize areas where an infected woodrat has recently died, thus perhaps maintaining spread of the parasite. Hall (1988) noticed a correlation between the spread of the gypsy moth (Lymantria dispar) and loss of woodrats in Pennsylvania. "There is a possibility that acorns make up a significant part of the food supply of the species in Pennsylvania. Acorns may be important as a winter food source since they can be stored for long periods of time. Studies conducted by the Pennsylvania Game Commission show that acorn production drops to zero for several years following defoliation. Gypsy moth infestation has resulted in considerable mortality of oaks, especially along the poorer soils of rocky ridge tops. These are the areas where many rocky sites are found, which are ideal woodrat habitats." In support of his argument, Hall noted that at three other sites where woodrats survived, other winter food sources were available. In a similar theory, McGowan (pers. comm., 1994) speculated that the 1930-1940s permanent loss of the American chestnut (Castanea dentata) may be a factor. This chestnut was extremely hardy and a bountiful producer of mast, and its previous distribution essentially mirrors the historic distribution of the woodrat. Loss of this stable and predictable food source may have led to the continuing woodrat population decline (LoGiudice 2006; Smyser et al. 2012b).Nawrot and Klimstra (1976) argued that the disappearance of a similar species, N. floridiana illinoensis, was likely due to two unusually severe winters. "Despite a tolerance of Neotoma to many environmental conditions, severe winter weather appears to be a major factor in sudden woodrat population declines. Fitch and Rainy (1956) recorded a drastic decline in Neotoma floridianaabundance in Kansas after two winters of below-average temperatures and prolonged snow and ice cover. Significantly, this decimated population was unable to make substantial gains and continued to decline gradually for several years." Weather also has been proposed as a factor in Neotoma magister decline, a view that is supported by the fact that the decline has been in the northern part of the range. Records in Pennsylvania and West Virginia over the past thirty years indicate "below normal" temperatures in critical months accompanying the observed shrinkage in range (Linzey pers. comm., 1994).In some areas, including caves popular with spelunkers, human disturbance has been implicated in the disappearance of woodrat populations (e.g., Kirkland 1986). These woodrats do seem to avoid areas of human habitation or heavy human use, but many sites where they have disappeared are remote and rarely visited by people. Habitat is generally inaccessible and undesirable for development, but strip mining of coal and limestone is a potential threat in many areas. Monty and Feldhamer (2002) stated that increased predation by great horned owls has been proposed as a threat, but owl predation seems highly unlikely as a reason for the decline. Populations often are small and isolated, hence highly susceptible to extirpation (Mengak pers. comm., 1994). disruption of genetic connectivity within metapopulations may also be a factor (LoGiudice 2006; Smyser et al. 2012b).
population: The total adult population size is unknown but likely is much larger than 10,000. Populations are localized and generally quite small (less than ten), apparently exhibiting a typical metapopulation structure. For example, in Pennsylvania the Allegheny Woodrat population consists of 78 disjunct metapopulations (Butchkoski 2004). This species is represented by a very large number of occurrences or subpopulations (probably more than 200). The number of occurrences or subpopulations with good viability probably is substantially smaller than the total number of extant occurrences.Populations in the northeastern United States have declined, while those in the southern portion of the range appear to have remained relatively stable. However, woodrats appear to be rare in Tennessee (Kennedy and Harvey 2001), and few specimens have been reported from Alabama, where present status is poorly known.The species has disappeared from Connecticut, New York, most of eastern Pennsylvania, and all but one site in New Jersey. This decline has apparently been occurring for many years. Early sources (e.g., Newcombe 1930) remarked on the woodrat's decreasing range and abundance, and the most recent reports from Connecticut date from the 1930s (Goodwin 1935). Such a decline might be expected in the wake of human settlement, but in recent decades, woodrat decline has been dramatic in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Maryland. Apparent extirpation has occurred in at least 100 sites in northern Virginia (Buhlmann pers. comm., 1992). Since the late 1960s woodrats in Pennsylvania have disappeared from sites where they once occurred, particularly in eastern and northwestern Pennsylvania; surveys of more than 360 sites from which woodrats have been reported yielded 20 metapopulations, but five of these metapopulation areas no longer support woodrats, and seven of them have fewer active colonies than in the past (C. Fergus, no date; www.pgc.state.pa.us, accessed April 2006). The species has disappeared from the southeastern portion of Pennsylvania and has declined in much of the rest of the state; at present, populations exist throughout much of Pennsylvania's south-central and southwestern counties, with a few remnant populations in eastern counties; mapped distribution indicates that the species no longer occurs in roughly half of the historically occupied range (Pennsylvania Game Commission website, woodrat information last updated in 2006).In New Jersey, several populations have been extirpated for at least 20 years; the single known remaining population has been relatively stable in recent years, based on trapping results in 1999–2001 (New Jersey Division of Fish and Wildlife).Woodrats were documented throughout their historical range in southeastern New York as recently as the mid-1960s, when they appeared to occupy all available habitat; those populations were extirpated by 1987; currently, the only woodrats in the state are immigrants that occasionally occupy a small patch of habitat on the New York-New Jersey border (this is the northern extreme of the habitat for the last remaining New Jersey woodrat population) (New York State Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy, 2005 revised draft). Reintroductions attempted in the early 1990s were unsuccessful.This species may be represented by only one population in Ohio, or possibly it is extirpated; recent surveys failed to locate woodrats there (W. Peneston pers. comm., cited by Mengak 2002).In Maryland, woodrat populations have been in decline for over two decades and continue to decline (Dan Feller, Maryland Natural Heritage Program pers. comm., cited by New York State Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy 2005 draft).In the early 1980s, extant populations in Indiana were reported from 20 sites (18 bluffs, two caves) adjacent to the Ohio River; in 1991–1992, live trapping surveys at 17 sites yielded a total of 101 woodrats at 12 (11 bluffs, one cave) of the 17 sites (Johnson 2002). Abundance in Indiana appears to have declined in recent decades. Population density for six sites in Indiana averaged 27.5/km of cliff habitat during the early 1980s (Cudmore 1985). During the 1990s density averaged about 11 individuals/km at 12 Indiana sites (Johnson et al. 1997).Woodrat populations in the core of the range in West Virginia (Castleberry 2000), Virginia (Mengak 2000), and Kentucky (Thomas 1998) currently appear to be secure.Cudmore (1983) estimated population densities of 8.3 to 71.9 woodrats per 1,000 m of cliff along the Ohio River in Indiana. According to Burt and Grossenheider (1976), populations of 5–8 adults per hectare are probably high.In Illnois, there was an increase in the amount of debris that was being built up into the river as aftermath of the 2009 derecho.
range: The range for this species extends throughout the Appalachian Mountains (Castleberry et al. 2006). It extends from western Connecticut, southeastern New York, northern New Jersey, and northern Pennsylvania southwestward through western Maryland, Tennessee, Kentucky, West Virginia, and northern and western Virginia (from the Blue Ridge westward) to northeastern Alabama (observed in several cave systems) and northwestern North Carolina (Hall 1981), with isolated populations north of the Ohio River in southern Ohio (where recent surveys failed to locate this species; W. Peneston pers. comm., cited by Mengak 2002) and southern Indiana (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). Although Hall (1981) showed Neotoma magister in the northwestern corner of Georgia, the Tennessee River is generally accepted as the southern range limit.Through the survey of distribution in the Appalachian Mountains (Gooley et al. 2018), from 2011–2015, organic signs of this species (latrines, fresh scat, fresh food caches, or maintained stick-nests) were a determining factor of their presence in the outcrop regions of the Northeastern and Midwestern United States. This specific survey took place in western Shawnee National Forest. Overall it has been determined that the presence of N. magister has increased in Southeastern Illinois, eastward into away from its remnant populations, once considered isolated.
conservationActions: Management guidelines resulting in the protection of Allegheny woodrat habitats are needed throughout the range. In particular, attention needs to be given to maintaining dispersal corridors among isolated populations. Continuing research on causes of the decline is also needed.Examples of protected occurrences include those in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Falls Ridge (a TNC preserve in Virginia), and the Deam Nature Preserve in Indiana. Many populations receive fairly good de facto protection in numerous areas with inaccessible cliffs and caves. Many additional occurrences are in state game areas and national forests and parks; these may afford some protection.Range-wide surveys are needed to better determine status and trends. Areas with woodrats should be protected from excessive human traffic. Mining and logging operations should not be permitted in areas with woodrat populations.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because its extent of occurrence is smaller than 4,125 km², but there is no data available to suggest how many locations there are. There is an inferred continuing decline in the area, extent of its habitat due to threats from continuing timber extraction and conversion of forest to coffee plantations.
habitat: The eastern slopes of the northern Sierra Madre Oriental, are typically steep and covered with vegetation varying from coniferous forest to cloud forest. Most sites from which Tamaulipan woodrats have been collected are within cloud forest (Alvarez 1963, Baker 1951, Vargas and Hernández 2001), one capture location was within tropical deciduous forst (El Pachón - Hooper 1953). N. angustapalata occupies etiher crevices among rocks that are covered with sparse vegetation growing from a deep layer of humus (Alvarez 1963, Baker 1951, Hooper 1953) or limestone caves (Hooper 1953). Individuals of this species are usually solitary, nocturnal, and active throughout the year (Ceballos 2014). They will mainly feed on seeds, other parts of plants and occasionally invertebrates (Ceballos 2014). They appear to reproduce year round and have litter sizes of 2-3 in the spring and 1-2 in the autumn (Ceballos 2014). Other mammals collected in the same habitats as N. angustapalata, include: Didelphis marsupialis, Philander opossum, Liomys irroratus, Peromyscus ochraventer, P. leucopus, Reithrodontomys mexicanus, Oryzomys couresi, O. champani, Oligoryzomys fulvencens, Sciurus aerogaster, S. deppei (Alvarez 1963, Baker 1951, Hooper 1953). The Tamaulipan woodrat has been found in baron owl (Tyto alba) and wood owl (Ciccaba virgata) pellets in Tamaulipas caves (Koopan an Martin 1959). Undated, subfossil skeletal fragments (owl pellets) of N. angustapalata were found 3 Tamauilipas caves (Koopan and Martin 1959). No fossils are known (Alvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.).
threats: This species is threatened by timber extraction and conversion of forest to coffee plantations (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.). Its narrow distribution is heavily impacted by human activities (Wilson et al. 2017).
population: This species is very rare and no population estimates or trend information are available (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and is restricted to the Sierra Madre Oriental regions in southwestern Tamaulipas and adjacent San Luis Potosí, México (Musser and Carleton 2005, Ceballos 2014, Wilson et al. 2017). It is only known from a few localities (Álvarez 1963, Birney 1973, Hutterer 1993) and is distributed from near sea level to elevations of 1,200 m asl (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: The Tamaulipan woodrat is known from only 14 museum specimens collected from only 12 localities. The total area of the geographical distribution of N. angustapalata is approximately 8,800 km2. N. angustapalata has a higher risk of extinction because of low density, restricted geographic distribution, and isolation of localities. Part of the distribution of Tamaulipan woodrat found within the Biosphere Reserve "El Cielo" (Alvarez-Castañeda pers. comm). The Mexican Government places N. angustapalata in a special protection category (NOM--059--Ecol--2011).

rationale: Although this species is known mainly from isolated records from a large area, it is listed as Least Concern because it is found in protected areas, expected to be widespread, and is thought to occur in rock outcrops, which are not under threat.
habitat: This species is poorly known. Thought to be found in rock outcrops. Two pregnant females were caught in September and February (Reid 2009).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown, but its habitat preference is thought to be for rocky outcrops, which are not under threat.
population: It is rare and local, also known from only a few specimens (Reid 1997).
range: This is species is distributed in higher elevations in Honduras and northwest Nicargua at an elevation of 1,000 m (Reid 2009).
conservationActions: It has been found in Salaqui National Park in Honduras. More information is required regarding the ecological requirements and possible threats faced by the species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is primarily restricted to habitats surrounding the Colorado River and its major tributaries, where its dens are typically found at the bases of cliffs and rock outcrops, and in high desert.
threats: There are no major threats known. It is sympatric with Neotoma albigula, which may limit its population numbers through competition for den sites.
population: This species is common.
range: The species' range appears to be uncertain (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is mapped to include western Arizona east of the Colorado River, and northwestern Sonora, Mexico. It ranges in elevation from sea level to 2,200 m.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures specific to this species. However, a portion of its range is within protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because its extent of occurrence is much greater than 20,000 km², it can be common within its range, and there are no major threats.
habitat: It is a habitat specialist found in heavy chaparral; hardwood, conifer, and mixed forests, typically in densely wooded areas with heavy undergrowth; riparian woodlands. It builds house of debris on the ground or in a tree; houses tend to be in situations that are shaded, relatively cool, and in good cover, and they may be used by many generations over several years. After breeding, males live in tree dens apart from females. One study found that each woodrat averaged 1.8 houses/home range. Loosely colonial, with partially overlapping home ranges; several individuals may live in the same area, though individuals (aside from females with young) typically live in separate houses. Adult home range averages around 2,000 sqm. Predators include hawks, owls, bobcat, coyote, long-tailed weasel, etc. Stick houses provide cover for many vertebrate and invertebrate commensals. Most young are born from February (especially in south) to May. Gestation lasts 30-37 days. Usually one litter per year. Litter size is 1-4, usually 2-3. Weaning begins at three weeks (Carraway and B. J. Verts 1991, Maser et al. 1981). Diet includes a wide variety of plants. Feeds on seeds, nuts, acorns, fruits, green vegetation, inner bark, and fungi. This woodrat stores food. It is primarily nocturnal.
threats: Generally populations are negatively affected by grazing and the removal of undergrowth or shrubby vegetation, but these are not major threats to the species overall.
population: This species is considered secure within its range (NatureServe). Population density is up to about 45/ha in optimal conditions; more typically 1-3 dozen/ha.
range: This species occurs in extreme western United States, from the Columbia River in western Oregon southwards to the inner Coastal Range of west-central California, and north Sierra Nevadas, east-central California.
conservationActions: The range of this species includes several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 100 km², it is found in only one location, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species is poorly known. The area around Perote is characterized by xeric shurb, pine-oak forest, cloud forest, and tropical rainforest in the deep ravines (Gonzales-Ruiz et al. 2006). Inhabits desert plains with vegetative cacti in the Valle de Oriental in Perote, Veracruz which is isolated (Gonzalez-Christen et al. 2002).
threats: This species is threatened by extensive conversion to agriculture, which may have already contributed to its decline and the isolation of its populations (Gonzales-Ruiz et al. 2006). Invasive, exotic species may also pose a threat.
population: This species is rare within its restricted range (Gonzales-Ruiz et al. 2006). The population is suspected to be declining due to habitat loss.
range: This species known from the type locality: Veracruz, Perote, (2,377 m), México (Musser and Carleton 2005), and it was also recently recorded in an area 40 km from southeastern Perote (Gonzalez-Christen et al. 2002). Its total geographic range is estimated to be less than 100 km², limited to the eastern volcanic slopes of Orizaba and Cofre de Perote (Gonzales-Ruiz et al. 2006).
conservationActions: This species is considered endangered by the Mexican government (NOM-059-ECOL-2001).

rationale: Listed and Least Concern because it is relatively widespread, reasonably common, adaptable and there are no known threats.
habitat: The species is found primarily at higher elevations, in rocky areas and riverine habitats, and also artificial stone walls in farmlands and artificial dykes (Abe et al. 2005).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is fairly common only in suitable habitat. The species is difficult to trap.
range: This species is endemic to Japan, and is only found on Honshu. It is found in the southern Kii Peninsula, as well as Chubu and Hokuriku Districts and northwards (Abe et al. 2005). It is found from sea level to the alpine zone in Tohoku District and the Kii Peninsula. In Chubu District, the species is found from 400 m asl to the alpine zone (Abe et al. 2005).
conservationActions: It is present in protected areas within its range.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is widespread, common, adaptable and there are no present threats.
habitat: It occurs in primary and secondary forest. It prefers wet areas, and is found also in conifer plantations and farmlands in lowland montane areas. It is absent entirely from alluvial plains.
threats: There are no major threats to this adaptable species.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species is endemic to Japan, and is found only on Honshu (Niigata and Fukushima Prefectures and southwards), Kyushu, Shikoku, and Dogo Island (Oki Islands). It is found from about 400 m asl to lowland montane and alpine zones (Abe et al. 2005).
conservationActions: It is known to be present in protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is common and widespread with no major threats.
habitat: It inhabits coniferous forests and birch forests often around river valleys, where it tends to prefer rocky areas, dense undergrowth and leaf litter, and is also found in dry peat-bogs, grasslands and subarctic dwarf shrub heathland. It has a herbivorous diet, feeding on vegetative parts of grasses, herbs, and dwarf shrubs, and on berries (Henttonen and Viitala 1982, Sulkava 1999). The species can sometimes be found in high densities in clear-cut areas, and is often found on plains (B. Sheftel pers. comm. 2006).
threats: There are not thought to be any major threats to this species at present. Declines in Fennoscandia may be linked to changes in forestry practices (H. Henttonen pers. comm. 2006).
population: It is a common species in northern Fennoscandia. The long-term trend is stable with cyclic fluctuations every 4-5 years (Sulkava 1999). In northern Fennoscandia (Fennoscandian taiga) and northern Russia it was previously common, but there have been declines since the mid-1980s (H. Henttonen pers. comm. 2006).
range: The grey-sided vole, Myodes rufocanus, has a large range in the northern Palaearctic, extending from northern Fennoscandia through northern Russia, including Siberia to Kamtchatka, the south Ural Mountains, Altai Mountains, and northeastern and northern Korea (Keima Plateau) and the islands of Sakhalin (Russia), and Japan (Sulkava 1999). It ranges as far south as northern parts of Mongolia and China (Wilson and Reeder 2005). In China it occurs from northern Xinjiang eastwards through Mongolia to the provinces of Jilin and Liaoning in northeast China. In Mongolia it is known from woodland habitats in Hangai, Hentii, Hövsgöl, Mongol Altai and Ikh Hyangan mountain ranges, and Mongol Daguur Steppe. There is an isolated population around Ikh Bogd Mountain in Govi Altai Mountain Range (Lkhagvasuren and Samiya 2004). In Japan, the subspecies Clethrionomys rufocanus bedfordiae is found on Hokkaido, Rishiri, Rebun, Daikoku, Teuri, Yagishiri, as well as Kunashir and Shikotan (South Kuril Islands) (Abe et al. 2005).It occurs from the coast to at least 1,170 m in northern Fennoscandia (Henttonen and Viitala 1982), and can reach elevations of up to 2,700 m asl in its Mongolian range, such as the Hangai Mountain Range.
conservationActions: It occurs in a number of protected areas within its wide range. The population trend should be monitored in the north-western part of the range.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it has a large distribution, is it not thought to be in decline, and there are currently no known threats to the species.
habitat: The species is found in montane forests on mainland Hokkaido (Abe et al. 2005). It is also found in conifer plantations, scrublands, and grasslands on Hokkaido. The species is found in grasslands and abandoned farmlands on Rishiri and Rebun Islands. In areas of co-occurrence with Clethrionomys rufocanus bedfordiae, the latter species is dominant.
threats: This species has low genetic diversity probably due to genetic bottleneck caused by a founder effect (Iwasa and Nakata 2011). Additionally, it has a fragmented distribution either because it has persisted on Hokkaido through past glacial periods by using several fragmented refugia (Kawai et al. 2013) or because its habitat preferences differ from the typical vegetation structure of Hokkaido and it fails to compete with M. rufocanus for resources (Iwasa and Nakata 2011).
population: The populations can be divided in at least 4 distinct clades that occupy different regions: Rishiri Island (which constitutes a separate lineage), and northern, central and southern Hokkaido (Kawai et al. 2013). The Southern Hokkaido phylogroup appears to have lower genetic variability than the other groups (Kawai et al. 2013). It is a naturally rare species.
range: Previously thought to be a Japanese endemic restricted to the islands of Hokkaido, Rishiri, Rebun, Shikotan and Shibotsu (Abe et al. 2005), it was recently recorded in Russia in the south of Sakhalin Island, Dolinsk district (Abramson et al. 2009). It is also thought that this species might be widespread through several islands of the Russian Far East (Abramson et al. 2009).
conservationActions: The species is present in protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in forest and woodlands (Smith and Xie 2008). Its diet consists of green vegetation, shoots and to a lesser extent seeds (Smith and Xie 2008). It is primarily nocturnal (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the provinces of Sichuan, Gansu, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Hebei, Beijing, Nei Mongol (Smith and Xie 2008), Henan and Hubei (CSIS 2008).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Songshan, Xinglongshan, Houhe, and Pangquangou Nature Reserves (CSIS 2008) and may be present in additional protected areas. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is nocturnal, arboreal and is found in mature and secondary rainforest, lowland and lower montane forest (Linares 1998).
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: This rodent is common in Venezuela (Linares 1998).
range: This species occurs in the moist lowland forest that follows an arc from Trinidad, through north and west central Venezuela, to central Colombia (Meta Department) (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is found from 10 to 1,500 m in Venezuela (Linares 1998).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas throughout its range.
