rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution in isolated pockets, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is an arboreal species; it occurs in primary montane forest (M. Gómez-Laverde and B. Rivas pers. comm.). It inhabits relatively undisturbed cloud forest and the forest-páramo ecotone in the Eastern Cordillera of the Andes (Patton et al. 2015).
threats: Species that live in cloud forests are threatened by anthropogenic pressure and habitat fragmentation (Ramirez and Quintero 2015).
population: It is a relatively common species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the eastern Cordillera of the Colombian Andes, from Norte de Santander (and the Páramo de Tamá in the Venezuelan border) southward to Cundinamarca and the Distrito Especial de Bogotá. A single specimen, provisionally referred to this species, was also found in the Serranía de la Macarena (Patton et al. 2015). It is known from elevations between 1,800 and 3,100 m asl.
conservationActions: It occurs in a number of protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is an arboreal and nocturnal species that is present in a wide variety of habitats, including primary and secondary Yungas forest, plantations and cultivated areas.
threats: There are no major threats to this species. It is a pest species in coffee plantations.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in the lower east Andean slopes and foothills, about 350 to 2,600 m, from La Paz Department, west central Bolivia, south to Jujuy Province, northwest Argentina (Tribe 1996, Musser and Carleton 2005); in Argentina between 500 m to 1,400 m.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is arboreal in primary montane forest and dry forest.
threats: There do not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: It is a relatively common species (R.P. Anderson pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the mountains of north and west Venezuela, Tobago (Trinidan and Tobago), and east Colombia (Musser and Carleton 2005). Extent of eastern distribution is uncertain.
conservationActions: The species occurs in a number of protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is often found in house plantations, gallery forest and Cerrado dry forest (Tribe 2015).
threats: There are no major threats at this time.
population: There is no information on population or abundance.
range: This species occurs in the eastern fringe of Amazonian rainforest, principally in Pará and Mato Grosso east of the Rio Xingu and as far south as Serra do Roncador, central Brazil (Musser and Carleton 2005, Tribe 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is nocturnal, arboreal, occurring in primary and secondary rainforests (M. Aguillera pers. comm.).
threats: There does not appear to be any major threats to this species.
population: It is relatively common (Linares 1998).
range: This species occurs in the highlands of south Venezuela (Bolívar and Amazonas States) and is likely to be present in neighbouring parts of north Brazil and west Guyana (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an altitudinal range of 300 to 2,800 m (Linares 1998).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This rodent is nocturnal, arboreal and is found montane forest (Linares 1998). This species is found in cloud forests, evergreen forest, some in orchids, and mainly in trees and vines, and a few under bushes and on rock ledges. They mainly prefer elevations between 2,000 and 3,350 m (Tribe 2015).
threats: Species that live in cloud forests are threatened by anthropogenic pressure and habitat fragmentation (Ramirez and Quintero 2015).
population: It is difficult to capture and sample as it is an arboreal species (Linares 1998).
range: This species is found in the Venezuelan Andes in the states of Merida and Trujillo at elevations above 2,000 m and also some in the eastern in the Tachira state. Populations have also been found above 1,300 m in the states of Falcon and Yaracuy states in the mountain ranges, and in the Distrito Capital in the states Aragua and Vargas in the Cordillera de la Costa (Tribe 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in a several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a wide distribution and it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Habitat loss is occurring throughout much of its range due to deforestation for the cultivation of illicit crops. Further information is needed to confirm the species presence in protected areas and the effect of habitat conversion on populations.
habitat: It is presumably an arboreal, nocturnal species. It is present in lower montane forest, cloud forest and east Andean slopes. It is not known if the species can persist in secondary habitats, although one specimen was collected from an abandoned shed (Tribe 1996).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation through conversion of land to agricultural use and illicit crops (e.g. coca).
population: It seems to be a rare species.
range: This species occurs at middle elevations in east Andean slopes, central Peru. It has an altitudinal range of 700 to 1,800 m (Tribe 1996, Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It has not been recorded from any protected areas, although there are seven protected areas within the general range of this species. Further research is needed into the distribution of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because, although it is seldom recorded, it has a relatively wide distribution, with no immediate threats to the known range and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is an arboreal species, which has been collected in undisturbed lowland evergreen forest. It has also been collected in disturbed forest.
threats: There appear to be no immediate threats to this species. It may be threatened in the future by general clearance of lowland tropical forest.
population: It seems to be an uncommon species.
range: This species occurs from the westernmost Brazil (Acre State) and lowlands of southeast Peru, perhaps including the valley of the Río Ucayali (Tribe 1996, Musser and Carleton 2005). It is known to occur from about 200 to 1,480 m.
conservationActions: It has been found in Manu Biosphere Reserve in Peru. Further research is needed into the distribution of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a wide distribution, it is characterized as common within parts of its distribution, has a presumed large population, occurs in some protected areas, and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in montane forests, scrub, bamboo, and in open and rocky meadows (Smith and Xie 2008).Reproductive periodicity occurs from early summer to late autumn (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species has been characterized as common along stream banks (Smith and Xie 2008).
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the provinces of Yunnan and Sichuan (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies elevations ranging from 2,500-4,800 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species is present in Changshanerhai Nature Reserve (CSIS 2008) and may be present in additional protected areas. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, although its current known range is less than 20,000 km2, it has a presumed large population, it occurs in a variety of habitats and there are no indications of a population decline severe enough for listing under a threat category.
habitat: This species occupies forests and meadows (Kaneko 1996). Reproductive period is from early summer to late fall (Kaneko 1996).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is an endemic of China, known only from the Omei (Emei) Shan range of Sichuan province (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies elevations ranging from 1,500-3,000m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species is present in Wawushan Nature Reserve (CSIS 2008), and likely present in Gonggashan and Labahe Nature Reserves. Mt. Emei was named a World Heritage Site in 1996 (UNESCO 2008). Further studies are needed into the abundance of this species. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, it has a presumed large population, it occurs in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It inhabits dense montane forest at high elevations, preferring steep slopes and banks (Smith and Xie 2008). There are few data regarding the natural history of this species.
threats: Deforestation is a threat to this species.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species occurs in southern China, the extreme northeast region of Myanmar (Smith and Xie 2008) and in the Zayu county, Tibet (Fu et al. 2012). In China, it is known from the area west of the Salween river valley in Yunnan province (Smith and Xie 2008). Its range may extend to southern Yunnan and the east-central regions of Myanmar (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occupies elevations ranging from 2,300-3,200 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Nujiang and Tongbiguan Nature Reserves (CSIS 2008), and is likely to be present in other protected areas. Further studies are needed into the abundance, distribution, natural history and threats to this species. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This vole's extent of occurrence (EOO) is 8,337 km² (i.e., less than 20,000 km² threshold for criterion B1) and it is known from fewer than ten locations. There is no current information on threats or the state of the species habitat, so it is not possible to determine whether the population is declining at present; however if data become available to indicate that the population is declining, the species would immediately qualify for the Vulnerable category. It is assessed as Near Threatened based on it nearly qualifying as threatened under criterion B1.
habitat: This species inhabits open and rocky meadows and stream banks in forests (Smith and Xie 2008). It is also found in broadleaf and conifer forests (Zeng et al. 2013). The species' reproductive period occurs from early summer to late fall (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: Currently there are no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China and occurs in the extreme northwest of Yunnan province (Mekong and Salween river valleys) (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies elevations ranging between 2,400-4,250 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
useTrade: No use and trade information is available for this species.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It may be present in protected areas. Further studies are needed into the abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Species at type locality was taken from semiarid thorn scrub bordering saline flats, a narrow ecotone between the Chaco and Monte extending from Catamarca to Rio Negro provinces (Mares and Braun 1996). This species is found in habitats at the northern end of the Bolsón de Pipanaco in or near creosote brush flats. It has been reported to be nocturnal, with little to no reproductive activity in the winter, and some reproductive activity in the summer (Braun 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is considered a rare species.
range: This species is known only from a few adjacent localities in the Bolsón de Pipanaco, an isolated valley in the Monte Desert of northwestern Argentina, at an elevation of about 1,000 m (Braun 2015).
conservationActions: It is found in one protected area.

rationale: Chinanteco Deer Mouse (Habromys chinanteco) is endemic to Mexico where it is known from only one small area in Oaxaca. It is assessed as Critically Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is only 84 km², all individuals are in a single location, and it is experiencing continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species occurs in humid cloud forests (Briones-Salas et al. 2011).
threats: The species is threatened by deforestation within its very restricted range (Rogers et al. 2007).
population: Chinanteco Deer Mouse is known from only one location (in southern Mexico), where it has a limited distribution (Briones-Salas et. al 2011). It is suspected to be declining because of habitat loss.
range: This species is only found in one location: on Cerro Pelón (2,080 to 2,650 m) in the Sierra Juarez, Oaxaca (México) (Carleton et al. 2002, Esther et. al. 2005, Briones-Salas et al. 2011).
conservationActions: There are no reported conservation measures currently in place for this mouse.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because it is experiencing a continuing decline in its extent of occurrence, area of occupancy and quality of habitat due to deforestation of its highland, mature forest habitat but does not currently meet the threshold for a threatened category under Criterion B.
habitat: This rodent occurs in naturally fragmented, highland, wet, montane forest in the pine-oak belt (Reid 1997; Rogers 2007) and favors mature oak forest with numerous epiphytes, mosses, and fallen trees (Reid 1997). It is nocturnal and semiarboreal; it is usually trapped on fallen logs or low branches. Females were non-reproductive in December in Guatemala (Reid 1997).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation (Rogers 2007).
population: This species can be uncommon to locally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species is known from the highlands of Chiapas, México, to northern Guatemala (León-Paniagua et al. 2007). It occurs at elevations of 1,950 to 3,110 m (Musser 1969). This species is now known to be in the SE Mexico (Sierra Madre de Chiapas) through Guatemala to extreme NW El Salvador. (U.F.J. Pardiñas, et al. 2017).
conservationActions: The species occurs in protected areas in Mexico and Guatemala (Sierra de las Minas Biosphere Preserve).

rationale: Slender-tailed Deer Mouse (Habromys lepturus) is assessed as Critically Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is only 86 km², all individuals are known from a single location, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species occurs on wet mountain slopes (Rogers et al. 2007). It is only known from above 2,500 m in cloud forest and prefers cool, wet climates with fern and lichen vegetation.
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation within its restricted range.
population: This species is considered rare. The population is suspected to be declining because of habitat loss.
range: Slender-tailed Deer Mouse is only known from Cerro Zempoaltepec (above 2,500 m), in Oaxaca (Mexico) (Carleton et al. 2002, Ceballos and Olivia 2005, León-Paniagua et al. 2007).
conservationActions: There are currently no conservation measures reportedly in place.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, although it is thought to be uncommon, it is very wide ranging, it occurs in many protected areas and there are no major threats.
habitat: It is found in a variety of habitats where moisture levels are high and where sedges and grasses provide both food and cover. Such habitats occur within high-elevation sedge-grass meadows in pine or spring forests, spruce-fir forests, wet meadows, sphagnum bogs, tundra, riparian areas within spruce forests, and in early successional grasslands associated with recently burned forests. Atypically, one subspecies occurs on sagebrush slopes in southern British Columbia.It occupies burrow systems up to one foot deep and surface runways. Young are born in nests that may be underground or on the surface in concealing vegetation. Breeds May-August. Gestation lasts probably three weeks. Litter size is 2-8 (average four). Several litters per year. At least some breed during the summer of their birth.Maintains a home range of probably less than one acre. Very sociable; may be found in small colonies. Feeds on grasses, sedges, and other herbaceous vegetation. Active day/night throughout the year.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: Its widespread distribution extends from Alaska to Labrador and south to portions of the northern United States, but populations are localized; population sizes are not known for any location, although nowhere does this mammal appear to be common. It is patchily distributed throughout the range. Population densities may range up to three dozen per acre.
range: This species is found in Labrador, Canada, west to central Alaska in the United States, and south to Washington, Montana, southeastern Manitoba and northern New England (see Clough and Albright 1987 for recent records from Baxter State Park, Maine, and from Mt. Moosilauke, Grafton County, New Hampshire). Its distribution is apparently spotty even in the centre of its range in central Canada.
conservationActions: In Montana two sites are in Glacier National Park and one is in a USFS Special Botanical Area. In Washington three sites are USFS Wilderness Areas.The majority of lower 48 state occurrences have been found in the past 15 years and more are likely to be located. In eastern Canada more work is needed and the extent of occupied habitat even within the centre of its range in western Canada is currently unclear.Little is known of the ecology of the species. Essentially all publications deal only with distribution or taxonomy. Much additional information is needed on population parameters, movements, and habitat requirements.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Collecting localities recorded so far from voucher-specimens suggest a broad distribution in the Lower Amazon and a high likelihood to occupy disturbed forest or secondary brush formations (Gonçalves and Oliveira pers. comm.).
habitat: This species is found in lowland moist forests of the Amazon River basin. It inhabits secondary growth forest and brush formations (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at present.
population: No population estimates are available for this species, but its records suggest stable population sizes (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
range: This species is distributed along the Madeira, Xingú, Tocantins and Tapajós river basins, in the Brazilian states of Mato Grosso, Rondônia and Pará (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
conservationActions: The range of this species overlaps numerous protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species has been found in submontane and montane vegetation. It occurs in forest and disturbed areas but on edge of forest, from sea level to 800 m elevation (Geise pers. comm.). It also occurs in wetlands (Bergallo pers. comm.).
threats: There are no major threats to this species throughout its range.
population: This species is relatively common to uncommon across a large range. It is not easy to collect (Bergallo pers. comm.).
range: The species occurs in the Atlantic Forest region of southeast Brazil, including Bahia, Espirito Santo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo States (Pereira et al. 2001, Hoffmann et al. 2002).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Itatiaia and Restinga de Jurubatiba Nationals Parks.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It ranges from lowland cerrado and mixed forest, into Yungas and montane forest and regrowth following logging. It is present in savannas, grassland and fields, in primary and secondary habitat including disturbed areas.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is a moderately common species.
range: This species occurs in the south central Peru to northern Bolivia, as far south as Cochabamba and east into west Santa Cruz Departments (Anderson 1997, Musser and Carleton 2005). It has an elevational range of around 400 to 2,500 m in Bolivia, and 500 up to 1,900 m in Peru.
conservationActions: It is present in many protected areas. No conservation measures are needed for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occursrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is nocturnal, diurnal, and terrestrial. It is present in primary and secondary Polylepis woodland and humid montane forest. It may be present in cultivated areas, although this requires verification. It feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates and may use its long claws to dig these from the litter.This species inhabits the Yungas (Andean humid montane forests) of Peru and Bolivia. The few reproductive data available suggest a breeding season at the end of the rainy season (March-April) (Hinokosa et al. 1987).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. It is somewhat adaptable to habitat disturbance.
population: It is a rare species in Peru, but is more common in Bolivia. Its geographical records suggest stable population sizes (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
range: It occurs in the stretch of humid montane forests along the eastern slopes of the Andes mountains in Peru and Bolivia, ranging from 600 to 3,500 m above sea level. Collecting localities of museum voucher-specimens are located in the southern part of Cordilllera de Carabaya (Puno, Peru), in Cordillera Real (La Paz, Bolivia) and in Cordillera Oriental (Cochabamba, Bolivia) (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
conservationActions: It is present in at least three protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in 1,800-2,700 m elevation range of humid montane forest and secondary vegetation (Musser and Carleton 2005).
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: This species is common.
range: This species occurs from east Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo to Rio de Janeiro, southeast Brazil (Bonvicino et al.,1998).
conservationActions: The species is found in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 29,000 km², which is above the 20,000 km² threshold for criterion B1. However, this species could rapidly become threatened under the criterion B because currently all individuals are in fewer than ten locations, there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, and this species does not exist in any protected areas. The species is under threat from urban expansion and tourism development. Further monitoring of this species is necessary to provide an accurate estimation of extinction risk.
habitat: This rodent occurs in wetlands, scrub, humid grasslands, sandy areas (Queirolo pers. comm.). This species is sympatric to Oxymycterus nasutus and ecological data on Uruguayan Oxymycterus was analyzed by Barlow (1969). However, Hoffmann et al. (2002) stated that these data need re-evaluation because both species were likely treated as one in Barlow's study.
threats: The major threats are habitat destruction, tourism development, and urban expansion. Habitat loss due to urban expansion along coastal Uruguay specifically presents a threat (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
population: This species is poorly known; there are only a few localities known.
range: This species is known from southwestern Uruguay, south of the Río Negro, in the departments of Soriano, Colonia, San José, Canelones and Maldonado (Oliveira and Gonçalves 2015).
conservationActions: This species is not found in any protected areas (at the moment national system of protected areas is being developed in Uruguay) (G. D'Elia. pers. comm)

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 6,693 km², it is currently known only from three locations, and there is ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat due mainly to agricultural expansion.
habitat: This vole occurs in mountain forests (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: The species' forest habitat is threatened by expanding agriculture and logging, although these threats are decreasing.
population: This species has been characterized as rare (Liu et al. 2005).
range: This species is endemic to China, where it is known from southern Gansu and northern Sichuan (Smith and Xie 2008). Two recent specimens were collected at elevations of 2,440 and 2,550 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008). A 2003 survey collected 16 specimens in Jiuhaigou National Nature Reserve (Liu et al. 2005), increasing the number of known localities to three.
conservationActions: The species has been recorded in Jiuzhaigou National Nature Reserve (Liu et al. 2005), but it is not known if it is present in any other protected areas. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species. In China, it has been regionally red listed as Vulnerable D2 (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species can be found on the lower wooded slopes and the adjacent dry grounds that are covered with mesquite. Its burrows are at the base of trees and under other available cover. Numerous trails have been noted leading from these burrows onto the wooded hillside. It prefers the foot of low cliffs and rocky ledges on the hillsides, and it is noted that it inhabits dense patches of agave (Genoways and Birney 1974). A female captured in February had a single embryo; and a lactating female accompanied by two young was found in September (Genoways and Birney 1974).
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: This species is relatively common to locally abundant in suitable habitat (Genoways and Birney 1974).
range: This species is known from south Sinaloa to Oaxaca; it is found in interior México along basins of Río Balsas to central Puebla and Río Tehuacán to north Oaxaca (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are several protected areas located within the range of this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Unlike other hamsters, this is an arboreal species, that occurs in deciduous forests of the mountainous habitats within its range (Smith and Xie 2008). It is nocturnal, and primarily active in spring and summer (Smith and Xie 2008). It is a herbivore, feeding on leaves and grasses (Smith and Xie 2008).Litter size is 6-8 (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the provinces of Gansu, Ningxia, Shaanxi (Smith and Xie 2008), and Sichuan (CSIS 2008). It generally occupies elevations between 1,000-1,400 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It may be present in protected areas. This species has been regionally Red Listed in China as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and occurrence in a number of protected areas.
habitat: It occurs in Yungas (Andean forests) at elevations between 800 and 2,500 m.
threats: This species is threatened by timber exploitation and cattle farming.
population: It is a common species but there are no data on its abundance.
range: This species occurs in mountain ranges in northwestern Argentina and south central Bolivia (Emmons 1997, Jayat et al. 2010). Its elevational range goes from 800 to 2,800 m (P. Jayat unpublished data). In Argentina, this species occurs at an elevational range from 1,500 to 2,600 m (Jayat et al. 2008).
conservationActions: It is found in at least two national parks and other protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This mouse is terrestrial, and mostly nocturnal. It probably feeds on insects, seeds, and vegetation. It nests in burrows and travels in tunnels under leaf litter. It is found in evergreen forest, and in montane habitats, grassy areas, especially with tall grass, young second growth, gardens, and clearings. Reproduction is between July and August in southern Peru, with litter size from two to seven (Patton 2015).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species; anthropic intervention could threaten some populations.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species occurs in upper montane forests along east Andean slopes, 1,200 to 2,400 m (Patton 2015), in Ecuador, Peru, and central Bolivia (Anderson 1997, Patton and Smith 1992).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It has been found in dense forest (Voss et al. 2002). This mouse is terrestrial, and mostly diurnal and crepuscular. It probably feeds on insects, seeds, and vegetation (Quiceno 1993).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is common, especially in secondary and altered areas (R. Anderson and M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.). Voss et al. (2002) captured 10 specimens of this species in the valley of the Rio Siato, Departamento Risaralda, Municipio Pueblo Rico, Vereda Siato, at 1,520-1,620 m, with 405 trap-nights.
range: This species occurs in the Cordillera Occidental of western Colombia (Musser and Carleton 2005); it also occurs in the Cordillera Central, Colombia (Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.). It has an altitudinal range of 1,300 to 3,000 m (Alberico et al. 2000).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Farallones de Cali, Tatamá, Las Orquideas in the Cordillera Occidental, and in Los Nevados National Parks and other protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population; occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is a nocturnal, terrestrial and solitary species. It feeds on insects, other invertebrates, seeds and vegetation. It is present in open grassland, Polylepis forest, and Paramo/Espeletia areas, at high elevations, as well as disturbed and cultivated areas (Linares 1998).
threats: The major threats are paramo and cloud forest destruction.
population: This species is common in some parts of its range and rare in others (M. Gómez-Laverde and B. Rivas pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the Andes of northwest Venezuela, east and central Colombia (Musser and Carleton 2005); it also occurs in south Colombia to Huila Department (Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.). It has an elevational range of 2,600 to 3,900 m (Soriano et al. 1998).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas including Chingaza National Park in Colombia, Sierra Nevada in Venezuela.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is present in grassland, shrubland, disturbed habitats and cultivated areas. It typically lives in holes at the base of shrubs.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is a very common species.
range: This species occurs in the Altiplano of southeast Peru to south central Bolivia (Musser and Carleton, 2005). It is found at elevations of 3,700 to around 5,000 m. In northwestern Argentina it is restricted to northernmost Salta Province mainly above 2500 m (Jayat et al. 2006, 2010)
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its abundance within its restricted distribution, its presumed large population, and because its habitat is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This rodent occurs in temperate climate Araucaria forests and Atlantic rainforest with fields at about 900 m altitude in above mean sea level.
threats: The species has no reported threats (Christoff and Langguth pers. comm.).
population: The species is abundant throughout the range (A. Christoff and A. Langguth pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs from southeastern Brazil (Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul States) to northeastern Argentina (Misiones Province) (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas in Argentina and Brazil (Itatiaia National Park, A. Langguth pers. comm.).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in bunchgrass, along the base of stone wall bordering agricultural plots, fragmented Polilepys and yungas (Patton et al. 2015). It feeds on arthropods and plan material (Solari 2007).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: It is a very common species.
range: This species occurs from the western Andean upper slopes of Ayacucho and Arequipa Departments through highlands of Cuzco and Puno in Peru, and then to Cochabamba in Bolivia (Patton et al. 2015). It occurs between 1,900 and 4,500 m (Myers et al. 1990, Patton and Smith 1992, Anderson 1997 Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas, including six in Peru.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in Yungas and cloud/foggy grasslands at elevations around 400 and 2,500 m (J.P. Jayat pers. comm.).
threats: No major threats known to the species.
population: There is no information available on populations.
range: This species occurs on eastern, lower Andean slopes, 400-3,000 m, from south central Bolivia (Tarija Province) (Anderson 1997) to northwestern Argentina, Jujuy to Catamarca Provinces (Mares et al. 1997, Ortiz et al. 2000a) and Tucuman and Salta provinces (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: There are at least 5 protected areas in the range.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because its extent of occurrence is not much greater than 20,000 km² (EOO is around 25,700 km²), the population is severely fragmented, and the extent and quality of its habitat are declining. It is therefore close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B.
habitat: The only habitat this species is known to occur in is cloud forest on the eastern Andean slopes of the Bolivian Andes (Pardiñas et al. 2015). It is not believed to occur, or persist, in modified habitat.
threats: Major threats to this species include clearance of cloud forest for cattle pasture. The range of the species is divided by a major road, along which human colonization is taking place, further fragmenting the habitat.
population: The species is localized, but is probably not especially rare.
range: This species is known only from the vicinity of the type locality and adjacent cloud forest areas in Cochabamba and west Santa Cruz Departments, central Bolivia. It has been recorded from about 1,800 to 3,100 m (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It may be marginally present in Amboro and Carrasco National Parks. There is a need to prevent further degradation of the species habitat.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in open grassland, disturbed sites, cultivated areas and in Yungas between in foggy grasslands (J.P. Jayat, pers. comm.).
threats: There are no major threats to this species, however, populations associated with Yungas forest are threatened by deforestation and agricultural activities.
population: This is an abundant species, however, there is no information available on the population of this species.
range: This species occurs in the Altiplano and eastern Andean slope from Puno Department of Peru to Chuquisaca Department in Bolivia (Patton et al. 2015). It is found from 1,130 to 4,360 m.
conservationActions: It is present in at least two protected areas in Peru. Further natural history research is needed into this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species inhabits dry Chaco areas.
threats: No major threats are known to the species, but the Chaco habitat has many pressures because of loss of habitat due to cattle and agriculture.
population: It is a common species in the Paraguay Chaco.
range: This species occurs in the Chaco of western Paraguay, southeastern Bolivia, and contiguous northern Argentina (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas in its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits forest and high elevation grasslands of the Yungas ecoregion as well as grasslands in the Chacoan ecoregion of Argentina. The reproductive activity begins in early spring (late August) (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
threats: Some populations are suspected to be threatened by logging and agricultural activities.
population: This species is described as being the most common species in its restricted range. Recent data concerning population trend are not available (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
range: This species is known from just a few localities in the Sierra de Santa Bárbara and the surrounding area, all in southeastern Jujuy province of Argentina. It is found at elevations between 900 and 2,400 m (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
conservationActions: It does not occur in protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 16,896 km²; it is known from fewer than ten locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat. The threats to this species are increasing as the foothills of the Andes and Andean valleys are increasingly targeted for logging and human settlement.
habitat: The few specimens of this species that are available were captured in very wet mid-montane forest on the steep slopes of the Urubamba Valley of Peru. There is no information available on the ecology of this species (Pardiñas et al. 2015). It is generally restricted to primary humid montane forest, and will persist in selectively logged areas but no clearcut. It is not found outside of forest habitats.
threats: It is threatened by commercial clearcut logging, and clearance of forest habitat through conversion to cropland and pasture.
population: The population abundance is not known, but it does not appear to be common.
range: The Silent Grass Mouse is only known from the vicinity of Machu Picchu in the mid-elevation montane forest of the Urubamba Valley in Cusco department, Peru. It is known to occupy elevations between 600 and 2,000 m (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
conservationActions: A small part of the range may be included in a protected area. Conservation of areas of suitable forest habitat are needed to preserve this species. Further research is needed into the population abundance of this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered due to its small area of occupancy (AOO = 112 km²), small number of locations (4-5), and continuing decline in the area, extent and quality of its habitat due to conversion of its native high elevation grassland habitat to agriculture.
habitat: This rodent is present in the shrubby paramo/forest ecotone, in subalpine Rain Forest, in grassy glades surrounded by subalpine Rain Forest, and in grassy paramo. All recorded captures were on the ground: in runways under dense bunch grass, among mixed grasses, and mossy shrubs, and under moss mats or low herbs. Several individuals of Neomicroxus latebricola were captured in broad daylight, between the time when traps were checked just after dawn and when they were rebaited in the late afternoon (Voss 2003).
threats: The major threats to this mouse are habitat loss and fragmentation, due to conversion of its native high elevation grassland habitat to agriculture.
population: It is rare and poorly known (D. Tirira pers. comm). Fewer than 50 individuals have been trapped and no formal attempts to estimate its population abundance have been done (Serrano pers. comm).
range: This species is known from only a few localities and is suspected to occur in the Cordillera Oriental above 2,800 m n north central Ecuador (Pichincha, Napo and Tungurahua Provinces) (Serrano pers. comm). It could occur in southern Colombia, but has not been yet recorded (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, as although it is known only from a few sites, and although it is seldom recorded, it does not appear to have any major threats, it may range more widely than is currently known, and it does not appear to be declining at a rate fast enough to qualify as threatened.
habitat: It is a terrestrial species. This species occupies moist bunch grass and disturbed shrub habitats at the upper edge of the elfin forest. It occurs in primary and secondary upper and lower Yungas forest habitat, Polylepis woodland, and high elevation elfin forest. It is very common along rock walls of old terraces and buildings and in thick clumps of grass and shrubs in the relatively more open and disturbed areas (Myers and Patton 1989, Salazar-Bravo et al. 2003, Tarifa et al. 2007). It has not been recorded yet from agricultural land.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species, however, in lower parts of its range it appears to be threatened by ongoing general habitat loss through conversion of natural habitat to agricultural land.
population: It may be a rare species, but it has been misidentified with similar specie (A. mimus and A. fumeus) in the past, therefore the abundance is not well known.
range: This species is found in the drainages between the Marcapata and Limbani on the east of the Andean slope in Cusco and Puno departments in southern Peru, south to the Cochabamba department in central Bolivia between elevations of 1,800 to 3,700 m (Myers and Patton 1989b, Yensen et al. 2002, Tarifa et al. 2007).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas in Bolivia. Further research is needed into the ecology and distribution of this species, especially with regards to its relationship with other Akodon species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. However, it is possibly a species complex and as further taxonomic research takes place, some threatened species from this complex may be identified.
habitat: This species has been captured in heavily wooded canyons as well as in open swamps at high altitudes in long grass or rushes. It has been described as occurring in dense, humid, but cool forests which comprise the cover of the lower slopes of the eastern Andes. It is also common in corn and potato plots (Pardiñas et al. 2015).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: This species is described as common and seems to have a stable population.
range: This species occurs on the eastern Andean slopes east of Río Marañón in Amazonas and northern San Martín departments of northern Peru. It is found in wet elfin forests between 1,900 to 2,860 m elevation (Pardiñas et al. 2015). Barnett (1999) and Moreno and Albuja (2005) recorded this species in Ecuador. It has an altitudinal range of 1,800 to 3,700 m.
conservationActions: It is present in at least three protected areas, such as Río Abiseo National Park, Cajas. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its abundance within its restricted distribution and because its habitat is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in dense subtropical gallery forests (Musser and Carleton 2005). In Taim, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, species were found in abundance in swamp forest habitats, and some specimens were captured in grasslands (Gonzalez et al. 1998). Breeding season is thought to occur from spring into autumn (Gonzalez et al. 1998).
threats: There are no threats affecting the species; its habitat is not being reduced (Gonzalez et al. 1998). Some populations may be affected by clear cutting in the future.
population: This species is collected less frequently than others and has a patchy distribution (A. Langguth pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in eastern Uruguay and extreme southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul state) (Musser and Carleton 2005). Species range may extend northward to the southern portion of the Atlantic Forest (Gonzalez et al. 1998).
conservationActions: The species occurs in Taim Federal Reserve (Gonzales et al. 1998).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. However, it is a species complex and as further taxonomic research takes place, some threatened species from this complex may be identified.
habitat: This species is found in a wide variety of humid and dry grassland and shrubland habitats. It can be found in secondary habitats, and has been recorded from traditionally cultivated areas to pine and ecucalipus plantations (Patton et al. 2015). This mouse is terrestrial, and mostly nocturnal. Its litter size is two per year, with two to four embryos (Barnett 1999). Its reproduction period goes from May/June to August/September.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this widespread and adaptable species.
population: It is the most common mouse in many parts of its geographical range (Barnett 1999). It is generally rarer in lowland areas, such as at the coast.
range: This species occurs in the Pacific lowlands and adjoining montane regions of north Ecuador to west central Peru (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from close to sea level to around 4,900 m (Patton et al. 2015). In Ecuador it has an altitudinal range of 2,200 to 4,160 m (Tirira 2011).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas in Ecuador and Peru. Further taxonomic research is needed for this species complex.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is generally associated with semi-desert and steppe habitats. It has been recorded from areas of clay and loess substrate, and can be found close to watercourses (Habibi 2003). It is a colonial species that lives in an extensive system of interconnected burrows (Habibi 2003).
threats: In view of the distribution over a wide area of suitable habitat, there seem to be no major threats to this species as a whole.
population: There is little information available on the abundance of this species.
range: This species is widely distributed in semi-desert, steppes, and mountainous areas of southern Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, central Afghanistan and northeastern Iran (Habibi 2003, Musser and Carleton 2005, Siahsarvie et al. 2005). In Afghanistan, it has been recorded between 1,500 and 3,400 m asl.
conservationActions: It is found in the periphery of Tandoureh National Park in the Kopet-dag Mountains of Iran (Siahsarvie et al. 2005). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, ecology, and threats to this little known species.

rationale: This species has a fairly large extent of occurrence (c.100,000 km2). Little information is available on population status or trends, but it does not appear to be under threat at present hence is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Habitats characteristic to the species are matted loess soils, sometimes found in loess-sandy semideserts in mountains. It is diurnal and colonial. It makes complex burrows, on ground exits connected by pathways. The species reproduces the whole year round with 2-3 months break in summer.
threats: No known major threats are known to this species.
population: There are no data available for population trend and status. Ecology of the species is similar to that of Blanfordimys afganus, which usually undergoes periodical population fluctuations.
range: Northern ranges of Pamir-Alay, namely Zeravshan, Gissar and Nuratau Ranges (Uzbekistan and Tajikistan), and Badakhshan Range (Afghanistan). It is distributed up to at least 1,500 m asl, in Afghanistan probably up to 3,000 m (Gromov and Erbaeva 1995)
conservationActions: It is not known if the species occurs in protected areas. Further research is needed about population trend and status, actions and threats.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it does not currently meet the thresholds for a threatened category. It could potentially be listed as Near Threatened in the near future because despite its large range, due to pressures on its habitat and the possibility of a species complex. This species is currently estimated to be in decline due to habitat loss caused by deforestation, and due to water pollution (the species is semi-aquatic). However, it is not currently declining at a rate sufficient to qualify for Vulnerable under criterion A. If further studies reveal this to be more than one species they will need to be assessed.
habitat: The distribution of this species (as it is currently recognized) spans over dissected mountainous terrain. It has been captured along the banks or streams of irrigation canals, and most abundantly in agricultural landscapes. The original habitat through the range of this species was most likely cloud forest (Voss 2015). It is nocturnal, terrestrial and semiaquatic and feed on crabs and other aquatic invertebrates (Voss 1988).
threats: The major threats to this species, outside of the protected areas in which it occurs, are loss of habitat due to deforestation and agriculture, as well as water pollution. However, the species seems to persist even in agricultural landscapes.
population: This species is not considered to be rare, but it is difficult to collect. Three different local populations are currently recognized which comprise the species; further population data are unavailable.
range: This species occurs in the Andes mountains of western Venezuela, in the eastern and western Andes of Colombia, and in the western Andes of northern Ecuador. It is known from elevations between 1,000 m and 2,800 m (Voss 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas in Venezuela. In Colombia, it occurs in Munchique National Park (Voss, 1988). Further taxonomic studies of this species are needed.

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened due to a restricted geographic range in an area threatened by deforestation, cattle and agriculture. The area of occupancy is approximately 5,000 km² and there is a continuing decline in quality and extent of habitat outside of protected areas, 10 locations (defined by threat). Due to continuing development of the regions the species will soon be exposed to water contamination and pollution, thus this situation needs to be studied and monitored.
habitat: The species occurs in tall rainforest and montane cloud forest (Voss 1988). All known specimens have been captured by hand in small streams or drainage canals bordered by lower montane forest. Captive individuals of this species consumed a variety of small, aquatic animals, but preferred pseudothelphusid crab (Voss 2015). It is nocturnal, terrestrial and semiaquatic (Voss 1988).
threats: In the western part of the distribution there is habitat destruction caused by deforestation and conversion to pasture (J. Ochoa pers. comm.). This species is susceptible to water pollution and contamination.
population: This is not a rare species where habitat remains, yet it is difficult to collect (J. Ochoa pers. comm.).
range: This species is known from a few scattered localities in the coastal cordilleras and adjacent hills of northern Venezuela. It occurs at elevations ranging from 700 m to 1,750 m (Voss 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas (J. Ochoa and M. Aguilera pers. comm).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because it is common within suitable habitat, has a presumed large population, occurs in protected areas and it is unlikely to be in decline.
habitat: This species is poorly known. It can be found in evergreen forest, forest edge, and in open areas (Reid 1997). It is mainly arboreal (Handley 1966). A female with four embryos was caught in February (Reid 1997).
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: This species is common in Panamá. It can be found in rural gardens, but does not persist in secondary forests.
range: This species occurs from east Panamá, including Azuero Peninsula, and perhaps adjacent Colombia (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from lowlands to 900 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: Most of its distribution in Panamá is in protected areas.

rationale: Although its extent of occurrence is probably less than 20,000 km2, this species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse can be found in highland and montane forest, forest edge, and clearings. Its biology is poorly known. It is mainly terrestrial but is sometimes caught on logs or low branches. It may be found among patches of bamboo near creeks (Reid 1997).
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: It is locally common (Reid 1997).
range: This species occurs from upper elevations in the Cordilleras Tilarán, Central, and Talamanca, Costa Rica, to the Chiriquí region, western Panamá (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from 1,300 to 3,350 m (Timm et al. 1989).
conservationActions: It occurs in protected areas in Costa Rica, including Volcán Irazu.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is poorly known. It can be found in or near evergreen forest. It was recorded in Nicaragua from a shaded coffee field; in Costa Rica it was found in deep rocky canyons and cloud forest (Reid 1997). It was trapped along fallen logs and at the bases of large trees in Nicaragua (Jones and Genoways 1970). Two pregnant females, with 3 and 4 embryos, were caught in June (Reid 1997). It is often in edge habitat.
threats: There are no major threats known for this species.
population: This mouse is generally rare and local (Reid 1997), but may be abundant is secondary growth.
range: This species occurs in allopatric populations in highlands of north central Nicaragua (Jones and Genoways 1970) and central Costa Rica (Musser and Carleton 2005). In Nicaragua it occurs from 1,100 to 1,250 m (Reid 1997) and in Costa Rica from 1,700 to 2,300 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It is located in mid-elevation national parks in Costa Rica, including Rincon de la Vieja national park.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered, because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 4,339 km², its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 500 km², its range is severely fragmented, and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its tidal marsh habitat, and the number of locations as well as the number of individuals.
habitat: The species' habitat consists of salt and brackish marshes, where plants provide a dense mat of cover, ideally around 30-50 cm high with a high percentage (e.g., 60%) of pickleweed (Salicornia) and complex structure of Atriplex and other species. The Salt-marsh Harvest Mouse is reliant on cover from vegetation to protect them from salt marsh tides and predators. Pickleweed is known to be an integral part of the Salt-marsh Harvest Mouse habitat; however, research suggests areas with mixed vegetation not dominated by pickleweed can be equally productive (Sustaita et al. 2011). The mouse needs access to refuge/cover on high ground, especially during highest tides in winter. It appears to be less dependent on cover in diked marshes than in tidal marshes (Geissel et al. 1988). In South San Francisco Bay, in diked marsh, harvest mice used more open and saltier pickleweed when vole populations were high, then moved into deeper and less salty pickleweed as vole populations declined (Geissel et al. 1988). In diked salt marshes, high densities of voles (Microtus) seem to force this species into marginal habitats or to become locally extirpated (Geissel et al. 1988). Grass dominated habitats saw few individuals. Densities of Salt-marsh Harvest Mice were higher in diked wetlands but with greater long term persistence in tidal wetlands. Both tidal and diked wetlands are capable of sustaining populations (Sustaita et al. 2011). Subspecies halicoetes builds ball-like nests of dry grasses/sedges on the ground. Subspecies raviventris does little nest building but may use accumulations of vegetation on the ground surface. Diet dominated by green vegetation. Will eat salt grass and pickleweed as well as some seeds. Diet influenced by availability of food plants. More green vegetation is eaten in winter. Primarily nocturnal but sometimes active during the day.Average litter size is 3.7-4.0 young. There may be only a single litter/year in R. r. halicoetes (breeds May-November) but multiple litters in R. r. raviventris (breeds March-November).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat destruction or disturbance due to development, residential encroachment, intrusion of fresh water into salt marshes, marsh subsidence, and predation (especially by house cats). In many marsh habitats, there is no higher ground to escape to during high tides. Habitat within the range of the southern subspecies (R. r. raviventris) has been more severely impacted than that of the northern subspecies (R. r. halicoetes).Most of the historical tidal marsh habitat has been lost as a result of filling for urban development and conversion to agricultural uses and commercial salt production. Upland vegetative cover adjoining tidal marshes is important cover for harvest mice during high tides and storms, but much of this habitat is no longer available due to clearing and conversion to intensive human uses. Remaining populations are relatively small, isolated, and may lack the size and full range of resources needed for long-term persistence.Threats include continued loss of habitat to development, pollution and other changes in water quality, and encroachment by exotic plant species (e.g., invasive cordgrasses, Spartina) that do not provide suitable habitat for salt marsh harvest mice. Most areas of remaining habitat support few to no mice because of backfilling, subsidence, or vegetation changes. Salt marshes are subject to subsidence and increased tidal coverage (flooding) as a result of groundwater pumping. This reduces the extent of the broad pickleweed zone favoured by harvest mice (Shellhammer 1998).Most of the remaining habitat is diked. Much of the habitat is managed for waterfowl and such management (e.g., lowered salinities) may not be compatible with the needs of harvest mice. Excessive inputs of fresh water (e.g., from discharges of treated municipal sewage) have altered salinity levels, marsh vegetation, and mouse food resources. See Shellhammer (1989) for a discussion of threats to diked marshes.Much of the East Bay shoreline from San Leandro to Calaveras Point is rapidly eroding. In addition, an estimated 600 acres of former salt marsh along Coyote Creek, Alviso Slough, and Guadalupe Slough has been converted to fresh- and brackish-water vegetation due to freshwater discharge from South Bay wastewater facilities; these areas likely no longer support populations of salt marsh harvest mice.Some habitat has been lost as a result of discing of non-tidal salt marsh. Discing of wetlands, an activity not regulated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, has been employed by interests seeking to obscure the Corps' jurisdiction and circumvent the Clean Water Act and the Federal Endangered Species Act.Some harvest mice are preyed upon by feral and free-ranging cats and non-native red foxes that roam salt-pond dikes or wander from residential areas now bordering many tidal marshes.Habitat may be threatened over the long term by the rise in sea level that is predicted to occur within the next century. In combination with reduced sediment supply caused by upstream dams and water diversions, sea level rise could result in major losses of tidal marsh habitat that would be very difficult to prevent or mitigate.
population: No exact population data have been found from recent surveys. Populations are small due to habitat destruction (Kays and Wilson 2009). Shellhammer et al. (1983) estimated a total population of a "few thousand animals at the peak of their numbers each summer." They also mapped 24 "principal populations." Recent figures are unavailable. The former, probably more or less continuous historical distribution has been fragmented, leaving harvest mouse populations restricted to discontinuous patches of suitable habitat. About 84% of historical tidal marshes of the San Francisco Bay area have been destroyed. Over 3,600 acres of habitat have been filled or degraded since the 1970s. Since 1982, hundreds of acres of non-tidal salt marsh in the South Bay have been disced and the damage continued into at least 1989 (California DF&G 1990).
range: The Salt-marsh Harvest Mouse is endemic to salt marshes bordering San Francisco Bay in California, USA (Kays and Wilson 2009). The subspecies raviventris inhabits the San Pablo bay at the south end of San Francisco bay, while halicoetes occupies the Suison bay at the north end. Occurrence within this small range is highly fragmented. The range encompasses salt marshes of the San Francisco Bay system (San Francisco, San Pablo, and Suisun bays), in central California (Shellhammer 1982). The remaining tidal marsh habitat in the San Francisco Bay Area is estimated to be 12,555 ha (=125 sq km). An unknown fraction of this habitat is actually occupied by this species.
conservationActions: Although populations occur in a number of protected areas, many are probably not large enough to ensure long term persistence. There was a recovery plan completed in 1984. However, the US Fish and Wildlife Service is developing a "Tidal March Ecosystem Recovery Plan," with R. raviventris to be included in this apparently updated plan.This mouse is protected to some extent by federal and state listings as Endangered. Several small marshes are protected in national wildlife refuges and other preserves, but few provide refuge and cover from the highest tides.Marshes and adjacent uplands need to be protected from development and degradation. Managed, diked marshes appear to be the key to the survival of the subspecies raviventris; future management prescriptions may include the possibility of a more patchy environment with some areas of high salinities plus the acceptance of some open areas within the managed areas (Geissel et al. 1988). Shellhammer (1989) questioned whether large enough areas of diked marsh can be acquired in the near future to protect this species in perpetuity. Up-to-date data are needed on range-wide habitat occupancy and relative abundance. Research is needed on the effects of plant salinities on water balance and habitat use of mice.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species range is found in high elevation pine/oak forest.
threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
population: This species is common in suitable habitat within its range.
range: This species occurs in the Cordillera Transvolcanica, from southeast Jalisco to west central Veracruz, México (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: This species' range falls partially into a number of protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 4,894 km², all individuals occur in fewer than five locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: The species particularly occurs in pine-oak habitats associated with cloud forests. It may occupy other montane regions in central Guerrero, but appears to be restricted in distribution (Bradley et al. 2004).
threats: The species is threatened by habitat fragmentation and deforestation by logging within its restricted range.
population: No information on population or abundance is available. Little is known about this recently described species.
range: This species is known from the montane region of central Guerrero, Mexico. It occurs at elevations greater than 2,150 m (Bradley et al. 2004). This species is only known from two localities: Filio de Caballo and Omiltemi de la Sierra Madre.
conservationActions: This species is not found in any protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because it has a limited range and an estimated area of occupancy is around 240 km². Additionally, its extent of occurrence and habitat quality are declining and fragmented due to continued deforestation within the species range and there are an estimated 2-5 locations.
habitat: This species is restricted to mature, broadleaf montane forest where it favours the coldest, wettest slopes, with abundant epiphytes and mosses. Its biology is poorly known; this species apparently is semi-arboreal (Reid 2009).
threats: Deforestation is a major threat to this species. Fire is a potential threat, for example in Sierra de las Minas National Park, due to the small extent of occurrence of the species.
population: This species is rare and localised (Reid 2009). No new information on population trends have been found since the 2008 assessment.
range: The Narrow-nosed Harvest Mouse is distributed from southeast Chiapas, Mexico to eastern Guatemala. It is found between 2,400 and 2,900 m (Rogers et al. 1983, Reid 2009).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Sierra de las Minas National Park in Guatemala, but does not occur in any known protected areas in Mexico. Its distribution has been reduced in recent years (Ceballos 2014). Very little is known about this species, research concerning its distribution, ecology, and biology is needed.

rationale: Although its extent of occurrence is probably less than 5,000 km2, this species is listed as Least Concern in view of its occurrence in a number of well-managed protected areas, and because it does not appear to be under threat and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This mouse can be found in wet, mature highland forest and in pastures at forest edge (Reid 2009).  Its biology is poorly known. It has been trapped on the ground in grass at the edge of wet forest on Irazu (Goodwin 1946), and in low vegetation in elfin forest. This mouse feeds on the nectar of a melastome (Blakea sp.), and may be one of several mouse pollinators for this plant (Lumer and Schoer 1986). A pregnant female was captured in July (Reid 1997).
threats: No major threats are known for this species.
population: This species is rare and local (Reid 2009).
range: In addition to previous assessment, the species is known from Volcán Barva, Volcán Irazú, and Cerro la Asunción in Central Costa Rica (Reid 2009). This species is patchily recorded in the Cordilleras Central and Talamancas, central Costa Rica (Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from 1,500 to 3,400 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It is located in national parks in well-protected forests. It needs taxonomic research.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is a species that should be monitored closely, however, because it is very habitat specific, only being found in mature and undisturbed humid and cool forests, which are becoming increasingly fragmented.
habitat: This mouse is restricted to mature and undisturbed montane forest with numerous ferns, mosses, and fallen trees (Reid 1997). It is semiarboreal. It may be trapped on logs or on the ground at the base of large trees.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss.
population: It is local but not uncommon in suitable habitat (Reid 1997).
range: This species is in isolated pockets in the highlands of north Michoacán and Distrito Federal, north Oaxaca, and central and south Chiapas, Mexico, and west central Guatemala (Musser and Carleton 2005). In Chiapas and Guatemala, it occurs from 2,200 to 3,100 m (Reid 1997).
conservationActions: It occurs in very few protected areas in Mexico, and in a poorly-protected park in Guatemala.

rationale: his species is listed as Near Threatened because the area of occupancy for this species is likely to be close to meeting the threatened threshold for criteria B2, it occurs in 8-10 locations and there is a continuing decline in the area and quality of its habitat. This species occurs in a limited portion of its restricted range, is confined to suitable undisturbed matorral habitat and in fragmented and not well conserved areas, but it is increasingly threatened by habitat loss due to agricultural activities and urban development.
habitat: This species occurs in shublands of the Chilean matorrall. Almost nothing is known about the ecology of this rodent. It is semi-fossorial and digs tunnels with burrow openings usually protected by rocks, shrubs, or fallen logs. Chelemys macronyx inhabits dense mesophitic forest and shrubby areas. This species appears to be rare, or at least very difficult to trap. Recently collected specimens come from Parque Nacional Fray Jorge, a protected area of arid Mediterranean thorn- scrub with remnants of fog forests at higher elevation near the city of Coquimbo, from disturbed forest along the Río Quino in the municipality of Victoria, Malleco province, and from dense thickets of throny bush, Trevoa trinervi, in Rinoconada de Maipú, Metropolitan Region (Bazán-Leon et al. 2015, Teta et al. 2015).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat destruction due to urban development, agricultural activities, viniculture and cattle activities.
population: This species is considered rare.
range: This species is known from only a few scattered localities in an apparently disjoint distribution in coastal central Chile. In the north, it is limited to the Coquimbo to Santiago regions and in the south to BioBio and Araucanía, and presumably Maule regions, with no records from the intervening O'Higgins region (Quintana 2009, Teta et al. 2015, Bazán- Leon et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (e.g. Parque Nacional Fray Jorge).

rationale: The Sichuan Vole is assessed as Near Threatened (NT) as it is known for certain from only a single patch in Sichuan with less than 50 km² of available habitat available. The region is under current development for tourism. The population is likely to be declining, but more data are required to confirm this. It is assessed as NT as it almost qualifies for a threatened category under criterion B.
habitat: It occurs in high altitude forests (Smith and Xie 2008). Although, a study by Wang et al. (2010) found this species near crop fields and concluded that this species may compete for space and food with Rattus edwardsi.
threats: In the past, logging in this region would have posed a threat. Today, the extent to which illegal logging occurs is not known but it continues to pose a threat to this species. In addition, part of this species habitat is being constructed as a skiing park so there is a high likelihood that this will affect population numbers (Liu pers. comm).
population: There is a lack of data regarding the population status of this species. However, a recent study found that this species occupied 20% of the community in the northwest region of Sichuan (Liu pers. comm).
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring only in the northwest region of Sichuan province (Smith and Xie 2008). The locality recorded by Zhang et al. (1997) in southern Yunnan requires confirmation, it is probably Microtus clarkei (Musser and Carleton 2005). This species occurs at elevations above 4,000 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008).
useTrade: The use and trade informations for this species are not known.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Wolong Nature Reserve (CSIS 2008) and is presumed to occur in WenchuanCaopo, Heishuihe, Fengtongzhai, Anzihe, and Longhixihongkou Nature Reserves. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Vulnerable A1ac (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: This rodent is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because all individuals are known only from four fossils and and one holotype from 1896, and there have been no new records since then.
habitat: This species occurs in Chacoan environment in and near freshwater (Wilson et al. 2017) and there are no details of its ecology (Patton et al. 2015).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown.
