Isarog National Park used to be logged particularly in the lowlands and lower montane forest, but this has ceased and the area appears to no longer be threatened by logging and most montane and mossy forest is currently undisturbed (Heaney et al. 2016). Given the severity of previous logging operations on the forest on the mountain, logging is a plausible future threat to the small mossy forest at high elevations.
population: The population appears stable, but it is geographically restricted (Musser and Freeman 1981). The species is more common on Mt. Isarog than Chrotomys gonzalezi or Archbold luzonensis. It is difficult to trap. It is common in mossy forest and less common in montane forest  (Heaney et al. 2016).
range: This species is only known from Mt. Isarog, Camarines Sur Province, Luzon (Philippines) (Heaney et al. 2002). Specimens of Rhynchomys found on Mt. Labo are provisionally assigned to this species, though more research is required (Heaney et al. 2016).
conservationActions: The species occurs in Mt. Isarog National Park (Heaney et al. 2016).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because this species is probably in significant decline (but probably at a rate of less than 30% over ten years) because of widespread habitat disturbance and ongoing conversion of forested areas to vegetable farms through much of its range, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2c.
habitat: This terrestrial species inhabits mossy forest (Heaney et al. 2002) and occurs in areas with wet leaf litter where it feeds on earthworms (Rickart et al. 2011). It was found to only be present at low disturbance mature forest at Balbalasang  (Rickart et al. 2007). It is has been trapped during the nocturnal/crepuscular period (Rickart et al. 2011).
threats: There has been some clearing for intensive agriculture, but also a lot of regeneration of ​secondary forest associated with a major decrease in the extent and frequency of burning in the Central Cordillera (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016). Rhynchomys soricoides has specific habitat requirements, which makes it relatively intolerant of disturbance (Ong and Rickart 2008), principally because forest loss causes the leaf litter to dry out and its food source is eliminated (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2006). On Mt. Data, which was one of the most disturbed sites surveyed in a study, the species was not detected where it historically had been found (Rickart et al. 2011). This is likely to be because the forest that does still occur on Mt. Data is quite small and is an isolated patch (L. Heaney pers. comm).
population: The species is moderately common in Balbasang National Park (Heaney et al. 2004, Ong and Rickart 2008), but described as uncommon in the Barlig- Mt. Amuyao region (Ong and Rickart 2008) and generally considered to occur at fairly low densities (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
range: This species, which is endemic to Luzon (Philippines), has been recorded from Mt. Data, Benguet province, and from montane and mossy forest from 1,600-2,150 m in Balbalasang, Kalinga province (Heaney et al. 1998) and on Mt. Pulag (Rickart et al. 2011) and on Mt. Amuyao between 1,990 m and 2,690 m asl. (Rickart et al. 2016). However, it is likely to occur throughout the Central Cordillera (L. Heaney pers. comm.), although surveys on Mt. Sto Tomas failed to detect the species (Reginaldo and de Guia 2014).
conservationActions: The species is found in a number of protected areas across its range, including in Mt. Pulag National Park (Rickart et al. 2011).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because whilst it is known from a fairly small restricted area on Mount Oku, its afromontane grassland habitat currently has no major threats identified.
habitat: It is found in afroalpine grass savanna above the montane forest zone and is only found in areas where there is abundant grass cover, including where there is grassland in woodlands and agricultural fields (E. Van der Straeten pers. comm.).
threats: There are no major threats to the species at present in its high elevation habitat, although it may be locally affected by livestock grazing of grasslands. It is plausibly threatened by future climate change related events.
population: The abundance, population size and trends for this species are not known.
range: This species is known from ten specimens collected by Eisentraut in the 1960s at Lake Oku on the Banso Highlands, on Mount Oku, western Cameroon at 2,100 to 2,300 m asl, and from more recent surveys of Mount Oku (Maisels et al. 2001, Denys et al. 2014). Collections in similar habitats in Nigeria have failed to find this species.
conservationActions: The area in which this species has been recorded is not protected. There is a need to monitor population trends of this species within its high elevation distribution.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, although it is seldom recorded, it occurs in an area of extensive, suitable habitat which appears not to be under significant threat, has a presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in dry savanna in northern Côte d'Ivoire and Mali (where it can be on rather rocky substrate), and was found associated with cultivated of fallow habitats in Guinea . The species is associated with the 'Sudan Savannah Zone'.
threats: There are no known threats to this species.
population: It is locally common in Côte d'Ivoire and Mali in suitable habitat.
range: This species occurs in northern Côte d'Ivoire, southern Mali, in Central Guinea and it is known from a single record in Senegal. The species is presumed to occur in Ghanabut no specimens have been recorded to date. In Mali and Guinea it has been recorded from 500 to 700 m asl.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Comoe National Park in Côte d'Ivoire.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This is a dry savanna species. Presumably the species can persist in areas with some disturbance.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: It is not abundant, but it is regularly found in suitable habitat.
range: This species has been recorded in the 'Guinea and Doka woodland' of central Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana (Van der Straeten 1975, Ziegler et al. 2002); it possibly also occurs in Sierra Leone. The distribution area is probably larger than is currently known.
conservationActions: There are a number of protected areas within the species range (e.g., Comoe National Park, Côte d'Ivoire, and Mole National Park, Ghana).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, it is reasonably common within its small range where the extent of occurrence is approximately 30,592 km2. Its native forest habitat may be threatened from deforestation, especially on the island of Biak. Further research into the response of this species to habitat degradation.
habitat: It has been recorded from tropical moist forest, at the forest edge, in rural gardens, and within villages. On Papua the species was found in lowland rainforest areas (Pattiselanno and Arobaya 2012).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation of native forest, especially on the island of Biak. It is possibly threatened by competition with the introduced Rattus rattus.
population: It is a reasonably common species.
range: This species is restricted to Yapen, Biak-Supiori, and Owi islands of Indonesia and has been found in Tamrau Highland Nature Reserve in the Saukorem District in Papua (Pattiselanno and Arobaya 2012). Its elevational range is from sea level to 600 m asl.
conservationActions: It is found in Tamrau Highland Nature Reserve (Pattiselanno and Arobaya 2012). Further studies into the habitat requirements, ecology, and threats to this species are needed; most importantly, research should focus on how it responds to habitat degradation.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population (it is abundant in suitable habitat), lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It has been recorded in lower elevation montane tropical forests.
threats: There are no known major threats to this species.
population: It is abundant in suitable habitat.
range: This species is widely distributed through the lower montane forests in the Central Cordillera of New Guinea (Papua Province, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea). It is found from 1,500 to 2,500 m asl.
conservationActions: It possibly occurs in Lorentz National Park. Further studies into its taxonomic status are needed (see Taxonomic Notes).

rationale: Listed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence of less than 20,000 km2, all individuals occur in fewer than ten locations, and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat primarily due to increased fire frequency associated with global warming. This species is confined to a very particular high altitude habitat that is tied to the remnant glaciers. This species could well become more threatened as these glaciers continue to retreat.
habitat: It is found in areas of alpine scrub and tussock grassland, often between rocks and other cover.
threats: This high-altitude species is considered to be at risk from the impacts of increasing fire frequency induced by global warming. There is mining activity in one of the protected areas where it is found. Animals are predated by hunting dogs in parts of its range.
population: It is believed to be reasonably common where it is found.
range: This species is known only from three localities in two areas of the island of New Guinea. It is found in the Central Cordillera of Papua Province, Indonesia where it has been recorded from around Lake Habbema and Mount Wilhelmina, and from Mount Jaya (Flannery 1995). These areas represent two of the last areas with glacial cover on New Guinea. It has an elevational range of 3,225 to 4,500 m asl.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: This species has been recorded from protected areas (e.g. Lorentz National Park). Other areas of suitable glacial habitat should be surveyed to locate additional populations of this restricted range species.

rationale: This species is known from a fewer than five locations and, based on current known occurrences, it may have a small extent of occurrence (the current calculated EOO is 2,937 km²). It is potentially at risk of continuing loss of habitat. It could therefore qualify as threatened under criterion B, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any long-term, comprehensive surveys in the area. It is possible that its distribution and extent of occurrence is significantly larger, which would potentially qualify this species for listing as Least Concern. Therefore, it is considered more appropriate to assess this species as Near Threatened, as it is likely to at least be approaching the thresholds of criterion B. Further research into its ecology, population and threats is needed.
habitat: Individuals have been recorded in primary montane tropical moist forest. This species’ original locality was characterised as an oak forest with many large trees over 30 m tall, as well as numerous dead trees covered by ferns and mosses, and regular mists (Taylor et al. 1982). It may be more tolerant of disturbed valley habitat than its congeners such as R. verecundus (see Cole et al. 1997). The only specimen captured by Cole et al. (1997) was found with burgundy-stained fur, indicating contact with fruit, and others have been trapped with the use of peanut butter, beetle larvae and sweet potato baits (see Burgin 2017). Overall, little is known about the natural history of this species.
threats: The forest within which this species lives has been degraded in parts of its range. From 1972–2002, 14,456 ha of highland forest was degraded in the south-eastern forests of Papua New Guinea (Shearman et al. 2009). Forest loss in Papua New Guinea is largely driven by subsistence agriculture and oil palm plantations, some of which is being pushed to higher elevations as lowland plantations expand and human populations increase (Gamoga et al. 2021). It is not known to what extent this species tolerates habitat change or degradation. Additionally, there may be competition with Rattus rattus at the lower edges of its elevational range.
population: Very little is known about its population. It may be locally abundant at certain sites but absent from others. At least 40 specimens have been collected.
range: Rattus vandeuseni is restricted to the mountains of south-east Papua New Guinea, where it is found at altitudes above 1,300 m asl. It is currently only known from specimens collected in the 1990s from Milne Bay Province on the slopes of Mt. Dayman, near Param and Munimun Village. Cole et al. (1997) described it as “presumed endemic to mid-montane forests of the eastern Owen Stanley Range”. Further survey work might reveal a wider distribution (e.g., it is possibly present on Mt. Simpson). It appears to replace the closely related but more widespread R. verecundus at around 1,300 m asl (Aplin et al. 2003). Its range is suspected to be very fragmented.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Further studies into the distribution, natural history, habitat status, and threats to the species are needed. Important areas of habitat for this species should be identified and protected.

rationale: This rat is listed as Near Threatened since its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 29,755 km² (larger than the criterion B1 threshold) and it is found in a single location where its native forest habitat is declining. Thus the species is close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B1, depending on how affected the species is to habitat disturbance. The range is probably not fragmented.
habitat: This species seems to be largely terrestrial (Helgen 2003). This species has been recorded from moderately disturbed mid-elevation rainforest in precipitous limestone country (Helgen 2003). This is the largest known rat on Seram.
threats: This species is threatened by logging, especially in lowland areas. There has been deforestation in lowland areas for cacao and oil palm, with large areas of forest cleared for plantation in 2009, but small scale shifting agriculture in upland community has little pressure on forest clearance (Sasaoka et al. 2014). There is conflict because of undefined boundaries of Manusela National Park, but the mixed tree gardens of surrounding communities may provide an important buffer zone for conserving biodiversity (Cosiaux 2014). It can persist in some moderately disturbed areas. It is also threatened by competition with the introduced Rattus rattus.
population: It is known from eight specimens collected at three sites (Helgen 2003).
range: This species has been recorded at three localities on Seram (Teloeti Bay on the south coast, near Piliana Village in south-central Seram, and on Gunung Manusela), the elevational range is from sea level to 1,830 m (Helgen 2003). Although the distribution is incompletely known, it almost certainly occurs throughout the island.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Manusela National Park. Studies are needed into the persistence of this species in modified habitats, and also into the general habitat use by the species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, although it has a patchy distribution, it has a relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, is tolerant of some degree of habitat modification, lacks major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Even if R. novaeguineae were split into separate species, they would all likely be considered Least Concern.
habitat: It has been collected in primary tropical moist forest, secondary forest, and grassland. It has been recorded in association with vegetation along stream and river banks in montane forest. It breeds year round; females give birth to between four and six young.
threats: There are no known major threats to this species.
population: It is a common species that can occur in dense populations.
range: This species has a patchy distribution within the central part of Papua New Guinea. It ranges from 740 to 1,520 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if this species is present in any protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern since, although its extent of occurrence is probably less than 7,000 km2, it is common and adaptable, it occurs in a number of protected areas, it is tolerant of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in a wide variety of primary and secondary montane habitats. Musser and Newcomb (1985) note that they "suspect that this species is terrestrial and lives in grass and dense shrubbery providing good cover that may occur either along forest margins or scattered through forest with an open canopy. Thick scrub cover adjacent to agricultural fields may also be good habitat".
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this relatively adaptable species.
population: It is presumed to be a common species.
range: This species has been recorded from only two localities in Lam Dong province, southern Viet Nam (Musser and Carleton 2005), Langbian Peak (12°03'N, 108°26'E) and Gougah.
conservationActions: It is present in protected areas across its range. Further studies are needed into the relationship between this taxon and Rattus losea.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, because it is widespread over a range of ​ elevations ​in eastern Mindoro, in both primary and secondary forest.
habitat: It is widespread over a range of ​ elevations ​in eastern Mindoro, in both primary and secondary forest (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
threats: Deforestation has occurred in the past, which was thought to have adversely affected this species (Heaney et al. 1998). There is continued illegal logging in the lowlands (M. Lepiten-Tabao pers. comm. 2006), however, the species has been recorded in both primary and secondary forest (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016), therefore it appears to be tolerant of some habitat disturbance.
population: It is common at a range of elevations and in both primary and secondary forest (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
range: This species is endemic to the Philippines, where it is known only from Mindoro island (Heaney et al. 1998). It is widespread over a range of ​ elevations ​in eastern Mindoro, in both primary and secondary forest (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
conservationActions: The species has been recorded in Mt. Iglit National Park.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered, because its extent of occurrence is estimated to be 1,067 km² and its area of occupancy is considered to be less than 500 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat.
habitat: Rattus montanus is a diurnal or crepuscular, terrestrial species. It occurs in tropical evergreen montane forest and wet grasslands (Molur et al. 2005).
threats: Habitat loss and degradation due to expansion of agriculture, fire and clear-cutting of forests have been observed to be the major threats for this species (Molur et al. 2005).
population: There is no information available on the population size or trends of this species (Molur et al. 2005).
range: This species is endemic to Sri Lanka in Central and Uva provinces, where it is restricted to four highly fragmented locations (Peak wilderness Sanctuary, Hakgala Strict nature reserve, Horton Plains, Nuwara Eliya and Ohiya) in the central highlands (Phillips 1980, Molur et al. 2005, D. Wickramasinghe in litt. 2005, W.L.D.P.T.S. de A. Goonatilake in litt. 2016). It occurs at elevations from 1,320 to 2,310 m asl (Molur et al. 2005).
conservationActions: The species is protected by Fauna and Flora Protection (Amendment) 45 Act, No.22 of 2009. It has been recorded from Horton Plains National Park, Hakgala Strict Nature Reserve, Peak wilderness Sanctuary. Phylogenetic studies, general field surveys, research into the natural history and monitoring of populations are recommended for this species (Molur et al. 2005).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, high tolerance to habitat disturbance, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This terrestrial species has been recorded in a wide variety of habitats, from primary mossy tropical forest, tropical scrubland and eucalyptus savanna, through secondary forest to rural gardens, and to some extent villages. The species does not appear to have a breeding season; females give birth to between two and four young (Flannery 1995b).
threats: There appear to be no threats to this adaptable species.
population: It seems to be a common species.
range: This species is present in eastern New Guinea and on the Huon Peninsula (Papua New Guinea), the Conflict Group of islands, Fergusson Island, Goodenough Island, Misima Island, Normanby Island, Sideia Island, Sudest Island and Woodlark Island (all Papua New Guinea) (Flannery 1995a). It occurs from sea level up to 2,800 m asl.
conservationActions: It is presumed that the species is present in some protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it is apparently a common and adaptable species.
habitat: This is an arboreal species, and very agile climber. It has been trapped on the ground in gardens on the edge of primary forest, and observed it climbing in understory plants. It spends its days in burrows, the entrances to some having been found placed in particularly bare areas in new gardens (Flannery 1995). Flannery (1995) also observed this species in cocoa plantations on Batjan.
threats: Although there is likely to be habitat loss taking place on the Halmahera islands due to logging and agriculture, this species seems fairly adaptable to human disturbance. It may be affected by competition with introduced murids, including Rattus rattus.
population: Flannery (1995) recorded it as common throughout its range.
range: This is the only murid endemic to the Halmahara Islands where it has been recorded from Morotai, Halmahara, and Batjan islands (Musser and Carleton 2005). All known localities are from low-lying areas, but there has been no survey work in higher-elevations in these islands.
conservationActions: It is not known whether it occurs in any protected areas. There are several proposed nature reserves on Halmahera, but the status of these is unknown.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it is common within its restricted distribution, it presumably has a large population, it may be adaptable to habitat modification, the distribution is fully within a well-protected area, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in montane and moss forest, and sub-summit dwarf forest and scrub (Musser 1986). It is not known if the species is present in disturbed habitats. As with related species, it may be readily adaptable to habitat modification.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: This species is common at altitudes between 2,130 and 3,810 m on Mt. Kinabalu (Medway 1977, Musser and Newcomb 1983, Musser 1986).
range: This species is known only from Mt. Kinabalu (Malaysia) in northern Borneo (Musser and Carleton 2005, Md Nor 2001, Musser 1986). It has been recorded between 1,524 and 3,810 m.
conservationActions: It is present in Mt. Kinabalu National Park. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy of this species. Surveys are needed to determine if it is present in other mountain areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as although it is probably undergoing decline due to the conversion of forested habitat to agricultural lands in parts of its range, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to warrant listing in a higher category of threat.
habitat: It has been collected from lowland secondary forest, and in rubber estates whenever traps were set low in trees. Several specimens were also taken on the ground (Muul and Lim 1971). These same authors noted that none were taken in deep primary forest.
threats: In the Sumatran part of the range, the major threat is likely to be loss of forest cover, with conversion of land to agriculture. Malaysian populations are probably more stable.
population: Muul and Lim (1971) collected large numbers in Selangor, Malaysia.
range: This species is known from the Malaysian Peninsula, Singapore, east Sumatra, Padang and Rupat (Musser and Newcomb 1983, Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas across its range.

rationale: This rat is listed as Near Threatened, because although it is considered abundant within its small range, its extent of occurrence is approximately 6,129 km² and there appears to be wide scale forest loss on Taliabu. The species is close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B1. Further studies are needed to determine if this species can persist in modified habitats.
habitat: This rat is present in lowland tropical forest, and has been collected in secondary growth and coco plantations, although it is not known if it can persist in these modified habitat and it is possible that the localities may have been close to relatively undisturbed forest.
threats: It may be threatened by habitat loss through logging and conversion of land to agricultural use. Taliabu has experienced drastic habitat clearance in the last few decades, in particular, primary lowland forest (Rheindt 2010). Forest fires have also caused large-scale forest destruction above 750 m asl on Taliabu (Rheindt 2010).  It is also potentially threatened by competition by introduced Rattus species.
population: It is a common species on Taliabu island.
range: This species is known only from Pulau Taliabu and adjacent Pulau Mangole in the Sula Archipelago (Indonesia), but is absent from Pulau Sanana, where only the introduced R. tanezumi and R. exulans are found (Flannery 1995, Musser and Carleton 2005). It occurs from the lowlands to possibly around 1,200 m.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Further research is needed into the response of this species to habitat disturbance.

rationale: Rattus burrus is endemic to the Nicobar Islands, India. It is assessed as Endangered, in view of its small extent of occurrence (EOO; estimated to be 2,841 km²) and area of occupancy (AOO; estimated to be less than 500 km²), with all individuals in fewer than five locations, and a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: This species occurs in tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests (Molur et al. 2005).
threats: The December 2004 tsunami was observed to be the most major threat for this species on the Nicobar islands. Post tsunami development, establishment and expansion of human settlements, conversion of forests into palm plantations are also serious threats to the species (S. Molur pers. comm).
population: There is little information available on the abundance of this species.
range: This species is endemic to the Nicobar group of Islands in India, where it is confined to the islands of Great Nicobar, Little Nicobar and Trinket (Molur et al. 2005, Musser and Carleton 2005). Rattus palmarum and R. anadamanensis occur on Car Nicobar Island and not R. burrus as previously believed (Musser and Carleton 2005). The total area of the islands is less than 1,500 km². and the species is fragmented into three populations on as many islands.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures in place; it is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Additional studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, general ecology and threats to this little-known species. Populations of this species should be monitored to record changes in abundance and distribution.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, although there have been some declines in habitat, it has a relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, occurs in a number of protected areas, and it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is associated with broad, flat, treeless alluvial floodplains of tidal rivers. The species moves seasonally from the floodplains to uplands because of flooding (Williams 2008). Females can produce nine or more young throughout the year depending upon the monsoonal rains (Williams 2008).
threats: Currently, there are no known major threats to this species. There has been some saltwater intrusion of floodplains that can change the vegetation. The effect of feral water buffalo on vegetation encourages saltwater intrusion throughout their range. Habitat loss is occurring through exotic plants, introduced shrubs and grasses. There is also pastoralism through cows. Cane Toads, which reach large numbers in their range, are seen as a potential threat.
population: It is generally an extremely common species where it is found; populations are eruptive (Williams 2008).
range: This species is restricted to the monsoonal subcoastal plains of the Northern Territory, Australia (Williams 2008).
conservationActions: This species is known from many protected areas, including Kakadu National Park.

rationale: This rat is assessed as Least Concern as it is found across a wide elevational range and appears to be abundant in suitable habitats. The area it inhabits is not currently under threat from human activities. Increased fire frequency due to global warming may be a future threat, but the impacts of fires on small rodents needs to be studied.
habitat: It is found in subalpine grassland, moss forest, and in the beech-moss forest zone (Taylor et al. 1982, Helgen 2007). Animals construct shallow tunnels leading to nests among tussock grass. The species is nocturnal (Helgen and Opiang 2013).
threats: The species has a relatively restricted range and is preyed upon by hunting dogs. It is potentially threatened by increased fire frequency induced by global warming.
population: Described as common in appropriate habitat (Helgen and Opiang 2013).
range: This species has been recorded from the upper slopes of Mount Giluwe and its associated peaks, Papua New Guinea (Flannery 1995) and from subalpine grasslands in the Kaijende Highlands (Helgen 2007). It has been recorded from 2,195 to 3,660 m asl, with most records being above 2,800 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if this species is present in any protected areas. Further studies into the distribution, natural history, and threats to this species are needed. In the Kaijende Highlands the area continues to support a largely intact mammal community whether there does not appear to be over-hunting (Helgen 2007).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It has been recorded from montane moss forest and alpine habitats.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: This is an extremely abundant species above 2,000 m asl.
range: This species is widespread in the mountains of central and western New Guinea (Papua Province, Indonesia). It has been recorded between 2,200 and 4,100 m asl.
conservationActions: There are a number of protected areas within its range (e.g. Lorentz National Park). Further taxonomic study is needed (see Taxonomic Notes).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and because its population is likely to be increasing. It is considered a pest in parts of its range.
habitat: The species is apparently found only in a variety of habitats in the lowland areas: from secondary forest, agricultural areas, plantations, gardens, scrub, to grassland (Sanborn 1952, Payne et al. 1985), while Esselstyn et al. (2004) found it in grassland-forest mosaic, selectively logged forest, rice fields, mossy forest, and the transition zone between mossy and montane forest.
threats: There are no major threats to the species.
population: This species is common and widespread.
range: This species is found on peninsular Thailand (south of the Isthmus of Kra), the Malaysian Peninsula, and Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo). In the Philippines, it occurs in the Palawan Faunal Region only being recorded from Arena, Bancalan, Busuanga, Calauit, and Palawan (Musser and Carleton 2005).It is also found on many smaller islands, including Tioman island, Enggano island (south-west of Sumatra) and the Maratua Archipelago (east of Borneo), as well as the smaller islands of Pandjang, Rabu Rabu, Sangka Laki, Bilang Bilangan, Eraban, and Miang Besar off the east coast of Borneo (Musser and Califia 1982). It is also found on Busuanga (Musser 1977).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas across the range.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of habitat modification (exploiting human-disturbed habitat), large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species can be found in low densities within primary tropical moist forest, but it is abundant at the forest edge and in rural gardens or open and grassy areas. Animals are often found in burrows. It breeds throughout the year with females giving birth to litters averaging between 2.7 and 3.4 young.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species, although there is competition with Rattus rattus.
population: It is a common species that can reach high densities.
range: This species is generally widespread on the island of New Guinea (Indonesia and Papua New Guinea), being absent only from the Vogelkop Peninsula (Indonesia), the southern lowlands, and parts of the far east of the island (Flannery 1995). Its elevational range is between 450 and 2,800 m asl.
conservationActions: The species is presumed to occur in some protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because it has not been recorded with certainty since three specimens were collected presumably between 1886 and 1888. There is apparently no local knowledge of the species. It is quite possibly extinct, however, Guadalcanal has not been adequately surveyed. Should this species still exist, it is almost certain to be very few in number.
habitat: It appears to have been a terrestrial species that may have inhabited caves (Flannery 1995). It probably lived in lowland tropical forests.
threats: The reasons for the decline and possible extinction of this species are not known. It may have been subject to overhunting and loss of suitable habitat; or competition, predation, and/or disease transmission from introduced species. Feral cats have been recorded from the area, and these could certainly have lead to the demise of this species.
population: It is known only from the holotype. Guadalcanal has not been adequately surveyed for this species (K. Helgen pers. comm.).
range: This species is known only from the holotype collected by C.M. Woodford presumably between 1886-1888 at Aola, Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands (Flannery 1995). There is apparently no local knowledge of the species. Tim Flannery reports seeing something which could be this species in 1989, but this sighting is unconfirmed (Flannery 1995).
conservationActions: Future surveys of Guadalcanal should be familiar with this species so that any remnant populations can be identified.

rationale: The King Rat is assessed as Endangered because it is endemic to Guadalcanal Island (Solomon Islands) which has an area of 5,336 km² and the species is absent from large parts of the island. Its area of occupancy (AOO) is likely to be less than 500 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and the extent of its forest habitat is declining.
habitat: This arboreal species has been recorded from primary tropical moist forest, including relict patches of native forest.
threats: It is presumably threatened by loss of habitat through deforestation for timber and conversion of land to cultivated use.
population: There are few recent records of this species. A specimen was captured in 1987 by Tim Flannery, found it in a "relict outlier of tall rainforest in the Poha Valley." Flannery (1995) reports that another two were found at Gold Ridge in 1989, but an intensive survey of Mount Makarakomburu in 1990 failed to locate the species. Roger James (pers. comm.) has had indications in interviews with the locals that the species may occur elsewhere on the island, but there are no specimens to confirm this anecdotal information.
range: This species is endemic to the island of Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands. It is absent from large parts of the island. It has been recorded at elevations of 20 and 600 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Directed field studies are needed to identify important sites for this species. Protection of these areas may be needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It occurs in primary and secondary tropical moist forest, closed sclerophyll forest, wet open woodland, swamps, and mangroves (Flannery 1995a, Moore 2008). It is generally not found outside of wooded areas. Females give birth to a litter of usually two or three young after a gestation period of 36 days (Moore 2008).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: This species is common.
range: This species is present on the island of Waigeo (Indonesia), the Kai Islands, the Aru Islands (Indonesia), the island of Yapen (Indonesia), and ranges widely through the lowlands of New Guinea (Indonesia and Papua New Guinea) (Flannery 1995a,b). It is present on Fergusson and Normanby islands (Papua New Guinea), and is present in Cape York and in north-eastern Queensland, Australia, to just south of Townsville; also on Hinchinbrook Island (Moore 2008). It ranges from sea level to 1,925 m asl (Flannery 1995a).
conservationActions: It is present in a number of protected areas. Further studies into the taxonomy of this species are needed to determine whether it is a species complex, possibly containing a number of restricted range species.

rationale: Conservation status assessment is difficult because the recent discovery of this species means that there is no historical context for population trends, and because there is no ongoing monitoring program. Recent research (Moore 2010) has provided some information on abundance and ecology. Most of the habitat is securely protected, and the species is unlikely to be threatened by the factors affecting many Australian mammals (introduced predators, changed fire regimes, habitat degradation due to livestock).Although the species' area of occupancy and its extent of occurrence are relatively small (and there are few locations and subpopulations), there is no evidence to indicate current decline or that marked decline is likely in the next 10 or so years. Hence it is not here considered threatened. However, modelling of climate change impacts suggests that a marked decline of habitat extent and quality is likely over the course of the next ca. 30-50 years. Hence it is likely to become threatened in the next few decades.It is here provisionally listed as Near Threatened as it almost qualifies as threatened under criterion B1ab(ii,iii,v)+2ab(ii,iii,v).
habitat: The Pygmy White-tailed Rat is a nocturnal rodent restricted to rainforests, where it is tightly associated with dense undergrowth vegetation and abundance of fallen logs on lower slopes and gullies and around headwater streams (Moore 2010). Unlike its larger co-occurring congener, the Giant White-tailed Rat U. caudimaculatus, it is entirely terrestrial (rather than also arboreal). Its diet includes seeds, invertebrates (mostly captured by tearing apart decomposing logs), sap (taken from chewing at the bark of tree buttresses), and aerial tree roots (Moore 2010).During the day it nests in burrows with entrances hidden under leaf litter, in holes at the base of trees or under creek banks (Moore and Winter 2008). Climate change and associated factors have been predicted to have a major detrimental impact on this species, acting directly or indirectly through reduction in rainforest area, habitat degradation due to increased incidence of severe cyclones, increased incidence of high temperatures, and reduced incidence of free water in mist (Winter 2004). The extent of its upland habitat is expected to decrease by 50% with a temperature increase of as little as 1oC (Williams et al. 2003, Moore and Winter 2008). The breeding season probably extends from November to April (Moore 2010). Longevity may be 4-5 years (Moore and Winter 2008), so generation length is taken here to be 2-3 years.
threats: Due to the narrow range of habitat used by this species, the headwaters of permanent creek systems in upland rainforest, the greatest threat to this species is global warming. Past clearing and fragmentation may have reduced its previous distribution and current selective logging may adversely affect populations outside the protected area (L. Moore pers. comm.). There is a prediction of 50% decline in extent of its upland habitat with a temperature increase of just 1 degree Celsius (Moore and Winter 2008).
population: There is no robust estimate of population size. Dickman et al. (2000) estimated the total population as 1001-10 000 individuals, although noted that ‘it is possible that population size is larger than indicated’. In a study that targeted ostensibly preferred habitat, Moore (2010) reported trap success of 0.17 individuals per 100 trap-nights (from a trapping effort of >22 000 trap-nights), with a density of 0.4 individuals/ha. Woinarski et al. (2014) estimated the population at 20,000 mature individuals, with low reliability.Dickman et al. (2000) considered that its population size was stable, although  also noted that it ‘has probably declined in the fragmented forest of the Atherton Tableland’.
range: This species is endemic to north-eastern Queensland, Australia. It is restricted to the Thornton Peak massif between 550 and 1,220 m asl elevation, the Mount Carbine Tableland above 900 m, and from the Lamins Hill/Mount Bartle of the Atherton Tableland (above 800 m). In the Atherton Uplands it may be distributed in areas of continuous tropical moist forest with a high rainfall, between Kuranda in the north and Herbert River Gorge in the south (Lee 1995). This species occurs in a discontinuous narrow north-south band: Moore (2010) estimated the latitudinal range was 155 km. Dickman et al. (2000) estimated the ‘current distribution size’ as between 101 and 1,000 km2. This distributional extent is unlikely to have changed since European settlement. However, its area of occupancy is presumed to have declined historically due to some (minor) habitat loss and impacts of subsequent fragmentation (Harrington et al. 2001). Dickman et al. (2000) estimated that its distribution had declined by between 1 and 25%. Woinarski et al. (2014) calculated AOO (based on no. of 2 km x 2 km cells with recent records) as 32 km2, but noted that this was likely to be a major under-estimate due to limited sampling within range; and they calculated EOO as 3,114 km2 (based on alpha hull encompassing known recent records), but again considered this to be an under-estimate.
conservationActions: Most of the population of this species is located within the protected areas of the Wet Tropics World Heritage Area. Its major threat is reduction in rainforest habitat extent and quality due to global climate change. There may be some limited scope to restore connectivity to now fragmented habitat.

rationale: Listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because it has not been recorded with certainty since three specimens were collected between 1886 and 1888. Anecdotal information suggests that the species survived until the 1960s. This species is quite possibly extinct, however, Guadalcanal has not been adequately surveyed (Lavery 2013). Should this species still exist, it is almost certain to be very few in number.
habitat: It seems as though this was a largely terrestrial species that was at one point found throughout much of Guadalcanal, including the dry northern lowlands and areas close to the coast. Later reports suggest that the species became restricted to mossy montane forest (Flannery 1995).
threats: The reasons for the decline and possible extinction of this species are not known. It may have been subject to overhunting and loss of suitable habitat; or competition, predation, and/or disease transmission from introduced species.
population: It is known only from three specimens collected between 1886 and 1888. Anecdotal information suggests that the species survived into the 1960s (Flannery 1995). Guadalcanal has not been adequately surveyed for this species (K. Helgen pers. comm.).
range: This species is known from three specimens collected by Charles Woodford between 1886 and 1888, at Aola, northern Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands (Flannery 1995).
conservationActions: Future surveys of Guadalcanal should be familiar with this species so that any remnant populations can be identified.

rationale: Listed as Near Threatened because this species is likely in significant decline (but probably at a rate of less than 30% over ten years) because of widespread habitat loss due to oil palm plantation expansion and logging through much of its range, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2c.
habitat: This is a terrestrial species, and there is little information available on its natural history. In general solitary animals have been collected, at least one of these was found in tropical forest regrowth (Flannery 1995).
threats: The threats to this species include deforestation for oil palm (this brings in predators like owls and snakes and competitor rats), and hunting for food by local people. Logging is most pervasive at low elevations within this species' range (for estimates of forest cover loss on New Britain for the period of 1989-2000, see Buchanan et al. 2008).
population: U. neobritannicus is a common species.
range: This little-known species is endemic to the island of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Surveys for this species on the adjacent island of New Ireland have not revealed any animals (Flannery 1995). It has been collected at 30 and 500 m Asl.
useTrade: This species is locally used for food.
conservationActions: It is not known if this species is present in any protected areas. Further studies into the distribution, ecology, and threats to the species are needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, lack of major threats, occurrence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Hunting is a threat locally.
habitat: It has been recorded from primary tropical moist forest, and also from degraded forest but probably not from secondary forest (unless it is very old forest). It has been recorded from stands of Pandanus. Animals have been reported from caves (Flannery 1995). Groups of up to 12 animals may be found roosting together in hollow trees, epiphytes, or Pandanus (Flannery 1995). Females have been found with four young.
threats: There are no major threats to this species. It is threatened by overhunting locally, and has disappeared from parts of its range. However, the species is widely distributed and populations have not been significantly impacted by hunting in other areas.
population: It is uncommon, occurring naturally at fairly low densities throughout its range.
range: This species is widely distributed through the Central Cordillera of the island of New Guinea (Indonesia and Papua New Guinea), from the Weyland Range in the west to Mount Dayman in the east. It is also present on the Huon Peninsula (Flannery 1995). It has been recorded from 850 to at least 3,000 m asl.
useTrade: It is hunted for food.
conservationActions: It occurs in Lorentz National Park, Indonesia and possibly others.

rationale: Listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) because its extent of occurrence is less than 100 km2, all individuals are in a single location, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat. This species is known only from a tiny island. There have been six recent collecting efforts that have failed to locate this species, so it may be possibly extinct. Its extent of occurrence and area of occupancy meet the criteria for CR B1 and B2. Even if it extends to adjacent islands within the island group, it would still qualify under CR B1 and possibly B2.
habitat: Nothing has been recorded about the natural history of this species. It presumably occurs in tropical moist forest.
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation. It is susceptible to changes in its habitat since it is known from a small island system.
population: There is no information available on population abundance of this species. According to Fisher and Blomberg (2011), the last sighting of Emma's Giant Rat was in 1946. Recent collecting efforts have not located this animal.
range: This species is known only from the holotype collected from Owi Island in the Paidaido Islands east of Supiori-Biak, Papua Province, Indonesia. It is probably a small island endemic.
useTrade: Emma's Giant Rat is not utilized.
conservationActions: It is not known if this species is present in any protected areas. Further field studies are urgently needed to locate any remaining populations and also to study the natural history of this little-known species.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered as it found only at high elevations on Seram island and it has a small extent of occurrence less than 1,700 km2. Known from less than five locations and the habitat is under threat from logging and the species is affected by competition with Rattus rattus.
habitat: There is little information available for this species. It has only been recorded from undisturbed primary tropical moist forest at altitudes from 1,500 to 1,800 m asl.
threats: Even if logging does not represent a threat at high altitudes, however, ongoing habitat degradation at lower altitudes will affect the quality of higher altitude habitat. Competition with the introduced Rattus rattus is believed to be a threat to this species.
population: It is known only from three specimens (Natural History Museum London) and an additional example in the Western Australia Museum (Helgen 2003). The species is not believed to be common.
range: This species is endemic to the island of Seram, in the Moluccan Islands of Indonesia. It is known only from two localities on Mount Mansuela.
useTrade: Use and trade informations are unknown.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from the Manusela National Park. Further studies into the distribution, natural history and threats to this species are needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its fairly wide distribution, large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. The availability of nest sites is not a limiting factor.
habitat: This species is found from lowland tropical moist forest to montane mossy forest at higher altitude, and occurs in secondary habitats wherever there are large trees with holes. It lives in small groups of four or five animals in tree hollows. Females give birth to a litter of two or three young and are highly fecund.
threats: There are no major threats to the species. It is locally hunted for food.
population: The population size of this species is not known, but it is more abundant than many other species in its range.
range: This species is present in eastern New Guinea (Papua New Guinea only) and also on the D'Entrecasteaux Group of islands where it has been recorded from Fergusson, Goodenough, and Normanby islands (Papua New Guinea). It ranges from sea level to 1,300 m asl.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from some protected areas. It is legally hunted in some of the protected areas. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy of this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its tolerance of habitat modification (it is found in severely degraded areas), presumed large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It has been recorded in areas of primary and severely degraded tropical moist forest. Animals generally live in tree hollows.
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. It may be threatened by competition with the introduced Rattus rattus. It is also hunted for food by local people, but this is not a major threat.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species appears to be restricted to the Owen Stanley Mountain Range of Papua New Guinea. It has been recorded between 1,200 and 2,300 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if this species is present in any protected areas. The degree to which this species is threatened by introduced rats should be studied.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found from tropical moist forest and possibly in secondary habitats. It presumably lives in small groups in tree hollows. Females produce multiple litters annually.
threats: There are no known major threats to the species. It is potentially threatened by competition for tree hollows from the introduced species Rattus rattus. Chiruromys vates is not specifically hunted for food, but would be killed if found.
population: It is a common species.
range: This species is patchily distributed in south-eastern New Guinea (Papua New Guinea only). It ranges in elevation from sea level to 1,500 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is considered to be moderately common and found on several islands. There is a suspected population decline based on a shrinkage in distribution due to habitat destruction and degradation and therefore monitoring this habitat loss will be important over the next 10 year.
habitat: The species inhabits lowland forest and tolerates some level of habitat disturbance. On Camiguin it has been found in disturbed agricultural land among secondary forest and disturbed montane forest (Heaney and Tabaranza 2006). In recent surveys in the lower elevations in Mt. Daguma (2009) and Mt. Apo (2013 and 2014) it was found in forest and forest edge, but was not captured in open and agricultural areas (M.R. Duya pers. comm. 2018).
threats: There is significant deforestation in the lowlands, and much of this species' habitat is gone. Habitat loss is ongoing in Mindanao (M.R. Duya pers. comm. 2018).
population: The population status of the species is not very well known as it is very difficult to trap (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2008). However, it has been found to be moderately common on Camiguin (Heaney et al. 2006) in recent surveys in the lower elevations in Mt. Daguma (2009) and Mt. Apo (2013 and 2014) it was quite common in forest and forest edge, but was not captured in open and agricultural areas (M.R. Duya pers. comm. 2018).
range: This species is endemic to the Philippines and occurs from sea level to 1,550 m on Camiguin (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2008, Heaney and Tabaranza 1995), Leyte, and Mindanao (Bukidnon, Cotabato, and Davao del Norte provinces) which represent two biogeographic regions. It is known from scattered records in the central parts of its range in Mindanao but is likely to occur throughout eastern Mindanao since it also occurs on Leyte (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2008).
conservationActions: More surveys using appropriate trapping techniques (with earthworms or drift fences) need to be undertaken at lower elevations to get a better sense of this species' population status. More research should also be carried out to determine if the species can persist in second growth forest.

rationale: The taxon is listed as Near Threatened because it nearly meets the requirements under criterion A2c since the proportional loss in population is suspected to be approaching 30% and because this species is threatened by inappropriate fire regimes, mainly for mainland populations, that are causing habitat loss. Future declines are likely to be buffered by its occurrence on nine Kimberley islands.
habitat: In its current range the Golden-backed Tree-rat occurs in rainforest patches on volcanic, lateritic, sandstone and floodplain surfaces, eucalypt-dominated savannah woodlands, Livistona palm woodlands, and rugged sandstone plateaux and screes. It is largely nocturnal, but individuals have been seen foraging shortly before dusk and soon after sunrise. In thick vegetation and near vertical rock faces, it is mainly arboreal (on trees or rocks) but spends time on the ground. In sparser vegetation and rocky areas, it spends most of its time on the ground. They have been observed denning in tree hollows and in rock scree. Individuals are known to travel up to 300 m from their refuge into open savanna to forage at night (R. Hohnen pers. comm). Flowers, fruits and termites were recorded as the main dry-season foods, but grasses, ants and beetles were occasionally eaten (Morton 1991). Pregnant females and juveniles have been recorded in August, October and November, suggesting a mid- to late-dry-season breeding period. The litter size is usually two, but one and three have been recorded (McKenzie and Kerle 2008). Longevity in captivity is 7 years (Weigl 1971 in AnAge 2012). Generation time is here assumed to be ca 3 years.
threats: This species is threatened by inappropriate fire regimes (severe, mainly mainland, fires less frequent on islands), which definitely affects mainland subpopulations and is increasingly likely to affect some islands where visitation is increasing, ameliorated by the rugged nature of much habitat that breaks up fire patterns and occurrence in rainforest patches, which burn infrequently. Another threat is predation by feral cats (moderate, mainland part of range), which has not been demonstrated, but is highly plausible on the mainland; however, this is somewhat ameliorated by the rugged nature of habitat, which offers some protection from cats, and by partially arboreal behaviour.
population: There has been no robust estimate of total population size. It is locally common at some Kimberley mainland sites and on islands. It was recorded at 15 out of 119 site surveys (13 %) conducted throughout the North Kimberley from 1994 to 2011, and at eight of 41 surveys (20 % sites) during the North Kimberley Land Conservation Initiative monitoring program in 2012 (I. Radford pers. comm). In 2012 the Golden-backed Tree-rat was recorded for the first time at a number of Mitchell Plateau sites that had been surveyed repeatedly from 2007 to 2012, suggesting this species may be expanding its range locally. If it persists in the Northern Territory, it is unlikely that its population size is greater than 1,000 individuals, and is almost certainly far fewer.
range: This rodent is endemic to Australia. Previously this species was known to occur in the Northern Territory (Parker 1973) at ‘Balanbrinni’ (probably Balbarini) in the upper McArthur in 1901; from Nellie Creek (in the upper Mary River) in 1903; and in Deaf Adder Gorge in 1969. Numerous recent surveys have failed to detect it (Palmer et al. 2003), but a recent assessment of Indigenous knowledge across the Top End of the Northern Territory has suggested that the final phase of its decline was very recent, with plausible records within the last five years (Ziembicki et al. 2013). In Western Australia it has disappeared from the Pilbara (McKenzie and Kerle 2008) and drier parts of the Kimberley (McKenzie 1981), with all known records since 1903 coming from the higher rainfall north-western Kimberley. Subfossil records from Cape Range show that it once had a Pilbara distribution (Baynes and McDowell 2011) and the type specimen came from near Roebourne in 1875 (McKenzie and Kerle 2008). It has disappeared from the south-west Kimberley but remains widespread and reasonably common in the near-coastal, high-rainfall north-west Kimberley from near Kalumburu south to the Yampi Peninsula (e.g. Kitchener et al. 1981). In the Kimberley, it also occurs on nine islands: Augustus with an area of 189 km², Carlia with an area of 4.2 km², Conilurus with an area of 2.5 km², Hidden with an area of 19 km², Jar with an area of 1.8 km², Lachlan with an area of 11.8 km², unnamed in Scott Strait with an area of 20 ha, Uwins with an area of 32.5 km² and Wollaston with an area of 8.6 km² (Abbott and Burbidge 1995, Gibson and McKenzie 2012). At Artesian Range it has been observed at seven of 10 survey sites spread over approximately 40,000 ha of plateau and riparian habitat adjacent to the Charnley River and Walcott Inlet.
conservationActions: A recovery plan for the Golden Bandicoot and Golden-backed Tree-rat (Palmer et al. 2003) includes the following actions that are relevant to this species: Establish cooperative management processes and procedures between various Government agencies and relevant Aboriginal landowners. Establish process and procedures for engagement of Traditional Owners and other stakeholders in Recovery Plan. Form northern Australian multiple species recovery group, collaborate across jurisdictions via multiple species recovery group. Establish population monitoring sites at two WA mainland sites (Mitchell Plateau and Yampi Sound Training Area). Determine population estimates for Uwins Island and establish monitoring sites. Sample historic locations of Golden-backed Tree-rat to determine if populations persist. Identify factors that are driving the decline in critical weight mammals through a landscape scale experiment based in the NT. Develop and disseminate educational and communication materials concerning fire and the introduction of feral animals, particularly cats, onto islands where the Golden Bandicoot and Golden-backed Tree-rat survives. Develop contingency plan in case of feral animal introduction onto island. Produce educational packages and communication material on the Recovery Plan for all stakeholder groups in the region. ‘Cat-watch Patrol’ local people with tracking skills employed to undertake tracking transects on Uwins and Augustus Islands to monitor presence/absence of cats, rats, dogs. Actions in the recovery plan have been partially implemented. Management arrangements with indigenous groups are being developed. The Department of Environment and Conservation is establishing monitoring sites at Mitchell Plateau. Some of the objectives in the Recovery Plan are being carried out by Australian Wildlife Conservancy on private and public conservation land in the Artesian Range, including monitoring to determine population trends (carried out at over 40 sites per year) and identifying the impacts of key threats (fire and feral Cats) on the Golden-backed Tree-rat.There is some regional fire management and feral animal control in the southern and northern parts of its range and management of fire at Artesian Range. Land on which the Golden-backed Tree-rats occurs includes indigenous land, national parks and land managed by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy. A research program on Golden-backed Tree-rats at Artesian Range (AWC/University of Tasmania) began in late 2012, to describe the impacts of fire patterns and feral Cats on their ecology and survival.Regular trapping is undertaken at Mitchell Plateau as part of the Kimberley Science and Conservation Strategy Landscape Conservation Initiative (Radford et al. 2011). Recently monitored annually (across c. 40 sites) by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy at Artesian Range Sanctuary, north-west Kimberley (S. Legge pers. comm).

rationale: Limited monitoring information for this species suggests a decline of 50% over a 10 year period (Woinarski et al. 2014). However, it is difficult to extrapolate this rate to the whole population, therefore a decline of 30% is assumed by Woinarski et al. (2014) and here. The Black-footed tree Rat is therefore assessed as Vulnerable under criterion A.
habitat: The Black-footed Tree-rat is a nocturnal rodent that dens mostly in tree hollows, but occasionally in dense foliage (notably of Pandanus), and occasionally in buildings. Most knowledge of its ecology derives from studies of the Kimberley and mainland Northern Territory subspecies (notably Friend and Taylor 1985, Friend 1987, Rankmore 2006). It forages on the ground and in trees, and individuals may make movements of at least 500 m from roost sites to foraging areas (Friend et al. 1992). Its diet comprises mostly fruits (including of the tough Pandanus spiralis) and seeds, but also includes some invertebrates, flowers and grass (Morton 1992, Rankmore 2006, Rankmore and Friend 2008). It occurs mostly in lowland open forests and woodlands dominated by Eucalyptus miniata and/or E. tetrodonta, particularly where these forests have a relatively dense shrubby understorey (Friend and Taylor 1985, Friend 1987). Such vegetation structure is typical of a regime with a low frequency or intensity of fires; and frequent, intense fires may also be detrimental by reducing the abundance of hollow-bearing large trees (Price et al. 2005).Breeding may occur throughout the year, but in the most intensively-studied population (in the Northern Territory) peaked in August-September (Friend 1987, Rankmore 2006). Litter size is small (1-3 young), and gestation period is 43-44 days, the longest recorded for an Australian rodent (Crichton 1969). The generation length is taken here to be 2 years, recognising young reach reproductive maturity at about three months (Crichton 1969), and longevity is probably 3-5 years.
threats: Major threats are predation by feral cats and habitat decline (due to inappropriate fire regimes and invasive pasture grasses) (Woinarski et al. 2014). In some areas, prime habitat is being cleared mostly for plantation forestry or horticulture, and intensification of livestock production; and the large home range of the species makes it susceptible to habitat fragmentation (Woinarski et al. 2014).
population: There are no published estimates of the number of individuals in any subpopulation, or overall. The Black-footed Tree-rat has a large home range (60-70 ha: Rankmore 2006, Rankmore and Friend 2008), so population density (and hence total population) is likely to be relatively low, and the species is unlikely to maintain viable populations in smaller now isolated bushland fragments or islands. This species has not been recorded since 1982 in the Kimberley, despite considerable survey effort, and there are few recent records from some locations where previously reported in north Queensland (Woinarski et al. 2014).The limited historic information suggests a pattern of decline since European settlement, but that the rate and extent of decline has increased recently. The species was still abundant in the Kakadu area in the 1980s (Friend 1987, Braithwaite and Muller 1997), but that is no longer the case (Woinarski et al. 2001, 2010). A recent decline for the subspecies endemic to Melville Island, M. gouldii melvillensis, has been associated with the loss of substantial areas of prime habitat to forestry plantation, since the 1990s (Firth et al. 2006).Woinarski et al. (2014) provided a population estimate of 30,000 mature individuals, noting that this had low reliability.
range: This species is endemic to tropical northern Australia, where it is distributed discontinuously from the Kimberley (Western Australia) to north Queensland, and occurs on one island (Melville Island, Northern Territory) (Lee 1995, Woinarski et al. 2014). Woinarski et al. (2014) noted that there had been no records from the Kimberley since 1982, despite considerable survey effort.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: Although the Black-footed Tree-rat is present in several protected areas (including Kakadu, Litchfield Garig Gunak Barlu National Parks), monitoring indicates that it is declining in even these areas, indicating reservation alone is insufficient to maintain populations. It requires active control of major threats (fire and feral cats). More studies are needed in Queensland and the Kimberley to resolve status and conservation requirements, and to establish effective monitoring programs.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This is largely an arboreal species. It is generally present in the tangled canopy of montane forest at altitudes between 2,100 and 2,700 m. It has been recorded form outside of forest on open hillsides where there are thickets of dense vegetation (Anthony 1941). However, it is not generally present in disturbed habitats.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to the species within its remote montane distribution.
population: It is known from very few specimens, and there is little information about the population abundance.
range: This species occurs in mountainous areas of southern China (western Yunnan, central and northern Sichuan, southern Gansu, and south western Shaanxi) extending into northern Myanmar (Musser and Carleton 2005, Smith et al. 2008).
conservationActions: It is presumably present in a number of protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because whilst it has a fairly limited range with an extent of occurrence of approximately 35,397 km² and there is continuing destruction and degradation of its habitat, it is not severely fragmented and nothing is known about number of locations.
habitat: It is an arboreal species, presumably of lowland tropical moist forest. Animals have been collected from tree-hollows, and it is likely that the species is dependent on tree hole availability.
threats: This species is threatened by severe habitat degradation, mostly because of conversion of forested areas to small-holder agricultural use. There has almost certainly been extensive logging, which poses a major threat to this hole nesting species.
population: It is only known from a few specimens.
range: This species has been recorded from the island of Salawati and the Vogelkop Peninsula in Papua Province, Indonesia on the island of New Guinea. The fossil record suggests that previously it was distributed throughout the western-most part of Papua Province. Its elevational range is sea level to a few hundred metres at most.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. There is a need to protect important sites for this species. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, although it is seldom recorded, it is likely that this species is difficult to trap, it has a relatively wide distribution, no known major threats, and it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is believed to be an arboreal species of lowland tropical moist forest (gallery and hill forest). It may be sensitive to habitat disturbance as it is rarely found close to areas inhabited by people. Animals have been collected in a tree hollow.
threats: There are possibly no major threats to this species, as it has a wide range in an area with a low human population density.
population: It is considered to be difficult to trap and is not known from many specimens.
range: This species is found on the island of New Guinea (Papua Province, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea). It is known from several large drainage basins, including the Fly River and lower Strickland River. It appears to be a lowland species. Elevation range is from sea level to 600 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population (although is uncommon), lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is known from tropical moist forest habitats. Animals have been found in tree hollows. A female with two young has been recorded (Flannery 1995).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. It is suspected that northern populations are under threat from general habitat loss, mostly from conversion of forest habitat to cultivated land.
population: It is generally uncommon (Flannery 1995).
range: This species is endemic to the island of New Guinea (Indonesia and Papua New Guinea), where it has a wide range in northern parts of the island from the Weyland Range (Papua Province, Indonesia) in the west to the Huon Peninsula (Papua New Guinea) in the east (Flannery 1995). It has been recorded from 400 to 1,500 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas, but the range coincides with some protected areas (e.g., Mamberamo). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, habitat status, and threats to this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because its primary habitat occurs at higher altitudes and is not yet encroached by vegetable farms. Lowland populations have been negatively affected by logging, mining and vegetable farms, but since it is believed that this does not constitute an important part of the species' range, it is not of great concern.
habitat: The species occurs in montane and mossy forest (Heaney et al. in prep.).
threats: On Mindanao, the species' habitat is being encroached on for vegetable farming from mid to high elevations. On Dinagat island it is particularly threatened by mining and deforestation. Lowland forest has been deforested, but since this species occurs primarily at higher elevations, this is less of a concern (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2006).
population: This species is probably common in primary montane and mossy forest, but has declined in the lowlands of Mindanao (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2006). On Leyte, the species is common in montane and ridgetop mossy primary forest from 700 m to 950 m and uncommon at 500 m in lowland forest there (Heaney et al. 1989, Rickart et al. 1993); on Mt. Kitanglad, Mindanao it is moderately common in montane and mossy forest from 1,600 m to 2,375 m (Heaney et al. in prep.).
range: This species occurs in the Philippines and is restricted to the Mindanao faunal region occuring on Dinagat, Mindanao (Bukidnon province) from 1,200 to 2,400 m, Leyte and Biliran islands (Musser and Carleton 2005). Its elevation range starts at 1,200 m upwards on Mindanao with highest densities occurring at 1,600 m. It is thought to be widespread on Mindanao and other islands.
conservationActions: There are records from protected areas.

rationale: The species is assessed as Endangered as it is has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 1,272 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and there is a continuing decline caused by habitat loss and destruction from agriculture, mining and illegal logging activities. The species is probably not tolerant of habitat disturbance.
habitat: This species occurs in lowland forest at around 350 m (Musser et al. 1998). It is not thought to be tolerant to major habitat disturbance. This species is nocturnal and probably arboreal (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
threats: The population of this geographically restricted species on Dinagat island has been particularly threatened by habitat loss caused by illegal logging since 1995 and more recently (2001-2007) several mining companies have started operating there. Suitable habitat for this species is found within the mining concessions. The local government is also very supportive of the mining companies because of their contribution to the local governments funds.
population: The species is known only from two specimens collected in 1975, and one individual in 1995 (Musser et al. 1998). There have been no subsequent surveys done specifically for this species, but other surveys in the area in the early 2000s failed to locate any additional individuals (B. Tabaranza pers. comm).
range: This species is endemic to the Philippines where it is known only from Dinagat island (Heaney and Rabor 1982). It is thought to occupy areas above 300 m. It may be more widespread than its current known range, occurring perhaps on Siargao and Bucas Grande, but there have been no adequate surveys to determine this (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
conservationActions: Little is known about this species and field research is badly needed (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016). Surveys are required to determine the geographic range of the species on nearby islands as well as its tolerance to habitat disturbance.

rationale: Listed as Vulnerable because of a population decline, estimated to be more than 30% over the last three generations, inferred from past and continuing habitat destruction.
habitat: It inhabits lowland forest. Wearn (pers. comm.) observed this species in steep, riverine primary forest.
threats: It is threatened by habitat loss.
population: This species is rare. It has never been trapped on the ground but has been observed (Wearn pers. comm.).
range: This species has been recorded in Borneo and in Palawan and Calawit islands (Philippines). However, it is very likely to be extinct on Calawit and it has not been found on Palawan in the most recent survey. Therefore, the Borneo population may be the only one remaining. However, Heaney et al. (2009) found a specimen captured in Abangan Province in the Philippines.
useTrade: Use and trade information is missing.
