Further, there are only four separated and small populations of Tehuantepec Jackrabbit (Lorenzo et al. 2006, 2018) and quantified population censuses from 2001–2016 have documented a severe decline (approaching 80% in the 10-year period beginning in 2006) in the population (Lorenzo et al. 2017), thus triggering the EN category under criterion A2. These censuses also indicate that the population undergoes extreme fluctuations. Ongoing decline in the quality and quantity of habitat utilized by the species, coupled with an increase in anthropogenic stressors further threaten this species. These stressors include overgrazing, burning of pastures, an increase in human settlements, poaching, and completion with domestic dogs. The isolation of the four subpopulations also contributes to the likelihood of increased inbreeding which can further jeopardize the fitness of these animals.
habitat: At present, the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is restricted to grasslands with open shrub and tree cover, and coastal grassy dunes which never exceed a 4-5 km wide strip along the shores of salt water lagoons on the north side of the Gulf of Tehuantepec. Tropical dry savannas of native grasses (Paspalum and Bouteloua) with an over story of sparse bushes (Byrsonima crassifolia, Opuntia decumbens, Opuntia tehuantepecana), and scattered trees (Crescentia spp.) are the vegetation communities selected by Tehuantepec Jackrabbits (Lorenzo et al. 2006). Tehuantepec Jackrabbits are also found in xeric shrub and coastal grassy dunes dominated by species like Donkey Grass (Jouvea pilosa), and grasslands associated with cacti (Opuntia spp.) and some shrub species such as Black Sage (Cordia curassavica), Manchineel (Hippomane mancinella), and Cuachalalate (Amphipterygium adstringens) (Carrillo-Reyes et al. 2010). Preference by adults was shown for areas with greater visibility for escaping predation during the hours they are active (Farías and Fuller 2009). Juveniles showed preference for areas with more over story. Both adults and juveniles chose areas with shrubbery for protection while resting (Farías and Fuller 2009). Low tolerance to habitat degradation (Lorenzo et al. 2006), suggests that preservation of the preferred habitat structure is important to the survival of this jackrabbit (Farías and Fuller 2009).A detailed analysis using satellite images from 2001 – 2014 of habitats by type in the region occupied by Tehuantepec Jackrabbits showed that their preferred savanna habitat declined by 16.5%, while unsuitable habitat increased dramatically (seasonal agriculture +24.5%; human settlements +26.6%; burned areas +142.8%; and areas without vegetation +38.3%) (Lorenzo et al. 2017). Savannas and forests have increasingly been converted to pastures for livestock, which increase trampling and loss of vegetation. The fires are set with the intention of promoting regeneration of grasslands, but they often become uncontrolled and then affect large parcels of land (Lorenzo et al. 2017).The diet of Tehuantepec Jackrabbits is highly diverse; 18 vegetal species are consumed in the dry season and 16 vegetal species in the rainy season (of the families Poaceae, Cyperaceae, and herbs) in Montecillo Santa Cruz. The highest percentages of consumption found were grasses (Bouteloua dactyloides, Cathestecum brevifolium, and Digitaria ciliaris) for both seasons of the year in that population (Lorenzo et al. 2011).Average home range size of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit in Montecillo Santa Cruz is 55 ha. Similar data from Santa María del Mar shows wide intraspecific variation, with a range from 0.20 to 152 ha with a high level of overlap between sexes and stations (over 70%). Therefore this population does not exhibit exclusive home ranges, suggesting that Tehuantepec Jackrabbits are not territorial (Farías et al. 2006, Carrillo-Reyes et al. 2010).The Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is polygamous. Over the course of the mating season, males mated with three females, but females only allowed a single male to mate (Rioja et al. 2008). The length of the breeding season may extend from February to December, with a peak in reproduction during the rainy season (from May to October) (Farías 2004, Rioja et al. 2008). Mean litter size is two, with a range of one to four embryos (Farías 2004). The total length is between 49.9–64 cm (Lorenzo et al. 2018). This species reaches maturity at six to seven months for both sexes (Farías 2004).The Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is primarily nocturnal, demonstrating more activity at 18:40 ± 2 hr. The greater part of this period (12 ± 3 hours), is occupied in feeding, interspersed with periods of grooming (with average duration of 12 ± 9 minutes), and socialization. Tehuantepec Jackrabbits feed in a solitary manner, as well as in groups of up to 13 hares eating together in an area with a radius equal to or less than 50 m, without showing evidence of aggressive territorial behavior (Carrillo-Reyes 2009).Can serve as a prey item for native carnivores.The Tehuantepec Jackrabbit co-exists with the Eastern Cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus). Its main native predators are Coyotes (Canis latrans) and Gray Foxes (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) (Farías 2004, López et al. 2009).
threats: The change in land use that occurs with the increase in human settlements has led to bad management and lack of control of productive activities, such as ranching and the burning of pastures for seasonal agriculture. The extent of occurrence of Tehuantepec Jackrabbits is jeopardized by habitat alteration and degradation by introduction of exotic grasses, human-induced fires, agriculture, cattle-raising activities, and human settlements in savannas. These activities have resulted in fragmentation of the habitat of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit, so that their existing populations are almost completely isolated, and most possess low genetic viability (Flux and Angermann 1990, Rico et al. 2008). Land use changes for activities such as livestock production and agriculture, as well as the expansion of human settlements, are already reducing the natural vegetation (savannas) of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit at a rate of 1.2% per year over a period of 26 years (1986-2012) with a total loss of 6,850.6 ha (Sántiz et al. 2016). Human-induced fires in the savanna accounted for 20% of adult deaths. Historically, excessive hunting is another anthropogenic factor that caused the decrease of population densities of this species, contributing to its current situation (Lorenzo et al. 2008, 2017, 2018). In addition, the species is shot by numerous parties of hunters coming from cities up to 200 km away to shoot deer by spotlighting at night. Poaching accounted for 13% of adult deaths, and for 6% of juvenile deaths.Possible species competing for food (Eastern Cottontail and cattle) and predators (Coyotes and foxes) of Tehuantepec Jackrabbits may be affecting their populations. Direct observations in Santa María del Mar point to domestic dogs (Canis familiaris), Rat Snakes (Masticophis mentovarius), and Deaf Snakes (Trimorphodon biscutatus) as the main predators of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit (Rioja et al. 2011). Predation was the major cause of mortality for radio-marked jackrabbits and accounted for 94% of juvenile deaths and 67% of adult deaths during a 29 month study. In San Francisco del Mar Pueblo Viejo and Aguachil, cattle and horses can act as potential competitors of food and transmitters of diseases of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit (Rioja 2008).
population: The four populations are each isolated from one other. Recently (2001-2016), densities of 1.4-4 jackrabbits per km² have been reported for the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit (Lorenzo et al. 2000, 2008, 2017), and drastic declines in density have been recorded over these 15 years of monitoring. These changes have been partially attributed to management practices such as prescribed burning and grazing (Lorenzo et al.2008, 2017). Average density (individuals/km²) ranged from 15.5 (range: 13-17.5; 2006-2010) to a low of 3.15 (range: 1.4-6; 2011-2016). The quantified census protocol that yielded these data support the documented decline of nearly 80% (Lorenzo et al. 2017).A phylogeography study showed that the four isolated populations are made up of two clades with low genetic diversity (Rico et al. 2008). The populations at Montecillo Santa Cruz, San Francisco del Mar Viejo, and Aguachil make up one panmictic clade, while the isolated, western-most population at Santa María del Mar makes up the second (Rico et al. 2008). Given this information, the two genetically diverse groups should be treated as evolutionary significant units with regard to future conservation measures (Rico et al. 2008).
range: The Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is currently restricted to four isolated populations around the Laguna Superior and Laguna Inferior of the Tehuantepec Isthmus, Oaxaca, Mexico: Montecillo Santa Cruz, San Francisco del Mar Pueblo Viejo, Aguachil and Santa María del Mar (Lorenzo et al. 2006, Lorenzo et al. 2018). According to Chapman et al. (1983) this species existed only from Salina Cruz, Oaxaca, to the extreme west of the State of Chiapas, Mexico. Tehuantepec Jackrabbits have not been found in Chiapas (Retana and Lorenzo 2002). The area occupied in the past was apparently 150 km², but increasing clearance for agriculture has destroyed much of its habitat. The former distribution of the Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is not documented in detail, but Nelson (1909) estimated its historic range as occupying the Mexican Pacific Coast on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec from Salina Cruz in Oaxaca to Tonalá in Chiapas, an area of perhaps only 5,000 km². Four populations of Tehuantepec Jackrabbit persist, and the current extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 769 km². This jackrabbit inhabits altitudes of no more than 500 m (Lorenzo et al. 2006).
useTrade: This species is hunted locally for subsistence and very occasionally taken as a pet.
conservationActions: The Tehuantepec Jackrabbit is listed as endangered in the Mexican Official Norm NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2010 (SEMARNAT 2010). Its conservation should focus on establishment of appropriate management strategies for grassland and savanna communities. Specifically, grasses should be controlled annually by fire; livestock-raising practices should be improved to avoid a negative impact on grasses; a program of reproduction of jackrabbits in protected enclosures should be developed; and a Communal Ecological Reserve in the form of a Wildlife Use and Management Unit, established and administrated by community authorities, with universities as technical advisory role, should be implemented (Lorenzo et al. 2017).

rationale: The Mountain Hare has a widespread distribution and populations appear to be stable across much of this area (Mitchell-Jones et al. 1999, Angerbjörn 2018). Isolated regions are experiencing population declines, but these are not significant enough to warrant listing the species as Near Threatened under the current Red List Criteria. It is confirmed as Least Concern.
habitat: The Mountain Hare inhabits tundra and taiga, particularly pine, birch, and juniper (Flux and Angermann 1990, Angerbjörn 2018). Moors and bogland are the preferred habitats for this species in Ireland and Scotland (Flux and Angermann 1990). However, L. timidus hibernicus will also utilize cultivated land, rich agricultural area, in Ireland (Thulin 2003). The Mountain Hare occupies lowland woodlands of open steppe in southern Russia along with reed belts around lakes (Flux and Angermann 1990). In Mongolia, it occurs in forests located on the Altai, Hingan, Hentei, Hovsgol, and Hangai mountain ranges (Mallon 1985).The diet of the Mountain Hare varies in relation to the type of habitat it occupies (Flux and Angermann 1990, Angerbjörn 2018). Calluna (heather) constitutes the bulk of the diet in Scotland, while birch, juniper, poplar, willow, and Vaccinium are selected in Europe (Flux and Angermann 1990). If present, L. timidus will consume palatable grasses and clovers (Flux and Angermann 1990).The Mountain Hare is a nocturnal species that will increase daytime activity during summer months (Flux and Angermann 1990). Home range for this species ranges according to locality (Flux and Angermann 1990). In Scotland, home ranges as small as 10 ha have been observed, while in Finland it was reported that home ranges could be as large as 305 ha (Flux and Angermann 1990).In areas where L. timidus and L. europaeus coexist, L. timidus will retreat to areas of higher elevation (Thulin 2003). The reason for this is believed to be competitive exclusion, L. timidus yields habitat to L. europaeus (Thulin 2003).Litter size of the Mountain Hare is variable (two to six) according to the number of litters and the latitude (Angerbjörn 2018). Gestation time is between 47-55 days ( Angerbjörn 2018). The breeding season is February to August (Macdonald and Barrett 1993). The Mountain Hare reaches maturity at one year of age. Longevity for L. timidus is nine years (Macdonald and Barrett 1993). Natural mortality for juveniles is 80%, while adult mortality is 58% (Macdonald and Barrett 1993). Total length of this species is 45.7-61.0 cm (Macdonald and Barrett 1993).L. t. hibernicus is the only endemic hare of Ireland (Reid and Montgomery 2007). Contrary to other mountain hare populations, this subspecies "occurs at all altitudes and can be found in most habitats throughout Ireland" (Reid and Montgomery 2007). L. t. hibernicus typically forages on grasses (Reid and Montgomery 2007).
threats: There are several potential threats identified for this species. The Mountain Hare has successfully hybridized with L. europaeus in areas where the latter has been introduced (Thulin 2003). The pathogens, European Brown Hare Syndrome (EHBS) and Tularemia, are considered problematic, but require research to determine how great an impact they inflict (Thulin 2003). Competitive exclusion occurring between the Mountain Hare and the European Hare could be restricting the distribution of the former (Thulin 2003). The discovery of an introduced population of L. europaeus to Ireland could pose a threat to L. t. hibernicus (Reid 2011). More recently abundance has been reduced by a lack of duration of snow cover caused by global warming (Pedersen et al. 2017).
population: The Mountain Hare is an abundant species within its range (Flux and Angermann 1990, Angerbjörn 2018). Populations appear to be stable across much of its geographic distribution, with fluctuations occurring in northern Europe and possible declines in the Alps (Mitchell-Jones et al. 1999). Population declines have been observed in Russia and in the extreme, southern portions of Sweden, the Mountain Hare has disappeared entirely (Thulin 2003). The Mountain Hare is found at low densities in tundra areas. In Northern Ireland, historical game bag records indicate that there has been a substantial decline in hare abundance (Dingerkus and Montgomery 2002). Populations of the Mountain Hare are subject to periodic crashes where the cause is potentially parasitism, predation, climate change, or starvation (Angerbjorn and Flux 1995, Petersen et al. 2017, Angerbjörn 2018).
range: The geographic distribution of the Mountain Hare extends from the Pacific Ocean in the east to the eastern edge of Poland and Scandinavia (Flux and Angermann 1990, Angerbjörn 2018). The northern most populations can be found at 75°N in Russia and Scandinavia, extending south to 40-50°N (Flux and Angermann 1990). Isolated populations are located in Hokkaido (Japan), Ireland, the Kurile Islands, Sakhalin, Scotland (Flux and Angermann 1990), and the Alps regions of Austria, Italy, Germany, France, Slovenia, and Switzerland (Mitchell-Jones et al. 1999). Introduced populations can be found in England, the Faeroes (Denmark), several Scottish islands (Flux and Angermann 1990). On Spitsbergen Island, introduced populations failed to persist (Flux and Angermann 1990).
useTrade: The Mountain Hare is a popular game species in most countries (Angerbjorn 2018).
conservationActions: Regional declines in Mountain Hare populations suggest that research be conducted to determine the cause(s). Several areas have been suggested: interspecific competition with L. europaeus, pathogenic impact, and the effects of hybridization (Thulin 2003). In Ireland, the cause(s) of population declines require investigation (Dingerkus and Montgomery 2002). The current situation of the endemic Irish Hare (L. t. hibernicus) needs to be investigated specifically (Reid 2011). In Mongolia, approximately 12% of the species' distribution occurs in protected areas (Clark et al. 2006) and has been recorded in Hustai National Park (Todgerel 2002). In China, it occurs in Honghe, Xingkaihu, and Sanjiang Nature Reserves.This species is listed under the Bern Convention, Appendix III as well as the European Union Habitats and Species Directive, Annex V (Mitchell-Jones et al. 1999). This species is regionally Red Listed as Least Concern in Mongolia (Clark et al. 2006).

rationale: The White-sided Jackrabbit is widespread in Mexico where there is a general lack of data regarding current population status. Studies and reports nonetheless indicate declines for populations in New Mexico, Durango, and elsewhere in Mexico (Flux and Angermann 1990, Best and Henry 1993, Traphagen 2011, Brown et al. 2018a,b). The White-sided Jackrabbit was listed as threatened by the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish in 1975 and remains at that status (New Mexico Department of Game and Fish 2006).. Reports by Mexican outfitters and ranchers, José Fernandez, José Treviño as well as the majority of literature references (Brown et al. 2018b) indicate major population reductions or absence within large areas of historic range where it was previously common. Detailed analyses have occurred in the US range, largely comparing the surveys of Bednarz (1977) with those of Traphagen (2011). Based on the total hectares of suitable habitat, it is estimated that only 9.8% of its former range in the US is currently occupied by White-sided Jackrabbits. This percentage is less than half that reported in 1976 (20.1%, Bednarz 1977). The US population has declined from an estimated 400 total animals to 58 from 1976 to 2010 (Bednarz 1977, Traphagen 2011). The total U.S. and Mexican population has been estimated to have declined from 12,950 to 2,101.5 over the same period, a decline of >40% per decade (Myles Traphagen, pers. comm.). The main stressor on the species appears to be habitat change (Brown et al. 2018b). Climate change and overgrazing has greatly altered the open grasslands favored by the White-sided Jackrabbit. These habitat changes are preferred by the Black-tailed Jackrabbit (L. californicus) which has led to the replacement of the White-sided Jackrabbit in several areas (Bednarz and Cook 1984, Best and Henry 1993, Desmond 2012). It is inferred that this will only exacerbate the issue of population decline based on recent surveys of the species in the US and in Mexico. Ancillary stressors include predation by feral dogs, illegal hunting, and vehicle collisions (including by US Border Patrol near the US/Mexico border). The species is listed as Vulnerable under criterion A2bcde.
habitat: The White-sided Jackrabbit is restricted to Madrean Plains grasslands in New Mexico (Flux and Angermann 1990, Brown et al. 2018a). In the area surrounding the valleys inhabited by this species north of the Nazas River, grazing has caused an increase of shrubs and a lower density of grasses, resulting in a replacement of White-sided Jackrabbits by Black-tailed Jackrabbits (Bednarz and Cook 1984, Desmond 2004). This problem has also been identified in Zacatecas (Mexico) where the White-sided Jackrabbit also lives in open plains grasslands. South of the Nazas River, as in Queretaro (Mexico), it is associated with tropic-subtropic savannas, cultivated areas and pastures (potreros) (Best and Henry 1993).Breeding season varies from the middle of April to August and the average litter size is 2.2 (range 1-4) (Anderson 1972, Bogan and Jones 1975, Bednarz 1977). The White-sided Jackrabbit is capable of producing up to three litters per year (Bednarz 1977). It is common to observe this nocturnal species in pairs, particularly during the breeding season (Flux and Angermann 1990). An average total length for this species is 55.0 cm (Best and Henry 1993). Unlike the Black-tailed Jackrabbit, which is a “see and flee” species, the White-sided Jackrabbit’s escape strategy is to remain motionless or course through dense grasses undetected. Their diet is thought to be exclusively grasses, but may consist of roots during dry seasons (Bednarz 1977). The White-sided Jackrabbit serves as a game species and a prey source for native carnivores.
threats: Changes in habitat due to grazing negatively impact the White-sided Jackrabbit by presumably increasing predation rates and resulting in encroachment by Black-tailed Jackrabbits (Flux and Angermann 1990, Desmond 2004). In some places, there is competition with Black-tailed Jackrabbits. Additional threats may include subsistence hunting, human perturbation and exotic predation. In some places, animal competition for grasses, habitat fragmentation and land clearings represent important threats to populations. A model generated for climate conditions in 2050 indicated a 60% range reduction from the current potential range for this species (Martinez-Villeda 2006).
population: In 1976, the density of the White-sided Jackrabbit was estimated at 1/31.6 ha in New Mexico, producing a maximum population of 340 animals (Bednarz 1977). Between 1976 and 1981, the restricted population in New Mexico experienced a nearly 50% decline due to habitat change (Flux and Angermann 1990). This decline was said to be accompanied by an increase in the presence of Black-tailed Jackrabbits and Desert Cottontails (Sylvilagus audubonii) (Best and Henry 1993). Historic population information for Mexico is scarce (Flux and Angermann 1990) but there has been an observed decline in most populations (Brown et al. 2018b). A survey conducted from 1998-1999 on the Madren Plains grassland in Chihuahua, Mexico found White-sided Jackrabbit densities of 0.01/ha and 0.06/ha, respectively (Desmond 2004). Reported density in the US in 2010 was 0.01/ha (Traphagen 2011). It is estimated that only ~ 60 White-sided Jackrabbits currently occur in the US (Traphagen 2011).
range: The White-sided Jackrabbit is essentially a Mexican endemic, distributed from extreme southwestern New Mexico (USA) to northern Oaxaca (Mexico) (Bailey 1932, Hall 1981, Best and Henry 1993, Villa-Ramirez and Cervantes 2003, Brown et al. 2018a). The White-sided Jackrabbit has been observed at an elevation of 2,550 m in Puebla and 750 m in Morelos (Best and Henry 1993). Lepus callotis gaillardi has a discontinuous distribution that extends from southwestern New Mexico, USA, to north-central Durango, Mexico (Best and Henry 1993). In Mexico, there are two isolated subpopulations: one in central Chihuahua and the other extending from south-central Chihuahua into Durango (Martinez-Villeda 2006). Its distribution in southwestern New Mexico is restricted to two locations in Hidalgo County at elevations between 1,500-1,600 m (Flux and Angermann 1990). In 1950, there was a potential sighting of two L. c. gaillardi on the west side of the Huachuca Mountains in Arizona (Hoffmeister 1986). The total range in the USA is estimated to be 5,837 ha (Traphagen 2010). The subspecies L. c. callotis is distributed from the central part of east Durango toward the plains of the central part of Mexico, along the axis Neovolcanic to northern Guerrero and Oaxaca (Best and Henry 1993, Villa-Ramirez and Cervantes 2003).
useTrade: The White-sided Jackrabbit is hunted for subsistence and sport in Mexico. Nonetheless, no systematic surveys or harvest estimates are conducted.
conservationActions: Research should be concentrated on determining population status, numbers and range, as well as efforts to establish trends and monitoring in populations both north and south of Nazas River. Population decline in New Mexico prompted the listing of White-sided Jackrabbits as “Threatened” in 1975 by New Mexico Department of Game and Fish (New Mexico Department of Game and Fish 2006). Efforts have been made to periodically monitor population status and trends in New Mexico, as well as, encouraging shrub control and non-detrimental grazing practices by landowners (New Mexico Department of Game and Fish 2006). Range reduction, indicated by climate change models, is expected to be most severe in the northern portion of this species' range. It is suggested that assessments be made of the population density of L. c. gaillardi and habitat transformation, to determine the impact future changes will have on its survival (Martinez-Villeda 2006).

rationale: Local extirpation of Lepus hainanus was noted in 1983 as a result of overharvesting (Lazell et al. 1995). The species is endemic to the island of Hainan and its extent of occurrence is 744 km². Original natural habitat has been consumed by human habitations and agriculture. This species survives only on artificially deforested lands currently used as deer ranches. Despite listing as a China Key List - II species in China, L. hainanus continues to be poached for meat and skin. L. hainanus may face competition from feral European rabbits.
habitat: Lepus hainanus inhabits grasslands of the western regions on Hainan (Flux and Angermann 1990). The eastern region of the island is not considered suitable for this species (Flux and Angermann 1990). In 1995, L. hainanus was found only at deer ranches close to ranger stations, which provide some protection from poaching. They are also found on flat, dry farm land that is scattered with second growth scrub or plantains (Flux and Angermann 1990). This species is characterized as tame, probably the result of few native carnivores present within its range (Lazell et al. 1995). L. hainanus is predominantly a nocturnal species, but is known to forage during the day (Flux and Angermann 1990). It is exclusively a ground-dweller (Luo 1988). L. hainanus reaches a maximum length of 40.0 cm (Lazell et al. 1995).
threats: Over harvesting and the expansion of agriculture present a major threat to Lepus hainanus (Flux and Angermann 1990). Greater than 90% of its original habitat has been destroyed. Artificially cleared deer ranches provide nearly all the extant habitat. As of 1995, poaching for meat and skins continued.
population: Formerly characterized as abundant, Lepus hainanus is now experiencing population declines (Lazell et al. 1995). In 1995 it was estimated at 157 ±68 km² at Da Tien and 62 (no replicates) per km² at Bang Xi. There are probably no more than two km² of optimal habitat remaining, so that total population may be no more than 250-500.
range: Lepus hainanus is endemic to the island of Hainan, China (Flux and Angermann 1990). Formerly, L. hainanus occupied most of the lowlands of Hainan Dao, except possibly in the northeast. In 1995 it was located only at Bang Xi and Da Tien deer ranches in the central west coastal zone. Historic locations of L. hainanus specimens were found from sea-level and approximately 300 m (Lazell et al. 1995).
useTrade: 90% of the total population is utilized. As of 1995, Lepus hainanus was still regularly poached and sold in village markets, and this activity continues in spite of its reduced numbers.
conservationActions: A China Key List - II protected species in China as of 1991, but as of 1995 there was no apparent law enforcement. No habitat has been conserved for this species. Recovery management is needed to reverse population declines (Luo 1988).

rationale: This species is an endemic of the Espiritu Santo and La Partida islands, Gulf of California, Mexico (Lorenzo et al. 2018a). The Black Jackrabbit qualifies for listing as VU D1 because the average number of censused mature individuals is less than 1,000.
habitat: Espiritu Santo Island is an uninhabited protected area, but it is a popular tourism destination and local fishermen often visit (Lorenzo et al. 2018a, 2018b). Despite this activity, the habitat of the Black Jackrabbit has not become fragmented or overly modified (Lorenzo et al. 2018a, 2018b). This species prefers open areas and is common on rocky slopes, mesetas, dunes, and sandy valleys (Cervantes et al. 1996). The Black Jackrabbit inhabits tropical scrub of cactus (Pachycerus, Stenocereus, and Opuntia) and shrubs (Prosopis, Ambrosia, and Acacia) in dunes with grasses and halophytic plants (Cervantes et al. 1996).The Black Jackrabbit is restricted to a habitat of xeric scrubland vegetation on rocky soil. The most important plants for the Black Jackrabbit are Lomboy (Jatropha cinerea), Goatnut (Simmondsia chinensis), Morning Glory (Jacquemontia abutiloides), Cape Thorn (Acacia capensis), Limberbush (Jatropha cuneata), Adam’s Tree (Fouquieria diguetii), and Copal (Bursera hindsiana). It is possible to observe the Black Jackrabbit in their “beds” in an attitude of rest and protection against the sun and the high temperatures, surrounded by dry grass under the branches of plants such as the Slipper Plant (Euphorbia lomelii) or under thorn bushes (Lorenzo et al. 2014, 2018a, 2018b).They are nocturnal and crepuscular, active from dusk till evening and then again at dawn (Cervantes et al. 1996, Lorenzo et al. 2018a). It forages on a wide variety of grasses (Aristida spp., Bouteloua spp., Panicum spp., Agrostis spp.), herbs, forbs, and will consume the fleshy part of short cacti (Stenocereus spp., Opuntia engelmannii, Pachycereus spp., and Mammillaria spp.) and young stems of shrubs (Prosopis spp.) (Cervantes et al. 1996, Lorenzo et al. 2014). The availability of each of these sources varies seasonally (Lorenzo et al. 2014, 2018a).The Black Jackrabbit shares its habitat with several mammals, such as the endemic mice (Chaetodipus spinatus lambi, Peromyscus fraterculus insulicola), Bryant’s Woodrat (Neotoma bryanti bryanti), White-tailed Antelope Squirrel (Ammospermophilus leucurus insularis) and Ringtail (Bassariscus astutus saxicola) (Lorenzo et al. 2014, 2018a,b).The Black Jackrabbit shares its habitat with several species that may be predators of both young and adult jackrabbits such as the American Kestrel (Falco sparverius), Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) and the Caracara (Caracara cheriway). In addition, there are reptiles such as the Speckled Rattlesnake (Crotalus mitchellii), Variable Sand Snake (Chilomeniscus stramineus), Baja California Striped Whipsnake (Masticophis barbouri), and Espiritu Santo Whiptail (Aspidoscelis espiritensis) (Lorenzo et al. 2014, 2018a,b). Introduced domestic goats (Capra aegagrus hircus) are potential competitors for food sources (Lorenzo et al. 2018a,b).Observational evidence of males with scrotal testes indicates that the reproductive season is primarily during the wet season (May-October), but may include some of the dry season (March-November) (Lorenzo et al. 2018a). Six adult, pregnant females contained two embryos each (one in each uterine horn) (Cervantes et al. 1996, Lorenzo et al. 2018a). The total length is 54.2-60.8 cm (Lorenzo et al. 2018a).Black Jackrabbits are primarily solitary, but they have been observed in groups of two (Lorenzo et al. 2018a).Black Jackrabbits are an important prey species for a number of native predatory birds and mammals.
threats: The major threats associated with the Black Jackrabbit are hunting for local subsistence, and probably loss and disturbance of habitat by exotic fauna.
population: The species is found throughout the islands. The total population is estimated to be 923 individuals (range 537-1,586) with an average population density of 11.4 individuals/km² based on a sampling area of 81 km² (Lorenzo et al. 2012, 2018a).
range: The Black Jackrabbit is known only from Espiritu Santo and La Partida islands in the Gulf of California (Thomas and Best 1994, Lorenzo et al.2018a). It occupies elevations ranging from sea level to 300 m (Nelson 1909). The extent of occurrence (EOO) for this species is 140 km² and the total area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 96 km² - the sum of the area of the two islands of occupancy. The actual AOO is smaller than this as the species does not occur on rocky cliff or other submarginal areas on the islands. The island areas were documented from the database found at http://mapserver.inegi.gob.mx/geografia/espanol/datosgeogra/extterri/frontera.cfm?c=154%29
useTrade: This species is hunted on Espiritu Santo Island (Cervantes et al. 1996, Lorenzo et al. 2018a).
conservationActions: The Black Jackrabbit is listed in the Mexican Official Norm NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2010 as a species subject to special protection (SEMARNAT 2010). Monitoring the impacts of hunting and competition from invasive domestic goats is recommended (Lorenzo et al. 2012, Lorenzo et al. 2018a).

rationale: Alaskan Hare is confirmed as Least Concern. Populations seem to be healthy, overall, although there seems to be little monitoring occurring at the moment.
habitat: The Alaskan Hare normally occupies open tundra (Flux and Angermann 1990, Beever 2018). Diet is likely to be the same as that of other arctic hares: Dwarf Willow, grasses, sedges and heath plants.The total length is 56.5-69.0 cm (Hall 1981). L. othus produces one litter per year (Best and Henry 1994). It averages 6.3 young per litter (Anderson and Lent 1977). Gestation length is approximately 46 days (Anderson and Lent 1977).
threats: Southern populations may be subject to habitat loss, perhaps climate change as well, although this is highly speculative.
population: Population is more or less continuous and is thought to be stable and healthy. Populations may undergo cyclic fluctuations. However, little/no monitoring of populations is ongoing.
range: The geographic range of the Alaskan Hare consists of west and southwest Alaska (Flux and Angermann 1990, Beever 2018). It occupies elevations from sea level to approximately 660 m (Flux and Angermann 1990). Previously, the distribution included the Chukotkan region of Russia, however, molecular phylogeny suggests that this population of hare is more closely allied with L. timidus (Waltari et al. 2004). The Alaskan Hare has not been studied extensively, probably because of its restricted and isolated distribution along the Arctic tundra region of western Alaska. The distribution is almost entirely north of treeline, including the North Slope of Alaska, although verifiable records of this range extension are lacking.
useTrade: This species is modestly used for food, and to a small extent the fur is used by natives. Five percent of the population is utilized.
conservationActions: Research is needed to determine the taxonomic status of this species in relation to L. arcticus and L. timidus. Research should also be conducted in the areas of habitat and population status, harvest levels, and trends. There are no known conservation measures in place at this time.

rationale: There is little known about the Ethiopian Hare, but it appears widespread within its extent of occurrence (EOO) and there are no data indicating that it is threatened, therefore it is assessed as Least Concern. However, research is needed in the areas of biology, distribution, reproduction, diseases and ecology. It is also recommended that research be undertaken to determine population status, in order to accurately assess the Red List status of this species.
habitat: The Ethiopian Hare inhabits scrub and forest edge (Happold 2013). Total length of this species is 45.0-54.0 cm (Happold 2013). The body weight of this species ranges from 1,704-2,278 g. The hind foot length of this species ranges from 9-11.0 cm. The ear length of this species ranges from 6.0-9.5 cm. The tail length of this species ranges from 7.0-10.7 cm (Tolesa 2014).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: There are no data currently available regarding the population status of the Ethiopian Hare.
range: The geographic distribution of the Ethiopian Hare extends across the western region of the Ethiopian Highlands (Yalden et al. 1986). Its range may extend into SE Sudan and NW Kenya (Happold 2013). The distribution of the Ethiopian Hare is allo- or parapatric with that of the African Savannah Hare (L. victoriae) (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). On the Shewa Highlands, it is sympatric with the Ethiopian Highland Hare (L. starcki) (Tolesa and Johnston 2018). At the eastern extent of its range it may be sympatric with the Abyssinian Hare (L. habessinicus) (Tolesa 2018). The Ethiopian Hare has also been recorded in south Oromia in Ethiopia (Tolesa 2014, Tolesa et al. 2017). It can be found at elevations ranging from 500-2,500 m (Happold 2013).
conservationActions: This species is present in Gambela National Park (Yalden et al. 1996). Though noted as present in Abiata Shalla Lakes National Park by Yalden et al. (1996), recent surveys only found the Abyssinian Hare in the park and adjacent areas, which is typical habitat for it and not the Ethiopian Hare (Tolesa 2014). There are few data available on this species. It is therefore recommended, that research be conducted on population/density, biology, reproduction, disease and ecology.

rationale: Koslov’s Pika was first described in 1884 and was subsequently not seen again until the 1980s (Smith et al. 1990). The China Red List currently classifies Koslov’s Pika, a Chinese endemic, as EN A2c (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). Previously it had been classified as Endangered – EN B1ab(iii) on the 2008 IUCN Red List assessment, and as Endangered – EN B1ab(i,ii,iii) on the China Red List (Wang and Xie 2004). Since those determinations additional occupied sites have been located farther west across the Kunlun Mountains (Smith et al. 2018), such that an extent of occurrence (EOO) classification cannot be validated for a threat category using criterion B. This is a very difficult species to assess. On the one hand, it is a burrowing pika, and in general burrowing pika species can occur at high population densities locally. On the other hand, numerous attempts to locate the species within the original eastern part of its range have failed to find any Koslov’s Pikas – leading to the decline (A2) criterion on the current Chinese Red List (Smith 1994; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). Known sites where the species occurs are widely separated, thus extreme fragmentation must be considered in any attempt to classify the status of the species (Li et al. 2006). There are also reports that Koslov’s Pikas have been subject to control (poisoning) measures by local pasture control agencies (Smith 1994), and it is likely that these activities are still being pursued.This assessment is based primarily on demonstrated declines in populations of Koslov’s Pika based on comprehensive surveys undertaken in 2011 and 2012 in the same areas where the species had been assessed in 1999 (Li et al. 2016). In the Dingzikou region at Aqik Lake, the 1999 census found Koslov’s Pika density reflected by 44 burrows/ha, while the 2011 and 2012 surveys found no active burrows. South of Tuzi Lake there were 152 burrows/ha in 1999, but only 3 family burrow systems with a maximum of 30-40 burrows/ha in 2011/2012. The vegetation in the region appeared highly degraded and only two animals were observed (Li et al. 2016). In the Arjinshan National Nature Reserve, at Fenchenkou (Wind Gap, the type locality for the species) no pikas were observed during a survey taken in 2016 (Li pers. comm). The newly mapped distribution for the species (four new sites in the western Kunlun Mountains – 800 km west of the Arjinshan region, verified by specimens from the British Museum in this region) was found to have only remnant populations of Koslov’s Pika – only 2-3 animals/ha (Li et al. 2016). Thus throughout the range of Koslov’s Pika populations have declined significantly 50% in the past decade. The assessment of EN A2c is based on these decline numbers coupled with demonstrated declines in habitat quality and increasing fragmentation.
habitat: This species occupies alpine meadow tundra and digs holes in the swelling mounds of saline loess on the Guldsha Pass (Büchner 1894). The burrows constructed by this species are shallow (Smith et al. 1990). Healthy populations of Koslov’s Pikas live communally at high densities (Li et al. 2006). Koslov’s Pika is characterized as general herbivore and is a diurnal species of pika (Smith et al. 1990, Smith et al. 2018). The total length of this species is 22.0-24.0 cm (Smith and Xie 2008). Only a single litter is produced each year (Zheng 1986), with four to eight young per litter (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: Koslov’s Pika populations may have been negatively affected by vertebrate control programs in the region (Smith 1994). Regional assessment in China indicated that this species is threatened by severely fragmented extent of occurrence and continuing decline in extent of occurrence, area of occupancy and area, extent and/or quality of habitat (Wang and Xie 2004; Li et al. 2006, 2016).
population: Koslov’s Pika was found to be locally abundant in survey taken in 1999 (Li et al. 2006). However, this species has been commonly characterized as rare (Lin et al. 2010). Recent surveys have documented severe declines in the number of extant populations as well as overall population density in the remaining censuses populations (Li et al. 2016).
range: Koslov’s Pika is endemic to China (Smith and Xie 2008). A 1999 survey concluded that O. koslowi occurs in three localities, "(i) the Valley of the Winds, where the type specimens were collected), (ii) the juncture of the Kunlun and Kala-Kunlun mountains, which is located south-east of Mount Kongke, and (iii) in the Arjin Mountain Nature Reserve, including the areas verified in 1984, 1988 and during the 1999. During recent surveys, it was verified that the distribution is nearly continuous between Aqik Lake, Yueya River and Tuzi Lake. The distance between these three limits is 800 km east to west, running parallel to the Kala-Kunlun mountains, where the distribution of Koslov's pika is limited and discontinuous (Li et al. 2016). This distribution also extends further west (Smith et al. 2018) than previously mapped for the species. This species was previously recorded in two additional localities, "Kuzyuk-Kakty Pass" and near Arkatag village by the Przehevalski expedition in 1884 (Smith et al. 1990). The locality of Ikhe-Tsaidemin Nur requires confirmation (Smith et al. 1990). This species occurs at elevations of 4,200-4,800 m (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: Research is needed in the areas of ecology, reproduction, population status, and distribution. Conservation measures should be drafted and implemented for this species. This endemic species was recently regionally assessed, in China, as Endangered under criteria A2c (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). This species occurs in Arjinshan Nature Reserve.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little or nothing is known regarding the behavior, ecology, and reproduction of Ochotona forresti (Smith et al. 1990). O. forresti inhabits mountain slopes at elevations of 2,600 to 4,400 m in the forest belt (Feng et al. 1986). These high altitude habitats are typically coniferous or mixed broadleaf and conifer forests and shrubland (Smith and Xie 2008). It is speculated that this species of pika creates burrows (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: The current population status of Ochotona forresti is unknown; there have been no ecological or natural history investigations of this species.
range: Ochotona forresti ranges from northwest Yunnan to northern Myanmar. The mapped range in Myanmar is totally speculative (Duckworth and Thaw pers. comm). Ochotona forresti occupies elevations of 2,600-4,400 m.
conservationActions: Due to the general lack of data regarding the population status, behaviour, ecology, and reproduction research in these areas should be undertaken. This species has been regionally assessed in China as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2016).

rationale: This species was discovered and named in the mid-1980s (Li and Ma 1986), and was subsequently investigated for a period of about 10 years (Li et al. 1991, Li 1997), including data gathered from a captive population (Li 2003, 2004; Li et al. 1993a,b). These investigations were followed by a hiatus of about 10 years, after which follow-up censuses were conducted during 2002 and 2003. These censuses found no pikas present in 57% of locations known to have been inhabited by the Ili Pika approximately 20 years earlier (Li and Smith 2005). Additionally, there had been a decline in the area of occupancy (AOO) within the suitable extent of occurrence (EOO) for this species (Li and Smith 2005). Evidence of the presence of Ili Pikas were found at only six of the 14 original known localities, they were missing from the type locality (Li and Smith 2005). Subsequent surveys in 2006, 2010, and 2014 have documented further overall decline in this species, both in number of sites occupied and population levels in occupied sites (Li and Smith 2015). Of the original 14 known occupied sites, eight found vacant in 2006 remained unoccupied through 2010. The 2014 census consisted of surveys of seven of the original 14 sites, five sites that were vacant in the surveys of 2002-03, 2006, and 2010 were not re-censused. Two sites were documented to have no pikas in one of the new censuses, but subsequently were found to be occupied. One new occupied site was located in 2014. Only one re-censused site was found to be occupied in all four surveys. The 2014 census found no pikas at two localities which were unoccupied in all four censuses, and evidence of pikas at three sites (Li and Smith 2015).During the majority of these surveys, pika occupancy was determined by sign (active green haypiles and scat piles); no living animals were seen. The first living Ili Pikas in 20 years were seen in 2014 (two animals at one locality). Subsequently, camera traps have verified the occupancy of pikas at some localities that had been determined to have pikas by sign only. The 2014 census included 3-16 people working in the field for 38 days on 10 separate trips covering 150 km. This survey included placement of 20 infrared camera traps that ran for periods of 3-6 months. Six of these camera traps were placed at previously known pika occupancy sites (Telimati Daban sites) in the southern range (see distribution map) for three months. These cameras took many images, but none of Ili pikas. Thus, although we conservatively have included this southern spur of the Tian Shan on the range map, it is highly likely that the pikas are extirpated there (Li and Smith 2015).The glaciers in the Tian Shan have melted considerably, and we consider global warming to be one potential influence in the observed decline of the Ili pika. Since the late 1980s their isolated habitat has become occupied by an increasing number of pastoralists (Ili Pika habitat was unoccupied by people in the 1980s), leading to an increase in sheep grazing and a concomitant decline in habitat quality. Nearly all native pastoralist families have mastiff dogs which have become an additional predator of the Ili Pika (Li and Smith 2015). Qualitatively the abundance of active sign has decreased greatly since the early investigations of the species in the late 1980s. Overall we estimate that there are less than 1,000 living Ili pikas, and no subpopulation comes close to having 250 individuals. Over the past decade we estimate that the overall Ili Pika population has decreased by over 50%, and that the root causes of this decline remain unabated.Our assessment expands that of the current China Red List classification of EN (A2c) (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016—an assessment that failed to address any of the literature by Li Weidong, the person who discovered and named the species and who has conducted all the recent population censuses), as we incorporated additional information that was accessed by those assessors.
habitat: The Ili Pika inhabits "talus areas on high cliff faces" (Li and Smith 2005). The species exhibits low population densities (Li and Smith 2005, 2018). Typically a diurnal species, but may exhibit nocturnal activity (Li and Smith 2005, 2015). This species constructs haypiles and is characterized as a generalized herbivore (Li and Smith 2005).
threats: The exact causes for recently observed population declines are not known, but it is speculated that an increase in grazing pressure and global atmospheric pollution resulting in climate change are negatively impacting the Ili Pika populations (Li and Smith 2005, 2015, 2018). Low population densities and reproductive rates coupled with the relatively limited ability to disperse impede the ability of the species to recover from declines (Li and Smith 2005). Increased human presence and thus sheep grazing pressure contributes to habitat deterioration, and the mastiff dogs owned by local pastoralist represent an additional predator on Ili Pikas (Li and Smith 2005).
population: Population declines have been observed for several locations inhabited by this species (Li and Smith 2005, 2015). The Ili Pika may be extirpated from Jilimalale, Hutubi South Mountains, Jipuk South, and Telimati Daban (Li and Smith 2005, 2015). Populations have declined in the regions of Jipuk and Tianger Apex (Li and Smith 2005, 2015). Even in occupied localities, the population density is very low and apparently declining.
range: The Ili Pika is endemic to China, known only from two spurs of the Tian Shan in Xinjiang, China (Li and Smith 2005, 2015, 2018). This species has a highly fragmented distribution, within a restricted geographic range (Li and Smith 2005, 2015). It is found at elevations between 2,800-4,100 m (Li and Smith 2005, 2018). Upon its discovery the Ili Pika was determined to occupy 14 locations, 12 in the north spur of the Tian Shan, two in the south spur. One additional site was found in 2014. It currently occupies only four of these sites, none of which are in the south spur, where current surveys have failed to find any sign of occupancy. The map portrays the envelope of possible occurrence of this species, given its habitat requirements, the rough terrain and difficulty of access dictates that the status of the species in much of this area is unknown.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for the Ili pika, with the exception of the formation of protected areas that may lead to a decrease in completion with domestic sheep and a reduction of predation by mastiff dogs. Research is needed in the areas of ecology, reproduction, and behavior (Smith et al. 1990). Furthermore, data are needed to assess the distribution and population status (Li and Smith 2005). A recovery plan should be implemented to prevent extinction (Li and Smith 2005). This species has been regionally listed, in China, as Endangered under criteria A2c (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).

rationale: This is a widespread species that is not known to be experiencing a decline, and is present in protected areas. The species is listed Least Concern.
habitat: Ochotona nubrica inhabits alpine and subalpine desert scrub, where it is assumed to be a burrowing form of pika, rather than talus-dwelling (Smith et al. 1990, Smith and Xie 2008). The subspecies O. n. lhasaensis occurs in alpine steppe (Smith et al. 1990).Ochotona nubrica forms well defined family group territories, but little is known about reproductive biology (Smith and Xie 2008). The total length of this species is 14.0-18.4 cm (Smith and Xie 2008). This species is characterized as a habitat generalist (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no threats to the status of Ochotona nubrica known at this time.
population: There are few data regarding the population status of this species. In Nubra Valley, the type locality, it was characterized as common by locals during a survey conducted in 1980-1986 and again in 1989-1991 (Mallon 1991).
range: Ochotona nubrica occurs in the trans-Himalayan region from the mountains in south Xizang, China, across the Tibetan plateau and into Ladakh, India (Smith et al. 1990, Smith and Xie 2008). The species occurs at elevations between approximately 3,000 to 4,500 m (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: This species may be present in Changthang and Karakoram Wildlife Sanctuaries in India (Mallon 1991), as well as Himalayan nature reserves in China. No conservation measures are currently in place for Ochotona nubrica and none have been proposed. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Jiang et al. 2016).

rationale: Historically, this was a widespread species with regional populations that were "common" to "very numerous" (Ognev 1966). However, Ochotona pusilla has experienced a distribution contraction within historical time (Smith et al. 1990). No data could be found to characterize the current status of the O. pusilla at the global level, but this species still occupies a considerable range. Until definitive evidence suggests a threatened status this species is listed as Least Concern. Efforts should be made to determine the current status European populations of O. p. pusilla, which was characterized as "rare" by the Red Book of the Bashkir Autonomous Republic, Soviet Union (Smith et al. 1990).
habitat: Ochotona pusilla is a burrow-dwelling species of pika that occupies steppe habitat, "found primarily in moist soil which is verdant with thick grass and bushes" (Smith et al. 1990). As a steppe dwelling species, O. pusilla is an excellent indicator for the general health of steppe ecosystems (Smith 1994). This species of pika constructs haypiles (Ognev 1966). It is unusual "in that it is frequently nocturnal" and "vocalizations are usually heard at late dusk and through the night" (Smith et al. 1990). The total length of this species is 15.3-21.0 cm (Sokolov et al. 1994). O. pusilla has one to thirteen young per litter (Smith et al. 1990). The number of litters per year varies according to the age of the female (Shubin 1965). Adult pikas can yield three to five litters per year, whereas yearlings only produce one to three litters (Shubin 1965; Smirnov 1982). Females will mature in four to five weeks, whereas males become mature after a year (Shubin 1965). The reproductive periodicity will vary yearly according the weather conditions (Sokolov et al. 1994). Gestation is approximately 22-24 days (Shubin 1965).
threats: Habitat modification is the likely cause for the recorded distribution decline (Smith et al. 1990). The species at one time extended west across the European steppes, and it may have been extirpated from this region due to agricultural intensification.
population: Population densities of Ochotona pusilla vary spatially and temporally and may vary according to habitat quality (Smith et al. 1990). Populations were described as "common" to "very numerous" for several regions within its distribution (Ognev 1966). The Red Book of the Bashkir Autonomous Republic, Soviet Union characterized some of the European populations of O. p. pusilla as "rare" (Smith et al. 1990).
range: This is a widespread species. Ochotona pusilla is known "from the upper Volga River and southern Ural Mountains south and east to the border of China," Kazakhstan, and Russia (Smith et al. 1990). The westernmost extent of O. pusilla is the easternmost edge of the European continent (Smith 1994). Despite its presence in Europe, it is routinely left off European mammal lists (Smith 1994). However, "the range of this species has contracted significantly in historical times" (Smith et al. 1990). A population was recently discovered in western China (Shayilawu et al. 2009). The past distribution extended into western Europe during the Pleistocene, with a new specimen record extending its northern-most presence to Cumbria county in the UK (Fisher and Yalden 2004). By the onset of the Holocene, O. pusilla still occurred in Hungary. This distribution moved eastward, so that by the 10th century it occurred in the Ukraine and by the 18th century it could be found “between the Don and the Volga” and finally, “only east of the Volga” by the 19th century (Smith 1994). The cause for distribution contraction has been two-fold: 1) naturally occurring climate change from the Pleistocene to Holocene; and 2) anthropogenic changes like overgrazing and agriculture (Smith 1994).
useTrade: In the past, Ochotona pusilla was trapped for its pelt primarily to make high quality felt (Smith et al. 1990). Trapping for this purpose no longer occurs (Smith et al. 1990).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. The subspecies Ochotona pusilla pusilla has been characterized as rare by the Red Book of the Bashkir Autonomous Republic, Soviet Union (Smith et al. 1990). Research should be conducted to determine the current status of the European populations of this subspecies.

rationale: Thomas’s Pika is a widespread, but rare and relatively unknown species that occurs in isolated mountains in central China. It may be threatened by pest control measures, but the effects of this are unknown. The past two China Red List assessments considered this Chinese endemic as Near Threatened (NT) (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016; Wang and Xie 2004). Wang and Xie (2004) indicate its NT status based on nearly meeting the Vulnerable (VU) criteria (A2c + 3c), Jiang et al. (2015, 2016) fail to indicate their criteria for their NT status listing. Because the species is endemic, there should be justification to list it currently as NT, but we fail to find any demonstrable data to support the species nearly meeting VU due to criteria A2c + 3c, and find it troubling that Jiang et al. (2015, 2016) fail to give any supporting evidence. Recent expeditions have determined that even previous collections putatively of Ochotona thomasi, upon genetic analysis turned out to be O. cansus, thus the form is even rarer than previously thought. This finding in the field – that the Thomas’s Pika cannot be clearly identified – further obscure any attempts for this poorly known form to be assigned a threatened category. Thus we retain the Least Concern (LC) designation for the present, and hope for studies to truly clarify the status of this species.
habitat: Thomas’s Pika inhabits meadows and shrubby areas, and is a diurnally active, generalized herbivore (Smith et al. 1990, Smith and Xie 2008, Smith et al. 2018).The ecology of Thomas’s Pika is not well known, but it is assumed to be similar to O. cansus (Smith and Xie 2008), a species that it closely resembles. Thomas’s Pika may live in small family groups (Smith et al. 1990, Smith et al. 2018).
threats: Because Thomas’s Pika has not been studied, little is known about the possible threats to its habitat and populations. It is possible that the species may be at risk due to the inadvertent killing of Thomas’s Pikas in an attempt to control other pest species that occur in its range (Smith et al. 1990, Smith et al. 2018).
population: Thomas’s Pika is known to be a rare species that occurs in isolated mountains, but nothing is known about the status of those populations (Smith et al. 1990, Smith et al. 2018). It has never been the subject of an ecological investigation. It is rarely encountered by scientists working in the range of this species.
range: Thomas’s Pika is endemic to China, occurring on the northeastern portion of the Qinghai-Tibetan plateau (Smith and Xie 2008, Smith et al. 2018).
conservationActions: No conservation measures are in place to protect Thomas’s Pika. Research is needed to determine the effects of pest control on the pikas, to establish whether any other threats exist, and to determine current population statuses. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2015, 2016; Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: Pentalagus furnessi has a small area of occupancy (334 km²) (Sugimura et al. 2000, Sugimura and Yamada 2004), and is located in four fragmented subpopulations (Yamada 2004) with two locations (Amami and Tokuno islands) that are experiencing a continuing decline in area of occupancy, area and quality of habitat, and number of mature individuals (Sugimura et al. 2000, Sugimura and Yamada 2004). The decline is attributed to invasive predators (Yamada and Cervantes 2005) and habitat loss caused by forest clearing (Sugimura et al. 2000) and resort construction (McDowell 1996). In the past 10 years its area of occupancy (AOO) has increased as invasive mongooses were controlled, but this is now declining to about the former AOO due to predation by feral cats.Currently (2016), there are an estimated 5,000 individuals on Amami island, the larger population, and 400 on Tokuno island, based on fecal pellet counts (Sugimura and Yamada 2004).
habitat: Pentalagus furnessi originally lived in dense primary forest, prior to widespread deforestation (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). No studies have been conducted to measure the impact of the deforestation that began in the 1950s on P. furnessi abundance, but old forest area was reduced by 70-90% of the area since 1980 by logging (Sugimura et al. 2000). The species currently lives in coastal cycad cover, mountain habitat with oak cover (Yamada and Cervantes 2005), broad leafed evergreen forests and cutover areas where perennial grasses dominate (Sugimura et al. 2000).Pentalagus furnessi has a diet of 12 species of herbaceous plants and 17 shrub species, consuming mostly acorns and the sprouts and young shoots of plants (Yamada and Cervantes 2005).The species burrows underground, usually in densely covered forest valleys (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). They are primarily nocturnal (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). The total length of males of this species is 45.1 cm. Females are on average 45.2 cm in length (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). P. furnessi has two breeding seasons each year (March-May and September-December), with a single kitten bred at a time (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). At birth, neonates are 15.0 cm in length (Yamada and Cervantes 2005).
threats: Pentalagus furnessi is threatened by invasive predatory species and human caused habitat destruction.The introduction of the mongoose (Herpestes javanicus), which probably occurred on Amami Island in 1979, has presented a serious threat to P. furnessi, which evolved in isolation in absence of large active predators (Yamada 2002). Feral cats and dogs on both islands present a similar threat (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). While mongooses have been largely controlled, feral cats now represent a major threat to this species.Habitat destruction, in the form of logging, has decreased the area of old growth forest to less than 10-30% of the area that existed in 1980 (Sugimura et al. 2000). Forest road construction, for the purpose of logging, encourages predator expansion in forests (Sugimura et al. 2000). Construction of resort facilities (e.g. golf courses) on Amami island have caused concern because the plans required destruction of rabbit habitat (McDowell 1996).
population: Total population size for Amami island, from estimates in 2003, was between 2,000 and 4,800 individuals, reduced from a 1993-1994 estimate of 2,500-6,100 individuals; a 2016 estimate is ca. 5,000. These estimates were based on fecal pellet counts (Sugimura and Yamada 2004). Tokuno, which has a much smaller area of occupancy, has three populations numbering 200, 100, and 100.
range: Pentalagus furnessi occurs only on the Japanese islands of Amami-Oshima (712 km² total land area) and Tokuno-Shima (248 km²), in Kagoshima prefecture, in the Nansei archipelago (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). The rabbit is estimated to have a distribution on Amami Island of 301.4 km² (Yamada and Cervantes 2005), and 33 km² on Tokuno, based on data collected using fecal pellet presence and suitable habitat (Sugimura et al. 2000). The area of both islands combined is 960 km², but less than half of the area constitutes suitable habitat (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). The rabbit’s distribution is fragmented into four separate populations, three of which are very small. (Yamada 2004). The elevational distribution is from sea level to 694 m on Amami and 645 m on Tokuna (Yamada and Cervantes 2005).Range size declined on Amami Island by 20-40% from 1977-1994 (Yamada 2008).
conservationActions: Pentalagus furnessi was declared a natural monument of Japan in 1921, and a special natural monument in 1963. These designations prohibited hunting and capture of the rabbits (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). The Center for Conservation of Amami Wildlife was established in 1999, and P. furnessi was listed under the Japanese Endangered Species Act in 2004 (Yamada and Cervantes 2005).Control of exotic predators has been addressed by a program started in 2005 by the Ministry of the Environment, which seeks to eradicate the introduced mongoose (Yamada and Cervantes 2005). Control of feral cats and dogs is also needed (Sugimura et al. 2000).Because of the limited area of P. furnessi’s natural range, habitat preservation is very important (Sugimura et al. 2000). The cessation of forest road construction would discourage the spread of predators into the rabbit’s range and restrict logging of mature forests. These logging practices destroy prime habitat for P. furnessi and fragment local populations (Sugimura et al. 2000). Government subsidies intending to support the local economy have inhibited rabbit conservation, as they have provided financial support for forest road construction (Sugimura 1988) and clearing for farmland (Sugimura et al. 2000). Ninety percent of the mature forest area is privately or locally owned, the remaining 10% is owned by the national government (Sugimura et al. 2000).

rationale: The Volcano Rabbit is endemic to a small region along the Transverse Neovolcanic Belt in central Mexico where it occupies a restricted and specialized habitat on five mountain massifs (Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). This range is becoming increasingly fragmented and the area of available suitable habitat is decreasing (Velazquez 1994, Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2016, Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018, Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018). This rabbit is being threatened by competition with grazing livestock, increasing frequency of fire, intrusion by humans (settlements, roads, etc.), and climate change. Models extrapolating its persistence in a metapopulation context under climate change indicate that it is likely to be severely impacted (Anderson et al. 2009). Its current EOO is 2,469 km², and an overestimate of the AOO is <444 km² (based on the sum of 19 relatively large habitat polygons, in which the species is further fragmented). The high level of current fragmentation and the multitude of ongoing threats are likely to lead to further decreases in area occupied. Thus, the Volcano Rabbit qualifies for Endangered status (EN B1ab(i,ii,iii,v) + B2ab(i,ii,iii,v)).Reports that the Volcano Rabbit has gone extinct in the vicinity of the Nevado de Toluca (Mexico Daily News 2018) are false. Native populations of the Volcano Rabbit have never been in the Nevado de Toluca. A colony was introduced in the 1970s and sometime later a single individual was captured and taken into captivity, since then there have been no verified records of the species in this area. The Nevado de Toluca is not included in the current distribution map for the species.
habitat: The Volcano Rabbit is a habitat specialist (Velazquez et al. 1993, Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). It is found at its highest density in a subalpine habitat containing bunchgrass (“zacaton”) and pine communities (Velazquez et al. 1993, Hunter and Cresswell 2015, Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2015). The largest remaining area of preferred habitat resides in the Iztaccihuatl-Popocatepetl National Park, between 3,400 and 4,200 m (Hunter and Cresswell 2015). A study conducted on the Iztaccihuatl volcano found that preference was shown for areas that had low occurrence of “closed forest, long grass, cattle grazing, hunting, bare ground and incline” (Hunter and Cresswell 2015). Contrary to previous findings, the study suggested that an increase of recent fire activity resulted in increased abundance of the rabbit, resulting from improved habitat quality from reduced competition to bunchgrass (Hunter and Cresswell 2015). However, regular use of fire to benefit cattle grazing is not recommended given that cattle grazing proved to be more detrimental to the Volcano Rabbit than the benefit of improved habitat quality (Hunter and Cresswell 2015). Further, prevalence of fire led to a decrease in population persistence (VORTEX modeling, Portales et al. 1997). A second study in the Ajusco-Chichinautzin Mountain Range found that, in addition to the previously mentioned factors, proximity to highways and population centers had a negative impact on abundance, although this study did not find a correlation with regard to slope (the effect of fire was not examined) (Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018).Until today, habitat fragmentation has not resulted in the loss of genetic variability, nor has it affected the genetic structure of Volcano Rabbit populations. The values of genetic diversity are similar in populations that live in a connected landscape and those that live in an unconnected one. In addition, gene flow has been detected even in isolated populations (Montes-Carreto et al., in press).The diet of the Volcano Rabbit is diverse. It is known to consume more than 70 plant species, although the rabbits consume with greater frequency zacatonales of the genera Muhlenbergia, Festuca, and Jarava (Cervantes and Martínez 1992, Martínez-García et al. 2012, Mancines-Arellano 2017). In areas where bunchgrass is less abundant, they give birth in cracks and abandoned burrows (Velazquez et al. 1993). It is unlikely that the Volcano Rabbit constructs burrows of its own (Fa and Bell 1990). Gestation time for this species is 38-40 days (Cervantes et al. 1990). It may be reproductively active year-round with a peak breeding season occurring "during the warm, rainy summer" (Cervantes et al. 1990). Litter size is one to three (Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). Adults in a captive breeding program weighed 400-600 g, with birth weights for females 25-27 g and males 32 g (Matsuzaki et al. 1982). Total length of newborns ranges from 8.3-10.6 cm (Cervantes et al. 1990). Mean total length of adults range between 26.8-32.0 (Cervantes et al. 1990). Most activity occurs in the morning and late afternoon (Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).A study conducted in the Itxa-Popo National Park found that the Volcano Rabbit makes up 12.5% and 5.5% of the prey base for the Bobcat (Lynx rufus) and Coyote (Canis latrans), respectively (Garcia et al. 2014). Additional predators include the Long-tailed Weasel (Mustela frenata), Red-tailed Hawks (Buteo jamaicensis), and rattlesnakes (Crotalus spp.) (Cervantes-Reza 1981, Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).
threats: The Volcano Rabbit is threatened by habitat destruction, caused by livestock grazing, agriculture and property development encroachment, logging, harvest of the “zacaton” grasses, and fires (98% of which are started by humans attempting to encourage new pasture growth) (Fa and Bell 1990). Its range is within 45 minutes of one of the world’s largest cities (Mexico City) and urban expansion has resulted in habitat loss (Fa and Bell 1990), which is ongoing. Today, suitable habitat for the Volcano Rabbit in the Ajusco-Chichinautzin Mountains covers 7,544 ha, equivalent to only 13.68% of the landscape, including 957 patches: 293 have a minimum area of 0.25 ha and only two are larger than 1,000 ha (Uriostegui-Velarde et al 2018). Though hunting is illegal, it continues because of lack of local knowledge of its protected status, and lack of enforcement (Cervantes et al. 1990, Fa and Bell 1990, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).Reduction of habitat quality associated to the presence of pasture lands, crops, and roads may have a stressful effect on the rabbits, as mean cortisol metabolites levels measured in its faeces were more than two times higher in highly degraded habitat compared to the low degraded habitat (Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2014). Climate change is likely to have severe consequences for this species. Anderson et al. (2009) predicted that the lower elevation range limit of the Volcano Rabbit may shift upslope by approximately 700 m during the next 100 years, which will reduce the area occupied by the species, as the mountain peaks currently lack suitable habitat.
population: An early estimate of the population of the Volcano Rabbit was 7,085 rabbits; 1,811 individuals in Pelado, 1,816 in Tlaloc, 3,458 in Izta-Popo and approximately 3,056 for the surrounding areas (Portales et al. 1997). Due to a variety of continuous and ongoing threats, its population is likely to be lower at the present time.Population densities estimated by line transects are variable between regions. Studies conducted on the Pelado Volcano indicated that densities ranged from 0.11 to 1.2 rabbits/ha according to habitat characteristics (Velázquez 1994); in the Biological Corredor Chichinautzin the density was estimated to be 4.2 individuals/ha (Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2016). Other studies have shown the relative abundance based on fecal pellet counts is also highly variable throughout its distribution, ranging from 0.1 to 3.1 latrines/m² in habitat on the Volcano Pelado (Velázquez 1994, Velázquez and Heil 1996), and 0.02 to 0.12 latrines/m² in Sierra Chichinautzin (Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2015).The only study that has monitored trends in population was conducted in a core population in the Sierra Chichinautzin based on density estimates using pellet counts (Guerrero et al. in press). This study indicated that Volcano Rabbit density declined from 4.2 individuals/ha in 2011 to <1 individual/ha in 2017.Initial studies indicated that the Volcano Rabbit occupied fragmented habitat, and that there were 16 discrete occupied habitat fragments (Portales et al. 1997); the current number of isolated habitat polygons is 19. More recent evaluation of the degree of fragmentation within occupied habitat polygons was able to discern significantly more fine-scale Volcano Rabbit habitat fragmentation (Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018). At the landscape level 957 patches of available habitat covering 75.44 km² were identified along the Ajusco-Chichinautzin Mountain Range (thus encompassing Tlaloc Volcano, Pelado Volcano, and Coajomulco forests), most (N = 293) of which had a minimum area of 2,500 m². Only two patches were larger than 1,000 ha. 144 plots were sampled intensively, and of these 50 contained no evidence of Volcano Rabbit presence (no latrines were located); on only five plots were there more than 100 latrines, indicating the presence of a highly viable population (Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018).
range: The Volcano Rabbit is endemic to Mexico, restricted to the Transverse Neovolcanic Belt, mainly in discontinuous patches on four volcanoes (Popocatepetl, Iztaccihuatl, El Pelado, Tlaloc) and the Sierra Chichinautzin (Rizo-Aguilar et al.2016, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). An initial estimate of area of occupancy (AOO) was approximately 386 km² based on occupancy on the four volcanoes (Velazquez 1994), although this area has subsequently been reduced to 335 km². Recent observations, based on latrine records and sightings in the Biological Corridor Chichinautzin, have added 109 km² to this distribution (Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2016). A recent survey in the Parque Ecoturístico Piedra Canteada, along the Tlaxcala/Puebla border, north of Iztaccihuatl, yielded a recent siting of Volcano Rabbits, but the extent is unknown (Ramírez-Albores et al.2014). As a result of the over 15 years continuous volcanic activity of the Popocatepetl Volcano, the distribution range has shifted and expanded, locally. Currently, the discontinuous EOO is 2,469 km². The whole range, however, is becoming increasingly fragmented as a result of human-induced and natural causes (Uriostegui-Velarde et al. 2018, Velazquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).The Volcano Rabbit occurs between 2,900 m and 4,250 m in elevation (Rizo-Aguilar et al. 2015, 2016), but its highest density is found between 3,150 m and 3,400 m (Velazquez 1994).
useTrade: In some areas, this species is hunted for food.
conservationActions: The Volcano Rabbit is listed under Appendix I of CITES (1973), although the species has never been involved in international trade and this listing is apparently an historical artifact. Hunting is illegal according to Mexican law, but poorly enforced (Fa and Bell 1990, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). It is listed as endangered in the Mexican Official Norm NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2010 (SEMARNAT 2010). It occurs within the protected areas Izta-Popo and Zoquiapan National Parks, but hunting, grazing, and grass burning persist within the park boundaries (Cervantes et al. 1990, Fa and Bell 1990, Velázquez et al. 1993, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).Captive breeding programs have been established with some success, but infant mortality in captivity is very high (Fa and Bell 1990).It is recommended that conservation measures focus on habitat management, particularly the control of burning and overgrazing of the bunchgrass “zacaton” habitat, and enforcement of the existing laws prohibiting hunting and trade of the Volcano Rabbit (Fa and Bell 1990, Hunter and Cresswell 2015, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). Management of the protected areas should be improved and education plans at local, national, and international levels should be implemented (Fa and Bell 1990, Portales et al. 1997, Hunter and Cresswell 2015, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018). Captive colonies, especially those in the zoos of Mexico City should be used to educate the public about the protected status of the Volcano Rabbit (Fa and Bell 1990, Velázquez and Gopar-Merino 2018).

rationale: The Tres Marías Cottontail occurs on four islands with a total land area of less than 245 km² (Cervantes 1997), thus the area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 245 km² and perhaps as small as 9.1 km². Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 1,015 km². The available habitat on the islands is declining due to increased pressure from human settlements, increased land converted to agriculture, and the introduction of game species which have caused strong ecological impacts due to completion for resources (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Cervantes 1997). As a result, Tres Marías Cottontail populations have declined historically and the only extant population in 1987 was reported to occur on the smallest island of San Juanito (9.1 km²; less than 5% of the total area of the islands; Cervantes 1997). Little-to-no work has been done on this species in the last 20 years. However, the TresMarías Islands were designated as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 2010 (Lorenzo et al. 2018). The species is confirmed as Endangered under criterion B.
habitat: The Tres Marías Islands where this species occurs are more arid than the mainland (<630 mm annual precipitation), and the resulting habitat is tropical dry deciduous and moist forest (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Cervantes 1997).
