The Tres Marías appears to inhabit both intact habitats and in areas of secondary succession, such as deserted ranches and fields (Nelson 1899), although they may be less abundant in forested areas (Cervantes 1997). On San Juanito, the species does particularly well in thorn scrub habitat (Wilson 1991). The Tres Marías Cottontail has only a few natural predators: Raccoons (Procyon loctor insularis), Red-tailed Hawks (Buteo jamaicensis), and Northern Crested Caracaras (Caracara cheriway) (Cervantes 1997). It is considered to be exceedingly tame, and on an 1897 biological expeditions it was noted that they could have collected over a hundred in a single night (Wilson 1991).Little is known about reproduction in this species, but an expedition in March 1978 documented 11 lactating females and two females with embryos (75 mm) (Wilson 1991). Total length is 48.0 cm (Cervantes et al. 2005).This species is a primary consumer and seed disperser, as well as a prey item for native carnivores.
threats: The Tres Marías Cottontail had few historical predators, and does not exhibit much fear of humans, which leaves it vulnerable to hunting (Cervantes 1997).Introduced agricultural, and game species, such as the White-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus), pigs (Sus scrofa), and domestic goats (Capra aegagrus hircus) exist on Maria Magdalena Island, and the Black Rat (Rattus rattus) was introduced to all islands. These species have caused strong ecological impacts and competition for resources (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Cervantes 1997).A federal prison located on Maria Madre Island has led to increased human settlement and development of the land, which has caused habitat disturbance that presents a threat to the Tres Marías Cottontail (Cervantes 1997).Habitat destruction has probably been the main cause of decline in the Tres Marías Cottontail. Populations used to be more abundant on the uninhabited islands of Maria Cleofas and San Juanito, but Maria Cleofas has been stripped of about half of its native vegetation in preparation for settlement (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).
population: Populations of the Tres Marías Cottontail are declining (Cervantes 1997). In 1897, the species was reported to be abundant on portions of San Juanito, María Madre, and María Magdalena Islands (Nelson 1897, Ramirez-Silva 2005). An expedition in March of 1978 located cottontails on all four islands, but noted that they were only abundant on the uninhabited San Juanito Island (Wilson 1991). However, a 1987 Oxford University expedition did not find any rabbits or evidence of activity on María Madre, María Magdalena, or María Cleofas (Cervantes 1997).
range: Distribution of the Tres Marías Cottontail is limited to the four Tres Marías Islands in Nayarit, Mexico (Cervantes 1997). The subspecies Suncus graysoni graysoni is native to María Madre (area = 145.3 km²), María Magdalena (70.4 km²), and María Cleofas (19.8 km²) islands, and the subspecies S. g. badistes occurs on San Juanito Island (9.1 km²) (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). The total area of the four islands is 245 km²; its area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 200 km² and its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 1,015 km². The species has been recorded from sea level to an elevation of 350 m (Cervantes 1997).
useTrade: The species is used for meat and fur.
conservationActions: The Tres Marías Cottontail is listed as Endangered in the Mexican Official Norm NOM-059-ECOL-2010 (SEMARNAT 2010). Detailed long-term study has strongly recommended the need to identify the current state of conservation, population status, and the basic biological characteristics of the species (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Cervantes 1997, Lorenzo et al. 2018).The island of María Magdalena was designated an ecological reserve by the Mexican government (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). In 2010 the Tres Marías Islands Biosphere Reserve was added to the UNESCO World Network (Lorenzo et al. 2018).Some vital actions to ensure survival of the Tres Marías Cottontail are to cease all forms of hunting, turn San Juanito Island into an ecological reserve, create a biological reserve on María Madre Island, and support scientific investigation to assess the rabbit’s present status and specific habitat conditions (Lorenzo et al. 2018).

rationale: Sylvilagus dicei is not a well-known species, yet evidence suggests that in some portions of its range there are numerous potential threats. Thus, this species is possibly threatened due to its restricted range and invasive predators. It qualifies for Vulnerable B1 based on its extent of occurrence (EOO = 6,271 km²), few locations, and inferred continuing decline in quality of habitat.
habitat: Very little is known about the ecology of Sylvilagus dicei, but it is presumed to be similar to S. brasiliensis, of which S. dicei was formerly a subspecies (Reid 1997). This species is most abundant in the paramo grasslands (such as those in the Chirropo massif) but also occurs in the shrublands and oak cloud forests surrounding and associated with these high elevation ecosystems (Schipper pers. comm).
threats: Threats that currently affect Sylvilagus dicei are poorly known (Chapman and Ceballos 1990) as few people have studied it. During several camera-trap studies in the paramo, high elevation grasslands and cloud forests of the Chirropo massif, the species was found to be relatively abundant throughout the region based on photographic evidence and scats (Schipper pers. comm.). However, interviews with locals in the area suggest that the species was previously more common than it is today, and likely had a larger distribution that extended down to lower elevations (which have since been converted to cattle pasture and other agriculture). The following are potential threats for S. dicei in the Talamanca mountain region of Costa Rica (Schipper pers. comm.):1. Coyotes - a non-native carnivore (natural range expansion south following cattle) and is likely the greatest consumer of S. dicei in the Talamancans. Probably less of a threat in forested areas, but in paramo and grassland their bones are in nearly every scat found.2. Fire - lower elevations of Talamanca are burned annually for range control, but the paramos burn periodically and completely over large areas (also human caused - accidental and intentional). This likely has a short term effect by removing forage and a longer term effect by removing hiding places.3. Habitat loss - coupled with fire is the reduction of forest habitat along the lower reaches of the species' range. This has the effect of range contraction, as it is already limited entirely to the Montane forest areas, which are being logged and cleared for pasture right up to the park border.4. Mesocarnivore population explosions - along the contact zone with S. dicei and humans there is intensive hunting of large mammal fauna, which has the indirect effect of increasing the number of mesocarnivores (coyotes, tayra, and other rabbit predators).
population: Very little is known about population status of Sylvilagus dicei.
range: Sylvilagus dicei occurs in a limited range only in the Cordillera de Talamanca of Costa Rica and in western Panama (Reid 1997) at high elevations (above 1,640 m in Cervantes, Costa Rica, to 3,800 m in Cerro Chirropo, Costa Rica). It occurs to 1,180 m at Rancho de Rio Jimenez in Panama (Diersing 1981).
useTrade: Sylvilagus dicei was hunted until 2012, when this activity was outlawed in Costa Rica, however the species may still be hunted for game or subsistence in rural areas.
conservationActions: A status survey is needed for Sylvilagus dicei. Owing to a lack of knowledge about the species it is recommended that research be conducted on population, biology/ecology, threats, and use.

rationale: The Mexican Cottontail was previously considered to be abundant throughout its range (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Cervantes et al. 2005). While recent declines have been documented within portions of the range (Lorenzo et al. 2018), the percentage of population reduction is unknown and the area of occupancy is substantial. The species is confirmed Least Concern.
habitat: Mexican Cottontails have quite broad ecological preferences, being found in tropical, semi-arid, and temperate forest, open forest, dense shrub, and grassland. From southern Sinaloa to western Michoacán, they occur along the coastal plain at sea level to the mountain slopes (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). In central Mexico they occur in pine and pine-oak forest, particularly with clumped understory grasses, xeric scrub dominated by Kidneywood Tree (Eysenhardtia polystachya), Shadbush (Amelanchier spp.) and Sumac (Rhus spp.), grasslands of Mexican Broomroot (Muhlenbergia macroura) and Peruvian Feather Grass (Stipa ichu), Alligator Juniper forests (Juniperus deppeana), and oak forests (Quercus spp.) (Lorenzo et al. 2018). In western Mexico they occur in pastures, dry deciduous forest, and areas of disturbed vegetation (Chapman and Ceballos 1990), they can also be found in upland valleys of tropical deciduous and mixed pine-oak (Lorenzo et al. 2018). Home range size is around 3.3 ha and 4.06 ha for both females and males, respectively, with overlap in ranges between the sexes (Vázquez et al. 2013, Rodríguez-Martínez et al. 2014).Although they are able to reproduce throughout the year, peak reproduction occurs during the warmer and wetter summer from March through October (Vázquez et al. 2006, Vázquez et al. 2007). Up to six young are produced per litter and gestation time is 28-34 days (Cervantes et al. 2005, Aguilar et al. 2014, Lorenzo et al. 2018). Total length for this species ranges from 48.5-51.5 cm (Cervantes et al. 2005).The Mexican Cottontail is sympatric with other Lagomorphs in portions of its range, including the Volcano Rabbit (Romerolagus diazi), Desert Cottontail (Sylvilagus audubonii), the Eastern Cottontail (S. floridanus), White-sided Jackrabbit (Lepus callotis), the Black-tailed Jackrabbit (L. californicus), and the Antelope Jackrabbit (L. alleni) (Cervantes et al. 2005). Mexican Cottontails are preyed upon by Coyotes (Canis latrans), Bobcats (Lynx rufus), Grey Foxes (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), Pumas (Puma concolor), Owls (Tyto spp.), Hawks (Buteo spp.), snakes and American Crocodiles (Crocodylus acutus) (Cervantes et al. 1992, Lorenzo et al. 2018).Mexican Cottontails are an important food source for native predators throughout their range. They are also primary consumers and seed dispersers, especially for Alligator Juniper (Lezama-Delgado et al. 2016).Although they engage in group feeding and running in pairs, this species can also be strongly aggressive and can be contained in a maximum group size of 3-4 females and 2 males within a 530 m2 habitat (Lorenzo et al. 2018).
threats: The Mexican Cottontail is threatened in some areas by overgrazing, hunting, habitat fragmentation, and habitat destruction, which has caused the decline of some populations (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). It is also vulnerable to human-induced fires and volcanic activity. Habitat reduction has been estimated to be between 13-23% over the last three generations (Cuarón and de Grammont pers. comm.). A climate change model generated for 2050, indicated that there will be 22% range reduction (primarily along the Pacific coast, impacting S. c. pacificus) from the current potential range of this species (Martinez-Villeda 2006).
population: The Mexican Cottontail was previously considered to be abundant (Chapman and Ceballos 1990), but has experienced recent declines in portions of its range (Lorenzo et al. 2018). It has been reported that the average density was 27 ± 5.4 individuals/km² in central Mexico at La Malinche National Park, Tlaxcala, which varies according to the rainy and dry seasons (Gonzalez et al. 2007). Recent declines have been associated with areas where overgrazing, hunting, and habitat degradation occur (Gilcrease 2014).
range: The Mexican Cottontail is endemic to Mexico and has the widest distribution of all endemic cottontails in Mexico. Its range extends from mid-Sinaloa, continuing south along the Pacific coast to Oaxaca, including the Axis Neovolcanic and western region of Veracruz (Lorenzo et al. 2018). Its altitudinal distribution ranges from sea level to approximately 4,300 m (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Presently there are three subspecies: S. c. cunicularius which occurs in the central portion if the distribution (Axis Neovolcanic into the states of Michoacán, Guerrero, and Oaxaca), S. c. insolitus occurring in the northern extent of the species’ distribution from mid-Sinaloa along the Pacific coastal plain to the south-central region of Jalisco, and S. c. pacificus which occurs from the southern region of Jalisco south along to the Pacific coastal plain to Oaxaca (Hall 1981).
useTrade: Mexican Cottontails are hunted for subsistence and sport and as a potential competitor with livestock (Lorenzo et al. 2018).
conservationActions: Although once abundant throughout its range, this species experiences pressure from habitat destruction, overgrazing, and hunting which have contributed to recent declines in portions of the range (Gilcrease 2014, Lorenzo et al. 2018). Due to potential loss of habitat resulting from global climate change, research should be conducted regarding population density and habitat transformation (along the Pacific coast for S. c. pacificus), to determine the impact on survivability (Martinez-Villeda 2006). Recent declines have been reported near the coast in Jalisco and in the state of Morelos (Lorenzo et al. 2018).

rationale: This species once had a widespread distribution across New England, USA. Suitable habitat for the New England Cottontail has declined by an estimated 86% since 1960, and the available habitat has become increasingly fragmented (Litvaitis et al. 2008, Fenderson et al. 2014). It is confirmed as Vulnerable because a population size reduction has occurred since 1994 and in the last ten years it is suspected to be greater than 30%. The decline is continuing due to further habitat destruction/modification and fragmentation resulting from urbanization and suburbanization, and competition with the expansion of the range of the New England Cottontail. Currently New England Cottontails occupy less than 15% of their historic range, and they are considered Endangered and are protected (no hunting) in Maine and New Hampshire. They are considered a game animal in the remainder of their range. There is a substantial effort underway to increase abundance of habitat in a large portion of the historic range of NEC. However, much of this effort will require years for managed lands to develop into suitable habitat, and a substantial portion will never be suitable given site characteristics. Likewise, introductions of captive-bred rabbits have had some modest successes and also failures. These have not offset continued losses. As a result, most populations continue to decline in the occupied range. The USFWS (2015) denied a petition to list the New England Cottontail as an endangered or threatened species and to designate critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act of 1973. This decision is controversial based on available data of population estimates, the misrepresentation of the historical range of the species, and failure to acknowledge that ongoing attempts to conserve the species have been over-stated.
habitat: The New England Cottontail occupies areas of open woods and shrubs (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998), often with sandy soils. This species is a habitat specialist. It historically occupied early successional forests that became abundant when farmlands were abandoned, and the maturation of these forests into closed-canopy stands caused decline of this species beginning in the 1960s (Litvaitis et al. 2008). It is typically found close to streams, swamps, ponds, or lakes in dense cover with a shrub dominated understory (generally >20,000 stems/ha), and will rarely venture more than 5 m from escape cover (Litvaitis et al. 2018). Radio-tracking suggests New England Cottontails are using the invasive Japanese Barberry (Berberis thunbergii) as an important cover type, particularly when Eastern Cottontail populations are present (Cheeseman 2017).Minimum patch sizes of 2.5 ha have been suggested for New England Cottontail populations, based on foraging efficiency in winter settings (Barbour and Litvaitis 1993). However, because summer home range size is greater, this may be too conservative of a target (Cheeseman 2017).The diet of New England Cottontails includes a variety of herbaceous plants, fruits, and seeds, and in the winter it consumes woody species (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998).Outside of the breeding season New England Cottontails are often solitary. They have an average litter size of 4.2 young/litter, the average female produces 2.5 litters during the mid-March through August breeding season (Litvaitis et al. 2018). Adults range in size from 38.6–43.0 cm (Litvaitis et al. 2018).
threats: The New England Cottontail is most threatened by habitat destruction (Litvaitis et al. 2008). Urban-suburban sprawl and industrial development expand into and fragment the habitat of this species. These areas are better suited to the Eastern Cottontail (S. floridanus). Recent genetic studies suggest this population isolation is leading to moderate-to-strong genetic drift in many portions of the range (Fenderson et al. 2011, Fenderson et al. 2014, Cheeseman 2017).New England Cottontails have historically declined due to maturation of second-growth forests and fragmentation of suitable habitat (Litvaitis et al. 2008). The conversion of native shrublands to other land uses, confusion with Eastern Cottontails by sportsmen, and lack of education on existence, biology, and habitat requirements of this species cause problems for the conservation of this species.Competition with Eastern Cottontails may also place pressure on New England Cottontail populations (Litvaitis et al. 2008). Decline in the New England Cottontail coincides with growth in Eastern Cottontail populations. Captive trials suggest that the species may not be exerting much competition (Litvaitis et al. 2008), however, telemetry estimates indicate that habitat usage for the New England Cottontail shifts where the two species overlap in distribution (Cheeseman 2017).
population: The New England Cottontail is rare to scarce in many portions of its range. Recent census efforts suggest that around 17,000 New England Cottontails exist in the wild, with the majority of these found in Connecticut and Massachusetts (10,000 and 4,600 individuals, respectively, USFWS 2015). Population estimates are smaller in New York (1,600 individuals) and Maine (700 individuals), and are extremely limited in New Hampshire (<180 individuals) and Rhode Island (<100 individuals) (USFWS 2015). However, these estimates may be overstated, as they assume rabbits occupy all known available habitat within focal areas, which is contravened by most field studies. Many rabbits in Maine, New Hampshire, western Massachusetts, southeast New York, and western Connecticut are found on small habitat patches (<3 ha), which probably only support 3-4 individuals per patch (Barbour and Litvaitis 1993, Litvaitis et al. 2008). As patches of less than 2.5 ha are likely population sinks (Barbour and Litvaitis 1993) many of these patches are unlikely to contribute to New England Cottontail population recruitment.Recent survey efforts have also suggested population decline since the early 2000s in the Merrimack River Valley of New Hampshire, northward from Manchester to Concord, and in northern Rhode Island (USFWS 2015). Historical estimates suggest that the New England cottontail peaked in abundance and distribution in the 1960s (Litvaitis et al. 2008), benefiting from succession that occurred on land cleared in the mid-19th and early 20th centuries (Foster et al. 2002). Across much of their range, including areas of eastern New York, genetic evidence suggests highly restricted gene flow, strong population fragmentation and genetic drift (Fenderson et al. 2011, Fenderson et al. 2014, Cheeseman 2017).
range: New England Cottontails historically occurred throughout southern Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Connecticut, eastern New York, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. Whitaker and Hamilton (1998) include a small region of southern Quebec. A study by Litvaitis et al. (2008) estimated that the current area of occupancy (AOO) in its historic range is 12,180 km², approximately 86% less than the occupied range in 1960. This study showed small patches of populations existing in coastal southeastern Maine, coastal and Merrimack River valley region of southern New Hampshire, southeastern New York, western and some of eastern Connecticut (east of Connecticut River), western Massachusetts, parts of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. Estimates suggest ongoing range contraction, with 2% of the range of New England Cottontails lost per year (Fenderson et al. 2014, USFWS 2015).
useTrade: Overall, numbers of cottontails harvested have not declined, but the percent of New England Cottontails in the harvest has. The species is hunted for sport, for food, and for ornamental/decorative goods. Cottontail hunting has been prohibited in Maine since 2004 and New Hampshire prohibits take of any cottontails in areas where the New England Cottontail occurs (USFWS 2015).
conservationActions: The New England Cottontail was recommended by Chapman and Stauffer in 1979 to be listed by the IUCN as a species of special concern due to the significant differences between it and the Eastern Cottontail, which is now sympatric in much of its range (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). In 2004 the United States Fish and Wildlife Service began consideration of this species to be listed as a threatened or endangered species (Litvaitis et al. 2006). Protection under the Endangered Species Act was declined based on known scattered occurrences across its range as well as presence within protected areas (Department of the Interior - Fish and Wildlife Service 2004). In 2006, a subsequent review found sufficient evidence to designate the species as a candidate and begin a warranted-but-precluded 12 month findings on the New England Cottontail (Department of the Interior - Fish and Wildlife Service 2006). In 2015 a decision not to list the New England Cottontail was made based on the assumption that populations had been artificially high due to age of succession in New England habitats and were subsequently declining as habitats aged (USFWS 2015). Very little good habitat for the New England Cottontail is protected, and tracts of scrub oak barrens should be purchased and protected. Conservation of critical habitat and establishment and management of “Important Mammal Areas” containing known populations, with appropriate publicity and public education programs have been implemented.The New England Cottontail is in need of more research, including surveying and population monitoring, research on nest sites, dispersal, habitat, use of corridors, response to climatic change and stochastic events, effects of sport hunting, competition with other lagomorphs, and response to invasive vegetative species (especially how invasive plants affect spread of parasites and disease).Captive breeding and reintroductions have been ongoing through work at the Roger Williams Park Zoo in Providence, Rhode Island. Success of these reintroductions has been mixed (McGreevy, T.J., pers. comm.).

rationale: Ochotona hoffmanni occupies a restricted distribution. It is also known from only two widely separated locations. The total area of these two mountain distributions is 1,242 km², and the Pika only occupies isolated rock outcroppings within each of these is widely separated mountains (estimated at 10%), and thus its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be around 124 km², which is also probably an over-estimate. Each population is subject to stochastic extinction, due to small population size, and climate change may make each of the isolated populations increasingly vulnerable to population loss.
habitat: The preferred habitat of Ochotona hoffmanni is rock and talus; there have been no detailed ecological studies conducted on this isolated form.
threats: This species is threatened by rising global temperatures. As a rock dwelling species, Ochotona hoffmanni is unable to disperse to more suitable habitat due to the intolerable ambient temperatures of connecting terrain.
population: Each population is subject to stochastic extinction, due to small population size. The current population status is poorly known.
range: Ochotona hoffmanni occurs in two restricted ranges. It occupies the subalpine regions of the Hentiyn Nuruu ridge of the Bayan-Ulan range in Mongolia, as well as the Erman Mountain range of the Russian Federation (Formozov et al. 1996, Formozov and Baklushinskaya 1999).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for Ochotona hoffmanni. There are very little data concerning the habitat, ecology, status of the population and its habitat. Research in these areas is recommended.

rationale: Annamite Striped Rabbit is categorised as Endangered based on the rates of decline inferred over the 10-year period (a period exceeding that of three generations) to 2018 (past), the 10-year period from 2018 (future), and any 10-year period including 2018 within it (ongoing). Illegal hunting pressure is extremely high throughout the species' known global range. This poaching is primarily accomplished with wire snares; is almost ubiquitous across the Annamite forests, even in protected areas; and has resulted in precipitous declines of almost all ground-dwelling mammal and bird species similar in size to or larger than this rabbit. There is no reason to believe that populations of Annamite Striped Rabbit have not suffered declines comparable to those of other similarly sized mammals in the Annamites. There are indications that it is more sensitive to hunting than are some comparably sized ground-dwelling mammal species. Best-case scenarios, incorporating insight for similar-size ground-dwelling mammal species, suggest that the global population of Annamite Striped Rabbit has declined by more than 50% over the 10-year time period to 2018. Camera-trapping indicates that although the species is still present in detectable numbers across much of its known range, it is nevertheless uncommon in areas that have undergone, or are currently experiencing, intense poaching pressure, compared with what can be ascertained of populations before the onset of intensive snaring. Although it is evidently more abundant than are some of the larger Annamite endemic mammal species such as Saola Pseudoryx nghetinhensis and Large-antlered Muntjac Muntiacus vuquangensis, indicating (even allowing for different pre-exploitation densities) that its populations have not been as negatively affected by snaring as have the ungulates, these latter species’ populations have been assessed as having recent rates of decline almost certainly over 90%. Moreover, Annamite Striped Rabbit appears effectively to be restricted to wet evergreen forest: this means that the vast majority of its range is in Viet Nam, where snaring pressure has been recently, and remains, remarkably high; therefore, a higher percentage of its global population  has been exposed to these high levels of snaring than for Annamite endemic or near-endemic mammals with more flexible habitat requirements and that extend further westward into Lao PDR, such as Owston’s Civet Chrotogale owstoni. As of 2018, it has been over 20 years (two assessment windows of time for this species under Category A) since intensive snaring started to sweep through the Annamite mountains, and it is likely that over 95% of Annamite Striped Rabbit’s occupied range has at some point experienced intensive snaring (i.e., over 100 snares per km², equating to 3,000 snare-nights per km², per month). Comparing the relative levels of decline at first wave of industrial snaring with those subsequently, and looking at geographic patterns of expansion of this snaring between the mid 1990s and 2018, the consensus assessment of surveyors and wildlife researchers active in the species's range is that in the 10 years to 2018 it declined by 50-65%. It is extremely unlikely that hunting pressure will decrease to a point that would allow widespread population recovery in the near future; continuing population declines extending into the next 10 years (from 2018) of comparable magnitude are suspected to be likely.
habitat: To date, no studies have focused on the ecology of Annamite Striped Rabbit. Nonetheless, some general natural history traits can be surmised from camera-trap records and villager information. It is clear that it occurs predominantly in wet evergreen forest, that which has little to no dry season (probably no month with rainfall below 40 mm; Rundel 1999). Most records come from low- to mid-elevation broadleaf forest. As an example of typical Annamite Striped Rabbit occurrence patterns, camera-trapping in three protected areas in Viet Nam, Phong Dien Nature Reserve (= NR), Khe Nuoc Trong proposed NR and Bac Huong Hoa NR, detected Annamite Striped Rabbit in broadleaf wet evergreen forest from 50 to 1,183 m asl (Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2017). There is one record in Viet Nam from close to the highest point in Bach Ma NP in forest with characteristics approaching montane evergreen forest, but still with an ever-wet climate (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016). One record in Lao PDR comes from the western portion of Xe Sap NPA where semi-evergreen and lower montane forests (following Rundel 1999) predominate (Lamxay 2013); however, intensive and extensive camera-trapping showed that the species is very localised and/or very rare in western Xe Sap NPA. The localised presence of Licuala and Lanonia palm species indicates small patches of ‘ever-wet’ habitat in this area (Timmins 2013) and the lower montane forest areas with a considerable Dalat Pine Pinus dalatensis component (Timmins 2013) are another clear indication that these lower montane forests have reduced dry seasons compared with most such forests in Lao PDR.Although Annamite Striped Rabbit has potentially a low detectability by camera-trapping as conventionally practised in Indochina, it appears to have been detected by all camera-trapping efforts of more than a few thousand camera-trap-nights in wet evergreen forest (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018). In stark contrast, it has never been camera-trapped by surveys of similar effort in areas of indisputable semi-evergreen and lower montane forest (following Rundel 1999) in Lao PDR. Particularly telling in this regard are the absence of detections from Nam Et – Phou Louey NPA, Nam Kading NPA, the Nam Ngiap catchment, the Nam Xang – Nam Chouan area, Phou Sithon ESCA, large regions of Nakai – Nam Theun NPA, and much of western Xe Sap NPA: these are all areas with varying degrees of Annamite faunal affinity. In Nakai – Nam Theun NPA the few detections were all in sites where, as with Xe Sap NPA, other indications suggest localised occurrence of wet evergreen forest (or forest strongly transitional with it). Potentially, many Lao populations function as sink populations, because most if not all wet evergreen forest in Lao PDR is likely to be to some extent ‘transitional’ with ‘drier’ semi-evergreen and lower montane forests, and thus is presumably suboptimal for this rabbit.Camera-trapping from the Hue SNR in central Viet Nam suggests that the species survives in secondary and heavily degraded forest (M. Le pers. comm. 2016).There is one report of Annamite Striped Rabbit occurrence far from wet evergreen forest, in western Khammouan province, Lao PDR. This was based upon the presentation of a Nesolagus timminsi image to local villagers and a positive response from the villagers that the animal was present in their area (Orlov et al. 2008, A.V. Abramov pers. comm. 2018). However, other independent evidence (R. J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018) indicates that identification of animal images (including mammals as distinctive as Tiger Panthera tigris and Saola) by local villagers is often not reliable. The area reported is a mosaic of karst and rural agriculture, far from wet evergreen forest. Occurrence in this area would, if confirmed, represent a substantial increase in the species’s known range, and would require a comprehensive rethink of biogeographic patterns of occurrence of not only this species, but other Annamite associates as well. On this survey, A. Abramov (pers. comm. 2018) reported also that they found small leporid tracks, and that villagers stated that the animal with which they identified the Annamite Striped Rabbit image was common in the area and an at least occasional pest of rice fields. Factors contesting occurrence in this region are the lack of any evidence of Annamite Striped Rabbit in western Lao PDR despite extensive camera-trapping and the absence of trade records of it in the several fresh wildlife meat markets around Khammouan's western karst: Kha-nyou Laonastes aenigmamus and several other small mammal species of karst are found in these markets quite frequently (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018). There is no confirmation from anywhere in its range of Annamite Striped Rabbit occurrence in any habitat remote from wet evergreen forest.Annamite Striped Rabbit appears to be strictly nocturnal: camera-trap records from seven protected areas in the central Annamites (Bach Ma NP, the Hue and Quang Nam SNRs, Phong Dien NR, Khe Nuoc Trong proposed NR, Bac Huong Hoa NR and Xe Sap NPA) were exclusively at night (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016, M. Le pers. comm. 2016, Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2017). It appears to be solitary: the aforementioned systematic camera-trapping in Bach Ma NP, the Hue and Quang Nam SNRs, and Xe Sap NPA showed predominantly lone individuals, with only two exceptions, both of duos (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016, M. Le pers. comm. 2016). Almost nothing is known about reproduction. A duo of kittens, estimated to be approximately one week old, was found in a shallow burrow in Phou Chomvoy Provincial Protected Area, Bolikhamxai province, Lao PDR, during the month of January (O. Vongsa pers. comm. 2015). A second duo of kittens, estimated to be 10–12 weeks of age, were found in Pu Mat NP in the month of May (Abramov et al. 2016).
threats: Annamite Striped Rabbit is threatened by poaching, with widespread snaring probably the most damaging form, although the species is also caught opportunistically by hunters, sometimes with the aid of dogs. Snaring operations range from the setting of a few snares to supply the camps of forest users not targeting ground-dwelling large mammals, to well-organised gangs focused on supplying such mammals to the national and international trade in wildlife meat and purportedly medicinal products. Indiscriminate wire snares have reduced populations severely of almost all ground-dwelling mammal species of rabbit-size or larger in the Annamites, and while Annamite Striped Rabbit may be slightly buffered from the effects of snaring operations by its small size and presumed small home range, there is both direct and indirect evidence that industrial-level snaring has reduced greatly its population. In Viet Nam, Timmins et al. (1999) mentioned a snared individual from just north of Phong Nha Ke Bang NP; a snared individual was found in Ha Tinh province (Dang et al. 2001); a skeleton was found in a snare by Timmins and Trinh (1999); remains were found in a snare in the same area of Ha Tinh (N. Furey pers. comm. 2002); and one was found in a brush-fence-style snare line in the Hue SNR (A. Tilker pers. comm. 2016). In Lao PDR, one was found dead in a wire snare close to eastern Xe Sap NPA (K. Thongasmouth pers. comm. 2013). At least four animals, all presumed to have been snared, were seen in the local market at Ban Lak-20 (= Ban Lak Xao) in the 1990s (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018). The numbers observed in snares or otherwise in trade gives no suggestion, relative to the frequency with which other sympatric species have similarly been observed, that snaring pressure is any less significant a threat to rabbits than it is to any other species of similar or larger size. The scarcity of records since about 2010 in many localities within the species’s range offers the most compelling evidence of snaring-driven declines. For example, in Bach Ma NP, where both past and current snaring levels have reached staggering magnitudes, Annamite Striped Rabbit appears as of 2018, on the basis of extensive camera-trapping, to be rare (see 'Population'). Although without pre-exploitation baselines it is not possible to prove declines in any particular area, the ecological conditions in Bach Ma NP resemble those in the Hue and Quang Nam SNRs (adjacent to Bach Ma NP), where Annamite Striped Rabbit densities are higher. It is thus reasonable to assume that without intensive hunting pressure, Annamite Striped Rabbit would be much more common in Bach Ma NP than at present, and that its rarity there is a consequence of hunting. Similar patterns of decline are evident at other localities in Viet Nam, including the Ke Go – Khe Net Lowlands: industrial-level snaring is likely to have caused the decline in this species there, as well as in a number of other ground-dwelling species. Although snaring numbers recorded by Willcox et al. (2015) are relatively low (fewer than 1,500 snares), this result came from a relatively small area of forest and during only approximately three months’ survey, indicating a high overall snaring intensity (D.H.A. Willcox pers. comm. 2018). Most wildlife was recorded at the very tops of the hills in the protected area, away from the main snare lines (D.H.A. Willcox pers. comm. 2018). Although information does not span the relevant period, the highest intensity of snaring may have ceased well before the 2010 surveys, given that large numbers of abandoned snares were not found. Mortality from hunting dogs occurs in some areas. Local reports from hunters operating near the Quang Nam SNR in central Viet Nam suggest that while hunters do not target Annamite Striped Rabbit with dogs, it is captured opportunistically while hunters walk the streams at night, and that such events may not be uncommon (A. Tilker pers. comm. 2016). Hunters report that when the species is illuminated by lamp-light it freezes, allowing the hunter to shoot the rabbit or the dogs to attack and kill it. Two separate encounters with two separate individuals in the same area of Quang Nam SNR, in which both animals were captured by hand (and then released unharmed), provide evidence for this behaviour (S. Woodfin pers. comm. 2015; A. Tilker pers. comm. 2015). Villagers from Ban Kalo, in Xekong province, Lao PDR, reported a similar opportunistic hunting of Annamite Striped Rabbit using local hunting dogs (A. Tilker pers. comm. 2014). While there is no evidence for a specific market demand for Annamite Striped Rabbit, and while it does not command the high prices of some species targeted for the wildlife trade such as pangolins Manis or some turtles, it is plausible that its meat can sometimes fetch a higher-than-average price because of novelty.Habitat degradation, loss and fragmentation are major threats only insomuch as they increase accessibility to hunters. Viet Nam’s aggressive road building policy, particularly in border regions, has in recent years increased accessibility to previously little-disturbed habitat for farmers and timber harvesters (semi-commercial and commercial logging operations), as well as for mammal poachers. Dams, which so far have had minimal impact, look set to increase in the future; they not only reduce habitat but also increase accessibility to commercial hunters and harvesters of other forest products, who take wildlife meat opportunistically whilst pursuing other activities. Similarly, the expansion of the road network in many border areas of Lao PDR (e.g., Salavan and Xekong provinces) will improve access into areas of Annamite Striped Rabbit range and, in the absence of functioning law enforcement, increase levels of snaring of mammals potentially to intensities similar to much of the species' Viet Namese range. Mining for gold, gems and other minerals seems to be on the rise, which results in habitat destruction and increased hunting levels.
population: Although population size and density have not been established anywhere in its range, Annamite Striped Rabbit appears to be noticeably less abundant in heavily hunted areas than in areas perceived on the basis of other evidence to have had lower hunting intensity. Observations and estimates of the intensity of hunting pressure across the species' known and presumed distribution in both range states indicates that at a landscape level this pressure is extremely high, with episodic deployment of snares in the region of dozens to hundreds of snares per km² over periods of years within almost every km² of suitable habitat in these landscapes. Although clear quantification of population size or decline rates is not possible, subjective assessment of available evidence, from camera-trapping of this species and trends in conservation status of other species in the same areas, suggests that substantial range-wide declines are very likely to have occurred. The clearest and most compelling information on the population trend of Annamite Striped Rabbit comes from a camera-trapping project in central Viet Nam. Because camera-trapping as conventionally practised in Indochina is often targeted at animals much larger than in Annamite Striped Rabbit, and for a variety of objectives, there is wide variation in its ability to detect this rabbit reliably. During this specific camera-trapping project in central Viet Nam the cameras were set consistently low enough to record rabbit-sized ground-dwelling mammal species reliably. Systematic such camera-trapping (totalling 6,805 camera-trap-nights) in Bach Ma National Park (= NP) in 2014-2015 at 53 camera-trap stations evenly spaced across the national park detected Annamite Striped Rabbit at only four (7.5%) of the stations, with a total of seven detections (defined as images of the species separated by at least 60 minutes from the previous image of the species at the same station) (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016). Most records came from the more remote and rugged parts of the protected area. More intensive camera-trapping in a core part of the protected area, at finer spatial scale, failed to record the species at 64 stations (8,256 camera-trap-nights), indicating that the species is either extremely rare or extirpated in this part of the protected area (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016).Camera-trapping in the Hue and Quang Nam Saola Nature Reserves (= SNRs), two contiguous protected areas adjacent to Bach Ma NP, conducted immediately after the Bach Ma NP survey, detected the species more often: it was recorded at 10 (of 39) stations with camera-traps spaced systematically over the protected areas, in a total of 5,933 camera-trap-nights, comprising 47 detections (defined as above). The detection of Annamite Striped Rabbit at 25.6% of the camera-trap stations is far higher than in the landscape-scale camera-trapping in Bach Ma NP, but well below the occupancy of other mammals generally taken to be more resilient to hunting, such as ferret badger(s) Melogale. A further 54 detections (from 14 [of 64] stations) was obtained in an intensive effort in the reserves’ core. This intensive camera-trapping recorded a minimum of 27 individuals, as identified by their unique striping patterns (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016). Unlike Bach Ma NP, the Hue and Quang Nam SNRs have some level of anti-poaching support (although snaring persists at high levels nonetheless), which could indicate that Annamite Striped Rabbit may be able to rebound in the presence of targeted anti-snaring efforts. However, no baseline survey was conducted in this area before anti-poaching activities began, so the population trend remains speculative.It is likely that the inferred differences in ground-dwelling vertebrate densities (including those of Annamite Striped Rabbit) between Bach Ma NP and the SNRs is caused by Bach Ma NP having been more ‘accessible’ to more hunters for a longer period of time, and so having experienced more sustained hunting pressure than have localities more distant from the high human population density and the high densities of ‘access’-oriented infrastructure that characterise the Viet Namese coastal lowlands. That this is the case largely hinges on the lack of evidence to suggest that Bach Ma NP's habitat quality is lower than that of the SNRs for any of the species apparently less abundant in the former than in the latter (such as Northern Red Muntjac Muntiacus vaginalis, the Roosevelts' Muntjac M. rooseveltorum taxonomic complex, Sambar Rusa unicolor, Crested Argus Rheinardia ocellata, Malayan Porcupine Hystrix brachyura, Masked Palm Civet Paguma larvata, Mainland Serow Capricornis milneedwardsii, and Crab-eating Mongoose Herpestes urva). Apparent patterns of decline from the Bach Ma NP / SNRs forest complex of other species known to be particularly sensitive to snaring, including Crested Argus, suggest that levels of accessibility and/or remoteness may explain distributions of ground-dwelling species, including Annamite Striped Rabbit, in this particular forest block (N. Wilkinson pers. comm. 2018). Ease of access is postulated commonly to affect the distribution and status of many quarry species in South-east Asia (e.g., Harrison et al. 2016), including Annamite species such as Owston’s Civet Chrotogale owstoni, Saola Pseudoryx nghetinhensis and Large-antlered Muntjac Muntiacus vuquangensis (Timmins et al. 2016a,b,c). All available evidence indicates that the current low densities of species such as Crested Argus in areas such as Bach Ma NP can be attributed confidently to substantial snare-induced declines, in many cases probably exceeding 90% over an approximately 20-year period starting in the late 1990s, because reasonably clear data on population status at the beginning of this period exist for these species (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018).It appears that Annamite Striped Rabbit occurs at densities broadly similar to those of other species that are considered to be sensitive to snaring and are thought to have declined over a similar time period by rates in excess of 50%. For example, in the combined landscape and intensive camera-trapping in Bach Ma NP mentioned above, representing 117 camera-trap stations and 15,061 camera-trap-nights, Crested Argus was detected at only two stations and Owston’s Civet at, at most, one (the image is insufficiently clear for consensus on its identification); some hunting-sensitive species were not recorded in this effort, including Saola, Sambar and Greater Hog Badger Arctonyx collaris. Species that are believed to be fairly robust to snaring pressure during this survey appeared to be at depressed levels but were nonetheless more frequently photographed than was Annamite Striped Rabbit: Common Palm Civet Paradoxurus hermaphroditus was detected at 48 stations, Asiatic Brush-Tailed Porcupine Atherurus macrourus at 44, and ferret badger(s) at 46 (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016). In sum, Annamite Striped Rabbit seems to be following other hunting-sensitive species into local extirpation in Bach Ma NP.Given that most of the habitat suitable for the species is in Viet Nam, and that most (perhaps nearly all) of it is probably under levels of hunting pressure not an order of magnitude different from those in Bach Ma NP, it is likely that Annamite Striped Rabbit densities are depressed to broadly similar levels across most of the species’s range. While this is largely a subjective extrapolation by those who have spent years surveying in the species's range, some other recent camera-trapping surveys provide support for the conclusion that the species occurs at low densities in core parts of its distribution (but see the caveat above about the risk of some styles of camera-trapping under-detecting the species). Patterns of hunting pressure and overall defaunation similar to those in Bach Ma NP were found in the Ke Go – Khe Net Lowlands by small carnivore-targeted surveys conducted in 2007, 2008 and 2010. In total, 1,171 camera-trap-nights (with cameras set at heights above ground suitable for detecting the rabbit) and 101 hours of spotlighting did not record Annamite Striped Rabbit. Furthermore, this work failed to record other species believed generally to be sensitive to snaring (Owston’s Civet, Sambar, Greater Hog Badger, Crested Argus), but did record species presumed to be more resilient to hunting, such as Common Palm Civet and Asiatic Brush-tailed Porcupine (Willcox et al. 2015). Targeted camera-trapping in Pu Mat NP in 2015, focused on two interior parts of the protected area, and representing 20 camera-trap stations and approximately 2,500 camera-trap-nights, yielded similar results: no Annamite Striped Rabbit was recorded (Tuan Vo pers. comm. 2017). A sighting of a female Annamite Striped Rabbit with young in 2017 shows that the species persists in Pu Mat NP (Abramov et al. 2016), but this single sighting does not provide evidence that its densities are not severely depressed in the protected area. A camera-trap survey in Ba Na – Nui Chua Nature Reserve (= NR) during 2016–2017, in which 23 camera-trap stations operated for more than one year, in an area adjacent to Bach Ma NP (and within the species’s historical distribution although potentially suboptimal habitat), also failed to record it, and likewise documented low encounter rates for mammals and galliform birds considered to be sensitive to snaring, with Owston’s Civet and Crested Argus recorded at only a single camera-trap station each, and no records of Greater Hog Badger (Hoang Quoc Huy pers. comm. 2018). Not surprisingly, the mammal community in Ba Na – Nui Chua NR appears to have undergone levels of defaunation similar to those at Bach Ma NP and the Ke Go – Khe Net Lowlands (Hoang Quoc Huy pers. comm. 2018).Surveys in Bac Huong Hoa NR in 2015 and 2016, totalling 134 stations and 5,294 camera-trap-nights, recorded the species at seven (5.22% of) camera-trap stations (Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2017). Surveys in Phong Dien NR in 2016, totalling 84 stations and 4,181 camera-trap-nights, recorded the species at three (3.57% of) stations (Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2017).  Surveys in Khe Nuoc Trong proposed NR from 2012 to 2017, totalling 1,018 independent stations and 33,500 camera-trap-nights, recorded the species at 54 (5.22% of) stations (Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2017). The proportion of stations at which the species was recorded by all three surveys is broadly similar to the results from Bach Ma NP.In Lao PDR, the species was camera-trapped only twice (at different stations; in 2007) in Nakai – Nam Theun National Protected Area (= NPA) during surveys from 2006 to 2011 covering four survey blocks, which comprised at least some suitable habitats for the species, with a total of 11,126 camera-trap-nights and 201 camera-trap stations (Johnson and Johnston 2007, Nam Theun 2 Watershed Management and Protection Authority pers. comm. 2011). Both stations were within 5 km of the international border. Interpretation of this result is confounded by several factors, notably that most of the NPA is probably unsuitable in forest-type for the species and has therefore never supported a sizeable population of it. Thus, even though intensive snaring had not yet affected much of the NPA by 2006–2011, there was no possibility of recording a high encounter rate with the species. Since 2011, no relevant camera-trapping has taken place to provide up-to-date information on conservation status of ground-dwelling animal populations in the parts of the NPA within which Annamite Striped Rabbit was recorded previously. However, since these two records in 2007, the trade-driven snaring pressure, especially within 5–10 km of the Viet Namese border (where lies most of the habitat suitable for the species in the NPA) has intensified. This suggests that, were surveys to be repeated, they would find severe declines among the more hunting-sensitive ground-dwelling species there (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2016, C.N.Z. Coudrat pers. comm. 2018). Populations of Annamite Striped Rabbit in these areas are, therefore, likely to have declined, possibly to local extinction.Surveys in the northern and central Annamites during 2012–2017 that focused on assessing hunting pressure (by direct observation of hunting signs, and determining the local status of hunting-sensitive quarry species through direct observation, encounters with animal signs, and opinions of local villagers) support strongly the assumption that the camera-trapping rates expressed above for Viet Nam are a true indication of depressed population density. Excepting surveys in Nakai – Nam Theun NPA, these surveys intentionally entered and assessed the least accessible, remotest, parts of each area (because species status is, often, strongly related to level of human access; Harrison et al. 2016). Although these surveys could not determine directly the current status of Annamite Striped Rabbit, past and current rates of snaring could be inferred along with the status of some of the presumed snaring-sensitive species listed above. In all Viet Namese areas surveyed, including the SNRs, Phong Dien and Bac Huong Hoa NRs and the Bach Ma NP extension, evidence was found that dozens to hundreds of snares per km² had been deployed over periods of multiple years. Encounter rates with ungulate signs in these same areas were well below those in areas with evidence of significantly lower hunting intensity, and calling rates of Crested Argus were vastly lower than the rates heard in ecologically similar forest in the 1990s.  Lao sites however showed considerably more variability in the past and ongoing intensity of snaring. A situation similar to that of Viet Nam was found in the eastern international border area of Nakai – Nam Theun NPA in Lao PDR. In other Lao sites, intensive snaring appeared to be or have been more heterogeneous (for instance, in Xe Sap NPA), although still affecting a majority of the area or in some areas a large minority of the area (generally, the parts closest to the Viet Namese border). Only one landscape, comprising Khoun Xe – Nong Ma Provincial Protected Area (PPA) and Laving Laveun NPA of Central Lao PDR, was found where a substantial proportion of the area showed no signs of current or past intensive snaring pressure. Even within this landscape, signs in border areas evinced snaring intensity not dissimilar to those in surveyed areas of Viet Nam. The areas surveyed included some such as Phou Sithon Endangered Species Conservation Area (ESCA) where, based on habitat and climactic factors, Annamite Striped Rabbit is almost certainly absent, and others such as Xe Sap NPA where occurrence is likely to be highly localised. Overall, given the likely distribution of suitable habitat for Annamite Striped Rabbit, only the Khoun Xe – Nong Ma PPA and Laving Laveun NPA landscape had a sizeable area of suitable habitat with relatively low hunting intensity at this time.Intensive snaring in the Annamites appears to have begun in the 1990s, when Saola, the Annamite large mammal species now closest to global extinction (Timmins et al. 2016c), was apparently still relatively frequently caught. Since then, surveys often find evidence of intensive snaring; concerns of its severity were already raised before 2000 (e.g. Timmins et al. 1999). However, snaring has not affected all areas simultaneously in similar ways. Instead, intensive snaring appears to have progressed wave-like through the forests of the Annamites, with the progression of the wave, albeit in a somewhat stochastic fashion, most likely related to factors such as access and initial resource abundance. Although there have been no studies of the dynamics, observations suggest that usually at the forefront of the wave (defined as initial entry of poachers to previously unsnared forest areas) snares are deployed intensively, up to thousands per km². Snaring at this density is likely to lead to rapid, extensive declines in all mammal species rabbit-sized and larger, and thus after a few years (perhaps shorter), with the ground-dwelling large mammal community probably typically depleted by more than 80% at a locality, poachers move on. The form of and damage from the next phase probably depends on the relative ease of access and the quantities of other valuable forest resources remaining in the area. In accessible areas (for example, those reachable in a single day’s travel from the nearest human habitation, such as all of Bach Ma NP), snaring probably continues at a sustained and significant level (in the order of dozens of snare-nights per km² per month) because of the low resource cost for snaring in the context of the abundance of other ‘marketable’ forest resources remaining. In areas that take greater effort to enter, for example, those more than a day’s travel away, the situation is probably more complex, although at least periodic episodes of snaring are likely to take place in association with directed poaching of high-value species. However, these remote areas may also remain snaring-free for a considerable time after the initial wave. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, encountering the forefront of this wave was commonplace during Annamite surveys, at which time large areas had not yet experienced intensive snaring at all. But during the 2012–2017 surveys outlined above, the front of the wave was found only in Lao areas, notably in Xe Sap NPA and Khoun Xe – Nong Ma PPA. In all Viet Namese areas the most intensive snaring had clearly passed, probably at least 5–10 years previously. Although continued snaring was found in all Viet Namese areas surveyed during this time, the levels were in most cases considerably less than those which typify the initial forefront of the wave, supporting the conclusion that in accessible forest areas relatively low intensity but widespread snaring occurs, whilst relatively remote areas receive generally more intensive but localised effort. In some cases, notably in Phong Dien NR and even more so the eastern border areas of Nakai – Nam Theun NPA, evidence of recent snaring was limited, though mammal densities appeared to be severely depressed.Considering observations of snaring from the late 1990s onwards, as of 2018 the core area of Khoun Xe – Nong Ma PPA is almost certainly by far the largest area of Annamite Striped Rabbit range remaining that has yet to experience intensive snaring. Overall, probably more than 95% of the species’s entire range has already experienced high to very high levels of snaring pressure. Given the still increasing demand for wildlife in the thriving illegal trade, and the very small percentage of the species’s range in Lao PDR that had not by 2018 experienced a significantly lower snaring pressure, and therefore is likely to retain healthier populations, Khoun Xe – Nong Ma PPA will almost certainly experience industrial snaring within the next five years unless there are unprecedented enforcement interventions.Intensive snaring has been ongoing in Annamite Striped Rabbit range for a little over 20 years, yet the Red List Criterion A assessment window is only for ten years, meaning that it is important to consider the portion of the decline that has occurred during 2008–2018. Although there is no baseline for the species's abundance at the start of intensive snaring, the likely progression and magnitude of decline over the quarter-century to 2018 can be proposed. Subjective assessments from wildlife surveyors active in the Annamite forests before industrial snaring indicate that local populations of all ground-dwelling species of mammals of rabbit-size and larger may be reduced initially by close to an order of magnitude (including species often considered ‘hunting-resilient’ such as palm civets and ferret badgers). After this, interpretation is more problematic, in part because some small patches seem to escape the ‘initial crest’ of the snaring wave. By 2008, the start of the time period relevant for assessing Annamite Striped Rabbit under Criterion A, intensive snaring had already probably affected around half, perhaps more, of the species's range, based on field observation up to that period (R.J. Timmins pers. comm. 2018).  Since 2008, such snaring has affected about 90%, perhaps more, of the range that as of 2008 had not been snared thus (that is, about 45% of the original range). Thus, as of 2018, no more than 5% of the species's original range has never been intensively snared. Assuming that initial Annamite Striped Rabbit population densities are reduced by well over half following landscape-scale intensive snaring, by 2008 populations had already declined by well over 50% in at least half of the species’s range. At this time, the bulk of the population therefore remained in areas not yet intensively snared. Under the foregoing presumptions, from 2008 the small proportion of the global population in the areas already heavily affected has by 2018 presumably declined at a reduced rate (perhaps below 50%), whilst the majority of the unaffected populations has undergone a substantial decline (of more than 50%). It is likely that a small fraction (5% or lower of the total population) did not experience any decline. An average, weighting population trend by the proportion of the global population in each category in 2008, results in a decline of 50% or more for the entire population for the ten years to 2018.These decline rates seem plausible given the evidence presented above, despite some uncertainty of the relative severity of decline rates during the initial wave relative to ongoing rates thereafter. Areas such as Bach Ma NP, Phong Dien NR, and the Ke Go – Khe Net Lowlands, with good evidence of intensive snaring before 2008, would now have Annamite Striped Rabbit populations substantially below 25% of their early 1990s levels. This inference fits with the general camera-trapping findings given above. The scenario also fits the information from the SNRs where, evidently, intensive snaring generally occurred later (some before, some after 2008). It does not contradict the general conclusion that the recent protection levels in the SNRs might have reduced decline rates substantially or even have lead to minor recovery there, given the strong evidence that substantial snaring activity had already swept through the SNRs before significant anti-poaching enforcement occurred there.Taken together, available evidence incorporating information from other similar-size ground-dwelling mammal species indicates that the total global population of Annamite Striped Rabbit has declined by more than 50%, plausibly up to 65% over the 10 years to 2018. The rate of decline that will be experienced in the future, now that about 95% of the species' global range has already undergone intensive snaring, depends largely upon the relative difference (if any) between the rates of decline during the first wave relative to the ongoing decline thereafter. Based on slender quantification (such as the numbers of snared Annamite Striped Rabbits found in the 1990s versus those found since 2008; see below), the current status in areas such as Phong Dien NR and Bach Ma NP may reflect substantial initial declines (perhaps of about 75%, maybe higher) but lower decreases since then (perhaps 30% or even lower, and perhaps even localised recovery). It is therefore possible that in the ten years to 2028 declines would not meet the 50% threshold. However, taking a precautionary viewpoint, particularly given the increasing trend in regional natural resource exploitation in general, and industrial snaring in particular, a further 50% decline is quite plausible in the future.
range: Annamite Striped Rabbit occurs at low and medium altitudes in the northern and central Annamite Mountains along the Viet Nam and Lao PDR border. In Viet Nam, it is believed to occur in six provinces (listed from north to south): Nghe An, Ha Tinh, Quang Binh, Quang Tri, Thua Thien Hue and Quang Nam. In Lao PDR it is believed to occur also in six provinces (from north to south): Xiangkhouang (unconfirmed), Bolikhamxai, Khammouan, Savannakhet, Salavan and Xekong. There are no records from the southern parts of the central Annamites or from the southern Annamites but these regions are not obviously ecologically unsuitable. The westward extent of occurrence in Lao PDR appears to be tied closely to localised climactic factors, with all indications suggesting that the species is strongly associated with wet evergreen forest. Fitting this, it has been confirmed in the Lao PDR only in areas close to the border with Viet Nam: a pattern shown by various other wet evergreen forest indicator species. The Annamite ridge forms most of the international border between the two countries and places most of Lao PDR in the rain-shadow of moisture-laden air masses from Viet Nam in the Lao dry season. The vast majority of habitat suitable for Annamite Striped Rabbit is therefore in Viet Nam. Most records come from below 1,000 m and the species has been recorded nearly down to sea level (50 m asl; Le Trong Trai pers. comm. 2018), although few low-altitude areas retain otherwise suitable habitat. The highest record traced was at 1,300 m asl (A. Tilker, A. Nguyen The Truong and A. Wilting pers. comm. 2016).
useTrade: Although there is no evidence of a targeted trade for the species, it is certainly hunted as part of the thriving wildlife trade that occurs across its known range. Given the paucity of information suggesting that the species has a high value for wildlife trade, it is likely that when caught, it often ends up in the local fresh wildlife meat markets, or is used for primary consumption. In fact, the first evidence of Nesolagus in mainland South-east Asia came from a subsistence market in rural Lao PDR (Surridge et al. 1999).
conservationActions: Although habitat loss and degradation have undoubtedly been factors in Annamite Striped Rabbit population declines from historical levels, the primary threat to the species is the intensive snaring that occurs across Annamite forests, and which is especially high in northern and central Viet Nam (which areas comprise most of the species's known range). It is difficult to convey the intensity of snaring in the Annamites: in many protected areas, hundreds of snares can be collected in a single day’s walk, and elaborate brush-fence-style snare lines can reach several kilometres in length (Gray et al. 2017, 2018). It is therefore no surprise that, as with other rare and threatened ground-dwelling Annamite endemic mammal species, the highest priority for Annamite Striped Rabbit is effective law enforcement to curtail the industrial-level snaring that occurs across the region, combined with efforts to reduce the demand for wildlife meat and products sold as medicines (the ultimate driver of snaring throughout the Annamites) amongst the increasing middle classes in Viet Nam, Lao PDR and further afield (whether or not this rabbit is ever traded further afield does not affect the merit of this recommendation, as it is simply one species among a large general catch, driven by market demand in not just Lao PDR and Viet Nam). The challenges to enacting effective protected area-based law enforcement are substantial: neither Viet Nam nor Lao PDR has a historical model upon which to base effective protected area management, and government support remains weak, involving laws and decrees that have, typically, little follow-up action. Protected areas across the species’s range remain little more than paper parks, and if the species is to survive in the wild, this situation must change fundamentally. Some success has been achieved by joint government- and NGO-led snare-removal teams operating in the Hue and Quang Nam SNRs in Viet Nam and in neighbouring Xe Sap NPA in Lao PDR, operating under the direction of the WWF ‘Carbon and Biodiversity’ (CarBi) project. Over a five-year period, these patrols have removed more than 75,000 snares from the SNRs and the eastern section of Xe Sap NPA (Gray et al. 2018). Notable as these achievements are, the level of snaring in all three protected areas remains extremely high, with snaring intensity plausibly reaching thousands of snare-nights per square kilometre per year (A. Tilker pers. comm. 2017). Therefore, although this joint management model provides some hope for future protection for Annamite Striped Rabbit from intensive snaring in at least one forest block, considerable increase in effectiveness is needed before any part of this forest complex could be considered safe for the species (or any other ground-dwelling Annamite endemic mammal). Most other protected areas known or likely to hold the species are probably at least as exploited and as of 2018 receive minimal law enforcement effort or snare removal.Because of the challenges that remain in the effective management of  protected area, it is vital that conservation stakeholders consider within the next few years the establishment a captive ‘insurance’ population of this species. Currently it is not held in captivity. Although it is true that the urgency to establish an insurance population of Annamite Striped Rabbit is lower than for some other Annamite endemic mammals, notably Saola Pseudoryx nghetinhensis, it would be prudent to secure an ex situ population of Annamite Striped Rabbit in the near future: the general snaring-driven declines are unlikely to slow in coming years. Establishing a captive population for Annamite Striped Rabbit should be less difficult than for the much larger and rarer Saola: unlike Saola, the rabbit still exists in detectable densities within several forest blocks in both Viet Nam and Lao PDR, and it should be much easier to capture, in part because of its habitat of becoming immobile when encountered with a headlamp at night. Indeed, as long as proper international expertise to oversee the care of captured individuals can be secured, there seems little downside in establishing an insurance population sooner rather than later.

rationale: This is a widespread species with no currently known population decline. The species is listed Least Concern.
habitat: Ochotona alpina occupies rocky regions and talus piles (Smith et al. 1990). Because this is a rock-dwelling species it occupies naturally fragmented habitat, as talus piles are generally separated by terrain that pikas rarely traverse. It prefers talus sites where vegetation is present (Smith et al. 1990). This species is a generalized herbivore that collects foodstuffs to create haypiles (Smith and Xie 2008). This pika is considered an important factor in the health of the ecosystem, as it is prey for sables in the region (Khlebnikova 1978). It has been noted that pika haypiles have been utilized by several species during winter months (Smith et al. 1990). Siberian wapiti (Cervus elaphus sibiricus) and reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) will eat from the haypiles during heavy snowfall (Smith et al. 1990). It has been reported that vegetation diversity and composition are largely influenced by the presence of this species (Khlebnikova 1978). It is primarily a diurnal species, but vocalizations can be heard at night (Ognev 1966). Reported mortality rates differ according to habitat type; 41% in alpine zones and 53% in forested areas (Smith et al. 1990). Longevity of O. alpina can be as high as six years, but is usually only three years in the northern extents of its range (Sokolov et al. 1994). O. alpina produces two litters per year, with an average of three young per litter (Smith and Xie 2008). Gestation is approximately 30 days and newborns are 5.8-6.0 cm in length (Sokolov et al. 1994). Total length is 15.2-25.1 cm.
threats: There are no known major threats at present.
population: There are few data regarding the current status of Ochotona alpina. Some isolated populations may be subject to stochastic variation in population size.
range: Octotona alpina occurs in the mountain ranges in western Mongolia, northern Xinjiang, eastern Kazakhstan, and southern Russia. O. alpina ranges in elevation from 400-2,500 m in the Altai Mountains (Ognev 1966), in China, O. alpina occurs at elevations greater than 2,000 m (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: In Mongolia, approximately 12% of the species' distribution occurs in protected areas (Clark et al. 2006). This species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern in Mongolia (Clark et al. 2006). In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004).

rationale: The species is confirmed Least Concern. This is a widespread species that is characterized as fairly abundant. The status of the subspecies Ochotona cansus sorella (not seen in the wild for 50 years) and O. c. morosa (an isolated population) required further investigation to determine their current status.
habitat: Ochotona cansus is a burrowing species of pika and one of the simplest among pikas (Smith et al. 1990). It occupies shrubland with adjacent alpine meadows (Jiang and Wang 1991, Smith and Xie 2008). This habitat consists of the deciduous shrubs Potentilla fruticosa and Caragana jubata (Smith and Xie 2008). It is excluded from open alpine meadows, where it is sympatric with O. curzoniae (Jiang and Wang 1991, Su 2001). Home range size fluctuates with seasonal variation (Jiang and Wang 1991). O. cansus is considered a generalized herbivore (Smith and Xie 2008) and is diurnal (Jiang and Wang 1991). Litter size varies with one to six young per litter and up to three litters per year (Smith and Xie 2008). The breeding season for this species is from early April through late August (Smith et al. 1990). Gestation last for 20 days (Smith et al. 1990). Total length is 11.6-16.5 cm (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: There are no known major threats for Ochotona cansus. It is speculated that application of chemical pesticides may have negatively affected the subspecies population of O. c. sorella, which has not been recorded in the wild for about 70 years (Smith et al. 1990).
population: Ochotona cansus is characterized as fairly abundant (Smith et al. 1990). The subspecies O. c. sorella is only known from a few specimens and has not been recorded in the wild for over 70 years (Smith et al. 1990). Additionally, the status of the isolated O. c. morosa population is unknown (Smith et al. 1990).
range: Ochotona cansus is endemic to China (Smith and Xie 2008). The geographic distribution extends from northern Xizang and Sichuan, up through central and eastern Qinghai to the southern regions of Gansu (Smith et al. 1990). Ochotona c. morosa occurs in Shaanxi (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies elevations of 2,700-3,800 m (Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: Ochotona cansus occurs in Luoshan (CSIS 2008) and Jiuzhaigou National Nature Reserves (Liu et al. 2005). There is little information regarding the current status of the isolated population of O. c. morosa, and it is therefore recommended that research be conducted to determine population numbers.

rationale: This is a widespread species that is unlikely to be experiencing a decline significant enough to warrant listing under a threat category. Ochotona collaris occurs in remote regions of Alaska (USA) and northwestern Canada, where it is unlikely to be negatively influenced by human activities (Smith et al. 1990). It is possible that some local declines have been exacerbated by localized impacts of global warming on snow cover and shrub encroachment, and more work needs to be conducted to determine the severity and generality of these responses.
habitat: Ochotona collaris is a typical rock-dwelling species of pika (Smith et al. 1990). Talus sites are often located in proximity to vegetation patches and meadows (MacDonald and Jones 1987). Home ranges for this species are typically 30 m in diameter (MacDonald and Jones 1987). O. collaris is a general herbivore that constructs haypiles (Smith et al. 1990, Franken and Hik 2004). However, individuals that occupy nunataks (rocky outcroppings) of the Yukon Territory in Canada will collect and forage upon the brain matter of dead birds to supplement their diet (Krajick 1998). Increased risk of predation did not alter vegetative selection, but did decrease the overall amount collected (Morrison et al. 2004). Ochotona collaris is a diurnal pika, active in the morning and late afternoon (MacDonald and Jones 1987, Morrison et al. 2009). The breeding season peaks from May to early June (MacDonald and Jones 1987), but can extend into July in some years (Franken and Hik 2004). The season is timed to allow parturition to coincide with the start of vegetative growth. Litter size for this species is two to six, with two litters produced per year (MacDonald and Jones 1987). A recent study suggests that a reduced breeding season, resulting from high latitudinal orientation, may limit this species to a single litter per year (Franken and Hik 2004). Young are weaned within three to four weeks and reach reproductive maturity by one year of age (Franken and Hik 2004). Gestation time is approximately 30 days (MacDonald and Jones 1987). Adult size is reached between 40-50 days (MacDonald and Jones 1987). The total length of this species averages 18.9 cm (Hall 1981), and mass is typically about 150 g (Franken and Hik 2004).Largely a philopatric settlement pattern, however individuals appear to be able to move over sufficient distances to maintain gene flow.  In the Ruby Range (Yukon) population, Zgurski and Hik (2014) reported that while this population declined abruptly during 2000 and 2003, it subsequently recovered and failed to show any genetic signature of having undergone a population bottleneck.  There was also no evidence for widespread inbreeding before or after the population declines. Using a spatial autocorrelation analysis, they documented positive fine-scale genetic structure (<250 m) in the population during seven out of the 12 years examined (N=442 individuals). Although the genetic structure was consistent with low average dispersal distances, there was also evidence that this population received immigrants from other surrounding populations, and that some of these individuals survived and bred.  So there is evidence that dispersal distances are adequate for preventing declines in genetic variability. On a broad landscape scale, little gene flow exists between separate mountain ranges (Lanier et al. 2015b).
threats: There are no known threats for Ochotona collaris, although it may be vulnerable to global climate change.
