range: The geographic range (in Arabia) includes isolated populations scattered across the entire peninsula. It is also found on the islands of Sardinia and Cypress. Geographic range in Africa is extensive and separated into two distinct regions of non-forested areas (Boitani et al. 1999, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2018). The southern extent of occurrence includes the following countries: South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique (Boitani et al. 1999, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2018). The northern extent of occurrence includes: Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Eritrea, South Sudan, Sudan, Egypt, Libya, Chad, Niger, Tunisia, Algeria, Burkina Faso, Mali, Morocco, Western Sahara, Mauritania, and Senegal. In areas where habitat is altered due to overgrazing by livestock, the Cape Hare’s range is expanding at the expense of hares that do not adapt as well (Flux and Angermann 1990).
useTrade: In South Africa, this species is hunted for food, fur and sport (Robinson et al. 2016). It has also been identified as a species utilized for traditional medicine in South Africa, as it is believed to have medicinal or curative properties (Maliehe 1993, Ntiamoa-Baidu 1997).
conservationActions: National legislation does exist:Protected by law in Jordan, UAE, Oman, and Bahrain. Hunting is permitted in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. Hares are present in all terrestrial protected areas.In Arabia, hare specific surveys are required to confirm if populations are still extant. According to colleagues who have visited Masirah Island, Oman for coastal surveys, there are no longer any hares there. If it is true, this would be of concern as it is possible that L. c. jefferyi is in fact a separate species. There were no representatives from Bahrain, however, from previous conversations with wildlife biologists from Bahrain it seems possible that L. c. atallahi may no longer exist there. It was also recorded, provisionally, as occurring in Qatar. There are still hares in Qatar but their taxonomy is uncertain.The area of occupancy for the Cape Hare includes sections of established protected areas in Africa (Boitani et al. 1999). Sustainable utilization of this species is recommended (Kryger et al. 2004). The development of conservancies to protect appropriate habitats for local subspecies and forms is also recommended. Taxonomic resolution at a species and subspecies level is required for the Lepus genus to ensure that localized or isolated populations and subspecies are conserved (Robinson et al. 2016).

rationale: The Yunnan Hare is widespread and occurs in protected areas. It is reported as being very common by local inhabitants of the region (Wu et al. 2000). It is likely that the population is secure due to its occurrence in remote regions in southwestern China (Flux and Angermann 1990). Isolation on mountains due to encroaching agriculture in surrounding valleys, may pose a threat, but more information is needed (Flux and Angermann 1990). On the other hand, Wang and Xie (2004), followed by Jiang et al. (2015, 2016), listed the species as Near Threatened on the China Red List, stating that it nearly met the criteria for VU A2cd+3cd. Given that the species' range is nearly entirely within China (a near endemic)—this could substitute as the global Red List category. There is no evidence that the extent of occurrence (EOO) has declined, it is unknown whether or not the area of occupancy (AOO) has declined recently by 30%. There is a likelihood that habitat quality has declined by 30%, given human population pressures in general across China, although no solid evidence exists for documenting this decline. There have been no ecological studies on the species in several decades. Similarly, actual or potential levels of exploitation are possible, but unknown. Thus we conservatively list the species as Least Concern, while noting that investigations are desperately needed to document the status of the Yunnan Hare.
habitat: There are few data regarding the habitat and ecology of the Yunnan hare (Flux and Angermann 1990, Wu et al. 2000). It is assumed that the Yunnan hare inhabits high montane pastures within its range (Flux and Angermann 1990). This habitat is thought to be similar to that of L. oiostolus in Tibet (Flux and Angermann 1990, Wu et al. 2000). Hunters have reported that each adult hare has three burrows, with male burrows smaller, shallower, and straighter and female burrows that are bigger and oval (Luo 1988). The Yunnan hare is diurnal, but ventures into cultivated fields at night to forage (Luo 1988). The Yunnan hare produces a litter size of one to four young, two to three times per year (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: Populations that occur on mountains may become isolated as agriculture expands into surrounding valleys (Flux and Angermann 1990).
population: Reports from local inhabitants of the region state that the Yunnan hare is very common (Wu et al. 2000), although modern pressure from an expanding human population and resulting habitat loss is likely.
range: The geographic distribution for the Yunnan hare is Yunnan, western Guizhou, and southern Sichuan in China (Smith and Xie 2008). It is found on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau at elevations of 1,300-3,200m (Wang et al. 1985, Smith and Xie 2008). Its presence has also been recorded in northern Myanmar (Wu et al. 2000).
useTrade: This species is hunted by local peasants (Wu et al. 2000).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the following nature reserves, Shilin (Yunnan), Changshanerhai, Daweishan, Jinpingfenshuiling (Yunnan), Nujiang, Gaoligongshan (Yunnan), and Tongbiguan (CSIS 2008). The Chinese regional Red Listing classifies the Yunnan Hare as Near Threatened nearly meeting criteria A2cd+3cd for listing as Vulnerable (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). Research is needed to determine this species' habitat, ecology, and population status (Wu et al. 2000).

rationale: The European Hare is confirmed Least Concern; it is widespread and abundant across its geographic range (Flux and Angermann 1990, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016, Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). There is evidence of population declines beginning in the early 20th century in association with the intensification of agricultural practices (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). It is listed under Appendix III of the Bern Convention in Europe (as “Lepus capensis (europaeus)” Council of Europe 1979). Several European countries have placed the European Hare on their Red List as "Near Threatened" or "Threatened" (Reichlin et al. 2006). There is increasing concern regarding the status of regional forms of this species (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016). However, the status in Europe and the European Union is “Least Concern” (Temple and Terry 2007).
habitat: The European Hare is a highly adaptable species that can persist in numerous habitat types from sea level to alpine areas (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). There is a positive association with hare abundance and habitat diversity (Smith, Jennings and Harris 2005). Various surveys have investigated habitat preferences of European Hares. As the study areas vary considerably, the results diverge also substantially. However, fallow land is preferred consistently in all studies, whereas residential areas are avoided (Schai-Braun et al. 2013, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016). When available, weeds and wild grasses are selected by the European Hare, however, intensified agro-practices have reduced this food source resulting in the selection of crop species (Reichlin, Klansek and Hackländer 2006, Schai-Braun et al. 2015).The European Hare averages three litters/yr, but can vary from one to five litters/yr (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016). Litter size can vary with respect to the season, smaller litters produced earlier in the season and larger litters later (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2018). The birth weight of the European Hare is approximately 100 g (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). Gestation is 42 days and reproduction occurs year round in suitable habitats. In northern ranges or higher altitude reproduction is restricted to summer (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). Physiological age is 8-12 years (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). Females reach maturity around 4-5 months Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018).
threats: A study reviewing available literature regarding population densities in connection with habitat that was identified as primarily farmland from 12 European countries, concluded that the primary cause of the European Hare decline was intensification of agriculture (Smith et al. 2005). It is inferred that this threat is pertinent to the species across its geographic range where farming is practiced. Smith et al. (2005) also identified negative associations with predation and precipitation in respect to abundance. However, "field size, temperature, precipitation, and hunting had no effect on density throughout Europe" (Smith et al. 2005). In Greece, Spain, France and Denmark, the restocking of hares from other regions or countries to complement hare densities for hunting has been identified as a threat to regional gene pools (Mamuris et al. 2001, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016). This issue has also been identified as a concern for the Cantabric population in Spain (Palacios et al. 2004). Disease is an additional threat to the European Hare and several have been identified as the principle sources of mortality (Lamarque, Barrat and Moutou 1996). These diseases are European Brown Hare Syndrome (EBHS), Pasteurellosis, Yersiniosis (Pseudo-tuberculosis), Coccidiosis and Tularaemia (Lamarque et al. 1996, Lavazza and Cooke 2018).Genetic diversity of the European Hare in the North Rhine-Westphalia region of Germany indicates that hare populations still retain sufficient diversity (Fickel et al. 2005). However, it is cautioned that restricted gene flow could eventually lead to allelic fixation and inbreeding depression within populations that become isolated (Fickel et al. 2005).
population: Populations of the European Hare have been experiencing declines in many areas across its geographic range in Europe (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). Natural population densities are about 2/100 ha, but can reach up to 275/100 ha in highly suitable habitats (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2016).A study conducted in the Czech Republic found mean hare densities were highest in habitat with the following characteristics (Pikula et al. 2004): elevation (sea level up to 200 m); annual snow cover duration (40-60 days); mean annual precipitation (450-700 mm); annual sunshine duration (1801-2000 hrs); mean annual air temperature (>10˚C).Population dynamics are mainly affected by juvenile mortality due to annual differences in weather conditions, mechanical activities in agricultural land, diseases, and predation (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018).
range: The current Eurasian distribution of the European Hare extends from the northern provinces of Spain, to introduced populations in the United Kingdom and southern regions of Scandinavia, south to northern portions of the Middle East, and has naturally expanded east to sections of Siberia. The south-eastern boundary of its range runs from the southern Caspian Sea south to the Persian Gulf (Flux and Angermann 1990, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016, Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). This species has been introduced as a game species extensively to countries across the globe, including eastern Australia, New Zealand, South America up to 28°S, Canada, and the United States (Great Lakes Area), as well as numerous islands in the Indian and Atlantic Ocean (Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018). This species can be found at elevations ranging from sea level up to 2,400 m (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016).
useTrade: The European Hare is recognized as an important game species throughout its historical distribution, including those areas where it has been introduced (Flux and Angermann 1990, Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016, Hackländer and Schai-Braun 2018).
conservationActions: The European Hare is recognized as an important game species throughout its distribution and as such conservation measures are required to halt declining populations (Flux and Angermann 1990). The recent decline of this species has garnered it protection under the Bern Convention as an Appendix III listing (Council of Europe 1979). In Norway, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, population declines have resulted in country-specific Red Listing as "near threatened" or "threatened" (Reichlin et al. 2006).Research is needed to determine population dynamics specific to habitat type and the effects habitat change has on life history parameters with regard to declines (Smith et al. 2005). There is a lack of understanding as to why hare numbers are low in pastoral landscapes and therefore, research should be conducted within this habitat type with particular emphasis paid to demography and behavioral ecology (Smith et al. 2005).When population declines are the direct result of agricultural intensification, which results in increased application of fertilizer, landscape homogeneity and mechanization, population declines of the European Hare can be countered by augmenting habitat to boost heterogeneity (Smith et al. 2005).In Spain, molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that the Cantabric population has unique mtDNA in relation to other European populations (Palacios et al. 2004). As an important hunting species, declining numbers have prompted the importation of non-Iberian hares (from France and elsewhere) to supplement hare densities (Palacios et al. 2004). In an effort to conserve this population's gene pool, a captive breeding program has been implemented (Palacios et al. 2004). As of 2003 this program has successfully bred leverets and in 2004 turned its focus to increasing genetic variability by introducing individuals from new localities (Palacios et al. 2004).

rationale: The species remains listed as Least Concern. This is a widespread species that occurs in protected areas; however, efforts should be made to ascertain the population status.
habitat: The Manchurian Hare is a forest dwelling Hare that prefers mixed forest to homogeneous conifer (Flux and Angermann 1990, Sokolov et al. 1994). It favours habitats that include the Manchurian Hazelnut (Corylus sieboldiana mandshurica) and Mongolian Oak (Quercus mongolica). This species avoids open habitat and human settlements (Flux and Angermann 1990). It is presumed that the ecology of the Manchurian Hare is equivalent to that of the snowshoe Hare (Lepus americanus), its New World ecological equivalent (Angermann 1966).The species is nocturnal, but it can display some activity at dawn. Nests are built in closed shelters, not in the open, and the hares are reticent to leave cover when disturbed. They have been known to utter a sneezing vocalization when scared.
threats: Forest clearing results in loss of habitat for the Manchurian Hare that promotes replacement by the Tolai Hare (L. tolai) (Flux and Angermann 1990).
population: Population density may be quite high, such as 27–55 per 100 ha (Sokolov et al. 1994). Population dynamics are unstudied.
range: The geographic distribution of the Manchurian Hare includes eastern China, the Ussuri region of Russia (Hoffmann and Smith 2005), and may extend into North Korea (Smith and Xie 2008). It is possibly parapatric with the Korean Hare (Lepus coreanus) in North Korea (Hoffmann and Smith 2005, Smith et al. 2018). It inhabits elevations between 300-900m (Flux and Angermann 1990).
useTrade: Some subsistence hunting. The species has experienced very minor commercial exploitation – as the skin is thin and rips readily. This activity is believed to have ceased.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Honghe, Liangshui, Xingkaihu, Laotudingzi, Baishilazi, and Sanjiang Nature Reserves. Research should be undertaken to address the lack of data regarding population for the Manchurian Hare. Research is also needed to determine the status of habitat for this species (Flux and Angermann 1990). This species was regionally Red Listed as Least Concern in China (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).

rationale: This is a widespread species that is characterized as very common. Although the species is subject to habitat destruction, intensive hunting and predation, it is confirmed as Least Concern because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The Indian Hare can be found in wide variety of habitats such as short grasslands, barren agricultural fields, crop fields, and forest roads. The species can be seen in forests of many types other than the mangroves and tall grassland habitats. However, one can see the species adjacent to forest areas in agricultural fields. Its diet consists primarily of grasses (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016, Molur and Nameer 2018).It breeds throughout the year, but the peak breeding season is during the monsoon season (Flux and Angermann 1990). Litter size is one to four, but can be higher (Gurung and Singh 1996). Forbs and grasses constitute the bulk of their diet (Flux and Angermann 1990). The Indian Hare is characterized as a shy species (Gurung and Singh 1996). It exhibits activity during crepuscular and nocturnal hours (Chakraborty et al. 2005).
threats: Major threats for the Indian Hare include habitat destruction and conversion of prime forest areas for agricultural purposes, as well as intensive hunting by locals for meat. Individual hares, especially the young ones living in the forest areas, are subjected to predation by carnivorous mammals and birds. The Indian Hare is also threatened by domestic predators, competition from livestock, and human set forest fires (Chakraborty et al. 2005).
population: The Indian Hare appears to be very common wherever they occur. However, the population in India is subjected to severe fragmentation due to expanding agricultural fields and pressure on forest in terms of fuel wood collection and sometimes illegal hunting.
range: The Indian Hare is distributed throughout India, except the high reaches of the Himalayas and mangrove areas within the Sundarbans in the state of West Bengal. The geographic distribution extends into eastern Pakistan, southern Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh excluding the Sundarbans (Flux and Angermann 1990, Molur and Nameer 2018). It is thought to occur in Bhutan as well, but exact locations are not known (Chakraborty et al. 2005). This species can be found at elevations ranging from 50-4,500 m (Chakraborty et al. 2005).This species has been introduced (as a single or several unidentified subspecies) to many islands Comoro, Mayotte, Madagascar, Réunion (including Gunners Quoin I), Mauritius (Alaléga Island), Seychelles (Cousin I), and Andaman Island in the Indian Ocean, and into New Guinea. The Gunners Quoin population of the Indian Hare has been eradicated (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016). The Indian Hare has been considered native to Java by McNeely (1981), but its origin there has been considered uncertain by Hoffmann and Smith (2005).
useTrade: Up to 40% of some populations of the Indian Hare are utilized. This species is hunted for meat, but is also removed to prevent crop damage (Flux and Angermann 1990).
conservationActions: This species is listed under the Schedule IV of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. No specific conservation action has been framed to protect the species in the wild in India. However, a number of individuals are present within sanctuaries and national parks and are somewhat protected from human intervention. Further taxonomic research is needed for this species, as well as increased public awareness (Chakraborty et al. 2005).The Indian Hare may be impacted from habitat fragmentation, habitat destruction (conversion of prime habitat to cultivated land), predation by non-native animals, competition with livestock, and human-induced fires.

rationale: The Woolly Hare is a widespread species that occurs in protected areas. There are no available data on population status, which should be addressed. The status of the Woolly Hare in India has been assessed as Endangered (B1ab(ii,iii)+2ab(ii,iii)) due to its restricted distribution, fragmentation, and decline in habitat area and quality there (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). However, it was assessed as Least Concern in Nepal (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). Recent Chinese Red List assessments consider the Woolly Hareto be Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). Globally, the species is Least Concern.
habitat: The Woolly Hare can be found occupying montane subtropical grasslands (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). It also inhabits, "upland grasslands of various types, montane meadows, shrub meadows, and alpine cold desert" (Smith and Xie 2008). Diet is predominantly grasses and herbaceous plants (Smith and Xie 2008). This species only moults once a year (Flux and Angermann 1990, Smith and Xie 2008). It is primarily nocturnal, but can be observed during the day (Smith and Xie 2008). They tend to avoid dense shrubby cover. Their major predators are large raptors and meso-carnivores (Smith et al. 2018).
threats: There has been an overall decrease in quality and total area of habitat available to the Woolly Hare in India resulting from destruction and fuelwood harvesting (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). In India, habitat destruction has resulted in population fragmentation and the inability to disperse (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). Subsistence harvesting by locals also poses a threat in India (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005), but this activity may have declined in China since guns were recently outlawed.
population: Woolly Hares occupy open grassland habitats where their density can range from 13-27 hares/km².
range: The geographic distribution of the Woolly Hare includes western and central China, northern regions of Nepal and India (Smith and Xie 2008, Smith et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is harvested for local subsistence and fur trade (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005).
conservationActions: This species is present in protected areas in Nepal (Annapurna, Makalu Barun, Sagarmatha, and Shey Phuskondo) (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). In China, it occurs in Qinghaihuniaodao, Wolong, Zhumulangmafeng, Meihualutiebu, and Jiuzhaigou National Nature Reserves (Liu et al. 2005). The status of the woolly hare in India has been assessed as Endangered B1ab(ii,iii)+2ab(ii,iii), due to restricted distribution, fragmentation, and decline in habitat area and quality (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005). However, it was regionally assessed as Least Concern in Nepal (Chakraborty, Bhattacharyya and Srinivasulu 2005) and China (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).

rationale: The Burmese Hare is confirmed as Least Concern, being common and widespread. Furthermore, populations appear to be stable or even increasing due to conversion of primary forest to scrubbier habitat favorable to the species.
habitat: The Burmese Hare occupies mostly low altitude dipterocarp forests, and plain non-forest habitats with numbers especially high in the grass and shrub vegetation of seasonally exposed large river channels. It can be found in rain/flood-fed low intensity rice fields, but avoids irrigated multi-crop rice fields which cover much of Thailand (Duckworth et al. 2008). The species appears to be absent from Nakai Plateau, Lao PDR, despite what appears to be suitable habitat (possibly due to high altitude) (Evans et al. 2000). It is also absent from Thung Yai Wildlife Sanctuary in Thailand, again despite suitable habitat at a relatively high altitude (Duckworth et al. 2008). For these reasons and the fact that there have been numerous field surveys for the species above 700 m without detecting the species (in Thailand and Lao PDR) the 1,300 m upper elevation limit may be too high, though a comprehensive examination of specimens is lacking (Duckworth et al. 2008). There are insufficient data regarding the home range and population density of the Burmese Hare (Flux and Angermann 1990). The Burmese Hare may have several litters per year with litter size ranging from one to seven (three to four average) (Lekagul and McNeely 1977). Gestation lasts approximately 35-40 days (Lekagul and McNeely 1977). It is estimated that the longevity of this species is six years (Lekagul and McNeely 1977). This species is crepuscular and nocturnal (Duckworth et al. 2008) It actively feeds at night on grass, bark and twigs (Lekagul and McNeely 1977).
threats: Extension of irrigated rice fields destroys habitat in localized areas (Duckworth et al. 2008). The species is heavily hunted, but this does not seem to constitute a major threat (Duckworth et al. 2008). Habitat in Lao PDR and Viet Nam is regularly burnt during the dry season (February-May), posing a threat to young that may be present (Duckworth et al. 2008).
population: This species is locally abundant.
range: The Burmese Hare occurs in central and southern Myanmar from the Chindwin River valley east through Thailand, Cambodia, southern Lao PDR, southern Viet Nam, and south into the upper Malay Peninsula (Myanmar, Thailand) (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016, 2018). This distribution may include the northern and central regions of Lao PDR, as signs of its presence in the wild and fresh kills in markets have been identified, but only to the genus level (Duckworth et al. 1994, Duckworth 1996). Distribution is enigmatic in the north and east, with few confirmed records. The Thai distribution would suggest that the species has spread with human-related forest loss in the northern highlands of Lao PDR, particularly one might surmise along the lowland valleys. The mapped range in Myanmar is largely speculative, further work is likely to show that the species is more restricted within this country. A collection expedition in Thailand (pre-1950's) recorded this species as occurring at 1,300 m on Doi Ang Ka (modern name Doi Inthanon) (Allen and Coolidge 1940). Further work is needed to determine the upper limit of this species.
useTrade: The Burmese Hare may be hunted/snared for food.
conservationActions: The Burmese Hare is found within protected areas throughout its range. Research is needed in the following areas: taxonomy, distribution, and behavior. The evident lack of hares within the mid-altitude ranges of central Indochina, despite suitable habitat, requires further investigation to determine potential taxonomic distinction between low and high altitude hare populations (Duckworth et al. 2008).

rationale: The Cape Scrub Hare is a fairly restricted species. Hunting pressure and habitat loss has reduced population, however the species is listed as Least Concern because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Population trend is expected to continue to decline by at least 20% for the next 100 years (Kryger et al. 2004).
habitat: The Cape Scrub Hare starts foraging at dusk and continues throughout the night (Flux and Angermann 1990). It, "prefers scrub or savanna woodland habitat with grass cover but easily takes to agriculturally developed areas" (Kryger et al. 2004). Home range is variable depending on habitat type and season (Kryger et al. 2004). It shows preference for green grasses, but also consumes leaves, stems, and rhizomes of dry and green grasses (Happold 2013, Robinson 2018). Reproduction is suspected to be year round with a peak breeding season occurring from September to February (Happold 2013).
threats: Habitat fragmentation resulting from agriculture, commercial plantations and development are threats to this species (Kryger et al. 2004). Hunting pressure has reduced population sizes in South Africa (Kryger et al. 2004). The Cape Scrub Hare may be threatened by intensive agricultural expansion and overhunting in the Western Cape (Happold 2013), but monitoring data are required to demonstrate this.
population: The Cape Scrub Hare is fairly common throughout its distribution (Robinson et al. 2016). Population trend for this species has been declining and is expected to continue to decline by at least 20% until the year 2104 (Kryger et al. 2004). While a slow decline has been predicted due to habitat loss and hunting pressure (Kryger et al. 2004), it is expected that land conversion from livestock to wildlife may benefit the species and counteract population declines by creating and reconnecting suitable habitat patches (Robinson et al. 2016). However, the status of scattered subpopulations and isolated subspecies is largely unknown, and may be threatened (Robinson et al. 2016). For example, populations are fragmented in the Western Cape Province (Robinson et al. 2016).
range: The geographic range of the Cape Scrub Hare is now restricted to the W and N Cape Provinces of South Africa with marginal distribution in the southwestern part of Namibia, based on the taxonomic restriction of the Cape Scrub Hare sensu stricto (Robinson 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food, fur and sport (Robinson et al. 2016). It has also been identified as a species utilized for traditional medicine in South Africa, as it is believed to have medicinal or curative properties (Maliehe 1993, Ntiamoa-Baidu 1997).
conservationActions: The Cape Scrub Hare occurs in several protected areas ,including both formally and privately protected areas (Kryger et al. 2004). Research in the following areas has been recommended: survey studies, taxonomic, genetic research, and life history (Kryger et al. 2004). Sustainable utilization has also been identified as a needed management measure (Kryger et al. 2004).

rationale: This is a widespread species that occurs in protected areas, but more information is needed to determine population and distribution status. The Chinese Hare is largely a Chinese endemic (with perhaps a small range in northeastern Viet Nam). As such this global assessment should parallel the Chinese Red List assessments of Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). However, southeastern China has experienced incredible human population growth and habitat loss for species such as the Chinese Hare, and there have been no recent studies of the Chinese Hare to allow an assessment as to how it has fared given the anthropogenic onslaught. Such studies are needed. Habitat loss and hunting appear responsible for the lack of recent data on the species from Viet Nam, the last reported sighting was in the 1990s (Schai-Braun and Hackländer 2016).
habitat: Records of the Chinese Hare suggest a relatively low altitudinal distribution. This species inhabits hilly expanses with open edge grassland and scrubby vegetation (Smith and Xie 2008). Constructs burrows. Diet consists of leafy plants, green shoots, and twigs (Smith and Xie 2008). It is nocturnal, but is occasionally active during daylight hours (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: In Viet Nam, the original range of the Chinese Hare was very small, in a heavily populated region. Habitat for this species is in decline and it is inferred from heavy hunting pressure on other species, that hunting is likely a major threat for this species in Viet Nam (Do Touk pers. comm). This threat is also likely in the increasingly heavily populated region in southeast China.
population: Populations of the Chinese Hare in Viet Nam are thought to be very small, with the last confirmed records from the 1990s. The species was surveyed recently in Viet Nam (by Phan Trong Anh) without detection (Do Touc pers. comm). There are no data regarding population for the remaining distribution for this species.
range: This species occurs in southeastern China from the Yangtse River southward. It is also found on Taiwan, with minor range in northeast Viet Nam (Hoffmann and Smith 2005, Smith et al. 2018). There are a few records of hares west of the range of this species and it is not known if they belong to the Chinese Hare or the Burmese Hare (Lepus peguensis) (Duckworth pers. comm). It can be found occupying bamboo at elevations up to 4,000-5,000m (Smith and Xie 2008).
useTrade: There is local subsistence hunting and it is sold in markets (Flux and Angermann 1990).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the following nature reserves, Niumulin, Wuyishan, Nanling, Heishidingkuoyelin, Damingshan (Guangxi), Dayaoshanshuiyuanlin (Guangxi), Shiwandashan, Leigongshan, Maolan, Jiugongshan, Taoyuandong, Dongdongtinghu (Hunan), Bamianshan, Mangshan, Poyanghuhouniao, Yanquan, Taohongling, Jinggangshan, Nanjiliedao, Qingliangfeng, Tianmushan, Gutianshan, Wuyanling, and Dawuling. Research should be conducted to determine the distribution and status of the Chinese Hare to investigate possible isolation due to increasing agricultural practices. This species was regionally Red Listed as Least Concern in China (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).

rationale: This species is confirmed as Least Concern; it has a restricted geographic distribution in Ethiopia, but has been considered abundant within its range (Boitani et al. 1999). Current data on its population status are lacking.
habitat: There are few data regarding the ecology of this species (Boitani et al. 1999, Tolesa and Johnston 2018). This species occupies grassland and Afro-alpine moorland habitats within its range (Boitani et al. 1999). Abundance of Ethiopian Highland Hares in the Bale Mountains National Park was found to be greatest in rocky grasslands and wetlands during the wet and dry seasons, respectively (Mekonnen et al. 2011). Diet during both seasons consisted mostly of monocotyledons with preference shown for Festuca spp., Agrostis gracilifolia and Carex monostachya (Mekonnen et al. 2011). Food selection varied more during the dry season to include dicots (Mekonnen et al. 2011). HB length of the Ethiopian Highland Hare is 44.0-54.5 cm (Happold 2013). The body weight of this species ranges from 1,692-2,963 g. The hind foot length of this species ranges from 10.5-12.3 cm. The ear length of this species ranges from 10.0-11.9 cm. The tail length of this species ranges from 9.5-13.0 cm (Tolesa 2014).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: The population status of the Ethiopian Highland Hare has been reported as being "relatively numerous" (Flux and Angermann 1990). Current data on the population status of this species are lacking.
range: The geographic distribution of the Ethiopian Highland Hare is restricted to the Ethiopian Highlands (Flux and Angermann 1990). It occurs on the Bale Mountains (Flux and Angermann 1990) as well as the central highlands of Shewa (Tolesa and Johnston 2018). In addition to the populations in the Bale Mountains and the northern Shewa, Tolesa (2014) recorded an Ethiopian Highland Hare population in the Gurage Zone (central Ethiopia). It is sympatric with the Abyssinian Hare (L. habessinicus) within parts of distribution (Tolesa and Johnston 2018). The Ethiopian Highland Hare occurs at elevations of 2,140 m to 4,380 m (Boitani et al. 1999).
useTrade: Species is likely harvested for subsistence.
conservationActions: Research is needed for the Ethiopian Highland Hare in the areas of biology, reproduction, population/density, diseases and habitat requirements (Flux and Angermann 1990, Tolesa and Johnston 2018). Ethiopian Highland Hares have been recorded from the Mount Kaka and Mount Hunkolo areas in southeastern Ethiopia (Girma et al. 2012). This species is recorded as "quite abundant and sufficiently represented in existing protected areas" (Boitani et al. 1999). It is present in Bale Mountains protected area (Yalden et al. 1996).Ecosystem Services: Is a prey species for mammalian predators, including the Endangered Ethiopian Wolf (Canis simensis), the Vulnerable Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) and the Vulnerable Leopard (Panthera pardus) (Wolf and Ripple 2016).

rationale: The White-tailed Jackrabbit is a widespread species, confirmed as Least Concern. Population status across its entire distribution is not currently known, but non-trivial declines have been observed over the past 150 years across much of its range (Brown et al. 2018). This cold-tolerant jackrabbit is now rare or extinct in portions of its former range in British Columbia, Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Missouri, and Washington (Applegate 1997, Brown et al. 2018). It is a species of concern in California (Williams 1986), and was reported to be absent from former habitats in the Yellowstone ecosystem (Berger et al. 2005, Berger 2008) - a status shown to be overly pessimistic by Gunther et al. (2009). The cause of this reduction is generally thought to center on the conversion of native prairie to shrub-steppe or agriculture and/or the arrival of expanding Black-tailed Jackrabbit populations better suited to human disturbance (Brown et al. 2018). It is unknown whether these declines and replacement by Black-tailed Jackrabbits have been the result of habitat changes or reflect a continuation of climatic shifts that have occurred throughout Holocene times (Brown et al. 2018). Therefore this species is declining and is clearly a species that should be carefully watched.
habitat: The primary habitat of the White-tailed Jackrabbit is open prairie and plains grassland, but this varies with locality (Flux and Angermann 1990, Beever et al. 2018). They are also found on montane and subalpine pastures among scattered evergreens to 3,100 m altitude in Colorado (Flux and Angermann 1990). Diet of this species is predominantly grasses and forbs, with shrubs during the winter (Lim 1987). The breeding season was recorded to extend from late February through mid-July in North Dakota (Flux and Angermann 1990). A similar breeding season was recorded in Wyoming (Rogowitz 1992). The season is shortened in the northern extent of its range to May through early July (Lim 1987). The gestation period is variable, one account sets it as low as one month and another as high as 43 days (Lim 1987). It is thought that elevation and latitude may influence total gestation time (Lim 1987). Breeding conditions and environmental factors influence the total number of litters produced each year (Lim 1987). Common litter size is recorded as four to five young. Longevity is unknown but speculated to be up to five years (Forsyth 1999).
threats: There are numerous hypothesized factors contributing to the decline of the White-tailed Jackrabbit, but the most prevalent appears to be the conversion of native prairie to shrub-steppe or non-grass agriculture. This habitat alteration has led to the exclusion of White-tailed Jackrabbits where the distribution expansion of Black-tailed Jackrabbits has occurred (Lim 1987, Brown et al. 2018).
population: The population density of White-tailed Jackrabbits varies greatly temporally and across the range of the species. In the shortgrass prairie region it has been reported at a density of 2.2 per square km, but densities as high as 43 – 71/km² have been recorded in Minnesota and Iowa, respectively (Beever et al. 2018).
range: The White-tailed Jackrabbit has a wide geographic distribution. Its historic distribution extended across the southern regions of Canada, including south-central British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, southwestern Manitoba and the extreme southwest of Ontario (Flux and Angermann 1990, Beever et al. 2018). The distribution within the USA included: Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Nebraska, Kansas, North and South Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, and Illinois (Flux and Angermann 1990, Beever et al. 2018). This distribution represented an expansion from its original distribution, which resulted from the creation of suitable habitat (Lim 1987). There is some debate to whether this species was introduced to Wisconsin (Lim 1987). Now, however, the range of the species is definitely contracting. Some treatments indicate that this species has been possibly extirpated from British Columbia, southern Nebraska, Kansas and Illinois, and some recent distribution maps exclude Missouri (Flinders and Chapman 2003). The White-tailed Jackrabbit is excluded from some areas of its range resulting from the expansion of the Black-tailed Jackrabbit (Lim 1987). This species was recorded at an elevation of 4,319 m on Mt. Bross, Colorado (Lim 1987). Its lower limit is recorded as 30 m on the Columbian plains (Lim 1987).
useTrade: This species has been hunted for sport and their fur is sold to fur buyers and mink ranchers (Flux and Angermann 1990, Brown et al. 2018).
conservationActions: Research should be conducted to ascertain the ecological role of this species within prairie and sage steppe ecosystems. Furthermore, efforts should be made to determine the species’ status, life-history, demography, and predator-prey relationships. Also this species be removed from the 'varmint' list produced by the State of Wyoming (Berger et al. 2006). More data are needed to understand the factors that operate when Black-tailed Jackrabbits and White-tailed Jackrabbits occur sympatrically (Flinders and Chapman 2003).The White-tailed Jackrabbit is classified as “possibly extirpated” in Kansas, southern Nebraska, and British Columbia, “imperiled” in New Mexico, “vulnerable” in California, “apparently secure” in Colorado, Montana, Nebraska, Oregon, South Dakota, and Wyoming, and “secure” only in Idaho and Nevada. The White-tailed Jackrabbit is a priority species in Washington where it is a “species of greatest conservation need” (Ferguson and Atamian 2012, Brown et al. 2018).

rationale: The Abyssinian Hare has been described as a widespread and abundant species (Flux and Angermann 1990) and it is confirmed as Least Concern. Its distribution may be increasing due to the effects of habitat change produced by overgrazing (Flux and Angermann 1990). Current data on the population status of the species are lacking.
habitat: The Abyssinian Hare occupies a variety of habitats from open grassland, steppe, and savanna, to desert regions, where some shrub is required for cover (Flux and Angermann 1990). Other Lepus species occupy areas where shrub cover is denser (Flux and Angermann 1990). It is suspected that the Abyssinian Hare is nocturnal, like the Cape Hare (Flux and Angermann 1990). HB length of this species is 40-55 cm (Happold 2013). The body weight of this species ranges from 1,415 -2,440 g. The hind foot length of this species ranges from 9.5-11.4 cm. The ear length of this species ranges from 9.5-12.0 cm. The tail length of this species ranges from 5.0-11.1 cm (Tolesa 2014).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: The Abyssinian Hare has been considered an abundant species (Flux and Angermann 1990), although data on the current population of the species are lacking.
range: The geographic distribution of the Abyssinian Hare includes Somalia (excluding the southern region), eastern Ethiopia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and minor distribution in Sudan and possible distribution in the extreme north of Kenya (Yalden et al. 1986, Tolesa 2018). It is suspected that this species' distribution is expanding into areas where overgrazing occurs (Flux and Angermann 1990). It is sympatric with the Ethiopian Highland Hare (L. starcki) within parts of its distribution in Ethiopia. This species can be found at elevations that range from sea level up to 2,000 m (potentially as high as 2,500 m) (Yalden et al. 1996).
useTrade: Subsistence hunting is likely.
conservationActions: This species is present in Awash National Park, Mago National Park, and possibly Yangudi-Rassa National Park (Yalden et al. 1996). Abyssinian Hares have been recorded from the Mount Kaka area in southeastern Ethiopia (Girma et al. 2012). It has been suggested that the range of the Abyssinian Hare may be expanding into areas where overgrazing occurs (Flux and Angermann 1990). Research to determine its true geographic distribution and population status should be conducted.

rationale: Though few data are available regarding population densities and distribution (Duthie and Robinson 1990), the Bunyoro Rabbit is a fairly widespread species. There have been fewer sightings of the species in comparison with early and mid-twentieth century reports (Happold 2013), suggesting it may be in decline. It is present in several protected areas. It is therefore confirmed as Least Concern.
habitat: The Bunyoro Rabbit exists primarily in moist savanna grassland, woodlands with rocky outcrops, and less prominently in forested areas (Duthie and Robinson 1990). They often dwell in rock crevices, and are associated in some areas with hyrax habitat (Kingdon 1974). It is a nocturnal feeder, foraging on flowers, newly sprouted grasses, and "much attracted to heavily grazed, newly mowed or burnt areas where the grass is short" (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Feeding occurs in small groups, but it is likely solitary when resting in forms (Happold 2013). The primary habitat of grassland is periodically burnt and grazed, which provides for a more frequent supply of sprouted plants (Kingdon 1974).Breeding probably occurs throughout the year (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Gestation is around 5 weeks (Kingdon 1974) with litters of one or two altricial young (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
threats: Little is known about the threats to the Bunyoro Rabbit. Though the grassland habitat is annually or biannually burnt leaving the rabbit vulnerable to predators, this pattern actually promotes vegetation growth included in its diet (Kingdon 1974). It is hunted locally and some of its habitat is utilized for cultivation of peanuts and rice, but little is known of the effects of these threats (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
population: The Bunyoro Rabbit is widespread and common within some parts of its range, including northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo and southern South Sudan, though little is known about abundance in other areas (Duthie and Robinson 1990). A decrease in sightings suggests that the population may be declining (Happold 2013, 2018)
range: Specimen records included in a 1974 report (Kingdon 1974) indicate that the Bunyoro Rabbit occurs in two separate areas of central Africa. This report and a later review (Duthie and Robinson 1990) concluded that the northern extent of the larger range stretches from southeastern Chad through southern South Sudan to northwestern Kenya, through most of Uganda (excluding the extreme southeast), western Rwanda and Burundi, northern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC, former Zaire), all of Central African Republic (Duthie and Robinson 1990, Kingdon 1974). The second area is predominantly in northwestern Angola and southwestern DRC (Kingdon 1974, Duthie and Robinson 1990, Boitani et al. 1999).A new survey of specimen distribution (Happold and Wendelen 2006) proposes that the distribution of the Bunyoro Rabbit is actually smaller than previous accounts have reported. Based on specimen records, there is no indication that it exists in Angola, southern DRC, northwestern Kenya, Rwanda, Chad, or Burundi. The accounts are restricted to Uganda, southern South Sudan, northeastern DRC, and eastern (and possibly central) Central African Republic (Happold and Wendelen 2006, Happold 2013).
useTrade: This species is hunted in Uganda with dogs and nets.
conservationActions: The Bunyoro Rabbit is found in protected areas within its range, including the Garamba National Park in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo and Murchison Falls National Park in Uganda (Duthie and Robinson 1990).It is possible that no form of additional protection may be required (Duthie and Robinson 1990), but more research regarding population size and trend, ecology, and the effects of threats should be conducted.

rationale: Though declining within its range, the Natal Red Rock Hare is known to be a widespread and abundant species (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Despite being widespread, it is patchily distributed within its distribution due to their restriction to areas of rocky habitat. While no estimate of population size or trend is available for this species, it is inferred to have a large population, given its extent of occurrence (Matthee et al. 2016). However, while its rocky habitats are largely inaccessible and unlikely to be transformed, increasing hunting pressure (inferred from expanding human settlements and anecdotal reports of decline), loss of foraging areas from agricultural expansion, and habitat degradation from overgrazing may be causing local declines and possible extinctions (Matthee et al. 2016). The Natal Red Rock Hare occurs in areas of high human population density and may be increasingly, locally threatened by hunting (Matthee et al. 2016). The species is easily hunted and is thought to be substantially utilized for subsistence or sport hunting (Matthee et al. 2016). There are greater than 10,000 mature individuals in the wild and the decline is projected to be 20% or more in the next 20 years (Matthee et al. 2004). It is also present in protected areas (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
habitat: The habitat of the Natal Red Rock Hare is naturally fragmented due to the distribution of suitable habitat (Duthie and Robinson 1990, Matthee et al. 2004). It is confined to rocky areas that provide shelter and occur in krantzes, rocky hillsides, boulder-strewn koppies, rocky ravines and amongst rocks in dry river beds (Skinner and Chimimba 2005). It is usually observed in tall, dense grassland on rocky slopes where grasses and shrubs grow among the rocks or at their bases (Happold 2013). They are nocturnal, relying on rocks for shelter during the day, although they have occasionally been flushed in thick grass where they presumably were resting. They defecate at specific sites (latrines), which is often the only evidence of their presence in an area. This is the largest of the rock hare species. This species lives in small colonies consisting of a few individuals. While not much is known about the reproduction of this species, it is likely to be similar to other red rock hares. Nests are typically built in shallow excavations and lined with fur from the mother’s belly and flanks over a grass and stick structure. This species probably breeds year-round and has one to two young per litter. The diet consists of sprouting grasses (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
threats: The Natal Red Rock Hare is found in a limited area in coastal and inland southern Africa. Here, human populations largely of lower income who hunt local fauna for subsistence are increasing, thereby increasing the threat to this otherwise abundant species (Matthee et al. 2004). Sport hunting with dogs may also be impacting this species, as empirical evidence suggests a wide range of species are affected and the sport hunters are indiscriminate (Grey-Ross et al. 2010). Hunting is suspected to be causing local declines (and possibly local extinctions) in this species but it is uncertain whether there is a net decline in the populations. Agriculture and habitat encroachment are also causing a decline (Matthee et al. 2004). For example, in KwaZulu-Natal, cane and fruit crops may be reducing the overall quality of foraging area for the rock hare (Matthee et al. 2016). Natural habitat is being lost at a rate of 1.2% per annum (between 1994 and 2011) in KwaZulu-Natal, primarily due to agriculture (Jewitt et al. 2015). Incidental predation on rock hares by domestic dogs may be increasing as a result of agricultural and rural settlement expansion (Matthee et al. 2016). Since the 1900's, 21-50% of total habitat has been lost and future loss (until 2022) is expected to remain between 21-50% (Matthee et al. 2004).
population: There is no population size or trend estimate available for this species (Matthee et al. 2016). The Natal Red Rock Hare is fairly common throughout its distribution, though the population is experiencing a decline due to encroachment of human settlements and increased hunting/trapping pressure in rural areas where the rock hare occurs (Matthee et al. 2004). Greater than 10,000 mature individuals exist (Matthee et al. 2004). There is a predicted decline in total population of 20% or more until the year 2022 (Matthee et al. 2004).
range: The Natal Red Rock Hare is near endemic to South Africa, with only a tiny part of its range in southern Mozambique in the Maputo Province (known from only two records there, Happold 2013). It is found in southeastern South Africa in the provinces of Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga (Duthie and Robinson 1990, Matthee et al. 2004), and in Swaziland in the Lumbobo and highveld regions where it is considered uncommon (Monadjem 1998). Although Meester et al. (1986) indicated that it occurs in eastern Lesotho, as it is found from sea level to 1,550 m in elevation (Duthie and Robinson 1990); it is unlikely to occur extensively in Lesotho. Thus, field surveys and specimens are needed to confirm its presence in the country (Lynch 1994). It does occur against the grassy slopes in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg (Pringle 1974). While it is not recorded from the Free State or northeast Eastern Cape (Lynch 1983, 1989), some specimens from the northeastern Eastern Cape possessed both Smith’s Red Rock Hare (P. rupestris) and Natal Red Rock Hare characters (Lynch 1994).Extent of occurrence is greater than 20,000 km², and area of occupancy greater than 2,000 km² (Matthee et al. 2004).
useTrade: This species is hunted for meat and sport. It is likely to be fairly important in subsistence communities where they are easily obtained. Maliehe (1993) specifically mentioned rock hares as being an important bush meat item in Lesotho and in Zululand, but this is likely to be true throughout its range. As a fairly slow-moving species, they are easily hunted with dogs. At night, they have a tendency to freeze when chanced upon in spotlights and can be easily shot or captured in nets (B. Wilson pers. obs.). During the day, it  is also possible to hunt them in their refuges, using a coiled piece of barbed wire that hooks and drags the animal out of its shelter (B. Wilson pers. obs.). While having a particularly warm and thick fur, pelts from these species are prone to hairslip and do not cure well, making them unsuitable for hardwearing fur items.
conservationActions: The Natal Red Rock Hare exists in abundance in national and provincial parks and wildlife refuges within its range, and protected seasonally as a game species by Provincial Nature Conservation agencies (Duthie and Robinson 1990). It is presumed to also occur on private protected areas and conservancies (Matthee et al. 2016). The main intervention at this stage is research to quantify potential threats, area of occupancy, population size and trends. Until such data have been collected, no specific conservation interventions can be proposed (Matthee et al. 2016). Sustainable utilization is recommended, as well as research in the areas of life history, genetics, and survey studies (Matthee et al. 2004).

rationale: Jameson’s Red Rock Hare is widespread and common within its range, and though some decline has occurred and continues, it is not severe and there are greater than 10,000 mature individuals in the wild (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004). Despite being widespread, it is patchily distributed within its distribution due to their restriction to areas of rocky habitat. While no estimate of population size or trend is available for this species, it is inferred to have a large population, given its extent of occurrence (Matthee et al. 2016). However, while its rocky habitats are largely inaccessible and unlikely to be transformed, increasing hunting pressure (inferred from expanding human settlements and anecdotal reports of decline), loss of foraging areas from agricultural expansion, and habitat degradation from overgrazing may be causing local declines and possible extinctions (Matthee et al. 2016).
habitat: Jameson’s Red Rock Hare occurs in rocky areas on hill or mountainsides with grass or scrub vegetation (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Tracts of unsuitable habitat cause natural fragmentation (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Much like the other members of the red rock hare family, this species is a medium-sized rabbit-like hare with thick, dense woolly pelage typically cinnamon-rufous in color. Where its range overlaps with that of Hewitt’s Red Rock Hare, it tends to occur in the drier low-lying mountain slopes where there are many jumbled boulders and rock crevices, whereas Hewitt’s is found at higher altitudes with fewer boulders and crevices and higher rainfall (Happold 2013). Generally nocturnal and solitary in nature, they can sometimes be seen in small groups when grazing. The diet consists of sprouting grasses (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Also characteristic of the genus are their flattened round dung pellets deposited on flat spaces amongst rocks (Lynch 1983). They use latrines established away from their resting sites. Rock hares are unique in their ability to run and jump over rocks and can run up steep rock faces to reach crevices when fleeing. Key vegetation types are those typical of mountainous and rocky terrain, including Afromontane and Afroalpine areas. This species breeds year round and has one to two young per litter (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
threats: This species is hunted for food and sport (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004). Hunting pressure is thought to be more severe in areas of high-density human settlements. For example, in the southern part of Jameson’s Red Rock Hare’s eastern range, intensive urbanization (Johannesburg, Pretoria, and surrounds) is likely to be impacting on local subpopulations (Matthee et al. 2016). Some decrease in habitat quality has occurred due to commercial plantations of pine and eucalyptus within this rock hare’s habitat (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004). The replacement of natural vegetation by forestry plantations in Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces will presumably reduce habitat quality for Jameson’s Red Rock Hare (sensu Armstrong and van Hensbergen 1996). Since the 1900s, 21-50% of total habitat has been lost and future loss is predicted to be greater than 20% until the year 2102 (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004).
population: Jameson’s Red Rock Hare is fairly common throughout its distribution (Duthie and Robinson 1990), but it may be experiencing local declines due to encroachment of human settlements and subsequent hunting pressure. Happold (2013) describes it as being very common in the granite hills of Matopos Hills in Zimbabwe and the sandstone formations of eastern Botswana. There is no evidence of gene flow between the two isolated populations (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004). Greater than 10,000 individuals exist in South Africa (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004). Future decline in total population is predicted to be 20% or more over an unspecified length of time (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004).
range: Jameson’s Red Rock Hare was first described from Observatory Hill, in what is now almost the center of Johannesburg. It occurs in northeastern South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, western Mozambique, and a separate, isolated population exists marginally in western Angola to central Namibia (Duthie and Robinson 1990; Happold 2013). There is no reason to suspect gene flow between the two isolated populations, which are some 900km apart, and taxonomic resolution is required. The extent of occurrence is greater than 20,000km², and the area of occupancy is greater than 2,000km² (Matthee, Collins and Keith 2004).
useTrade: It is likely to be fairly important in subsistence communities where they are easily obtained. Maliehe (1993) specifically mentioned rock hares as being an important bush meat item in Lesotho and in Zululand, but this is likely to be true throughout its range. As a fairly slow-moving species, they are easily hunted with dogs. At night, they have a tendency to freeze when chanced upon in spotlights and can be easily shot or captured in nets (B. Wilson pers. obs.). During the day, it is also possible to hunt them in their refuges, using a coiled piece of barbed wire that hooks and drags the animal out of its shelter (B. Wilson pers. obs.). While having a particularly warm and thick fur, pelts from these species are prone to hairslip and do not cure well, making them unsuitable for hardwearing fur items.
conservationActions: In South Africa, Jameson’s Red Rock Hare occurs in national and provincial parks and wildlife refuges, and is seasonally protected by Provincial Nature Conservation agencies as a game species (Duthie and Robinson 1990). It is presumed to also occur on private protected areas and conservancies (Matthee et al. 2016). The main intervention at this stage is research to quantify potential threats, area of occupancy, population size and trends. Until such data have been collected, no specific conservation interventions can be proposed (Matthee et al. 2016).

rationale: Smith’s Red Rock Hare is a widespread species, but patchily distributed due to their restriction to areas of rocky habitat (Matthee et al. 2016). While no estimates of population size or trend are available for this species, it is inferred to have a large population, given its extent of occurrence (Matthee et al. 2016). However, while their rocky habitats are largely inaccessible and unlikely to be transformed, increasing hunting pressure (inferred from expanding human settlements and anecdotal reports of decline), loss of foraging areas from agricultural expansion, and habitat degradation from overgrazing may be causing local declines and possible extinctions. This species is easily hunted and thought to be substantially utilized for subsistence or sport hunting (Matthee et al. 2016). For example, anecdotal reports from the Northern Cape suggest Smith’s Red Rock Hare has declined over the past 30 years. Emerging threats to Smith’s Red Rock Hare may be increased competition with Rock Hyraxes (Procavia capensis) following the decline of raptors in the region, grazing pressure from goats and sheep, and increased predation from mesocarnivores due to lack of holistic management (Matthee et al. 2016). Population size in South Africa is greater than 10,000 mature individuals and this species is common within portions of its distribution in South Africa (Matthee et al. 2004). The species is confirmed as Least Concern.
habitat: Smith’s Red Rock Hare occurs on rocky slopes and the tops of rocky outcrops of mountains and hills, where grass or scrub vegetation occurs (Duthie and Robinson 1990, Matthee et al. 2004). Areas of unsuitable habitat cause some natural habitat fragmentation (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Their distribution range is typically at lower elevations than Hewitt’s Red Rock Hares (P. saundersiae) (Happold 2013). Nests are characteristically built in shallow excavations and lined with fur from the mother’s belly and flanks over a grass and stick structure. Breeding is restricted to warmer months during which time a female could produce three to four litters. Litter size is one to two young (Duthie and Robinson 1990) and the young are born naked. Gestation time is 35-45 days (Happold 2013). The diet consists of sprouting grasses (Duthie and Robinson 1990).
threats: Hunting of Smith’s Red Rock Hare poses a threat to the species (Matthee et al. 2004). Habitat loss due to building houses on rocky outcrops also occurs, but this is not currently considered a serious threat (Matthee et al. 2004). Additionally, agricultural and rural settlement expansion may be increasing incidental predation on rock hares by domestic dogs. Sheep farming is also impacting Smith’s Red Rock Hare. In areas where there is intensive sheep farming, the species may face grazing competition (B. Wilson pers. obs.). Additionally, as a consequence of available food resources, many sheep-farming areas also report higher than normal rates of predators such as Black-backed Jackals (Canis mesomelas) and Caracals (Caracal caracal), which is exacerbated by indiscriminate and non-holistic predator control methods (Minnie et al. 2016). These predators pose a threat to the rock hares when at abnormally high numbers. There has been a greater than 20% loss of habitat since the 1900's and future loss is predicted to continue at the same rate until the year 2022 (Matthee et al. 2004).
population: This species is characterized as abundant in the Springbok and Kuruman areas of its distribution (Matthee et al. 2004). The majority of anecdotal reports collected from farmers across the Northern Cape report a decline in numbers over the past 30 years (B. Wilson unpubl. data.). It has a population size of greater than 10,000 in South Africa (Matthee et al. 2004, Happold 2013), but verification is needed. In South Africa, population decline of greater than 10% is predicted to occur by the year 2022 (Matthee et al. 2004). There is no data regarding the status of the east African distribution.
range: Smith’s Red Rock Hare occurs in South Africa (Free State, North-West, and Northern Cape provinces) and in a separate population in southwestern Kenya, central Tanzania, eastern Zambia, and Malawi (Duthie and Robinson 1990, Boitani et al. 1999, Matthee et al. 2004). The two populations are separated by 1,200 km and thus require taxonomic resolution (Happold 2013). Although previously thought to no longer occur in Namibia (Bronner et al. 2003, Happold 2013), there is one confirmed record from Keetmanshoop (C. Matthee unpubl. data). Field surveys are needed to determine the continued existence, extent, and viability of the Namibian population. The species is restricted to rocky outcrops, so the exact area of occupancy is probably lower than indicated from its wide extent of occurrence. Much of the habitat in the region of the distribution map is characterized by isolated rocky outcrops. The extent of occurrence is greater than 20,000 km², and the area of occupancy is greater than 2,000 km² (Matthee et al. 2004).
useTrade: The main threat to rock hares is hunting, both for bushmeat and for sport. Hunting pressure is thought to be more severe in areas of high-density human settlements. Sport hunting with dogs may also be impacting this species. Hunting is suspected to be causing local declines (and possibly local extinctions), but it is uncertain whether there is a net decline in the population. As a fairly slow-moving species, they are easily hunted with dogs. At night, they have a tendency to freeze when chanced upon in spotlights and can be easily shot or captured in nets (B. Wilson pers. obs.). During the day, it is also possible to hunt them in their refuges, using a coiled piece of barbed wire that hooks and drags the animal out of its shelter (B. Wilson pers. obs.). While having a particularly warm and thick fur, pelts from these species are prone to hairslip and do not cure well, making them unsuitable for hardwearing fur items.
conservationActions: In South Africa, Smith’s Red Rock Hare occurs in national and provincial parks and wildlife refuges, and is seasonally protected by Provincial Nature Conservation agencies as a game species (Duthie and Robinson 1990). Sustainable utilization is recommended, as well as research in the areas of status surveys and life history (Matthee et al. 2004). Long-term monitoring should be established to quantify subpopulation trends. Few data exist for the east African distribution and research should be conducted in the areas of threats, population and habitat status. Taxonomic revision is also suggested for this species.

rationale: The Swamp Rabbit (Sylvilagus aquaticus) is a species with a wide distribution, and though the area of suitable habitat is declining in most areas due to human development of land, population viability analyses suggest long term persistence (Robinson et al. 2016). It occurs in many protected areas (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2006). The species is confirmed Least Concern.Swamp Rabbits are considered endangered in the state of Indiana and a species of special concern in Missouri and South Carolina (Indiana Department of Natural Resources 2017, Missouri Department of Conservation 2018, Nielsen and Berkman 2018).
habitat: Swamp Rabbits occur in swampy, lowland, or river bottom areas, always near water (Chapman and Feldhamer 1981). They are always associated with water and will swim to escape predators and hunters (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). In Illinois, bottomland hardwood forest habitat is preferred, as are areas of brushy habitat and canopy cover (Zollner, Smith and Brennan 2000a, Scharine et al. 2009, Scharine et al. 2011, Berkman et al. 2018). Use of early successional bottomland habitats suggests that restoration efforts could help maintain populations (Crawford et al. 2018). Because of their habitat preferences, Swamp Rabbits have been suggested as an indicator of quality bottomland forest habitat (Hillard et al. 2017). Despite their preference for lowlands, adjacent upland areas may provide important habitat during seasonal flooding (Vale and Kissell 2010). Radiotracking studies suggest that Swamp Rabbits avoid open areas, such as residential areas, agricultural areas, and roads (Crawford et al. 2018). Swamp Rabbit occupancy and detectability increase in larger tracts of habitat (Fantz et al. 2017). In timber habitat Swamp Rabbit density is around 2 rabbits/ha (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).Swamp Rabbits prefer a diet of sedges and also feed on grasses and forbs (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).Females have litter sizes from one to six, and produce two to five litters per year (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Gestation is 35-40 days (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998) and females reach sexual maturity at 152 days of age.
threats: Swamp Rabbits are a favorite game species, though their speed, ability to swim, and habitat preferences offers some protection from hunters and predators (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). Hunting is regulated by individual state wildlife agencies (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). While hunting is not a major threat to stable populations (Nielsen and Berkman 2018), Swamp Rabbits appear to have a sensitivity to harvest in the late season (winter) (Bond et al. 2004). Population viability modeling suggests that changes in fecundity and catastrophic flooding may pose the greatest risk to the species (Robinson et al. 2016).Habitat loss has been the greatest cause of decline of Swamp Rabbits. In Missouri in 1973, a decline of suitable habitat from 850,000 ha to 40,000 ha was recorded over the previous 103 years (Korte and Fredrickson 1977). The habitat was converted from forest to cropland. Changes to waterways and resulting flooding also negatively impact the availability of habitat for Swamp Rabbits (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).Habitat fragmentation is an issue associated with human encroachment upon Swamp Rabbit habitat. Many Swamp Rabbit populations exist on small tracts of private property, impeding dispersal and creating difficulties for management (Scheibe and Henson 2003).Flooding of wet forested areas has a negative impact on Swamp Rabbit populations, but floods in some areas induce dispersal (Scheibe and Henson 2003).
population: Swamp Rabbits are an important game species in much of their range and are hunted for meat, fur, and sport. They are known to be locally abundant in some areas but appear to be declining in others (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Barbour et al. 2001, Scheibe and Henson 2003). Few studies have been conducted to determine the abundance or decline of Swamp Rabbits.In Missouri, the overall area of suitable habitat is decreasing, but there are still several viable populations within the known range, and there is some indication that new populations have recently been naturally established, possibly due to dispersal facilitated by flooding (Scheibe and Henson 2003). In Louisiana, there are large tracts of suitable habitat and it is an important game species (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).In South Carolina, the Rabbit Hunter Survey data from 2016-2017 show that there is an increase in rabbits jumped/hour, 1.35 (2007-2008) to 1.58 (2016-2017), but of the rabbits harvested only 1.72% were Swamp Rabbits (South Carolina Rabbit Hunter Survey, 2016-2017).Three population viability analyses (PVA) have provided insight into local population trends of Swamp Rabbits at the northern fringe of their range. In southern Illinois, the PVA suggested a 0% chance of quasi-extinction (90% metapopulation decline) of Swamp Rabbits within 25 (or even 50) years. Changes in fecundity values and the effects of catastrophic flooding had the greatest effect on extinction risk, and changes in no other parameter yielded any appreciable impact. Removing the largest patches from the population increased the 25-year risk of extinction to 4%, whereas any other modifications to the habitat did not change the extinction risk (Robinson et al. 2016). Roy Nielsen et al. (2008) found southern Indiana Swamp Rabbits existed as a metapopulation that appeared to be stable. Metapopulation dynamics were best characterized as being stationary, but habitat area was an important factor in extinction rates, occupied patches were significantly larger than unoccupied patches. In Missouri, more than 50% of available habitat patches were predicted to contain rabbits after 1000 years, both patch area and patch isolation were significantly related to patch occupancy and play key roles in the incidence of Swamp Rabbits (Pajda-De La O et al. 2013).
range: Swamp Rabbits occur in the southeastern United States in eastern Texas and Oklahoma, most of Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, the western tip of the Florida panhandle, western Georgia, western Tennessee, far western Kentucky, the northwestern tip of South Carolina, the southwestern tip of North Carolina, far southern Illinois, southwestern Indiana, and the south sections of Missouri (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).There are two recognized subspecies of Swamp Rabbits: S. a. littoralis, which occurs in a narrow fragment of habitat along the southern gulf coastal from Mississippi to Texas, and S. a. aquaticus, which occupies the northern section of the range and is more common in dense forest (Chapman and Feldhamer 1981, Chapman and Ceballos 1990).
useTrade: The species is hunted for sport, meat and fur.
conservationActions: Hunting of Swamp Rabbits is managed individually by state wildlife agencies (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Because Swamp Rabbits occurs in many instances on small tracts of private land, management becomes problematic (Scheibe and Henson 2003). Increasing the area of continuous tracts of suitable habitat may be key to Swamp Rabbit conservation (Scheibe and Henson 2003, Fantz et al. 2017).Swamp Rabbits are currently found in three managed areas in Missouri: Mingo National Wildlife Refuge (NWR), Duck Creek Conservation Area, and Donaldson Point Conservation Area (Scheibe and Henson 2003). It also occurs in White River NWR in Arkansas, Panther Swamp NWR, Mathews Brake NWR, Hillside NWR, and Morgan Brake NWR in Mississippi, Atchafalaya NWR in Louisiana, Deep Fork NWR in Oklahoma, and Chickasaw NWR in Tennessee (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2006).

rationale: The Desert Cottontail is confirmed as Least Concern, it is widespread and common, occurs in a large contiguous area, is a habitat and dietary generalist, and none of the subspecies are known to be significantly declining. However, a recent survey of long-term harvest information based on data from all western United States state game and fish agencies indicated a consistent downward trend in the numbers of all western United States cottontails (primarily S. floridanus, S. audubonii, S. nuttallii – these species tend not to be separated in agency databases, but the Desert Cottontail is a major component of these databases (Brown et al. 2018).
habitat: The Desert Cottontail inhabits arid and mountain regions from woodlands, grasslands to deserts at low elevations (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Laundré 2018). They appear to avoid midday heat and are active in the twilight hours of dawn and dusk as well as at night (Hoffmeister 1986). They prefer habitat with a high density of cover, rarely venturing out into more open areas (Laundré 2018).The breeding season begins in December or January for a length of seven to nine months. Mean litter sizes vary among populations, between 2.6-3.6 young per litter, which is small for the genus (Chapman and Willner 1978).The diet of the Desert Cottontail varies depending on habitat and cover. Forbs are the most dominant forage type, followed by grasses and then shrubs (Laundré 2018).Early evidence indicated that the Desert Cottontail is short-lived and one study found that no rabbit lived past the age of 19 months, while most rabbits lived less than one year (Chapman and Willner 1978).
threats: The Desert Cottontail is widespread and common in many parts of its range, including Mexico, but cattle grazing and habitat loss due to land clearing may affect some populations (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Brown et al. 2018). Predation by invasive alien species, including domestic dogs and cats, presents a threat in some areas populated by humans (Chapman and Willner 1978).The Desert Cottontail is hunted for sport and local subsistence and as an important game species it is managed by individual states in the USA, where it is not considered to be under threat (Brown et al. 2018).Human-induced fire may represent a threat for some populations.
population: Little specific data regarding population density and abundance exists, but the Desert Cottontail is known to be common throughout most of its range in Mexico and is not considered to be threatened by state game agencies in the USA (Brown et al. 2018). A report in 1947 showed that a population in the San Joaquin Experimental Range in California had a population density that fluctuated over three years (1939-41) of 4.7, 1.6, and 2.9 individuals per hectare (Chapman and Willner 1978). A study in northeastern Colorado showed a density of 16.3 individuals per hectare (Flinders and Hansen 1973).In the Reserva de la Biosfera de Mapimi in Durango, Mexico, the Desert Cottontail population is declining (Portales 2004).
range: The Desert Cottontail occurs in the western USA and north and central Mexico. In the USA the western boundary is the Pacific Ocean and in the east it barely extends into the Great Plains. The far northern extent of the range almost reaches Canada in eastern Montana and southwestern North Dakota, extending south through Wyoming, western South Dakota, Nebraska, and Kansas, the panhandle of Oklahoma, and western Texas. Except for extreme mountainous areas, the range includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, south and central Utah, southern Nevada, and all but northern California (Laundré 2018). In Mexico, the range includes all of Baja California, Baja California Sur, most of Sonora and Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo Leon, western Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosi, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, eastern Durango, northern Sinaloa, north-eastern Jalisco, northern Guanajuato, northern Queretaro, central Hidalgo, Tlaxcala, north-central Puebla, and a small area in western Veracruz (Vargas Cuenca and Cervantes 2005).The Desert Cottontail occurs from below sea level in Death Valley, California, to 1,800 m or higher (Chapman and Willner 1978, Laundré 2018).
useTrade: It is hunted for food and sport.
