conservationActions: The Desert Cottontail is managed a game species in the USA by individual state wildlife agencies. None of the subspecies are known to be under threat and no new conservation measures are needed, although Brown et al. (2018) stress that habitat management plans to increase shrub cover are needed, as well as curtailing potential detrimental impacts of agricultural chemicals in the range of the species.

rationale: This is essentially a new assessment, considering the Tapetí to be a highly restricted form rather than to cover most of South America, due to refinement of Sylvilagus species limits across South America (Ruedas et al.2017, Ruedas and Smith 2018). The known geographic range of the species is confined to the northern portion of the Atlantic Forest Biome in the Pernambuco Endemism Center (CEPE). Ecological niche modelling of this species suggests that its available habitat is restricted to between 500-700 km² (Ruedas et al. 2017, Ruedas and Smith 2018). This region suffers from ongoing habitat loss, high levels of fragmentation, and increased development, aspects that further restrict the habitat available for occupancy by the Tapetí. The CEPE has lost 94.4% of its forest cover, and most forest fragments are less than 10 ha (Mendes Pontes et al. 2016). The most comprehensive study of all mammals in the region found that all large mammals were regionally extinct, and of extant species the Tapetí was one of the three least abundant with sighting rates below a detectable level (Mendes Pontes et al.2016). Thus a conservative estimate of the current area of occupancy (AOO) is less than 400 km², and likely far less. Thus the Tapetí appears to be Endangered (EN) following criteria B2ab(ii,iii).
habitat: No dedicated studies have been conducted on this newly identified species within its geographic range.
threats: Habitat loss by deforestation and human settlement poses a threat to this species, 94.4% of the forest cover in the geographic range of this species has been lost (Mendes Pontes et al. 2016).
population: The only recent attempt to measure the population size of the Tapetí determined that their density was so low that sighting rates fell below a detectable level (Mendes Pontes et al. 2016).
range: The Tapetí, as currently described, occupies the Pernambuco Endemism Center within a narrow band along Atlantic coastal Brazil in the northern portion of the Atlantic Forest Biome. Ecological niche modeling of this species suggests that its occupied range (AOO) is restricted to between 500-700 km². It is unknown whether the species range will be found to extend farther south within the Atlantic Forest Biome (Ruedas et al. 2017, Ruedas and Smith 2018).
conservationActions: Protection and restoration of tropical forest cover are needed to conserve this species.

rationale: The Eastern Cottontail is confirmed as Least Concern; it is the most widely distributed species of Sylvilagus and is abundant throughout its range (Chapman, Hockman and Ojeda 1980, Nielsen and Berkman 2018). This species has been introduced in regions of North America and Europe, and is expanding its range by displacing other Leporids (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).
habitat: The historical habitat of Eastern Cottontails was diverse, including deserts, swamps, glades, prairies, rain forests, boreal forests, hardwood forests, and woodlands (Chapman et al. 1980). In developed areas, they survive well in farmland, pasture, and hedgerows (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).The diet of Eastern Cottontails is variable, depending on the type of habitat and the season, including woody plants in the dormant season and herbaceous plants in the growing season (Chapman et al. 1980). Breeding season varies depending on elevation and latitude, with breeding activity beginning later at higher elevations and northern latitudes (Chapman et al. 1980). Average gestation time is 28 days and size at birth ranges from 3.06-5.06 cm (Lorenzo and Cervantes 2005). Litter sizes are 3-5 with 3-4 litters per year (Lorenzo and Cervantes 2005). Total length ranges from 33.5-48.5 cm (Lorenzo and Cervantes 2005).
threats: Although abundant, subpopulations of Eastern Cottontails are at risk human perturbation, habitat change, predation from invasive alien species, and from hunting pressure (sport and local subsistence) throughout its range. In some locations it is threatened by livestock competition and habitat fragmentation.
population: Eastern Cottontails are abundant, widespread, and highly effective colonizers. New populations of Eastern Cottontails have been successfully introduced outside their range, and in some cases, they have been known to displace native Leporids, including the New England Cottontail (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Litvaitis et al. 2008, Nielsen and Berkman 2018). Peak densities have been recorded at 20 individuals/ha, but they are more commonly found in densities of less than 10/ha (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).In Virginia, the population has declined over the past 50 years or so. This decline may be due to the loss of early successional habitat that is being turned into farmland and is exacerbated by an increase in the cottontail's predators. In most years, populations of adult cottontails experience 60-80% mortality, but mortality rates in some populations can be as high as 95% (Nielsen and Berkman 2018). However, in areas where there is good habitat there are still abundant populations (Virginia Department of Game and Inland Fisheries 2008).
range: The Eastern Cottontail is widely distributed throughout the USA (eastern USA east of the Rocky Mountains, portions of southwest and northwest), Central America (central and eastern Mexico, southwestern Guatemala, southern Honduras, El Salvador, central Nicaragua, northwestern Costa Rica), and occurs in southern Canada (Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec) and the northern part of South America (Colombia and Venezuela) (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).Eastern Cottontails can survive in diverse habitats, allowing the range to spread quickly (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). They have more recently been introduced to Italy and other areas outside of their historical range (Nielsen and Berkman 2018).
useTrade: The species is hunted for food and sport hunting.
conservationActions: The Eastern Cottontail is the most important regulated game animal in the USA. While Eastern Cottontails have declined since the mid 20th Century due to agricultural changes (Mankin and Warner 1999a,b), they have also been introduced widely outside their original range (Nielsen and Berkman 2018). They can present a threat to sympatric species, such as the New England Cottontail (S. transitionalis) in north-eastern USA (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Litvaitis et al. 2008).Research is needed regarding taxonomy, distribution, population size, and to determine how the Eastern Cottontail affects other species.

rationale: The Mountain Cottontail is confirmed as Least Concern, it is common throughout most of its range (Beever and French 2018), and does not appear to be experiencing significant decline. However, a recent survey of long-term harvest information based on data from all western United States state game and fish agencies indicated a consistent downward trend in the numbers of all western United States cottontails (primarily S. floridanus, S. audubonii, S. nuttalii – these species tend not to be separated in agency databases, Brown et al. 2018). Additionally, the Mountain Cottontail has presumably become extirpated from much of its former range in South Dakota due to displacement by the eastern cottontail, is considered vulnerable in Arizona and British Columbia, only apparently secure in New Mexico, Oregon, South Dakota, Montana, and Saskatchewan (Beever and French 2018). It is classified as secure in the remaining part of its range. Thus, while still widespread and abundant, these declines indicate that this species should be carefully monitored.
habitat: The Mountain Cottontail occurs in a variety of habitats throughout its range. In the north it primarily occupies sagebrush habitat, while in the south it occurs more frequently in forested areas (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).The Mountain Cottontail feeds on sagebrush and juniper all year where this vegetation occurs, but grasses are preferred when available in spring and summer (Chapman 1975). The breeding season is variable throughout its range (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).The habitat of the Mountain Cottontail is highly linked to escape cover, including dense brush, rock crevices, and holes in the ground. While they can be active at any time of the day, activity is highest at night or during crepuscular hours (Beever and French 2018).
threats: The Mountain Cottontail has been replaced by the Desert or Eastern Cottontail in several eastern extensions of its range (Beever and French 2018).
population: The Mountain Cottontail is a common species throughout most of its range (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). The species has a varying population density from 0.06 to 2.5 per hectare in central Oregon, where it inhabits juniper scrublands (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). In the northern (British Columbia) extension of its range densities vary from 0.23 to 0.43/ha.
range: The Mountain Cottontail occurs in the western USA in the intermountain area, from just north of the Canadian border in southern Alberta and Saskatchewan to northern New Mexico and Arizona, and from the eastern Rocky Mountains to the eastern Cascade-Sierra Nevada Range, extending north just into British Columbia (Chapman 1975, Beever and French 2018). The range of the Mountain Cottontail has been largely taken over by S. floridanus in south-eastern North Dakota (Genoways and Jones 1972). The species once extended as far east as Texas, but there it has now been replaced by the Desert Cottontail (Beever and French 2018).
useTrade: The species is utilized for food and sport.
conservationActions: The Mountain Cottontail is a common game species managed by individual state wildlife agencies, which regulate bag limits and hunting seasons, although it – along with other Sylvilagus species – tends to be declining in abundance (Brown et al. 2018).

rationale: The Appalachian Cottontail is known to be a rare species and occurs in patchy fragments throughout its range. It was listed on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species as NT – Near Threatened in 2008 (Barry and Lazell 2008). The most robust populations are in West Virginia, where habitat is decreasing due to enchroachment of exotic plants and habitat conversion, out of the 21 localities known in the state only nine have had documented sightings in the last 20 years (West Virginia Division of Natural Resources). Across the southern poritions of the range (Alabama and Georgia) the species is considered to be critically imperiled due to loss of habitat and is known from fewer than five localities in either state (Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources. 2015, Georgia Biodiversity Portal). Across the range the Appalachian Cottontail thought to be declining, but because of the lack of data regarding the status of populations of this species it is difficult to assess how severe that decline is, but at least a 25-30% in the last ten years is suspected. In light of this uncertainty, a change of status from Near Threatened to Vulnerable A2ce is not justified at this time, and new surveys on the status of this species are necessary (Barry 2018).
habitat: The Appalachian Cottontail is found at high elevations with conifers and ericaceous species in the central to southern Appalachian Mountains, mixed oak forests and early successional (recent clearcut) habitats with dense, ericaceous vegetation (Bunch et al. 1997, Chapman 1999) or blackberry thickets (Bunch et al. 1997). They have also been recorded from old growth forest with dense understory (Bunch et al. 1997, Bunch and Dye 1999). Dense understory that provides concealment and thermal cover is important (Laseter 1999). Individuals also have been observed near openings in rocky outcrops (Barry 2018).Appalachian Cottontails have been found in a patchy distribution across western North Carolina. In locations where Eastern Cottontails are present, preliminary data suggest the Appalachian Cottontail is less widespread, possibly due to competitive exclusion. Surveys in 2018 documented the species at elevations ranging from 1000 to 1800 m in varied habitats, including spruce-fir forest, northern hardwood forest, oak forest, cove forest, and shrub-dominated balds (Leisl Erb, pers. comm.).They feed on ferns, grasses, forbs, shrubs, and, unique among cottontails, conifer needles (Chapman 1999). Early March through early September is the breeding season for this species, and breeding is synchronous (Chapman 1999, Barry 2018). Gestation is 28 days and an average of 24 young/female are born annually (Chapman 1999).
threats: Threats to the Appalachian Cottontail include:Destruction, fragmentation, and maturation of habitat (Barbour and Litvaitis 1993). Urban and suburban development.Indirect encroachment on habitat by Eastern Cottontails (S. floridanus), which thrive better in developed areas and require less cover than Appalachian Cottontails (Barbour and Litvaitis 1993).Indiscriminate hunting may result from lack of knowledge by sportsmen or because Appalachian Cottontails are phenotypically similar to Eastern Cottontails (Chapman 1999). Lack of education on existence, biology, and habitat requirements of this species.
population: Appalachian Cottontail populations are highly fragmented, and in much of the range the species is considered rare, except in portions of eastern Tennessee and the Monongahela National Forest in West Virginia (Laseter 1999), and western North Carolina (www.dpr.ncparks.gov/mammals/view.php?species_id=34 ). Densities at Dolly Sods, West Virginia, reached a high of 0.7 individuals/ha, and densities in eastern Tennessee reached 0.8 individuals/ha (Laseter 1999). In the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, on the Tennessee side, only three records exist and none have been recorded since 1960.
range: The Appalachian Cottontail occurs in discontinuous upland patches (commonly 570-1,300 m, but with one report as low as 274 m) in the eastern United States including central Pennsylvania, western Maryland, western Virginia, eastern West Virginia, eastern Tennessee, eastern Kentucky, western North Carolina, northwestern South Carolina, northern Georgia, and northern Alabama including along the Interior Low Plateau (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998, Campbell et al. 2010).The type locality is Dolly Sods, West Virginia (Tucker and Grant counties) in Monongahela National Forest, which is an important source population.
useTrade: The species is hunted for sport, meat, and fur.
conservationActions: Conservation measures proposed to prevent the decline of the Appalachian Cottontail include:Conservation of critical habitat and establishment and management of “Important Mammal Areas” (as in Pennsylvania) containing known populations, with appropriate publicity and public education programs.Additional surveying and population monitoring.Research on nest sites, dispersal, habitat, use of corridors, response to climactic change and stochastic events, effects of sport hunting, competition with other lagomorphs (i.e. Eastern Cottontail and Snowshoe Hare), and response to invasive vegetative species.Development and implementation of state management plans.Public education and awareness programs, particularly to educate the sportsmen public about the habitats that the Appalachian Cottontail favors, to distinguish from the habitat that the game species Eastern Cottontails prefer, as the two species are easily confused (Chapman 1999).

rationale: The Brush Rabbit is abundant throughout most of its range, and most populations do not appear to be experiencing significant decline (Chapman and Ceballos 1990).The subspecies S. b. riparius has been listed as an endangered species by the state of California, USA (State of California 1994) and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Williams et al. 2004) due to decline primarily caused by habitat degradation, wildfire, and flood (Kelly 2018a,b). Additionally, three Mexican forms appear to be at risk: 1) S. b. exiguus is considered threatened and in need of immediate conservation actions, its current situation is unknown and it is probably extinct (Lorenzo et al. 2013); 2) it is possible that the southern form S. b. peninsularis may be extinct due to anthropogenic activities (Lorenzo et al. 2013); and 3) S. b. cerrosensis from Cedros Island, off the west coast of Baja California Sur is under intense pressure from predation by feral dogs, it is listed in danger of extinction in the Official Norm NOM-059 of Mexico (SEMARNAT 2010, Cortés-Calva el al. 2013, Lorenzo et al. 2014, Lorenzo-Monterrubio et al. 2018, Álvarez-Castañeda and Lorenzo 2016).
habitat: The Brush Rabbit requires dense brush cover, occupying disjunctive bramble clumps, with the size of the clumps affecting home range size and suitability for occupation (Chapman 1974). Home ranges are small (less than 2,000 m2) and are dependent upon habitat uniformity (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). The bramble habitat contains runways and occasionally burrows formed by other species (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Their diet consists predominantly of grasses, but it will consume alternative vegetation when seasonally available (Chapman 1974). The breeding season for the Brush Rabbit varies from north to south, but appears to be uniform in length (Chapman 1974). In California, the species breeds from December to May or June, and in Oregon between February and August (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Litter size varies regionally, with an annual mean of 2.87 in Oregon, 3.50 in north and central California, and 4.00 in west-central California (Chapman 1974). Fecundity of the Brush Rabbit is lower than other Sylvilagus species, producing about 15 young annually (Chapman 1974). Gestation time is approximately 27 days (Cervantes et al. 2005).The subspecies S. b. riparius occupies both old-growth riparian forest, dominated by Valley Oak (Quercus lobata) and riparian communities dominated by thickets of willows (Salix spp.), wild roses (Rosa spp.), blackberries (Rubus spp.), and other successional trees and shrubs and when available dense tall stands of herbaceous plants adjacent to patches of riparian shrubs in the northern San Joaquin Valley, California. S. b. riparius stays close to dense stands of vegetation into which it retreats for escape, resting and nesting. They do not normally burrow or use burrows (Williams and Basey 1986, Williams 1988, Williams and Hamilton 2002). S. b. riparius eats a great variety of woody and herbaceous plants, preferring green foliage of shrubs, grasses and forbs. Much of its foraging is concentrated at the edge between thickets of woody plants and more open ground with herbaceous plants. A favored habitat is willow thickets along stream banks (Orr 1940, Chapman 1974, Kelt et al. 2014).The area of highest abundance of the Cedros Island Brush Rabbit, S. b. cerrosensis is characterized by xeric scrubland vegetation with dominance of chamizo (Atriplex spp.), in association with sacrocaule and coastal desert scrub in the southwest part of the island composed by Limberbush (Jatropha cuneata), Oregano (Lippia palmeri), Fourwing Saltbush (Atriplex canescens), agaves (Agave shawii, A. sebastiana) and other shrubs (Lorenzo et al. 2014, Lorenzo-Monterrubio et al. 2018). S. b. cerrosensis shares its habitat with other endemic mammals, such as the San Diego Pocket Mouse (Chaetodipus fallax anthonyi), Bryant’s Woodrat (Neotoma bryanti bryanti), the Cedros Island Cactus Mouse (Peromyscus fraterculus cedrosensis), and Cedros Island Mule Deer (Odocoileus hemionus cerrosensis) (Lorenzo et al. 2014, Lorenzo-Monterrubio et al. 2018). All the records of S. bachmani south of 30°N, not including the insular population (Cedros Island) are associated with mesic vegetation habitats, some of which are oases (Cervantes et al. 1999, Lorenzo et al. 2013).
threats: Hunting for food and the clearing of land for human settlements pose a threat to Brush Rabbits, but the extent and severity are not quantified (but see select Mexican subspecies below).Decline in numbers and threats of extinction of subspecies S. b. riparius stem principally from actions involved in developments of irrigated agriculture in the San Joaquin Valley of California. Foremost of these developments were stream impoundment, channelization of streams on the valley floor and the San Joaquin River Delta, and clearing and cultivation of natural communities. Riparian communities in the San Joaquin Valley have been reduced to about 1% of their historical extent, are found almost entirely within the levees of channelized streams. Most existing patches have been extensively degraded by wood cutting, livestock, invasion of exotic species, greater levels of flooding within levees, and lack of natural riverine processes (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 1998, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2000).Principal existing threats to S. b. riparius can be summarized in order of importance as: 1) stochastic environmental processes, wildfire and flood; 2) additional habitat loss and degradation due to urbanization and conversion to agriculture; 3) increased predation from domestic and feral cats and dogs due to urban development adjacent to existing inhabited sites; and 4) genetic and demographic stochasticity in small populations. While all of these are proximate threats, wildfire and flood are probably the most severe threats to the population at Caswell MSP. A less imminent threat is natural successional processes that are reducing habitat quality. Because the park has multiuse objectives, and because up-stream impoundments have greatly modified the natural flooding regime, secondary successional patches, especially those caused by scouring floods, are disappearing from the Park. The changes are noticeable and may be associated with the decline in S. b. riparius within the park (Williams and Hamilton 2002).For the South Delta metapopulation of S. b. riparius, wildfire is a serious threat to each subpopulation, but would unlikely affect all subpopulations simultaneously. Flooding poses a more immediate metapopulation threat, because the entire area is approximately at sea level or below, rivers are channelized, and there are few or no refugia above flood level. Over the past several decades there have been numerous breaks in levees and widespread flooding. The most recent were in 1997, 2006, and 2011. Typically, the only areas not flooded are built-up areas for railroads, levee tops, multilane highways and other developed sites. Likely these areas will be inundated at some time in the future when flooding is greater than it has been in recent decades. Urbanization also is viewed as an imminent threat because most of the known populations are adjacent to areas undergoing development planning, with construction slated to begin within 1-10 years. However, this threat may be mitigated by appropriate design and management of conservation lands set aside for Brush Rabbits and other organisms (Williams and Hamilton 2002).The re-introduced population on the San Joaquin River NWR, like the populations at Caswell MSP and South Delta, is threatened by wildfire and flood, but major conservation actions to mitigate impacts of the flooding have been implemented at the refuge. See below.S. b. cerrosensis from Cedros Island, off the west coast of Baja California Sur is under intense pressure from predation by feral dogs (Cortes-Calva et al. 2013, Álvarez-Castañeda and Lorenzo 2016). On Cedros Island there is a population of 2,696 inhabitants, whose main activity is obtaining salt from the salt flats of Guerrero Negro (INEGI 2010). There are vast areas covered with organic (lobster shells) and inorganic (glass bottles, metal material) garbage. Additionally, feral cats (Felis sylvestris) and feral dogs (Canis lupus) in large numbers occupy also the habitat where S. b. cerrosensis occurs. S. b. cerrosensis was abundant about 20 years ago, however poaching has been excessive and reduced the rabbit population to a situation that is currently critical (Lorenzo et al. 2014).S. b. peninsularis may be extinct or close to extinct due to anthropogenic activities – the widespread building of infrastructure to support a growing tourist industry, using all the water of the river for the urban development, creating more desert areas in which the Desert Cottontail (Sylvilagus audubonii) is more common (Lorenzo et al. 2013).S. b. exiguus from the central desert of the Baja California peninsula has always been rare and now may be declining due the process of desertification in the peninsula, in which the mesic environment has been more optimal for desert species such as the Desert Cottontail and Black-tailed Jackrabbit (Lepus californicus).
population: Except for the Riparian Brush Rabbit (subspecies riparius) which is state (California) and federally listed as endangered (Williams et al. 2004), and the forms S. b. cerrosensis on Cedros Island, and S. b. exiguus and S. b. peninsularis on the Baja California peninsula, the Brush Rabbit is considered common where it is known to exist, throughout Oregon, California, and Baja California (Chapman and Ceballos 1990, Kelly 2018a).The S. b. riparius population at Caswell Memorial State Park in San Joaquin County, California, USA, was statistically estimated in 1993, when there were 241 rabbits (approximate 95% confidence interval = 170-608) (Williams 1993). Similar censuses were conducted in 1997-2004, resulting in capture of 0 (1997) to 16 (2002) rabbits. Capture rates in the best year (2002) were only 27% of that of 1993, and captures and recaptures were too few in any one year since 1993 to use capture-recapture population models to meaningfully estimate population size (Williams et al. 2004).Population censuses for the S. b. riparius South Delta metapopulation have not been conducted because of restrictions on activities on private land. However, capture rates for short-term assessments of presence and to capture breeders for a controlled propagation program suggested that this metapopulation have remained at fairly high densities since its discovery in 1998. Capture rates for the South Delta metapopulation varied from 127% to 626% of the capture rate of the Caswell MSP population in 1993. The South Delta population probably consists of about 300-600 rabbits at peaks in population cycles).Censuses have also not been conducted for the re-introduced population of S. b. riparius on the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge. However, visual and camera surveys suggest that the population is quite robust and now reaches into the thousands when conditions are optimal—due to the quality and quantity of available habitat.In 2012 the population density of S. b. cerrosensis was estimated to be 1.21 individuals/km² and the number of individuals estimated as 145 in an area of 120.7 km² (Lorenzo et al. 2014).
range: The Brush Rabbit is distributed along the Pacific coast of North America. It reaches the Columbia River in the north (Oregon-Washington border) and in the south it extends to the southern tip of Baja California. It extends east from the Pacific Ocean to the western Sierra Nevada mountain range (Chapman 1974, Kelly 2018). It occupies an elevational range of 0-2,070 m (Chapman 1974).The subspecies S. b. riparius occurs only in Caswell Memorial State Park (MSP) on the Stanislaus River, and the South Delta area of the San Joaquin River, including Paradise Cut and Tom Paine Slough. The park size is 253 acres, and population on the South Delta occurs on privately owned land (Williams and Hamilton 2002). Even though there is other ideal habitat for S. b. riparius in MSP, they are unable to reach it because there is no connecting habitat above flood level in MSP (Sandoval, Williams, and Colliver 2006).In Caswell Memorial State Park, Stanislaus River, San Joaquin County, California, USA, S. b. riparius occurs in about 90% of the park's 102 ha when populations are high, but about 20-40% of the Park at other times (Williams 1988, 1993).The South Delta population of S. b. riparius, in the vicinity of Mossdale and Lathrop, San Joaquin County, CA, USA, exists on about 122 ha of private land within an area of about 2,927 ha. Populations are found along Paradise Cut, Tom Paine Slough, Grantline Canal, and the San Joaquin River. Rabbits also are found along the narrow right-of-ways of two railroads running through the area. Habitat for S. b. riparius is distributed in discontinuous, narrow strands of riparian vegetation along streams, sloughs, and railroad beds adjacent to intensely cultivated fields. Most land in this area is planned for urban and industrial development within the next 1-10 years. Existing habitat is periodically cut or burned for weed and flood control (Williams and Hamilton 2002).The re-introduced population of S. b. riparius is located in the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge in Stanislaus County, California. This refuge has about 285 ha of habitat for Brush Rabbits. An additional few hundred hectares have been restored from cropland to natural, riparian vegetation. Refugia from flooding, vegetated mounds and berms, have also been established throughout the refuge for rabbits and other terrestrial wildlife (Kelly 2018a, b).The former range of S. b. peninsularis was from the Magdalena Bay region to the tip of the Baja California peninsula, although specimens are known only from two localities, Santa Anita and Cabo San Lucas separated by only 32 km. Recent intensive field work failed to locate any of the rabbits, and the area has been severely modified by tourist developments. The last known specimens of this subspecies were obtained only in the first quarter of the 20th century (Lorenzo et al. 2013).The range of S. b. exiguus is in the central desert of the Baja California peninsula, where it is known from only eight localities. While recent intensive surveys have found desert cottontail rabbits to be common, no Brush Rabbits were observed at these sites. While the region only exhibits low human impact, it nevertheless appears that the exiguus subspecies is of conservation concern (Lorenzo et al. 2013).S. b. cerrosensis is restricted to lowlands of Cedros Island, Baja California on the Pacific-north coast of Mexico. Cedros Island is a “mountain in the sea” so less than the 15% of the island is optimal habitat for S. b. cerrosensis, in addition with the presence of packs of feral dogs that in recent years have been controlled.
useTrade: This species is hunted for food and sport. <2-5% of the total population is utilized, because their brushy preferred habitat is unsuitable for hunting.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for the species as a whole.The San Joaquin Valley population of subspecies S. b. riparius has been listed by the state of California as an endangered species (U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2000), and has been the subject of a recovery plan involving habitat management and captive breeding (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 1998, Kelly 2018b).The following timeline includes recent conservation measures implemented for S. b. riparius:1) Distribution and status review in 1986 (Williams and Basey 1986).2) Listing as a California Species of Special Concern (Williams and Basey 1986).3) Ecology and habitat management plan for Caswell Memorial State Park developed (Williams 1988).4) Populations estimate made for Caswell MSP in 1993, the only known population at the time (Williams 1993).5) Listed as an endangered species by the State of California in 1994 (State of California 1994).6) Featured species in the multi-species Recovery Plan for Upland Species of the Service (Williams and Hamilton 2002).10) Habitat acquisition and restoration begun by multi-agency CalFed Program with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service as the land owner and manager, starting in 2000 and continuing to date (Williams et al. 2004).11) Controlled propagation facility constructed beginning in 2001 and completed in 2002 by U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (Williams et al. 2004).12) Controlled propagation of Riparian Brush Rabbits initiated in December 2001 with 3 males and 3 females in one large outdoor pen that contained semi-natural habitat conditions (Williams et al. 2004).13) The re-introduced population of Riparian Brush Rabbits on the San Joaquin River NWR was started with the release of 49 young rabbits from the controlled propagation facility between July and October 2002 (Williams et al. 2004).14) By the end of 2002, controlled propagation expanded to three breeding pens resulting in larger numbers of rabbits being released on the refuge, many fitted with radio-collars to get detailed information on survivorship, dispersal, and habitat use (Williams et al. 2008, Hamilton et al. 2010, Kelt et al. 2014).15) Major spring flooding of the San Joaquin River in 2006 resulted in the mortality of nearly all Brush Rabbits on the refuge. The extent and severity of flooding was mapped so that locations could be chosen for the placement of large mounds of dirt that would be vegetated with brushy species and thereby serve as temporary refuges for rabbits during floods. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service also vegetated miles of bare river levees on the refuge with brushy species to provide additional upland cover for the rabbits (Kelly 2018b).16) Major spring flooding of the San Joaquin River occurred again in 2011 and 2017, but because of the habitat management restoration measures taken following the 2006 flood, the population rebounded quickly in both years and despite high levels of flood-related mortality (Kelly 2018b).17) In late 2005 and early 2006, rabbits were also released on the privately owned Faith Ranch, which is under conservation easement, and runs downriver along the San Joaquin River from the refuge boundary towards Caswell MSP. Later in 2006, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service acquired the Buffington property, which connects the Faith Ranch to Caswell MSP, thereby creating more than 20 continuous river-miles of riparian habitat for the Brush Rabbit (Kelly 2018b).18) By the time the breeding and reintroduction program was suspended in December 2013, a total of 1,496 Riparian Brush Rabbits had been released on the refuge, that includes releases on the Faith Ranch and the Buffington property (Kelly 2018b).19) The rabbit populations at Caswell MSP and on the San Joaquin River NWR continue to be monitored (Kelly 2018b).Although S. b. cerrosensis is fully protected on Cedros Island, along with all native wildlife (SEMARNAT 2010), there is an urgent need to assess the pressures of habitat destruction and poaching on this subspecies. Cedros Island needs to correct its management of open industrial garbage dumps and to eradicate feral cats and dogs as soon as possible. The control of feral dogs began at the end of 1980 by personnel of the National Institute of Ecology in collaboration with local fishermen (McChesney and Tershy 1998), but the dogs were not eradicated because the effort was not constant. It is necessary to develop research projects to determine population dynamics, reproduction, ethology and other aspects of the biology and ecology of this subspecies (Lorenzo et al. 2014, Lorenzo-Monterrubio et al. 2018).S. b. cerrosensis is an endangered subspecies according to the Official Norm NOM-059 of Mexico (SEMARNAT 2010). rationale: The Marsh Rabbit (Sylvilagus palustris) is a widespread species, known to be abundant in some parts of its range, particularly in Georgia (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). Only populations is the southern Everglades (Sovie et al. 2016) and the subspecies S. p. hefneri are experiencing severe decline and restricted area of occupancy.The Lower Florida Keys subspecies (S. p. hefneri) appears to meet IUCN Red List Criteria B1ab(ii) and B2ab(ii) for Critically Endangered. First, based on surveys conducted from 2001-2004 by C.A. Faulhaber and N. Perry of Texas A&M University (2003), the subspecies' extent of occurrence is 90 km², and the area of occupancy is less than 10 km². More recently, Schmidt et al. (2012) identified 1025,92 ha of potential habitat only 624 ha of which were occupied (Schmidt et al. 2011). Also, these populations are "severely fragmented." This subspecies has been known to disperse as far as 2 km (Forys and Humphrey 1996), so most patches within the Keys are likely part of the same "subpopulation." All of these subpopulations are relatively small (less than 250 mature adults) and isolated from one another. Finally, the area of occupancy has declined over the past 10 years. A distribution survey conducted between 2001 and 2003 found a net loss of nine of the 76 patches identified in surveys conducted from 1988-1996 (Faulhaber 2003). Because the rabbit occurs in a network of patches, local extinctions and recolonization occur (Forys 1995, Forys and Humphrey 1996, Faulhaber 2003, Schmidt et al. 2011). However, most of the recently extirpated patches are unlikely to be recolonized due to habitat fragmentation, isolation and sea-level rise (Faulhaber 2003, Schmidt et al. 2012).
habitat: The Marsh Rabbit is common in fresh and brackish wetlands marshes and close sources of freshwater (Tomkins 1935, Chapman and Ceballos 1990). They has also been documented in grassy fields, mangroves, hammocks, fallow tomato fields, costal berms, and along canals, ditches, roadsides, and cultivated fields (Carr 1939, Schwartz 1952, Layne 1974), but they are generally never far from a water source. It is a nocturnal species that often walks as opposed to hopping and is a good swimmer (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Home range size varies greatly (0.3 to 32.8 ha), possibly based upon the quality of the habitat (McCleery et al. 2018).Reproduction occurs all year for Marsh Rabbits, with up to seven litters annually per each adult female, with 3 to 5 young per litter (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Gestation is approximately 30-40 days (McCleery et al. 2018). Their diets include a variety of aquatic plants, herbaceous material from shrubs, trees, and woody plants, cultivated crops (Chapman and Willner 1981), as well as grasses, sedges, and flowers (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). They will also consume crawfish molts and plastrons from box turtles (McCleery et al. 2018).The Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit is usually found in saltmarsh/buttonwood transition zones and freshwater marshes within the Lower Keys (Forys, Frank and Kautz 1996, Faulhaber 2003). The saltmarsh/buttonwood transition zone forms the transition between lowland mangrove areas and upland hardwood hammocks and pineland. This transition zone can be subdivided into: 1) an intertidal marsh, occurring at lower elevations and characterized by low halophytic vegetation; 2) a grassy saltmarsh, which occurs at slightly higher elevations and is dominated by grasses and Cyperaceae; and 3) buttonwood transitional vegetation, consisting of grasses and Cyperaceae with an open canopy of buttonwood transitional habitat for foraging and daytime resting sites (Forys 1995). Forys (1995) found that the grassy saltmarsh was commonly used for nests. Rabbits also forage in the intertidal marsh and mangroves, and they occasionally use mangroves for daytime form sites (Forys 1995, Faulhaber 2003).Freshwater wetlands used by the Lower Keys subspecies are usually dominated by Sawgrass (Cladium jamaicense) and often include patches of buttonwood trees (Conocarpus spp.) or other hardwoods (Faulhaber 2003). Faulhaber (2003) noted that rabbits on Boca Chica Key inhabited disturbed mesic grasslands dominated by Schizachyrium gracile, with patches of invasive exotic Lead Tree (Leucaena leucocephala) used for cover. Historically, they were also found on coastal beach berms (United States Fish and Wildlife Service 1999).This subspecies exists in small patches of habitat spread throughout the Lower Keys (Forys and Humphrey 1996). Adult rabbits establish permanent home ranges within these patches, with same sex ranges rarely overlapping (Forys 1995). The average home range reported by Forys and Humphrey (1996) was 3.96 ha, while data collected by Faulhaber (2003) suggests a mean home range of 1.2 ha. Females reproduce year-round, with a mean of 3.7 litters per year and 1-3 young per litter (Forys 1995). The reproductive rate of the Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit may be lower than that of other subspecies, Holler and Conaway (1979) noted a mean of 5.7 litters per year with 2-4 young per litter for the upper Keys and Florida subspecies (S. p. paludicola). Young leave the nest after about 2 weeks and often disperse from their natal patch after 8-10 months (Forys 1995). Dispersal appears to be male-biased, and dispersing rabbits tend to use thick cover and native vegetation types rather than disturbed areas (Forys 1995).Known predators include invasive Burmese Pythons (Python bivittatus), feral and domestic cats (Felis domesticus), Bobcats (Lynx rufus), Raccoons (Procyon lotor), Coyotes (Canis latrans) raptors, Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus), Cottonmouths (Agkistrodon piscivorus), and Americn Alligators (Alligator mississippiensis) (Howe 1988, Forys 1995, McCleery et al. 2015, McCleery et al. 2018).
threats: The Marsh Rabbit is considered an agricultural pest in some areas, especially in sugarcane fields of southern Florida (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). They are hunted in the southern United States (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). Over the last twenty years, Marsh Rabbits have essentially disappeared in the southern part of Everglades National Park (Dorcas et al. 2012), a pattern that is best explained by predation from invasive Burmese Pythons (Python molurus vivittatus) (Sovie et al. 2016).The Lower Keys subspecies was listed as endangered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 1990. The primary reason cited for listing the species was the loss and fragmentation of its habitat due to human development. From 1959 to 2006, 47% of the Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit's habitat was lost to sea level rise and another 8% was lost to human development. Human development has also resulted in increased isolation for some patches, reducing the likelihood of recolonization. Although the rate of habitat loss has slowed since the rabbit received legal protection, habitat destruction and fragmentation remain significant threats to the species' persistence (Faulhaber 2003). LaFever et al. (2007) modelled the potential impact resulting from oceanic rise, due to thermal expansion only, on Marsh Rabbit habitat. They found that the three most important factors impacting potential change were: the rate at which sea-level rise impacts the ability of flora migration upslope, the magnitude in terms of the overall oceanic rise and whether it is great enough to reach Marsh Rabbit habitat, and whether or not humans abandon low-lying habitat, where abandonment would facilitate greater ease of upslope migration by vegetation. They recommended multiple management strategies for the local ecosystem: consideration of land-use planning, use of bioclimatic reserve systems in conjunction with corridors (LaFever et al. 2007). More recent vulnerability assessments (Reece et al. 2013) concluded the Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit to be highly likely of extinction by 2100 due to sea level rise, lack of freshwater, and barriers to dispersal.Additional threats to the subspecies include mortality from pythons, cars, and cats (both domestic and feral). Cars and cats accounted for more than half of the mortalities observed by E.A. Forys on Boca Chica in the early 1990s (Forys 1993). Faulhaber (2003) estimated that just over half of occupied local populations are reasonably likely to have current or future impacts due to cats. A recent population viability analysis supports this assertion, indicating that without predator control, habitat improvement efforts may result in a negligible increase in the chance for persistence (LaFever 2006). The subspecies is also threatened by habitat degradation from invasive exotic plants, trash dumping, mowing and off-road vehicle use (Forys 1993). If left unchecked, invasive exotic vegetation can render patches unsuitable for rabbits. Management efforts have reduced the threat of invasive exotic vegetation on some government-owned properties, but invasive exotic vegetation remains a problem on privately-owned land parcels and even on some government properties. Currently, trash dumping and off-road vehicle use appear to be less of a problem than in the past (Forys 1993, Faulhaber 2003).It has been suggested that Red Imported Fire Ants (Solenopsis invicta) (Forys 1993) and elevated Raccoon (Procyon lotor) densities also pose a threat to the subspecies (Schmidt et al. 2010). Historically, poaching may have contributed to the rabbit's decline, but poaching does not appear to be a major threat at the current time. Feral hogs degraded habitat and may have caused the extirpation of rabbits on Little Pine Key, but hogs were removed from the islands in the 1990s (Wilmers 2003).
population: Other than the Lower Keys subspecies, little is known about the populations of Marsh Rabbits, but it is locally abundant in favorable habitat, with the largest populations occurring in Georgia (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998). However, recent studies of road kill mortality in Georgia suggest populations may be declining (Bosch, Benson and Mead 2016).Once common in the Lower Keys, the Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit is now rare and has become extirpated on several islands within its range. In 1999, the United State Fish and Wildlife Service estimated that only 100-300 adults remained (Faulhaber 2003). A widened search led to the discovery of additional occupied habitat patches from 2001-2003. However, the overall population size remains low. In 2003 estimates suggested that the population contains 200-700 mature individuals, with no key containing more than 250 mature individuals (Faulhaber 2003). A Population Viability Analysis using data collected from 1991-1993 predicted that the subspecies would have a 100% probability of extinction in 50 years (Forys 1995, Forys and Humphrey 1999). Population estimates based on pellet counts and live trapping in 2007-2008 suggested a total of 371 individuals across the subspecies, largely concentrated in the western keys (Schmidt et al. 2011).The Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit occurs in small patches of wetland vegetation on 4 larger keys and several smaller surrounding islands. A distribution survey conducted between 2001-2003 mapped 220 patches of occupied (n=102) and potential (n=118) habitat ranging in size from 0.1-51 ha. The median patch size was 2.4 ha (interquartile range = 0.7-5.1 ha) (Faulhaber 2003). In 2011, out of 150 surveyed patches (of 228 identified possible patches), 73 patches were occupied (Schmidt et al. 2011). Dispersal among these patches is likely frequent enough that these local populations do not fit the IUCN's definition of "subpopulations." Lower Keys Marsh Rabbits have been known to disperse as far as 2 km (Forys and Humphrey 1996), so most patches within keys are likely part of the same "subpopulation." Parameters estimated from 22 years of patch survey results suggest that populations on Sugarloaf, Saddlebunch, and Boca Chica Keys are relatively stable, with higher patch occupancy, while populations on Big Pine Key may be slowly declining and exhibit lower patch occupancy (Eaton et al. 2014). It additionally appears that brackish coastal patches have and will continue to be lost to sea level rise (Schmidt et al. 2012).Although the species is thought to be an excellent swimmer (Tomkins 1935), genetic differentiation among islands is only moderate, with the major distinction being between Big Pine Key and the other three larger keys (Crouse 2005, Tursi, Hughes and Hoffman 2013). Rabbits on Big Pine Key and its surrounding islands are isolated from rabbits on Boca Chica, Saddlebunch, and Sugarloaf keys, likely due to extirpation on the intervening islands (Faulhaber et al. 2007). Moreover, rabbits have not naturally recolonized the keys between Big Pine Key and Sugarloaf Key, indicating that the interchange of dispersers among keys is probably low.
range: The Marsh Rabbit occurs in the south-eastern coastal lowlands of the United States from the Dismal Swamp of southeastern Virginia, through eastern North Carolina, southeastern South Carolina, southern Georgia, southern Alabama, and most of Florida, excluding the extreme southeast but including the Florida Keys (Chapman and Willner 1981, Chapman and Ceballos 1990).The Lower Florida Keys subspecies is restricted to the Upper and Lower Keys of Florida (Chapman and Ceballos 1990). Historically, the subspecies probably occupied all keys with suitable habitat in the Lower Keys. Currently, they can be found on only 4 of the larger keys (Boca Chica, Saddlebunch, Sugarloaf, and Big Pine Keys) and on some of the surrounding smaller keys. More than 50% of the total occupied habitat was found on Big Pine and Boca Chica Keys during a 2001-2005 survey (Faulhaber et al. 2007). This survey also concluded a net loss of occupied patches compared to a conglomerate of surveys conducted between 1988-1995 (Faulhaber et al. 2007). The greatest loss of occupancy occurred on Saddlebunch Keys (Faulhaber et al. 2007). There is a gap in the rabbit's current distribution between Big Pine Key and Sugarloaf Key and the rabbit has been extirpated on Key West (Faulhaber 2003). Fecal pellets of this subspecies were discovered in a single patch on No Name Key in 2001 but have not been located on the island since (Faulhaber 2003). The Lower Keys subspecies exists in small patches of brackish and freshwater wetland habitat, which are under threat from sea level rise (Schmidt et al. 2011, Schmidt et al. 2012). Distribution surveys identified 1025,92 ha of potential habitat, of which 624 were occupied (Schmidt et al. 2011, Schmidt et al. 2012). However, because the subspecies exists on habitat patches that are prone to colonization and extinctions, the area of occupancy varies through time. These estimates are conservative, as they only included areas of known use (e.g. areas with fecal pellets or sightings of individuals). The greatest abundance of the subspecies occurs on Boca Chica, Saddlebunch, Sugarloaf, and Big Pine Keys (Schmidt et al. 2011).
useTrade: The species is hunted for sport, meat, and fur; considered an agricultural pest in South Florida.
conservationActions: Policy-based Actions: The Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit subspecies was listed as endangered by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service in 1990. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (1999) have developed and are in the process of implementing a recovery plan for the subspecies. Restoration and predator control measures have been implemented to address issue with feral cats and habitat quality (Cove et al. 2018). However, there is currently little management action to address the growing threat of invasive pythons to Marsh Rabbit population in south Florida. Research Actions: The distribution and size of the population has not been estimated in 10 years (Faulhaber 2003, Schmidt et al. 2011). The ecology of the Lower Keys Marsh Rabbit is fairly well known (Forys and Humphrey 1996), but there is a growing need to understand nestling/juvenile mortality and dispersal (Faulhaber 2003). Further research should also examine the movements, habitat use, behavior and fitness across the highly modified landscapes of the lower Florida Keys. Three emerging threats that also require further understand: how Marsh Rabbit populations respond to sea-level rise, emerging pathogens such as the Primary Screw-worm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) and invasive predators (pythons and tegus). A population viability analysis model was developed for the subspecies (Forys and Humphrey 1999) but current distribution data demography and environmental data would improve the model's predictive capability. For the mainland population there is a need to understand the ecological consequences of the Marsh Rabbits local extirpation in south Florida, to determine why they are so vulnerable to invasive pythons and if antipredator behaviors and traits are developing in populations exposed to pythons for over 20 years. Habitat-based actions: Approximately two-thirds of local populations occur entirely on publicly-owned and military land (Faulhaber 2003). Faulhaber (2003) estimated that nearly 500 ha of privately-owned land could be purchased to ensure the protection of existing occupied and potential habitat patches and the area immediately surrounding these patches. Further land acquisition would help protect connectivity between local populations. Efforts to control invasive exotic vegetation are ongoing in rabbit habitat under public and military ownership.Species-based Actions: A pilot reintroduction program was initiated for the subspecies with mixed success (Faulhaber et al. 2006, Schmidt et al. 2011). While initial translocation of wild-caught Marsh Rabbits had a 100% and a 81% survival rate for the individuals released on Water Key and Little Pine Key only the latter population appears to have persisted (Schmidt et al. 2011). As the source population was likely from the eastern not the western populations of rabbit there may be mixing these genetically distinct clades if the animals leave the island.

rationale: The Desert Hare is a widespread species. There are no data available on population status, but it is presumed that the population is not declining at a rate sufficient to qualify it for listing under a threat category, although increased population pressure throughout central Asia may be a concern. The species has been assessed as Least Concern in China (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).
habitat: Desert Hares occur in grassland or scrub areas of desert, semi-desert, and steppe habitats (Smith and Xie 2008, Smith et al. 2018). This species is primarily crepuscular, but can be observed during the day (Smith and Xie 2008). Diet varies including "herbaceous plants, seeds, berries, roots and twigs" (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: The threats to this species are not known, although population pressure is likely to impact hare habitat, and the threat of unsustainable subsistence harvest is also likely.
population: There are no data regarding the population.
range: The geographic distribution of the Desert Hare includes Afghanistan and northern Pakistan, extending east through northwestern China, southern Mongolia (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). It is allo- to parapatric with the Tolai Hare (Lepus tolai), except in the Tien Shan range where is thought to be sympatric with it (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). Desert Hares can be found up to elevations of 3,500-4,000m (Smith and Xie 2008).
useTrade: The species is used likely subsistence hunting.
conservationActions: No conservation measures are currently in place for the desert hare. Research should be conducted to ascertain population status, as well as taxonomic studies (see Taxonomic Notes) to elucidate species status. This species was regionally Red Listed in China as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).

rationale: The Tolai Hare is a widespread species that occurs in many protected areas, has a large population size, and has no known widespread major threats. Much of its range is in China, which has regionally assessed the Tolai Hare as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). However, data on Tolai Hare populations are lacking, and the increased human population and concomitant habitat loss may be instrumental in causing a decline in the Tolai Hare; studies are needed to accurately determine the status of this species.
habitat: The Tolai Hare inhabits semi-desert, mountain-steppe, forest steppe, and rocky habitats (Tsevegmid and Tsendjav 2004, Sokolov et al. 1994). It also occurs in grasslands and forest meadows (Smith and Xie 2008). The Tolai Hare does not occupy true forests. It is a nocturnal species (Sokolov et al. 1994, Smith and Xie 2008). Diet consists of roots, grass, and other herbaceous plants (Smith and Xie 2008). Tolai Hares take shelter under shrubs, under rocks, or by digging shallow pits. When fleeing predators they run in a straight line, and are able to jump a length of 2.5–3m (Sokolov et al. 1994).
threats: Hunting (for meat, skins, and for traditional medicines) has been identified as a threat to the Tolai Hare in Mongolia (Clark et al. 2006).
population: In Mongolia, populations are characterized as large, with no apparent decline (Clark et al. 2006). In Russia, the population density can reach 10–30 individuals per 100ha (Sokolov et al. 1994). One study looked at Mongolian commercial harvest data obtain from Dornad Aimag between 1932-1993, which did not indicate any apparent change in Tolai Hare takes (Reading et al. 1998). The authors specify that the data may or may not provide a valid indication of population trends (Reading et al. 1998). In southern Uzbekistan, pelt takes decreased from 8,751 in 1959 to 595 in 1977 (Volozheninov 1980). It is inferred that this species is sufficiently abundant in China, where is it categorized as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004, Jiang et al. 2015, 2016).
range: The geographic distribution of the Tolai Hare extends from the northern and eastern shores of the Caspian Sea, south to Iran, east through Afghanistan, Kazakhstan, and southern Siberia, as well as the "Middle Asia republics to Mongolia, and W, C, NE China" (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). This species was observed at an elevation of 2,400 m on Yihe-Bogdo, Mongolia (Ognev 1966). In China, it is usually located at elevations between 600-900m (Smith and Xie 2008), although it has been reported to occur as high as 4,900 m (Smith et al. 2018). Evidence of a single specimen in south Asia may extend the distribution as far south as Jammu and Kashmir, India (Chakraborty et al. 2005).
useTrade: Historically the Tolai Hare was trapped for food and pelts. The utilization of the hares for fur has ceased, and the only offtake currently is by subsistence hunting.
conservationActions: In Mongolia, approximately 12% of the species' distribution occurs in protected areas (Clark et al. 2006) and has been recorded in Hustai National Park (Todgerel 2002). This species is present in many nature reserves in China. In China, it is regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004; Jiang et al. 2015, 2016). It has also been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern in Mongolia (Clark et al. 2006).

rationale: Ochotona turuchanensis is listed as Least Concern; it is a widespread species, although very little is known about its current status. It is reported as abundant on the Putorana plateau in Russia, and likely so across its remote distribution.
habitat: Ochotona turuchanensis is a rock-dwelling species of pika, although not typically so. Throughout the major part of its range, it lives in flat taiga where it occupies cavities between buried stones. Here, it constructs runways in moss and behaves very secretly. This is an herbivore that demonstrates preference in which plants it consumes. It is diurnal, avoiding nighttime activity due to low temperatures . Reproductive periodicity extends from mid-June through late August . Females have 3.4 ± 1.4 (n=8) embryos (Lissovsky 2004). Juveniles begin to appear in mid-July (Lissovsky 2004).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: There are few data on the current population status of this species. On the Putorana plateau in Siberia, Russia, Ochotona turuchanensis is considered abundant.
range: The geographic distribution of Ochotona turuchanensis extends from the southern expanse of the Yenesei River to Lake Baikal and the middle region of the Lena River in Russia. O. turuchanensis is widely sympatric with O. hyperborea over much of its range.
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. Research should be conducted to determine the current population status, as little data are available in this area. Furthermore, more data are needed regarding the biology and ecology of Ochotona turuchanensis.

rationale: This species has a widespread distribution (Flux and Angermann 1990). The African Savannah Hare has been characterized as a "successful species over much of Africa" (Flux and Angermann 1990), and current analyses give no indication that it is threatened (Awadi and Ben Slimen 2018). The species is confirmed as Least Concern.
habitat: There are few data regarding the ecology of the African Savannah Hare (Boitani et al. 1999). Where it and the Cape Hare are sympatric, the African Savannah Hare occupies scrubbier and more montane habitat (Flux and Angermann 1990). Diet for this species varies according to habitat (Flux and Angermann 1990). It is suspected that this species is able to thrive in agricultural landscapes (Robinson et al. 2016). This is a nocturnal species (Happold 2013). Female hares were found to be breeding during all months of the year, with an average litter size of 1.6 (Flux and Angermann 1990). HB length is 41.5-57.5 cm (Awadi and Ben Slimen 2018).
threats: The threats to this species include habitat loss and fragmentation as a result of urban sprawl, agricultural encroachment, commercial plantations, and infrastructure development for tourism (Drew et al. 2004). Additionally, these species are threatened by hunting pressure through both recreational sport hunting, as well as subsistence hunting for bushmeat and fur. While agricultural and urban expansion may not necessarily cause direct declines, they may increase hunting pressures. Hunting pressure is likely to cause local subpopulation declines (Robinson et al. 2016).
population: There are no known data regarding the current population status of the African Savannah Hare. However, it has been characterized as a "successful species over much of Africa" (Flux and Angermann 1990). There is a small, isolated population in western Algeria (Flux and Angermann 1990, Hoffmann and Smith 2005).
range: The African Savannah Hare occupies a large geographic distribution within Africa (Awadi and Ben Slimen 2018) including the sub-Saharan region, Atlantic coast (Western Sahara, Mauritania, Senegal, The Gambia, and Guinea), the Sahel to the western-most regions of Ethiopia and Kenya, and south to the northeast regions of South Africa, Botswana and Namibia (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). In western Algeria, a small isolated population has been identified (Flux and Angermann 1990, Hoffmann and Smith 2005). There is a recent report of African Savannah Hares in southern Morocco near Tantan (Moores and Brown 2013). This species is sympatric with the Cape Hare, allo- to parapatric with the Cape Scrub Hare and the Abyssinian Hare (L. habessinicus) (Hoffmann and Smith 2005). However, taxonomic uncertainty limits confidence in geographical distribution with Happold (2013) stating that the species is not found in southern Africa (being instead replaced by the Cape Scrub Hare) (Robinson et al. 2016).
useTrade: It is hunted recreationally for sport, bushmeat and fur at a subsistence level in South Africa, Lesotho and Swaziland. However, this is not expected to have a substantial effect on the population (Robinson, Relton and Child 2016).
conservationActions: Available data on the ecology for the African Savannah Hare are included in many treatments, but are restricted to select areas of its distribution (Boitani et al. 1999). Research specific to this species' ecology should be conducted. Research regarding the isolated population in western Algeria should be conducted (Flux and Angermann 1990). It occurs within numerous protected areas, including both formally and privately protected areas. Sustainable utilization is recommended. The development of conservancies to protect appropriate habitats for local subspecies and forms is recommended. Taxonomic resolution at a species and subspecies level is required to ensure that localized or isolated populations and subspecies are conserved (Robinson, Relton and Child 2016).

rationale: Ochotona argentata was previously known only from three highly restricted areas in the Helan-Shan range, each occupying an area of 3 km² (Formozov et al. 2004). Past deforestation within its range has reduced total available habitat for this species (Formozov et al. 2004). Logging is suspected to be ongoing within the Helan Shan range. The current (new) range map includes additional localities made available from surveys by an ornithologist working in this isolated mountain range (Li pers. comm.), thus expanding the extent of occurrence (EOO) for this species from past assessments (to 107 km² – close to but not reaching the criterion B1 threshold for Critically Endangered). We know of no ongoing assessments of the population status of this species, so no population size reduction can be assessed.
habitat: Ochotona argentata is restricted to rocky outcrops in a small forest located on a ridge of the Helan Shan mountain range (Formozov et al. 2004). It is a rock-dwelling species that will also occupy mine shaft entrances (up to 20 m deep) (Smith and Xie 2008). It constructs haypiles out of available vegetation (Smith and Xie 2008). Total length of this species is 20.8-23.5 cm (Smith and Xie 2008).
threats: Deforestation within the range of O. argentata has resulted in loss of habitat (Formozov et al. 2004). Logging is suspected to be ongoing within the mountain range. Ochotonids are sensitive to thermal changes within their habitat and rock-dwelling pikas can be likened to insular populations that are unable to disperse to more suitable habitat, because connecting terrain cannot be easily traversed due to intolerable ambient temperatures. It is therefore inferred, that future climate change will negatively impact the survival of O. argentata.
population: There are no known data on current population status of O. argentata; however, it is inferred that deforestation is likely to cause declines as a result of habitat loss.
range: Ochotona argentata is endemic to Ningxia province in China (Smith and Xie 2008). It occupies a highly restricted geographic range within the Helan Shan range of Ningxia, China, where it occurs along mountain top ridges.
conservationActions: This species is currently listed as Vulnerable D2 under the regional assessment in China (Wang and Xie 2004). Due to its highly restricted extent of occurrence and area of occupancy, it is recommended that efforts be made to conserve remaining habitat for this species. Additionally, research efforts should be made to remedy the lack of data regarding biology, ecology, current habitat and population statuses.

rationale: This species is confirmed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Habitat preferences for Hewitt’s Red Rock Hare are considered similar to those of other Pronolagus species (Happold 2013). It prefers rocky hillsides and outcroppings, and "rock crevices and boulders are an essential component of the habitat" (Happold 2013). Where its range overlaps with Jameson’s Red Rock Hare (P. randensis), it occurs at higher elevations in areas that have fewer boulders and crevices and higher rainfall (Happold 2013). Habitat loss has been occurring over the last 100 years and is anticipated to continue to decline in total area by <20% over the next 20 years due to commercial plantations (Matthee et al. 2004).While not much is known about the reproduction of this species, it is likely to be similar to other red rock hares. Breeding is restricted to warmer months during which time a female could produce three to four litters of one to two altricial (naked) young on each occasion (Matthee et al. 2016). Total length ranges from 38.0–53.5cm (Happold 2013).
threats: The main threat to rock hares is hunting, both for bushmeat and for sport. Hunting pressure is thought to be more severe in areas of high-density human settlements. For example in Lesotho, it is threatened due to hunting pressure from herders with pack dogs (Lynch 1994). Additionally, agricultural and rural settlement expansion may be increasing incidental predation on rock hares by domestic dogs. Hunting is suspected to be causing local declines (and possibly local extinctions), but it is uncertain whether there is a net decline in the population. Long-term monitoring should be established to quantify subpopulation trends.
population: Populations are considered fairly abundant throughout its distribution (Happold 2013), but rarely collected (Lynch 1989). Population for Hewitt’s Red Rock Hare has been estimated at >10,000 mature individuals (Matthee et al. 2004). The population is characterized as having declined in the past, and is predicted to continue declining in the future at a rate of <10% over the next 20 years (Matthee et al. 2004).
range: Hewitt’s Red Rock Hare is endemic to southern Africa (Happold 2013). It is a widely distributed species that occurs in the southern and eastern regions of South Africa (including portions of Western Cape, Free State, Northern Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo Province, and Mpumalanga), as well as Lesotho and western parts of Eswatini  (Matthee et al. 2004).
useTrade: This species is hunted for meat and sport. It is likely to be fairly important in subsistence communities where they are easily obtained. Malieha (1993) specifically mentioned rock hares as being an important bush meat item in Lesotho and in Zululand, but this is likely to be true throughout its range. As a fairly slow-moving species, they are easily hunted with dogs. At night, they have a tendency to freeze when chanced upon in spotlights and can be easily shot or captured in nets (B. Wilson pers. obs.). During the day, it is also possible to hunt them in their refuges, using a coiled piece of barbed wire that hooks and drags the animal out of its shelter (B. Wilson pers. obs.). While having a particularly warm and thick fur, pelts from these species are prone to hairslip and do not cure well, making them unsuitable for hardwearing fur items.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as the species remains widespread in Africa, and the total world population well exceeds 10,000 mature individuals. There is a continuing decline in populations outside protected areas (and even within some protected areas) due to persecution and habitat loss, although this is not sufficient to warrant listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Spotted Hyaenas are present in all habitats including semi-desert, savanna and open woodland, dense dry woodland, and even montane habitats, such as in the Aberdares, Mt Kenya, and the Ethiopian Highlands, up to 4,100 m altitude (Young and Evans 1993, East and Hofer 2013). It is absent from, or present at very low densities in, extreme desert conditions, the highest altitudes on mountains, and tropical rainforests, although they may make deep incursions into forested areas where logging roads provide access (Kingdon 1977, Henschel and Ray 2003). In many parts of their range, they occur in close association with human habitations. Although long periods may elapse between drinking, Spotted Hyaenas are at least somewhat dependent on water, and Tilson and Henschel (1986) recorded an instance where a clan dispersed after the only water source in their range dried up. Often considered just scavengers, Spotted Hyaenas are in fact effective and flexible hunters as well (Kruuk 1972, Höner et al. 2002); damage to domestic stock mainly involves cattle, sheep, and goats and varies widely in intensity (Hofer 1998). The ecology of the species is reviewed by Holekamp and Dloniak (2010) and East and Hofer (2013).
threats: Outside protected areas, populations are subject to persecution by humans through culling (shooting and spearing), trapping and poisoning. Such activities may sometimes occur within the boundaries of conservation areas: mortality due to wire snares set to catch wild herbivores for meat is an important cause of adult mortality in the Serengeti, where snares kill around 400 adult Spotted Hyaenas each year and are responsible for more than half of all adult mortality (Hofer et al. 1996). Apparently only since the mid-1970s has game meat hunting rapidly expanded, as more people have moved within walking distance of the boundaries of protected areas such as in the north and west of the Serengeti (Hofer 1998). Entire clans of Spotted Hyaenas may be killed by poisoning (Holekamp et al. 1993), and many individuals are killed when hit by vehicles. Spotted Hyaena populations in protected areas may be decimated by authorities when they are considered a threat for other wildlife species such as lions, cheetahs and rhinos. Government officials and managers may also allow local human residents within protected areas to kill Spotted Hyaenas when they are suspected or known to have preyed upon livestock. The numbers killed by licensed sport hunters are probably small as they are not considered an attractive species. It is also killed for food, medicine and witchcraft (Hofer and Mills 1998b). A further threat is posed by the decline in densities of wildlife species consumed by Spotted Hyaenas due to habitat loss caused by increased human settlement, overgrazing by livestock, and game-meat hunting by humans.
population: Viable populations exist in a number of countries and a tentative estimate of the total global population is between 27,000 and 47,000. The largest known populations occur in the Serengeti ecosystem in Tanzania and Kenya (7,200-7,700 in the Tanzanian sector and 500-1,000 in the Kenyan sector) and the Kruger National Park in South Africa (1,300-3,900).Population densities based on systematic censuses vary substantially, from 0.006 individuals per km² in Namibia to 2.4 individuals per km² in the Ngorongoro Crater in Tanzania (Hofer and Mills 1998b, Holekamp and Dloniak 2010, Höner et al. 2012). Low population densities occur in semi-desert areas in southern Africa (0.006-0.05 individuals per km²), such as the Namib (Tilson and Henschel 1986) and Etosha Pan (Gasaway et al. 1991). High densities occur in savanna and some open woodlands in Tanzania and Kenya, as well as in montane forests (0.32-2.4 individuals per km²), such as Selous Game Reserve (Creel and Creel 1996), Aberdare National Park (Sillero-Zubiri and Gotelli 1992) and Ngorongoro Crater (Höner et al. 2012). Most populations in protected areas in southern Africa and several populations in eastern Africa are considered to be stable.There is evidence that a few populations have increased during the past years. In Eritrea, there were no confirmed records of the species until the 1990s, but since then, Spotted Hyaenas have been recorded throughout the country and the population is believed to be increasing (F. Hagos pers. comm. 2014). Similarly, in Chad, the population of the largest national park has experienced a two-fold increase during the last few years (Olléová and Dogringar 2013). In contrast, many populations in eastern, central and western Africa, are considered to be declining, even in protected areas, mostly due to an increase in human-wildlife conflict during which humans poison and cull Spotted Hyaenas, and due to incidental snaring (Hofer and Mills 1998b, Holekamp and Dloniak, pers. obs.). In Gabon, substantial efforts to find Spotted Hyenas revealed that single individuals from The Republic of Congo may enter Gabon from time to time, but there is no evidence of a resident population in Gabon (Bohm 2012, Henschel et al. 2014).
range: Spotted Hyaenas are relatively widely distributed in Africa, south of the Sahara. Their current distribution is patchy, especially in West and Central Africa, with populations often concentrated in protected areas. More continuous distributions persist over large areas of Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Botswana, Angola, Namibia, and parts of South Africa. Künzel et al. (2000) reported that Spotted Hyaenas are still widespread in Djibouti, and Grubb et al. (1998) noted the same for Gambia. Long-term studies on Spotted Hyaenas and recent surveys have confirmed their presence in Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Ethiopia, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya, Malawi, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, The Republic of Congo, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe (Vermeulen 2007, Henschel et al. 2014, Höner et al. 2012, East and Hofer 2010, Holekamp and Dloniak 2010, T. Aebischer pers. comm. 2014). In Eritrea, Spotted Hyaenas have not or only very rarely been sighted until 2007, but they are now regularly sighted throughout the country (F. Hagos pers. comm. 2014). It is thus likely that Spotted Hyaenas established a small population in Eritrea. Spotted Hyaenas may occasionally enter Gabon from The Republic of Congo but there is no evidence to suggest that there is a resident population in Gabon (Bohm 2012, Henschel et al. 2014). Hofer and Mills (1998a) reported the species as extinct in Algeria where they may have occurred in the Ahaggar and Tassili d’Ajjer. There is also no confirmed evidence of their occurrence in Egypt, Lesotho, Liberia, Libya, Tunisia, or Morocco, and no recent records from Togo.
useTrade: In at least two locations in Ethiopia, live, wild Spotted Hyaenas are utilized by locals for tourism. Tourists pay to feed Spotted Hyaenas by hand, and some believe that the hyaenas take away bad spirits and that feeding them will cure various ailments. Hair and scraps of skin are often collected from dead animals and are used as talismans. In several areas in Tanzania, Spotted Hyaenas and their body parts are utilized for witchcraft. In Nigeria, local people earn money by keeping Spotted Hyaenas and showing them to spectators on exhibition walks.
conservationActions: Legal classification varies from “vermin” (parts of Ethiopia) to fully protected in conservation areas. Thus, while it is fully protected in the Serengeti National Park in Tanzania, the Spotted Hyaena may be legally shot by sport hunters in the adjacent Maswa Game Reserve. In some protected areas, Spotted Hyaenas may be legally killed by resident humans when they have preyed upon livestock.

rationale: Listed as Near Threatened as the global population size is estimated to be below 10,000 mature individuals, and experiences ongoing deliberate and incidental persecution coupled with a decrease in its prey base such that it may come close to meeting a continuing decline of 10% over the next three generations. It almost qualifies as threatened under criterion C1.
habitat: In most of its range the Striped Hyaena occurs in open habitat or light thorn bush country in arid to semi-arid environments (Hofer 1998, Alam et al. 2014, Wagner 2013). These animals avoid open desert (such as the centre of the Arabian desert and the Sahara, though they may occur at low density in the central Saharan massifs), dense thickets and forests.
