Capture for the purposes of public display is no longer permitted under Australian law.
conservationActions: As a recently described new species, Australian Humpback Dolphins have not been listed under any national and International listing. Previous conservation assessments as S. chinensis are summarized in Table 2. The most recent assessment of the conservation status of humpback dolphins (as S. chinensis ) in Australia, concluded the species should be listed as Data Deficient (Woinarski et al. 2014). In 2012 The Australian Federal Government commissioned a comprehensive review of the current knowledge and conservation status of Australian tropical inshore dolphins (Beasley et al. 2012) and a Draft Coordinated Research Strategy to address knowledge gaps and assess their national conservation status (Parra et al. 2012). These reports led to a technical workshop attended by researchers, statisticians and government and indigenous representatives to review the proposed research objectives identified in the draft research strategy, and agree on research priorities that would allow the assessment of the conservation status of Australian inshore dolphins at a national level. The resulting research strategy (DSEWPaC 2013) identified three specific research objectives applicable to Australian snubfin and humpback dolphins: (1) to conduct a broad-scale assessment of their extent of occurrence and area of occupancy (2) to conduct dedicated multi-year studies of their distribution, abundance and habitat use at selected sites across northern Australia with differing levels of threatening processes; and (3) to undertake a spatial and temporal risk assessment of current and projected threatening processes. Sampling and statistical methods to achieve these objectives have been recently described in Brooks et al. (2014). Following these advances, the Australian Federal Government released in 2014 the Whale and Dolphin Protection Plan, which includes a National Dolphin Conservation Plan. This plan aims to guide research and conservation assessment of Australian Humpback Dolphins and snubfin dolphins by supporting research into their ecology and major threats over the next three years. Multiple-use marine protected areas in Western Australia (e.g. Shark Bay and Ningaloo Reef Marine Park), the Northern Territory (e.g. Garig Gunak Barlu), and Queensland (Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, Dugong Protected Areas; Moreton Bay Marine Park) cover a substantial portion of the known and presumed habitat of Australian Humpback Dolphins in Australian waters and may provide some protection for humpback dolphins. To improve the quality of water discharged into the Great Barrier Reef, in 2008, the Australian Government invested $200 million in The Reef Rescue initiative to help farmers in the Great Barrier Reef catchments to improve farming practices to reduce sediment and nutrient run-off. In Australia, humpback dolphins have also been identified as a conservation value in Commonwealth waters around Australia in the North, North-west and Temperate East Marine bioregional plans (DSEWPaC 2012a, b, c). These plans were developed under section 176 of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC Act) and are aimed at improving management and decision making in relation to Australian marine biodiversity and resources. Biologically Important Areas (i.e. areas where species of conservation value displays important behaviors such as breeding, foraging, resting and migration) for the conservation of humpback dolphins were identified using available information at the time and expert scientific knowledge about species’ distribution, abundance and behavior in these regions. National Guidelines for Whale and Dolphin Watching and for interaction with seismic explorations provide some protection for inshore dolphins (DOE 2005, 2008). Strategies to reduce the entanglement and death of Australian Humpback Dolphins in nets set by The Queensland Shark Control Program for protection of bathers include the use of acoustic alarms, mixed use of nets and drumlines, overall reduction in the number of nets, and establishment of mammal rescue squads (DPI 2001, Gribble et al. 1998).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened as the mean global population size is estimated to be below 10,000 mature individuals, and it experiences a measure of deliberate and incidental persecution such that it may come close to meeting a continuing decline of 10% over the next three generations (24 years). It almost qualifies as threatened under criterion C1.
habitat: The Brown Hyaena is found in dry areas, generally with annual rainfall less than 100 mm, particularly along the coast, semi-desert, open scrub and open woodland savanna with a maximum rainfall up to about 700 mm. It shows an ability to survive close to urban areas. It is predominantly nocturnal in its activity (Hulsman et al. 2010). The Brown Hyaena is independent of drinking water, but needs some type of cover in which to lie up during the day. For this it favours rocky, mountainous areas with bush cover in the bushveld areas of South Africa (Skinner 1976). It is primarily a scavenger of a wide range of vertebrate remains, which is supplemented by wild fruit and other plant material, insects, birds’ eggs, and the occasional small animal which is killed; their impact on domestic livestock is usually very small (Mills 1998, 1990; Maude and Mills 2005; Schiess-Meier et al. 2007). On Namibian farmlands, Brown Hyaenas often scavenge from leopard kills (Stein et al. 2013). Along the Namib Desert Coast, Brown Hyaenas are successful hunters of Cape Fur Seal pups (e.g. Wiesel 2006, Wiesel 2010). Populations of Brown Hyaenas in non-protected areas comprise a significant proportion of the global population, suggesting that such areas are likely to be important for their sustained conservation (Kent and Hill 2013, Lindsey et al. 2013, Stein et al. 2013). Working in areas occupied by pastoralist herders, Maude and Mills (2005) found, that, although Brown Hyaenas feed on carcasses of livestock, there was no evidence to suggest that Brown Hyaenas hunted livestock, or any other significantly sized mammals. Thus the persecution of them because of perceived livestock predation is unjustified. The dietary benefit derived by the Brown Hyaenas from the presence of subsistence pastoralists and their livestock carcasses, may be the primary reason that Brown Hyaena populations are viable in cattle areas (Maude and Mills 2005).
threats: Outside protected areas, the Brown Hyaena may come into conflict with humans, and they are often shot, poisoned, trapped and hunted with dogs in predator eradication or control programmes, or inadvertently killed in non-selective control programs (Mills 1998). Brown Hyaena body parts are used in traditional medicine and Brown Hyaenas are also often unintentional victims of lethal problem animal control through poisons and poaching through snares (I. Wiesel, C. Edwards, L. Boast and R. Yarnell pers. comms. 2014). Lethal control remains the most predominant form of conflict resolution. The Brown Hyaena is regarded as a threat to livestock in some areas, and over 72% of livestock owners in Namibia believe that the Brown Hyaena is responsible for losses (Lindsey et al. 2013), despite the finding that Brown Hyaenas very seldom prey on livestock (Maude and Mills 2005). In South Africa's North West Province 40% of livestock owners regard the Brown Hyaena as a problem animal (Thorn 2008), but in the North West Province, only 6% of surveyed farmers admit to having killed Brown Hyaenas on their property (St John et al. 2011). Persecution in small stock areas in Namibia has lead to the local extinction of Brown Hyaenas in the southeastern parts of that country, where increasing conflict may lead to further population decline.
population: The total population size on the continent has been estimated as at a minimum of 5,000 to 8,000 individuals, with Botswana having the largest population (an estimated 3,900 animals; ,Hofer and Mills 1998b). However, numbers for Botswana may be higher, as one density study for the Central Kalahari Game Reserve, Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park and Makgadikgadi Pans estimates the park's Brown Hyaena population at 2,253 animals (G. Maude pers. comm.). Winterbach and Winterbach (2014) estimate Botswana's total population in 2014 between 2,799 and 5,271 animals.  A recent national population estimate for Namibia puts the number of Brown Hyaenas at 566-2,440 animals (Stein et al. 2013). Thorn (2008, unpublished PhD thesis) estimates South Africa's population at 1,007 (31-2,316) animals. No recent population size estimates are available for Zimbabwe, Angola, Mozambique, Lesotho or Swaziland. Mean density of Brown Hyaenas on farmlands in Botswana was 2.3 per 100 km2 based on camera trap data, and 2.88 per 100 km2 based on spoor surveys (Kent and Hill 2013). Thorn et al. (2009) estimated population density in Pilanesberg National Park, South Africa, at 2.8 per 100 km2.
range: This species is endemic to southern Africa with a marginal extension into the arid parts of southwestern Angola, southeastern Botswana, and the northern and western Cape regions of the Republic of South Africa. Almost 90% of the Brown Hyena population in Botswana occurs in the Southern Conservation Zone (Winterbach et al. 2014). The range of the Brown Hyaena has shrunk significantly since the end of the 18th century when it was last recorded from Table Bay in the extreme southwest of the continent (Hofer and Mills 1998a, Mills 1990). They remain widespread in southern Africa, and in recent years in South Africa have been recorded from the extreme south in the Western Cape (Gansbaai and Bredasdorp), possibly vagrants from a small population in the Little Karoo (Yarnell et al. 2013). Thorn et al. (2011a) found that Brown Hyena distribution in northern South Africa was larger than in previous estimates. However, in farm land in this same area, Brown Hyaena occupancy was estimated at 0.748 (±SE 0.1), and estimated overall density in agricultural land (0.15/100 km2, ±SE 0.08), which was an order of magnitude lower than in protected areas (Thorn et al. 2011b). Boast and Houser (2012) also found that Brown Hyena distribution in Ghanzi, Botswana was larger than previously believed. Several re-introductions have taken place in South Africa's Eastern Cape (e.g., Shamwari Game Reserve; Slater and Muller 2014), and sightings have since been recorded there (e.g., Hayward et al. 2007). Other range expansions have also been recorded from South Africa (Thorn et al. 2011a). Recent studies from Zimbabwe show a range expansion into the north/northwest region of the country (E. van der Meer pers. comm. 2014) and into the east (R. Groom pers. comm. 2014). They seem to be absent from southeast Namibia (I. Wiesel pers. comm. 2014) and the Zambezi region (former Caprivi Strip; L. Hanssen pers. comm. 2014). No recent records are available from the central and western parts of South Africa's Northern Cape Province. Records from Malawi are erroneous (see discussion in Ansell and Dowsett 1988).
useTrade: The bones and other parts of Brown Hyaenas are used for traditional medicinal and ritual purposes. Animals are also hunted by trophy hunters.
conservationActions: Brown Hyaenas occur in a number of large conservation areas, including: Namib-Naukluft, Skeleton Coast, Tsau//Khaeb (Sperrgebiet) and Etosha National Parks (Namibia), Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (South Africa, Botswana), Makgadikgadi National Park (Botswana), Pilanesberg National Park (South Africa), Shamwari Game Reserve (Eastern Cape, South Africa), and the Central Kalahari Game Reserve (Botswana). A recent study from Botswana suggested that a significant proportion of the global Brown Hyaena population is found in non-protected areas, and that these animals can also tolerate land-use changes under some circumstances (Kent and Hill 2013). Boast and Houser (2012) found that Brown Hyaenas occurred evenly on game and cattle farms in Botswana, and in Namibia 54.5% of farm owners reported Brown Hyaena presence (Lindsey et al. 2013). Increased efforts to educate farmers and pastoralists about the fact that Brown Hyenas pose very little risk to livestock is likely to enhance conservation of these animals.

rationale: Assessed as Least Concern as it is a widespread and common species with no major threats.
habitat: Inhabits arid and semi-desert vegetation zones where suitable roosts and food are available. Recorded in semi-desert grassland with areas of Acacia scrub in oases with gardens and orchards surrounded by sandy desert and hamada, in gorges of wadis with some Tamarix and oleanders (Nerium oleander). Roosts in dry caves, ruins, underground tunnels (including catacombs), mosques and old buildings, and sometimes in fissures, small crevices and among boulders. The species is sendentary and it stores fat in autumn for the winter months.
threats: Human disturbance in roost sites and pesticide use against locusts are the main threats
population: The Egyptian Mouse-tailed Bat (Rhinopoma cistops) appears to be particularly abundant near oases. However, both distribution and abundance are undoubtedly insufficiently investigated because the roosts and suitable habitats are often unreachable. Colonies range in size from a few bats up to several hundred, maximum is about 1000 individuals (Egypt). This species is assumed stable throughout its distribution range. Population information remains unknown for most of its African distribution.
range: Occurs across arid northern part of Africa and western Arabia, north to Israel and Syria, south to South Sudan. Occurs up 1,100 m Asl in the Maghreb and western Arabia.
conservationActions: No specific measures are known or are in place, but occurs in protected areas across the range. A study on the impacts of pesticides is required, especially ways in which the impact might be minimised.

rationale: Rhinolophus willardi is listed as Endangered under criterion B1ab(i,iii,v) because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 3,588 km², and all individuals are from a single unprotected region (forest patches within the Misotschi-Kabogo highlands) where there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
habitat: Rhinolophus willardi is known from unprotected forest patches in the montane forests of the Misotschi-Kabogo highlands (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013). The two nearby capture sites were at 1,880 m and 1,950 m asl. The species is assumed to roost in caves and mines, similar to other species in the R. maclaudi group.
threats: This species is known only from one (1) location (two nearby capture sites) in unprotected forest patches the Misotschi-Kabogo highlands (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013). This area is destabilized by regional conflict which is contributing to unregulated forest clearing, habitat degradation and loss. The species likely roosts in caves and mines, which are heavily disturbed within the region.
population: Currently there is no information on the species population size, but it is suspected to be decreasing due to unregulated forest clearing within its limited range. Further, cave roosting bats are heavily hunted and the roosts disturbed in the region.
range: Rhinolophus willardi has been been recorded from one (1) location (two (2) nearby capture sites) in unprotected forest patches in the Misotschi-Kabogo highlands, north of Kalemie, Kilicha River, western shore of Lake Tanganyika, South Kivu Province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013).
useTrade: The species is thought to be hunted in its cave roosts, a common practice in this region of Africa.
conservationActions: This species is in urgent need of conservation attention since it is only known from one location in unprotected forest patches in the Misotschi-Kabogo highlands, a region destabilized by conflict. Research is needed into the species distribution, population size and trends, habitat, ecology, and threats.

rationale: Rhinolophus kahuzi is assessed as Endangered under criterion B as it is only known from one (1) location (Kahuzi-Biega National Park) and has an area of occupancy (AOO) of ca 120 km² and an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 155 km². Given the ongoing conflict in the region, it is assumed that its overall EOO, AOO, population, and roosting/foraging habitats are declining from unregulated logging and over-harvesting for food.
habitat: The type specimen was collected at 2,600 m above sea level, and is the only known record of this species. It was recorded in mixed Afrocarpus and Nuxia forest on the slopes of Mt Kahuzi (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013). The species is assumed to roost in caves as is typical of similar species in the Rhinolophus maclaudi group where it is subject to disturbance and hunting. Further, there is unregulated forest harvest in the area related to the ongoing conflict in the region.
threats: This species is only known from the type locality, the Mt Kahuzi area (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013), where its habitat is assumed to be declining due to unregulated forest clearing that are typical patterns associated with conflict zones in the region. Further, its risk of extinction is exacerbated as the species is only known from this one (1) location where the species is assumed to be under great pressure from over-harvesting as a food source in its cave roosts; a common practice in this region.
population: Rhinolophus kahuzi is known from a single specimen collected from the western slopes of Mt Kahuzi (at 2,600 m). The species population size is unknown and is assumed to be declining as it is in a conflict zone where there is unregulated forest clearing that is removing important forest habitat and from over-harvesting of the species for food (a typical pattern in this region, especially given the ongoing conflict).
range: Rhinolophus kahuzi is known from a single specimen collected at 2,600 m in elevation from the western slope of Mt Kahuzi, Kahuzi-Biega National Park, South Kivu Province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2013). Its area of occupancy (AOO) is ca 120 km² and its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 155 km². Furthermore, given most species in the R. maclaudi group have highly restricted distributions, we are conservative in assuming that the distribution of R. kahuzi is limited to this one (1) location in the Mt Kahuzi region until additional data confirms otherwise.
useTrade: The species is assumed to be over-harvested for food as this is a typical pattern in this region of Africa.
conservationActions: This species is in urgent need of conservation attention. Despite the fact that it is known to occur within a protected area, the region has been destabilized by conflict. Additional research on the species distribution, habitat, ecology, population and threats is needed to inform effective conservation actions within the national park and the broader region.

rationale: Rhinolophus thailandensis is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The species is known to roost in limestone caves and forages in (sub) tropical moist forest habitats (Francis 2019, Ellis 2020). It is known to inhabit the lowlands (80m amsl) as the highlands (1,790 m amsl) (Ellis 2020).
threats: There are unlikely to be major threats affecting the species throughout its range. Deforestation due to logging, agriculture, plantations and urbanisation is probably affecting some populations. Roost cave disturbance is likely negligeable given the remoteness of its known locations of occurrence.
population: Little is known but the population is assumed to be stable.
range: The species is endemic to Thailand.
useTrade: The species is not known to be hunted, used, or traded.
conservationActions: Rhinolophus thailandensis is currently only known from protected areas (e.g. Chiang Dao Wildlife Sanctuary, Khlong Wang Chao National Park, Pha Daeng National Park; Ellis 2020). Little is known about this species and additional research is needed to determine the species distribution, population status and trends, and ecology. Further research is therefore required to establish conservation action plans.

rationale: This very rare bat has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 26,865 km², occurs in only three locations, is severely fragmented, and is experiencing a decline in the extent and quality of its habitat. Therefore it is listed as Near Threatened approaching Vulnerable (VU) under criteria B1ab(iii).
habitat: All three areas where this species has been recorded are located in the seasonal and mesic subtropical monsoon climate belt, which possess a large elevational gradient ranging from about 500 m to 3,500 m asl. Record localities are comprised between 500 m to 1,800-1,900 m asl.
threats: This species is under threat due to loss of habitat as a result of cave development for tourism and deforestation for logging and agriculture.
population: Although Yunnan and Guizhou are relatively well represented by records of Rhinolophus specimens, it is known from only five specimens collected over a 45 years span.
range: This species is known only from Yunnan and Guizhou Province in China (Zhou et al. 2009). The elevations of two localities are at 1,500 m and 1,980 m Asl. All three localities are in mountainous regions. The type locality of R. xinanzhongguoensis is Wumulong, Yongde County, Yunnan Province, China.
conservationActions: Immediate study is needed to ascertain its geographic range and population size to assess potential conservation concerns.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, which overlaps several protected areas, and although its distribution and populations have not been properly assessed it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Usually found in well preserved montane forests of the eastern and central cordilleras of Colombia (Solari et al. 2013). However, it may be found in lowland forests near savanna, as low as 130 m in Guyana, Suriname and northeastern Peru (Lim et al. 2008, Calderon and Pacheco 2012). Like its congeners, it is a frugivorous species best described as a nomadic frugivore (Soriano 2000).
threats: Given its wide distribution, and preference for montane habitats, this species does not seem threaten by major impacts at the moment.
population: Relatively common over 1,000 m, at the eastern and central cordilleras of Colombia (Solari pers. obs.). In Guyana and Suriname this is the most abundant species of the genus in highland forests, being absent in coastal forests, and uncommon in interior lowland forest and savanna (Lim et al. 2008).
range: Dermanura bogotensis is known from northern South America  including eastern and central Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname (Lim et al. 2008). There is a record from northeastern Peru (Calderon and Pacheco 2012). It is not known from French Guiana (Simmons and Voss 1998) and northern Brazil (Sampaio et al. 2003, Martins et al. 2006). Previously, it was considered a subspecies of D. glauca (Simmons 2005) but phylogenetic analyses (Lim et al. 2008, Solari et al. 2009) proved they are different species.
conservationActions: The distribution range of the species overlaps several protected areas, including national parks, natural reserves, forest reserves and protective zones. Its distribution needs to be clearly determined in parts of the Colombian and Venezuelan Andes.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because of its wide geographic distribution, including large sections of continuous native forests, and natural abundance at local scale. There is no major threats to these habitats or the species itself.
habitat: Dermanura rava inhabits dry and wet forests of western Ecuador and northwestern Peru, although it seems to prefer dry forests (Pacheco et al. 2009, Carrera et al. 2010). In Colombia, it is present from the Pacific lowland forests of the Chocó to the dry valleys of the Cauca and Magdalena rivers (Solari et al. 2013). This small frugivore may be found in open areas too, being able to move long distances every night to get to its key resources, typically fruits (such as Ficus sp.).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown.
population: In western Ecuador, this species inhabits dry and wet forests, being more commonly collected in dry forests (Carrera et al. 2010). This is a common species along the interandean valleys of western Colombia (Solari, pers. obs.).
range: This species is found from southeastern Panama through the Pacific versant of Colombia and Ecuador, western and central Colombia, and northwestern Peru (Pacheco et al. 2009, Solari et al. 2009, Carrera et al. 2010, Solari et al. 2013).
conservationActions: A couple of national reserves exist in northwestern Peru, where the southern limit of the species is reached. Also, small natural reserves protect the Tropical dry forests of western Ecuador (Carrera et al. 2010). A few protected areas occur in western Colombia, including natural reserves and national parks.

rationale: This species in currently known from Eastern Sarawak, Central and Eastern Kilimantan, where habitat loss is ongoing due to intensive deforestation. Since Rhinolophus proconsulis can be affected by habitat loss in less than five locations and its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 2,665 km², it is listed as Endangered (EN) under criterion B1ab(iii).
habitat: This species has been captured while roosting in or exiting from limestone caves (Abd Rahman et al. 2011, Hill 1959). Like other members of the genus, it is a gleaning insectivore specialized to forage in dense vegetation (Hill 1992, Struebig et al. 2010).
threats: Human disturbance of caves in which this species roosts could pose a threat and should be minimized (Wiles and Brooke 2009). This species forages in dense vegetation so is particularly vulnerable to the rampant deforestation currently occurring across Borneo (Struebig et al. 2010).
population: This species is known from only nine localities. Population sizes and trends are currently unknown.
range: This species has to date only been recorded from the original site of collection, Bungoh Cave (Hill 1959); from Wind Cave, Padawan, Kubah, Fairy Cave, and Jambusan Cave (Abd Rahman et al. 2011) in Sarawak, Malaysia; and from two sites in Central Kalimantan and one site in East Kalimantan (Struebig et al. 2010).
conservationActions: No conservation actions are in place for this species. More research to determine population size, distribution and trends would be helpful.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern (LC) on the basis of its widespread distribution in Sulawesi, its stable population trend and the absence of threats affecting the whole population. Deforestation and human disturbance of roost sites, however, could still adversely affect populations at a local scale.
habitat: This species is a gleaning or aerial insectivore, as are all members of the genus (Hill 1992).  It is possible that it roosts in caves although more likely a tree rooster. This species has been mistnetted in slightly disturbed rainforest lowland to lower montane forest (Bergmans and Rozendaal 1982).
threats: While this species is not currently under threat throughout its range, deforestation and human disturbance of roost sites could adversely affect local populations (Wiles and Brooke 2009).
population: The species is recorded from throughout the island of Sulawesi (Hill 1992); no data are available at the current time with respect to population sizes and trends, however, although these parameters are unknown, populations are assumed to be large and stable.
range: The species as currently defined has been found across the island of Sulawesi (Hill 1992).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: In China and Vietnam, this species is commonly found in montane forests. It usually roosts in colonies and lives in natural or artificial caves.
threats: Urban constructions are the main threats for the population declines of this species, as they caused destruction of forests and caves which the species depends for predation and roosting.
population: The species global population is currently suspected to be in decline, due to habitat fragmentation and loss of key roost sites, but not at a rate to qualify as a threatened species.
range: This species is widely distributed in Southern China and Vietnam. Recently, it has been recorded from six provinces in China, including Hunan, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi, Yunnan and Guizhou (Sun et al. 2016, Gong et al. 2017) and three provinces in Vietnam, including Vinh Phuc, Tuyen Quang and Thanh Hoa (Tu et al. 2017).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution range across Indochinese subregion and being observed in relatively large colony in many caves.
habitat: It is found in caves, limestone areas and in several forest types, from lowland to hill evergreen forest (Soisook et al. 2008). Female individuals were found pregnant in late February and lactating in May (Soisook et al. 2008).
threats: The major known threat to this species, as well as other cave bats, is habitat destruction, i.e. limestone quarrying, and forest conversion.
population: In Thailand, a few individuals of this species are often captured in the same harp trap when trapping is undertaken near karst habitat.  A relatively small size of colony, with about 10 to 50 individuals, was observed in day-roost cave (P. Soisook, unpublished data). However, a colony of about 1,200 individuals was recorded roosting torpid in a cave in western Thailand (Robinson et al. 1995).
range: This species is known from Myanmar, Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand (north of the isthmus of Kra) (Soisook et al. 2008). It is also recorded from Lao PDR (Thomas et al. 2013). It is very likely to be occurred in China but current record is referred to Rhinolophus stheno (Zhang et al. 2009).
conservationActions: There is no conservation action or scheme in-place specifically for this species, although in Thailand it is being considered to be listed in the National Wildlife Protection Act (P. Soisook, pers. comm.).

rationale: Balionycteris seimundi is assessed as Least Concern because it is widespread, it can be common in suitable habitat, it has been found in secondary forest and rubber plantations, and its populations are unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species occurs in primary lowland rainforest from sea level up to 1,500 m asl, and is also found in mangroves (Hodgkison and Kunz 2006). It roosts in epiphytic ferns, zingers, active arboreal nests of ants and abandoned arboreal termite nests (Kingston et al. 2006). It is widely distributed in Peninsular Malaysia but not recorded in abundant, usually forms small harem groups. Furthermore, it has also been reported from rubber plantations managed by villagers which retain vegetative structure (A. Suyanto pers. comm.).
threats: This species is locally threatened throughout much of its distribution by deforestation for agriculture, logging and plantations, and as a result of fire. In Peninsular Malaysia, habitat loss due to forest conversion for agriculture, housing and public infrastructures development is the main threat to the populations.
population: In Peninsular Malaysia, it is common in primary lowland rain forest (T. Kingston pers. comm.) and was also recorded in hilly dipterocarp forest at Taman Negara Pahang (Tan et al. 2015). The species population is assumed to be stable in protected areas within Peninsular Malaysia and there are no data to document declines outside the region’s protected areas. However, the species habitat has been reduced to 63.62% of what was historically available (DWNP 2017) and may provide insights of possible decreasing of populations outside the protected areas. More studies are needed to be conducted at outside the protected areas.
range: Formerly, this species was recorded as a subspecies of Balionycteris maculata in Peninsular Malaysia. It is widespread in Peninsular Malaysia (Tan et al. 2015, Lim et al. 2017) and it is expected that the southern Thailand populations are the same species. However, further studies are needed to reconfirm the species in Thailand, Sumatra, and Riau Archipelago.
conservationActions: This species occurs within several reserves and protected areas, including production forests in Peninsular Malaysia (Hodgkison and Kunz 2006, Tan et al. 2015). No direct conservation measures are currently taken for the species as a whole. However, further studies are needed to monitoring the changes of population in abundance and distribution.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered because it is a Mindoro Island endemic with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 1,589 km², it is only known from four localities, and the species is threatened from hunting by local communities, faces habitat loss and degradation, and is disturbed from recreational mountaineering.
habitat: There is limited information on the ecology and habitat requirements for D. microleucopterus. Since the species was described from Mt. Siburan, is has been captured on Mt. Halcon in secondary lowland and secondary lower montane forests. In Mts. Iglit-Baco National Park, Calintaan, Occidental Mindoro, individuals were captured in a disturbed lowland forest adjacent to grassland, agroforest and kaingin area. And in the Mt. Tallulah Peak area, Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro (140-180 m asl), individuals were captured in lowland forest with semi-evergreen structure. Additional research is required to expand and refine the understanding of the species ecology.
threats: This species is only known from four areas on Mindoro Island and is threatened by local subsistence hunting for food, habitat loss and degradation, and disturbance brought about by tourism (mountaineering activity in Mt. Halcon). At this stage the precise threats to the species are not clear.
population: Very little information is known about the population status of the species as limited numbers of individuals only have been captured from four localities on Mindoro Island. It is inferred that the number of mature individuals is declining given the ongoing hunting of the species and decline in the extent and quality of its habitat.
range: Desmalopex microleucopterus is a Mindoro Island endemic (EOO is 1,589 km²) and has only been documented from four localities, including Mt. Halcon, Bayanan, Oriental Mindoro (450 and 1,480 m asl), Mts. Iglit-Baco National Park, Calintaan, Occidental Mindoro (120-250 m asl), Mt. Tallulah Peak, Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro (140-180 m asl), and Mt. Siburan (100 m asl, Type Locality). Additional information is needed to refine the understanding of the species distribution across Mindoro.
useTrade: The species is hunted for local consumption.
conservationActions: While most of the current known distribution for the species is outside of any known protected area, it has been found in the Mounts Iglit-Baco National Park which is also recognized as an ASEAN Heritage Park. It is unknown what percent of the species is found within the protected area. While there is no species-level conservation plan in place, a conservation management plan has been drafted for the Mt. Halcon area and is awaiting approval by local communities. There are no active monitoring activities in place. Further work is needed to determine the distribution, abundance, ecological requirements, threats and conservation needs of this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is regularly recorded from woodland (including miombo woodland), savanna, bushland, arid or semi-desert grassland habitats and mosaics of these general habitat types.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species as a whole. Some populations may be threatened by overharvesting for subsistence food.
population: This is a common species.
range: This species is largely distributed in Central Africa and East Africa, in general more easterly distributed (at lower altitudes) than E. labiatus. It appears to range from southern and eastern South Sudan, Ethiopia and Somalia, and from here south into eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania (including the island of Zanzibar), being recorded as far south as Malawi, northwestern Mozambique and northern Zambia. It occurs at altitudes from sea level to 1,950 m (at Solai Valley, Kenya).
useTrade: This species is harvested for the bushmeat trade.
conservationActions: This species has been recorded from many protected areas. No direct conservation measures are currently needed for the species as a whole. Additional research is needed into the impact of possible overharvesting of animals on some populations.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is typically associated with lowland tropical moist forest, although it has also been recorded from swamp forest and mosaic forest-grassland habitats (Bergmans 1997). It appears to be confined to forest with a closed canopy, but within this habitat it has been recorded suspended from plantain leaves, shrubs and inside human habitations (Rosevear 1965, Weber et al. 2009). In Cameroon and Benin, it is common within banana plantations (Grubb et al. 1998, Weber et al. 2009). Little is known about roosting behavior, however, it does not seem to roost in groups. This obligate nectivorous bat species in Africa feeds on nectar as well as pollen of several plants (Petterssen 2005, Weber et al. 2009).
threats: It may be locally threatened by habitat loss and degradation, often resulting from conversion of land to agricultural use or the harvesting of timber and firewood.
population: The species is locally abundant.
range: This species ranges throughout much of West Africa. It is distributed from Sierra Leone and Guinea in the west, through to Ghana and western Togo in the east, although the eastern limit is not currently known and the species may extend further into western Nigeria (Nesi et al. 2013). It is probably safe to speculate that the distribution of M. azagnyi does not overlap that of M. woermanni but the exact location of the change-over is under dispute and could be anywhere between the Dahomey Gap (eastern Togo–western Nigeria) and the Cameroon Volcanic Line (eastern Nigeria-western Cameroon). The records from Benin (Djossa et al. 2008, Weber et al. 2009) and Nigeria (Happold 1987) may refer to either of the two species, or both (if the two species are shown to occur sympatrically).
conservationActions: This species has been recorded within a number of protected areas and also survives outside of such areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because its extent of occurrence is greater than 20,000 km², it is very common, and its populations are not declining fast enough for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is generally found in the primary forest at elevations up to 2,100 m asl (Maryanto et al. 2012)
threats: Deforestation is occurring throughout the species' range.
population: This species is common and widely distributed in Sulawesi (Maryanto et al. 2012).
range: This species known from greater Sulawesi, Talaud, and Wowoni Islands, Indonesia (Maryanto et al. 2012).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in some protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The species is found in lowland rainforests of Equatorial Africa. It has been recorded roosting in vegetation. There is little information currently available on the natural history of this species. It is not known if the species can persist in degraded, or secondary, forest habitats. Females are highly philopatric, whereas males are more prone to disperse. In addition, the Congo River and other large rivers constitute strong biogeographic barriers for females. Flying over large rivers is probably too risky for females of this small bat species (Hassanin et al. 2015).
threats: Threats to this species are currently unknown.
population: This species is a rarely recorded in western Equatorial Africa, but it seems to be more common (at least locally) in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Based on mitochondrial divergence, two different subspecies have been described: Scotonycteris bergmansi bergmansi in western Equatorial Africa (at elast in southern CAR, Republic of the Congo, Gabon, and Equatorial Guinea), and Scotonycteris bergmansi congoensis in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
range: This species occurs in Equatorial Africa, where it is known from the rainforests of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Republic of the Congo, southern Central African Republic, and Democratic Republic of the Congo.
conservationActions: This species is undoubtedly present in the Campo Ma'an National Park, a protected area located near the type locality. Further studies are needed to better understand the distribution, natural history and threats of this species.

rationale: Scotonycteris occidentalis is assessed as Least Concern due to the species relatively large distribution and with threats that are likely not resulting in a population decline that would warrant a threatened listing at this time. The species current distribution is restricted to areas of the Upper Guinean Forest of West Africa (Ghana, Cote d’Ivoire, Liberia, and Guinea) and Nigeria, an area larger than 20,000 km². However, the species is known from only a few sites, and it remains unclear how widespread it is between known localities.
habitat: Subtropical and tropical moist lowland forests are of major importance to S. occidentalis. The species roosts singly in forests and has been captured up to 1,000 m asl on mount Nimba (Fahr 2013). Although it appears dependent on intact forest, the species has been captured in forest fringes and edges, perhaps during movement between forest patches. It is often collected in lowland forest understory in mist-nets, but reports of captures from ground to canopy level suggest the species forages along the entire vertical column (Fahr 2013).
threats: The threats to the species are not fully understood. Major threat likely include forest fragmentation, degradation, and loss due to small scale logging, shifting agriculture, and housing/urban expansion. The species is likely threatened by forest fragmentation, disturbance and habitat loss.
population: Population status and trends for S. occidentalis are unknown. Among fruit bats, the species is one of the less common species to capture during forest surveys.
range: Currently, this species is known to be restricted to the forest zone of four countries: Ghana, Cote d’Ivoire, Liberia, and Guinea in the Upper Guinean Forest of West Africa and southwestern Nigeria. Populations from southwestern Nigeria are recognized here as S. occidentalis with individuals being larger (morphometrics) at Omo Forest Reserve (Happold and Happold, 1978-part I) and Okomu National Park (Tanshi et al. 2019) than southeastern Nigeria (Tanshi,. unpubl. data). Note that Happold and Happold 1978-part II suggests that their captures refer to zenkeri (with occidentalis recognized as subspecies at the time) despite reporting a mean forearm length (Happold and Happold, 1978-part I) that fits better with occidentalis (Hassanin et al. 2015).
conservationActions: There are no species-specific conservation actions currently in place for the species. The species is known from protected areas. Research is needed to further illuminate taxonomy, population status and trends, life history and ecology, and threats.Research neededTaxonomy: surveys and biogeographical molecular analysis in Nigeria are needed to support morphological reports as a final confirmation of S. occidentalis in southwestern Nigeria (Hassanin et al. 2015). Similarly, molecular analysis will help to resolve the potential role of the Dahomey gap as a barrier between populations in Upper Guinea forest and the southwestern Nigeria population. The eastern limits of the species re the role of Niger Delta and River Niger is also in need of resolution.Population size and distribution: surveys in localities west of its current known range in Guinea is crucial for understanding the full extent of the species range. It is essential to conduct population assessment across its range and establish to what extent the species is dependent on undisturbed forest. Finally, a species distribution analysis will aid identification of areas of occupancy and assessment of protection needs.Life history and ecology: across its range, intensive understory forest surveys and telemetry are necessary to understand home range and roosting habits. Conservation Actions NeededSite and area protection: although the species is known from protected areas across its range, many of these protected areas face immense threats from shifting agriculture that leads to conflict between farmers and protected area managers as seen in Okomu National Park, Nigeria.

rationale: This newly described species is known from at least six widely distributed localities in Kenya including several protected areas (Brooks and Bickham 2014) and occurs in close association with human altered landscapes, roosting in buildings. While currently listed as LC, further studies are needed to clarify taxonomic status.
habitat: This species occurs in a wide range of savanna and woodlands habitats. Its ecology is poorly known, but it is captured in human-altered landscapes suggesting that it is tolerant of habitat disturbance.
threats: The major threat is persecution of roosting sites.
population: Population size is not known but is presumably large since it occurs in anthropomorphic environments.
range: Currently only known from Kenya where it is widely distributed from the coast north and westwards to western Kenya.
conservationActions: This species is known to occur in Tsavo National Park and may occur in other protected areas in Kenya.

rationale: This newly described species is known from at three widely distributed localities in Ethiopia (Brooks and Bickham 2014), and possibly occurs widely throughout the country (Largen et al. 1974) and may occur in protected areas.
habitat: This species occurs in savanna and woodland habitats. Its ecology is almost entirely unknown.
threats: The major threat is persecution at roosting sites.
range: Currently only known from Ethiopia, west of the Rift Valley. Specimens of Scotophilus are also known from east of the Rift Valley (Largen et al. 1974) but it is not known if this eastern population belongs to S. ejetai or S. andrewreborii.
conservationActions: This species is not currently known to occur in any protected areas. However, other medium-sized Scotophilus species in eastern and southern Africa occur in close association with human-altered landscapes and if this is the case with S. ejetai, then it is unlikely to need specific protection.

rationale: This newly described species is known from two extremely widely distributed localities in Kenya and Ghana (Brooks and Bickham 2014), and the species is likely to occur in between. More research is needed across its region and requires examination of existing museum material to determine its full distribution.
habitat: This species probably occurs in a wide range of savanna and woodland habitats. Its ecology is poorly known, but it is captured in human-altered landscapes suggesting that it is tolerant of habitat disturbance.
threats: The major treath is persecution of roosting sites.
population: There is no information about population size, but it is presumably large since it occurs over a large area and in anthropogenic environments.
range: Currently only known from western Kenya and Accra, Ghana.
conservationActions: This species is not currently known to occur in any protected area, but specimens of Scotophilus within the range of this newly described species have been recorded from several protected areas.

rationale: This newly described species is known from three localities in coastal Kenya including one protected area (Brooks and Bickham 2014). It may occur in close association with human altered landscapes.
habitat: This species appears to occur in woodland and forest habitats of coastal Kenya. Its ecology is poorly known, but it may utilize human-altered landscapes.
threats: The major threat is persecution of roosting sites.
population: There is no information about population size and trend.
range: S. trujilloi is currently only known from coastal south-east Kenya, but may also occur in north-east Tanzania and southern Somalia.
conservationActions: This species is known to occur in the Shimba Hills National Park and may occur in the other protected areas in Kenya.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because, although there is not much information on the population status or ecology of this species, it is unlikely to meet any of the criteria for Vulnerable or higher listing. Its known extent of occurrence is quite large, with reported records from 15 localities ranging from northern Thailand to northern Vietnam to southern Vietnam. There are no data on population size, but there is no reason to believe it is less than 10,000 individuals given the wide distribution. Although the population has likely declined due to loss of forested habitat, it is unlikely to have declined at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little is known of the ecology of this species, and no roosting sites have been reported. All published records with ecological information indicate specimens were captured in harp traps set across trails through forest. The type series was caught in wet evergreen montane forest, with extensive bamboo understorey at 1,300m altitude. Another Lao specimen was caught in an area of mixed pine savannah, semi-deciduous and broadleaf evergreen forest at 500m altitude. One Vietnamese individual was caught in premontane secondary forest at 700m. A specimen in Thailand was caught near a stream in hill evergreen forest at an altitude of 700m.
threats: Forestry practices and clearing of forests for agriculture have likely resulted in past and ongoing loss of habitat, but without information on the specific habitat requirements of this species, it is not possible to estimate the magnitude of habitat loss.
population: There is no reliable information on population sizes of this species, which has been reported so far from 15 widely distributed localities. Typically, only a few individuals have been captured at each locality, but as the species likely roosts alone or in small groups, this does not provide a basis for estimating population size.
range: This species has so far been reported from 15 localities, in northern Thailand (Soisook 2013), Laos (Francis and Eger 2012, Ruedi et al. 2012 [as Murina sp. A], Thomas et al. 2013) and Vietnam (Francis and Eger 2012, Son et al. 2015). The type locality was near the Nam Pan in the Annamite Mountains, Bolikhamxai Province, Lao PDR (18°28’N, 105°05’E, alt. ca. 1,300 m)
useTrade: No reported records of trade. The species likely roosts alone or in small groups in trees or other vegetation, and hence is likely rarely harvested.
conservationActions: No specific information for this species, but it would likely benefit from efforts to protect remaining wet evergreen and mixed forests in the region.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered because, based on its known habitat preference (i.e., plain lowland rainforest), this rare species has a very small area of occupancy (AOO) and extent of occurrence (EOO); EOO and AOO are both currently estimated to be less than 4 km². It is also threatened by habitat loss due to agricultural activities throughout the whole area where it has been recorded.
habitat: This species occurs in cluttered, moist, plain-lowland Malaysian-type evergreen forest at an elevation of 340-370 m (Soisook et al. 2013). It is found hunting on small insects in cluttered understorey at approximately 2-3 m above ground (P. Soisook, unpub. data). Roosting habit is unknown but it is very likely that it roosts in leaves or hollow trees.
threats: The major threat to this species is the habitat loss as the lowland forest, although legally protected, is being disturbed and converted to agricultural land.
population: As this bat is usually captured singly and is known only from very few records, it seems impossible to estimate the current population size. However, it is very likely that the population size is very small.
range: The Bala Tube-nosed Bat is known only from the lowland rainforest of Bala Forest, Hala Bala Wildlife Sanctuary, Narathiwat Province, south Thailand (Soisook et al. 2013). Although a lot of sampling efforts have been made in different localities of the wildlife sanctuary (P. Soisook, unpublished data), as well as in peninsular Malaysia (e.g. Kumaran et al. 2016), it has not been found outside the vicinity of the type locality. Both its EOO and AOO fit well within one 4 km² grid cell; the actual area this species is known from is between 0.06 and 1 km².
conservationActions: Currently there are no conservation actions or schemes in place for this species. However, it is being considered for inclusion in the National Wildlife Protection Act (P. Soisook, pers. comm).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Although this species is believed to have a small extent of occurrence, there is no evidence of population decline. Recreational activity may cause disturbance to one hibernaculum, but the effect to its population is likely to be negligible.
habitat: This bat occurs in various lowland and montane forests. An abandoned bunker on a mountain top (3350m Asl) is used annually by up to ten individual bats as a hibernaculum during a period from November to late March/early April (Cheng, H.-C. pers. comm.). One record was made to a female which gave birth to two pups in June; a few more records were made to nursing females in July (Cheng et al. 2015).
threats: The abandoned bunker that provides the hibernaculum to the focal species is open to the public for recreation activities.
population: Despite its wide altitudinal range of occurrence, this species is associated with rarer and geographically more sporadic records in Taiwan compared to other congeneric species there. Nothing is known about its population structure, size and trends in Taiwan.
range: This species is endemic to Taiwan where it has a wide altitudinal range of distribution, from sites close to the sea level to a site as high as 3,350 m Asl.
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas, including at least two national parks. However, no specific conservation action is taken.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Although this species is believed to have a small extent of occurrence, there is no evidence of define threats and/or population decline. However, climate change may cause reduction of suitable habitats and population decline in the future.
habitat: This species is found in broadleaf and mixed forests with nature or planted conifers. Its ecology remains largely unknown. A record was made to a female which gave birth to two pups in May (Cheng et al. 2015). A few other observations were made to nursing females from mid-May to mid-July (Kuo, C.-H. pers. obs.).
threats: In response to global warming, suitable habitats of this highland dwelling species are expected to shift and shrink towards mountain tops of Taiwan, and thus become more isolated from each other in addition to a reduction in the total extent (Kuo 2012). Therefore, population decline and fragmentation of this species in the future are expected.
population: Geographical-based genetic structure presents among subpopulations in Taiwan, which could reflect isolation by distance (Kuo et al. 2014).
range: This species is endemic to Taiwan where it occurs in mountain regions with elevations predominantly from 1400 to 2700 m Asl (Kuo et al. 2009, 2014). It was occasionally found in regions with elevations higher or lower than the former altitudinal range.
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas, including three national parks. However, no specific conservation is taken.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern. Although this species is believed to have a small extent of occurrence, there is no evidence of population decline.
habitat: This species occurs in various lowland and montane forests. Pregnant females are recorded annually from mid-April to mid-May while nursing ones are recorded from mid-May to the end of July (Cheng et al. 2015; Kuo, H.-C. pers. obs.). It mainly feeds on insects of the orders Coleoptera, Lepidoptera and Hymenoptera (Lu 2013).  Behavioral experiments showed that this bat can perform aerial hawking in addition to glean prey from the substrate; additional experiments revealed that this bat used olfactory cue to aid locating prey (Liao 2013).
threats: This species may not be particularly under threats apart from  having a restricted extent of occurrence.
population: The Central Mountain Range stretching North-South across Taiwan presents as a barrier against gene flow in the East-West direction between populations on the opposite sides of the mountain range (Kuo et al. 2014).
range: This species occurs in hill and mountain regions of Taiwan with elevations lower than 2,200 m Asl (Kuo et al. 2009, 2014).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas, including three national parks. However, no specific conservation is taken.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern. Although there is not much information on the population status or ecology of this species, it is unlikely to meet any of the criteria for Vulnerable or higher listing. It has been reported from at least 10 widely scattered localities from Central Laos and Vietnam to south Laos and Cambodia, such that the known extent of occurrence exceeds 20,000 km2.  There are no data on population size, but there is no reason to believe it is less than 10,000 individuals, although it does appear to be less common than several other Murina in the region. Although the population has undoubtedly declined due to loss of forested habitat, it has been caught in more than one forest type, and there is no evidence that it has declined fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little is known of the ecology of this species, and no roosting sites have been reported. Records from Lao PDR and Vietnam for which habitat information was reported were captured in harp traps set across trails in wet evergreen hill forest in the Annamite mountains at altitudes of 830m to 1,140m. A specimen from Cambodia was caught in semi-deciduous forest at an altitude of 290m. Most sites involved capture of 1 or 2 individuals, suggesting it likely occurs mainly singly or in small family groups.
threats: Populations have likely declined over the past several decades due to clearing of forest for agriculture or settlements, but without reliable information on habitat specificity, including the extent to which it can use disturbed forests, it is not possible to estimate the extent of habitat loss for the species.
population: No estimates are available on population size. The species has been caught at 10 localities, with one or two individuals at most sites, but likely occurs in many other locations in between.
range: The species has so far been reported from 10 localities (Francis and Eger 2012, Son et al. 2015) from central Laos and central Vietnam south to Cambodia and south Vietnam. The type locality was Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Khammouan Province, Pha Deng, ~8 km E of Ban Navang (17°57’N, 105°23’E), altitude 1,140 m.
useTrade: No records of trade in this species. Presumably roosts individually or in small groups, like other members of the genus, which would make it unlikely to be readily captured in significant numbers for consumption or trade.
conservationActions: Has been reported from reserves or biodiversity conservation areas in all three countries.

rationale: Murina eleryi is assessed as Least Concern due to its relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, its tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Several aspects of the wing morphology and echolocation call design of Murina eleryi collectively suggest its adaptation to foraging in highly cluttered airspaces such as forest interiors and other densely vegetated environments. The species likely roosts in foliage but its occurrence in heavily degraded forest areas also indicates that it is capable of tolerating a degree of habitat disturbance (Furey et al. 2009). In northern Vietnam and likely also neighbouring territories, M. eleryi bears young at the start of the wet season (May–September) and completes weaning in July (Furey et al. 2010).
threats: The current pattern of records of Murina eleryi demonstrates a strong association with forest, therefore forest clearance undoubtedly presents a threat. However, like several other Murina species, M. eleryi is capable of tolerating some habitat disturbance.
population: The species has a presumed large population and, while it is thought to have some tolerance of habitat modification, it is suspected to be experiencing a low level population decline.
range: This species was described based on specimens from Kim Hy Nature Reserve (Bac Kan province), Khau Ca area (Ha Giang province) and Phu Yen district (Son La province) in northern Viet Nam (Furey et al. 2009). Francis and Eger (2012) reported records from the Bolikhamxai, Houaphan and Khammouan provinces of Laos and specimens from Quang Nam province (Viet Nam) and Shiwandashan National Reserve, Jing Xin County Nature Reserve (Guangxi province) and Shuipu Village (Guizhou province) in China, whereas Son et al. (2015) reported records from Phia Oac - Phia Den Nature Reserve (Cao Bang province), Xuan Son National Park (Phu Tho province), Xuan Lien Nature Reserve (Thanh Hoa province), Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park (Quang Binh province), Ngoc Linh Nature Reserve (Quang Nam and Kon Tum provinces) and Ba To area (Quang Ngai province) in Viet Nam. Liu et al. (2014) and Xu et al. (2014) assessed specimens from the Hunan, Guangdong (Qixi Mountain), Guizhou, Jiangxi (Jiulianshan National Natural Reserve) and Guangxi provinces in China. This pattern of records suggests the species is widely distributed in Viet Nam and adjacent areas of Laos and China, although possibly largely in montane forested regions.
conservationActions: There are no species-specific conservation actions known for the species. Given its broad range, it is assumed the species is found in at least one protected area. Research is needed into the species population, trends, ecology, and threats from deforestation.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: In northern Myanmar, it has been found altitudes ranging from 615 to 1,230 m asl (Bates and Harrison 1997). In Southeast Asia, it appears to have been recorded from somewhat disturbed areas.
threats: The threats to this species are not well known, although it is unlikely to be threatened throughout its range. Although it is definitely threatened by deforestation (generally resulting from logging operations and the conversion of land to agricultural and other uses), it has been recorded from some modified habitats and seems to be somewhat adaptable in parts of its range.
population: It has only been caught in small numbers in all parts of the range (Francis pers. comm., Csorba pers. comm.).
range: Widespread in the Indo-Burma subregion, with only scattered records from China. The boundary between the closely related forms M. feae and M. jaintiana is not known.
conservationActions: It is present in a number of protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as EN under criterion B1ab(i,ii,iii) as it is known from only Dalat Plateau in southern Viet Nam, with an estimated extent of occurrence of 782 km². The species has only been recorded from Bi Dup – Nui Ba National Park in the northeast portion of the plateau. Over 30% of the plateau has been logged and forest loss and degradation is continuing throughout much of the area.
habitat: Murina harpiolodes is found in mountainous mixed subtropical forest where it is quite moist throughout the year as there is no pronounced dry season. Nightly temperatures in that area could be relatively low, especially in the end of winter. Little is known about foraging behaviour and diet composition of this species. A young individual with not fully ossified epiphyses of wing bones was once captured in the second half of April suggesting that the birth took place in March (Abramov et al. 2009, Kruskop 2013).
threats: Forest loss and degradation are the main threats to this species, with more than 30% of the species' known range on the Bi Dup – Nui Ba National Park (Lam Dong Province) being affected. The species has a limited distribution area. The use of any chemical on nearby agricultural lands pose a threat to the Murina harpioloides population.
population: The population of Murina harpiolodes is unknown, but is thought to be declining as over 30% of its forested habitat has been lost. The population size is thought to be given the species small distribution range on the Dalat Plateau in southern Viet Nam.
range: Murina harpiolodes is only known from one location on the Dalat Plateau in Viet Nam (Lam Dong Province), where it occurs from 1,400 to 1,800 m asl (Kruskop 2013, Son et al. 2015). There is possibility, that this bat also inhabits forested areas at same elevations in neighbouring provinces Dak Lak and Khanh Hoa.
useTrade: This bat is not used in commercial trade, local cuisine or local medicine.
conservationActions: All known records of Murina harpiolodes were made in Bi Dup – Nui Ba National Park (Lam Dong Province) or nearby it. The territory of this Park is situated close to the large Chu Yang Sin National Park (Dak Lak Province) and Hon Ba mountain Nature Reserve (Khanh Hoa Province), where populations of Murina harpiolodes have yet to be documented. Currently, a large part of the potential distribution range of the species is situated in protected areas which offers the species some protection. Additional studies of the species' distribution, ecology, reproduction, foraging behaviour are required.

rationale: Barbastella darjelingensis is assessed as Least Concern as it has a wide range, part of which is located in sparsely populated regions, so it is difficult to assume threats to its existence in the near future. However, careful research is needed over most of the range, as the species may include cryptic taxa, which may have a higher threat status.
habitat: Strictly nocturnal species. Little is known about its habits, but, by analogy with other barbastelles, it is probably solitary or forming small colonies and feeding on middle-size flying insects. Known mainly from mountain areas up to elevation of ca. 2,350 m ASL. Inhabiting mountainous temperate and subtropical forests. In Vietnam it was found foraging over stream in a deciduous forest at the elevation of ca. 2000 m ASL (Kruskop and Shchinov 2010), in India animals were captured in an oak forest and over a forest clearing (Chakravarty et al. 2020). Day roosts probably in natural and artificial caves and caverns, rock crevices or in hollows under tree bark.
threats: This species can be threatened by uncontrolled visits and development of underground cavities that serve as roosts for it, as well as the destruction of habitats and the use of pesticides in the surrounding agricultural lands.
population: Considering its wide range there seems to be little information available about the population of this species. According to published records, this species is highly sporadic, with low density of population, however it could be an artifact caused by distribution in hard-to-reach areas. The species population is presumed stable.
range: As accepted here, the species has a vast distribution range from eastern Afghanistan (Benda and Gaisler 2015) through northern India, Nepal, Bhutan, south China, to Laos, northern Vietnam and Taiwan (Bates and Harrison 1997, Smith and Xie 2008, Kruskop 2013). Known distribution connected with the mountainous areas of moderate elevations.
useTrade: This species has no commercial value and not known to be involved into commercial trade. It most probably plays certain role as a natural controller of forestry pests, but due to low population density its influence on agriculture in this respect is negligible.
conservationActions: No special conservation actions are known to date. Special research for revealing of possible cryptic taxonomic diversity and clarifying of the species natural habits are recommended.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern due to its wide distribution and no known major threats. In its eastern range, the species is naturally not abundant.
habitat: Found in a wide range of arid and semi-arid habitats including steppe in lowland areas and rocky mountains. A crevice-dwelling species, it inhabits buildings, ruins (including tombs), and natural rock crevices throughout the year.
threats: Little is known about threats to the species; however the habitats in some parts of its range are degrading. As this species lives in crevices in ruins, tourism-related developmental activities and disturbance will have negative impact on their populations.
population: Appears to be generally rare to uncommon although reported as locally common.
range: A palaearctic species, occurring in central Asia to India.
useTrade: Nothing is known about its use and trade.

rationale: Eptesicus anatolicus is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large and stable population. If it is declining, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Eptesicus anatolicus inhabits mostly Mediterranean shrubby habitats, avoiding mountains and forested areas in the West and more arid habitats in the East (e.g. Iran) (Benda et al. 2012, von Helversen 1998). Its roosting preferences are unknown, but one maternity roost has been found in Turkey in a building crevice, comprising 15 to 20 individuals. (Albayrak and Asan 1999).It is known to forage around streetlamps in Turkey and in the vicinity of urban areas on Rhodes (Benda et al. 2012, A. Lefebvre pers. comm.). It feeds on a range of insects. Orthoptera, Coleoptera, Odonata and Lepidoptera where the most common orders of insect preyed on in Iran whereas E. anatolicus seemed to feed almost exclusively on Carabidae (Coleoptera) in Turkey (Benda et al. 2012).
threats: Understanding of the threats to the species is limited as the ecology of the species is poorly known. This species, unlike E. bottae, seems to rely on Mediterranean habitats which are highly at risk because of climate change, mainly because of the increased occurrence of fires (Barredo et al. 2016) as well as urbanisation, especially in coastal areas (Cuttelod et al. 2009).
population: This is a widespread, but relatively unknown species. It appears to be generally common, especially along the coast of South Anatolia as well as the Greek Islands. It appears to be quite rare in Lebanon from where there are very few records (Benda et al. 2016). The population is presumed to be stable.
range: This is a Middle eastern species distributed along a belt of Mediterranean habitats spanning from Rhodes and other Dodecanese Islands (Symi and Megisti) (Greece) to Iran (Spitzenberger 1994, von Helversen 1998, Hanak et al. 2001, Benda et al. 2016, Benda et al. 2018, Benda and Uhrin 2017, Mensoor 2020). The unique record in Northern Cyprus is believed to be an accidental record (Benda 2007, Benda 2018). It has been recorded from sea level to 1,310 m (Benda et al. 2012).
conservationActions: This species is protected on the Greek Islands under the Bonn convention which needs to be updated to reflect taxonomic changes (NOTE: it is listed as Eptesicus bottae in said legislation). This species does not occur in protected areas.More research is needed to better understand the species’ ecological needs and the dynamics of its populations in order to develop adequate conservation plans.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, because it is widespread, relatively adaptable and there are no major threats.
habitat: This taxon inhabits varied habitats from semi-desert and steppe habitats to tropical forests. Usually roost in shaded areas, such as the cracks of rocks or buildings. Sometimes found in frontal parts of caves. Generally solitary or found in small groups. It is thought that its diet may include butterflies and moths. Nothing much is known about its ecology.
threats: There are no major threats to the species throughout its range.
population: There is no information on population sizes at present.
range: The species is widespread and is currently found in from China, Taiwan, Laos PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, India, Pakistan and Iran.
useTrade: This species it not included in trade and has no commercial value.
conservationActions: This bat requires no special conservations actions besides conservation activities common for all bats of the temperate zone. Its range does include a few protected areas in its range.

rationale: The species is locally abundant and widespread. Regional trends are difficult to determine due to the lack of reliable data but it seems that there are no reasons to consider the population to be declining globally.
habitat: The species uses mainly crevices in rocks as a natural roost. This characteristic has allowed this bat to make frequent use of bridges and other similar human-made constructions with crevices-like openings etc., being directly favoured by the availability of these frequent human constructions. It is an ecologically plastic species found in a variety of habitats from semi-desert to temperate and subtropical dry forest, Mediterranean-type shrub-land, farmland and suburban areas. As in other serotines, favoured feeding areas include pasture, open woodland edge, gardens, and forested regions. It's a trophic generalist species, feeding on a variety of sources from beetles to moths and flies. Most maternity colonies (between 20 and 100 females) are found in human constructions and buildings and naturally in rock fissures. It is a sedentary species with annual movements of less than 40 km and females showing high fidelity to the roosts (Ibáñez 2007).
threats: No specific threats are known for the species although it can accumulate biocides due its feeding habits in agricultural areas (Guillén et al. 1991).
population: There are no estimates of the population figures for the species. Nevertheless, it is reported to be very abundant locally and in some areas of Southern Spain is considered one of the commonest species with density values up to 7.5 individuals per km2 (Ibáñez 2007). Lifespan is not well known but annual survival rate of adults was found to vary across colonies with an average value around 0.70 (Papadatou et al. 2011). This species is the main host of a differentiated strand of rabies virus in Iberia (Vázquez-Morón et al. 2011).
range: The species is known to occupy the warmer southern half of the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean fringe along the African coast from Morocco all the way to Lybia, from where it was originally described. The Iberian and Moroccan populations seem quite close genetically suggesting recent contacts through the Gibraltar Strait (Juste et al. 2009).
conservationActions: No specific actions seem to be required to guarantee the species’ future. E. isabellinus is profiting from most of the man-made constructions that are being used more and more often as roosting places making the species quite common in urban areas.

rationale: This newly described species is known from several different portions of western dry deciduous forests, where, based on frequency of capture, it appears to be relatively common (Goodman et al. 2015). It has been found within and at the edge of several protected areas.  This species is known from relatively intact dry deciduous forest, as well in degraded habitats, in both cases often netted over water pools, and it is presumed not to be strictly forest-dependent.  As it is difficult to separate in the hand from other sympatrically occurring vesper bats known from western Madagascar, it is presumed to have a broader geographic distribution than currently documented.
habitat: This species occurs in different non-forested habitats, as well as forested zones. Its ecology is poorly known, but it occurrence in human-altered landscapes suggests that it is tolerant at some undefined level of habitat disturbance.
threats: The forested habitats in the region of Madagascar this species is known are under considerable pressure associated with logging for wood products and clearing for swidden agriculture (Zinner et al. 2014).  It is presumed that these habitat modifications have an impact on this species, but as it is known to not be strictly forest dependent, it is difficult to assess if these pressures form a major threat.
population: Not known but presumably substantial as it has been captured at several different geographically separate sites and in degraded habitats that have been modified by human actions.
range: Currently only identified from the central and south central portions of western Madagascar. Its known elevation distribution is from near sea level to 870 m (Goodman et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This species is known to occur in the general vicinity of the Kirindy Forest north of Morondava, which is part of the Menabe Antimena (Kirindy CNFEREF) protected area; the Zombitse-Vohibasia National Park; the Kirindy Mitea National Park; and Amoron'i Onilahy (Sept Lacs) protected area (Goodman et al. 2015).

rationale: Hypsugo lanzai is listed as Endangered under criterion B1ab(iii) as its extent of occurrence is smaller than 4,000 km² and the limited habitat on the island is declining due to increased storms (e.g., cyclones) caused by climate change, and unplanned development.
