habitat: Grevy’s Zebras live in arid and semi-arid grass/shrubland where they can gain access to permanent water (Klingel 1974; Rubenstein 1986; Rowen and Ginsberg 1992; Williams 2002, 2013; Kebede 2013). They are predominantly grazers, although browse can comprise up to 30% of their diet during times of drought or in those areas that have been highly transformed through overgrazing (Kartzinel et al. 2015). Breeding males defend resource territories (water and food being the key resources) of 2–12 km²; the home range size of non-territorial individuals can be as large as 10,000 km² (Williams 2013). They are extremely mobile and individuals have been recorded to move distances of greater than 80 km, with movements determined by the availability of resources; lactating females, for example, can only tolerate one or two days away from water (Klingel 1974; Rubenstein 1986; Rowen and Ginsberg 1992; Williams 2002, 2013). Hence when pastoral livestock monopolize water, Grevy’s Zebras suffer. They often mill around watering points in the late afternoon waiting to drink, thus reducing foraging time. By drinking predictably at night they are prone to predation by lions and in some areas when co-habiting with plains Zebras, they are preferentially attacked (Rubenstein 2010). During the dry season, when they are dependent on permanent water, Grevy’s Zebra may stay nearer to water and tend to be more concentrated. However, in the Alledeghi Wildlife Reserve in Ethiopia, they are more concentrated during the wet season in order to avoid the pastoralists and livestock that move into the area during that season (Kebede et al. 2012).Between 2010 and 2014 the population of Grevy’s Zebras inhabiting the Mpala, Ol Jogi and Pyramid Conservancies in central Laikipia County, was monitored three times per year. During this period on average the population consisted of: 33% adult males of which 17% were territorial and 16% were bachelors; 40% adult females; 8% juveniles, half males and half females; and 19% infants of which 8% were males, 8% were females and 3% were of undetermined sex (Rubenstein and Brown pers. obs.). Therefore 33% adult males + 40% adult females gives 73% of the population as mature. Given that population projection models show population stability is maintained when the percentage of recruits (juveniles and foals) reach 30% (Rubenstein 2010), the Laikipia Grev’s Zebra population appears to be in relatively good demographic health (between 2004 and 2014). A decade of data on sightings of Grevy's Zebra numbers as well as age and sex class from scouts in the Meibae, Westgate, Sessia, Laisamas, Ngili West and Kalama Conservancies show an that the percentage of recruits (foals and juveniles) has increased from 9% to 22% of the population, with the 2016 Great Grevy's Rally showing a Kenya-wide age structure of 28% recruits. This indicates that this population is approaching sustainability.
threats: Kenya’s Grevy’s Zebra Technical Committee recently assessed and ranked the threats to Grevy’s Zebras. In decreasing order they include: 1) Habitat degradation and loss induced by extremely heavy grazing by livestock (Rubenstein 2010, Low et al. 2009); 2) Competition with livestock, especially over access to water and high quality rangeland (Rowen and Ginsberg 1992; Williams 2002, 2013); 3) Local hunting for meat as well as medicinal and cultural purpose; 4) Disease from contact with unvaccinated livestock, especially with respect to anthrax and babesiosis (Hawkins et al. 2015); 5) Hybridization with plains Zebras, although genes currently only flow from Grevy’s to plains Zebras (Cordingley et al. 2009); 6) Predation (Rubenstein 2010); 7) Anticipated land conversion for resort development and other large-scale initiatives for economic expansion.In Kenya, hunting for skins in the late 1970s was the likely cause of the initial precipitous decline in numbers. Recent data suggest that numbers continued to decline because recruitment was limited by low levels of infant and juvenile survival. This was a result of competition for resources – both food and water – with pastoral people and their domestic livestock (Williams 1998). However, a low level of hunting of Grevy’s Zebra for food and, in some areas, medicinal uses continues (Williams pers. comm. 2002). Furthermore, access to existing water sources continues to decline in some regions and the water supply in critical perennial rivers has been reduced, most notably in the Ewaso Ng’iro River where over-abstraction of water for irrigation schemes has reduced dry season river flow by 90% over the past three decades (Williams pers. comm. 2002).In Ethiopia, the Grevy’s Zebra population was in a declining trend during the last 30 years, due to habitat loss/fragmentation, drought, poaching and potential competition with livestock. Habitat loss, drought and poaching were considered to be the major threats. Illegal killing of Grevy’s Zebra was the primary cause of the decline (Kebede 2013). The Alledeghi Wildlife Reserve population is small and genetically isolated. Initial population genetics research on the mtDNA control region revealed two new haplotypes that so far are not found in any other Grevy’s Zebra populations. The nucleotide diversity levels for both the Alledeghi and the southern Ethiopian populations were extremely low (Kebede et al. 2014).Recently, Muoria et al. (2007) recorded an outbreak of anthrax in the Wamba area of southern Samburu, Kenya, during which more than 50 animals succumbed to the disease. Further research on disease prevalence is revealing that Grevy’s Zebra are a reservoir for Theileria and Babesia (tick borne disease), and the first case of West Nile Virus has been found in one individual; the first detected in a wild equid (Hawkins et al. 2015). Disease represents a significant potential threat to fragmented and small populations of endangered species.
population: Grevy's Zebra suffered a severe population reduction between the late 1970s/early 1980s and the early 2000s, declining from a global population of around 15,600 individuals in the late 1970s/early 1980s (Williams 2002) to around 2,000 individuals in 2004. Since then there have been some signs of population recovery, with the population remaining roughly stable over the last 10 years. Over the last three generations (a generation is approximately 10 years) there has been a population reduction of about 54% from an estimated 5,800 Grevy's Zebra in the 1980s to ~2,680 animals currently.The most recent estimates put the total population of Grevy's Zebra remaining in the wild in Kenya and Ethiopia at less than 2,000 mature individuals, based on 73% adults in well studied populations (Rubenstein and Brown pers. obs. 2014). This number consists of approximately 2,350 individuals in Kenya (1,716 mature animals) in 2016 and about 230 individuals in Ethiopia (168 mature animals) in 2012. The largest regional population numbering around 1,300 individuals (949 mature) is in the centre of the Samburu region of central Kenya. In Kenya, the Grevy’s Zebra population declined from around 13,700 in 1977 (Dirschl and Wetmore 1978) to 4,300 in 1988 (KREMU 1989). They then declined further to 2,400-2,700 in 2000 (Nelson and Williams 2003) and 1,570-1,980 in 2004 (KWS 2012), to an estimated population size of 1,470-2,140 in 2006 (B. Low pers. comm. 2007); a decline of 85-90% over 29 years. In 2008, the population was estimated to consist of 2,400 individuals, indicating that either counting techniques had improved or that the population had stabilized or even increased, or a combination of the two (Mwasi and Mwangi 2007, KWS 2012). An assessment of all existing counts carried out by Kenya’s Grevy’s Zebra Technical Committee in 2012 estimated that by 2011 the population in Kenya was approximately 2,500. In January 2016 a comprehensive census of Grevy's zebra in five counties in Kenya was conducted (“The Great Grevy’s Rally”). The census comprised of 350 people (members of the public, conservancy members, rangers and scouts from conservancies and National Parks and Reserves, and scientists) driving over 25,000 km² recording Grevy's zebras using GPS enabled cameras. Over 40,000 photos of Grevy's Zebra were taken. The photographs were sent to the US-based IBEIS team to process the images, identifying unique individuals seen on days 1 and 2 as well as the number seen on day 1 that were re-sighted on day 2. From these three values population size estimates could be computed. In the future, such analyses will be performed by Kenyan scientists once the software is made publicly available. From the sight-resight analysis the population was estimated to be 2,250 individuals (95% CI of +/- 93; KWS 2016). For the first time, Laikipia county has the highest number of Grevy’s Zebras (supporting over half of Kenya's Grevy's Zebra population), surpassing Samburu and Isiolo counties, the traditional heartland of the species. An additional 80-100 animals were estimated in Tsavo, Oserian, Meru National Park, and the Laisamas area - areas that were too dangerous or inaccessible to survey during the census period (KWS 2016). The total Kenya population in 2016 is therefore estimated to be ~2,350 individuals. The population will be re-censused in August 2017. It is expected that the Kenyan population of Grevy's Zebra will remain stable, or may increase due to conservation efforts.In Ethiopia, Grevy’s Zebra declined from an estimated 1,500 (or a possible maximum of 1,900) in 1980 to approximately 600 in 1995 (Rowen and Ginsberg 1992, F. Kebede pers. comm. 2007), to approximately 100 in 2003 (Williams et al. 2003). In 2006, the population in Ethiopia was estimated to be approximately 130 (F. Kebede pers. comm. 2007). The trend from 1980 to 2003 (23 years) suggests a decline of roughly 94%. Counts and ‘sight-resight’ population analyses of the largest population suggest that by 2011 Ethiopia’s population had increased to approximately 230 individuals (Kebede et al. 2012, Kebede pers. comm. 2014). However this population is mainly in the Alledghi Wildlife Reserve (196 +/- 53 animals, declined from 600 in 1970) and very few individuals remain in Chew Bahir (22 animals, declined from 1,500 in 1970) and Borana (10 animals) (Williams 2002, Kebede pers. comm. 2014).  The population in Ethiopia is expected to at best stay stable, and is likely to decline.The density and area of occupancy of Grevy’s Zebra fluctuates seasonally as animals move in their search for resources. During the dry season, when they are dependent on permanent water, animals tend to be more concentrated. However, given that they can move up to 35 km from water even during the dry season, their densities are never high. They are most abundant and most easily observed in the southern portion of their range in southern Samburu and Laikipia counties, Kenya.
range: Grevy's zebra is only found in the Horn of Africa, specifically Ethiopia and Kenya. Grevy's Zebras have undergone substantial reductions in range. Historically, they ranged east of the Rift Valley in Kenya to southwestern Somalia, and in northern Ethiopia from the Alledeghi Plain through the Awash Valley, the Ogaden, and north-east of Lake Turkana in Ethiopia to north of Mt. Kenya and southeast down the Tana River in Kenya (Bauer et al. 1994). Currently, Grevy’s Zebra have a discontinuous range, and are found from the eastern side of the Rift Valley in Kenya to the Tana River. Currently there is a small, isolated population in the Alledeghi Plains northeast of Awash National Park (N.P.) in Ethiopia. From Lake Ch’ew Bahir in southern Ethiopia, the population extends to just north of Mt. Kenya although a few animals are found further southeast along the Tana River. A small introduced population survives in and around Tsavo East N.P. in Kenya.Grevy's Zebra are considered to be extirpated from Somalia, where the last confirmed sightings date to 1973. There are no confirmed records that the species ever occurred in Eritrea or Djibouti (Bauer et al. 1994, Yalden et al. 1986). Sightings in South Sudan are questionable and need to be verified (Williams 2002, 2013).
useTrade: In Kenya, Grevy’s Zebras are only hunted at subsistence level for meat and medicinal uses; commercial trading of skins has ceased. In Ethiopia, killing of Grevy’s Zebra for meat and medicine is the primary cause of the decline (Kebede 2013).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. Grevy's Zebra are legally protected in both Kenya and Ethiopia, although in the latter, official protection has been limited. Changing attitudes of local pastoralist populations towards the species has had dramatic effects on improving the ranging, foraging and drinking capabilities of Grevy’s Zebras. Scout programs in which community members participate in gathering essential data on the ecology and behaviour of their populations not only generates income, it transforms the scouts into Grevy’s Zebra champions which in turn helps change community attitudes and gather essential information when populations are at risk (Low et al. 2009). In addition, in Kenya Grevy’s Zebras have been protected by a hunting ban since 1977. While under the Wildlife Conservation and Management Act No 376 of 1976 (Part II of the First Schedule), Grevy’s Zebra was listed as a ‘Game Animal’ (Williams 2002); there is a chance that they will be up-listed to a legally ‘Protected Animal’ in Kenya.At present, protected areas form less than 0.5% of the range of Grevy’s Zebra. In Ethiopia, the protected areas are nominal (Alledeghi Wildlife Reserve, Borena Controlled Hunting Area and Chew Bahir/Chalbi Wildlife Reserve). In Kenya, the Buffalo Springs, Samburu, Shaba N.R. complex and the private and community land wildlife conservancies in Isiolo, Samburu and the Laikipia Plateau provide a core and crucial protection of Kenya’s southern population of Grevy’s Zebra (Williams 2002). On the Laikipia Plateau, protection and reduced competition with domestic livestock, have seen Grevy's Zebra numbers increasing since they first expanded into this area in the early 1970s (Williams 2002, 2013). In addition, changing attitudes in Samburu county, the centre of its distribution, has enabled Grevy’s Zebra to share resources more equitably with livestock, thus increasing the proportion of infants and juveniles (Low et al. 2009).Habitat restoration through grass re-seeding and planned livestock grazing is targeting core habitat areas in Grevy’s Zebra range. Close monitoring of Grevy’s Zebra body condition during prolonged droughts is carried out by scouts and additional water provision made to ensure continued access to declining water sources (http://www.grevysZebratrust.org/water-management.html). In addition, supplementary feeding of Grevy’s Zebra during extreme drought is being piloted in Kenya (Grevy’s Zebra Disease Response Committee, 2013), and appears to have prevented a population decline during the 2011 drought in the conservancies of central Samburu County (Low and Rubenstein pers. obs).Kenya has completed its second conservation strategy for Grevy’s Zebra (KWS 2012). It has 5 strategic objectives: 1) Coordination and implementation of the conservation and management strategy; 2) Enhancement of stakeholder partnership in Grevy’s Zebra conservation; 3) Enhancement of Grevy’s Zebra conservation and habitat management; 4) Establishment of a program for monitoring and managing Grevy’s Zebra population health; and 5) Enhancement of transboundary Grevy’s Zebra conservation.In September 2016  a workshop involving Grevy’s zebra biologists, conservationists and the governors of the five counties where Grevy’s zebras live will be convened by Kitili Mbathi, the Director General of the Kenya Wildlife Service, at the Mpala Reseach Center. The workshop will explore options that will move the populations from ‘ sustainable’ to increasing’ and identify actions that the governors can commit to that will help make this happen. Future actions to increase numbers might include: restoration of grasslands, improved water access, addressing high lion predation rates in Meru County, and developing local capacity and supporting citizen science monitoring. Ethiopia has held two workshops on the status and conservation of the Grevy’s Zebra. Research and community-based conservation is on-going in the Alledeghi Wildlife Reserve. The Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority in collaboration with the IUCN/SSC Equid Specialist Group will be developing a national species action plan in the near future.

rationale: The Romanian Hamster is endemic to Europe, occurring in Romania and Bulgaria. It has a restricted range, but its extent of occurrence is much larger than 20,000 km². The area of occupancy is not known but is suspected to be approaching the 2,000 km² threshold for Vulnerable. The ongoing decline in the number of active localities in Bulgaria meets the threshold for category Endangered A2c, with a population reduction of 50% estimated. However, data is not available for the Romanian range of this species. An overall population decline of 30% is suspected to have occurred within the past 10 years, therefore this species is assessed as Vulnerable A2c.
habitat: Relatively recent research suggests that this is a crepuscular species displaying little activity during daylight hours (Simeonovska-Nikolova and Dekov 2013). It is found in relatively dry habitats including barren, rocky steppe and steppe grassland, Medicago, Taraxacum and cereal fields, vineyards, gardens, and scrubby slopes (Vohralík 1999). A potential distribution model also predicts that their range overlaps with Central European mixed forests (Chisamera et al. 2012). Its diet is probably similar to that of other hamster species.
threats: The main threat to this hamster is habitat loss and degradation as a result of intensive agriculture. The agricultural utilisation of abandoned fields and steppe-like habitat is very likely to have a negative impact on the species (V. Vohralik pers. comm. 2006), although the species does inhabit some anthropogenic habitats. In Dobrudja intensive agriculture is ongoing (I. Coroiu pers. comm. 2006), and agricultural intensification may have increased since the accession of Romania in the European Union.
population: The Romanian Hamster is uncommon throughout its small range. Population densities fluctuate, but outbreaks are localised and infrequent. Long-term population trends have not been quantified but are believed to be declining. In Romania, the population was estimated at around 3,000 mature individuals (Murariu 1995). Approximately 50% of populations recorded prior to 2000 are no longer active in Bulgaria (N. Nedyalkov, unpublished data).
range: Mesocricetus newtoni is a European endemic species. Its range is restricted to lowlands (up to 460 m) along the right bank of the lower Danube River in northern Bulgaria and southeastern Romania, Dobrudja (Vohralík 1999). Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is much larger than 20,000 km² and the area of occupancy (AOO) is not known, but it is suspected to be close to 2,000 km².
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention and Annex II and IV of the EU Habitats Directive.Appropriate protection of this species' habitat from intensive farming is needed. Research and monitoring is required to determine population trends in this poorly-known species; if there is evidence of declines, appropriate conservation measures should be instated (Nechay 2000). The species is included on the Red Lists of Romania and Bulgaria and is protected by Romanian legislation. The Romanian Hamster became one of the target species in the LIFE20 NAT/BG/001162 project, which is likely to include an ex-situ element for future reintroductions.

rationale: Roach's Mouse-tailed Dormouse is found within a restricted range (its area of occupancy (AOO) is smaller than 2,000 km² ); there are recent records from Anatolia, European Turkey, Bulgaria and Greece, but these involved required intensive survey effort to collect (involved years of collecting effort) and the surveys failed to record the species across areas of suitable habitat where it was previously recorded, indicating a declining population and that this species is increasingly rare. It is known from more than 30 sites, however the failure to record the species in areas of suitable habitat and the conversion of potential habitat to agriculture, mean its remaining population is now thought to be severely fragmented and its AOO and population size are subject to ongoing decline. The decline in availability and quality of habitat and severe fragmentation of what habitat remains, combined with its small AOO qualifies Myomimus roachi for Vulnerable (VU B2ab(ii, iii)).
habitat: This species inhabits scrub and semi-open habitats with trees or bushes such as orchards, vineyards, hedgerows in arable land, and river banks. Although it is found in some extensively managed agricultural habitats, it is absent from intensively farmed areas. It is more terrestrial than other dormice, and its diet consists for the most part of seeds. The most recent recording of the species was caught on an old (about 40–50 years old) oak tree (Quercus spp.) at 1.8 m height within semi-open grassland with shrubs: blackthorn (Prunus spinosa), Jerusalem thorn (Paliurus spina-christi) and single trees or small forest patches of Quercus sp. (about 40–50 years old) and pear trees (Pyrus communis) (Nedyalkov et al. 2018).In Turkey the species has been often caught on mulberry trees, walnut trees and figs (Kurtonur and Ozkan 1991). It seems that M. roachi is active only for very short time; only for four months. In the wild, specimens have caught between May-August (only a few caught in the end of April). It has very low reproductive potential as during the active period (in the wild and in captivity) it is recorded to reproduce only once; in captivity two females produced five and six young respectively (Kurtonur and Ozkan 1991, Buruldağ and Kurtonur 2001, N. Nedyalkov pers. comm. 2020). Roach's Mouse-tailed Dormouse is omnivorous eating different type of food with inclination towards insects (mole-crickets, grasshoppers, butterflies, moths), but also consumes seeds (sunflower, peanuts, wheat) and fruits (apricot, apple, pear, mulberry) (Buruldağ and Kurtonur 2001). Myomimus roachi is found to co-occur with two other glirids: the Forest (Dryomys nitedula) and Edible dormouse (Glis glis), with which probably compеtеs for foods and shelters (Kurtonur and Ozkan 1991, N. Nedyalkov pers. comm. 2020).
threats: The range of this species is in decline. In European Turkey, most of its habitat has been transformed by agriculture. In spite of intensive searches the species has not been found in Turkey over the last five years. It is clear that the range is shrinking.It is very difficult to determine what is happening with the range because it is the exact habitat preferences are not known. It has been declining since the Pleistocene. Only 50 animals are known in collections. The region in European Turkey and Bulgaria is intensively cultivated, with very little natural habitat remaining. Much of the Bulgarian population is threatened by the construction of dams along the Tundzha River (Milchev and Georgiev 2012). Climate change, even following mild projections, could cause the extinction of this species (Levinsky et al. 2007).
population: Little is known about this restricted-range species. In Turkish Thrace there are only definite records from a small number of sites and despite intensive survey effort the species has rarely been recorded (SW Asia workshop 2005). The most recent record of this species was from 2017 near the Sakar Mountain in Bulgaria; however, surveys failed to record the species at any other location in Bulgaria where it is thought to be present, indicating a declining and increasingly fragmented population (Nedyalkov et al. 2018). Cranial remains of 15 specimens were determined among 30,532 mammals in Barn Owl (Tyto alba) pellets in 35 localities from 2000 to 2008 and 32,941 mammals in Eagle Owl (Bubo bubo) pellets in 59 localities from 1988 to 2011 in SE Bulgaria making up just 1% of the mammalian prey base (Milchev and Georgiev 2012). Due to the large survey effort that has gone into this species and paucity of recordings, it is thought to be extremely rare.Throughout its distribution the vast majority of suitable habitat has been converted to intensive agriculture, and the species' range is severely fragmented and subject to ongoing losses (SW Asia workshop 2005).
range: Endemic to the Mediterranean region. Roach's Mouse-tailed Dormouse is found in Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey (both European and Asian Turkey). Recently, the presence of this dormouse in Greece has been confirmed on the base cranial remains found in owl pellets (Kiamos et al. 2019). It is mainly a lowland species (0–400 m asl.). This species is found in Thrace (Kurtonur and Ozkan 1991) and western Turkey (Storch 1978). The species is present, though extremely rare, in Bulgaria, with its known range in the south and south east of the country.  The exact limits are unknown in western Anatolia, where the species is presently known from only three separate localities. The species was first described as a fossil species in 1937, and was only described as an extant species in the late 1940s. Subfossil information from southern Turkey and Israel indicated a larger range over the last few thousand years.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendices II and III of the Bern Convention; and in Appendix II on the Habitat directive 91/43/EEC. Surveys are needed to determine if and where the species can still be found, and sites where the species is found should be strictly protected. Myomimus roachi is strictly protected species, according national laws in Bulgaria and Turkey. This species is found in the Gallipoli Peninsula National Park. 6 of the 15 known recent localities in Bulgaria where this species occurs are protected areas (Milchev and Georgiev 2012); five more protected areas cover older records whose current status is unknown.  Even in protected areas, annual fires can damage the population and destroy areas of habitat. There is an action plan for the species in European Turkey (Özkan and Paksuz 2015).

rationale: The species is restricted to two sites on sand dunes, both of which are threatened by encroaching human settlements (building for tourist complexes). The localities occur on either side of a city and the population is therefore fragmented into two locations. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 507 km² and its area of occupancy (AOO) will be less than this, but data are currently unavailable to determine its AOO. Given the ongoing threat to its habitat, this species qualifies for at least Endangered (EN B1ab(iii)). More precise information on the distribution of this species could result in uplisting to Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species is found in sandy habitats close to the coastline, mainly dunes sprinkled with Juniperus phoenicea and Retama monosperma.
threats: The species is threatened by disturbance of its coastal habitat by tourism, especially during the summer months. In addition, the development of infrastructure for the tourist industry is leading to human disturbance for this species.
population: The population size for this species is unknown, but it is probably naturally small (due to the restricted habitat). It is likely to be declining as a result of habitat loss and mainly disturbance associated with human infrastructure building (Ndiaye et al. 2012). A recent survey failed to detect species at the type locality, meaning that the last specimen captured in the sand dunes south of Essaouira dates back to the early 1980s (Ndiaye et al. 2012).
range: A Moroccan endemic, this species is restricted to around 30 km of sandy habitats north and south to Essaouira (north of High Atlas).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures in place. There are no protected areas within its range.

rationale: Eastern Tur is listed as Near Threatened. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is above the threshold of 20,000 km², however the species is known from fewer than 10 locations and there is continuing decline in population size underway; it is suspected that a decline of  >10% will occur over the next three generations (estimated at 21 years). Therefore, the species almost qualifies as Vulnerable under criterion B1. This is a difficult species to assess because of its unclear taxonomic status. Its range is relatively small and it is a narrow endemic regardless of its taxonomic status; observed and projected declines justify maintaining the category Near Threatened.
habitat: Eastern tur inhabit elevations between 1,000 and 4,000 m a.s.l. Although the mountains in their range can reach 5,000 m asl, Tur seldom rise above 3,500 m asl. They live in forests found up to 2,600 m, and in subalpine and alpine meadows and rocky talus slopes at higher elevations. Animals avoid thick forests on gentle slopes, but stay readily in open forests growing on steep precipitous slopes. During winter, the proportion of animals dwelling below timberline increases (Veinberg 1984). On average, 34% of Eastern tur lived in the forest throughout the year in Georgia (Ekvtimishvili 1952). Some forest-dwelling populations in Azerbaijan may be completely (Vereshchagin 1938), or more possibly semi-isolated from subalpine and alpine zones. In summer, adult males typically inhabit higher altitudes than females and young (Veinberg 1984). During the harsh winters, tur concentrate on sunny slopes; during the summer, animals expand their distribution to slopes of different exposures (Veinberg 1984, Zalikhanov 1967, Magomedovet al. 2001). Seasonal migrations rarely exceed 5 km (Veinberg 1984, Zalikhanov 1967). Eastern tur consume 256 plant species in Daghestan (Abdurakhamanov 1977). Animals form mixed, adult male-female groups in November, just prior to rut. These disband by mid-January or the beginning of February at the latest and adult males and females live separately until the next rutting season (Veinberg 1984). Females give birth predominantly to just one kid (Veinberg 1984). Proportion of kids may exceed 20% in Azerbaijan (Kuliyev 1981) and Daghestan (Magomedovet al. 2001), but reach only 16.5% in North Ossetia, while yearlings make above 7% there (Veinberg 1984). Sex ratio favours males in protected populations (Weinberg 2002a). Mortality is about 60% in juveniles (Veinberg 1984), and about 20% in animals 1-9 years old, being higher in males than females (Magomedov et al. 2001). Yearly changes of overall group size depends on the reproductive cycle. Rugged and precipitous terrain reduces group size (Veinberg 1984, Weinberg 2004). Mean group size also correlates with population density (Magomedovet al. 2001). Overall mean group size is below 10 in North Ossetia (Veinberg 1984), but reached ca. 78 in Azerbaijan (Kuliyev 1981). Average population density varies from 0.15 to 17 animals/km² (Weinberg 2002c). Eastern Tur serve as prey to wolf Canis lupus and lynx Lynx lynx, and are also killed by snow avalanches. However, the significance of these factors differs along the species ranges. Snow avalanches cause most natural deaths among adult animals in the Central Caucasus (Veinberg 1984, Zalikhanov 1967) but not so in less snowy Daghestan, where wolf is the main natural enemy (Magomedov et al. 2001). Golden eagles Aquila chrysaetos and, supposedly, bearded vulture Gypaetus barbatus hunt newborn and small juveniles (Magomedov et al. 2001, Veinberg 1984). Eastern Tur coexist with Caucasus chamois Rupicapra r. caucasica on the northern slope in the Central Caucasus and on the southern slope in the Eastern Caucasus (mainly Azerbaijan), but the latter is much less numerous; in Daghestan and Chechnya, it is sympatric with the wild goat Capra aegagrus, which dominates in the forest but seldom rises above timberline (Weinberg 1999).
threats: Poaching and livestock grazing are the major threats to the Eastern Tur, combined with the impacts of severe winters. Poaching is probably the most significant cause of the recently observed serious declines. Livestock grazing results in competition for resources, especially with domestic sheep and goats. The species is also impacted by habitat loss and degradation (NACRES 2017, Weinberg et al. 1997).
population: Following a period of increase between the 1940s and 1960s numbers have since declined. In the late 1960s and early 1970s the total numbers were estimated to be between 25,000 to 30,000 animals (Kuliyev 1981, Ravkin 1975), but by the late 1980s had declined by >30% to between 18,000 and 20,000 head, of which ca 2,000 occurred in Georgia (Weinberg et al. 1997). The latest data suggest that there are no fewer than 3,000 animals in Georgia (Kopaliani and Gurielidze 2009; Georgian Biodiversity Database 2013, Ilia State University 2014). In Azerbaijan, in mid-1940s about 2,000 Tur had been harvested annually (Vereshchagin 1947) and if these data are accurate, at least 20,000 animals should have inhabited the country at that time. There was a decline since then. In 2006-2007, 5,300 Tur have been counted on the southern slope, and 1,000 more could occur on the northern slope (Guliyev, Weinberg and Askerov 2009). Since then, an overall census has not been carried out in Azerbaijan, but results of surveys conducted in summer 2013 came up with estimates of more than 13,000 animals (Yarovenko and Weinberg 2013), which might be too optimistic. Final assessment for nowadays could be the following: total population in Azerbaijan hardly exceeds 10,000, more likely it is about 7,000-8,000 animals. Of these, less than 2,000 occurred in Zakatala and about 1,300 in Ilisu Nature Reserves in 2018 (A. Muradov, pers. comm). Magomedov et al. (2001) suggested that there were up to 20,000 Tur in Daghestan alone, but this may be too optimistic, and later estimates are 15,000 tur (Babaev et al. 2017). In Russia, besides Daghestan, there are up to 4,000 tur in North Ossetia, including about 1,000 Tur in North-Ossetian Nature Reserve (Weinberg 2018), about 8,000 animals in Kabardino-Balkaria (Akkiev 2018). Even though, the taxonomic status of this latter population remains unclear and maybe just a half of this number belongs to C. cylindricornis inhabiting the Kabardino-Balkarian Highland Nature Reserve, the rest being hybrid (see Weinberg, Akkiev and Buchukuri 2010). At least some 2,000 Eastern Tur occur in Chechnya and Ingushetia. Currently, Eastern Tur numbers definitely grew since the beginning of 2000s in the Central Caucasus, after local conflicts stopped and political and social situation stabilized in the countries involved, and the total numbers are about 31,000–32,000 animals now.
range: This species is endemic to the central and eastern part of the Great Caucasus along the borders of Russia, Georgia and Azerbaijan between 800 and 4,000 m a.s.l. Its range on the north slope begins around the headwaters of the Baksan river east of Mount Elbrus (about 43º10’N, 42º30’E), or slightly more eastwards, at the headwaters of Bezengi river (43º03’N, 43º01’E) (Weinberg, Akkiev and Buchukuri 2010), which approximately corresponds to the headwaters of Inguri river on the south slope in Georgia, and stretches for some 500 km eastwards along both slopes of the Greater Caucasus up to eastern offshoots of Gyumyushlyu mountain of Babadagh mountain massif (40º57’N, 48º29’E). The range is much wider on the northern slope than on the southern slope due the peculiarities of topography. It is more or less continuous with separate locations mainly in the easternmost part of the range in Azerbaijan. Possible geographic barriers are major river valleys cutting across the range and hampering gene flow, like Ardon river valley in the narrowest part of the range in North Ossetia (42º45’N, 43º59’E), or Terek river valley in North Ossetia and Georgia (42º38’N, 44º38’E), and depressions between separate mountain massifs in Azerbaijan. The distribution is widest (up to 60 km) in Daghestan (Magomedov et al. 2001) because of the Caucasus Side Range being widest there, while being most narrow in North Ossetia (ca 12 km) (Weinberg 2002c).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food by local human communities.
conservationActions: It is included in Category III in the Georgian Red List (Decree 2014) and thus legally protected there. Hunting, including foreign trophy hunting, is forbidden in Georgia, but is permitted under license in Azerbaijan and Russia (Daghestan, North Ossetia). This species of Tur is found in several Nature Reserves: about 4,000 in Kabardino-Balkarian (Russia), 1,000 in North-Ossetian (Russia), 700 in Lagodekhi (Georgia), and 2,000 in Zakatala (Azerbaijan). Other protected areas with this species include Alania National Park (Russia), Tushetian and Kazbegi Strict Nature Reserves (Georgia), and Ilisu Nature Reserve with Kakh Sanctuary and Ismailly Nature Reserve together with a sanctuary of the same name, and the newly founded Shakhdagh National Park (Azerbaijan). Strangely enough, there are no nature reserves or national parks in Daghestan, the principal area of the species range harboring the largest part of the population. Conservation measures proposed include: 1) create new reserves, particularly in Daghestan on the border with Georgia and Azerbaijan neighboring with Lagodekhi and Zakatala Nature Reserve respectively;2) improve the effectiveness of existing protected areas for prevention poaching and human alteration of habitat;3) strictly enforce protection measures outside the four-month hunting season; if controls are successful and the population responds, then4) consider the possibility of increasing the annual hunting quota, 5) systematic population monitoring.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Endangered (EN)EU 27 regional assessment: Not RecordedThe Podolian Mole Rat (Spalax zemni) is endemic to Europe, where it is restricted to Ukraine. The population has undergone a severe contraction with up to 50% of the range loss in the past decade. While population densities are high in the southern part of the range, in the northern and western parts most of the subpopulations have gone extinct. The causes of these declines are not understood. The species is assessed as Endangered under criterion A2ac at the Global and European scope. It has not been reported in the EU 27 region.
habitat: The species dwells in steppe and partially in the forest-steppe zones. It prefers open landscapes with black soil. It is abundant in ravines, pastures, and along highways. In agricultural areas it normally has lower densities, but the species can be found in all types of crops (winter cereals, maize, alfalfa, vegetables, sunflower, rapes etc.). It is a typical underground rodent that builds extensive tunnel systems. It usually comes to the surface in late spring to disperse and is capable of moving hundreds of meters underground to pass through ploughed land where no food is available.
threats: Causes for the dramatic decline in northern and western parts of the range are not understood. In the south it is often persecuted as a pest by farmers. Some subpopulations in Mykolaiv and Kherson Regions suffered from military activities during the ongoing conflict that commenced in 2022. Isolated populations, especially in Western Ukraine, are threatened by the habitat loss due to urban development.
population: Population densities are high in the southern part of the range, but in the northern and western part most of the subpopulations have gone extinct, which equates to around 50% of the population.
range: The species is endemic to Ukraine, where it occurs in the northern part of the Steppe zone, west of the Dnieper River and extends to the western bank of the Tylihul River (Zagorodniuk et al. 2017). S. zemni is widely distributed westwards from the Dnieper, including a stable population on Khortytsia Island, which appears to be the distribution boundary between it and S. microphthalmus (Korobchenko and Zagorodniuk 2016). In the past, it had a wider distribution from the shores of the Black Sea (subfossil remains from the ancient Greek city of Olvia) to Kyiv city (middle of 20th century). The subpopulation of this species in the Lower Dnieper Sands had been cut off by the migrating watercourse of the Dnieper River and is considered to be a separate species, Spalax arenarius, although genetically, subpopulations from both sides of the Dnieper River are very close (Hadid et al. 2012). It experienced severe range contraction with most of the northern and western populations going rapidly extinct. Modern distribution lies between the cities of Mykolaiv, Kropyvnytskyi, Dnipro and Zaporizhia. A single isolate in western Ukraine (Ivano-Frankivsk Region) is currently known to be active still.
useTrade: The species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: In Ukraine it is a protected species and listed in the Red Book of Ukraine as Vulnerable (as of 2021). It occurs in several regional-level protected areas. Site protection, as well as species reintroductions in the northern and western parts of the range are recommended conservation methods. Research into the population trends and threats faced by this species are also recommended.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This species has a restricted range, but there is no evidence of population or range decline and the core range is protected. Currently, it is considered Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 member states, however, if new information suggests that population, range, or habitat quality is declining, uplisting to Near Threatened or Vulnerable should be considered. This species is included in the Red Data Book of Ukraine (Zagorodmyuk 2009) in general and in the Ukrainian Carpathians in particular (Potish and Bashta 2011).
habitat: The Tatra Vole is found in two types of habitat: first, humid areas in climax upper montane spruce forest with dense understory and numerous fallen logs; and second, humid rocky meadows in the subalpine zone. The species is never found outside natural habitats (e.g. in agricultural land) (Jurdíková et al. 2000, Martínková et al. 2004, Rudá et al. 2010a). Reproduction is slow according to rodent standards: both sexes attain sexual maturity in their second year, the reproductive season lasts about 140 days (April-September), litters are small (number of embryos = 1-4, mean = 2.46) and an average female putatively delivers 7.87 cubs per season. These voles are vegetarian, feeding primarily on green leaves of dicotyledonous plants (Krystofik and Danko 2012, Kryštufek 2017).
threats: Low genetic variability can be a potential threat to long-term survival of the species. Estimated values of the effective population size are below the population size threshold recommended to minimise inbreeding depression and maintain sufficient evolutionary potential (Rudá et al. 2010b). Otherwise, there are no thought to be any major threats causing significant declines at present. The species requires old, mature forests below the timberline, hence any logging in those areas would be harmful. Its habitat in the subalpine zone, above the timberline should be safe in the near future. Much of its range in the Slovak and Polish mountains falls within protected areas, and there are no thought to be any major developments planned in this area in the near future. However, forest habitat is sometimes lost through natural events (e.g. in 2004 a big storm in the High Tatras destroyed a large 1-2 km wide belt of forest at about 1,000 m above sea level, within the range of the vole (N. Martínková pers. comm. 2006).
population: It is a rare species that occurs in isolated subpopulations, for example in Slovakia one study observed low abundance and population densities (Rudá et al. 2010a). In the study in West Tatra Mts average population density over 12 years was 1.1 ± 0.73 individuals/hectare and no major population fluctuations or population outbreaks are known. Home range sizes are small and average 586 m2 in females and 836 m2 in males; the longest recorded movement was 260 m. Furthermore, the Tatra vole was not found in Beskid Zywiecki Mts. and Babiogorski National Park, Poland, during 2010-2013 monitoring (Wazna and Cichocki 2013) and confirmation of its presence is needed. There is very little information on the current status of subspecies Microtus tatricus zykovi in the Eastern Carpathians and subspecific status of the southern Carpathians isole is unknown. The range fragmentation appears partly natural, as the species is restricted to an intrinsically fragmented habitat type (high mountains), but fragmentation may have been exacerbated by the loss of woodland in mountain valleys through human activities in historical times.
range: The Tatra Vole is a European endemic species, native to the Carpathian Mountains arc between Tatra Mts., Beskidy in Slovakia, south-western Poland, and the Ciucaș Mts. in southern Romania. The most obvious large-scale gaps are between the western fragment in Slovakia and Poland and the eastern fragment in Ukraine and northern Romania; another gap is in Romania where Ciucaș Mts. (the Curvature Carpathians) is a far southern isolated subpopulation (Martínková and Dudich 2003, Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).The vertical range of localities is 600-2,343 m; the majority of records however are the mountains between 1,100 and 1,700 m, hence the distribution is fragmented at various scales.
useTrade: This species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention. The core range of the species' range in Slovakia and Poland falls within protected areas. Habitat and population monitoring is required to ensure that the species is stable and not declining. The Carpathians in Romania should be carefully surveyed to see if the large distribution gap is genuine.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as this species is widespread and common. It may be declining in some areas due to habitat destruction, particularly on the eastern extent of the range, but there is currently no evidence of a significant range-wide population decline that would warrant listing in a higher category of threat.
habitat: This species inhabits all strata of lowland and montane tropical moist forest, swamp forest and other lowland forest types. It is most common in secondary and colonising forests, and along the margins of these forests (Pimley & Bearder 2013). Its diet shows distinct seasonal variation: gums are dominant during drier periods, with insects, snails and fruits (such as figs, Musanga, Parinari, Uapaca and Myrianthus) eaten during the rainy seasons (Nekaris 2013). P. edwardsi are solitary animals, but do display some degree of sociality (Pimley et al. 2005). Charles-Dominique (1977) recorded females ranging over 3-9 ha, and males over 9-40 ha with their ranges overlapping that of one or more females; however, Pimley et al. (2005) found no significant difference in the range area of P. edwardsi between males (mean = 30.6 ha ± 2.97) and females (mean = 31.5 ha ± 7.25) with most overlap being between ‘paired’ males and females, which were found in close proximity and engaged in more social behaviours with each other than with other individuals (Pimley et al. 2005). Females give birth to one young annually. P. edwardsi in Gabon live to at least nine years of age (Charles-Dominique 1977).
threats: Perodicticus edwardsi are known to be widespread in secondary and primary forests, and even in disturbed forest near human habitation. There are probably no major threats resulting in a range-wide population decline, but localised declines are likely taking place due to habitat loss from clear-cutting and intensive agriculture, particularly on the eastern extent of the range. P. edwardsi is hunted and recorded in the bushmeat trade (Cameroon, Congo and DRC), pet trade (DRC and Nigeria) and in traded for traditional practices (Congo), although in small quantities (Svensson & Friant 2014, Svensson et al. 2015).
population: The species is widespread and common. Density averages 8–10 animals/km² at Makokou, in north-east Gabon (Charles-Dominique 1977) and 4.7 animals/km² in mixed secondary forest and farm bush on Mt. Kupe in Cameroon (Pimley 2002). In Angola, encounter rates of 0.83-1.80 animals/km were observed in moist, primary and secondary forest habitats (Bersacola et al. 2015).
range: Pseudopotto edwardsi occurs from the Niger River in Nigeria east through Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea (mainland), Republic of Congo, then south of the Congo River through the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as far east as Irneti and as far south as Angola. It occurs from sea level up to about 1,500 m asl. Pseudopotto martini, originally described as a new genus but here included in the synonymy of  P. edwardsi, is known from only one skeleton (which came from a specimen that died at Zurich Zoo) and two skulls, as well as some undocumented sightings around Mount Kupe, Cameroon, at 820–940 m altitude. However, P. martini was not observed on Mt Kupe during a two-year field study when only P. edwardsi (some with long tails) were recorded (E. Pimley pers. obs. 2000).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources  (as P. potto). This species is present in many protected areas throughout its range. However, further surveys are needed to determine the true conservation status of P. edwardsi, and careful research is required to better understand the impacts of habitat conversion and hunting on its populations.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern, Perodicticus ibeanus is widespread and locally common. To some extent, it is adaptable to habitat alteration caused by humans as long as sufficient fragments of forest remain within farm bush for refuge (Mittermeier 2013, Pimley & Bearder 2013). As a low density, non-gregarious, small bodied primate, P. ibeanus are vulnerable to local declines where habitat is lost due to human activities. There is no evidence, however, of a significant range-wide population decline that would warrant listing in a higher category of threat.
habitat: Perodicticus ibeanus inhabits all strata of lowland and montane moist forest, swamp forest and other lowland forest types. It is found in western Kenya at low densities in gardens and coniferous plantations adjacent to secondary forest (E. Pimley, pers. obs. 2006). This species is most common on the forest edge, flooded primary forest, secondary forest, colonising forest and riverine forest (Kingdon 1971, Charles-Dominique 1977, Wolfheim 1983, Pimley 2002, Pimley & Bearder 2013). Mean annual rainfall in its geographical range is 60–230 cm (Butynski & de Jong 2007). This species is omnivorous and forages in all forest strata but prefers the canopy. It forages mainly on ripe fruit, gum, nectar and invertebrates, but it also eats moss, frogs and bird’s eggs (Kingdon 1971, Charles-Dominique 1977, Wolfheim 1983, Pimley 2002, Pimley & Bearder 2013).
threats: Perodicticus ibeanus is widespread in secondary and primary forests, and in disturbed forest near human habitation. The main threat is habitat loss (Pimley & Bearder 2013). There are probably no major threats resulting in a range-wide population decline. Local  declines are, however, taking place due to habitat loss from clear-cutting and intensive agriculture that are related to fast growing human populations over much of the geographic range. In northern DRC, pottos are traded in small numbers for pets and body parts for various indigenous medicinal and witchcraft practices (Svensson et al. 2016). This species is easily detected by torch light and is thus readily located by hunters.
population: Perodicticus ibeanus is widespread and locally common, but occurs at low density over large areas. Densities range typically between <2 and 28 individuals/km². The encounter rates from several sites are presented in Butynski and de Jong (2007).
range: Perodicticus ibeanus ibeanus (Eastern Potto) ranges from east and south of the Ubangi River, and north and east of Congo River, Democratic Republic of the Congo, eastwards to east of the Lualaba River, then northwest to Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda to southwest Kenya (Kakamega Forest, Nandi Forests and surrounding forests). Occurs at 600-2,300 m asl (Butynski and de Jong 2007). Perodicticus ibeanus stockleyi (Mount Kenya Potto) is known only from one specimen collected in 1938 on Mount Kenya, central Kenya (Butynski and de Jong 2007).
conservationActions: Perodicticus ibeanus is an Appendix II CITES species and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (as Perodicticus potto). Present in many protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is declining rapidly and is thought to be undergoing further habitat degradation and increased pressure from hunting, particularly in Ghana. It is presumed to have declined by at least 50% over the past 27 years, although this decline may have been even more severe.
habitat: Cercocebus lunulatus occurs in primary and secondary forests, gallery and swamp forests, as well as mosaic habitats in the Guinean savanna zone. It is diurnal and largely terrestrial, but will also use the forest canopy. In gallery forest along the Comoé River in Burkina Faso, Galat and Galat-Luong (2006) observed this mangabey eating the fruits of the liana Saba senegalensis; at this site, a group of nine individuals was counted, while groups of up to 23 individuals were seen in the past in Comoé National Park, Côte d’Ivoire (Fischer et al. 2000). In the Tanoé swamp forest in Côte d’Ivoire, a mean group size of 5.13 (range: 1.53–8.73) was reported during a 3-month survey conducted in 2009 (Gonedelé Bi, unpublished data 2009).
threats: The species is hunted for its meat, both for local consumption and for the commercial bushmeat trade. Unregulated hunting has probably been the major cause of its decline. Illegal timber exploitation and mining is on the increase, which is leading to further habitat loss and fragmentation as a result of logging, the clearing for agriculture and charcoal, the demand for firewood, and fire. Cercocebus lunulatus has also been killed because of its crop raiding. In Ghana, many forests have been converted to rubber plantations. In Côte d’Ivoire, in the last decade, several forest reserves and protected areas that the species formerly inhabited have been completely converted into plantations, resulting in the local extirpation of the species and other primates in these forests (Bitty et al. 2015). In the remaining forests that still harbour the species, hunting and forest encroachment are affecting this monkey's survival. These threats are ongoing.
population: This species has a very patchy distribution and is now rare at all the sites where it still survives. At one of these sites, the Ankasa Conservation Area in Ghana, Gatti (2010) reports an encounter rate of 0.002 groups per km. Surveys conducted in 2012 in the Ankasa-Tano Community Forest, Western Region of Ghana, reported an encounter rate of 0.006 groups per km. In 2011, about 60 individuals were counted in a survey conducted by D. Osei in the Cape Three Point Forest Reserve. In April 2016, about 20 individuals were encountered during a survey conducted by D. Osei in the Ankasa Community forest (Osei et al. 2015). Although it was observed in the Comoé Lébara Reserve in 2005, in 2012, a survey of five protected areas across the southern border of Burkina Faso, including Comoé-Lébara Reserve, did not encounter this mangabey, although interviews in a nearby village suggested that it might still be present (Ginn and Nekaris 2014).The most important population of the species is probably that in Tanoé swamp forest in Côte d’Ivoire, where groups of up to 300 individuals were seen in past surveys. In 2009, a density of 12.3 individuals per km² was estimated for the Tanoé Forest, during a 3-month survey (Gonedelé Bi, unpublished data, 2009). In Port Gauthier and Dassioko Sud forest reserves in central coastal Côte d’Ivoire, the species was encountered at low rates of 0.004 and 0.009 groups per km, respectively (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2014).
range: Cercocebus lunulatus once ranged from the Nzo-Sassandra River system in western Côte d’Ivoire to just west of the Volta River in Ghana. The current presence of this species in southwestern Burkina Faso is uncertain (Ginn and Nekaris 2012). In Cote d'Ivoire, it occurs in the Comoé National Park and the Tanoe-Ehy Community Forest; its continued presence in the Dassieko Classified Forest is uncertain. In Ghana, the forested area it once occupied has been drastically reduced from its past distribution (Grubb et al. 1998) and the species is now restricted to the Western Region, apart from one population discovered in 2017 in the Atewa Forest Reserve situated in the Eastern Region of the country. In the Western Region, the species has declined dramatically since at least the 1970s, and has been extirpated from the Bia National Park, Krokosua Hills Forest Reserve, the Mamre Forest Reserve, and other protected areas and forest reserves. Recent surveys have shown that the species may now be restricted to Cape Three Points Forest Reserve and the Ankasa-Tano (or Kwabre) Community Forest (Danquah and Tetteh 2016); a population in the Ankasa Conservation Area appears to be on the verge of extirpation (Ossei et al. 2015).
useTrade: This species is hunted for bushmeat.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (as Cercocebus atys). European Union listed in Appendix I.Cercocebus lunulatus occurs in Comoé National Park, Côte d’Ivoire, but its survival there has been jeopardized by the combined effects of civil conflict and hunting; it has also been recorded from Ankasa Conservation Area, Dadieso Forest Reserve, Yoyo Forest Reserves, Cape Three Points Forest Reserve, and the Ankasa-Tano Community Forest in Ghana, and in Dassioko Sud Forest Reserve and Port Gauthier Forest Reserve in Côte d’Ivoire.

rationale: Previously assessed as Near Threatened, Cercocebus atys is now listed as Vulnerable as the population is estimated to have declined by at least 30% over the past 27 years (equivalent to three generations). The causes of the decline are intensive hunting across its range, combined with habitat loss and degradation resulting from the expansion of commercial and subsistence agriculture. This estimate is based on the results of foot surveys in both protected and non-protected areas, surveys of bushmeat markets, and interviews with hunters and farmers (e.g., Gonedelé Bi et al. 2012, Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016, Binczik et al. 2017, Soiret et al. 2019). The declining population trend is predicted to continue at the same or an accelerated rate.
habitat: Cercocebus atys is found in primary and secondary forests, gallery forest, swamp forest (including mangrove) and mosaic habitats in the western part of the Guinean forest zone. Sooty Mangabeys are large, predominantly terrestrial monkeys typically found in large multimale, multifemale groups (McGraw and Zuberbühler 2007). Groups of mangabeys at Tai National Park consist of up to 100 individuals (McGraw and Zuberbühler 2007), with males averaging 11 kg and females 6.2 kg (Oates et al. 1990). They forage mainly through leaf litter on the forest floor, and the staples of their diet include fruits, seeds and invertebrates, with seeds making up 68% of the diet and invertebrates making up 26% (Bergmüller 1998, McGraw and Zuberbühler 2007). Sooty Mangabeys are able to process food items that are too hard for other fruit eating monkeys to consume (Daegling et al. 2011). They show evidence of spatial memory skills when searching for fruit from Anthonata fragrans trees (Janmaat et al. 2006). They are known to raid farms, and are tolerant of some degree of habitat degradation in the absence of hunting (Binczik et al. 2017). The home range of a Sooty Mangabey group is estimated at 4-6 km² (1.54–2.32 mi²), but can be as large as 6.5 km² (2.5 mi²) (Galat and Galat-Luong 1985, McGraw and Zuberbühler 2007).In Côte d’Ivoire's Taï National Park, Sooty Mangabeys intermingle with groups of Western Red Colobus (Piliocolobus badius) and Diana Monkey (Cercopithecus diana) for approximately 5% and 10%, respectively, of total observation time (Taï Monkey Project unpubl. data 1990–2001).Monkey species associating with Sooty Mangabeys will often descend to lower canopy levels because of the latter's ability to detect predators approaching from the ground (McGraw and Bshary 2002). Sooty Mangabey vocalisations include a number of twitters, grunts and whoop calls (Range and Fischer 2004).
threats: Cercocebus atys is threatened by hunting and habitat loss. Forest habitat is being lost through farming, logging, firewood harvesting and mining, all of which are being accentuated by a high rate of human population growth. According to FAO 2015 data, Cote d'Ivoire, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia and Sierra Leone lost a combined 6% of their forest-woodland area over 25 years (1990–2015). The species is locally hunted for meat, and this is an increasingly important threat with ongoing forest fragmentation, because animals can be located more easily by hunters in small forest fragments. Increasing hunting pressure and bushmeat traffic is affecting the species in Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone (Kümpel et al. 2008, Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016, Brncic et al. 2015). Cercocebus atys is the most hunted primate species in the Forécariah/Kounounkan region of coastal Guinea bordering Sierra Leone (Dufour 2013), and the species is among the most hunted primates in the Sime Darby oil palm concession in central Liberia (Béné et al. 2013b,c). A survey in Liberia's Nimba County revealed that Sooty Mangabeys were the most common primate in bushmeat markets, representing 3.03% of all market prey (Bene et al. 2013b,c).Sooty Mangabeys are natural reservoir hosts of Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV). Despite a high prevalence in the wild population, the virus has no detectable impact on the survival or health of this host species (Silvestri et al. 2003). Sooty Mangabeys do not develop AIDS despite high levels of SIV infection because of several genetically-based mechanisms that enhance immune function (Palesch et al. 2018). Cercocebus atys can contract leprosy (Rojas-Espinosa and Løvik 2001), and Type 2 diabetes is more common in mangabeys than in other primate species (Jones et al. 2014).The bushmeat trade, the practice of keeping monkeys as pets, and the growing number of people living near wild Sooty Mangabeys significantly increases the risk of transmission of multiple zoonotic diseases (Mossoun et al. 2015)
population: Current, comprehensive data on the abundance and distribution of Sooty Mangabeys throughout much of their six-country range are lacking; however, available evidence suggests the species has declined across most of its distribution. In Côte d’Ivoire, the species has been extirpated in most of its range, except for the Taï National Park and the sacred grove of Gbepleu near the town of Man in western Côte d’Ivoire (S. Gonedelé Bi pers. obs. 2015). In Taï National Park, a survey by Covey (2009) estimated population density to be 4.35 groups/km² and N’Goran et al. (2012) estimated that approximately 63,000 individuals reside in the park. Recent surveys failed to detect the species in the Dodo Coastal Forest of southwestern Côte d’Ivoire (Soiret et al. 2019) and the Tonkpi region of west-central Côte d’Ivoire (Kramoko et al. 2017).During nationwide surveys of Liberia, Sooty Mangabeys were the second most common monkey detected on line transects (Junker et al. 2015). Surveys of four counties (Gbarpolu, Bomi, Bong and Grand Cape Mount) comprising the Sime Darby Plantation (oil palm, rubber) reported Sooty mangabeys present, although specific locality information were not published (Béné et al. 2013a). Several surveys carried out over the last ten years in the Mount Nimba region confirm the presence of Sooty Mangabeys there (Béné et al. 2013b,c, Granier 2016). In southeastern Liberia, surveys in the Grebo-Sapo Corridor reported a Sooty Mangabey encounter rate (groups/km) of 0.08 (Furnell et al. 2015a). The species appears to still be common in Sapo National Park (Vogt, 2011, Oates 2011) though it is hunted regularly (Greengrass 2016). Encounter rates in the Putu Range (0.09) are significantly lower than those inside Sapo National Park (0.19) (Vogt, 2011). During a 4-month survey in 2015, Sooty Mangabeys were heard but not seen in the newly-created Grebo-Krahn National Park (Furnell et al. 2015b).In Guinea in 1992, the species was often encountered during a 10-day field visit to the Kounounkan region, near the small town of Moussayah, Forécariah Province (Barnett et al. 1994). However, it was rarely encountered during a rapid assessment of the primate fauna conducted in 2005 in Sangaredi sub-prefecture in northwestern Boké Préfecture (Eriksson and Kpoghomou 2006). During site visits in 2017 and 2018, Sooty Mangabeys were observed in several areas in the Fouta Djallon region (R.A. Mittermeier pers. comm. 2017, C. André pers. comm. 2018).Recent surveys confirm Sooty Mangabeys near the village of Beli in the Boe region of Guinea-Bissau (Binczik et al. 2017) and they are present in Cantanhez Forest National Park (Garriga et al. 2018); however, their presence elsewhere in Guinea-Bissau is no longer certain (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003, Minhos et al. (2013).In Sierra Leone, the population of C. atys in Gola Forest National Park may have actually increased in the last 20 years. In 1985, before Sierra Leone’s 1991-2001 civil war, Davies (1987) had 0.14 encounters per km with this species (sightings and calls combined), while in 2006–2007 Klop et al. (2008) had an encounter rate based on sightings and vocal detections of 0.45 per km. It is not possible, however, to translate such encounter rates accurately into population density estimates, especially in the case of a species like C. atys whose calls carry for a considerable distance in the forest, and whose calling patterns can be affected by many factors. A nationwide survey of chimpanzees in Sierra Leone revealed Sooty Mangabeys mostly in the northern part of the country where human population numbers are lower (Brncic et al. 2015). Surveys carried out in the Moyamba and Port Loko districts of Sierra Leone during 2013–2014 identified Sooty Mangabeys as crop-raiders (Garriga et al. 2018).
range: This species ranges from Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia to the Nzo-Sassandra system in Cote d'Ivoire. It occurs between sea level and at least 1,000 m asl; possibly higher in the Loma Mountains in Sierra Leone.
useTrade: The species is hunted for bushmeat across its range. The price of a freshly killed adult male in areas bordering the Cavally River (Cote d'Ivoire and Liberia) is equivalent to approximately US $5 (Covey and McGraw 2014). Prices are substantially higher in towns and cities that are more distant from rural areas.
conservationActions: Cercocebus atys is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. European Union listed in Appendix I.Cercocebus atys occurs in a number of protected areas including Taï National Park (Côte d’Ivoire), Sapo National Park, Grebo-Krahn National Park and Gola National Park (Liberia), Tiwai Island Wildlife Sanctuary, Gola Forest National Park and Loma Mountains National Park (Sierra Leone), and the Cantanhez Forest National Park (Guinea-Bissau).The species is also conserved in Gbepleu sacred grove in western Côte d’Ivoire near the town of Man.

rationale: Perodicticus potto is listed as Near Threatened because although this species is still relatively widespread, its forest habitat is rapidly being destroyed and converted across a large part of its range. In the nine West African countries where the species is known to occur, forest cover over the last three generations (27 years, given a P. potto generation length of 9 years, Pacifici et al. 2013) has declined by more than 20% (FAO 2015), while human population has more than doubled (United Nations 2019). Also, P. potto is increasingly hunted for food and is traded for traditional practices (Svensson and Friant 2014, Svensson et al. 2015, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2016). Although data on declines in P. potto populations are not available, due to an absence of systematic surveys, it is likely that the population has declined by at least 20% over the last three generations (27 years). This species is likely to qualify for the threatened category of Vulnerable in the near future.
habitat: This species inhabits the mid- to upper strata of lowland tropical moist forest, swamp forest and other lowland forest types, both primary and secondary, as well as plantations. In Côte d’Ivoire, P. potto was observed mainly in younger, more disturbed forests (Pimley pers. obs. 2013). However, the opposite has been observed in other parts of their range where they more commonly encountered in mature forests (Oates pers. obs. 1966–2009). There is very limited information on the diet of P. potto, but Oates (1984) reports that P. potto consumes gum, fruits and insects. Pottos are predominantly solitary animals, but display some degree of sociality, with mothers and young maintaining contact by means of olfactory communication and occasionally high frequency vocalisations (Bearder et al. 2003). Pottos in Taï National Park, Côte d’Ivoire, were found in proximity of another potto for 30% of observations, with a proportion of this time spent allogrooming, which suggests that the species may also associate in pairs, as observed in P. edwardsi in Cameroon (Pimley pers. obs. 1998–2000).
threats: Perodicticus potto is endemic to West Africa, and although the species is known to survive in some disturbed forest near human habitation their entire range falls within a part of Africa where human population is growing rapidly and habitat destruction is rampant. In the nine West African countries where the presence of P. potto has been confirmed, the United Nations Population Division estimates that the combined human population increased in the 27 years from 1992 to 2019 from 154 million to 311 million, an increase of 102% (United Nations 2019). Associated with this increase in human population and the spread of settlement, agriculture, timber harvesting and development projects, forest cover in these same nine countries is estimated by FAO (2015) to have fallen from 671,880 km² in 1990 to 530,900 km² in 2015—a forest loss of 21%. Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone are among three of 10 countries in the world that had the fastest annual acceleration of tree cover loss in the 2001–2014 period, based on an analysis of satellite imagery, with Sierra Leone recording the world’s second greatest annual forest loss rate of 12.6% (Petersen et al. 2015).Perodicticus potto is also hunted, mainly for subsistence, but the species occurs in the commercial trade as well. It has been observed in the bushmeat trade (Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Nigeria), in the pet trade (Nigeria, Liberia and Togo) and in the trade for traditional medicines and practices (Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana) (Svensson and Friant 2014, Svensson et al. 2015, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2016). In the forest zone of West Africa, smaller mammals began to feature more commonly in the bushmeat trade more than a decade ago, as larger-bodied wild mammals have become scarce (Swensson 2005). This trend is now impacting on species such as P. potto, whose decline is suggested by a recent reduction in the number of pottos seen in western Nigeria in the possession of hunters or in bushmeat markets (R. Ikemeh pers. comm. 2016).
population: Perodicticus potto has been considered to be relatively widespread and abundant suitable habitat within its geographical range; however, population density data on the species throughout its range are lacking. Given accelerating rates of habitat destruction and increasing hunting pressure, it is inferred that the population is declining, and the subspecies juju in Benin, Togo and Nigeria is Endangered (see Perodicticus potto juju).
range: This species has a wide range in West Africa, with confirmed presence in SE Senegal, SE Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, S Togo, S Benin and SW Nigeria (Oates 2011, Nekaris 2013, Pimley and Bearder 2013). Perodicticus potto may also occur in the Gambia and Guinea-Bissau, but this is yet to be confirmed (Nekaris 2013, Pimley and Bearder 2013). For Guinea-Bissau, decades of field surveys and a recent survey of bushmeat markets using molecular markers failed to find the presence of the species (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 1996, Minhós et al. 2013).There are two subspecies: the nominate P. p. potto is found in West Africa from SE Senegal, SE Guinea, Sierra Leone to the Volta River in Ghana (there are no confirmed records for the Gambia, Guinea-Bissau and most of Guinea); P. p. juju  is found from the east bank of the Volta River in SE Ghana through southern Togo and southern Benin to the west bank of the Niger River in Nigeria.
useTrade: Perodicticus potto is hunted, mainly for subsistence, but the species occurs in the commercial trade as well. It has been observed in the bushmeat trade (Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Nigeria), in the pet trade (Nigeria, Liberia and Togo) and in the trade for traditional medicines and practices (Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana) (Svensson and Friant 2014, Svensson et al. 2015, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2016).
conservationActions: Perodicticus potto is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. This species is present in many protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: Papio cynocephalus is listed as Least Concern, as the species is widespread and common, present in numerous protected areas, and there are no major range-wide threats believed to be resulting in a significant population decline.
habitat: The Yellow Baboon lives primarily in open and woodland savanna. Over much of its range, it is associated with fire-climax Miombo (Brachystegia) woodland. Both in this zone and especially to the northeast of its range, the species may also occupy dry bushland, thickets, steppes, and the coastal littoral (including mangroves). Fever Trees (Acacia xanthophloea) and Tortilis Trees (A. tortilis) are often used as both sources of food and shelter (Altmann et al. 2013). The Yellow Baboon typically forages in extended, well-spaced troops that may occasionally number up to 300 animals, though more typically average 30 to 80 individuals. The species is not territorial but, instead, uses home ranges that may overlap with other troops’ ranges. They drink almost daily, so their ranges tend to include a water source within a half-day’s journey (Altmann et al. 2013). Like other members of the genus, Yellow Baboons are opportunistic omnivores. They primarily feed on the seeds, flesh, and pods of the leguminous trees including Acacia, Albizia, mopane (Colophospermum), and tamarind, all of which are seasonal staples. They also feed on grasses, shoots, fungi, lichens, and a range of animal prey, including invertebrates, lizards, birds, reptile and bird eggs, and small mammals. The latter include other primates, such as Vervet Monkeys (Chlorocebus pygerythrus) and Northern Lesser Galago (Galago senegalensis) (Altmann et al. 2013). Yellow Baboons prefer foods with unusual chemistry, suggesting that this species has acquired special digestive adaptations. Such adaptations may help to explain why the boundaries of the species’ distribution do not follow specific geographic discontinuities but coincide closely with the distribution of a plant community (Jolly 1993, Kingdon 1997). Although Yellow Baboons exhibit clear preference for woodland life, they can persist in secondary and highly fragmented vegetation, including areas that have been cultivated. In fact, some troops have adapted to living close to humans and regularly visit garbage dumps for foraging. While wild-foraging groups may spend approximately 70–75% of their time foraging and travelling up to 10 km per day, baboon troops that exploit garbage dumps forage for only 35–40% and travel only 2–4 km per day (Muruthi et al. 1991). Extensive review and summary of the Yellow Baboon’s anatomy, behaviour and reproduction may be found in Altmann et al. (2013) and Zinner (2013).
threats: There are no major threats to this species across its range, although some populations may be under pressure from agriculture and development projects. As other wildlife species decline and human populations increase, a potential increase in hunting pressure may be likely and trapping due to crop-raiding. Both Papio anubis and P. cynocephalus are naturally infected with Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, the bacterium that causes human yaws and closely related to the bacterium that causes syphilis (T. p. pallidum) (see Harper et al. 2012, Chuma et al. 2019). In Papio sp., the infection appears to spread through sexual contact and is associated with open lesions in and around the genitalia of both sexes. The degree of morbidity varies, including some cases of deaths occurring in the Tanzania’s Gombe National Park’s Olive Baboons, when the genitalia are so badly damaged that urinary flow was obstructed (Wallis and Lee 1999). Although the current hunting pressure and incidence of disease do not constitute “major threats”, both phenomena merit attention and monitoring.
population: This species is widespread and locally common, but patchily distributed over its extensive range.
range: The Yellow Baboon ranges from southern Ethiopia into Somalia, coastal Kenya, and northeastern Tanzania southwards to the Zambezi valley, where they are found in Malawi, northern Mozambique, and the far eastern part of Zambia (Jolly 1993). There are hybrid zones with Papio anubis near Sultan Hamud (2°02'S, 37°23'E) and Amboseli National Park in Kenya and Mkomazi National Park in Tanzania. As mentioned above, baboons in the broad clinal hybrid zone between Laikipia District, just to the northeast and east of Mt. Kenya, and the Lower Tana River, Kenya coast are intermediate in appearance; they become increasingly “yellow-like” in their phenotypes towards the Kenya Coast (De Jong and Butynski 2009, Zinner 2013). Yellow baboons are sympatric with Chlorocebus pygerythrus, Erythrocebus patas and Cercopithecus mitis. There are two subspecies: P. c. cynocephalus occurs in the central and southeastern parts of the range including Zambia east of the Luangwa, Malawi, northern Mozambique, and most of Tanzania and P. c. ibeanus is found in far southeastern Ethiopia, southern Somalia, and southeastern and coastal Kenya.
useTrade: Hunting of Yellow Baboons is not widespread, although occasional reports occur. As with other members of this genus, the species is often persecuted for crop-raiding activity as indicated in reports of trapping and killing by farmers in Tanzania’s Nguru (Doggart and Loserian 2007) and Nguu Mountains (Ceppi and Neilson 2014).
