Previous export of this species for use in medical research has apparently declined in recent years, although no current records are available.
conservationActions: This species is currently listed under Appendix II of CITES. It is listed as Vermin under the African Convention and is thus subject to legally sanctioned trapping and killing in certain areas. This may result in local extinction, if not controlled (Altmann et al. 2013).Yellow Baboons are present in many protected areas. These include, for example, Amboseli National Park and Tsavo East National Park in Kenya; Ruaha National Park, Mikumi National Park, Udzungwa National Park, Mkomazi National Park, and Selous Game Reserve in Tanzania; and Liwonde National Park in Malawi. They are susceptible to the spread of Treponema pallidum, which can have debilitating or even deadly consequences. Thus, research and ongoing monitoring for hunting pressure and disease transmission is recommended in assessment of the species’ long-term future. The effect of global climate change should be monitored; Altmann et al. (2002) noted measurable woodland loss in Amboseli since the 1970s, associated with temperature increases in the area. Thus, research into their habitat use, range, boundaries and reasons for separation into distinct subspecies could be useful for conservation planning.

rationale: Southern Patas Monkey is listed as Critically Endangered because there are estimated to be no more than 40 to 100 mature individuals left in the wild, with no more than 50 mature individuals in each of the two populations thought to persist. Erythrocebus baumstarki has a small extent of occurrence (EOO may be as small as 12,300 km²) and fragmented geographic distribution. A rapid population reduction has been observed. One, probably two, of the three historic (pre-2009) populations are now extinct. The geographic distribution of the one confirmed remaining populations (currently in an area of approximately 11,500 km² in the western Serengeti) appears to be about 56% the size that it was in 1995 (20,536 km²) and now comprises two fragments. The current number of E. baumstarki is probably between 80 and 200 individuals; the number of mature individuals may now be no more than 40 to 100 individuals. The EOO, area of occupancy (AOO), and population size are expected to continue to decline as the causes (mainly habitat degradation, fragmentation, and loss, but also hunting and reduced access to water) are ongoing and unlikely to be reversed in the foreseeable future.
habitat: Erythrocebus baumstarki is a medium-sized, diurnal, largely terrestrial, monkey. Occurs mainly in semi-arid acacia woodland, particularly Whistling Thorn Acacia (Acacia drepanolobium) woodland (De Jong et al. 2009). The habits and ecology of this species are poorly known but are likely similar to those of E. p. pyrrhonotus in northwestern Uganda (Hall 1965) and central Kenya (Chism and Rowell 1988, Isbell 1998, 2013).
threats: The main threats to E. baumstarki are habitat degradation, fragmentation, and loss due primarily to agricultural expansion and intensification (both crops and livestock), charcoal production, fire, and ‘development’ activities (e.g., settlements, roads; De Jong et al. 2009, Loishooki et al. 2016), but also hunting and loss of access to water. In Grumeti Game Reserve, western Serengeti, Whistling Thorn Acacia woodlands are disappearing due to over-stocking by livestock (G. Tolchard pers. comm. 2019).Bushmeat is a serious problem in the western Serengeti (K. Snyder pers. comm. 2020) and a threat to E. baumstarki (Loishooki et al. 2016). The pelt is used in traditional ceremonies (including dances and witchcraft). Hunted in retaliation for crop raiding (Loishooki et al. 2016). Hunted by domestic dogs in Burko Masailand Hunting Concession (D. Hurt pers. comm. 2019) and, probably, other places.The human population is doubling every 20-30 years over much of the range of E. baumstarki. ‘Rate of Natural Increase’ of the human population in Tanzania is 3.0%, compared to a worldwide rate of 1.1% (PRB 2019). Over the past decade, the western boundary of the Serengeti-Mara Ecosystem experienced a sharp human population increase, including a four-fold increase in some of the higher rainfall areas (Veldhuis et al. 2019).The human population growth rate is also high in the Arusha-Kilimanjaro region (TNBS  2020). Patas habitat is being increasingly converted into cropland in the densely settled areas at the western boundary of the protected areas of the western Serengeti (Serengeti National Park, Maswa Game Reserve, Keijereshi Game Reserve, Grumeti Game Reserve, Ikorongo Game Reserve, Ikona Wildlife Management Area). Due to a shortage of grazing land, pastoralists move their livestock illegally into protected areas (Veldhuis et al. 2019). As such, there is ever increasing competition between people and E. baumstarki for habitat and water (De Jong et al. 2009, G. Tolchard pers. comm. 2019). Within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, the human populations increased nine-fold in just 46 years (from 8,700 in 1966 to 79,000 in 2012) while the number of livestock in 2012 was 300,000 (IUCN 2014).
population: Old records indicate that Erythrocebus baumstarki has, historically, always occurred at low densities.Numbers of E. baumstarki are in rapid decline. In 2009, there were <900 individuals in Tanzania (De Jong et al. 2009). Currently, it can be assumed that the remaining global population (now limited to Tanzania) has between 80 and 200 E. baumstarki remaining in the wild. Given that about half of the individuals in populations of E. patas are mature (Hall 1965, Struhsaker and Gartlan 1970, Chism and Rowell 1988), the number of mature E. baumstarki is probably between 40 and 100.One, probably two, of the three historic (pre-2009) populations are now extinct (of those that existed before 1995). The Serengeti population appears to be in rapid decline. Twenty-one encounters with Erythrocebus in Tanzania have been documented since January 2009. Nineteen of these records are from the western Serengeti (1-24 individuals/encounter), one from Ngorongoro Conservation Area (one individual, 2012), and one from the Arusha population (one individual, 2014). Some western Serengeti groups were likely counted more than once. Ten of the western Serengeti records were obtained during a survey completed in 2015 (Loishooki et al. 2016). Ten of the 21 records are for solitary individuals and 11 records are for groups. Group size for five of the 11 groups is unknown, six groups comprised 2-24 individuals (83 individuals in total; mean = 12.2 individuals/group). Assuming that all six groups were encountered only once, the total number of individuals in Tanzania between January 2009 and December 2019 was between 93 (83 individuals and five uncounted groups with a minimum of two individuals) and 203 (83 individuals and five uncounted groups with a maximum of 24 individuals. It is highly likely, however, that some solitary individuals and groups were encountered more than once, particularly as the distance between some encounters was small (<100 m). It may be that there are groups in Tanzania that have remained undetected.
range: Erythocebus baumstarki is endemic to central north Tanzania. In March 2006, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong identified an E. baumstarki skin, from an unknown location in Kenya (specimen ZD.1934.4.7.1, labelled as “Erythocebus patas”), in the Natural History Museum (London). This specimen was collected by Lord Rothschild sometime prior to 1935, presumably in southern Kenya. Patas are known in southern Kenya from the Masai Mara-Loita Hills region and from the Namanga-Amboseli-Tsavo West-Athi River region (De Jong et al. 2008). Although these sites are contiguous with sites for E. baumstarki in northern Tanzania (De Jong et al. 2009), and the Patas of southern Kenya can be safely presumed to be baumstarki, we are not aware of any photographs or specimens of Patas from southern Kenya. Thus, specimen ZD.1934.4.7.1 appears to be the only confirmation that the population of Patas in south Kenya is/was a population of baumstarki.During a primate survey in the Loita Hills (southern Kenya) in 2012, unverified verbal reports of at least one group of E. patas were received from local people. Otherwise, there are no post-2004 records for Patas from southern Kenya (F. Allan, T. Allan, Z. Cockar, S. Dloniak, D. Grammaticas, S. Hatfield, B. Heath, J. Heath, P. Reynolds, H. Saunders pers. comm. 2019-2020, Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs.). The last records that we are aware of for Patas in southern Kenya are from south of the Chyulu Hills in 1996 (R. Bonham pers. comm. 2004) and from Tsavo West National Park in 2006 (J. Mutiso pers. comm. 2008). Given the 14-year absence of records for Patas from southern Kenya, it appears that E. baumstarki has been extirpated from Kenya.With the extirpation of E. baumstarki from Kenya, this species is now endemic to central north Tanzania. Here it occurred in three populations as of 1995: Serengeti ecosystem (including western Ngorongoro Conservation Area and Grumeti Game Reserve), southwest of Mount Kilimanjaro, and southwest of Arusha (De Jong et al. 2009) with a total geographic distribution of ca 37,400 km² (De Jong et al. 2009, R. Knocker pers. comm. 2012, Y. de Jong & T. Butynski unpubl. data 2019). Today, the Kilimanjaro population probably no longer exist (C. Foley pers. comm. 2019). The most recent evidence for the Arusha population is from 2014 when a Patas was killed by a domestic dog in Burko Masailand Hunting Concession (D. Hurt pers. comm.). Preliminary data suggest that the historic geographic distribution of the Serengeti population (ca. 20,500 km²) declined to ca. 11,500 km² (56% of historic range) as of 2019, and fragmented into two populations; one in western Serengeti (last encounter in 2019; Loishooki et al. 2016, R. Hoare pers comm 2010, Lomo Tanzania Safari, D. Hurt G. Tolchard pers. comm 2019) and one in western Ngorongoro Conservation Area (last and only encounter in 2012; R. Knocker pers. comm 2012). The Ngorongoro Conservation Area record (Naibardat Hill), the first record of E. baumstarki in the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, is, however, of a single encounter with what seemed to be a solitary individual (R. Knocker pers. comm. 2012). The extent of occurrence for this species is somewhere between 12,300 km² (Y. de Jong & T. Butynski unpubl. data 2019) and 31,267 km² (estimated using a minimum convex polygon around polygons on the submitted distribution map).Erythrocebus baumstarki has an altitudinal range of 800–1,580 (De Jong et al. 2009).
useTrade: Most killing of Southern Patas Monkeys is persecution/control resulting from resource competition. Bushmeat is a serious problem in the western Serengeti (K. Snyder pers. comm. 2020) and a threat to E. baumstarki (Loishooki et al. 2016). The pelt is used in traditional ceremonies (including dances and witchcraft). Hunted in retaliation for crop raiding (Loishooki et al. 2016). Hunted by domestic dogs in Burko Masailand Hunting Concession (D. Hurt pers. comm. 2019) and, probably, other places.
conservationActions: All 21 records for Erythocebus baumstarki since 2009 are from protected areas [Serengeti National Park (N=16), Ngorongoro Conservation Area (1), Grumeti Game Reserve (1), Ikorongo Game Reserve (1), Ikona Wildlife Management Area (1), Burko Masailand Hunting Concession (1)]. There are currently no conservation activities in place that focus on E. baumstarki. Enhance support for the conservation of E. baumstarki in Serengeti National Park, Ngorongoro Conservation Area, privately protected areas, and hunting concessions. Put into place, and fund, conservation, research, and monitoring activities that focus on E. baumstarki. Bring the plight of E. baumstarki to wide national and international attention so the urgent actions for its conservation are funded and implemented.

rationale: Allochrocebus lhoesti has undergone a significant population decrease in the past and continues to decline. Most of this species' range is in a region of intense conflict, which has exacerbated the known threats, which are mainly bushmeat hunting and habitat loss due, in large part, to artisanal mining. It is suspected that these declines will continue in the face of ongoing political turmoil, and will result in an overall population reduction of more than 30% over a 30-year time frame from 1995 to 2025 (given a 10-year generation period), qualifying the taxon as Vulnerable A4cd.
habitat: L’Hoest’s Monkey is semi-terrestrial and restricted to the lowland, submontane and montane forests of the Albertine Rift in eastern DRC and western Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda. The species forms one-male-multi-female groups that travel long distances on the ground and forage mainly in lower forest strata (Kaplin and Moermond 2000, Ukizintambara 2010). They are omnivorous with a diet consisting of terrestrial herbaceous vegetation, invertebrates, mushrooms, fruits, flowers and small vertebrates. In areas close to cultivated land, such as the periphery of Bwindi Impenetrable and Nyungwe national parks, these monkeys enter fields and gardens to forage on crops. They are found in small groups averaging 10 to 17 individuals, although larger bands of up to 37 individuals have been observed (Tashiro 2006). This species is often sympatric with Owl-faced Monkeys Cercopithecus hamlyni, especially west of the Albertine Rift. It is among the most important primate prey of leopards Panthera pardus in the Ituri Forest (Hart et al. 1996).
threats: Much of the geographic range of l’Hoest’s Monkey has seen significant human population growth, displacement and armed conflicts that have put pressure on natural resources. Deforestation is taking place on the eastern edge of the main block of the species' range in DRC, primarily as a result of agricultural expansion. This monkey is hunted for meat in parts of its range and is particularly vulnerable to both snaring and shotgun hunting. Bushmeat specimens have been seen at Wanie Rukula, Pembeliba and Kindu, which might come from Lualaba in DRC (J. Hart pers. obs. 2016). Expansion of artisanal mining and shifting cultivation pose additional threats, especially in eastern DRC. Mining is of particular concern as mining operations can open up formerly remote areas to exploitation and settlement, leading to habitat loss. Mines are also centres of commercial bushmeat trade and a stimulus for poaching in protected areas (Spira et al. 2019).
population: Current population size is unknown, but the abundance of l'Hoest's Monkey in DRC is certainly decreasing due to hunting. Widespread in the lowland forest block of eastern DRC, but only locally common in the Mikeno Sector of Virunga National Park and Epulu in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve (the latter is probably one of the largest protected populations). It is also common in Bwindi and Nyungwe national parks.
range: Allochrocebus lhoesti ranges from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), east of the Lualaba River through the Ituri Forest and south to the Itombwe Massif, to Burundi, Rwanda and western Uganda (southwest Kigezi District and the Ruwenzori mountains). The species still occurs in Lualaba, along the eastern bank of the Congo River, but the southern limits of its range are poorly defined. Isolated populations occur east of the main block of the range and include Virunga and Kahuzi-Biega national parks (DRC), Kibira National Park in Burundi, Nyungwe National Park in Rwanda, and Kibale Forest National Park, Kalinzu Forest Reserve, Ruwenzori Mountains National Park, Maramagambo Forest Reserve and Bwindi Impenetrable National Park in Uganda. This species occurs up to 2,900 m asl.
useTrade: This species is hunted with guns and is trapped by snaring for bushmeat.
conservationActions: Allochrocebus lhoesti is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (as Cercopithecus lhoesti). It is protected by national legislation in Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda, and listed as a partially protected species in DRC. The most important action needed to protect this species is control of bushmeat hunting through effective law enforcement. Protected areas that are important for the conservation of l’Hoest’s Monkey include: Kahuzi-Biega, Maiko and Virunga national parks and Okapi Wildlife Reserve in DRC; Kibira National Park in Burundi (restricted to the northern sector of Mabayi; Hakizimana 2014); Nyungwe National Park in Rwanda; and Bwindi Impenetrable, Kibale and Ruwenzori Mountains national parks and Kalinzu and Maramagambo forests in Uganda.

rationale: Cercopithecus lowei is listed as Vulnerable because populations throughout its geographic range are estimated to have declined by at least 30% over the past 27 years (three generations, if average generation time is about nine years). Considering the species' now patchy distribution and low population densities at many sites, and that population decline in unprotected areas has been extreme, the total population of this monkey could now number fewer than 10,000 mature individuals. This population decline has occurred mainly as a result of unregulated hunting, habitat loss, habitat degradation and habitat fragmentation due to agriculture, cattle-ranching, human settlement and mining. Hence, the taxon qualifies as Vulnerable under criterion A.
habitat: Lowe’s Monkey has been found in a wide variety of tropical forest types, including lowland forest, gallery forest, mangroves and forest-savanna mosaic zones. It has been found in secondary forest, farmland and farmbush. Cercopithecus lowei is active mainly in low (<5 m) forest strata and on the ground. Its locomotion is a mix of quadrupedal walking and running. Leaping and climbing are less common, and dropping is rare (Schubert 2011). Home range estimates from 1.5–40 ha were given by Bourlière et al. (1970). In Adiopodoumé, Côte d’Ivoire, a group varied in size from 6-16 individuals, while in Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary, Ghana, average group size was 16.6 (s.d.=3.8, N=13). Cercopithecus lowei has a large repertoire of vocalisations. One of the most prominent calls is the adult male's loud call, which consists of low-frequency double booms followed by a series of higher-frequency hacks (Bourlière et al. 1970).
threats: The greatest threat to the Lowe’s Monkey is from hunting, using firearms and snares (Oates 2011, Danquah et al. 2012). Lowe’s Monkeys are hunted as food for personal consumption and for the bushmeat trade, and their loud vocalizations make them an easy target for hunters. A recent market survey indicated that C. lowei and Perodicticus potto are now the two top primate species found in bushmeat markets in Côte d’Ivoire (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2017), in part reflecting the scarcity of other species. The monkeys are also captured as pets, both in live-traps as adults or as young when the mother is killed for the meat trade.Habitat loss and fragmentation due to conversion of forests and farmbush into cocoa, palm oil and rubber plantations is an almost equally important threat to this species. Since 2000, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana have lost 17% and 13% respectively of their forest cover (Global Forest Watch 2019). Between 1988 and 2007, at least 23,000 km² of the Upper Guinean rainforest in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana were cleared for cocoa farms, and the clearing of forests for cocoa production continues in both countries. In Côte d’Ivoire, the annual deforestation rate between 2000 and 2015 was estimated to be 2.69%, with an average forest loss of 2,500 km²/year (BNETD 2016), and many of the ~180 forest reserves in the geographic range of C. lowei have already been converted into plantations and human settlements. In some parts of Ghana, surface mining for gold, diamonds, bauxite and other metals also threatens the species’ survival, even in farmbush areas (E. Wiafe, pers. obs. 2015).
population: Although firm data are lacking, the total population of this monkey could number fewer than 10,000 mature individuals. Cercopithecus lowei now has a patchy distribution and low population densities at most of the sites where it still occurs (Gatti 2010, Danquah et al. 2012).In Ghana, at the Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary (BFMS) in Kintampo South where the species is protected by a traditional belief system (Wong and Sicotte 2006), the population size in the BFMS proper was estimated to be 181 individuals per km² in 2012 (Elgart 2016). However, a 2009 survey of several protected areas in southwestern Ghana found C. lowei at low encounter rates (0.04–0.4 groups per km²; Danquah et al. 2012).In Côte d’Ivoire, the most important population is found in the Tanoé swamp forest, where a density of 11.7 groups per km² was reported by a survey conducted in 2009 (Gonedelé Bi, unpublished data), but very low encounter rates (0.03–0.33 groups per km²) were reported (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2014) for several community forests and protected areas (that have not been converted into cocoa plantations). Strong poaching pressure and habitat degradation continue in most protected areas, presenting a serious threat to the survival of of C. lowei populations (Bitty et al. 2015).Considering the foregoing information, it is evident that the total population of C. lowei has declined by more than 30% during the last three generations, hence qualifying this taxon for a Vulnerable threat category.
range: Cercopithecus lowei once ranged from the Cavally River on the Côte d’Ivoire-Liberia border in the west to the Volta River in Ghana in the east (Oates 2011). Galat-Luong et al. (2013) reported observing this species as far north as 6°34'30°N in the Forêt classée de Duékoué, east of the N'zo River and west of Sassandra River. Between the Cavally and Sassadra-N'zo rivers in western Côte d’Ivoire, monkeys resembling C. campbelli were observed, as well as individuals with coat patterns intermediate between C. lowei and C. campbelli, indicating that this is a zone of hybridization (Booth 1955, Oates 1988).
useTrade: This species is hunted for local consumption and local trade.
conservationActions: Although it was once widespread, and is able to persist in modified habitats if hunting pressure is low, Cercopithecus lowei population declines in unprotected areas has been extreme, and the species now survives mainly in protected areas. Law enforcement against hunting is weak or lacking even in many protected areas; nonetheless, populations appear to be stable in a few well-protected areas. For example, the results of surveys carried out in 1993 and 2009–2010 (Oates et al. 2000, Wiafe 2016) indicate that conservation efforts in Kakum National Park, Ghana, in the last 20 years have been effective.Cercopithecus lowei is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.

rationale: This species’ Red List status has been upgraded to Near Threatened from Least Concern in the 2008 assessment in view of the fact it has been experiencing ever-increasing hunting pressure and populations are suspected to be declining, but at the rate of less than 30% over a period of 36 years (based on the generation period of 12 years). The habitats throughout its range have experienced ≥30% loss and degradation, and human population size in the range countries increased by 120% during the same period. The species, however, still has a wide distribution, is adaptable and can persist in some degraded habitats such as farmbush as long as hunting pressure is low or non-existent. The predicted future trajectory for populations of Cercopithecus campbelli is an accelerated rate of decline as larger-bodied primates are being depleted from their shared forests
habitat: Campbell’s Monkey is found in a wide variety of habitats, including lowland forest, gallery forest, mangroves, woodland, woody savanna and farrow lands (Oates 2011, Campbell 2013). It also occurs in secondary forest, in areas of subsistence agriculture, and in farmbush. The highest elevation area where this species occurs is the lower latitudinal locations (up to 600 m) in the Guinea Highlands. The estimated home range size for two groups in Taï NP was 52 ha and 67 ha (Buzzard and Eckardt 2007). C. campbelli mainly feeds on fruits and insects. In Taï NP, the diet of this species was found to be 46% fruits, 33% animal matter and 8% leaves (Buzzard 2006). Foraging for insects often involved unrolling curled-up leaves.The typical group structure is a one-male group, but the species is sometimes found in multi-male groups, and all-male groups outside heterosexual groups have been observed (Galat and Galat-Luong 1985, Buzzard 2006). In Taï NP in 1976, mean group size was 11.4 individuals (5–33, N=8) (Galat and Galat-Luong 1985), but had decreased to 9.3 (N=3) in 2001 (Buzzard and Eckardt 2007). Group size in Guinea-Bissau ranged from 1–20 (Gippoliti and Dell'Omo 2003). On Tiwai Island, mean group size recorded in 1982–1984 was 14 (Oates et al. 1990).This species is preyed upon by Leopards (Panthera pardus), Western Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus), and Crowned Hawk-eagles (Stephanoaetus coronatus) (Zuberbühler and Jenny 2002).
threats: Cercopithecus campbelli has been impacted by, first and foremost, bushmeat hunting, and secondly, habitat loss. Due to its relatively small body size, it was not a prime target for hunters until quite recently, but because the larger-bodied primates such as the Upper Guinea Red Colobus (Piliocolobus badius) and the King Colobus (Colobus polykomos) have been decimated or even extirpated from many areas due to unregulated hunting, even this small-bodied guenon (adult male ~4.5 kg) has now become a target for hunters. In Mount Nimba, Liberia, Bené et al. (2013) monitored hunters’ activities in 2009–2011 and found a high rate (0.7 per km) of encountering hunters carrying the carcasses of this species. In Konobo District in Liberia on the border with Côte d’Ivoire, an unsustainable level of hunting is taking place (Covey and McGraw 2014). During Tweh et al.’s (2015) primate surveys, conducted across Liberia in August-December 2010, hunting signs (empty cartridges, gunshots, poachers’ camps, and snares) were the most frequently observed anthropogenic signs. Due to unregulated hunting, logging and mining operations, the Lagoas de Cufada NP in Guinea-Bissau is becoming an “empty forest” (Starin 2010). Minhós et al.’s (2013) study using a DNA bar-coding method estimated that 1,550 individual primates, which included C. campbelli, sold in two markets in Guinea-Bissau, were consumed by the inhabitants during the 2010 dry season. Hunting pressure has been exacerbated by an increase of 120% in human population size in the habitat countries during the last three decades (World Bank 2019).Habitat loss through deforestation and forest fragmentation is due to creation of road networks, agriculture and mining (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003, Starin 2010, Minhós et al. 2013, Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016). This species once thrived in disturbed habitats and farmbush, but many of these habitats have been converted to plantations of non-native species.
population: Cercopithecus campbelli is still common in some areas, although its total geographic range has been reduced by deforestation, forest fragmentation and forest conversion. In Senegal, other than the fact that this species is present in the Parc National de Basse Casamance and several forest reserves, information on this species is scarce (P.I. Ndiaye pers. comm. 2019). In Guinea-Bissau, the species is still widespread except in the highest latitudinal areas in the northeast (Limoges 1989 cited in Gippoliti and Dell'Omo 2003, Minhós et al. 2013), but Bersacola et al.’s (2018) survey in 2015 at Dulombi and Paiai in Dulombi National Park found low encounter rates of 0.38 and 0.18 groups per km, respectively. This species is widespread and still common also in many parts of Guinea, even though hunting pressure is increasing, while many forests are fragmented and degraded (Campbell 2013, WCF 2015a).In Sierra Leone, C. campbelli occurs at Tiwai Island Wildlife Sanctuary (hereafter Tiwai), the Gola Forest National Park, Loma Mountains Forest Reserve (FR), Bumbuna in northern Sierra Leone, where the hydroelectric dam is being upgraded, and several other protected areas. Encounter rates vary between 0.02 to 0.54 groups per km (Brncic et al. 2015, Ganas-Swaray et al. 2017). In the early 1980s, population density at Tiwai was 39-44 per km² (Oates et al. 1990). In Gola Forest NP, surveys made before and after the 1991–2001 civil war obtained various group sighting data (Davies 1987, Klop et al. 2008, Lindsell et al. 2011). For example, Klop et al. (2008) reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 groups per km for their surveys conducted between October 2005 and June 2007, but the use of different survey methods and the manner in which auditory and visual sighting data were presented in different reports make it impossible to gauge with precision any changes in population numbers of this species. Nevertheless, Lindsell et al. (2011) concluded that primates “continue to have healthy populations in the forest… and showed little or no sign of reduced abundance". For this reason, the data are still insufficient to assess the current status of this species across the rest of Sierra Leone.In Liberia, this species occurs in a number of protected areas including North Lorma National Park, Gola National Park, Grebo-Krahn National Park, Krahn-Bassa National Forest, and Sapo National Park. Group encounter rates obtained in the early 2000s in all of these forests were in the range of 0.10–0.33 (Waitkuwait 2003, Barrie et al. 2007, Vogt 2011, WCF 2015b).In Côte d’Ivoire, C. campbelli occurs in several protected areas including Goulaleu and Krozialé Forêt Classées (FC or Classified Forests), Taï National Park, Goin-Débé FC, Cavally FC (Zuberbühler and Jenny 2002, Normand 2010, Kramoko et al. 2017) and community forests. However, Campbell’s Monkey appears to have been extirpated from Monogaga FC, Rapide Grah FC, Mont Péko NP, Kani-Bandaman Rouge FC, Séguéla FC and Koba FC, as all were converted into cocoa plantations (Bitty et al. 2015). The most important population is found in Taï NP, where a density of 24.4 individuals per km² was reported more than 15 years ago (Zuberbühler and Jenny 2002). More recent surveys conducted in Goin-Débé FC found that encounter rates had declined from 1.65 groups per km in 2007 to 1.31 in 2009–2010, and from 3.08 to 1.93 in Cavally FC (Normand 2010). Outside the protected areas in Côte d’Ivoire, this species persists even in areas where hunting occurs regularly (Soiret et al. 2019).
range: Campbell’s Monkey ranges from the Gambia and Senegal, just north of the Casamance River in the west, through Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia to the Cavally River on the Côte d’Ivoire-Liberia border in the east (Oates 2011). Between the Cavally and Sassandra-Nzo Rivers in western Côte d’Ivoire is a region where individuals of this species and of Cercopithecus lowei occur, as well as individuals with intermediate features (Oates 1988, 2011). This species also occurs on the island of Caravela in the Bijagos Archipelago of Guinea-Bissau (Gippoliti and Dell'Omo 2003).
useTrade: Campbell’s Monkey is hunted for bushmeat in all its range countries (see Threats). It costs 2,000 CFA (equivalent of US$ 3.6 as of 2019) to purchase four or five pieces of monkey meat at a market in Bissau, Guinea-Bissau (Starin 2010), while a small individual of this species is sold for about 3,000 CFA (US$ 5.3), and an adult male for 5,000 CFA (US$ 8.8) in markets in southwestern Côte d’Ivoire (S. Soiret pers. comm. 2019).
conservationActions: Cercopithecus campbelli is listed on Appendix II of CITES and Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.This species occurs in many protected areas in its geographic range (e.g., Gola Forest NP, Loma Mountains NP, and Tiwai Island in Sierra Leone; Sapo NP and Grebo NP in Liberia; Taï NP in Côte d'Ivoire), but anti-poaching enforcement is poor in Sapo NP and in the northern sections of Taï NP away from the research station. Rigorous law enforcement against poaching and in protected areas is needed throughout the range. Protection is sometimes improved where there is a permanent presence of researchers (e.g. southern Taï NP).

rationale: Previously assessed as Vulnerable, Cercopithecus diana is now listed as Endangered. Based on deforestation rates in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, and Ivory Coast, this species has lost at least 30% of its primary habitat over the past three generations (~1990-2018). Due to the combined negative impacts of hunting, which has resulted in the extirpation of a number of subpopulations and reduced others to levels that may not be viable over the long-term, C. diana numbers are suspected to have undergone a decline of 50% or more over this time period.
habitat: This largely arboreal species lives in the canopy of primary and old secondary lowland moist forest, and riverine and gallery forests. It is rare in degraded forest, but it appears that it can survive in lightly-logged forest where the canopy is relatively intact. This species occurs from just above sea level in Sierra Leone to at least 1,300 m asl in the Loma Mountains, Sierra Leone. Diana Monkeys feed mainly on fruits, arthropods and flowers; leaves become seasonally important when other items are less available (Buzzard 2006, Whitesides 1989). They spend much of their time in association with other primate species, which may be an anti-predator strategy (Whitesides 1991, Noë and Bshary 1997). Humans are the main predators on Diana Monkeys (Koné and Refisch 2007, McGraw 2007). Other important predators include Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), Leopards (Panthera pardus), and African Crowned Eagles (Stephanoatus coronatus) (Boesch and Boesch 1989, Shultz and Noë 2007, Oates 2011).
threats: Cercopithecus diana is threatened by hunting, and habitat degradation and loss.The relatively large body size of this species and the value of its meat and skin make it a preferred game species across its range in Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea. Subsistence hunting is widespread and laws against commercial hunting and other illegal activities (mining, habitat encroachment) inside protected areas are poorly enforced throughout the C. diana range. The increasing scale of commercial hunting poses the greatest threat (Béné et al., 2013c; Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016). Although Diana Monkeys adopt certain behaviours to minimize mortality due to hunting (Bshary 2001, Koné and Refisch 2007), they are now rarely found in areas with high hunting pressure, compared to areas where hunting pressure is relatively low (N’Goran et al. 2012). In Côte d’Ivoire, the species has been extirpated from almost all the protected areas within its Extent of Occurrence (>80%).In addition to hunting pressure, large-scale deforestation in the region, through mining, logging, conversion to agricultural land and charcoal production, continues to reduce the habitat available to this species (McGraw 1998, Tweh et al. 2014, Bitty et al. 2015, WCF 2015).  Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea each lost between 14 and 21% of their total forest cover between 2001 and 2017, and dominant drivers of loss continue (www.globalforestwatch.org).Combining the significant loss of suitable habitat with intense poaching pressure, it is suspected that the total population of C. diana has declined by more than 50% during the last three generations.
population: Cercopithecus diana is now a rare and declining species throughout most of its range. Populations are affected by habitat loss through agricultural expansion (cocoa, oil palm, rubber, rice), intensive commercial logging, and by hunting for bushmeat (Lindsell et al. 2011; Gonedele Bi et al. 2012; Béné et al. 2013a,b,c; Covey and McGraw 2014; Greengrass 2016). In Côte d’Ivoire, the species has been extirpated from almost all (>80%) the protected areas within its extent of occurrence (EOO). In the Taï NP where a viable population occurs, an estimated 97,000 individuals were reported in 2006-2008 based on survey data (N’Goran et al. 2012); a number that has almost certainly declined since that time. Within Taï NP, Diana Monkey abundance is strongly influenced by hunting pressure and this monkey is nearly 100 times more common near research stations and tourist sites than areas where hunting is unchecked (N’Goran et al. 2012). Outside Taï NP, a 2007-2010 biomonitoring survey reported the species in two reserves (Cavally, Goin-Debe) at a very low encounter rate (0.08–0.2 grp/km) with a decrease in the encounter rate ranging from 0.2 to 0.16 grp/km in Cavally FR and 0.08 to 0 grp/km in Goin Debe FR (WCF 2010). The ongoing hunting pressure, habitat encroachment and human settlement with these forest reserves pose severe threat to the survival of remaining populations. Currently, viable populations are found in Tiwaï Island Wildlife Sanctuary, Gola Forest National Park and Loma Mountains National Park in Sierra Leone; Sapo National Park in Liberia. Surveys within the Grebo-Sapo Corridor of southeastern Liberia reported a Diana Monkey encounter rate (N/km) of 0.31 (Furnell et al. 2015). The ongoing strong hunting pressure, habitat encroachment, and mining within these areas pose severe threats on these populations (Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary 2012, WCF, 2015).
range: This species is found in the forests of Upper Guinea in West Africa, ranging from coastal southeastern Guinea to Sierra Leone, Liberia, and southern Côte d'Ivoire (west of the Sassandra River).
conservationActions: Cercopithecus diana is threatened by habitat loss and hunting pressure, and is listed on Appendix I of CITES and on Class A of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. The species is found in the following protected and semi-protected areas: Cote d'IvoireTai National Park (330,000 ha)Cavally Classified Forest (64,200 ha)Goin-Debe Classified Forest (133,100 ha)Sierra LeoneTiwai Island Wildlife Sanctuary (1,200 ha)Gola Forest National Park (71,070 ha)Loma Mountains National Park (33,200 ha)LiberiaSapo National Park (180,400 ha)

rationale: The Roloway Monkey (Cercopithecus roloway) is listed as Critically Endangered, compared to Endangered in the previous assessment, because the species has suffered greatly from uncontrolled hunting for the bushmeat trade, as well as losing a considerable amount of its original habitat to logging and agriculture over the past ~30 years (ca three generations), leading to a population decline that is estimated to have exceeded 80%. The species is no longer found in most parts of its historical range, resulting in a major decline in its area of occupancy (AOO) as a consequence of ongoing hunting pressure, and habitat conversion and destruction. The species is at high risk of local extinction at three of the only four sites where it has been reported recently.An estimated population reduction of >80% in three generations (1991–2018) qualifies this species as Critically Endangered under criterion A. The causes of the reduction, although largely understood, have certainly not ceased and are not easily reversible.
habitat: This highly arboreal species was once confined to moist evergreen and moist semi-deciduous primary and old secondary lowland forests and swamp forests. Field studies on its ecology and behaviour are scarce. A group of 14–15 individuals in Bia National Park, Ghana, had a home range of 190 ha, and a diet of fruits (including mature seeds), insects and leaves (Curtin 2002). A mean group size of 6.85 (range: 2.89–11.85) and a population density of 36 individuals per km² were recorded in parts of the Tanoé swamp forest in Côte d’Ivoire during a survey in 2009 (S. Gonedelé Bi, unpublished data).
threats: This species is threatened by hunting and habitat degradation and loss. The relatively large body size of this species, its conspicuousness and the value of its meat and skin make it a preferred target of hunters. Large-scale deforestation in the region, through logging, conversion to agricultural land and charcoal production, continues to reduce the habitat available to this species, especially in Côte d’Ivoire (McGraw 1998, McGraw and Oates 2007, Bitty et al. 2015). Between 2001 and 2017, Côte d’Ivoire is estimated to have lost 17% of its tree cover (Global Forest Watch 2019) and this loss has been exacerbated by a large increase in the human population in the southern forest zone and the spread of cocoa farming, including illegal cocoa cultivation within protected areas (Bitty et al. 2015, Higonnet et al. 2018). In Ghana, hunting for the commercial bushmeat trade has decimated populations of Roloway Monkeys; recent surveys have failed to find any surviving groups in two national parks (Bia and Nini-Suhien) and in several forest reserves where it formerly occurred (Gatti 2010, Oates 1999, Osei et al. 2015). Even though relatively large areas of suitable habitat remain in these theoretically protected areas, laws against hunting in these areas have been poorly enforced. The species has probably undergone a decline of more than 90% in Ghana.
population: Cercopithecus roloway is now extirpated from most of its original range and it is likely that fewer than 2,000 individuals survive in Cote d’Ivoire and Ghana. Primatologists have been documenting its decline since the mid-1990s (Struhsaker and Oates 1995; Oates et al. 1997; Abedi-Lartey 1998, 1999; Oates 2006; Gonedelé Bi et al. 2008, 2012, 2014; Gatti 2010; Wiafe 2013; Bitty et al. 2015; Osei et al. 2015). The Tanoé forest in southeast Cote d’Ivoire seems to still support a population of the species (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2008), as does the adjacent Kwabre forest in southwest Ghana (Osei et al. 2015). A very small number of individuals may have survived in central coastal Côte d’Ivoire: two individuals were sighted in a mixed species group in Dassioko Sud Forest Reserve in 2012, and in 2013 a specimen was retrieved from a poacher in Petit Jacqueville, a remote camp on the outskirts of Port Gauthier Forest Reserve (S. Gonedelé Bi, pers. obs. 2016).
range: Cercopithecus roloway is endemic to Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana. It once occurred from the Sassandra River, Côte d'Ivoire, north and east to Goaso in the Brong-Ahafo Region and east to the Pra River, Ghana (Oates 1988, Grubb et al. 1998, Oates et al. 2000). There is an historical museum record and some reports of this species in Togo to the east of Lake Volta (see Campbell et al. 2008 for a summary), but recent surveys failed to document the persistence of the species in Togo and there is considerable doubt about the provenance of the museum specimen. The last forests where this rare primate species still exists are located in central coastal and southeast Cote d’Ivoire (Dassioko Sud and Port Gauthier forest reserves, Tanoé forest) and southwest Ghana (Kwabre forest).
useTrade: Roloway Monkeys have long been hunted to provide meat for local consumption. Roloway Monkey carcasses have historically been traded as bushmeat for commercial gain, along with the carcasses of many other forest mammal species in West Africa. The relatively large size of this monkey and the value of its meat and skin make it a preferred target of hunters. However, the rarity of Roloway Monkeys means that their meat will now be only a very small component of any local diets and will no longer be a significant component of any trade.
conservationActions: The Roloway Monkey is one of the most threatened monkeys of the Upper Guinean Forest block (Oates 1996). It has previously been recorded from a number of protected areas across the region. However, recent surveys failed to confirm the presence of Roloway in several forest reserves in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana.In Côte d’Ivoire, the Roloway Monkey has been extirpated from almost all the protected areas and forest reserves where it was recorded in the past. In the late 1990s, surveys documented the species in the Yaya Forest Reserve, Niégré Forest Reserve, Bolo Ouest Forest Reserve, Marahoué National Park, but more recent surveys report its extinction from these forests (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2008, 2012, 2014; Bitty et al. 2015); only the Tanoé forest is confirmed to still harbour a small population. A couple of individuals were observed during a survey of the Dassioko Sud Forest Reserve in 2012, and its probable survival in Port Gauthier Forest Reserve has been reported by local residents, but follow-up surveys in these two forests have not yet confirmed its continuing survival (S. Gonedelé Bi, pers. obs. 2016).In neighbouring Ghana, recent surveys failed to confirm the presence of the species in the few forest reserves that were suspected to be its last refuges in the country including Krokosua Hills Forest Reserve, Ankasa Conservation Area, Bia National Park (Oates 2006, Gatti 2010, Osei et al. 2015) and Dadieso Forest Reserve (Wiafe 2013). Only the swampy community-owned Kwabre forest has been confirmed to still harbour a population of this monkey (Osei et al. 2015).Conservation programmes that involve local communities living around the Tanoé and Kwabre swamp forests have been developed and need to be strengthened, along with the appropriate involvement of national government agencies and international conservation organizations. Further careful surveys are needed in Tanoé and Kwabre, along with surveys to ascertain whether any viable populations survive elsewhere.This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES and on Class A of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.

rationale: A Red List status of Vulnerable was proposed for this species at the time of its description (Hart et al. 2012). Currently, Cercopithecus lomamiensis is known to occur over a small extent of occurrence (which is likely to be smaller than 20,000 km²), which—despite its remoteness—is exploited by commercial bushmeat hunters supplying regional urban centres, in particular Kisangani. The largely terrestrial Lesula is vulnerable to snare trapping and hunting with dogs, indeed the first specimens collected originated from hunters (Hart et al. 2012). The Lomami National Park, patrolled by armed park guards, protects only 20% of the Lesula’s known range. Outside the park, hunting is largely uncontrolled.
habitat: Cercopithecus lomamiensis is a medium-sized monkey. The species occupies closed-canopy terra firma forest. It is uncommon or absent from secondary forests. Cercopithecus lomamiensis is terrestrial, although it does climb in the lower and middle forest strata. Based on camera trap studies in Lomami National Park, group size is usually 5–15 individuals; however, 30 animals were identified in one series of video recordings. Group size at a hunted site is lower (also based on a camera trap study), with a maximum of 11 individuals detected (McPhee 2015). Foods include fruits gathered from forest floor and herbaceous vegetation, in particular meristems of Megaphrynium spp. C. lomamiensis has been recorded feeding on the ground on fallen fruits beneath foraging groups of arboreal primates.
threats: Cercopithecus lomamiensis is threatened over most of its range by uncontrolled commercial bushmeat hunting. Cercopithecus lomamiensis is particularly vulnerable to snares set for duikers and bushpigs, although it is not targeted. C. lomamiensis population densities are lower in heavily-hunted areas relative to patrolled protected areas with similar forest habitats.Localized habitat loss caused by shifting agriculture affects the species’ range, in particular at its northern limits in the Opala area. Habitat loss through further expansion of subsistence shifting cultivation and commercial growing of upland rice is likely to increase in the future.
population: Cercopithecus lomamiensis occurs widely across its known range and can be locally abundant in some areas (Hart et al. 2012). Total population size is unknown, but thought to be more than 10,000 individuals.
range: The range of Cercopithecus lomamiensis is estimated at 19,600 km² in eastern-central Democratic Republic of Congo. Most of this range has very little human settlement or disturbance at present; however, localized habitat loss is occurring on the northern limits in the Opala region. The species was unknown before 2007, and range loss to shifting cultivation and levels of hunting before that date are not known.
useTrade: Outside Lomami National Park, hunting is largely uncontrolled.
conservationActions: The species is not listed specifically by CITES, but is included in Appendix II as a member of the genus Cercopithecus. The government of Tshopo Province has designated C. lomamiensis a protected species at provincial level; however, C. lomamiensis should be considered for designation as a totally-protected species at the national level.Most of the known range of C. lomamiensis is in Tshopo Province (formerly Oriental Province) in eastern-central DRC. It occurs in the Lomami National Park, where patrols protect about 20% of its known geographic range.

rationale: Cercopithecus denti is listed as Least Concern, as it remains widespread, despite being hunted across its range for consumption in rural areas and for the commercial bushmeat trade. It is also threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to shifting agriculture and human settlements, and large parts of its geographic range are exploited by artisanal miners, thus its population is likely to be decreasing.
habitat: C. denti is a small, arboreal guenon that occurs across a wide range of forest types. In the core of its geographic range, it lives in low- to mid-elevation tropical forest, including closed primary mixed forest, secondary and riverine forest (Thomas 1991). In the eastern part of its range, it occurs in submontane to montane forests up to 2,000 m asl, and sometimes occurs at 2,400 m (Detwiler pers. obs. 2004–2005).C. denti is yet to be the focus of a systematic behavioural ecology study, but its diet is mostly fruit and arthropod prey (Thomas 1991), and Kingdon (2015) adds flowers, caterpillars, shoots and leaves. Group size estimates range from 7 to 21 individuals (Thomas 1991), and the species forms mixed-species associations with C. ascanius, C. mitis stuhlmanni, C. mitis doggetti, Lophocebus albigena, Colobus guereza and Piliocolobus oustaleti (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013, Detwiler pers. obs. 2004–2005, Hicks pers. obs. 2004–2008).
threats: Cercopithecus denti is threatened throughout its range in DRC by subsistence and commercial shotgun hunters who target small, diurnal monkeys. Field biologists have identified fresh kills of C. denti along trade routes to the Kindu and Kisangani markets (Hart pers. obs. 2016, Hicks pers. obs. 2016). A bushmeat study conducted in the main market in Kisangani documented a significant increase in the hunting of small diurnal monkeys, including Cercopithecus, from 2002 to 2008–2009 (2,221 and 8,228 carcasses, respectively) (van Vliet et al. 2012). During both study periods, the two main trade routes for carcasses entering the Kisangani market were Ituri and Lubutu (van Vliet et al. 2012), both of which are core forest areas for C. denti. In a second, more recent study, which investigated urban and rural bushmeat consumption in the greater Kisangani region, small monkeys were among the top three types of bushmeat reported to be preferred and eaten by children (van Vliet et al. 2014).Cercopithecus denti is likely also sold in bushmeat markets in the southeastern part of the range, the South Kivu area, but it is difficult to confirm species identity, as the carcasses are sold without skin as “monkey” (K. Guschanski pers. comm. 2016). In this area, the Centre de Rehabilitation des Primates de Lwiro cares for wildlife confiscated by park rangers and conservationists, and C. denti is one of the monkey species living at Lwiro (K. Guschanski pers. comm. 2016). The most likely reason for the presence of this species at Lwiro is that young C. denti are captured by hunters when the mother is killed.Expanding artisanal mining poses a growing threat to C. denti over large areas of its geographic range – in Maniema, North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri and Haut-Uélé provinces – and illegal mining is established in several of the largest protected areas that support populations of this species, notably Kahuzi-Biega and Maiko national parks, and Okapi Wildlife Reserve. Mining sites that occur far from established roads and villages pose a particularly significant threat, as these sites are often provisioned by resident bushmeat hunters who target primates.In addition to an increase in hunting pressure, C. denti is impacted in parts of its range by habitat loss through deforestation, agriculture and human settlement (Potapov et al. 2013). Increased rates of deforestation are also associated with artisanal mining in eastern DRC (Butsic et al. 2015).
population: Cercopithecus denti is likely common throughout the core area of its range. There are no recent survey data for the Ituri Forest, but the species is still common (Hart pers. obs. 2012), and data from surveys conducted in 1986 provided density estimates of 2.41 groups per km² and 23.1 individuals per km² (Thomas 1991). South of Ituri, Hall et al. (2003) reported C. denti population densities of 12.55 and 17.34 individuals per km² at two survey sites in the Itebero lowland sector of Kahuzi-Biega National Park (KBNP; survey data collected 1994–1995). Despite ongoing security issues, encroachment by artisanal miners, and human settlement in the lowland sector of KBNP, C. denti’s occurrence was confirmed in a survey of the Itebero sector in 2012, and in the Kasese sector of the park in 2013 (K. Guschanski, pers. comm. 2016).Hicks (pers. obs. 2004–2008) found that the species’ occurrence varied from rare (≤0.10 encounters per km walked) to common (0.50 encounters per km walked) at multiple survey sites in the forests south of the Uélé River.Outside DRC, the only confirmed populations occur in Semuliki National Park, Uganda, and in Nyungwe National Park (including Cyamudongo) in Rwanda. In Nyungwe, C. denti is rare due to the small area of the lower elevation forest that is its preferred habitat (Detwiler pers. obs. 2004–2005, B. Kaplin pers. comm. 2016).C. denti is known to hybridize with both C. (mitis) doggetti and C. ascanius (Detwiler pers. obs. 2004–2005, Detwiler et al. 2005). A recent genetic study confirmed the identity of a wild C. denti x C. ascanius hybrid living in a small forest fragment near Gisakura (Nyungwe NP headquarters) in Rwanda (Detwiler et al. 2013).
range: Cercopithecus denti is found in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, east and north of the Congo-Lualaba River, extending north to the Uélé River. The species’ western limit is thought to be the lower Itimbiri River (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013). In a series of primate surveys in northern DRC, C. denti was not encountered at any of the eight sites north of the Uélé River, but was observed at three sites (Aketi-Akuma, Buta and Lebo) north of the upper Itimbiri/Rubi River (Hicks pers. obs. 2004–2008). The eastern limit of the species’ range includes the forests of the Albertine Rift in DRC, Rwanda and Uganda, and possibly Burundi (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013). It extends east into Semuliki National Park, an extension of the Ituri Forest in western Uganda, and into Nyungwe National Park, including the Cyamudongo forest, in southwestern Rwanda (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013, B. Kaplin, pers. comm. 2016). The species’ southern limit in DRC is not well known, but likely reaches the forest-savanna ecotone south of Kindu, at approximately 3°S (Hart pers. obs. 2016). In the southeast, C. denti is reported to range to the area of Kabambare, approximately 04°42' S (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013). Sarmiento and Kingdon (2013) also reported a small extension of its range into northern Burundi, along the Ruzizi Plain, but the current status of this population is not confirmed.
useTrade: Hunted for local consumption and commercial bushmeat trade.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.Several populations occur in protected areas, including Kahuzi-Biega National Park, Maiko National Park, Semuliki National Park, Nyungwe National Park, Okapi Wildlife Reserve and Rubi-Télé Hunting Reserve.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because although it has a small extent of occurrence (< 5,000 km²), the species is locally common and there are no major threats to the species.
habitat: This species is restricted to sandy soils and sparsely vegetated regions of Isla Cerralvo and the Los Planes Basin on the adjacent mainland of the southern Baja California Peninsula. On Isla Cerralvo, the species is most common on the flat, sandy southwestern part of the island and less common on slopes and ridges. It is found far up sandy arroyos with a sandy floor, suggesting that sandy soil is a more important aspect of the habitat than is a flat, open environment (Álvarez-Castañeda and Rios 2011).
threats: There are no obvious or imminent threats, outside of the common threats to all island populations in the region: a restricted distribution (although this one also occurs on the adjacent mainland), and introduced feral animals (cats, rats, goats, pigs) and invasive plants.
population: There is no information about the population of this species.
range: This species occurs in northwestern Mexico (Isla Cerralvo in the Gulf of California and Los Planes Basin on the adjacent mainland of Baja California Sur (Álvarez-Castañeda and Rios 2011).
conservationActions: No conservation actions are reported for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is widely distributed, locally common, and unlikely to be declining at a rate which merits a threatened listing.
habitat: This species inhabits open, sandy deserts of the eastern Mesa Central in once continuous, now isolated patches of short grass with clumps of prickly pear cacti (Opuntia, Cactaceae).
threats: Much of the natural habitat of this species in the sandy basins of the eastern Mesa Central has been ploughed and dryland farmed for decades. Extant populations persist on small, isolated patches of native habitat, often clustered around rocky knolls where ploughing is impractical (D. J. Hafner, pers. obs).
population: This species is relatively common throughout its range; however, the population is considered extinct in the Valley of Mexico.
range: This species is known only from the Mexican Plateau, where it has been collected in the states of Aguascalientes, Durango, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Querétaro, San Luis Potosí, and Zacatecas (Fernández et al. 2012).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures reported for this species.

rationale: This species is reassessed as Vulnerable because it has an extent of occurrence greater than 5,000 km² but less than 20,000 km² (EOO = 7,709 km²), and its area of occupancy is less than 2,000 km² (AOO = 1,786 km²). Its geographic range is fragmented with no or limited movement between forest fragments, and there is a continuing decline in the species' EOO, AOO, area and quality of habitat, and number of mature individuals remaining. In addition, Piliocolobus gordonorum is hunted illegally in parts of its range.
habitat: Piliocolobus gordonorum inhabits a variety of forest habitats, including lowland old-growth, secondary and montane forests of the Udzungwa Mountains, and miombo Brachystegia woodland adjacent to old-growth or secondary forest in the lower parts of Mwanihana Forest and elsewhere (Struhsaker et al. 2013). Group size is highly variable, ranging from 7–83 (Struhsaker et al. 2004). Groups are smaller in forests that are small (<5 km²), dominated by deciduous trees, and/or are heavily degraded by human activities, compared to groups living in large, intact and relatively mature blocks of moist, mixed evergreen and semi-deciduous forest (Struhsaker et al. 2004). Recent ecological modelling analyses show the importance of basal area and other vegetative features for P. gordonorum, and preference for lowland to sub-montane zones, relative to montane and upper montane zones (Barelli et al. 2015, Cavada et al. 2016).
threats: Piliocolobus gordonorum is threatened by illegal hunting and by habitat loss due to logging, conversion to agriculture, collection of firewood, and charcoal production. The population in Magombera, in Kilombera Valley, was severely affected by the construction of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway (in 1972–1975) which bisected Magombera Forest, and through selective logging and agricultural expansion. The presence of the railway facilitated agricultural encroachment into the reserve, and increased the number of bush fires. Agriculture was responsible for a decline in the reserve’s size from 15 km² in 1955 to less than 11 km² by 1979. The area was threatened with total destruction in 2002 when the Government of Tanzania agreed to relocate squatters there from the nearby Kilombero Sugar Estate. Fortunately, the international conservation community appealed to the Government of Tanzania, which averted destruction of the forest, which contains >1,000 red colobus (Struhsaker 2005).  The local Wahehe people hunt P. gordonorum, particularly in the western and south-western parts of the range (Struhsaker et al. 2013). This is evident from long-term monitoring in the southern Uzungwa Scarp Nature Reserve, where a marked decline has occurred over the last 10 years (Rovero et al. 2015, F. Rovero, unpubl. data).
population: The total population of Piliocolobus gordonorum is difficult to determine with precision due to the many difficulties of counting arboreal primates (Marshall et al. 2008), but it is clearly in the tens of thousands. Efforts to census the species using systematic distance sampling have increased steadily in recent years. Rovero et al. (2009) reviewed existing knowledge and proposed population sizes ranging between 25,000 and 35,000 individuals. Araldi et al. (2014) conducted systematic transect censuses in four major forest blocks (Magombera, Matundu, Mwanihana and Uzungwa Scarp) estimated 45,000–50,000 individuals using distance sampling. These authors, however, did not consider variations in detectability (due to group size, habitat structure, etc.) and density (due to habitat and human disturbance factors), which are important for obtaining precise estimates (Cavada et al. 2016). The large Ndundulu-Luhomero forest may also contain thousands of individuals, given that the encounter rate from a recent survey across Ndundulu averaged 0.59 groups/km walked (N. Cavada and F. Rovero unpubl. data), which is within the upper side of the range of values recorded in other forests (0.08–0.62 groups/km walked; Araldi et al. 2014). In conclusion, while a precise estimate is still unavailable, the total population of P. gordonorum likely ranges between 30,000–40,000 individuals. Yet, some populations, such as in Uzungwa Scarp are under heavy pressure from poaching and are in rapid decline (see below and Rovero et al. 2015).
range: Piliocolobus gordonorum is restricted to the Udzungwa Mountains in Tanzania, including Udzungwa Mountains National Park and several adjacent forests, most of which have protected status as a Forest Reserve (FR) or a Nature Reserve (NR) status: Kilombero NR, Matundu FR, Uzungwa Scarp NR, Nyanganje FR, Kiranzi-Kitungulu and New Dabaga/Ulangambi (Marshall et al. 2010, Jones 2013, Struhsaker et al. 2013). However, in the recent decades, numerous small forests outside the park have been lost or severely degraded, such as New Dabaga/Ulangambi FR (Marshall et al. 2005). The only viable population in Kilombero Valley along the eastern base of Udzungwa Mountains is in Magombera Forest. During the past decade, it has been extirpated from small forest patches such as Kalunga (Struhsaker 2005, 2010). There has been no recent assessment of its presence in gallery forest along the Msolwa River south of the railway to its confluence with the Kilombero River, including the Ibiki and Msitu ya Kinjugu forests (Struhsaker et al. 2013). Given the agricultural intensification and expansion that have occurred in recent years, it is unlikely that these small patches hold viable numbers. The altitude range is 250–2,200 m, with density being lowest at higher elevations (Marshall et al. 2005, Struhsaker et al. 2013, Barelli et al. 2015, Cavada et al. 2016).
useTrade: Hunted illegally. Meat is eaten and traded.
conservationActions: Piliocolobus gordonorum is listed as Class A under the African Convention, and under Appendix II of CITES. At present, only about half the range of this species is effectively protected in Udzungwa Mountains National Park. As such, this population is reasonably secure. The remaining habitat is in forest reserves or nature reserves, or is not protected as it is on public land. This species is nominally protected by law in Tanzania as ‘Presidential Game’. Better enforcement of these laws is essential in areas where the species is hunted. Conservation priorities for this P. gordonorum are: 1) Greatly improved management of the forest reserves and nature reserves; 2) Clarification of the conservation status of Magombera Forest, provision of effective management and allocation of formal and on-the-ground protection; 3) Prevention of fire in order to promote forest expansion and establishment of corridors among forest blocks, thereby facilitating the dispersal of forest-dependent species, including P. gordonorum; 4) Generally, improve law enforcement to prevent poaching, fires, encroachment and  illegal logging. Struhsaker et al. (2004, 2013) outlined recommendations for future research.

rationale: Piliocolobus preussi is listed as Critically Endangered (CR) as this species is estimated to have declined over the last three generations (ca 30 years). This is due to unsustainably high levels of mostly illegal hunting throughout its range, habitat loss and reduced habitat quality outside protected areas from timber exploitation and small- and large-scale industrial agriculture. An 80% decline in monkey sightings was recorded between 1990 and 2016 in the Korup National Park, the species’ stronghold. Although data are lacking on monkey populations outside protected areas, this species is known to be extremely vulnerable to hunting pressure and loss of mature, high canopy forest. The primary driver of these threats—human population growth—is expected to increase into the foreseeable future. The taxon is suspected to have undergone an overall population reduction of more than 80% over the past three generations and is listed as CR under criterion A2d. The causes of this decline have not ceased, nor will they in the foreseeable future.
habitat: Preuss’s Red Colobus inhabits mature, high canopy, lowland, mid-altitude and sub-montane moist forest up to 1,000 m asl (Butynski and Kingdon 2013), where it spends most of its time in the upper canopy. Preuss’s Red Colobus is highly folivorous, often feeding from trees that are exploited for timber. Group sizes of 20–60 animals have been observed in Korup (Edwards 1992, Linder 2008, S. Nguedem pers. comm. 2015), with some counts exceeding 100 individuals (D. Okon pers. comm. 2015).
threats: The major threat to Preuss’s Red Colobus is unsustainable and hunting, which is mostly illegal (e.g., Dowsett-Lemaire and Dowsett 2001, Linder and Oates 2011). In Korup National Park, P. preussi made up a relatively large proportion of the total primate offtake (22% of carcasses) in a recent study (Linder and Oates 2011). Hunting sign encounter rate has increased through time in southern Korup NP from 0.28 signs/km (86 signs along 196.5 km walked) in 2001–2002 (D. Okon pers. comm. 2015) to 0.41 signs/km (155 signs along 382.2 km walked) in 2013–2015 (Linder et al. 2015). Between 2013 and 2014, nearly 300 P. preussi were killed by 30 surveyed hunters living within 3 km of Korup (Astaras and Linder 2016). Offtake surveys of hunters in a village in northeast Korup NP indicated that Preuss’s red colobus represented 2.4% of the 824 animals killed by hunters in June 2016 (Hofner 2016). Fa et al. (2006) counted 494 Preuss’s Red Colobus carcasses for sale in rural Cameroonian bushmeat markets and 284 Preuss’s Red Colobus in rural Nigerian bushmeat markets between August 2002 and January 2003. Most of these red colobus carcasses were recorded in markets close to Korup NP. In addition to the threat from hunting, red colobus habitats have suffered and continue to suffer from forest loss and declining habitat quality, driven primarily by logging and small- and large-scale agriculture (Waltert et al. 2002, Forboseh et al. 2007, Linder 2013, Schoneveld 2014, B. Morgan pers. obs. 2016), resulting in a 3.8% decrease in tree cover since 2000 (Global Forest Watch 2019). Forests directly to the north and east of Korup NP have been and continue to be selectively logged, as have forests in the Makombe-Ndokbou area. One of the most exploited timber species in southwestern Cameroon is Lophira alata (Namuene 2014), a tree species that red colobus monkeys rely on for food. Large-scale industrial oil-palm plantations located adjacent to Korup NP and Ebo Forest threaten the integrity of forests in both areas. Underlying these threats is an increasing human population, leading to increasing demands for bushmeat and other natural resources. The human population growth rate in Cameroon and Nigeria is high and has been increasing from ~2.0% annual growth rate in the early 1960s to 2.6% in 2017–2018 (World Bank 2019).  The so-called “Anglophone Crisis” in the South West and North West Regions of Cameroon further exacerbates the threats listed above. Since 2017, conservation activities in Korup NP (SW Region) have been suspended due to civil unrest, which has forced a substantial proportion of the human population to flee into the forest. This has likely led to increased pressure on forest resources in and around Korup NP, including increased hunting of red colobus monkeys.
population: Based on extrapolation of a known number of groups in a circumscribed area in southern Korup National Park and an average group size of 24–33 individuals, there are estimated to be between ~3,300 and 4,600 red colobus monkeys in Korup NP, the remaining stronghold for this species (J. Linder and C. Astaras, unpublished data 2018).  Sighting frequency of Piliocolobus preussi in northeastern and southern Korup is relatively low and has declined through time. In northeastern Korup, group sighting frequency has declined from 0.07 groups/km (eight groups sighted; survey effort = 112.3 km) in 1990 (Edwards 1992) to 0.05 groups/km (four groups sighted; survey effort = 73.7 km) in 2004–2005 (Linder and Oates 2011) to 0.03 groups/km (two groups sighted; survey effort = 59.2 km) in 2014 (C. Jost Robinson pers. comm. 2016) to 0.02 groups/km (one groups sighted; survey effort = 60 km) in 2016 (Hofner 2016).  Similarly, in southern Korup, group sighting frequency has declined from 0.06 groups/km (11 groups sighted; survey effort = 196.5 km) in 2001–2002 (D. Okon pers. comm. 2015) to 0.05 groups/km (10 groups sighted; survey effort = 211.7 km) in 2004–2005 (Linder and Oates 2011) to 0.02 groups/km (nine groups sighted; survey effort = 382.2 km) in 2013–2015 (Linder et al. 2015) to 0.01 groups/km (1 group sighted on 99 km walked) in 2016–2017 (C. Astaras and J. Linder unpublished data 2018).  In the Oban Division of Cross River National Park, group sighting frequency calculated for the period between December 2014 and December 2017 was 0.001 groups/km (Abanyam 2018). Groups of Preuss’s Red Colobus were sighted in the Makombe-Ndokbou forest in 2000 (Dowsett-Lemaire and Dowsett 2001) and 2002 (B. Morgan pers. obs.) and in the Ebo Forest in 2012 (E. Abwe, pers. obs.). However, systematic line transects in the Ebo Forest since then have yielded no further signs of red colobus monkeys. Similarly, surveys conducted in 2018 in the Makombe and Ndokbou forests failed to detect any signs of red colobus monkeys. These results suggest that Preuss’s Red Colobus may now be extremely rare in the Ebo-Makombe-Ndokbou forest block.
range: Preuss’s Red Colobus is present in Korup National Park and surrounding forests in southwestern Cameroon (Forboseh et al. 2007, Linder and Oates 2011), and in the contiguous Ikpan block of the Oban Division of Cross River National Park in the southeastern corner of Nigeria (Abanyam 2018). This red colobus also occurred in the Ebo Forest just north of the Sanaga River (Dowsett-Lemaire and Dowsett 2001, Morgan et al. 2012), although last observed there in 2012 (E. Abwe pers. obs. 2019). At least until fairly recently, Preuss’s Red Colobus still persisted in the Makombe-Ndokbou forest to the north and northeast of Ebo Forest, where they were seen in both 2000 (Dowsett-Lemaire and Dowsett 2001) and 2002 (B. Morgan pers. obs. 2016). However, surveys conducted in 2019 failed to detect the presence of red colobus in Makombe-Ndokbou.
useTrade: This species is hunted unsustainably throughout its range, and most of this hunting is illegal. Preuss’s Red Colobus is commonly found in hunter offtakes (Linder and Oates 2011, Astaras and Linder unpublished data 2018) and in bushmeat markets near to Korup National Park (Fa et al. 2006).
conservationActions: This taxon is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. P. preussi is present in Korup National Park (1,260 km²) and its perimeter in Cameroon, with a small number residing in the adjacent Oban division of Cross River National Park (Nigeria). It has also been recorded in the Ebo Forest, which is proposed as a new national park, but its present status in Ebo Forest is unclear.

rationale: Piliocolobus pennantii is listed as Critically Endangered as this species has a very restricted range on the island of Bioko (approximately 160 km²), and is suspected to have undergone a decline of more than 80% over three past generations (1986-2016), mainly due to heavy hunting impact across its limited range.
habitat: Piliocolobus pennantii is a largely arboreal species found in lowland and mid-montane tropical moist forest, and marsh forest in the southwestern sector of the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve. These are considered ‘monsoon forests’, receiving over 10,000 mm of rain per year (Oates et al. 2004). This monkey is reported to occur from sea level through montane forests into Schefflera forests at elevations of 1,800 m or higher (Butynski and Koster 1994, González-Kirchner 1997); however, Cronin et al. (in review) observed it from only 0–1,200 m, and suggested that they are likely not found higher than that based on habitat suitability modelling.Abundance of P. pennantii is concentrated in the southwestern region, and especially in the lowland forests near Playa Moraka (Cronin et al. 2016, Cronin et al. in review), which suggests that it may have a preference for lowland tropical moist forest, contrary to González-Kirchner (1997), who suggested it preferred montane forest. It is locally abundant in parts of its range (e.g., the forests near Playa Moraka), but abundance drops significantly outside core areas (Cronin et al. in review).Group size is variable. In a brief survey, Struhsaker (2000) estimated that group size ranged from 5–30 animals, with a mean of 14 individuals. Using data from 506 encounters; however, Cronin et al. (in review) observed a maximum group size of 20 individuals and a mean group size of 2.85 animals (2.64–3.07) across its entire range, and 3.08 animals (2.71–3.52) in the crater of the Gran Caldera, where primate populations are most likely as close to ‘natural’ as is possible on Bioko due to isolation and very low hunting pressure.
threats: The major threats to this species are hunting (e.g., Cronin et al. 2015b, 2016), development and habitat degradation. Cronin et al. (2015b) reported that 1,754 individuals were available in the Malabo bushmeat market between 1997 and 2010. P. pennantii was hunted at a lower rate than most of the other diurnal primate species due to its isolated distribution in remote areas of the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve. It is, however, the primate species most vulnerable diurnal to hunting pressure on Bioko (Cronin et al. 2016). Hunting has continued unabated in the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve since 2010 (e.g., Cronin et al. 2016), and the recent completion of a road bisecting the reserve has eroded much of the isolation that had passively protected wildlife populations (Cronin et al. 2015a), and contributed to increased hunting activity in the reserve (D.T. Cronin, unpublished data, 2015, 2016). There are also plans for a significantly greater military presence in the near future at Ureca, the only village entirely within the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve, and construction of a large base is already underway to accommodate its personnel. This represents a potentially grave threat for P. pennantii and other wildlife in the reserve, as Cronin et al. (2016) reported that military staff in Ureca were the only gun owners and perpetrators of gun-hunting in the area around the village at the time of the study (2011–2012). This situation is still generally the case, but hunting activity has been augmented by hunters from outside the reserve visiting the area to hunt as a result of the road (D.T. Cronin, pers. obs. 2015, 2016). An increased number of arms and military personnel at Ureca are very likely to lead to increased hunting of primates, including P. pennantii.
population: There are probably fewer than 1,200 animals remaining on Bioko, and Cronin et al. (in review) estimate a >80% decline in numbers between 1986 and 2016. Piliocolobus pennantii is encountered at a rate of 0.26 groups/km (3.92 groups/km²) on Bioko, but abundance is highly localised (Cronin et al. in review). At Moraka in the remote southwest, abundance was 0.49 groups/km, but at Ureca near the limit of its range, abundance was 0.16 groups/km. Hunting and recent road development and the associated increasing in anthropogenic disturbance in the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve are contributing to declining population numbers and a reduction in its extent of occurrence.A past reduction of more than 80% is suspected over the last three generations based on bushmeat hunting and market surveys (Cronin et al. 2015, 2016) and the fact that this species is most favoured by bushmeat hunters.
range: Piliocolobus pennantii is endemic to the island of Bioko, Equatorial Guinea, where it is now restricted entirely to the southwest of the island with a range of approximately 160 km² in the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve (Cronin et al. in review). P. pennantii was thought to have persisted in the Iladyi valley in southeastern Bioko until recently, and in Pico Basilé National Park in northern Bioko into the early 1990s (Butynski and Koster 1994, González-Kirchner 1994, IUCN 2016), but there have been no records in subsequent studies in either area (Nowak and Rioso Etingue 2007, Butynski and Owens 2008, Grande-Vega et al. 2013, Cronin et al. 2013, Cronin 2014) and interviews with hunters who have worked extensively on Pico Basilé report not having seen it for ≥30 years (M. Grande Vega, unpublished data).
