Earlier reports detailed P. pennantii at elevations ranging from 0-800 m and potentially up to 1,800 m (Butynski and Koster 1994, González-Kirchner 1997), but Cronin et al. (in review) estimate its current elevational range is more likely between 0-1,200 m.
useTrade: From 1997 to 2010, 1,754 Piliocolobus pennantii carcasses were available for sale in the Malabo bushmeat market (Cronin et al. 2015b). During the final period of the survey (November 2007 through September 2010), the average change in the rate of P. pennantii carcass availability per month was increasing by approximately one carcass/month, i.e., the general offtake pattern was gradually increasing. The average price paid in the Malabo market for an adult P. p. pennantii in 2008 was about US$50 (Cronin et al. 2014).
conservationActions: P. pennantii receives some measure of protection under both national and international legislation. Its population is entirely within a legally-recognised protected area (IUCN 1b Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve), in which hunting is prohibited (Republic of Equatorial Guinea 2003). Furthermore, the hunting, sale and consumption of all primates was banned by Presidential Decree in October 2007 (Republic of Equatorial Guinea 2007). However, there is no management plan in place for the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve, and the National Institute for Forestry Development and Protected Area Management (INDEFOR-AP) has a very limited budget, with few staff and low capacity with which to effectively manage the reserve. Internationally, this taxon is also listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. The remaining populations of P. pennantii on Bioko are confined to approximately 160 km² Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve (510 km²); however, there is almost no control of hunting in these protected areas. Butynski and Koster (1994) provided the contemporary baseline for the status of Bioko’s primates, including P. pennanti, and there has been continual monitoring of primate populations on Bioko by the Bioko Biodiversity Protection Program (BBPP) since the early 2000s (Hearn et al. 2004, 2006, Cronin et al. 2010). More recently, there have been numerous systematic survey efforts throughout Bioko, especially in the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve, in order to assess primate abundance and hunting intensity (e.g., Cronin et al. 2016), including targeted surveys for P. pennantii (Cronin et al. 2013). This work has led to an increased understanding of the distribution and population density of P. pennantii and shed light on both the threats it faces and the urgent need for effective measures to protect the species (Cronin et al. 2017, in review). In order to effectively conserve primates on Bioko, Cronin et al. (2017) have proposed (i) the development and implementation of a management plan for the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve; (ii) the strengthening of the legal basis for protection and management of the GCSR; (iii) greater involvement of INDEFOR-AP in the GCSR; (iv) increased enforcement; and (v) a more proactive government approach to conservation, especially towards primate hunting. Also called for is a ban on shotgun hunting, as has been argued before (Albrechtsen et al. 2004, Hearn et al. 2006), as well as the implementation of bushmeat spot checks at existing checkpoints at key transit intersections. An area-based prioritization scheme was also recently developed using primate species richness as its basis (Cronin et al. in review), in which the ‘critical zone’ will encompass almost all of the range of P. pennantii. The ‘critical zone’ delineation has been adopted into the Equatoguinean ‘National Biodiversity Strategy & Action Plan for the Conservation of Biological Diversity’ (Engonga Osono et al. 2015); however, the completion of this plan has not yet resulted in the development of a comprehensive management plan for the reserve, nor has the plan bolstered government support for its conservation. The BBPP has many projects underway in the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve, including primate monitoring, alternative livelihoods, educational programmes, professional development training (i.e., ecoguard training), the development of a Nature Centre in the village of Ureca, and partnering with INDEFOR-AP to foment their active involvement in the reserve and its day-to-day management. A United Nations Development Programme (UNEP) Global Environmental Facility (GEF) project is also ongoing on the island with the goal of strengthening Equatorial Guinea’s system of protected areas. This project is helping to support BBPP’s efforts in Ureca, as well as working towards gaining recognition of Bioko Island as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

rationale: This species is assessed as Critically Endangered as it is estimated to have undergone a decline of more than 80% over the past three generations (ca 30 years) due to heavy hunting impact across its limited range in the Niger Delta, compounded by habitat loss and degradation. It persists in small pockets of fragmented and degraded forest but has been extirpated from most parts of the area where it was previously reported to be present (Ikemeh 2015). Piliocolobus epieni does not occur in any formal protected area, and although some conservation efforts have been attempted they have been significantly hampered by insecurity in the Niger Delta, a lack of political will, and a lack of consensus amongst key local communities over the scope of proposed conservation programmes. Therefore the decline of the species is expected to continue. Immediate conservation attention is required if P. epieni is to be saved from extinction.
habitat: It is a largely arboreal species restricted to freshwater swamp forest. Its diet is dominated by young foliage from large and medium-sized trees, with seeds being seasonally important. The Niger Delta red colobus flourishes only in areas where their favoured food trees occur in large patches (Werre 2000), and their populations are therefore very sensitive to the loss of these trees.
threats: The major threats to this species are habitat degradation and loss; hunting is reported to be relatively rare and opportunistic (Ikemeh 2015).  Artisanal-scale logging has seriously degraded the habitat of P. epieni, removing many important red colobus food trees, such as Hallea ledermannii (Werre and Powell 1997, Grubb and Powell 1999). These threats have further intensified during the last decade as a result of growing human population and migration, and increased economic activities accompanied by a rise in income levels. A survey in 2013 found that many of the forests across the range of P. epieni now lacked any large trees, and that even medium-sized trees were scarce, while an analysis of remote-sensing imagery indicated annual rate of forest loss across this range of 1.2% between 1991 and 2013  (Ikemeh 2015)
population: Piliocolobus epieni was discovered only in 1993, and was then quite common within its limited range, but surveys over the following 15 years suggested significant declines as a result of habitat loss and degradation from logging, and from hydrological changes resulting from oil industry activities (Werre and Powell 1997, Grubb and Powell 1999, M. Isoun and D. Otobo pers. comm. 2009). A survey in 2013 found no evidence (from sightings and local reports) for the presence of Niger Delta Red Colobus at 10 of the16 sites where Werre (2000) had recorded their presence in the mid-1990s (Ikemeh 2015). The current population may now only number in the hundreds (Ikemeh 2015).
range: The historical range of Piliocolobus epieni extended from the Forcados-Nikrogha Creek and the Sagbama-Osiama-Agboi Creek in the marsh forest of the Niger Delta, Nigeria (Grubb and Powell 1999, Werre 2000). Recent surveys suggest that remaining populations are now highly fragmented, and concentrated in an area of approximately 200 sq. km in the central south-eastern part of their original range (Ikemeh pers. comm. 2019).
conservationActions: This taxon is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.   Protection of the remaining habitat of this taxon is an urgent priority, along with serious efforts to control hunting. Piliocolobus epieni is not represented in any protected area, although a forest reserve, Apoi Creek, near Gbanraun had been proposed for upgrading to national park status. Additional sites have also been proposed that could protect viable populations of the species (Ikemeh 2015), but there has been a lack of political will to implement these recommendations. Conservation efforts have also been hampered at a local level, particularly in the Apoi Creek area, where key communities have disagreed over land rights and the scope of conservation programmes that can be implemented. In the long run, any conservation action must include close monitoring of surviving populations and their habitats.

rationale: Piliocolobus semlikiensis has an extent of occurrence of ~78,500 km² and an area of occupation of ~54,400 km², but forest loss is ongoing across its range. Total forest loss is estimated at 4,430 km² (8.1% of the range) over 17 years (2001–2018; GFW 2019), which is 1.7 generations for this monkey (generation time for the genus is estimated at 10 years; Pacifici et al. 2013). This species occurs in eastern DRC, where the rate of forest cover loss is increasing: since 2014, it has been ~1% per year. Prior to that, annually rate of loss was 0.25–0.4% (GFW 2019).Projecting backwards three generations (to 1990) goes beyond the last 17 years for which forest loss data are available; however, we know that forest loss was occurring before 2001. Extrapolating 0.25-0.4% annual loss to the decade 1990–2000 gives an additional 2.5-4%  lost. Therefore, we estimate an overall range loss of 12–14% between 1990 and 2020.Added to forest loss is increasing hunting for bushmeat. Monkey meat is eaten in rural locations and traded commercially for consumption in towns and cities, and the bushmeat trade is a serious threat to red colobus monkeys across Central Africa (Struhsaker 2010). Red colobus are targeted for because of their large size, which affords a good return to a hunter for the cost of a shotgun cartridge. Red colobus live in relatively large groups (Struhsaker and Grubb 2013), and their behaviour when faced with a hunter tends to be to observe rather than flee – which affords very easy, multiple targets for the hunter. Hunting pressure was high throughout the areas surveyed in the last few years: Maiko National Park (Amsini et al. 2006a,b), Usala (S. Nixon pers. comm. 2019) and Okapi Wildlife Reserve (Vosper et al. 2012, Madidi et al. 2019).In 2019, there were roughly three times more people in DRC than in 1990 (mean human population growth 1990–2018 was ~3% annually). In addition, once intact blocks of forest are increasingly fragmented and made far more accessible to hunters: in DRC, 4.2% of forests classified as intact were lost between 2000–2013 (Potapov et al. 2017). Finally, the ability of the ever-increasing proportion of urban dwellers to pay much higher prices for bushmeat has created a highly lucrative market for commercial hunters, driving ever more rapid extraction of bushmeat from the regions’ forests. At present, 44% of the human population in DRC lives in towns and cities (World Bank 2019), compared with 27% in 1980, and this upward trend has been the case since 1960 (when it was 22%).Because red colobus monkeys are large-bodied and bring a higher profit per cartridge than smaller species, it is preferentially selected by hunters and tends to be eliminated or at least greatly reduced in abundance before other, smaller monkeys. Red colobus now appear to be very rare, even in protected areas.Thus, there is a combination of 12–14% of total habitat loss, plus 4.2% loss of intact forest, plus the increased demand for bushmeat, plus increased access too remote areas and an increased incentive for hunters to supply bushmeat to towns and cities. Piliocolobus semlikiensis is therefore suspected to have undergone a population decline exceeding 30% during the past three generations (1990–2019). The taxon is listed as Vulnerable under criterion A2cd, as the decline has been ongoing for some time and will continue into the future; causes have not ceased (indeed, the intensity of the causes is increasing), nor will they in the foreseeable future.
habitat: Little is known of this species but all observations have been in forest habitats – terra firma, swamp forests and along rivers. The animals live in groups. It is assumed, that like other red colobus, they are primarily folivores.
threats: The Semliki Red Colobus is directly threatened by habitat loss and hunting, and indirectly by the creation of easy access routes into huge areas of previously remote forests and increasing human populations.The species is subject to habitat modification, as intact forest is converted to farmland and “farm bush,” which can be seen clearly in Tyukavina et al. (2016) and Harris et al. (2017). In DRC, over 90% of forest loss is due to shifting agriculture (Tyukavina et al. 2018). Since 2001, there has been a trend towards gradually increasing annual forest loss, especially since 2013–2014 (GFW 2019).Hunting for bushmeat is increasing throughout the range. The meat is eaten by rural populations, traded to miners (Spira et al. 2019), or sold in urban markets. Road access into once-remote forests – even around protected areas – has hugely increased during the last 20–30 years (Kleinschroth et al. 2019), facilitating increased hunting and transport of bushmeat for commercial trade in both local markets and distant urban centres (Abernethy et al. 2013, 2016; Ziegler et al. 2016).Human populations in the range of the taxon are growing at roughly 2.7% annually, and this rate will not slow down in the near future (United Nations 2019, World Bank 2019).
population: The Semliki Red Colobus is targeted by hunters due to its large size. In recent years, they have rarely been seen, despite intensive survey efforts. They were recorded eight times in Maiko National Park in 2005 (both in the north and the south of the park: 380 and 300 km of effort, respectively; Amsini et al. 2006a,b). In 2007, red colobus vocalisations were heard on three separate transects close to the Ituri River (which forms the limit between P. semlikiensis and P. oustaleti), but which side of the river the vocalisations emanated from was unclear (WCS unpubl. data 2005–2007). Also in 2007, they were seen only once in the Usala area (which lies between Maiko National Park and Tayna Natural Reserve), although teams walked over 200 km of recces (Nixon et al. 2007). In the past, two groups were observed in Virunga National Park (Struhsaker 2010), but they were not recorded during surveys of the Semliki forest, Virunga National Park in 2008 (S. Nixon pers. comm. 2019) – the site of the taxon’s type locality. Finally, they were not found in Mt. Hoyo Reserve by Plumptre et al. (2015), but were apparently recorded in that area in 2018 (D. Kujirakwinja pers. comm. 2019).
range: The geographic range (area of occurrence) of Piliocolobus semlikiensis covers approximately 54,400 km². This is a forest-dwelling, Central African taxon and the vast majority of its range is in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) although, given the known distribution, it is possible that they could (rarely) occur in the contiguous forests of Semuliki and Rwenzori national parks, western Uganda. However, they were not recorded in Semuliki during a recent survey (Nixon et al. 2019) and there are no records in Rwenzori to date.The southern limit of P. semlikiensis is roughly 1° S, comprising the Lowa River (to the southwest) and further east, its tributary, the Oso River. The northern limit is roughly 1.2° N, comprising the Nduye River (at the northeastern edge of the range of this taxon), which then runs west and joins the Ituri River that in turn becomes the Aruwimi River, which completes the northern limit. The eastern limit is the Albertine Rift, especially the northern sector of Virunga National Park, with a possible extension into Uganda, as noted above. The western limit is unclear but can be described as a very rough north-south line veering west towards the south at about 27.9° E. The reason for this vague boundary is that this taxon, as defined here, incorporates what has been described as a “hybrid swarm”, flanked to the west by P. langi and to the south by P. lulindicus and P. foai, with possible contribution from P. oustaleti in the north.
useTrade: The species is illegally hunted for local consumption and sale to bushmeat markets. The level of offtake is probably declining as remaining populations are reduced and those remaining are mostly remote and depleted (and hence more costly to hunt).
conservationActions: This taxon is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. In DRC, the taxon (as Procolobus badius) is on the totally protected list (may not be hunted) (Enerunga 2006).It occurs in Maiko and Virunga national parks. It should also occur in Tayna Natural Reserve and Kisimba Ikobo Primate Reserve, and was found in Okapi Wildlife Reserve in the past. Efforts to control the killing of red colobus and trade in bushmeat would have a positive impact on remaining populations, especially in areas where mining and increasing settlement do not occur.The first conservation action plan for red colobus monkeys will be published in 2020. The plan identifies priority areas for conservation and recommends range-wide and taxon-based actions to prevent red colobus extinctions. Range-wide conservation priorities include actions that aim to improve government investment in wildlife conservation, expand and improve protected areas, determine taxon-specific distribution and abundance, engage with local human populations and integrate them into conservation activities, remove barriers that prevent local access to human healthcare and family planning, and raise awareness of the plight of red colobus.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered, based on a precipitous reduction in extent of occurrence (EOO) in the past 30 years that is expected to continue into the future. Piliocolobus foai is threatened by uncontrolled hunting and habitat loss in an area that has seen high levels of civil unrest in the past 30 years. The geographic range described by Colyn (1991) was approximately ~23,000 km². Since then, surveys have shown that this species remains in only two small and isolated populations and currently has an EOO of ~6,700 km², representing a 70% decline since the range was defined in the 1990s. Furthermore, only a single sighting was recorded between 2003 and 2019 in for one of the populations (D. Kujirakwinja pers. comm. 2019). Given past trends of uncontrolled hunting that have not stopped, it is extremely likely that P. foai will be extirpated from Itombwe Nature Reserve in the near future, if it even still exists there.The two known locations for P. foai are 1) Kabobo and Ngandja Reserves and adjacent Luama Hunting Reserve (together comprising the Kabobo Massif protected area complex) where it occupies an area of forest of about 1,200 km²; and 2) Itombwe Nature Reserve, where numbers have declined dramatically during the past 30 years due to habitat loss and hunting.Piliocolobus foai has not been recorded in Kahuzi-Biega National Park in the past three decades, and is thought to be no longer present in this area.The Kabobo Massif, the location of the only confirmed population, has had low levels of human impact; it has been protected historically because civil conflicts meant that human settlement in the region has been low (Plumptre et al. 2008, 2010). Establishment of the Kabobo Massif protected area complex (Rainforest Trust 2016) has contributed significantly to the conservation of Foa's Red Colobus. Nevertheless, human populations are currently increasing in the area. Hunting and habitat degradation associated with artisanal mining are occurring, particularly in Luama Hunting Reserve (A. Plumptre and D. Kujirakwinja pers. comm. 2019).In addition to habitat loss, a major threat is hunting: P. foai is targeted for bushmeat across its range. Because red colobus monkeys are large-bodied and bring a higher profit per cartridge than smaller species, they are preferentially selected by hunters and tend to be eliminated or at least greatly reduced in abundance before other, smaller monkeys. They live in relatively large groups (Struhsaker 2010, Struhsaker and Grubb 2013), and they have a tendency to observe humans rather than flee – which affords hunter with very easy, multiple targets. Hunting pressure was high in all areas surveyed in the recent past, and is associated with the expansion of artisanal mining and insecurity during periods of civil unrest.Monkeys are eaten in villages and traded commercially for consumption in towns and cities; the bushmeat trade is a serious threat to red colobus monkeys across Africa (Struhsaker 2010). In the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), there were approximately three times more people in 2019 than in 1990 (3% mean annual human population growth in DRC 1990–2018). The ability to pay much higher prices for bushmeat by the increasing proportion of urban dwellers in DRC has created a highly lucrative market for commercial hunters, which is the increasing rate of bushmeat extraction. At present, 44% of the human population in DRC lives in towns and cities (World Bank 2019), compared with 27% in 1980, and this upward trend has been the case since 1960 (when it was 22%). Given the human population growth, increasing human access to previously intact forest, uncontrolled hunting and the vulnerability of red colobus to hunting, this species is expected to continue declining.Piliocolobus foai is listed as Endangered under criterion A2cd due to a 70% decline in its extent of occurrence (EOO) in the recent past and hunting for bushmeat. The causes are not reversible, have not ceased, nor will they in the foreseeable future.
habitat: Piliocolobus foai occurs in primary montane and submontane forest from 800 to 2,270 m asl. In Itombwe, it is restricted to evergreen closed forests; in Kabobo, it also occurs in adjoining gallery forests on the escarpment above Lake Tanganyika. It is not known to range far into gallery forests or the forest islands west of the escarpment (Plumptre et al. 2008).
threats: Piliocolobus foai populations have been reduced or extirpated from over 50% of the species’ range by hunting and by range loss due to habitat conversion and degradation during the past 30 years. Hunting certainly contributed to the loss of the taxon from KBNP, and remains a threat in Itombwe Nature Reserve, where the species is now apparently almost extirpated.For the past two decades, eastern DRC has been the theatre of entrenched conflict promulgated by a multiplicity of rural militias, a number of whom are based in the region’s protected areas, including Itombwe Nature Reserve and the Kabobo Massif. This has not had an entirely negative impact. Rebels based in the Kabobo Massif prevented widespread occupation by farmers, herders and miners for two decades from the late 1970s through the fall of the Mobutu regime in 1997 (Plumptre et al. 2008, 2010). As security returned, incursions in the landscape increased (Plumptre et al. 2016). Elsewhere, however, occupation by militias and brigands has made management and protection of these protected areas difficult or impossible, favouring resource extraction and use by hunters, miners and pastoralists.Outside protected areas, habitat loss and degradation are due primarily to shifting cultivation and smallholder farming, small-scale logging, charcoal production and conversion of forest to pastures. Deforestation in DRC increased by a factor of 2.5 between 2011 and 2017 (Harris et al. 2017). Forest loss and associated degradation has been particular severe in the range of P. foai, the region of DRC where human population densities are highest.Small-scale (artisanal) and industrial-scale mining threaten the remaining forests in eastern DRC. Notably in the Itombwe Massif, where artisanal miners have reached even the most remote areas of this site. Since 2011, a major Canadian-registered, international gold mining company, Banro, has been operating concessions totalling 2,616 km² in and around Itombwe, and the company has outstanding requests for prospection within the boundaries of the Nature Reserve (Thierry Regards 2019).In the Kabobo Massif, fires set for hunting and to clear land for agriculture are among the main threats to the evergreen montane forests favoured by P. foai (Plumptre et al. 2016).
population: No population estimates are available for P. foai, which has a restricted range that is threatened by habitat degradation and hunting.The species was described as uncommon in the Itombwe Massif in the early 1990s (Doumenge and Schliter 1997). It was recorded in 1996 in lower montane formations between 1,220 and 1,850 m asl by Omari et al. (1999), who noted low overall encounter rates of primates in the massif (0.1 groups/km) and widespread evidence of hunting. Subsequent surveys and patrols between 2003 and 2019 yielded only a single observation of P. foai from Itombwe (Plumptre et al. 2010, D. Kujirakwinja pers. comm. 2019).Rahm and Christiaensen (1963) and Rahm (1964) reported the species in what are now the highland sector and corridor of Kahuzi-Biega National Park (KBNP). Specimens attributed to P. foai were collected in this same region (Colyn 1991); however, there are no recent records of this species from surveys in this area (Inogwabini et al. 2001, Spira et al. 2015).The last remaining stronghold for P. foai is the Kabobo Massif Reserve Complex, where it was recorded several times during surveys conducted in 2008 (Plumptre et al. 2008). It is threatened here, nonetheless, and rare in the Luama Hunting Reserve (Plumptre et al. 2010).
range: Endemic to the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Piliocolobus foai (sensu stricto, Colyn 1991) is restricted to montane forest habitats and does not occur west of the Albertine Rift highlands in areas of lower elevation. Historically, the species’ ranged through montane and submontane forests (900–2,800 m asl) in the Albertine Rift, from Kahuzi-Biega National Park (KBNP), south through the Itombwe Massif to Mt Kabobo (Rahm 1964). Colyn (1991) suggested, although without confirmed specimens, that P. foai ranged south to the Lukuga River (800 m asl); however, there is now very little if any remaining suitable habitat in this region, which borders on the city of Kalemie. Specimens from Irangi, west of the KBNP highlands, have been attributed to P. ellioti (Rahm and Christiaensen 1963). West of the Albertine Rift highland forests, red colobus populations show intergradation between P. foai and P. lulindicus and possibly other forms, and are considered to be hybrids (Colyn 1991).Piliocolobus foai is currently known from only two widely-separated locations. In the Kabobo region, it occurs in an area of ~1,200 km² of evergreen and gallery forests on the Lake Tanganyika escarpment (Plumptre et al. 2008, unpubl. data 2019). In the Itombwe Massif, it was recorded in 1996 (Omari et al. 1999), but patrol teams have reported only one sighting since 2003 (D. Kujirakwinja pers. comm. 2019).
useTrade: Uncontrolled hunting for local consumption and sale to bushmeat markets is a significant threat to Foa's Red Colobus. Levels of offtake are probably declining as numbers of this monkey are reduced.
conservationActions: All red colobus are protected by CITES (Appendix 1I). They are also listed as totally protected species by national laws in DRC (Enerunga 2006).The most important hope for the conservation of P. foai is the establishment and protection of the Kabobo Massif Reserve Complex, composed of the Kabobo and Nagandja Natural Reserves (Rainforest Trust 2016).Efforts to control the killing of red colobus and trade in bushmeat would have a positive impact on remaining populations, especially in areas where mining and settlement do not occur.The first conservation action plan for red colobus monkeys will be published in 2020. The plan identifies priority areas for conservation and recommends range-wide and taxon-based actions to prevent red colobus extinctions. Range-wide conservation priorities include actions that aim to improve government investment in wildlife conservation, expand and improve protected areas, determine taxon-specific distribution and abundance, engage with local human populations and integrate them into conservation activities, remove barriers that prevent local access to human healthcare and family planning, and raise awareness of the plight of red colobus.

rationale: Sciurocheirus alleni was previously assessed as Least Concern, because although S. alleni is forest-dependent, it can flourish in secondary forests. Recently, rapidly rising human population densities, accompanied by large-scale forest conversion in the larger, mainland part of the range in Nigeria and Cameroon, are rapidly reducing the area occupied by S. alleni and, therefore, its numbers. The trend in habitat loss is expected to continue into the future, and to accelerate. Therefore, the status of S. alleni is changed from Least Concern to Near Threatened. A population decline of at least 20% is probable in the 12-year period from 2010 to 2022 (approximately equal to three generations, with an estimated generation time of 4 years), nearly meeting criterion A4c.
habitat: Found in lowland and montane primary and secondary forest; also recorded in farmbush. A nocturnal species that forages on the ground, and in the low- and mid-canopy.
threats: The major threat to Sciurocheirus alleni is ongoing habitat loss in southeastern Nigeria and southwestern Cameroon. The estimated rate of forest loss in Nigeria increased from 2.7% per annum 1990–2000 to 5.0% per annum 2000–2015 (FAO 2015) and is likely to continue to accelerate. Large-scale agricultural projects for crops, such as oil palm in the Southwest Region (Linder 2013), as well as rapid urbanization around the city of Douala, have led to major loss of habitat in Cameroon, and this loss is projected to continue. Habitat loss is also the primary threat to S. alleni on Bioko. Although occasionally hunted on Bioko (Cronin et al. 2015), hunting does not represent a significant threat to the species.
population: This species is locally common in appropriate habitat. The highest densities are recorded in montane forest, with lower densities in primary lowland forest (Ambrose and Pimley 2013). Density in secondary forest on Mount Kupé, Cameroon, of about 14 animals/km² (Pimley 2002, Pimley et al. 2005). Encountered at the rate of 1–2 individuals/hr at various elevations on Bioko Island (Ambrose and Pimley 2013); at 0.48 individuals/hr in lowland forest in Korup National Park (Bearder and Honess 1992); and at 0.43 individuals/hr in lowland forest at Rhoko near Cross River National Park in Nigeria (Bearder and Oates 2009).The species is likely to be declining in many parts of its range due to rapidly growing human population, large-scale forest conversion, shifting agriculture, smallholder farming and small-scale resource extraction. It is suspected that the global population of Allen's Galago will undergo a reduction of at least 20% over the three generation period between 2010 and 2022.
range: Sciurocheirus alleni is present on Bioko Island (Equatorial Guinea) and on the African mainland in the coastal moist forest zone between the Niger River, southeast Nigeria, and the lower Sanaga River, central Cameroon, including the mountains of southwestern Cameroon (Ambrose and Pimley 2013). There are two subspecies: S. a. alleni is endemic to Bioko, while S. a. cameronensis is present in southeastern Nigeria and western Cameroon.
useTrade: Given their small size (300 g), S. alleni is not hunted in significant numbers for meat, even though they occur in areas with very high levels of hunting for the bushmeat trade. Sporadically for sale in the Malabo bushmeat market and a roadside bushmeat stall on Bioko Island (Cronin, pers. obs. 2011). Between 1997–2010, 160 individuals for sale in were counted in the Malabo market (Cronin et al. 2015). Not seen on markets in the Cross-Sanaga region (Fa et al. 2006).
conservationActions: Sciurocheirus alleni is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It is recorded from Cross River National Park and Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary (Nigeria); Korup, Bakossi and Mount Cameroon national parks, and Banyang-Mbo Wildlife Sanctuary (Cameroon); and Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve and Pico Basilé National Park on Bioko.

rationale: Listed as Vulnerable because of observed extreme declines at two major roosting areas (Mount Suswa and Ithundu caves, Kenya) within the past two decades (Kock et al. 2005). It remains unclear whether these populations have continued to decline in recent years.
habitat: Individuals of O. harrisoni are associated with high altitudinal areas and have been recorded from a variety of tropical to semi-arid habitats in northeast Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. These include woodlands and shrublands of the Arabian Peninsula and Eritrea, montane grasslands, woodlands and forests of Ethiopia, xeric grassland and shrublands of Djibouti and the bushlands and thickets of Kenya (Olsen et al. 2012).The species has a preference for roosting in mountain-associated cave systems and lava caves. Tightly-packed clusters of individuals congregate in the Mount Suswa and Ithundu lava caves system of the Rift Valley and Chyulu Hills in Kenya (Kingdon 1974; Kock et al. 2005), the Sof Omar karst cave system of Ethiopia (Largen et al. 1974), the Hud Sawa caves at the Al-Rayadi Al-Gharbi Mountains in Yemen (Al-Jumaily 1999), the Day Forest National Park at the Goda Massif Mountains in Djibouti (Hill and Morris 1971) and within a disused railway line tunnel near Asmara in Eritrea (Kock and Zinner 2004).While it seems as though there is no direct evidence of migration in this species, marked seasonal absence from some areas and from major colony sites during the dry season has prompted the suggestion of migration (e.g., Mutere, 1973). Animals are known to make long distance foraging flights during the dry season.
threats: The leading threat to this species appears to be roost disturbance. Major colonies in East Africa, such as the population at Mount Suswa (Kenya), seem to have disappeared through disturbance of their cave habitats (Hutson et al. 2001). Threats to these caves include guano mining (with associated changes to the cave microclimate), blocking of entrances, recreational caving and general tourism activities. It is possible that the collection of 4,954 bats by Mutere (1973) as part of a reproductive study may have contributed to a decline of the Kenyan populations.
population: The species is usually found roosting in caves and disused tunnels in colonies of 500 or more individuals. Major colonies of this species known from caves in East Africa, including Ithundu and Mount Suswa, have declined severely and now harbour very few bats (Hutson et al. 2001).
range: This species is restricted to northeast Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. It has been recorded from Yemen (Hud Sawa cave, Ar-Rayadi Al-Gharbi Mountains) on the Arabian Peninsula (Al-Jumaily 1999, Hutson et al. 2001), Djibouti (Mount Day), Ethiopia (Sof Omar limestone cave), Kenya and Eritrea (in a disused railway tunnel 8 km east of Asmara). It is typically found at high elevations from 1,000 m asl.
conservationActions: There is a need to reassess the status of all known roosts (and to locate additional localities) to ascertain numbers and status of colonies, so that key sites can be identified (for further discussion see Ralph et al. 2015). Disturbance of key localities should be restricted or managed to reduce the impact on colonies. An IUCN Species Action Plan was developed for O. martiensseni sensu lato (Hutson et al. 2001); this action plan requires revision given the reviewed species limits of O. martiensseni (Lamb et al. 2008, Richards et al. 2012) and the description of new northeast African species, O. harrisoni (Ralph et al. 2015).

rationale: The species is listed as Near Threatened because its population is likely declining at a rate of 20% to 30% over the last 15 years (proposed generation length of 5 years based on similar species, Pacifici et al. 2013) due to past and continuing disturbance of human activities to the roosting caves and degradation and loss of foraging habitat in forests.
habitat: The distribution of this species ranges from northern to southern Vietnam in three remarkably disjunct areas, including: the undisturbed forests in the limestone karst of Cat Ba National Park, secondary forests in a mountainous area in Chu Mom Ray in central Vietnam (Thong et al. 2012), and lowland forests in Cat Tien in southern Vietnam (Thong 2012). It is likely that to occur in areas that lie between these three isolated sites. There is no information about roosting sites of the species in northern and south-central regions. A cave roost in southern Vietnam is the only known roosting site of a group up to 30 individuals. Recordings of the species in Cat Ba and Chu Mom Ray suggests that the species forages along trails under the forest canopy.
threats: Threats to the species in northern and south-central Viet Nam are unclear but the roosting site in southern Viet Nam is likely disturbed by cave visiting and ecotourism. Foraging habitats in forests also face continued degradation and loss due to harvest.
population: Little is known about the population size of this species, but it is likely that the population is declining due to disturbance of tourism and habitat changes. Four individuals were captured in Cat Ba National Park, two individuals from Chu Mom Ray National Park (Thong et al. 2012) and several individuals from Cat Tien National Park (Thong 2012). It was observed in a group of less than 30 individuals inhabiting a cave in Cat Tien National Park (Thong, unpublished data). It is thought that there are at least two subpopulations, one in Cat Ba National Park in northern Viet Nam and at least one in south central and southern Vietnam. A series of surveys between 2014 and 2018 in both Cat Ba and Cat Tien National Park provided no additional information about the species.
range: This species has only been recorded from three disjunct national parks, namely Cat Ba, Chu Mom Ray (Thong et al. 2012) and Cat Tien (Thong 2012). It is probable that the species range is includes at least some areas that lie between these isolated sites.
conservationActions: All known localities of the species are situated within national parks, where forests are legally protected. Conservation campaigns have been implemented at Cat Ba National Park but outcomes are uncertain. The unscientific development of ecotourism in all three national parks, particularly in Cat Ba, appears as a critical threat to foraging habitats and roosting sites of the species.

rationale: The species is listed as Vulnerable under criterion C2a(i); total population size is estimated at 4,700 individuals in 14 caves in peninsular Thailand and the number of individuals in each cave varies between 3 and 800 individuals. The species is subject to continuing decline due to habitat disturbance.
habitat: This species roosts in limestone cave with the colony size of 3-800 individuals. It was found sharing the cave with Hipposideros armiger, H. larvatus, H. diadema, Megaderma lyra, Eonycteris spelaea.
threats: All roosts are in limestone outcrops and surrounded by rubber, oil palm plantations, or temples and villages. Most of the roost caves are outside protected area, and many caves are disturbed by monk and other human activities, and limestone quarrying.
population: The total number population estimated is 4,700 individuals in 14 caves in seven provinces of peninsular Thailand. The number of individuals in each cave varies between 3 and 800 individuals. The species is subject to continuing decline due to habitat disturbance.
range: The species is found in the Chumphon, Surat Thani, Nakhon Sithammarat, Phang Nga, Krabi, Trang and Phattalung provinces of peninsular Thailand.
conservationActions: The species is under the national list of protected wildlife. However, as the roosts are mostly outside protected area, it is at risk by disturbance and habitat loss.

rationale: Hipposideros alongensis is listed as Vulnerable because it is only found within the karst habitats in northeastern Viet Nam, number of mature individuals is smaller than 10,000 (estimate of 8,000 to 10,000 bats). The species has been observed in caves in groups up to 500 individuals (Thong et al. 2012). All colonies in caves across the known distributional range has been declining due to disturbance of roosting sites and loss of foraging habitats. The species comprises two distinct subspecies (H. a. alongensis in karst islands in Ha Long Bay, including Cat Ba archipelago, and H. a. sungi within fragmented karst forests in mainland of northeastern Viet Nam). The largest colony of each subspecies are both in serious decline, from ca 500 individuals to less than 200 individuals and every known colony appears to be continuously in decline since 2008 and ca 130-150 individuals in a colony in Cat Ba island (Kruskop 2013).
habitat: The species has been known as cave-dweller, recorded from different habitats ranging from cultivated areas with fruit tree gardens to secondary and primary forests within karst landscapes (Thong et al. 2012), and mangrove (Thong et al., unpublished data). It was observed foraging in group along trails, streams and under forest or fruit tree canopies with a height from ca 1 m to less than 10m from water surface or ground (Thong et al. unpublished data).
threats: Tourism, particularly the visiting of caves as well as habitat loss are major threats to the species. Electronic lights and artificial construction of gates and routes within caves have significantly and negatively impacted on the roosting sites of the species. Clearance of vegetation surrounding the cave with the largest colony of the species in Cat Ba island and development of cave tourism have led to loss of habitat of the species (Thong et al., unpublished data). The occasional, illegal hunting of the species by local people in some mainland areas within the distributional range of the species, has also caused population declines.
population: The largest colony of the species, in Cat Ba island, was included in Thong et al. (2012). It had an estimated population size of up to 500 individuals, this had dramatically declined to ca 130-150 individuals (Kruskop 2013) and even less than 80 individuals in 2017 (Thong et al., unpublished data). The current population of the species is estimated at fewer than 9,000 individuals and number of individuals at every known caves has declined remarkably since 2008 (Thong et al., unpublished data).
range: The species comprises two distinct subspecies (Hipposideros alongensis alongensis in karst islands in Ha Long Bay, including Cat Ba archipelago, and H. a. sungi within fragmented karst forests in mainland of northeastern Viet Nam). Topal (1993) included a record of the species from “Yu Do”, Yen Bai province, north-west Viet Nam, without geographical coordinates, which was subsequently cited in Can et al. (2008). However, this record is uncertain since there is no locality named “Yu Do” in Viet Nam (Thong et al. 2012).
useTrade: Illegal hunting of the species by local people in some mainland areas.
conservationActions: The species is not listed in any lawful or legal document of Viet Nam. Conservation actions including public awareness is essential in the Cat Ba archipelago (Thong 2007, Thong and Furey 2008). Previously colonies and roosting sites in caves in Cat Ba island were well conserved and almost undisturbed. However, rapid development of cave tourism in the Cat Ba archipelago, Ha Long Bay and other areas have threatened the species since 2010. Strategies for the conservation of the species which highlighted its endemic values were undertaken at national workshops and meetings but received little attention from local authorities.

rationale: This bat is listed as Critically Endangered because, despite a series of intensive surveys that have been continuously undertaken over the last 15 years (Soisook et al. 2015), this rare species is still only known from very few collections within a very small area around the type locality. Its area of occupancy (AOO) and extent of occurrence (EOO) are both less than 4 km². It is also threatened by habitat loss throughout the whole area where it has been recorded.
habitat: This species was observed roosting in a hollow tree (species unknown) and foraging on a large beetle in lowland moist evergreen rainforest (Soisook et al. 2015). It was also known to use a man-made building as a shelter during a rainy night. Two out of three specimens were caught in mist net set in forest gap at between two and three metres above ground.
threats: The major threat to this species is the habitat loss as the lowland forest, although legally protected, is being disturbed and converted to be agricultural area.
population: As this species is known only from three specimens collected during the last 15 years, it is believed to be extremely rare. It is not possible to estimate the population size but presumably decreasing due to the loss of forest area.
range: This species is known only from a very small area of Bala Forest, south Thailand. Both its EOO and AOO fit well within one 4 km² grid cell. The actual area this species is known from is between 0.03 and 1 km².
conservationActions: There has no conservation action or scheme currently in place. However, the species is being considered to be included in the list of National Wildlife Protection Act (P. Soisook, pers. comm).

rationale: Hipposideros nicobarulae is assessed as Endangered under criterion B2ab(iii) as it is known only from the Nicobar group of islands of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, India and its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be between 44–52 km² across at least 11 islands (Douangboubpha et al. 2011, Aul et al. 2014). Its area of occupancy, extent and quality of habitat, and the number of locations/subpopulations are declining. The overall population and number of mature individuals is inferred to be declining due to habitat degradation and loss. Its range is severely fragmented and the species is distributed in 3-5 locations, which are assumed to represent subpopulations, based on the spatial distribution of the islands. It is vulnerable to climate change related effects (sea level rise, strong cyclones); it is suspected to have been significantly impacted to the mass destruction of its habitat from a tsunami in 2004.
habitat: This species is known to roost in caves (Aul et al. 2014) and as a mixed sex colony in a sea cave (Douangboubpha et al. 2011). It has also been recorded from an abandoned military establishment (Hill 1967) and is assumed to forage in tropical lowland forest habitat. Deforestation is negatively impacting the species forest foraging areas and its cave roosts are inferred to be declining from disturbance. The 2004 tsunami razed over 95% of the Nicobar Islands' mangrove forests (Reddy et al. 2016).
threats: Hipposideros nicobarulae had its lowland foraging habitats severely damaged by the 2004 tsunami and its coastal cave roosts in the Nicobar Islands were partially or completely submerged, either killing bats or forcing them to vacate the caves (Aul et al. 2014). The species is impacted by periodic (May-June) in-cave disturbance due to poachers coming from Myanmar and Thailand to harvest edible swiftlet nests (Aul et al. 2014). Deforestation degrades and eliminates important foraging habitats (Reddy et al. 2016). Climate change brings threats from sea level rise and increased frequency of stronger cyclones where a single storm could severely damage both cave roosts and foraging habitats.
population: The population and number of mature individuals are suspected to be declining due to disturbance at cave-roosts, and loss and degradation of habitat. Its range is severely fragmented and the species is distributed in 3-5 locations, which are assumed to be subpopulations, based on the spatial distribution of the islands. Research and monitoring is needed to confirm the status, distribution, and trend of the species.
range: Hipposideros nicobarulae is endemic the Nicobar Islands, India. It is found on at least 11 islands including: Camorta Island, Trinket Island, Katchal Island, Little Nicobar Island, Great Nicobar Island, Tillanchang Island, Chowra Island, Bompoka Island, Teressa Island, and Nancowry Island (Douangboubpha et al. 2011) with a total land area of ca 1,840 km². Its is located in 3–5 locations (subpopulations) based on the spatial distribution of the islands, and its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be between 44–52 km² and is declining.
useTrade: The species is not traded or hunted.
conservationActions: The species likely occurs in two (2) protected areas on Great Nicobar and Tillangchong islands. Protection of known roosts from all forms of disturbance and its foraging areas are top priorities. Establishment of proactive conservation programme involving local stakeholders and identiﬁcation of a ﬂagship species (Aul 2006). Additional research is needed to ascertain the current status of this species, threats, and its habitats.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species generally inhabits riparian habitats in low-lying woodlands and savanna. Vonhof and Kalcounis (1999) indicate that this species is characterised as a tree-roosting bat preferring small trees and shrubs. Populations have been recorded roosting in caves and mines (Skinner and Chimimba 2005). It is known to be roosting in large numbers alongside other species in coral caves in coastal Kenya. as well as to be roosting in caves alongside other species in near Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this widespread species as a whole. The species is locally threatened in parts of its range by disturbance of roost sites and mining activities. Populations have been recorded roosting in caves and mines (Skinner and Chimimba 2005).
population: Some colonies of this bat can be quite large, with up to half a million animals recorded in the Koalin Mines of Tanzania. In peripheral parts of the range, such as Zimbabwe, colonies are often much smaller.
range: This species is widely distributed ranging through much of East Africa, with records from Djibouti in the north to central Mozambique and east Zimbabwe. The species has also been recorded in Central Africa from the Congo and Central African Republic border, south Congo, Angola and possibly Gabon. This species has also been recorded in Malawi in 2015 and 2016, captured in mist nets in Liwonde National Park and Satemwa Tea estates in the shire highlands.
conservationActions: There appear to be no direct conservation measures in place. It occurs in several protected areas in Mozambique (Monadjem et al. 2010a) and Tanzania. Further taxonomic studies are needed for specimens of Triaenops from the Albertine Rift.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Roosts of Glischropus species within stalks of dead bamboo were reported for G. javanus by Chasen (1939) from Java and for G. tylopus by Kofron (1994) from Brunei. The type locality of G. bucephalus, Seima Biodiversity Conservation Area, includes large stands of giant bamboo. Another bamboo specialist group, Tylonycteris spp. also occurs in significant numbers at the site (Csorba 2011). In Thailand, a male individual of Glischropus was caught at the edge of lowland wet evergreen forest, 100 m Asl (Bumrungsri, pers. comm. in Csorba 2011).
threats: The species most probably roosts in stems of giant bamboo species and the destruction of bamboo forests poses a threat.
population: The species is widespread and may be locally abundant where large bamboo stands are present.
range: Glischropus species north of the Isthmus of Kra are belonging to this species. It has a rather wide distribution area, specimens were reported from Cambodia, Myanmar, Lao PDR, Thailand and Vietnam (Bates et al. 2005, Csorba 2011, Francis et al. 1999, Francis et al. 2010, Guillen et al. 1997, Kruskop 2013).

rationale: This newly described species is known from seven sites in the northern and western portions of Madagascar (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013; Goodman unpublished data), many of which are within existing protected areas. This species is apparently not forest-dependant and by extrapolation not subjected to any important habitat degradation or other human pressures.
habitat: A species that at least in the west uses caves for day roost sites, many of these sites are in vicinity of native forests, specifically within or adjacent to dry deciduous forest. It is known from two localities in more mesic humid forests. It presumably forages in areas that are more open or close to the forest edge and it is suspected that this species is not forest dependant.
population: Not known.
range: Known from different sites in northern and western Madagascar and across an elevational range from 5 to 600 m above sea level (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013).
conservationActions: This species is known from several protected areas: Bemaraha, Loky-Manambato, Masoala and Namoroka.

rationale: This newly described species is known from numerous sites in the dry southern portion of Madagascar (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013); a few of these localities are within existing protected areas. This species is apparently not forest-dependant and may not be very sensitive to any important habitat degradation or other human pressures.
habitat: A species that uses caves for day roost sites, and in several cases, these caves are in close vicinity to native forest. However, a few known localities are without exposed sedimentary rock and presumably, it employs hollow trees for day roost sites. Most of these localities are within or adjacent to dry deciduous forest or spiny bush. However, several of the capture sites are distant from native forest and it is suspected that this species is not forest dependant. It presumably forages in open areas or those close to the forest edge.
population: Not known.
range: Known from different sites in the dry portion of southern Madagascar and across an elevational range from 0 to 950 m above sea level (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013).
conservationActions: This species is known from several protected areas, which include: Isalo, Kirindy Mité, Mikea, and Tsimanampetsotsa.

rationale: This newly described species occurs at several sites in the western half of Madagascar (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013); it is also known from a few specimens obtained on Anjouan Island in the Comoros Archipelago (Goodman et al. 2010). It is apparently not forest-dependant and may not be subjected to any important habitat degradation or other human pressures.
habitat: A species that uses caves for day roost sites. On Madagascar, it is found in areas with dry deciduous forests and on Anjouan Island with notably more mesic forest habitats (Goodman and Ramasindrazana, 2013; Goodman et al. 2010).
population: Not known.
range: On Madagascar known from numerous sites spanning the northern half of the western portion of the island and across an elevational range from 40 to 1350 m above sea level (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013). In the Comoros, this species is known from two sites on Anjouan Island and within the elevational range from 220 to 690 m above sea level (Goodman et al. 2010).
conservationActions: On Madagascar, this species is known from several protected areas, which include Ankarana, Namoroka and Bemaraha. To our knowledge the sites this species occurs on Anjouan Island are not under any special protection.

rationale: This newly described species is known from several sites in the northern portion of Madagascar (Goodman et al. 2015), most of which are montane and apparently not subjected to any important habitat degradation or other human pressures. It is notably common at several of these sites.
habitat: A species that uses caves for day roost sites, many of these caves are in close proximity to native forests. In certain cases day roosting sites are in isolated forest fragments. Most of these sites are within or adjacent to montane humid forest, although one is found in the upper end of lowland humid forest. It is suspected that this species is not forest dependant.
population: Not known.
range: On the basis of the recent species description, it occurs in montane areas of northern Madagascar and across an elevational range from 810 to 1570 m above sea level (Goodman et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This species is known from several protected areas, which include Marojejy, Montagne d’Ambre, Ambohitantely, and Bemanevika.

rationale: This newly described species is known from numerous sites in the eastern portions of Madagascar (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013), several of which are within existing protected areas. This species is apparently not forest-dependant and by extrapolation not subjected to any important habitat degradation or other human pressures.
habitat: The day roost site of this species is unknown, but presumed to be in rock crevices and tree hollows. It presumably forages in areas that are more open or close to the forest edge. Most of the sites it has been captured are in close vicinity to native humid forests and it is suspected that this species is not forest dependant.
population: Not known.
range: Known from different sites in eastern Madagascar and across an elevational range from 5 to 1300 m above sea level (Goodman & Ramasindrazana 2013).
conservationActions: This species is known from several protected areas, which include Masoala, Sahafina, and Andohahela.

rationale: This species is known from very few sites only, all representing underground spaces threatened by human activities. Currently it is listed as Near Threatened because actual levels of disturbance are likely to lead the habitat of this species to decline of at least 30% in the next 15 years.
habitat: The Maghrebian Bent-wing Bat inhabits the Mediterranean arboreal (subtropical dry forest, Mediterranean-type shrubland) vegetation zone. It is known to roost in caves. The species stores fat in autumn for the winter months.
threats: Threats to the species are mainly human disturbance of roost sites, and perhaps the use of pesticides against insects.
population: This species has been found in the Mediterranean and steppe habitats of the Maghreb.
range: This species possibly occurs across the Mediterranean part of North Africa, but it is known only from central and south-western Morocco and northern Tunisia.
conservationActions: No specific measures are known to be in place for this species, but it occurs in protected areas across its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered under criterion D as it is known from one site and from only colony of ca 150 individuals.
habitat: Presumably it forages at arid and semi-desert vegetation zone of southern Arabia; the colony roost represents/represented a new but uninhabited town house.
threats: The main threats to this species are human disturbance in the roost site and the roost destruction (i.e., the use of the house as a living one).
population: The only known colony contained ca 150 individuals during the last check in 2007.
range: This species is known from one site, Ash Sheher town, Hadramaut province, south-eastern Yemen, ca 65 m asl.
conservationActions: No specific measures are known or are in place.

rationale: This new species is known only from a single specimen. Rhinolophus species from Sulawesi, almost invariably endemic, have been shown to have either widespread or restricted distributions, with widespread species documented based on survey work. Extensive scientific collecting and survey work in the nearby area have resulted in no novel records for R. belligerator, underscoring the likely rarity of this species. The current distribution in Sulawesi refers to the local distribution of R. arcuatus, from which this species has been split.Since R. belligerator has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 1,742 km² and it is experiencing an ongoing decline in its habitat within a single location, it is listed as Endangered (EN) under criterion B1ab(iii).
habitat: Based on the limited information accompanying the specimen, specific information regarding habitat and ecology of this species is unknown at this time. However, other members of the genus are gleaning insectivores capable of highly manoeuvrable flight (Hill 1992).
threats: Deforestation and disturbance of roosts in caves affect closely related members of the genus (Wiles and Brooke 2009). Ongoing civil strife in the area is thought to have contributed to strong declines in undisturbed habitat and wild animal populations.
population: It is not possible to assess population trends at this time as this species is only known from a single specimen, collected in 1987 (Hill 1988, Patrick et al. 2013).
range: This species currently is only known from Permana Cave near Poso, Sulawesi Tengah Province, Sulawesi, Indonesia (Hill 1988), although it is conceivable that it could be found in the Kasiguncu lowlands area as well.
conservationActions: More research on habitats, ecology, and population size and trends is needed for this species.

rationale: Dyacopterus rickarti is listed as Endangered under criterion B2ab(iii) as the species is restricted to a few mountain ranges on Mindanao Island and Northern Luzon, Philippines. Its population is highly fragmented and it is only known from seven captures in six locations (four in Mindanao and two in Luzon). Its area of occupancy is 36 km². There is also continuing loss in area, extent and quality of habitat in the mountains where it has been captured.
habitat: Before 2007, this species was initially categorized as Dyacopterus spadiceus, which is also found in neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Data from Helgen et al. (2007) showed differences from this species to that of other Dyacopterus species. Limited records for this species are from montane forest habitats generally above 1,000 m asl to 1,680 m asl, suggesting it is restricted relatively high elevations on montane to mossy forest. However, the Mt. Pangal capture in Northern Sierra Madre is the lowest elevation record for this species at 550 m asl and is characterized as a lower montane forest. Records from New Bataan and Mt. Mahuson and Mt. Apo National Park were from degraded habitats, which may indicate that this species can tolerate some level of disturbance. In Mt. Apo National Park, for example, this species was captured in a net placed in a cultivated area. More research needs to be done on distribution extent and ecological requirements of this species to determine specific conservation needs of this endemic fruit bat. If it is similar to Dyacopterus spadiceus, this species may require cave habitats.
threats: The primary threats to the species is from past and ongoing forest habitat degradation and loss through the intrusion of agriculture, recreation/ecotourism, and rural communities into its known range. If the species is documented to use caves, like the similar Dyacopterus spadiceus, then we expect cave disturbance to be a significant threat as it is prevalent throughout the Philippines. While there are currently no records of hunting of this species, given its size, it is likely taken when other species are hunted in an area. More data are needed to ascertain the degree of threat from hunting.
population: Very little information is available about the population status for this species due to the limited data available. It is rarely captured, mostly at high elevations, and may be mistaken for similar species. More data are needed to determine population size and trends, and threats to this species.
range: Dyacopterus rickarti is a Philippine endemic species that has only been documented from seven (7) sites in six (6) locations, including Abra Province (550 m asl), Mt. Malibato, Opol, Misamis Oriental (altitude unrecorded), Mt. Kitanglad National Park, Sumilao, Bukidnon (1,450 m asl), Mt. Apo National Park, Davao City (1,185 m asl), Mt. Puting Bato, New Bataan, Compostela Valley (1,680 m asl), and Mt. Mahuson, Arakan Valley Conservation Area, Arakan, North Cotabato (1,260 m asl). Its area of occupancy (AOO) is 36 km². Additional information is needed to refine the understanding of the species distribution across the Philippines.
conservationActions: The current distribution of this species is at relatively high elevations, 550 m asl and above, which are mostly forest areas protected under Philippine law. But with continued intrusion of agriculture, recreation/ecotourism, and communities, habitats of this species must be protected. More research is needed to determine distribution, population, abundance, ecological requirements, threats, conservation and management of this species.

rationale: This bat is listed as Near Threatened (nearly meets criterion A2b) based on an estimated past population size reduction of 25-30% over the past 17.4 years (three generations; generation length = 5.8 years, Pacifici et al. 2013) across its range. In Taiwan, the species has undergone continuous declines of >90% in several of the largest known colonies and estimated losses of >70% of known individuals in the last 30 years and similar patterns are suspected throughout its range.
habitat: Habitat use, roost ecology and natural history for the species at global scale are poorly known. In Taiwan, the species has been known to roost in foliage of 35 plant species, mainly broad-leaved trees (e.g. Terminalia catapapa, Dimocarpus longan, Hibiscus tiliaceus and Swietenia mahagoni) and in buildings during breeding seasons (Chang 2007). Records are from small secondary forest fragments and settlements in rice paddy-dominated landscape in the lowland during breeding season. It has been recorded using nature caves and abandoned tunnels in mountain area with elevations over 1800 m as hibernacula in India (Chakravarty et al. pers. comm.) and in Taiwan (Heng-Chia Chang, pers. obs). In Pakistan, few individuals were captured in a mountainous landscape dominated by agriculture lands, forest patches and grassland in warm temperate zone (Mahmood-ul-Hassan and Salim 2015). In Taiwan, a well-studied maternity colony began to form in late March, and number peaked in May when pregnant females gave birth with one offspring during May to June. The bats left the maternity roost sites between mid-August and early October for hibernation sites (Shen and Lee 2000). The species is reported mainly feeding on small flying insects, including coleopterans, lepidopterans, dipterans, hemipterans (Yang 1996) and foraging in rice paddy (Ying-Yi Ho, unpubl. data) and riparian grassland (Joe Chun-Chia Huang, pers. obs.) in the lowland.
threats: Not much is known about the global threats of the species due to its general rarity. In Taiwan, the causes responsible for the wide and dramatic decline of this species are also unclear. However, several potential threats have been proposed. The continuous loss of arable land and uses of pesticide may have threatened the species by loss of food source. Several types of pesticide residue were detected from the faeces of this species (Heng-Chia Chang and Chia-Jung Tsai 2013). Since the species is at least partly cave-dwelling during winter hibernation, hence the disturbance of hibernacula and climate changes can be threats. Two roadkill incidences of the species reported from Taiwan (https://roadkill.tw/) indicate it is potentially risked by the expansion of road systems and increasing vehicle volume within its distribution range. A dead bat found near wind farm in coastal area in western Taiwan suggests the development of wind energy farms may threaten this species. Domestic cats might be another threat as a cat-killed incidence is found in Taiwan (Heng-Chia Chang, pers. obs). Observations in the field show the presence of artificial light could suppress its emerging from the roost (Yang 1996). It also tends to avoid artificial light during foraging in the night (Joe Chun-Chia Huang and Ying-Yi Ho, pers. obs.) suggesting light pollution may cause degradation of habitats quality, disturbances to the roost and interference to the migration movement. As it roosts among foliage, logging also threaten its populations. This species has conspicuous colouration, hence it may be used as ornament.
population: It is a generally rare although widely distributed species from northern South Asia to southeastern China and Taiwan (Csorba et al. 2014). It usually roosts as a few to tens animals, although under specific circumstances it can be relatively numerous, with up to over a thousand individuals in a single house roost (Heng-Chia Chang, pers. com.). In Taiwan, continuous and dramatic declines have been observed at all its largest known colonies. The three colonies containing >100 individuals all experienced a colony size decrease, from ~120-250 to 20 or less. (Heng-Chia Chang and Ying-Yi Ho, unpub. data). Similar trends of decline were also widely found in ~70% of other smaller colonies (Heng-Chia Chang unpub. data).
range: The species has a rather wide distribution from Afghanistan to Taiwan. Bates and Harrison (1997) and Mandal et al. (2000) report the species from Afghanistan, India (Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Sikkim, Assam, Meghalaya and Karnataka). It occurs also in Nepal (Mahalaxmi and Dhaulagiri), Pakistan, China (Tibet and Jianxi) and Taiwan. The species has one record from northern Vietnam (Csorba et al. 2014, Mahmood-ul-Hassan and Salim 2015). Earlier records of the species from the Laos, Philippines, Indonesia, North and South Korea, Tsushima Island (Japan) as well as China’s provinces of Fujian, Jilin, Shanghai and Sichuan are referable to other species (Csorba et al. 2014).
useTrade: This species has a colourful pelage and may be used as an ornament.
conservationActions: The species is listed as vulnerable in Taiwan (Cheng et al. 2017). There is no direct conservation assessment in the other countries within its distribution. In Taiwan, all known hibernacula are found in protected forest areas. The protection of roosts and foraging habitats is important for this species. Since the population in Taiwan is migratory, the connectivity between its breeding habitats and winter hibernacula sites therefore is critical for this species as well. Studies on migratory movement and influences of pesticides to its survival are necessary. Further monitoring to understand the intensity of the incidences by wind turbines, vehicle collision and cat kill is also recommended.

rationale: The Galápagos Fur Seal population declined by 46–67% over three generations from 1988 to 2018, the last year census data are available. Since 2018, the population might have stabilized, but no data exist for this time period. However, it is very likely that the reduction over the last three generations still exceeds 50%. Generation length for this species is between 8 and 11.7 years, with a best estimate of 10 years. The causes of the reduction are partly understood, have not ceased, and may not be reversible. Impacts from El Niño events and infectious diseases continue to threaten the population. Galápagos Fur Seals qualify for listing as Endangered under criterion A2b.
habitat: Galápagos Fur Seals are the smallest and the least sexually dimorphic of the otariid seals. Adult males are 1.1–1.3 times longer and 2.0–2.3 times heavier than adult females. They are small and compact, and adult males are stocky in build. Pups are blackish brown. Pups moult their natal coat for one that resembles that of the adult female when they are about 4-6 months old.The few adult males measured to date have been 1.5–1.6 m long and weighed 60–68 kg. Adult females have curvilinear lengths of 1.1–1.3 m and an average weight of 27–28 kg, with a maximum of 33 kg.Pups are 3.4 kg at birth and an average of 11.3 kg when they are 12 months old (Trillmich 1987). Galápagos Fur Seals are believed to mature at an age of about 5 years. Females usually produce a pup each year thereafter, but successfully rear a pup only every other year, for most of the rest of their lives.Males do not become large enough to compete for a viable mating territory until they are considerably older than the average age of maturity of females, but exact age information is lacking. Males hold mating territories that average 200 m², which are large compared to the average size of territories held by other otariid males; this is particularly notable given the Galápagos Fur Seal's small size.Galápagos Fur Seals occur on nearly all of the islands in the archipelago occasionally. Breeding colonies are found at 11 sites across seven different islands in the west and north of the archipelago (Páez-Rosas et al. 2021). They prefer to haul-out on rocky coasts with large boulders and ledges that provide shade and the opportunity to rest in crevices and spaces between rocks. They have a pupping and breeding season that lasts from mid-August to mid-November on Fernandina. The peak of pupping at this site occurs between the last week of September and the first week of October. Pupping on other islands can occur at different times (Trillmich pers. obs.), but no systematic data are presently available.Colonies are located close to pelagic foraging areas and the average duration of female trips is the shortest for any fur seal with a mean trip length of 1.5 days in the cold season (May to November and up to 4 days in the warm season (December to April) (Trillmich and Kooyman 2001, Jeglinski et al. 2013, Villegas-Amtmann et al. 2013). Foraging occurs pelagically 10 to 70 km off the coast around Fernandia Island. The mean depth of foraging dives is 26–32 m with a duration of less than 2 minutes (Horning and Trillmich 1999, Jeglinski et al. 2013). The maximum dive depth recorded is 115 m, and the longest duration is 5.7 minutes. Mothers visit their pups around 300 times before weaning, with attendance periods lasting 0.5-1.3 days. Weaning occurs at 12-36 months, with the exact age depending on marine productivity patterns over time. Pups that are born prior to the weaning of an older sibling rarely survive, with most starving to death because the older pup dominates access to their mother; a few are directly killed by the older sibling (Trillmich and Wolf 2008). In exceptional cases, offspring that are known to have been 4-5 years old were still nursed by their mothers, as in Galápagos Sea Lions (Childs et al. 2026).In the water, particularly near haul-outs, Galápagos Fur Seals raft in postures typical of many of the southern fur seal species. There is no evidence of migration, and they do not seem to spend prolonged periods of time at sea, except for males immediately before the period of territory tenure.Galápagos Fur Seals consume a variety of small squids including Onychoteuthis banksi, and a number of species of ommastrephids (Clarke and Trillmich 1980). A variety of fish species are also consumed, mostly myctophids and bathylagids (Dellinger and Trillmich 1999). They feed almost exclusively at night, exploiting vertically migrating prey species as they swim closer to the surface. Niche overlap between juvenile Galápagos Sea Lions (Zalophus wollebaeki) and Galápagos Fur Seals has been documented at Fernandina (Jeglinski et al. 2013), but in the most recent census, Fur Seals outnumbered Sea Lions by five to one at shared colonies in the west (Paez-Rosas et al. 2021). Among adults, interspecific competition seems to be rather limited due to the different foraging strategies (Páez-Rosas et al. 2012). Predators of Galápagos Fur Seals include sharks (Moreira-Mendieta et al. 2024) and orca.
threats: Hunting was prohibited (but not necessarily stopped) in 1934, and additional protection was provided in 1959 when more than 80% of the Galápagos Archipelago was declared a National Park (Trillmich 1987).Galápagos Fur Seals have experienced serious declines due to ocean warming caused by El Niño events (Salazar 2002, Alava and Salazar 2006) and associated reductions in marine productivity, and this threat is likely to intensify under global warming (Trillmich and Dellinger 1991, Wang et al. 2017, Cai et al. 2014). El Niño events dramatically elevate mortality rates of all age classes, particularly juveniles, and cause population declines; this is due to the dramatic decline in productivity around the archipelago during these events (Trillmich and Limberger 1985). Oceanographers differ in their predictions of how the frequency and intensity of El Niño events may change with climate warming. Cai et al. (2014) suggest that the total number of El Niño events will decrease slightly, but the total number of extreme events will double as global warming continues. In contrast, Santoso et al. (2013) predict a doubling of the frequency of El Niño events with global warming. In the historical long-term perspective offered by Cobb et al. (2013) the frequency of El Niño during the last 50 years is unusually high, but still within the range of variability observed over the last 7,000 years. The most likely projection is that El Niño events will become more frequent, and likely more extreme, in the immediate future (Thirumalai et al. 2024). In their review of otariid extinctions, Gerber and Hilborn (2001) conclude that for species subject to El Niño impacts, the concern about species recovery should focus on changes in the frequency of El Niño events.Tourism in the Galápagos is intense and tourist numbers are increasing, but well regulated, and Fur Seals are fully protected. Episodes of entanglement in local net fisheries have been reported and are thought to be increasing (Alava and Salazar 2006). An increasing number of fast travelling fiberglass boats with strong outboard engines create risks of collisions with Fur Seals resting at sea. Feral dogs on Isabela Island, which killed Fur Seals of all ages, have been exterminated.Like all fur seals, Galápagos Fur Seals are vulnerable to oil spills because of their dependence on their pelage for thermoregulation. Although there is limited large vessel traffic in the Galápagos Archipelago, particularly in the areas of greatest fur seal abundance, numerous small and medium sized vessels operate in the area that could release moderate quantities of oils, fuels, and lubricants if involved in a marine accident. Contaminant levels are low at present, but need to be monitored (Alava et al. 2011).
