Infectious diseases are a risk for all colonially breeding pinnipeds including Galápagos Fur Seals (Alava et al. 2024).The Galápagos Fur Seal population will always be vulnerable to a variety of threats because of the species' breeding distribution is restricted to a small island archipelago (Cai et al. 2014, Wang et al. 2017). Complete assessment is hampered by limited data being available, hence a new census of the entire population of the Archipelago is urgently needed.
population: Age-structure data are not available for the Galápagos Fur Seal, so generation time cannot be calculated precisely. With sexual maturity attained at about 4–6 years of age and a maximum longevity of approximately 20 years, the average age of reproducing individuals may be anywhere between 8 and 11.7 years (based on generation length estimates for other Arctocephalus species; Pacifici et al. 2013), but the best estimate is about 10 years (similar to the generation time reported for Arctocephalus gazella by Forcada et al. 2008). The number of mature animals in the population is likely to be about two-thirds of the total.Whalers and sealers harvested Galápagos Fur Seals indiscriminately during the 19th century and there were few left by 1900 (Trillmich 1987). Although there was little documentation, the population recovered substantially during the 20th century. In 1977–1978, the first systematic census efforts were conducted; 9,785 fur seals were counted and total abundance was estimated to be 30,000, using correction factors that took lunar stage and time of day when counts were made into account (Trillmich 1987). This would represent about 20,000 mature individuals. In November 2001, 2,733 fur seals were counted at haul-outs and rookeries in the Galápagos Archipelago (Alava and Salazar 2006). By accounting for the probability that animals could be seen at a distance, total abundance was estimated to be 6,000–8,000. This corresponds to 4,000–5,300 mature individuals. The last census of the whole archipelago was conducted in 2018 (Páez-Rosas et al. 2021) when a total of 3,093 Galápagos Fur Seals were counted. Although only 300 additional individuals were seen at this census compared with Alava and Salazar (2006), the authors arrived at a population estimate of 13,000. This would mean that their correction factor (4.2) was very different from both Trillmich in 1978 (3.07) and Alava and Salazar in 2001 (2.2–2.9, Alava and Salazar (2006)). Applying a correction factor in the range of 2.2 to 3 would yield between 6,800 to 9,300 individuals.Population estimation methods differed in the studies outlined above, but comparisons of these three estimates indicate a reduction of 56–77% over a period of 40 years (four generations). Alava and Salazar (2006) also provided count data for specific rookeries in 1977, 1978, and 2001. If the average numbers of individuals counted per site in 1977 (345.5) and 1978 (395.6) are compared to 2001 (79.2), this suggests a reduction in abundance of 77–80%. The population seems to have recovered somewhat since 2001, at least on the western side of Fernandina Island (Trillmich, pers. obs). The abundance of Galápagos Fur Seals was assessed most recently in 2018—and at that time it seemed that the population was stabilizing. Nevertheless, over three generations or the last 30 years with available data (1988–2018), the population decline can be estimated at 46 and 67%, based on an exponential decline between 1988 and 2018 (3 generations) with an annual rate of decline between 2.1 and 3.7%. The reasons for the reduction are not clearly understood, but this species has been exposed to recurrent El Niño events for thousands of years and recent trends are likely tied to 1982/83, 1997/98, and 2015 El Niño events (Trillmich and Limberger 1985, Trillmich and Dellinger 1991, Alava and Salazar 2006, Páez-Rosas et al. 2021).
range: Galápagos Fur Seals are observed throughout the Galápagos Archipelago. Lactating females make trips of relatively short-duration trips, which usually take them 10–20 km out to sea, but during the warm season trips last longer and go further offshore. Foraging by males outside the breeding season is unknown. Most breeding colonies are located in the western and northern parts of the Archipelago, close to productive offshore upwelling areas. Vagrants are occasionally observed in southern Mexico during El Niño events (Aurioles-Gamboa et al. 2004) and also in Colombian waters (Barragan-Barrera et al. 2024). Pups have been reported to be born on the coast of mainland Ecuador, but this has not been confirmed.
useTrade: Whalers and sealers harvested Galápagos Fur Seals indiscriminately during the 19th century and there were few left by 1900 (Trillmich 1987). The population recovered substantially during the 20th century (Trillmich 1987). Galápagos Fur Seals were protected under Ecuadorian law in the 1930s, and since 1959 with the establishment of the Galápagos National Park, by the Administration of the Park. Currently there is no direct use or trade.
conservationActions: Galápagos Fur Seals were protected under Ecuadorian law in the 1930s, and since 1959 with the establishment of the Galápagos National Park, by the Administration of the Park. The waters around the islands are also protected by a 40 nautical mile no fishing zone. Tourism is regulated and most visitors are escorted by a trained Park Naturalist. The species is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: The Leopard Seal does not meet the criteria for any threatened category under the IUCN Red List framework. The most recent genetic assessment (Bender et al. 2023) estimated a female effective population size of ~12,188 individuals. Under the assumption of a 1:1 sex ratio, this would constitute a total effective population (mature individuals) of ~24,376 individuals and an inferred global population size of ~79,000 individuals. These estimates rely on several assumptions (see Population section), and although the global population is more than twice the previous census-based estimates—which covered around three quarters of the Antarctic coast (approximately 35,500 individuals; Southwell et al. 2012)—it is likely an underestimation. At present, there is no evidence of a global decline. However, substantial uncertainty remains regarding overall abundance and population trends due to limited data for this species across much of Antarctica. Therefore, a collective effort to improve population size estimates for the Leopard Seal is needed. Given their strong dependence on ice and the ongoing warming and retreat of sea ice in the Southern Ocean, climate change likely represents the most critical threat to Leopard Seals (and their prey). Despite these risks, the lack of evidence for population decline supports maintaining the species' current classification as Least Concern.
habitat: Leopard Seals exhibit reverse sexual dimorphism, with females in some cases being up to 50% larger than males (Kienle et al. 2022). Adult males typically measure 2.7–3.3 m in length and weigh up to 324 kg, while adult females range from 2.9–3.6 m, with large individuals possibly reaching 3.8 m and weighing up to 540 kg (Jefferson et al. 2008, Rogers 2009, Kienle et al. 2022). At birth, pups measure 1–1.6 m and weigh 30–35 kg (Jefferson et al. 2008, Rogers 2009). Sexual maturity is likely reached at ~4 years for females and ~4.5 years for males, and longevity is estimated to be over 26 years (Kooyman 1981, Rogers 2009).Breeding likely occurs between November and March (Gwynn 1953, Southwell et al. 2008, Kienle et al. 2024), peaking from mid-November to early December (Shirihai 2002), although little is known about their breeding behaviour. Mating is thought to occur in the water (Rogers 2018). Females give birth to a single pup annually, usually on ice floes (Rogers 2009, Acevedo et al. 2017), though births on land have also been reported (van der Linde et al. 2022). Pups are generally born between September and late December, although pupping could span from late August to early January (Southwell et al. 2003, Jefferson et al. 2008, van der Linde et al. 2022). Timing of births seems to vary regionally: births in South Georgia occur from late August to mid-September, while the peak number of births in Chile occurs in October–November (van der Linde et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2024). Pups are likely weaned at about four weeks of age, with female oestrus occurring around the time of weaning. Male Leopard Seals do not remain with female–pup pairs. Maternal investment remains poorly understood, though recent observations of post-mortem attentive behaviour (PAB) suggest stronger maternal attachment and energetic investment than previously thought (Sperou & Borras-Chavez et al. 2025).Leopard Seals are generally solitary, both on ice and at sea (Southwell et al. 2003, Forcada and Robinson 2006). Their diet includes krill, fish, squid, penguins, a wide range of seabirds, and pups of other seals, including Crabeater, Southern Elephant, and fur seals (Casaux et al. 2009, Southwell et al. 2012, Krause et al. 2015, Botta et al. 2018, Krause et al. 2020). Diet composition varies by year, season, mass, age and location (Laws 1984, Krause et al. 2020, Sperou et al. 2023). As apex predators, Leopard Seals exert strong top-down control on penguin colonies and fur seal aggregations in the Southern Ocean (e.g., Ainley et al. 2005, Forcada et al. 2009, Krause et al. 2022). Importantly, the species has shown a remarkable degree of specialisation at the level of the individual. In some cases, only a few highly specialised individuals may drive prey population declines (Krause et al. 2022, Sperou et al. 2025).The Leopard Seal's diverse feeding strategies are facilitated by their extreme swimming abilities, aided by hydrodynamically efficient forelimbs, and elongated flippers compared to other phocids (Hocking et al. 2021, Rogers 2018, Robbins et al. 2019). For large prey such as penguins and seals, they employ a grip-and-tear strategy: grasping prey and tossing it through the air and smashing it against the water surface to tear it apart (Hiruki et al. 1999). For smaller prey such as krill, they use suction and filtering in combination, the later achieved with their specialised dentition (Hocking et al. 2013). Leopard Seals are frequently observed patrolling penguin rookeries and fur seal colonies to ambush prey (Hiruki et al. 1999). Other strategies include food caching (Krause and Rogers 2019), kleptoparasitism, and scavenging (Krause et al. 2015). Outside Antarctica, their diet is poorly documented: in southern Patagonia, they have been reported feeding on fish and Magellanic Penguins (Spheniscus magellanicus) (Markham et al. 1971), while Leopard Seals in New Zealand have been observed eating seabirds and chondrichthyans (McKinlay et al. 2014, van der Linde et al. 2021).Although capable of travelling long distances (>800 km; Staniland et al. 2018, Kienle et al. 2022), most individuals remain near foraging areas (Rogers et al. 2005, Meade et al. 2015, Kienle et al. 2022). Staniland et al. (2018) and Kienle et al. (2022) tracked individuals moving between South Georgia and Antarctic waters, but other than these few animals, there is little evidence of individuals moving between Antarctic and Subantarctic regions. Leopard Seal dives are generally short and shallow, with most dives lasting 2–5 minutes and reaching <48 m (Nordøy and Blix 2009; Krause et al. 2015, 2016; Kienle et al. 2022). The deepest and longest dive recorded was 1,256 m and 25 minutes (Kienle et al. 2022).
threats: Although no direct exploitation currently affects Leopard Seals, several indirect threats may pose risks to the species. The impacts of climate change remain a primary concern. While Learmonth et al. (2006) considered its effects on Leopard Seals as unknown, evidence from other wide-ranging Southern Ocean predators indicates that both climate change and expanding fisheries could have significant consequences for the species (Hindell et al. 2020, Hückstädt et al. 2020). Potential impacts include the loss of pack-ice habitat critical for pupping, resting, predator avoidance, and access to preferred prey (penguins, other ice seals, krill, and fish). All of these resources are expected to decline as sea ice declines. Demographic reconstructions suggest that population fluctuations in Leopard Seals have historically tracked ice expansions and contracting periods, reinforcing concerns under projected future warming scenarios (Bender et al. 2023, Nebenführ et al. 2025). Broader ecosystem effects of Antarctic sea ice loss, general climate warming, and sea-level rise on circulation, productivity, and marine resources also remain uncertain. In Chile, 76% of all historical Leopard Seal sightings occurred in ice habitats, with 100% of births recorded on ice floes (Borras-Chavez et al. 2024). These findings highlight climate change in Patagonia as a pressing regional threat, especially given the transition of many marine-terminating glaciers into land-terminating systems (Dussaillant et al. 2019).Disease is another potential threat. Leopard Seals have tested positive for antibodies to canine distemper virus (CDV), though the impacts of an outbreak remain unknown. The prevalence of the Seal Louse (Antarctophthirus ogmorhini) is reported to be low in Leopard Seals compared with Crabeater, Weddell, and Elephant Seals (Soto et al. 2025). Given their largely solitary habits, except during breeding, pathogen transmission within the species is likely to be slow or restricted to certain seasons (Bengtson et al. 1991, Soto et al. 2025).The arrival of the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) to Subantarctic islands and the Antarctic continent imposes an important threat to the species, particularly considering the significant impact that has been reported in other phocid species of the region such as Southern Elephant Seals (Mirounga leonina; Campagna et al. 2024). Assessing and monitoring the prevalence of HPAI in Leopard Seals is advised.Tourism in the Antarctic and Subantarctic has increased steadily over the last three decades, reaching record levels of more than 120,000 cruise tourists during the 2023/24 season (Senigaglia et al. 2025). The effects of increased vessel activity, including noise, disturbance from ships, and close approaches by small boats or visitors, on Leopard Seal behaviour, distribution, and foraging remain unknown. There is some risk of direct injury from vessel collisions or crushing in ice fields.Interactions of Leopard Seals with fisheries are not currently reported as significant in Antarctica. However, commercial krill harvest could represent a potential threat if continues to be conducted on a large scale, as it may reduce prey availability. Outside Antarctica, unpublished reports indicate Leopard Seals have been deliberately shot by fishermen in Chilean and Argentine Patagonia (La Segunda 2013, Negrete et al. 2019).Finally, pollution is an emerging concern. Microplastic debris (<5 mm) has been identified in Leopard Seal scats in Antarctica, with plastics representing the predominant debris type. Leopard Seals also appear to ingest larger microplastic particles than Weddell and Crabeater Seals (Cebuhar et al. 2024).
population: Due to their wide distribution across Antarctic and Subantarctic waters, and their strong association with pack ice, population assessments of Leopard Seals are logistically difficult, costly, and rarely undertaken. Standard sighting surveys yield little information due to the inaccessibility of their habitats and the species' cryptic behaviour (Southwell et al. 2012). Early global estimates ranged from 100,000–300,000 individuals (Scheffer 1958) to 220,000–440,000 (Laws 1984), but these figures were highly speculative and based on very limited sampling. Using ship- and aerial-based sighting surveys conducted between 1968 and 1983, Erickson and Hanson (1990) estimated a global population size of ~300,000 Leopard Seals in the pelagic pack ice of the Southern Ocean, although this number also has substantial uncertainty (revised in Southwell et al. 2012). The most recent census estimate (Nc) was conducted over multiple years (1997–2000) by the Antarctic Pack Ice Seal (APIS) initiative of the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR). Leopard Seal counts were reported from approximately three-quarters of the continent, totalling around 35,500 individuals, with large confidence intervals associated with each regional assessment: 15,000 (3,500–65,000) in the 150°W–100°W sector, 13,200 (3,700–23,100) in the 90°W–30°W sector, and 7,300 (3,700–14,500) in the 64°E–150°E sector (revised in Southwell et al. 2012). However, the APIS census did not include/report estimates for most of the Indian Ocean sector and therefore, it does not constitute a full circumpolar assessment.Based on genetic drift models, Bender et al. (2023) inferred a Nc of 78,632 individuals (95% CI: 54,438–106,868) calculated from an effective population size (Ne) of 24,376 (95% CI: 16,876–33,126), which is derived from a female effective population size of 12,188 individuals (95% CI = 8,438–16,563). Several assumptions underlie this genetic approach: first, it assumes a 1:1 sex ratio and calculates the number of mature individuals by multiplying the female effective population by two, reaching a rough estimation of ~ 24,376 mature individuals (i.e., reproductive males and females). Second, to calculate Nc (complete population), the authors used a mean Ne/Nc ratio value (0.31) derived from a multispecies pinniped analysis (Peart et al. 2020). However, the use of a more conservative number, such as the median Ne/Nc ration (0.13) reported by Peart et al. (2020), would have considerably affected the final census number (complete population) obtained. Finally, they also assumed that the genetic diversity at their study site is representative of the species' overall range, which is supported by a recent study (Nebenführ et al. 2025). Nonetheless, caution is warranted when interpreting the number of mature individuals (~24,500 individuals), as genetic drift models also assume all individuals reproduce successfully, which is unlikely to be true in natural populations.The estimates of Bender et al. (2023) are far lower than early speculative figures (Scheffer 1958, Laws 1984, Erickson and Hanson 1990) but fall within the range of more recent survey-based estimates covering at least three-quarters of the Antarctic coastline (Southwell et al. 2012). Bender et al. (2023) acknowledged that better estimations of the Ne may be reached if based on genome-wide data and by increasing the sample size to represent other areas of the species' distribution. Nonetheless, we suggest that the estimate of approximately 79,000 individuals proposed by Bender et al. (2023) represents a reasonable minimum population size for the species, with a considerable degree of uncertainty around this number and likely to be an underestimation. Overall, population estimates based on effective population sizes are expected to represent a conservative approximation of total population size.
range: Leopard Seals are widely distributed throughout coastal waters around the Antarctic continent and surrounding pack ice areas, with some individuals occurring north to Subantarctic and South American waters, where they establish seasonal or long-term residency in some areas. Leopard Seals haul out on ice as well as on land, often preferring ice floes near shore when available (Kooyman 1981, Rice 1998, Bengtson 2002, Borras-Chavez et al. 2024). They also occur at most Subantarctic islands, including having a year-round presence in Kerguelen (Borsa 1990), Heard and McDonald Islands (Gwynn 1953, Brown 1957), and Auckland and Campbell Islands (King 1983). They have been recorded seasonal at Macquarie, Marion and Falkland/Malvinas and South Georgia Islands (Rounsevell and Eberhard 1980, King 1983, Borsa 1990, Walker et al. 1998, Jessopp et al. 2004, Bester et al. 2006, Forcada and Robinson 2006, Staniland et al. 2018, Ross et al. 2025). The northernmost multi-year resident (and breeding site) group is in the Laguna San Rafael National Park, Northern Patagonia, Chile (van der Linde et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2024).Vagrant, largely juvenile individuals, have been reported in relatively warmer temperate waters, reaching as far north as the tropics (Rounsevell and Pemberton 1994, Rogers et al. 2005, Stewart et al. 2020, Borras-Chavez et al. 2024). The northernmost confirmed vagrant observation to date comes from Rarotonga, Cook Islands (Berry 1960), and they have also been observed on oceanic islands such as the Juan Fernandez Archipelago and Easter Island, in the southeast Pacific Ocean (Aguayo-Lobo et al. 2011, Hucke-Gaete et al. 2014, Stewart et al. 2020), Pitcairn Island in the central South Pacific (Stewart and Grove 2014); as well as the Gough (Wilson et al. 2006) and Tristan da Cunha archipelagos in the South Atlantic (Bester et al. 2017). Additional vagrant occurrences have been recorded in South Africa (Courtney-Latimer 1961, Best 1971, Vinding et al. 2013), central and northern Chile (Aguayo-Lobo et al. 2011, Borras-Chavez et al. 2024), Argentina (Rodríguez et al. 2003, Ferrer et al. 2018), Brazil (Ferreira et al. 1995, Velozo 2007), New Zealand (Hupman et al. 2019) and Australia (Shaughnessy et al. 2024).
useTrade: There is no evidence of current direct use or trade of Leopard Seals within their normal Antarctic range (Jefferson et al. 2008, Rogers 2018). A small number of individuals have historically been taken for research purposes, and some were previously killed for dog food; however, there has never been any substantial catch of the species in Antarctic waters (Reijnders et al. 1993). Historical accounts also indicate hunting of Leopard Seals alongside Elephant Seals in Patagonia, Chile (Torrejón et al. 2013), but this practice is no longer permitted.
conservationActions: The Leopard Seal is protected under the Antarctic Treaty and the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals, which regulate any potential commercial harvest (Reijnders et al. 1993). In addition, all countries and overseas territories where Leopard Seals are considered year-around or seasonal residents, have local protection measures for the species.

rationale: Weddell Seals face threats common to all Antarctic pack ice seal species, including the impacts of global climate change, increased human presence through tourism and fisheries activities, and the introduction of emerging infectious diseases into Antarctic waters. However, due to their broad geographic distribution and large estimated population size, and no evidence of population decline, the Weddell Seal is currently assessed as a species of Least Concern.
habitat: Due to their high site fidelity to their breeding colonies, some of which are located within easy reach of Antarctic research stations, certain Weddell Seal populations have been studied extensively over several decades. As a result, Weddell Seals are among the most intensively researched pinniped species. Adult Weddell Seals typically weigh between 300 and 550 kg, with some individuals reaching up to 600 kg. Females are generally larger than males, attaining lengths of up to 3.3 m and weights exceeding 500 kg, while adult males reach approximately 2.9 m in length. The species has an average lifespan of around 18 years, although the oldest known female reached 31 years of age, while the oldest recorded male lived to 28 years (Macdonald et al. 2025).Female body mass varies significantly throughout the year, with notable weight loss occurring postpartum and during lactation (Shero et al. 2015a). Most females reach sexual maturity between 4 and 11 years of age, although this varies geographically: from 4–5 years at Signy Island to 7–8 years in Erebus Bay (Hadley et al. 2006). Males typically begin breeding at 7–8 years of age. Weddell Seals breed in areas of stable, predictable land-fast ice, congregating in loose aggregations along recurrent cracks, leads, and near access holes to the water at specific sites; they also breed on land at a few locations (Testa et al. 1990). The behaviour of animals breeding in the pack ice or the Subantarctic islands is not well known.Annual reproductive rates vary between 53% and 88% (Lake et al. 2008). Parturition occurs from mid-October to early November, following a gestation period of approximately 10 months (Shero et al. 2018). While the occurrence of embryonic diapause has been proposed for the species, as in other pinnipeds, recent evidence suggests that, in Weddell Seals, diapause may be very brief (as short as two weeks) or entirely absent (Shero et al. 2015b).Newborn pups are about 1.5 m long and average 30 kg (Rotella 2023). Adult female Weddell Seals nurse their pups for seven to eight weeks, and they resume foraging after 1–2 weeks of fasting post-parturition, while lactating, displaying a mixed capital-income breeding strategy (Wheatley et al. 2008). Females enter oestrus approximately one week before weaning their pup, and copulation occurs underwater. During the breeding period, males establish and defend underwater territories by controlling access to breathing holes and cracks in the ice.Satellite telemetry movement data have been collected across much of the Weddell Seal's range in Antarctic waters, providing valuable insights into their air-sea behaviour. Weddell Seals' habitat utilisation and movement patterns vary significantly across their distribution, exhibiting strong site-specific differences.Individuals from the Ross and Weddell seas disperse over several hundreds of kilometres, utilising areas over deep water both on and beyond the continental shelf (Photopoulou et al. 2020, Goetz et al. 2023). In contrast, Weddell Seals in regions such as Adélie Land, and Princess Elizabeth Land exhibit more restricted movements, typically remaining within a range that encompasses a few hundred kilometres over the narrow continental shelf (Heerah et al. 2017), whereas seals tagged in the South Shetland Islands, western Antarctic Peninsula, spend up to 10 months within an area of 18 km² (A. Piñones pers. comm.).The diving behaviour of Weddell Seals has been studied extensively. While most dives last between 12 and 15 minutes and reach depths of 100–350 m, the longest recorded dive lasted 96 minutes, and the deepest reached 904 m (Heerah et al. 2013). Their diel diving pattern, characterised by shallower dives at night and deeper during the day, suggests a diurnal foraging strategy (Testa 1994). Weddell Seals are generalist predators, and their diet varies regionally (Lake et al. 2008). Notothenoid fish (icefishes), particularly Antarctic Silverfish (Pleurogramma antarcticum) dominate their diet in many regions. Other common prey types include Antarctic Toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni), myctophid fishes, and cephalopods (Plötz et al. 1991, Goetz et al. 2017). Recent observations using animal-borne cameras have identified crustaceans as the most frequently consumed prey by lactating adult female Weddell Seals in McMurdo Sound (Foster-Dyer et al. 2024). Although individuals inhabiting stable land-fast ice regions may benefit from reduced predator exposure, those in the pack ice are more susceptible to predation by Killer Whales (Orcinus orca) and Leopard Seals (Hydrurga leptonyx) (Stirling 1969a, Visser et al. 2008).Weddell Seals that remain in land-fast ice areas actively maintain breathing holes by abrading and grinding the surrounding ice. They do so by biting the ice and vigorously swinging their heads from side to side, using their teeth to wear it away (Stirling 1969a,b). This behaviour incurs a physiological cost: seal inhabiting areas where frequent ice abrasion is necessary exhibit increased tooth wear, which might impact their life expectancy.
threats: Weddell Seals were a significant source of food for both expedition members and sled dogs during the early periods of Antarctic exploration and continued to be used as dog food in McMurdo Sound until the 1990s. These harvests led to localised population declines; however, since the cessation of exploitation, populations in affected areas have recovered. Currently, there are no immediate or significant threats of direct exploitation to the species.As with other Antarctic ice seals, global climate change represents the most significant threat to Weddell Seal populations. Sea ice provides habitat for pupping, resting, predator avoidance, and access to foraging areas. However, due to their generalist foraging strategy, Weddell Seals might exhibit a degree of adaptability to environmental change, potentially more so than other Antarctic pack-ice seal species. Learmonth et al. (2006) suggested that Weddell Seal populations may decline with rising temperatures if Antarctic sea ice is substantially reduced. In contrast, Proffitt et al. (2007) reported that localised cooling and increased sea ice extent in the Ross Sea were associated with reduced reproductive success and lower weaning mass among Weddell Seals in McMurdo Sound. Habitat models project that Weddell Seals may be capable of buffering the direct impacts of environmental change and could even gain a competitive advantage via warming over other Antarctic mesopredators, such as penguins (Wege et al. 2021). Furthermore, the existence of breeding populations on land (e.g., South Georgia) suggests some capacity for environmental plasticity. Sea ice reductions can also increase the detectability and vulnerability of Weddell Seals to natural predators, thereby potentially increasing the chance of predation. Overall, the effects of global climate change on Weddell Seals remain poorly understood and are likely to vary regionally.Seasonal tourism in the Antarctic and Subantarctic regions has increased steadily over the past three decades and has now reached all-time high levels, following a rapid recovery after the COVID-19 pandemic. The impacts of increased vessel noise, disturbance from ship traffic, and the close proximity of tourists in small boats or on land and ice on Weddell Seal behaviour, distribution, and foraging remain poorly understood. There is also a risk of physical injury to a small number of individuals due to vessel collisions or crushing by icebreaking ships.Currently, there are no reports of significant interactions between Weddell Seals and fisheries. However, expansion of existing fisheries targeting Antarctic Toothfish and krill, as well as the potential development of new commercial operations, may affect food availability and increase the risk of incidental bycatch.Plastic pollution is an emerging concern in Antarctic waters. Microplastics have been detected throughout the Southern Ocean food web and have been identified in the faeces of Weddell Seals and other Antarctic phocids (Cebuhar et al. 2024).  Additionally, the increasing human presence, through tourism, fisheries, scientific research and military operations, raises the likelihood of introducing novel exogenous pathogens to the Antarctic ecosystem. Weddell Seals may be particularly vulnerable as they are among the few species of Antarctic phocids that form breeding colonies, which attract birds that feed on dead pups and the afterbirths, and the seals also congregate to moult. Notable, Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI), recently detected in Antarctic birds and marine mammals, poses a cross-species transmission risk, including potential mammal-to-mammal spreading (Banyard et al. 2024).
population: The global population of Weddell Seals has been estimated to range between 200,000 and 1,000,000 individuals (Erickson and Hanson 1990, Southwell et al. 2012), although there is considerable uncertainty surrounding these numbers. As a widespread species inhabiting remote and inhospitable regions, population assessments of Weddell Seals are logistically challenging and expensive and, therefore, rarely conducted. Data collected during the Antarctic Pack Ice Seals (APIS) project in the 2000s suggested that the total population may exceed one million individuals (Southwell et al. 2012). These survey-based estimates are likely inflated due to methodological limitations. More recently, the first direct global population survey using high-resolution satellite imagery estimated the total population to be approximately 202,000 individuals (95% Confidence Interval: 85,345–523,140), placing it at the lower end of previous estimates (LaRue et al. 2021). Although discrepancies in Weddell Seal population estimates arise primarily from methodological differences rather than actual declines, their magnitude highlights the urgent need to obtain reliable abundance estimates for all pack-ice species in polar regions.
range: Weddell Seals are circumpolar and widespread in Antarctic waters and represent the world's southernmost breeding mammal. They are commonly associated with land-fast ice, where they congregate to form breeding colonies and haul out during the moult, but the species also occurs offshore in the pack ice zone, extending northward to the seasonally shifting limits of the Antarctic convergence. The species ranges from the South Georgia Islands in the north to the edge of the Ross Sea Ice Shelf in the south. Small populations are also present in the South Orkney, South Sandwich, and South Shetland Islands. Vagrant individuals have been recorded in Subantarctic and temperate regions, including Argentina, Bouvet Island, Chile, the Falkland/Malvinas Islands, Heard and McDonald Islands, Juan Fernández Islands, Kerguelen Islands, New Zealand, South Africa, and Uruguay.
useTrade: Weddell Seals served as an important source of food for men and dogs throughout the early periods of Antarctic exploration (Stirling 1971) until the final removal of dogs from the continent in the 1990s. Local populations no doubt suffered declines from these harvests, but the Murdo Sound population has recovered in the 30 years since harvests ended in the 1980s (Testa and Siniff 1987).
conservationActions: The Weddell Seal is not listed as endangered or threatened. They are protected by the Antarctic Treaty and the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals, and any future commercial harvest would be regulated by those international agreements.

rationale: The distribution of the Southern River Otter has declined drastically due to combined pressures from the destruction of habitat, removal of vegetation, river and stream canalization, and extensive dredging (Medina 1996, Medina-Vogel et al. 2003). At present, poaching is a minor problem but still occurs, particularly south of 43°S latitude where control of hunting is difficult to implement. Extirpation of the Southern River Otter began in local basins but has become widespread. The lack of re-establishment of the species is probably due to high mortality or reproductive failure following the dispersal of otters into unsuitable areas (Medina 1996). This is resulting in a population that is becoming increasingly fragmented and more susceptible to local extinctions through habitat destruction, human disturbance, predation by domestic dogs, and demographic or environmental stochastic events. Genetic studies have confirmed a lower genetic diversity in the northern freshwater subpopulations in comparison to those from the south confirming a past bottleneck probably due to anthropogenic factors (Centron et al. 2008, Vianna et al. 2011). The species has suffered a suspected past population decline of ≥50% over the last 30 years or three generations (based on Pacifici et al. 2013) in its range countries due to habitat loss and degradation, water pollution, overhunting for the pelt trade, and direct persecution due to retaliation (Chehébar 1990). Accelerating habitat destruction and degradation throughout the Southern River Otter's range is the greatest threat to the species, and is suspected (based on current trends) to lead to a future ≥50% reduction in population size over the next 30 years (three generations based on Pacifici et al. 2013) for those subpopulations using rivers and lakes (freshwater habitats), and for the subpopulations using the southern fjords and islands (marine habitats) the population decline may be due to the impacts of intensive fishery activities. Therefore, based on the suspected population decline in the past and future, the species is categorised as Endangered under criteria A2cd+3cde.
habitat: The Southern River Otter is distributed in the southern temperate forest of South America. This species presents a distribution associated with inland waters in the northern parts of its range, and marine habitat in the southern part of its range. In freshwater habitats otters are associated with the presence of macro-crustaceans from the genus Aegla spp. and Sammastacus spp. (Aued et al. 2003, Cassini et al. 2009, Sepúlveda et al. 2009), which are the otter’s main prey (Medina 1997, Medina-Vogel and Gonzalez-Lagos 2008, Fasola et al. 2009, Rodríguez-Jorquera and Sepúlveda 2011, Franco et al. 2013). Other species of crustaceans, fish and amphibians are also in the otter’s diet but are of marginal occurrence. The species uses rivers with abundant vegetation (Chehebar et al. 1986, Medina-Vogel et al. 2003) and inhabit diverse types of wetlands including Andean lakes, rivers of different sizes, ponds and estuaries. A study using telemetry described an average home range of 11.3 km, with solitary behaviour and a low spatial overlap between individuals of same sex suggesting intrasexual territoriality (Sepúlveda et al. 2007). In the marine range the species uses the marine rocky coast with abundant vegetation cover and low exposure to wind and waves (Sielfeld 1992, Sielfeld and Castilla 1999). In this environment the Southern River Otter is sympatric with the Marine Otter (L. felina), but the latter is segregated by its use of more wave-exposed coastal areas (Sielfeld 1992, Ebensperger and Botto-Mahan 1997). The diet in the marine environment is composed of coastal fish of the genera Harpagifer, Patagonotothen, Eleginops, Cottoperca and crustaceans of the genera Munida, Taliepus, Cancridae, Galatheidae, Lithodidae, Lithodes, Paralomis and Campylonotus (Sielfeld and Castilla 1999, Valenzuela et al. 2013). In general, for both marine and inland waters the Southern River Otter seems to be a specialized aquatic bottom forager preying on slow benthic fish and crustaceans.
threats: The Southern River Otter habitat is very sensitive to anthropogenic impacts (Medina-Vogel et al. 2003, Sepúlveda et al. 2009, Valenzuela et al. 2013). In those subpopulations inhabiting freshwater environments, the high demand for water by human activities such as agriculture, human use, etc. is altering watercourses through canalization and drainage and loss of riparian vegetation. These activities are promoted to increase the amount of agricultural lands but are impacting those otter subpopulations distributed in lowlands, particularly in the Central Valley and the Coastal Range of Chile (Medina-Vogel et al. 2003, Sepúlveda et al. 2009). In the case of Andean lakes, where the species occurred historically, the high level of urbanization and tourism has been proposed as the main causes responsible for the local extinction of the species in those areas (Medina 1996). Other threats are poaching (Medina 1996, Espinosa 2012), predation by free-ranging domestic dogs (Espinosa 2012) and transmission of diseases such as Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) (Sepúlveda et al. 2014). Free-ranging dogs are an important threat to carnivores because of predation and disease transmission (Vanak and Gompper 2009), and are present in rural and protected areas where the Southern River Otter occurs (Sepúlveda et al. 2014). Implementing dog population control measures as well as vaccination programmes are an important measure to mitigate the impact of dogs on this species (Sepúlveda et al. 2014). In several parts of the otter's distribution range, hydroelectric dams are installed or are planned to be built in the near future but no research on the potential impact of these on the otters has been conducted so far. The presence of wild exotic salmon and the salmon farming industry are suggested as a potential threat to otter prey leading to potential competition between otters and salmon (Medina 1996, Aued et al. 2003, Cassini et al. 2009) but no studies have confirmed this as yet. In relation to the invasive American Mink (Neovison vison), although several studies have investigated competition between these mustelids and river otters (Medina 1997, Aued et al. 2003, Fasola et al. 2009, Valenzuela et al. 2013), there is no clear evidence of a negative effect of the mink on the otter. Indeed, current studies in the marine part of the range suggest a negative effect of otters over minks by habitat (Valenzuela et al. 2013) and temporal segregation (Medina‐Vogel et al. 2013). The invasive mink is a potential vector of CDV to otters given their behavioural similarities and sharing of latrines (Sepúlveda et al. 2014).
population: Most studies on this species have been made based on indirect signs of the species, hence, there are no estimates of population or subpopulation size. The freshwater subpopulations have been studied more than those in marine environments. Monitoring of signs such as spraints or tracks has been implemented particularly for the population in Nahuel Huapi National Park in Argentina by the Administration of National Parks for over 30 years (Chehebar 1985, Chehebar et al. 1986, Chehébar and Porro 1998, Aued et al. 2003, Cassini et al. 2009, Pozzi and Chehebar 2013). A relatively stable otter distribution has been observed in this area with some marginal expansion outside the Nahuel Huapi Park in the Limay River (Carmanchahi et al. 2006). In this population recent volcanic activity during 2011 could have disrupted freshwater ecosystems, consequently affecting the otter population, but there are no studies on the subject, which are of utmost urgency. Freshwater subpopulations have been described as fragmented and comprised of seven isolated subpopulations (Medina 1996) but subsequent surveys have identified presence in areas previously thought not to have otters (Rodríguez et al. 2008); it is not clear if this is the result of a recent recolonization or sampling bias in earlier studies, and more research is needed. A radio-telemetry study in the Queule River found densities of 0.25 otters/km of river (Sepúlveda et al. 2007). Studies of the marine population in Chile indicate that the otter distribution in this environment would be continuous and abundances estimated are 0.57 otters/km of coast (Sielfeld 1992). Studies based on indirect signs in marine populations in Argentina, indicate two separate subpopulations, one in Isla de Los Estados (Provincial Reserve) and the other in Bahia Lapataia, Tierra del Fuego National Park, in the Beagle Channel (Valenzuela et al. 2012). During 1910–1954 a total of 38,263 otter pelts (Lontra felina and L. provocax) were exported from Chile but after that period no exports exist due to the implementation of different laws and international agreements (Iriarte and Jaksic 1986).
range: The Southern River Otter occurs in Chile and Argentina in freshwater and marine environments. The freshwater distribution is located in the northern part of the otter’s range and was historically wider in both countries. In Chile, river otters occurred from Cachapoal River (34ºS) (Gay 1847, Reed 1877) up to the Peninsula de Taitao (46ºS) with a continuous distribution in rivers and lakes (Medina 1996). The current distribution in Chile has been strongly restricted from north to south due to land use change and human colonization (Medina 1996), as a consequence, the otter populations are only found at present from the Imperial River (38ºS) (Rodríguez-Jorquera and Sepúlveda 2011) to the south.  In Argentina freshwater subpopulations were distributed historically from the Neuquen Province (36ºS) to the Lake Buenos Aires (46ºS) and mostly associated with water courses from the Andean Range and the steppe (Valenzuela et al. 2012). The present freshwater distribution in Argentina is mostly restricted to the Limay watershed, mainly within the Nahuel Huapi National Park (Chehebar 1985, Cassini et al. 2010, Valenzuela et al. 2012). Southern River Otter subpopulations that inhabit marine environments are distributed along the Pacific coast of Chile from 46ºS to Tierra del Fuego in Chile (Cabrera 1957, Redford and Eisenberg 1992, Sielfeld 1992, Malmierca et al. 2006). In Argentina, marine subpopulations are present only in the Archipielago Fueguino in Los Estados Island and the Beagle Channel (Malmierca et al. 2006, Valenzuela et al. 2012, Valenzuela et al. 2013). Marine river otters in Argentina are probably a continuous subpopulation of the main otter subpopulation in Chile (Sielfeld 1992).
useTrade: The species is hunted for their pelts which are used to make clothing.
conservationActions: The Southern River Otter is listed on CITES Appendix I and listed on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) Appendix I. In Chile, the conservation status is listed by the Reglamento de Clasificación de Especies as Endangered in VI, VII, VIII, IX, XIV and X Districts and as Data Deficient in XI and XII Districts (Chile 2011). In Chile, the Subsecretaria de Pesca is the governmental agency responsible of their conservation and management. In those populations inside official protected areas the Corporacion Nacional Forestal is responsible for their conservation. National Action plans in Chile are developed by the Minisiterio del MedioAmbiente, but despite its conservation status, no Action Plan exists for this species at present, which is the most urgent conservation action priority. Hunting is prohibited since 1929 in Chile (Iriarte and Jaksic 1986) and the governmental agency responsible for hunting permits and enforcement is the Servicio Agricola y Ganadero. In Argentina, the conservation status is Endangered (EN A3cd) (Valenzuela et al. 2012). At national level, the governmental agency responsible of native wildlife conservation and management is the Secretaría de Ambiente y DesarrolloSustentable de la Nación through the Dirección de Fauna Silvestre. The Administración de Parques Nacionales (National Parks Administration) is responsible for conservation of those populations inside the national protected areas, where the species is classified as Special Value Species (APN 1994.). The two populations in Argentina from freshwater and marine habitats are mostly inside national protected areas. Because of the several agencies involved in the management of the species a strong coordination with clear responsibilities and a work agenda is a major urgency in the short term. Actions recommended for both Chile and Argentina are: To develop a Conservation Bi-National Plan for the species; To develop specific National Conservation Plans for each country; To develop validated Monitoring Programmes in protected and unprotected lands; particularly in Chile where there is no such activity in any population; and To reinforce the importance of environmental impact assessment projects in relation to the species in order to adequately determine: a) presence of otter population in areas of projects, and b) in those projects requiring to implement adequate actions to incorporate: 1) measures of monitoring, 2) mitigation and 3) compensation activities. There have not been any reintroduction attempts, which could be an appropriate conservation action considering the success of such plans in North American and European species. Although otters are one of the most appealing species in zoo/aquarium exhibitions providing good opportunities for education and awareness about conservation issues in aquatic environments, no known individuals of the Southern River Otter are currently in captivity and there are no historical records for any captive animals.

rationale: The last comprehensive estimate of total abundance for the species (650,000 animals) dates from the mid 1990s. From the 1950s until 2023, changes in the abundance of Southern Elephant Seals have varied between populations and subpopulations, with some being stable, others increasing, and yet others experiencing steady declines. However, the overall population number globally did not likely change substantially between the 1990s and 2022. In contrast, since 2023, Southern Elephant Seals have experienced dramatic declines in abundance in parts of their range due to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). Mortality rates of more than 90% of newborn pups and possibly more than 50% of adult females have been reported for colonies in the South Atlantic. Modelling of one of these subpopulations indicates that it will take decades to recover. Demographic impacts are also suspected for the two subpopulations on Iles Kerguelen and Heard Island. The disease has now spread to four of the five major Southern Elephant Seal subpopulations, which together are responsible for over 90% of global pup production, intensifying the threat from HPAI. Relatively low levels of antibodies have been found in surviving animals. Furthermore, novel strains of the virus have been recorded in South America, acting as a possible source of further outbreaks in the adjacent Antarctica and Southern Ocean. Additionally, the fifth major subpopulation (Macquarie Island, where HPAI has not been identified) has experienced a slow but sustained decline in numbers over the past few decades due to other factors. A population reduction of more than 30% is suspected, where the causes of the reduction may not have ceased. This reduction is based on subcriteria (b) an index of abundance appropriate to Southern Elephant Seals and (e) the effects of pathogens. Thus, a reclassification of this species from Least Concern to Vulnerable is supported under criterion A2.
habitat: Southern Elephant Seals are the largest of all members of the Carnivora, with adult males reaching masses of 2–4 tons and lengths of up to 4.5 m, while adult females reach masses of 400–900 kg and lengths of 2.8 m. Newborn pups weigh between 40 and 46 kg (Laws 1993).Females have their first pups between the ages of three and six years. Males are reproductively mature from four or five years of age, but they only become socially mature between the ages of six and ten (Laws 1956, Carrick et al. 1962a, McCann 1981, Pistorius et al. 2001, Kirkman et al. 2004). Although longevities of 23 years have been recorded for females at Macquarie Island (Hindell and Little 1988), most individuals in this species do not live to be that old. On Marion Island, fewer than 5% of females survive beyond 13 years of age, and fewer than 5% of males beyond 10 years (de Bruyn 2009).Southern Elephant Seal adult females spend more than 85% of the year at sea, while the figure is approximately 80% for adult males (Carrick et al. 1962a, Hindell and Burton 1988, McIntyre et al. 2010). Further, both sexes spend some 65% of their lives below 100 metres (McIntyre et al. 2010). Dives mostly range from 200 to 400 metres deep, with durations of 20 to 30 minutes, but dive depth and duration vary seasonally and between the sexes. The maximum recorded depths are below 2,000 metres (Costa et al. 2010, McIntyre et al. 2010). The Southern Elephant Seal’s marine habitat includes areas over sea mountains, frontal systems, current lines and shifting marginal ice-edge zones. They are thought to be sensitive to fine-scale variation in bathymetry and ocean surface properties, such as sea-ice concentration and sea-surface temperature (Bailleul et al. 2007, McIntyre et al. 2010, Van den Hoff et al. 2014).Over the past two decades, animal-borne devices deployed on Southern Elephant Seals have collected critical oceanographic and at-sea habitat data. The Southern Ocean historically has been poorly studied due to its relative isolation and the difficulty of operating remote sampling instruments in ice-covered waters, so the seal generated data has been important in extending our knowledge of the Southern Ocean with concomitant new knowledge of at-sea behaviour and habitat use of the species (Boehme et al. 2010, Roquet et al. 2013, Hindell et al. 2016, Treasure et al. 2017).The diet of Southern Elephant Seals consists primarily of squid and myctophid and notothenid fish, with juveniles and adult females consuming Antarctic Krill (Euphausia superba) when foraging in Antarctic waters. It varies interannually and regionally (Brown et al. 1999, Piatkowski et al. 2002, Bradshaw et al. 2003, van den Hoff et al 2003, Cherel et al. 2008, Newland et al. 2011, Lübcker et al. 2017, Bester and Connan 2022). Southern Elephant Seals participate in four types of terrestrial periods during the course of their lives. They are born ashore and spend the first few weeks of life on land. All individuals haul out to moult annually. This alternates with one or more annual autumn-winter haul-out periods in immatures, and the breeding season for adults (Laws 1956, Carrick et al. 1962b, Kirkman et al. 2004). The breeding season takes place in the austral spring and is highly synchronised. Adult males haul out first, followed by the adult females. Polygynous breeding aggregations of up to a thousand females are formed, which are defended by males. While the females spend approximately a month ashore, the most successful males can be ashore up to three months. Females give birth 2–3 days after hauling out. They suckle their pups for three weeks; remaining ashore throughout the lactation period. Mating takes place shortly before weaning. The pups remain ashore for several weeks following weaning (Laws 1956, Carrick et al. 1962b, McCann 1981, Bonner 1989). While their primary predators are Killer Whales (Orcinus orca) (Reisinger et al. 2011), pups are also vulnerable to predation by Leopard Seals (Hydrurga leptonyx) (Gwynn 1953).
threats: The most serious and urgent threat facing Southern Elephant Seals is the arrival of novel diseases. Currently, HPAI is the disease of greatest concern. This virus recently has been recorded at four of the five largest subpopulations, which together supported more than 90% of global pup production prior to 2023 (Hindell et al. 2016, Laborie et al. 2023, Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025). The 2023 outbreak has resulted in substantial reductions in the abundance of at least two of five major subpopulations (Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025) in Peninsula Valdés and South Georgia, which supported some 54% of the global population before the outbreak (Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025). At Peninsula Valdés, HPAI has resulted in the mortality of almost an entire cohort, and the subsequent breeding season had a 67% reduction in reproductive females. Modelling indicated that the subpopulation would take decades to recover (Uhart et al. 2024, Campagna et al. 2025). The impact on the South Georgia subpopulation resulted in a 47% reduction in the number of adult females hauling out to breed between 2023 and 2024. However, this was only for a study area comprising 15.6% of the subpopulation. Since HPAI mortality varied between colonies at this site (Bamford et al. 2025), the reported reduction may not be generally applicable to the entire subpopulation. HPAI was also recorded at two further subpopulations among the five largest—at Îles Kerguelen and Heard Island—during the 2024 and 2025 breeding seasons (Clessin et al. 2025, MAFF 2025). These sites are responsible for approximately 46% of global pup production (Hindell et al. 2016, Laborie et al. 2023). While the demographic impacts on these colonies are, as yet, unreported or unknown, it is possible that they will be substantial based on the response at other colonies. Currently, HPAI has been confirmed for Southern Elephant Seals at six subpopulation sites (Bennison et al. 2024, Uhart et al. 2024, Clessin et al. 2025, MAFF 2025, SCAR 2025). It is suspected to be affecting a further subpopulation and has been confirmed in sympatric birds at the locations of a further two subpopulations (DFFE 2025, SCAR 2025, Steinfurth et al. 2026). It is unknown if it has infected seals at the remaining four subpopulations. Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza is an ongoing threat to Southern Elephant Seals. Recent work indicates that little antibody response has yet been detected in subpopulations that have been exposed to the disease (Moutinho 2025), as in other species of pinnipeds (Younger et al. 2026). Furthermore, both multiple and novel strains have been recorded in South America, the Southern Ocean and Antarctica (Ogrzewalska et al. 2025, Vanstreels et al. 2025, Younger et al. 2026). These could result in further mass mortality events.Other diseases are also a concern. Seals share their coastal habitat with a variety of seabirds, one of the taxa that is responsible for spreading HPAI in the Southern Ocean (Younger et al. 2026). In addition, seals that haul out on mainland sites may encounter domestic and wild animals and be exposed to a variety of diseases (Lavigne and Schmitz 1990). Morbilliviruses are a potential threat (Bester 2014). They have resulted in several outbreaks in other species of pinnipeds (Di Guardo et al. 2005). Southern Elephant Seals are also at risk from rabies. The disease is now endemic in Cape Fur Seals (Arctocephalus pusillus pusillus) (Van Helden 2024). Vagrant Southern Elephant Seals visit the southern African coastline. Here, they occasionally come into contact with Cape Fur Seals and sometimes haul out at Cape Fur Seal colonies (Penry et al. 2013, Bester et al. 2022). If they do so to moult, they could be in contact with Cape Fur Seals for up to a month. The effects of climate change on Southern Elephant Seals are not known but may well impact prey populations or alter marine habitats (Learmonth et al. 2006, Kovacs et al. 2012). It has been suggested that the declines in some Southern Elephant Seal subpopulations over the past forty years possibly are due to reductions in prey availability. However, it is unknown if this is influenced by climate change. It is also possible that the reduction in sea ice cover due to climate change may benefit Southern Elephant Seals (van den Hoff et al. 2014).Due to the isolation of Southern Elephant Seals from human population centres and areas important to commercial fisheries, other threats and conflict are not considered important. However, intensive fishing could deplete important prey stocks in the future (Hanchet et al. 2003). Southern Elephant Seals are also subject to entanglement in marine debris (Hofmeyr et al. 2002, Campagna et al. 2007, Jepsen and de Bruyn 2019), and increases in plastics at sea could have demographic impacts.
population: Southern Elephant Seal abundance has fluctuated widely over the past few thousand years, with some populations becoming extinct and new ones being founded in prehistoric times. In addition, several populations became extinct in historic times (Berg et al. 2025). Since the 1950s, changes in abundance have varied between populations and subpopulations, with some being stable, others experiencing steady increases, and yet others experiencing steady declines (Boyd et al. 1996, Pistorius et al. 2011, Hindell et al. 2017, Galimberti and Sanvito 2020, Laborie et al. 2023, Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025). Since 2023, some populations have been heavily impacted by Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) (Laborie et al. 2023, Bamford et al. 2025). Southern Elephant Seals have therefore been subject to dramatic changes in distribution and abundance over relatively short periods of time (Berg et al. 2025).Southern Elephant Seals are thought to occur in four distinct populations, each of which consists of a number of subpopulations, corresponding to an isolated island, archipelago, or mainland site. These populations (and included subpopulations) are 1) the South-West Atlantic (Peninsula Valdés), 2) the South Atlantic (South Georgia, Falkland Islands, South Orkney Islands, South Shetland Islands, Bouvetøya, Gough Island), 3) the Indian Ocean (Îles Kerguelen, Îles Crozet, Heard Island, the Prince Edward Islands) and 4) the Pacific Ocean (Macquarie Island, Campbell Island, Antipodes Islands) (Gales et al. 1989, Hoelzel et al. 1993, Slade et al. 1998, Hoelzel et al. 2001, Corrigan et al. 2016). A handful of small to medium-sized colonies (hundreds of individuals) have been identified along the coast of Southern Chile in the Southeastern Pacific (L. Huckstad pers. comm.). Movement between populations does occur but is rare (Fabiani et al. 2003, Reisinger and Bester 2010, Chua et al. 2022). Over-exploitation is thought to be responsible for extirpation of Southern Elephant Seals from: St. Helena Island, Tristan da Cunha, Islas Juan Fernández, the Bass Straights, and New Zealand (Carrick and Ingham 1962, Wace and Holdgate 1976, Bester 1980, Berg et al. 2025), while a further population at Victoria Land on the Antarctic coast became extinct prior to human discovery (Hall et al. 2006). Range-wide estimates for Southern Elephant Seal abundance exist up to the mid 1990s when the global population comprised circa 650,000 animals (SCAR EGS 2008) [about 325,000 mature individuals]. In recent years, good estimates exist for only parts of the range. Since the 1990s, a slow decline has been experienced in some parts of the range. This has been arrested in some areas, while in others the decline has continued. These slow changes have been followed by recent catastrophic impacts of HPAI experienced during the 2023 and 2024 breeding seasons, which have resulted in almost complete mortality of entire cohorts of pups, as well as mortality in older age classes.Updated estimates are available for some subpopulations (Pistorius et al. 2011, Hindell et al. 2017, Laborie et al. 2023, Bamford et al. 2025, de Bruyn 2025). In the 1990s, more than half of pup production was thought to take place at South Georgia (Boyd et al. 1996, SCAR EGS 2008). At the time, Îles Kerguelen was thought to be responsible for a further 21% (Authier et al. 2011). However, recent estimates suggest that, prior to 2023, South Georgia and Îles Kerguelen were each responsible for approximately 40% of global pup production (Laborie et al. 2023). A further three subpopulations—at Peninsula Valdés, Heard Island and Macquarie Island—supported more than 5% of global pup production each (Lewis et al. 1998, Slip and Burton 1999, Van Den Hoff et al. 2014). The remaining nine islands or island groups were responsible for a total of some 3% of global pup production. The Peninsula Valdés subpopulation experienced growth for 60 years, with a mean annual increase of 1–3% from 1970 to 2010 (Ferrari et al. 2013). In 2022, 18,000 reproductive females hauled out during the breeding season (Campagna et al. 2025). However, this area was severely impacted by HPAI during the 2023 breeding season, with an estimated 97% of pups dying (Uhart et al. 2024). Some 67% fewer reproductive females hauled out for the following breeding season, indicating that HPAI also had a major impact on adults, and possibly an impact on fertility rates (Campagna et al. 2025). Modelling indicates that the outbreak has had a severe demographic impact, with this subpopulation forecast to take decades to recover (Campagna et al. 2025). Subpopulations of the South Atlantic population were considered to be either growing or stable in recent times, though comprehensive estimates are lacking (Boyd et al. 1996, SCAR EGS 2008, Gil-Delgado et al. 2013). The most important of these subpopulations, at South Georgia, was thought to account for more than half of the world’s abundance (Boyd et al. 1996) of Southern Elephant Seals, but subsequent reassessment of other subpopulations indicates that it was more likely responsible for circa 40% of the global population (Laborie et al. 2023). Assessment of the three largest colonies at South Georgia (comprising 15.6% of the subpopulation total) indicates that abundance remained stable from 1995–2022 (Bamford et al. 2025). However, this site was heavily impacted by HPAI during the 2023 breeding season. An assessment of the three largest colonies in 2024, indicated a 47% reduction of breeding females compared to 2022, and a 33.7% decline compared to the long-term average, indicating that it is likely that significant numbers of adult females died during the epidemic (Bamford et al. 2025). It was noted that the impact was not uniform between colonies (Bamford et al. 2025). The remaining five subpopulations in the South Atlantic population are all much smaller, with fewer than a thousand breeding females each. The largest colony in the Falkland Islands subpopulation experienced a period of stability from the mid-1990s to 2002. This was followed by a recorded 4.49% annual increase until 2018 (Galimberti et al. 2001, Galimberti and Sanvito 2020). Numbers of Southern Elephant Seals at Gough Island have declined since 1975, and this subpopulation was functionally extinct in 2019, with only two pups being born (Jones et al. 2020). At Bouvetøya during the 1998/1999 summer, pup production was estimated at less than 100 (Kirkman et al. 2001). Breeding continued, at least until 2014/2015, though current numbers are unknown (pers. obs.). For the South Shetland Islands, few recent estimates exist, and available counts cover only portions of the subpopulation’s range (Gil-Delgado et al. 2013, Fudala and Bialik 2022, Negrete et al. 2022). However, abundance was thought to be fluctuating (SCAR EGS 2008). Pup production at the South Orkney Islands was last assessed in 1985 when it was estimated at less than 100 (McCann 1985). HPAI in Southern Elephant Seals has been found at two of these smaller subpopulations. Demographic impacts in the Falkland Islands have been relatively minor. Mortality of an estimated 1.2% of pups and a single adult male was recorded at the main colony. However, the following breeding season, a 5.6% decline in the number of breeding females was recorded (F. Galimberti pers. comm.). HPAI has been recorded further in a Southern Elephant Seal at the South Shetland Islands (SCAR 2025). It has also been recorded or is suspected in sympatric seabirds at all sites except Bouvetøya, where its presence is unknown (SCAR 2025, Steinfurth et al. 2026). The demographic impacts of the disease on most of these smaller subpopulations are unreported. The Indian Ocean population contains large subpopulations at both Iles Kerguelen and Heard Island, and two smaller subpopulations at the Îles Crozet and the Prince Edward Islands. Southern Elephant Seals in this region declined in abundance through the 1990s, followed by periods of intermittent stabilisation or increase (Guinet et al. 1999, Slip and Burton 1999, Bester and Hofmeyr 2005, Authier et al. 2011, Pistorius et al. 2011, Laborie et al. 2023). The causes of the declines are not completely understood and may have differed between island groups. However, evidence indicates that the low survival of adult females and of pups was important and varied interannually with climatic conditions (Guinet et al. 1999, McMahon et al. 2005b, Pistorius et al. 2011, Hindell et al. 2016). The largest subpopulation in this stock, at the Îles Kerguelen, is one of the two largest globally and is thought to account for 40% of total pup production (Laborie et al. 2023). The first complete census at this site took place in 2018, estimating that over 100,000 females bred on the island, and that previous counts had been underestimates (Laborie et al. 2023). Until recently, the population was increasing, with a mean annual growth of 1.6% for selected colonies (Laborie et al. 2023). An unusual mortality event due to HPAI was detected in November 2024 (Clessin et al. 2025), but the demographic impact has not yet been reported. Within the Indian Ocean stock, the subpopulation at Heard Island accounts for some 6% of the species' total abundance. It declined by some 50% from 1949 to 1985, and then remained stable until 1992, when pup production was thought to be 17,000–18,000 (Slip and Burton 1999). While subsequent assessments are lacking, abundance is thought to have remained stable (Hindell et al. 2016) until recently. HPAI was associated with an unusual mortality event at Heard Island in October 2025 (MAFF 2025), but the demographic impact of this disease event is unknown. Two further, substantially smaller subpopulations are found in the Indian Ocean Sector. Over a thousand pups are born annually at the Prince Edward Islands. The colonies on the largest island in the group, Marion Island, declined by 83% from 1951 to 1997 (Pistorius et al. 1999, McMahon et al. 2009). However, between 1997 and 2023, abundance increased by 47% (de Bruyn 2025). Numbers have also increased on the adjacent and rarely surveyed Prince Edward Island (Mammal Research Institute unpublished data, in de Bruyn 2025). While HPAI has yet to be detected in Southern Elephant Seals at this site, it has been recorded in sympatric species of birds (DFFE 2025). The final subpopulation of the Indian Ocean stock inhabits the Îles Crozet. Abundance here also declined until the mid-1990s (Guinet et al. 1999). However, after 1994, the population experienced a mean annual growth rate of 5.1% and tripled in size. HPAI was first detected in Southern Elephant Seals at this site in October 2024. At monitored sites, pup mortality exceeded 50%, and dead adults were also found (Clessin et al. 2025), likely having an important demographic impact at this site.The Pacific population consists of a large subpopulation at Macquarie Island supporting some 5% of global abundance, and two smaller subpopulations at Campbell Island and the Antipodes Islands. The Macquarie Island subpopulation has experienced a slow but persistent decline of 1.45% annually from 1949 to 2015 (Hindell et al. 2016). It has been suggested that this decline is possibly linked to the extent of sea ice, and its impact on habitat quality (Van den Hoff et al. 2014, Hindell et al. 2016). The subpopulations at Campbell and Antipodes Islands are both very small and thought to be decreasing (McMahon et al. 2005a, Hindell et al. 2016). A few reproductive and moult haul outs have been identified along the fjords and channels in the Southeastern Pacific along the coastline of Southern Chile, each with a few hundred pups being born each year (L. Huckstadt pers. comm.). HPAI has yet to be detected in the Pacific region. Generation length for Southern Elephant Seals has been calculated at 9.5 years (Pacifici et al. 2013). The total abundance over three generations from 1996 is inferred to have been stable or to have increased up to 2023 (SCAR EGS 2008, Authier 2011, Pistorius et al. 2011, Van den Hoff 2014, Laborie et al. 2023, Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025). But the impact of HPAI events in the last couple of years has led to major declines in two of the five largest subpopulations (Peninsula Valdés, South Georgia; Bamford et al. 2025, Campagna et al. 2025), and two further subpopulations (Îles Kerguelen, Heard Island) have been impacted, though the extents of their declines are currently unknown (Clessin et al. 2025, MAFF 2025). The fifth (Macquarie Island) has yet to be impacted but is experiencing a slow long-term decline for other reasons (Van den Hoff et al. 2014, Hindell et al. 2016).
range: Southern Elephant Seals inhabit the waters of the Southern Ocean in a nearly circumpolar distribution. Their foraging range is between approximately 40°S and the Antarctic continent. Although most of their haul-out sites are on Subantarctic and Antarctic islands, seals from a few sites in South America and the Antarctic Peninsula use sites along the coasts of southern Argentina and Chile (Campagna and Lewis 1992) and others come ashore in Antarctica (Murray 1981, Heimark and Heimark 1986, Bester 1988). Vagrants are regularly recorded on the coasts of northern South America (Alava and Carvajal 2005, De Moura et al. 2010), southern Africa (Kettlewell and Rand 1955, Oosthuizen et al. 1988, Bester et al. 2022), Australia and New Zealand (Mills et al. 1977, Taylor and Taylor 1989). The most distant vagrant was recorded at Oman on the Arabian Peninsula, some 9,000 km from the nearest possible point of origin (Johnson 1990).The extent of occurrence for this species is estimated at approximately 91,000,000 km². Its area of occupancy within this range has not been determined but is much larger than the criterion B2 thresholds.
useTrade: Southern Elephant Seals were hunted for hundreds or thousands of years by indigenous societies in New Zealand, Australia and South America, but this is no longer the case (Berg et al. 2025). More recently, they have been subject to intensive commercial harvests starting in the early 19th century and not ending until 1964 at South Georgia (McCann 1985). They were prized for the large quantity of blubber that could be rendered to a valuable oil (Laws 1960). These harvests led to the severe reduction of some subpopulations and the extinction of others (McCann 1985, Berg et al. 2025). Southern Elephant Seals were last commercially harvested in 1964 (McCann 1985).
conservationActions: Exploitation of seals within the Antarctic Treaty area (south of 60°S) is regulated by the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals, while to the north of this area, the Convention on Antarctic Marine Living Resources and various national measures protect islands and continental areas on which the species breeds and occurs. The Falkland Islands Dependencies Conservation Ordinance provides protection for Southern Elephant Seals on South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands (Reijnders et al. 1993). Seals on the Prince Edward Islands are protected by virtue of the status of these islands as a special nature reserve, their location within a marine protected area, and also by the South African Seabirds and Seals Protection Act 1973 and the Marine Living Resources Act 1998 (PEIMP 2010). Southern Elephant Seals in Australian areas are protected by the Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (AFMA 2023). New Zealand subpopulations are protected by the Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978 and the Wildlife Act 1953 (Fisheries New Zealand 2009). The most recent range-wide comprehensive estimate of abundance dates from the mid-1990s (Boyd et al. 1996, Hindell et al. 2016). While more recent estimates exist for some parts of the range (Jones et al. 2020, Laborie et al. 2023, Campagna et al. 2025, de Bruyn 2025), other areas are only partially covered (Galimberti and Sanvito 2020, Bamford et al. 2025) or estimates are outdated (Slip and Burton 1999, Kirkman et al. 2001, SCAR EGS 2008, Hindell et al. 2016). In the light of the current threat posed by novel strains of HPAI, updated abundance estimates are essential for estimating status and trends. The risks posed by novel pathogens indicate the importance of biosecurity regulations at terrestrial haul-out sites occupied by Southern Elephant Seals. Even though seals and seabirds (and not humans) are thought to have been important natural vectors of infection by HPAI (Ogrzewalska et al. 2025, Younger et al. 2026), biosecurity measures may assist in reducing the transfer of novel diseases. Finally, vaccination of Southern Elephant Seals against HPAI might need to be tested. Vaccines against the disease have proved effective in generating an immune response in King Penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus) (Lejeune et al. 2025) and are being tested in the congeneric Northern Elephant Seal (Anthes 2025).

rationale: The Ross Seal is assessed as Least Concern, even if it remains the least studied Antarctic seal and is likely the most poorly understood species within the family Phocidae. The scarcity of data, particularly the absence of reliable population estimates, hinders accurate assessment of the species' conservation status. Nevertheless, available evidence suggests that the Ross Seal is the least abundant of the Antarctic pack ice seal species. Its life history is closely tied to the availability of sea ice, which is declining due to global climate change, raising concerns that the species may already be experiencing population declines, the magnitudes of which are unknown.
habitat: Ross Seals are the smallest of the four Antarctic phocid species at maturity. They exhibit slight sexual dimorphism, with females being slightly larger than males. Based on a limited sample of measured individuals, adult males range from 1.67–2.10 m in length and weigh between 129 and 216 kg, while females measure between 1.96 and 2.5 m and weigh between 159 and 204 kg in mass (Skinner and Klages 1994, Wege et al. 2021). Ross Seal pups are estimated to measure approximately 1 meter in length and weigh around 16 kg at birth (Shaughnessy and Jones 2019). Measurements of eight suckling pups examined in November ranged from 109 to 138 cm in length and 40 to 75 kg in mass. Age at sexual maturity is estimated to be 3–6 years (Atkinson 1997), and they can live to at least 20 years (Skinner and Klages 1994).Most Ross Seal pups are likely born in November, with a peak in births occurring from early to mid-November (Southwell et al. 2003). Weaning is estimated to occur at approximately one month of age, although little is known about the mother-pup relationship. Nursing pups have been observed swimming between ice floes. Mating is presumed to occur in the water, although direct observations are lacking. While the species has traditionally been considered polygynous, genetic evidence does not support this hypothesis and instead suggests a monogamous mating system (Curtis et al. 2011).Ross Seals are typically found singly on the ice. Moulting is believed to occur in January, during which time individuals appear to fast, similar to most phocine seals (Skinner and Klages 1994). During summer months, Ross Seals exhibit a diel haul-out pattern, with the majority observed hauled out on the ice around midday (Ray 1981, Bengtson and Stewart 1997, Southwell 2003, Wege et al. 2021). Satellite telemetry studies indicate that Ross Seals are pelagic foragers, spending extended periods in the open ocean, often in association with the Antarctic Polar Front (Blix and Nordøy 2007, Arcalis-Planas et al. 2015, Wege et al. 2021). They return to the pack ice to breed in October-November (Blix and Nordøy 2007), and subsequently to moult deep in the pack ice in January–February. Recent studies using at-sea movement data from satellite tags have provided new insights into the habitat preferences of Ross Seals. In the Amundsen Sea, satellite-tagged Ross Seals travelled long distances away from the pack ice into open waters during late summer. These individuals showed limited use of the pack ice and exhibited a preference for water temperatures ranging from -1.8°C to 2°C (Arcalis-Planas et al. 2015). Individuals from the Dronning Maud Land sector in the Weddell Sea exhibit a preference for at-sea habitats characterised by sea surface temperatures ranging from -1°C to 2°C, open waters away from the sea ice edge, shallow mixed layer depths during summer, deeper mixed layer depths in winter, and relatively slow current velocities (Wege et al. 2021). A few studies have examined the diet of Ross Seals through stomach content analysis, revealing a diet composed primarily of cephalopods, followed by fish and other invertebrates, including Antarctic Krill (Euphausia superba) (Ray 1981, Skinner and Klages 1994).
