The status of this species in captivity is difficult to determine, owing to taxonomic confusion with E. rufus. However, both E. rufus and E.rufifrons are found in a number of collections world-wide.

rationale: A population reduction of ≥30% is predicted to occur over a three-generation time period (30 years) in the future, based on continuing and projected decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, in addition to ongoing and projected exploitation through unsustainable hunting pressure. The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species is 6,991 km² and extremely fragmented. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: Total length of 54.7- 66.6 cm and an average weight of 900g. Its dorsal fur is gray-brown, and ventral fur is white with a reddish-brown tail (Zaramody et al. 2006, Mittermeier et al. 2008). It is an inhabitant of primary humid lowland and montane rainforest, as well as secondary and disturbed forest formations. This species is nocturnal and arboreal. The diet consists mainly of mainly leaves (approximately 98%), along with some flowers and fruits (Faulkner and Lehman 2006). Young leaves of Harungana madagascariensis and Syzygium sp. made up 67.5% of their diet at Vato in Ranomafana (Faulkner and Lehman 2006). One study at Ranomafana showed that resting occupied 59.5% of nightly activity, feeding 22%, traveling 13.5%, and grooming 5%. Home range is estimated to be on average 1 ha (P. Wright pers. comm.).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to shifting agriculture, in addition to hunting.
population: Population densities at Ranomafana tend to be higher in secondary forests and disturbed habitats (Lehman et al. 2006), though a more recent study found the opposite trend with encounter rates positively related to canopy height (Herrera et al. 2011).Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss and degradation. A population reduction of ≥30% is predicted to occur over a three-generation time period (30 years) in the future, based on continuing and projected decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, in addition to ongoing and projected exploitation through unsustainable hunting pressure.
range: This species occurs in south-eastern Madagascar. The precise limits of the distribution of this species, and in particular its relationship to Avahi meridionalis and A. ramanantsoavanai in the south, are as yet undetermined. It is currently known from south of the Mangoro / Nesivolo river systems in the forests of Manara, Vatoalatsaka, Sangalampona, Mahasoarivo and Ranomafana. The southern extent of the range remains unclear (Zaramody et al. 2006, Mittermeier et al. 2008).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is sometimes hunted for food; however, its bitter taste is not widely appreciated.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. Based on the description of Zaramody et al. (2006), this species is presumably present in three national parks including Ranomofana National Park, Andringitra, and Midongy du Sud. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers approximately 874 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: Lepilemur wrightae is an inhabitant of mid-altitude rainforest. Currently, it is only known to occur in Kalambatritra Special Reserve and Beakora Forest. This species is primarily nocturnal and folivorous (Rowe and Meyers 2016). Like other species within the Lepilemur genus, holes in large trees serve as sleeping sites for L. wrightae (Rowe and Meyers 2016). Groups of 1-3 individuals (2 adults, 1 juvenile) have been seen foraging together. This species is known to defecate in communal areas known as latrines (Irwin et al. 2004).
threats: The entirety of this species’ known distribution is classified a “red zone” due to illegal activities, including Marijuana cultivation and cattle rustling (Rowe and Meyers 2016). Wild grassfires lit by humans are a threat. Beakora Forest is currently unprotected.
population: Population numbers are thought to be in decline due to habitat loss. There are an estimated 72 individuals per km2 (Rakotonirina et al. 2017).
range: This species is currently known from Kalambatritra Special Reserve in south-eastern Madagascar, west of the Mananara River and north of the Mandrare River (Louis et al. 2006), as well as the unprotected Beakora Forest (Irwin et al. 2001, Rakotonirina et al. 2017). Further studies need to be conducted to determine the precise limits of its distribution, especially relative to Lepilemur leucopus and L. fleuretae. The extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated at 874 km2.
useTrade: Little is known about whether this species is hunted.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. It is known to occur in Kalambatritra Special Reserve and the unprotected Beakora Forest (Irwin et al. 2001, Louis et al. 2006, Rakotonirina et al. 2017). Further work is now urgently needed to clarify the distribution and taxonomic limits of this Lepilemur species. Beakora Forest south of Kalambatritra Special Reserve should be protected, although densities in Beakora are lower than Kalambatritra. Because this region is considered a “red zone” security should be improved for the protection of this area.

rationale: The extent of occurrence of this species covers less than 500 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As a result, it is suspected that there has been a population reduction of 80% in the past, and that it will increase to between 80% and <90% in the future. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: Avahi cleesei occurs in sub-humid, dry deciduous forests close to the western Tsingy precipices, in the larger Tsingy crevasses or gorges, and forests along small seasonal rivulets and seasonal swamps close to the Bemaraha massif (Thalmann and Geissmann 2006). Avahi cleesei's total length ranges from 55.2 to 67.5 cm. Its average weight ranges from 750 to 1,300 g (Thanlmann and Geissmann 2005, Zaramody et al. 2006, Lei et al. 2008). Its woolly dorsal fur is brown-gray, and its thin ventral fur is light gray whilst the fur on the tail varies between individuals. White patches on the dorsal surface of the hindlimb is unique to this species.
threats: This species is primarily threatened by continued habitat loss. Thalmann and Geissmann (2005, 2006) noted that the disturbed forest close to the village of Ankinajao (outside the park), which supported a substantial number of individuals in 1994, had been cut completely by 2003. Continued loss of habitat within the borders of Tsingy de Bemaraha between 2002 and 2007 was noted near the village of Ambalarano (E. Louis, Unpubl.). The sub-humid forest at the base of the escarpment of the Tsingy de Bemaraha is under continuous pressure from bush fires that reduce it in many places every year. Such sub-humid forests are the only habitat in which Avahi cleesei is known to occur so far.
population: Thalmann and Geissmann (2000) describe Avahi as being generally rare in the Bemaraha region, where the forests it inhabits tend to have a high proportion of evergreen trees (secondary forest growth). Ironically, local population densities appear to correlate negatively with levels of habitat disturbance, meaning that higher population densities seem to be found in disturbed habitats.The extent of occurrence of this species covers less than 500 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As a result, it is suspected that there has been a population reduction of 80% in the past, and that it will increase to between 80% and <90% in the future.
range: This species is known only from the Tsingy de Bemaraha region of western Madagascar, north of the Manambolo River (Thalmann and Geissman 2005). Currently, Avahi cleesei is known only from within Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, where it has been sighted in two localities, in the forest of Ankindrodro (19°08′S, 44°49′E;) and the type locality (18°59′S, 44°45′E), a forest 3–4 km east-northeast of the village of Ambalarano at the base of the western Tsingy precipice (Thalmann and Geissmann 2006). The forest near where Avahi species was previously outside the reserve’s boundaries in 1994, is in the heavily disturbed forest in the surroundings of the village of Ankinajao (19°03′S, 44°47′E; Thalmann and Geissmann 2000). However, the forest was destroyed, and no woolly lemurs have been found there since 2003 (Thalmann and Geissmann 2006). The forest of Ambalarano has also seen a significant decline as documented from expeditions there between 2002 and 2007 (E. Louis, Unpubl.). The northern limit of its range is unclear; however, there has been no evidence offered of its occurrence between the Sambao and Betsiboka Rivers (Thalmann and Geissmann 2005). The estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 500 km² at an elevation 27 – 82 metres above sea level (avg. 36 metres).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: There is no trade or general use of this species. It is quite rare with habitat loss being the most significant threat for this species.
conservationActions: Avahi cleesei is listed on CITES Appendix I. The only protected area in which it is known to occur is Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park and Strict Nature Reserve. Given the extremely small known range of Cleese’s Woolly Lemur, surveys that were recommended in 2012 are still urgently needed to identify additional populations and/or individuals. As with all Avahi species, it is not kept in captivity long-term successfully.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 2,954 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also thought to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of the lowland rainforest and wet littoral forest. This species is mainly nocturnal but has its peaks of activity at twilight and exhibits sporadic diurnal activity in certain environmental conditions (Balestri 2018). This species has been studied in the Ste Luce Conservation Area and in the lowland humid forest of Ampasy in the northernmost portion of the Tsitongambarika Protected Area. Home range size varies from 2.5 to 3.5 ha at Sainte Luce (Norscia and Borgognini-Tarli 2008) and from 4.59 to 10.39 ha at Ampasy (Balestri 2018). This species is pair-living and has a strictly folivorous diet with a total of 43 plant species used over a 7 month period at Sainte Luce. The diet breadth was only slightly broader in Ampasy with 48 plants species used over a 10 month period (Balestri 2018). Young leaves are preferred over mature leaves and the species seems to tolerate tannins well. One of the main predictors of the species abundance in littoral forest fragments is tree size (Norscia et al. 2012).
threats: This species is mainly threatened by habitat loss and degradation from ongoing shifting agricultural practices and logging of precious wood. Opportunistic hunting is an additional minor threat for the species (Campera et al. 2017).
population: Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss and hunting (Bollen and Donati 2006). Densities in littoral forest fragments are relatively high ranging from 55 to 240 individuals/km² (Norscia 2008). In inland rainforest areas densities seem to be at the lower range of the previous figures. A density of 16.7 individuals/km2 has been reported in the wet portion of the Andohahela National Park (Feistner and Schmid 1999), while 32.0 individuals/km2 have been recently observed in the Northern part of the Tsitongambarika Protected Area (Balestri 2018). Densities between 24 and 95 individuals/km² have been recorded in the southern part of Tsitongambarika (Norscia et al. 2006, Asity Madagascar pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs in the wet forests of south-eastern Madagascar. The southernmost  limit of the species seems to be the transitional littoral forest of Petriky, south of Tolagnaro, (G. Donati pers. obs.), north to Parcel 1 of Andohahela National Park, the Tsitongambarika Protected Area and the littoral forest fragments of Sainte-Luce Conservation Area and Mandena Conservation Area (Zaramody et al. 2006). Further studies are required to determine the exact northern distribution, and especially its limits in relation to neighbouring species (Avahi peyrierasi and A. ramanantsoavanai). A recent study suggests the possible presence of the species at the Beampingaratsy Protected Area (Ligue Pour la Protection de la Nature pers. comm.; ETCTerra, 2018). The EOO is estimated to be around 2,954 km².This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: Opportunistic hunting is a threat for the species (Campera et al. 2017).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. This species is known to occur in Andohahela National Park (Parcel 1), the Tsitongambarika Protected Area, the Sainte-Luce Private Reserve, and in the Mandena Conservation Zone, east of Tolagnaro (Fort-Dauphin). Further studies are required to determine the exact northern distribution range of this species. This species is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be less than 1,195 km2. This species geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As such, a population reduction is thought to have occurred, be ongoing, and to occur in the future. Based on these criteria, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of dry deciduous forest. As with the genus Lepilemur, this species is presumably largely folivorous.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation of its habitat due to shifting agriculture.
population: Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss. It is suspected that a 50% reduction in the population has occurred in the past three generations (21 years) due to habitat degradation. Given that the threats facing the species have not abated, it is suspected that the rate of population decline will continue into the future as well.
range: This species is found between the Betsiboka and Mahavavy du Sud Rivers in western Madagascar. The southern extent of the range across the Mahavavy du Sud River is yet to be clarified (Andriaholinirina et al. 2006). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 1,195 km2. Lepilemur aeeclis is found from 12-63 metres above sea level (avg. 52.5 metres). This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: There is no use or trade for this species that is known, except possibly as an occasional food source.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. It is not known from any protected areas except at Antrema which offer some degree of protection; it is found in the Anjahamana and Antrema Classified Forests. Further work is now needed to clarify the distribution and taxonomic limits of the recently described Lepilemur species, especially in relationship to unknown holotype localities of Lepilemur dorsalis and Lepilemur grandidieri. There is an urgent need for field assessments of population numbers and basic biology of this species.

rationale: There is a suspected population reduction of ≥30% in this species over a three generation period. Causes of this reduction (which have not ceased) include continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, and exploitation through hunting. Between 1999-2005 habitat loss in the Tsitongambarika Protected Area has been 1.74% per year (Andriamasimanana 2008). A population reduction of ≥30% is also suspected to be met in the next 27 years (over a three generation time period) due to the same causes. These causes have not ceased, and will to a large extent not be easily reversible. Of note, it has been estimated that there will be a 21% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015). Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of subtropical moist lowland and montane forest (up to 1,600 m). The species exhibits a cathemeral activity pattern and lives in small social groups ranging from 2 to 9 individuals, sometimes with one or two breeding adult females and one or two adult males (Eppley et al. 2015b, 2016b, 2017c, 2017d). Home range sizes are variable, ranging from 6.60 – 18.39 ha (Eppley et al. 2016b). At Kalambatritra Special Reserve and Mandena Conservation Area, individuals exhibit latrine behaviour (repeated group defecation at specific sites); groups defecate in turn, with adults going first followed by juveniles. It is thought that this likely serves some communicatory function, possibly for demarcating territory and mate-guarding (Eppley et al. 2016b). Similar to other bamboo lemur species, Hapalemur meridionalis is classified as a folivore (Eppley et al. 2011, 2016a). In Mandena, groups have been observed to spend significant amounts of time on the ground, foraging terrestrially on various grass (Poaceae) and reed (Cyperaceae) species within the littoral forest, in open-canopy areas, and within marsh / swamp areas (Eppley et al. 2011, 2016a). These flooded forest and marsh habitats appear to be important for the individuals populating the littoral coastal forest (Eppley et al. 2015a), with groups even observed in the reed marshes along the estuaries by Evahtra. Within the littoral forest, this species has been recorded to feed on 72 different species from 37 plant families (Eppley et al. 2016a). Though the majority of their diet is composed of terrestrial grasses, piths, and liana stems/leaves, they also consumed 34 different fruit species (Eppley et al. 2011, 2016a). This species often selects for resting sites with large diameter at breast height (DBH) within the degraded littoral forest (Eppley et al. 2017b). Brief observations from more continuous humid forests (e.g., Andohahela National Park, Tsitongambarika Protected Area) have noted this species feeding on various woody and liana bamboo species (Feistner and Schmid 1999; T. Eppley pers. comm.).
threats: The principal threat is habitat loss due to slash and burn agriculture, illegal timber extraction, charcoal production, and large-scale mining. Hunting is also a threat, with locals targeting this species as it appears to crop-raid often in agricultural areas (Campera et al. 2019; Eppley pers. comm.). This species is occasionally kept as a pet (Reuter and Schaefer 2017).
population: The population size of this species is not known, but population is suspected to be undergoing decline. There is a suspected population reduction of ≥30% in this species over a three generation period. Causes of this reduction (which have not ceased) include continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, and exploitation through hunting. Between 1999-2005 habitat loss in the Tsitongambarika Protected Area has been 1.74% per year (Andriamasimanana, 2008). In addition, this species is shown to be negatively impacted by habitat fragmentation (Eppley et al. 2020). A population reduction of ≥30% is also suspected to be met in the next 24 years (over a three generation time period) due to the same causes. These causes have not ceased, and will to a large extent not be easily reversible. Of note, it has been estimated that there will be a 21% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).Surveys in Andohahela National Park reported an encounter rate of 0.27 individuals/km (Feistner and Schmid 1999), while in the Tsitongambarika Protected Area reported encounter rates were 0.52 ind./km at Ivohibe, 0.23 ind./km at Antsiriky, and 1.10 ind./km at Ivorona (Birdlife International 2011). More robust surveys in the Ampasy valley, a relatively undisturbed lowland rainforest in the northern section of the Tsitongambarika Protected Area, indicate densities of 18±5 (10-33) individuals per km2 (Campera et al. 2019). The number of mature individuals is suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss and hunting (Mittermeier et al. 2010, Campera et al. 2019).
range: This species is found in south-eastern Madagascar. The southernmost of the Bamboo Lemurs, the type locality is the forestry station of Mandena, located approximately 10 km north of Tolagnaro in coastal south-eastern Madagascar (Warter et al. 1987, Warter and Tattersall 1994). The precise range is unclear, but it is known from the forests of Mandena Conservation Area, Tsitongambarika Protected Area, Andohahela National Park (Parcel 1), and Ambatosirongorongo/Malahelo in the extreme south, while also inhabiting the Midongy du Sud National Park, Manombo, Kalambatritra, Pic d' Ivohibe, Andringitra and Ranomafana further to the north (Feistner and Schmid 1999, Mittermeier et al. 2010, Birdlife International 2011, Eppley et al. 2011, Nguyen et al. 2013, Rakotonirina et al. 2017). Rabarivola et al. (2007) noted that an animal from Atsimo appeared to be a heterozygote between this species and Hapalemur griseus, and it is possible that this species extends as far north as Ranomafana National Park (E.E. Louis Jr. pers. comm.). In Andohahela animals were observed at 1,500 m, but were absent at higher elevations (Feistner and Schmid 1999). Upper elevation limit are unclear as animals from 1,600 m on the Andringitra Massif are either H. meridionalis or hybrids between H. griseus and H. meridionalis. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be approximately 33,967 km2. It has been estimated that there will be a 21% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food (Nguyen et al. 2013; Campera et al. 2019). Through village interviews, it was reported that 75.4% participants had eaten this species within the Tsitongambarika Protected Area (Campera et al. 2019). This species is occasionally kept as a pet (Reuter and Schaefer 2017).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. This species is known to occur in four national parks (Andohahela,  Andringitra, Midongy du Sud, and Ranomafana), three special reserves (Kalambatritra, Manombo and Pic d' Ivohibe), the Tsitongambarika Protected Area, and in the Mandena Conservation Zone, east of Tolagnaro (Feistner and Schmid 1999, Rabarivola et al. 2007, Mittermeier et al. 2010; E.E. Louis Jr. pers. comm.). There is a need for further survey work to determine the full distribution, population status, and ecology of this species. This species is threatened mainly by habitat loss due to the regular burning of forest to clear pasture for livestock and shifting agriculture, as well as illegal timber harvesting from protected areas. Hunting should also be considered a major threat as this species is known to crop-raid which puts them at further risk from humans attempting to protect their crops (Campera et al. 2019, Eppley pers. comm.). Southern bamboo lemurs are able to survive in degraded habitats and this species is presumably edge tolerant (Eppley et al. 2015a,  2017a). It has been observed to utilize the invasive paper-bark tea tree (Melaleuca quinquenervia) within the littoral forest area of southeast Madagascar. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence of this species covers approximately 14,376 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also thought to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of the primary eastern humid rainforests. It is nocturnal and arboreal. This species has not been systematically studied in the wild.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation.
population: Population numbers are thought to be in decline due to habitat loss and degradation from shifting agriculture, timber harvesting, and frequent cyclones. In Manombo, very few infants and/or juveniles have been recorded over the past few years (GERP, unpublished report).
range: This species occurs in south-east coastal Madagascar. Currently it is known only from the area of its type locality, the Manombo Special Reserve and Agnalahaza Forest (Zaramody et al. 2006; Andriantompohavana et al. 2007). Further studies are required to determine its exact distribution, and especially the limits with regard to neighbouring species (Avahi peyrierasi and A. meridionalis) (Mittermeier et al. 2008). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 14,376 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. The only protected areas in which it occurs are the Manombo Special Reserve and the nearby Agnalazaha Forest (Zaramody et al. 2006; Andriantompohavana et al. 2007), which is now being managed by the Missouri Botanical Garden (Rylands et al. 2018 notes it is found in: Reserve Speciale de Manombo, Agnalazaha, Reserve de Ressources Naturelles d'Agnakatrika, and Reserve de Ressources Naturelles d'Ankarabolava). Further work is urgently needed to confirm the distribution, population status, ecology, and threats to this species. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 70 km2. This geographic range is undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also known to be in decline (though the number of births are increasing). Based on these premises, the species continues to be listed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of moist lowland rainforest.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from shifting agricultural practices, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
population: Population densities in Manombo Special Reserve are 45 individuals/km2, and 23 individuals/km2 in Manombo Classified Forest. There is an approximate total known population size of 1,386 individuals (Ingraldi 2010). Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss.
range: This species currently is known from the Manombo Special Reserve region in south-eastern Madagascar. The precise northern and southern limits of the range are unknown, but it could range south of the Manampatrana River and north of the Mananara River (Louis et al. 2006). The estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 70 km2.
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. Present in the Manombo Special Reserve (Louis et al. 2006). An ongoing research and conservation action are now active in the study sites to scale up the status of the Lepilemur jamesorum.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 1,100 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits dense primary forest fragments in mountainous areas.
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation in its already restricted distribution due to unsustainable farming practices, logging and hunting.
population: Almost all sampled populations of Microcebus bongolavensis show genetic evidence for a relatively rapid crash in population size. This crash is likely to have occurred within the last 500 years, thus coinciding with accelerated deforestation due to human population expansion in Madagascar (Olivieri et al. 2008). Present day populations are also suspected to be in decline due to declines in habitat quality and extent of occurrence.
range: This species is known only from three small forest fragments in the area around Port-Bergé, between the rivers Mahajamba and Sofia in north-western Madagascar (Olivieri et al. 2007). Prior to recent taxonomic revisions, the mouse lemurs in this region were assumed to be Microcebus ravelobensis. It may also be present in the Bongolava Classified Forest. The estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 1,100 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forests (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: It is listed on CITES Appendix I. The species is found in the Ambodimahabibo Classified Forest, and may be present in the Bongolava Classified Forest as well. Consideration should be given to establishing a protected area that includes the latter, it being the only relatively large forest fragment left within the known range. Further surveys are needed to determine the full extent of its range and population status, and to confirm the taxonomic distinctiveness of this taxon. This species is not being kept in captivity (I.J. Porton pers. comm. 2010).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 2,614 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Although population totals and density estimations now available since the last assessment in 2012 are considered high compared to other sportive lemurs, there are discrepancies between the surveyed site densities that cannot be explained by purely environmental reasons; therefore, hunting could potentially be considered as a reason for these differences. A future reduction of >50% is suspected due to ongoing threats. Based on these premises, the species continued to be listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits primary and secondary tropical moist, gallery and dry deciduous lowland forest. It is presumably largely folivorous. As with all sportive lemurs, reproducing their diet in captivity is currently impossible; thus, no sportive lemurs have survived a permanent captive scenario.
threats: Habitat loss and hunting are the immediate threats to the sportive lemurs in the Daraina region, especially linked to the illicit mining for gold. Furthermore, the effects of mining activities on the forest should be evaluated and its effect of diurnal and nocturnal lemur species.
population: Population declines are suspected, with a suspected 30% rate of decline in the past increasing to at least 50% population declines in the next three generations. These declines are suspected due to continued hunting and habitat loss, as well as illicit mining and deforestation activities in region.In Salmona et al. (2014), the authors presented 2011 dry season survey data for the ten main forest fragments of the Loky-Manambato region, estimating Lepilemur milanoii densities and population sizes. Although the results suggest reasonably high sportive lemur densities in the region, there also revealed important discrepancies between forest fragments with densities ranging from 49.8 ind./km² in Antsaharaingy to 590.5 ind./km² in Ampondrabe. For the region Loky-Manambato, the authors estimated a population size of ~52,000 individuals, but this estimate does not include the forest cover populations between the Loky River and Andrafiamena, an area that has been reported to host both Ankarana and Milanoii sportive lemurs (Louis et al. 2006).
range: This species is found in northern Madagascar, known primarily from the Daraina region, south of the Loky River. There is an additional population occurring in the Andrafiamena Forest, living sympatrically with Lepilemur ankaranensis in this now protected forest. Field studies are needed to determine how these two species share the same forest as this population is the only area where two Lepilemur species evidently occur in sympatry (Louis et al. 2006). The estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is 2,614km2 at elevations 18 – 378 metres above sea level (avg. 167 metres).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: As sportive lemurs have been documented to remain part of the bushmeat frequently eaten by locals in other regions (Jenkins et al. 2011), Daraina and the Loky-Manambato region is no exception to this situation. Hunting in the region has been documented with not only crowned lemurs, but also with the sportive lemurs (i.e. in Solaniampilana; Salmona et al. 2014). The continued illicit gold mining efforts in the Daraina region should be considered linked to any potential hunting pressure. Therefore, as with the documented hunting of crowned lemurs for the restaurants in Sambava, hunting in this region should be taken seriously, particularly in areas with gold and rock mining activities.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I and is found within two protected areas. This species is known to occur in the Loky-Manambato Protected Area (Daraina), as well as in the Andrafiamena (Anjahakely) Protected Area, which is slated to become a national park. Further work is now urgently needed to clarify the distribution and taxonomic limits of the recently described Lepilemur species, it would be important to determine whether the differences in Lepilemur densities observed in Daraina are due to the historical poaching since no simple environmental correlate could be linked to these discrepancies. It would be important to repeat these surveys in this region and extend it over other neighbouring regions. Furthermore, studies should be conducted on the sympatric L. milanoii and L. ankaranensis population to determine the extent of this dual existence within the forest habitat between the Loky River to Andrafiamena region.

rationale: Given the impact of habitat loss within the range of this species, it is likely that Microcebus griseorufus is currently in decline. Despite this threat, the species is still thought to be relatively common within its range. Based on these premises, M. griseorufus is listed as Least Concern. Further information on hybridization, population status, habitat loss, and threats may warrant listing this species in a more threatened category in the future.
habitat: Microcebus griseorufus is found in spiny desert, dry thorn scrub, and gallery forest habitats (Rasoazanabary 2004). It is sympatric with M. murinus at Beza-Mahafaly and in the Mikea Forest, whereas in Berenty it is found in spiny forest patches but not in the immediately adjacent gallery forest that is occupied by the former species. It tolerates a wide range of habitats including coastal shrub (Steffens et al. 2017). This species feeds mainly on gums during the dry season, in arid habitats, and during periods of drought, but seems to bounce against the dry limits of its tolerance in the spiny bush (Bohr et al. 2011). In the wet season and in more humid forests it feeds on fruits and gums in equal proportions. Flowers and arthropods are also part of its diet, especially in arid habitats and in the dry season. Mating takes place during the rainy season (normally between September and November). Gestation in one wild female lasted 52 days. Females usually raise only one litter per year, consisting of only one or two offspring, although up to three young have been reported. Alloparenting has been observed. Young males disperse. Home range size varies from 0.33 ha in the dry season to 0.55 ha in the wet season (Génin 2008; Mittermeier et al. 2010 and references included therein).
threats: The most significant threats to this species include forest loss due to charcoal production and commercial maize production.
population: This is a relatively common species. Hybridization between Microcebus griseorufus and M. murinus has been noted in south-eastern Madagascar in two ecologically different contact zones. One hybrid zone is located in the transitional zone between dry spiny bush and humid littoral forests south of the southern tip of the Anosy Mountain Range west and east of Ankilivalo (S 25.112 E 46.689) (Gligor et al. 2009). The second hybrid zone is located in the western rainshadow of the Anosy Mountain Range where there is a mosaic of dry spiny bush and gallery forests. Most hybrids in this area have been observed at Mangatsiaka (S 24.9660 E 46.5574) (Hapke et al. 2011).Given the impact of habitat loss within the range of this species, it is likely that M. griseorufus is currently in decline. Despite this threat, the species is still thought to be relatively common within its range.
range: This species is found in southern and south-western Madagascar, where it ranges from Lamboharana south to the Toliara (= Tuléar) region, to the Beza-Mahafaly Special Reserve (south of the Onilahy River) in the south-east, and to Tsimanampetsotsa, Berenty, and Petriky in the extreme south (Mittermeier et al. 2010). The species occurs from sea level to 250 m.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. It is known to occur in the Tsimanampetsotsa National Park, Beza Mahafaly Special Reserve, the Berenty Private Reserve, Mikea and Andohahela (Mittermeier et al. 2010; Rakotondranary et al. 2011). It may be present as well in two other national parks (Isalo and Zombitse-Vohibasia), but this has yet to be confirmed.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered as it has been suspected to have undergone a population reduction of ≥80% over the past 21 years (three generations, assuming a generation length of seven years) due primarily to continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, and exploitation through unsustainable levels of hunting (e.g., Seiler et al. 2010, 2012). This cause has not ceased and will to a large extent not be easily reversible. A future population reduction of ≥80% over a 21 year period is also suspected due to the same cause. Furthermore, the area of occupancy of Lepilemur sahamalaza covers only between 12 and 472 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in extent of occurrence, area of occupancy and in quality of habitat of the remaining areas (Seiler et al. 2013a). The number of subpopulations and mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline.
habitat: The Sahamalaza Peninsula is part of a transition zone between the Sambirano region in the north and the western dry deciduous forest region in the south. The species inhabits both primary and mature secondary forests. Irrespective of the differences in overall structure and habitat parameters of the forest fragments in Ankarafa, the microhabitat in sportive lemurs’ home ranges as well as around sleeping sites was similar in all measured habitat parameters, as were all measured parameters for the different sleeping trees (Seiler et al. 2013b, 2014). Sahamalaza Sportive Lemurs chose the locations of their home ranges on the basis of different habitat variables, with abundance of sleeping sites and feeding trees as well as tree density and canopy cover being the most important factors (Seiler et al. 2014). Tall trees with large crowns, a high density of small trees, and dense canopy were particularly important for sleeping site choice (Seiler et al. 2013b). The Sahamalaza Sportive Lemur is a highly folivorous generalist herbivore and has been observed to feed on at least 42 different tree species, preferring the abundant species Clitoria lasciva, Mangifera indica, Garcinia pauciflora and Sorindeia madagascariensis and occasionally adding fruits of Ficus tiliaefolia, spiders, insects and insect larvae to its diet. It has prolonged periods of resting during its activity periods (Seiler et al. 2014). Home ranges covered an area of 1.4 ha (nightly ranges of 0.5 ha) and did not overlap between adult individuals (Seiler 2012). The very few sociopositive interactions between individuals took place between mother and kin. Although the small number of observed individuals makes it hard to finally conclude on the social organization of the Sahamalza Sportive Lemur, the low level of social interaction and cohesiveness suggest that the Sahamalaza Sportive Lemur has a very low degree of social complexity and is likely to be solitary (Seiler 2012). During daylight hours the Sahamalaza Sportive Lemur rested alone (except mother-infant pairs) in tree holes or in tree tangles (Seiler et al. 2013b). Tree holes used as sleeping sites were usually found in Bridelia pervilleana, whilst tree tangle sleeping sites are mostly located in Sorindeia madagascariensis. Individuals resting in tree holes usually sat at the entrance rather than inside the hole, possibly to increase sun exposure. During diurnal observations, 5-14 % of the sportive lemurs’ behaviour was active, although the animals never leave their sleeping sites or feed. Comparing the proportion of active behaviour between individuals resting in tree holes and those in tree tangles, animals in tree holes to have significantly higher levels of activity (Seiler et al. 2013b). Resting Lepilemur sahamalaza recognized predator vocalizations as indicators of increased predation risk, discerned vocalizations of different predators, and employed species-specific anti-predator behaviours (Seiler et al. 2013c). Furthermore, the studied Sahamalaza Sportive Lemurs were able to use information on predator presence and predator type in referential signals of different surrounding species, thereby taking advantage of the possibility of early predator detection through interspecific communication (Seiler et al. 2013d).
threats: Although some of the known distribution is within a protected area, forest clearing for agriculture, and timber-cutting for charcoal and construction continues at high rates, especially since the onset of the political crisis in Madagascar in 2009. The species is also subject to increasing levels of hunting (Seiler et al. 2012).
population: Population declines are suspected. This species is suspected to have undergone a population reduction of ≥80% over the past 21 years (three generations, assuming a generation length of seven years) due primarily to continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, and exploitation through unsustainable levels of hunting (e.g., Seiler et al. 2010, 2012). This cause has not ceased and will to a large extent not be easily reversible. A future population reduction of ≥80% over a 21 year period is also suspected due to the same cause. The number of subpopulations and mature individuals are also suspected to be in decline. Olivieri et al. (2005) recorded an encounter rate of 4.17 individuals/km2 in the forest of Ankarafa. This high encounter rate could be due to recent loss of habitat, forcing all animals to concentrate in the few remaining forest fragments. Ruperti (2007) recorded a mean density of 280 individuals/km2 in Ankarafa. Most recent data on Lepilemur density (Seiler et al. 2013a) suggests densities ranging from only 7 to 23 individuals/km2 in the same area. The differences between density estimations are most likely due to different methods of data collection. Whereas Ruperti measured lemur density inside one-hectare plots (one for each fragment), Seiler et al. counted all individuals found during 12 months of field work. Another factor that may have contributed to the differences is ongoing habitat alteration. During the study period from 2009 to 2011, various observations were made of illegal logging (often hardwoods), slash-and-burn agriculture and poaching of the sportive lemurs on the Sahamalaza Peninsula (Seiler et al. 2010, 2012).
range: Lepilemur sahamalaza is restricted to the Sahamalaza Peninsula. The precise range of this species is not known, but inferring from the biogeography of this area of Madagascar and from the distribution of the sympatric Eulemur flavifrons, the northern boundary of the range is likely to be the Andranomalaza (Maetsamalaza) River, and the southern boundary the Maevarano River (Mittermeier et al. 2010). While the extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 514 km2, the area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be between 12 and 472 km2. The three remaining forest blocks of the Sahamalaza Peninsula and their unique fauna are in grave danger of disappearing, despite having been under official protection since 2007. The forests are already extremely degraded and highly fragmented; nonetheless, bush fires and tree-felling are activities that are routinely pursued and accepted within the local society (Seiler et al. 2010, 2012). In 2010, the Ankarafa Forest measured only about 185 ha, divided into six fragments (10, 10, 13, 22, 30 and 100 ha; Seiler et al. 2010). In 2014, the Anabohazo forest covered a total area of ~5,000 ha (Randriatahina et al. 2014).
useTrade: The species is hunted at increasingly high rates by the local human population since the onset of the political crisis in Madagascar in 2009, due to an almost complete lack of law enforcement. The level of hunting is likely to be unsustainable (Seiler et al. 2012).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. The species is present in the Sahamalaza–Iles Radama National Park (Aire Protégée Terrestre, Marine et Côtière) which is part of the country's protected area network managed through Madagascar National Parks (MNP). The Sahamalaza Peninsula is also a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve (declared in 2001). The Association Européenne pour l'Etude et la Conservation des Lémuriens (AEECL), together with MNP and the local communities, is carrying out a community-based natural resource management programme to ensure a better protection of the very few remaining forest fragments in the park (Schwitzer et al. 2006). Further work is needed to clarify the exact distribution and taxonomic limits of the recently described Lepilemur species.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 3,000 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: Lepilemur betsileo is an inhabitant of the eastern rainforests. This large sportive lemur has a head-body length of 25 cm, a tail length of 28 cm, and a total length of 53 cm (Mittermeier et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to ongoing agricultural practices, use and modification of biological resources, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
population: Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss. A population size of 2,315 was estimated based on the IUCN range by Herrera et al. (2018) but the species has not been studied in the wild (Mittermeier et al. 2010).
range: This species is currently known from the Fandriana region in central-eastern Madagascar. The southern and northern extents of the range need to be confirmed, but are believed to be between the Mangoro/Onive and Namorona Rivers (Louis et al. 2006). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be less than 3,000 km2. Herrera et al. (2018) estimated the occupied area as 1,167 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. Present in the Fandriana Classified Forest (Louis et al. 2006). Further work is still needed to confirm the distribution and taxonomic limits of the species.

rationale: The extent of occurrence of Lepilemur petteri is estimated at 32,647 km2. This EOO is based on new information, establishing a much larger distribution than what defined in the original description in Louis et al. (2006). Furthermore, although this range would be normally considered quite large, the spiny forest habitat in south-western Madagascar has become severely fragmented, decreasing in area by 28% from 1950 to 2000 and undergoing the highest annual rate of deforestation (1.2%) during the 1990’s than any other forest type or region in Madagascar (Harper et al. 2007). This trend has persisted between 2000 to present, continuing the decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Past, and ongoing rates of decline in this species are suspected to be >30% over three generations, but trends in the future are suspected to get worse, and reductions in the next 3 generations could be >50%. Therefore, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: Petter’s Sportive Lemur is an inhabitant of spiny forest and dry forest in south-western Madagascar. As with other sportive lemurs, Lepilemur petteri is presumably largely folivorous, nocturnal and arboreal. At Beza-Mahafaly, L. petteri has been found to spend roughly 50% of the night resting and/or self-grooming, 30% feeding and 10–15% travelling. They rest significantly more and travel significantly less in the cooler, dry season. Social behaviour, vocalizing, and other behaviours make up 5% of their nocturnal active time. The activity of this species does not seem to be correlated with nocturnal illumination, although the animals seem to use the highest stratum of the forest less frequently during full-moon nights (Nash 1998, 2000, 2007).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from shifting agricultural practices.
population: Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss and the agriculture shift of habitat. It is suspected that the population has undergone a 30% reduction in the past three generations (21 years) due to extensive habitat loss (observed/documented by satellite imagery). The spiny forest habitat in south-western Madagascar has become severely fragmented, decreasing in area by 28% from 1950 to 2000 and undergoing the highest annual rate of deforestation (1.2%) during the 1990’s than any other forest type or region in Madagascar (Harper et al. 2007). Looking forward, it is suspected that population reduction rates will be greater than 50% in the next three generations, due to ongoing threats faced by the species.
range: Located in south-western Madagascar, this species was initially described in 2006 from a single locality, the Beza-Mahafaly region, which then set the species distribution from south of the Onilahy River and west of the Linta River (Louis et al. 2016). Further distribution studies (unpublished data; E. Louis pers. comm.) were completed over the following eight years, determining the western extend of Lepilemur petteri to be south of Toliara (Onilahy River), the eastern distribution defined as west of the Mandrare River, the northern extent from the Onilahy River, bordering the northern extent of the Mahafaly Plateau to the Linta River, extending easterly in the forest fragments to the Mandrare River. Due to deforestation, L. petteri has been essentially extirpated from the coastal forest south of the Mahafaly Plateau. Petter’s Sportive Lemur's distribution previously included a major portion of the distribution of L. leucopus which is now found in the Nord-Ifotaka NAP, Ankodida NAP, and the two Andohahela National Park spiny forest parcels, east of the Mandrare River, continuing westward into the Andohahela NP intermediate transitional zone parcel, and finally easterly bounded by the Anosy Mountain which includes the Andohahela National Park’s humid eastern rain forest parcel (L. leucopus does not extend into the eastern rain forest of Andohahela. But L. fleuretae occupies this ecosystem).   The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated as 32,647 km2 at an elevation range from 146 – 169 metres above sea level (avg. 157 metres).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: There is no suspected trade or general use, including active bushmeat or hunting of this sportive lemur.
conservationActions: Lepilemur petteri is listed on CITES Appendix I. This species is known to occur is the protected areas of Beza-Mahafaly Special Reserve, Tsimanampetsotsa and the Mahafaly Plateau Protected Area, along with the adjacent classified forests within its distribution. Further efforts to determine population numbers and densities, along with restoration of the spiny forest which it continues to reside, especially using advanced techniques for the Alluaudia and other spiny trees that this species utilizes.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 10,335 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As a result, it is suspected that the population has declined by at least 30% in the past, and that this rate of decline continues into the future. The number of mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of the eastern humid rainforests; limited research has been committed to this species and population and density information is not available.
threats: Hunting of this species is unsustainable (Golden 2005). Surveys documented 0.15 Lepilemur seali per household per year with 1,155 households in the region. The density of sportive lemurs is unknown, and they have a low reproductive rate; therefore, sustainability cannot be evaluated. Population numbers need to be defined based on regional densities due to the high hunting. Habitat degradation due to slash and burn agriculture is also a threat.
population: Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss across its currently known distribution. It is suspected that the population has declined by at least 30% in the past, and that this rate of decline continues into the future.Hunting of lemurs is high in this region (Golden 2005) and the geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. It has been estimated that there will be a 8% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).
range: This species is found in north-eastern Madagascar. Known only from the Anjanaharibe-Sud region, ranging south of the Antainambalana River at least as far as the Fananehana River and including the Makira region (Craul et al. 2008). Additional surveys are needed to determine the northern and southern extents of the distribution (Louis et al. 2006). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 10,335 km2 at an elevation from 982 – 1,047 metres above sea level (avg. 1,013 metres).  It has been estimated that there will be a 8% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: There is no commercial trade of this species; however, subsistence hunting is active and high in this region of Madagascar.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. It occurs in Anjanaharibe-Sud Special Reserve and northern Makira Protected Area. Further work is now urgently needed to clarify the distribution and taxonomic limits of the recently described Lepilemur species both north and south of its current known distribution (Ramaromilanto et al. 2009).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of Lepilemur tymerlachsonorum covers less than 75 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As a result, population declines of at least 80% are suspected to have taken place in the past and to continue into the future. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits primary and secondary tropical moist lowland forests that are subject to a dry season each year. It appears to be more common in secondary forest. In dense primary forest this species favors tree holes for sleeping; however, it was determined in a recent study in Lokobe that they spend more time resting in vegetation tangles in more open deciduous forest (Sawyer et al. 2015). It feeds on leaves, supplementing with some fruit, and bark. Births occur from August through November, mothers typically producing a single offspring. Predators include the Madagascar Harrier-hawk Polyboroides radiatus and the Madagascar Buzzard Buteo brachypterus (Mittermeier et al. 2010 and references therein).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from unsustainable agricultural practices, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
population: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of Lepilemur tymerlachsonorum covers less than 75 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. As a result, population declines of at least 80% are suspected to have taken place in the past and to continue into the future.Population density has been estimated at 63.2 individuals/km2 in Lokobe National Park (Bederu 2014).
range: This species is found in north-western Madagascar, its range currently confined to the Lokobe National Park region and agricultural fragmented forests on the island of Nosy Be. Furthermore, this may or may not be the species that formerly occurred on the island of Nosy Komba as well; in any case sportive lemurs have not been observed there in recent years (Roberts and Daly 2014). Zinner et al. (2007) found that some specimens from the mainland were identical in mitochondrial DNA sequence data to the type of Lepilemur tymerlachsonorum; however, this study only utilized partial d-loop or control region sequence data, truncated from the dataset which was utilized to describe this species. Mitogenomic studies did not support this finding (E. Louis, unpublished data). The locations of the holotypes of L. dorsalis and L. grandidieri still need to be determined so that the distribution and taxonomic designations of sportive lemurs on Nosy Be and other regions in north-western Madagascar can be established. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is highly restricted, estimated to be less than 75 km2 in elevations from 12 – 35 metres above sea level (avg. 15 metres).
useTrade: Individuals are caught by locals for illegal sale to tourists; unfortunately, this practice is lethal to sportive lemurs as they do not survive captivity due to diet restrictions.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. In areas where logging has reduced the availability of sleeping sites, researchers have provided nesting boxes. Individuals are still frequently caught by locals for illegal sale to tourists. The only protected area in which it occurs is the Lokobe Strict Nature Reserve. Further work is now urgently needed to clarify the distribution and taxonomic limits of the recently described Lepilemur species.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 2,350 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Therefore, there are thought to be declines in population (both in the past and in the future) at a rate of >50% over three generations. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species occurs in dry deciduous forests and in moist evergreen forest. The natural history of this species remains poorly studied by comparison to that of sportive lemurs inhabiting western and southern Madagascar. Adults seem to remain solitary during nightly bouts of foraging for leaves. Tree holes and vine tangles are preferred daytime shelters. The Madagascar ground boa is known to prey upon sportive lemurs in their sleeping sites. A study of this species in degraded secondary forest fragments south of Montagne d’Ambre National Park found that the animals eat a high proportion of fruits during the rainy season when fruits are abundant, whereas they only eat leaves during the dry season. The fruits of five plant families were consumed: Moraceae, Verbenaceae, Rubiaceae, Pittosporaceae, and one that was not identified. The species has also been observed to feed on latex (Mittermeier et al. 2008 and references therein).
threats: The major threats to this species are forest loss, particularly for charcoal (such as in Analamerana and Andrafiamena), and hunting (exacerbated by mining in the region for sapphires). It is occasionally kept as a pet within Madagascar (Reuter and Schaefer 2017).
population: A past population decline of 50% (over the last three generations) is suspected due to loss of habitat (confirmed through site visits and drone footage) and hunting. It is suspected that this rate of population decline will continue three generations into the future. Population densities have been variously estimated between 150 and 550 individuals/km² (Ratsirarson and Rumpler 1988, Hawkins et al. 1990), the higher figures coming from more humid forest environments such as Ankarana. However, utilizing these population densities from three decades ago to calculate current projected population numbers based on the Area of Occupancy (AOO) values are most likely going to grossly overestimated, given the observed declines in habitat area and quality (Mittermeier et al. 2008).
range: This species is found in northern Madagascar in the forests of Ankarana, Andrafiamena, and Analamerana, from 5 - 434 metres in elevation (avg. 167 m). This species has been documented to be sympatric with Lepilemur milanoii in the Andrafiamena or Anjahakely Classified Forest (Louis et al. 2006, Salmona et al. 2014). Field studies are needed to determine how these two species share the same forest. This population represents the only area where two Lepilemur species evidently occur in sympatry. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 2,350 km2. It has been estimated that there will be a 6% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015). This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food. Hunting has become more serious in recent years, with the appearance of large numbers of itinerant sapphire miners in the Ankarana region and the charcoal enterprises for Analamerana. It is occasionally kept as a pet within Madagascar (Reuter and Schaefer 2017).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. The species is found in the surrounding areas west of Montagne d’Ambre National Park and in three special reserves (Analamerana, Ankarana, and Fôret d’Ambre), as well as in the Andrafiamena Classified Forest (Mittermeier et al. 2008, Louis et al. 2006, Salmona et al. 2012). Improved management and protection of Analamerana is urgently required, and long-term scientific presence within the existing reserve is encouraged. Andrafiamena included within a protected area with excellent management will provide an opportunity to study Lepilemur ankaranensis and L. milanoii. Surveys to determine densities and population numbers should follow the studies from the early 1990’s.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 2,850 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of the eastern lowland rainforest. It has not yet been studied in the wild. There have been reports of this species being hunted in Betampona, and individuals being sold to tourists (on RN2) (Borgerson pers. comm.).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from shifting agriculture. There have been reports of this species being hunted in Betampona, and individuals being sold to tourists (on RN2) (Borgerson pers. comm.).
population: This species is in decline due to habitat loss and destruction.
range: Microcebus simmonsi is known only from the regions of Betampona, Zahamena and Tampolo in north-eastern Madagascar, the type locality is at 965 m asl (Louis et al. 2006, 2008). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be restricted to less than 2,850 km2. This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: There have been reports of this species being hunted in Betampona, and individuals being sold to tourists (on RN2) (Borgerson pers. comm.).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. It is currently known only from two strict nature reserves (Betampona and Zahamena) and Zahamena National Park. In 2009 there were four individuals of this species in captivity, all in the Tsimbazaza Zoo in Antananarivo, Madagascar (E. E. Louis Jr. pers. obs.).

rationale: This species’ extent of occurrence (EOO) is limited to Zombitse-Vohibasia, an area less than 276 km². It has been estimated that there will be a complete loss of the species' range by 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015). Moreover, this geographic range is severely fragmented, undergoing continued decline in area and quality of habitat due to subsistence harvesting of natural materials, artisanal mining, and frequent fires. Lemurs in this region are subject to significant hunting pressure. The species has been assessed as Endangered, but it is likely that with new information this species will be considered Critically Endangered.
habitat: No field studies are known for this recently described species (Lei et al., 2009). They inhabit the dry and deciduous forests of the Zombitse region and are presumed to be folivorous, as with other Lepilemur spp. Individual(s) return daily to the same tree roost to sleep during the daytime and so can be consistently observed if the roost is located. They are sympatric with the Red-tailed Sportive Lemur (Lepilemur ruficaudatus), which has only recently been observed in the same range as L. hubbardorum (Fanomezantsoa Andrianirina pers. comm.).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from shifting agriculture, subsistence resource use and small-scale mining, frequent forest/agricultural fires, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting. Shotguns, spears, hatchets, and dogs are used to hunt wildlife in this area. It has been estimated that there will be a complete loss of the species' range by 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).
population: Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss and significant hunting pressure (see Siers 2007). One individual Lepilemur hubbardorum was seen (by Bornbusch, S.) during a walking tour of the Zombitse-Vohibasia National Park. National Park guides stated that sightings are rare, with only a handful of individuals observed in the park within the areas that they frequent. In the 2 years mid-2016 to mid-2018, eight L. hubbardorum roosts have been identified in an approximately 40,000 m² area of the National Park (Fanomezantsoa Andrianirina pers. comm.). It is not known how many animals use one roost or if all roosts identified were occupied by L. hubbardorum. An adult individual L. hubbardorum was seen and photographed at a known tree roost in the park during July 2018 (LaFleur, M. pers. obs. 2018).
range: This species is only known to occur in the Zombitse-Vohibasia region, an area of south-western Madagascar that is north of the Onilahy and south of the Fiherena river. Surveys are needed to confirm the east/west boundaries of the species. The EOO (extent of occurrence) is estimated as less than 276 km². It has been estimated that there will be a complete loss of the species' range by 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food.
conservationActions: This species is listed in Appendix 1 of CITES. The only area where the species is known to occur is in the Zombitse-Vohibasia National Park. Data are needed on the ecology, distribution, and density of the species.

rationale: The extent of occurrence of this species covers less than 1,470 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of the eastern humid rainforests. It is nocturnal and arboreal. Primarily it differs from other members of the Avahi genus by having a reddish-brown dorsal coat and grey underline. It has a total length of 48-58.9 cm with an average weight of 900-1,200 g (Andriantompohavana et al. 2007, Mittermeier et al. 2008).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation.
population: Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss.
range: Currently Avahi betsileo is known in the Bemosary Classified forest (Fandriana), from high altitudes only. The regional distribution is tentatively set from south of the Mangoro River and north of the Mananjary River until its full distribution can be confirmed (Andriantompohavana et al. 2007, Mittermeier et al. 2008). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be less than 1,500 km².This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
conservationActions: It is listed on CITES Appendix I. This species is not known to occur in any official protected areas but is found in Bemosary Classified forest (Fandriana), which provides some degree of protection (Andriantompohavana et al. 2007, Mittermeier et al. 2008). There is a need for further survey work to determine the geographic range and population status of this species. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 143 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing extensive decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. This is leading to suspected population declines that are above 80% both in the past and in the future. The number of mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits dense primary forest fragments in mountainous and coastal areas.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to urbanization, agricultural practices, livestock farming, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
population: A population decline is suspected in this species due to an extensive decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. This is leading to suspected population declines that are above 80% both in the past and in the future. The number of mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline. Encounter rates in forest fragments near Anjajavy and between Antsohihy and Analalava are low. In 2010, Lepilemur grewcockorum were found to be present in only 3 of 11 sites (Anjajavy, Ambarijeby, and Bekofafa) in the Région Sofia. If present, its abundance ranged from 0.8 to 1 individual per km (Randrianambinina et al. 2010). The population is declining due to habitat loss and degradation as well as hunting. Forest loss in Région Sofia from 1990 to 2000 was 10% or 75,000 ha; from 2000 to 2010: 3% or 20,000 ha. Thus, forest lost during three generations of L. grewcockorum was 13% or 95,000 ha. Forest loss has increased again since 2009 due to political crisis and lack of law enforcement. Hunting is not quantifiable, but likely to be unsustainable due to high human population pressure (population growth of 2.7% annually). Future decline is likely to accelerate due to higher human population pressure and political instability. If the decline rate were to grow back to 1990-2000 levels, it would equal 20% loss during three generations through forest loss alone, not including hunting. The total population is divided into several isolated subpopulations without any genetic exchange. Subpopulations are likely to be small due to a high degree of habitat fragmentation (Mittermeier et al. 2008 and references therein).
range: It is currently known from the Anjiamangirana region in north-western Madagascar. Louis et al. (2006) gave the range as north of the Mahajamba River and south of the Maevarano and Sofia River. Formerly, the sportive lemurs found in this part of Madagascar were thought to be Lepilemur edwardsi. More recently, Craul et al. (2007) have described L. otto from between the Mahajamba and the Sofia, making the Sofia River effectively the southerly limit of L. grewcockorum. Clearly, the limits between L. edwardsi, L. otto, and L. sahamalazensis remain unresolved. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 143 km2 with an elevation of 172-361 metres above sea level (avg. 279 metres above sea level).
useTrade: The species is hunted at increasingly high rates by the local human population since the onset of the political crisis in Madagascar in 2009, due to an almost complete lack of law enforcement. The level of hunting is likely to be unsustainable.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. This species is known to occur in the Anjiamangirana Classified Forest as well as in a proposed 50,300 ha conservation area on the Bongolava Massif; however, there is no effective protection due to lack of enforcement. Management authority of either site should be directed at a strong organisation well versed in working with communities, leveraging the biodiversity to restore the habitat for mutual benefits. Restoration and timber use forest need to be mutually inclusive programmes, tied to the forestry department and local government agencies. Population evaluations of the primary sites should be conducted immediately.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species is 3,770 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also thought to be in decline, partly due to hunting. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of dry deciduous forests.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss, bushfires, habitat degradation from unsustainable agricultural practices and from hunting.
population: Population numbers are thought to be in decline due to habitat loss, fragmentation and hunting.
range: So far it is known from its type locality of Ambodimahabibo and from three other sites in north-western Madagascar (Craul et al. 2007, Mahaboubi et al. 2015). The distribution is limited by the Mahajamba River in the west and the Sofia River in the north (Craul et al. 2007). The species is bounded by Lepilemur grewockorum to the north (north of the Sofia), and by L. edwardsi to the west (west of the Mahajamba). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 3,770 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. It occurs in the 60,589-ha conservation area “Forest corridor of Bongolava”. More surveys are required in this heavily deforested and fragmented region to obtain information about the location, connectivity and viability of the remaining populations, so that appropriate local conservation measures can be proposed.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 1,100 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
