habitat: This species is known to inhabit the Antafondro Classified forest and perhaps the high elevations of the Tsaratanana Special Reserve (Louis et al. 2008). Research should be done on their ecology, as no specific information is available. They are thought to be nocturnal and arboreal but have not yet been studied in the wild.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from unsustainable agricultural practices.
population: This species is suspected to be in decline due to habitat degradation and loss.
range: This species is mainly found in the Antafondro Classified forest, in north-west Madagascar (Andriantompohavana et al. 2006, Louis et al. 2008). Its distribution is thought to range from the south of the Andranomalaza River to the north of the Maevarano River, but further research is required in order to establish its exact range (Louis et al. 2008). This species used to be misidentified with Microcebus sambiranensis in the past. The estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) is less than 1,100 km2. This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forests (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
conservationActions: This species is not known to occur in any protected areas, but is found in the Antafondro Classified Forest and perhaps also at high-elevations in the Tsaratanana Special Reserve (Louis et al. 2008). It is not known to be kept in captivity (I.J. Porton pers. comm. 2010).

rationale: Microcebus arnholdi's area of occupancy (AOO) covers between 500 and 1,004 km2, and its extent of occurrent (EOO) covers 13,577km2. Its geographic range is severely fragmented and covers about 8 locations, and is undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. It is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: This species inhabits northern rainforest (Louis et al. 2008, Sgarlata et al. in prep). It has not yet been studied in the wild, hence no specific information is known on their ecology nor behaviour, except that they are nocturnal and arboreal.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from various sources, including slash and burn agricultural practices.
population: The population density of Microcebus arnholdi is estimated to vary between 124 and 200 individuals/km2 (Sgarlata G.M., Le Pors B., Chikhi L., unpublished data). The population is likely to be in decline due to habitat loss.
range: After its discovery, Microcebus arnholdi was thought to occur exclusively in the montane forest of Montagne d'Ambre National Park and Foret d’Ambre Special Reserve (Louis et al. 2008). However, Weisrock et al. (2010) reported that an individual sampled close to Ambanja, further south of Montagne d’Ambre, was genetically associated to the Microcebus species occurring in Montagne d'Ambre. Now, new unpublished mitochondrial genetic data suggest that M. arnholdi exists also in one forest fragment close to Montagne d’Ambre and in several forests between the Loky and Fanambana Rivers, south-east of Montagne d’Ambre (Sgarlata et al. in prep). The area of occupancy (AOO) is now estimated to be between 500 and 1,004 km2. It occurs between 56 and 990 m of altitude (Sgarlata et al. unpublished).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forests (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
conservationActions: It exists in four protected areas: Montagne d'Ambre National Park and Foret d’Ambre Special Reserve (Louis et al. 2008), Northern COMATSA Protected Area and in the Binara forest, part of the Loky-Manambato Protected Area (Sgarlata. et al., in prep). It is not being kept in captivity.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species is estimated at 1,183 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing a continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits lowland rainforests. It has not yet been studied in the wild, so little is known about its behaviour and ecology.
threats: Habitat loss due to the rapid rate of deforestation from unsustainable agricultural practices in the region is a major threat to this species. Hunting does occur locally.
population: Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss and degradation.
range: This species is found in north-east Madagascar. This recently-described species is known from its type locality near the village of Anjiahely in the Makira region, about 26 km west of Maroantsetra (Radespiel et al. 2008) and from the island Nosy Mangabe (Louis and Lei 2016). The precise limits of its distribution and its relationship to neighbouring taxa remain to be determined. It occurs sympatrically with Microcebus mittermeieri at Anjiahely (Radespiel et al. 2008). It has a restricted extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated at 1,183 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forests (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: The species is hunted locally.
conservationActions: This species is found in the Nosy Mangabe Special Reserve (IUCN cat IV) and Makira Natural Park (IUCN cat II), which is currently under Wildlife Conservation Society management. This species is not kept in captivity (ISIS 2009).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 400 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. Even though the region where Lepilemur hollandorum is located has a human occupancy of approximately 223,000 people in approximately 30,000 households, the bushmeat survey of households that exploit the sportive population in the form of hunting revealed that 0.22 L. hollandorum/household in 2013 which converts to as many as 6,765 L. hollandorum may be eaten each year. As a result, the species is suspected of undergoing declines of at least 80% in the past and into the future. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Critically Endangered.
habitat: This species inhabits lowland rainforest. There is a significant decline in forest habitat and quality due to agricultural shifts to vanilla, palm and other cash crops in the region. Although there is no specific information available, it is presumed that this species largely folivorous as is the case with other sportive lemurs.
threats: Habitat loss to agricultural shifts and hunting are the major threats to the lemur biodiversity in the Mananara-Nord Biosphere Reserve in north-eastern Madagascar. A mean of 0.22 Lepilemur hollandorum are eaten per household per year (Golden and Borgerson, unpubl. data); therefore, an estimated 64 L. hollandorum were eaten by members of 287 households during the prior year. The Mananara region is home to a human population of approximately 223,000 people (INSTAT 2015). Excluding all major cities, this is a rural human population of 120,000 individuals or approximately 30,000 households (given a local median household size of 4 individuals per household). Therefore, as many as 6,765 L. hollandorum may be eaten each year. While this hunting is likely unsustainable, we currently lack the information on L. hollandorum density necessary for sustainability analysis.
population: The species is suspected to be undergoing population decline. The northern two of three parcels that form the Mananara-Nord Biosphere Reserve, Ivontaka and Ivontaka-Sud, are heavily damaged by agricultural shifts and deforestation. Therefore, surveys have documented this species only in Ivontaka-Sud and Verezanantsoro parcels. Population numbers continue to decline due to habitat loss and hunting. Hunting estimates for bushmeat are estimated to be over 6,000 sportive lemurs per year. Although these estimates are seemingly unsustainable, the humid environment of this region precludes a sustainable agriculture of domestic fowl as livestock. Therefore, the utilization of lemur populations, especially the easily hunted sportive lemurs which sleep during the day in tree holes and vines, creates the potential for dramatic declines in this species’ densities and overall population numbers. Given these threats, and that the extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 400 km², the species is suspected of undergoing population declines of at least 80% in the past and into the future.
range: This species is found in north-eastern Madagascar and is known from the Mananara-Nord region, with the only confirmed reports so far coming from the Ivontaka-Sud and Verezanantsoro (Ambinanibeorana) parcels of the Mananara-Nord Biosphere Reserve. The northern and southern limits of the range are still undefined, though they are tentatively assumed to be the area south of the Fahambahy or Mananara Rivers and north of the Simianona, Sandratsio, or Maningory Rivers, respectively (Ramaromilanto et al. 2009). Additional surveys are required to determine the full extent of the distribution. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is still estimated to be less than 400 km2, at elevations between 279 – 374 metres above sea level (avg. 299 metres).
useTrade: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from shifting agriculture, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. The only area in which this species is known to occur is the protected Mananara-Nord Biosphere Reserve. Further work is urgently needed to confirm the distribution, population status and densities, and ecology of this Lepilemur species and to verify if hunting is occurring at the estimated rate, along with any other threats in the region.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species is estimated to be 2,544 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also thought to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: Lepilemur scottorum inhabits primary lowland and littoral rainforest, but can also be found in selectively logged habitats despite potentially being negatively affected by high levels of habitat disturbance (Sawyer et al. 2017, Fenosoa et al. 2018). Its abundance was highest in the primary lowland forest where Garcinia commersonii was abundant. As rosewood (Dalbergia spp.) has been recorded as a key dietary resource for Lepilemur spp. (Ganzhorn et al. 2001), it may be that the continued illegal extraction of Dalbergia spp. from the Masoala peninsula is negatively impacting L. scottorum abundance (Sawyer et al. 2017). It is presumably largely folivorous and nocturnal. In primary forest habitat, they use tree holes as sleeping sites.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to ongoing shifting agricultural practices and illegal timber harvesting, in addition to relatively low levels of subsistence hunting.
population: Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss from shifting agriculture (including fires) and illegal logging, in addition to hunting pressure and frequent cyclones. Density estimates were recorded at 25.2 individuals/km2 near Ambodiforaha (Sawyer et al. 2017), compared to 33 individuals/km2 recorded by Sterling and Rakotoarison (1998).
range: This species is found in north-eastern Madagascar. It is currently known only from Masoala National Park (Lei et al. 2008; Mittermeier et al. 2010). Additional surveys are needed to determine the eastern and northern limits of its range. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 2,544 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: While generally not targeted by hunters because of their bitter taste, Lepilemur scottorum is occasionally opportunistically hunted using slingshots and found objects (Borgerson 2016).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. The only protected area in which this species is known to occur is Masoala National Park. Further work is urgently needed to confirm the distribution, population status, ecology, and threats to Lepilemur scottorum throughout the Masoala National Park and adjacent unprotected habitats. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species is 2,544 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. The number of mature individuals is also suspected to be in decline. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: Avahi mooreorum has a distinct white patch on the posterior surface of the hindlimb is the main visual characteristic for this species. Its total length ranges from 57.8 to 70.3 cm, with an average weight of 920 g, it is lighter than A. laniger. Its overall pelage is a mix of different browns with gradual lightening towards the base of the tail (Andriantompohavana et al. 2007, Lei et al. 2008). A. mooreorum inhabits primary lowland and littoral rainforest, selectively logged habitats as well as agricultural mosaics, it is currently only known from lowland rainforest (up to 274 m asl) (Sawyer et al. 2017). High density of this species is positively associated with high abundances of Garcinia commersonii and Eugenia spp. in the primary lowland rainforest (Sawyer et al. 2017). In areas of increased disturbance, they use lower forest stratum, which may increase the threat of hunting pressure (Fenosoa et al. 2018). It is presumably largely folivorous, as well as nocturnal and arboreal as individuals have not been observed active during daylight hours or exhibiting terrestrial activity. Avahi mooreorum have been observed in groups of up to 4 individuals. In disturbed areas, solitary individuals are seen frequently, whereas pairs are most frequently observed in undisturbed habitat. This is possibly a response to lower resource availability in areas of high disturbance (Sawyer et al. 2017). In primary forest areas, they sleep in clumps of dense foliage during the daytime.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation due to ongoing shifting agricultural practices and illegal timber harvesting, in addition to relatively high levels of subsistence hunting.
population: Density estimates were recorded at 93.8 individuals/km2 near Ambodiforaha (Sawyer et al. 2017), compared to 25 individuals/km2 recorded by Sterling and Rakotoarison (1998). These contrasting findings may be an indication of the localized success that the creation of Masoala National Park in 1997 has had on the Avahi population. Despite the localized high density in the main tourist area, this species is in decline due to habitat loss from illegal logging and shifting agricultural practices, frequent cyclones and fires, as well as unsustainable levels of hunting.
range: It is found in north-eastern Madagascar, where it is currently known only from Masoala National Park (Lei et al. 2008, Mittermeier et al. 2010). Further surveys are required to confirm the northern extent of this species within this protected area and, possibly, in intervening forest fragments between Makira Natural Park (where Avahi laniger has been confirmed to occur) and the Masoala Peninsula (Mittermeier et al. 2010). The Extent of Occurrence is estimated to be 2,544 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: Avahi mooreorum is hunted opportunistically using slingshots and found objects (Borgerson 2016, unpub. data).
conservationActions: Listed on CITES Appendix I. It is known to occur in one protected area (Masoala National Park). It would appear that the Avahi mooreorum population around Ambodiforaha is quite healthy and likely the result of the creation of Masoala National Park (Sawyer et al. 2017). As this village is the park’s main tourist entry point, lemur populations here are abundant. Further work is needed to confirm the distribution, population status, ecology, and threats to Avahi mooreorum throughout the Masoala National Park and adjacent unprotected habitats. It is not being kept in captivity (C. Schwitzer pers. comm. 2018).

rationale: Given that Cheirogaleus medius’ geographic distribution is now considered to be constrained to western dry deciduous forests and given the fact the Menabe region has been undergoing unprecedented rates of deforestation, it is very likely that C. medius is currently in decline (Hudson et al. 2019). Therefore, the species is assessed as Vulnerable based on a suspected future decline of 30% due to decline in habitat quality and EOO, as well as due to potential exploitation. Further information on population status, and threats may warrant listing this species in a more threatened category in the future.
habitat: Cheirogaleus medius inhabits western dry deciduous forests. Fruits, flowers, seeds and the tender parts of plants are dietary staples, with invertebrates being eaten in small amounts and small vertebrates taken on occasion. C. medius, like other dwarf lemur species, accumulates large quantities of fat within weeks in preparation for hibernation. At Kirindy, during the prehibernation fattening period, dwarf lemurs consume mostly fruits with high sugar content, which is then converted to fat deposits, thus the name fat-tailed dwarf lemur (Fietz and Ganzhorn 1999). Individual home ranges approach 1-2 ha. Small family groups consist of the reproductively active female-male pair and their offspring from one or two breeding seasons. During the day, which is the resting period, individuals occupy tree holes with up to five individuals occupying a single shelter (Fietz and Dausmann 2006). The breeding season occurs from September to November, leading to a gestation period of about two months. One to four (usually two) offspring are born in December or January. Full sexual maturity is reached during the second year of life (Mittermeier et al. 2008). Longevity record in captivity is 29 years at the Duke Lemur Center, NC, USA (Blanco and Zehr 2015).
threats: Threats include habitat loss, primarily due to slash-and-burn agriculture, charcoal extraction, and bushfires; in addition to hunting.
population: Although Cheirogaleus medius was considered to be a widespread and abundant species, there has been recent concern about low densities and lack of sightings at sites under protection, where this species has been studied long term, e.g. CNFEREF Kirindy. Given that C. medius’ geographic distribution is now constrained to western dry deciduous forests and given the fact the Menabe region has been undergoing unprecedented rates of deforestation, it is very likely that C. medius is currently in decline (Hudson et al, 2019). As such, it is suspected that, due to a decline in habitat quality and Extent of Occurrence (as well as due to potential exploitation of the species), that a population reduction of at least 30% will occur over the next three generations (21 years).Prior estimates ranged between 40-400 individuals/km² (see Mittermeier et al. 2008 and references therein). In central Menabe, densities were recorded at 140 individuals/km2. C. medius co-occurs with Microcebus berthae; they are found in higher densities when together. C. medius is able to live in fragments of 200-300 ha.
range: The updated geographic range of this species is limited to the dry forests of western Madagascar, from Tsingy de Bemaraha to the north to Zombitse to the south. Ranges from sea level to 800 m. More generally, this species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. Its presence is reported at Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, CNFEREF Kirindy, Kirindy Mitea National Park, Analalava and Zombitse. There are ~25 individuals of Cheirogaleus medius housed at the Duke Lemur Center, North Carolina, USA as of 2019.

rationale: Given the continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, in addition to fragmentation throughout its range, this species is assumed to be in decline. This species has been reported to be hunted, most severely in the northern range. Based on habitat decline and actual levels of exploitation, and using the precautionary principle, Cheirogaleus major is listed as Vulnerable. Further studies into population status, geographic distribution, and threats may warrant listing this taxon as Endangered in the future.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of Madagascar’s eastern lowland forests where conditions of water and food availability are not as seasonally severe as in the drier western deciduous forests. During the active season, this species occupies tree holes or nest-like structures (Blanco, per.obs., Lahann 2007). The species prepares for hibernation by storing excess fat in its tail, but they have shorter hibernation periods than other dwarf lemur species. Cheirogaleus major hibernates inside tree holes and/or underground burrows (Blanco et al. 2018). Home ranges of adult females extend ~4 ha and appear to include those of adult males and juveniles as well (Lahann 2007). Sleeping groups of up to three adult animals have been observed both in tree holes and clumps of vegetation. Mating behaviour ensues shortly after emergence from torpor in October and November, females giving birth to two to three infants in January after a gestation of about 70 days (Petter-Rousseaux 1964). However, a number of observations of this species, cited here and elsewhere in this account, were made in Andasibe (= Périnet), and probably refer to C. crossleyi.
threats: This species is presumably undergoing localized declines due to habitat loss from slash-and-burn agriculture. There is also evidence of hunting, with particularly high hunting pressure in northeastern Madagascar, at a rate of ~0.38 per year/household in places like Masoala, Makira, Mananara and <0.01 individuals per year/per household in Kianjavato forest (Borgerson, 2016, Borgerson et al. 2018, Brook et al. in press).
population: Population densities have been estimated at 59–110 individuals/km2 in different locations. However, it should be noted that a number of these observations were made in Andasibe (= Périnet), which would mean that they may refer to Cheirogaleus crossleyi. It is suspected that population numbers are declining. C. major shows a negative edge effect (densities are lower in closer proximity to the forest edge) (Lehman et al. 2007). It is suspected that this species is undergoing a population decline (over a 24 year period) of at least 30% due to continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, in addition to fragmentation throughout its range. For context, Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018). In addition, this species has been reported to be hunted, most severely in the northern range.
range: This species is found in north-eastern, eastern-central and south-eastern Madagascar. In the north-east, Cheirogaleus major has been found at Marojejy National Park, Makirovana-Tsihomanaomby complex, Masoala and Makira (Blanco, pers. obs., Brooke et al. in press, Williams et al. 2019). In the eastern rainforests, it has been found in Mananara, Tampolo, Sahafina and Andasibe (Lei et al., 2014, McLain et al, 2017, Razafindrasolo, pers. obs.) According to Groeneveld et al. (2009), C. major is found from the south-eastern tip of the island near Tolagnaro (= Fort-Dauphin) potentially all the way up to near the northern tip, with an additional, small population isolate in the central-west. The southern limit of its distribution is particularly interesting, since two other dwarf lemur species can also be found in the same general region, although not to date in the same forests. Andreas Hapke has found C. major in the humid forests of the Vohimena and Anosy mountains and the littoral forest at Mandena, and believes it might also occur in Sainte-Luce, but this has yet to be confirmed (Hapke et al. 2005). C. major generally occupies low elevation rainforests, whereas C. crossleyi can occupy low as well as high elevation sites. These species can be found to live in sympatry (Williams et al. 2019).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018). C. major shows a negative edge effect (densities are lower in closer proximity to the forest edge) (Lehman et al. 2007).
useTrade: There is evidence of hunting, with particularly high hunting pressure in north-eastern Madagascar, at a rate of ~0.38 per year/household in places like Masoala, Makira, Mananara and <0.01 individuals per year/per household in Kianjavato forest (Borgerson, 2016, Borgerson et al. 2018, Brook et al., in press).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. This species is relatively widespread but additional taxonomic revision is pending. It is reported to occur in four national parks: Andasibe-Mantadia, Mananara-Nord, Marojejy, Masoala, one strict nature reserve, Betampona and Makira Natural Park, as well as in the Mandena Conservation Zone, east of Tolagnaro. More recently, based on genetic analysis, Cheirogaleus major has been found in Makirovana/Tsihomanaomby (NE Madagscar) living in sympatry with C. medius-like and C. crossleyi. The population of C. major at Tsihomanaomby, however, differs morphologically from that of Marojejy National Park, particularly in fur coloration, with more grey-brownish coat in the former compared to reddish-brownish in the latter (Blanco, pers. obs., Williams et al. 2019). Population densities in some of these locations seem to be comparatively low, and C. major shows a negative edge effect (densities are lower in closer proximity to the forest edge) (Lehman et al. 2007).

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers less than 5,200 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline because of human pressures, including slash-and-burn agriculture. Even though this species is found in three protected areas, Ranomafana National Park, Andringitra National Park, and the COFAV corridor, it can also be found in unprotected forest fragments that are decreasing in area. This species seems to be abundant at forest edges. Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: Microcebus rufus is reported to occur in rainforests, and also in secondary forest formations, bamboo forests, old plantations and even Eucalyptus groves. This species sleeps in tree holes and leaf nests during the day and has been observed to use old bird nests. Mating takes place in September and October, and 1-3 young are born following a two month gestation period (see Mittermeier et al. 2008, and references therein). The majority of females go into oestrus the first week of October and have 2-3 offspring which are kept in leaf nests (Blanco 2008). One male travelled over 1 km one night and returned the next night (P.C. Wright pers. obs.). Genetic evidence shows that individuals can disperse across a road and a river, a distance of 1 km (C. Karanewsky per. obs.).
threats: The principal threat to this species is habitat loss due to slash-and-burn agriculture.
population: Microcebus rufus has an estimated density of 23.52 individuals/km2 with a total estimated population of 7,762 within Ranomafana National Park (Wright et al. 2012). Population numbers are suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss.
range: The range of this species was tentatively considered to include much of the eastern rainforest, at least from Tolagnaro in the south to Tsaratanana in the north. However new studies have led to the discovery of new eastern mouse lemur species, thereby reducing the range of Microcebus rufus (Louis et al. 2008). The range is now assumed to extend from Ranomafana National Park to Andringitra National Park only (E.E. Louis Jr. pers. obs.). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to measure less than 5,200 km2.This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. This species is present in Andringitra National Park, Ranomafana National Park (Feistner and Schmid 1999, Wright and Porter 2004, Louis et al. 2008). Some individuals are in captivity (Zurich Zoo, University of Hanover, Stanford University, etc).

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable, as it has a small range with an extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 13,670 km², and its habitats are being lost and becoming more fragmented due to aridization across the whole region.
habitat: Very little information is available; the species is known only from the type locality in a city garden. The species occupies grasslands that border cultivated farms, grape gardens and foothills in altitudes ranging from 1,100 m up to more than 2,000 m asl (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2017).
threats: There is increasing aridity in the region at lower latitudes, for example where the most southern ridge of the Microtus species is, which causes fragmentation of the species' habitats (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2017).
population: No data area available on population size or trends for this species.
range: This vole is restricted to the type locality and a series of around four specimens. A second survey was conducted in the same area and failed to find the species although found closely related to Microtus socialis (Krystufek and Kefeliojlu 2002). The type locality was in a garden within the city of Shiraz (Iran) described over 80 years ago, and so the species may be threatened if it is restricted to the vicinity of the type locality (D. Kock pers. comm. 2008).Recent work identified the species from two localities (Mamasani and Bamo National Park) in Fars province, but it seems that the species has really restricted range between these two locations and that populations are severely fragmented both due to climate changes and increasing of the aridity in the area and by anthropogenic activities (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2017).
conservationActions: Since the species is known from at least one protected national park, there is still hope to rescue the populations from the extinction, however, further research is need on its ecology, population size and threats to the species in the region (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2017).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 18,600 km², it occurs in fewer than 10 locations, and the extent of its habitat is decreasing because of deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture, specifically cattle ranching.
habitat: This species inhabits dense humid forest, Puna grassland, Subalpine rain páramo or Montane rainforest (Osgood 1914, Thomas 1926, Leo and Romo 1992). Specimens have been found in bare or shrub rocky places, shrubby places bordering streams, or at the border of continuous humid montane forests (Leo and Romo 1992). This species is terrestrial and nocturnal. It occurs in cloud forest and close to paramo (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture, specifically cattle ranching.
population: This species is locally common to frequent (V. Pacheco pers. comm).
range: This species is endemic to Peru. It is limited to northern Peru (Amazonas, San Martin, and La Libertad departments), east of the Marañón river in the Cordillera Oriental, at elevations between 3,050 and 3,660 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Abiseo National Park (V. Pacheco pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species has been found in montane forest, on rocky and wooded hillsides. It is thought to be terrestrial (S. Anderson 1997). It is present in primary and second growth forest (V. Pacheco and J. Vargas pers. comm.).
threats: Some populations of this species are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is locally common (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is restricted to montane forests in the Andes in the La Paz department of northwestern Bolivia, from 2,360 to 3,300 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in Cotapata National Park (J. Vargas pers. comm).

rationale: Although this species has a relatively narrow distribution it is listed as Least Concern as it is tolerant to some degree of habitat modification and occurs within three National Parks and it is not declining at a rate that merits a higher threat listing.
habitat: This species is terrestrial and its preferred habitat is páramo (Gómez- Laverde et al. 1997); a pregnant female was found in local wet season (July), and its diet is composed mainly of young leaves and other green part of plants (Lopez-Arévalo et al. 1993). It does not occur in unnatural grassy areas created for pasture (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
threats: The biggest threat to this species is habitat conversion into unnatural pasture outside protected areas (Rivas and Gómez-Laverde 2008).
population: It is a relatively common species (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm.).
range: This species' distribution is constrained to the Cordillera Oriental of the Andes in central Colombia, in the departments of Boyacá and Cundinamarca. It has an elevation range from 2,550 to 3,500 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: It occurs in several protected areas (M. Gómez-Laverde pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits mainly montane forests, where they are found apparently in low abundance (Medina et al. 2012, V. Pacheco pers. comm). Its diet is composed primarily of monocots (89.2%) plus a few arthropods (< 5%; Noblecilla and Pacheco 2012).
threats: Some populations of this species are affected by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is rare (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species is endemic to Peru, its range extends from Amazonas to Cuzco Departments, in montane forests on the eastern Andean slopes. It occurs at elevations between 1,400 to 3,400 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (V. Pacheco pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its abundance within its restricted distribution, its presumed large population, its occurrence in protected areas and because its habitat is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The habitats of this species include upper montane elfin forest and the edge of cloud forest (Salazar- Bravo and Yates 2007; O. P. Pearson field notes, MVZ archives; V. Pacheco pers. comm.). Individuals had been captured on the ground, but most of the time in the arboreal strata (Salas et al. 2013). T. oreas’ diet had a very high frequency of intact seeds and arthropods (Sahley et al. 2015).
threats: Some populations of this species are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture.
population: This species is considered rare (Pacheco and Vargas pers. comm.), but it is presumed it has a large population.
range: This species inhabits eastern montane forests from northern Peru (Amazonas department) to central Bolivia (Cochabamba department). Its altitudinal range is 2,460 to 3,650 m  (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas, such as Madidi National Park, in Bolivia, and Manu National Park, in Peru (V. Pacheco and J. Vargas pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a large distribution, is common, adaptable, and does not appear to be in decline.
habitat: Observed habitats include pristine and secondary upper montane forests, Queñua Andean forests (Polylepis weberbaueri), and montane bamboo forests (V. Pacheco pers. comm., L. Luna pers. comm.). Specimens had been captured in tall shrub mixed with short and slender trees, among small trees (about 5 m high), densely covered by mosses and lichens, and the ground by short grasses browsed by cattle, in forest with trees reaching heights of 10 to 25 m high, and with numerous species of shrubs, epiphytes, tree ferns, and vines (V. Pacheco,pers. obs.), and near a stream (L. Luna pers. comm.). Pacheco (pers. obs.) observed that these rodents are excellent and agile climbers.
threats: Some populations are threatened by deforestation, fragmentation, and agriculture (Pacheco and Vargas 2008).
population: This species is locally common (V. Pacheco pers. comm.).
range: This species occurs along montane forests in the Andes of Ecuador and northern Peru, at elevations between approximately 1,150 and 3,350 m (Pacheco 2015).
conservationActions: This species does not occur in any protected area (V. Pacheco pers. comm). Further surveys are needed on ecology, habitat requirements and conservation.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because it is widespread and common in a major portion of its range. Its population is currently stable and so is not declining fast enough for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found mainly in high desert (sagebrush, shadscale, greasewood). In southwestern Idaho, highest densities were in winterfat-Sandberg's bluegrass communities, with intermediate densities in big sagebrush-dominated communities and lowest densities in shadscale communities; scarce in communities dominated by exotic annuals (Yensen et al. 1992). It generally occurs in well-drained soils, especially embankments, often around desert springs and irrigated fields. This species makes extensive burrow systems and young are born in a nest chamber in an underground burrow. This species breeds late January-early March, depending on locality. Drought may suppress breeding. Gestation lasts 24 days and females typically have a litter size between 5-10 with one litter per year. Males mature as yearlings or as two year-olds; females breed as yearlings (Rickart 1987). This species' mean home range was estimated at 1,357 m² and they will form colonies but families and individuals live separately. Compared to other ground squirrels, it has high fecundity and low adult survivorship and is short-lived (Rickart 1988). Their diet includes herbaceous vegetation (grasses, forbs, and exotic annuals), and seeds; it may also eat some shrub parts and animal matter. They will often feed on crops. Emerges from dormancy in late winter or early spring (males before females) but returns to dormancy during May-July, when grasses dry out.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat conversion to agriculture and rangeland degradation. A decline in the late 1980s in the Snake River Birds of Prey Area in southwestern Idaho was due to widespread conversion of desert shrublands to exotic annual-dominated communities by wildfires (Yensen et al. 1992). It is also subject to local shooting and poisoning as an agricultural pest (Wilson et al. 2017).
population: This species forms colonies more than 30 adults/ha. Although densities of 331/ha (adults and juveniles) have been reported, this figure is likely to be an overestimate. Studies showing 3-32 adults/ha (not including juveniles) are likely to be more representative.
range: This species occurs in southeastern Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada and Utah (Wilson et al. 2017).
conservationActions: This species is not known to occur in any protected areas.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable as it has a restricted extent of occurrence (8,806 km² ), occurs in 3-5 locations and there is a continuing decline in its extent of occurrence, area, extent and quality of its habitat due to agricultural expansion, urban development and introduced grass species.
habitat: This species is found in high desert sagebrush (Artemisia) regions and cultivated fields (Wilson et al. 2017) and is only active for 4-5 months, spending most of the year hibernating in underground burrows (Scheffer 1941). The active season begins from late January to late February and extends until late May to late June. The diet is largely green vegetation, with Sandberg's bluegrass (Poa secunda), western tansymustard (Descurainia pinnata), lupine (Lupinus laxiflorus) and woollypod milkvetch (Astragalus purshii) occurring most frequently in their diet (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011). This species fulfills several important ecological functions, including affecting soil structure and fertility through their burrowing, providing burrow habitats for other wildlife, and serving as prey for numerous predators (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011).
threats: Much of this species' geographic range has been converted for agriculture and urban development; less than 10% of habitat in its native distribution remains and many historical sites no longer contain individuals (Yensen and Sherman 2003, Wilson et al. 2017). Its remaining shrub-steppe habitat is being degraded by cheatgrass and other exotic annuals (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011). Studies of closely related species in Idaho found a strong negative relationship with cheatgrass since it is not a reliable year-to-year food source (Yensen et al. 1992). This species is also threatned by poisoning and shooting in some locations where farmers and fruit growers consider this squirrel a pest  (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011). Disease and droughts are other potential threats to this species  (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011).
population: The species occurs in concentrated colonies and presumably as scattered individuals distributed across the landscape. No comprehensive population surveys of this species has been conducted. However, overall abundance appears to have undergone a significant decline (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011).
range: This species occurs only in Washington, between the Yakima and Columbia Rivers south of the Wenatchee Mountains (Yensen and Sherman 2003).
conservationActions: Little research and few conservation actions have been aimed specifically at this species (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife 2011). Most individuals reside on privately owned land (Wilson et al. 2017). The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife acquired approximately 17,500 acres of shrub-steppe habitat east of Ellensburg in 2006-2007. This included some habitat for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered, as it is only known from two mountain tops, with an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 4,092 km2, where there is ongoing loss of forest habitat on the lower slopes due to conversion of land to agricultural use, and the extraction of timber for firewood and building materials.
habitat: This species is associated with tropical montane forest.
threats: There is deforestation on the lower slopes of the species mountain habitat through conversion of land to agricultural use, and the extraction of timber for firewood and building materials.
population: There is little information available on the abundance of this species. It is known only from a few specimens.
range: This species is only found on Mt. Lefo and Mt. Oku, Cameroon.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. There is an urgent need to effectively conserve remaining areas of montane forest in Cameroon.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence is less than 20,000 km², its range is severely fragmented, and there is an ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, as well as the number of locations and subpopulations and number of mature individuals due to persecution and other human disturbances. This species is also subject to extreme fluctuations in the number of locations and subpopulations and number of mature individuals.
habitat: Urocitellus endemicus originally inhabited shrub-steppe communities dominated by big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata), perennial bunchgrasses (especially Poa secunda, Pseudoregnaria spicatum, Festuca idahoensis, Elymus elymoides, and Hesperostipa comata), and diverse forbs especially Lupinus spp. (Yensen 1991, Yensen and Sherman 1997, E. Yensen personal observations). Approximately 43% of their historic range has been converted to agriculture or urban use (E. Yensen, unpublished data). They survive in degraded shrub steppe invaded by exotic annuals (e.g., Bromus tectorum, Taeniatherium asperum, Sisymbrium altissimum, Poa bulbosa) (Barrett 2005, Lohr et al. 2013). They feed primarily on forbs with some grasses (Tarifa and Yensen 2004, Tarifa and Yensen in prep).Mating occurs soon after spring emergence; Gestation lasts about 3.5 weeks; juveniles remain in the burrow until weaned approximately 3.5 weeks after birth. Litter sizes are about 6 weaned young per litter (based on placental scar counts). There is one litter per year (Yensen and Sherman 1997). They prefer soils with higher percentages of silt and sand, greater perennial grass cover, and more mesic north and east aspects with more remnant native vegetation. They tend to avoid areas with high cover of exotic annuals and lower plant species diversity (Lohr et al. 2013).
threats: Threats include recreational shooting and poisoning. Although no longer a candidate species, it is a state protected species (as of 2017) and a Bureau of Land Management "sensitive species", but the State of Idaho authorizes kill permits to land owners (Bosworth, 2017). Idaho Department of Fish and Game will monitor and perform habitat occupancy modelling for the foreseeable future (Bosworth 2017). Other threats include habitat degradation; the species is more abundant in areas with remnant native vegetation, especially on east and north aspects with better moisture retention (Lohr et al. 2013). Fat storage for hibernation, overwinter survival, and overall fitness are higher at sites with more native species (Barrett 2005, Lohr 2013).
population: Urocitellus endemicus populations have fluctuated considerably over the past four decades. Their numbers were low in the early 1980s, high later in the decade, very low in the late 1990s-early 2000, then increased coincident with candidate status for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act (Yensen 2001). Populations were relatively stable from 2005 to 2015. In 2015, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, citing the stability under protection, removed the species from candidate status (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2015).
range: This species is known only from Gem, Payette, and Washington Counties in southwestern Idaho, USA (plus one sight record from extreme southern Adams County). The historic geographic range is estimated at 2,400 km² making it the second smallest of any ground squirrel in the world (Yensen 1991, Yensen and Sherman 2003a, and E. Yensen unpub. data).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is widespread, there are no major threats, and its population is not declining fast enough for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: Recorded habitats for this species include arid and semiarid shrub-grass associations, openings in montane coniferous forests dominated by sagebrush (Washington), willow-fringed creeks, marshes (Oregon), bunchgrass associations, sagebrush-aspen associations (California), sagebrush-grass associations (Nevada), alkaline shrubland (Utah) (Hoffman et al. 1969, Williams 1984, Cornely et al. 1992). Diet probably resembles other shrews, feeding primarily on insects and other small invertebrates (worms, molluscs, centipedes, etc.). It is active throughout the year, and may be active at any time throughout the day or night, but probably most active during morning and evening hours.
threats: There are no known threats to this species.
population: Neither population numbers nor area of occupied habitat is known. Verts and Carraway (1998) suggest that the apparent rarity of this shrew is primarily an artifact of little sampling effort.
range: This species is known from Western North America, from the Columbia Plateau to the northern Great Plains (Junge and Hoffman 1981, Cornely et al. 1992, Long and Hoffmann 1992). Recorded occurrences include northeastern California (Shohfi et al. 2006), northwestern and northeastern Nevada (Ports and George 1990), central and eastern Oregon, southeastern Washington, south-central British Columbia (D. Nagorsen pers. comm.), west central Idaho, Montana (east to the North Dakota border), northwestern and southwestern Wyoming, west central Colorado (Long and Hoffmann 1992), and the south shore of the Great Salt Lake; there are no records for Snake River Plain of southern Idaho or from the bulk of the Great Basin in Nevada or Utah south of the 40th meridian. It has been recorded from elevations of about 1,280-2,550 m asl.
conservationActions: This species is known from Sheldon National Antelope Refuge, Nevada (Hoffmann and Fisher 1978), Timpie Spring Waterfowl Management Area, Utah (Tomasi and Hoffman 1984) and Lassen Volcanic National Park, California (Shohfi et al. 2006). There is a need for more pitfall trapping across western North America to determine the species' population status and range. Since its habitat needs are poorly known, this is critical to protecting the species.

rationale: The African Wolf is widely distributed across the northern and north-eastern parts of the African continent, and while it is known to be declining in parts of its range, there is no evidence that these declines would be sufficient for the species to meet the thresholds for listing as threatened.
habitat: Due to its tolerance of dry conditions and its omnivorous, adaptable diet, the African Wolf is able to occupy semi-desert, short to medium grasslands and savannas (Moehlman and Jhala 2013). In Ethiopia, the species has been recorded at elevations up to 3,800 m in the Bale Mountains of Ethiopia (Sillero-Zubiri 1996) down to sea level in Eritrea (Moehlman and Hayssen 2018). In Ethiopia, the species feeds on rodents, insects, carcasses and occasionally predates on livestock (Atickem et al. 2017, Gutema et al. 2018).
threats: The African Wolf is probably declining slowly across parts of its range due to lack of habitat and indiscriminate predator control programmes. The species is considered as a key livestock predator in many parts of the Ethiopian Highlands (Atickem et al. 2017) and elsewhere. They are frequently found in close proximity to human settlement (Yirga et al. 2017) possibly due to higher food availability from human waste and livestock prey. However, extended urbanization may also affect the availability of shelter, especially for breeding. The African Wolf also may occasionally be hunted as a game species and eaten, as has been recorded in Morocco (F. Cuzin pers. comm. 2007).
population: In the Serengeti National Park, Tanzania, densities can range as high as two adults per km² (Moehlman 1983, 1986, 1989).
range: The African Wolf is widespread in the northern and north-eastern parts of Africa, occurring from Senegal and Morocco in the west to Egypt, Ethiopia and Somalia in the east, then ranging southwards to northern Nigeria, northern Cameroon, northern Central African Republic and northern Tanzania (Jhala and Moehlman 2004, Gaubert et al. 2012, Moehlman and Jhala 2013, Moehlman and Hayssen 2018). The species has only recently been recognized as distinct, on morphological and molecular grounds, from the Eurasian Golden Jackal (Canis aureus) and hence the range of the Golden Jackal in Africa as previously understood is here taken to represent the range of the African Wolf.
useTrade: There is no significant trade in African Wolf products, although skins and tails are very occasionally sold.
conservationActions: Legal protectionNot included on the CITES Appendices.Presence in protected areasThe African Wolf is present in a great number of protected areas across their range, including the Serengeti-Masai Mara-Ngorongoro complex in East Africa. CaptivityNot commonly held in conservation breeding programmes.Gaps in knowledgeMost of what is known of the biology of this species comes from studies in the Serengeti and more recently from the Guassa Highlands of Ethiopia. There is otherwise little quantitative information available on densities, habitat use, and ranging patterns in relation to food availability. Information on dispersal, survival and mortality factors of adults, pups and dispersing individuals is needed. Aspects of disease in relation to population dynamics and transmission need to be better understood.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough (especially at higher elevations) to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is a terrestrial species that is presumably found in forest and scrubland at higher elevations.
threats: The threats to this species are not well known. It may be threatened by habitat loss at lower elevations.
population: It is probably a fairly common species.
range: This poorly known species is found in the highlands of the island of Borneo. It has been recorded between 940 and 3,360 m on the slopes of Mt. Kinabalu, and possibly occurs throughout the upland forests of the island (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has been recorded in Bukit Belalong, Brunei, by Yasuma and Abdullah (1997).
conservationActions: This species occurs in Bukit Raya National Park (Musser and Carleton 2005) and Mt. Kinabalu National Park. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, ecology, and threats to this poorly known species.

rationale: The Eurasian Harvest Mouse is listed as Least Concern because the species has a very wide distribution, is common and adaptable, and faces no major threats.
habitat: It is present in a wide variety of habitats, including alpine grasslands, tall grass fields, bamboo stands, wetlands, reedbeds, and clearings and edges of humid forest. It has also adapted to a variety of anthropogenic habitats, including gardens and arable land (in the wetter north-western parts of its range), drainage ditches, and grain or rice paddies (Spitzenberger 1999). It has a high tolerance of disturbed habitats (Haberl and Kryštufek 2003). Its diet includes seeds, green vegetation, insects, and birds' eggs.
threats: There are no major threats throughout its range. In Europe the species is common in wetlands (e.g., rice fields) and other habitats (e.g., abandoned agricultural land). There are no serious threats to the survival of the species, although local population declines have occurred in some areas as a result of loss and degradation of wetland habitats (Spitzenberger 1999).
population: Population declines have been noted in many parts of Europe. However, populations of this species fluctuate drastically, and some reported declines may in fact have been part of a natural fluctuation (Trout 1978, Haberl and Kryštufek 2003). The species is hard to trap and is often not recorded even when it is present (Haberl and Kryštufek 2003). However, nests may be found quite easily by experienced observers (R. Juškaitis pers. comm. 2006). It is considered to be common in South Asia.
range: The harvest mouse has a large range in the Palaearctic and Indomalayan regions, where it occurs from northern Spain and Great Britain through Europe, eastern Fennoscandia, and Russia to northern Mongolia, China, the Korean peninsula, northeast India, Myanmar and Viet Nam (Corbet 1978, Panteleyev 1998, Spitzenberger 1999); also Japan and Taiwan. It is present on the border between southern Sweden and south-east Norway, where it is regarded as possibly introduced (van der Kooij et al. 2001, Wilson and Reeder 2005, van der Kooij et al. in litt. 2006). In Europe, it is largely absent from Iberia, southern part of Italy, and the Alps. It is typically a lowland species, although it occurs at altitudes of up to 1,700 m asl in Europe (Spitzenberger 1999). It is restricted to the northern parts of Mongolia, including Mongol Altai, Hövsgöl, Hentii and Ikh Hyangan mountain ranges, Mongol Daguur Steppe and Eastern Mongolia. In Japan, the species is found on Honshu (Miyagi and Niigata Prefectures southwards), Shikoku, Kyushu, as well as the Oki Islands (Dogo, Nishinoshima, and Nakanoshima), Awaji, Teshima, Innoshima, Osaki-kamishima, Tsushima, Shimoshima (Amakusa Islands), Fukue (Goto Islands), and Kuchinoerabu (Osumi Islands) (Abe et al. 2005). The species is likely found more widely on small islands in the vicinity of the known distribution in Japan (Abe et al. 2005). The species is found from sea level up to 1,200 m asl in Japan.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas across its range. In Japan, the species is listed as threatened in a number of regions.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. The previous published assessment was based on the old taxonomic concept. Acomys spinosissimus has now been split into four separate species: A. spinosissimus, A. selousi, A. muzei, and A. ngurui.
habitat: This species is found on rocky outcrops in savanna woodland. It is an insectivorous species. It is not known if the species can persist in disturbed or modified habitats.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: The species is very common in the southern parts of the range, but less common further north.
range: Acomys spinosissimus occurs widely across Zimbabwe and in Mozambique. It appears to be restricted between the Zambesi and Limpopo Rivers.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from a large number of protected areas in all the countries of its range, including Kruger National Park and a number of private conservation areas. However, it is apparently not in the Selous Reserve in Tanzania.

rationale: The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species has been updated to be 6,934 km2. This geographic range is severely fragmented and is undergoing continuing decline in area of occupancy, extent of occurrence and in quality of habitat. The number of subpopulations and mature individuals is also known to be in decline. It has been estimated that there will be a complete loss of the species' range by 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015). Based on these premises, the species is listed as Vulnerable.
habitat: This species is an inhabitant of intact and degraded forest fragments from sea level to 780 m. The species has been found in fragments of between 50 and 400 ha in size.
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from unsustainable farming practices, logging and hunting.
population: Population densities vary between 2.2 and 5.0 individuals/ha (which is low compared to other mouse lemur species), and the highest densities are found in disturbed forest fragments which may be due to crowding or edge effects (Randrianambinina et al. 2010). Almost all sampled populations of Microcebus danfossi show genetic evidence for a relatively rapid crash in population size. This crash is likely to have occurred within the last 500 years, thus coinciding with accelerated deforestation due to human population expansion in Madagascar (Olivieri et al. 2008). It is suspected that there is a declining population, including a decline in the number of mature individuals in the population, due to a decline in extent and quality of habitat.
range: It is known from sixteen forest fragments between the rivers Sofia and Maevarano in north-western Madagascar (Olivieri et al. 2007, Randrianambinina et al. 2010). Although this species was already reported to occur at Anjajavy on the basis of census data, recent genetic analysis confirmed this species assignation (Blanco, unpublished). Prior to taxonomic revisions in 2007, the mouse lemurs in this region were assumed to be Microcebus ravelobensis. Randrianambinina et al. reported an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of ~7,600 km2 in 2000; however, forests have been severely fragmented over the last 8 years, and it EOO is estimated to be 6,934 km2. It has been estimated that there will be a complete loss of the species' range by 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forests (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted.
conservationActions: It is listed on CITES Appendix I. It is known to occur in the Bora Special Reserve, as well as in the Anjiamangirana and Andalirano Classified Forests. However, it is believed that it will have little chance for long-term survival without additional conservation measures; such efforts should include the strengthening of infrastructure within Anjiamangirana I Forest, and the establishment of other protected zones in the forest fragments at Marosakoa, Anjajavy, Ambarijeby and Bekofafa. The species does also occur in Anjajavy forest, an area comprising ~10,000 hectares (including private Reserve ~1,200 ha and ~8,000 ha of recently protected area). Further surveys are needed to determine the full extent of its range and population status, and to confirm the taxonomic distinctiveness of this taxon. According to I. J. Porton, this species is not being kept in captivity (Mittermeier et al. 2010 and references therein).

rationale: Listed as Endangered based on a suspected population reduction of at least 50% over the past 45 years (three generations), primarily due to logging, agricultural encroachment, and hunting, and a suspected continuing decline over at least 15 years (one generation) into the future. Continuing habitat loss, fragmentation and impacts of wildlife trade also threaten this species.
habitat: Nomascus annamensis inhabits broadleaf evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, at elevations of between 100-1,200 m asl. The species is frugivorous but also consumes significant proportions of leaves, young shoots and flowers. They are also known to feed on Finlayson’s Squirrel (single record by an adult female) and lizards. Food sharing has been observed (Geissmann 1995, Duc et al. 2016). This species is diurnal and arboreal. Individuals have an activity budget of: 32% inactive, 30% traveling, 26% feeding, 10% social and 2% other. They generally live in monogamous family groups an have a home range of around 50 ha (Frechette et al. 2017).
threats: Habitat loss, habitat degradation, hunting, pet trade. In Cambodia’s Virachey National Park, large areas have been cleared for rubber plantations in recent years, particularly on its eastern side, and the area is also subjected to illegal logging for luxury timber. In addition, road building along Cambodia’s northern border with Lao PDR is contributing to further habitat degradation and increased accessibility to remote parts of this landscape (P. Sinovas pers. comm. 2020). In Viet Nam, habitats for Nomascus annamensis are heavily fragmented due to logging and agricultural encroachment, and a high population density of humans continues to threaten this species’ habitat and population numbers.Lack of enforcement and hunting with guns presents quite a danger to the conservation of the taxon throughout its range. The species is used in traditional 'medicine', for food, and in the pet trade (Duckworth et al. 1999, Geissmann et al. 2000, Duc et al. 2015, Rawson et al. 2011). In recent years, the amount of logging and the use of guns in Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Park has increased (McGrath and Behie in prep.). In 2017, through interviews with local people in five villages adjacent to VSSPNP, it was found that the most sought-after primate species in VSSPNP for use as a pet was N. annamensis, with 43.75% of participants willing to keep one as a pet. Despite this, N. annamensis is rarely hunted in Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Park, which may be due to a lack of hunting equipment, as this was the most frequently reported as the reason for not hunting other primates in the area (McGrath and Behie 2019). Interviews conducted in 2019 with local communities along the southern edge of Virachey National Park to understand prevalence of primate hunting found that N. annamensis was generally not targeted and only very rarely caught (FFI unpublished data). Virtually no species-specific information on international trade is available as, until 2013, the species was not recognised as a separate taxon by CITES. According to the CITES trade database, reported trade to date consists of low levels of scientific samples from Viet Nam to Germany in 2016 and 2018 (P. Sinovas pers. comm. 2020). In general, within the range of N. annamensis, gibbons are traded for their meat, and, to a lesser extent, as pets. Cross border trade of wildlife, especially from Lao PDR and Cambodia into Viet Nam occurs. Hunting, in particular, is a major threat in both Viet Nam and Lao PDR.In addition to losses suffered due to hunting for food and medicinal purposes, as well as live capture for the illegal pet trade, this species is impacted by historic and ongoing significant tropical forest loss throughout its range. According to the most recent Global Forest Watch reports, since declining populations were first noted in 2001, Viet Nam has lost 16% of its forest cover to date and could lose as much as 56% by the year 2045 if current rates continue. Lao PDR has also lost 16% of its forest cover to date and could lose as much as 52% by the year 2045 if current rates continue, and Cambodia has already lost 25% of its former forest cover to date and could lose as much as 70% by the year 2045 if current rates continue.
population: More than 220 groups were recorded in Viet Nam between 2000 and 2015 (Rawson et al. 2011). Key populations occur in Dak Rong and Phong Dien Nature Reserve. Minimum group counts from protected areas in Viet Nam include: Dak Rong 56 groups; Phong Dien 26 groups; Thua Thien Hue Saola Nature Reserve 14 groups; Bach Ma 8 groups; Song Thanh 15 groups; Chu Mom Ray 14 groups; Kon Ka Kinh 9 groups (42 estimated); and Kon Cha Rang 13 groups (20 estimated) (Rawson et al. 2011). Recent surveys in Ba To District and An Toan NR recorded 21 and 9 groups, and an estimated population of 52 and 22 groups, respectively (Duc et al. 2016)In Cambodia, Virachey National Park holds a highly significant population, likely larger than any in Viet Nam (Traeholt et al. 2005, Rawson et al. 2011). Acoustic surveys conducted in Virachey National Park in 2018 recorded 332 groups (excluding solo males) in 20 survey sites across the park; preliminary analysis of the data give an estimate of over 2000 groups for Virachey, representing the largest known population within a single protected area and a key global stronghold for the species (FFI unpublished data). A 2010 population survey in adjacent Veun Sai and Siem Pang districts (now Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Park) estimated approximately 500 groups (Rawson et al. 2012). A subsequent analysis of the same data from Veun Sai-Siem Pang reported that 77 groups had been detected and gave an estimated population density of 0.32 calling groups/km2, but concluded that no population estimate could be given for the entire park as variance due to inter-array variation in the encounter rate could not be accounted for (Kidney et al. 2016). In a 2019 survey of the same locations, 92 N. annamensis calling groups were detected (solo males excluded) across 13 sites located at least 4 km apart throughout Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Park (McGrath and Behie in prep).No recent population data for Lao PDR exists although, again, populations could be significant including in In Xe Pian NPA, where an estimated population of 400-6,720 groups exist (Duckworth et al. 1995). According to Thien et al. (2017), in central Viet Nam, sound recording in eight protected areas, of which 171 individuals were of N. annamensis (73 males and 98 females), gave a total estimate of 71 groups. Recorded group densities for Dak Rong Nature Reserve were 0.6 groups/km2, and 0.21 and 0.11 group/km2 in the Ba To District and An Toan NR, respectively (Duc et al. 2015). However, these populations have been heavily suppressed.
range: In Lao PDR, Nomascus annamensis is distributed in the south of the country (16°00’-16°03’ N), East of Mekong River up to the Banhiang River in Savannakhet Province. N. annamensis occurs in the central and southern provinces of Attapu, Champasak, Salavan, Savannakhet and Xekong (Thinh et al. 2010, Chuong et al. 2018). Lao PDR may support the largest global populations of N. annamensis, although there is little population data for the country (Duckworth 2008), although the largest known population is in Cambodia.In Cambodia, N. annamensis occurs north of the Srepok River (about 13°30’ N) in Stung Treng and Rattanakiri Provinces (Thinh et al. 2010). The largest Cambodian population may be in Virachey National Park (Traeholt et al. 2005, Rawson et al. 2011), while the contiguous Veun Sai-Siem Pang Conservation Area forest block south of this park supports approximately 500 groups (Rawson et al. 2012).In Viet Nam, N. annamensis is distributed from approximately the Thach Han River (about 16°40’-16°50’ N) in Quang Tri Province in the north of its distribution to the Ba River (about 13°00’-13°10’N), which flows through Gia Lai and Phu Yen Provinces, in the south. (Rawson et al. 2011). N. annamensis occurs in the protected areas of Bac Huong Hoa and Dakrong Nature Reserves, Quang Tri Province; Phong Dien, Hue Saola Nature Reserves and Bach Ma National Park, Thua Thien Hue Province; Song Thanh Nature Reserve, Sao la Quang Nam Nature Reserve Quang Nam Province; Chu Mom Ray National Park, Kon Tum Province, and Kon Ka Kinh National Park, An Toan Nature Reserve Gia Lai Province.
useTrade: Hunting for food and 'medicinal' purposes is a major threat in Viet Nam and Lao PDR, as well as live capture for the illegal pet trade. Gibbons do not appear to be targeted by communities around Virachey National Park and captures are very rare. In Cambodia, hunting does not appear to be the main threat at present (P. Sinovas pers. comm. 2020).
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix I and is presumably legally protected in Viet Nam (Appendix 1b of Decree 32, 2006) and in Lao PDR (Category 1 protected species in accordance with the Wildlife Law (2007) and Decree 81/PM of 2008) and under the Law on Forestry (2003) in Cambodia, although the taxon is not included on species lists due to its relatively recent description.Found in the following protected areas: Dak Rong, Phong Dien, Saola, Ba Na-Nui Chua, Song Thanh, Ngoc Linh, Kon Cha Rang and An Toan Nature Reserves and Bach Ma and Chu Mom Ray National Parks, Bac Huong Hoa Nature Reserve, Viet Nam; Dong Phou Vieng, Xe Sap, Xe Bang Nouan, Phou Xiengthong, Dong Amphan, Dong Houa Sao, Xe Pian National Protected Areas in Lao PDR; and Virachey and Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Parks and Western Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia.According to Thien et al. (2017) in central Viet Nam, the species occurs in the following protected areas: Bac Huong Hoa NR (10 groups), Dakrong NR (7 groups), Phong Dien NR (10 groups), Bach Ma NP (13 groups), Hue Saola NR (8 groups), Song Thanh NR (2 groups), Chu Mom Ray NP (14 groups) and Kon Ka Kinh NP (7 groups).Most N. annamensis populations receive little protection. A five-year (2011-2015) conservation project by WWF in the ‘Central Annamites’ and ‘Southern Laos’ landscapes includes N. annamensis as a priority species for the development of protection and monitoring activities (Duc et al. 2015, 2016). Conservation International has a project based on protection and ecotourism (gibbon viewing) in Veun Sai-Siem Pang NP, Cambodia. Fauna & Flora International has a project in Virachey National Park to better understand the N. annamensis population and strengthen management of the protected area (P. Sinovas pers. comm. 2020). Controlling hunting of N. annamensis is one of the most important actions for all remaining populations of this species. Environmental impact studies should be conducted for all proposed dam and road construction projects and areas proposed for economic land concessions in sites with confirmed populations of N. annamensis, and measures to avoid or mitigate development impacts should be implemented by relevant district and provincial agencies (Duc et al. 2015, 2016; Rawson et al. 2011).

rationale: The Tarim Red Deer is regarded provisionally here as a separate species from Cervus elaphus and C. canadensis (see the Taxonomic Notes section). The total population size is estimated at approximately 2,500 individuals, although no recent estimates have been obtained for the populations in China. Although the population in China is small and probably declining, this is offset by the increasing trend of the species in Central Asia, which represents the majority of the species’ population (approximately 75%). Numbers in India are very small, and thus are numerically not significant for determining species-level population trends. Its extent of occurence (EOO) is >1,000,000 km² and although its area of occupancy (AOO) is not known, it is not likely to approach the threshold of <2,000 km² to qualify for Vulnerable or Near Threatened. To the best of our knowledge there is no continuing decline or extreme fluctuations in the EOO, AOO, area, extent and/or quality of habitat, number of locations or subpopulations or the number of mature individuals. This species is therefore listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Cervus h. bactrianus and C. h. yarkandensis inhabit riparian forested corridors surrounded by desert environments. Some significant groups of C. h. bactrianus inhabit reed bushes with very limited tree cover. Although the main habitat of C. h. bactrianus is riparian forests, its diet includes grasses, sedges and shrubs, and tree shoots to a minor extent. Its diet is very limited most of the year (e.g. when inhabiting reeds and brush). As opposed to other red deer subspecies, which consume branches preferably of young deciduous trees of up to 15 mm thick, C. h. bactrianus eats only branches of willow, poplar, some other riparian forest species and saxaul in deserts up to 5 mm thick.Cervus h. hanglu inhabits deciduous woodland, upland moors and open mountainous areas (sometimes above the treeline), natural grasslands, pastures and meadows (Koubek and Zima 1999).It primarily uses mixed oak forests, followed by Morus and riverine habitats during the winter and mixed oak forests and coniferous forests during the summer, where food availability is greatest (Ahmad et al. 2015). In woodland, its diet consists mainly of shrub and tree shoots, but in other habitats it also consumes grasses, sedges and shrubs.Generally found in mountainous areas, where it spends summers in alpine meadows and winters in valleys. On more level terrain, it seeks wooded hillsides in summer, open grasslands in winter.
threats: In Central Asia C. h. bactrianus has declined due to illegal hunting and loss of habitat; although much of the remaining forest is legally protected, illegal logging, forest loss due to fires and illegal grazing of livestock remain problematic (Karlstetter and Mallon 2014, Pereladova 2013).Poaching, by both civilian and military personnel, was identified as the main cause of the decline of the Hangul in the past and present (Shah et al. 2011). The Wildlife Department are at present unable to patrol and implement protection activities due to the occupation of Dachigam National Park by insurgents and the armed forces, thus poaching may very likely have increased as a result (M.K. Ranjitsinh pers. comm. 2016). Incursion of nomadic livestock herders and predation of fawns by their guard dogs is reportedly also a significant problem that is not being effectively dealt with and competition for grazing grounds with livestock and the associated risk of disease transmission are also significant threats. The Hangul C. h. hanglu population in the Dachigam landscape also appears to have low genetic variation in comparison to other species (Mukesh et al. 2015) and thus could be susceptible to the effects of inbreeding.In China C. h. yarkandensis is threatened by agricultural expansion, oil exploration and most significantly, by hunting (Jianfang et al. 2006).
population: Cervus h. bactrianus known from the basins of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers underwent a rapid decline in the 19th century and disappeared from Syr Darya by 1900. In the mid 1960s the population consisted of 350-500 individuals; special reserves were established for the protection of C. h. bactrianus and populations were restored in parts of its former range.
