conservationActions: Dugongs are covered under three international conservation conventions: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Convention on the International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and the Convention on Migratory Species of Wild Animals (also known as CMS or the Bonn Convention). Dugongs are also included in the Coral Triangle Initiative (CTI), goal five (Threatened Species). Additionally, the Convention on Wetlands (the Ramsar Convention) protects some important Dugong habitats.To date, there has been little effective management intervention to reduce anthropogenic impacts on the Dugong, apart from legislative protection which is almost ubiquitous throughout its range. Protected area initiatives aim to protect Dugongs in many range states (Marsh et al. 2011) and are most developed in Australia. Most of the marine protected areas outside Australia with the potential to protect Dugongs are ‘paper parks’ where laws and regulations exist but are not implemented. Strategic Action Programmes/Strategic Plans/Action Plans to protect Dugongs have been developed by countries in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region (Gerges 2002), Indonesia (de Iongh et al. 2009a, 2009b) and South Pacific Regional Environmental Programme (SPREP; Gillespies 2005). However, effective enforcement of conservation regulations is a problem throughout most of the region because of poverty, lack of resources and personnel. The most pressing need is for alternative sustainable livelihoods that address poverty and provide incentives for conservation. The most promising initiative is the UNEP Dugong, Seagrass & Coastal Communities Initiative (see http://www.cms.int/en/publication/dugong-seagrass-and-coastal-communities-initiative).

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered as it is suspected to have undergone a decline in both population and range size exceeding 50% over the past 30 years (three generations) across its already restricted range, mainly as a result of increasing habitat loss and degradation in the Nigeria/Cameroon highlands, and also from hunting throughout its range. This population reduction is ongoing at a similar rate.
habitat: This species is found in primary and secondary lowland, submontane, and montane forest, but occurs mainly in montane and submontane moist forest above 800 m (Butynski 2013). They were the most common monkey in the afro-alpine forest zone on Mount Oku, Cameroon in a study by Beeson et al. (1996). It is more rarely found in lowland forest (e.g., to 450 m in the Caldera on Bioko (Butynski and Koster 1994, Hearn et al. 2006) or to 100-300 m in the Idenau forests near Mt. Cameroon) (Gartlan and Struhsaker 1972), and on Bioko it shows a preference for Schefflera forest (González-Kirchner 2004, Hearn et al. 2006). It can also occur in isolated forest patches within montane grasslands (Butynski 2013). It inhabits areas with approximately 2000-9000 mm annual rainfall; among the wettest sites in Africa (Butynski 2013). They have been found in polyspecific groups with Cercopithecus nictitans (Beeson et al. 1996). They have semi-terrestrial habits and are found usually in the understorey of the forest (Gartlan and Struhsaker 1972, González-Kirchner 2004). Little is known about feeding behaviour, but the study in Oku showed that about half the diet was fruit and seeds, about 40% shoots, and the rest was flowers, other plant material and a small quantity of insects (Beeson and Lea 1994, Beeson et al. 1996, Butynski 2013). This species lives in groups of 2-19 animals, consisting of one or more males and several females with their young; at Mt. Oku, group size was usually 10 or fewer (Beeson et al. 1996, Butynski 2013).
threats: This species’ population size and distribution have been severely affected by habitat loss and fragmentation resulting from logging and agriculture and hunting. By the 1990s, available habitat for A. preussi  was already greatly reduced on the mainland (Oates 1996). For example, Cameroon’s forests have been severely eroded by cultivation, fire and collection of wood for fuel (Charlotte 2010, de Wasseige et al. 2012, Megevand et al. 2013). Intact highland forest, in which the species is most abundant, is converted across its range to grazing land, farmland and “farm bush” (e.g., Tyukavina et al. (2016)). Forest loss in the most recent year available (2014) was higher than in all previous years (from 2001) in Cameroon, and highest in 2011 and 2014 for Nigeria (World Resources Institute 2016).In some places human population density can reach 300 people per km² (WorldPop 2016), and human population growth in the three range states of the taxon is estimated to continue at roughly 2.7% annually for at least several decades (United Nations 2015, World Bank 2016). Throughout the highlands of the Cameroon volcanic line, much of the previously intact forest has been cleared for agriculture, and these forests suffered greatly in the 1980s and 1990s when the rise in coffee price first led to rapid clearing of the afro-alpine forests of the Cameroon highlands for growing coffee and subsequently—despite the price falling again—led to further clearing by farmers in the hope of future profits (Sunderlin et al. 2000). As a result, little montane forest remains in the mainland part of this species’ range and the largest remaining afroalpine forest block of West Africa is the Kilum-Ijim Forest Reserve which contains Mount Oku (Maisels et al. 2001).This species is highly susceptible to human predation because it is semi-terrestrial and relatively large-bodied. Hunting has led to a decline in its population across its range, but particularly on Bioko (Cronin et al. 2017). It was locally common in the Ndokbou, Kilum-Ijim, and Ebo Forests, and now populations have been extirpated as a result of overhunting (Dowsett-Lemaire & Dowsett 2001, Maisels et al. 2001). An intensive survey in 2009 in the Bakossi Mountains National Park failed to find any although they had been present some years earlier (Fonkwo et al. 2011). The montane and sub-montane forests of the Cameroon highlands are the last stronghold for A. preussi on the mainland, but firm data are not currently available on its rate of population decline. While it has been recorded in protected areas in Cameroon and Nigeria (e.g., Takamanda National Park and Cross River National Park), most of the remaining Cameroonian forest in the region lies outside protected areas, and are currently being eroded as a result of cultivations, bush fires and fuel wood collection (Oates et al. 2004). Hunting is also most severe outside protected areas and this monkey is disproportionately targeted given its large size and semi-terrestrial behaviour which make it easily accessible to hunters. The ongoing quest to convert forests to large-scale palm oil plantations in the region is likely to worsen these threats in the coming decade (Linder 2013). On Bioko, hunting intensity is high, including within the two protected areas, and recent infrastructure development has increased accessibility of remote areas of Bioko’s forests and core areas of the range of A. preussi on the island. A road leading to the summit of Pico Basilé was expanded and greatly improved between 2005-2010. This has greatly facilitated hunting within the reserve, primarily by hunters from Basile Fang, a village at the base of the road, which was founded in 2005 by professional hunters from continental Equatorial Guinea, Rio Muni (Grande Vega et al. 2013). In late 2014, a road bisecting the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve was completed, eroding much of the isolation that had passively protected wildlife populations, including A. preussi, in the remote Gran Caldera de Luba (Cronin et al.  2015, Cronin et al. 2016), and contributed to increased hunting activity within the reserve (D.T. Cronin, unpublished data, 2015-2016).
population: There has been no comprehensive population survey of this species, except on Bioko where the species has undergone declines exceeding 65% over a 30-year period between 1986 and 2016 (Cronin et al. 2017). On the mainland, the species is uncommon and highly fragmented. Between 1992 and 1994, Beeson et al. (1996) studied a population of the species in the Kilum-Ijim forest area in northwest Cameroon, reporting that it was the most common guenon in the afro-montane forest on Mt. Kilum. However, just seven years later, Maisels et al. (2001), reported that A. preussi remained near Mt. Kilum, but that numbers had fallen since the time of Beeson et al.’s (1996) study. Gadsby found Preuss’ guenon to have the highest relative abundance of all diurnal primates in restricted areas where they occurred (Boshi-Okwangwo and Mt. Cameroon), but that they were unknown in contiguous, lowland forest containing the same complement of conspecifics (1990, 1992). SMART-based ranger patrols facilitated by WCS in Boshi-Okwangwo from March 2011 to January 2018 recorded 21 separate sightings of the species, representing only 5% of all sightings of diurnal primates made.
range: This species has a restricted distribution (five separate population fragments) in southwestern Cameroon, southeastern Nigeria, and on Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea (three fragments). The total area of all eight fragments is approximately 17,300 km². Its population centres on highlands, including the Cameroon Highlands and Mount Cameroon. It is found from 100-3,000 m, but mainly above 1,000 m, and is most abundant in montane and sub-montane forest up to at least 2,500 m asl (Oates 2011, Butynski 2013). Its range on the mainland extends from the highland areas along the Nigeria-Cameroon border near the Cross River drainage in the north to the Sanaga River in the south, and from the southern slopes of the Obudu Plateau in Nigeria east to the proposed Ebo Forest National Park in Cameroon (Littoral Region) (Oates 2011, Butynski 2013).Its population is fragmented across highland sites throughout the region in Cameroon (the Bamboutos Mountains, Mt. Oku and the Kom-Wum Reserve, Mt. Kupe, Rumpi Hills, Takamanda National Park, Mt. Cameroon National Park, Bakossi National Park, Banyang-Mbo Wildlife Sanctuary, Kagwene Gorilla Sanctuary, Mone River Forest Reserve, Mawambi Hills forest, and the proposed Ebo Forest National Park, Nigeria (Okwangwo Division of Cross River National Park, the Obudu Plateau and the Sankwala Mountains), and Bioko Island (Pico Basilé National Park and the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve [including Pico Biao and the Gran Caldera de Luba]). Its range also includes isolated patches of forest in the grasslands of the Cameroon Highlands. Careful surveys failed to find it in Korup National Park, even at the highest point (just over 1000 m) (Linder 2008). This species is divided into two subspecies: A. preussi preussi, on the mainland, and A. p. insularis, which is restricted to Bioko Island.
conservationActions: This species is listed as Class B under the African Convention, and under Appendix II of CITES. Nationally, it is completely protected in Cameroon, and in Cross River State, Nigeria. The hunting, sale, and consumption of primates are forbidden in Equatorial Guinea by Presidential Decree. The species occurs in the Okwangwo Division of Cross River National Park (Nigeria), the Obudu Plateau and the Sankwala Mountains, and in the Bakossi National Park, Takamanda National Park, Mount Kupe, Kom-Wum Reserve, Kilum-Ijim Forest Reserve, Kagwene Gorilla Sanctuary, Mone River Forest Reserve, Mawambi Hills forest, the proposed Ebo National Park, Banyang-Mbo Wildlife Sanctuary and the Mt. Cameroon National Park (Cameroon). On Bioko, it occurs in the Pico Basilé National Park and the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve (Equatorial Guinea). Monitoring of the status and distribution across its range are needed, especially on the mainland.  Much of the montane forest area of the Cameroon highlands, the most important remaining habitat for this species, is now formally protected on paper, but requires urgent conservation action on the ground.

rationale: Piliocolobus badius is listed as Endangered, as the species is estimated to have undergone a decline exceeding 50% during the past three generations (ca 30 years). Insufficient survey data preclude the estimation of a total population size for Piliocolobus badius; however, recent surveys report significant population declines and/or local extirpations. The scale of the decline is inferred from rates of human-induced habitat loss, and evidence of unsustainable rates of hunting. Already small and isolated Western Red Colobus populations are expected to continue declining given that these threats are ongoing and in most places are not being countered, and indeed are likely to increase, driven by the demand for natural resources from a rapidly growing human population in West Africa.
habitat: This is a predominantly arboreal species found in a variety of forest types including primary, secondary, and gallery forest, woodland savanna, tree and shrub savanna, mangroves and residential gardens (Starin 1991, Galat-Luong and Galat 2005, Struhsaker 2010, Butynski et al. 2013). In general Western Red Colobus prefer mature old growth moist forest, where they use the main canopy at 20-40 m height (50% of time, Galat-Luong 1983), and typically travel on the larger branches (McGraw 1998); however, the northern populations also spend time travelling, resting, playing, feeding and grooming on the ground (Starin 1991).Their diet is dominated by fruit, seeds and young leaves (Galat and Galat-Luong 1985, Starin 1991, Davies et al. 1999, Korstjens 2001). Multimale-multifemale groups, range in size up to 90 individuals (Butynski et al. 2013), with an average of 26 individuals in Abuko Nature Reserve (Starin 1991), 37 individuals (Galat-Luong 1983) and 53 individuals (Korstjens et al. 2007) in Taï National Park.
threats: The two major threats to Western Red Colobus are hunting and habitat loss.Red colobus are extremely vulnerable to hunting pressure (Refisch and Koné 2005; Struhsaker 2005, 2010; N’Goran et al. 2012; Covey and McGraw 2014), and subsistence and commercial hunting have heavily impacted populations of this West African species. Estimates from surveys at bushmeat markets on the Liberia-Côte d’Ivoire border and around Sapo National Park in southeastern Liberia reveal that primates – including P. b. badius – are being hunted at rates that are almost certainly unsustainable (Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016). In Côte d’Ivoire, where hunting is especially intensive, this monkey is reported to have disappeared from all areas except Taï National Park, and possibly the Cavally Classified Forest to the north of Taï National Park (Sanderson et al. 2015) and in relic forest in the Tonkpi region, near Côte d’Ivoire’s border with Guinea and Liberia (Kramoko et al. 2017).It is estimated that in Guinea-Bissau almost 200 red colobus are hunted during each dry season to supply the two urban bushmeat markets and the meat is consumed in dedicated bushmeat restaurants (Minhós et al. 2013). In Guinea, the intensity of hunting has increased since 2000, with bushmeat also coming from Niokolo Koba in Senegal to supply the city of Conakry and large towns (Galat-Luong and Galat pers. obs. 1983–2000). In addition, skins are used in animistic practices and traded in dedicated markets (Sá et al. 2012).Offtake levels are likely increasing due to increased hunting associated with significant human population growth and habitat degradation. Hunting has increased due to heightened demand for bushmeat, increasingly fragmented and smaller forest blocks, and improved access to forest interiors through logging (Laurance et al. 2015, Sloan et al. 2016). Indeed, the human population has increased by more than 100% in the seven range countries since 1990 (Worldometer 2020).Deforestation through logging, charcoal production, mining and clearance for agricultural land, including industrial-scale plantations, has occurred over much of the species range (McGraw 1998, Bitty et al. 2015, WCF 2015).In the P. b. badius subspecies’ range, analysis of satellite imagery of tree cover shows that Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea were among the 10 countries with the fastest annual rate of forest loss in the world in the 2001–2014 period (Petersen et al. 2015). According to Global Forest Watch, Côte d’Ivoire lost about 17% of its forest cover between 2000 and 2015 with an annual deforestation rate of 2.69% – among the highest in the world. Many areas in Côte d’Ivoire designated as protected areas no longer contain forest and have been largely or completely converted to plantations (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2012, Bitty et al. 2015). A list of countries with the largest increase in primary forest loss during 2018 includes two P. badius badius host countries in the top 10: Côte d’Ivoire was ranked second (26% increase) and Liberia (12% increase) was ranked sixth. When the world’s countries are ranked by the amount of primary forest lost as a percentage of the country’s total, Côte d’Ivoire is second (1.88%) and Sierra Leone is sixth (1.23%) (all forest loss data GFW 2019).In the P. b. temminckii subspecies’ range, 16.2% (>15,000 km²) of forest habitat has been lost in the past 17 years (2001–2018, GFW 2019; 1.7 generations for this taxon). Total forest lost during this period varied between 9.2% in Senegal and 16.6% in Guinea. With the exception of Gambia, rates of forest loss have more than doubled since 2013 in all range countries (GFW 2019). However, forest loss would have been occurring continuously long before 2001; extrapolating the lowest estimate of forest loss (9.2%) to the decade 1990–2000, gives an estimated total of 22% of suitable habitat lost over three generations.Degradation and loss of natural habitat also lead to increasing human-wildlife-human conflict (e.g., Starin 1989; Struhsaker 2005, 2010; Galat et al. 2009). Furthermore, large areas in the range of P. badius were impacted by civil conflict between 1989 and 2011, and this negatively impacted Western Red Colobus populations in Côte d'Ivoire, Liberia, Senegal and Sierra Leone.For additional information on threats, see the two Piliocolobus badius subspecies assessments.
population: Western Red Colobus are patchily distributed and many populations are small and isolated. No overall population estimate is available due to the paucity of survey data; however, a significant decrease in total population size since 1990 is inferred based on: (1) recent surveys have reported significant population declines and/or extirpation from certain areas (e.g., A. Galat-Luong and G. Galat pers. obs. 1974–2002; Starin 1989; Gonedelé Bi et al. 2006, 2012, 2014; Wright et al. 2006; Bene et al. 2013; Bitty et al. 2015; M. Mayhew pers. obs. 2015–2019; Minhós et al. 2016; Bersacola et al. 2018); (2) unsustainable exploitation for bushmeat consumption or cultural/medical practices indicated by hunting and offtake rates (e.g., Galat-Luong and Galat pers. obs. 1983–2000; Starin 1989, 2007; N’Goran et al. 2012; Sá et al. 2012; Minhós et al. 2013; Covey and McGraw 2014; Greengrass 2016); (3) increasing demand for natural resource driven by the growing human population, with a more than 100% increase in human population in the seven range countries since 1990 (Worldometer 2020); and (4) a significant decrease in suitable habitat (WCF 2015, Peterson et al. 2015).In Côte d’Ivoire, the only forest certain to still contain red colobus is Taï National Park, with a population estimated at approximately 97,000 individuals (N’Goran et al. 2012). Additional surveys are needed to confirm reports that they still occur at other locations.In Sierra Leone, red colobus are now rare in most of their former habitats, although recent work suggests there may be over 5,000 red colobus in Gola Rainforest National Park. They are still present on Tiwai Island, and reported in Loma Mountains National Park, Kambui Hills Forest Reserve and Kangari Hills Forest Reserve (Brncic et al. 2010, 2015).In Liberia, a significant population is found in Sapo National Park, and their presence was recently confirmed in the Grebo-Krahn National Park (Furnell et al. 2015a) and the corridor linking it to Sapo (Furnell et al. 2015b). Elsewhere in Liberia, red colobus have been reported in North Loma National Forest (Barrie et al. 2007), Foya Natural Forest, Gola Forest National Park and the Tonglay and Norman Community Forests and the Putu Range adjacent to Gola Forest National Park (S. Jones pers. comm. 2018, J. Oates unpubl. data 2019).In northwestern Guinea, a few individuals were reported in Boulléré/Sangarédi sub-prefecture during a rapid survey conducted by Eriksson and Kpoghomou (2006).Based on surveys conducted over the last 20 years, the known population of P. b. temminckii is estimated to total approximately 2,500 individuals. Relatively large populations are still found in: Abuko Nature Reserve (Starin 2017) and the forest around Sambel Kunda, Central River Region (Mayhew et al. 2019) in Gambia; Cantanhez Forest National Park, Guinea-Bissau (Minhós et al. 2016); Delta du Saloum National Park (Fathala Forest Reserve and nearby mangroves) and Niokolo Koba National Park, Senegal (A. Galat-Luong and G. Galat pers. obs. 2000, Galat-Luong and Galat 2005). All other known populations are each estimated to contain fewer than 60 individuals.For more details, see the two Piliocolobus badius subspecies assessments.
range: Piliocolobus badius has a fragmented geographic range, from southwestern Senegal and the Gambia, south and east to the Nzi-Bandama River system in western Côte d'Ivoire (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 1996, 2003; Groves 2007, Oates 2011, Butynski et al. 2013).Piliocolobus badius badius occurs in fragmented populations in Sierra Leone, southern Guinea, Liberia and western Côte d'Ivoire. Piliocolobus badius temminckii occurs in southwest Senegal, the Gambia, much of Guinea-Bissau and northwestern Guinea.The exact boundary between the two subspecies is not known. Harding (1984) reported that individuals from the Kilimi area of northwestern Sierra Leone have coat colouration resembling typical temminckii, while further south and east in Sierra Leone only typical badius colouration is observed (J. Oates pers. obs. 1979–1991). In the past, Piliocolobus badius and P. waldroni met at the Bandama River in Côte d'Ivoire.For more details, see the two Piliocolobus badius subspecies assessments.
useTrade: Subsistence and commercial hunting have heavily impacted most populations of this species. Hunters report that red colobus are easily hunted (Struhsaker 2005, Ferreira da Silva 2012). Commercial hunting has been reported in most range countries (Ferreira da Silva 2012, N’Goran et al. 2012, Sá et al. 2012, Minhós et al. 2013, Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016), although hunting is rare in Senegal (Galat-Luong and Galat pers. obs. 1983–2000). In Gambia, red colobus are rarely hunted for meat, but they are often killed as a crop-protection measure (Starin 1989), and their body parts are used for traditional practices (Starin 2007).Bushmeat trade takes place in both rural and urban areas, and trade estimates strongly suggest unsustainable levels of exploitation that, if not controlled, will continue to result in  extirpation of this taxon in parts of its range. Indeed, commercial hunting in Guinea-Bissau may have been contributing to its rarity in Cufada Lagoons Natural Park (Ferreira da Silva 2016) and disappearance of groups in Cantanhez Forest National Park (Minhós et al. 2016). Estimates from surveys at bushmeat markets on the Liberia-Côte d’Ivoire border and around Sapo National Park in southeastern Liberia reveal that primates are being hunted at rates that are almost certainly unsustainable (Covey and McGraw 2014, Greengrass 2016). For example, it was estimated that approximately 9.5% of the 9,400 primate carcasses brought annually from Liberia’s Konobo District to one bushmeat market on the Cavally River were red colobus (Covey and McGraw 2014).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.Western Red Colobus have been recorded in a number of protected areas including: Taï National Park and possibly the Cavally Classified Forest in Côte d'Ivoire; Abuko Nature Reserve, Kiang West National Park, River Gambia National Park and Tanji Bird Reserve in the Gambia; Badiar National Park and the Forêt classée de N’dama in Guinea; Cantanhez Forest National Park, Cufada Lagoons Natural Park and Dulombi-Boé-Tchetche Complex in Guinea-Bissau; Gola Forest National Park, Grebo-Krahn National Park, North Lorma National Forest and Sapo National Park in Liberia; Niokolo Koba National Park and Saloum Delta National Park in Senegal; and Gola Rainforest National Park, Loma Mountains National Park, Outamba-Kilimi National Park and Tiwai Island Wildlife Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.The first conservation action plan for red colobus monkeys will be published in 2020. The plan identifies priority areas for conservation and recommends range-wide and taxon based actions to prevent red colobus extinctions. Range-wide conservation priorities include actions that aim to improve government investment in wildlife conservation, expand and improve protected areas, determine taxon-specific distribution and abundance, engage with local human populations and integrate them into conservation activities, remove barriers that prevent local access to human healthcare and family planning, and raise awareness of the plight of red colobus.

rationale: Lepus coreanus is a widespread species. There are no published reports of population declines, so it is assumed that L. coreanus is not at risk. However, it is recommended that research regarding population status, biology, and ecology should be conducted.
habitat: The Korean Hare is a generalized herbivore, and its diet includes the bark of shrubs. Their feeding on cultivated crops has led to their being considered a pest species in some regions. The species occupies various habitats across its geographic distribution from plains to mountains (Flux and Angermann 1990, Smith and Xie 2008, Smith and Jo 2018). They used to pose a problem to barley growing near the mountains in Gyeonsangnam Province and have girdled half the peach trees that were growing on a five hectare farm in Jeollanam Province (Flux and Angermann 1990). Due to low density, recent damages on agriculture have been rarely reported (Jo 2018) A study conducted in Mt. Chirisan National Park, South Korea, indicated that Korean Hare abundance was positively associated with the percent of shrub cover within a given landscape (Rhim and Lee 2007). Huang et al. (2014) and Son et al. (2017) determined that hare abundance was greater in habitat conditions with significant cover and understory in larch forests. Their density can be greater in Japanese larch plantations compared with natural deciduous forest. Populations are negatively impacted when percent edge increased, which is an indicator of higher levels of fragmentation (Lee and Rhim 2017). Korean Hares do not dig nor occupy burrows but use several resting forms (Smith and Jo 2018).
threats: The threats to this species are potential for overharvest, and increased habitat loss and fragmentation.
population: This species has been considered common in Korea (Flux and Angermann 1990, Smith and Xie 2008). The density of the Korean Hare varies according to habitat (Flux and Angermann 1990). Values ranged from no presence on urban areas, up to 1.0/sq. km on hills, and 1.8/sq. km on mountains (Jo 2018). Population density peaked in 2001 as 12.3/sq. km but it has drastically declined to 1.4/sq km in 2017 (Jo 2018). As indicated above, overharvesting and habitat loss has led to a decrease in the population in recent decades.
range: The geographic distribution of the Korean Hare encompasses the entire Korean Peninsula, as well as southern Jilin, China (Smith and Jo 2018).
useTrade: The Korean Hare used to be trapped for food (Flux and Angermann 1990).
conservationActions: The 2005 hunting ban was a pro-active attempt to stop the decline in Korean Hare populations. Ulsan and Gwangju metropolitan cities have designated the Korean Hare as a protected species. In 2018, the Ministry of Environment, South Korea designated Korean Hare as a candidate of Endangered Species. After five years of assessment, the government will decided the designation of Korean Hare as Endangered Species.

rationale: Based on habitat loss alone, Tarsius spectrumgurskyae is considered Vulnerable in that at least 30% of its habitat has been converted in the past 20 years (approximately three generations). From 1990 to 2000, about 15.26% of the forest habitat on the island was converted to agriculture (A. Salim pers. comm.), and since that time at least an additional 10% has been lost.
habitat: This species has been studied in the field by Gursky. It occurs in primary, secondary and mangrove forests, forest gardens, and a variety of other habitats of varying degrees of human disturbance that provide adequate shrubby cover.  Feed mainly on insects such as moths and crickets, small vertebrates such as frog and lizards. The diet is 100% live animal prey, mostly insects with some small vertebrates.  Like all tarsiers it shows extreme adaptations for vertical clinging and leaping (VCL) in the understory of suitable tropical habitats, often 0 m or less from the ground.Nocturnal and arboreal social primates, they likely live in small, monogamous or polygamous groupings of 2–11 individuals, often sharing their home range with more than one adult of the same sex. Prefers dense vegetation or tree cavities for sleeping. Normally one sleeping site and 2-3 alternative sites used. Nocturnal as they are, their activity period commences a little after sundown and ends a bit before dawn. Activity during night is characterized by periods of inactivity and foraging.  A little before dawn, these animals sing their ‘territorial duet’ before getting back to their sleeping sites. These tarsiers can survive and adapt to small scale agro-forestry, areas of selective logging, and disturbed forests (Estrada et al. 2012).
threats: The primary threat to this species is loss of habitat loss due to illegal logging. Other threats include agricultural pesticides and predation by domestic animals (dogs and cats). In addition, some animals are entering the pet trade. There has been extensive loss of lowland forest habitat; however, the species has some tolerance to forest conversion, although population densities decrease drastically with the level of habitat degradation and loss—from 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat to 45 individuals/km² in degraded habitats (Merker 2003).
population: This taxon has been studied in the wild, and in good habitat it had an estimated population density of 156 individuals/km² (Gursky 1997). Merker (2003) found the closely related species, Tarsius dentatus, to have population densities up to 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 190 individuals/km² in slightly disturbed habitat, 130 individuals/km² in moderate disturbance, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitat.
range: Tarsius spectrumgurskyae is found in Sulawesi, from the northern tip of the northern peninsula to the Isthmus of Gorontalo.
useTrade: Some animals are recorded in pet trade.
conservationActions: Tarsiers are protected by national law and international treaties, including CITES Appendix II. Found in several conservation areas including the Greater Tangkoko area and others; however, there needs to be improved management of the currently protected areas to ensure the ongoing survival of the species. Public education to overcome the misconception that tarsiers are crop pests would be a step forward in improving conservation measures for the species. In fact the species might actually be beneficial to crops, as they eat, and may even have a dietary preference for, some real crop pests such as large grasshoppers.

rationale: This species is considered Vulnerable. Continued loss of suitable habitat on Sulawesi, and the combined threats from habitat loss, conversion, degradation, pet trade, attacks by feral dogs and cats, and persecution are suspected to have contributed to the decline in the population by over 30% over the last 22.5 years (three generations), and is suspected to continue at the same rate into the future.
habitat: Tarsius fuscus has been observed in the karst forests of Bantimurung National Park, but is assumed, like other species of the genius Tarsius to be found in a variety of primary and secondary habitats, particularly rural gardens / agroforestry. These tarsiers are unusual in that they are known to make their nest sites near the entrances within the honeycombed matrix of small karst caves.
threats: It is assumed that the primary threats to Tarsius fuscus are similar to those for other species of the genus Tarsius: habitat loss, habitat degradation, use of agricultural pesticides and herbicides, predation by domestic and feral cats and dogs.
population: This species has not been studied. The closely related species, Tarsius dentatus, was found to have densities of 270 individuals/km² in pristine habitat, 190 individuals/km² in slightly disturbed habitat, 130 individuals/km² in moderately disturbed habitat, and 45 individuals/km² in heavily disturbed habitat (Merker 2003).
range: Tarsius fuscus occurs on the southwestern peninsula of Sulawesi, presumably south of the Lake Tempe Depression. This species is assumed to occupy the same range as Macaca maura, but it is only known in the published literature from Bantimurung National Park. Tarsier duet recordings from Tanjung Bira are probably referable to T. fuscus, but Nietsch (pers. comm.) thought they might be a distinct species.
useTrade: Not known.  Many species of the genus Tarsius are found as backyard pets and in the pet trade, though they rarely live longer than a few weeks.
conservationActions: The species is included on CITES Appendix II. Tarsiers are protected by national law and international treaties, including CITES Appendix II. There has been almost no systematic study of this species, but based upon other tarsiers from Sulawesi, all of which are at least Vulnerable, and M. maura, which is believed to share the same (or even larger) range, and which is Endangered, it seems safe to conclude that this species is Vulnerable. The species occurs in Greater Maros Conservation Area.

rationale: Although the Mainland Serow occupies a distribution range encompassing over eleven countries, its populations are fragmented, isolated and in rapid decline due to poaching, habitat loss and destruction throughout its range. These factors, together with unavailability of reliable data on the abundance and distribution of this species, make it difficult to implement effective conservation actions for long-term conservation. Therefore, the Mainland serow qualifies as Vulnerable because of a decline exceeding 30% over three generations as inferred from local surveys, decline in occupied area and habitat quality as well as actual levels of exploitation. The species requires urgent conservation actions.Capricornis sumatraensis sumatraensis is assessed as Vulnerable (VU A2; C1) because this subspecies is believed to be in significant decline driven by both over-hunting and serious habitat loss.Capricornis sumatraensis milneedwardsii and C. s. thar were previously assessed as Near Threatened. New data and information suggest that these subspecies are experiencing significant declines in population size, range size and their habitat over the last decade, and continuing significant declines are expected to occur in future due to intensive human impact. Both of these subspecies are therefore assessed as Vulnerable (VU A2; C1).
habitat: The mainland serow is a forest dwelling mammal, and inhabits mountain slopes with rugged steep hills and rocky places from 100 m to 4,000 m (Li et al. 2014, Phan et al. 2014, Paudel et al. 2015, Buzzard et al. 2018, McShea et al. 2018). It is also recorded in temperate coniferous forests and broadleaved forests in Nepal (Paudel et al. 2015) and northwest Yunnan, Southwest China (Buzzard et al. 2018) and in the dense thickets of Rhododendron and Vaccinium in Vietnam (Abramov et al. 2006). It also inhabits lowland montane forests with gentler terrain, including flat areas with shrubs (Li et al. 2012). The serow occurs also on small offshore islands, such as Cat Ba Island in north Vietnam (Phan et al. 2014) and coastal small islands along the Northern Peninsula in Thailand (S. Lovari pers. comm).While the mainland serow are sensitive to human disturbance, they seem to tolerate moderately degraded forests and small isolated limestone hills and cliffs in both natural karst scrubland and even disturbed habitats (Lekagul and Mcneely 1988). Studies have found that serow occupancy is positively correlated with distance to roads, distance to villages and distance to trails indicating its preference for areas inaccessible to human encroachment (Li et al. 2012, Phan et al. 2019). The serow prefers closed canopy habitats to open ones, at relatively high altitudes in coniferous and rhododendron forests (Li et al. 2014, Buzzard et al. 2018). However, the species prefers open canopy to closed canopy, in low altitude limestone forests (Phan et al. 2019).This species normally winters in the forest belt, on flat and hilly slopes, while they move to higher-elevation cliffs and high slopes in the summer season (Wu and Zhang 2004, McShea et al. 2018). In addition, the separation of habitat selection of this species in winter and summer is based on vegetation type, tree dispersion, slope, elevation, rock dispersion, tree size, slope position, canopy and water sources. However, shelter, and concealment opportunities, as well as distance from water, were not found to be significantly influenced by season (Wu and Zhang 2004).The species feeds on a wide range of leaves and twigs of at least 33 different plant species in the Cat Ba Island, Vietnam (Phan et al. 2012), and 34 plant species in the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal (Giri et al. 2011). Most of these plant species are shrubs and low growing trees and thus serow is categorised as a typical browser.The Mainland Serow is active at almost any time, especially at dawn (Li et al. 2018b). They shelter under overhanging cliffs and rocks Lovari and Locati 1984). This species may naturally occur at rather low density, compared to other sympatric bovid species such as Goral and Takin (McShea et al. 2018). It is mostly solitary and probably territorial (McShea et al. 2018), marking the boundaries of its territory e.g. with dung piles (Lovari and Locati 1994). Several individuals are sometimes seen in the same area, but they feed some distance apart (Lekagul and McNeely 1988). The breeding season occurs on late October and November, and a single kid is born after a seven-month gestation period and will stay with its mother for almost a year (Lekagul and Mcneely 1988).
threats: Currently, the Mainland Serow is facing two main threats, i.e. over-poaching and habitat loss. Over-poaching, especially using snares to supply local and regional markets with meat, horns and other body parts has caused a rapid decline of this species in Southeast Asia (Steinmetz et al. 2010; Shepherd and Krishnasamy 2014; Leupen et al. 2017). Forest encroachment and clearance in protected and non-protected areas where this species exists are likely to have had a significant impact. In addition, most of the plant species consumed by the serows are medicinal herbs and edible sources for humans and thus they have been massively exploited by local people (Giri et al. 2011; Phan et al. 2012). These threats may determine a decrease in the numbers of serows and an increase in the fragmentation of populations, causing high risks of local extirpations over its range.In China, poaching, primarily through snares, is considered the top threat to wild serow, especially in eastern China where a very dense human population occurs. Die-offs caused by sarcoptic mange, typically during late winter to early spring, when the animals are weak, have been widely reported in western China, which may lead to abrupt decreases or even elimination of local serow populations (McShea et al. 2018). In addition, the meat, fur and other body parts of this species are highly prized by local people for food and medicinal purposes, and thus the species faces severe poaching pressure within its Chinese range (Shackleton, 1997).Serows are also significantly threatened by widespread poaching, illegal trade and habitat loss in South-east Asia. In Cambodia, logging, hunting, habitat loss and vast numbers of landmines are the main threats to the species. Illegal commercial hunting, particularly snaring, remains the major threat to the ground-dwelling mammals in Cardamom Rainforest Landscape and is possibly impacting populations of most such species in the landscape (Gray et al. 2017). The removal of more than 109,000 snares from the Southern Cardamom National Park and Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary between 2010 and 2015 was hard evidence of the risks which serows may face (Wildlife Alliance, unpublished data). In addition, local law enforcement is also minimal (Gray et al. 2017). Cambodia has also experienced the most rapid deforestation rate globally, between 2001 and 2014, and approximately 1,150 km² of the protected areas in Cardamom Rainforest Landscape have been lost to Economic Land Concessions for industrial agriculture (Davis et al. 2015), thereby reducing the mountainous habitat for mammals, including the serow in the whole country (Gray et al. 2017). In Lao PDR, serow horns, skull bones, leg bones and other body parts are used for traditional medicine and were recorded in 59 shops, and these items should be derived from a minimum of 150 serows (Leupen et al. 2017). There is a cross-border trade in almost all parts of the serow from Lao PDR to Thailand, Vietnam and China. However, the effects of this entire disturbance are unknown in Lao PDR (Salter and  Phanthavong, 1997; Duckworth et al. 1999). In Vietnam, the serow is frequently hunted for bush meat and for commercial purposes. Vietnam is a significant consumer of wildlife meat, including serow and thus wild meat is sold in many local markets and serow bones are purchased to make medicines (Shairp et al., 2016; Nijman and Shepherd, 2017). Over 23,000 snares were discovered and removed by forest rangers in Hue-Quang Nam Saola Reserve in 2015 (Gray et al. 2018). The result of this hunting is a significant decline in the populations of this species in almost all protected areas in Vietnam (Do Tuoc. pers. comm. 2011). In Thailand, loss of habitat caused by logging and land clearing for agriculture, and poaching for meat and medicinal purposes are the major threats for this species (Lovari, 1997). In addition, poaching for the trade in trophies (skins and horns), and the collection of non-timber forest products also negatively impact on the species and damage its habitat, which has resulted in the species being threatened in almost all forested areas in Thailand (Lyam et al. 2006). Furthermore, the remaining habitat for wildlife in Thailand is highly fragmented presently and mostly too small to support viable populations of wildlife species (Lyam et al. 2006). In Myanmar, too, the major threats to the serow include hunting, poaching, habitat degradation, and loss from deforestation. Wildlife items are widely used in the local pharmacopeia, and serow items were recorded for sale in 25 medicine shops in Mon State, south Myanmar (Nijman and Shepherd 2017). Habitat degradation and deforestation are the main consequences of human activities such as timber harvesting and agriculture, and fires in the country (Salter and Shackleton 1997).In Indonesia, habitat destruction threatens the long-term survival of the Sumatran serow. The principal causes of habitat destruction are slash-and-burn agriculture practices by highlanders and shifting cultivators, as well as the indiscriminate extraction of timber for export to the West. Serows are caught in snares as well as shot, for local consumption of the meat, and for use of body parts in traditional medicines (Holden 2014). Poaching occurs inside and outside protected areas. Sources living around protected areas in Sumatra, such as the Gunung Leuser National Park, Aceh, claim that hunting continues to increase as illegal logging roads have opened up parts of the park, allowing access to previously inaccessible areas. Locals claim that populations of serows have been declining. Trade of body parts, especially the horns, is conducted openly in some places, such as in the town of Pancur Batu, North Sumatra. Enforcement action against individuals trading Serow parts does not occur in these locations.In Malaysia, the Sumatran Serow faces several primary threats from habitat destruction caused by limestone quarrying and poaching for illegal commercial trade (Shepherd and Krishnasamy 2014). Serows also suffer from substantial poaching for its meat and body parts that are used for medicinal and purportedly magical purposes (Rahman 1997). The species is threatened by the widespread setting of snares and it is targeted species whenever poachers have access to its rugged habitats (Krishnasamy and Or 2014). Over the past two years, enforcement authorities have taken action against individuals involved in illegal hunting of this species, and as a result, trade of this species is not carried out openly, as it is in other areas of its-Southeast Asian range. Very little information on current population sizes of this species exists. Local people living near serow habitat state that populations seem to be declining, due to hunting and to mining activities (limestone and quartz). Eighteen out of 165 restaurants, that served bushmeat in Peninsular Malaysia, offered the meat of this species (Shepherd and Krishnasamy 2014).In the Himalayan range, habitat destruction and resource competition with livestock are key-threats to the Mainland serow throughout its range, even in protected areas. Disease transmission (sarcoptic mange and goat pox) seems to be a rising concern wherever serow overlap with domestic livestock, particularly sheep. Herders have reported finding dead serow with symptoms such as extremely dry skin, with rupturing and bleeding across the body, hair loss and foaming in the mouth in Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal, Uttarakhand (Khanyari et al. 2019). In Arunachal’s Tawang district, a recent outbreak of goat pox has severely impacted serows. According to local people, goat pox emerges every few years in the region when serow and goral populations reach high densities (Janaki Mohan pers. comm. 2020), although the other way round looks rather more likely.Poaching remains a serious threat to serow in most parts of Himalayan range. Most hunting in Himachal is subsistence only and is done particularly in winter months when the animals are seen more easily. In Arunachal, the serow is widely hunted both for subsistence and for sale. In Upper Siang district, gun hunting is rare and local hunters lay snare traps near salt licks. Datta-Roy (2019) noted that hunting in these community forests is strictly controlled by village institutions.Infrastructure development, including dams and highways in Sikkim and Arunachal, which may be the species strongholds, are a rising cause of large-scale habitat destruction.Habitat disturbance and poaching are the greatest threats to its survival also in Bangladesh, both related to slash and burn cultivations (Khan 1985). Over-hunting, habitat destruction by human and livestock, and habitat fragmentation are main threats to the serow population decline in Nepal (Aryal 2009, Giri et al. 2011). In Bhutan, the species is rarely hunted and populations appear to be stable.
population: There are no estimates of the total population size and trend of the Mainland serow throughout its range. It is believed that populations have been fragmented and significantly declined through time, and its distribution range has been gradually reduced due to the loss of habitat and intervening forest clearance, with excessive poaching in many areas.Subspecies Capricornis sumatraensis sumatraensis: No population estimates have been made on the Sumatran Serow. In Indonesia, this sub-species was recorded by camera traps in some national parks, such as Kerinci Seblat and Bukit Barisan Salatan, however, the status of this species is already very rare in these national parks because of deforestation and illegal poaching (Pakpahan et al. 2016, Dwiyahreni Asri pers. comm. 2020). For example, the serow was considered 'rare' in Kerinci Seblat National Park, based on camera-trap surveys in 2005 and 2006 (Leader-Williams et al. 2006) and hundreds of thousands of hour camera-trap surveys in Sumatra in six years, only one photo-trapped at 2,700 m on a volcanic peak (Holden 2014). Also, in Malaysia information on the status of serow is not available, but it is considered threatened and significantly declined in Peninsular Malaysia (Shepherd and Krishnasamy 2014). A total of 30 artificial salt licks were developed in 10 protected areas in Malaysia, and they were monitored in 2011 and 2013 but this sub-species rarely visited these artificial salt licks (Magintan et al. 2015).Subspecies C. s. mildneedwardsii: Populations of this sub-species in southeast China (south of the Yangtze river) are small and isolated, and this subspecies’ general distribution range falls within regions with relatively dense human populations which are well-exploited economic areas (Sung et al. 1997). Camera-trapping surveys conducted in numerous reserves across this region indicated that serow is the least detected ungulate species and its abundance is extremely low (Chen et al. 2016, Li et al. 2018a). Although no population estimates have been made in this area, numbers are believed to be decreasing and its distribution range has gradually been reduced. In southwest China, serow populations are generally considered stable in most well-managed nature reserves, whereas there are cases of a decrease observed in some reserves following the rapid increase of free-ranging livestock over the last few decades (Li., unpublished data). While co-existing with other meso-large bovid species, such as Takin and Goral, in forest ecosystems, serows have the lowest detection and relative abundance according to camera-trapping surveys (Li et al. 2012, Li et al. 2014).In Cambodia the population status of this sub-species is unknown and serows are probably naturally restricted to the hilly and mountainous terrain that surround the Mekong and Tonle Sap central plains. An intensive camera-trap survey was conducted within Phom Prich Wildlife Sanctuary in eastern Cambodia in 2008 and 2009, and 23 species were recorded, including four large ungulate species but serow was not recorded (Gray and Phan 2011). In addition, camera-trap detection levels of this sub-species were low and restricted to the Cardamoms, south-west Cambodia and Virachey National Park, north-eastern Cambodia (Gray et al. 2017). In Lao PDR, data on population size and trend of this sub-species are unavailable. However, the sub-species showed a low detection rate in camera-trap surveys in Xe Sap National Protected Area, in southern Lao PDR (Tilker 2014) and has a density of 0.22 individual/km² in Nam Et-Phou Louey National Protected Area in northern Lao PDR (Vongkhamheng et al. 2013). In addition, this sub-species is potentially considered at risk in Lao PDR (Duckworth et al. 1999). In Thailand, the population and status of this sub-species is unknown and showed a low detection rate in camera-trap surveys, in Dong Phayayen - Khao Yai Forest Complex, in southern Thailand (Lyam et al. 2006). Serows had a very low detection rate in Kuiburi National Park, in south-western Thailand (Steinmetz et al. 2009) and in Thung Yai Naresuan Wildlife Sanctuary, in western Thailand (Steinmetz et al. 2010). In Vietnam, population numbers are unknown, an exception being about 26 individuals left in the Cat Ba Island, in north Vietnam (Phan et al. 2014). This sub-species was recorded in almost all protected areas from northern to southern central areas of Vietnam, but populations are small and scattered, and numbers are probably low (Nguyen Xuan Dang and Le Xuan Canh, 2009; Dang Ngoc Can et al. 2008). It is believed that populations in the northern highlands are heavily depleted in number and the populations are highly fragmented. However, they are likely to be more present in most protected areas along the Annamite mountains of central Vietnam. For example, five monitoring programs used 591camera traps in Pu Mat National Park in central Vietnam and recorded 94 photos of serows from 2016 to 2018 (Tran Xuan Cuong pers. comm. 2019).Subspecies C. s. thar:  No counts have been made in Bangladesh, but numbers are believed to be very low. In addition, serows have not been detected by camera-trap surveys from 2011 to 2015 in the Sangu Reserve Forest in the southeastern, Bangladesh (CCA 2016). In Bhutan’s Jigme Singye Wangchuck National Park, Wang (2010) used distance sampling to estimate serow density of 0.36 individuals/km². In India, the population size of this sub-species is not available, but its density seems to be fair in good habitat: within Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary (Uttaranchal) it has been estimated at 1.6 serow/km² within suitable habitat (Green 1987). This sub-species was frequently detected using camera traps from 2008 to 2010 in Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve, Sikkim (Bhattacharya et al. 2012). In Arunachal’s Dibang Valley, Nijhawan (2018) estimated serow densities from camera trapped data using at 0.62 (0.26-1.46) and 0.25 (0.10-0.59) individuals/km2 in two separate community forests and 0.19 (0.08-0.49) individuals/km2 in Dibang WLS. No  population estimates exist from J&K or Himachal and the species is encountered very rarely in camera trap studies indicating naturally rare populations even in protected areas. In Himachal, populations are reportedly declining in most areas though local herders report easy detections during winter months (November-February). In Nepal, no estimates of population size are available, but density within the Annapurna Conservation Area has been estimated at 1.17 individual/km², significantly declined over the last few decades (Aryal 2009).
range: The Mainland Serow occurs across eleven countries, including China, Southeast Asia and Himalayan range. Subspecies Capricornis sumatraensis sumatraensis is found in Indonesia (Sumatra), Malaysia (Peninsular Malaya), Thailand (south of about 9°S latitude) (Grubb, 2005). In Indonesia, this sub-species is restricted entirely to the volcanic mountain chain of the Bukit Barisan mountains in Sumatra, especially in the Aceh highlands in the north, the Kerinci highlands in the centre and the Barisan Seletan highlands in the south (Dwiyahreni Asri pers. comm. 2020). It is also found scattered through Peninsular (West) Malaysia, but concentrated in the northern states, especially Kelantan, Perlis and Perak. The species has been recorded in 50 areas in Peninsular Malaysia (Rahman 1997), but the species has significantly decreased in these areas (Shepherd and Krishnasamy 2014).Subspecies C. s. mildneedwardsii occurs in much of Myanmar, Cambodia, south and central China (extends to eastern Himalayas and Indo-Burma), Lao PDR, Thailand, and Viet Nam (Grubb 2005). The sub-species is widely distributed through much of central and south-eastern China, including southern Shaanixi, southern Gansu, southeastern Qinghai, western Sichuan, eastern Tibet, Yunnan, Guangzi, Guizhou, Chongqing, Guangdong, Jiangxi, Hubai, Hunan, Anhui, Zhejiang, Fujian provinces. However, this sub-species is replaced in parts of northern Myanmar by Capricornis rubidus (Smith and Xie 2008).Records show a more or less continuous distribution along the ranges of the Hungduan mountain system. East of this region, populations occur in adjacent mountain areas of Qinling (Southern Slope), Shaanxi and Guizhou (Zhen 1982). A few populations exist in the north-western Hengduan Mountains of Yushu and Nangqqian (Qinghai) (Li et al. 1989). This subspecies has a comparatively widespread distribution from eastern to southern China, through western and southern Zhejiang, northern Fujian, most of Jiangxi, eastern Guizhou (Luo et al. 1985), northern Guangdong, eastern and south-western Guangxi, eastern and southern Yunnan, where it inhabits low mountains and foothills. It may also occur in south-western Sichuan, as indicated by specimens from the adjacent mountains of Jijiang.Two subspecies (C. s. sumatraensis and C. s. milneedwardsii) originally were widely distributed throughout Thailand, but they are now restricted to steep, forested limestone hills and cliffs, in areas relatively inaccessible to human encroachment (Lovari, 1997). Therefore, their populations are highly fragmented, with a low density (Lovari 1997, Lyam et al. 2006, Steinmetz et al. 2009). The dividing line between the ranges of C. s. milneedwardsii and C.s. sumatraensis is unclear, but it is suspected to fall somewhere in the Chooporn or Suratchathani Provinces (Grubb 2005).The historic distribution of C. s. milneedwarsii in Lao PDR almost certainly included the vast majority of the countries, the majority of which is hilly to mountainous (Lekagul and McNeely1988). Currently in Lao PDR the sub-species is restricted to rugged terrain areas, especially along the Annamite mountain range of eastern central and southern Lao PDR (Vongkhamheng et al. 2013, Tilker 2014). In Cambodia the species is probably naturally restricted to the hill and mountainous terrain that surround the Mekong and Tonle Sap (lake) central plains (Gray and Phan 2011, Gray et al. 2017). In Viet Nam the serows were recorded in almost all protected areas from northern to the south-central areas of the country, especially where forested limestone mountains and cliffs occured (Nguyen Xuan Dang and Le Xuan Canh 2009). During mammal surveys from 1999 to 2008, serows were found in the northern Vietnam, including Ha Giang, Cao Bang, Lai Chau, Tuyen Quang, Bac Kan, Phu Tho, Thai Nguyen, Vinh Phuc, Quang Ninh, Hai Phong, Hoa Binh and Ninh Binh provinces; in the northern central areas of Vietnam, such as Thanh Hoa, Nghe An, Ha Tinh, Quang Binh, Quang Tri, and Thua Thien Hue; in the central areas of Viet Nam, including  Quang Nam, Kon Tum, Gia Lai, Dak Lac, Dak Nong and Lam Dong provinces, and in the southern central areas of Vietnam, including in Binh Dinh, Binh Thuan and Ninh Thuan provinces (Dang Ngoc Can et al. 2008). The species has also been recorded from offshore islands in the north, e.g. Cat Ba (Phan et al. 2014). However, there is no further information available on its distribution status and it is believed that this sub-species has significantly declined due to poaching in Viet Nam.The general distribution in Myanmar appears to follow the forested mountain ranges surrounding the central plains. Its distribution in the northwest is believed to stretch through the Chin Hills from the border with India, probably as far south as 20ºN in the Arakan Yoma range. A larger distribution area occurs in the mountains in the north (Kachin state) and in the mountains east of about 96ºW, to Myanmar’s borders with China, Lao PDR and Thailand (Grubb 2005).Subspecies: C. s.thar is known to occur in east and southeast Bangladesh, Himalayas (Bhutan, northern India including Sikkim and Nepal), China (Tibet only), northeast India (provinces east of Bangladesh), and probably into western Myanmar (Grubb 2005). This sub-species is widespread though sparsely distributed throughout the Himalayas from Jammu and Kashmir through Nepal and Bhutan till the eastern side of Arunachal Pradesh. Its distribution is generally fragmented and throughout the majority of its range in India, it naturally occurs in low density. In the state of Jammu and Kashmir, its presence has been confirmed through camera traps and direct sightings from the districts of Srinagar (Dachigam National Park, Brien-Nishta Wildlife Conservation Reserve), Kishtwar (Kishtwar National Park), Ganderbal/Anantnag (Overu-Aru Wildlife Sanctuary), and Baramulla (Tangmarg-Gulmarg valleys) (Sathyakumar et al. 2013, Tawqir Bhat pers. comm. 2019, Munib Khanyari pers. comm. 2019). In Himachal Pradesh, Pandey (2002) reported that the species is found extensively in the Sutlej and Beas River catchments in the state. More recently it has been confirmed from the districts of Shimla (Rupi Valley, Narkanda Valley, Dodra-Kwar region), Lower Kinnaur (Bhaba valley), Kullu (Great Himalayan National Park including Thirthan, Sainj, Parvati and Jeeva Nala), Kangra (Barabangal region), Chamba (Lower Bharmour and Upper Dalhousie region though believed to be nearly extinct in this area) (Munib Khanyari pers. comm. 2019). They are occasionally sighted in abandoned farmland in these areas. In Uttarakhand, serow presence has been confirmed via camera-trap surveys from Rudraprayag (Kedarnath Forest Division, Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary) (GTF et al. 2019) and Pauri Garhwal (Lansdowne Forest Division) (Pawar et al. 2018), distribution in the rest of the state remains uncertain, but the species is likely be present in forest patches from 500 to 3,500 m in elevation. The serow is widely distributed across Sikkim where camera-trap surveys have confirmed populations in East Sikkim Wildlife and Forest Division (Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, Kyongnosla WLS), North Sikkim Forest Division and Khangchendzonga NP (Sathyakumar et al. 2011, Bhattacharya et al. 2012; Srivastava and Kumar 2018). In West Bengal, it is extant in Darjeeling Wildlife Division (Singalila National Park) and Gorumara Wildlife Division (Neora Valley National Park) (GTF et al. 2019). In Assam, the species occurs in hilly tracts on the north bank of Bramhaputra river and has been reported from the districts of Kokrajhar (Ripu and Chirang Reserve Forests), Sonitpur (Nameri National Park), rare but seen in winter in Lakhimpur (Ranga, Kakoi and Dulung Reserve Forests), and Dhemaji (Subansiri Reserve Forest) (Choudhury 2003).In Arunachal Pradesh, the sub-species is widely distributed across protected areas and community owned forests from lowland forests up to 3,500 m. Camera-trap surveys, where it is often captured, and hunter interviews have confirmed populations in the districts of Lower Subansiri (Hapoli Forest Division, Talle Valley WLS), Upper Siang (Yingkiong Forest Division), West Kameng (Eaglenest WLS), Tawang and West Siang (Yorde Rabe Subse WLS), Lower Dibang Valley, Dibang Valley (where it is frequently recorded in very steep terrain), Lohit, Anjaw and Changlang districts. In Namdapha Tiger Reserve, the species overlaps with C. rubidus. No records of C. s. thar have emerged south of Tirap and Longding districts in Arunachal. C. rubidus is found in the hill tracts south of Brahmaputra and appears to be the only serow species from southwards from Nagaland into Bangladesh.Serow appears to be widely distributed in Nepal across its community forests and protected areas and has been reported form Annapurna Conservation Area (ACA), Sagarmatha National Park (NP), Makalu Barun NP and CA, Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve, Langtang NP, Khaptad NP, Rara NP and perhaps in Shey-Phoksundo NP and Chitwan NP. They have also been reported from Kanchanpur, Taplejung, Ramechhap and Illam districts. The only serow-focused research conducted in the country by Aryal (2008) in Annapurna Conservation Area found that the species prefers altitudes between 2,500 and 3,500 m and slopes between 20-40 degrees. The species also appears to be widely distributed in Bhutan up to an altitude of 3,500 m. It is regularly camera trapped in subtropical and temperate zones of Royal Manas, Black Mountain and Jigme Singye Wangchuck National Park.In China, this sub-species occurs in the forest belt between 2,000 and 3,000 m only in the narrow area on south slope of Qomolangma on the border with Nepal. Observations of serow running across highways are not infrequent. A population is found in the Yaluzangbu Grand Canyon National Nature Reserve, where it inhabits sub-alpine forests and has been recorded in camera-trap surveys and by wildlife photographers (Wen et al. 2014, Wu et al. 2016, Mcshea et al. 2018). In Medog county, southeast Tibet, China, the Himalayan Serow is the most detected bovid species by camera-trap surveys (Wen et al. 2014, Wu et al. 2016).
conservationActions: The Mainland serow is listed in Appendix I of the CITES (The Convention of International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora), which prohibits international commercial trade of the species, its body parts and derivatives. In Indonesia, the species has been protected by law since 1932. A total of 3,083,308 ha of serow habitat are under some form of protection in a system of protected areas that includes three national parks, three game reserves, three nature reserves and two protected forests. The species is afforded fully legal protection in Peninsular Malaysia under Wildlife Conservation Act, 2010, which means that hunting this species is prohibited. The serow is classified as Category II on the State Key Protected Animal List, under the Wildlife Protection Law of China (Smith and Xie 2008), and Potentially at Risk in Lao PDR (Duckworth et al. 1999). However, it seems that there is no actual legislation aimed at conserving the serow in Cambodia, Myanmar and Thailand. In Vietnam, the animal is listed as IB (hunting prohibited) in the Endangered and Rare Species List in Degree 32, in 2006, and Endangered (E) in the Vietnamese Red Book, in 2008. The serow is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act of India and Forest and Nature Conservation Act of Bhutan which bans all hunting. In Nepal its hunting is banned by law (Wegge and Oli 1997). The serow is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act of India (WLPA, 1972) and Forest and Nature conservation act of Bhutan which bans all hunting. In Nepal too, it’s hunting is completely banned by law (Wegge and Oli 1997).So far, there have been just a few research projects focused on the distribution and status of serows throughout its range, except several studies, e.g. in Cat Ba Island, Vietnam (Phan et al. 2014) and in Annapurna Conservation Area, (Aryal, 2008). Camera-trap surveys were conducted by conservation organisations (e.g. WWF, FFI and WCS) in protected areas throughout Southeast Asia to monitor and assess the distribution status of wildlife animals, including serows. For example, in Vietnam, WWF cooperated with Song Thanh Nature Reserve and Bac Hai Van Nature Reserve to monitor wildlife animals through establishing camera-traps, and recorded the presence of serows in these reserves (Mai Sy Luan pers.comm. 2020). Similarly, FFI and SVW conducted a camera-trap survey in Pu Mat National Park to monitor wildlife and recorded the evidence of serows (Tran Xuan Cuong, pers.comm. 2020). WWF-India, Wildlife Institute of India (WII), Nijhawan (2018) and by the Nature Conservation Division of The Department of Forest and Park Service of Bhutan have conducted widespread camera trapping surveys in India and Bhutanese Himalayas. However, these data have not been made available for focused research on this species.More research on distribution and status as well as the impact of hunting and trading of Mainland Serows throughout its range is urgently needed. In addition, relevant information on the ecology and behaviour of this species should be published and brought to the attention of relevant enforcement agencies, conservation organisations and the public, to advertise the threats that this species is facing, and increase the efforts to save it from further local extinctions.

rationale: Nycticebus kayan is listed as Vulnerable as there has probably been more than a 30% reduction in population over the past three generations (approximately 21-24 years) and there is a continuing decline based on harvesting for the pet trade, hybridization, and extensive habitat loss from deforestation for oil palm plantations and forest fires.
habitat: The species is nocturnal and arboreal as other slow lorises (Nycticebus spp.). Slow Lorises in Borneo are found in a range of habitats from heavily degraded to pristine rainforest, plantations, and lowland and montane forests (Nekaris et al. 2008, Thorn et al. 2009). To date there have been no wild studies of this species. This species is known to be venomous (Madani and Nekaris 2014).
threats: Burning of habitat and conversion, especially to palm oil plantations, almost certainly represents a threat to this species. Although it is relatively adaptable to anthropogenic habitats, and so it might less affected by forest loss than some other primate species, forest loss has been so severe in the region that it is likely to have had some negative impacts. Forest fires of 2015 on Borneo have been the worst since 2004, and acres of forest have been burned, leading to a significant decrease in the habitat of this species.The species is collected locally for use as pets; subsequent uncontrolled release of pets in some areas is also a threat. Such animals may also be caught and used by tourists as photo props. In 2015, an individual of the species was confiscated by authorities and brought to Singapore Zoo, showing that international trade is also a threat. Hybridization poses a real threat to this species both in the wild and for confiscated individuals in rescue centres. Lack of law enforcement further threatens slow loris species across their range (Nekaris and Starr 2015, Nijman et al. 2014).The occurrence of N. menagensis in the illegal wildlife trade suggests that N. kayan is at risk of exploitation by the illegal wildlife trade.
population: Miard (unpublished) encountered Nycticebus kayan in the Mulu district of Sarawak and at the tip of Borneo, Kudat district in Sabah. This species is suspected to be in declining due to loss of habitat from deforestation, forest fires and the illegal pet trade.
range: Nycticebus kayan is located in central and northern Borneo (Brunei, Sarawak, Sabah, and East Kalimantan). Its southern range extends to the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan and the Rajang River in Sarawak. It is found as far north as the tip of Borneo in Sabah. It spans the width of Borneo, east to west, but unlike its neighbour (N. menagensis), it appears not to be found along the east part of Sabah. It is sympatric with N. menagensis in East Kalimantan Sabah and Sarawak.
useTrade: The species is collected locally for use as pets; subsequent uncontrolled release of pets in some areas is also a threat. Such animals may also be caught and used by tourists as photo props. In 2015, an individual of the species was confiscated by authorities and brought to Singapore Zoo, showing that international trade is also a threat. Hybridization poses a real threat to this species both in the wild and for confiscated individuals in rescue centres. Lack of law enforcement further threatens slow loris species across their range (Nekaris and Starr 2015, Nijman et al. 2014).
conservationActions: This species is protected by Indonesian law (No. 5 of 1990), the Malaysian (Sabah) Wildlife Conservation Act (2010) Act 716 (Nekaris & Starr, 2015) and in Sarawak (Malaysia) with the Wild Life Protection Ordinance, 1998 (Chapter 26). It is also included in Appendix I of CITES. Following the description of three new species on Borneo, surveys to assess the status of this species are required. There is a particular need for field guides for this and other nocturnal Indonesian primate species, as they are often confused in rescue centres and elsewhere. There are a number of protected areas throughout its range, though its status there is uncertain. Long-term monitoring of populations and increasing available data on the species ecology, behaviour and habitat requirements should be a top priority for this species. Establishing education across its range is also important in order to address issues with the illegal use of slow lorises in the illegal wildlife trade.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct). A combination of historic forest loss and continued degradation has resulted in less than 20% of former suitable habitat remaining for Nycticebus bancancus. Since it was last seen in 1937, it may already be Extinct; more surveys are needed to find this species. Species distribution modelling and a gap analysis have revealed that any remaining subpopulations of N. bancanus will be highly fragmented. Due to mass conversion of the island of Bangka for oil palm over the last 20 years, the species is suspected to have experienced a decline of at least 80% over the last 24 years (three generations).
habitat: The species is nocturnal and arboreal as other slow lorises (Nycticebus spp.). Slow lorises are found in a range of habitats from heavily degraded to pristine rainforest, plantations, and lowland and montane forests and thus the species should still occur in forest patches on the island (Nekaris, 2014).
threats: This species was last reported from the wild in 1937; if it is still extant then burning of its habitat and conversion to agriculture (especially to palm oil plantations) is its greatest threat. The occurrence of Nycticebus menagensis in the illegal wildlife trade suggests that N. bancanus is likely also at risk of exploitation by the illegal wildlife trade. However, this risk will be less since Bangka is relatively isolated from other Indonesian islands. At the same time, slow lorises are often caught during forest conversion due to their tendency to cling to trees rather than flee (Nekaris and Starr, 2015), meaning that they may still occur in trade. Lack of law enforcement further threatens slow loris species across their range (Nijman et al. 2014).
population: If it is still extant, this species is highly likely to be declining due to loss of habitat from extreme deforestation largely due to oil palm plantations, leaving Bangka with less than 20% of its forest cover.
range: Nycticebus bancanus is only known from the island of Bangka, Indonesia. The Bangka population is allopatric to all other slow lorises. It is possible the species also occurs on Belitung, but no records are available. The species has not been reported from the wild since 1937 and field studies are required to confirm its presence on the ground.
useTrade: If it is still extant, this species is likely to occur in trade as other Loris species are traded. Further studies are required to understand the use and harvest of this species.
conservationActions: This species is protected by the Act of the Republic of Indonesia No. 5 of 1990 Concerning Conservation of Living Resources and Their Ecosystems which prohibits to catch, injure, kill, store, possess, nurture, transport and trade protected animals in alive or dead condition. Exceptions from prohibition can only be made for purpose of research, science, salvage of the animal species or in case the animal endangers the human life. It is also included in Appendix I of CITES. Surveys to assess the status of this species are required. Long-term monitoring of populations, and increasing available data on the species ecology, behaviour and habitat requirements should be a top priority for this species (Nekaris and Starr 2015).Establishing education across its range are also important in order to address issues with the illegal use of slow lorises in the illegal wildlife trade. There is a particular need for field guides for this and other nocturnal Indonesian primate species especially in local languages, as they are often confused in rescue centres and elsewhere.

rationale: Nycticebus borneanus is listed as Vulnerable as there has been a more than 30% reduction in population over three generations (approximately 21-24 years) based on harvesting for the pet trade and extensive habitat loss. Although it is adaptable to anthropogenic change, forest loss has been so severe that it is likely to have had some negative impacts, with Borneo losing a third of its forest in less than 25 years, as also due to extensive fires.
habitat: As for other as other slow lorises (Nycticebus spp.), this species is nocturnal and arboreal. It has been observed in dipterocarp forest at Bukit Batikap Protected Forest, Central Kalimantan (Van Berkel 2011). Slow Lorises in Borneo are found in a range of habitats from heavily degraded to pristine rainforest, plantations, and lowland and montane forests (Nekaris et al. 2008, Thorn et al. 2009).
threats: Burning and habitat conversion, especially to oil palm plantations, almost certainly represents a threat to this species. The Slow Loris species studied so far are relatively adaptable to anthropogenic change, although forest loss has been so severe that it is likely to have had some negative impacts, with Borneo losing a third of its forest in less than 25 years (Rautner and Hardino, 2005). Forest fires of 2015 in Borneo have been the worst since 2004, and acres of forest have been burned, leading to a significant decrease in the habitat of this species. In Indonesia, habitat fragmentation, deforestation and the lack of data available on the species habitat requirements are seen to be the most significant risks to this species.The occurrence of Nycticebus menagensis in the illegal wildlife trade suggests that N. borneanus is also at risk of exploitation by the illegal wildlife trade. The species has not yet appeared in photographs of rescued individuals (Nekaris, pers. obs.). Legal penalties for illegal hunting, trafficking or selling lorises across their range are often not enforced, and the current penalty is not seen as a significant deterrent. In Indonesia, this species has specific uses in traditional medicine and ceremonies. Hybridization poses a real threat to this species both in the wild and for confiscated individuals in rescue centres.Lack of law enforcement further threatens slow loris species across their range (Starr and Nekaris 2015, Nijman et al. 2014).
population: The only survey data available to date for this species is from a survey in Bukit Batikap Protected Forest, Central Kalimantan, where the species was recorded at densities of 0.05 individuals/km (Van Berkel, 2011). This species is believed to be in decline due overexploitation and loss of habitat from deforestation and forest fires.
range: Nycticebus borneanus is found in central south Borneo (West, South, and Central Kalimantan, but excluding the extreme southwest), south of the Kapuas River, extending as far east as the Barito River. This species may occur sympatrically with N. kayan or with N. menagensis (Munds et al. 2013).
useTrade: In Indonesia, this species has specific uses in traditional medicine and ceremonies. Hybridization poses a real threat to this species both in the wild and for confiscated individuals in rescue centres. Legal penalties for illegal hunting, trafficking or selling lorises across their range are often not enforced, and the current penalty is not seen as a significant deterrent.Lack of law enforcement further threatens slow loris species across their range (Nekaris and Starr, 2015; Nijman et al., 2014).
conservationActions: This species is protected by Indonesian law and is included in Appendix I of CITES.
