rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large populations, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate of required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: In Thailand, the species was captured either within limestone caves or in their vicinities or in an area that includes limestone outcrops. The surrounding vegetation varied from seasonal hill evergreen, hill evergreen, moist evergreen, lowland rain evergreen, lowland evergreen, lowland tropical rain, mixed deciduous, mangrove to disturbed forests. It is tolerant of highly disturbed habitat, including cultivations (Douangboubpha et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation, generally changing forest plantations (B. Douangboubpha pers. comm.).
population: In Thailand, it has been found roosting in colonies up to hundreds of individuals (Douangboubpha et al. 2010).
range: The species is known from peninsular Thailand and Malaysia to Sumatra (Indonesia) and Teratau and Tioman Islands (Malaysia) (Douangboubpha et al. 2010).
conservationActions: This species occurs in a number of protected areas.

rationale: The Vangunu Giant Rat is assessed as Critically Endangered because it is endemic to Vangunu Island, Western Province, Solomon Islands, which has an area of 544 km². Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is restricted to the unlogged lowland forests of southern Vangunu, an area approximately 77 km² in size. It is known only from a single locality that has now been logged, and the area and extent of its lowland forest habitat is rapidly declining due to logging.
habitat: Little is known about the habitat requirements or ecology of this species. It appears to inhabit primary lowland forests only. The holotype was collected from a tree (Dillenia salomonensis) that was felled during a commercial logging operation in lowland primary forest. Uromys vika reportedly nests in these trees as they readily from hollows within the branches—it does not eat the fruits of this tree (H. Judge pers. comm). The holotype reportedly emerged from within a nest constructed amongst epiphytic ferns. This species feeds on ngali nuts (Canarium indicum), which are common within the historic village sites that lie amongst tracts of primary forest. A faecal pellet collected on southern Vangunu in November 2011 was thought to belong to this species and contained traces of Canarium nut and fragments of unidentifiable rodent hair. Wider diet is unknown.
threats: This species is threatened primarily by logging. It seems completely reliant on primary forests and prefers to nest in Dillenia salomonensis, which is a prized commercial timber tree. This species may be hunted opportunistically but does not appear to be specifically targeted.
population: This is a rare species and population size is unknown. Periodic surveys targeting this species have been undertaken since January 2010 using rodent traps, motion-activated cameras, spotlighting, and active searches of tree hollows. These efforts have been unsuccessful.
range: This species (known only from the holotype) was captured from a felled tree in lowland forest being logged on southern Vangunu (Lavery and Judge 2017). It is likely restricted to lowland forests with a range recorded as sea level to 400 m. The species possibly occurs on New Georgia, Kolombangara and Gatokae as these islands were interconnected together during the Pleistocene, but this requires confirmation.
conservationActions: This species does not occur within any legislatively protected areas. There is an urgent need to protect any remaining populations of this rare species. The remaining area of primary forest adjacent to the type locality is protected under a community conservation agreement and recognised as the Zaira Community Resource Management Area. This community has a long-term goal to register their area under the Solomon Islands Protected Areas Act.

rationale: Miss Waldron's Red Colobus is listed as Critically Endangered as the species is estimated to have undergone a population decline of more than 80% in the 30 years (approximately three generations) up until the last authenticated specimen (killed by a hunter) was found in 2002. Calls of what are believed to be this animal were heard in early 2008, but no wild animal has been seen by an experienced field-worker for 40 years. Therefore this monkey is regarded as possibly extinct. Its disappearance from its former range in the forests of eastern Côte d’Ivoire and western Ghana was almost certainly caused by excessive hunting for the bushmeat trade, combined with a loss of mature forest habitat.
habitat: Miss Waldron’s Red Colobus was restricted to tropical moist and semi-deciduous forest, and swamp forest, where it typically used the upper canopy (Martin 1991). Two groups studied in Bia National Park in Ghana in the 1970s comprised 34 and 58 individuals, had home ranges of 100–140 ha, and had a diet consisting predominantly of leaves but also fruits, seeds and flowers (Martin 1991).
threats: The major causes of the decline of the species were hunting and habitat loss (Oates et al. 2000). Both subsistence and commercial hunting (for the bushmeat trade) heavily impacted populations of this species, and improved access to forest interiors via logging roads increased hunting pressure. Deforestation through logging, charcoal production, cocoa farming and clearance for agricultural land (including industrial oil palm and rubber tree plantations), occurred over much of the species range in the last 50-60 years.
population: There have been no confirmed sightings of Miss Waldron's Red Colobus in the wild since 1978 and surveys carried out from 1993 to the present have failed to produce a sighting of living individuals (Oates et al. 2000, McGraw 2005, Oates 2011). The last evidence for the survival of a small population came from the Tanoé Swamp Forest between the Ehy lagoon and the Tanoé River in extreme south-eastern Côte d'Ivoire (McGraw and Oates 2002, McGraw 2005, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2008), near which a skin was found in possession of a hunter in 2002 and where calls by what is believed to be Miss Waldron's Red Colobus were heard in March 2008 by a team of scientists from the Centre Suisse de Recherches Scientifiques en Côte d’Ivoire (I. Koné pers. comm. 2008).
range: Piliocolobus waldroni ranged from the Nzi-Bandama River system in south-eastern Côte d'Ivoire to south-western Ghana, but did not reach the Volta River (Oates et al. 2000, McGraw 2005, Oates 2011). Its numbers were declining in Ghana 60 years ago, when Booth (1956) predicted its extinction in the near future. The last evidence for the monkey’s survival came from swamp forests between the Ehy lagoon and Tanoé River in south-eastern Côte d'Ivoire (McGraw 2005, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2008).
useTrade: This species was known to be heavily hunted.
conservationActions: This taxon is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.

rationale: Molecular phylogenetic studies (e.g. Faulkes et al. 2010, 2017) indicate that the Hanang Mole-rat is a relict species of the Fukomys genus with a restricted distribution and declining, fragmented populations. Based on the available evidence, this species qualifies for “Endangered” status under the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria.Quantitative data indicate that some subpopulations are in decline, particularly in the Hanang region, and would fall under criterion A2, and it is likely that this extends to the population as a whole. Certainly, the subpopulations occurring in the agricultural land that surrounds both Mt Hanang Nature Forest Reserve and Nou Forest Reserve are potentially threatened due to human activities, and to the fact that the mole-rats will eat some cultivated crops like sweet potato and thus constitute a pest species. They may also be culled for use in traditional medicines.Under both criteria B1 and B2, the evidence appears to be strong for qualification as Endangered. The Hanang Mole-rat has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 645 km² (i.e., <5,000 km²) and an area of occupancy (AOO) of 64 km2 (<500 km2), as calculated using Geocat (Bachman et al. 2011) with a cell width of 2 km (which is a realistic estimate given the subterranean lifestyle of the species). In both cases this is supported by “a. severely fragmented” (they are in small and isolated subpopulations), and “b. observed and inferred continuing decline” in (ii) area of occupancy, (iii) area, extent and quality of habitat, (iv) decline in the number of locations or subpopulations and (v) number of mature individuals. With increasing human population growth and transport infrastructure such as tarmac roads dividing up the landscape and the limited dispersal patterns of mole-rats, fragmentation and isolation of subpopulations are projected to increase.We estimate that the population size meets criterion C, under C2a(i) “number of mature individuals in each subpopulation <250”, and criterion D “population size estimated to number fewer than 250 mature individuals” or 125 colonies.Therefore, the final assessment of this species is Endangered (EN) A2acd; B1ab(ii,iii,iv)+2ab(ii,iii,iv); C2a(i); D.
habitat: Fukomys hanangensis (the Hanang Mole-rat) is a small to medium sized example of the African mole-rat genus Fukomys, with an average adult weight of 83 g. As with other members of the genus, the Hanang Mole-rat has a completely subterranean lifestyle, and is a social cooperative breeder, where the young exhibit natal philopatry and reproduction is restricted to a single adult breeding pair (i.e. a high “reproductive skew”) within the social group (or colony). So far, a maximum group size of eight has been recorded for the Hanang Mole-rat (Faulkes et al. 2017). Each colony represents one breeding “unit”, and so “population size” (as defined by the IUCN) is equivalent to the number of colonies multiplied by two (Faulkes and Bennett 2013, Faulkes et al. 2017). Generation time for the Hanang Mole-rat is estimated to be around 3–6 years given their life history strategy and extrapolating from a related species in the genus - F. damarensis where for the latter, long term field studies have revealed a generation length (average age of parents/breeders) for females of 6.2 years (Schmidt et al. 2013). Immigration is known to occur in other Fukomys species, thus occasionally giving rise to mixed-kin social groups (e.g. F. damarensis; Burland et al. 2004), but dispersal has not been quantified in the Hanang Mole-rat. High constraints on dispersal within their subterranean niche has been suggested as a major factor in promoting natal philopatry, group living and cooperative breeding in African mole-rats (Faulkes et al. 1997, 2013). Social groups cooperate in digging foraging tunnels from their burrow systems in search of underground roots, corms and tubers that form the staple diet of mole-rats. The occurrence of mole-rats is therefore dictated by the presence of suitable plants and shrubs with subterranean food resources.The type locality of the Hanang Mole-rat is Jorodom Village, (04°29.510′ S; 035°24.519′ E) in farmland on the slopes of Mt Hanang. The specimen was trapped in a valley at an altitude of 1,957 m (6,422 ft) above sea level. The local subpopulation at Jorodom and neighboring villages around Mt Hanang now appears to be in decline. The Hanang Mole-rat occurs in uncultivated grassy fields and boundary hedges within the agricultural areas and small subsistence farms that surround Mt Hanang Nature Forest Reserve and Nou Forest Reserve. Soil type is classified as “Calcic Cambisol” (FAO Soil Unit: Bk) at Hanang and as “Distric Nitosol” (FAO Soil Unit Nd) at Nou (The FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World 1974–1980). Their burrows may extend into cultivated fields where they may also forage for suitable food such as sweet potato. Mole-rats have also been caught deep within the forest reserves at both Hanang and Nou, in naturally occurring open patches of habitat containing grasses, ferns and other small plants and shrubs. These areas may represent important refugia given the intensity of farming in this region of Tanzania. Burrow systems have been observed above the forest line on Mt Hanang and an animal recently caught as high as 3,097m – although active mole-hills were found as high as 3,199 m. Limited dispersal, the encroachment of human agriculture and other activities, and patchy habitat availability has led to population fragmentation and sub-structuring. At both Hanang and Mbulu/Nou, the Hanang Mole-rat is sympatric with the subterranean dwelling root rat Tachyoryctes splendens, and at the latter site both species can occur in close proximity, leading to potential competition for resources and further pressure on the population.
threats: The presence of mole-rats on farmland may lead to conflict and threaten the population. At least around Mt Hanang, the local people may use mole-rats in traditional medicine, and they may be considered an agricultural pest. In general, their habitat is at risk from the expansion of the human population in the area.
population: Surveys of this cooperatively breeding rodent conducted in February 2010 that built on some original sample collections in the Hanang area in 2006 revealed that there are more colonies of the Hanang Mole-rat in the subpopulations in Mbulu District than Hanang District (Babati District was not surveyed at this time). Animals can be caught by several non-lethal methods, and subterranean burrows can be reliably identified by the presence of active (freshly produced) mole-hills, highly characteristic of the species. Each colony is a discrete family/breeding group with one breeding pair. The difference in abundance between Mbulu and Hanang Districts was also observed in May 2019, during the most recent major fieldwork in the area (where we were assisted by many locals). In 2010, there were 2–5 colonies per subpopulation in Hanang versus 1,014 per subpopulation in Mbulu. Moreover, at Hanang, the area of patches of uncultivated grassland within agricultural land providing habitat for the mole-rat tends to be smaller (normally less than 0.5 hectares). In Mbulu District, such areas tend to be larger at 0.5-1.5 ha. Interviews conducted with village elders at Hanang (in 2010) also suggested a declining population due to extensive agriculture in the land surrounding and abutting the Mt Hanang Nature Forest Reserve. Subopulations in Mbulu and Babati Districts were not fully surveyed in 2019, but due to agricultural pressure the potential for mole-rats to be viewed as a pest species is the same as at Hanang. Thus, there is no reason to assume that the decline in population size and natural habitat differs greatly among the districts. Furthermore, we failed to find mole hills around Babati town (in 2019), and on the edges of Nou Forest between Dongobesh and Dareda on the way to Babati (in early 2020), although mole-rats were known to locals in the past. The best quantitative information is currently from around Jorodom Village at Hanang from over the past 10 years (three generations is estimated at 9-18 years), which produces a value for decline in population size of 66%.In 2019 after extensive searching we have identified another site on the south-western slopes of Mt Hanang around the village of Gendabi, where 4–5 colonies were recorded (with animals captured from three). During an ascent of Mt Hanang from the town of Katesh (1,921 m) to the summit (3,420 m), on emerging from the main forest block we found evidence of approximately 12 colonies in small grassy fields from (2,569 m; -4.462747 Lat., 35.391548 Long.) to (3199 m; -4.447174 Lat., 35.387026 Long.). We confirmed that these were the Hanang Mole-rat by sequencing the mitochondrial cytochrome-b gene in one animal captured at (3,097 m; -4.452347 Lat., 35.387560 Long.). This individual was found to have an identical haplotype to other specimens from the Hanang area (Haplotype B in Faulkes et al. 2010, 2017).
range: Occurs in the Manyara Region of Tanzania on and around Mount Hanang in Hanang District, including the adjacent villages of Gendabi, Gitting and Jorodom, and extending 40 km further north and slightly east along the Rift Valley through the town of Dareda in Babati District; and into Mbulu District in and around the Nou Forest Reserve and surrounding villages to the west of the forest, including Eyasirong hamlet and Mongahay village. In Nou Forest, the Hanang Mole-rat can be found where open patches of grassland occur.
useTrade: Around Mt. Hanang, the local people use mole-rats in traditional medicine and ceremonies involving "cleansing rituals", which leads to a degree of preservation, but also occasional sacrifice.
conservationActions: There is no known ex situ collection of the Hanang Mole-rat in captivity. Listing of Hanang Nature Forest Reserve and Nou Forest Reserve and surrounding countryside as Key Biodiversity Areas would add further levels of protection and conservation. The forest reserves at Hanang and Nou, and associated “conservation areas” around the village of Gendabi on the west of Mt Hanang offer some protection.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, despite increasing hunting and persecution of this taxon. Cercopithecus agilis usually occurs at low density and a significant population decrease is suspected; however, data needed to quantify the threats and any resulting declines are lacking.
habitat: In the west of its range, this species is generally found in riparian or periodically-flooded swamp forest (Gautier-Hion and Brugière 2005). In Odzala-Kokoua National Park in Congo, they use seasonally-inundated and riverine habitats and occasionally the Marantaceae-dominated terra firma forests (Maisels 1995, 1996). In the area east of Makokou in Gabon, they were found in riverine forests (Quris 1975). By contrast, a study group at Mondika in CAR spent most of its time in terra firma mixed forest, and was never observed along the Mondika River, nor in swamp forest along the Ndoki River (Shah 2003), whereas a group at Bai Hokou, also in CAR, spent some time along rivers and streams (N. Shah pers. obs. 2003). Cercocebus agilis also uses open-understorey Gilbertiodendron dewevrei dominated forest (Shah 2003, Devreese 2011). In the north of its range, the species will use the gallery forests in savanna-forest mosaics of northern CAR (Fay 1988), and in the east (e.g., Okapi Wildlife Reserve), it uses terra firma forests, but will sometimes forage on crops (Kambale Saambere 1999). These monkeys are usually active in lower strata (0–10 m) of the habitat (Quris 1975, Shah 2003), although they spend less time on the ground than other Cercocebus spp. (Shah 2003). Home-range size was estimated to be ca 3 km² in Dzanga-Sangha in CAR (Shah 2003), and 2 km² in Gabon (Quris 1975).Agile Mangabeys have strong dietary preferences for fruit, seeds and monocotyledon shoots, and can bite through the hard shells of some fruits, such as Strychnos (Shah 2003). They also prey on animals up to the size of infant Peters’ Duikers (Knights et al. 2008, Shah 2013).In CAR, mean group size was 21 at Mondika, but a habituated group at nearby Bai Hokou numbered 135 animals, and on occasion it reached 330 individuals (Devreese et al. 2013). In northeastern Gabon, group size ranged between 8 and 18 (Quris 1975). In Odzala-Kokoua National Park (Congo), group size was usually >20 (Maisels 1996). In Ituri (DRC), it was 24 (Kambale Saambili 1999), in Ngotto Forest (CAR) it was 20 (D. Brugière, pers. comm. 2013). Groups of 50–200 have been observed in southeast Cameroon (Usongo and Fimbel 1995), northeast Gabon (Quris 1975) and northeast DRC (Kambale Saambili 1999).
threats: Cercocebus agilis is hunted throughout its range for bushmeat and sometimes persecuted for crop raiding. Because these monkeys spend a fair proportion of time on the ground, they are vulnerable to snaring – a method of hunting used throughout its geographic range. Snares are usually set for forest antelopes and rodents, but can catch any terrestrial animal.At the western, northern and eastern edges of its range, this species is threatened by habitat loss caused by deforestation for timber and firewood. An analysis of forest loss suggests that 1.3% of the forest in its range was lost between 2001 and 2016 (13,368 km² of the 1 million km² range). However, because this taxon occurs primarily along rivers, this may be an underestimate of the true loss of habitat, as forest loss in the savanna-forest mosaic will be concentrated along rivers and galleries.
population: Few data exist on abundance relative to human pressure, but even in 1996, in the more westerly part of its range (Lobéké NP, Cameroon), the abundance of C. agilis was an order of magnitude lower than the smaller-bodied, sympatric guenons at that site, and it was recorded only at distances of over 20 km from a road (an indicator of high hunting pressure), whereas smaller-bodied primate species still occurred close to the road (WCS unpublished data 1996). In the most easterly part of its range, in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve, encounter rates on surveys declined by an order of magnitude (WCS unpublished data 2018) over the last decade. This is attributed to increased hunting pressure, due to easier access along a much-improved main road, to the influx of large numbers of people into the area for artisanal mining, and to ongoing civil unrest in eastern DRC.Densities of Agile Mangabeys appear to be highly variable, presumably influenced by both habitat type and hunting pressure. Population density in Gabon has been recorded at between 6.7 and 12.5 individuals/km² (Quris 1975). At Mondika in Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park (Congo), density was 6.9 individuals/km² (Shah 2003). In Odzala-Kokoua National Park (Congo), group size was usually at least 20, and there were between 0.5 and 2 groups/km² (10–40 animals/km²), depending on the habitat type (Maisels 1996). In the Ituri Forest (DRC), densities varied between 2 individuals/km² (Thomas 1991) and 38 individuals/km² (Kambale Saambili 1998). In the Ngotto Forest (CAR), densities varied between 7.2 and 41 individuals/km² – variation here was related to hunting intensity by humans (D. Brugière pers. comm. 2013).
range: The geographic range of Cercocebus agilis is not well known, despite covering about 1,010,000 km². This species occurs in Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), northeast Gabon and northern Republic of Congo. It remains to be confirmed whether it still occurs in Equatorial Guinea.The most westerly subpopulation, which may be isolated, appears to be in Campo Ma’an in southern Cameroon, as recorded by three different surveys (Etoga and Foguekem 2008, 2009; Nzooh Dongmo 2015). The Agile Mangabey is, therefore, expected to occur in Equatorial Guinea; however, since the 1960s, when a single adult female was recorded by Sabater Pi and Jones (1968), no survey has re-confirmed the presence of this species (Larison et al. 1999, Puit and Ghiurghi 2004, Sunderland 2005, Ruffler et al. 2012).The northerly range limit is the forest ecotone from north of the Dja Biosphere Reserve in Cameroon, perhaps at 5°N, across to the Ubangui River, the gallery forest areas in CAR, up to about 9° N (Fay 1988). East of 22° E, the northern limit is likely around 6° 45’ N across to about 30°E, including the area of DRC southwards to at least the Tshopo River.The southern limit is the right bank of the Congo River, probably from its confluence with the Tshopo (J. Hart pers. obs.) westward to the Sangha-Congo confluence at 1°6’ S. The range is then limited by the southwestern edge of the swamp forests (around 0°18’S up to just south of Odzala National Park (NP) at about 0°30’ S, and continues westwards across Gabon to Cameroon – west of the Dja Biosphere Reserve, near Sangemelima at around 11°30’ E (Gautier-Hion et al. 1999).
useTrade: This species is hunted throughout its range for bushmeat.
conservationActions: Cercocebus agilis is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. Nationally, it is listed as partially protected in Cameroon, Congo and DRC. The hunting, sale, and consumption of primates are forbidden in Equatorial Guinea by Presidential Decree. It is on List C of Annex 2 to Ordinance 84.045 of 1984 in CAR, and not mentioned in Gabon’s protected species list. Cameroon, Gabon and Congo are currently revising their protected species lists.To determine the western limits of its distribution, it is recommended that people familiar with both the call and appearance of C. torquatus, C. agilis (and Lophocebus albigena) undertake surveys in Campo Ma’an National Park and the areas between there and Dja Biosphere Reserve to be sure whether or not the two Cercocebus spp. are indeed sympatric. If C. agilis is confirmed there, then it may well also still occur in Equatorial Guinea and efforts should be made to look for this species there also.Agile Mangabeys have been recorded in a number of protected areas; here we cite only the most recent survey information available:Cameroon: Lobéké NP (Nzooh Dongmo et al. 2016a); Boumba Bek NP and Nki NP (Nzooh Dongmo et al. 2016b); Mengame Gorilla Sanctuary (Ekobo 2006); Dja Biosphere Reserve – already uncommon in 2009 (Latour 2010) and not recorded in 2015 (MINFOF/IUCN 2015; Campo Ma’an NP (Nzooh Dongmo 2015). Not recorded in Abong Mbam or Deng Deng in 2001 (Fotso et al. 2002), nor in Deng Deng in 2012 (Maisels et al. 2013a).CAR: Dzanga-Ndoki NP (N’Goran et al. 2016), Mbaéré-Bodingué NP (Brugière et al. 2005); Zemongo Reserve (Roulet et al. 2007), Chinko Reserve (R. Hickisch & T. Aebischer, unpublished data 2016).Congo: Nouabalé-Ndoki NP and Lac Télé Community Reserve (Brncic et al. 2018); Odzala-Kokoua NP (Maisels et al. 2013b).DRC: Bili-Uéré Hunting Domain (Hicks 2014), Garamba NP (Hillman-Smith et al. 2014), Okapi Wildlife Reserve (Wildlife Conservation Society, unpublished data 2018).Gabon: an early study of this species (Quris 1975) recorded its presence south of the Ivindo River (just to the east of what is now the north of Ivindo NP). C. agilis has not been recorded in protected areas of Gabon since. However, Shah (2013) mentions personal communications from well-informed scientists (L.J.T. White and S.A. Lahm) suggesting that Agile Mangabeys may still occur in Ivindo NP, Minkébé NP and Mwagna NP.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered A3d+4d as declines of >80% are suspected over a time frame of three generations (looking forward three generations [2019-2040] and looking forward two generations and backwards one generation [2012-2033] based on indiscriminate hunting and poaching across the species range for local and international use which has been demonstrated to cause the extirpation of the species at some sites and areas. This is compounded by the likelihood that governance and law enforcement changes on a level needed to prevent the overexploitation of the species are unlikely to occur within two or arguably three generations time, that derivatives of this species are used in traditional medicine in China, both legally and illegally, and being promoted as a means of economic growth in the country and along the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) which could increase demand for the species and its parts, and there is currently weak evidence that demand reduction efforts in key consumer countries for Asian pangolin products and derivatives are effective, which theoretically could lead to a reduction in harvest.Currently, only Hong Kong and Taiwan, and potentially Bhutan, are parts of the range where overexploitation is not thought to be a threat to the species.
habitat: This species is found in a wide range of habitats, including primary and secondary tropical forests, limestone, bamboo, broad-leaf and coniferous forests, grasslands and agricultural fields (Chao 1989, Gurung 1996). The species digs its own burrows, or enlarges passages made by termites (Wu et al. 2005. Newton et al. 2008). Mro hunters in Bangladesh reported that a pangolin can excavate up to 15 burrows in a single night (presumably feeding burrows) and that resident burrows can extend up to 10m deep (Trageser et al. 2017). This study also revealed that like the Indian Pangolin, the Chinese Pangolin will create an earthen wall once in a resident burrow which likely aids in predator avoidance (Trageser et al. 2017). Indications are that home ranges are relatively large. In Taitung, Taiwan, the home range of a male was estimated 96.0 ha (100% MCP) or 66.6 ha (90% Fixed Kernel; n = 1) and 14.3-30.3 ha (100% MCP) or 15.9~19.6 ha (90% Fixed Kernel) for females (n = 6) (Lin, 2011) The Chinese Pangolin is solitary, primarily nocturnal (sometimes crepuscular), and largely terrestrial although it is fully capable of climbing trees and, like other pangolins, swims well (Heath and Vanderlip 1988; Chao 1989). Little is known about the species' life history, although in China (including Taiwan [Province of China]), young (normally one and occasionally two) are reportedly born from August to February (Allen and Coolidge 1940, Liu and Xu 1981, Shi and Wang 1985, Chao 1989, Chao et al. 1993, Chin et al. 2011). Hunters in Viet Nam reported that they never find this species in trees and it seems likely that it is far more terrestrial than the more arboreal Sunda Pangolin (see Newton et al. 2008). Lin (2011) reported that there are two type of burrows that Chinese Pangolin use, namely feeding burrows and resident burrows. Feeding burrows are created by feeding on subterranean termites and are mainly used once. Lin found no statistically significant difference between the frequency of forest and more open habitats. Resident burrows are used for shelter and resting and sleep. A male pangolin can occupy ~80 resident burrows in its home range and a female has ~30-40 resident burrows. Different individuals may use the same resting burrow but very rarely on the same day. Sun et al. (2018) reported the nursing period of the wild Chinese Pangolin was 157 days. The infant pangolin was observed exiting the nursing burrow alone at 11 weeks old and exploring behaviors such as s soil scraping and licking were recorded. In addition, the exploring behaviours were observe while the mother had left the burrow. The growth rate of was estimated at a constant rate of 1.2 cm/week during the nursing period, which was much faster than the only record from a hand-reared individual (0.7 cm/week; see Sun et al. 2018). The diet consists of ants and termites and it has been noted that in China, there appears to be a close correlation between the Chinese Pangolin's distribution and that of two termite species (Coptotermes formosanus and Termes (Cyclotermes) formosanus) which are assumed to form a major component of the diet (Allen and Coolidge 1940). Individuals are prey selective but known prey species include Anoplolepis gracilipes, Camponotus mitis, C. nicobarensis, C. variegatus dulcis, Polyrhachis demangei, Aphaenogaster exasperata, Crematogaster dohrni, and termite species Macrotermes barneyi : this is based on analysis of stomach contents (see Lee et al. 2017).
threats: The primary threat is indiscriminate hunting and poaching, both targeted and untargeted, for local and international use, with the latter primarily driven by demand in China, and the species is subject to very heavy collection pressure across much of its range (Wu and Ma 2007, Newton et al. 2008, Thapa 2013, Challender et al. 2015, Nash et al. 2016, Trageser et al. 2017, D'Cruze et al. 2018). As has occurred historically, exploitation for nutritional, medicinal and spiritualistic purposes takes place locally (Anon 1999, Nash et al. 2016, Trageser et al. 2017, D'Cruze et al. 2018). However, evidence suggests that local use is now frequently forgone in favour of entering animals into national and international trade given their high financial value (Newton et al. 2008, Thapa 2013, MacMillan and Nguyen 2014). International use involves trafficking of the species and its derivatives despite the species being included in Appendix I of CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. Challender et al. (2015) estimated that between 2000 and 2013 international trafficking in this species potentially involved ~50,000 individuals, though the actual number between 2000 and 2018 is higher (see Challender et al. 2019). In China and Viet Nam, the meat is consumed conspicuously as a luxury wild meat for which affluent consumers are willing to pay high prices (Shairp et al. 2016). This species also appears in both Chinese and Vietnamese traditional medicinal literature which prescribes the use of scales in traditional medicines to treat skin conditions, improve blood circulation and to stimulate milk secretion in lactating women (e.g., Chinese Pharmacopeia Commission, 2015). In China, pangolin scales also appear to be prescribed for these and other ailments, and cancer (Yu and Hong 2018), through designated outlets such as hospitals, but also through traditional medicine retailers. Since 2009 the Chinese government has released an average of 26.6 tonnes of pangolin scales from (presumably) government stockpiles on to a legal market for scales in the county (CBCGDF 2016), and which are certified through a certification system. However, this mechanism is undermined by ongoing illegal trade and availability of scales in traditional medicines shops in China (Xu et al. 2016). Ongoing but illicit availability is also the case in Viet Nam (Challender et al. 2015).Other threats include infrastructure development, habitat loss and fragmentation, and pesticide use. In China, major developments including hydropower stations and mining also pose a threat.Taiwan and Hong Kong are exceptions where populations are not threatened by heavy hunting or poaching. The threats here include predation by feral dogs, roadkill and development, i.e. conversion of land for human use. In Taiwan, research suggests that Chinese Pangolins can become trapped in burrows or tree hollows, and is a cause of mortality, as is their capture in gin traps (Sun et al. 2019).
population: There is very little information available on population levels at any level (local, national or global) with few exceptions, and there is a paucity of research on abundance. This species is rarely observed, principally due to its increasing rarity, but also because it is secretive, solitary and primarily nocturnal. Evidence indicates it has been extirpated from parts of its current range as a result of over-exploitation, and is otherwise in steep decline across most of its range (Zhang 2008, Nash et al. 2016, Trageser et al. 2017). An exception is Taiwan where populations are suspected to be stable and potentially increasing. China comprises the largest range state for this species, but populations have suffered severe declines in recent decades. Between the 1960-1980s up to 160,000 Chinese Pangolins were harvested annually in China for consumptive use resulting in all but the commercial extinction of the species by the 1990s (SATCM 1996, Zhang 2008). We et al. (2004) estimated that populations declined by 88-94% between the 1960s and 1990s. In 2002, Wu et al. (2002) estimated populations in China to comprise 50,000-100,000 individuals, and in 2008 China’s then National Forestry Administration (NFA; though now National Forestry and Grassland Administration [NFGA]) estimated the national population to comprise 64,000 individuals. In contrast, Zhang et al. (2010) estimated the population in China in 2008 to comprise between 25,100 and 49,450 individuals. Also in 2008, the NFA (2008) estimated the population of Guangxi Province at 990 individuals with a density of 0.043 individuals/km². Interviews as part of research in China in recent years indicate this species is present but very rare in the border areas of Guangxi and Yunnan provinces (P.L.B. Chan, unpubl. data), but at some sites (e.g., Dawuling Natural Reserve and Luofushan Natural Reserve), new burrows have not been seen in approaching twenty years indicating extirpation, and it is suspected that the species has been extirpated from Jiangsu, Henan and Shanghai Provinces (Wu et al. 2005, Zhang et al. 2010). Between 2015 and 2016, more than 20 natural reserves were surveyed in southern China, but found no fresh burrows or live individuals (F. Zhang and Q. Wang, unpubl. data). Li et al. (2018) estimated that in eastern China (Fujian, Jiangxi and Zhejiang Provinces) the species’ range contracted by 52% between 1970s and 2000s, and populations are now largely confined to the Wuyi Mountains. On Hainan Island, extensive field research between 1997 and 2013 and interviews with hunters and local people indicate the species is of very low abundance and likely commercially extinct (Nash et al. 2016, P.L.B. Chan, unpubl. data). In Hong Kong SAR, the species is present but is considered rare (G. Ades, pers. comm).In Taiwan (P.R. China) reports from the late 1980s and early 1990s suggest that populations of the nominal subspecies, the Formosan Pangolin were decreasing due to overexploitation from hunting and populations are were greatly reduced (Chao  1989, Chao et al. 2005). After the Taiwanese government established the Wildlife Conservation Act in 1989 it appears that domestic consumption was significantly reduced. Evidence suggests populations are stable if not increasing in Taiwan and poaching is no longer the main threat. In southern Taiwan Pei (2010) estimated densities of 12-13 individuals/km². Kao et al. (2019) estimated very approximately that the meta-population in Taiwan may comprise 15,000 individuals - though this estimate should be treated with extreme caution given significant knowledge gaps in parameters used to inform the models used to produce this estimate.The species is very rare in Viet Nam. There are records from the past three decades from various protected areas, including Ba Na NP (Frontier Viet Nam, 1994), Cuc Phuong NP, Khe Net Nature Reserve and in Ke Go Nature Reserve (see Newton et al. 2008). However, hunters in three areas of Viet Nam reported that although they still find the Chinese Pangolin it is extremely rare and populations have declined dramatically in the last two decades (i.e. in the 1990s and 2000s; see Newton et al. 2008). In Khe Net and Ke Go, hunters reported that numbers of Chinese Pangolins were lower than those of the Sunda Pangolin probably because the former is easier to capture. If this is the case, then in places where both species occur, populations of the former are likely to be more heavily depleted (Newton et al. 2008).The species has been so heavily hunted in Lao PDR that field sightings are exceptionally rare. There were field sightings of an individual in Nam Theun Extension PNBCA (Proposed National Biodiversity Conservation Area) in 1994-1995, and an individual was seen in a village in Nakai-Nam Theun NBCA during the same period (Duckworth et al. 1999). There are unverified camera trap records from Nakai-Nam Theun NBCA in the early 2010s (Coudrat, 2017). In Bangladesh, Chinese Pangolins in the southeast may have disappeared (Trageser et al. 2017), however, there are still a few areas where they exist, such as within the Chittagong Hill Tracts where there is an absence of high-skilled hunters (Trageser et al. 2017). In this area, there was consensus among hunters interviewed that populations in the south has been extirpated as a result of overexploitation from poaching since 2014 (Trageser et al. 2017). Populations in Bangladesh are suspected to be declining. This species was reported in the 1980s as common in the undisturbed hill forests of Arunachal Pradesh, however, little is known about the total population in India (Tikader 1983, Zoological Survey of India 1994). However, trafficking figures suggest this species is under severe hunting pressure in Northeast India (Misra and Hanfee 2000, Mohapatra et al. 2015, D'Cruze et al. 2018).Surveys conducted in the Royal Nagarjung Forest in Kathmandu, Nepal, in the early 1990s determined that there was a healthy population there (Gurung 1996). Nepal's population has been loosely estimated at 5,000 individuals but is suspected to be declining as a result of overexploitation (Jnawali et al. 2011).There is little information on the status of the species in Thailand and Myanmar. There is a potential record from Hkakaborazi NP in northern Myanmar form post-2000 (Rao et al. 2005).
range: This species occurs in the Himalayan foothills of Nepal, southern Bhutan, north and northeastern India, northeast, northwest and southeastern Bangladesh, northern and western Myanmar, to northern and Annamite regions of Lao PDR and northern Viet Nam, part of northwestern Thailand, and across southern China. In China it occurs south of the Changjiang (Yangtze River) and on Hainan, Taiwan (P.R. China) and Hong Kong SAR. The species has likely been extirpated from parts of its current range, the limits of which are poorly known and may never be elucidated, due to high levels of exploitation historically. However, Taiwanese pangolin populations have stabilized in the last two decades and may even be increasing. The species occurs at high altitudes, especially in the southern and western parts of its range. In Nepal it has been recorded up to 3,000 m asl (A. Khatiwada, unpubl. data), though also occurs at much lower altitudes, for example in Hong Kong and likely in the northeast of its range. Its latitudinal range is thought to overlap considerably with that of the Sunda Pangolin Manis javanica. Where this is apparent it is hypothesized that the Chinese Pangolin occurs in hills and mountains and the former is more generally found at lower altitudes (Duckworth et al. 1999). In Viet Nam interviews with hunters in 2007 (see Newton et al. 2008) suggested that the two species can be found in the same areas of forest, and that the differences between them are ecological, relating to diet and habitat use, rather than altitude, but ecological differences between the species have yet to be fully elucidated. In China the species' distribution extends from the southern border as far north as the Changjiang, including on the island of Zhoushan at the mouth of the Changjiang (Allen and Coolidge 1940). Its distribution extends to the provinces of Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Hunan, Guangdong, Huibei, Chongqing, Shanghai, and Fujian, and in the Autonomous Regions of Guangxi Zhuang, Tibet, and Hainan Island. Zhai (2000) suggest the species occurs in Xichuan county of Henan province, which would be the only record north of the Changjiang, but they provide little detail and this requires verification. In Hong Kong, the species has been recorded from the central and northeast New Territories and Lantau Island, but not on the smaller outlying islands (Shek et al. 2007); it occurs here at low altitudes (Reels 1996). In Taiwan (P.R. China), the species occurs on the periphery of the Central Mountain Range, the Western Foothill Range, the Taoyuan Tableland, the Ouluanpi Tableland, the East Coast Mountain Range, the Tatun Volcano Group, Taipei Basin, Puli Basin, and the Pingtun Plain (Chao 1989, Chao et al. 2005). The upper limit of occurrence in Taiwan is around 2,000 m asl (Chao 1989).Beyond China, the species is distributed in northern and central Vietnam, from Ha Giang province as far south as Quang Tri Province, but is absent from the northeast coast (Newton et al. 2008). The species is found in Cuc Phuong National Park, Khe Net Nature Reserve, and Ke Go Nature Reserve, and Ba Na National Park (Newton et al. 2008). In Lao PDR, the species has been recorded in the north and central parts, but there are too few locality records to determine the geographic and altitudinal range of the species in the country with any accuracy (Timmins and Evans 1996; Duckworth et al. 1999). The species is plausibly widespread in northern Myanmar, although there are few records and its exact distribution is not well known (Salter 1983, Corbet and Hill 1992). There is a record from Karen State in the early 2010s (Moo et al. 2017). Rao et al. (2005) report a sighting of the Sunda Pangolin in Hkakaborazi NP in northern Myanmar, but there is uncertainty over the species' identification (M. Rao, pers. comm.) and it is plausibly and perhaps more likely the Chinese pangolin. There are few records from Thailand but include those from Doi Inthanon (formerly Doi Angka) in Changwat, Chiang Mai (northern Thailand), sometime in 1937 and 1939 (Allen and Coolidge 1940) and Doi Sutep, Chiangmai (northern Thailand) in 1901. In Bangladesh, the species occurs in northern, northeastern and southeastern parts of the country, including in the border areas with northwestern Myanmar and India’s Assam, Meghalaya and Mizoram states. Two Chinese Pangolins were captured from northwestern Bangladesh in recent years but which is thought to be the result of flash flooding from India. The species has reportedly been extirpated from most protected areas in southeastern Bangladesh. However, it does occur in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (southeast), Lawachara National Park and adjacent protected areas (northeast), and Thakurgao (northwest) but has been extirpated from some areas due to poaching since around 2014 (Trageser et al. 2017). In northern Bangladesh, it may be restricted to the India-Bangladesh border area only (Trageser et al. 2017). The species is marginally present in northern India e.g. Vamiki Tiger Reserve, Bihar (Maurya et al. 2018). There are photographic records of the species in Bihar and it has been recorded in northeastern India (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Sikkim and the northern part of West Bengal) (Tikader 1983, Zoological Society of India 2002, Srinivasulu and Srinivasulu 2012). Chinese Pangolins also exist in Kaziranga-Karbi-Anglong landscape and Manas-Bhutan landscape and there are recent (post-2015) camera trap records from Manas National Park, India (D. Lahkar, unpubl. data), and reports of the species being present near Sirohi Wildlife Sanctuary, Bunning Wildlife Sanctuary and Yangoupokpi-Lokchao Wildlife Sanctuary of Manipur, India (J. Sethy, unpubl. data). The species appears to be sympatric with the Indian Pangolin (M. crassicaudata) in the Neora Valley National Park (Mallick 2010) and Manas National Park (Lahkhar et al. 2018; Goswami and Ganesh 2014). The species occurs in southern Bhutan (though potentially central and western areas only) and Nepal, where it is typically located between 555-1740 m Asl, though there are records from 3000m Asl (A. Khatiwada, unpubl. data). A nation-wide survey of pangolins (see DNPWC and DOF 2018) in Nepal unveiled the occurrence of Chinese Pangolin throughout Nepal largely distributed in human dominated landscapes outside the protected areas, though it does occur in protected areas as well. This suggests that Chinese Pangolins are distributed across eastern, central and mid-western Nepal and the Mid hills of central Nepal harbors likely strongholds for the species. It has been recorded as present in the lower elevation belt of the Kangchenjunga Conservation Area, the Gaurishankar and Annapurna Conservation Areas, Makalubarun, Sagarmatha, Chitwan, Parsa and Shivapuri-Nagarjun National Parks, the Salyan district in western Nepal (Khatiwada et al. 2019).  It has been also recorded in the Suklaphanta NP in southwest Nepal within the last four years and in Jajarkot district in mid-west Nepal (H.S. Baral, unpubl. data). In Nepal, its distribution appears to overlap with the Indian pangolin in the south and west. The Chinese Pangolin occurs from Inner Terai to hills and mountains while the Indian Pangolin is confined to lower altitudes; however, ecological differences between are not fully understood.
useTrade: This species has been hunted at a local level historically, both for the consumption of its meat as a protein source, and for its scales for use as an ingredient in traditional medicines among other spiritual and ritualistic uses (Anon 1992, Zhang 2008, Wu and Ma 2007). It has also been subject to international trade historically. Based on trade data from CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, this has principally involved scales or traditional medicines containing scales, as well as skins between the 1970s and the year 2000 (Challender et al. 2015; Heinrich et al. 2016). However, following population declines in China up to the mid-1990s (see Zhang 2008), a heavy unrecorded and seemingly illicit international trade in live pangolins has occurred between Southeast Asia and China since which has involved this species (Li and Li 1998, Newton et al. 2008, Wu and Ma 2007). In the year 2000, CITES introduced zero export quotas for wild-caught specimens of this species traded for commercial purposes. Despite this, illegal trade has continued post-2000 which is largely driven by market demand in China and mainly involves live animals and scales originating from Southeast and South Asia based on available evidence (Wu and Ma 2007, Challender and Waterman, 2017). Trade in this species in particular appears to come from Myanmar (Challender and Waterman 2017). Although local use of pangolins also continues today, evidence suggests that this is often forgone in favour of selling the animals into trade, which is primarily destined to China (Newton et al. 2008).  In China, as well as Viet Nam, pangolin meat is consumed conspicuously as a luxury wild meat dish for which affluent consumers are willing to pay very high prices (Shairp et al. 2016). This species also appears in both Chinese and Vietnamese traditional medicinal literature which prescribes the use of scales in medicines to treat skin conditions, improve blood circulation and to stimulate milk secretion in lactating women (Chinese Pharmacopeia Commission 2015). In China, pangolin scales also appear to be prescribed for these and other ailments, and cancer (Yu and Hong 2018), through designated outlets such as hospitals, but also through traditional medicine retailers, as in Viet Nam. Since 2009 the Chinese government has released an average of 26.6 tonnes of pangolin scales from (presumably) government stockpiles on to a legal market for scales in the county (CBCGDF 2016), and which are certified through a certification system. However, this mechanism is undermined by ongoing illegal trade and availability of scales in traditional medicines shops in China (Xu et al. 2016). Ongoing but illicit availability is also the case in Viet Nam (Challender et al. 2015).Other consumer countries include the United States which imported large quantities of derivatives including the Chinese Pangolin between 1985 and 20111 based on CITES trade data (Challender and Waterman 2017).There is ongoing local use across the species' range though quantifying this across the species' range is challenging. In Bangladesh, tribal communities believe that the use of pangolin meat can reduce their illness and the scales can keep away evil spirits. Local physicians also sell the scales by promoting their supposed supernatural medicine value, occasionally in cities. Trade routes exist between Bangladesh and Myanmar and pangolins are trafficked along these routes, mainly destined to China. In Sindhupalchowk district of Nepal, scales are worshipped as an incarnation of God during Tihar festival and are kept in homes to avoid evil spirits (P. Kaspal, unpubl. data). In Nepal, jhakris, local traditional healers have been using the pangolin for its supposed medicinal benefits for generations, but it is only recently that a booming trade has developed around the species which is threatening the specie. The species continues to be exploited locally for consumptive use in China (Nash et al. 2016), Viet Nam (Newton et al. 2008), Bangladesh (Trageser et al. 2017), northeastern India (D'Cruze et al. 2018) and Nepal
conservationActions: The species is present in a number of protected areas across its range including in Bangladesh: Chittagong Hill Tracts, Lawachara National Park and adjacent protected areas (Trageser et al. 2017); China: Dawuling Natural Reserve; India: Vamiki Tiger Reserve (Maurya et al. 2018), Manas National Park (D. Lahkar, unpubl. data), Sirohi Wildlife Sanctuary, Bunning Wildlife Sanctuary and Yangoupokpi-Lokchao Wildlife Sanctuary (J. Sethy, unpubl. data), and Neora Valley National Park (Mallick 2010); Nepal: Kangchenjunga, Gaurishankar and Annapurna Conservation Areas, Makalubarun, Sagarmatha, Chitwan, Parsa, Shivapuri-Nagarjun, and Suklaphanta National Parks, and Royal Nagarjung Forest; Vietnam: Cuc Phuong National Park, Khe Net Nature Reserve, Ke Go Nature Reserve, Ba Na National Park, Lung Day (Cao Bo Province), Ha Nang Nature Reserve, and Pu Luong Nature Reserve (Newton et al. 2008). There are older records from Lao PDR - Nam Theun Extension Proposed National Biodiversity Conservation Area (NCBA) and Nakai-Nam Theun NCBA (Duckworth et al. 1999), and a dated record from Doi Inthanon National Park, Thailand. Whilst the Chinese Pangolin is protected by national legislation in virtually all range states there and is included in CITES Appendix I, there remains a need to ensure effective enforcement and judicial proceedings in range states where hunting and poaching, trafficking and trade occur (Challender and Waterman 2017). Additional interventions are also needed including efforts to reduce demand for pangolin products among consumers in key markets and ensure local community buy-in to conservation efforts within and around key sites.   Research is required into the population status of this species, including population parameters and its ability to withstand current and projected hunting and poaching pressures. More comprehensive research is also required to quantify hunting pressure and national and international utilisation of this species.

rationale: The Zanzibar Red Colobus has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of less than 5,000 km² and an area of occupancy (AOO) of less than 500 km² (376 km², Davenport et al. 2019). Low recruitment, forest loss, illegal killing, human population growth and economic development in the species’ geographic range all justify a projected reduction of the population, its EOO and AOO. Therefore, we apply a categorization of Endangered based on criteria B1 and B2.
habitat: This species lives primarily in areas of ground-water forest, and scrub forest on coral rag along the southern and eastern sides of the island; it is also found in mangrove swamp (Struhsaker and Siex 1998). Most (68.1%) occur in primary and secondary forest, 17.4% in scrub/thicket, 4.5% in shamba, 4.5% in mangrove, 3% mixed vegetation, and 2.6% (Davenport et al. 2019). The Zanzibar Red Colobus is not territorial and lives in multi-male groups, with a mean of 17.1 individuals per group. Mean group sizes are significantly higher in protected areas (20.6) than outside (12.8) (Davenport et al. 2019). Young leaves and leaf buds account for more than 50% of the diet. In forest-dwelling groups, unripe fruit accounts for an additional quarter of the diet, whereas for groups living in agricultural areas, leaves from herbaceous species are the second most eaten item (approximately 15% of the annual diet). Some groups feed on mangrove leaves, and populations on coral rag appear to subsist on a drier, coarser diet than recorded for any other red colobus (Siex 2003).
threats: The species is increasingly threatened by habitat destruction from agricultural expansion, human development, timber felling and charcoal production. Forest destruction in protected areas remains a problem. Since the eradication of the Zanzibar Leopard, humans have been the main predator. Hunting of primates (the Zanzibar Red Colobus included) for consumption by humans and dogs, and in retribution for crop damage is widespread across Zanzibar (Davenport et al. 2019).The species has been extirpated from Bambi, Jendele, Kichwele and Nungwi forests in the last 35 years. Only one group survives in each of Dunga, Kibele and Maji Mekundu.Tourism and residential developments have destroyed habitat in Chwaka, Fumba, Jambiani, Kiwengwa, Mchangamle, Michamvi, Nungwi and Uroa.
population: The total population estimate—established by sweep census—is approximately 5,862 individuals (Davenport et al. 2019), some 3.4 times the mean of all previous estimates. The Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Bay population consists of 2,907 individuals and Kiwengwa Forest Reserve has 628, with 366, 344, 309, 234 and 200 animals in Mchangamle, Ukongoroni, Masingini Forest Reserve, Uzi/Vundwe and Kitogani respectively (Davenport et al. 2019). Only 103 individuals exist in the proposed Jambiani-Muyuni Forest Reserve, but 134 and 139 survive in thickets and shambas (gardens) of Jambiani and Pete (Davenport et al. 2019).
range: This species is endemic to Unguja Island in the Zanzibar Archipelago, where it occurs at elevations of 0–110 m asl (Siex and Struhsaker 2013). Zanzibar Red Colobus may once have occurred on the mainland, but certainly no longer. On Unguja, it is found mainly in the central part of the island in Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Park and nearby Ukongoroni, Kitogani and Dunga (Davenport et al. 2019); in the northeast in Kiwengwa Forest Reserve; and in the southern coral rag forests of Kizimkazi and Mchangamle, Muyuni and Uzi and Vundwe Islands. Also found in isolated populations in coral thickets along Unguja’s eastern coast from Uroa to Cheju, and Michamvi to Jambiani (Davenport et al. 2019). On the west coast there is a small isolated group in the mangroves of Maji Mekundu. A group of 23 individuals were translocated to Masingini Forest Reserve near Stone Town in 1974 (Struhsaker 2010). It is not known if the species formerly existed there. By 2015, this population had grown to 309 individuals (Davenport et al. 2019). In 1973, 14 animals were introduced to Ngezi Forest Reserve, Pemba Island (Struhsaker and Siex 1998), where there are now 35-40 animals; however, discussions are on-going about their removal due to their ‘exotic’ nature and limited genetic variability.
useTrade: Killed illegally as retribution for crop raiding, removal of wildlife to legitimise clearance of forest patches, and to make a political statement about benefit sharing. The carcasses are usually fed to domestic dogs.
conservationActions: Listed on Appendix I of CITES and as Class A under the African Convention. Piliocolobus kirkii is nominally protected under Tanzania’s Forest Resource Management and Conservation Act of 1996. About 69% of the total population lives in protected areas: 50% in Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Park (55 km²), 11% in Kiwengwa Forest Reserve, 5% in Masingini Forest Reserve, 1% in Bungi Usalaama army camp and 2% in Jambiani-Muyuni proposed Forest Reserve. The remaining 31% of the population is highly threatened, with most groups already isolated. Greater protection for Uzi and Vundwe islands and Mchangamle has been recommended.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it is widespread and abundant, and there are no major threats believed to be resulting in a range-wide decline of the species.
habitat: The Chacma Baboon occupies all types of woodland, savanna, steppes and subdessert, montane regions (such as the high elevations of the Drakensberg), Cape Fynbos and Succulent Karoo. Cliffs, hills or large trees are necessary night-time retreats. In some habitats, such as in the Namib Desert, habitat choice is influenced by predation risk. This species is totally dependent on drinking daily, and water availability limits its overall range in Namibia. However, one troop in the Kuiseb Canyon, Namib Desert, balanced its water requirements with moisture from nearby plants and conserved water by resting and sleeping during the hottest part of the day. Through this adaptation to their arid environment they temporarily overcame restrictions imposed by the need for regular drinking and were observed to survive without water for up to 11 days and even longer. In dry localities, artificial water supplies have allowed substantial expansion of territory. This species is an opportunistic omnivore and shows a local preference for bulbs, shoots, roots, seeds or fruits. Invertebrates, small vertebrates, seashore life, fungi and lichen are eaten as and when available. Occasionally, they take small antelopes or the young of species like Impala Aepyceros melampus. Crops (maize, tomatoes, citrus and root crops) are raided in settled areas. Lambs and small stock are taken in some ranching areas. They are also known to predate on smaller monkeys.  Troops average between 20 and 50 animals, but may total up to 130 individuals. Multi-male hierarchies are normal, though smaller troops may only have a single male (in one study in the Drakensberg, one-male groups made up 50% of groups recorded above 2,100 m).
threats: There are no major threats to this species, although problem animals may be shot as vermin. Local population extinctions are known from many farming areas. With changes in land use, populations are also becoming increasingly fragmented. Animals are also hunted and body parts of dead baboons are offered for sale in markets in South Africa for traditional medicinal use, but this is not considered a major threat.
population: This species is common and widespread. Densities can range from 3 or 4 up to 40/km² in some protected localities.
range: This species ranges all over southern Africa, up to the Zambezi valley (and including south-west Zambia; see Kingdon 2013), Caprivi and southern Angola littoral. Altitudinal range is from sea level to >2,100 m. One region of exclusion is the central Kalahari Desert in South Africa. There are two subspecies: P. u. griseipes occurs in south-west Zambia, Botswana (Okavango Delta), Zimbabwe and Mozambique, south of the Zambezi River; P. u. ursinus occurs in the remainder of the range south of the Limpopo River, in all provinces in South Africa and throughout Namibia.
conservationActions: It is listed under Appendix II of CITES. Occurs in numerous protected areas across its range.

rationale: Extensive habitat destruction, habitat degradation and intensive hunting throughout its geographical range have led to an inferred decline of more than 80% of the species’ population over the past 27 years (three generations, average generation time of nine years), based on evidence of an 87.2% reduction in encounter rates of C. vellerosus in six sites in Ghana in the last 31 years (Martin & Asibey 1979; Magnuson 2002; Gatti 2010) and the disappearance of the species from about 80% of known sites across its range in Côte d’Ivoire since 2004 (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2014). Between 1975 and 2013, the range countries of Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria have experienced an extensive (25-58%) loss of forest (CILSS 2016) and between 2000 and 2012 protected areas in three range countries (Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria) have seen a significant (4.0-6.7 % per annum) decline of forested areas (Spracklen et al. 2015). The high degrees of threat that this species is facing justify upgrading its threat status by two categories compared to the 2008 assessment.
habitat: Found in lowland rainforest, swamp forests, semi-deciduous forests and in gallery forests in the savanna zone. At Kikélé Forest in Benin, Djègo-Djossou et al. (2015) report that the diet of an habituated group consisted of 60.3% leaves, 33.3% fruits, 6.4% other items (seeds, flowers and  tree bark). At Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary (BFMS) in Ghana, the species is reported to eat mainly leaves of trees and lianas, along with a small quantity of fruits and seedpods (Kankam and Sicotte 2013).  The Kikélé fissioned into two groups in 2018, one of which contains two adult males in a group of 19 individuals, while the other contains one adult male and one adult female (R. Chabi Ota pers. comm.). At BFMS and in Bia National Park (Ghana), groups were either one-male or multi-male and average group size was between 10 and 15 (range 3–38); home-range size varies between 11 ha and 48 ha (Wong & Sicotte 2006). Groups encountered during surveys in Togo in 2014-2015 varied in size between 4 and 20 (Segniagbeto et al. 2017) while surveys in Kwabre Swamp Forest found small groups of between 3 and 5 (Danquah and Tetteh 2016).
threats: Colobus vellerosus is threatened primarily by hunting and secondarily by habitat loss (McGraw 2005). Accelerated hunting pressure is discernible from reported changes in hunters’ behaviour in the species’ range countries. Thirty years ago, hunters in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire almost always hunted only larger-bodied animals, but now they are mostly hunting smaller-bodied animals because of the depletion of large primates like C. vellerosus (Decher and Kpelle 2005, Gonedelé Bi et al. 2016). The region the species inhabits has a dense and rapidly growing human population; forest destruction and fragmentation have been extensive, and the hunting of wildlife is uncontrolled in most places, although at several sites the monkeys are held sacred (e.g., Kikélé sacred forest in Benin, Dinaoudi sacred grove in Côte d’Ivoire, Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary in Ghana). Even in sacred groves, however, the future of this species is uncertain, because traditional beliefs are no longer well respected and habitat degradation is ongoing (S. Gonedelé Bi pers. obs. 2014). In both Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, more than half of the closed forest in the forest reserves has been converted to plantation or farmland, or cleared and left bare (Bitty et al. 2015). In Comoé National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, several groups remain, but hunting pressure and mining occur although some patrol is in place. At the border of Benin and Togo, the proposed construction of the 147MW Adjarala storage hydropower station on the Mono River is threatening the future of this species in the Togodo protected area; approximately 2,315 hectares of the forest will be submerged under water
population: In Côte d’Ivoire, surveys conducted in the last three decades indicate that Colobus vellerosus has been extirpated from almost all the protected areas where it formerly occurred (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2012) except the Comoé National Park in the northeast where several groups were observed in December 2018–January 2019 (S. Gonedelé Bi and R. Matsuda Goodwin pers. comm. 2019). This species also occurs in a community forest (Tanoé-Ehy swamp forest) and two sacred groves (Dinaoudi and Grébouo 1). In Tanoé-Ehy, a few groups were observed (S. Gonedelé Bi, pers. obs. 2018). In Dinaoudi and Grébouo 1, not more than 45 individuals in total remain.In Ghana, more than 50% of protected areas that contained C. vellerosus in the 1970s no longer contain it. There has been on the average 87% reduction in encounter rates of this species in six forest reserves in the last 30 years, suggesting an equivalent reduction in population size. On the other hand, Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary and its surroundings were home to 365 individuals in 2007 (Kankam and Sicotte 2013). Although no systematic census has been conducted since then, this population appears to be stable, while at least two groups of this species survive in Kakum National Park where law enforcement has been strengthened in the last 10 years (Wiafe 2016). Danquah and Tetteh’s (2016) survey in the Kwabre swamp forest in the southwest of the country in February 2009 reported the average encounter rates of 1.5 group/km (logged areas) and 1 group/km (unlogged areas) for C. vellerosus, but R. Horwich (pers. comm. 2015) reported that the species became much scarcer in recent years. In Mole National Park, the relative abundance of the species reported by patrol guards shows a 69% decline between 2001 and 2006 (Burton 2010). The continued occurrence of this species at Bui and Digya National Parks is uncertain given the fact that the former has been extremely deforested and there is no evidence of the bushmeat of this species sold in the markets near the latter park.In Togo, this species occurs in Togodo protected area near the Benin-Togo border, Fazao-Malfakassa National Park, and the Yikpa-Dzigbe community forest where a few small groups at each site were observed; it has been extirpated from Missahohe (Kpalime), Assime Forest and Assoukoko forest (Segniagbeto et al. 2017).In Benin, a habituated group of about 18 individuals and another unhabituated group of three individuals live in Kikelé sacred grove; the Lama forest has one group consisting of 10-15 individuals. Other forests where this species was once reported occurring are Mt. Kouffé, Pénéssoulou, Wari-Maro, Lokoli Forest, Bonou, Upper Ouémé River Forest and Boukou.In Nigeria, although surveys at eight localities in southwestern Nigeria in December 2015-January 2016 found no individuals, small isolated populations may still remain in Old Oyo NP and Opara Game Reserve (Kazeem 2017).Colobus vellerosus is probably extinct in Burkina Faso (Ginn and Nekaris 2014).Overall, we estimate that only about 850-1,150 individuals currently occur at known sites. By including areas where surveys have not yet been conducted or incompletely performed, our estimate of the total remaining population size of this species is less than 1,500 individual
range: Colobus vellerosus ranges eastward from between the Sassandra and Bandama Rivers in Côte d'Ivoire through Ghana, Togo, and Benin to western Nigeria. Its current distribution is extremely fragmented and within the Bandama-Sassandra interfluvial zone in Côte d'Ivoire, Grébouo 1 sacred forest is the only site where this species still occurs (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2014). A few local biologists and forest rangers have recently reported that this species still occurs in the Old Oyo National Park and Opara Game Reserve in western Nigeria (Kazeem 2017), but this needs verification. A subpopulation that was once located between the Bandama and Sassandra Rivers, and sometimes referred to the subspecies dollmani, probably represented a hybrid zone with C. polykomos (Oates & McGraw 2009). Recent surveys in this interfluvial region indicate that “dollmani” has been extirpated and that the remaining population of the black-and-white colobus in that area is more similar to C. vellerosus, based on pelage patterns (Gonedelé Bi et al. 2014).
useTrade: Subsistence hunting for bushmeat occurs for this species (national rather than international commercial value).
conservationActions: C. vellerosus is listed as Class A under the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources and under Appendix II of CITES. Range countries should enact tougher laws against the hunting of threatened species and strictly enforce them. In order to more accurately grasp the size and density of populations of this species, systematic surveys should be conducted in Mole NP, Digya NP, Atewa FR in Ghana, and Old Oyo NP, Opara Game Reserve, and Kainji Lake NP in Nigeria. Currently, the Centre Suisse de Recherches Scientifiques en Côte d’Ivoire (Swiss Centre for Scientific Research)(CSRS) and the Action pour la Conservation de la Biodiversité Côte d'Ivoire (ACB-CI) in Côte d’Ivoire, and West African Primate Conservation Action (WAPCA) in Ghana have initiated conservation efforts for C. vellerosus and other threatened primates in Tanoé-Ehy Community Forest in Côte d’Ivoire and in the nearby Kwabre Forest in Ghana by involving local communities (Koné 2015). CSRS and ACB-CI are also currently conducting surveys in the Comoé National Park. In Togo, the Togolese Association for Nature Conservation (AGBO-ZEGUE) is making an effort to contribute to the preservation of the habitats of the species in Togodo National Park (G. Segniagbeto pers. comm. 2016). We recommend developing primate tourism in the Kikélé Forest (Benin) and Comoé National Park (Côte d’Ivoire). Because there are no ex situ conservation programs targeting C. vellerosus, we encourage the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria to establish a captive-breeding programme for this species

rationale: The European Rabbit is a widespread colonizer and is considered a pest outside its natural range, where eradication of the rabbit is priority for conservation (Cooke 2014, Cooke, Flux and Bonino 2018). However, only the natural range of Spain, Portugal, and southern France are considered in this global assessment. Assessment of the European Rabbit is filled with contradictions (Lees and Bell 2008, Delibes-Mateos et al. 2011). The European Rabbit is an important game species in Spain, Portugal and France, and the agriculture sector considers the species a pest (not a typical situation for a putatively Threatened species). On the other hand, it is an important ecosystem engineer (Galvez-Bravo et al. 2009) and a keystone species within its native range (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2008), serving as the dominant prey item for the highly endangered Iberian Lynx (Lynx pardinus) and the Spanish Imperial Eagle (Aquila adalberti) (Ferrer and Negro 2004). However, from 1950 onwards, the European Rabbit declined dramatically throughout its native range to densities less than 10% of those found earlier in the 20th century mainly due to the irruption of viral diseases (Myxomatosis in the fifties and Rabbit Hemorrhagic disease, RHD, in the nineties), and habitat loss (Moreno et al. 2007, Delibes-Mateos et al. 2009a, Villafuerte et al. 2017). Other factors such as human induced mortality or predation may have played a role in rabbit decline, at least locally. On balance this situation led more than one decade ago to a classification of the European Rabbit as Vulnerable in Spain and Near Threatened in Portugal (Cabral et al. 2005, Villafuerte and Delibes-Mateos 2008). In recent years many rabbit populations, particularly in natural habitats, have continued declining (some have even become extirpated), while others, mostly in human-modified landscapes, have increased in numbers leading to an increase in complaints by farmers concerning crop damage caused by rabbits (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2014a).Most recently, beginning after 2010, a new wave of disease (a new variant of RHD virus – GI.2/RHDV2/b) has swept through many rabbit populations causing massive declines. In an area that traditionally held the highest rabbit densities within Doñana National Park (i.e. Coto del Rey) – which thus held a core population of Iberian Lynx – there was a decline of greater than 80% during 2012-2014. In low-density rabbit areas within the park similar declines have been reported (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2014b). Rabbit density in the proximity to Yeguas River in Andújar and Cardeña Natural park in southern Spain, where the largest Iberian Lynx population lives, the rabbit density declined from more than 3.5 rabbits/ha in 2010 to less than 1 rabbit/ha in 2013 (a decline of approximately 75%). Also, rabbit abundance decreased by 57% between 2010 and 2014 in 26 localities surveyed in the Córdoba province (southern Spain), only 11% of these populations experienced a positive trend in the study period (Guerrero-Casado et al. 2016). The Andalusian government through censuses that started in 2004, has shown that rabbit density has decreased on average by more than 50% in 2016, despite the increase in abundance detected in some agricultural areas, where rabbits have to be controlled to avoid crop damage (www.juntadeandalucia.es). Hunters have similarly noted the decreased abundance of rabbits based on declines of 70-80% in the hunter bags in some estates compared with recent years (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2014b). In summary, the recent overall estimated 60-70% decline in populations of European Rabbits over the past decade has been followed by decreases of 65.7% in Iberian Lynx and 45.5% in Spanish Imperial Eagle fecundities (Monterroso et al. 2016). These new data lead to a re-evaluation of the previous assessment of the European Rabbit as NT, to EN – Endangered A2abce reflecting that populations have experienced or are experiencing declines mainly due to the recent impact of GI.2/RHDV2/b. The A3 criteria has not been applied because European Rabbits have been known to develop immunity to epizootics of prior viral diseases, it is hoped that a similar recovery will occur following this epizootic.
habitat: The European Rabbit prefers a mixed habitat of Mediterranean oak savanna or scrub-forest, or areas with around 40% cover for shelter from predators and open areas that support their diet of grasses and cereals (Moreno and Villafuerte 1995, Calvete et al. 2004). Nevertheless, in the Iberian Peninsula, rabbits are increasingly found at high densities in intensively-managed farmland areas (Barrio et al. 2010). The European Rabbit builds warrens in soft soil (Calvete et al. 2004), but finds shelter in scrub in rocky areas, though predation risk is higher in above ground dwellings (Villafuerte and Moreno 1997). The natural range of the European Rabbit on the Iberian Peninsula is warm and dry, rarely occurring above 1,500 m (Fa et al. 1999). The rabbits are territorial and tend to live and forage in colony groups of up to 20 adults (Mitchell-Jones et al. 1999), and are crepuscular (Lombardi et al. 2003).The European Rabbit can breed throughout the year (uncommon in lagomorphs), though this is limited by climate and resource availability (Bell and Webb 1991, Villafuerte et al. 1997). They raise altricial young between three and six at a time, which leave the warren in under a month (Gibb 1990). Females reach sexual maturity on average in 3.5 months, males in 4 months, and can live up to 9 years (Macdonald and Barrett 2001), though many succumb to predation and other perils much earlier. Up to 75% of young rabbits are killed by predators before they establish a territory (Gibb 1990). Annual mortality is usually higher than 50% (e.g. Cowan 1983, Webb 1991), but it can be highly variable among years, seasons, and habitats (Lombardi et al. 2003, Moreno et al. 2004). The head-body length is 34-50 mm (Macdonald and Barrett 2001).The European Rabbit is an ecosystem engineer and a keystone species (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2007, Galvez-Bravo et al. 2009). The diet of the Iberian Lynx consists of 80-100% rabbits (Delibes et al. 2000), the Imperial Eagle consumes 40-80% of its diet in rabbits (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2008), and the decline of the European Rabbit has been linked to the near extinction of these two predators (Ferrer and Negro 2004).The European Rabbit is responsible for landscape modelling that supports vegetation growth typical to Spain and Portugal and creates habitat for wildlife species (e.g. Galvez-Bravo et al. 2009). Its presence increases species richness (Delibes-Mateos et al. 2008) and increases soil fertility (Willott et al. 2000).
threats: The greatest force behind the decline of the European Rabbit has been two diseases that appeared in the 20th century. Myxomatosis is a South American virus, primarily spread by insect (mosquito and flea) vectors, that was intentionally introduced by a farmer in the mid-1950s in France to control the rabbit population (Lavazza and Cooke 2018). An estimated 90% of European Rabbits perished due to myxomatosis after the first outbreaks in the 1950s (Muñoz 1960), after that, the disease became endemic to Iberia, where it currently affects most rabbit populations (Villafuerte et al. 2017). After symptom onset, death results in an average of 13 days.
