It is found at altitudes of 1,465 to 3,965 m asl.
conservationActions: It is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Vulnerable because its extent of occurrence is approximately 16,941 km², its distribution is severely fragmented, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its Cyperus swamp habitat in the Albertine Rift.
habitat: It is a nocturnal species mostly confined to high altitude marshes within bamboo and montane forest. It is specialized for climbing on stems of marshy grass and other plants. The species has not been recorded from human habitats. Two pregnant females have been recorded with three embryos each, and a nest with four young has been found (Nowak 1999).
threats: The small geographic range of the species has experienced considerable habitat destruction in recent years and has a very high human population density.
population: In some swamps it may be common, but not many specimens have ever been collected.
range: This species is endemic to the Albertine Rift valley in southwest Uganda, western Rwanda, Burundi and extreme eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where it occurs in or very close to Cyperus swamps above 2,000 m asl. (J. Kerbis Peterhans and T. Demos pers. comm).
conservationActions: The species is found in Kahuzi-Biega National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kibira National Park in Burundi and in Mgahinga Gorilla National Park and Nyungwe National Park in Uganda. Research is needed into population numbers, the species range, biology, ecology, habitat status, threats, and potential conservation measures. Populations of this species should be monitored. Further management of the protected areas in which the species occurs is needed.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This is an arboreal and nocturnal species. In South Asia it occurs in dry deciduous forests and evergreen forests. In addition to natural forest, it has been recorded from plantations. It is found to occupy tree canopies and holes (Molur et al. 2005). On Hainan Island it has been found only in large patches of forest, where it was considered abundant (Smith and Xie 2008). On Taiwan it is most abundant in hardwood compared with coniferous forest (Smith and Xie 2008). In South-east Asia it is widespread in lowland and hill evergreen broad-leaveed forest, up to about 1000 m, and probably also inhabits deciduous dipterocarp forest (e.g. Duckworth 1998).
threats: There are no major threats to this species overall. In Southeast Asia, the species seems to be very resilient to hunting, habitat degradation and fragmentation, but it cannot tolerate deforestation excpt for when the forest is replaced by tree plantations. Thus, it is likely to be in overall reflecting the rate and distribution of deforestation. In South Asia, habitat loss and degradation resulting from logging, shifting cultivation, expansion of human settlements and forest fires have been proposed as threats to this species (Molur et al. 2005) but this is likely to be so at only the most local of scales. It is hunted for local consumption and medicinal purposes almost throughout it range.
population: It is locally abundant in Southeast Asia where suitable habitat protection is in place (Duckworth et al. 1994; Duckworth 1998; Evans et al. 2000). It could be in local decline in a few areas in India where it is under heavy hunting pressure (Nandini R. pers. comm. 2006).
range: This widely distributed Asian species is found in South Asia, southern and central China, and mainland Southeast Asia. In South Asia, it is seemingly patchily distributed in Bangladesh, India and Sri Lanka (e.g. Choudhury 2013). In China, it has been recorded from Hainan Island, Yunnan, Sichuan and Shaanxi (Smith and Xie 2008). It is present on the island of Taiwan. In Southeast Asia, it is distributed over much of the mainland, being only absent from the Malay Peninsula (as it is from the entire Sundaic subregion). In South Asia it has been recorded from 500 to 2,000 m asl; in Southeast Asia it is known from the plains up to 1,000 m asl (Duckworth 1998).
useTrade: It is hunted for food and medicine purposes.
conservationActions: Currently, there are no species-level conservation need other than taxonomic clarification. It occurs in numerous protected areas in Southeast Asia. In India it is present in Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary in Andhra Pradesh; Valmiki Tiger Reserve, Kaimur Wildlife Sanctuary in Bihar; Bandipur National Park, Nagarhole National Park in Karnataka; Chinnar Wildlife Sanctuary, Parambikulam WS, Peechi-Vazhani Wildlife Sanctuary, Periyar Tiger Reserve, Thathekad Bird Sanctuary in Kerala; Bori Wildlife Sanctuary, Kanha National Park in Madhya Pradesh; Phulwari Wildlife Sanctuary, Sitamata Wildlife Sanctuary in Rajasthan; Kalakkad-Mundunthurai Tiger Reserve in Tamil Nadu. In Sri Lanka it is known from Horton Plains National Park, Knuckles Forest Reserve in Central Province and Sinharaja Forest Reserve, Sabaragamuwa (Molur et al. 2005). The species is included in the Schedule II (Part II) of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. A taxonomic review of populations currently allocated to this species is needed. Once this has occurred, surveys to define the range of the constituent units, and monitoring of any of those which might be at risk, will be needed.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable as its population is suspected to have declined by over 30% over the past 40 years (three generations is 36–39 years) across its entire distribution range primarily due to hunting and habitat loss. For example, the species is now considered extinct in Bangladesh, and in India the species is generally not found outside protected areas except for in a few forest reserves. This decline is predicted to continue at the same rate or higher over the next three generations or 40 years. The species is likely to face increasing threat of population decline from the ongoing and projected threats from increasing habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation due to infrastructure development, new settlements, expanding monocultures, and slash-and-burn cultivation, from hunting for consumption and the traditional medicine industry, and from isolation stresses. Nationally, in Thailand this species is listed as Endangered.
habitat: This species ranges from tropical semi-evergreen forest to tropical wet evergreen forest and tropical moist deciduous forest (Chetry 2020). It prefers dense tropical semi evergreen forests (Chetry 2002, Choudhury 2001), but can persist in disturb secondary forests and those adjoining human-modified habitats. Srivastava and Mohnot (2001) report it from lowland semi evergreen forests to monsoon and montane forests. In India, it occurs at elevations of 50–1,300 m (Chetry 2002; Molur et al. 2003; Choudhury 2001, 2002; Srivastava and Mohnot 2001), between 200 and 2,200 m in Myanmar (Htun pers. comm.), and up to 2,400 m in China (X. Jiang pers. comm.). In Viet Nam, Lao PDR and Cambodia it is predominantly found above 400 m, while in karst limestone environments it is found in much lower elevations (R. Timmins pers. comm.). Climate varies from tropical to subtropical across this macaque's distribution. The species is good swimmer, but is terrestrial and diurnal. It spends 73-83% of its time on ground for feeding (Chetry 2002), where it feeds primarily on seeds, fruits, flowers, stem cortex, bulbs, shoots rhizomes, roots and to lesser extent on young and mature leaves, small vertebrates and insects. It will also raid crops for potatoes, sweet potatoes, turnips and rice. This species has a generation length of 10–12 years (Molur et al. 2003). It occurs widely in the hill and mountain areas of Viet Nam, Lao PDR and Cambodia (R. Timmins pers. comm.). In Thailand, it is widespread but discontinuous, in forests associated with limestone hills and outcrops, and other forest habitats (R. Boonratana pers. comm.). In China, it is found in broadleaved evergreen forests, and sometimes in secondary forests close to farmlands (X. Jiang pers. comm).Long-term study in India reported that the species consumes 23.65% of time feeding on seeds, 21.81% on fruits, 14.22% on leaves and twigs, and 10.35% on roots and tubers. Moreover, they spent 8.09% of their time feeding on bamboo shoots, and 7.79% feeding other minor food items (Chetry and Chetry 2015).Stump-tailed Macaque is very selective over the lodging trees. In India, it has been found to use only six species of tree for lodging: Artocarpus chama, Ficus bengalensis, Castopnopsis indica, Ficus religiosa, Mangifera sylvatia and Ficus benjamina (Chetry and Bhattacharjee 2004, Chetry et al. 2020).Home range, as measured in Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary (Assam, India), ranges from 387 to 587 ha, and day travel ranges from 90 to 4.5 km (Chetry 2002, Chetry et al. 2007, Chetry and Chetry 2020). Daily movement differs from one place to another: for example, in Yunnan, China daily ranges are 2–3 km. Group size can be as small as 2-3 individuals or as large as 60 individuals.
threats: Habitat disturbances affecting this species' survival include selective logging, timber and firewood collection for charcoal, building roads, dams, power lines and fisheries, deliberately setting fires, fragmentation, and soil loss/erosion. These animals are hunted and traded for food, sport and traditional “medicine”, and accidental mortality due to trapping occurs. There is a local trade for bones, meat for food, and live animals as pets (Molur et al. 2003). The species is hunted as a pest in Khasi and Garo hill in “Paan Jhum” area in Northeast India (Srivastava 1999, Chetry and Chetry 2020).In India, much of its habitat is affected by Jhum cultivation (shifting or slash-and-burn agriculture; Srivastava and Mohnot 2001). It has also been indiscriminately hunted over almost its entire distribution in India (Srivastava and Mohnot 2001). Its vulnerability to hunting is due to its large body size and terrestrial habit (Chetry and Chetry 2020, D. Chetry and J. Das pers. comm.).In Viet Nam, this species is heavily targeted for use in traditional “medicine,” both nationally and for trade with China. Agriculture, hydropower and mining developments are the other threats that need to be watched.Within Lao PDR, Viet Nam and Cambodia, hunting levels for food and for trade are also very high. Habitat loss is a relatively lower threat compared to hunting (R. Timmins pers. comm.), but increasing fragmentation is expected with ongoing and future planned hydropower projects (and associated road access, power lines, and timber extraction).In Cambodia, where Stump-tailed Macaques are found only in three of 24 sites, concession mining and land mining are existing threats even in protected areas.In Lao PDR, the species suffers from opportunistic hunting in their area of occurrence across the country for supply of bones for “medicinal” use in Viet Nam and China is threatening the population. Logging, gold mining and shifting cultivation are accounted as some direct threats. Other threats include extensive poaching and earlier were used in manufacturing polio medicine. Poaching for traditional medicine is still on unabated and therefore pressing the remaining population. Absence of any new conservation measure is in not helping the situation either.In Myanmar, logging and timber extraction are major threats. Commercial rubber plantations, hunting, and trade of animal parts with China are all major threats to this species. In China, hunting and habitat loss have reduced in population of this species, and it is locally extinct in some places. Over hunting might have extirpated the population in Guangdong Province. Habitat loss from plundering of evergreen broad leaf forest is a serious threat. In Thailand, habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation are major threats, while hunting is prevalent, but not a significant threat to the species (R. Boonratana pers. comm.). Until 1976, until the ban on international trade in 1976 of primates, trade and export of Stump-tailed Macaque was well and active. The United States of America alone imported ca 30,000 primates from Thailand, mostly macaques, for use in biomedical research and some were famously sold as ‘miniature chimpanzees’. The population in peninsular Thailand was thus significantly reduced due to this trapping for trade and export.
population: Populations of this species are critically threatened in India, declining in Myanmar and Viet Nam, probably stable in China, and the species is listed as Endangered in Thailand. There are some declines in Lao PDR and Cambodia. Future declines are predicted to be faster in Lao PDR, Viet Nam, India, Myanmar and China due to habitat loss and/or hunting. Populations in South Asia and in Myanmar are few and are fragmented (Molur et al. 2003, S.Htun pers. comm.). This species is suspected to be extinct in Bangladesh, having last been recorded there in 1989 (M. Feeroz pers. comm.).The population is declining rapidly in India except in the few protected areas; in fact, the species is extirpated outside the protected areas except in few reserve forests (D. Chetry and J. Das pers. comm). It is very scarce all over its range in northeastern India. It was previously reported as common in the mountains of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram  and Tripura but currently only found in few isolated locations (Chetry 2002,Choudhury 2001). In India, it is found in the following protected areas:  Arunachal Pradesh, Namdapha National Park, Kamlang Wildlife Sanctuary, Assam-Barail Wildlife Sanctuary and Reserved Forest, Innerline Reserved Forest, Hollongapar Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary, Meghalaya-Balpakram National Park, Nokrek National Park, Narpuh wildlife Sanctuary, Mizoram-Murlen National Park, Phawngpui Nationa Park, Dampa Tiger Reserve, and Lengteng Wildlife Sanctuary (Chetry 2018, Chetry and Chetry 2020, Chetry 2002, Choudhury 2002, J. Das and D. Chetry pers. comm.). In India, <1,000 individual are estimated on the south bank of the river Brahmaputra and east of Dibang River in northeast India; the species is critical in India (D. Chetry and J. Das pers. comm). In China, the species is still common in western Yunnan, though the populations are thought to be lower in the eastern portions of its range, but recent record suggest that there is still existence of the species in Bangladesh (Dr. Md. Farid Ahsan pers. com.). In 2015, 23,000 individuals were estimated in China’s National survey on mammal populations (Long and Jiang pers. comm), albeit in several fragmented subpopulations. Li et al. (2018) estimated ~3,700 individuals. The population of this species should be larger than 3,700 in China (Pengfei Fan pers. comm.). In many places, populations have gone extinct locally (Chang pers. comm.).There are no available population estimates for this taxon in Lao PDR, Viet Nam, Cambodia and Thailand (R. Boonratana pers. comm.). The population is probably large as the species is frequently encountered throughout its distribution in these countries, although populations are mostly fragmented and isolated.
range: This species is found in Cambodia, southwestern China [Guangdong, Guangxi, Hunan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Fujian and Yunnan provinces (Li et al. 2018)], northeastern India (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Tripura states), Lao PDR, northwestern Peninsular Malaysia (Perlis), northern Myanmar, Thailand, and Viet Nam. It appears that some occur on the border between Tripura and Chittagong Hill Tracks as confirmed in February 2016. The macaques were on the both sides of the border. Once widespread, the species in Thailand currently persists in a few isolated locations in the western, central and southern parts of the country (Treesucon 1988, Malaivijitnond and Hamada 2005). Formerly it was also found in eastern Bangladesh, but the species has vanished from most parts of its former range in Bangladesh. In China, it is found south of 25°N. The species has been introduced to Hong Kong. In northeastern India, it was long believed to be restricted to the south bank of the Brahmaputra River (Choudhury 1988, Chetry 2002). The Namdapha–Kamlang landscape is also on the south/east bank of the Brahmaputra and is a known stronghold of the species. However, it is to be seen whether it occurs north of the Lohit River, a major tributary of the Brahmaputra from where there are unconfirmed reports. Srivastava and Mohnot (2001), J. Das (pers. comm.) and Chetry et al. (2003) report possible records of this species from Namdapha National Park, though they were morphologically distinct from other representatives of the species, and could represent an undescribed subspecies. Introduced in Hong Kong.It is suspected that its area of occupancy (AOO) and extent of occurrence (EOO) are undergoing rapid decline due to ongoing and planned infrastructure development, which is causing habitat degradation and loss. For example, in Perlis (Malaysia), there has been a 24% decrease in tree cover since the year 2000 (Global Forest Watch 2020).
useTrade: The species is hunted for food (subsistence and exotic), traditional medicine industry, pet trade, and sport, cultural and traditional hunting.
conservationActions: Internationally, this species is listed under Appendix II in CITES. Regionally, India lists it as schedule II under the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Srivastava and Mohnot 2001) amended up to 2002. In Indian context the species facing severe threats with few populations left and needs revision of the Indian status so that in can get better protection. The species is also protected in national wildlife acts of Lao PDR, Viet Nam, Thailand, Cambodia, Malaysia, and Myanmar.Stump-tailed Macaques are found in a number of protected areas throughout their range, including: Nokrek National Park, Balpakram National Park, Kamlang Wildlife Sanctuary, Hollongapar Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary, Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, Murlen National Park (India); HuaiKhaKhaeng Wildlife Sanctuary, ThungYaiWildlife Sanctuary, PhuKhieo Wildlife Sanctuary, KhaoKrapuk-Khao Tao Mo Wildlife Non Hunting Area, KhaoSok National Park, KhaoLuang National Park (Thailand). They occur in Namdapha Wildlife Sanctuary (India), Perlis State Park (Malaysia; Syamil et al. 2019) and in Nam Ha National Biodiversity Conservation Area (Lao PDR). The population in the protected areas in India are increasing (D. Chetry and J. Das pers. comm.).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: In South Asia, this species is found from arid zones to wet and humid areas. It is equally abundant in forested areas and in rural landscapes, but in urban landscapes its populations are declining (B. Srinivasulu and C. Srinivasulu pers. comm. 2018). It roosts in hollows of trees, holes, crevices and cracks in walls and ceilings of old buildings, dead leaves of trees. In Southeast Asia this is a largely forest species inhabits primary and secondary hill, montane and montane mossy forest (Heaney et al. 1998). It is adapted to highly disturbed habitats, gardens, and mangrove forests (P. Bates pers. comm. 2006). In Vietnam this bat was found, besides natural landscapes, in Casuarina growth close to sea shore and in Hanoi city in urban area (Kruskop 2013). It is an early flyer, with a varied flight pattern from a jerky flight with many twists and turns to a slow fluttering and floating flight to an erratic flight as the evening progresses. Its diet is varied and seasonal. It feeds on beetles, cockroaches and wingless ants in winter, on a wide variety of insects in summer and on winter termites, moths, hymenopterans, dipterans and beetles during monsoon. There are two breeding seasons one in February-March and the other in July-August and between one to three young are born (Bates and Harrison 1997).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this widespread and somewhat adaptable species. However, increase of deforestation and urbanization, at the current rates of these processes, can affect individual populations of this species.
population: In South Asia, this species is widely distributed and common. It is widespread and moderately common in the Philippines (Heaney et al. 1998). It is locally very common in Myanmar and Lao PDR (Bates et al. 2005). This species is quite common in some areas of Vietnam, occurring even in large cities, including Hanoi, though there it is much less abundant as ecologically similar P. abramus.
range: This widespread species is found throughout much of South Asia, southeastern China and Southeast Asia. In South Asia, this species is presently known from Afghanistan (Laghman and Nangarhar Provinces) (Benda and Gaisler 2015), Bangladesh (Chittagong and Sylhet divisions), India (Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal), Nepal (central and mid-western), Pakistan (North West Frontier Province, Punjab and Sind) and Sri Lanka (Central, North Central, North Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, Uva and Western provinces) In those areas it has been recorded form sea level to 769 m asl (Molur et al. 2002). It is present over much of southeastern China, including the island of Hainan (Smith and Xie 2008). In Southeast Asia, it is found throughout the mainland, from northern Vietnam (Tu et al. 2016) ranging into Indonesia (Sumatra, Java, Bali, Lombok, Sulawesi, Seram and Serasan), the island of Timor (East Timor and Indonesia), Borneo (Indonesia, Malaysia and possibly Brunei, the species is possibly more widespread than currently known [C. Francis pers. comm.) and the Philippines, where it has been recorded on Cebu (Paguntalan pers. comm. 2006), Luzon (Rizal Province), Mindanao (Taylor 1934), Negros, and Sibuyan (Heaney et al. 1998) where it occupies an altitudinal range from sea level to 800-1,700 m (P. Bates and L. Heaney pers. comm. 2006). However, similar to other widespread Oriental pipistrelles, allocation of some mentioned population to P. coromandra requires further studies.
useTrade: There are no evidences that this species was used in commercial trade, in local cuisine or in local medicine. Like other insectivorous bats, P. tenuis plays certain role as natural regulator of some forestry and harvest pests. Living in lowland populated areas, it may have impact to some extent on populations of mosquitos and other disease vectors. In some parts of India, individuals of this species are killed and preserved for display in sealed photo frames which are then exported outside of the country (B. Srinivasulu, pers. comm., 2018).
conservationActions: In Southeast Asia the species has been recorded from many protected areas. In South Asia, the species has been recorded from protected areas in India like Satpura National Park in Madhya Pradesh, Agasthiyamalai Biosphere Reserve in Tamil Nadu (Vanitharani 2006) and Nagarjunasagar Srisailam Tiger Reserve in Andhra Pradesh (C. Srinivasulu pers. comm. 2008). In Vietnam this species occurs in several protected areas, including Bugiamap, Cattien, Yokdon and Bavi National parks. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, reproduction and ecology of this species.

rationale: Listed as Vulnerable as the species is suspected to be undergoing a population decline of ≥30% over a period of 24 years (three generations) including both past and future, primarily due to continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat, in addition to exploitation through unsustainable hunting pressure. These causes have not ceased, and will to a large extent not be easily reversible.
habitat: This species appears to be restricted mainly to primary forest habitats, as high as 2,400 m on the Tsaratanana Massif, as well as primary and secondary coastal rainforest. It does not appear to tolerate degraded habitat well (Tecot 2008). Its activity pattern is characterized as cathemeral, and it can be more frequently recorded during nocturnal than diurnal transects (Holmes et al. 2015). Group size varies from two to six individuals, the typical group containing an adult pair and their offspring (Overdorff and Tecot 2006, Tecot et al. 2016). Home range size has been estimated at 12-15 ha. Young are typically born in September and October (Tecot 2010), after a gestation period of 123–127 days. One infant is usually born per year or in alternate years to each group and mortality is approximately 50%; twinning occurs frequently (Tecot 2010). Weaning occurs at 6–7 months. They are very specialized frugivores, and an important seed disperser (Wright et al. 2012), although they also consume leaves, flowers and invertebrates, which can be important food sources at certain times of year (Overdorff 1993, Tecot 2008).
threats: The main threat is habitat loss due to slash-and-burn practices and illegal logging. The species is also subject to hunting, which can be heavy in certain areas, such as Mantadia and surrounding forests. It is occasionally kept as a pet within Madagascar (Reuter and Schafer 2017).
population: Population numbers are suspected to be undergoing a population decline of ≥30% over a period of 24 years (three generations) including both past and future, primarily due to continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat (Vieilledent et al. 2018, Morelli et al. 2019), in addition to exploitation through unsustainable hunting pressure. These causes have not ceased, and will to a large extent not be easily reversible. In particular, this species is shown to be negatively impacted by habitat fragmentation (Eppley et al. 2020).Eulemur rubriventer has an estimated density of 5.46 individuals/km2 with a total estimated population of 1,802 within Ranomafana National Park (Wright et al. 2012), and an estimated density of 6.65 individuals/km2 at Tsinjoarivo (Rakotomalala et al. 2017). Densities vary across regions, and so cannot be assumed to be as high in other areas as in Ranomafana National Park, and many sites apparently have low or zero densities. For example, E. rubriventer is the only lemur species to have been extirpated in the relatively large (4,000 ha) lowland rainforest fragment of Andriantantely (Randriahaingo et al. 2014, King and Ravaloharimanitra 2017), despite persisting in at least two smaller fragments elsewhere in the same region (Sahafina and Ambodilongo; King and Ravaloharimanitra 2017). Similarly it has been reported as having been extirpated from the 500 ha lowland rainforest fragment of Vohibe in the Nosivolo protected area (Andrianandrasana et al. 2013).
range: The range of Eulemur rubriventer extends from northern Madagascar’s Tsaratanana Massif south along the thin strip of east coast rain forest to the Pic d'Ivohibe and the Manampatrana River (Irwin et al. 2005, Mittermeier et al. 2010), although at one time it ranged further south. It does not occur on the Masoala Peninsula. It ranges from 70-2,400 m asl. Over its relatively large range the Red-bellied Lemur is sympatric with four other Eulemur species: E. albifrons in the northern part, E. fulvus toward the middle, and E. rufifrons and E. cinereiceps in the southern part. However, this species appears to be thinly distributed and restricted to intact forests, and is usually considerably rarer than other sympatric Eulemur; additionally, there are signs that this species is becoming rarer.It has been estimated that there will be a 76% reduction in the species' range from 2000 to 2080 due to climate change alone (Brown and Yoder 2015).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).
useTrade: This species is hunted for food. It is also occasionally kept as a pet within Madagascar (Reuter and Schafer 2017).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. Though relatively widespread this species appears to be uncommon everywhere, and has declined drastically in number in recent years. It is known to occur in seven national parks (Andringitra, Andasibe-Mantadia, Makira, Marojejy, Marolambo, Ranomafana, and Zahamena), two strict nature reserves (Tsaratanana and Zahamena), six special reserves (Ambatovaky, Analamazaotra, Anjanaharibe-Sud, Mangerivola, Marotandrano, and Pic d' Ivohibe) and other newer protected areas in lower protection categories (Corridor Ankeniheny-Zahamena, Corridor Forestier Fandriana-Vondrozo, and Maromizaha) (Mittermeier et al. 2010, Nicoll and Langrand 1989, Schmid and Smolker 1998). Other populations are found in community-based conservation sites: four groups were located in Vohitrarivo bamboo forest (east of Ranomafana National Park), where they are being monitored by the NGO Helpsimus, and additional groups in Didy forest. Unprotected groups close to the Ankeniheny-Zahamena Corridor are being monitored by local communities supported by The Aspinall Foundation, as are groups occurring within the Corridor itself. The Aspinall Foundation is also proposing to reintroduce the species to the lowland rainforest fragment of Andriantantely in the Brickaville District, from where it has been extirpated in living memory (King and Ravaloharimanitra 2017). As of 2019, there were approximately 165 individuals reported in zoological collections worldwide, most of them in Europe (ZIMS 2019). Over 140 are held by EAZA institutions, with the population managed for various roles including as an insurance population and as a source for reintroduction or other conservation translocation projects (Johann et al. 2018). Additional captive animals not included in the above figures are held in Madagascar, including approximately 45 in recognised facilities (E. Robsomanitrandrasana in litt. 2016) and probably small numbers in illegal captivity (Reuter and Schafer 2017).

rationale: The threat status of Euoticus pallidus has been raised from Least Concern in the previous assessment (in 2008) to Near Threatened because it is suspected that due to a rapid rate of forest conversion, especially in eastern Nigeria and western Cameroon, Euoticus pallidus has lost at least 20% of its habitat (and likely also at least 20% of its population) in the last 15 years [about three generations, based on an estimated generation length of 5 years given by Pacifici et al. (2013)], thus nearly meeting criterion A2c. This habitat loss will almost certainly accelerate into the future until most individuals remain only in protected areas.
habitat: Euoticus pallidus is usually found in the mid to high canopy of tropical moist forest, including secondary forest. It feeds on tree gums and resins. It appear to be largely confined to lower elevations, perhaps due to a paucity or absence of gum-producing trees at higher elevations (above 1,600 m asl) (Oates pers. obs. 2016). It gives birth to a single young annually.
threats: The primary threats to Euoticus pallidus are the loss, degradation and fragmentation of its habitat through conversion of forest for subsistence and commercial agriculture, and extraction of timber. Underlying these pressures are high and rapidly increasing human populations over a major part of the species’ range, combined with economic development. Statistics from the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization show an increase in the rate of forest loss in Nigeria from 2.7% per annum 1990–2000, to 5.0% per annum 2000–2015 (FAO 2015). This trend is likely to accelerate until most forest remains in protected areas only. In addition to subsistence farming, there are a growing number of large-scale agricultural projects for crops, such as oil palm, in southeastern Nigeria and southwestern Cameroon (Linder 2013), while major road projects are planned or in progress that will devastate areas of community forest habitats that are suitable for E. pallidus (Torto 2016).
population: Euoticus pallidus is a relatively uncommon species, although encountered regularly at some sites. It has been encountered at rates of 0.6–1.9 individuals/km in Nigeria and Cameroon (0.2–0.9/hr), and 0.1–0.4 individuals/hr at Moka, Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea (Bearder and Honess 1992, Ambrose and Perkin 2000, Schlossman 2006, Bearder and Oates 2009, Croce 2009, Oates 2011, Stokes 2011, Ambrose and Oates 2013). Although this species occurs in both primary and secondary forest, it is rarely encountered in highly disturbed habitats. As a result of habitat loss and fragmentation across its range, this species is certainly declining in numbers. However, it is rarely, if ever, targeted by hunters.It is suspected that the global population of Euoticus pallidus has declined by at east 20% over the last 15 years (three generations) due to the rapidly growing human population across its range, resulting in large-scale forest conversion, shifting agriculture, smallholder farming and small-scale resource extraction.
range: Euoticus pallidus is patchily distributed in areas of lowland and montane moist forest from the Niger River in Nigeria to the Sanaga River in Cameroon, as well as on Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea. There are two subspecies: E. p. pallidus is endemic to Bioko Island, where its range is <2,000 km², while E. p. talboti occurs in Nigeria and Cameroon.
useTrade: This species is rarely targeted by hunters.
conservationActions: Euoticus pallidus is listed on Appendix II of CITES. Present in several protected areas including: Cross River National Park (Nigeria), Korup, Takamanda and Mt. Cameroon national parks, and Banyang-Mbo Wildlife Sanctuary (Cameroon); and Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve and Pico Basilé National Park (Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea). E. pallidus populations in these protected areas are relatively secure.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable as it is known from an area of less than 2,000 km² (area of occupancy is 1,388 km²), triggering criterion B2. Paragalago orinus occurs in the montane and submontane forests of the Eastern Arc Mountains, which are under threat of clearance and degradation from agriculture and timber harvesting. The geographic range is: (a) severely fragmented and (b) there is continuing decline in the (i) extent of occurrence; (ii) area of occupancy; (iii) area and quality of habitat; and (iv) number of locations where the taxon occurs; and (iv) number of mature individuals. The known range of Paragalago orinus is under severe threat, as there is continuing loss and degradation of the species’ habitat.
habitat: It is found in the mid to high canopy of submontane and montane tropical forest. It is presumed to give birth to one or two young per year. There is some evidence that this species tolerates secondary forest that still maintains a canopy. Trees and interconnected vine structures are needed as they feed and build nests in vines as well as utilising tree holes for daytime refuge and raising young.
threats: The main threat to this species is habitat loss through deforestation for timber, and conversion to agricultural land. Deforestation and degradation is occurring in habitat occupied by P. orinus. Between 1975 and 2000 5% (210 km²) of evergreen forest and 43% (2,060 km²) of miombo woodland were lost in the Eastern Arc Mountains (Green et al. 2013). Average annual loss in estimated to be 0.1% per year in protected areas to 0.5% per year (Green et al. 2013). The most threatened habitat is an estimated 450 km² of forest in Rubeho, East and West Usambara and Uluguru Mountains, which is not formally protected. Habitat in National Parks and Nature Reserves is well protected and can be considered stable.
population: This species has a widespread but fragmented range, and is present at low densities.
range: This species is present in many of the Eastern Arc Mountains of Tanzania. It has been recorded from the West and East Usambara, the Uluguru, the South Nguru, the Udzungwa, and the Rubeho mountains. Similar forms have been recorded from Rungwe Mountain in the Southern Highlands of Tanzania, and Misuku Hills of northern Malawi (S. Bearder pers. comm.). It was previously thought to occur in the Taita Hills, Kenya (Perkin et al. 2002), but this is now thought to be as the Kenya coast dwarf galago Paragalago cocos (S. Bearder, pers. comm.). The species appears to occur at elevations from 600 to 2,300 m. It is sympatric with Otolemur garnettii and narrowly sympatric with P. zanzibaricus.
useTrade: Paragalago orinus is not hunted.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It is present in a number of protected areas throughout the range, including the Udzungwa Mountains National Park and the Udzungwa Scarp Forest Reserve, both in Tanzania. Further studies on the taxonomy, population range and numbers, and threats to this species are needed.

rationale: Unlike other Papio species, Guinea Baboons have undergone a range contraction over recent years, in the face of large-scale agricultural expansion, persecution, and hunting. The decline is possibly on the order of about 20-25% in the past 30 years (a three-generation period). Their adaptability to a wide variety of habitats has enabled them to remain locally common in many areas where the species occurs. The species is currently listed as Near Threatened, under criterion A2cd.
habitat: This species inhabits woodlands, savanna, and Sahelian steppe, always within reach of water (e.g., Vale et al. 2015b). It also inhabits gallery forests and secondary forest in the south of its range. In Guinea-Bissau, the species has been observed using mangrove forests for sleeping and foraging. Rich food resources and good protection in the Niokolo Koba National Park in Senegal allow often large aggregations of one-male units, numbering 10-200 (sometimes >500) individuals, to forage together. This population exhibits a multi-level system similar to Hamadryas Baboons. Therefore, there are sometimes small groups, other times larger groupings (Fischer et al. 2017; Patzelt et al. 2011).In Guinea-Bissau, groups of approximately 100 individuals have been observed, but foraging groups seem to be smaller (approximately 30-50 individuals). Guinea Baboons eat seeds, shoots, roots, fruits, fungi, invertebrates, small vertebrates, and eggs. Where agriculture has expanded, rice, maize, yams, groundnuts, and other cultivated crops are also taken (Sá et al. 2012).In Mauritania, given the general arid conditions of the Tagant, Assaba, and Afollé mountains, Guinea Baboons are typically found close to bodies of water, especially near rock pools (locally known as gueltas) along mountain rivers (Brito et al. 2010).The realized ecological niche of Mauritanian populations is apparently distinct from that of southern populations, a consequence of the unusually arid conditions of Mauritania (Vale et al. 2015a). In a regional analysis of biogeographical traits of the mammals of West Sahara-Sahel, Guinea Baboons exhibited very low niche breadth suggesting high specialization within the region (Vale et al. 2016).
threats: Outside the Niokolo-Koba National Park, this species has undergone widespread declines due to extensive agricultural expansion, tree-felling, and direct hunting for crop protection and for meat in Guinea and Mali. In the past, large numbers were exported for laboratory use, particularly from Senegal.  In Mauritania, the main threats are climatic oscillations and competition with human activities for water resources. Past droughts have resulted in rock pools drying out, which has caused local extinction of other fauna (Trape 2009, Brito et al. 2011, Vale et al. 2015b). Several rock pools are overexploited by herdsmen, which causes water-shortage during the dry season, fecal contamination by domestic animals, and increased activities for excavating pools or pumping water. Local studies are needed to quantify pressures and threat risks to baboon populations in Mauritania.Baboon populations in Guinea-Bissau have been declining due to habitat degradation and/or loss and hunting, since the 1970s (Cá 2008) and the 80s (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Ferreira da Silva 2012). The species has been hunted for meat consumption and trade, for the trade of skins for traditional medicine and magic practices, in hunting events organized by the military during moments of political instability and killed by farmers during crop-foraging episodes (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003, Casanova and Sousa, 2007, Ferreira da Silva 2012, Costa et al. 2013, Minhós et al. 2013, Sá et al. 2012, Ferreira da Silva et al. 2014). In the south of the country, where baboons are believed to be relatively common (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003), residents claim to see baboons less frequently and hunters state that baboons are becoming increasingly hard to find, particularly in the last two decades (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Cá 2008, Ferreira da Silva 2012, Costa et al. 2013, Amador et al. 2014). In the south, baboon meat has been frequently used as a source of protein in replacement of domestic meat in southern sections of the country (Costa et al. 2013) and hunters stated during interviews that they would hunt one or two baboons per day, four or five times a week (Ferreira da Silva 2012). In the capital city, primate carcasses are sold whole in meat markets to private customers and to specialized restaurants (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Starin 2010, Ferreira da Silva 2012, Minhós et al. 2013). Data collected at two of the bushmeat markets in Bissau suggested the trade of a minimum of 283 baboons per dry season (from November to May; Minhós et al. 2013). Urban bushmeat vendors base the carcass prices on the specimens’ body size. Thus, male baboons, being the largest of all primate species traded at the Guinea-Bissau bushmeat markets, are sold at a price 60% higher than any other primate carcass (approximately 22-33 USD vs. 8-16 USD for baboon females and carcasses of any other primate species (Minhós et al. 2013). Baboon meat is consumed in specialized urban bushmeat restaurants as a snack while alcoholic beverages are served (Minhós et al. 2013, Ferreira da Silva et al. 2018). Probably as a consequence of hunting practices towards adult females, it is also very common to observe young individuals being kept as pets, even within protected areas (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Hockings and Sousa 2011). Human hunting practices have been proposed as a factor shaping the population structure and dispersal patterns of Guinea baboons (Ferreira da Silva et al. 2014; Ferreira da Silva et al. 2018). The population size of Guinea baboons for southern Guinea-Bissau (encompassing the protected areas of Cantanhez Forests National Park, Cufada Lagoons Natural Park, Dulombi National Park and Boé National Park) has been estimated in 2 399 to 3 981 reproductive individuals using molecular tools (Ferreira da Silva et al under review).As mentioned above, Guinea Baboons are reportedly kept as pets in some parts of their range and their skins have been observed as part of ju-ju practices in The Gambia (C. Barlow, pers. obs. 2017).
population: Guinea Baboons are reported to be common in many parts of their range (e.g., The Gambia, Senegal, northern Guinea, and southeastern Guinea-Bissau, within protected areas) and, although patchily distributed, appear to be relatively abundant in a few additional locations. Nevertheless, in Guinea-Bissau, baboons are rare outside protected areas. Human activity (hunting, habitat encroachment) appears to be impacting population numbers in most locations. As such, a population reduction of 20% over the past three generations is suspected.In Senegal, group size can temporarily reach several hundred individuals (Patzelt et al. 2011). In Mauritania, group size ranges from less than 10 individuals up to 50 individuals, but most groups contain fewer than 20 (Brito pers. obs. 2016).
range: The Guinea Baboon, a monotypic species, is endemic to West Africa. It ranges from southern Mauritania and western Mali, through parts of The Gambia and Senegal, to Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, and northwestern Sierra Leone. The northern limit of this range is not well known, but appears to have shifted south due to decreasing rainfall (Verschuren, in Galat-Luong and Galat 2013). Furthermore, recent surveys confirm the species ranges further east than has been previously suggested (Kopp et al. 2014, Vale et al. 2015a).Niokola Koba National Park, in Senegal, remains a stronghold for the Guinea Baboon. Outside the protection of the national park, however, their numbers appear to be declining in the country (D. Zinner, pers. obs. 2016). Some fragmented populations still occur in other regions, e.g., the Réserve Naturelle Communautaire du Boundou in eastern Senegal (Kopp et al. 2014, Kopp 2015) and parts of Casamance (Galat-Luong et al. 2006). Specifically, they exist in upper and middle Casamance, but are not in the Parc Basse Casamance (J. Carter, pers. comm. 2017). The range of a reintroduced group of the species in Saloum has expanded in recent years (Galat-Luong and Galat 2013).Guinea Baboons are abundant in northern Guinea, in the Fouta Djallon area, where there is a local taboo against eating this species. However, hunting pressure in the southern and eastern parts of Guinea has driven the numbers down where populations are highly fragmented and mainly restricted to the peaks of hills and mountains. Baboons have been observed in the area north of Siguiri in Guinea, but it is unclear whether those occurring south of the Niger River are Guinea or olive baboons (G. Kopp, pers. obs. 2012).In Mali, Guinea Baboons are found in the Boucle du Baoulé National Park, but outside this area their numbers have decreased drastically. Faecal samples collected in western Mali were identified as those from Guinea Baboons, but recent assessment of southern Mali indicates little evidence of their presence there (G. Kopp, pers. obs. 2012).Their presence in Sierra Leone was previously uncertain (Grubb et al. 1998) but was confirmed in mid-2020 to be common in the north (S. Bell pers. comm.). In addition, P. anubis is also found in the north and northeastern part of the country (Wallis, unpublished report). Papio papio and P. anubis both inhabit the Outamba Kilimi National Park in Sierra Leone.In The Gambia, Guinea Baboons occur in Kiang West National Park LRR, Gambia River National Park (Baboon Islands) CRR, and possibly Bao-bolon Wetland Reserve North Bank Region (north of the river). They are also present in some forest parks, e.g., Kunkilling Community FP CRR south of the river (C. Barlow, pers. obs. 2017). Since 1998, Guinea Baboons have appeared at Pirang Bonto Forest Park and at Kiti forest, both forest fragments in Western Division, coastal Gambia south of the river (C. Barlow, pers. obs., 2020). They are common and locally abundant outside protected areas in some areas of The Gambia.In Mauritania, the Guinea Baboon is restricted to the southern mountain massifs of Tagant, Assaba and Afollé (Brito et al. 2010, Vale et al. 2015a, 2016). Ecological niche-based modelling of the distribution of Guinea Baboons suggests that Mauritanian populations may be isolated from southern populations and that Tagant/Assaba populations may be isolated from those in the Afollé Mountains (Vale et al. 2015a).In Guinea-Bissau, the Guinea Baboon is present in the south and east sections of the country (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003; Casanova and Sousa 2007; Cá 2008; Ferreira da Silva et al. 2014). The species is relatively common in the Cantanhez Woodlands National Park, Cufada Lagoons Natural Park, and Dulombi -Boé - Tchetche Complex (DBT), but is rare outside protected areas (Ferreira da Silva, pers. obs. 2016) and absent from areas near urban centers (the capital city - Bissau - and towns, such as Buba, Bafatá and Bambadinca. Ferreira da Silva, pers. obs. 2016). The species is not reported occurring in the northwest part of the country (Limoges 1989).Along its eastern (and possibly southern) limits, the Guinea Baboon has likely hybridized with the larger olive baboon (Papio anubis); intermediate individuals have been observed in Mali (Pollock in Sharman 1981), but little is known about this hybrid zone (Sarmiento 1998, Zinner 2013, Kopp 2015, Teixera 2016).
useTrade: This species has undergone widespread declines due in part to direct hunting for crop protection and for meat in Guinea and Mali. In the past, large numbers were exported for laboratory use, particularly from Senegal.  In Guinea-Bissau, baboon populations have been declining due partly to hunting since the 1970s (Cá 2008) and the 80s (Casanova and Sousa 2007). The species has been hunted for meat consumption and trade, for the trade of skins for traditional medicine and magic practices, in hunting events organized by the military during moments of political instability and killed by farmers during crop-raiding episodes (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003, Casanova and Sousa, 2007, Ferreira da Silva 2012, Costa et al. 2013, Minhós et al. 2013, Sá et al. 2012, Ferreira da Silva et al. 2014). In the south of the country, where baboons are believed to be relatively common (Gippoliti and Dell’Omo 2003), residents claim to see baboons less frequently and hunters state that baboons are becoming increasingly hard to find, particularly in the last two decades (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Cá 2008, Ferreira da Silva 2012, Costa et al. 2013, Amador et al. 2014). In the south, baboon meat has been frequently used as a source of protein in replacement of domestic meat in southern sections of the country (Costa et al. 2013) and hunters stated during interviews that they would hunt one or two baboons per day, four or five times a week (Ferreira da Silva 2012). In the capital city, primate carcasses are sold whole in meat markets to private customers and to specialized restaurants (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Starin 2010, Minhós et al. 2013). Data collected at two of the bushmeat markets in Bissau suggested the trade of a minimum of 283 baboons per dry season (from November to May; Minhós et al. 2013). Baboon meat is consumed in specialized urban bushmeat restaurants as a snack while alcoholic beverages are served (Minhós et al. 2013). Probably as a consequence of hunting practices, it is also very common to observe young individuals being kept as pets, even within protected areas (Casanova and Sousa 2007, Hockings and Sousa 2011).Guinea Baboons are reportedly kept as pets in some parts of their range and their skins have been observed as part of ju-ju practices in The Gambia (C. Barlow, pers. obs. 2017).
conservationActions: The Guinea Baboon is listed as Class B under the African Convention, and under Appendix II of CITES. This species is protected in the Niokolo-Koba National Park (Senegal), where densities of 2-15 individuals/km² have been estimated, in the Boucle du Baoulé National Park (Mali), and in Outamba-Kilimi National Park (Sierra Leone).In Mauritania, populations from the Tagant mountain are included in the Ramsar site “Lac Gabou et le Réseau Hydrographique du Plateau du Tagant” (Tellería 2009). Populations distributed in the Assaba and Afollé mountains are unprotected. Because the mountain rock pools are considered local biodiversity hotspots, these mountains have been identified as priority sites for the conservation of biodiversity in the Sahara-Sahel (Vale et al. 2015b, Brito et al. 2016).At least on paper, the Guinea Baboon is fully protected under the Guinea-Bissau law and has been included in the Red List of threatened species of Guinea-Bissau since 2004 (MAFCP/DGFC 2004).

rationale: Papio kindae is listed as Least Concern, as the species is widespread and common, present in several protected areas. While there are no major range-wide threats believed to be resulting in a significant population decline, continued monitoring is warranted.
habitat: Throughout most of their range, Kinda Baboons occur in miombo (Brachystegia) woodland with seasonally flooded grasslands (dambos) and patches of evergreen forest (mushitu). They appear to spend less time in open grasslands than do other baboon species (Weyher, unpublished data; Zinner 2013). On average, this species lives in wetter (average precipitation is approximately 1000 mm) environments. Studies using niche modelling found that the environments Kinda Baboons inhabit may be distinct compared with other baboon species (Fuchs et al. 2018).There have been no systematic studies of their diet content, but Kinda Baboons are omnivorous, with a preference for fruits. In one study, Kinda Baboons spent about 35% of their time feeding, 14% travelling, 32% resting, and 19% in social activities (Weyher, unpublished data). In that study, higher temperatures were associated with more time spent feeding and travelling and less time in social activity and resting (Weyher, unpublished data).As with the Yellow, Chacma, and Olive Baboons, females form a close social bond; most adult grooming partnerships occur between females. However, male-female relationships and female-female relationships of Kinda Baboons differ substantially from those seen in Yellow, Chacma, and Olive Baboons, suggesting that the social structure of the Kinda Baboon constitutes a further variant of baboon social structures (Weyher et al. 2014). Compared with other baboons, the Kinda Baboon exhibits relatively low degrees of sexual dimorphism in body size and canine tooth, with large relative testis size, leading to the suggestion that they have evolved under reduced direct, and increased indirect, male-male competition (Petersdorf et al. 2019).
threats: There are no major threats to this species across its range, though some populations may be under pressure from agriculture and development projects. As other wildlife species decline and human populations increase, a potential increase in hunting pressure may be likely in some areas.The closely related Papio anubis and P. cynocephalus are naturally infected with Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, the bacterium that causes human yaws and closely related to the bacterium that causes syphilis (T. p. pallidum) (see Harper et al. 2012, Chuma et al. 2019). In Papio spp., the infection appears to spread through sexual contact and is associated with open lesions in and around the genitalia of both sexes. The degree of morbidity varies, including some cases of deaths occurring in the Tanzania’s Gombe National Park’s Olive Baboons, when the genitalia are so badly damaged that urinary flow was obstructed (Wallis and Lee 1999). The presence of this disease has not been confirmed in the Kinda Baboon, but their range is known to be previously endemic for yaws (Knauf et al. 2018).Thus, although the current hunting pressure and potential incidence of disease are not known to constitute “major threats,” both phenomena merit attention and monitoring.
population: This species is widespread and locally common, but patchily distributed over its extensive range. No populations numbers are available, but in the absence of extensive surveys the species is assumed to be stable at present.
range: The Kinda Baboon occurs in southwestern Tanzania as far north as the Mahale Mountains National Park, in southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, western Zambia (west of the Luangwa River), and in northern Angola. Kinda Baboons hybridize with Chacma Baboons and Yellow Baboons in their respective Zambian contact zones.
useTrade: The hunting of Kinda Baboons for food is practised by some but not all ethnic groups within the species' range. As with other members of this genus, the species may be persecuted for crop-raiding.
conservationActions: This species is listed under Appendix II of CITES (as Papio cynocephalus) and is considered as Vermin under the African Convention (as a subspecies of Papio cynocephalus). It is present in many protected areas, including Upemba and Kundelungu National Parks in DR Congo and West Lunga, Kafue, Kasanka, and South and North Luangwa National Parks in Zambia.As mentioned earlier, there are currently no reports of major range-wide threats resulting in a significant population decline of Kinda Baboons, although they are likely at risk in some areas where encroachment by local humans may be impacting their habitats and where crop-raiding behaviour by the baboons may be met with retribution killings. This may lead to local extinction in some areas. Consequently, impacts of human-baboon interactions should be monitored.As noted in the Threat section, research and monitoring for hunting pressure and disease transmission is recommended in assessment of the species’ long-term future. Also, Weyher (unpublished data) found that temperature and humidity significantly predict activity patterns of Kinda Baboons. Thus, as for all African mammals, the effect of global climate change should be monitored.Research and ongoing monitoring for hunting pressure and disease transmission is recommended. Additionally, research into their range, boundaries, and behaviour could be useful for conservation planning.

rationale: Alouatta belzebul is considered VU A4cd, based largely on threats to its Amazonian populations (more than 95% of the total), which are suspected to have already declined over the course of one generation (2007-2018) and are suspected to continue declining by more than 30% over the course of the current and subsequent generations (2019-2040) due to a loss of a third or more of suitable forest habitat and the impacts of medium- to heavy-hunting, which have been found to reduce population densities of large-bodied Neotropical primates upwards of 50%.
habitat: This species occurs in a mix of habitats including lowland Amazon rainforest, Marajó várzea forest, and fragments of the northern Atlantic Forest. It is not restricted to primary habitats and presents tolerance to environmental changes and disturbances, being found in mining areas in Parà (Carvalho 2010) and occupying small size regenerating fragments in Atlantic Forest (Fialho et al. 2014).The howler monkeys are the large leaf-eaters of the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted for their chewing leaves through shearing. Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the under surface at the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaws which surround the enlarged larynx and hyoid apparatus, a resonating chamber. It is with this enlarged and highly specialized voice box that they produce their howls (grunts, roars and barks). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1-2 km (Drubbel and Gautier 1993).They can usually be seen in groups numbering from four or five or up to 11 or so individuals. There is usually only one dominant male in the group (occasionally two), others being sub-adults, or juveniles, along with a harem of two to five females. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), the howler monkeys generally have quite small and broadly overlapping home ranges, of 5 ha up to 45 ha, depending on the type of habitat (Neville et al. 1988). Pina et al. (2002) studied two groups of 5-6 and 7-9 individuals (each with just one adult male and two adult females), in Caxiuanã (Pará), with home ranges of 13.5 ha and 18.05 ha, respectively. Bonvicino (1989), in Atlantic Forest (Pacatuba, Paraìba), recorded home ranges between 4.45 ha and 9.50 ha.Howlers are the only New World primates which regularly include mature leaves in their diet, although softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when they are available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the keys to their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruit is the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, moss, stems and twigs, and termitaria. The diet of two A. belzebul groups in the Caxiuanã National Forest was studied by Souza et al. (2002). They were largely folivorous but would switch to fruits whenever available, especially during the wet season. Size:Adult male: HB 44-68 cm, TL 54-74.5 cm (n=18); adult female: HB 30-64.5 cm; TL 45-70 cm (n=23) (Gregorin 1996)Adult male weight 4.7 kg (4.1-5.2) (n=8); adult female weight 3.2 kg (2.9-3.6) (n=6) (for Atlantic Forest individuals - CPB, unpublished data)Adult male weight 7.27 kg (n=27), adult female weight 5.52 kg (n=26) (Peres 1994)Adult male weight 6.5-8.0 kg (mean 7.3 kg, n=27), adult female weight 4.85-6.2 kg (mean 5.5 kg, n=26) (Ford and Davis 1992).
threats: More than 95% of the Alouatta belzebul population is located in Brazilian Amazonia, versus the Atlantic Forest region. Amazonian forests are projected to be reduced by as much as 40% by the year 2050 due to illegal deforestation, hydroelectric projects, road-building, cattle-ranching and cattle-ranching if current conditions do not change (Soares-Filho et al. 2006). In addition, studies have shown that densities of large-bodied Amazonian primates such as Alouatta spp. are often reduced by as much as 50-75% in areas of heavy hunting (Peres and Palacios 2007). In the Atlantic Forest region, where habitat loss and fragmentation has been due largely to the expansion of sugar cane plantations, remaining small forest patches are vulnerable to stochastic and demographic effects.
population: It is inferred and suspected that the current distribution of the taxon is reduced relative to its historical extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO), as much of its distribution in the Amazon region is included in the “Arc of Deforestation” and in the Atlantic Forest, its AOO is now extremely small and fragmented. The Guaribas Biological Reserve, for example, is an area of confirmed local extinction where the species has recently been reintroduced.Alouatta belzebul is extremely common in some areas (such as Marajó, Pará), but very rare in the Atlantic Forest portion of the range. The total population size in the Atlantic Forest is inferred to be less than 500 individuals and not more than 250 mature individuals, distributed in 18 isolated areas: one in Rio Grande do Norte, ten in Paraíba, one in Pernambuco and six in Alagoas (Fialho et al. 2014). The largest population in the Atlantic Forest is probably found in Pacatuba locality (Paraiba). However, it appears that the Amazonian population has more than 10,000 mature individuals.At the north of the state of Tocantins, near the municipality of Estreito, population abundance for the species over four forest fragments from 65 to 900 ha, is calculated to range from 1.35 to 3.72 individuals/10 km. For this region the estimated total population is about 141 individuals, living in altered isolated forest fragments.
range: Alouatta belzebul is endemic to Brazil presenting a disjunct distribution, with a group of populations in the eastern portion of the Amazon and another in the Atlantic Forest.The Amazonian population has its eastern boundary in the “Mata dos Cocais” in the states of Maranhão and Tocantins, where the geographic distribution coincides with the limits of the Amazon biome. The Xingu River is apparently the western boundary. In the north the species is limited by the Amazon River, although there are records of populations in southern Amapá (Gregorin 2006) and Oriximiná, Pará (Bonvicino et al. 1989). The latter may be a mistake because Oliveira et al. 2009 reported that the species occurring in Oriximiná was A. macconnelli, widely distributed on the northern bank of the Amazon River. Further surveys are needed at the headwaters of the Xingu and in the Xingu-Iriri interfluve to establish what species of Alouatta occur in these areas. At the northern end of the state of Tocantins, the species is sympatric with A. caraya with isolated populations north of the city of Babaçulândia, where Fabiano R. de Melo and Raony M. Alencar (pers. comm.) found a mixed group (A. caraya female with A. belzebul male), demonstrating the existence of a small contact zone in the region.The Atlantic Forest population currently occurs in 18 forest fragments, one in Pernambuco, one in Rio Grande do Norte (northern limit) and the remainder in the states of Paraíba and Alagoas. The southern limit is marked by São Francisco River, the eastern by the Atlantic Ocean and the western by Coruripe locality (Coruripe, AL) (Fialho et al. 2014).The extent of occurrence (EOO) for this species in Amazon region is larger than 800,000 km² and in the Atlantic Forest its EOO is approximately 16,600 km². The area of occupancy (AOO) of the Amazon population exceeds 2,000 km²; that of the Atlantic Forest population is estimated to be less than 160 km² (Fialho et al. 2014).
useTrade: Alouatta belzebul is a local livelihood species and it is used as food by humans.
conservationActions: Alouatta belzebul is one of the five species included in the Brazilian government conservation action planning system: Plano de Ação Nacional para a Conservação dos Primatas do Nordeste (ICMBio 2012). It is listed on Appendix II of CITES and listed as Endangered -A2cd+B2ab(ii)(iii)+C2a(i)- on Brazilian Red List (MMA 2014).The species has been recorded from the following protected areas: Atlantic Forest:Rio Grande do Norte: Mata da Estrela RPPN (2,039 ha) (Fialho et al. 2014);Paraíba: Guaribas Biological Reserve (4,052 ha) (re-introduced), Fazenda Pacatuba RPPN (266 ha), Engenho Gargaú RPPN (1,058 ha) and Terras Indígenas Potiguaras (Indigenous and Community Conserved Area) (Fialho et al. 2014);Alagoas: Murici Ecological Station (6,131), RPPN Reserva Santa Tereza (100 ha) (Fialho et al. 2014).Amazon:Pará: Caxiuanã National Forest (317,946 ha) (Jardim and Oliveira 1997; Pina et al. 2002), Tapirapé Biological Reserve (99,272 ha) (Rylands and Bernardes 1989), Carajás National Forest (392,725 ha) (Carvalho et al. 2014), Tapirapé-Aquiri National Forest (196,501 ha), Igarapé Gelado Protected Area (23,285 ha) ( Carvalho unpublished data).Maranhão: Gurupí Biological Reserve (271,197 ha) (Rylands and Bernardes 1989) e Quilombo do Frexal Extractive Reserve (9,338 ha) (Fialho unpublished data).Tocantins: Araguaia National Park (562,312 ha) (Ibama 2001).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern given its relatively large distribution and lack of any major threats driving a significant range-wide decline.
habitat: This species is found in the llanos (plains), in deciduous forest patches and gallery forest. Long-term studies of this species have been carried out at Hato Masaguaral, Guarico, in seasonally inundated "bajo llanos". Troth (1979) describes the vegetation on the ranch. It is otherwise known from the biogeographic region of the North coast range (approximately 62ºW to 69ºW), where there are humid rain forest patches, either lowland tropical or pre-montane, resulting from orographic rainfall. Some mountains rise to elevations exceeding 2,000 m and in some ranges there are true montane cloud forests (Eisenberg and Redford 1979). The Howler Monkeys are the large leaf-eaters of the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted for their chewing leaves through shearing. They spend up to 70% of their day lying and sitting about quietly among the branches, fermenting leaves in their enlarged caecums. Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the under surface at the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaw which surrounds the enlarged larynx and hyoid apparatus, a resonating chamber. It is with this enlarged and highly specialised voice box that they produce their howls (grunts, roars and barks). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1-2 km (Drubbel and Gautier 1993).Howler groups are usually small, ranging in size from 2-16 animals and averaging 4-10 (Neville et al. 1988). Mean group size in Hato Masaguaral, Guarico State, Venezuela, ranged 7.7 to 10.5 at various times in the period 1969 to 1984 (Crockett and Eisenberg 1984). Mean numbers of adult males per group ranged 1.1 to 1.8, and adult females from 2.3 to 2.9. Group size in another ranch in the llanos, Hato El Frío, was 7.6 (Braza et al. 1981). In the red howlers, there is usually only one dominant male in the group (occasionally two), others being sub-adults, or juveniles, along with a harem of two to five females. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), the Howler Monkeys generally have quite small and broadly overlapping home ranges, of 5 ha up to 45 ha, depending on the type of habitat (Neville et al. 1988). The large groups of A. palliata may have home ranges extending to 60 ha (Estrada 1982), whereas in the llanos of northern Venezuela, home ranges of A. arctoidea can be as small as 4 ha (Sekulic 1982). Howlers are the only New World primates which regularly include mature leaves in their diet, although softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when they are available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the keys to their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruit is the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, moss, stems and twigs, and termitaria.Crockett and Rudran (1987a,b) examined seasonal variation in births in red howlers from northern Venezuela, and found that they were less frequent during the early wet season (weaning would occur at the time of greatest food shortage). Oestrus lasts 2-4 days, with intervals between oestrous periods of about 17 days. Interbirth intervals are generally about 16.6 months, although they may be shortened by the death of an infant to about 10.5 months (Crockett and Sekulic 1984). Crockett and Rudran (1987a,b) reviewed long-term demographic data on births at Hato Masaguaral, examining seasonality and interannual and habitat differences. Mean gestation length is 191 days (range 186-194, n=6) (as for A. seniculus seniculus in Crockett and Sekulic 1982).Size: As for Alouatta seniculus, VenezuelaAdult male 6.31 kg (n=64) (Rodríguez and Boher 1988)Adult female 4.67 kg (n=46) (Rodríguez and Boher 1988).
threats: The main threat to this species is hunting.
population: Between 15 and 118 individuals/km² have been recorded in Venezuela (Defler 2003). Rudran and Fernandez-Duque (2003) report on 30 years of demographic data on this species at the Hato Masaguaral, Guarico State, Venezuela. Habitats there include a continuous gallery forest along the Río Guarico and forest patches in seasonally inundated grasslands. Populations on the ranch ranged from a peak of 346 in 1989/1990 to 99 in 1999; population densities from 223 to 58 individuals/km². Population increases were found to result in part from increases in group size and in part from increases in the numbers of groups. The authors found that density was a good predictor of the size of established and new groups. A gradual increase from 146 in 1970 to 346 in 1989/1990 was partly due to habitat regeneration. The decline in the population from 1990 to 1999 was believed to result from disease and food shortage, the latter resulting in stress, longer distances travelled to find food, less nutritious diets, and increased susceptibility to botfly infestations. Short-term fluctuations were related to rainfall, drier years reducing population growth. Crockett and Eisenberg (1986) and Crockett (1996) examine particular aspects of demography, habitat and group size in this species.
range: Alouatta arctoidea is endemic to Venezuela. Its range, following Hill (1962) and Bodini and Pérez-Hernández (1987), is along the Venezuelan coast, east of Lake Maracaibo from Falcón to the state of Miranda. Bodini and Pérez-Hernández (1987) indicated that the howler monkey north of the Río Orinoco and west through Apure basin north of the Rio Meta, widely distributed throughout the Venezuelan llanos, is a distinct, as yet undescribed, form. Linares (1998), however, considered it to be A. arctoidea. Linares (1998) descibed its range as the Cordillera Oriental, Cordillera Central and the Coro System along northern Venezuela, extending south throughout the llanos to the Río Orinoco, between 10 m and 1,160 m asl. To date, the species is known only from Colombia, but it may extend into Colombia in Arauca.
useTrade: Aloutta arctoidea is a local livelihood. It is used as food by humans.
conservationActions: This species occurs in a number of protected areas, including:El Avila National Park (85,192 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)Henri Pittier National Park (107,800 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)Aguaro-Guariquito National Park (569,000 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)Sierra Nevada National Park (190,000 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)Guatopo National Park (92,640 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)Macarao National Park (15,000 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982)El Guacharo National Park (15,500 ha) (Venezuela, INPARQUES, 1982).Cinaruco-Capanaparo National ParkParia National ParkTuruépano National ParkMochima National ParkLaguna de Tacarigua National ParkSan Esteban National ParkYuribí National ParkTirgua National ParkGuache National ParkCueva Quebrada del Toro National ParkSierra San Luis National ParkTerepaima National Park This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES (as Alouatta seniculus).

rationale: Despite its large range, occurrence in numerous nature reserves in several countries, and apparent adaptation to modified habitats, Alouatta caraya is considered Near Threatened due to a suspected population reduction of 25-30% over 36 years (three generations; 2004-2040) due to ongoing loss of suitable habitat, hunting pressure, and the susceptibility of this species to disease outbreaks (e.g. yellow fever).
habitat: Alouatta caraya is found in deciduous, seasonally deciduous, mixed evergreen, gallery, and xeric forests, as well as in forest patches in savanna habitats. Today, it occupies forest patches throughout a large part of the Cerrado of central Brazil, and the Pantanal of Mato Grosso. It occupies deciduous forest (caatinga alta) in some areas in southern Piaui, western Bahia and north-western Minas Gerais. In Rio Grande do Sul occurs in mixed evergreen forest (Araucaria), forest patches in savanna, seasonal deciduous forest (Codenotti et al. 2002; Codenotti and Silva 2004) and gallery forest. In Argentina, it specializes in semi-dry deciduous forests and gallery forests as well as the typical island forests of the Chaco (Arditi and Placci 1990; Brown and Zunino 1994). In Bolivia, it is found in the Chaco and Chiquitano forests, and gallery forest and forest islands in the Beni. In Paraguay, Stallings (1985; Stallings et al. 1989) reported that A. caraya occurs throughout the eastern forests and gallery forests of the southern and western Chaco along the ríos Paraguai and Pilcomayo, and the numerous small rivers that drain the Chacoan plain. It can also be found in sporadic xeric forests, continuous with gallery forests.Mean adult male weight ranges from 6.42 kg (n=58, Rumiz 1990) to 7.77 kg (n=9, Svoboda et al. 2006), while mean adult female weight ranges from 4.33 kg (n=117, Rumiz 1990) to 5.13 kg (n=12, Svoboda et al. 2006). Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the under surface at the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaw that surrounds the hyoid apparatus, a resonating chamber, and enlarged larynx that produces their howls (grunts, roars and barks) (Kitchen et al. 2015). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1-2 km (Drubbel and Gautier 1993; Cunha and Byrne 2006).Howler monkeys have a folivorous-frugivorous diet (Crockett and Eisenberg 1987). The molar teeth are particularly adapted for their chewing leaves through shearing. Although they regularly include mature leaves in their diet, softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when they are available. Howlers spend up to 70% of their day lying and sitting in the canopy, while their enlarged caeca ferment the leaves. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the keys to their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruit is the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, moss, stems, twigs and bark. A few groups inhabiting orchards near human habitations were reported to eat bird eggs (Bicca-Marques et al. 2009).Behavioral and ecological field studies have been carried out mostly in Argentina and Brazil (see reviews by Bicca-Marques 2003, Oklander et al. 2011, Arroyo-Rodríguez et al. 2015, Cristóbal-Azkarate et al. 2015, Dias and Rangel-Negrín 2015, Fortes et al. 2015, Martínez-Mota et al. 2015).
threats: Alouatta caraya is threatened by habitat loss due to agricultural development and cattle ranching in the Brazilian cerrado, soya farming in the Bolivian Chiquitano, and small-scale farms and cattle ranching in Argentina. Studies in Brazilian Amazonia suggest a loss of suitable forest habitat approaching 40% by the year 2050 if current conditions remain unchanged (Soares-Filho et al. 2016).  Subsistence hunting also occurs throughout much of this species' range.  In studies of hunting impact in Amazonia, Peres and Palacios (2007) have shown that large-bodied primates such as Alouatta species may experience declines in population density upwards of 50% in areas of moderate to heavy hunting. In addition, significant population declines have been reported following outbreaks of sylvatic yellow fever in Brazil (Veiga et al. 2009; Bicca-Marques and Freitas 2010, Almeida et al. 2012, Freitas and Bicca-Marques 2013, Silva et al. 2013) and Argentina (Holzmann et al. 2010).
population: Although widespread, Alouatta caraya is patchily distributed, and densities vary widely. In Argentina, Brown and Zunino (1994) recorded high densities in a number of sites: Chaco forest, Formosa, 111 individuals/km²; Chaco forest, Corrientes, 90 individuals/km²; gallery forest, 63 individuals/km²; and inundated forest 283 individuals/km². Arditi and Placci (1990) carried out surveys in gallery forests of the Chaco in Argentina (Riacho Pilagá, Estancia Guaycolec) and found lower numbers than those reported by Brown and Zunino (1994) resulting from surveys in the 1980s: 11.7 individuals/km². Dvoskin et al.
