(2004) repeated the surveys there in 2001 and found that numbers had increased to 26 individuals/km².  The highest densities (88–425 individuals/km²) occur in flooded forests and there have been numerous surveys of Alouatta caraya in this forest type of Argentina (Pope 1968; Rumiz 1990; Thorington Jr et al. 1994; Zunino et al. 1996, 2001; Kowalewski and Zunino 2004). In the dry Bolivian Chaco, in the gallery forest of the Parapeti river, it was found at 15-18 individuals/km² (Ayala 2011). Codenotti et al. (2002; see also Codenotti and Silva 2004) located small and isolated populations, composed mostly of single groups, in forest fragments of up to 50 ha in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Densities in these small fragments ranged from 17 to 650 individuals/km². Similarly, Silva and Codenotti (2007) found densities ranging from 30 to 500 individuals/km² in small fragments in the municipality of Tupanciretã, Rio Grande do Sul. In the state of Paraná, Brazil, Aguiar et al. (2011) found densities of 40 to 260 individuals/km².Overall, it is suspected that the population will suffer a reduction of 25-30% over 36 years (three generations; 2004-2040) due to loss of suitable habitat, subsistence hunting and population extirpations caused by disease (e.g. yellow fever).
range: This is a wide-ranging species occurring throughout most of central-western Brazil (with range expanses to the north, northeast and south; Ludwig et al. in press), eastern Bolivia (Wallace et al. 2013), eastern Paraguay (Stallings 1985), northeastern Argentina (Brown and Zunino 1994) and potentially reaching northwestern Uruguay (Villalba et al. 1995). It inhabits moist semi-deciduous, deciduous or higher altitude habitats within the Cerrado, Caatinga, Chaco, Pantanal, Pampa and Atlantic Forest biomes, mostly in gallery or floodplain forests and marginally in more humid forests of the Amazon.The range of Alouatta caraya partly overlaps that of other howler species. It occurs in sympatry with A. guariba clamitans in the states of Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul in south Brazil (Aguiar et al. 2007, 2014; Bicca-Marques et al. 2008) and the Province of Misiones in Argentina (Agostini et al. 2008). Hybridization is suspected in these contact zones. In the state of Rondônia, Brazil, the species occurs in sympatry with A. puruensis (Alves 2006, 2013). Alencar and Melo (2013) report a potential contact zone with A. belzebul in the state of Tocantins, Brazil. In Beni and Santa Cruz departments of Bolivia, the species is found in sympatry with A. sara (Buntge and Pyritz 2007, Wallace and Rumiz 2010).
useTrade: Alouatta caraya is still subjected to subsistence hunting.

rationale: Despite its relatively large range and occurrence in several protected areas, Alouatta discolor must be considered Vulnerable (VU A4cde). Loss of suitable habitat, which is likely to approach 40% by 2040 throughout the core of its range if current conditions do not change, ongoing hunting pressure, and the susceptibility of this species to disease outbreaks (e.g. yellow fever) is likely to cause the population to decline by more than 50% over 37 years (three generations; 2003-2040).
habitat: Alouatta discolor is found in lowland terra firma and seasonally inundated rain forest (igapó), palm swamps, and secondary forest (Pinto 2002, Pinto and Setz 2004). Although relatively common in much of its geographical distribution, it can be rare in some areas. In a preliminary survey conducted in Jamanxim National Park, A. discolor was the most frequent species (Buss et al. 2013). In the region of Tapajós National Forest, along the BR-163 highway, Spix's howlers are more abundant in forest fragments in relation to continuous forest (Ferrari et al. 2003). However, the species is rare further south to the Serra do Cachimbo, between the BR-163 and the Tapajós River.Howler monkeys are the most folivorous of the New World primates. The contribution of leaves to the diet of Howlers varies across their geographical distribution, depending on characteristics of habitat and fluctuations in food availability (Rylands and Mittermeier 2013). Compared with the diets of the other Howlers, A. discolor has one of the highest rates of frugivory (Pinto 2002; Pinto and Setz 2004). For a group studied for one year in Paranaita, Rio Santa Helena, ripe fruits made up most of the diet in all months but one. The annual diet was 55% ripe fruit and some unripe fruit (0.6%), 19.8% young leaves, 5.7% flowers, 5% mature leaves, 4.4% bark, 3.2% decaying wood, 0.5% soil from termitaria, and small amounts of twigs, petioles, and orchid pseudobulbs (Pinto 2002; Pinto and Setz 2004). Alouatta discolor lives in unimale-multifemale or multimale-multifemale groups, with 2–9 individuals. In the study in Paranaita, home range of a group with 7–9 individuals was 69 ha (Pinto 2002; Pinto and Setz 2004). Seasonal migration from terra firma to igapó was observed in the flood season, during the peak fruiting in the igapó (Pinto 2002).Adult male weight is 6.5–8.0 kg; adult female weight is 4.8–6.2 kg (Glander and Pinto 2013).
threats: The main threats to Alouatta discolor include deforestation driven by logging, agriculture (mainly soybean expansion), cattle ranching, mining, expanding rural settlements, and energy and transportation matrix development (i.e., paving of the Cuiabá-Santarém highway (BR-163), which bisects its range north to south, and the Transamazon highway (BR-230), which bisects its range west to east), as well as limited subsistence hunting. Soares-Filho et al. (2006) project that close to 100 mammal species in Brazilian Amazonia will lose more than 40% of their tropical forest habitat within protected areas and as much as 80% outside of those areas by the year 2050 due to the expansion of cattle and soy industries, and the construction of all-weather highways into the region’s core.  This projection is based upon assumptions that the current rates of deforestation and highway construction will continue, compliance with legislation requiring forest reserves on private land will remain low, and new protected areas will not be created. According to Azevedo-Ramos et al. (2006), approximately 60% of Amazonian primate ranges fall outside of protected areas.  Construction plans for the Tapajós Hydroelectric Complex (Ravetta 2008, Buss et al. 2017) include a number of dams within the range of Alouatta discolor, including two along the Jamanxin River that are projected to flood an estimated 65,000 hectares of tropical forest habitat within four protected areas in which this species presently occurs: Jamanxin National Park, Itaituba I National Forest, Itaituba II National Forest, and the Tapajos Environmental Protection Area (Fearnside 2015). Based on surveys (1987-2005) of more than 100 sites, in areas where Amazonian howler monkeys are subjected to medium levels of hunting, population densities are reported to have declined by as much as 50% (Peres and Palacios 2007). In addition, the potential for population declines in howler monkeys due to disease outbreaks (e.g., sylvatic yellow fever) is significant (e.g., Bicca-Marques and Freitas 2010; Almeida et al. 2012).
population: There are no published density estimates available. By the year 2040, loss of suitable habitat is likely to approach 40% throughout the core of its range if current conditions not change. This, in combination with medium-to-heavy hunting pressure, and the susceptibility to disease outbreaks (e.g. yellow fever), could easily result in a population decline of at least 50% over 37 years (three generations; 2003-2040) for this species.
range: The type locality for Alouatta discolor is given as Forte Curupá (= Gurupá), Pará, Brazil but Gregorin (2006) explained that this was on the southern margin of the Rio Amazonas, not on the Island of Gurupá (opposite), which is occupied presumably by Alouatta macconnelli.Aloutta discolor occurs along the south bank of the Rio Amazonas, from the right bank of the Tapajós and Juruena rivers to the Xingu and Iriri rivers; the range extends east of the Xingu River near its mouth to Gurupá Island (Gregorin 2006). The species is also present in the interfluvium Juruena-Teles Pires, where it was registered a group living in sympatric with A. puruensis on the left bank of the Santa Helena River (Pinto and Setz 2000).Bonvicino et al. (1989) indicated that A. discolor occurs on the Islands of Marajó and Caviana, and Mexiana, but here we follow Fernandes (1994), Ferrari and Lopes (1996), and Gregorin (2006) who agree that Alouatta belzebul is the howler occurring there.Between the lower Xingu in the west and the Tocantins the identity of this species is in doubt (A. Rylands pers comm.).
useTrade: Alouatta discolor is a local livelihood and it is used as food by humans.
conservationActions: The following protected areas are within the range of the species: Tapajós National Forest (549,067 ha); Jamanxim National Park (859,797 ha), Itaituba I National Forest (220,639 ha); Itatiuba II National Forest (427,366 ha); and Altamira National Forest (724,965 ha), Tapajós Environmental Protected Area (2,060,332 ha), Jamanxim National Forest (1,301,683 ha), Trairão Environmental Protected Area (257,526 ha), Riozinho do Anfrísio Extractive Reserve (736,340 ha), Cristalino Private Reserve of Nature Patrimony (670 ha).It is listed on Appendix II of CITES.

rationale: Although it is present in a wide range in the Atlantic Forest, Brown Howler Monkey has suffered from extensive habitat loss and fragmentation. It is suspected that the predominant scenario of small isolated subpopulations may aggravate the synergistic demographic and genetic effects of the already severely fragmented habitat. Also, the species suffers hunting pressure at different levels within its distribution range. Furthermore, it is highly susceptible to yellow fever, and an outbreak in 2008-2009 killed many individuals in southern Brazil. Lots of its subpopulations are impacted by urban expansion and infrastructure development, leading increasingly to vehicle and power line accidents and the predation by dogs. The yellow fever epidemic, coupled with ongoing habitat degradation, hunting pressure and other threats, has resulted in ongoing population decline, suspected to be at least 30% over three generations (36 years; 2008-2044). Thus, the species is listed as Vulnerable (VU) under criterion A4ce.
habitat: The species is an inhabitant of lowland, submontane and montane forest along the Atlantic coast of Brazil. It extends inland to the mesophytic, semideciduous, seasonal forest in the states of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Paraná (Mendes 1985, 1989; Chiarello 1993, 1995, 1999; Rylands et al. 1998; Marques 2001). In Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul, it occurs in the highly seasonal, subtropical and temperate, mixed broadleaf/Araucaria forest (Schneider and Marques 1999; Buss 2001). Aguiar et al. (2007) recorded it in periodically flooded, seasonal, semideciduous forest in the floodplains of the Rio Paraná in Paraná State. In Rio Grande do Sul it occurs also in seasonal deciduous forest fragments (Fortes 2008). Buss et al. (2009) reported the occurrence of A. g. clamitans in different vegetation types at Itapuã State Park, i.e. meso-hygrophilous, hygrophilous and sub-xerophilous forests. Only in Rio Grande do Sul individuals of this taxon have been found on forested sandbanks (psammophilous forest; Fialho 2000), and in the Banhado dos Pachecos Wildlife Refuge it occurs in swamp forest (Bicca-Marques, unpublished data).  There are no reports that the species was observed in mangroves. The taxon is not restricted to primary habitats, suggesting that the species is tolerant to environmental changes and human disturbances.The howler monkeys are the large leaf-eaters within the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted for chewing leaves through shearing. Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the underside of the tail tip. The most characteristic feature is the deep lower jaw, which encompasses the enlarged larynx and the hyoid apparatus, forming a resonating chamber. With this enlarged and highly specialized voice box howler monkeys produce their howls, grunts, roars and barks. Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard at distances of 1-2 km, particularly in the early morning (Drubbel and Gautier 1993). Brown Howler Monkeys live in groups of four to five individuals, reaching a maximum of 13 individuals (Alves and Zau 2007, Di Fiore et al. 2011, Jardim 2005, Ingberman et al. 2009, Miranda and Passos 2005). Ingberman et al. (2009) reported a mean group size of 4.5 (range: 1 to 6) individuals in 10 observed groups in the Ilha do Cardoso State Park. The authors compiled data from 16 additional studies, finding mean group sizes ranging from 1.8 to 9.4 individuals, and a maximum group size of 13 individuals. In Forest Hemlock in Rio de Janeiro State, Alves and Zau (2007) observed a mean group size of 5.8 (range: 3 to 8) individuals, based on four groups, each with a single adult male. Miranda and Passos (2005) reported 5 groups with a mean group size of 6.3 individuals (range: 4 to 10), including 1 to 2 adult males and 1 to 3 adult females.There is usually only one dominant male in each group (occasionally two) with a harem of two to five females. Others males are either subordinate younger males, sub-adults, or juveniles. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), howler monkeys have generally small and broadly overlapping home ranges. Home range size, however, varies depending on the type of habitat type (Neville et al. 1988). Bicca-Marques (2003) mentions a variation in home size ranging from 3.9 to 33.0 ha (mean ± SD = 10.2 ± 8.1, N = 11). Fortes (2008) studied a group that used two small forest fragments summing not more than 1 ha. Miranda and Passos (2011) documented variation in home range size reaching from 1.8 to 33 ha (mean ± SD = 10.0 ± 7.9, N = 15). A more recent review reported an average home range size of 13.0 ha (SD = 15.9; Fortes et al. 2015).Howler monkeys are the only New World primates that regularly include mature leaves in their diet, although softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the key factors for their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. In many regions mature fruits are another important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus), but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, mosses, stems, twigs, and even termites.Size:Mean adult male weight: 6.73 kg (N=4); mean adult female weight: 4.35 kg (N=5) (Smith and Jungers 1997).
threats: Widespread forest loss and fragmentation throughout its range are the main threats to Alouatta guariba. Its distributional range largely correlates with the most densely populated regions of Brazil. Only 12% of the original forest coverage is remaining in these areas, fragmented into almost 250 forest fragments, 83.4% of which are smaller than 50 ha (Ribeiro et al. 2009). It is suspected that the current scenario of small isolated subpopulations, may progressively aggravate the synergistic, demographic and genetic effects of the severely fragmented habitat, including the increase of inbreeding. However, the species is able to survive in quite small forest fragments if there is no hunting. Especially in the northern part of its range it suffers from hunting pressure at different levels (Canale et al. 2012). Furthermore, the species is highly susceptible to yellow fever, and an outbreak in 2008-2009 killed a large number of individuals, with local extinctions recorded in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil (Almeida et al. 2012, Fialho et al. 2012), and Misiones, Argentina (Holzmann et al. 2010). This epidemic resulted in lethal aggression from local communities due to a fear of direct transmission from howler monkeys (Bicca-Marques and Freitas 2010). In addition, many subpopulations are affected by urban expansion and infrastructure developments. This includes accidents with vehicles and power lines and predation by dogs (Printes 1999, Pasquotto et al. 2002, Galetti and Sazima 2006, Fries et al. 2007, Lokschin et al. 2007, São Paulo (Cidade) 2011, Buss 2012).
population: Although the size of the total remaining population is unknown, there are a fair number of population estimates throughout the range of this species and it is suspected that the number of mature individuals exceeds the threshold of 10,000 individuals. Pinto et al. (2009) reported at least eight subpopulations with more than 500 individuals, estimated by using linear transect surveys in the Atlantic Forest area of southern and southeastern Brazil. Most of those studies were carried out in very small forest fragments. González-Solís et al. (2001) provided a summary, listing 11 sites (forests; ranging from 50 ha to 100,000 ha) where brown howlers were counted.Densities can be very high. When not hunted, densities can vary, even within very small forest fragments due to being folivorous and their dietary flexibility. In a 50-ha site at Lageadinho in São Paulo State, group size was 6-12 individuals, and the density was estimated as 98 individuals/km² (Torres de Assumpção 1983). Chiarello (1993) recorded a density of 177 individuals/km² at the Santa Genebre Reserve (259 ha) in São Paulo State. Density estimates at the Caratinga Biological Station (survey area ranging from 570 to 800 ha) in Minas Gerais, varied from 92 to 149 individuals/km² (Mendes 1985, 1989; Hirsch 1995). Lower densities, e.g. 10.1 individuals/km², were recorded by Pinto et al. (1993) in the Augusto Ruschi Biological Reserve (4,000 ha) in Espírito Santo State. Hirsch (1995) estimated densities of 1.8 to 49.0 individuals/km² in the Rio Doce State Park (32,210 ha) in Minas Gerais. González-Solís et al. (2001) estimated only a density of 0.79 individuals/km² in four contiguous protected areas of the Serra do Paranapiacaba in the state of São Paulo, totalling about 140,000 ha (i.e., the state parks of Intervales, Turístico Alto Ribeira and Carlos Botelho, and the Xitué State Ecological Station). Surveys by Chiarello (1995) in the Linhares Forest Reserve, Espírito Santo failed to register howlers even though they were present. During later surveys in the same reserve, Chiarello (1999) recorded an encounter rate of 0.15 groups/10 km. Schneider and Marques (1999) estimated a density of 92-125 individuals/km² in the southern part of the range of this species, in mixed broadleaf/Araucaria forest in the Aracuri-Esmeralda Ecological Station. Buss (2001) estimated 65 to 85 individuals/km² in the Itapuã State Park. Ingberman et al. (2009) reported 10.6 individuals/km2 or 2.4 groups/km2 in Cardoso Island State Park. The same authors compiled data from 16 studies using different methods and obtained values ​​from 0.4 to 260 individuals/km2. Pinto et al. (2009) mentioned a variation in population density reaching from 0.3 to 176.8 individuals/km2 (N=20). Chiarello and Melo (2001) surveyed seven forest fragments in Espírito Santo, varying in size from 210 to 24,250 ha, and found the species in very low abundance. In two of these fragments (Sooretama Biological Reserve: 24,250 ha; Rio Preto National Forest: 2,822 ha) only by vocalization, in two others (Linhares Forest Reserve: 21,800 ha; M7/317: 260 ha) by a single encounter. Lower densities seem to occur in large and continuous forests. On the other hand, higher densities are found in small, isolated or peri-urban forest fragments.The above quoted density estimates are mainly the result of a number of behavioural and ecological field studies conducted on this species. The study sites chosen are those where howler monkeys were found to be numerous and visible. Thus, the high densities reported are undoubtedly at the top end of the possible range and do not reflect a situation typical for the entire distributional range of the species. At localities where they are hunted they will occur in much lower densities, or not at all. In some areas they are scarce even though hunting is minimal or absent (for example, the Rio Doce State Park or the Augusto Ruschi Biological Station). The reason for low population densities in these areas is generally sought to be disease epidemics, especially yellow fever.In Misiones, Argentina, densities of both A. guariba and A. caraya are extremely low, probably as a result of the dramatic habitat fragmentation observed in the last few decades, and due to repeated yellow fever outbreaks (1966, 2008-2009).
range: Alouatta guariba inhabits a large part of the Atlantic Forest, along the coast of eastern Brazil. Its distributional range extends from Rio de Contas in southern Bahia (formerly south of the Rio Paraguaçu) (Neves et al. 2015a, b), south to the basin of the Rio Camaquã, in the state of Rio Grande do Sul (Printes et al. 2001), and further to the extreme North of Argentina in the province of Misiones (Crespo 1954; Rylands et al. 1998; Di Bitetti et al. 1994; Rylands 1994; Marques 2003). Alouatta g. clamitans occurs in sympatry with A. caraya in the states of Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul in southern Brazil (Aguiar et al. 2007, 2014; Bicca-Marques et al. 2008) and in the Province of Misiones in Argentina (Agostini et al. 2008). Hybridization between these two taxa is suspected in the contact zone and was observed in captivity (Jesus et al. 2010). Kinsey (1981) argued that the Rio Doce separated the northern subspecies (Alouatta g. guariba) from the southern subspecies (A. g. clamitans). However, throughout a large part of their range, i.e. north of the Rio Doce, howler monkeys were indistinguishable from those to the South of the river (S. Mendes pers. comm.). Surveys by Rylands et al. (1988) resulted in the discovery of groups just south of the lower Jequitinhonha River, which were all pale gold in colour, whereas further west, north of the middle Jequitinhonha, groups in deciduous forests showed sexual dichromatism typical of clamitans occurring further south (females dark brown, males golden brown). North of the Jequitinhonha River, only a few records of brown howler monkeys were reported, and only a few viable populations remain (Neves et al. 2015a,b). If the uniformly pale howlers of the lower Jequitinhonha are, in fact, a distinct subspecies (the nominate subspecies), then the populations must be minuscule. However, the validity of the two subspecies remains doubtful. Also, recent genetic analysis, comparing populations from the south of the species’ range in the states of Santa Catarina, São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro suggest a strong subpopulation differentiation within clamitans (Jerusalinsky 2001, Harris et al. 2005, Martins et al. 2011).
useTrade: The species suffers from high hunting pressure for consumption or for cultural use (to remove the hyoid bone used in rituals and folk medicine)..
conservationActions: Some initiatives focus on the conservation of the southern subspecies, Alouatta guariba clamitans, since the early 1990’s, implementing research and management actions. The Projeto Bugio (Howler Project) is an initiative of the Indaial Biological Research Center (CEPESBI), maintained by the Municipality of Indaial and the University Foundation of Blumenau (FURB). Since 1992 they have conducted research, environmental education, management of individuals and conservation activities in the northern region of the Santa Catarina State (Projeto Bugio 2016). In 1993 the Programa Macacos Urbanos (Urban Monkeys Program), linked to the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul and recently recognized as a Nucleus of Universitary Extension (NEMU/UFRGS), implemented a transdisciplinary approach towards the species conservation (Jerusalinsky et al. 2010). Actions implemented include: creation of new protected areas (Printes et al. 2010), environmental education activities (Teixeira et al. 2011) and the installation of rope bridges in the south of the city of Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul State, by the Urban Monkeys Program (NEMU/UFRGS) to minimize road kills, dog attacks and electric shock accidents with public power lines (Lokschin et al. 2007; Teixeira et al. 2013).The municipality of São Paulo has developed a number of reintroductions and environmental education activities of local communities (São Paulo (Cidade), 2009a; São Paulo (Cidade) 2009b; Alencar Jr. et al. 2011; São Paulo (Cidade) 2012).The northern subspecies, Alouatta guariba guariba, was included in the Central Atlantic Forest National Action Plan, elaborated by ICMBio and collaborators in 2010, establishing a series of conservation strategies by means of research and management of the species and its habitats. As part of these strategies, the Projeto Barbado-Vermelho (Red-Howler Project), coordinated by IESB in cooperation with the National Center for Research and Conservation of Brazilian Primates (ICMBio/CPB) and the Uiraçu Institute, is developing research and management actions. The program is supported by the Rain Forest Trust, the Primate Action Fund (CI), and the Mohamed BinZayed Fund. The activities include the release of howler monkeys that were illegally kept in captivity (Serra Bonita, Camacan, Bahia), and the management of a complex of private reserves with more than 2.000 hectares (Neves et al. 2015a, b). rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern given its widespread, although incompletely known (relative to A. seniculus) distribution and a lack of any major threats that could result in a significant population decline.
habitat: This species is found in evergreen rain forest. Along the Rio Juruá, and undoubtedly elsewhere in its range, it tends to be more common in seasonally flooded forest (várzea) than in terra firma forest (Peres 1997, Queiroz 1995).The howler monkeys are the large leaf-eaters of the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted to chewing leaves through shearing. They spend up to 70% of the day lying or sitting among the branches, fermenting leaves in their enlarged caeca. Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the underside of the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaw which surrounds the enlarged larynx and hyoid apparatus, forming a resonating chamber. With this enlarged and highly specialized ‘voice box’ the howler monkeys produce their howls (grunts, roars and barks). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1-2 km (Drubbel and Gautier 1993).Group size is usually four to 11 individuals (rarely 14 individuals). In the red howlers, there is usually only one dominant male in the group (occasionally two), others being sub-adults, or juveniles, along with a harem of two to five females. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), the howler monkeys generally have quite small and broadly overlapping home ranges of 5 to 45 ha, depending on the type of habitat (Neville et al. 1988).Howlers are the only New World primates, which regularly include mature leaves in their diet. Although softer and less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the key factors for their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruits are the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, mosses, stems and twigs, and sometimes termites. Oestrus lasts 2-4 days, with intervals between oestrous periods of about 17 days. Inter-birth intervals are generally about 16.6 months, although they may be shortened by the death of an infant to about 10.5 months (Crockett and Sekulic 1984). Mean gestation length is 191 days (range 186-194, n=6) as for A. seniculus (Crockett and Sekulic, 1982), considered here to be A. arctoidea.Size: As for Alouatta seniculus, Brazil:Adult male 7.62 kg (n=28) (Ayres 1986)Adult female 6.02 kg (n=34) (Ayres 1986).
threats: This species is under a strong pressure of hunting throughout its range, even inside the protected areas. Aquino and Encarnación (1994) reported that populations of red howlers have declined in the lower parts of the selva alta (high forest) in the Peruvian Amazon as a result of colonization by humans, hunting and deforestation, noting particularly the valley of Chanchamayo (Department of Junín) where the species has been extirpated.
population: Peres (1997) estimated the following population densities in terra firma forest in the Brazilian Amazon: Kaxinawá Reserve: 9.2 individuals/km²; Altamira: 4.6 individuals/km²; Barro Vermelho I: 1.0 individuals/km²; Fortuna: 5.3 individuals/km²; Vira Volta: 4.7 individuals/km²; Riozinho: 8.4 individuals/km². In várzea (white-water flooded forest), the densities tend to be higher: Sacado do Condor: 24.7 individuals/km²; Nova Empresa: 35.7 individuals/km²; Barro Vermelho II: 15,6 individuals/km²; Lago da Fortuna: 35.7 individuals/km². Queiroz (1995) estimated a density of 38 individuals/km² at Lago Mamirauá, between the Rios Japurá and Solimões.
range: Gregorin (2006) reported that this species occurs throughout the upper Amazon of Brazil in the states of Acre and Amazonas, to the south of the Rio Solimões. If A. seniculus amazonica is a junior synonym of A. juara, A. juara would be the species to the north of the Rio Solimões, west of the Rio Negro, extending into Colombia and into large parts of the Peruvian Amazon, perhaps north of the Rio Inuya (A. puruensis to the south of the Río Inuya).There is no information regarding the range limits of A. juara and A. seniculus (Colombian Andes and Venezuela; type locality: Cartagena, Bolivar, Colombia). They were therefore presented in one map.In Colombia, A. seniculus is absent from the Pacific and the desert of the Guajira Peninsula, and has not been reported from the Department of Nariño (Defler 2004). Otherwise, it is present throughout the country, except in non-forested areas and mountainous regions above app. 3,000 m asl (though it has been reported at 3,200 m in the Central Andes). In Venezuela, Bodini and Pérez-Hernández (1987) suggest that the howler monkey north of the Rio Orinoco and west through the Apure Basin north of the Rio Meta is a distinct, as yet undescribed, form of red howler. By contrast, Linares (1998) labelled it as A. arctoidea, also occurring along the north coast of Venezuela.In summary, Alouatta juara / A. seniculus occur west of the Juruá and Envira Rivers through the Peruvian Amazon north of the Rio Inuya, further north along the Andean Cordillera into Ecuador and into Colombia, including the Cordillera Central and the Cordillera Oriental in Venezuela around Lake Maracaibo, west of the Serra de Merida.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern given its relatively large distribution and lack of any major threats resulting in a significant range-wide decline that would warrant listing the species in Near Threatened or a threatened category.
habitat: Alouatta nigerrima is found in tall evergreen terra firma forest, seasonally inundated forest and forest patches in savanna areas, as well as secondary forest in abandoned rubber plantations. The howler monkeys are the large leaf-eaters of the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted for their chewing leaves through shearing. They spend up to 70% of their day lying and sitting about quietly among the branches, fermenting leaves in their enlarged caecums. Like the spider monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the under surface at the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaws which surround the enlarged larynx and hyoid apparatus, a resonating chamber. It is with this enlarged and highly specialised voice box that they produce their howls (grunts, roars and barks). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, can be heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1-2 kms (Drubbel and Gautier 1993).Black howler groups number four or five or up to 11 or so individuals. There is usually only one dominant male in the group (occasionally two), others being sub-adults, or juveniles, along with a harem of two to five females. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), the howler monkeys generally have quite small and broadly overlapping home ranges, of 5 ha up to 45 ha, depending on the type of habitat (Neville et al. 1988). Howlers are the only New World primates which regularly include mature leaves in their diet, although softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when they are available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the keys to their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruit is the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, moss, stems and twigs, and termitaria.Oestrus lasts 2-4 days, with intervals between oestrous periods of about 17 days. Interbirth intervals are generally about 16.6 months, although they may be shortened by the death of an infant to about 10.5 months (Crockett and Sekulic 1984).
threats: Hunting and habitat loss are localised threats, but human population density is relatively low, and neither is likely to be driving significant range-wide declines.  It is not known if the rarity of this species along the left bank of the middle and upper Tapajós is largely a result of hunting by gold miners or some natural factor within its range, perhaps involving competition with related atelids, spider monkeys and woolly monkeys. Under any circumstances the species is heavily hunted, as are other atelids in the Amazon, Ateles spp. and Lagothrix spp.
population: There is no information available on population densities.
range: Alouatta nigerrima occurs south of the Rio Amazonas in Brazil, west from the rios Tapajós and Juruena, to the Rios Madeira and Aripuanã, to about 9ºS. There are outlying populations north of the Rio Amazonas in the region of Oriximiná and Óbidos on the lower Rio Trombetas (Napier 1976) and just south of the Rio Amazonas-Solimões, midway between the rios Madeira and Purus, at the Lago Janauacá (A. Rylands, pers. obs.; Langguth et al. 1987; Bonvincino et al. 1989; Gregorin 2006; R. Sampaio, unpublished data).Surveys are needed along the lower Purus to investigate the contact zone with the Purus Red Howler Monkey, A. puruensis, to the west and south. Local people say that the southernmost known locality is Igapó-Açu (R. Sampaio, pers. comm.). Red howlers, presumably, A. puruensis, occur on both sides of the Aripuanã, at the Cachoeira de Dardanelos, Aripuanã, 10°10’S, 59°27’W). Black howlers are known from a little north of there, along the Rio Aripuanã. The extent of occurrence for this species is greater than 20,000 km², and the area of occupation is, therefore, greater than 2,000 km².
conservationActions: This species is present in Amazonia National Park (1,084,895.62 ha) (Ayres and Milton 1981; Rylands and Bernardes 1989; Branch 1983; A. L. Ravetta, unpubl, data), Tapajós-Arapiuns Extractive Reserve (677,513.24 ha), Amanã National Forest (540,417ha) (A. L. Ravetta, unpubl. data). The Jatuarana National Forest (837,100 ha) and Pau Rosa National Forest (827,877 ha) are within its known range. It is listed on Appendix II of CITES.

rationale: Alouatta palliata is considered Vulnerable (VU A4cd), as a population reduction of 30% or more is inferred over the course of 30 years or three generations. This is based upon Global Forest Watch data for southeastern Mexico south through Central America, into western Colombia and Ecuador, and extreme northern Peru. The data suggests that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has impacted the previous generation (2003-2018), 19% of this species’ suitable habitat is likely to be lost by the year 2048. Combined with continued evidence of hunting, both for the pet trade and for bushmeat, these threats put Alouatta palliata above the threshold for Vulnerable status.
habitat: Alouatta palliata occupies several distinct vegetation types, including mature evergreen forests, deciduous and riparian forests, mangroves, and anthropogenically disturbed forests (Neville et al. 1988, Baumgarten and Williamson 2007). Although mantled howlers spend most of their time resting (65-74%), their daily activities vary considerably according to season and food availability (Glander 2013).The diets of Mantled Howler Monkeys have been extensively studied across the distribution range of the species in Central America. In average mantled howlers spend 21% of their time feeding (range 8–40 %, Dias and Negrin 2015). They mainly consume fruits and leaves, but the relative proportions vary by study site, with some populations being mostly folivorous while others have a more equal share of fruits and leaves in their diets. Other food items include flowers, petioles, buds, etc. (see Dias and Negrin 2015 for a detailed review of howler diets).Group size varies considerably, with some locations reporting sizes of 40 or more individuals in a single group (in Mexico and Costa Rica), although the average group size is 15.2 individuals (Dias and Negrin 2015). Groups include multiple males and females, with a sex ration of 1.79 females per male (Chapman and Balcomb 1998). Group home ranges vary between 8 and 75 ha (see Arroyo-Rodriguez et al. 2015, and references therein).Mean adult male weight ranges from 5.80 ± 0.69 kg in Mexico (Kelaita et al. 2011), 5.79 ± 0.58 kg in La Pacifica, Costa Rica, 6.57 ± 0.48 kg in Santa Rosa, Costa Rica, and 7.56 ± 0.73 kg in BCI, Panama (Glander 2006), while mean adult female weight ranges from 4.39 ± 0.48 kg in Mexico (Kelaita et al. 2011), 4.73 ± 0.62 kg in La Pacifica, Costa Rica, 5.16 ± 0.54 kg in Santa Rosa, Costa Rica, and 6.45 ± 0.55 kg in BCI, Panama (Glander 2006).Behavioural and ecological field studies have been carried out mostly in Mexico, Costa Rica, and Panama and at a lesser extent in Nicaragua and Ecuador (see recent reviews in Kowalewski et al. 2015a,b).
threats: Threats to this species include habitat loss and fragmentation, as a consequence of economic activities, as well as hunting for the pet trade.
population: Alouatta palliata is patchily distributed throughout its range and its densities vary widely. In Mexico a number of studies have reported variable densities between 23.29 (Estrada 1982) and 105 ind./km² (Serio-Silva & Rico-Gray 2002). In Costa Rica, population densities between 4.9 and 30 ind./km² have been estimated for A. p. palliata (see Di Fiore et al. 2011) and 0.2 and 0.1 groups/km² were reported in protected areas (see Glander 2013). In Nicaragua this subspecies is known to occur in densities of 0.21 individuals/ha in fragmented habitats (Williams-Guillen et al. 2008). Densities above 90 ind./km² are reported for A. p. palliata and A. p. aequatorialis in Panama (Chiriqui 1,050, Baldwin and Baldwin 1972, 1976; and BCI 91.7, Milton 1982, respectively). In Colombia, Ramírez-Orjuela and Sánchez-Dueñas (2005) estimated between 0.7 and 1.5 ind./km² for A. p. aequatorialis, but Glander (2013) comments that there are reports of 20 ind./km² in the same general region in Colombia. Population density of A. p. trabeata in the Azuero Peninsula shows great variability, with some areas holding up to 42 ind./km², whereas other areas having as low as 0.5 ind./km² (Average 5.2 ind./km², Méndez-Carvajal 2013). The density of the Coiba Island howler (A. p. coibensis) was estimated to an average of 4.1 groups/km² (17.6 ind/km²) and a total population of 472 individuals (Mendez-Carvajal 2012).A population reduction of 30% or more is inferred over the course of three generations. This is based upon Global Forest Watch data (Global Forest Watch 2020) for southeastern Mexico south through Central America, into western Colombia and Ecuador, and extreme northern Peru. The data suggests that, should forest loss continue at the same rate that has been seen since 2003, close to 30% of this species’ suitable habitat is likely to be lost by the year 2048. In addition, the species is threatened by hunting.
range: Alouatta palliata is distributed from the southern portion of the state of Veracruz in Mexico, and extends south through the Mexican states of Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco, throughout Central America and the Pacific Coast and western slopes of the Andes in Colombia and Ecuador, reaching the Tumbes region in northern Peru.There are five recognized subspecies:Alouatta palliata palliataThis subspecies is distributed from southern Guatemala to western Panama. However, the limits separating A. p. palliata from A. p. aequatorialis are not clear. Lawrence (1933) cited a specimen of A. p. palliata from Cotó, extreme western Panama, and Hill (1962, p.106) mentioned that specimens from Sevilla Island, western Panama, collected by J. H. Batty were “manifestly” A. p. palliata. Hall (1981), on the other hand, lists Sevilla Island, and Puerto Cortez, Costa Rica, as marginal records for A. p. aequatorialis. Lawrence (1933) comments that many individuals from Panama are intermediate. Based on mitochondrial DNA analyses, Cortés-Ortiz et al. (2003) reported two clades separating A. p. palliata/A. p. coibensis/ A. p. mexicana from A. p. trabeata/A. p aequatorialis, and mentioned that these two clades were divided around the Sona Peninsula in western Panama (Cortés-Ortiz et al. 2003). Consistent with this view, recent analyses of individuals from Limones in Punta Burica Panama (Cortés-Ortiz unpubl.) show that their mitochondrial DNA haplotypes cluster with those from A. p. palliata from Costa Rica. To the north, A. p. palliata extends through Costa Rica, Nicaragua and Honduras reaching the south margin of Rio Dulce in southern Guatemala, where it may be sympatric with A. pigra (Curdts 1993, Baumgarten and Williamson 2007). It is not known to currently occur in El Salvador (Burt and Stirton 1961), but it is likely that it occurred there in the past (Daugherty 1972).Alouatta palliata mexicanaThe distribution of A. p. mexicana ranges from southern Veracruz state in Mexico extending southeast to northeastern Oaxaca (Ortiz-Martínez et al. 2008), western Tabasco, and northern Chiapas (see Serio-Silva et al. 2006). In Tabasco A. p. mexicana is sympatric with A. pigra (Smith 1970) and hybridization has been confirmed in that region (Cortés-Ortiz et al. 2007, 2015b). Serio-Silva et al. (2006) reported the presence of A. p. mexicana in Campeche, Mexico, based on the observation of individuals with atypical white hairs on the flanks of their bodies. Cortés-Ortiz et al. (in prep.) have analysed mitochondrial and nuclear DNA from individuals in Campeche with similar coloration patterns and concluded that they are A. pigra, and not A. palliata or hybrid individuals. The reason for the presence of white hairs in the pelage of A. pigra individuals remains unclear. Although several published maps include the range of this subspecies extending into the highlands of Chiapas and north-central Guatemala, a study by A. Cuarón (unpublished) revealed that its range is restricted to western Chiapas, central and western Tabasco, southern Veracruz, and northeastern Oaxaca. Baumgarten and Williamson (2007) argued that A. palliata could have occurred on the Pacific side of the highland massif of northern Central America. There are historical records that suggest the presence of A. palliata (putatively A. p. mexicana) in this region in Mexico (Estrada and Coates-Estrada 1984) and Guatemala (Handley 1950), but no current populations are reported.Alouatta palliata aequatorialisAlouatta palliata aequatorialis occurs in eastern Panama extending through the Serranía del Darién (Anthony 1916, Lawrence 1933) to western Colombia, Ecuador and into the Tumbes region of northwestern Peru (Aquino and Encarnación 1994; Encarnación and Cook 1998; Tirira 2001, 2007). In northern Colombia A. p. aequatorialis is sympatric with A. seniculus in the left banks of the Peye and Atrato rivers in the department of Chocó and perhaps east of the Atrato River, south to the río Sinú (Zuñiga Leal and Defler 2013).Alouatta palliata coibensis This howler monkey is known only from Coiba Island and neighbouring Jicarón Island, off the Pacific coast of Panama (Milton and Mittermeier 1977, Méndez-Carvajal 2012).Alouatta palliata trabeataThis subspecies is endemic to the Azuero Peninsula, Panama (Froehlich and Froehlich 1987, Rowe 2000, Mendes-Carvajal 2005).
useTrade: This species is hunted for bushmeat and also live captured for the pet trade. Pet trade is a common and well-known threat to howler monkeys.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable as, although it is widely distributed, it is facing increasing pressures from hunting and habitat loss which are suspected to have resulted in an ongoing population reduction exceeding 30% over the past three generations (30 years), with similar (and possibly increasing) rates of decline suspected to occur in the future. Further survey work is needed to clarify the distribution limits of the species relative to Alouatta sara in Bolivia.
habitat: This species is found in lowland, evergreen rain forest. Along the Rio Juruá, and undoubtedly elsewhere in its range, it tends to be more common in seasonally flooded forest (várzea) than in terra firma forest (Peres 1997). In the middle Rio Guaporé region, A. puruensis was observed only in igapó forests (Alves 2013).The howler monkeys are the large leaf-eaters of the South American primate communities. The molar teeth are particularly adapted for their chewing leaves through shearing. They spend up to 70% of their day lying and sitting about quietly among the branches, fermenting leaves in their enlarged caecums. Like the spider and woolly monkeys, they are prehensile-tailed, with a naked patch of skin on the under surface at the tip. Their most characteristic feature is the deep jaw that surrounds the enlarged larynx and hyoid apparatus, a resonating chamber. It is with this enlarged and highly specialized voice box that they produce their howls (grunts, roars and barks). Howling sessions, usually involving the entire group, are heard particularly in the early morning and are audible at distances of 1 to 2 km (Drubbel and Gautier 1993).Red howler groups are usually small, ranging in size from 2 to 16 animals and averaging 4 to 10 (Neville et al. 1988). There is usually only one dominant male in the group (occasionally two), others being sub-adults, or juveniles, along with a harem of two to five females. Unlike the spider monkeys, and related to the large proportion of leaves in the diet (up to 50% of the annual diet), the howler monkeys generally have quite small and broadly overlapping home ranges, of 5 ha up to 45 ha, depending on the type of habitat (Neville et al. 1988). Howlers are the only New World primates which regularly include mature leaves in their diet, although softer, less fibrous, young leaves are preferred when they are available. Their folivory and ability to eat mature leaves is undoubtedly one of the keys to their wide distribution and the wide variety of vegetation types they inhabit. Mature fruit is the other important food item, especially wild figs (Ficus) in many regions, but they also eat leaf petioles, buds, flowers (sometimes seasonally very important), seeds, moss, stems and twigs, and termitaria.Oestrus lasts from 2 to 4 days, with intervals between oestrous periods of about 17 days. Interbirth intervals are generally about 16.6 months, although they may be shortened by the death of an infant to about 10.5 months (Crockett and Sekulic 1984). Mean gestation length is 191 days (range 186-194, n=6) (as for A. seniculus in Crockett and Sekulic 1982)Size: As for Alouatta juara, BrazilAdult male 7.62 kg (n=28) (Ayres 1986)Adult female 6.02 kg (n=34) (Ayres 1986).
threats: Increasing habitat loss and hunting are taking place throughout the majority of this species' range. Very low natural population densities in terra firme forests (Peres 1997) make this species more susceptible to anthropogenic threats. Future levels of habitat loss and extraction are expected to increase with the repair and reopening of the BR 319 highway (Fearnside and de Alencastro Graça 2006). Additionally, there is evidence that the species is restricted to the portions of the interfluvia near rivers, occurring at low abundances in terra firme forests. The reopening of the highway will also connect the eastern portion of its distribution to the arc of deforestation. Therefore, the impact of the highway may be stronger than anticipated by a simple look at its wide geographic distribution. Outbreaks of sylvatic yellow fever may also cause high mortality in its populations, seriously compromising their recovery and long term viability.
population: Peres (1997) estimated population densities of howler monkeys at a number of sites on the right (east) bank of the Rio Juruá (presumably A. puruensis): Vai Quem Quer (terra firme forest), 1.0 individuals/km²; Igarapé Jaraquí (terra firme forest), 5.5 individuals/km²; Penedo (terra firme forest), 2.6 individuals/km²; Boa Esperança (várzea), 89.7 individuals/km². In the Guaporé Biological Reserve, on the right bank of the Rio Guaporé, the estimated population density of A. puruensis in igapó forest was 0.5 individuals/km² (Alves 2013).A population reduction exceeding 30% over the past three generations (30 years) is suspected to be ongoing, with similar (and possibly increasing) rates of decline is suspected to occur in the future. These declines are due to hunting and habitat degradation and loss.
range: This red howler monkey extends west from the lower Rio Madeira (left bank) and the Rio Aripuanã across the basin of the Rio Purus to the Rios Juruá and Envira, as postulated by Gregorin (2006). It occurs in northern Rondônia to the Rios Mamoré-Guaporé (Alves 2013), and the species has been observed in the Teles Pires basin (Pinto and Setz 2000), but the southern limits to its range in Brazil are unclear. It is not clear whether it is the form in north-west Bolivia. According to Anderson (1997), only Alouatta sara occurs in Bolivia.There is suspected habitat degradation and loss across the species range.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered based on a small population size and continuing decline driven primarily by hunting and habitat loss. It is estimated that there are fewer than 2,500 mature individuals remaining in the wild, and that there are no subpopulations with more than 250 mature individuals.
habitat: Alouatta ululata occurs in Babaçu forests, semi-deciduous and dry forests and in mangroves located in areas characterized by Caatinga and Cerrado Biomes. The taxon is not restricted to primary habitats, however, it shows little or no tolerance to anthropogenic disturbance in the environment, mainly because the species’ high sensitivity to hunting (Pinto and Roberto unpublished data; Freire Filho et al. 2018; Freire Filho and Palmeirim 2019).Like all other species of the genus, A. ululata is a folivorous and frugivorous species, occupying and defending small home ranges (territories). Pinto and Roberto (unpublished data) estimated the home range of a troop in the dry forest of Caxingó, Piauí, to be between 7 and 14 hectares. In the mangrove areas of Igarapé dos Periquitos, Ilha Grande, Piauí, it was observed an average home range size of 7.96 ha (± 5.53) with a minimum of 1.26 ha and a maximum of 20.27 ha. Freire Filho and Bezerra (in prep.) have registered two groups with 16.05 and 3.22 hectares, respectively, in the arboreal caatinga region.
threats: Only a few populations survive in a region which has a long history of human occupation, resulting in high levels of forest loss and human pursuit (hunting for bush meat). Hunting pressure on this taxon varies in intensity. In Ceará the species survives only on hill tops and steep slopes, where populations are inaccessible to hunters and where the forest is protected by law. The sugarcane plantations along the middle and lower Parnaíba, rural settlements and charcoal production represent additional threats. A reduction in rainfall and rising temperatures in the region, due to climate change, could be the dominant threat in the long term.
population: All known populations are small and isolated. Pinto and Roberto (unpublished data) observed the group composition of six troops in the dry forests of the municipality of Caxingó (Piauí). The mean group size ranged from seven to ten individuals with an average of 8.33 (± 1.36) individuals. The same authors estimated the group size in Igarapé of Periquitos region, a mangrove area in the municipality of Ilha Grande, Piauí, to range from 2 to 14 individuals with a mean of 5.85 (± 2.63) individuals. Freire Filho and Bezerra (in prep.) monitored two groups in an arboreal caatinga environment in São Miguel do Tapuio (Piauí), and recorded one with four mature individuals and another with six. By sensing the populations in this site, these authors estimated the subpopulation has between 100 and 150 mature individuals (Freire Filho and Bezerra, in prep). This and the Parnaíba River delta are the areas with the largest subpopulations of the species, recorded so far (Ferreira et al., in prep.; Freire Filho and Bezerra, in prep.). Despite existing in other parts of Piauí and Ceará states, subpopulations are small and isolated. Therefore, it is plausible to infer that the size of the total remaining population does not exceed 2,500 mature individuals and that there are no subpopulations with more than 250 mature individuals.
range: Endemic to Brazil, Alouatta ululata occurs in three states of north-east Brazil: Maranhão, Piauí and Ceará. Its range was recently elucidated through the efforts of the Centro Nacional de Pesquisa e Conservação de Primatas Brasileiros of the Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade (Oliveira et al. 2004, Ferreira et al. 2007, Ferreira et al. in prep.). The type locality is Miritiba, now called Humberto de Campos, on the coast of Maranhão just east of Rio Itapecurú, which seems to mark the western range limit. Freire Filho et al. (2018) established a set of enclaves in Auiá locality as the eastern limit of the species’ range, Coreaú city in Ceará state.  Guedes et al. (2000) recorded two further localities in the Serra da Ibiapaba in the municipality of Ibiapina. Ferreira et al. (2007, in prep.) found the species to occur further south than was previously recognized, extending at least to the Parnaíba River, near the municipality of Floriano, Piauí. Piauí is also the state with highest population densities. Another isolated A. ululata population occurs in the Acopiara region, Ceará, very distant from any other populations (Ferreira et al., in prep.).
useTrade: Aloutta ululata is used as food by humans.

rationale: The species is listed as Least Concern although deforestation occurs throughout many parts of its range, particularly in Brazil. The population is not believed to decline fast enough to qualify for a higher threat category. However, agricultural development to produce soy beans and other products represents a growing threat to this species.
habitat: Night monkeys typically occur in primary and secondary forest (including disturbed forest and selectively logged forest), seasonally flooded and terra firma lowland forest, and sub-montane and montane (cloud forests) in Colombia and the Andes up to 3,200 m above sea level (montane forms of night monkeys are Aotus lemurinus and Aotus miconax) (Hernández Camacho and Cooper 1976, Aquino and Encarnación 1994, Defler 2004). In the Chaco, Aotus a. azarae occurs in dry, semi deciduous forest patches and gallery forest, where annual rainfall can be as low as 500 m a year (Wright 1985; Stallings et al. 1989; Brooks 1996; Fernández-Duque et al. 2002). Aotus a. boliviensis is found in semi-deciduous and evergreen lowland forests in Bolivia and up to at least 1,250 m above sea level in some parts of the Andes. Aotus a. infulatus inhabits lowland evergreen forests in southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, but forest patches and gallery forest in the Cerrado (bush savanna) of the Pantanal in Mato Grosso. Aquino and Encarnación (1994) reviewed the habitat and forest preferences of the genus. Night monkeys are nocturnal, being most active at dawn and dusk. The only exception is Aotus azarae azarae of the Chaco in southern Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina, which is cathemeral (irregularly active at any time of night or day). They are frugivorous, but their diet includes also nectar, flowers (seasonally important for A. a. azarae in the Chaco), and small animal prey such as insects (Wright 1989; Fernández-Duque 2007). Aotus azarae has been observed to include a significant portion of leaves in its diet (Ganzhorn and Wright 1994; Wright 1985; Arditi and Placci 1990; Giménez and Fernández-Duque 2003). They are socially monogamous and form family groups of 2 to 5 individuals, comprising of an adult pair and 1 to 4 offspring of different age (infant, juveniles and sometimes a subadult). However, a significant number of adults are solitary. These may be subadults that left their natal groups or older adults which were evicted from their groups by competitors (Fernández-Duque and Huntington 2002; Fernández-Duque 2004). Normally, the male cares for the infants, but the females occasionally provide alimentation and care for the litter during the first week after the birth (Wright 1984; Dixson 1994). In the wild, male A. azarae reach adult weight when about 4 years old, and age at first reproduction is about 5 years (Juárez et al. 2003; Fernández-Duque 2004). Single offspring are the rule and the birth interval is 8 to 10 months (Wright 1985). Night monkeys are territorial—groups occupy overlapping territories of 5-18 ha (depending on species and location) (Wright 1978; Fernández-Duque 2007). Wright (1989) points out that home ranges of Aotus azarae azarae could be bigger than those of A. azarae boliviensis. For instance, Wright (1989) gives 5 ha for Paraguay, but Schwindt et al. (2004) and (Arditi 1992) reported 4 to 10 ha in Argentina and 12 ha at Guaycolec, Formosa Province in Argentina, respectively. The intrinsic morphological similarities among species of the genus Aotus and the slight variation in their phenotypes make the identification of various subspecies difficult. However, differences in body coloration, geographic distribution and phylogenetic analysis need to be considered to finally establish the taxon’s’ taxonomic status and to obtain more information on its ecology and conservation status.
threats: Threats to this species in the Brazilian Cerrado, in the Bolivian Chaco-Chiquitano forest, and the Paraguayan Chaco include habitat loss due to agricultural development for soy beans and cattle ranching. In Argentina it also includes small-scale farming and cattle ranching, and in Bolivia urban development around Santa Cruz de la Sierra. Minimal subsistence hunting occurs in Bolivia, for consumption and as bait for fishing. In Brazil, the main threats identified for the taxon were fire, agriculture, livestock keeping, urban expansion, deforestation, habitat disconnection, habitat reduction and mineral extraction. These are general threats for the taxon across its geographic range and there is no specific information available about the intensity of these threats affecting single populations (Rímoli and Rylands 2015).
population: Population density estimates for this species vary across different studies. Estimates are mainly available from Argentina, Paraguay and Bolivia. Across its range, the species is relatively common, but due to its nocturnal and crepuscular behavior it is usually ignored in primate abundance surveys. Only a few reliable estimates of population density are available for any of the subspecies. Aquino and Encarnación (1994) reviewed population structure and densities for the genus. In the eastern Formosa Province (Guaycolec) in Argentina, densities in gallery forests can be as high as 60 individuals/km² (Fernández-Duque et al. 2001). Elsewhere in the Formosa Province, relatively lower densities were established: 32.3 individuals/km² (Zunino et al. 1986), 25.0 individuals/km² (Arditi and Placci 1990), 64.0 individuals/km² in gallery forests (Fernández-Duque et al. 2001), 12.8-29 individuals/km² (Fernández-Duque et al. 2007), 15.0 individuals/km² (Brown and Zunino 1994), and 29.0 individuals/km² (Rathbun and Gache 1980). In Teniente Enciso in Paraguay, Stallings et al. (1989) estimated population density as 8.9 individuals/km², while for Agua Dulce, Stallings et al. (1989) reported 14.4 individuals/km². In Bolivia, Ayala (2011) reported 15.3-26.6 individuals/km² along the Rio Parapeti in the Bañados de Izozog depression (Ayala 2011). From the Bosque Chimanes, in Beni, 13-18 individuals/km² were reported (Rumiz and Herrera 2000) and Wallace et al. (2000) estimated popualtion density to range from 0.8-7.4 individuals/10 km² in the Reserva de Vida Silvestre Ríos Blanco y Negro.
range: The taxon is not endemic to Brazil, but occurs in Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008). In Brazil it is present in the Pantanal of the states of states of Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, where it is resident and native (Cáceres et al. 2008; Fernández-Duque et al. 2008; Melo and Damasceno Jr. 1998; Melo and Amorim 2003; Melo and Antunes 2004; Melo et al. 2004; Melo and Martins Vincensi 2004; Tomas and Mourão 2007; Tomas et al. 2010, 2011). In Paraguay, Azara’s night monkeys are found in the dry southern and western parts of the Chaco (excluding the extreme West where no Primates occur) and west of the Paraguay River (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008). Its presence extends further to the South-west of the Rio Paraguay and across the Rio Pilcomayo in Bolivia and Argentina, and to the South of the Rio Bermejo and Rio Negro in the Argentinian provinces of Formosa and Chaco (Rathbun and Gache 1980, Hershkovitz 1983, Stallings 1985, 1989; Zunino et al. 1986; Stallings et al. 1989). In the West, its distribution extends along the Cordillera Oriental, but the limit to the North is not clearly defined (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008). According to Hershkovitz (1983), the species can occur in Bolivia’s Bañados de Izozog. Presumably, the current distribution is reduced relative to its historical extent. It is suspected that Azara’s night monkeys also occurred in southwestern Mato Grosso, in northwestern Mato Grosso do Sul (Corumbá and Ladário Municipalities) and along the border between Brazil and Bolivia (Tomas & Mourão 2007, Tomas et al. 2010, 2011 ).
useTrade: Common in local pet trade
conservationActions: This species is listed in the appendix II of CITES. Further study on the species would provide more detailed information about threats and conservation actions for future assessments. Actions for conservation are restricted to regions in which the subspecies occurs, for instance, in protected areas such as national parks, indigenous territories, conservation units and reserves, including: Brazil: Municipal Natural Park of Piraputangas (1,300 ha), Corumbá, Mato Grosso do Sul, single record (Rímoli unpubl. data) Argentina: Plicomayo National Park (51,889 ha) (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008) Bolivia: Kaa-Iya Gran Chaco National Park (3, 441,100 ha) (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008) Otuquis National Park (102,600 ha) (in range) San Matías Natural Area of Integrated Management (2,918,500 ha) (in range) Beni Biological Station (135,000 ha) (Garcia and Tarifa 1988) Paraguay: Tinfunque National Park (280,000 ha) (Fernández-Duque et al. 2008) Defensores del Chaco National Park (780,000 ha) (Stallings 1985, 1989)Further studies on this species should be carried out in order to provide more accurate future assessments.

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable based on the rate of loss of habitat across its range, causing a suspected population decline at a rate greater than 30% over the past three generations (24 years). As forest loss continues this species should be closely monitored.

Aquino and Encarnación (1994b) reviewed the habitat and forest preferences of the genus.Night monkeys are nocturnal; they are most active at dawn and dusk. They are frugivorous and their diet includes fruits, nectar and flowers, leaves, and small animals prey such as insects (Wright 1989, Fernandez-Duque 2007). Aotus azarae and Aotus zonalis has been observed to include a significant portion of leaves in their diet (Hladik and Hladik 1969, Ganzhorn and Wright 1994, Giménez and Fernandez-Duque 2003). Preliminary studies on the diet of grey'-legged night monkeys in Remedios, Antioquia, included at least 40 different fruit species (Link et al. unpubl.data).They are socially monogamous, living in small groups of an adult pair and offspring of different ages (infant, one or two juveniles and sometimes a subadult. In A. a. azarae a significant number of adults range alone and both sexes disperse. Solitary adults were observed by Villavicencio Galindo (2003) in the northern Colombia. Night monkeys are territorial and groups occupy overlapping territories of 5-18 ha (depending on species and location) (Wright 1978; Fernandez-Duque 2007). Males cares for the infants (carry them; Rotundo et al. 2005). Wright (1994) and Fernandez-Duque (2007) reviewed the behaviour and ecology of the genus.Captive male A. lemurinus reach sexual maturity when 2 years old, and captive female A. vociferans and A. nancymaae first breed when 3-4 years old (Dixson 1983, Fernandez-Duque 2007). In the wild, male A. azarae reach adult weight only when about 4 years old, and age at first reproduction is about 5 years of age (Juárez et al. 2003, Fernandez-Duque 2004). A female A. azarae was found to breed for the first time at 58 months of age (Fernandez-Duque et al. 2002). Single offspring are the rule. Wright (1985) recorded births between August and February for A. nigriceps in Peru (Manu National Park), and Aquino et al. (1990) indicated a birth season between December and March) for A. nancymaae in north-eastern Peru. In the Argentinean Chaco, A. azarae shows a peak of births between March and June (Fernandez-Duque 2007).Size:Adult male weight average 1.0±0.2 kg (n=20), adult female weight 0.923±0.063 kg (n=16) (Dixson 1983).Adult male weight average N.A., adult female weight 900±70 g (n=2) (Link unpubl. data).
threats: Aotus griseimembra remains threatened in Colombia and Venezuela, partly because of habitat loss due to large-scale cattle ranching, agro-industries (e.g., oil palm) and mining. Most of the natural habitat within the species’ historical distribution were transformed and less than 20% of its habitat remains in the lowland forests and wetlands of the Magdalena River basin (Link et al. 2013). An even smaller proportion of natural habitat is left in northern Colombia (Miller et al. 2004) and northwestern Venezuela (Portillo-Quintero and Urbani in press). The pet trade and subsistence hunting pose additional threats to wild populations.
population: Aquino and Encarnación (1994) reviewed population structure and densities for the genus. There are no studies on the population status of Aotus griseimembra in Colombia or Venezuela, but Portillo-Quintero and Urbani (in press) reported that at least 30% of the species’ natural habitat was lost over the course of the last three generations (approximately 24 years) and that they occur in low densities in the Socuy and Guasare River basins. In Colombia, they are still locally common in lowland inter-Andean forests since they can survive temporarily in small forest fragments. However, the rapid destruction of their habitat and the loss of connectivity between populations certainly drive a severe population decline. Grey-legged Night Monkeys are usually found in groups of 2-5 individuals, including a reproductive pair and their offspring (Link and De Luna unpublished data).
range: The geographic distribution of Aotus griseimembra includes the lowland forests on both banks of the Magdalena River and the valleys of the Cauca and São Jorge Rivers in northern Colombia (Hernandez-Camacho and Cooper 1976; Defler 2003, 2004). It extends north to the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, partly including the Guajira Peninsula and eastwards across the Sierra de Perija to Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela (Hernandez-Camacho and Cooper 1976; Bodini and Pérez-Hernández 1987; Linares 1998; Defler 2003, 2004). In Venezuela grey-legged night monkeys are restricted to the north-western areas of the country, specifically in the south-west of the Lago de Maracaibo Basin in evergreen forest and in the seasonally flooded forest of the piedmont of the Eastern Andes (Portillo-Quintero and Urbani in press). There is only scant information on the altitudinal distribution of Aotus griseimembra and its distribution limits with Aotus lemurinus.
useTrade: Aotus griseimembra is used both as food by humans and for pet trade.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its wide range, suspected large populations, and because there are no major threats believed to be resulting in a significant population decline at present. However, given ongoing development projects, the species does require close population monitoring, particularly in its western distribution.
habitat: Aotus nigriceps occurs in lowland tierra firme and seasonally flooded tropical forest. It’s is not restricted to primary forest habitats, being adaptable to modified/disturbed and fragmented habitat. Aotus are socially monogamous, living in small groups of an adult pair and offspring of different ages (infant, one or two juveniles and sometimes a sub-adult. Both sexes disperse. Males carry and care for the infants (Rotundo et al. 2002, 2005). Lone adults were observed by Villavicencio Galindo (2003) in northern Colombia and in Peru by Shanee et al. (2014). Night monkeys are territorial—groups occupy overlapping territories of 1.3-18 ha (depending on the species and location) (Wright 1978; Fernandez-Duque 2011; Shanee et al. 2014). In Cocha Cashu, Manu National Park, Peru, Wright (1989) recorded home range size for A. nigriceps of 7 to 14 ha. Wright (1994) and Fernandez-Duque (2011) review the behaviour and ecology of the genus. Diets of night monkeys are variable, A. nigriceps have been observed to consume insects (15% of dietary intake) fruits (75%), leaves and flowers (10%) (Wright 1985, 1994). Arboreal food sources include Moraceze (Ficus spp.). Inga marginata, Annonaceae, Bombacaceaea, Sapindaceae (Wright 1985; Arditi 1992).Night monkeys reach sexual maturity at 3.3-5 years of age (Fernandez-Duque 2011) and can live for 20 years (Ross 1991; Aquino & Encarnacion 1994). Single offspring are the rule with a 4.5 month gestation period (Wright 1981) and 1 year inter-birth interval (Fernandez-Duque et al. 2008). Wright (1985) recorded births between August and February for A. nigriceps in Peru (Manu National Park), and Aquino et al. (1990) indicated a birth season between December and March for A. nancymaae in north-eastern Peru. Size:Adult male weight 0.875 kg (n=1), adult female weight 1.04 kg (n=2) (Smith & Jungers 1997; Peres 1993a).
threats: A wide ranging species of the upper Amazon, there are currently no major threats believed to be resulting in a significant population decline. However, in Brazil populations have been depleted over large areas in the states of Acre and Rondônoia, and with infrastructure development along major development corridors (Porto Velho - Cuiabá and Porto Velho - Manaus and the Rio Madeira itself), it is likely that large tracts of forest will be lost in the future. Similarly in much of northern and central Peru widespread deforestation from immigration and infrastructure development is reducing the possible area of occupancy for this species. Aotus nigriceps is also commonly found in local wildlife markets in the Peruvian Amazon.
population: Wright (1981, 1985) estimated a density of 36-40 individuals/km² at Cocha Cashu, Manu National Park. 2.45 groups/km² (8.8 ind./km²), rio Urucú, Tefé, Amazonas (Peres 1993); 5.49 groups/km² (24.73 ind./km²), São Domingos, Sena Madureira, Acre (Peres 1988); 11.1 groups/km² (31.1 ind./km²), rio Urubamba-rio Tambo, Peru (Aquino et al. 2013). Aquino and Encarnación (1994b) reviewed population structure and densities for the genus. At REBIO Guapore (Rondonia), A. nigriceps the average group size is 2.7 ± 0.6 ind./group (min-max=2-3) (Alves 2013), similar to observed in the lower region of rio Urumbamba, close to the border of Acre (2.8 ind/group) (Aquino et al 2013). In Peru, Wright (1989) reported group sizes of 2-5 ind. The current estimated population size for this species in Brazil is greater than 10,000 mature individuals.
range: Aotus nigriceps occurs throughout a large part of the central and upper Amazon, south of the mainstream and along the right bank of the Rio Jutaí in the west. In the east, it extends to the rios Tapajós and Juruena in the south west of Para and north west of Mato Grosso in Brazil (Aotus azarae infulatus occurs to the east of the rios Tapajós and Juruena). It also occurs throughout the state of Rondônia, restricted to east of the Rio Guaporé. In Bolivia, it occurs north of the Río Madre de Dios in the Department of Pando (Hershkovitz 1983; Brown and Rumiz 1986; Anderson 1997), extending to the south-eastern and central Peruvian Amazon, west through the Río Ucayali basin to the Andean foothills west of the Rio Huallaga in San Martin (Shanee et al. 2013; 2015) where it meets the distribution of Aotus miconax (Aquino and Encarnacion 1994a; Shanee et al. 2013; 2015). The current extent of occurrence for this species in Brazil is estimated at 1,100,650.77 km².
useTrade: Night monkey species, including A. nigriceps, are fairly common in the local pet trade in Amazonian regions of Peru and Brazil.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its wide range, presumed large populations, and because there are no major threats believed to be resulting in a significant population decline at present.
habitat: Night monkeys typically occur in primary and secondary forest (including disturbed forest and selectively logged forest), seasonally flooded and terra firma, lowland forest, submontane forest (Hernández-Camacho and Cooper 1976; Defler 2003, 2004). Aquino and Encarnación (1994b) reviewed the habitat and forest preferences of the genus.Night monkeys are nocturnal: they are most active at dawn and dusk. The only exception is Aotus azarae azarae of the Chaco of southern Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina, which is cathemeral (active during night and day). They are frugivorous; their diet includes fruit, nectar and flower (seasonally important for the A. a. azarae in the Chaco), leaves, and small animals prey such as insects (Wright 1989; Fernandez-Duque 2007).They are socially monogamous, living in small groups of an adult pair and offspring of different ages (infant, one or two juveniles and sometimes a subadult. In A. a. azarae a significant number of adults range alone. They may be subadults that have left their natal groups or older adults which have been evicted from their groups by competitors (Fernandez-Duque and Huntington 2002; Fernandez-Duque 2004). Both sexes disperse. Males care for the infants (carry them) (Rotundo et al. 2002, 2005). Lone adults were observed by Villavicencio Galindo (2003) in northern Colombia. Night monkeys are territorial—groups occupy overlapping territories of 5-18 ha (depending on the species and location) (Wright 1978, 1981; Fernandez-Duque 2007). Wright (1994) and Fernandez-Duque (2007) review the behaviour and ecology of the genus.Captive male A. lemurinus reach sexual maturity when 2 years old, and captive female A. vociferans and A. nancymaae first breed when 3-4 years old (Dixson 1983; Fernandez-Duque 2007). In the wild, male A. azarae reach adult weight only when about 4 years old, and age at first reproduction is about 5 years of age (Juárez et al. 2003; Fernandez-Duque 2004). Single offspring are the rule. Wright (1985) recorded births between August and February for A. nigriceps in Peru (Manu National Park), and Aquino et al. (1990) indicated a birth season between December and March for A. nancymaae in north-eastern Peru.Size:Adult male weight average 1.2 kg (n=1), adult female weight 1.0 kg (n=1) (Fernandes 1993).
threats: This is a wide-ranging species, and there is no evidence of any particular threat other than habitat loss.
population: In Bolivar, Colombia, Green (1978) estimated a density of 0.5 groups/km² or 1.5 individuals/km². Aquino and Encarnación (1994b) reviewed population structure and densities for the genus.
range: Based on a specimen collected at Maipures, near the mouth of the Río Tomo on the Río Orinoco, Defler and Bueno (2007) indicated that the night monkeys of eastern central Colombia north of the Río Guaviare are probably A. brumbacki.Hershkovitz (1983) proposed that A. trivirgatus was the form in Colombia between the Rios Vaupés and Inirida, but Defler (2003, 2004) indicated that A. vociferans occurred in this region and that A. trivirgatus as such is restricted to the east of the Ríos Negro, lower Guainia, and Atabapo and, below the mouth the Río Atabapo, the Río Orinoco. To the north, in Venezuela, A. trivirgatus occurs south of the Río Orinoco and east as far the middle Rio Caroni. The extension east beyond the Río Caura is based on just one locality on the upper Caroni (Bodini and Pérez-Hernandez 1987, Linares 1998). A. trivrigatus is confined to north (left bank) of the Rio Negro to its mouth, extending east, north of the Rio Amazonas, as far as the Rio Trombetas. North it reaches the Serra da Pacaraima, but does not it seem extend into Guyana. In the state of Roraima, the Rio Mucajaí is indicated by Hershkovitz (1983) as marking its northern limits.
