However, there have been no published studies looking at changes in Mainland Clouded Leopard density or abundance over time from anywhere in the species’ range (which includes a number of high-profile Tiger Reserves and Tiger Protected Areas).Estimating the global population of Mainland Clouded Leopard is difficult with little consistent range-wide data however it is highly likely that there are fewer than 10,000 mature individuals. Published density estimates for the species, from protected areas in the Indian Subcontinent, northern Myanmar, Malaysia, and Thailand, vary between 0.3 and 5.14 mature individuals per 100 km² (Borah et al. 2014, Petersen et al. 2020b). There are no published density estimates from Cambodia, China, Lao PDR, or Viet Nam. However, in many sites in which the species has been detected (often as by-catch from camera-trap efforts focusing on tigers) there are insufficient detections to estimate density suggesting densities may be lower than those reported in the literature. The range-wide models of MacDonald et al.(2019) estimated approximately 558,000 km2 of high-quality Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat across the species’ range (Macdonald et al. 2019) which was revised to ~370,000 km² using more recent forest cover data (Petersen et al.2020a). An average density between ~1.8 and 2.7 individuals per 100 km² across all high-quality habitat (dependent on the year of forest cover estimation) would be required for a global population of >10,000 mature individuals. Given likely absence due to hunting (See Geographic Range / Population / Threats) in some of these areas, and the low camera-trap detection rates in many other places, this range-wide density estimate seems too high. As such this assessment believes that the likely Mainland Clouded Leopard population is <10,000 mature individuals. However, estimated, as opposed to inferred, rates of population decline are required to trigger Vulnerable under criterion C1. Long-term monitoring of Mainland Clouded Leopard abundance within sites are recommended in order to more accurately observe or estimate rates of population change and this, potentially, trigger criterion C1 in future assessments.
habitat: The Mainland Clouded Leopard is intermediate in size between large and small cats, with wild females from Thailand weighing 11.5 (Austin and Tewes 1999) to 13.5 kg (Grassman et al. 2005), and males 16 (Grassman et al. 2005) to 18 kg (Austin and Tewes 1999). Its coat is patterned with distinctive large cloud shaped markings, its canines are exceptionally elongated, as is its tail - for a large cat (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002). The Mainland Clouded Leopard is highly arboreal and strongly associated with forest habitat, particularly primary evergreen tropical rainforest, but there are also records from dry and deciduous forest, as well as secondary and logged forests. They have been recorded in the Himalayas at elevations above 3,500 m (Can et al. 2020, Y. Ghimrey in litt., 2020).Less frequently, they have been found in grassland and scrub, dry tropical forests and mangrove swamps (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Radio-tracking studies in Thailand have shown a preference for forest over more open habitats (Austin et al. 2007, Grassman et al. 2005). There is some evidence from Peninsular Malaysia for the ability of animals to persist amidst an agricultural matrix of certain land uses, including rubber (Mukri et al. unpub.; A. Giordinao in litt., 2020).A study in Thailand's Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary found that Mainland Clouded Leopards preyed upon a variety of arboreal and terrestrial prey, including hog deer, slow loris, brush-tailed porcupine, Malayan pangolin and Indochinese ground squirrel (Grassman et al. 2005). Other observations include mainly primate prey, but also muntjac and Argus pheasant (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Mainland Clouded Leopards are primarily nocturnal, with crepuscular activity peaks (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007).Two radio-telemetry studies in different parks in Thailand found that adult male and female Mainland Clouded Leopards had similar home range sizes between 30-40 km² (95% fixed kernel estimators), with smaller intensively used core areas of 3-5 km² (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007). While both studies found substantial home range overlap between males and females, as is typical of most felids, Grassman et al. (2005) also found that the ranges of their two radio-collared males overlapped by a significant amount (39%). Although both studies found similar home ranges, Mainland Clouded Leopards in Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary travelled approximately twice the average daily distance (average 2 km) than Mainland Clouded Leopards in Khao Yai National Park (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007).Mainland Clouded Leopards may occur at higher densities when densities of the larger cats, tigers and leopards, are lower (Lynam et al. 2001, Grassman et al. 2005, Petersen et al. 2020b).
threats: Mainland Clouded Leopards prefer closed forest (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007), and their habitat in Southeast Asia is undergoing amongst the world's fastest deforestation rates (0.6% per year between 1990 and 2010; Stibig et al. 2014). A recent modelling paper estimated a range-wide decline in the area of habitat categorised as strongholds for Mainland Clouded Leopard (defined as large contiguous areas of high-quality habitat where the species could survive over the mid-to-long term) of 34% between 2000 and 2018 (Petersen et al. 2020a). In addition to direct habitat loss the degradation of habitat and loss of functional connectivity is likely impacting many Mainland Clouded Leopard populations and, with future infrastructure development, particularly in Myanmar, this is likely to become a significant issue (Kaszta et al. 2020). A boom in large number of hydropower projects and rural roads in Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat is also a potentially significant threat in Nepal (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018).Nevertheless, the biggest drive of population decline in Mainland Clouded Leopard during the assessment period was likely mortality due to illegal hunting – both targeted hunting for trade and incidental capture in indiscriminate hunting snares. The low number of detections or absence of the species from areas of suitable habitat particularly within Myanmar and Indochina indicates the scale of this threat. For example, in Cambodia the most recent records of the species from two apparently suitable sites (Western Seam Pang and Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuaries) were of individuals captured in ungulate hunting snares. The rapid spread of snaring across Lao PDR and Cambodia, during the assessment period (and in Viet Nam largely prior to the current assessment) is likely the biggest cause of population decline during this period.The Mainland Clouded Leopard is also hunted for the illegal wildlife trade. Large numbers of skins have been seen in market surveys, and there is also trade in bones for medicines to supplement the tiger bone trade, meat for exotic dishes and live animals for the pet trade (Hunter 2011). Wild animals are likely to be the primary source, but there is also some illegal trade from captive animals (Nowell 2007). For more details of trade driven threats see Use and Trade above.Additional possible threats to Mainland Clouded Leopard which may require further research and analysis include prey depletion. This is potentially a threat in Indochina and China but seems likely to be a less significant issue elsewhere in the range. Can et al. (2020) also highlighted the potential impact of climate change on Mainland Clouded Leopard particularly on higher elevation populations in central Nepal.
population: The continued expansion of camera-trapping (including a number of studies targeted on Mainland Clouded Leopard) across the species’ range means that we have a better understanding of Mainland Clouded Leopard population and densities than in the previous assessment in 2016. At least six studies have published density estimates for Mainland Clouded Leopards with estimates varying between 0.3 individuals per 100 km² (across large areas of Southern Bhutan: Penjor et al.2018) to 5.14 individuals per 100 km² Dampa Tiger Reserve, India (Singh and MacDonald 2017). However, in the majority of locations across the species’ range there are too few camera-trap detections to estimate density and in other, apparently suitable sites (see Geographic Range) there have been no recent records. Camera-trap detection rates and naïve /modelled camera-trap occupancy vary extensively across the species’ range. This variation is likely linked to both sampling design and ecological conditions (e.g. lower intrinsic carrying capacity for Mainland Clouded Leopard in high elevation areas in the northern and western extremes of the range; Can et al. 2020) and anthropogenic pressures particularly poaching. In their range-wide camera-trap analysis MacDonald et al. (2019) reported naïve occupancy (from the 39 of 45 studies which detected the species) of between 0.02 and 0.44.In Peninsular Malaysia, documented declines in tiger abundance during the assessment period (WWF Tigers Alive Initiative, in litt. 2020) and evidence of targeted poaching of large cats, particularly using cable snares, suggests Mainland Clouded Leopard populations will have declined in the past 21 years. On at least two recent occasions (in 2017 and 2018) organized Vietnamese poaching gangs in Malaysia have been apprehended with body parts of at least two Mainland Clouded Leopards, as well as tiger, bear and wild boar body parts (TRAFFIC 2019). Forested landscapes supporting Mainland Clouded Leopard in Malaysia receive less targeted protection than in some other range countries (e.g. Thailand, Nepal, India) and all occupied habitat is under, at least some, poaching pressure. In Manas Tiger Reserve in India the encounter rate of Mainland Clouded Leopard from camera-trapping has declined in recent years (J. Borah, in litt. 2020) though the extent to which this is due to behavioural changes following tiger recovery is unclear. In Thailand there are recent records from at least 14 protected areas in seven forest complexes (Petersen et al. 2020a) but evidence that densities are lower in more accessible and heavily hunted areas (Petersen et al. 2020b).Camera-trap density estimates of Mainland Clouded Leopard exclude cubs (e.g. Petersen et al.2020b) thus we assume that published density estimates refer to mature individuals. Extrapolating published densities across the 558,000 km² of ‘good quality’ Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat modelled by MacDonald et al. (2019) would give a global population of between 1,600 and 29,000 adult individuals. Though a number of the areas identified as high-quality habitat in this paper (e.g. in parts of Viet Nam and Lao PDR) are unlikely to support the species due to hunting and habitat loss (Petersen et al.2020a). Nevertheless, the global Mainland Clouded Leopard population is probably incorporated within these bounds (e.g. 1,600–29,000) but is likely much more towards the lower end (see also Assessment Rationale) with range-wide average densities of ~1.0 individual per 100 km² more realistic. This would give a population of between ~5,580 (based on MacDonald et al. 2019 available habitat) and ~3,700 (based on Petersen et al. 2020a available habitat) mature individuals. Given continued habitat loss, fragmentation, and hunting across the range the population is inferred to be continuing to decline. Long-term monitoring of Mainland Clouded Leopard abundance within sites are recommended in order to more accurately observe or estimate rates of population change and this, potentially, trigger criterion C1 (i.e. <10,000 mature individuals and observed, estimated, or projected decline of >10% in three generations) in future assessments.
range: The Mainland Clouded Leopard is found from the Himalayan foothills in Nepal through Mainland Southeast Asia into China (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Mainland Clouded Leopard is extinct on the island of Taiwan (Chiang et al. 2015) and numbers are very low, and the species may be close to extirpation, in Viet Nam (Wilcox et al. 2014), China, and Bangladesh.BhutanWith a forest cover of 60%, the vast majority of the available habitat in Bhutan is suitable for the Mainland Clouded Leopard. However, due to the rapid increase in latitudinal elevation, Mainland Clouded Leopards have a much higher probability of occurring in the southern forested areas both inside and outside of protected areas than the northern forested areas (Penjor et al. 2018). Using an occupancy sampling framework, Mainland Clouded Leopard data gathered from the national tiger survey showed that the species was predicted to occur across the majority of the National Parks and connecting wildlife corridors including the Wangchuck Centennial National Park, Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary, Jigme Dorji National Park, Bundling Wildlife Sanctuary, but with the highest probability in the southern protected areas of Royal Manas National Park (Tempa et al. 2013), Phipsoo Wildlife Sanctuary, Phrumsengla National Park, Jomotshankha Wildlife Sanctuary, Jigme Khesar Strict Nature Reserve, and Jigme Singye Wangchuck National Park (Lungten et al. unpub. data). NepalMainland Clouded Leopard were believed to be extinct in Nepal until 1987, when two cubs were captured alive by local communities in southeast Nepal (Dinerstein and Metha 1989) with the first camera-trap record, from Shivapuri Nagarjuna National Park in 2010 (Ghimirey and Acharya 2016). The expansion of camera-trapping studies across the country has subsequently demonstrated that Mainland Clouded Leopard occurs relatively extensively in eastern Nepal from the Terai in the south (e.g. Chitwan and Parsa National Park) up to the Nepal-Tibet (China) border in the north (e.g. Langtang NP) and as far west as Annapurna Conservation Area. Confirmed records for the species have been made from the protected areas of Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, Manaslu Conservation Area, Annapurna Conservation Area, Langtang National Park, Shivapuri Nagarjuna National Park, Chitwan National Park and Parsa National Park and from the districts of Khotang. Records west of Annapurna (e.g. Kailali district Ghodaghodi Lake, Api-Nampa Conservation Area) have been questioned. Annapurna remains the westerly extent of the species’ known global distribution (Ghimrey and Acharya 2016). However, recent seizure of a pelt that supposedly originated in Pyuthan district provides a possibility of pushing the westernmost limit further west by around 100 km (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018). In addition, an interview with a Nepalese park ranger produced a credible firsthand observation of a Mainland Clouded Leopard in Khaptad National Park (A. Bashyal and A. J. Giordano unpub. data). In Langtang National Park Mainland Clouded Leopards have been detected from altitudes as high as 3,498 m (Can et al. 2020).IndiaMainland Clouded Leopard occurs widely in northeastern India as far west as Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar (Shafi et al. 2019) with recent records from protected areas in at least Sikkim (Bashir et al. 2011), West Bengal (Jhala et al. 2020), Assam (Borah et al. 2014), Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, and Mizoram (Mukherjee et al. 2019). Mukherjee et al. (2019) reported on camera-trap studies from 10 sites across five northeast Indian states with Mainland Clouded Leopard present from six sites. The extensive camera-trapping and surveys for the 2018 All India Tiger Census recorded Mainland Clouded Leopard from Kaziranga, Nameri and Manas Tiger Reserves, Assam; Pakke, Kamlang and Namdapha Tiger Reserves, Arunachal Pradesh, Buxa Tiger Reserve, West Bengal, and Dampa Tiger Reserve, Mizoram (Jhala et al. 2020). Published Mainland Clouded Leopard density estimates from Manas National Park (Borah et al.2014) and Dampa Tiger Reserve (Singh and MacDonald 2017) of 4.7 and 5.1 individuals per 100 km2 are amongst the highest recorded across the species’ range.BangladeshMainland Clouded Leopard likely persists in very small numbers in suitable mountainous habitat in part of the Chittagong Hill Tracts of southeast Bangladesh with at least one camera-trap photograph from Sangu-Matamuhuri Reserve Forest collected by parabiologists between 2011 and 2015 (Creative Conservation Alliance 2016).MyanmarThe vast majority of Myanmar is ecologically suitable for, and within the historic range of, Mainland Clouded Leopard. However, as a result of hunting and habitat loss, the species is now likely very thinly but widely distributed across the dense evergreen forests particularly of northern (e.g. Kachin / Sagain) and southern Myanmar (e.g. Kayin, Taninthayi; Zaw et al. 2014, Greenspan et al. 2020). Zaw et al. (2019) reported widespread occurrence in Kachin (Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary, Hkakaborazi National Park Imaw Bum, Bumphar Bum Area, Hphonkanrazi Wildlife Sanctuary, Myit Sone Area) and Sagaing States (Htamanthi Wildlife Sanctuary, Alaungdaw Kathapa National Park Proposed Mahamying Wildlife Sanctuary, Mt. Saramati Area) in the north of the country with an apparently more reduced distribution in Rakhine (Rakhine Yoma), Bago (Bago Yoma) and Shan States (Paunglaung Area). Recent camera-trapping coordinated by the Kawthoolei Forestry Department (KFD) has recorded Mainland Clouded Leopard from a number of protected areas in Kayin State, including Kweekoh Wildlife Sanctuary, Kadoh Mae Nyaw Wildlife Sanctuary, Yoe Mu Kyo (proposed Wildlife Sanctuary), Megatha Wildlife Sanctuary, Maw Kee (proposed Wildlife Sanctuary), and various unprotected forested areas, including the newly formed Salween Peace Park (Moo et al. 2018; KFD unpub. data). However, the species has not been detected in some apparently suitable areas, such as Tu Ter Lor Wildlife Sanctuary and Klermu Thoepli Wildlife Sanctuary, and the number of individuals detected in any area was low (Moo et al. 2018, KFD unpublished data) with a patchy distribution throughout the region (Greenspan et al. 2020). Mainland Clouded Leopard appears widespread in Tanintharyi with recent records from most camera-trapping studies across the landscape, such as Tanintharyi Nature Reserve, Kaser Doh Conservation Landscape, Ler Mu Lah, and Lenya Reserve Forests (KFD unpub. data).Lao PDR: Mainland Clouded Leopard were historically distributed throughout Lao PDR but the species has experienced significant declines prior to, and during, the assessment period driven by intensive hunting, most notably snaring. The most significant Mainland Clouded Leopard population remains in Nam Et Phou Louey NPA where the species is the most widely distributed large carnivore, although a decrease in density was detected between 2013 and 2017, suggesting its future in the park is not secured unless snaring is reduced (Rasphone 2018). In the rest of Lao PDR, Mainland Clouded Leopard has become extremely rare and is likely extirpated from many apparently suitable areas of forested habitat. For example, extensive camera-trap surveys within Nakai Nam Theun National Park since 2018 has not detected the species (which had been present in low numbers between 2007-2011, Coudrat et al. 2014; Coudrat, in litt. 2020). Mainland Clouded Leopard remains present in some Karst limestone protected areas, such as Phou Hin Poun NPA, where there has been less pressure from hunting (Brakels and Somdachit, 2020). West of the Mekong there are a couple of recent camera-trap records from Nam Poui NPA (2016/17; F. Guegan, in litt. 2020). There are no recent records from southern Lao PDR (e.g. Xe Sap NPA or Xe Pian NPA) and if Mainland Clouded Leopard persist in southern Lao PDR they likely do so in extremely low numbers.ChinaThe Mainland Clouded Leopard historically had a wide distribution in China, south of the Yangtze, but recent records are few, habitat is fast disappearing, illegal hunting of this species has been prolific and its current distribution in China is poorly known and appears largely restricted to areas in Yunan Province along the border with Lao PDR and Myanmar (Wozencraft et al. 2008, B.P.L. Chan, in litt. 2020). In a review of recent felid camera-trapping across 28 protected areas and 10 provinces / autonomous regions across China (939 camera-trap stations and 283,239 trap-nights) between 2007 and 2019 Mainland Clouded Leopard were detected in three sites: Medog County, Tibet Autonomous Region and two of four protected areas (Yiwu and Tongbiguan) in Yunnan Province (Liu et al. 2020). In a review of recent range-wide records Petersen et al. (2020a) found published records of Mainland Clouded Leopard from only one (Medog County) of 25 camera-trapping studies in the species’ predicted range. More recent camera-trapping from the Chinese Felid Conservation Alliance appear to have detected Mainland Clouded Leopard from a number of additional sites in Yunnan province, thus a more thorough assessment of the status of the species in China is required (A. Giordano in litt. 2020). ThailandMainland Clouded Leopards appear to be widely distributed throughout Thailand’s highly fragmented forests based on the results of a recent literature review (Petersen et al. 2020a). As is common elsewhere across the species range, most records in Thailand are derived from tiger survey bycatch data; therefore, generalizations about possible occurrence in unsurveyed areas should be made cautiously. Recent published camera-trap records (2010 onwards) confirm the presence of at least one individual in most major forest complexes (i.e., WEFCOM, Kaeng Krachan FC, Khlong Saeng-Khao Sok FC, Hala Bala FC, Eastern FC, Dong-Phayayen-Khao Yai FC, and Phu Khieo-Nam Nao FC). The species status in less frequently surveyed areas, however, is uncertain. Specifically, there are a lack of recent published records from the relatively unexplored forest complexes in northern (i.e., Lum Nam Pai-Salawin FC, Sri Lanna-Khun Tan FC, Doi Phu Kha-Mae Yom FC, Mae Ping-Om Koi FC, and Phu Meang-Phu Thong FC), northeastern (i.e., Phu Parn FC and Phanom Dongkrak-Pha Tam), and southern Thailand (i.e., Khao Luang FC and Khao Bantad FC).CambodiaMainland Clouded Leopard historically occurred throughout Cambodia’s evergreen and semi-evergreen forests and was likely only absent from the lowlands surrounding the Tonle Sap. However, the species has declined significantly in both distribution and abundance in the past 20 years with post 2014 records from only Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary and Virachey National Park in the northeast, and the Cardamom Rainforest Landscape in the southwest. The latter two sites (Virachey and the Cardamoms) represent the largest and most inaccessible evergreen forest landscapes in the country. Mainland Clouded Leopard have been recently (post-2018) recorded from camera-traps in multiple locations in Virachey National Park (McCann et al. 2020) and at least four protected areas in the Cardamom Rainforest Landscape (Botum Sakor National Park, Central Cardamom National Park, Southern Cardamom National Park, and Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary (Gray et al. 2017). These two landscapes represent the last strongholds for Mainland Clouded Leopard in Cambodia, although in all sites the number of camera-trap records were insufficient to estimate density. Elsewhere in Cambodia Mainland Clouded Leopard have become extremely scarce and may be extirpated. In the Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary complex, Stung Treng Province, a single Mainland Clouded Leopard was photographed by camera-traps in April 2016 and a pregnant female was captured alive in a snare in February 2020 (J. C. Eames in litt. 2020). In the Eastern Plains Landscape, Mondulkiri Province, Mainland Clouded Leopard was last camera-trapped in December 2012 (from Phnom Prich Wildlife Sanctuary), with no documented records from the more extensive evergreen forests of Seima Wildlife Sanctuary since 2006 (when an individual was released alive from a snare) whereas the last camera-trap record was obtained from March 2003 (WWF-Cambodia, in litt. 2020). In the Northern Plains Landscape of Preah Vihear, the species was last detected on camera-traps from Chepp Wildlife Sanctuary in 2014 however one Mainland Clouded Leopard was camera-trapped from Phnom Dongrak, on the border with Thailand, in November 2020 (L. Grassman, in litt., 2020). There are no recent records from Prey Long Wildlife Sanctuary (WCS-Cambodia, in litt. 2020). In the adjacent Phnom Tnaout Wildlife Sanctuary apparent Mainland Clouded Leopard tracks were recorded in 2014 but have not been found subsequently (S. Davis, in litt. 2020).Viet NamMainland Clouded Leopard was historically widespread throughout the evergreen forests of Viet Nam however there are no recent records and the species is likely close to extinction from the country due to industrial levels of snaring and other hunting. The last documented record of Mainland Clouded Leopard from Viet Nam was from Pu Luong (a protected area dominated by karst limestone forests and thus protected, to some extent, from snaring) in December 2003. In their country-wide review of the status of wild cats, Wilcox et al. (2014) documented only two other (earlier) confirmed records of Mainland Clouded Leopard across the country between 1995 and 2013. Whilst there is possibility of dispersal into remote areas of Viet Nam from Lao PDR (A. Giordano in litt., 2020) camera-trap studies since 2013 across the country from at least 19 protected areas, including Pu Luong, have not detected the species.MalaysiaMainland Clouded Leopards are still relatively widespread across Peninsular Malaysia (Perhiltan 2017), and can be found all the way from the north of the country bordering Thailand, to the most southern state of Johor. They predominantly occur within the Central Forest Spine map (DTCP 2009), a ~51,000 km² landscape which forms the majority of Peninsular Malaysia’s remaining forests, which includes large protected-area complexes (e.g., Belum-Temengor, Taman Negara, Endau Rompin), as well as Forest Reserves (e.g., Pasoh FR, Ulu Muda FR, Pasir Raja Selatan FR, Tanum FR, Sungai Yun FR), and Linkage areas (Primary Linkage 7, Primary Linkage 8, Tan et al. 2017, Rostro-García et al. unpub. data). Much of it is contiguous, and the areas outside it are relatively small and fragmented – even if they still harbor Mainland Clouded Leopards they might not persist over the long-term.
useTrade: Mainland Clouded Leopard exploitation for pelts is well documented in several countries, and the species’ parts remain noted in trade. Whilst some market surveys are recording fewer Mainland Clouded Leopard items since ~2010 this may represent trade moving underground and becoming more difficult to detect particularly in notorious borders markets in Myanmar. Population declines and local extinctions may also be contributing to declines in the number of Mainland Clouded Leopard occurring in trade. Recent (2016/17) surveys in Mong La, Special Region 4, Shan State, Myanmar found 11 Mainland Clouded Leopard skulls and 4 full skins (Sapai Min, in litt. 2020) compared to 54 skulls in December 2013 and 17 skulls and 5 full skins in February 2009 (Nijman and Shepherd 2015). In contrast, at Tachilik, Shan State on the Myanmar-Thailand border 2016/17 surveys found 8 full skins and 17 Mainland Clouded Leopard skulls (Sapai Min, in litt. 2020) compared to 22 skulls and 4 full skins in February 2006 (Nijman and Shepherd 2015). Mainland Clouded Leopard trade is also reported in other range states with a seizure of 19 Mainland Clouded Leopard skins in Phnom Penh, Cambodia in October 2014 (S. Gauntlett, in litt. 2020). A recent study in Nepal found a total of at least 51 individual Mainland Clouded Leopards in trade in just over 30 years (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018) whilst in Northeast India six cases of Mainland Clouded Leopard seizures were reported between 2015 and 2020; five were of skin and one of teeth and bones (J. Borah, in litt. 2020) and three cases of illegal poaching of Mainland Clouded Leopard were recorded from Bhutan in 2013/14 (W. M. Wong, in litt. 2020). These seizures and surveys likely represent a small proportion of the trade in Mainland Clouded Leopard parts in Asia, and highlight that wild off-take (either targeted poaching or through capture in indiscriminate hunting methods such as snares) is likely causing declines in many populations.
conservationActions: Included on CITES Appendix I and protected by national legislation over most of its range (Nowell and Jackson 1996). However, in all countries, particularly in Southeast Asia, the interpretation of the law protecting Mainland Clouded Leopard is imperfect and can be undermined by corruption. Fines and punishments also need to be increased. Despite co-occurring with tiger in many protected areas, and the growth of camera-trapping studies, there are no published temporal trends in Mainland Clouded Leopard population size or density. This remains a research priority and such information would strengthen future assessments and implementation of conservation activities.The species occurs in many protected areas, although direct exploitation, range fragmentation, and reduction in habitat quality have caused Mainland Clouded Leopard declines within protected areas across its range. Improving the effectiveness of Protected Area management through implementing the Zero Poaching tool-kit (http://zeropoaching.org/) and achieving Conservation Assured Tiger Standards (CA|TS; Pasha et al. 2018) is likely to significantly reduce threats impacting Mainland Clouded Leopard populations within protected areas.Given that much Mainland Clouded Leopard occurs in transboundary conservation landscapes the species should be considered in transboundary conservation planning (Farhadinia et al. 2019).

rationale: Cyclopes didactylus is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, its tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The common silky anteater has a head-body length of 20 cm and a tail of 16.5–29.5 cm length. It weighs around 300 grams. The general colour is brownish yellow, with a grey rump, legs, and tail. There is an irregular but distinctive dorsal stripe, with evident dorsal and ventral black stripes. Cyclopes didactylus can be found in evergreen tropical, mangrove, and secondary forests. The subpopulation in north-eastern Brazil is restricted to tropical moist lowland forests in the Atlantic Forest biome. It has been observed in red and white mangrove habitats. Not much is known about the ecology of this arboreal anteater. On Trinidad Island, population density has been estimated at 4.6–5.5 individuals per km². This is an opportunistic forager that almost entirely feeds on ants, but can also ingest beetles. No termites have been identified in any dietary study of Cyclopes (Miranda et al. 2009). Female common silky anteaters usually give birth to a single young per year, usually in September-November, after a gestation of 120–150 days.
threats: The species is affected by habitat loss, especially in the Brazilian Atlantic forest where large areas of native forests have been replaced by sugarcane plantations. In Suriname, the indigenous people from the hinterland consider that the species brings bad luck, because of which they always kill it when they find one (M. Pool pers. comm. 2022).
population: The population status and trend of C. didactylus are not known, but presumably the tendency is stable. The population density has been estimated at 4.62-5.50 individuals/km2 in a mangrove swamp on Trinidad Island (Bhagratty et al. 2013). It is quite abundant, but difficult to observe in the Brazilian Amazon (F.R. Miranda pers. comm. 2022).
range: The Common Silky Anteater is known from eastern Colombia, eastern and southern Venezuela, Trinidad Island, the Guianas, and northern and northeastern Brazil, with the southern limit being the São Francisco River. Cyclopes didactylus has a genetically separated subpopulation (i.e., a disjunct distribution) in Brazil. One is limited to the northeast of the Brazilian Amazon (state of Pará), towards the Brazilian states of Maranhão and Piauí, and the other is a disjunct subpopulation in the northeastern Atlantic forest, including the states of Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and Alagoas.
useTrade: Silky anteaters are sometimes captured and kept as a pet species in the country of origin.
conservationActions: Cyclopes didactylus is present in a number of protected areas.

rationale: Cyclopes dorsalis is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: The Central American Silky Anteater has a head-body length of 18.5–21.5 cm, a tail of 17­–22.5 cm length, and it weighs 155–275 grams. Its colour is quite different from the other Cyclopes species: its general colour is yellowish-brown, with the tail and limbs being more yellowish. There is no dorsal stripe, but a strongly developed and extensive sternal stripe (Miranda et al. 2018). This nocturnal and arboreal species occurs in mangrove forests and tropical rainforests. No information is available on the diet of this species, but it is presumably an opportunistic insectivore that mainly feeds on ants. Adults are solitary; the home range of a male overlaps the home range of three females (Montgomery 1983). Gestation length is 120-150 days; a mother with her half-grown offspring was recorded in February (McCain 2001).
threats: The threats to this species are unknown. It is probably affected by habitat loss, especially due to the degradation of mangroves.
population: The population status and trend of C. dorsalis are not known, but presumably the population is stable.
range: The Central American Silky Anteater occurs from southern Mexico through the Atlantic slope of Honduras to the inter-Andean valleys of Colombia and along the Pacific coast of Colombia and Ecuador.
useTrade: Silky anteaters are sometimes captured and kept as a pet species in the country of origin.
conservationActions: Cyclopes dorsalis is present in a number of protected areas. The species is listed as Vulnerable in Honduras (Wildlife Conservation Society 2021).

rationale: The species description of Cyclopes rufus is based on seven records, all of them in the state of Rondônia, Brazil, an area with high deforestation rates. Unconfirmed photographic records suggest that the species may also be present in the north of Bolivia, and it is possible that it also occurs in southeastern Peru. Deforestation due to the expansion of cattle ranching and large-scale agriculture is the main threat to the species. In addition, mining and hydroelectric dams also represent impacts. Nevertheless, the currently available information suggests that habitat loss is unlikely to equate to a reduction in population size that would warrant its listing in a threatened category. Therefore, Cyclopes rufus is listed as Least Concern, with a strong recommendation for urgent research and monitoring of the situation.
habitat: No specific data are available on the size of Cyclopes rufus, but assuming that it is similar in size to other silky anteaters, it would have a head-body length of around 20 cm, a tail of similar length, and it would weigh around 300 grams. Its fur colour is unique; the dorsum has a distinct reddish tone, and the tail and limbs are more yellowish red. There are no ventral or dorsal stripes. This nocturnal and arboreal species occurs in the Amazon forest. Its diet consists almost entirely of ants. Other than that, its ecology is unknown.
threats: The species is affected by habitat loss, as its area of distribution suffers from environmental degradation (mainly due to livestock and agroindustry) and the effects of large hydroelectric dams (Proyecto MapBiomas 2024). Considering only Brazil, where the species has confirmed records, it lost almost 26% of its habitat between 2000 and 2022. When including Bolivia and Peru, where the species may occur, the habitat loss is 21% in the same period. As a strictly arboreal species, such habitat loss is even more concerning for its survival (P.M. Santos pers. comm. 2024).The frequent and more aggressive forest fires in the last 5 years in Bolivia and in part of Brazil are threatening all anteater species (Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021, Noss et al. 2010, Silva et al. 2020).
population: The population status and trend of C. rufus are not known, but presumably it is decreasing.
range: Cyclopes rufus is endemic to western Brazil, where it occurs in the western Amazon basin. Its northern limit may be the Amazon river, but its southern limit of distribution is unknown. For example, unconfirmed photographic records suggest that the species may be present in the north of Bolivia (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021). It is possible that it also occurs in southeastern Peru.
useTrade: Silky anteaters are opportunistically captured and kept as a pet species in the country of origin, especially in rural areas (Noss et al. 2010).
conservationActions: It is not known whether the species is present in protected areas.

rationale: Cyclopes xinguensis is endemic to Brazil. Its distribution is limited to the north by the Amazon river, to the east by the Xingu river and to the west by the Madeira river. The southern limit of the distribution is still unknown. Despite the incidence of habitat loss, mining and hydroelectric dams, mainly in the extreme north of its range, it is considered that such threats do not imply a risk of extinction for the species in the near future. Therefore, C. xinguensis is listed as Least Concern (LC), with a strong recommendation for urgent research and monitoring of the situation.
habitat: No specific data are available on the size of Cyclopes xinguensis, but assuming that it is similar in size to other silky anteaters, it would have a head-body length of around 20 cm, a tail of similar length, and it would weigh around 300 grams. The dorsum of this silky anteater is grey, its rump yellow, the belly pale yellowish, and the tail grey. There is an evident dorsal stripe, while the ventral stripe is indistinct and irregular.The Xingu Silky Anteater occurs in the Amazon rainforest. No information is available on the ecology or diet of this arboreal species, but it is presumably an opportunistic insectivore that mainly feeds on ants. Gestation length of the genus Cyclopes is 120-150 days.
threats: The threats to this species are unknown, but it is probably affected by habitat loss due to the construction of hydroelectric dams. There is also environmental degradation due to the significant deforestation in this part of the Amazon, driven by the expansion of livestock ranching and agriculture (Proyecto MapBiomas 2024). Fieldwork is urgently needed to assess to what extent these threats are affecting the Xingu silky anteater.The species lost 13% of its habitat between 2000 and 2022 (P.M. Santos pers. comm. 2024). As a strictly arboreal species, such habitat loss is even more concerning for its survival.
population: The population status and trend of C. xinguensis are not known.
range: The Xingu Silky Anteater is endemic to the eastern Brazilian Amazon region. Its northern, western, and eastern limits are probably the Amazon, Madeira, and Xingu rivers, respectively, while the southern limit of its range is unknown. Known records exist for Amazonas, Pará and Mato Grosso states.
useTrade: Silky anteaters are sometimes captured and kept as a pet species in the country of origin.
conservationActions: There are few conservation Units in the region, and it is not known whether the species occurs in any of them.

rationale: Presbytis canicrus is considered Endangered in light of a continuing decline of the population caused by extensive habitat loss, fragmentation and hunting. Habitat loss (which is assumed to roughly equate to the rate of population size reduction) has been around 50% in the past 20 years, and in the next 10 years will certainly be well over the 50% threshold (30-year time period, which is three generations for this species). Where the species remains, it is heavily hunted. The geographical boundaries of this species are unknown, thus it should be reassessed once this becomes clearer.
habitat: Lowland to hill dipterocarp rainforest in elevations of 1,000 m with occasional records up to 1,600 m and possibly higher. Densities of Presbytis canicurus were slightly lower in riparian forests (18.4 ind/km²) compared to interior dryland forest (22.3 ind/km²); they were sympatric with White-fronted Langur (P. frontata) and Maroon Langur (P. rubicunda) (Rodman 1978).Miller’s Grizzled Langurs eat mainly young leaves and leaf shoots (66%), unripe fruit (28%) seeds, flowers, bird eggs and nestlings, mineral mud which results in the formation of stomach concretions. They are diurnal and arboreal, spending most of their time in upper canopies, at heights of 20 m for 62% of the time, and in lower canopies, 10-20 m above the ground for 29% of the time. Groups consist of a single male, 2-4 females, and young. Mean group size is eight individuals.
threats: Formerly, this species had a large population (in Kutai National Park), but its population has been considerably reduced due to forest fires in El Nino years during the 1980s and 1990s (Groves and Roos 2013). This should therefore be considered a threat and conservation should include this natural factor.Clearance of habitat for oil palm plantations fragments the continuity of forest and canopy cover. They are therefore required to descend to the ground to reach other parts of forests, making them vulnerable to stray dog attacks and poaching for their bezoar stones. Acacia and Gmelina plantations have replaced some high altitude forests in Gunung Beriun in addition to clear-cutting for oil palm plantations. Setiawan et al. (2009) suggest the possibility of local extinction in Kutai due to such persistent threats.Habitat loss and hunting continue to threaten the viability of the newly discovered population in Wehea. The positive news from the area is that it is protected locally by Wehea Dayak as protected land, where tree felling, fires and forest produce harvesting are prohibited. The forest is also patrolled by the Wehea Dayak rangers. Together with other forests, Wehea Forest forms a contiguous potential habitat for Presbytis canicrus (Lhota et al. 2012).
population: Recent discoveries in the Wehea Forest and studies through camera traps on salt licks have shown that Presbytis canicrus was recorded at a rate of just 0.2 individuals/day (Lhota et al. 2012). However, at a different salt lick, this was the most often seen (0.7 individuals/day); this site is protected by provincial and customary law.Surveys in Kutai National Park, eastern Borneo, found only one group of individuals on the riverbank of the Baai River, in Karangan, East Kalimantan. Camera traps confirmed the presence of the species in Wehea Forest, East Kutai district, East Kalimantan and their frequent occurrence at mineral springs or sepans. The presence rate in small sepan and large sepan in Wehea is 0.21 and 0.03 respectively (Lhota et al. 2012).
range: Presbytis canicrus is endemic to Borneo, where it is confined to an area of east Kalimantan, from the Kayan and Sembakung (=Sebuku) rivers in the north, south and southwest to the Makakam River (Groves and Roos 2013). The western boundary of its range is not well known, but it certainly occurs east of the Apau Kayan and the Kauan Mentarang National Park.
useTrade: This species is captured for 'bezoar' stones (visceral secretions used in traditional medicine).
conservationActions: This langur is included in CITES Appendix II. It was first classified as Endangered on The IUCN Red List in 2008 (as Presbytis hosei canicrus). The species is legally protected in Indonesia (as P. aygula canicrus). The geographical boundaries of the species are unknown. The formerly large population in Kutai National Park is much reduced.

rationale: Jungle Cat remains probably the most common cat species in South Asia (India, Nepal, Bangladesh), where the majority of the global population occurs and despite likely extensive declines in mainland Southeast Asia, where the species is now extremely scarce and largely restricted to remote lowland deciduous dipterocarp forest (Duckworth et al. 2005, Gray et al. 2014), it is unlikely that globally averaged declines are sufficient to merit Near Threatened status. Population declines and range contraction are also of concern elsewhere in the species’ range particularly in Egypt (Glas 2013), southwest Asia (Abu-Baker et al. 2003), the Caucasus (IUCN 2007), central Asia (Habibi 2004) and parts of Turkey (Ogurlu et al. 2010). However, very little new information has been obtained from these regions since the previous assessment. Nevertheless, ongoing collation of records, particularly from South Asia, is needed and evidence of declines, particularly outside protected areas may merit reassessment.In India, there is evidence of continued, and likely accelerating, habitat loss and ongoing poaching for both skins and, potentially, as a result of conflict with farmers (Choudhury 2010, Chowdhury et al. 2015, S. Mukherjee in litt. 2014, H.S. Baral in litt. 2014, D. Jathana in litt. 2014). The Jungle Cat's preference for open scrub and grassland in South Asia makes the species more susceptible to habitat loss than cat species which also utilise denser evergreen forests.The majority of the suitable Indian habitat is classified as ‘wasteland’ which legally eases conversion into any other form of use particularly industrialisation and urbanization – the latter has been identified as a particular threat in India given the pace of urbanisation of agricultural and unprotected forest areas (S. Mukherjee in litt. 2014, D. Jathana in litt. 2014). Hybridisation with domestic cats is also a potential, although unproven, threat. There remains uncertainty as to how the species will respond to habitat loss, and potential interactions with hunting and persecution. Therefore, further research is recommended, particularly in the Indian subcontinent, in order to gather additional data for a more thorough future assessment of the species' likely trends in response to habitat loss. Generally, more information on the species' ecology, distribution and status is needed across its range.
habitat: The Jungle Cat, despite its name, is not strongly associated with the classic rainforest "jungle" habitat, but rather with wetlands - habitats with water and dense vegetative cover, especially reed swamps, marsh, and littoral and riparian environments - scrubland, and deciduous dipterocarp forest (Gray et al. 2014). Water and dense ground cover can be found in a variety of habitats, ranging from desert (where it is found near oases or along riverbeds) to grassland, shrubby woodland and dry deciduous forest, as well as cleared areas in moist forest (Nowell and Jackson 1996).Areas with extensive deciduous dipterocarp forest and at least scattered surface water are the species predominant known habitat in Indochina. However, areas such as the Nakai Plateau which support other forms of savanna-like vegetation may support the species. It is probably absent from all closed canopy forests, including rainforest. The species may make use of agricultural areas with a low intensity of human use and which retain patches of scrub (Duckworth et al. 2005). In Iran, the Jungle Cat was found in a variety of habitats such as from plains, agriculture lands and mountains but was mostly found in shrub lands and woodlands (Sanei et al. 2016). In the Republic of Dagestan (Russian Federation), the favourite habitat of it was reed thickets, thorn bush thickets and thick lowland forests near water bodies (Yarovenko 2014). An analysis of habitat preferences, from camera-trap photographs, in eastern Cambodia demonstrated a strong preference for deciduous dipterocarp forests with no encounters (c.f. Leopard cat) in other forest types (Gray et al. 2014).Jungle cats have adapted well to irrigated cultivation, having been observed in many different types of agricultural and forest plantations throughout their range, such as sugar cane plantations in India. In Israel, they can be found around pisciculture ponds and irrigation ditches. Vereschagin (1959) noted that the Jungle Cat's use of the semi-arid plains of Azerbaijan increased with the development of a local irrigation system and decreased with its abandonment. However, mowing the seasonally flooded riverine tugai vegetation (trees and shrubs with dense stands of tall reeds and grasses) of this region for livestock fodder, as well as ploughing it under for agriculture, is known to be associated with the decline of Jungle Cat populations in the European-central Asian parts of its range (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Apparently, Jungle Cats are also able to tolerate urban environments to some degree as they have been found on the campus of Pulchowk Engingeering College in the middle of Lalitpur, Nepal (Basnet et al. 2017).In India, in a study in the Pench Tiger Reserve, Madhya Pradesh, the Jungle Cat was mostly active in the night hours (Majumder et al. 2011), whereas in Cambodia, Jungle Cats were found to be more active during the day (Gray et al. 2014). Jungle Cats feed mainly on prey that weighs less than one kilogram. Small mammals, principally rodents, are the prey most frequently found in faeces and stomach contents (Adhya 2014, Majumder et al. 2011). A study in India's Sariska reserve estimated that Jungle Cats catch and eat three to five rodent per day (Mukherjee et al. 2004). Birds rank second in importance, but in southern Russia waterfowl are the mainstay of Jungle Cat diet in the winter. With overwintering populations of waterfowl congregating in large numbers on unfrozen rivers and marshes, the Jungle Cat hunts among reed beds and along edges of wetlands, searching for injured or weakened birds. Other prey species are taken more opportunistically, including hares, nutria, lizards, snakes, frogs, insects, and fish (Majumder et al. 2011, Ogurlu et al. 2010, Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Patel 2011). In India, they have been seen to scavenge kills of large predators such as the Asiatic lion. In a study in southern Uzbekistan, the fruits of the Russian olive made up 17% of their diet in winter. While Jungle Cats specialize on small prey, they are large and powerful enough to kill young swine, subadult gazelles, and chital fawns (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002).Density estimates from natural tugai habitat in Central Asia range from 4-15 individuals per 10 km², but where this vegetation type has declined due to development density it does not exceed 2 cats per 10 km² (Nowell and Jackson 1996).
threats: The biggest threat to Jungle Cat is habitat loss particularly industrialisation and urbanisation of low intensity agricultural areas and scrubland in the Indian subcontinent. Habitat destruction for agricultural purposes and infrastructure development are also issues in Turkey and Iran (Ogurlu et al. 2010, Sanei et al. 2016). In Turkey, wetlands are mainly threatened by dam constructions and irrigation projects (Avgan 2009, Gerngross 2014). Additionally, environmental pollution and illegal hunting are threatening the Jungle Cat in Turkey too (Ogurlu et al. 2010). Also in Iran, illegal killing of Jungle Cats by shooting or trapping is a threat (Sanei et al. 2016). Jungle Cats can do well in cultivated landscapes (especially those that lead to increased numbers of rodents) and artificial wetlands. However, reclamation and destruction of natural wetlands, ongoing throughout its range but particularly in the arid areas, still pose a threat to the species, as density in natural wetlands is generally higher (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Nevertheless, the species' response to urbanisation and degradation of low intensity agricultural landscapes is unclear and merits further research.Unselective trapping, snaring and poisoning around agricultural and settled areas have caused population declines in many areas throughout its range (Abu-Baker et al. 2003, Duckworth et al. 2005). Moreover, some farmers consider the Jungle Cat a pest which takes poultry (Abu-Baker et al. 2003).  Some illegal trade is taking place in Asia such as in India, Myanmar, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nepal as well as in Egypt (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Habibi 2004, Shepherd and Nijam 2008, Choudhury 2010, Glas 2013, Chowdhury et al. 2015, Altaf et al. 2017, Min et al. 2018, McEvoy et al. 2019). The scarcity of Jungle Cat in mainland Southeast Asia is likely the result of high levels of hunting in open and accessible deciduous dipterocarp forest (Duckworth et al. 2005).
population: In Europe, the Jungle Cat is of marginal occurrence, with small populations in Cis-Caspian region and the Caucasus along the Caspian Sea. The European population has been rapidly declining since the 1960s. There were no records of this species in Astrakhan State Reserve (Russian Federation) since the 1980s. In Northern Ossetia (Russian Federation) only about 150 animals were recorded (Kuryatnikov and Varziev 1983). In the Republic of Dagestan (Russian Federation), the number of Jungle Cats was estimated at 105 animals in 2009, at 216 in 2010, at 177 in 2011, at 110 in 2012 and at 307 animals in 2013, showing population fluctuations (Yarovenko 2014). Marked population fluctuations are characteristic of this species in this region, probably because of absence of adaptations to cold winters. Despite these fluctuations the long-term trend in Europe is of decline in both population and in area of occupancy. Data from Russia suggest that there are about 500 animals left in the wild (Prisazhnyuk and Belousova 2007). A very small population persists in Georgia (I. Macharashvili pers. comm. to K. Tsysulina 2007). This species is considered threatened in a number of range states in Europe and the Caucasus, and is included in the Red Books of the Russian Federation, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia (IUCN 2007). In Israel’s National Red List the Jungle cat is listed as Vulnerable (Dolev and Perevolotsky 2004).In southwest Asia the species is considered rare and threatened (Abu-Baker et al. 2003, Habibi 2004). However, the Jungle Cat is considered common in some parts of its range, primarily in India (Mukherjee 1998, Patel 2011), but also in Pakistan and Bangladesh (Duckworth et al. 2005). In the respective National Red Lists, the Jungle Cat is listed as Near Threatened in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and as Least Concern in Nepal where its population is estimated to exceed 10,000 individuals (Jnawali et al. 2011, IUCN Bangladesh 2015, Ratnayaka 2018). In China’s National Red List it is listed as Endangered (Jiang et al. 2016). Generally in Southeast Asia, it appears quite rare in comparison to sympatric small cats (Duckworth et al. 2005). This rarity appears to be a relatively recent phenomenon associated with unselective trapping and snaring, especially in Lao PDR and Thailand as well, where it was described as common by Lekagul and McNeely (1977) but has since suffered drastic declines and is rarely encountered (Duckworth et al. 2005, Lynam et al. 2006). There are a number of recent camera-trap records from the Eastern Plains Landscape protected area complex in eastern Cambodia (Gray et al. 2014) and this area likely remains the stronghold of the species outside South Asia.
range: The Jungle Cat has a broad but patchy distribution. In Africa, it is found only in Egypt, along the Nile River Valley south to Aswan, and in El Faiyum, Farafara, Dakhla and Kharga oases (Glas 2013). In Southwest Asia its occurrence is highly localized around riparian vegetation and permanent water sources. It occurs through Israel, Lebanon, northwestern Jordan, western Syria, into southern Turkey, and in Iraq. In Iran, it is reported from large parts of the country except in the centre and some regions in the west and along the Persian Gulf. In the north, it is found from the provinces of Khorasan, Golestan and Mazandaran westwards along the Caspian Sea coastline and Hyrcanian forests to the West Azerbaijan Province (Abu-Baker et al. 2003, Sanei et al. 2016).In Turkey, the Jungle Cat has a fragmented distribution and seems to be quite widely distributed in the south of the country but to be restricted especially to wetland areas (Gerngross 2014). Jungle Cat presence was recently recorded around the Büyük Menderes Delta, Aydin Province, in the Akyatan Wildlife Conservation and Development Area, Akyatan Lagoon, Adana Province, and close to Manavgat, Antalya Province (Avgan 2009, Gerngross 2014). However, its status in Turkey is not known (Avgan 2009).The Jungle Cat is found in the Caucasus mountains (up to 1,000 m) including Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia. It occurs west and south of the Caspian Sea as well as south and east of the Aral Sea and associated river valleys. In Central Asia, it is found in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Afghanistan (T. Rosen and R. Kulenbekov, pers. comm. 2020). In 2017, the Jungle Cat was recorded in the Chuy region in northern Kyrgyzstan. How or if this presence record is connected to the distribution range of the species in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan is still unknown.The Jungle Cat’s distribution extends into South Asia from Pakistan through almost all of India as well as Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal ranging up to 4,000 m in the Himalayan foothills (Jnawali et al. 2011). The Jungle Cat occurs through Southeast Asia including Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos PDR and Viet Nam, to southern China, but is absent from Malayan peninsula south of the Isthmus of Kra (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Its range in Indochina is poorly known. Duckworth et al. (2005) reviewed the few historical distribution records from Indochina and added several recent ones from Lao PDR, Cambodia and Viet Nam.
useTrade: Some illegal trade (and killing) continues in India (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Choudhury 2010) and elsewhere in South Asia (Chowdhury et al. 2015, H.S. Baral in litt. 2014) as well as in Egypt (Glas 2013) and Afghanistan (Habibi 2004). India formerly exported large numbers of Jungle Cat skins before the species came under legal protection (over 300,000 were declared as being held by traders there when export was banned in 1979; Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Choudhury 2010). In India and Pakistan Jungle Cats are sometimes used for medicinal and/or ornamental purposes (Vijayakumar 2015, Altaf et al. 2017). In Myanmar, Jungle Cats were found on sale at markets, albeit rarely in comparison with other felid species detected, and reported to be regularly hunted in a nationwide hunter survey in 2018 (Shepherd and Nijam 2008, Min et al. 2018, McEvoy et al. 2019). The skin of a single Jungle Cat was also among seized wildlife parts between 2003 and 2013 in Kathmandu Valley, Nepal (Dangol 2015).
conservationActions: The Jungle Cat is listed on CITES Appendix II. It is protected from hunting in some range states (India), but in many it receives no legal protection outside protected areas (Nowell and Jackson 1996). The species now receives legal protection from all hunting and trading within Afghanistan after being placed on the country’s 2009 Protected Species List. Furthermore, given the amount of habitat loss occurring in riparian and wetland areas in Afghanistan, this species should be considered a research priority.The ecology and status of the Jungle Cat is poorly known (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Sunquist and Sunquist 2002). In Southwest and Southeast Asia, where it is considered rare and declining, more research needs to be undertaken to gain knowledge of current distribution, both in and outside of protected areas (Abu-Baker et al. 2003, Duckworth et al. 2005). Some farmers consider the Jungle Cat a pest which takes poultry (Abu-Baker et al. 2003), and conservation measures should include better protection for domestic fowl and halting of indiscriminate poisoning and trapping. The Jungle Cat would also benefit from improved protection of natural wetlands and reedbeds, particularly in the more arid parts of its range, and improved legislation prohibiting fur trade.The Jungle Cat was recorded in 13 protected areas in Iran (Sanei et al. 2016). There are recent Jungle Cat records from protected areas in India as from Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, Andhar Pradesh, Dihang-Dibang Biosphere Reserve, Biligri Rangaswamy Temple Tiger Reserve, Mundumalai Tiger Reserve and from Mana National Park (Behera and Borah 2010, Borah et al. 2012, Choudhury 2010, Kalle et al. 2013, Kumara et al. 2014). In 2013, its presence was recorded in Chitwan National Park, Nepal (Lamichhane et al. 2014). There are also a number of recent records from protected areas from eastern Cambodia such as from the Phnom Prich Wildlife Sanctuary and Mondulkiri Protected Forest (Channa et al. 2010, Gray et al. 2014) as well as from Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary in Thailand (Borries and Koenig 2014) and from the Shwesettaw Wildlife Sanctuary, Myanmar (Linnell et al. no date). However, all protected areas in Cambodia are insufficiently managed and threatened by habitat loss, degradation, and hunting.

rationale: Rhinolophus hillorum is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion A (VU A2c+4c) due to inferred and projected continuing decline in the number of mature individuals of 30% over three generations (22-year periods covering 2000–2022 and 2015–2037, based on a generation length of 7.5 years; Pacifici et al. 2013). The species’ forest habitat quantity and quality have been severely reduced and damaged due to past and unprecedented rates of deforestation (logging and conversion to agriculture) and increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires throughout the species range.
habitat: Rhinolophus hillorum primarily inhabits tropical moist montane forests, with the occasional capture from forest edge, tropical high-altitude grasslands, and pastureland at high altitudes (Fahr 2013, Wilson and Mittermeier 2019, Tanshi et al. 2021). It was captured in forest understory using harp traps and in mist nets set over a small stream on the Obudu Plateau at CRNP in Southeast Nigeria. The species is an insectivorous bat that forages in cluttered forest spaces (Tanshi et al. 2021) and may also perch-hunt (Fahr 2013).This species roosts in caves, mines, and other features that offer similar conditions (e.g., bridges; Verschuren 1976, Brosset 1984, Fahr et al. 2006) and has been recorded sharing roosts with R. simulator, R. guineensis, Lissonycteris angolensis (Brosset 1984), and on one occasion with Rousettus aegyptiacus (B.O. pers. obs.). It roosts in small colonies of 3-10 individuals (Verschuren 1976). A recent survey in Cross River National Park, Nigeria (CRNP) reports the highest relative abundance (15 individuals over seven sampling nights) of the species at 1,750 m asl, where it was also the most abundant bat species in the forest understory (Tanshi et al. 2021). Little information is available on its reproductive ecology. It is known to birth one pup per reproductive circle, the number of reproductive pulses in a year is unknown (Fahr 2013); one pregnant female from Liberia was captured in July (Verschuren 1976). Pacifici et al. (2013) estimated its generation length at 7.5 years. It is a small species with the following morphological characteristics (Fahr 2013); FA = 52–57 mm (mean = 54.5 mm, n = 17), and weight = 16.5–25.0 g (mean = 20.2 g, n = 9).
threats: The major threats to this species are forest fragmentation, and habitat degradation and loss through conversion to small-holder farms, wildfires, mining and quarrying, intensive logging, housing and urban development and ranching (Fahr and Ebigbo 2003, Fahr 2013, CEPF 2015). Forest cover loss across the range of R. hillorum is estimated at above 1.2 Mha between 2001 and 2020 (Global Forest Watch 2022), highlighting the significance of habitat loss for this species. Within its range in Nigeria, logging is ongoing at an unprecedented rate due to a renewed interest in Bubinga wood and poor law enforcement (Bukie et al. 2021, Eludoyin et al. 2021, B.O pers. com). Other threats affecting the species' range include climate change and severe weather (CEPF 2015). Further, wildfires have intensified across its range in Nigeria, potentially driving significant population declines through the direct loss of its roost and foraging habitat. Hunting for food is an assumed threat for this species (Fahr 2013) that needs to be confirmed. It is also likely threatened by cave disturbance, and sometimes a by-catch from the hunting of the cave-dwelling fruit bat species Rousettus aegyptiacus, a species with which it shares roosts. In addition, armed conflict in southern Cameroon further threatens the habitat of this species.
population: Little is known about the population size and trend of R. hillorum, although the number of mature individuals is inferred and projected to have a continuing decline in the number of mature individuals of at least 30% over three generations (22-year periods covering 2000–2022 and 2015–2037, based on a generation length of 7.5 years; Pacifici et al. 2013). The decline is due to habitat degradation and loss across its range from deforestation (logging and conversion to agriculture) and wildfire. Given its fragmented distribution, the species’ population is assumed to be structured in at least three subpopulations, all of which are declining. It is known to roost in small colonies of  ≤10 individuals (Verschuren 1976, Brosset 1984, Fahr et al. 2006).
range: The species is endemic to the major highland areas of the Upper (Guinea and Liberia) and Lower (Nigeria and Cameroon) Guinean Forest of West Africa (Fahr et al. 2006, Fahr 2013, Tanshi et al. 2021). Given these two areas are separated by about 2,000 km of mostly lowland habitats, the species is considered to have a highly fragmented distribution in at least three (3) broad locations. It is a highland species, primarily found at elevations between 800 and 1,950 m asl. The suitability of lowland areas for this species is unknown, as the only lowland record came from the vicinity of mountains in Cameroon (Fahr 2013). A recent survey that spanned all elevational gradients across two mountains in Southeast Nigeria only reported R. hillorum above 800 m asl (Tanshi et al. 2021).
useTrade: Although the species is presumed to be hunted for food and locally traded as bushmeat (Fahr 2013), an extensive hunting survey in 2017–2020 in Southern Nigeria did not confirm its hunting or trading (Obitte, unpublished data).
conservationActions: There are no conservation actions specifically targeting R. hillorum. However, the species is found in three protected areas; Cross River National Park and Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary in Nigeria (Tanshi et al. 2021), and Bali-Ngemba Forest Reserve in Cameroon (Cotterill 2002), but these protected areas are threatened by logging and encroachment from small-holder farms (Enuoh and Ogogo, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2022). Enforcement of anti-logging laws is critical, especially in Cross River National Park where timber extraction is at its highest within protected areas (Bukie et al. 2021, Eludoyin et al. 2021, B.O. pers. obs.). In addition, locals need to be educated on the dangers of irresponsible farming practices such as unsupervised brush-burning, encroachment of small-holder farms into protected areas, and bat hunting.Extensive surveys are required to establish the species' distribution, movement ecology, and to quantify its population size, trends, and habitat use. Furthermore, molecular data is needed to resolve the taxonomy of the specimens from Sudan and the Sapoba Forest Reserve in Nigeria. In addition, surveys are required to understand the extent of hunting and the bushmeat supply chain for this species across its range.

rationale: Mops petersoni is assessed as Near Threatened because its population is suspected to have declined by 25–29% over the last 15 years (three generations; GL = 5 years; Pacifici et al. 2013) because of ongoing loss of its primary forest habitat. It is close to meeting the threshold for criterion A2c
habitat: The species is known only from rainforest, at one locality in Ghana and five in Cameroon (El-Rayah 1981, Smith et al. 1986). It is likely to occur where suitable rainforest habitat exists and likely to extend into the Northern Rainforest–Savanna Mosaic (Happold 2013). It has not been recorded from disturbed areas.
threats: The species is considered to be threatened by loss and degradation of forest habitats within its known range, largely through the conversion of land to agricultural use and the extraction of firewood and timber.
population: It is considered to be a very rare species.
range: This little-known species has only been recorded from Ghana and Cameroon (with type locality of "15 km S Kumba") and there are no records from the intervening countries of Togo, Benin, and Nigeria. A specimen from Sierra Leone, formerly identified as Tadarida petersoni (Koopman 1989), is now considered to represent Mops brachypterus (Grubb et al. 1998, Happold 2013).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species and it is not known if the species is present within any protected areas. There is a need to maintain areas of suitable forest within the range of this species. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, breeding biology and general ecology of this bat.

rationale: Styloctenium wallacei is assessed as Near Threatened (nearly meets the threshold for criterion A). This species is suspected to have declined over the past 15 years (three generations, GL = 5 years, Pacifici et al. 2013) at a rate of 25–29% due to widespread forest loss and hunting throughout much of its range on Sulawesi and adjacent islands.
habitat: Styloctenium wallacei is most closely associated with tropical rainforests up to 1,800 m asl and has also been encountered in mixed-gardens (e.g. cocoa, rambutan, and durian plantation) (Maryanto et al. 2011, Yusti 2015, Widayati and Nurjana 2018, Widayati et al. 2020). This species is a solitary, nectarivorous species that also feeds on fruits (Maryanto et al. 2011).
threats: Degradation and the loss of forest habitats due to logging and small-scale agriculture are the primary drivers of the species decline. Further, it is at risk of bushmeat hunting for local consumption in North Sulawesi close to Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park (Mickleburgh et al. 2009, Ransaleleh et al. 2020).
population: Population data on Styloctenium wallacei are not available as the species is usually encountered in very small numbers (1–2 individuals), which is often much lower compared to other Pteropodid bats in Sulawesi. The species population is suspected to be declining by an estimated 25–29% due to forest loss and hunting (Mickleburgh et al. 2009, Ransaleleh et al. 2020). It is unknown if the species' distribution reflects a single location or if it comprises a single population.
range: This species has been recorded from throughout Sulawesi, including the nearby Buton Island and the Togian Islands (Bergmans and Rozendaal 1988, Maryanto et al. 2011, Yusti 2015, Patterson et al. 2017, Mubarok et al. 2018). The species is suspected to occur on Selayar Island (Heinsohn 2002), but that has yet to be confirmed. Styloctenium wallacei has been found from sea level up to 1,800 m asl (Maryanto et al. 2011, Widayati and Nurjana 2018, Widayati et al. 2020). The type locality for this species is Macassar, Sulawesi, Indonesia.
useTrade: The species is threatened by hunting for bushmeat for local consumption in North Sulawesi close to Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park (Mickleburgh et al. 2009, Ransaleleh et al. 2020).
conservationActions: While S. wallacei occurs in Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2011), Lambusango Forest Reserve (Patterson et al. 2017), and Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park (Ransaleleh et al. 2020), there are no known species-specific conservation initiatives in place for it. Forests where the species is known from should be protected, and degraded forests should be restored. Additional research is needed to inform the species distribution, its population status and trends, and the extent of the threats, including the impacts of hunting on the species. Insights into the species ecology are needed to better inform the species conservation and management.

rationale: This langur is listed as Endangered. The population is suspected to have declined by more than 50% over the last 36 years (three generations), due to a combination of habitat loss and hunting. Currently, fewer than 2,500 mature individuals are estimated to be remaining.
habitat: It occurs in primary, secondary evergreen, semi-evergreen, mixed deciduous forests, and also in limestone areas, limestone karsts, in Lao PDR. It is sympatric with Trachypithecus francoisi and Pygathrix nemaeus. It is largely folivorous, but is known to feed on figs, bamboo shoots, flowers, seeds and gums. Breeding and birthing through the year but birthing peaks during November-April. The author and his co-workers discovered a high dietary diversity of 148 plant species and 27+/-8 (range 15-51). Females disperse from natal groups and shortly after entering a new group can take over as the dominant female.  In a study on female receptivity to male and mate choice, Lu et al. (2012) found that the females were more receptive towards adult males during the peri-ovulatory period and towards adolescent males during the post conceptive period. Adult males were more aware of periods of fertility than adolescent males. Females of the species might employ such strategies to confuse paternity.
threats: In Viet Nam and Lao PDR the major threat to this langur is hunting (Nadler et al. 2003, 2004).
population: Population densities at Nam Nao National Park Phu Kieo Wildlife Sanctuary were 23-38 ind/km², average of 3.4 groups/km². According to Xuelong Jiang (unpubl.) more than 2,000 individuals exist in Wuliangshan and a total of 5,000 in China. The largest populations in Viet Nam exists Xuan Lien Nature Reserve with about 150 individuals and in Mu Cang Chai Species and Habitat Conservation Area with 50-80 individials (Nadler and Brockman 2014). Home range of 73.7-93.4 ha with groups as large as 14-20 individuals. Peng Fei et al. (2012) studied groups as large as 90 individuals in Wuliangshan, China, that increased from 81 individuals at the start of the study.
range: Indochinese Gray Langur (Trachypithecus crepusculus) occurs in southwestern China (East of Salween, also the western limit and south of Xishuanbanna, southern Yunnan Province), northern Myanmar, northern Thailand (south to Raheng and west to Bay of Bengal coast), northern and central Laos, northern Viet Nam, south of the range of Phayre’s Langur (Trachypithecus phayrei) (Groves and Roos 2013).
useTrade: This langur is hunted for meat in Viet Nam.
conservationActions: It is protected in Viet Nam under the wildlife protection law, Decree 32/2006, and as endangered, precious and rare species prioritized for protection in Decree 160/2013, but under the synonym Trachypithecus (phayrei) barbei.Indochinese Gray Langur occurs in the following protected areas:Viet Nam: Pu Mat and Ben En National Parks, Pu Luong, Xuan Lien, Muong Ne Nature Reserves and Mu Cang Chai Species and Habitat Conservation Area (Nadler and Brockman, 2014)Laos: Phou Dendin, Nam Et-Phou Louey, Phou Khaokhoay, Nam Kading National Biodiversity Conservation Areas, Phou Gnouet Production Forest. Thailand: Nam Nao National Park, Huai Kha Khaeng and Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuaries.China: Ailaosjan, Huanlianshan, Wuliangshan, Xishuangbanna, Fenshuiling, Niuluohe, Caiyanghe, Lancangjiang National Nature Reserve.

rationale: Presbytis percura is only found in a number of isolated and unprotected lowland forests, and faces extinction in the wild based on large-scale forest loss in Riau Province (Rizaldi et al. 2019). Riau experienced the highest rate of deforestation in Sumatra and 63% of the natural forest have been lost between 1985 and 2008 (Uryu et al. 2010). Additionally, forest fires linked to the ENSO events, and open burning of forest land for agricultural purposes destroy millions of hectares of land in Indonesia on an annual basis, and Riau is often one of the worst impacted areas, owing in part to its high concentration of peatland (World Bank 2016). The scattered forest remnants and agroforests where P. percura were found might no longer remain without conservation actions on the ground. Individuals of this species were also killed by local communities when they fed on fruit crops such as rambutans, durians and mangosteens. We thus infer that the area of occupancy, extent of occurrence and quality of habitat of P. percura have declined to such an extent that the population size has reduced by ≥80% over the last three generations since 1984 (Nijman et al. 2020) for the closely-related P. melalophos). We also suspect this rate of decline will continue into the future, thus fulfilling the IUCN conditions for Critically Endangered (CR A2cd A3cd A4cd).
habitat: Presbytis percura is generally found in mixed mangrove, primary freshwater, riverbank, primary lowland logged, scrub-grassland riverbank, and secondary riverbank habitats. This species has adapted to feed on non-native Rubber Trees (Hevea brasiliensis) which were introduced into their habitat in Sumatra nearly 100 years ago. Plantations of fast-growing rubber were first introduced in Jambi, Sumatra in 1904 and subsequently expanded rapidly as a cash crop in the eastern coast from the 1920s (Stoler 1995). Today, rubber plantations in Sumatra continue to grow in the forms of rubber forest and rubber monoculture. Six out of nine groups of P. percura were observed in rubber forests and individuals were feeding on rubber seeds and leaves (Rizaldi et al. 2019).
threats: Presbytis percura faces a high risk of extinction in the wild. Its natural habitats are rapidly converted to agricultural land. Compared to other provinces in Sumatra, Riau experienced the highest rate of deforestation, where 63% of the natural forest have been lost between 1985 and 2008. Riau also produced more palm oil and paper pulp (Uryu et al. 2010). These land use changes have resulted in highly fragmented forest remnants and degraded habitats that are surrounded by oil palm, rubber, and forest plantations (e.g., Acacia spp. and Eucalyptus spp.) within the range of P. percura. Additionally, forest fires due to hot weather conditions and open burning for agricultural purposes destroy millions of hectares of land in Indonesia on an annual basis, and Riau is often one of the worst impacted areas, owing in part to its high concentration of peatland (World Bank 2016). Individuals of this species were also killed by local communities when they fed on fruit crops such as rambutans, durians and mangosteens.
population: There is no estimate on population size in the wild for this species.
