conservationActions: Some individuals have been recorded from national parks and the species is listed as Endangered (EN) in the Japanese Red List (Ministry of the Environment 2014).The issue of wind development and bats is being reviewed by the conservation committee of the Japanese Mammalogical Society to explore future actions. Research is needed on the population, ecology, life history and threats to the species to inform sustainable conservation.

rationale: The species is listed as Vulnerable under criterion B2ab(iii). Although its extent of occurrence is greater than 20,000 km², its area of occupancy (AOO) is 1,770 km². It is a rare species, with a severely fragmented range, and there is ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat (loss of suitable tree hollows).
habitat: Although this species characteristically uses tree cavities as roosts, all reported roosts have been found in buildings (Fukui 2015).
threats: Human disturbance at roost sites in buildings is a threat. It is exacerbated by the destruction of habitat resulting in loss of suitable tree hollows.
population: There are only around 20 records for this species, collected from seven localities, and very little information is available. There has been little survey work, but Eptesicus japonensis is probably patchily distributed across Japan. It is thought to be very rare. Maternity roosts have been found only in buildings in Norikura Highland, Nagano Pref. Up to 200 pregnant females assemble to form maternity colonies in June (Fukui 2015).
range: Eptesicus japonensis is endemic to Japan and is known from the base of the northern Japan Alps, southern Japan Alps, Mount Hakusan and Mount Fuji, Chichibu Mountains, Nikko and Oze (Fukui 2015). It has mostly been recorded from elevations above 700 m asl.
conservationActions: This species is present in protected areas. More information is needed on the species' range, population status, habitats and ecology. It is listed as Vulnerable (VU) in the Japanese Red List (2014).

rationale: This assessment is based largely from Woinarski et al. (2014). Categorisation is difficult because very little is known of Mormopterus eleryi. It has a very large extent of occurrence, but probably a much smaller area of occupancy (associated mostly with riparian areas in arid and semi-arid regions); its population size is poorly known and cannot be estimated reliably; and some decrease in population size is inferred from substantial loss of habitat in part of its range. The current inability to estimate population size precludes the use of criterion C, but on inference of a small population size and continuing decline, it is considered here as Near Threatened (nearly meets criterion C2a(i)).
habitat: Pennay (2006) noted of Mormopterus eleryi that “nothing is known of its ecology”.  It has been recorded mostly from open woodlands (Reardon and Pennay 2008, Pennay et al. 2011, Milne and Pavey 2011), particularly near watercourses and riparian areas (Pennay 2006).  The few observations indicate that it flies relatively low to the ground (Reardon and Pennay 2008, Milne and Pavey 2011).  During the day it shelters in tree hollows (typically with very small entrances), with group sizes of 4–15 individuals being reported (Pennay 2006, Reardon and Pennay 2008).Females aggregate in maternity roosts (Pennay 2006).  Reproduction is likely to be seasonal, with births in November-December (Reardon and Pennay 2008). The generation length is taken here to be 4-5 years, recognising that for insectivorous bats, reproductive maturity is at about 10 months, and longevity about 8-10 years, and with generation length taken as the midpoint of these values.
threats: Habitat loss and degradation through a combination of grazing, wildfire, and large-scale native vegetation clearance (the latter especially in central Queensland) has in the past, and will continue to be the main threat to this species.
population: There are no estimates of the population size. Roosts of up to 15 individuals have been reported (Pennay 2006, Reardon and Pennay 2008). Pennay (2006) reported that it was readily trappable at sites where present, and so suggested that the very few captures across its extensive range represented real absences or rarity. Reardon and Pennay (2008) considered it “sparse” and “rare”. Pennay et al. (2011) noted that it was “the least known and reported bat” in New South Wales. There is no information on trends in population size (Pennay et al. 2011), but broad-scale vegetation clearance in substantial portions of its range (notably inland Queensland and, less so, inland New South Wales) over the last 12-15 years is the basis for a strong inference of decreasing population size. For example, in the Queensland portions of the Mulga Lands and Brigalow Belt bioregions ca 27,000 km² of native woodland was cleared over this period (DERM 2013).
range: The range of the Bristle-faced Free-tailed Bat is poorly known. There are few records scattered across a vast area of inland Queensland, central New South Wales and central Australia (including far northern South Australia) extending westward to near the Western Australian border in central Australia (Reardon and Pennay 2008, Reardon et al. 2008, Pennay et al. 2011, Milne and Pavey 2011). There are major disjunctions within this known range, which may represent real gaps (Reardon and Pennay 2008). Within this extensive range, its area of occupancy is likely to be far more circumscribed because of an assumed narrow habitat specialisation to riparian areas (Pennay 2006).
conservationActions: For the New South Wales portion of its range, management is guided by a Priorities Action Statement (Lunney et al. 2011). Some records are from conservation reserves (e.g., Gundabooka National Park, Pennay 2006), where some threats are managed (Scott 2012). It is listed as a Vulnerable species in South Australia under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972, with no specific recovery programme implemented.  It is not listed in the Northern Territory or Queensland. Development of conservation actions for this species require further information and study, particularly on the following: 1) resolving the extent of distribution and apparent gaps; 2) estimating population size and trends; 3) developing a better understand of key threats and their relative impacts; 4) determining their ecological requirements; and 5) conducting a population genetic study to determine population structure and genetic diversity.

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered under criterion B2ab(iii) because its area of occupancy, based on the area of known roost sites, is less than 500 km². These critical roost sites are where the species occurs for 12 hours out of every day. Its range (and population) is severely fragmented as the roosts are on multiple islands separated by significant water gaps. In addition, there is a presumed continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat through the loss and degradation of forested foraging areas and disturbance at caves throughout its range.
habitat: This species roosts in caves and mines, with colonies numbering over several hundred bats. This species forages over forests and feeds mainly on Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera and Diptera (Fukui et al. 2009). Female give birth single young in early June.
threats: Roost disturbance from humans/tourists (e.g., some caves have electricity lined in for tourist activities), and the threat of development around caves represent the main threats. Above several caves roosted by this species on the Ishigaki island, a new airport has been constructed. Population monitoring in these caves is conducted every year before and after construction. However, population trend cannot be estimated because the number of roosted individuals has highly fluctuated so far (Kara Karst Scientific Committee 2014, New Ishigaki Airport Bat Monitoring Committee 2015).
population: There were many large maternity colonies in the past, but now many appear to have become small or extinct. On Okinawa Island, one maternity colony of 10,000 females is known. On Iriomote Island, a maternity colony with 1,000 newborn youngs is known (Ministry of the Environment 2014). There may be one breeding colony on Tokunoshima, but there is no information for Amami-Oshima. There is no known breeding colony on Ishigaki.
range: This species is endemic to Japan where it is known from Amami-Oshima, Tokuno-shima, Okinoerabu Island, Okinawa Island, Kume Island, Ishigaki, and Iriomote islands (Sano 2015). In 1933, the species was collected from Kii Peninsula (Honshu), but it now appears to be extinct there (Maeda 1978, 1982).
conservationActions: No breeding colonies are known from protected areas. Near the new airport, an artificial cave has been constructed as an alternative roost, but only few individual roosted so far. It is listed as Endangered (EN) in the Japanese Red List (Ministry of the Environment 2014).

rationale: This species has a large extent of occurrence and area of occupancy, uses a broad range of habitats, is presumed to have a large population size, occurs in many protected areas, and is recorded regularly throughout much of its range. There is no empirical data on population trends for this species but because natural roosting and foraging habitat has been cleared or modified in many areas of its range, it is reasonable to infer that there has been an historical and continuing reduction in population size in some areas. Listed here as Least Concern but there is uncertainty about the direction, rate and magnitude of trends in population size.
habitat: Recorded localities for Ozimops petersi are from chenopod shrublands, mallee, myall, mulga, grasslands, ephemeral watercourses in desert (dunes and stoney) as a well as agricultural lands (Churchill 2008). Natural roosts are in tree hollows with narrow hole or fissured entrances. Also reported roosting under corrugated iron roofs. Forages in open spaces above the canopy or between trees but also observed foraging on the ground (Richards et al. 2008). Ozimops petersi gives birth to a single young each year in November or December.
threats: Habitat of Ozimops petersi has ongoing threats from land clearing and degradation associated with wheat, cattle and sheep farming, plus wildfires and burning regimes that are responsible for tree hollow loss.
population: The population size is unknown but expected to be large, likely in excess of a million individuals. This species is recorded commonly across much of its range. Pennay et al. (2011) suggested that the species may be under-reported because usually only males are identified (based on penis morphology) but even males would have been confused with O. ridei before the taxonomic revision in 2014.
range: A widespread species found in arid to semi-arid regions in the southern half of the Australian continent. There appears to be a gap in its distribution between Western Australian records and those in central and eastern Australia that coincides with a genetic disjunction between these populations (Reardon et al. 2014).The western population records are from the Coolgardie and the eastern Murchison bioregions, but understanding of the full extent of the distribution is currently limited because female Ozimops petersi and O. kitcheneri are difficult to distinguish based on their external morphology. There are many unassigned records in the Wheatbelt and Mallee bioregions of Western Australia that may be attributable to O. petersi. There are no records from the vast Nullarbor region. The eastern population has its current western extent near the South Australian/Western Australian border. The species is uncommon south of the Murray River in South Australia and Victoria. The eastern limit is not clear because O. petersi and O. ridei have been confused prior to the 2014 taxonomic revision, so many past records attributed to both species in eastern New South Wales need to be re-assessed. In addition, female O. petersi and O. planiceps are difficult to distinguish based on external morphology. Field identification of male Ozimops is more reliable because of diagnostic penile morphology (Van Dyck et al. 2013, Reardon et al. 2014). The likely eastern boundary coincides with the base of the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range.Representatives of this species in the Northern Territory are significantly larger, an observation that led them to be assigned formerly to O. lumsdenae (as O. beccarii in Milne and Pavey 2011). However, these are part of the same genetic clade as the eastern populations of O. petersi.
useTrade: This species is not used in trade.
conservationActions: No specific conservation programmes are directed at this species but it occurs in many national parks and conservation reserves.

rationale: Pteropus ennisae is assessed as Vulnerable under criteria B and C (VU B1ab(i,ii,iii,v); C2a(ii)). The species is endemic (with one location/population) to New Ireland Island, Papua New Guinea and its extent of occurrence is 19,581 km². Its population is small (estimated to be between 9,000 and 10,000 mature individuals) and is inferred to be declining as the rate of habitat loss and degradation over the past three generations (24 years; Pacifici et al. 2013) is likely exceeds 10%. A habitat loss of ca 25% over the past three generations (24 years) is due to logging and deforestation on New Ireland Island (observed rates of 1.34% p/a from 1972 to 2002, and 0.966% p/a from 2002 to 2014; Shearman et al. 2009, Shearman and Bryan 2015). There is no indication that the rate of habitat loss will decline or cease.
habitat: This is an uncommon species. Individuals have been recorded in lowland and hill forests, secondary forest, bordering gardens (Lavery 2019). It is frugivorous and has been reported feeding on clusters of figs (Ficus spp.). It roosts alone or in small groups in vegetation (Flannery 1995, Bonaccorso 1998) and is largely solitary (Lavery 2019). Presumably, females give birth to a single pup, with one captured female being found lactating and another carrying a near-term foetus in June–July during an Australian Museum expedition (Lavery 2019). Male lactation has been reported in this species. Lifespan averages 8–10 years and reaches maturity at 1–2 years of age.
threats: New Ireland is recognized as a region that lacks significant environmental governance and is highly vulnerable to climate change, which would further exacerbate habitat loss issues. Although data are limited, the species is suspected to be impacted (loss of roost and foraging habitat) by human activities in coastal areas and mangrove forests. Logging and land use changes are believed to have resulted in substantial loss of habitat, particularly at low elevations: 40.1% of the forested area of New Ireland Island was logged or cleared in the period 1972–2002 (Shearman et al. 2009), and a further 11.6% over the period 2002–2014 (Shearman and Bryan 2015). There is no indication that the rate of deforestation will decline or cease. The species has been observed to have some tolerance of habitat loss and disturbance, however the degree of tolerance is unknown (Lavery 2019). The species may also be hunted opportunistically for food and persecuted as a perceived threat to subsistence gardens. The impacts of climate change, induced droughts and associated wildfires are also likely to impact the species. The ongoing forest degradation and loss, and risk of strong tropical cyclones that can lead to the destruction of forests and food supplies can cause major fluctuations in flying fox populations, presenting a possible significant threat to the species.
population: The species is endemic (with one location/population) and its population is small (estimated to be between 9,000 and 10,000 mature individuals) and is inferred to be declining due to deforestation and habitat degradation on New Ireland. The species is uncommonly found in low densities over its geographic range, as it is not a colonial species like more commonly studied flying foxes.
range: This species has been recorded from, and is endemic to, the island of New Ireland in the Bismarck Archipelago of Papua New Guinea (Flannery 1995, Bonaccorso 1998). It has been recorded from sea level to 1,200 m asl. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 19,180 km².
useTrade: This species may be taken opportunistically for subsistence purposes.
conservationActions: There are no species-specific conservation programs. Pteropus ennisae is not explicitly listed on Appendix II of CITES. However, P. capistratus is listed on Appendix II of CITES and P. ennisae was previously included in this species; CITES needs to be updated in the near future to reflect the new taxonomy. The species is likely to occur within at least one of the three Key Biodiversity Areas on New Ireland (http://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/kba-data) but does not occur in any protected areas as there are none recognized on the island. Additional research is needed to determine important roosting and foraging sites, ecology, life history and threats for this species.

rationale: This species is endemic to the Atlantic Forest Biome sensu lato in the states of MG, ES, SP, PR, SC and RS in Brazil and in the Argentinean provinces of Iguazú and Missiones. Major threat factors are related to loss, fragmentation and disconnection of the habitat, urban expansion, increase in roads and energy matrix, hunting and hybridization. It is suspected that these factors are leading to a population reduction of about 30% within three generations (48 years). For these reasons the taxon was classified as Near Threatened (NT) approaching the A4cde criteria.
habitat: Sapajus nigritus inhabits lowland, sub-montane and montane tropical and subtropical forest of the Atlantic coast of Brazil and also in gallery forest. The taxon is tolerant to environmental changes and disturbances, occurring in secondary forests and utilizing pine and eucalyptus plantations and also inhabits fragments close to corn, bananas and cassava fields (Ludwig et al. 2006) and sugar-cane fields (Rímoli 2001, Rímoli et al. 2008).Capuchins are insectivore-frugivores, including a wide range of plant species, a variety of fruits, seeds and arthropods, frogs, nestlings and even small mammals in their diet, supplemented by stems, flowers and leaves (Ludwig et al. 2005, Mittermeier et al. 2013). They are extractive manipulative foragers and can use tools to access larvae and nuts (Izawa 1979, Fernandes 1991, Rocha et al. 1998). The home range recorded for 3 groups in the Iguazú National Park, Argentina was 161±77 ha (range 81-293 ha) (Di Bitetti, 2001); for one group in Paraná, Ludwig et al. 2005 estimated a 56 ha home range; in São Paulo home ranges of 117 ha (Izar et al. 2007), 5 ha and 10 ha (Freitas et al. 2005) and 465.3 ha (Izar and Sato 1999) were estimated; and in Minas Gerais, Rímoli 2001 estimated 268 ha.Group sizes range from 11 to 23 (Aguiar 2006, Silveira et al. 2005), although Lynch & Rímoli (2000) noted a maximum group size of about 30 animals at Caratinga Biological Station, Brazil. The number of females exceeds the number of males. Males disperse from their natal groups, but females are usually philopatric; females may also transfer groups especially when groups divide or there is a change of the alpha male (Mittermeier et al. 2013). The top ranking male is dominant to the top-ranking female. However, the ranks of the lower ranking individuals are not always easy to determine (Lynch 2001, Izar 2006). Subordinate males may be peripheral (Freese & Oppenheimer 1981, Fragaszy et al. 2004), but also may form close bonds with other group members (Lynch 2001).Movement Patterns: Terrestrial (range behavior with day range movement ranging from 750 m in Dry Season to 3000 m in Wet Season, in a forest fragment in Atlantic Forest (Rímoli 2001).Congregatory: Social groups. Group sizes range from 11 to 23 (Aguiar 2006, Silveira et al. 2005) to 24-29 individuals (Lynch and Rímoli 2000, Rímoli 2001, Lynch 2001)
threats: Although quite wide ranging, the species is nonetheless subject to habitat reduction, loss and degradation, besides fire, rural settlements, increasing road and agriculture matrix, predation by exotic species, hunting and gathering across its range. Another threat is hybridization with congeneric species (Lynch Alfaro et al. 2014). The species is considered a crop pest in some areas (in sugar cane and pine plantations). Otherwise, it is generally scarce except in the larger protected areas.
population: Total remaining population is not known and it is unclear whether the number of mature individuals of this taxon is greater than 10,000.Di Bitetti (2001) recorded a population density of 16 individuals/km² in the Iguazu National Park, Argentina. In Brazil the population density is recorded at 3.5 ind/km² (González-Solís et al. 2001), 24.5 ind/ km² (Bernardo and Galetti 2004) and 5.6 ind/km² (Freitas et al. 2005) in São Paulo; 7.71 ind./km² in Minas Gerais (Costa et al. 2012); 29 ind/km² in Parque Estadual Mata dos Godoy (Rocha 2001); 54 ind/ km² and 94 ind/km² in Ibiporã (Ludwig et al. 2005); 66 ind/km² in Parque Estadual Vila Rica do Espírito Santo (Vidolin and Mikich 2004); 51 ind/km² in adjacent shores of Paraná River in Paraná state (Aguiar et al. 2011) in Paraná and 0.35 groups/km² in Parque Estadual do Turvo in Rio Grande do Sul (Fialho and Setz 2007).
range: Sapajus nigritus occurs in the states of Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. It extends into the northern most tip of the Argentinean provinces of Iguazú and Missiones (east of the Paraná River). The limits are the Doce River in the north, the State of Rio Grande do Sul in the south (that is not defined yet), the Atlantic Ocean in the east and the provinces of Iguazú and Misiones in Argentina in the west.

rationale: Chlorocebus dryas is a rare animal with widely-dispersed occurrences within a poorly defined geographic range. Since the 2008 Red List assessment of Critically Endangered, there has been a significant increase in the known range and population size of C. dryas, with the discovery of a new population at the eastern limits of Congo’s central cuvette, as well as an additional occurrence (skin of an individual killed by a hunter) at Djombolanda village, Yahuma Territory, 36 km east of Kokolopori. Fourteen occurrences of this species are now known, seven in the Kokolopori-Wamba-Djombolanda area and seven in the Lomami-Lualaba interfluve area. At each site, the total number of groups ranges from 1 to 6, and group size ranges from 2 to 15 individuals (Kuroda et al. 1985, Alempijevic et al. 2018). Although the precise limits of this species' distribution are not known, it is uncommon and very localized wherever it has been found. Average group size is ~9 individuals, with approximately 50% mature individuals in 26 groups estimated to occur across 14 known occurrences. This results in an overall population size estimate of less than 250 adults, therefore C. dryas qualifies as Endangered under criterion D. Further surveys are urgently needed to assess the distribution and population status of this species.
habitat: The habitats and ecology of Chlorocebus dryas are not well known. It is reported to use secondary lowland moist forests of a range of ages, riparian forests and swamp forests (Kuroda et al. 1985, Lokasola 2014). It seems to avoid primary forest (Hurley and Lokasola 2007). The Lomami-Lualaba monkeys were observed in old secondary and riparian forests. The two southernmost locations for C. dryas in the Lomami National Park and adjacent buffer zone, are small riverine galleries bordered by open seasonally-inundated savannas. It is considered a highly cryptic species, hiding in thickets in dense secondary forest. Chlorocebus dryas are frequently found in proximity to human settlements, ranging even up to the edges of gardens in Kokolopori (Lokasola 2014). Dryas Monkeys were detected more often in secondary forest than riparian forest, with particularly high encounter rates along the edges of old gardens in Bafundo (Alempijevic et al. 2018). Chlorocebus dryas is arboreal and regularly found in the sub-canopy and lower strata of the forest. In four multi-strata camera trap surveys, 97% of Dryas Monkeys were detected in mid-to-low strata at between 2 and 10 m (Alempijevic et al. 2018). It is also found on the ground, foraging on herbaceous vegetation (Kuroda et al. 1985, Lokasola 2014), although Dryas Monkeys were not detected by terrestrial camera traps (Alempijevic et al. 2018). Dietary items include fruits, young and mature leaves, shoots, pith, seeds, insects and mushrooms (Lokasola 2014, Alempijevic et al. 2018). Chlorocebus dryas live in small social groups (most estimates are fewer than 15 individuals) with one adult male, although additional adult males have been observed in one group (Kuroda et al. 1985). Chlorocebus dryas occur in mixed-species associations, especially C. ascanius, which also use the lower strata in disturbed sites (S. Kuroda pers. comm. cited in Butynski 2013, Alempijevic et al. 2018). There are few data available on behaviour and vocalisations (Butynski 2013). No loud calls are known, though contact calls have been recorded by camera traps (Alempijevic et al. 2018). Adult males have a striking blue scrotum and perineal area (Alempijevic et al. 2018). This colourful genital region is characteristic of terrestrial forest guenons (C. hamlyni and C. lomamiensis), as well as Allochrocebus, Cercopithecus and Erythrocebus (Hart et al. 2012, Cramer et al. 2013).
threats: Kuroda (cited in Butynski 2013) states that expanding shifting agriculture also poses a threat. However, Dryas Monkeys are thought to prefer secondary forest over undisturbed forest types. The main threat to this species is hunting, which is illegal. Chlorocebus dryas was documented in Wamba, Kokolopori, Djombolanda, Bafundo and Djekoshilo through hunter kills. Hurley and Lokasola (2007) and Kuroda (cited in Butynski 2013) state that the species is under pressure from poaching in Wamba and Kokolopori, and Kuroda reports declines in populations since the 1980s (Butynski 2013). In 2014, Sakamaki et al. (2016) confirmed that C. dryas occurs in the Wamba research area, however, it was not encountered during a recent primate census at the site. The Lukuru Foundation has been surveying bushmeat in the area since 2009, and the species was never reported until 2014, when one dryas kill was seen in Bafundo. Since 2014, two additional hunter-killed Dryas Monkeys have been recorded in Bafundo. However, it may be difficult to assess accurate hunting levels for such a small primate that may be eaten locally, and not traded in regional markets. Nevertheless, the impacts of even very small numbers of removals from such a small population represent a serious threat. Given that commercial bushmeat hunting occurs in most of the species’ known range, the threat is ongoing.
population: Chlorocebus dryas occurs in widely-separated, isolated populations that contain small numbers of animals. It is unlikely that there is direct contact between the known eastern and western populations. At the Kokolopori-Wamba locations, Kuroda et al. (1985) and Hurley and Lokasola (2007) reported that group sizes typically ranged from 2-15 individuals. Butynski (2013) quotes Kuroda as recording six groups of C. dryas, ranging from 2-10 individuals along 1.5 km of transect in the Wamba area. At Bisandu village in the Kokolopori Bonobo Nature Reserve, Lokasola estimated that a total of 31 individuals occurred in three different groups (Yembo group: eight individuals; Bepila group: 12 individuals; Bolendela group: 11 individuals). Recent camera trap surveys in Lomami National Park suggest that two groups occur at Camp Bartho in the park interior and three groups occur in the park’s buffer zone near Bafundo village (Alempijevic et al. 2018). Between one and five individuals were detected by camera traps in each event. It is estimated that 26 groups occur in the 14 known occurrences, with an average group size of ~9 individuals, of which ~50% are mature individuals. This results in an overall population size estimate of less than 250 adults.
range: This species is limited to the Congo’s central basin in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The current range is known from two widely-separated areas, with 14 known occurrences. Area of occupancy is not known within its potential range.
useTrade: Chlorocebus dryas is hunted for local consumption. Due to its small body size, it is not likely to yield a high market value. Hunting is known to occur in both major areas of occurrence, but the degree to which C. dryas is being targeted is not known. Dryas carcasses have not been seen in local or regional bushmeat markets.
conservationActions: Chlorocebus dryas is hunted throughout its range and only three of the 14 known occurrences are within the boundaries of Lomami National Park. One is in the Luo Scientific Reserve, another is in the newly recognised Iyondji Community Bonobo Reserve, and four are in Kokolopori Bonobo Reserve. Priorities for this species are further survey work to identify additional occurrences and to better estimate overall population size and area of occupancy.Chlorocebus dryas is listed on Appendix II of CITES.

rationale: Assessed as Endangered, Piliocolobus bouvieri is suspected to have undergone a population decline of at least 50% over the past three generations (1990-2019),primarily due to poaching and to a lesser degree, habitat loss. This species is downlisted from Critically Endangered as its known geographic range now includes previously unknown populations in northern Republic of Congo. Bouvier’s Red Colobus was first recorded west of the Sangha in 2007, 2014 and 2015 (Devreese 2015). It has also been found in the Lesio-Louna Reserve (Ndzai et al. 2019). The taxon was thought likely to have been wiped out since the 1970s in the southern part of its range. Hunting continues throughout its range, and habitat change (due to clearing of forests for charcoal) is intensifying in the south. Although surveys have been intensive, records of the continuing presence of this species are few and far between.
habitat: Bouvier’s Red Colobus is a largely arboreal species that lives in riverine and swamp (seasonally- or permanently-flooded) forests.
threats: The major threat to Piliocolobus bouvieri is hunting. All red colobus species are slow-moving and easily hunted (Struhsaker 2005), as illustrated by a female observed with her infant in northern Congo who remained clearly visible for 15 minutes (Devreese 2015). During this same survey, Devreese (2015) reported evidence of a single hunter claiming to have killed more than 60 red colobus during a single hunting trip. Devreese also identified a substantial commercial trade along the Likouala and Sangha rivers, although this trade may have decreased in recent years due to a perceived threat of contracting Ebola virus disease (Devreese 2015). The immigration of a workforce into logging concessions and access facilitated by logging roads will lead to increasing hunting pressure on wildlife in the northern part of this species' range. In the southern part of the range, Bouvier’s Red Colobus are hunted in and around the Lesio-Louna Reserve (Ndzai et al. 2019). As yet, there is little habitat transformation, but this is likely to change over time, as there is a very high demand for charcoal from Brazzaville (the capital city) and perhaps also from Kinshasa (the capital of DRC, population 12 million).
population: Population size is unknown, but because Bouvier’s Red Colobus is a large-bodied, slow-moving, group-living species, it is certainly declining due to illegal hunting. Local decreases in numbers have been recorded in the south of their range, in and around the Lesio-Louna Reserve, where they are hunted (Ndzai et al. 2019).
range: Piliocolobus bouvieri is found in the swamps of northern Republic of Congo and riverine forests in the south of the country. Previously, it was known to occur on the right bank of the Congo River, only along the lower reaches of the Alima to the mouth of the Likouala-aux-Herbes (i.e., west of the Sangha River), and the tributaries of the lower Congo River (Gautier-Hion et al. 1999, Butynski et al. 2013). However, in 2007, 2014 and 2015, the species was recorded on five occasions in the north, in a large logging concession of Ngombe and in Ntokou-Pikounda National Park, in the area west of the Sangha River and east of the Bokiba (Lingoue) and Likouala rivers in Congo (Devreese 2015). In 2016, a troop was recorded in the south of Lesio-Louna Reserve, in gallery forest along the Loubilika River, in the least accessible area of the reserve, about 45 km west of a main road that links Brazzaville to towns to the north and about 65 km east of a smaller road system south of the source of the Lefini River (Ndzai et al. 2019; although earlier targeted surveys in the north of Lesio-Louna Reserve and the south of Lefini Reserve had failed to find this species; Downer 1998, Ikoli et al. 1998).
useTrade: Hunted illegally for local consumption and commercial sale at bushmeat markets.
conservationActions: This taxon is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. The range of Piliocolobus bouvieri overlaps with the Lefini Reserve. This taxon is a priority for further survey work to determine whether it remains extant in the wild.

rationale: Goodman's Mouse Lemur (Microcebus lehilahytsara) has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of at least 66,800 km² and an area of occupancy (AOO) of 10,000–15,000 km². Presence of this species has primarily been reported from the central and eastern highlands of Madagascar. More than ten populations have been identified, which occur over a highly fragmented range. The population is inferred to be undergoing a continuing decline of ca 25% over three generations (approximately 17 years), based on ongoing habitat loss and degradation, an apparent increase in hunting rates, and the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on conservation efforts in the country. The species is assessed as Near Threatened (nearly meeting VU under criteria A2, A3 and A4).
habitat: The species inhabits rainforests, although some individuals have also been observed in patches of old Eucalyptus plantations where they move through the understory without descending to the ground (Ganzhorn 1987). In the Central Highlands, the species persists in small to very small relict forest fragments surrounded by a forest-grassland savannah matrix (Andriamboloson et al. 2021). In Andasibe, the species is mainly solitary at night and feeds on fruits and insects in shrubs and low trees as well as in the upper canopy of the forest (Ganzhorn 1988, 1989). At Ambavala and Anjiahely (i.e., its northern range), where it can be found in sympatry with M. jonahi and M. macarthurii, respectively, this species can be found in forest habitats of all levels of degradation as well as fallow vegetation adjacent to forest edges (Radespiel et al. 2008; Schüßler et al. 2018; D. Schüßler pers. obs.).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat degradation and loss from unsustainable agricultural practices, charcoal production, logging, mining (both industrial and artisanal), and hunting. Repeated vegetation burning has starkly contributed to forest loss in the Central Highlands, whereas the main threats to remaining rainforests further east mainly stem from slash-and-burn agriculture. Madagascar's largest mine is located within the species' range.
population: Home ranges in males (0.22–0.42 ha) were slightly smaller than in females (0.21–0.30 ha) in Mantadia National Park (Randrianambinina 2001), but larger ranges have been documented in males (0.97–3.97 ha) and females (0.22–1.62 ha) in the Ankafobe Forest fragments (Andriamboloson et al. 2021). Population densities estimated by Ganzhorn (1988) (when the species was still believed to be Microcebus rufus) were 110 +/- 34 individuals/km² at Andasibe. At Tsinjoarivo, M. Blanco (pers. comm.) estimated population densities at 132 individuals/km² in a forest fragment and 80 individuals/km² in a continuous forest site. At Ankafobe, population density was estimated at 219 individuals/km² (Andriamboloson et al. 2021). As other rainforest mouse lemurs, the species is believed to occur in lower densities than Microcebus species in western dry forest (Setash et al. 2017).A continued decline of the population is inferred though it is hard to estimate the rate of decline, though it could be inferred as c. 25% over the past three generations and ongoing into the next three generations. In the past three generations (ca 17 years), population decline is inferred based on a suspected continuing decline of the species' area of occupancy as well as a decline in area, extent and quality of its habitat. For example, from 2000 to 2020, the Alaotro-Mangoro Region in Madagascar lost 30% of its tree cover while the Sava Region has lost 23% during that same time period (Global Forest Watch 2022) (these being two regions where the species is known to occur). Given the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on conservation initiatives in Madagascar (due to reduction in eco-tourism and reduction in funding), we suspect that habitat degradation will continue at the same rates into the future (particularly outside protected areas). There is also evidence that hunting of this species could be increasing.
range: The type locality of this species is the region of Andasibe, Madagascar, based on nine animals caught in the Analamazaotra Forest Station in Andasibe (Kappeler et al. 2005, Roos and Kappeler 2006, Dolch 2008). Apart from occurring in other protected areas in the immediate surroundings (Analamazaotra Special Reserve, Mantadia National Park, Maromizaha Forest, Vohimana Forest), it also occurs as far west as Ambohitantely Special Reserve (Rasoloarison et al. 2013) and smaller fragments such as Ankafobe Forest (Blanco et al. 2016, Yoder et al. 2016). Analyses of samples from Tsinjoarivo Classified Forest have also been identified as Microcebus lehilahytsara (Yoder et al. 2016), meaning that the southern limit of its distribution might be the Onive/Mangoro river complex. The northernmost collection locality of the merged ranges of M. lehilahytsara and the junior synonym M. mittermeieri lies in Marojejy National Park (Poelstra et al. 2021). Although intermediate locations are successively filled with observations (e.g., Marotandrano Special Reserve, Weisrock et al.2010; Ambavala near Mananara Avaratra, Schüßler et al. 2020a; highlands of Makira Natural Park, D. Schüßler pers. comm.), notable absences have been recorded for lowlands (e.g., Manarana-North National Park, Ambodiriana near Manompana (Schüßler et al. 2020a) and certain highland areas, such as Zahamena Strict Nature Reserve and National Park, where it is replaced by M. jonahi and M. simmonsi, respectively (Roos and Kappeler 2006, Schüßler et al. 2020a). M. lehilahytsara was deemed to be a “highland specialist”, only found at altitudes >825m a.s.l., in its southern range (Weisrock et al. 2010, Radespiel et al. 2012). However, recent observations at a few places of lower altitudes in its northern range (e.g., at 350 m asl in Marojejy National Park and Anjiahely or at 233 m asl in Ambavala; Schüßler et al. 2020a), as well as absences from adjacent lowlands make the species' distribution irregular and not well understood to date. Its neighbouring species to the south, south-east and east are M. jollyae and M. rufus (Louis et al. 2006), M. marohita (Rasoloarison et al. 2013) and M. gerpi (Radespiel et al. 2012), respectively. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be ca 66,800 km2.There is likely to be an ongoing decline of the species' area of occupancy as well as a decline in area, extent and quality of its habitat. For example, from 2000 to 2020, the Alaotro-Mangoro Region in Madagascar lost 30% of its tree cover while the Sava Region has lost 23% during that same time period (Global Forest Watch, 2022) (these being two regions where the species is known to occur). Given the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on conservation initiatives in Madagascar (due to reduction in eco-tourism and reduction in funding), we suspect that habitat degradation will continue at the same rates into the future (particularly outside protected areas).
useTrade: The species appears to be occasionally (and randomly) trapped for both food and the pet trade. Around Makira Natural Park, opportunistic capture of mouse lemurs occurs mainly during preparation of fields for shifting cultivation (i.e., cutting of fallow vegetation; D. Schüßler pers. obs.). Reuter et al. (2019), surveying the frequency with which lemurs are kept in country (including areas where Microcebus lehilahytsara occurs), found that Microcebus spp. only make up 2.2% of all lemurs kept as pets, but suspect them to be under-reported because of their "non-lemur like" appearance. Jenkins et al. (2011), in another household survey, found that Microcebus spp. were the seventh-most popular bushmeat in the Moramanga and Anosibe An’ala Districts (which are both within the geographical range of M. lehilahytsara).
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. It occurs in several protected areas (Rylands et al. 2018, Schüßler et al. 2020a), including two National Parks (Mantadia, Marojejy), four Special Reserves (Analamazaotra, Ambohitantely, Marotandrano, Anjanaharibe-Sud) and Makira Natural Park. Some sites where it occurs have recently been gazetted as new protected areas (e.g. Ankeniheny-Zahamena, Anjozorobe-Angavo, Mangabe-Ranomena-Sahasarotra, Tsinjoarivo, Maromizaha), are in the process of becoming protected areas (e.g. Ankafobe, Torotorofotsy) or are managed by local communities for conservation (Ambavala; Schüßler et al. 2018). The species is kept in only a few zoological institutions, with a significant breeding colony of several dozen individuals being kept in the Masoala exhibit of Zoo Zurich (Jürges et al. 2013, Karanewsky et al. 2015).

rationale: Gray's Sportive Lemur (Lepilemur dorsalis) is assessed as Endangered due to suspected population due to habitat loss (Mittermeier et al. 2008) at a suspected rate of 30% in the past with this increasing to a suspected rate of 50% in the future due to increases in threats including habitat loss (and hunting). For example, the species could well lose 45% of tree cover in its range over the next three generations, in addition to which it faces threats from hunting. Habitat fragmentation due to deforestation and agricultural shifts has impacted population numbers and densities in the geographic range of this species.The extent of occurrence (EOO) of this species covers 7,082 km². This geographic range is severely fragmented and undergoing continuing decline in area, extent and quality of habitat. This is leading to suspected declines in population numbers.
habitat: Prior to the completion of the molecular work that resolved distribution of this species, it was thought to be the subject of only brief field studies. However, studies by Wilmet 2018; Wilmet 2019, Wilmet, Devillers, and Beudels-Jamar 2017 and Wilmet et al. 2017 in Ampasindava (previously described as L. mittermeieri) expands the knowledge of this species. It inhabits humid forests that are subject to a short dry season each year, as well as sub-humid forests that are subject to a long dry season. In dense primary forest, it appears to favour tree holes for daytime sleeping, but it will seek out vegetation tangles in more open deciduous forest. Births occur from August through November, mothers typically producing a single offspring. It is presumably largely folivorous (Mittermeier et al. 2008 and references therein).
threats: The main threats are believed to be habitat loss due to rice, cocoa, and coffee cultivation, as well as illegal logging and hunting. Its geographic distribution on Ampasindava presents major threats to its habitat from mining concession for rare earth metals.
population: Population densities for this species have been recorded to range between: 0.16–0.3 individuals/km². Population numbers are in decline due to habitat loss (Mittermeier et al. 2008) at a suspected rate of 30% in the past, with this increasing to a suspected rate of 50% in the future due to increases in threats including habitat loss and hunting. Future population decline in the Ampasindava peninsula were previously estimated as being at least 80% (Wilmet et al. 2020). Habitat fragmentation due to deforestation and agricultural shifts has impacted population numbers and densities in the geographic range of this species.
range: This species has a highly restricted distribution. It is found in the Sambirano region of north-western Madagascar, centring on Ambanja. The extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated at 7,082 km² with an elevation range from 100 to 370 m asl (average 154 m asl).This species is likely affected by national trends in forest habitat loss: Madagascar lost 37% of its forest cover from 1973 to 2014, with an annual deforestation rate of 1.1%/year from 2010 to 2014. Almost half of Madagascar's forest (46%) is now located within less than 100 metres from the forest edge (Vieilledent et al. 2018).In the two regions that overlap with the species' range (Diana and Sofia), 19% of tree cover was lost from 2001 to 2020 (Global Forest Watch, 2022). However, rates of tree cover loss within the species range appear to be higher than those across the wider region. For example, within the Ampasindava peninsula, the deforestation rate has been evaluated at 2.27% per year between 2005 and 2010 and at 3.14% between 2010 and 2014 (Wilmet et al. 2020). There is also the development of the rare earth mining project (around 320 km²) that will impact on this species. If we presume that the deforestation rate continues at ca 3% over the next three generations (ca 15 years), the species will lose ca 45% of its remaining tree cover in its range.
useTrade: This species is sometimes hunted for food.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix I. It is known to occur in the Ampasindava Manongarivo Special Reserve, and possibly Tsaratanana Strict Nature Reserve and Nosy Be. With the resolution of the type locality of Lepilemur dorsalis, a comprehensive distribution and extensive molecular investigation should be considered a priority conservation narrative for this species due to the lack of population information and its northern and eastern distributions.

rationale: Javan Surili (Presbytis comata) is listed as Vulnerable because its population size is well below 10,000 mature individuals, with no more than 1,000 mature individuals within each subpopulation. This species may be re-assessed as Endangered in the future given that its estimated population size (lower end estimate of 2,300 mature individuals with ca 300 mature individuals in the largest subpopulation) is on the threshold for being considered Endangered under criterion C. In addition, it is suspected that there is a continuing decline of ca 10–20% in the number of mature individuals within three generations (30–36 years) due to excessive hunting, deforestation and fragmentation; however, criterion C1 is not used because suspected continuing decline is insufficient to trigger this criterion (more data are needed to estimate rate of decline).
habitat: This species was historically found from sea level to around 2,500 m (Nijman 2017) but is now mainly restricted to mountain habitat fragments.It is folivorous, but will also consume fruits, flowers, and seeds (Ruhiyat 1983).Prefers middle and upper layers of forest canopy. Found in primary and secondary forests, edges and interior. Lowland forests, forests on steep slopes, hills and upper montane forest.Ruhiyat (1983) found the species to be largely folivorous at altitudes between 1,400 and 1,650 m asl, with 65.2% of the diet comprising leaves and flowers (59.1% young leaves, 5.6% mature leaves, 7% flowers) and only 14.2% comprising fruits and seeds (13.5% fruit, 0.7% seeds). This is similar to that reported by Sujatnika (1992) from similar altitudes (1,250–1,550 m a.s.l.) on Mt. Gede-Pangrango, i.e., 65.0% young leaves, 5.0% mature leaves, 17.0% flowers, 6.4% fruits, and 2.3% seeds. At lower elevations, the species is more frugivorous. Sugiarto (2006) studied the species at 700 m a.s.l. on Mt. Pangrango where 38.2% of the diet comprised fruits and seeds and 59.6% leaves.Preferred leaves are sourced from Ficus pubinervis, Passiflora lingularis, Elaeagnus triflora, and Schefflera aromatica. Preferred fruits include Premnda parasitica, Saurauia and Castanopsis argentea (Ruhiyat 1983).No set breeding season. Natal coat is medium to dark grey or black.Arboreal, diurnal. In Gede Pangrango National Park activity budget is 51% resting, 23% foraging and feeding, 21% travelling and 5% engaging in social and other activities. Three to four feeding bouts, travel in the upper canopy, sleep in high trees and ridges.Single adult male or two in a group. Sometimes form mixed species groups with Javan Langur (Trachypithecus auratus) (Nijman 2017).
threats: Presbytis comata is threatened by habitat destruction, such that many, but not all, of the remaining populations are now confined to montane forest patches. The species once occurred across extensive lowland areas. Hunting is a persistent threat in many of the remaining population fragments.
population: Total population size estimated at 5,000–12,000 individuals, of which 2,300–5,500 are adults.There are approximately 30 isolated populations (which have been isolated from each other for decades, and sometimes for more than 100 years). The population size has been estimated at between 2,285 (Supriatna et al. 1994) and 2,500 animals (MacKinnon 1986), which included a small number of individuals included in P. fredericae. Nijman (2017) gave an overview of population sizes for eleven of these isolated populations. Excluding Ciremay-Kuningan-Pemabarisan, six of these populations (from west to east Ujung Kulon, Rawa Danau, Mts Halimun-Salak, Mt Gede-Pangrango, Kawah Kamojang, Mt Patuha), hold an estimated 640-720 groups. With an average group size of 7.2 individuals, this translates to 4,600–5,200 individuals. Including the populations on Ciremay-Kuningan-Pemabarisan the numbers are 1,040–1,420 groups and 7,500–10,200 individuals. Potentially sizeable populations, such as Sanggabuana, Masigit-Kareumbi, Mt Tangkuban Perahu-Burangrang, Cibanteng-Cikepuh (Supriatna et al. 1994), not included in the above estimates, would add to this total.Densities differ somewhat by altitude, with Nijman (2017) summarising it as 0.4-0.6 groups/km² in the lowlands (<500 m asl), 0.5–2.4 groups/km² in hill forest (500–1,000 m asl), 0.1–2.4 groups/km² in lower montane forest (1,000–1,500 m asl), and 0.35–5.8 groups/km² in montane forest (>1,500 m asl). Group sizes are negatively correlated with altitude. Giving equal weight to groups at different altitudes, an average group contains 3.3 adult individuals.
range: This species is found in western Java, as far west as either Mt Sawal in West Java or Mts Pembarisan in Central Java.
useTrade: The species is targeted to a limited extent for the domestic pet trade, as well as some hunting for food.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. Most remaining populations in western Java exist in nature reserves where they are mostly safe from habitat disturbance and hunting. These sites include Ujung Kulon National Park, Mt Halimun-Salak National Park, Gede-Pangrango National Park and possibly Mt Ciremai National Park. Also occurs in a number of Strict Nature Reserves, including Telaga Warna, Mt Malang, Mt Simpang, Mt Papandayan, Kawah Kamojang, Rawa Danau, and Cibanteng. Most populations seem to have stabilized, and although they are fragmented, some retain large numbers of individuals.Nevertheless, this species is severely threatened with habitat loss and to a lesser extent by hunting. Total population estimated at 5,000-12,000 individuals in c. 30 isolated population. Threatened with habitat degradation, these langurs are now restricted only to the montane habitats while once they were found extensively in the lowland areas. Gradual degradation of forests through illegal logging, felling for building materials though occasionally, tree felling to obtain orchids and pitcher plants, firewood collection. They are also persecuted for crop raiding.

rationale: The Javan Fuscous Langur (Presbytis fredericae) is assessed as Vulnerable (VU A3cd) based on a suspected reduction in population size of at least 30% over the next three generations (ca 33 years), due to ongoing deforestation and habitat fragmentation, and hunting pressure. A least one of the known subpopualtions is suspected to now be extirpated. The minimum population size estimate for this species is less than 2,500 mature individuals, and it is suspected that it will face at least a 20% decline in the next two generations (ca 22 years). The small population size and suspected decline suggests that this species may actually qualify for Endangered under criterion C1, however more data are needed to confirm the rate of decline before criterion C1 can be used for this species.
habitat: This is an arboreal, diurnal species, which was historically found from sea level to around 2,565 m (Nijman 2017) but is now mainly restricted to mountain habitat fragments, with the only lowland population occurring in the western part of Mts Dieng.It is folivorous, but will also consume fruits, flowers, and seeds. Suryana (2010) studied the species at 500–600 m a.s.l. in Mts. Dieng and found it to feed largely on fruits and seeds (i.e., 24.9% seeds, 17.2% fruits and seeds, 8.9% fruits) and to a lesser extent on leaves and flowers (i.e., 35.8% young leaves, 4.0% mature leaves, and 1.6% flowers).Prefers middle and upper layers of forest canopy. Found in primary and secondary forests, edges and interior. Lowland forests, forests on steep slopes, hills, montane and upper montane forest.There is no set breeding season for this species. Natal coat is medium to dark grey or black.A single adult male or two occur within a group. The species sometimes forms mixed species groups with Javan Langur (Trachypithecus auratus) (Nijman 2017).
threats: Presbytis fredericae is threatened by habitat destruction, such that many, but not all, of the remaining populations are now confined to montane forest patches. It is suspected to be extirpated from at least one of these isolated subpopulations. The species once occurred across extensive lowland areas. Hunting is a persistent threat in many of the remaining population fragments.
population: Total population size estimated at between 5,000–17,000 individuals, of which 2,300–7,800 are mature individuals.There are four to eight isolated subpopulations. Excluding Ciremay-Kuningan-Pemabarisan, these subpopulations may hold 300 groups (Mt Slamet), 400–600 groups (Mts Dieng), 20–40 groups (Mt Merbabu), and possibly 10–20 groups in Mt Muria, totalling 730–960 groups. With an average group size of 7.2 individuals, this translates to 5,300–6,900 individuals. Including the populations on Ciremay-Kuningan-Pemabarisan the numbers are 1,770–2,380 groups and 12,700–17,000 individuals.Densities differ somewhat by altitude, with Nijman (2017) summarising it as 0.5 groups/km² in the lowlands (<500 m asl), 0.5–2.4 groups/km² in hill forest (500–1,000 m asl), 1.7 groups/km² in lower montane forest (1,000–1,500 m asl), and 0.9 groups/km² in montane forest (>1,500 m asl). Group sizes are negatively correlated with altitude. Giving equal weight to groups at different altitudes, an average group contains 3.3 adult individuals.A population decline of ca 20% over the next two generations (ca 22 years) is suspected. Of the five main subpopulations, three subpopulations are either already extirpated or could be extirpated in the near future by fires. There are only two subpopulations that are not under high levels of threat, and both of these are not formally protected. For example: 1) Mt. Lawu is unprotected and the species have not been seen there since 1995 so may no longer be present; 2) at Mt. Merbabu there is a small and fragile population within a National Park which is found in a small of forest high up on the mountains. This area suffers from forest fires and a large fire could cause a local extinction of the 20-40 groups. Two areas - Mt. Slamet and Mts. Dieng - are home to 300 and 400-600 groups, respectively, but are largely unprotected. Both of these areas are experiencing ongoing forest loss (though rates of loss in Mt. Slamet are currently low).
range: This species is found in central Java, on Mt Merbabu, Mts Dieng and Mt Slamet (all in the province of Central Java), and possibly Mt Muria (Central Java), Mts Pembarisan (Central Java), Kuningan and Mt Ciremay (West Java). The species was also known from Mt Lawu on the border of Central and East Java, but it has not been recorded there since 1995.It is suspected that the extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, and habitat quality are all declining.
useTrade: The species is targeted to a limited extent for the domestic pet trade and hunted for food.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. Most remaining populations in Central Java are not included in the conservation area system, but the forest in all sites is protected for watershed reasons (hutan lindung) or is managed by the state forestry department PERHUTANI. These langurs occurred in mountains habitats Mt Slamet, Mts Dieng, Mt Merbabu, Mt Muria (possible presence), as well as in the lower regions of the eastern Mts Dieng, down to ~250 m asl.They are threatened by the gradual degradation of forests through illegal logging, felling for building materials though occasionally, tree felling to obtain orchids and pitcher plants, firewood collection. They are also persecuted for crop raiding.

rationale: Trachypithecus margarita is assessed as Endangered as it is known to be impacted by past and ongoing loss of habitat and the effects of hunting. The population size is suspected to have declined by over 50% in the last 36 years (three generations). If the current threats continue the population will continue to decline in the future.
habitat: The Annamese Silvered Langur occurs in lowland, evergreen, semi-evergreen, mixed deciduous, riparian, gallery forest. They are sympatric with doucs throughout most of their range. Most observations were reported between 100 and 650 m asl while the highest elevation recorded (650 asl) is on the Lang Biang Plateau (ca 12°05’N, 108°30’E; Elliot 1909). Similar to the other congeners of the cristatus group, this langur is primarily folivorous. The species was reported to consume young leaves at 54.4% and mature leaves at 7.1% followed by fruit at 29.9%, and flowers at 7.7% (Tran Van Bang 2013). At least 33 plant species from 19 families were used by the Annamese langurs in Takou NR with a preference of species from Moraceae (Tran Van Bang 2013). The species is known to come to the ground to eat soil (Rawson and Luu Tuong Bach 2011). Breeding appears to occur throughout the year but infants with orange pelage are most often seen between November and May (Hoang Minh Duc pers. obs.).Monge (2016) says "home range size reached 256 ha, being larger in the dry season than in the rainy season, likely because of different food availability. The high canopy was most frequently used, although juveniles used the mid-canopy more frequently. Langurs preferred mixed deciduous forest during the rainy season but avoided it during the dry season, probably for a lack of canopy to hide and feed".
threats: Logging has a detrimental effect on the ranging of the T. margarita (Gonzalez-Monge and Behie 2019).Major threats include: habitat loss due to land use changes, especially in Eastern Cambodia (Moody et al. 2011) and the Central Highland in Vietnam, hunting, use in traditional medicine, and pet trade. In Viet Nam they were common in the Central Highlands in the early 1980s but intensive hunting has extirpated them throughout much of their range (Hoang Minh Duc, pers. obs.). In Lao PDR, suitable habitat for the species has largely been converted for agriculture. Remaining suitable habitat is fragmented and has been under severe hunting pressure. The demand for monkey bones in Viet Nam has likely driven more intensive hunting of the species in the last few decades. The species has been recorded in the international animal trade (Singh et al. 2006)."Langurs were strongly affected by logging, moving higher in the canopy as intensity increased, and abandoned areas of their home range where it was most destructive. While T. margarita tolerates human disturbance, loggers target key tree groups and law enforcement must be maintained" (Monge 2016).
population: No population estimate is available for the species throughout its geographical range. Hoang Minh Duc et al. (2012) reported at least 60 individuals in Takou NR, Binh Thuan Province in Viet Nam. While they have been observed in a few other areas in the past few years including Cat Tien NP (Dong Nai Province), Yok Don NP (Dak Lak Province), Chu Mom Ray NP (Kon Tum Province), and Kon Ka Kinh NP (Gia Lai Province), no population estimates are available.The largest population is found in Cambodia, mostly in the “deciduous/evergreen forest mosaics of the Northern and Eastern Plains” (Moody et al. 2011: 24). An estimated population of 900–5,000 was reported to the Seima Conservation Area (Nut Menghor et al. 2015). The Annamese Silvered Langur is the scarcest monkey species in Lao PDR; there is no known large population across its Lao range (Timmins et al. 2013). The association of the species with lowland semi-evergreen habitats that are easily accessed means that it has been under great hunting pressure in Lao PDR. In addition, lowland plains in south Lao PDR have been heavily converted to agriculture land. A population of Annamese Silvered Langur in Dong Sakee Sacred Forest (ca. 180 ha) in Dong Phou Vieng National Protected Area, Lao PDR comprising about 90 individuals (Vongkhamheng et al. 2014) are not hunted by local communities, due to traditional beliefs that the animals being reincarnation of the dead; however, it is likely that this tradition will not hold through the generations and outsiders not sharing this belief can easily hunt the animals that are easy to approach (Coudrat 2011, Timmins et al. 2013, Vongkhamheng et al. 2014). In other fragmented suitable habitats in its Lao range, the Annamese Silvered Langur is already believed to have been extirpated from overhunting (Timmins 2009).
range: This species is known from eastern Cambodia in Ratanakiri and Mondulkiri provinces, southern Lao PDR (N limit 16°23’N) (Timmins et al. 2013) and south-central Viet Nam (N limit of 14°30’N), with Mekong probably being the western limit. In Viet Nam, records north of 16°37'N are doubtful and need confirmation (Roos et al. 2013). The southernmost record was reported in Ba Ria—Vung Tau Province at 10°24’N (Tran Van Bang pers. comm.). Silvered Langurs also occur along the Mekong River in northern Cambodia, in particular along the braided section of the Mekong between Stung Treng and Kratie Towns (Bezuijen et al. 2009). It is not yet clear if these populations are attributable to T. germaini or T. margarita.
useTrade: The species is hunted for use in traditional 'medicine' and the pet trade.
conservationActions: This species is listed in CITES Appendix II. In Viet Nam, the species is legally protected under Appendix 1B of Decree 32 (2006) and Appendix I of Decree 160 (2013) under the name of Trachypithecus villosus.In Cambodia: all Silvered Langurs are listed as Common in the Ministerial Declaration (Prakas No. 020) on Classifications and List of Wildlife species (2007) under the name of Semnopithecus cristatus. This species is legally protected under Chapter 10 of the Forestry Law (2002) and within protected areas managed by the Ministry of Environment under the Protected Area Law (2008).In Lao PDR: The species is considered At Risk in Lao PDR and is legally protected under the ‘Prohibited’ category of the list of threatened species, and the Wildlife and Aquatic Law (2007).Protected areas of occurrence (Zinner et al. 2013): in Lao PDR: Dong Phou Vieng, Xe Bang Nouan, Xe Pian, Dong Hua Sao National Biodiversity Conservation Areas and Bolaven Southwest Proposed National Protected Area.In Viet Nam: Cat Tien, Yok Don, Chu Mom Ray, Kon Ka Kinh National Parks, Ta Kou Nature Reserve and Chu Prong Proposed NR.In Cambodia: Virachey National Park, Veun Sai forests, Mondulkiri Protected Forest, Lomphat Wildlife Sanctuary, Phom Prich Wildlife Sanctuary, Seima Protection Forest, Phom Nam Lyr, and Snoul Wildlife Sanctuaries.

rationale: There is no information on global abundance or trends in abundance, but True’s Beaked Whales are locally common in the western North Atlantic (see Supplement for definitions). Plausible categories range from Near Threatened (NT) to Least Concern (LC). Least Concern is chosen as the appropriate category, given that regular sightings suggest of True’s Beaked Whales are common in some parts of their known range.
habitat: The biology of True’s Beaked Whale is poorly known. They inhabit deep, offshore, temperate waters. Along the US eastern coast, nearly all beaked whale sightings occur in water deeper than 1000 m (McLellan et al. 2018). In surveys conducted by the US National Marine Fisheries Service in 2018 and 2019, sightings of True’s Beaked Whales occurred over an average seafloor depth of 2,425m (±305m, n=171 sightings; Cholewiak et al. 2021). Dive data collected from a digital acoustic recording tag placed on one animal for 13 hours documented 9 foraging dives, with a maximum dive depth of 1037m (±89.6m) (Cholewiak, pers obs.). In the eastern North Atlantic, these whales are sometimes observed in the deep water of the Bay of Biscay (Robbins et al. 2019). Little is known about their diet. Hernandez-Milian et al. (2017) reported that 102 of 104 prey remains identified from two adult females that stranded separately in Ireland were small (75% < 100 mm) fish; 2 unidentified cephalopods were also present. The fish identified included 23 species of at least 13 families of mostly bathy- or meso-pelagic forms, usually found in waters 200-800 m deep.
threats: Little specific information is available on threats to True’s Beaked Whales.There has never been a directed fishery for this species. Drift gillnets and longlines (both active and abandoned) are abundant and widespread in the ocean, and mesoplodonts, including True’s Beaked Whales, are known to become entangled and drown due to incidental bycatch (Nishimura and Nishiwaki 1964, Julian and Beeson 1998, Waring et al. 2009).Beaked whale including True’s Beaked Whales were taken between Georges Canyon and Hydrographer Canyon in a pelagic drift gillnet fishery that operated in US waters between 1989 and 1998. The fishery was permanently closed in 1999. This has eliminated the only reported source of incidental fishery mortality for this species in the western North Atlantic, but one fishery-related mortality from New York was reported among six animals that stranded between 2013–2017 off the northeast US coast (Hayes et al. 2020). As of 2020, total U.S. fishery-related mortality can likely be considered to be insignificant and approaching zero (Hayes et al. 2020).In recent years, there has been increasing evidence that loud underwater sound, such as from active sonar and seismic operations, can be harmful to beaked whales (Cox et al. 2006). In particular, the use of mid-frequency active sonar from naval vessels has been implicated in numerous atypical mass strandings of beaked whales, including several Mesoplodon species (Balcomb and Claridge 2001, Wang and Yang 2006, D’Amico et al. 2009, Filadelfo et al. 2009). The exact cause of the strandings is unknown, but stranded individuals sometimes suffer from chronic and acute tissue damage due to in vivo formation of gas bubbles, possibly resulting from decompression sickness (Frantzis 1998, Jepson et al. 2003, Fernández et al. 2005).Ingestion of plastic in the ocean by marine organisms is a widespread and increasing problem, and possibly a significant cause of mortality among cetaceans, especially beaked whales (Simmonds 2012, Fossi et al. 2018, Lusher et al. 2018). The specific threats include macroplastic items that can physically block the digestive tract and lead to death (Secchi and Zarzur 1999), and microplastics (<5 mm; Baulch and Perry 2014, Lusher et al.2015) that can leach toxic chemicals (Baini et al. 2017). Plastics have been found in the digestive tracts of stranded True’s Beaked Whales (Gassner et al. 2005, Lusher et al. 2015).Organochlorine residues have been identified in other mesoplodonts (see Miyazaki et al. 1987, Bachman et al. 2014, Anezaki et al. 2016) and is a health hazard of unknown significance. However, the residue levels in beaked whales are much lower than in other small cetaceans (Cockcroft 1999).Mesoplodonts are relatively small whales that normally live far offshore; mortality from ship strikes would be difficult to document, but some possible cases have been reported (Waring et al. 2009).Predicted effects of global climate change on the marine environment may affect True’s Beaked Whales, although the nature and severity of impacts are unclear (Learmonth et al. 2006).
population: There are no estimates of global abundance or trends for True’s Beaked Whales. They are cryptic and skittish in the field and difficult to distinguish from congeners (M. bidens, M. densirostris and M. europaeus). However, sightings have become regular in some parts of their range (Cotter et al. 2019, McLellan et al. 2018, Cholewiak et al. 2021.) such that for a beaked whale, the species is common (see Supplement for definitions). An abundance estimate of 10,107 (CV=0.27) Mesoplodon spp. beaked whales was generated from two vessel surveys conducted in U.S. waters of the western North Atlantic during the summer of 2016 (Hayes et al. 2020). The abundance estimate for True’s Beaked Whales from these surveys was 2,562 (CV=0.28; Palka 2020).
range: Knowledge of the geographic range of True’s Beaked Whale comes almost entirely from stranding records. The northernmost records of stranded individuals in the western North Atlantic are from the Isles de la Madeleine, Gulf of St. Lawrence, Canada (Einfeldt et al. 2019) and St. Anne’s Bay, Nova Scotia (Moore 1966). The southernmost stranding was from Flager Beach, Florida (Moore 1966). MacLeod (2000) reported, without details, a record from Bermuda. There is also an unconfirmed record from San Salvador, Bahamas (Anon. 1981). In the eastern North Atlantic, specimens are known mainly from Ireland, with 13 strandings between 1899 and 2014 (Coombs et al. 2019). Other strandings include: Kearvaig Bay, Scotland (Kitchener et al. 2020); and Bidart, France (Barriety 1962). It has been recorded as far south as Islas Canarias and the Azores (Aguilar de Soto et al. 2017, Steiner et al., 1998, Vonk and Martin 1988). A purported stranding from the Outer Hebrides was a misidentified Ziphius cavirostris (Herman, 1992) as was another one from the Mediterranean Sea (Öztürk et al. 2016). Between known stranding locations in the eastern and western North Atlantic, a continuous at-sea distribution across the North Atlantic has been assumed, but not confirmed, for this species. Remote passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) data are starting to provide additional information on at-sea distribution and movements. Analyses of PAM data collected along the shelf break of the US eastern seaboard from 2016-2019 detected True’s Beaked Whales at six sites from Heezen Canyon off Georges Bank, through Wilmington Canyon, Delaware (Cohen et al. 2022).  Seasonal variation in detection rates were observed, with lowest rates of detection during fall months. True’s Beaked Whales were not acoustically detected at five sites from Cape Hatteras south to Blake Spur, off central Florida (30˚N, 76.5˚W) suggesting that they are distributed primarily north of Cape Hatteras in the western North Atlantic. The majority of the strandings are also north of Cape Hatteras.
conservationActions: The species is listed in Appendix II of CITES. Research is needed to identify and assess the impacts of threatening processes on these whales. True’s Beaked Whales are also covered by the Agreement on the Conservation of Small Cetaceans of the Baltic, North East Atlantic, Irish and North Seas (ASCOBANS) and the Agreement of the Conservation of Cetaceans in the Black Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Contiguous Atlantic Area (ACCOBAMS). The species is also listed in the Memorandum of Understanding Concerning the Conservation of the Manatee and Small Cetaceans of Western Africa and Macaronesia (Western African Aquatic Mammals MoU).

rationale: Bradypus tridactylus is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution. The species is affected by habitat loss due to deforestation resulting from land use change and urban sprawl. However, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category, as deforestation rates are not as high as in other parts of the Amazon. A reassessment will be necessary if rates of deforestation increase within its range.
habitat: Bradypus tridactylus is found in lowland and montane tropical moist forest. In Suriname and French Guiana the species has not been observed in mangroves, but it occurs in the swamp and marsh forests immediately adjacent to them (M. Pool pers. comm. 2022; B. de Thoisy pers. comm. 2022). It has been recorded on tepuis (table-top mountains). Adult sloths are light to dark grey with a unique pattern of darker areas. The head and throat range in colour from white to orange-yellow. Males can be distinguished from females by their dorsal patch of shorter hairs consisting of a central black line pattern in combination with orange-yellow hair. This dorsal patch has a unique pattern for each individual. The dorsal patch only forms around the age of around one year prior to which the animals cannot be sexually distinguished from external features. Both males and females reach reproductive age at three to six years. A single young is born after a gestation of six months (Taube et al. 2001).
threats: In Suriname, sloth densities seem to be higher in the coastal zones, and habitat loss due to urban sprawl and land conversion for agriculture are especially affecting this part of the country. In addition, sea level rise may affect the species in the future, as it occurs very close to the coast. There was a major drought in 2019 that significantly affected the species, as trees lost their leaves, the main food source of pale-throated three-fingered sloths (M. Pool pers. comm. 2022). If droughts become recurrent due to climate change, this may become a threat to the species.In French Guiana the species occurs very close to the coast, but no signs of local disappearance have been observed there. However, human population is exploding along the Marowini River, and deforestation rates are very high there. It is probable that the species is locally declining in that area (B. De Thoisy pers. comm. 2022).In Brazil, deforestation is more frequent in the Amazon Basin, where this species does not occur. There is not much information about habitat changes within the range of B. tridactylus in this country, but it is estimated that the species lost 2% of its habitat within Brazil (N. Moraes-Barros pers. comm. 2022; P. Marques Santos pers. comm. 2022).
population: Population density estimates vary from 1.7 animals per km² in French Guiana (Taube et al. 1999) to 221 animals per km² in Manaus, Brazil (Chiarello 2008). At least 130 individuals were found in an isolated forest fragment of 0.07 km² during a recent rescue in Suriname (Pool et al. 2016).
range: Bradypus tridactylus occurs in the Guiana Shield region, from Venezuela south of the Orinoco (although its distribution crosses at the delta region) into northern Brazil (south to the Amazonas/Solimões), through to Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana. It does not occur south of the Amazon river. A recent review using molecular phylogeny pointed out that several specimens of B. variegatus were misidentified as B. tridactylus, particularly in north-central Brazil where the two species are sympatric (Moraes-Barros et al. 2011).
useTrade: This sloth is sometimes hunted for food, and its bones are used for medicinal purposes by some tribal peoples in Suriname.
conservationActions: Bradypus tridactylus has been recorded from many protected areas.

rationale: Bradypus variegatus is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution including a large part of the Amazon forest, presumed large population, and its occurrence in a number of protected areas. Although there are threats, such as habitat loss due to deforestation, wildfires, illegal trade, and the use of wild individuals for selfie tourism, they are not thought to be causing significant declines in the global population. They may, however, do so at the local level and warrant listing of the species in a threatened category in regional Red Lists.
habitat: Bradypus variegatus has been recorded from a number of forest types including seasonal mesic tropical forest, semi-deciduous forest (inland Atlantic Forest), cloud forest, and lowland tropical forest. In Bolivia, it is frequently observed in Cecropia trees. It inhabits cacao (Theobroma cacao) plantations in Costa Rica (Vaughan et al. 2007, Ramirez et al. 2011). Indeed, regenerating forests, such as those disturbed by shade cacao plantations, might provide positive population growth for this species (Garcés-Restrepo et al. 2019). This sloth species produces one litter of one infant at intervals of at least 19 months (T. Plese pers. comm. 2010). Mating period varies depending on the year and geographical region, but occurs mainly in spring (i.e., from July to November in South America and from February to May in Central America).The species has the ability to withstand habitat changes (Queiroz 1995). It can be considered as synanthropic; individuals that lose their habitats partially or totally are able to use the resources offered by vegetation fragments in urban areas (Bezerra et al. 2020, Andrade et al. 2020), both in preserved or restored areas (parks, reserves) and those used for urban afforestation. This fact refers mainly to the Atlantic Forest region of Brazil, as it has become a very critical environment for the survival of B. variegatus due to the high degree of anthropization related to the growth of numerous cities along the coast of Brazil.
threats: As for other species, severe habitat degradation and fragmentation seems to be the main threat to Bradypus variegatus. Some subpopulations, especially in Colombia and the Atlantic Forest in Brazil, are declining due to deforestation leading to severe habitat degradation and fragmentation. This is particularly true for the subpopulation of the Atlantic Forest, where forest cover within its distribution in the Biome does not exceed 33% (P.M. Santos pers. comm. 2021).
