Additionally, deforestation in the Biome increased by more than 20% in the period 2018/2019 (SOS Mata Atlântica 2020), which could result in additional population declines. In Brazil, the estimated habitat loss that occurred within the species' EOO was 13.65% (P.M. Santos, pers. comm. 2022), in 32.28 years, approximately 3 generations (Pacifici et al. 2013). In Bolivia, the agro-industrial expansion was accompanied by large forest fires in 2019, 2020 and 2021, which affected around 5 million hectares. Although their impact on sloths has not been quantified, there are reports of sloths that died burned or were found suffocated.Furthermore, sloths are hunted by local indigenous communities. Wild-caught individuals, especially offspring, are sold as pets to tourists in Colombia (Moreno and Plese 2006) as well as in Bolivia (E. Aliaga-Rossel pers. comm. 2021) and Honduras (M. Turcios pers. comm. 2021). This illegal trade is increasing and represents a cause of concern due to its impact on the wild populations. The species is handled by tourists in Central and South America, including the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon, as an attraction for the “selfie” market (Carder et al. 2018).Mortality on roads also occurs. For instance, the increase in paved roads in Bolivia has resulted in a high mortality of brown-throated three-toed sloths in some tropical areas (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021). The lowest levels of genetic diversity of the species were observed in the Atlantic Forest; they were similar to the levels observed in the Critically Endangered Bradypus pygmaeus (Silva et al. 2018).
population: Population densities of B. variegatus have been estimated at 2.2 to 6.7 animals per hectare in the Brazilian Amazon (Queiroz 1995), 0.5 to 0.7 animals per hectare in the Atlantic forest of northeastern Brazil (Andrade et al. 2020), 8.5 animals per hectare in Panama (Montgomery and Sunquist 1975), 0.6 to 4.5 animals per hectare in the tropical dry forest of Colombia (Acevedo and Sanchez 2007) and 0.7 animals per hectare on Isla Palma, Valle, Colombia (Carvajal-Nieto et al. 2013). No demographic information is available from the remaining area of distribution. Bradypus variegatus is commonly found in public squares, where densities can reach 12.5 animals per hectare (Manchester and Jorge 2009).Recent phylogeographic studies reveal that B. variegatus from the Central American, Western Amazon and Atlantic forests constitute distinct and unique evolutionary units that are distinguishable by molecular and morphological traits. More recent molecular studies indicate the existence of four to six genetically differentiated haplogroups (Silva et al. 2018, Ruiz-Garcia et al. 2020). Atlantic forest populations have been isolated from Amazonian populations for thousands of years (late Pleistocene) and should be regarded as an evolutionary significant unit, distinct from the Amazonian clade (Silva et al. 2018).
range: Bradypus variegatus ranges from Honduras in the north, through southern Central America. In South America, it ranges from Colombia into western and southern Venezuela, and south into Ecuador, eastern Peru and Bolivia, into Brazil and northern Argentina (where it is now considered to be extirpated). Its distribution overlaps with B. torquatus in the central part of the Atlantic forest (Hirsch and Chiarello 2012). In Brazil, the species currently occurs in forested areas of the Amazon, Atlantic forest, and possibly in the contact zones between these biomes and Cerrado. There are historical records of B. variegatus in the Caatinga biome (Moraes-Barros unpublished data 2010). B. variegatus was recently recorded for the first time in the Cerrado sensu stricto, in Minas Gerais State, Brazil (Garcia et al. 2017).There are no confirmed records for B. variegatus in the Pantanal biome of Brazil or Bolivia, but the species might occur in the contact zones between this biome and the Amazon forest to the north. Additional field studies are necessary in order to properly define the current species distribution in the Cerrado, Caatinga and Pantanal.The southernmost distribution of this sloth in Brazil was reported by Cabrera (1957) as the state of Rio Grande do Sul, which could, however, not be confirmed (Gardner 2007). It is historically absent from the state of Santa Catarina (Brazil) and northeastern Argentina; the southernmost confirmed record of the species is near Londrina, in the state of Paraná, Brazil, but today it is considered extinct in this state (Mikich and Bernils 2004). The last record from Argentina was collected in Jujuy province and dates back to 1916 (Vizcaíno et al. 2006), but field studies specifically aiming at this species are lacking from this country. Bradypus variegatus is found from sea level to at least 2,500 m asl (Ureña et al. 1986, Allgas et al. 2015).
useTrade: In Brazil, especially in the northeastern region and in the Amazon, and in Colombia the common sloth is hunted and sold in public markets as food, medicine, and as a pet species. The illegal trafficking of the species seems to be increasing in Bolivia, where it is sold as a pet or exhibited in private gardens. This seems to be a common practice although it is illegal to keep wildlife as a pet (Presidencia del Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia 2021). In several touristic sites, B. variegatus is used by locals to entertain visitors.
conservationActions: Bradypus variegatus is present in many protected areas. It is included in CITES Appendix II. The species is listed as Endangered in Honduras (Wildlife Conservation Society 2021).

rationale: Choloepus didactylus is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population and its occurrence in a number of protected areas. The species is affected by several threats, especially habitat loss due to wildfires and land use change. However, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Choloepus didactylus is found in tropical moist lowland and montane forest. In Suriname and French Guiana it does not occur in mangroves. Two-toed sloths have nocturnal and solitary habits. Gestation length seems to be approximately 10 months (Eisenberg and Maliniak 1985) but estimates are quite variable.There is little information on the diet of wild individuals (Chiarello 2008). A rather unusual observation in the Amazon of north-eastern Peru recorded an adult individual descending to the forest floor to feed on a human latrine (Heymann et al. 2011).
threats: The species is affected by habitat loss due to deforestation for large-scale agriculture, logging, exploration for mining and other activities, and urban sprawl (especially in Suriname). In Brazil, habitat loss within the species' extent of occurrence (EOO) as a result of the increase of pasturelands and soybean crops has been estimated at 9.4% (P.M. Santos pers. comm. 2022).It is also affected by wildfires, which can kill the animals or affect them indirectly through habitat loss. The species is illegally sold as a pet species in several parts of this range, but the impact of this activity is difficult to quantify.Because they are usually found high in the canopy, motionless and virtually invisible, they are not as commonly hunted as armadillos or anteaters, and there are taboos against their consumption by some native groups. They are probably hunted opportunistically, but there is no serious bushmeat trade.
population: In French Guiana, C. didactylus has been found at densities of 0.9 animals per hectare (Taube et al. 1999). In the Brazilian Amazon, estimated densities range from 0.13 individuals per hectare (Manaus region) to 0.88 animals per hectare in the flooded forests (Mamirauá Reserve; Queiroz 1995, Chiarello 2008).There is evidence suggesting a differentiation between western and eastern populations; the diploid numbers range between 2n = 52–54 and 2n = 64–65 (Moraes-Barros 2018). A taxonomic reevaluation is needed to ensure the proper conservation of the species.
range: Choloepus didactylus ranges through Venezuela (the delta and south of the Río Orinoco) and the Guianas (French Guiana, Guyana, and Suriname) south into Brazil (Maranhão state west along the Rio Amazonas/Solimões) and west into the upper Amazon Basin of Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. Additional visual records from southeastern Pará State, Brazil, need to be confirmed. Its southern limit in the western Amazon of Brazil is unclear. It occurs in the southern departments of Colombia, with its northern limit being the departments of Meta and Guainía. It ranges from sea level up to 2,400 m asl (Britton 1941).
useTrade: Choloepus didactylus is probably hunted opportunistically, but there is no serious bushmeat trade. The illegal trafficking of the species seems to be increasing in Bolivia, where Choloepus didactylus is captured and sold as a pet. Although it is illegal to keep wildlife as pets (Presidencia del Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia 2021), this practice seems to be increasing.
conservationActions: Choloepus didactylus is present in many protected areas.

rationale: Choloepus hoffmanni is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and its occurrence in a number of protected areas. The species is affected by several threats, especially ongoing deforestation, wildfires, hunting, and illegal trade. It is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category at the global level. However, some subpopulations could potentially be assessed as Near Threatened or Vulnerable. In Brazil, for instance, the species is listed as Near Threatened.
habitat: Choloepus hoffmanni is largely found in lowland and montane tropical forest, both deciduous and mixed-deciduous. In Central America, it occurs in evergreen and semi-deciduous tropical moist forest, as well as in secondary forest, but it is rare or absent in lowland dry forest. In Costa Rica, it is able to use cocoa plantations (Theobroma cacao) as habitat (Vaughan et al. 2007, Peery and Pauli 2012) and frequently ventures into relatively open pastures in search of isolated feeding trees (Vaughan et al. 2007). In Nicaragua the species has been observed in dry grassland with thorny shrubs and trees (Genoways and Timm 2003).These sloths are rather solitary. Preliminary studies in Honduras using camera traps have shown that their activity budgets consist of sleeping (61.3%), feeding (19.4%), preening (16.1%), and defecating (3.2%) (Martínez et al. 2020).In cocoa farms of Costa Rica, the mating system involves a mixture of polygyny with promiscuity, the sex ratio is female-biased and male home ranges vary from 1.1 to 139.5 ha (Peery and Pauli 2012). Their herbivore-omnivore diet consists mainly of leaves, fruits and sap of some trees. In the tropical moist forests of Honduras, they feed on Cecropia sp. and Inga oerstediana (Martínez et al. 2020).Further studies are needed to ascertain the existence of genetic differentiation among subpopulations or subspecies (Ruiz-Garcia et al. 2018).
threats: Some subpopulations, especially those in Colombia, Central America, Bolivia and Brazil, are declining due to severe habitat degradation and fragmentation. In Honduras, this habitat degradation is due to extensive cattle ranching and agricultural crops (Martínez et al. 2020, Turcios-Casco et al. 2020). In Bolivia, it is related to large wildfires to clear areas for the expansion of agricultural crops (E. Aliaga-Rossel pers. comm. 2022). The wildfires may kill the animals directly (through burning or suffocation by the smoke) or affect them indirectly through habitat loss.In Brazil, the few known occurrence records for Choloepus hoffmanni come from the Amazon’s arc of deforestation, responsible for 75% of the total deforestation in the biome. In Brazil, habitat loss within the species' EOO as a result of the increase of pasturelands and soybean crops has been estimated at 28% in 3 generations (P.M. Santos pers. comm. 2021; according to Pacifici et al. 2013, generation length is 14 years).These sloths are also hunted by indigenous communities. Wild-caught individuals, especially offspring, are sold as pets to tourists in Colombia (Moreno and Plese 2006) and Honduras (Martínez et al. 2020, Turcios-Casco et al. 2020). This illegal trade is increasing and represents a cause of concern due to its impact on the wild population. Individuals inhabiting small forest patches of fragmented forests may fall victims of domestic dogs or other terrestrial predators (Sibaja-Morales and Cartín-Núnez 2017). In agroforests in Costa Rica, Hoffmann’s Two-toed Sloths are exposed to pesticides. Electrocution is also an increasing cause of concern in urban areas of Costa Rica (A. Aguilar-Borbón, pers. comm. 2022).
population: Choloepus hoffmanni occurs at densities of 1.05 animals per hectare on Barro Colorado Island, Panama (Montgomery and Sunquist 1975). It has been found at densities of 0.3 to 1.5 animals per hectare in the Andean region of Colombia, while densities in the lowlands of northern Colombia were 0.2 to 0.83 individuals per hectare (Alvarez 2004, Acevedo and Sanchez 2007).
range: Choloepus hoffmanni has two disjunct subpopulations. The northern subpopulation ranges from northern Honduras south into northwestern Ecuador and western Venezuela. The northernmost record was described by Martínez et al. (2020) in Los Naranjos in Colón department, Honduras. The southern subpopulation is found from north-central Peru through extreme western Brazil (south-western Amazonas, Rondônia, Acre and Mato Grosso states) to northern Bolivia. Its range within Brazil remains unclear, and further surveys are needed. There is a doubtful, outlying record for this species from the Rio Aripuanã, Mato Grosso state, Brazil (Fonseca and Aguiar 2004). There is another outlying and more recent record for the species for the region of Cristalino, in northern Mato Grosso, Brazil (Rocha et al. 2012). However, since this record was based on visual detection only and the authors did not provide pictures or a detailed description of pelage coloration of the sighted sloth, the validity of this record should be considered with care until further information could confirm it.This species ranges from sea level to 3,300 m asl in Costa Rica; up to 1,925 m asl in Panama; and up to 1,150 m asl in the southern Andes of Venezuela. In Colombia, the species is found in the biogeographical regions of the Andean zone, Caribbean and Chocó, more specifically in the departments of Cauca, Chocó, Cundinamarca, Nariño, Quindío, Sucre, Valle del Cauca, and Santanderes from sea level up to 3,200 m asl (Alberico et al. 2000, Moreno 2003, Morales-Jiménez et al. 2004, Acevedo and Sanchez 2007).
useTrade: In some parts of its range, C. hoffmanni is hunted for food and to be sold as a pet to tourists. For example, two thirds of the records known from Honduras correspond to animals confiscated from illegal trade, ex situ conservation centres (most of them from illegal trade), skins from hunted animals, and animals promoted to be sold to tourists (Martínez et al. 2020, Turcios-Casco et al. 2020).For some indigenous cultures, it is among the primary prey (Voss and Fleck 2017).
conservationActions: Choloepus hoffmanni is present in many protected areas. Further research is needed to establish whether there are taxonomic differences between the two disjunct populations. The species is listed as Endangered in Honduras (Wildlife Conservation Society 2021).

rationale: Myrmecophaga tridactyla is widespread geographically, but there have been many records of population extirpation, especially in Central America (where it is considered the most threatened mammal) and the southern parts of its range. The low reproductive rates, large body size, along with threats to habitat loss and degradation in many parts of its range, have proved to be significant factors in its decline. The Giant Anteater is currently listed in a threat category in virtually all regional and national Red Lists. A population loss of at least 30% over the past 10 years has been estimated based on local extinctions, habitat loss, and deaths caused by fires and road kills. Based on this decline and past threats that are still ongoing today, it is likely that the population has suffered an overall reduction in population size of at least 30% but less than 50% over the last three generations (suspected to be around 21 years; Desbiez et al. 2020). Because of the real threats to this species and the noticeable declines, a precautionary assessment of Vulnerable is given. More data and population monitoring are required for this species, and a reassessment is recommended as soon as additional information becomes available.
habitat: This terrestrial anteater is found in tropical moist forest, dry forest, mangroves, swamp and marsh forests, savanna habitats and open grasslands. It has also been reported from the Gran Chaco (Meritt 2008, Noss et al. 2008, Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021), timber plantations (Kreutz et al. 2013), and areas in regeneration after having been used for agriculture and cattle ranching (Martinez et al. 2020). Recent camera trap data suggest that the species may be more abundant in areas of upland forest in the Brazilian Amazon than previously thought (Prestes et al. 2022). Giant anteaters require large areas (>10 km2) for their survival (Noss et al. 2010), which should contain forested patches (Giroux et al. 2021). Genetic analyses suggest that the Pantanal and Cerrado subpopulations share similar genes (Miranda et al. 2022). The establishment of forested corridors between biomes is thus fundamental for this habitat generalist.Animals are generally solitary. Once per year, the female gives birth to a single young. Gestation length is 171 to 184 days (Bartmann 1983, Patzl et al. 1998, Knott et al. 2013). The mother carries the offspring on its back for approximately six months. Data from captive animals in European zoos show several females reproducing for the first time at 18-22 months, and the oldest known reproductive captive dams were 20-24 years old (unpublished report provided by I. Schappert). For wild females, sexual maturity is usually indicated as being around 2 years. Population data of wild giant anteaters are limited. A giant anteater baseline population viability model built using multi-data sources estimated the age at first breeding at 2 years, maximum lifespan at 15 years, and generation length at around 7 years (Desbiez et al. 2020).
threats: Myrmecophaga tridactyla is at risk from habitat loss in parts of its range, and this is a significant threat to Central American populations in particular. Where this species inhabits grassland habitats (especially where termite mounds can be found at high densities) it is particularly susceptible to fires. Although they are a natural process in part of the species range, these fires have increased in intensity and frequency. In addition, intentional wildfires to transform forests and grasslands to pasture management for cattle as well as land use change for agroindustry areas to plant soybeans and other crops are increasing in several countries, especially in Brazil and Bolivia, and the number of giant anteaters burned is high (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021).The subpopulation in the Pantanal of Brazil has suffered significant declines due to the direct and indirect effects of intentional fires. One study estimated that the wildfires in 2020 alone killed over 220,000 giant anteaters (Thomas et al. 2021). Although this number might be an overestimate considering the low population density of giant anteaters in the Pantanal, there is no doubt that the impact on the Pantanal subpopulation has been significant. The genetic implications of the significant declines in this subpopulation need to be assessed. The loss of suitable habitat has also led to an increase in disease transmission from cattle to giant anteaters.Urban sprawl is also a problem, as it is causing the species to appear on the streets of large cities; this has been observed in Brazil (Miranda et al. 2022). Roadkills are another significant threat; a population viability analysis estimated a 46% probability of extinction over 100 years in the Brazilian Cerrado (Desbiez et al. 2020).Animals are sometimes attacked by dogs. Giant anteaters are hunted for food throughout their distribution and are additionally hunted as a pest, for pets or for illegal and legal trade in some parts of their range. In Bolivia, there is evidence that illegal traffickers of jaguar fangs are also demanding giant anteater claws. In Guyana, they are killed for use as a medicine and for reasons of superstition, as some people believe they bring bad luck; there also seems to be some illegal international trade.
population: Myrmecophaga tridactyla is locally uncommon to rare. It seems, however, to be relatively common in the Argentine Chaco region, where its main predator is virtually extinct (Quiroga et al. 2016). In Suriname the species is regularly seen in the coastal rainforests, including urbanized areas. Habitat loss and degradation, roadkills, hunting, and wildfires have been substantially affecting the populations. There have been many records of population extirpation, especially in Central America and in the southern parts of its range.A Population Viability Analysis showed that vehicle collisions reduce stochastic growth rate of a subpopulation in Brazil by half (Desbiez et al. 2020).
range: Myrmecophaga tridactyla has been recorded from northeastern Honduras in Central America, south through the lowlands of South America to the Gran Chaco region of Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina. Within Central America, the species has disappeared from much of its range, with recent sightings generally confined to highland regions. The giant anteater is considered the most threatened mammal of Central America; it seems to be extinct in Belize, Guatemala, and possibly Costa Rica. It is not listed in Owen and Girón's (2002) checklist of mammals of El Salvador. In South America, this species seems to be extinct in Uruguay (Fallabrino and Castiñeira 2006) and in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil (Cherem et al. 2004). Its presence in Ecuador west of the Andes needs to be confirmed.
useTrade: In some areas, giant anteaters are hunted for food; this is especially true in the Caatinga area of Brazil. Their skin is used to manufacture harnesses and other leather products, as well as for medicinal use (Ferreira et al. 2013). In the Argentine Chaco, giant anteaters are sometimes captured to be used as pets or for the illegal trade. In Bolivia there is evidence that illegal traffickers of jaguar fangs were also offering to buy giant anteater claws (Nuñez and Aliaga-Rossel 2017). In Suriname, although it being a fully protected species under the law, there is evidence of this animal being hunted for food. Furthermore, McCain (2001) reported that individuals were captured in Honduras with the purpose of being sold as pets in Asia.
conservationActions: Myrmecophaga tridactyla is listed on Appendix II of CITES. It has been recorded from many protected areas. It is listed on several national Red Data lists, and is protected as a national heritage species in some provinces in Argentina. There is a need to regulate or to improve fire management practices, especially in cattle ranching practices, and within the regions of grassland habitat occupied by this species. Population and genetic data, as well as habitat use information, are needed, especially for areas that are being subjected to land use change.The species is listed as Regionally Extinct in the Brazilian states of Rio de Janeiro (Bergallo et al. 2000) and Espírito Santo (Chiarello et al. 2007). It is classified as Critically Endangered in Paraná (Instituto Ambiental do Paraná 2010) and in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil (Fontana et al. 2003). It has been successfully reintroduced in Iberá, Corrientes province, Argentina (Jiménez-Pérez et al. 2016). More recently, a reintroduction program has been initiated by Instituto Tamandua in the Pantanal of Brazil.

rationale: Tamandua mexicana is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, its tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Tamandua mexicana is found in tropical and subtropical dry and moist forest, including mixed deciduous and evergreen habitats. It can also be found in mangroves and grassland with some trees. It can survive in secondary forests and in disturbed habitats. The most common coloration is tan with a black vest on back and sides (Wetzel 1985) but uniformly tan individuals without vest also occur. Tamandua mexicana can move, feed and rest on the ground and trees (Lubin and Montgomery 1981, Montgomery 1985). This anteater feeds mainly on ants and termites, but it has also been observed consuming palm fruit (Attalea butyracea) (Brown 2011).The females give birth to one young at any time of the year (Reid 1997).
threats: Habitat loss, roadkills, wildfires and hunting are affecting this arboreal anteater, but the scope of these threats is unknown. In rural Ecuador, T. mexicana is persecuted due to the local belief that it attacks domestic dogs (Tirira 2007). It is used as a pet species in southern Mexico (Lira-Torres 2006), and indigenous people may hunt it for food in some areas (Espinoza et al. 2003, Méndez-Cabrera and Montiel 2007, Urquiza-Haas et al. 2011).
population: Tamandua mexicana is common in appropriate habitat. It is, however, considered uncommon in Ecuador (Tirira 2007, 2008). Population density estimates vary from 0.06 individuals per hectare in Costa Rica (Guariguata et al. 2002) to 0.13 individuals per hectare in Panama (Montgomery 1985). Its home range has been estimated at 25 hectares in Central America and Ecuador (Montgomery 1985, Tirira 2007) and 70 hectares in Panama (Eisenberg 1989).
range: Tamandua mexicana ranges from southern Mexico in the north of its range, through Central America as far south as northwestern Peru and northwestern Venezuela. It ranges from sea level to 2,000 m Asl, although most sightings have been recorded in areas below 1,000 m Asl (Cuarón 2005; Cuervo-Díaz et al. 1986; Eisenberg 1989; Morales-Jiménez et al. 2004; Tirira 2007, 2008; Nuñez-Perez et al. 2011). It has been introduced in Guanaja island and possibly other islands of Islas de la Bahía department, Honduras (M. Turcios-Casco pers. comm. 2022).
useTrade: In some parts of this range, this small anteater is used as a pet species or hunted for food.
conservationActions: The population of T. mexicana in Guatemala is listed on Appendix III of CITES. It is listed as Vulnerable in Mexico. The species has been recorded from several protected areas, among them Soberanía National Park (Panamá), Machalilla National Park, and the Ecological Reserves Arenillas, Cotacachi-Cayapas, Mache-Chindul and Manglares Churute (all in Ecuador; Tirira 2007).

rationale: Tamandua tetradactyla is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Tamandua tetradactyla is adaptable to a variety of habitats, including gallery forests adjacent to savannas, lowland and montane moist tropical rain forest (Eisenberg 1989), as well as mangroves and coastal environments, such as restingas (Molina 2021). It also occurs in degraded or disturbed forests, forest fragments, periurban forests and even urban settings. Typically, this solitary species has pale tan or golden fur with a black vest, but uniformly tan to black colouration also occurs (Wetzel 1985). Recent studies have shown that significant morphological differences exist between the subpopulations north and south of the Amazon River (F. Miranda pers. comm. 2013). It mainly feeds on ants and termites, but also attacks bee nests to eat honey (Emmons and Feer 1990). The female gives birth to a single young once per year (Silveira 1968).
threats: In some portions of its range the Southern Tamandua is hunted for meat, attacked by domestic dogs, or sold as a pet species (Aguiar and Fonseca 2008, Noss et al. 2008, Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021, D.A. Meritt Jr. pers. comm. 2010). Habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation, wildfires, and especially road traffic represent major threats in some portions of the range. In Uruguay, T. tetradactyla is affected by habitat loss due to land use change (Coitiño et al. 2013). Many southern tamanduas died during the severe wildfires in Bolivia in 2019-2021; some individuals that fled the fires were killed by poachers (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021).
population: Tamandua tetradactyla is a relatively common species. Although there are few estimates of population density for this species, they vary from between 0.43 and 9 individuals/km2 (Noss et al. 2010).
range: Tamandua tetradactyla is found to the east of the Andes from Colombia, Venezuela, Trinidad Island, and the Guianas (French Guiana, Guyana, and Suriname), south through Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay to northern Uruguay and northern Argentina. It ranges from sea level to 2,000 m Asl (Emmons and Feer 1990).
useTrade: Tamandua tetradactyla is sometimes (inappropriately) used as a pet species or consumed. Some indigenous communities in the north of Brazil use their meat for food (Leeuwenberg 1997, Bodmer and Pen Jr. 1997). In the Caatinga region of Brazil, the species is used for various purposes, including as food and medicine, as a pet species, for ornamentation, and for religious purposes (Alves et al. 2016). In Bolivia, its claws are sometimes illegally sold as handicrafts. The skin is sometimes used to make leather products. Tamanduas that are found in the wild are donated or sold to private persons or zoos, and may be involved in wildlife traffic.
conservationActions: Tamandua tetradactyla is present in many protected areas. Further systematic studies on T. tetradactyla are needed to investigate population densities and dynamics in different parts of its range. Studbooks for captive tamanduas exist in some range countries (Brazil: Projeto Tamanduá; international: ALPZA), and a population management plan has been established in AZA zoos.

rationale: Bradypus pygmaeus is listed as Critically Endangered under criterion B (CR B1ab(ii,iii)+2ab(ii,iii) as this species has a very restricted range, being found only on one very small island less than 5 km² in size, and there is likely a continuing decline in the quality of habitat and area of occupancy due to habitat degradation.
habitat: This is the smallest of all sloths, and is found both in mangrove patches and on the interior of Isla Escudo. Although previously thought to exclusively inhabit the red mangroves of the island, recent tracking studies have found the sloths on the interior of the island, in dense tropical rainforest. Because of the difficulty of censusing cryptic canopy mammals, their density and abundance in the thicker forests is unknown. Nothing is known about their reproduction, lifespan, home range, or diet, although it is suspected that it primarily, if not exclusively, feeds on mangrove leaves. Its population is likely larger than previously estimated, but is still limited due to its restricted habitat range.
threats: Although the island is uninhabited, there are seasonal visitors (fishermen, campesinos, lobster divers, tourists, and local people) who harvest timber to maintain wooden houses on the island. Preliminary studies suggest a reduced level of genetic diversity for pygmy sloths compared to its putative population of origin, the common sloth population from mainland Panama. This is expected, considering the history of species diversification and isolation on the island. However, signs of a more recent population bottleneck were also detected (Silva et al. 2018, N. Moraes-Barros pers. comm. 2013). These results highlight the need of a continuous evaluation of the population status, trends, and additional studies considering a possible scenario of endogamic depression if the (already low) population size decreases any further.Despite having been designated as a protected landscape through a governmental resolution in 2009, a number of domestic and international efforts have been mounted to develop tourism infrastructure on the island. The increased interest in using the island for touristic purposes exponentially increases the number of local visitors and tourists. On the other hand, the intentions of local indigenous people to build permanent settlements on the island have increased the number of permitted constructions, putting the pygmy sloths and their habitat at risk (D. Smith pers. comm. 2022). The current status of the island’s custody is vague; a governmental resolution, and thus the protected status of the island, cannot be revoked, but no government staff has been appointed specifically to enforce protection of the island. Ongoing disagreements between the local Ngäbe bugle Comarca, regional politicians, and the Panamanian government are further complicating long-term protection of the island and the pygmy sloths. Additionally, as pygmy sloths have become more widely recognized internationally, there is growing interest in collecting them for captivity.
population: There is no accurate information available on the total population size of Bradypus pygmaeus. Previous censuses only searched for sloths in mangroves, which comprise less than 3% of the island. Censusing cryptic, slow moving arboreal mammals in dense forest is challenging and limited; however, B. pygmaeus has been observed in the interior forests of the island. The population size is most likely between 2,000 and 2,500 individuals (D. Smith pers. comm. 2022). In any case, it is extremely small for an entire species (Voirin et al. 2015).
range: Bradypus pygmaeus is known only from Isla Escudo de Veraguas, in the islands of Bocas del Toro, Panama. Sloths on the younger islands of the Bocas del Toro archipelago are conspecific with Bradypus variegatus. Isla Escudo de Veraguas has a total area of approximately 4.3 km² and is about 17.6 km from the mainland of Panama. For the Red List assessment, the parameters area of occupancy (AOO) and extent of occurrence (EOO) are larger than the total island area because of the methods used to measure these (IUCN Standards & Petitions Committee 2022). Its AOO is 8 km² (total area within two occupied 2x2 km grid cells); and its EOO is 5 km² (based on a minimum convex polygon around the entire island), however this is raised to 8 km² because EOO should not be smaller than the AOO (IUCN Standards & Petitions Committee 2022).
useTrade: The species is not utilized. Although it was previously thought that locals would eat pygmy sloths, this was recently disproven.
conservationActions: Bradypus pygmaeus is endemic to a single island of Panama, which is protected as a wildlife refuge and is contained within the Ngäbe bugle Comarca. There is a need to improve the enforcement of this protected area. A comprehensive conservation plan is underway, bringing together the local community, wildlife authorities in Panama, and the national and international scientific community to protect the island, using the pygmy sloth as a flagship species.The pygmy sloth is listed on CITES Appendix II (Notification to the Parties 2013/052, 20 November 2013).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due to its relatively large range, and because there is no evidence that it is undergoing a decline that would warrant listing in a threatened category.
habitat: An inhabitant of igapó (seasonally flooded forest), but also seen in terra firme (rainforest), (Haugaasen and Peres 2005). Average group size at Lago Uauaçú was 3.3 individuals.
threats: There are no known major threats to this species at present.
population: Very little is known about the population status of this species. Apparently it prefers riparian forests. It has been recorded at population densities of 0.4 individuals/km² in terra firme forests and 1.8 individuals/km² in igapó (Haugaasen and Peres 2005).
range: This species occurs in the State of Amazonas, Brazil, south of the Rio Solimões between the Rios Purús and Juruá, south as far as the Rio Tapauá or even the Rio Pauiní (if the species reported to occur in between the Rios Tapauá and Pauiní does not represent a new form).
useTrade: This species is used as a pet in rural communities.
conservationActions: Present in Abufari Biological Reserve (233,864 ha) (Rylands & Bernardes 1989), RESEX Catuá-Ipixuna (217,486 ha) (Moraes et al. 2006) e Tefé National Forest (865,126 ha) (Rossato et al. 2011). Also present in the Maratu and Tatutu Amerindian Reserves.This species is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Myotis escalerai, a European endemic bat, has a relatively restricted distribution in southern Europe, where it is known from the Iberian Peninsula, the Balearic Islands (Majorca, Menorca, and Ibiza), and the northern slopes of the most eastern French Pyrenees and an isolated record from eastern France. The species is possibly present in Andorra and Gibraltar.It is a strict cave-dweller that is confined to a limited number of sites, any threat to roosts will probably imply large-scale adverse demographic effects. There is substantial evidence of significant loss or alteration of roosting sites, including several of major importance. The picture in Spain is unclear because in some areas moderate increases have been recorded, but year-to-year variations of bat numbers in caves typical of this species (Quetglas 2016) may affect the reliability of monitoring. The Spanish Red List assessed this species as NT (Quetglas 2007); more recently, M. escalerai was assessed as VU in France (UICN France et al. 2017) and in Portugal (A. Rainho pers. comm. 2022). Overall, there are elements to suspect a past population reduction that may still be ongoing in part of the M. escalerai geographic range mostly due to a loss of roosting sites approaching, but not exceeding 30%, on which basis the species is assessed as NT in Europe approaching VU under criterion A2c.
habitat: Myotis escalerai is found in a variety of habitats and climatic conditions, from coastal arid zones to beech and pine forests in the mountains (e.g., Quetglas 2016). This is allowed by the existence of climate-adapted genotypes that are predicted to respond differently under climate change (Razgour et al. 2019). The species is a strict cave-dweller that may form large maternity colonies in caves or artificial underground sites, numbering up to > 1,000 females: the bats may hang to the cave walls or roost in crevices inside the cave (Quetglas 2016). Crevices in buildings may also be occasionally used. In winter, the bats seem to disappear in the caves, and the only two hibernacula known hosted ca. 180 bats; roost fidelity seems lower than in other cave-dwelling bats, judging from the interannual variation in roosting bats (Quetglas 2016).During the activity period (spring to fall), this species uses mainly both natural caves and similar man-made roosts such as mines and tunnels, although it has been found also in small holes in trees or even bridges. During the mating season (fall) it makes swarming at the entrance of caves together with other Myotis species.Little or nothing is known about the species' habitat selection, yet it is thought to be similar to M. nattereri; it hunts frequently in forest sites (Quetglas 2007). Myotis escalerai feeds on a broad range of arthropods, especially Lepidoptera, Diptera and Araneae, and much of its prey is not volant at night and is therefore likely taken by gleaning. Although its diet is very similar to that of M. crypticus, the diets of the two species overlap less in syntopy, probably due to a shift in foraging strategy since the amount of prey that does not fly at night is smaller in M. escalerai (Novella-Fernandez et al. 2020). The species is most probably sedentary, considering the absence of long-distance movements in Spain and Portugal reported before M. escalerai was recognized as a distinct species and at that time regarded as a regional characteristic of M. nattereri s.l. (Hutterer et al. 2005).
threats: Two large breeding colonies in caves known since the '80s have disappeared due to landslides or incorrect gating (Quetglas 2016), as have many others in buildings and other human constructions (J. Juste pers. comm.). In general, the species seems to be significantly threatened by roost loss, degradation or disturbance.
population: This is a widespread and quite abundant species in Spain (Quetglas 2007), but it is confined to a relatively small number of sites. Nurseries include several dozens to hundreds of females, up to 1,284 females (Ibáñez and Nogueras 2014). Over half of the Spanish subpopulation is concentrated in Andalusia and Levante (Quetglas 2016). The Andalusian subpopulation is increasing (J. Juste pers. comm.) and a moderately positive trend has also been observed in the Valencian Community (Machado Silvera 2017). The picture in Spain, however, is unclear because although in some areas moderate increases have been recorded, year-to-year variations of bat numbers in caves typical of this species (Quetglas 2016) may affect the reliability of monitoring. On the Balearic Islands, M. escalerai is frequent, but although several records are available for Majorca, only one nursery including few individuals and a male roost are known; in Menorca, two nurseries account for ca. 850 bats, and in Ibiza, the species is widespread (reviewed in Quetglas 2016). In Portugal, records previously identified as M. nattereri before M. escalerai was accepted as a valid species are now considered to be M. escalerai. It is widespread across the country (more abundant in the north) but the number of individuals is likely to be low and declining, and the subpopulations are scattered in a few locations (F. Amorim pers. comm.). In France, a decreasing trend is suspected, and the species is assessed as VU (UICN France et al. 2017).Overall, it is suspected that a past population reduction has taken place, and this may still be ongoing in part of the M. escalerai geographic range mostly due to a loss of roosting sites.
range: Myotis escalerai is endemic to Europe, where it is restricted to the Iberian Peninsula, the Balearic Islands (Majorca, Menorca, and Ibiza), the northern slopes of the most eastern French Pyrenees (Ibáñez et al. 2006, Evin et al. 2009, Salicini et al. 2011, 2013; Razgour et al. 2015), and with an isolated record from eastern France. The species is possibly present in Andorra and Gibraltar (and not included in the range map for the species).The highest known altitude recorded is 1,900 m asl (J. Juste pers. comm. 2022). The range of altitudes where this species can be found varies between 0 and 1,900 m asl. The AOO and EOO have not been estimated based on the available locality records, but they are expected to exceed the threshold for a threatened category.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: Myotis escalerai is protected by national legislation in the countries where it occurs. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the EUROBATS Agreement and the Bern Convention. It is listed under Annex IV of 92/43/EEC Habitats Directive. The species does not yet feature among those included in the Article 17 reporting made within the framework of this Directive and the 2013-2018 report still shows data for M. nattereri for Portugal, Spain and France. However, at least for the first two countries, the assessment mostly refers to M. escalerai since the other cryptic species, M. crypticus, has a very restricted range in Iberia and M. nattereri sensu stricto does not occur there. In Spain, the EU conservation status of M. nattereri s.l. according to Article 17, report is unfavourable - inadequate, whereas in Portugal this is unknown.The conservation of this species requires the strict protection of underground and overground roosting sites. A better assessment of its current distribution is also needed.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC) EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)In general, Myotis nattereri appears widespread and not particularly rare in much of its range. There is little information about population trends, but generally speaking, there is no decreasing trend at the European or EU scales, with an increasing trend detected by Haysom et al. (2013). On this basis, the species is assessed as Least Concern at both scales.It is worth mentioning, however, that M. nattereri is regarded as at risk in certain countries: for instance, in Finland, it is classified as EN (Hyvärinen et al. 2019), it is classified as NT in Sweden, and as CR in Moldova (where a new observation was made in the 2019-2021 monitoring campaign after 20 years of lack of records: Moldova 2021) and in Norway (Artsdatabanken 2021).Careful monitoring to produce estimates of population trends is strongly recommended for the many countries where such data are unavailable, as well as molecular analyses to unveil taxonomy and potential hybridization in regions of potential sympatry with M. crypticus or in the contact zones between such species.
habitat: Myotis nattereri forms maternity colonies in tree hollows, spaces beneath loose bark and in bat boxes, but also in crevices in buildings and bridges, and frequently in cattle stables as well as in hollow blocks. Nurseries number 30-80 individuals, but in buildings, they can include up to 200 females. It hibernates in underground habitats (caves, cellars and mines), usually solitary or in small clusters of 2-5 individuals (Simon et al. 2012), but > 300 bats hibernate in Nietoperek, Poland (EUROBATS 2019). The species is a foraging generalist that hunts by foliage gleaning and aerial hawking close to vegetation in many habitats such as meadows, pastures, orchards, broadleaved woods, open coniferous forests and riparian areas, which may be locally very important (reviewed in Kyheröinen et al. 2019). It also hunts inside sheds, where it detects copulating flies through passive listening and gleans them off the walls (Siemers et al. 2012).Radiotracking studies have shown that bats show different foraging ranges in different landscapes, but generally cover distances of a few km from the roost. In Germany, average distances of 1.5 km were found (Simon et al. 2004), while in the UK, the bats mostly foraged within 3 km of the roost, and the longest recording distance was 5.8 km (Smith and Racey 2008). The diet of this species is broad but is dominated by diurnal dipterans in summer (reviewed in Kyheröinen et al. 2019), whereas winter prey comprises much non-volant arthropod prey, Aranea, Isopoda and lepidopteran larvae (Hope et al. 2014). Myotis nattereri is deemed to be sedentary, but it might be a facultative migrant, and the longest seasonal movement recorded was 157 km in Germany (Hutterer et al. 2005).
threats: Simon et al. (2012) summarises the main threats to this species in Europe. These include roost loss due to abandonment of cattle husbandry (stable housing), but also renovation of buildings, bridges, and cattle stables used by these bats as roosts; agricultural intensification and the spread of pesticides; intensive forestry leading to the disappearance of suitable roost trees; loss of hibernacula due to collapse, closing or conversion of e.g. ice cellars, bunkers and other underground habitats, as well as disturbance to wintering roosting sites. The species is affected adversely by artificial illumination at night (Voigt et al. 2018) and road casualties (Fensome and Mathews 2016).
population: Myotis nattereri is widespread in Europe, but the overall population size is unknown, and the trend is uncertain for most countries. Among major range states outside the EU, Moldova and Belarus reported negative population trends (Moldova 2018, Shpak 2018), whereas it is rather stable in Ukraine (Ukraine 2018) and Russia (S. Gazaryan pers. comm. 2019). It has not been observed in Norway since 2010 (Henriksen and Hilmo 2015, Artsdatabanken 2021).According to the combined prototype European hibernating bat indicator (Haysom et al. 2013), a moderately increasing trend was observed in recent years, based on data from Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, Slovakia, and the United Kingdom. Although the population in France does not raise conservation concerns, its trend is unknown (UICN France et al. 2017). In the UK, the Natterer’s Bat Hibernation Survey showed statistically significant increases at the Great Britain level and in England and Wales, but no change in Scotland, possibly due to the small sample size considered (Bat Conservation Trust 2021). In Ireland, where the species is widespread but not common, the current population size and trends are unknown but assumed to be stable (Marnell et al. 2019).
range: Myotis nattereri sensu stricto is part of the M. nattereri complex, characterized by highly diverged lineages. The following components of the complex occur in Europe: M. escalerai (Ibáñez et al. 2006), M. crypticus (Juste et al. 2019), and Myotis sp. C (Puechmaille et al. 2012), the latter not yet formally described and endemic to Corsica. The range of altitudes where M. nattereri can be found varies between 0 and 2,000 m asl. The AOO has not been estimated, but based on the available locality records, it is expected to exceed the threshold for a threatened category.Myotis nattereri occurs across a broad European range: it is found north and east of the Alps, including the British Isles, Switzerland, France, Germany, Scandinavia, the Baltic states, the Balkans, the Carpathians and entire Eastern Europe up to the Urals in European Russia; it is considered to be endemic to the European region at present. However, the existence of hybrids in secondary contact zones between this species and the sibling Myotis crypticus as well as the lack of comprehensive molecular assessment across the entire range of the species makes the picture still unclear in certain regions.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: Myotis nattereri is protected by national legislation in most of the main range states. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the EUROBATS Agreement and the Bern Convention. It is listed under Annex IV of 92/43/EEC Habitats Directive. According to the 2013-2018 art. 17 reporting made within the framework of this Directive, the conservation status of this species in the EU is classified as unfavourable-inadequate in all Biogeographic Regions except the Continental and the Atlantic Regions, where it is favourable. However, the other cryptic species occurring in Europe are not assessed separately, so this evaluation has mixed data regarding all such species (for example, Iberian data were used, but in Iberia, only M. escalerai and M. crypticus occur).The preservation of this species requires strict protection of its underground and overground roosting sites, as well as the general conservation of habitat quality in forest, riparian and agricultural foraging sites, maintaining forest unevenness, decaying trees, as well as reducing the use of pesticides and artificial illumination.

rationale: The Azorean Bat (Nyctalus azoreum) is endemic to Europe, where it is restricted to the Azores Archipelago (Portugal), where it has a small population and range. The species' population has been estimated at between 2,000-5,000 individuals, and the most abundant subpopulation features < 1,000 individuals. The population is inferred to be undergoing continuing decline because of the disturbance and destruction of colonies, the loss and degradation of natural and semi-natural habitats, and pesticide use. There is no direct information on dispersal between islands, but genetic research suggests that dispersal is restricted, and so the population is precautionarily regarded as being severely fragmented. For these reasons, it may be approaching the Endangered category but at present, in the absence of more detailed population information, it is assessed as Vulnerable under criteria C2a(i) and B2ab(iii).
habitat: Nyctalus azoreum hunts on the wing in practically all habitats, including forests, pastures, water sites and human settlements, often ca.25 m above ground, favouring natural lagoons and urban areas with streetlights (Rainho 2021). However, detailed information on its foraging ecology and diet is unavailable. Roosts are found in trees, rock crevices in cliffs, and buildings (Rainho et al. 2002). Besides being active at night, bats also forage in the daytime, probably in response to the absence of diurnal avian predators.
threats: Human disturbance and the loss of roost sites are likely to be the main threats (Dechmann and Ruczynski 2020). Habitat loss and degradation, the use of pesticides, and the spread of exotic plant species may also have a detrimental effect on the species. It is suspected that the extreme scarcity of the species on Santa Maria is attributable to habitat loss and degradation. This species is particularly vulnerable to roost disturbance because it flies during the day, making colonies often easy to find (A. Rainho pers. comm.).
population: Previous population estimates of Nyctalus azoreum suggested that the overall population was somewhere between 1,750 (based on daytime counts) and 23,650 (night-time counts) individuals (Speakman and Webb 1993, in Dechmann and Ruczynski 2020). Surveys in 2002, 2003, and 2004 found the species to be quite abundant on São Miguel, Faial, Terceira, and São Jorge, but rare on Graciosa and extremely rare on Santa Maria. It is absent from Flores and Corvo (Rainho et al. 2002).There is no quantitative information on population trends, but it is suspected that the species may be declining in some islands because of habitat degradation, disturbance, destruction of or exclusion from roosts (both in trees and buildings). The total population is estimated at 2,000-5,000 individuals, and fewer than 1,000 individuals on São Miguel, where the species is most abundant (Cabral 2005). There is marked genetic differentiation between subpopulations on central and eastern islands in the archipelago, indicating that they have evolved in relative isolation for a long time (Salgueiro et al. 2004).
range: The Azorean Bat (Nyctalus azoreum) is restricted to the Azores Archipelago (Portugal), where it occurs on all islands except Flores and Corvo (Dechmann and Ruczynski 2020) from sea level to, at least, 1,150 m (Rainho 2021). The AOO (= 1,060 km2) was estimated using 2x2 km grid cells.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: Nyctalus azoreum is protected by national legislation in Portugal as well as by the Eurobats Agreement and Bern Convention. It is included in Annex IV of the EU Habitats Directive. An ongoing LIFE+ project (LIFE17 IPE/PT/000010) has, among its objectives, to increase the knowledge needed for the conservation of this bat species. This species needs substantial monitoring and ecological work to identify precisely population size, trends and conservation requirements. Its protection certainly implies the preservation of roosting and foraging sites, as well as the reduction of pesticide spread.

rationale: This European endemic species has an area of occupancy (AOO) of 400 km2, and has undergone a strong decline in habitat availability and quality. Its distribution is, overall, severely fragmented because the different subpopulations occur on oceanic archipelagos between which gene flow is extremely unlikely to exist. As such, the species qualifies as Endangered (EN B2a,b(iii)). Whilst the species' stronghold on Madeira has experienced a notable population decline, estimated to be over 20% in two generations (using a generation length of 5.2 years, as recommended by Pacifici et al. 2013), however, there is little information available regarding the situation of the species on the Canary and (even less so) on the Azorean islands. Therefore past and future rates of decline cannot be estimated, although the overall population size is suspected to be small, with less than 2,500 mature individuals. Therefore, Endangered (EN) under criterion C1 can not at present be applied.
habitat: The species forages over a wide range of habitats, including aquatic habitats, woodland, and farmland, as well as in parks and gardens (reviewed in Rocha 2020). It also feeds near streetlamps (D. Russo pers. obs.). The diet has not been analysed, but prey likely includes moths, small beetles, mosquitos, caddisflies, and flying ants, all caught on the wing. Nursery colonies often roost in wall cracks or under roof tiles but have also been found in bird nest boxes (reviewed in Rocha 2020).
threats: The species is exposed to significant habitat loss and degradation, probably including pesticide spread in agricultural sites. On Madeira, floods and mudslides as well as large-scale wildfires have affected adversely formerly important foraging sites. Roost disturbance, destruction, or renovation are also major threats. Such factors are especially serious as they affect small insular populations. Although this is a house-dwelling bat species, heavy urbanization is still unlikely to be tolerated and therefore also a risk since the Madeiran urban territory is rapidly developing. Finally, predation by domestic cats has been documented (Rocha 2015).
population: Although no exact estimates of population size are available, the overall number of mature P. maderensis individuals is likely < 2,500. A strong population decline is reported at least for Madeira. The subpopulation on the island is small and rapidly declining, following the large-scale events that adversely affected the species' habitat, such as floods and mudslides as well as the large-scale wildfires. Direct persecution, such as the exclusion of entire nursery colonies from human-made roosts, has been reported (S. Teixeira pers. comm.), and bat activity has declined by >80% in many key habitat sites on the island. The situation of Azorean and Canary Island subpopulations is practically unknown in terms of population size and trends, but the species is unlikely to be abundant on those islands.The population is considered to be severely fragmented because the different subpopulations occur on oceanic archipelagos between which gene flow is extremely unlikely to exist. This is supported by Teixeira et al. (2023), whose research classification each island subpopulation as separate Evolutionary Significant Units (ESUs).
range: This species is endemic to the European Macaronesian Islands (Spain and Portugal). In the Madeiran Archipelago, it is recorded from across Madeira and Porto Santo, but with only a single record from the Desertas Islands (Teixeira et al. 2023) in Portugal, and from a small number of records in the Azores Archipelago; the identity of pipistrelle bats in the Azores was uncertain, but it was first confirmed on Santa Maria Island based on molecular analysis (Trujillo and González 2011), with very small numbers of records now known from Corvo, Flores, Graciosa, Pico, Santa Maria, and São Jorge islands (Teixeira et al. 2023). In the Canary Islands, it is known from the western Canary Islands of La Palma, La Gomera, El Hierro, and Tenerife (Rocha 2020, Teixeira et al. 2023).All the recorded islands are regarded as separate locations (13 locations). It is found from sea level to 2,150 m on the Canary Islands, although it prefers lowlands on Madeira (Fajardo and Benzal 1999), where it is known up to 1,500 m asl (Rocha 2020). The AOO was estimated using 2x2 km grid cells.
useTrade: The species is not traded or used.
conservationActions: Pipistrellus maderensis is protected by national legislation in Portugal and Spain as well as by the Eurobats Agreement and Bern Convention. It is included in Annex IV of the EU Habitats Directive. It is one of the Eurobats' priority species for autoecological studies since very little is known about its ecology and even distribution and population size and trends. This species requires basic research to inform management, including distribution, a genetic assessment of subpopulations on the different islands, population size and trends, spatial ecology, and diet. Protection of roosting sites as well as known foraging habitats is paramount to preserving P. maderensis.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This species is considered to be endemic to Europe, although the identity of former subpopulations from West Asia require further taxonomic study. There is no evidence or suspects of significant declines across most of its range, and a stable trend was recorded in underground sites of countries that took part in the prototype European bat indicator project (Van der Meij et al. 2015). Consequently, the species is assessed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 Member States. No regional adjustment is applied at the EU level.
habitat: In summer, this species mainly roosts in deciduous trees, including rot cavities, woodpeckers’ holes, and other cavities such as those generated by a lightning strike in the main trunks or large branches. Roosts are usually located >5 m above ground but can sometimes be found close to ground level (reviewed in Ancillotto and Russo 2020). The species may also roost in buildings. Hibernacula are often caves but also human-made underground sites and only occasional tree cavities. Buildings are also often used both in summer and winter. This is mainly a forest forager that frequently gleans prey from the foliage or hunts on the wing. May also forage in gardens and parks, but typically trees are present at foraging sites. A recent study that was done in the Italian Apennines (Ancillotto et al. 2022) showed that high forest stands were the most preferred habitat type, whereas coppice, conifer stands, and pastures were the least preferred, and that trails and clearings were used as landmarks for commuting.Plecotus auritus typically covers short distances from the roost (e.g., max 1.6 km in the Italian Apennines: Ancillotto et al. 2022). The diet mostly consists of moths, but also scarabeids, crane-flies, and caddis-flies, along with other arthropods that are gleaned off the substrate such as diurnal flies, spiders, harvestmen or even isopods (reviewed in Ancillotto and Russo 2020). This is a sedentary species whose seasonal movements cover a few km (Hutterer et al. 2005).
threats: Colonies are put at risk by unsustainable forest management removing potential roost trees as well as destruction or renovation of buildings used for roosting. Other threats comprise predation by domestic cats, light pollution and pesticides whose indirect effects, such as the reduction in insect prey such as moths, may be significant (reviewed in Ancillotto and Russo 2020). However, there is no evidence of population decline for this species, and whether the above factors may or not have demographic implications for this species is unknown.
population: Plecotus auritus subpopulations can be assigned to three clades, probably resulting from postglacial colonisations that originated from Iberian and Balkan refugia: the Iberian clade (P. a. begognae), found south of the Ebro River in Spain, and a western” and an eastern clade found in the remaining mainland Europe (reviewed in Ancillotto and Russo 2020). No strong genetic differentiation characterises subpopulations across the Swiss-French Alps and Italy (Andriollo et al. 2018). The species mates in autumn at swarming sites, where genetic diversity is much higher than in the summer colonies, probably due to an extra-colony mating strategy at swarming sites (Veith et al. 2004). The species tends to be more common in the northern sections of its range and may be locally frequent.
range: Plecotus auritus has a typically Palearctic distribution, but following taxonomic revision (see Taxonomic Notes), it is endemic to Europe, with a range spanning from Iberia in the west to European Türkiye and the Ural Mountains in the east.The range of elevations where this species can be found varies between 0 and 2,350 m asl. The AOO and EOO have not been estimated, but based on the available locality records, they are expected to greatly exceed the threshold for a threatened category.
useTrade: This species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: It is protected by national legislation in most main range states, except Russia. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) and EUROBATS Agreement. It is included in Appendix II of the Council of Europe’s Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats (Bern Convention). It is also included in Annex IV of the EU Habitats and Species Directive. Important habitats are partially protected by Natura 2000 sites and national networks of protected areas.Although the species is not at risk, it may benefit from sustainable forestry in roosting areas to save potentially suitable trees from logging. Avoidance of light pollution and indoor confinement of domestic cats where this species is present, as well as restrictions in the use of agricultural insecticides, may favour its persistence.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)EU 27 regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)The most recent conservation status assessments at the national level available for Plecotus austriacus differ considerably among European countries. While the species is regarded as at high risk in England, with a population of ca. 400 individuals (Razgour 2020) and is classified as CR in Sweden (SLU Artdatabanken 2020) and Switzerland (Bohnenstengel et al. 2014), it is assessed as LC in France (UICN France et al. 2017) and as NT in Italy (Rondinini et al. 2022), Spain (Palomo et al. 2007), and Portugal (A. Rainho, in litteris). Art. 17 reporting under the 92/43/EC for years 2013-2018 provides a generally unfavourable/inadequate conservation status. The species has an area of occupancy (AOO) of 1,468 km2, which is less than the 2,000 km² threshold required for the Vulnerable (VU) classification under criterion B2. Although one (b) of the three additional conditions required is met, the species fails to meet the minimum requirement of two out of three additional conditions to qualify for VU status. Therefore, the species does not currently meet the criteria for VU status under criterion B2. The most likely picture is that a population decline is ongoing, as supported by the bat indicator implemented by Haysom et al. (2013). This decline approaches but does not overcome the 30% threshold. As such, the species is assessed as Near Threatened reaching criterion A2c.
habitat: The ecology of Plecotus austriacus is summarised by Razgour (2020), upon which much of the following description is based. This is a sedentary species that usually moves < 30 km between summer and winter quarters and up to 5 km from summer roosts to foraging sites (see also Hutterer et al. 2005). Habitat use varies significantly according to the geographic region considered.The species occurs in urban areas in Central Europe, in warm lowlands and unforested mosaic landscapes, while in Southern Europe it is also found in open forests and less associated with urban sites. Forests are also used in Slovakia, Germany, and Italy (D. Russo, pers. obs.). In the UK, habitat use varies according to reproductive conditions but in general, the species forages in semi-improved to unmanaged lowland grasslands (including meadows and marshlands), woody riparian vegetation, and broadleaf woodlands. In Central Europe, gardens, parks, orchards, streetlights, and towns are also used for foraging. While forests are avoided in certain areas such as Switzerland, they are used somewhere else (Germany and Belgium). Summer roosts often occur in buildings, but caves can be used in the south, while underground artificial and natural sites, as well as rock crevices, are used to hibernate. The diet is dominated by moths, captured on the wing in open spaces or along edges in low flights, but a small amount of diurnal prey is also caught, suggesting that gleaning may occur yet much more rarely than in Plecotus auritus (Razgour 2020).
threats: Loss of roosting opportunities in buildings during renovation and refurbishment works, intentional evictions, and closure of roost entrances are the main threats to this species. Disturbance in winter quarters (caves, tunnels, abandoned mines) by visitors/vandalism, pesticide use, and wood treatment in attics and roofs. It also suffers from a decline in insect abundance due to intensive agriculture, forestry, and horticulture (Simon et al. 2012). The species is sensitive to light pollution at roosts, commuting routes, and habitats (Voigt et al. 2018). Fragmentation of foraging areas and loss of linear structures that are utilized for commuting may impair habitats, especially around maternity colonies (Kyheröinen et al. 2019). At high risk of collisions with vehicles (Fensome and Mathews 2016). Climate change and severe weather such as droughts in the Mediterranean are also significant threats.
population: Based on counts at hibernacula, Haysom et al. (2011) estimated a decline in grey long-eared bat populations across Europe. In Germany and England, summer population densities of Plecotus austriacus have been estimated at 0.001, at 0.05 bats/ha in the Czech Republic. Population declines observed in Germany have been related to agricultural organochlorides, while changes in farming practices have probably been the cause of a 30-fold population decline in England in the past hundred years, where a colony crash related to adverse weather was also recorded due to an unusually cold winter (reviewed in Razgour 2020). In Britain, former estimates of a total population of 1,000 individuals are now seen as optimistic, given effective population size estimations of Ne=82 (63–112) and new comprehensive surveys, also carried out by e-DNA, suggesting that the true population size may be of ca. 400 bats.
range: Plecotus austriacus is endemic to Europe. Its distribution spans from the Mediterranean region, where it is relatively widespread, north to 51° and 53° N (Britain, Germany, and Poland), east to Ukraine, and the western and northwestern coasts of the Black Sea. The species has colonised several Mediterranean (Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, and the Balearic) islands, as well as, in the Atlantic, Madeira (reviewed in Razgour 2020).The area of occupancy (AOO; 1,468 km2) was estimated using 2x2 km grid cells. The range of altitudes where this species can be found varies between 0 and 2,250 m asl.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: Plecotus austriacus is protected by national legislation in most range states. There are also international legal obligations for the species' protection through the Eurobats Agreement and Bern Convention. It is included in Annex IV of the 92/43/EC Habitats Directive. According to the 2013-2018 art. 17 reporting made within the framework of the above-mentioned Directive, in the Alpine, Atlantic, Black Sea, Mediterranean, Pannonian, and Steppic biogeographic regions the conservation status is unfavourable-inadequate, in the Continental biogeographic region is unfavourable-bad, and in the Macaronesian biogeographic region (reported by Portugal only) is unknown (but all three prospect parameters are classified as poor).To conserve this species, roosts should be strictly protected and foraging sites should be carefully managed, including traditional farmland. Pesticides may cause direct mortality as well as prey decline, so their use should be limited or avoided where possible. The adverse effects of artificial lighting at night and road development should be mitigated.

rationale: The Sardinian Long-eared Bat is endemic to Europe, where it only occurs on Sardinia. Based on the systematic monitoring of known colonies, the species has undergone a well-documented, steep population decline by ca. 30% in one generation (7.6 years; Pacifici et al. 2013), and models predict a continuous decline in the next decades, with extinction likely occurring between 2040-2085 (Ancillotto et al. 2021). In 2022, the population numbered 150 mature individuals according to counts made at the few known nurseries (M. Mucedda pers. comm. 2023). There is no serious protection taking place, so the factors that have caused such a decline are likely to persist or worsen. On this basis, the species is classified as Critically Endangered (CR) under criterion C1.
habitat: The scarce information about the Sardinian Long-eared Bat’s ecology is reviewed in Kiefer et al. (2020). The species occurs in the karst region of central Sardinia. Females give birth to one pup in the second half of May in nurseries comprising 50–300 bats in caves or buildings. Males may roost in the same nursery sites, but they do so separately from females. Caves are typically surrounded by holm oak trees and juniper shrubs. The species hibernates in caves or buildings. Nothing is known about habitat preferences, diet, or spatial use.
threats: The species is highly threatened by roost disturbance, heatwaves and alteration of precipitation regime caused by climate change, and wildfires, often caused by humans and favoured by especially hot and dry summers (Ancillotto et al. 2021). There is no serious protection ongoing and if roosts are not strictly protected and wildfires are not effectively prevented, Sardinian long-eared bats will face extinction in the next few decades.
population: The species was first described in 2002 (Mucedda et al. 2002) and from then until 2020 the population showed a 4.01% mean annual decrease, crashing from ca. 950 individuals in 2003, to ca. 340 total population to be confirmed in 2020, overall decreasing by 63.4% in 17 years (Ancillotto et al. 2021). At present, the population numbers ca. 150 mature individuals according to monitoring data (M. Mucedda pers. comm. 2023). Between 2013 and 2020 the population experienced a ca. 30% decline (Ancillotto et al. 2021) and the negative trend is ongoing. The worst and best-case scenarios modelled by Ancillotto et al. (2021) predicted extinction between 2040 and 2085.
range: The Sardinian Long-eared Bat (Plecotus sardus) is endemic to the island of Sardinia, where it is restricted to the island's centre, from the coast to the interior, extending west to the Omodeo Lake (Kiefer et al. 2020). So far detected at 24 sites on the island, including 18 roosts and 6 sites where the species' presence was established by mist netting. AOO was estimated using 2x2 km grid cells. The range of altitudes where this species can be found varies between 0 and 1,030 m asl.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is included in Annex IV of the 92/43/EC Habitats Directive and is also protected under the Bern Convention and the EUROBATS Agreement. There is an urgent need for the strict protection of roosts and habitats used by this bat, but to date, no serious efforts have been undertaken. Research is also a priority: no habitat use study is available so protection of foraging sites is hampered by the lack of sufficient information. The species urgently needs ecological research aimed at developing and implementing an Action Plan.

rationale: The Canary Long-eared Bat (Plecotus teneriffae) is endemic to the Canary Islands (Tenerife, La Palma, and El Hierro). The population has shrunk since the 1950s and the decline is ongoing due to roost disturbance, pesticide spread and forest loss. Wildfires are also a major threat, and climate change will exacerbate their impact. There is no reason to believe that the declining population trend has halted or that the decline will reverse in the future. The endemic status of Plecotus teneriffae, along with the small area of occurrence (3,000 km2 or less) and the confinement to two locations, makes this species at serious risk. The overall population is small, with only three (small) maternity colonies previously known, one of which has recently disappeared. The population is considered to be severely fragmented. Surveys on La Palma showed, in 2012, an almost 50% reduction in distribution, and, in 2016, only six bats were observed. Trujillo (2007) wrote that the total population was estimated between 500 and 2,000 bats. Considering the above data, clearly suggesting a likely ongoing further, significant population decline, the current population probably numbers a few hundred mature individuals. The estimated Area of Occupancy (AOO) for the species, based on the only two remaining maternity colonies, is 8 km2. Moreover, the species' habitat has been considerably fragmented due to wildfires and the loss of roosting sites. Based on these factors, the conservation status of the species has been assessed as Critically Endangered under criterion B2ab(ii,iii,v).
habitat: Plecotus teneriffae uses a range of habitats, but it is primarily associated with pine forests (Pinus canariensis) and transition zones between pine forests and laurel forests or Fayal-Brezal heather, but also hunts to a smaller extent in mixed and laurel forests and other habitats (reviewed in Razgour 2020). It mostly hunts by foliage gleaning and, according to the limited data available, it mainly preys upon moths. The species roosts in crevices and uses volcanic tubes, caves, water mines, and abandoned buildings (Razgour 2020). Sedentary, P. teneriffae moves not more than tens of km between roosts (Hutterer et al. 2005).
threats: The Plecotus teneriffae population has declined since the 1950s when it was affected by aerial fumigation to control pests (Benzal and Fajardo 1999) and the decrease has continued due to roost disturbance, probably the use of pesticides in agriculture, and forest loss and fragmentation.Although wildfires are not mentioned explicitly as a threat in the (scarce) available literature, they are likely to be a serious problem for the main habitat (forest and woody vegetation) used by this species. The Canary Islands have been strongly affected by wildfires in the last decades. For example, in 2021 and 2022 wildfires ravaged forest areas on La Palma and Tenerife islands, and in 2006 ca.1,400 ha of forest burned in a large wildfire on El Hierro. Wildfires are predicted to exacerbate in the next years due to climate change-driven variations in weather (Carrillo et al. 2022). Occasional harvesting by private collectors has taken place in the past (Trujillo 2002).
population: Plecotus teneriffae has a small population size. Maternity colonies are typically small (10-30 bats). Only two maternity colonies are known, respectively in a cave on La Palma and on Tenerife islands. On La Palma, the species has shown a drastic decline and the above-mentioned maternity colony (the largest known, numbering 61 bats in 1988) has disappeared. Moreover, a survey carried out in 2012 on that island showed an almost 50% occurrence reduction and, in 2016, only six bats were captured (Trujillo 2012, 2016: in Razgour 2020). Trujillo (2007) wrote that the total population was, at the time of writing, estimated between 500 and 2,000 bats.
