(2010) indicated extremely low genetic diversity. Based on single gene fragments, Yang et al. (2012)  detected five haplotypes present in the population. A more recent study (Wang and Zhou, 2021) reported 11 haplotypes in the population. A study has established the whole genome sequence of R. brelichi using genome 2nd generation sequencing technology. The genetic diversity of Guizhou snub-nosed monkeys was found to be  extremely low (generally lower than other Rhinopithecus species, Zhou et al. 2016).
range: The Grey Snub-nosed Monkey is endemic to southwestern China, where it is restricted to the Fanjingshan National Nature Reserve in the Wuling Mts, Guizhou Province. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is smaller than 100 km² within the 419 km² National Reserve. The species’ area of occupancy (AOO) is ca 27.8 km² within a 41.1 km² area of the park (based on an analysis of the area of remaining suitable habitat that is accessible to the species; Guo et al. 2020). This has been calculated on the basis that certain parts of the park are either inaccessible to the species due to recently-installed infrastructure (e.g., an aerial tram) or because of lack of suitable habitat (Guo et al. 2020).There is another smaller nature reserve (the Yangxi Provincial Nature Reserve) close to the Fanjingshan National Nature Reserve, which is 218 km² in size and remains is largely unexplored. This would be the only other area where a population of Guizhou Snub-nosed Monkeys could exist, but its presence has never been confirmed here.
useTrade: This monkey is occasionally hunted for meat and use in traditional medicine.
conservationActions: This species is included in CITES Appendix I. It is also listed as a Category I species under the Chinese Wildlife Protection Act of 1989. The publication of the latest population sizes and group numbers by the reserve or the authorities is an urgent conservation priority.

rationale: Malagasy Giant Jumping Rat (Hypogeomys antimena) is endemic to Madagascar and is only found in two subpopulations within primary forest habitat of the Menabe-Antimena Protected Area. The species is assessed as Critically Endangered following recent estimated global population declines of 88% over a 12-year period (three generations for this species). Declines in the northern subpopulation are estimated to be as high as 92%. Due to recent deforestation data (2019), the species has an estimated extent of occurrence of 470 km². Habitat loss due to illegal land clearing for maize and peanut production are the predominant threats to the species. However, population declines are suggested to be occurring faster than the loss of forest itself, despite being one of the main drivers of the species’ population size.
habitat: This is the largest extant rodent in Madagascar. It inhabits dry deciduous coastal forest (mixed with baobabs) with a sandy floor permanently covered by dry leaf-litter. Animals live in monogamous social units and both sexes are territorial. The animals occupy a family burrow with a complex of tunnels. They are nocturnal, and forage on the forest floor for fallen fruit, seeds, and leaves. It is also known to dig for roots and tubers and to strip bark from saplings. Mating takes place in the rainy season, and the females give birth to one young per litter; females can give birth twice within the reproductive period. Males leave the parental burrow and territory at the age of around one year (before the next breeding period) and can reproduce immediately. However, female offspring show delayed dispersal and stay with their parents for two reproductive seasons. Females are probably not sexually mature before the age of two years (Sommer et al. 2002, Sommer 2003).
threats: The historical decline of this species has been partly through climatic change leading to increased aridification of south-western Madagascar, and also the extensive modification of suitable habitat by humans since their arrival on the island. Current areas of habitat are threatened by slash and burn agriculture, charcoal production, burning for cattle pasture and logging (Sommer 2003). The illegal destruction of primary forest habitat in recent years, even within the boundaries of protected areas, for maize and peanut production is one of the most significant causes of deforestation and subsequent habitat loss (Wilmet et al. 2020). There is a road that now cuts through the middle of the species' range and has divided the range. This species has declined with the introduction of feral dogs and cats, by predation and also potentially transmission of lethal toxoplasmosis. This species could be susceptible to hantavirus, which has been shown in some rodents in eastern Madagascar.
population: Within the largest forest fragment in the southern forest area, the Kirindy Forest/CFPF, field studies between 1990 and 2000 documented a rapid population decline. Whereas the population size was constant between 1992 and 1996 (54 animals/100 ha), the population density declined by about 40% between 1997 and 1999 (33 animals/100 ha) and in 2000 by about 60% of the original density (22 animals/100 ha) (Sommer and Hommen 2000). In a population viability analysis, Sommer et al. (2002) used a calculated median of 23 active burrows per 100 ha in suitable habitat to estimate the southern subpopulation (15,000 ha) with 6,900 adults and the northern subpopulation (4,000 ha) with 18,40 adults. Surveys undertaken in 2005 estimated the combined size of the two H. antimena subpopulations to be ca 36,000 individuals, considerably larger than previously assumed. There was no evidence that active burrow density across the species’ known range changed between 2000 and 2005. H. antimena was not uniformly distributed, with higher densities of active burrows found in forest with the highest canopy in areas furthest from forest edges (Young et al. 2008). However, a recent re-evaluation of the population status of H. antimena between 2007–2019 suggested an alarming total population reduction of 88% across both parts of the species’ range (Wilmet et al. 2020). The study estimated the current population size of H. antimena by calculating the density of active burrows along transects previously determined by Young et al. (2008). Current global estimated population size for the species is 5,036 (95% CI = 2,746–9,404) mature individuals, with a substantial population decline of up to 92% occurring in the southern Kirindy subpopulation (Wilmet et al. 2020).
range: This species is endemic to Madagascar, where it is restricted to the west of the island in a narrow coastal zone. The southern limit is now the Tomitsy River (until recently it ranged south to the Andranomena River) up to the Tsiribihina River in the north (Sommer 2003). In the last century, the species ranged from the Morondava River to the Tsiribihina in the north, but the species has lost significant portions of its range and is now found in two isolated range segments within the Menabe-Antimena protected area (separated by the Mandroatra River). The current Extent of Occurrence (EOO) is 470 km². The species is predicted to have an elevation range of 40-100 m asl (Goodman and Raherilalao 2013).Subfossil remains indicate that over the past 1,400 years, the range of H. antimena extended at least 475 km further south (Goodman and Rakotondravony 1996).
useTrade: Although this species was known to be consumed as a food source historically, there is no recent evidence that H. antimena is targeted and hunted as a subsistence source of protein.
conservationActions: The majority of the distribution of the species is within the Menabe-Antimena Protected Area. A successful captive-breeding programme for this species has been established in Jersey Zoo by the Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust (see Wright et al. 2003). There is need to investigate potential pathogens, and to control feral dogs and cats. Due to the high decline of the species, an action plan to identify how to save the species should be developed.

rationale: Myotis nimbaensis is assessed as Critically Endangered under criterion B (CR B1ab(iii,v)+2ab(iii,v)) as its extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both estimated to be 4 km². The species is only known from a single location (Guinean side of the Nimba Mountains) where there are only two (2) confirmed roosts, both in abandoned adits within an active mine site. While acoustic monitoring has detected M. nimbaensis visiting a further six (6) adits within the mining enclave, existing roost sites are unstable and collapsing, likely causing further decline in EOO, AOO, and quality of remaining habitat. Combined with the threat of future mining operations and wildfires, continuing decline in the extent and quality of its roosting and foraging habitat is projected.
habitat: While there is still little known about the distribution and natural history of this insectivorous species, it is thought to be highly specialized and restricted to roosting in subterranean features in the high-altitude grasslands of the Nimba Mountains. Existing roosts are shared with two other insectivorous bat species, Hipposideros lamottei and Rhinolophus guineensis. Based on echolocation call data recorded for this species (broad bandwidth, steep frequency-modulated pulse calls with a peak frequency of 42.5 kHz), its foraging habitat is thought to consist of high-altitude grassland, montane savanna, and gallery forest habitats along headwaters of the Zié, Gouan, and Zougué rivers in the northern Guinean Nimba Mountains between 1,200 and 1,500 m asl (Simmons et al. 2021). Although its relatively long call duration may suggest M. nimbaensis is not specialized for gleaning its insect prey, its call structure is similar to that of Myotis lucifugus which is both an aerial hunter and gleaner (Ratcliffe and Dawson 2003).
threats: The only known population is highly threatened due to the instability and high likelihood of structural collapse of current mining adits and decline in size and quality of foraging habitat due to wildfires caused by slash-and-burn agriculture and hunting to smoke out small mammals in lowland areas that could easily impact the species small range. There is also an imminent threat of iron ore mining activities that will severely impact existing roosting and foraging sites.
population: The global population is limited to one location within an active mining concession, with current roost sites unstable and collapsing. Currently, there is no information available on the abundance of this species, as current records are based on the capture of two individuals and acoustic monitoring data. While the number of mature individuals is unknown, its total population size is suspected to be very small as only a few individuals were acoustically detected at the entrances of its roosts (Simmons et al. 2021). An ongoing decline in the species’ population is suspected, as there is a continuing loss in the extent and quality of roosting and foraging habitat. Whether additional roosting populations exist, and where these may be located, are unknown. While populations would have occurred in natural cave features in the past, habitat disturbance has likely reduced the suitability of these locations.
range: This species is endemic to Africa and is known only from the Guinean region of the Nimba Mountains (Simmons et al. 2021), an isolated mountain range in West Africa that straddles the borders of Guinea, Liberia, and Côte d’Ivoire. While it has only been recorded roosting in two mine adits, extensive field surveys and acoustic monitoring has only detected species' presence between 1,200 and 1,500 m asl, covering an area smaller than 3 km². Extensive surveys on the Liberian side of the Nimba Mountains (Monadjem et al. 2016), lowland areas of the Guinea side of the Nimba Mountains (Bat Conservation International, unpublished data), as well as other high elevation sites in Guinea (Fahr and Ebigbo 2003, Fahr et al. 2006) have failed to detect M. nimbaensis at any other location. Only found at this one location, all evidence to date suggests that M. nimbaensis is highly dependent on the availability of subterranean features and restricted to high-altitude grassland, montane savanna, and gallery forest habitats on the Nimba Mountains.
useTrade: This species is not known to be used or traded.
conservationActions: All evidence to date suggests that M. nimbaensis is only found within the current mining concession and was identified as part of the environmental and social impact assessment for the Nimba Iron Ore Project. As part of ongoing conservation initiatives led by the Société des Mines de Fer de Guinée S.A (SMFG), community outreach projects are taking place in lowland areas of Guinea that surround the mountain to reduce the threat of wildfires. Work is also underway to identify suitable areas outside of the proposed mining footprint where new subterranean features can be created for the bats to occupy and provide long-term protection from future mining activities.Further research is needed to determine life history traits such as distribution, population size and trend, ecology, and specific habitat requirements so that more informed conservation management actions can be implemented. Furthermore, ongoing monitoring should continue to build a better understanding of distribution and seasonal movement patterns and provide a baseline to assess the effectiveness of efforts to provide new roosting habitat for the bats to occupy.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The Tasmanian Dusky Antechinus is mostly found in rainforests and eucalypt forests, especially where there is dense cover and thick leaf litter (Baker et al. 2015). Like A. mimetes (the Mainland Dusky Antechinus), it hunts arthropods and worms in moist soil and leaf litter.Breeding is in September-October (Green 1972, Baker et al. 2015).
threats: The impact of threats is not well established. Feral cats are widespread and abundant across much of the distribution, and may be increasing in response to decline in abundance of Tasmanian devils over the last few decades (Cunningham et al. 2020). Timber-harvesting occurs in parts of the range. The incidence of extensive high-severity wildfires is increasing under climate change. Species in the dusky antechinus group are particularly disadvantaged by severe and frequent fire, which removes dense understorey vegetation and results in drying of the vegetation and soil (e.g. Newsome et al. 1975, Recher et al. 2009).
population: There are no estimates of density, population size or population trajectory for this species. It is likely to be undergoing some decline associated with increasingly unfavourable fire regimes.
range: Following taxonomic revision (Baker et al. 2015), this species is now considered restricted to Tasmania where it is widespread ('other than the far south-east on Tasman Peninsula': Baker et al. 2015). Abbott and Burbidge (1995) also report it from Bruny Island.
conservationActions: The Tasmanian Dusky Antechinus is present in many protected areas. There are no other targeted conservation actions for this species. It is not listed as threatened under Australian legislation.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its relatively wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is probably undergoing gradual (and episodes of sharp) local decline in association with increasing incidence of unfavourable fire regimes and with some ongoing clearing and predation.
habitat: The Mainland Dusky Antechinus occurs in forest and shrubland, including alpine heathland. It prefers areas with moist soil such as long-unburnt gullies, with a dense understorey of ferns or shrubs. The species does not occur in secondary forest, and areas subject to recent, severe wildfires (e.g. Newsome et al. 1975 found that it became locally extinct for two years after fire). It hunts mainly insects - including larvae, spiders, and earthworms in leaf litter and soil.
threats: Threats to some populations of this species include predation by feral cats and red foxes (Woolley et al. 2019; Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021, 2022), clearing, timber-harvesting, and increasing drought and wildfire associated with climate change. Legge et al. (2021) reported that around 30% of the distribution of this species was burnt, much of this area at high-severity, in the 2019-2020 Black Summer wildfires of south eastern Australia.
population: There is no robust population estimate for Mainland Dusky Antechinus. However, the species is unlikely to be declining to the extent required for a threatened category. The species can be locally common. Most demographic studies have reported population densities of around ten per hectare (Fisher et al 2001, Recher et al. 2009). Legge et al. (2021) reported that around 30% of the distribution of this species was burnt, much of this area at high-severity, in the 2019-2020 Black Summer wildfires of south-eastern Australia: this presumably led to at least short-term population declines.
range: The Mainland Dusky Antechinus is restricted to mainland south-eastern Australia, extending from south-eastern Queensland to western Victoria. Of the two recognised subspecies, Antechinus mimetes insulanus is restricted to the Grampian Range (Gariwerd National Park and surrounds) in western Victoria.
conservationActions: The Mainland Dusky Antechinus is present in many protected areas including National Parks. There are no targeted actions for the conservation of this species. It is not listed as threatened under Australian legislation.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, although it is patchily distributed, it has a wide distribution, presumed large population, occurs in (and most of the range is within) protected areas, and is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. However, continued monitoring and research into threats is needed.
habitat: This species occurs in low rocky cliffs, hills, and gorges, with vegetation ranging from hummock grasslands to rainforests (e.g. Ondei et al. 2020).
threats: The impacts of any plausible threats to this species are not well resolved. Based mostly on studies of the closely related Petrogale wilkinsi, it is likely that habitat quality is optimised with a regime of small low-intensity fires that result in a fine-scale mosaic of vegetation types and ages-since-fire (Telfer and Garde 2006, Radford et al. 2015, Radford et al. 2020). One study found this species was abundant in long-unburnt areas (Ondei et al. 2020). Hence, it is likely to be disadvantaged by regimes of frequent, extensive and high intensity fires - although the rugged nature of its habitat may moderate some fire impacts. Feral cats are known predators of rock-wallabies (Woolley et al. 2019), but are relatively uncommon in at least some of the more rugged areas inhabited by this species (Hohnen et al. 2016).
population: The Western Short-eared Rock-wallaby is locally common (e.g., Fisher and Woinarski 2002, Ondei et al. 2020), though patchily distributed. There are no data on density, no robust evidence of population size and no estimates of population trajectory (although there is some limited monitoring at some sites: e.g., Mornington Marion Downs Wildlife Sanctuary: Lowe et al. 2023). The species appears to have persisted at all known sites. The population size is most likely >10,000 mature individuals, given that it is at least locally abundant; but any population estimate has a high degree of uncertainty.
range: This species is endemic to northern Australia, where it occurs in rocky areas of the Kimberley (Western Australia) and western Top End (monsoonal areas of the Northern Territory) as far east as the Daly River. It was formerly considered to occur also across the Top End, but Potter et al. (2014) recognised that these eastern populations as a distinct species, P. wilkinsi. Abbott and Burbidge (1995) listed no records from islands. Potter et al. (2014) reported it from two islands (Monsmont and Bullanyin) within the man-made Lake Argyle. Two subspecies are recognised: P. brachyotis brachyotis from the Kimberley to just west of the Victoria River; and P. b. victoriae from a restricted area east of the Victoria River (including Bradshaw and upper Fitzmaurice River).
conservationActions: This species is locally common in several conservation reserves (e.g., Purnululu, Drysdale River, Mirima, Gregory, Mornington Marion Downs Wildlife Sanctuary) and Indigenous Protected Areas. Priority research and management needs include: long-term monitoring at more sites, research into impacts of possible threats (and their management), and research into responses to fire regimes. Management is producing favourable fire regimes at some sites (Legge et al. 2011).

rationale: The Greater Glider is endemic to Australia. The species is assessed as Endangered (EN A2ab+4abc), based on evidence of recent and likely future rates of population decline and decline in habitat quality. The population of the Greater Glider is declining because of habitat loss, fragmentation, extensive fire, climate change, and some forestry practices. The species is particularly susceptible because of slow life history characteristics, specialist requirements for large tree hollows (and hence mature forests), and relatively specialised dietary requirements. Across its broad range, the population size and rate of decline is incompletely known, but several large-scale monitoring programs have demonstrated substantial declines. A large-scale (ca 160 monitoring sites across the Central Highlands, Victoria), long-term (1997 to 2024) monitoring program reported declines of about 80% in the probability of occurrence of this species (Lindenmayer et al. 2021, 2024). A substantial monitoring program in a conservation reserve in coastal New South Wales reported a complete loss of the monitored subpopulation over the period 2002 to 2010 (Lindenmayer et al. 2011). Smith and Smith (2020) reported major declines in lower altitude forests of the Blue Mountains, with sampling in 2015–2016 failing to record the species in seven of 20 sites at which it was known in the 1980s. An ongoing monitoring program (from 2014) in forests of northern New South Wales reported a 60–70% decline in probability of detection, with decline coinciding with low rainfall years (Goldingay et al. 2022). At woodland sites in central Queensland first sampled in 1973–1976 and re-sampled in 2001–2002, abundance declined by 89% (Woinarski et al. 2006). Large areas of the habitat of the Greater Glider were affected by the catastrophic bushfires of the summer of 2019/2020. A systematic analysis using mapping of fire severity classes over the species' distribution linked to expert elicitation to estimate effects on abundance concluded that there was an overall population decline of >20% one year after the fires, which is expected to increase to >30% within three generations after the fires (Legge et al. 2022). Subsequent sampling indicates that these fires did indeed cause major reductions in population size (Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024).The Commonwealth of Australia Threatened Species Scientific Committee (TSSC 2022a), taking into account both the effects of the 2019/20 bushfires and other evidence on declines not related to those events, estimated that the overall rate of decline exceeds 50% over three generations (21 years). Current declines are likely to continue, as the causes of decline are still operating. This estimate of decline rate applies to the subspecies P. v. volans. There is no monitoring of populations of the northern subspecies P. volans minor. However, the northern subspecies is subject to many of the same threats as P. v. volans, and is also likely to be in decline. The subspecies P. v. volans represents the great majority of the distribution of P. volans (approx. 95%, Woinarski et al. 2014). It is therefore unlikely that a lower decline rate of P. v. minor could offset the declines recorded by monitoring of P. v. volans and justify an assessment of Vulnerable (VU) rather than EN (the subspecies P. v. minor is treated as a full species by the Australian Commonwealth and is listed as VU under Commonwealth legislation (TSSC 2022b), on the basis that modelling of the impacts of climate change indicated that populations might decline by approximately 30% over the next three generations (Kearney et al. 2010), together with its small area of occupancy and number of locations).
habitat: The Greater Glider is an arboreal marsupial of eastern Australian eucalypt forests and woodlands. Typically, it is most abundant in taller, montane, moist eucalypt forests, that have relatively old trees and abundant hollows (Andrews et al. 1994; Smith et al. 1994a,b; Kavanagh 2000; Eyre 2004; van der Ree et al. 2004; Vanderduys et al. 2012). The species' distribution may be patchy even in suitable habitat (Kavanagh 2000). The Greater Glider favours forests with a diversity of eucalypt species, due to seasonal variation in preference for food tree species (Kavanagh 1984).The species is primarily folivorous, with a diet mostly comprising eucalypt leaves, and occasionally flowers and buds (Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Kavanagh and Lambert 1990, van der Ree et al. 2004). It feeds on a limited number of eucalypt species, and preferences for tree species vary regionally. Forests with high diversity of tree species are most valuable, because diversity compensates for seasonal differences in foliage production and nutrient composition among species. Approximately 85% of the Greater Glider’s water requirements are provided by consumed leaves (Foley et al. 1990). Free water is presumably obtained from dew condensation on leaf surfaces (Rübsamen et al. 1984).During the day the Greater Glider shelters in tree hollows, requiring large hollows in large, old trees (Henry 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Lindenmayer et al. 1991, Smith et al. 2007, Goldingay 2012). In the Grafton/Casino, Urbenville and Urunga/Coffs Harbour Forestry Management Areas (FMAs) in northern New South Wales, the abundance of Greater Gliders on survey sites was significantly greater on sites with a higher abundance of tree hollows (Andrews et al. 1994, Smith et al. 1994a,b). In the Grafton/Casino FMA, the Greater Glider was absent from surveyed sites with fewer than six tree hollows per hectare (Smith et al. 1994a). In southern Queensland, Greater Gliders need at least 2-4 live den trees for every 2 ha of suitable forest habitat (Eyre 2002). Comport et al. (1996) found that individuals used 4-6 different dens over the course of a month.Home ranges are typically relatively small (1–4 ha: Henry 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Comport et al. 1996, Gibbons and Lindenmayer 2002, Pope et al. 2005), but are larger in forests of lower productivity and woodlands that are more open (to 16 ha: Eyre 2004, Smith et al. 2007, McGregor et al. 2023), and larger for males than for females (Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Pope et al. 2005). Home ranges of males are mostly non-overlapping (Henry 1984, Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Pope et al. 2005).The greater glider is highly sensitive to forest clearance (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969a), and to intensive logging (Kavanagh and Bamkin 1995, Kavanagh and Webb 1998, Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Kavanagh et al. 1995), although responses vary according to landscape context and the extent of tree removal and retention (Kavanagh 2000, Taylor et al. 2007). The species is also sensitive to wildfire (Lunney 1987, Andrews et al. 1994, Lindenmayer et al. 2011, Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024), and local populations are slow to recover following major disturbance (Kavanagh 2004) because of low rates of increase and low immigration rates due to limited dispersal capacity. In Urbenville FMA of northern New South Wales, the abundance of Greater Gliders on survey sites was significantly greater in forests that were infrequently burnt (Andrews et al. 1994).Greater Gilders are sensitive to effects of habitat fragmentation (Eyre 2006, McCarthy and Lindenmayer 1999ab, Lindenmayer et al. 2000, Taylor and Goldingay 2009), because they have relatively low persistence in small forest fragments and disperse poorly across vegetation that is not native forest. Modelling suggests that they need native forest patches of at least 160 km² to maintain viable populations (Eyre 2002).Females give birth to a single young, from March to June (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b, McKay 2008). Sexual maturity is reached in the second year (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b). Longevity has been estimated at 15 years (Harris and Maloney 2010), so generation length is ca 7 years (TSSC 2023a). The relatively low reproductive rate (Henry 1984) may render small, isolated populations in small remnants prone to extinction (van der Ree 2004, Pope et al. 2005).
threats: The most significant threats are increased intensity and frequency of bushfires (linked to climate change); increased temperature and changed rainfall patterns due to climate change; inappropriate prescribed burning; habitat clearing and fragmentation; and timber harvesting.Increased intensity and frequency of bushfiresLarge losses or declines, including disappearance of local populations, have been documented following high-severity fires (McLean et al. 2018, Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024). These effects may be the result of direct mortality from lethal heating or suffocation, or loss of key habitat features and resources. Following the 2009 Victorian bushfires, 79% of large living trees with cavities died in the affected Eucalyptus regnans (Mountain Ash) forests; recruitment of new cavities takes many years (Lindenmayer et al. 2012). Populations have disappeared after major fires. The effects of fire can be compounded by habitat fragmentation, because the species does not readily disperse over gaps in forest habitat and so is slow to recolonise areas recovering from fire. No individuals were recorded for 19 years after a fire in an isolated area of habitat in Royal National Park near Sydney (Andrews et al. 2014). Recurring fires can therefore cause progressive regional decline in the proportion of forest habitat occupied. Indicators of forest fire danger in southeastern Australia point to an increase in the threat of severe fire in the near future, driven mainly by climate change (Boer et al. 2020). More than 23% of the temperate forests of southeastern Australia were burnt in the 2019-2020 fire season. The conditions that cause these extreme fires are intensifying.Increased temperatures and changed rainfall patternsMean temperatures across the distribution of Greater Glider have risen by 1.4 degrees over the past century, and heat waves have become longer and more frequent (BOM and CSIRO 2020). In the southern part of the range, winter rainfall has declined by 12% since the 1990s, but summer rainfall remains unchanged. These trends are projected to continue under moderate and high emissions scenarios (CSIRO and BOM 2021). A unique physiology and strict eucalypt diet make the Greater Glider vulnerable to high temperatures and low water availability (Rübsamen et al. 1984). Prolonged exposure to temperatures over 40°C is likely to lead to high mortality (Rübsamen et al. 1984). Moore et al. (2004) suggested that the preference of Greater Gliders for higher elevations is because they are sensitive to heat and must expend energy and water to cool themselves at ambient temperatures over 20°C. Increased night-time temperatures have been implicated in the decline of abundance in Victorian subpopulations (Wagner et al. 2020). At lower altitude (<500 m) sites surveyed in the Blue Mountains, increasing mean annual temperatures were considered to be the cause of declines of Greater Gliders (Smith and Smith 2018, 2020). A marked reduction in detection rates was reported for greater gliders in forests in northern New South Wales during periods of drought (Goldingay et al. 2022).Water stress limits growth in forest eucalypts (Matusick et al. 2013) and reduces availability of browse. Combined with high temperature this may cause heat stress, drought stress and mortality (Vic SAC 2015). Extended droughts in a warmer climate are likely to reduce the quality of available foliage (e.g. young foliage is more palatable than older foliage; McKeirnan et al. 2014) for Greater Gliders, and could therefore reduce reproduction rates (DeGabriel et al. 2009, Kearney et al. 2010). Above temperatures of 35℃, Greater Gliders need to dissipate >100% of metabolic heat production by evaporative means (Rübasamen 1984). At the same time, they reduce their food intake, leading to rapid expenditure of their energy and water stores (Beale et al. 2018, Youngentob et al. 2021). This can lead to death of both young and adult gliders, or reduced growth in milk-fed young (Youngentob et al. 2021). Climate projections and biophysical modelling of the Greater Glider in the northern portion of its range (that is, for the subspecies P. volans minor) predict a severe range contraction and increase in fragmentation of the remaining range under a 3°C temperature increase (Kearney et al. 2010).Inappropriate prescribed burning practicesIn Victoria, loss of hollow-bearing trees due to mechanical site-preparation works associated with prescribed burning may reduce suitable habitat for the Greater Glider. This impact occurs primarily in foothill forests close to settled areas. Trees that are assessed as potentially hazardous (if they were to catch fire) are routinely removed from the perimeter of planned burns on public land in Victoria. They are also removed from bushfire control lines during and after bushfire suppression activities (DELWP n.d). Although not all hazardous trees are hollow-bearing, many are.Too intense or frequent planned burning may contribute to population losses or declines in the southern part of the Greater Glider’s range. Bluff (2016) reported that hollow-bearing trees affected by fire during planned burns were 28 times more likely to collapse than those that were not burnt. Parnaby et al. (2010) found that following low intensity prescription burns in the Pilliga forests (NSW), mean collapse rates for burnt hollow-bearing trees were 14-26%. This was consistent with the collapse rate of 25.6% found by Bluff (2016). A survey following a planned burn at Tallarook Range (NSW) in 2021 found that a large number of potential Greater Glider habitat trees were burnt, with “many destroyed” (N. Stimson 2021, pers. comm. 26 June, cited in TSSC 2022a).After fires, trees with large hollows are often felled for safety reasons (along roads, fire trails and walking trails) within Greater Glider habitat (DECCW 2011). Andrew (2001) reported that 120 hollow-bearing trees were felled after the 1994 bushfires in Royal National Park by NPWS due to concerns over public safety.Habitat clearing and fragmentationThe Greater Glider is absent from cleared areas and has little dispersal ability to move through cleared areas between fragments (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b; McCarthy and Lindenmayer 1999a,b; Lindenmayer et al. 2000; Eyre 2006; Taylor and Goldingay 2009). Population viability in small remnants is low due to the species’ low reproductive output and susceptibility to disturbance and edge effects. Extensive land clearing for development and agriculture has led to fragmentation of habitat in some areas, e.g. the Tumut area of NSW (Pope et al. 2005) where small subpopulations exist in a pine matrix. About 30 years after clearing in the Tumut area, Lindenmayer et al. (1999) found that the occupancy rate of Greater Gliders in remnant patches was 21% compared to 38% in the surrounding native forest, indicating limited recolonisation. The probability of occurrence was significantly greater in large remnants. Genetic analysis in the Tumut population by Taylor et al. (2007) indicated that some immigration into patches was occurring, but there were lower levels of immigration and genetic mixing in patches further (>1 km) from continuous forest.Timber harvestingThe sensitivity of Greater Gliders to timber harvesting has been well documented. Although much habitat across the species’ range is found in conservation reserves (Smith and Smith 2018, Wagner et al. 2020), where timber harvesting is excluded and the removal of hollow-bearing trees is subject to constraints, much prime habitat coincides with areas suitable for timber harvesting (Braithwaite 1984). There is a progressive decline in numbers of hollow-bearing trees in some production forests, as harvesting rotations become shorter and dead stags collapse, and hollow-bearing trees are not replaced due to lack of recruitment (Ross 1999; Ball et al. 1999; Lindenmayer et al. 2011, 2012).The degree of impact depends on forest type and timber harvesting intensity, with larger declines in more heavily logged sites (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b, Lunney 1987, Kavanagh et al. 1995, Kavanagh and Webb 1998, Kavanagh 2000, McLean et al. 2018). In the Central Highlands of Victoria, where clear-felling is undertaken, Lindenmayer et al. (2017b) found that the rate of loss of hollow-bearing trees greatly exceeded the rate of recruitment. The area of clear-felled forest adjacent to wildlife corridors was also found to increase the chance of collapse of hollow-bearing trees, possibly due to the greater exposure of stems to elevated wind speeds at corridor edges. However, models investigating the impacts of forest disturbance on the Greater Glider in the same area found that timber harvesting in the surrounding landscape was not a significant influence on the probability of occurrence of the species (Lindenmayer et al. 2020).Recovery of subpopulations following timber harvesting is slow. Subpopulations in south-east New South Wales had not recovered 8 years after timber harvesting in sites retaining 62%, 52% and 21% of the original tree basal area (Kavanagh and Webb 1998). In the regrowth Mountain Ash forests (Central Highlands) of Vic, Greater Gliders (southern and central) were absent post-timber harvesting until the forests were >38 years old (Macfarlane 1988).Concerns about the conservation of greater gliders in production forests has been a high-profile issue and timber harvesting has been subject to many legal challenges (Wardell-Johnson and Robinson 2022). Partly as a consequence, the Victorian government ceased harvesting of native forests in 2024.
population: There is no reliable estimate of population size. Lunney et al. (2008) considered that the species had a ‘presumed large population’ and was ‘locally common’. In New South Wales, Kavanagh (2004) considered it ‘widespread and common … particularly in north-eastern New South Wales’. Density estimates in Victoria range from 0.6 to 2.8 individuals/ha (Henry 1984, van der Ree et al. 2004), and across its broader range from 0.01 to 5 individuals/ha (Kavanagh 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Maloney 2007). In a locally abundant population in the northern part of the species range, Comport et al. (1996) estimated a density of 2.6-5.8 animals/ha. Population estimates are available for some sites: Goldingay et al. (2022) estimated that there were more than 2,400 mature Greater Gliders in a 157 km² national park in northern New South Wales. Cripps et al. (2021) estimated that there were 24,575 greater gliders (of all ages) in the 259 km² Strathbogie Ranges in Victoria. These estimates of density together with the wide distribution of the species demonstrate that the total population is well over 100,000.Populations that have been monitored over the last 10 years or more show consistent evidence of decline, in some cases to local extinction. For example, declines in occupancy and detection rate in standardised surveys have been recorded for over more than two decades of monitoring in the Victorian Central Highlands (Lumsden et al. 2013, Lindenmayer 2020, Lindenmayer et al. 2024). There have been losses of subpopulations in NSW within the Jervis Bay and Blue Mountains areas (Lindenmayer et al. 2011, Smith and Smith 2018). In addition, the species was badly affected by the 2019–2020 bushfires, which severely affected much of its forest habitat in southeastern Australia. Post-fire surveys have indicated that in areas of high fire severity there is zero to very low occupancy (Smith and Smith 2022). A systematic analysis using mapping of fire severity classes over the species' distribution linked to expert elicitation to estimate effects on abundance concluded that there was an overall population decline of >20% one year after the fires, which is expected to increase to >30% within three generations after the fires (Legge et al. 2022).
range: The Greater Glider occurs in the eucalypt forests of eastern Australia, mainly along the east coast and near-coastal ranges, from sea level to approximately 1,200 m asl. It has a broad distribution from the Windsor Tableland in Queensland in the north, to the coast of Victoria in the south. There is a gap in distribution in the region of the Burdekin River, separating a small north-eastern portion of the range extending from Townsville north to the Windsor Tableland, from a much larger southern portion that extends southward from around Rockhampton. These two disjunct areas of distribution are considered as distinct subspecies, P. volans minor in the north and P. v. volans in the south. The westernmost occurrence is in the Wombat State Forest in central Victoria.
conservationActions: The Greater Glider occurs in many conservation reserves across its extensive range. In production forests, some logging prescriptions have been imposed to reduce impacts upon this species. The Victorian government ceased logging in native forests in 2024.The species is listed as Endangered (as ‘greater glider (southern and central) Petauroides volans’) and Vulnerable (as ‘greater glider (northern) P. minor’) under Australian law, with conservation advices to guide management (Threatened Species Scientific Committee 2022a,b). However, such management and legal protection has been ineffective at halting decline (Ashman et al. 2021).

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Vulnerable (VU)EU 27 regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)This European endemic species is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B1ab(i,ii,iii,iv) globally and for the European region. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be smaller than 20,000 km² (EOO = 13,455 km²). The species occurs at ca 10 locations, and agricultural intensification can be expected to impact the whole population over a short time in the near future, causing continued declines in habitat quality, extent of occurrence, area of occupancy and number of locations. A number of subpopulations have already gone extinct in the Ukrainian part of its range. When this species was assessed in 2008, its EOO was thought to be much greater; since then its taxonomy has been revised and Spalax antiquus and S. istricus (formerly included in S. graecus) are now recognised as separate species, resulting in the EOO now being much smaller. In Romania, the Bukovina Blind Mole Rat subpopulation appears to be stable at present, although agricultural intensification may potentially become a threat in the near future. Population decline and range reduction occurred in Ukraine and is expected to continue. Population monitoring is urgently required, as is research to determine the extent to which agricultural intensification is a threat and to determine its area of occupancy.In the EU 27 region, this species occurs at six locations with an EOO below 20,000 km², however no continuing declines in population or habitat quality have been confirmed. Therefore it is assessed as Near Threatened as it is close to qualifying as Vulnerable under criterion B.
habitat: The species inhabits steppe grassland, pastures, orchards and arable lands. In Ukraine, it can be found in the suburban area. Overall, it avoids very arid areas (Nowak 1999). Individuals aggregate in winter but disperse in summer (Kryštufek 1999). The Bukovina Blind Mole Rat is a fossorial species, digging extensive and elaborate tunnel systems with nesting chambers, storerooms and latrines (Nowak 1999). It feeds on bulbs, roots, tubers, and other underground parts of a range of plants (Nowak 1999). Mole rats of the genus Spalax can be distinguished from all other rodents by the lack of any external openings for the eyes, although small eyes are present under the skin (Nowak 1999).
threats: This species is persecuted as a pest by farmers and gardeners. It can be subject to road kills. Causes for local declines in the northern part of the range are not understood. Agricultural intensification is causing declines in habitat quality.
population: The species has a small range, within which it occurs at densities of approximately one to three individuals per hectare (although densities of up to 23 individuals per hectare have been recorded) (Nowak 1999, Kryštufek 1999). In Ukraine, it is verified to exist in the southwestern suburbs of Chernivtsi city. Most other populations recorded in the past are now extinct. In Romania approximately 40 small localities are recorded across Iași, Botoșani and Suceava counties (Hegyeli, unpublished data).
range: The Bukovina Blind Mole Rat is a European endemic species, known only from a few sites in Romania (Suceava and Iasi) and south eastern Ukraine (Chernivtsi). Its range is very fragmented. It occurs in lowland and upland areas up to 300 m. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 13,455 km² and it occurs in 8-10 locations. A contraction of north-eastern populations in Ukraine has caused declines in the EOO, where several subpopulations from Ukraine have gone extinct, leading to the decrease in the area of occupancy (AOO), though exact calculations of the AOO are subject to further studies.
useTrade: The species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: It is listed in the Resolution 6 of the Bern Convention. In Ukraine, it is included in the Red Book as Vulnerable (2021). In the Romanian Red Book, it is listed as Vulnerable. One of the populations in Ukraine is protected in a regional protected area Maliovanka with Emerald Network status 'Nominated'.This species could benefit from habitat protection and management, and species reintroductions could be considered. Further research into the population and habitat trends of this species, as well as identifying the cause of the declines in the northern part of its range is recommended.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) under criteria B1ab(i,ii,iii) because its estimated extent of occurrence (EOO), if the species is still extant, is somewhere between 4-17 km² and if it still occurs in the few, scattered localities it was previously recorded from, its population is likely to be severely fragmented. There has been a decline in the quality and quantity of its habitat. The area of occupancy and extent of occurrence has also declined. Moreover, despite recent survey efforts, there have been no records of this species since 1983. The species may already be extinct.
habitat: The species has never been studied but is possibly similar to Méhely’s Blind Mole Rat (Spalax antiquus). The species has been reported from areas covered by steppe and forest-steppe grasslands (Méhely 1909).
threats: Historically, blind mole rats (both Nannospalax and Spalax) were regarded as agricultural pests. Agricultural intensification and the conversion of its habitat into ploughed fields is a threat to this species (Németh et al. 2009).
population: The population status is poorly known, as no data has been recorded in the last 40 years despite recent search efforts (Németh et al. 2013). If the species still exists in the scattered localities it was previously recorded from, it is very likely severely fragmented.
range: This European species is endemic to Romania (Chişamera et al. 2014, Csorba et al. 2015). Specimens have been reported from Oltenia and Muntenia in southern Romania from hilly and flat terrain, covered by steppe and forest-steppe habitats (Méhely 1909). The species is endemic to a well-defined geographical region, between the mountain chain of the Carpathians and the river Danube. The type locality is Bârza, Olt County, Romania (Méhely 1909). Presently, no subpopulations are known to exist. Previous records were reported from three localities (Bârza, Horezu Poenari and Prundu) in southern Romania but presence has not been reconfirmed in recent surveys. The species has likely become extinct in those areas (Németh et al. 2011).
useTrade: The species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: There are no direct conservation actions for this species. Further taxonomic studies are required to confirm the identity of the species with respect to S. graecus, and it is possibly similar to Méhely’s Blind Mole Rat (Spalax antiquus). Research and surveys are required to confirm the current distribution and population size of the species.The species does not have legal protection at a European level (and is subject to inefficient application of the Romanian legislation).

rationale: Grey Slender Loris is assessed as Near Threatened. The species has a wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, and is presumed to have a large population. However, it is facing threats from deforestation and/or hunting across its range, and although the species has a wider distribution in India than in Sri Lanka, suspected declines due to various threats in the two countries indicates that the species is not Least Concern as it was previously thought to be. The population is suspected to be declining, but at a rate approaching, but not yet meeting, the threatened category thresholds.
habitat: This species occurs in tropical primary and secondary rainforests, dry semi-deciduous forests, scrub, swamp, acacia, bamboo, edge, and montane cloud forest up to 2,000 m asl. Understory in dry forests and canopies in wet forests. Also found in home gardens, tea plantations, hotel gardens probably surviving mainly on insects. Two long term studies have been conducted on the ecology and behaviour of this species in India, and one such study has been conducted in Sri Lanka (Nekaris and Bearder 2006, Radhakrishna and Singh 2004). The highest densities of lorises on Sri Lanka occurred in the dry zone forests; also, the presence of species of this genus is positively associated with insect presence, and negatively associated with secondary forest with little undergrowth (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004, Kumara et al. 2006).Loris lydekkerianus malabaricus is found to occur more in cardamom plantations and in degraded and stunted rainforests than in primary rainforests (Kumara et al., 2006). This species is characterized by a multi male/multi female social system of spatial overlap (Sasi and Kumara 2014, Radhakrishna et al. 2011).Loris lydekkerianus lydekkarianus seems to rely heavily on undergrowth, and is often found in secondary growth forest (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004, Radhakrishna and Singh 2002). Singh et al. (1999) found that relatively scrub forests and adjoining croplands are the preferred habitat types of lorises in the Dindigul Forests of Tamil Nadu, India. Loris are social with the 38% of activity in association with other individuals (Nekaris et al. 2013). Though primarily insectivores, L. l. lydekkerianus was found to include plant material, fruits and seeds in their diet (Radhakrishna and Kumara 2010). There is inter-species home range variation: Mysore Slender Loris adult males ranging 3.6 ha and  1.6 ha for adult females. Roving males can have home range as large as 117 ha. Ranges might overlap for males but not so for females which are almost ‘exclusive’ (Nekaris et al. 2013).Prior to taxonomic revision in 2020 (Nijman et al. 2020), three subspecies were recognised in Sri Lanka: L. l. grandis, L. l. nordicus and L. l. uva. These are no longer recognised as separate taxa (and are now synonyms of L. l. lydekkerianus), however since this Red List assessment was carried out in 2015, populations previously identified as these taxa are referred to by their former subspecies names below.Loris lydekkerianus nordicus is apparently able to survive well near human habitations (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2003), as it was found more often associated with disturbed human habitation than with forest (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004); similar trends in India were found by Singh et al. (1999) and were associated with agricultural pest abundance. Loris l. nordicus and L.l. lydekkarianus seem to rely heavily on undergrowth, and are often found in secondary growth forest (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004, Radhakrishna and Singh 2002). This species is characterized by a multiple-male/multiple-female social system of spatial overlap. They sleep in groups of up to seven individuals and interact commonly throughout the night (Nekaris 2006, Radhakrishna 2001). Loris lydekkerianus nordicus is very well studied in captivity (Schulze and Meier 1995). They are primarily insectivorous (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004) and are apparently able to survive well near human habitations (Nekaris and Jayewardene, 2003), as L. l. nordicus was found more often associated with disturbed human habitation than with forest (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004).Loris lydekkerianus grandis much prefers undisturbed forests than disturbed forests and this may cause its patchy distribution. It is found in a wide variety of habitats, including low wet evergreen forests, moist mixed evergreen forests, dry riverine forests, mid-elevation evergreen forests and a small portion of montane evergreen forests (Gamage et al. in press). Phillips kept grandis in captivity, reported it feeding on tree frogs, geckoes, and various kinds of insects, and it was mainly carnivorous (Phillips 1998, Nekari and Jayawardena 2004).Loris lydekkerianus uva is very rare but common in pristine undisturbed moist mixed evergreen forests (Gamage et al. 2017).
threats: Severe habitat loss in Sri Lanka and India threatens this species (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2003, Nekaris and Schulze 2005, Nekaris and Bearder 2006). Other threats include road kills, electrocution on uninsulated power lines, capture for pet trade and use in traditional “medicine,” and killing due to superstitious beliefs (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2003).Loris lydekkerianus malabaricus: occasional hunting (very rare) and habitat loss in some areas of its distribution are the main threats to this subspecies.Loris lydekerianus lydekkerianus: major threats include habitat loss outside protected areas, frequent road kills, electrocution on uninsulated power lines, capture for pet trade and use in traditional “medicine,” and killing due to superstitious beliefs, logging and clearance of forests, superstitious sensibilities as loris cry bringing misfortune, loris sighting resulting in spinsterhood, in Theni (Kanagavel et al. 2013), loris parts as cure-alls (Radakrishna et al. 2011). Prior to taxonomic revision in 2020 (Nijman et al. 2020), three subspecies were recognised in Sri Lanka: L. l. grandis, L. l. nordicus and L. l. uva. These are no longer recognised as separate taxa (and are now synonyms of L. l. lydekkerianus), however since this Red List assessment was carried out in 2015, populations previously identified as these taxa are referred to by their former subspecies names below. Loris lydekkerianus grandis: major threats are habitat loss and degradation of habitat due to expansion of agriculture, urbanisation, encroachment by villagers, illegal logging, firewood extraction, cardamom plantation, forest fire in the Uva region, and invasive alien species (Gamage et al. 2017, Gamage et al. in press).Loris lydekkerianus nordicus: major threats are habitat loss and degradation of habitat due to expansion of agriculture, urbanisation, encroachment by villagers, illegal logging and invasive alien species (Gamage et al. 2017, Gamage et al. in press). Additional threats: occasional road kills and electrocution (Nekaris and Jayawardena 2004).Loris lydekkerianus uva: habitat loss from agriculture, plantations, development and human settlements is causing severe fragmentation, deforestation and degradation (Gamage et al. 2017).
population: The population is suspected to have declined by 20–25% over the past few generations. Furthermore, it is suspected that this rate of decline will continue into the future. Population reductions are suspected to have occurred primarily due to habitat degradation and loss, as well as due to a number of other threats. The encounter rate of L. l. malabaricus in Talakaveri is 0.21/km, in Pushpagiri Wildlife Sanctuary it is 0.28/km, and in Sharavati Valley Wildlife Sanctuary 0.35/km. Relative abundance of L. l. malabaricus in Kerala is <0.2 lorises/km, except Aralam Wildlife Sanctuary, Konni, Thiruvanthapuram, Nemmara, and Chimmoney. The encounter rate for L. l. malabaricus is 0.21 animals/km (Sasi and Kumara 2014, Radhakrishna et al. 2011).Although Loris lydekkerianus lydekkerianus is widely distributed, it is highly fragmented, except for a few places where populations are contiguous due to habitat contiguity. The density is very high in certain fragments due to lack of space for the dispersal; for example, 0.16 individuals/ha in Devrayandurga State Forest to 2.57 individuals/ha in Ippadi State Forest with highest density of 165 individuals /km² in Tumkur Forest Division. Ujjaini, Ippadi, Nagavalli, and Savanadurga have high densities of Slender Lorises at 1.85 individuals/ha. Such high densities are found in small patches and therefore cannot be extrapolated to area of occurrence. In some localities of the Eastern Ghats, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, the population densities of L. l. lydekkerianus are rather high, although not as high as in Dindigul region (Singh et al. 2000, Kumara et al. 2016).Prior to taxonomic revision in 2020 (Nijman et al. 2020), three subspecies were recognised in Sri Lanka: L. l. grandis, L. l. nordicus and L. l. uva. These are no longer recognised as separate taxa (and are now synonyms of L. l. lydekkerianus), however since this Red List assessment was carried out in 2015, populations previously identified as these taxa are referred to by their former subspecies names below.Nekaris and Jayewardene (2003, 2004) carried out a survey of Slender Lorises in Sri Lanka. In this study population densities of the animals were estimated using animal encounter rate (ex: animal/km). According to these authors, L. l. nordicus had an encounter rate of mean 3.6 loris/km (range 0.33 to 50/km), whereas L. l. grandis was encountered at a mean of 0.42 /km (range  0.11 to 3.3/km). The greater prevalence of L. l. nordicus than L. l. grandis had been noted earlier by Petter and Hladik (1970) who estimated a density of one loris per ha (100/km²) for L. l. nordicus in the dry zone forest at the Polonnaruwa Sanctuary, but far fewer L. l. grandis at 0.2 loris/ha (18/km²) in the wet zone hills of Udawattakelle Santuary of Kandy. Local populations that were formerly identified as L. l. nordicus can be relatively high; for example, in the protected forest surrounding the Smithsonian Primate Research Station at Polonnaruwa, densities may reach 3-5 loris/ha (300–500/km²) (WPJ Dittus, pers comm), somewhat greater than the density of 1/ha observed in the Polonnaruwa Nature Sanctuary (Petter and Hladik 1970).Loris lydekkerianus grandis much preferred undisturbed forests than disturbed forests, which may cause its patchy distribution (Gamage et al. in press). According to Nekari and Jayawardena (2004), mean abundance is 0.42 /km (range  0.11 to 3.3/km). Phillips kept L. l. grandis in captivity and reported it feeding on tree frogs, geckoes, and various kinds of insects, and it was mainly carnivorous (Phillips 1998, Nekaris and Jayawardena 2004).Nothing much is known about the population of L. l. uva except that it is suspected to be declining due to severe threats to the habitat.
range: The species occurs in southern and eastern India (Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu) and Sri Lanka.It is suspected that the extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both declining for the species due to ongoing habitat degradation and loss. For example, India has lost 19% of tree cover from 2002 to 2019 (Global Forest Watch 2020). Meanwhile, Sri Lanka lost 5.7% of its total tree cover during the same time period (Global Forest Watch 2020).
useTrade: This species is traded in India due to superstitious beliefs among many locals. Lorises are used for various dubious practices such as selecting horoscopes, sacrifices, black magic, and to ward of evil eye. In some instances lorises are caught and killed for improving eyesight in humans (Smitha Daniel, pers. comm.).
conservationActions: This species is listed in CITES Appendix II, and classified under Schedule I of the Indian Wildlife Act (1972). In India, very few populations are found in protected areas, and the majority of the population occurs in private lands and commercial plantations (M. Singh pers. comm.).In Sri Lanka, the species is listed under the Flora and Fauna Protection Ordinance Act No. 2 of 1937 amended in 2009. In Sri Lanka able to formulate a Conservation Strategy for the Slender Lorises of Sri Lanka 2016-2025 by the Slender Loris Conservation Project (SLCP), Zoological Society of London (ZSL) & Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) Sri Lanka and this will publish in the year 2016. Further studies of behaviour and ecology are needed to better understand the habitat requirements of all the slender loris taxa (Nekaris and Jayewardene 2004). Singh et al. (1999) also suggests more detailed surveys in different forest blocks and habitat types in order to obtain quantitative data on densities and distribution. In Sri Lanka a conservation education programme has been launched in order to increase awareness about the taxa (Nekaris 2003).Loris lydekkerianus malabaricus: periodic monitoring and population assessments as there are no major threats. Over the past decade, since the last assessment the status has improved primarily due to increase in protected area coverage and improved management.Loris lydekkerianus lydekkerianus: in Karnataka, L. l. lydekerianus is found outside protected areas. The subspecies could well survive on road side trees and hardly come into conflict with human beings in the area. Managing such areas harbouring high densities of lorises by regulating deforestation and mitigating further degradation could help much in conserving the loris in the area. Converting Eucalyptus plantations into economically viable loris corridors by planting native Acacia spp., Caesalpinia spp., and Azadirachta indica could benefit both farmers and lorises (Das et al. 2011).

rationale: Northern Pig-tailed Macaque is listed as Vulnerable as its population is suspected to have declined by over 30% over the last three generations (36-39 years) across its entire distribution range due to multiple threats. This decline is predicted to continue at the same rate or higher over the next three generations. Ongoing threats from increasing habitat loss due to development, new settlements, agriculture, plantation, and other activities, and from hunting for various reasons, the species is likely to face a higher threat of decline unless specific actions are taken to ensure its survival. Nationally, in India this species is listed as Endangered, and in Bangladesh it is Critically Endangered.
habitat: This is a predominantly arboreal animal. It is diurnal and frugivorous. It occupies tropical evergreen and semi­-evergreen forest, tropical wet evergreen forest, tropical  moist deciduous forest, coastal forest, swamp forest, low elevation pine forests (in Lao PDR and China) and montane forest, including degraded forests. In China the species occupies elevations between 50­2,000 m (Molur et al. 2003, Choudhury 2003). In Lao PDR and Viet Nam the species is associated with low lands, usually below 500 m. Its generation length is 12-­13 years (Molur et al. 2003). According to secondary information and recent records, populations in Myanmar live between 190­-400 m (S. Htun pers. comm).Dark evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, tropical, subtropical and deciduous forests in plains, foothills, hills. (50-2,000 m). Found in lowland primary, secondary forest, pine, dry dipterocarp, coastal swamp, montane forest. Frequently observed in riparian forests in western Thailand and Laos, occasionally near human settlements, cultivated fields where it once relatively common (back in 1990), even in highly degraded regions. Known to share associations with Assamese macaques (Macaca assamemensis) western Thailand and the ranges of the two species were observed to overlap in Assam. Range overlaps also with Stump-tailed and Rhesus macaques besides langurs and Hoolocks (Anwaruddin Choudhury in litt., July 2019).This species eats more than 91 kinds of plants such as mature and tender leaves, leaf buds, leaf petioles, seeds, stems, climbers, roots, flowers, flower buds, inflorescences, bamboo shoots, and gums, insects, larvae, termite eggs and spiders. They also feed on post-harvest Rice paddy in NE India and fruits and vegetables by slash and burn agriculture of the hill tribe. Habituated groups have also been observed to beg for food and feed on biscuits as in Khao Yai National Park, Thailand.In NE India, winter-spring breeding has been observed. Females are sexually receptive in August-December, but some might continue through to February. Birthing occurs in mid-January, early May, and a few in June. Swellings occur during breeding, as in Lion-tailed Macaques (Macaca silenus). Gestation period is 171-180 days (Choudhury 2008).This species is primarily arboreal, but it may use both terrestrial and arboreal pathways; individuals flee from danger through trees and not by ground. They use the ground when crossing clearings, roads, to forage, feed in degraded areas and also feed on crops. Seasonal fluctuations dictate the time spent on the ground feeding on crops. One site reported macaques spending over 20% of their time feeding on the ground on sugar cane left overs by elephants (Elephas maximus). Detailed observation of the species in eastern and central Assam in 1992-1994 and 2004 recorded three peaks of feeding and long mid-day rest, shorter mid-morning rest spells, resting 45%, feeding 23.5%, locomotion 17-19.4%, grooming 6-8%. Actual time spent feeding 153-229 mins/day. Spent 65% of feeding time in January on harvested paddy.In Assam (Tikleswari, Borajan) the macaques raids the vegetable gardens, crop field and villages (D. Chetry and D. Das pers. comm).Home range is 83-347 ha, with about 25-48% overlap (Choudhury 2008). Daily movement is 690-2,240 m, influenced by weather and availability of fruits: where fruiting trees were far apart, the daily movement increased. Multi-male, multi-female groups of 12-40 individuals are seen (Choudhury 2008). Estimated group size in Laos rarely exceeds 20-30 individuals. There are few records of groups numbering 50-150 individuals in KhaoYai National Park in Thailand, DakLak Province in Viet Nam and DhouPhouVieng National Biodiversity Conservation Area in Laos. It may be the case that two or more groups were feeding together.Niche occupation studies by Feroz (2012) in Bangladesh indicated the mean group size of 19.8 (13-26) individuals, with a density of 2.5-6.9 individuals/km2 as studied in 21 sites.  They spent only about 1% of their time on the ground and about 85% of their time on mid canopy and in 97.6% of the cases found inside the forest as opposed to the sympatric M. mulatta that is found outside forests in farms and gardens. Direct competition was found to be scarce between the species and the overlap or sharing of resources was only found to be 22.4%. Of the 101 plant species used between both the species, only 42.6%  shared (Feroz 2012).In KhaoYai National Park,Thailand these macaques preferred tall sleeping trees (mean 20.9+/- SD 4.9 m) and ‘high sleeping places’(15.8+/- SD 4.3 m) and tend to reuse the sleeping site, an anti-predator strategy (Albert et al. 2011).
threats: Habitat disturbances affecting the future survival of this species include: selective logging; timber and firewood collection for making charcoal; building roads, dams, power lines; and deliberately setting fires. These threats lead to  forest fragmentation and soil loss/erosion. Specifically, a decrease in habitat quality has been due to the loss of fruiting trees and sleeping sites through monocultures and plantations, selective felling, and a subsequent increase in canopy gaps. These animals are hunted and traded for food, sport and traditional “medicine”, and accidental mortality due to trapping occurs. There is a local trade for bones, meat for food and the live animals as pets (Molur et al. 2003). Habitat loss and poaching are the major threats in India and Bangladesh. There has been a reduction in forest in Assam by over 10% in two years between 2001 and 2003 (Forest Survey of India 2003) and the rate of habitat loss has not reduced. Recent forest cover survey report of Ministry of Environment Forest and Climate Change, Government of India suggest that the dense forest cover in the distribution range is decreasing 2011-2013.In Lao PDR, Viet Nam and Cambodia, hunting for food and trade is the primary threat, but as a predominantly lowland species habitat  loss likely is also a major threat to the  species. In Thailand, the males of this species are exploited for picking coconuts by the industry. Sometimes, a well-trained macaque is sold for 1,000 USD. They are also in demand by resorts for show (R. Boonratana pers. comm). In Myanmar, hunting, trade, habitat loss in varying degrees, shifting cultivation in the north, logging in the east and south, and rubber plantations are the major threats (S. Htun pers. comm).In China, hunting, habitat loss and disturbance are major threats. There is a perceptible change in habitat quality that has an impact on the species (Huang et al. pers. comm).
population: In China, the species’ population is estimated to be less than 1,700 individuals (Jiang and Long pers. comm). No information is available on the status of the population dynamics, but it is suspected to be in decline. A very small population occurs in Bangladesh, which is isolated from the neighbouring Indian locations. This habitat is degrading rapidly, thereby causing a continuing decline in mature individuals in the country (Molur et al. 2003). A group density of 0.07 individuals/km² was recorded in Namdapha National Park, India, by Chetry et al. (2003). There is no precise information available on population numbers in Myanmar. In India the population is <1,500 individuals and populations are declining rapidly (Chetry and Das pers. comm.) but in one protected area (Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary) it is increasing. Choudhury (2003) stated that there may have been around 24,000 of these macaques in India at the turn of this century. The population has apparently declined owing to habitat loss.Niche occupation studies by Feroz (2012) in Bangladesh indicated the mean group size of 19.8 (13-26) individuals, with a density of 2.5-6.9 individuals/km² as studied in 21 sites. The mean of seven groups in Assam was 23.3 (range: 16-33) (Choudhury 2008); however, the largest group observed was of 43 macaques in Radhakishorepur reserved forest, Tripura in 2016 (Choudhury in press).It is also declining steadily in Myanmar.  The animals are very patchily distributed in Myanmar. The species is widely distributed and common in large forest blocks remaining in southern and central Lao PDR, but it is much scarcer in northern Lao PDR and Viet Nam (R. Timmins pers. comm). It is widely distributed through the remaining forest areas of Cambodia. Populations are stable in Thailand. Declines are due to different threats in different countries. There have been declines of more than 30% in the last 30­-35 (three generations) years in India, Bangladesh, China, Viet Nam and Myanmar. There are perceptible declines in Lao PDR and Cambodia, but the rates are close to or lower than 30%. In most of the countries, the species is predicted to decline at a rate higher than 30% over the next three generations due to increasing trends in habitat loss, persecution, and trade.
range: This species occurs in eastern Bangladesh, Cambodia, southern China (southwestern Yunnan), northeastern India (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura (Choudhury 1988, 2013)), Lao PDR, Myanmar (including the Mergui Archipelago), Thailand (from about 8°N and including adjacent islands), and central and southern Viet Nam. There might be a gap in the distribution in central and northeastern Myanmar between about 20 and 25°N, where it has not been recorded except on the coast at Arakan. In India found north to the Brahmaputra River (Groves 2001).Records from Xizang (China) are probably misidentified rhesus macaques (MacKinnon in press). It has recently been recorded from Namdapha National Park in northeastern India (Chetry et al. 2003). The precise taxonomic boundary between M. leonina and M. nemestrina is not well defined. There are populations of the two taxa found on either side of the distribution limits in the Isthmus of Kra, but many of these populations are the result of release by humans. The two species hybridize in a small area of southern peninsular Thailand, as well as on the islands of Phuket and Yao Yai (Groves 2001). In Viet Nam, there are historical records from as far north as Nghe An province, but there is uncertainty whether the species was ever found north of this province. It is widely distributed throughout the lower elevations (below 500 m) of Lao PDR and Cambodia (R. Timmins pers. comm.). It is found over much Myanmar except in areas of human settlements.
useTrade: In Thailand, the males of this species are exploited for picking coconuts by the industry. In almost throughout its range, the species is hunted for meat and for 'medicine'. Hunting is rampant in areas of development mainly for food.
conservationActions: This species is listed under CITES Appendix II. It is listed as Schedule III in the Bangladesh Wildlife (Preservation) (Amendment) Act, 1974, Category I under the Chinese Wildlife Protection Act (1989), and as Schedule II under the Indian Wildlife(Protection) Act, 1972 (Chetry et al. 2003), amended up to 2002. In Indian context the species facing severe threats with few populations left and needs revision of the Indian status so that in can get better protection. Northern pig­tailed macaques are known to occur in numerous protected areas, including Chunati Wildlife Sanctuary, Lawachara National  Park, Rema ­Kelanga Wildlife Sanctuary (Bangladesh); Daxueshan Nature Reserve, Nanguanhe Nature Reserve, WuliangshanNature Reserve, Xishuangbanna Nature Reserve (China); Balpakhram National Park, Dampa Wildlife Sanctuary, Dibru­Saikhowa National Park, Fakim Wildlife Sanctuary, Garampani Wildlife Sanctuary, Holongopar Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary, Gumti Wildlife Sanctuary, Intanki National Park, Kamlang WildlifeSanctuary, Lengteng Wildlife Sanctuary, Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, Murlen NationalPark, Namdapha National Park, Ngengpui Wildlife Sanctuary, Nongkhyllem Wildlife Sanctuary, Bherjan-Boorajan-Podumoni Wildlife Sanctuary, Phawngpui Blue Mountain National Park, Sepahijala Wildlife Sanctuary, Siju Wildlife Sanctuary, Trishna Wildlife Sanctuary, Yangoupokpi­ Lokchao Wildlife Sanctuary (India); Pidaung Wildlife Sanctuary (Myanmar); Doi Suthep Pui National Park, Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary (Thailand); Cat Tien National Park, Pu Mat National Park (Viet Nam). The species possibly occurs in Nam Ha National Biodiversity Conservation Area (Lao PDR) (M. Richardson pers. comm.; Molur et al. 2003). In India, it has been recorded in at least 29 protected areas (Choudhury 2016).The species is considered Critically Endangered in Bangladesh and Endangered in India.Destruction and degradation due to encroachment, monoculture tree plantations, fisheries, slash and burn shifting cultivation, by hill tribes (cultural minorities). They are also killed for food by Hill tribes in NE India as they have access to automatic firearms. Poaching rampant in Assam-Mizoram border. Poaching rampant in Assam-Mizoram border. In China, it is variously described as rare and endangered and thought to number to ca1,000 about the year 2000. The species was classified as Vulnerable in the Red Data Book of Viet Nam in 1990. Poaching for traditional medicine is now a threat to all primates in the country and no new conservation program is in place.Other direct threats include logging, gold mining, shifting cultivation by the hill tribe minority, development of economy and infrastructure resulting in habitat loss and degradation, hunting for food by villagers, hunting for traditional medicine to supply bone to the Viet Nam for use in medicine. Although in their incipient stage, agriculture, mining and hydropower are causing significant damages in terms of forest loss. In Cambodia, the species is reported only in five out of 24 provinces: use in traditional medicine, loss of habitat from logging, and trade are major threats in the region. In Myanmar, logging, plantation, aquaculture, hunting for food and pets, political unrest in cultural minority states impact primates. Timber extraction, large scale farms and plantations, irrigation, hydroelectric projects, highway construction, mineral exploration, resettlement programs for hill tribes, recreation and tourism, have significantly reduced forest cover in Thailand. Shifting cultivation of hill tribes and ethnic Thais have cleared large forests. Illegal hunting for sale (market hunting) and poaching for food near villages could have a direct effect on primate population in Thailand, including Macaca leonina. The Western Conservation Corridor, western Thailand may offer protection to both habitat and wildlife.

rationale: Considering the extensive habitat loss and fragmentation from changing land use such as large scale conversion to plantations, small-holder farming, limestone quarrying and potentially the construction of dams that has taken place within the range of Trachypithecus germaini, and the fact that the population is under high hunting pressure for traditional medicine and pet trade, it is suspected that the population size is quite small, fragmented and in decline, probably at a rate of more than 50% over three generations (approximately 36 years). It therefore qualifies for listing as Endangered. Since the threats are continuing and there is a lack of conservation 'will' politically and amongst the public, it is suspected that the decline will continue at the same rate if not more over the next three generations.
habitat: The Indochinese Silvered Langur occurs in lowland, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests on Phu Quoc Island, and forest on karst areas, mangrove forest and inundated Melaleuca forest in mainland Viet Nam (Hoang Minh Duc et al. 2012b, Hoang Minh Duc pers. obs.).
