High ambient temperatures constrain wild dogs’ hunting opportunities (Rabaiotti and Woodroffe 2019), and periods of hot weather have been linked to increased pup mortality, extended inter-birth intervals, lower adult survival, and altered phenology (Woodroffe et al. 2017, Rabaiotti et al. 2021, Abrahms et al. 2022). These demographic impacts of high temperatures help to explain why the energy-intensive pup-rearing period coincides with the coolest part of the year (McNutt et al. 2019). Projecting the potential impacts of climate change indicates that even quite probable carbon emission scenarios may be sufficient to prompt wild dog population collapse (Rabaiotti et al. 2023). Unfortunately, although this threat is well understood and not reversible in the short term, wild dogs’ short generation time means that it is projected to operate too slowly to trigger threat criteria under “projected decline” (Rabaiotti 2019).
population: Population estimates drew upon the best available evidence for each area of resident range. Where on-the-ground monitoring projects were in place, these projects were asked to provide up-to-date subpopulation size estimates (numbers of packs, and numbers of animals aged ≥12 months), for their areas of operation, these estimates drew on a range of data sources including tracking known individuals and packs with GPS-collars, visual monitoring, camera trap surveys, tourist photos, spoor surveys, and extrapolation from intensive study areas to nearby areas. Where there was no alternative data source, subpopulation size estimates were derived by multiplying the area of the resident range polygon by a conservative estimate of adult population density, with the number of packs then estimated using a mean pack size of 10 adults (McNutt and Silk 2008, Woodroffe et al. 2019). Mature individualsFor African wild dogs, the estimation of numbers of mature individuals is complicated by the species’ cooperative breeding behaviour, which means that many sexually mature individuals do not reproduce and hence do not contribute genetically to the next generation (Malcolm and Marten 1982, Creel et al. 1997, Girman et al. 1997a, McNutt and Silk 2008, Woodroffe et al. 2019). For this assessment, the number of mature individuals was estimated from the number of packs, by assuming that every pack contained a single alpha female and a single alpha male, while a proportion of packs also contained subdominant breeders in addition to the alphas. We used published data to calculate, separately, the average number of subdominant females, and the average number of subdominant males, reproducing each year, in addition to the alpha pair. Across seven study areas in Botswana, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, and South Africa, behavioural observations indicated that 32 of 343 litters were born to subdominant mothers (Frame et al. 1979, Girman et al. 1997b, Creel and Creel 2002, Spiering et al. 2010, McNutt 2019). As there were 32 litters born to subdominants and 311 born to alpha females, we inferred that, on average, there were 32/311 (0.103) subdominant breeding females for every alpha female. This value compared well with available genetic evidence (from two of the study subpopulations, Girman et al. 1997b, Spiering et al. 2010) which showed that, in South Africa, 10 of 137 pups had subdominant mothers, indicating that subdominant females produced 0.079 pups for every pup born to an alpha female.Male reproductive success can be measured only using genetics. In the same two genetic studies (Girman et al. 1997b, Spiering et al. 2010) 27 of 115 pups had subdominant fathers, indicating that subdominant males fathered 0.307 pups for every pup fathered by an alpha male.On the basis of this evidence, we estimated the number of mature individuals per subpopulation from the number of packs as:Mature individuals = Number of alpha females (= number of packs) + Number of subdominant breeding females (= number of packs x 0.103) + Number of alpha males (= number of packs) + Number of subdominant breeding males (= number of packs x 0.307).The estimate for each subpopulation was then rounded to the nearest whole number, and summed across all subpopulations to give a global population estimate. Trend in population sizeThe global estimate for the number of African wild dogs in the current assessment (2025: 1,676 mature individuals) exceeds the estimate for the previous assessment (2012: 1,409 mature individuals). However, this difference reflects two important changes, unrelated to real population trajectories. First, several additional wild dog subpopulations were discovered since the previous estimate, including those in south-eastern Angola (Funston et al. 2017), western Angola (Overton et al. 2020), and eastern parts of the Central African Republic (Aebischer et al. 2020). The addition of these subpopulations contributed to an increase in the global population estimate, but this change reflected a more accurate estimate rather than actual population growth. Second, for this assessment we slightly altered our method for estimating number of mature individuals. In contrast with the previous (2012) assessment, we based our estimate on the numbers of packs per site, rather than the numbers of adults, both because pack number can be easier to estimate in the field, and because it is more meaningful as a measure of population size (Woodroffe, O’Neill and Rabaiotti 2019). Additionally, the number of genetic studies available to inform our estimates of the number of subdominant breeders per pack increased from one (Girman et al. 1997a) to two (Girmanet al. 1997a, Spiering et al. 2010). For females, the rate of subdominant reproduction reported in the newer study (7.0% of pups with subdominant mothers, Spiering et al. 2010) was similar to that from the older study (7.8% of pups with subdominant mothers, Girman et al. 1997a), and was also consistent with behavioural data from seven sites. In contrast, for males the rate of subdominant reproduction could only be measured from genetics (rather than from behaviour as for females), and was found to be much higher in the newer study (27.9% of pups with subdominant fathers, Spiering et al.2010) than in the older study (10.3% of pups with subdominant fathers, Girman et al. 1997a). Unlike the older study (Girman et al. 1997a), the newer study came from a small, isolated subpopulation (Spiering et al. 2010) where limited opportunities to disperse and form new packs may have encouraged subdominant reproduction, and it is not clear to what extent it was representative of wild dog subpopulations more generally. However, as both studies had small sample sizes, we chose to include them both to draw upon the widest possible array of data to inform our estimates. However, we are aware that, in so doing, we may have inflated the estimated number of mature individuals, the global total (1,676 mature individuals) would have been 8% lower (1,543 mature individuals) had we drawn only on the older study of subdominant paternity. Indeed, the global total would have been 17% lower (1,392 mature individuals) had we ignored subdominant reproduction, as in the 2001 assessment.To avoid bias introduced by these methodological differences, we estimated recent population change by (i) restricting comparisons over time to sites with subpopulation size estimates in both 2012 and 2025, and (ii) comparing the estimated numbers of adults (animals aged ≥12 months) between the two time points, rather than the numbers of mature individuals, as this measure was estimated at both time points.On this basis, we estimated a 17% decline over the past three generations (15 years). The comparison period includes the population crash in Kenya’s Ewaso ecosystem (Mutinda et al. 2017), loss of wild dogs from Zambia’s Liuwa Plain (Zambia Carnivore Programme 2016) and the WAP Complex in West Africa (IUCN/SSC in review), and multiple whole-pack deaths in South Africa (Du Plessis 2016, Loots et al. 2017) and Tanzania (Grumeti Fund 2018). Across Africa, threats to wild dog populations are growing rather than declining, as human impacts on formerly wildlife-friendly habitats expand. As time passes, we expect there to be less habitat, fewer prey, more snares, more roads, and more domestic dogs and so more disease transmission. Facing this mass of threats, we expect wild dogs to continue the pattern of decline observed in recent years.Extreme fluctuationsWild dogs experience dramatic “boom and bust” population dynamics. Litter sizes are large, allowing populations to grow rapidly when conditions are favourable (e.g., Pole 2000, Woodroffe 2011a, Davies-Mostert et al. 2015). However, episodes of very high mortality are also relatively frequent, and are typically linked to disease outbreaks (e.g., Alexander et al. 2010, Goller et al. 2010). Since the last assessment there have been multiple episodes of this type (e.g., Du Plessis 2016, Zambia Carnivore Programme 2016, Grumeti Fund 2018, Loots et al. 2018, van Schalkwyk et al. 2019), including an epidemic of canine distemper virus which killed an estimated 20 packs in Kenya’s Laikipia County (part of the Ewaso ecosystem) within a three-month period in 2017 (Mutinda, Cook and Kinya 2017). For perspective, 23 of the 31 wild dog subpopulations remaining in Africa are estimated to number et al. 2000, Hofmeyr et al. 2004, Grumeti Fund 2018), as well as prompting two reintroductions to replace populations lost to disease (Masenga et al. 2017, African Parks 2021).Historical accounts show that disease-related wild dog die-offs are not a recent phenomenon. The earliest accounts document the loss of wild dogs from what is now the northern part of South Africa’s Kruger National Park during an epidemic attributed to “pulmonary distemper” in 1920, thought to have been transmitted by domestic dogs and to have entered from neighbouring Zimbabwe (Stevenson-Hamilton 1939). This die-off in the northern part of Kruger was followed in 1926 by the emergence of another disease (thought to be rickettsiosis) which led to wild dogs’ disappearance from the southern part of the park by 1931 (Stevenson-Hamilton 1939). Wild dogs were reported to have recolonised from neighbouring Mozambique in 1934 (Stevenson-Hamilton 1947), but rapidly disappeared again, with population recovery only beginning in earnest in 1948 (Reich 1981). A similar pattern has been observed elsewhere. Hoier (1955), noted wild dogs’ sudden appearance in, and equally sudden disappearance from, Albert National Park (now Virunga National Park in DRC), and proposed infectious disease as the cause. Wild dogs disappeared from Kenya’s Laikipia County during the 1980s in association with a disease outbreak, before recolonising two decades later (Woodroffe 2011a). Likewise, wild dogs disappeared from the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem on the Kenya-Tanzania border in a disease outbreak in 1990-1 (Gascoyne et al. 1993, Alexander and Appel 1994), returning after a decade (Marsden et al. 2011). The disappearance of wild dogs from the northern sections of Kruger National Park in the late 1990s may also have been caused by disease (Endangered Wildlife Trust 2017), this subpopulation recovered recently, after remaining low for two decades (Nicholson et al. 2020).These periods of very rapid disease-related decline, followed by prolonged absence and then recovery, are consistent with two other elements of African wild dogs’ life history. First, the very long-range movements of dispersers (Fuller et al. 1992, Davies-Mostert et al. 2012, Masenga et al. 2016, Cozzi et al. 2020, Woodroffe et al. 2020, Sandoval-Seres et al. 2022, Beytell et al. 2024) make it possible for them to detect and colonise (or recolonise) suitable habitat, even when it is located at some distance from resident populations. Second, wild dogs are capable of rapid population growth. Because litters are large, packs can easily double or even triple in size within a single breeding attempt (e.g., Mills 1993, Woodroffe et al. 2019) and, where environmental conditions are favourable, populations may grow rapidly. For example, wild dogs recolonising Kenya’s Laikipia County grew from one pack to 19 packs in eight years (Woodroffe 2011a), those establishing South Africa’s managed metapopulation grew from 17 individuals to 202 in seven years (Davies-Mostert et al. 2015), and two packs reintroduced to Mozambique’s Gorongosa National Park in 2018-9 (Bouley et al. 2021) had grown to 11 packs by late 2024 (Mercia Angela, pers. comm.). Other species with excellent dispersal abilities and high reproductive rates are adapted to exploit environmental conditions which are unpredictable and ephemeral (e.g., pioneer tree species which colonise and rapidly exploit gaps in rainforest canopy), and it may be the case that African wild dogs’ facility for (re)colonisation may indicate a similar adaptation. While the ephemeral resource to be exploited is likely to involve habitat with abundant prey and/or few competitors, one source of such habitat is land vacated due to disease mortality.Wild dogs’ “boom and bust” life history is relevant to their conservation (and hence to their red list assessment) for three reasons. First, rapid die-offs due to disease have occurred in large populations (e.g., Kruger in 1920 and Laikipia in 2017) as well as small populations, and inside protected areas (e.g., Serengeti in 1991 and Kruger in 2016) as well as outside, showing that neither population size nor protected status is sufficient to avoid sudden die-offs. Accounting for this additional risk is an important element of evaluating red list status. Second, although long-distance dispersal would, in the past, have allowed wild dogs to recolonise habitat vacated following disease die-offs, the habitat fragmentation typical of today’s human-dominated landscape acts as a barrier to dispersal (Cozzi et al. 2013, Jackson et al. 2016, Cozzi et al. 2020, O'Neill et al. 2020, O’Neill et al. 2022), impeding natural recolonisation and thus intensifying the impact of infectious disease on metapopulation persistence. Third, even if natural or assisted dispersal can return wild dogs to sites devastated by disease, other anthropogenic threats (including human-wildlife conflict, prey loss, climate change, and other infectious diseases) are all likely to hinder subpopulation recovery.In our view, this evidence of repeated disease-related die-offs, followed by natural recolonisation and recovery, makes the “extreme fluctuations” criterion appropriate to this species.
range: African Wild Dogs historically were distributed across Africa, south of the Sahara. However, as people degraded and destroyed natural habitat, wild dogs were extirpated across most of their historical range. Today, wild dogs are known to persist in just 8% of their historical range, with approximately two-thirds of this land lying outside IUCN Category I-IV protected areas (IUCN/SSC 2016, IUCN/SSC in review, IUCN/SSC in prep). The global wild population is estimated to number below 700 packs globally.African Wild Dog status varies across different regions of Africa. Their numbers are most robust in Southern Africa, where approximately 17% of the species’ historical range still supports breeding packs, comprising roughly two-thirds of the global population (IUCN/SSC 2016). The single largest subpopulation inhabits the Kavango-Zambezi (KAZA) Transfrontier Conservation Area, spanning northern Botswana, eastern Namibia, south-eastern Angola, south-western Zambia, and western Zimbabwe: KAZA alone supports nearly a third of the world’s African wild dogs (IUCN/SSC 2016). In eastern Africa, approximately 10% of historical range is still occupied by breeding packs, supporting nearly a third of the global population, the biggest subpopulation is in the Selous/Nyerere complex of southern Tanzania, which is thought to connect to Southern Africa via a corridor to northern Mozambique (IUCN/SSC in review). In Central Africa, wild dogs remain in just 5% of their historical range, with the largest subpopulation in and around Chinko National Park in the Central African Republic (IUCN/SSC in review). In West Africa the situation is even more serious, with a single remaining subpopulation in Sénégal’s Niokolo Koba National Park, covering just 0.2% of the region’s historical range and representing less than 0.5% of the global population (IUCN/SSC in prep-b). Most of North Africa falls outside wild dogs’ historical range, and the species is believed to be extinct in this region (IUCN/SSC in review).
useTrade: Across most of its geographical range, there is minimal consumptive use of this species. Evidence of localised traditional use has been reported in Zimbabwe (Davies and Du Toit 2004), but this is not reported from other areas. There is a low level of international trade in captive animals from South Africa to zoos worldwide, but no recent reports of animals being taken from the wild to support this trade.
conservationActions: Conservation action for African wild dogs is guided by regional strategies for southern Africa (IUCN/SSC 2016), eastern Africa (IUCN/SSC in prep), and North, West, and Central Africa (IUCN/SSC in review). These regional strategies each cover 10 years, and each has been updated at least once (IUCN/SSC 2008, IUCN/SSC 2010, IUCN/SSC 2012). Many range states have chosen to use their corresponding regional strategy as a template for developing National Action Plans (e.g., Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute 2016).Given the central threat from habitat loss, habitat conservation is the most important action needed to prevent wild dog extinction. Wild dogs require habitat conservation at scales seldom considered for other species, making them an excellent flagship for very large protected areas (e.g., South Africa’s Kruger National Park), protected area complexes (e.g., Tanzania’s Selous Game Reserve/Nyerere National Park), and Trans-Frontier Conservation Areas (e.g., KAZA). These three areas together support over half of the world’s wild dogs, and maintaining their integrity is the top priority for wild dog conservation. Wild dogs can also persist at scale outside protected areas, where land use is conducive, for example the pastoralist areas of northern and eastern Kenya support important populations almost entirely on community land, while combining private ranches in Zimbabwe into multi-owner conservancies fostered impressive recoveries, and persistence, of wild dogs on private land. Education, at all levels of society, is important to explain, justify, and promote the prioritisation of wildlife conservation at such scales.Although wild dog conservation is compatible with some hunting offtake of other species (e.g., in well-managed hunting reserves), indiscriminate hunting with snares has devastating impacts on wild dogs, which are highly susceptible to accidental capture. Control of snaring is a vital element of wild dog conservation (Becker et al. 2013), while removal of snares from the environment, antipoaching, and support for alternative livelihoods may all reduce snaring impacts on wildlife, removal of snares from injured animals may also play an important role in preventing population decline (Banda et al. 2023). Where snaring is a major concern, close monitoring of packs fitted with tracking collars can help with detecting and removing snares.Where wild dogs share the landscape with people, livestock farming is likely to be the primary human land use, creating opportunities for livestock predation and hence human-wildlife conflict. Approaches to mitigating human-wildlife conflict include conserving wild prey, as well as encouraging forms of livestock husbandry which deter predation (e.g., Rasmussen 1996, Woodroffe et al. 2005, Woodroffe et al. 2007b).Infectious disease is a biologically complex and hence challenging threat to wild dogs. Across much of Africa, rabies persists in domestic dog populations, and mass vaccination of domestic dogs is an effective way to protect local people and domestic animals, as well as wild carnivores, from a devastating disease (Cleaveland et al. 2003, Cleaveland et al. 2006, Prager et al. 2013, Hayes et al. 2022). However, wildlife likely play a key role in the persistence of canine distemper virus (Craft et al. 2008, Prager et al. 2012, Prager et al. 2013, Viana et al. 2015), meaning that domestic dog vaccination is unlikely to be as effective for distemper as it should be for rabies. Vaccination of wild dogs themselves has been shown to be both safe and effective against both pathogens (Reuben et al. in prep, Woodroffe et al. in prep, Gold et al. in review), the Canid Specialist group is current preparing guidelines to support wild dog managers in deciding which intervention is most important under which circumstances. As for snaring, monitoring using tracking collars is a vital tool for detecting and responding to disease outbreaks.Reducing the impact of road mortality on wild dogs is best achieved by avoiding routing major roads in and near wild dog habitat. Where such roads are already in place, measures such as signage and speed bumps may help to reduce impacts. Elsewhere in the world, over- and under-passes are used to reduce road mortality for both people and wildlife, such approaches are not yet widely practised in Africa, but could be valuable where road improvement or construction in or near wild dog habitat is unavoidable.As climate change is a global phenomenon, only global action to reduce carbon emissions can entirely avoid or reverse its negative consequences for African wild dogs. However, analyses suggest that weather impacts on adult wild dogs operate, at least in part, by increasing their susceptibility to existing causes of mortality such as disease and human wildlife conflict (Rabaiotti et al. 2021). Hence, climate impacts might be mitigated, to some extent by addressing other threats to wild dog populations.As is apparent from the narrative above, wild dog conservation action is often species-specific, hence it can only be implemented where wild dogs are known to occur. Important wild dog populations remained undetected in Angola and CAR until recent years, and it is possible that some other populations are yet to be confirmed. Surveys are much-needed, especially in areas identified in conservation strategies as “possible range” (IUCN/SSC 2016, IUCN/SSC in prep, IUCN/SSC in review). Likewise, monitoring of key populations is crucial to targeting conservation interventions, assessing their efficacy, and identifying new threats.Participants in strategic planning have identified few areas of “recoverable range”, where natural recolonisation or reintroduction could be considered (IUCN/SSC 2016, IUCN/SSC in prep, IUCN/SSC in review). While conserving existing populations should be prioritised over attempting to restore lost ones, reintroduction may have an important role to play in certain areas. Methods for reintroduction have been developed and honed in South Africa, in the course of establishing and maintaining a "managed metapopulation" of very small subpopulations across an array of small, fenced reserves, none of which would be viable on its own but which, under intensive management, has proven very successful when viewed as a single unit (Davies-Mostert et al. 2015). The methods developed in managing the metapopulation have been applied to reintroductions outside South Africa, most notably the successful restoration of wild dogs to Mozambique’s Gorongosa National Park (Bouley et al. 2021), which numbered 11 packs at the most recent estimate. Thus far, reintroductions have been restricted to southern Africa, translocations further afield should be guided by (ongoing; Ramage et al. in prep) studies of wild dog sub-specific taxonomy and evolutionarily significant units (Hoelzel 2023), as has been agreed recently for lions (Becker et al. 2022, Bertola et al. 2022).While it is now well-established that wild dog translocations should rely on wild-reared animals which have the survival skills needed for life in the wild, captive populations also have an important role to play in wild dog conservation. Developing guidelines for managing disease would have been far more difficult had it not been possible to evaluate vaccines and vaccination protocols in captivity before trialling them in the wild (e.g., Connolly et al. 2013, Connolly et al. 2015, Wahldén et al. 2018). Likewise, accelerometry collars used to better understand the impacts of prey loss and climate change were evaluated first in captivity (English et al. 2023). Zoos play a vital role in educating and inspiring people worldwide to care about wild dogs, and provide a vital stream of funding to support conservation action in the field.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)EU 27 regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)The Italian Water Vole is endemic to Europe. A population reduction of 20-25% is suspected to have occurred in the past 10 years, due to the decline of the subpopulations found in some parts of its range and the continuous reduction and fragmentation of the quality of the riparian habitat, bringing the species close to the qualifying as Vulnerable (A2ce). It is therefore assessed as Near Threatened both globally and for the EU 27 member states.
habitat: This species prefers habitats similar to those of Arvicola amphibius therefore it inhabits the riparian areas of waterways, swamps, canals, ponds, lakes, especially with abundant herbaceous vegetation. It feeds on plants that it finds in aquatic and riparian areas. Ecology information is not yet available but is probably similar to A. amphibius.
threats: The most important threats to this vole are the alterations of waterways, with particular regard to the overbuilding of embankments and the frequent maintenance and removal of riparian vegetation. The reduction or fragmentation of the habitat produces an excessive fragmentation of the populations. Moreover, freshwater habitat conditions in the region may be worsening: it is estimated that 46.2% of freshwater habitat types in Italy are threatened (Gigante et al. 2018) and in the reporting period 2013-2018, it was estimated that 66.6% freshwater habitats in Italy were not of a favourable conservation status (https://biodiversity.europa.eu/countries/italy). Further threats include the use of rodenticides as well as the possible competition with Rattus norvegicus and Myocastor coypus, and predation by Neogale vison. N. vison is now well established in northern and central Italy (Loy et al. 2019), with the water vole one of its main prey species (Mori and Mazza 2019).
population: There is a lack of data on the size and trend of populations, but significant reductions have been observed in some lowland areas. Based on declines in habitat quality, as well as threats of predation and competition, it is likely that this species has undergone a reduction of 20-25% over the previous ten years.
range: This species is endemic to Europe, where it occurs in peninsular Italy, marginally in southern Switzerland (Ticino) and possibly western Slovenia (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). It is found from sea level up to 1,600 m (Pardinas et al. 2017).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is currently not legally protected but it is present in some protected areas. Habitat protection and site management could benefit this species.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This is a very widespread and common species with no widespread threats. It is assessed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 Member States.
habitat: It is found in a wide variety of open habitats including moist meadows, pastures, forest-steppe, moist forest and sometimes agricultural areas, rarely in forest plantations. It feeds mainly on the green parts of grasses and herbaceous plants and is a serious agricultural pest in some areas (Zima 1999). Females produce three to four litters per year.
threats: There are no known widespread threats to the species.
population: It is a common species throughout much of its range, with population densities of over 1,000 individuals per ha reported in peak years. Population densities may fluctuate markedly from year to year. The species is probably increasing in some parts of its range (B. Krystufek pers. comm.)
range: Microtus arvalis is a European endemic species with a large range that extends from Spain across much of western, central and eastern Europe to central European Russia (Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005, Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). Isolated subpopulations occur in the Iberian Peninsula, on Guernsey and on the Orkney Islands (where it was introduced prehistorically). It is absent from much of southern Europe, Fennoscandia, northern Russia, Iceland and the British Isles (except the Orkney Islands). The species occurs from sea level to 2,600 m (Spitzenberger 2001).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is present in many protected areas. It is often considered a pest as it damages crops.

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered under criterion B1 as it has a small extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 4,896 km², the population is considered to be severely fragmented and presumed to be declining as a result of habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation, as well as interspecific competition with or predation by invasive alien species, littering and/or exposure to agricultural chemicals. Research is urgently needed to gather robust population data.
habitat: The Canary Shrew is mainly known from malpaís (barren lava fields with sparse vegetation), where it likely makes use of rich underground structures and lava tubes that experience less temperature fluctuation and higher humidity relative to external conditions. It seems to be adapted to the hot and dry conditions of these plains (Hutterer et al. 1992, Stone 1995), but it is found in many habitat types, such as sandy plains, ravines and barren mountain crests. The shrew is also sometimes found in gardens and abandoned arable land (Palomo et al. 2007). It feeds on insects and other invertebrates, and can depredate Atlantic Lizards (Gallotia atlantica) sometimes bigger than itself owing to venom in its saliva used to immobilise prey (López-Jurado and Mateo 1996).
threats: This species has a highly restricted distribution. Rapid urbanisation and infrastructure development in and around its range are causing loss and fragmentation of suitable habitat, and desiccation may also be a problem (Hutterer 2004). The use of chemicals in agriculture and residential areas are also thought to be a threat (C. Schuster pers. comm. 2022). Introduced cats (Felis catus) sometimes depredate Canary Shrews (Palomo and Gisbert 2002). Other introduced species, e.g. the North African Hedgehog (Atelerix algirus) and rodents such as the Barbary Ground Squirrel (Atlantoxerus getulus) are also present and may outcompete the Canary Shrew (Schuster 2014). In particular, accidental transportation of the White-toothed Shrew (Crocidura russula) from Gran Canaria may pose significant threat (Román et al. 2021) – the White-toothed Shrew is thought to be competitive and dominant, and can displace other shrew species. Finally, littering poses a notable risk to the Canary Shrew since individuals can easily become trapped and die in discarded bottles (Schuster 2014).
population: Few data are available on abundance and population trends of this species, though it is assumed to be decreasing (European Environment Agency 2020) given continued habitat loss and increasing numbers of introduced cats (C. Schuster pers. comm. 2022). Surveys undertaken in 2014 failed to capture the Canary Shrew in at least four protected areas formerly occupied by this species in Fuerteventura (Schuster 2014), but also registered the species in two previously unknown locations – continued monitoring is required to confirm occupancy status. The results of trapping surveys undertaken in recent years in Fuerteventura, Lanzarote and Mount Clara suggest that the Canary Shrew is more abundant on Mount Clara (C. Schuster pers. comm. 2022). This may be because Mount Clara is uninhabited and lacks invasive alien species (Palomo et al. 2007). The population is considered to be severely fragmented as it occurs on four islands with no dispersal between them. Mount Clara holds a very small population.
range: The Canary Shrew (Crocidura canariensis) is endemic to the eastern Canary Islands, where it is currently found on Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, and the islets of Lobos and Mount Clara. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 2,480 km². In Fuerteventura, there are no records of presence of this species in the south of the island, though this may be due to a limited number of surveys undertaken here. Fossil evidence indicates that it previously occurred on La Graciosa and Alegranza (Hutterer 1999), but it has never been trapped on either of these islands and is presumed to have gone extinct (Palomo and Gisbert 2002, Rando et al. 2011). Remains of this species found in owl pellets collected on La Graciosa and Alegranza are believed to result from the movement of owls between different islands (Palomo and Gisbert 2002). Overall, the distribution of the Canary Shrew may be severely fragmented as a result of anthropogenic-associated habitat loss further to existing natural barriers to dispersal (R. Hutterer pers. comm. 2006, C. Schuster pers. comm. 2022).
useTrade: This shrew species is not subject to trade and it is not utilised in any way.
conservationActions: The Canary Shrew is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention and Annex IV of the EU Habitats and Species Directive, and is also protected under Spanish law. It is found within a number of protected areas in Fuerteventura (including Corralejo, Betancuria, Malpaís Grande, and Cuchillos de Vigán), in Lanzarote (including Timanfaya National Park, in several protected areas of Natura 2000 and Canary Protected Areas Web), and in Lobos and Mount Clara (the latter islands are protected as a whole) (Schuster 2014). Research is needed to determine the ecological and conservation requirements of this species (Stone 1995), especially interactions with invasive alien species and the availability of insect prey. Recommended conservation measures include reducing the use of pesticides and agrochemicals, controlling feral cats and preventing further introductions of alien species to small islands such as Mount Clara (Palomo et al. 2007).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because it has a wide distribution with a large extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 212,199 km2, it is thought to be common, and there are no known major threats to the species.
habitat: The species is found on steppe grasslands.
threats: There are no major threats to the species.
population: Populations undergo fluctuations in density; in mountainous areas populations are patchy and density varies.
range: This species is found in southeastern Transbaikalia (Zabaykalsky Krai) of Russia and the districts of Dornod and Hentiy in adjacent Mongolia (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022). The range is well-delimited by tributaries of the Amur: Ingoda and Shilka in the north and Ulidza and Argon in the south (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022). It is found between 530–1,100 m asl (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation efforts for this species.

rationale: This species has a large population size and an extremely wide distribution, with an Extent of Occcurrence of approximately 19,431,310 km2. There are no indications of a a decline in population and there are no known widespread major threats to the species. It is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: This species inhabits tundra, plains and mountain steppes and meadows. In the forest zone (including mountain forests) and semideserts it occupies open grassy areas. It reaches maximum density in cereal and grass steppes, and alpine and water meadows. It lives in groups, during periods of high population density it may form colonies. It feeds on various wild and cultivated plants, but tends to prefer legumes. The reproductive period lasts throughout the warmer months of the year; in tundra zones reproduction often starts under snow cover (in Karsk tundra in February-March). It can have up to five litters per year in the southern parts of its range, and up to four in mountainous and northern areas. Litter size is usually up to 12 young. It is a considerable pest of crops in Siberia and Kazakhstan and pastures in Central Asia. It is a natural carrier of several diseases including encephalitis, plague and rabbit fever.
threats: There are no major threats to the species.
population: Populations undergo fluctuations in density. In mountainous areas populations are patchy and density varies.
range: This species is distributed across the tundra and forest-tundra region of northern Asia from the White Sea to the Kolyma River. It occurs in several separate regions: the steppes of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, SW Siberia, Yakutia, Mongolia and northern China. It occurs at altitudes from sea level up to 4,355 m asl (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
conservationActions: The species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species has a wide range and large extent of occurrence (EOO) of 18,124,520 km2. It is not considered to be facing any major threats at present, nor undergoing any significant decline. It is therefore listed as Least Concern.
habitat: It occurs in a wide range of habitats including grasslands, woods, upland heaths, dunes, marshes, peat-bogs and river-banks, tending to prefer damp areas. It also utilises a number of anthropogenic habitats including meadows, field-margins and young forestry plantations, but is absent from heavily grazed areas (Zima 1999). Marginal habitats support lower population densities (da Luz Mathias et al. 2017). The field vole is predominantly herbivorous, feeding on grasses and herbaceous plants, and gnawing bark in the winter. Exceptionally, animal prey (e.g., dipteran larvae) are taken (Krapp and Niethammer 1982).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species over much of its range.
population: It is generally common in suitable habitats (e.g., Cheprakov and Chernousova 2020), although it may be locally rare at its periphery in, e.g., eastern Siberia (Kryštufek 2017) and also less abundant in marginal habitats (da Luz Mathias et al. 2017). In some areas, population density fluctuates markedly over a cycle of approximately three to five years (e.g., central Scandinavia and the Czech Republic; Gouveia et al. 2015, da Luz Mathias et al. 2017). In peak years it can cause damage to pastures, orchards and forestry plantations (Zima 1999).
range: The Short-tailed Field Vole is a widespread Palaearctic species, ranging from western Europe eastwards through Scandinavia to the Alps, into Russia to Lake Baikal in southeast Siberia, Mongolia and northwest China (da Luz Mathias et al. 2017). It is present in Great Britain, central and northern parts of the continent, but it is absent from Iceland, Ireland, the Mediterranean region and southern Europe (Zima 1999, Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005, Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). Populations previously known from southern Europe are now considered to comprise two separate species, Microtus lavernedii and Microtus rozianus (Paupério et al. 2012 and Kryštufek 2017). Microtus agrestis occurs from sea level to 2,100 m asl in the Alps (Spitzenberger 2002).
conservationActions: The species is present in a large number of protected areas throughout its wide range. No specific conservation measures are required. In some areas, this species is considered to be a forestry pest (da Luz Mathias et al. 2017).

rationale: The Portuguese Field Vole is endemic to Europe, where it occurs in the Iberian Peninsula. The species does not fall into any category of threat due to the size of its range and the information on the status of its subpopulations, as in Portugal the species is abundant and considered not threatened. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species prefers humid grassland habitats, marshlands and reed beds (Pardinas et al. 2017, Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
threats: The species is not threatened in Portugal (Pardinas et al. 2017). However, the preferred habitats of this species are affected by climate changes (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
population: No population data is available for this species. However, in north Portugal the species is known to be abundant (Pardinas et al. 2017).
range: The Portuguese Field Vole (Microtus rozianus) is endemic to northern Portugal and northwest Spain, where it is found from sea level up to 1,775 m (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: No specific conservation measures are needed at this stage. It is thought to occur in at least one protected area. Research is needed to develop an understanding of population size and trends of this species.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This is a European endemic species that is widespread and common with no major threats. Although the fragmentation and decline of habitats could represent a threat, this species is assessed as Least Concern for both Europe and for the EU27 Member States.
habitat: Habitat requirements are similar to those of Microtus agrestis. It is found in damp grassland, and young forestry plantations rich in grass (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). The species is also found along streams surrounded by thick vegetation (Pardinas et al. 2017).
threats: According to Pardinas et al. (2017) the fragmentation and decline of habitats by urban and agricultural development could represent a threat to this species.
population: No data on population size and trends is available.
range: Microtus lavernadii is an European endemic species and its range consists of two fragmented subpopulations. The western subpopulation extends through northern Spain, Andorra, and southern and central France (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). The eastern subpopulation occurs through south-western Switzerland, north-eastern Italy, southern Austria, Slovenia, western Hungary, northern Croatia, and marginally Bosnia and Herzegovina and north-western Serbia (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). Altitudinal range varies from sea level up to 2,600 m.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is found in some protected areas across its range. There are no immidiate needs for conservation measures.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This European endemic species is relatively widespread, with a presumed large global population, no major threats, and no known declines. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU 27 Member States.
habitat: It inhabits meadows, open woodlands, forest edges, and woodland clearings, preferring open areas with dense herbaceous vegetation to mature forest. In the high mountains it is also found in Dwarf Pine Pinus mugo, and in the coastal lowlands it occurs dry meadows, vineyards, and hedgerows (Kryštufek 1999). It typically produces two to three embryos per litter.
threats: There are no major threats affecting this species. It is sometimes considered a pest and is controlled through poisoning.
population: This vole is locally common in at least parts of its range, and there is no evidence of population decline (Kryštufek 1999).
range: Microtus liechtensteini (Liechtenstein’s Pine Vole) is endemic to Europe, where it occurs in southwest Austria, northeastern Italy, southern Germany, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia. In Austria, it is found in isolated localities and also found along the Italian and Slovenian border (Spitzenberger 2002). Its altitudinal range is from sea level to 1,875 m (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: This species is found in protected areas. No specific conservation actions are recommended as no major threats are affecting this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, because it is relatively common, widespread, with a relatively large extent of occurrence (EOO is 221,468 km²), is tolerant of a range of manmade and natural habitats, and is facing no major threats at present.
habitat: It inhabits dry grasslands, such as dry meadows and pastures (Kryštufek 1999), shrublands and croplands, and is associated with well-drained soils (Amr et al. 2018). It occurs in colonies with 40 or more burrow systems per 1,000 m2 (Shehab et al. 2018) that may also be used by the Grey Dwarf Hamster (Cricetulus migratorius) and Tristram’s Jird (Meriones tristrami) (Shehab et al. 2018).
threats: No major threats are known.
population: Microtus guentheri is common in certain habitats, such as agricultural open meadows (Shehab et al. 2018). In these areas it can occur in high abundances to the point that it is considered a pest species, as observed in Israel (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2007) and Jordan (Amr et al. 2018).
range: Microtus guentheri is found in southeast Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, and northwest Jordan (see Kryštufek et al. 2009, Mahmoudi et al. 2015, Thanou et al. 2019). The populations in the Balkans and in the Cyrenaican Plateau of Libya, previously attributed to M. guentheri, are now recognised as distinct species: M. hartingi and M. mustersi, respectively (Thanou et al. 2019). M. guentheri may occur up to 500 m above sea level (Kryštufek 1999, Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005), but clarification of records is required following the aforementioned taxonomic revisions.
conservationActions: It is not known whether this species occurs in any protected areas. Nonetheless, no conservation measures are recommended at present, given that this species is considered an agricultural pest in multiple parts of its range.

rationale: This European endemic species is restricted to Sicily (Italy). The species is common and widespread across the island without any major threats known or conservation requirements, therefore it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The habitat and ecology are similar to those found in Microtus savii and M. brachycercus. The species is therefore found in open, uncultivated and cultivated areas.
threats: There are no major threats known.
population: The species is widespread throughout the island with populations abundant and stable.
range: The species is endemic to the island of Sicily in Italy (Bezerra et al. 2016), where the species is found from sea level up to 1,905 m (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: No specific conservation measures are needed.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)Microtus savii is a widespread and abundant species with no major threats. The population trend is stable, therefore it is listed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 Member States.
habitat: It is found in the majority of terrestrial habitat types, with the exception of high mountains, dense woodlands, and some very sandy, rocky or wet areas. It occurs in many anthropogenic habitats including pastures, arable land, gardens, and urban areas (Contoli 1999).
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This is a widespread and abundant species, dominating small mammal communities within its range, and representing a key food source for many predators. Periodic population explosions occur in cultivated areas, and the species can be considered an agricultural pest. The long-term population trend appears to be stable (Contoli 1999).
range: Savi's Pine Vole (Microtus savii) is endemic to Europe, where it is found in central and northern Italy (except the extreme northeast) (Bezerra et al. 2016). It also occurs marginally in southern Switzerland and may occur in southeastern France (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). It occurs from sea level up to 2,800 m (Amori et al. 2008).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is found in protected areas. It requires no specific conservation measures.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is a widespread with an estimated extent of occurrence of 9,004,682 km2, it is a common species, and there are no known major threats.
habitat: Principal habitats in the Arctic zone are moist tundra, bogs, and dwarf birch shrubs; further south in the boreal zone Middendorf’s Vole occupies wet meadows in the flooding river valleys and inside broad-leaf woodland (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022). Lives in colonies with shallow burrows in dry areas. Nest chambers are usually sited on hillocks, on the ground, or on shrub branches. The species feeds on sedges, leaves and stalks in summer and roots in winter. Reproduction occurs from May to August, and in favourable years, from March until October. Females that have overwintered can give birth to up to three litters per year. In the Urals fecundity is lower than in Yakutia.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: The distribution is sporadic and the animal is uncommon (Kostenko 2000).
range: The species is found in arctic and subarctic waterlogged tundra from the Ural Mountains to the Kolyma lowlands (Russian Federation). It has an elevation range from sea level to 2,060 m asl (Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is endemic to Europe, where it is restricted to southern mainland Italy with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 14,692 km². The species is divided into two subpopulations without the possibility of these coming into contact with each other due to the lack of suitable habitats over a large area, these are considered to be two locations. Although the northern subpopulation is expanding, the habitat is subject to reduction due to fires, especially in the southern areas and in those at lower altitudes of the remaining range. In addition, there is competition of the northern population with the introduced invasive C. finlaysonii which could potentially fragment its distribution and compete with the Calabrian Black Squirrel. The species could therefore potentially qualify as threatened under B1ab(iii), but, given its population expansion in the north and overall stable population status, and since its habitat is not threatened in its entirety, it is considered more appropriate to list this species as Near Threatened.
habitat: The species inhabits coniferous and deciduous forests.
threats: Possible threats to the survival of this species include destruction and reduction of the forest habitat due to fire, and competition with the introduced species Callosciurus finlaysonii with which it has already come into contact.
population: This species is stable with the northern subpopulation expanding.
range: Sciurus meridionalis is endemic to the southernmost part of the Italian Peninsula (Calabrian region) with two separate subpopulations. The southernmost subpopulation occurs in the Aspromonte Massif while the northern one occurs in the Sila Massif, the coastal chain and the Pollino Massif in the southern Apennines (Wauters et al. 2017). The EOO is 14,692 km². It is found from sea level up to 1,700 m.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species is present in some protected areas. Population and habitat monitoring is required.

rationale: This species has a large population size and a wide distribution, with a considerable extent of occurrence of 41,804,212 km2 and it occurs in many protected areas throughout its wide range. In Britain and Italy, the population has declined significantly following widespread habitat loss and out-competition, however, such declines have not yet been observed across major areas of this species range. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern, but population and threat monitoring is recommended.
habitat: The Eurasian Red Squirrel is found in coniferous forests, deciduous woods, mixed forests, parks, gardens, and small stands of conifers, from lowland to subalpine areas. Urban environments can support denser populations (Fingland et al. 2022). The Eurasian Red Squirrel nests in cavities or constructs spherical dreys from leaves, pine needles, and twigs placed high in the canopy. It is primarily herbivorous and will consume seeds, acorns, fungus, bark, and sapwood, although it occasionally takes animal prey (young birds and eggs) (Shuttleworth et al. 2015). It scatterhoards foods to provide a winter food store, aiding the reforestation process (Zhang et al. 2020). Young are born most often in February–April and May–August, with 1–6 individuals per litter (Wilson et al. 2016).
threats: In Britain and Italy the population has declined significantly following widespread habitat loss and out-competition by the introduced Grey Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) from North America in the 19th century (Gurnell and Pepper 1993, Wauters et al. 1997, Bertolino and Genovesi 2003). Now that the Grey Squirrel has become established on the European continent, it is possible that it may also spread through much more of the Eurasian Red Squirrel's range. Grey Squirrels can carry the “squirrelpox” virus (SQPV), which can present asymptomatically but is fatal to Eurasian Red Squirrels (Carroll et al. 2008). When the virus is present, the Grey Squirrel can replace the Eurasian Red Squirrel up to 25 times faster than the normal replacement rate (Rushton et al. 2006). Additional threats include the use of this species in the fur and pet trade Stubbe (1965), though these threats remain unquantified. In urban areas, road traffic accidents are also a notable cause of mortality (Fingland et al. 2022).
population: Although it is described as common throughout most of its range (Gurnell and Wauters 1999), there have been well-documented population declines and range contractions in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Italy and Finland (Gurnell and Pepper 1993, Wauters et al. 1997, O'Teangana et al. 2000, Selonen et al. 2010, Turkia et al. 2017). Typical densities range from less than 0.1 to 1.5 individuals per hectare (Gurnell and Wauters 1999). However, it is sufficiently common in some parts of its range to the extent that it is considered a forestry pest owing to its habit of stripping bark and feeding on conifer buds.
range: The Red Squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris) has a large range in the Palaearctic, extending from the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain and Portugal in the west, through continental Europe, Russia, Mongolia, and northwest and northeast China to the Pacific coast (Panteleyev 1998, Gurnell and Wauters 1999). It has been introduced into multiple areas of Russia, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Lithuania, and Northern Kazakhstan (Pavlov et al. 1973), and introductions in the Caribbean have also occurred (Wilson et al. 2016). In Europe, it is widespread in most areas, with the exception of the Iberian peninsula (where it is absent from the southwest) and Great Britain (where it has almost completely disappeared from the south-east). It occurs only sporadically in the Balkans, and is absent from the majority of Mediterranean islands. It is found from sea level up to 3,100 m asl in the Alps (Spitzenberger 2002).
useTrade: This species has been used for clothing and as a pet, though limited information is available and it is not clear to what extent it may be taken from the wild/traded for these reasons. In Mongolia, unsustainable hunting for skins for the international fur trade was a known threat in the mid-1900s, though current hunting levels are unknown.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention, and it occurs in many protected areas throughout its wide range. It is listed on the Chinese Red list as Near Threatened, and on the British Red List of Mammals as Endangered (Mathews and Harrower 2020). Urban areas may be suitable refugia for the Eurasian Red Squirrel, provided good-quality greenspaces are provided and Grey Squirrel populations are managed (Fingland et al. 2022).

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)EU 27 regional assessment: Not RecordedThis species does not reach the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion B, yet it is known to exist from 13 severely fragmented locations with an ongoing decline in the number of locations and area of occupancy (AOO). The AOO is close to 2,000 km², although there is some uncertainty as to whether it is below this value. If the negative trend in AOO continues, this species will likely become threatened. The species is endemic to western Russia and eastern Ukraine, and is not present in the EU27 member states. This species is assessed as Near Threatened as it almost qualifies as threatened under criterion B2.
habitat: This is a poorly studied species. It is active from May until October and hibernates in winter. It feeds on insects (i.e. moth, grasshoppers), flowers and seeds of steppe grasses. In the past, it was recorded in arable lands (Ognev 1947), but all later observations are strictly connected to pristine steppe habitats. It is found in sandy steppes along the rivers Don and Seversky Donets. In the northern part of the range it is recorded in true steppes with domination of Stipa spp. on rich chernozem soils. The Tsimlyansk Birch Mouse is mainly active at night, but is occasionally recorded in the daytime.
threats: The species is impacted by agricultural activities and by livestock. Habitat loss is occurring due to the loss of grasslands, with suitable habitat being converted into crop fields or artificial forest plantations.
population: This is a poorly known species. It is known to exist from 13 recent (and one probably extinct) subpopulations (M. Rusin, unpublished data). The density in the largest subpopulations (Tsimla and Archedinsk Sands) may reach up to five specimens per 100 pitfall traps. It is considered to be severely fragmented as the subpopulations are isolated from each other due to loss of grassland habitat.
range: This species occurs in western European Russia (Voronezh, Volgograd, Kursk, Belgorod and Rosotov regions) and in the Luhansk Region of Ukraine. It may also be found in small isolates in the Kharkiv region, but it has never been recorded there.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: This species is included in the Red book of Ukraine as Vulnerable. In Russia it is included to the Red books of: Voronezh (DD), Kursk (NT) and Rostov (DD) Regions under the name of S. severtzovi. Most of the recent occurrences are found within the protected areas, including Luhansk Nature Reserve (Triokhizbenka Steppe), Rostov Reserve (Tsimlyansk Zakaznik), Central-Chernozem Reserve, Belogorye Reserve (Yamskaya Steppe, Stenki Izgorya) and several other protected areas. Conservation action and further research is needed for this species. Suggested measures include habitat protection and restoration, and reintroductions, as well as further research into the population trends and threats faced by this species.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) (CR (PE)) EU 27 regional assessment: Not RecordedSevertzov's Birch Mouse is endemic to European Russia, where it was known to exist from two isolated subpopulations in the Voronezh Region. It is listed as Critically Endangered under criterion A2c and Possibly Extinct. The type locality was only recorded in 1921 (Ognev 1947). Yu. Kovalskaya failed to find any Sicista in the type locality between 1990-2000 (Yu. Kovalskaya pers. comm. 2016). Later in 2007 she found a new subpopulation 50 km to the east of the type locality (Kovalskaya et al. 2011). A subsequent intensive survey in 2014 failed to record any Birch Mice in the latter subpopulation. No specimen of S. severtzovi is kept in captivity. There is a high probability that the species has already gone extinct. The previous assessment of S. severtzovi included subpopulations now attributed to another species, S. cimlanica (Kovalskaya et al. 2011, Lebedev et al. 2020). The species is assessed as CR A2c because of the likely extinction of all previously known populations. The species is not recorded in the EU 27 region.
habitat: Both known localities occur within natural steppes. The species is poorly studied, only several specimens were recorded from two isolated localities.
threats: The major threat to the species is believed to be habitat destruction and turning natural steppes into croplands. No other threats are possible to identify because the species is close to extinction with no living specimen recorded since 2007.
population: This species is known from two isolated subpopulations in the Voronezh Region. Several specimens were captured by Yu. Kovalskaya in 2007, but a later survey in 2014 failed to record the species there. There is a chance that the species has already gone extinct, therefore a 99% population decline is inferred.
range: Severtzov's Birch Mouse (Sicista severtzovi) is endemic to European Russia, where it is restricted to a small population in the Voronezh region. The current status of the subpopulations is uncertain, and it is not known if the species is still extant. A single locality was reported by Kovalskaya et al. (2011), but this has not been confirmed by later surveys. The species was known from a maximum of two localities: the type locality, and then later found in one more locality 50 km to the east; both localities are currently most likely not active.
useTrade: This species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: No conservation measures are available to the species. An urgent search for any surviving colony is required with further strict protection of the site and ex-situ breeding if it is found. This species is listed as Data Deficient in the Red book of Voronezh Region.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern given its relatively wide extent of occurrence of 120,147 km2, presence across many localities and lack of evidence indicating a decline severe enough to warrant listing in a threatened category. However, it may be threatened by habitat loss, and information about its population is lacking. More research is therefore needed.
habitat: The species has been found in tall herb subalpine meadows (Cserkész et al. 2019).
threats: Specific threats to the species are not well-documented, but its preferred habitat (tall herb subalpine meadows) may be at risk from overgrazing and frequent mowing. Habitats near human settlements could face further pressure from rural development and road construction projects. Additionally, climate change could have adverse effects if it leads to habitat desiccation (T. Cserkész pers. comm. 2024).
population: No information is available on its population abundance or trends, however, based on limited trapping data for this and other species in the tianshanica group, it does not appear to be rare within its preferred habitats, which are also widespread in the Tien Shan Mountains (Holden et al. 2017).
range: It is known from the type locality of Rudnichny village, Kokcy-valley, Zhetysu Alatau (Dzungarian Alatau), Kazakhstan at an elevation of 1,310 m asl (Cserkész et al. 2019). It was formerly considered falling within Sicista tianshanica, of which several records obtained from the Zhetysu Alatau (i.e., Borokhudzir, Koktal, Kokcy, Kora, Aktogul river valleys) may actually represent S. zhetysuica (Cserkész et al. 2019). These occurrences are reported from 1,500 m asl (Shenbrot et al. 1995), but taxonomic confirmation is needed.
conservationActions: Surveys are needed to clarify this species' distribution and population. Geno- or karyotyping of the captured specimens are also needed to verify this species' presence in areas of uncertainty, i.e., further north of the Zhetysu Alatau where S. tianshanica has previously been recorded (Cserkész et al. 2019).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a wide range, with a large Extent of Occurrence and is relatively common. It occurs in a number of protected areas and is not known to be facing any major threats.
habitat: It is often associated with human habitation (Andreychev and Kuznetsov 2020), tending to be found in parks, gardens, and even buildings. It can be found in a wide variety of other habitat types, including woodland, forest edge, reed vegetation, river banks, and agroecosystems (Nistreanu 2011, Sheftel 2018). It is widespread in Crimea and present in majority of habitats (Tovpinets and Evstafiev 2010). In the desert zone it lives in oases and river valleys (Sokolov and Orlov 1980, Zaytsev et al. 2014) and also occurs on saline soils (Snitnikov 1936). It has been reported from steppes in Central Asia and Mongolia (Kuznetsov 1948, Sokolov and Orlov 1980). It feeds on insects and, to a lesser extent, plant material (Sheftel 2018). This species is most active at night, and forms nests under leaf litter, grass, log piles or similar (Sheftel 2018).
threats: No major threats are known.
population: It is considered common across most of its range, but not abundant (Sheftel 2018). In surveys undertaken in Crimea between 1980–2016 (Evstafiev 2016), it was recorded more frequently than the Bicoloured Shrew (Crocidura leucodon) at a ratio of 1 C. leucodon : 22 C. suaveolens. In the steppe forest zone in Ukraine, it is the most abundant shrew species, both in natural and agricultural habitats (I. Zagorodnyuk pers. comm. 2006). Relative numbers (shrews/100 trap nights) in Ukrainian surveys have previously varied between 0 and 0.44 over five years (Abelentsev et al. 1956); averages for four 5-year periods were 0.07–2.82 (Evstafiev 2016). In a steppic landscape of the Central Volga River, abundances are the highest in forests in gullies and flooplains; the species is rare in open upland habitats and recorded only in years of high density (Shlyakhtin et al. 2009).
range: The Lesser White-toothed Shrew (Crocidura suaveolens) has a widespread distribution, occurring in eastern Europe through to Russia and south towards the Caucasus. Its range extends eastwards to northern China and Mongolia (Sheftel 2018). However, the borders of its range and its status in countries at the edge of its distributional limits are unclear. It has been recorded to at least 800 m asl in Ukraine (Kuruts 2004) and up to 3,600 m asl in the Pamir Mts. (Zaytsev et al. 2014).
conservationActions: All Soricidae are protected under Appendix III of the Bern Convention. It occurs in numerous protected areas within its range. It is included in the Red Books of several administrative regions of the Russian Federation: Kaluga, Mordovia, and Chuvashia (Zaytsev et al. 2014). Given the recent taxonomic split of the C. suaveolens species group into three species, biological, ecological and distribution data for each of the newly recognized species should be studied.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because it has a wide range, large Extent of Occurrence of 10,492,245 km2, and there is no evidence to suggest any severe decline. Given the recent taxonomic revision of this species, further genetic, population and distribution studies would be beneficial.
habitat: It inhabits a wide range of habitats including vineyards, olive groves, terraced farmland on hillsides, dry Mediterranean shrubland, coastal sand dunes, rocky areas in mountains, and damp densely-vegetated patches near to water, including tidal marshes and coastal areas (Biedma et al. 2019). On the Isles of Scilly, where there are no other shrew species, footprint tunnels surveys recorded it in all surveyed habitats - foreshore, coastal grassland, scrub and heathland (Mathews et al. 2018). It tends to avoid dense forests (Vlasák and Niethammer 1990, Libois et al. 1999), exhibiting a preference for habitat patches with structural features typical of recently cut woodland, such as high shrub cover and low tree height (Mortelliti and Boitani 2009). Small, soft-bodied insects form a major part of its diet (Vlasák and Niethammer 1990), though it will occasionally consume molluscs, amphipods, annelids and small vertebrates (Palomo et al. 2007).
threats: Pesticides and herbicides may have a negative impact on the species in agricultural habitats (Libois et al. 1999), but at present this does not seem to be a major threat.
population: Much of the knowledge available for this species was collected under the assumption it occurred as the Lesser Shrew (C. suaveolens), thus, updated population data pertaining to Gueldenstädt's Shrew would be beneficial. Gueldenstädt's Shrew is considered relatively common in eastern parts of its range where it is more continuously distributed (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018). In Iran, it has been recorded more often than other shrew species (Yusefi et al. 2019). It is less common in the west (e.g. France, Spain and Portugal), occurring at much lower densities than its congener the Greater White-toothed Shrew (C. russula), for example (Libois et al. 1999).
range: Gueldenstädt's Shrew (Crocidura gueldenstaedtii) is found from the north and west coasts of the Iberian Peninsula and eastwards through Italy to the Balkan peninsula. It is present on some Atlantic and Channel islands, and on most eastern Mediterranean islands including Cyprus, Crete, Corsica, Menorca, Elba, and Capraia. It also occurs in the Caucasus and southwestern Asia (including Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Iraq, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, western Iran) where it has been recorded up to 2,470 m. The southernmost edge of its distribution passes through the Sinai Peninsula of Egypt. Its unusual distribution might be the result of varying range expansions following global cooling, but is more likely to result from occasional introduction by mariners and traders in ancient times (Dubey et al. 2007, Mittermeir and Wilson 2018).
conservationActions: All Soricidae are protected under Appendix III of the Bern Convention. No specific conservation actions are recommended, but this species would benefit from further genetic studies to solidify its taxonomic status, as well as population and distribution research.

rationale: This species is endemic to Europe, where it is restricted to mainland parts of Spain and Portugal, reaching the Pyrenees in the north, but absent from France and Andorra. There is no evidence to suggest this species is undergoing any widespread decline, though local reductions are likely given changes in habitat (A. Hinckley pers. comm. 2022). At present, this species is assessed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 Member States (which encompasses its entire range) though it would benefit from further research of its abundance, trends, distribution and threats, particularly in the south of the Iberian Peninsula where this species may have disappeared from previously occupied sites (Hinckley and Leonard 2022).
habitat: A semi-aquatic species, the Iberian Water Shrew prefers small streams, ponds and riparian habitats (Bencatel et al. 2019) though can also reach locations far from the waterside (Rychlik 1997). It feeds predominantly on invertebrates such as insect larvae, spiders and worms (Palomo et al. 2007). In the northern extent of its range, it exists in sympatry with the larger Eurasian Water Shrew (N. fodiens), appearing to occupy different microhabitat niches, with the Iberian Water Shrew favouring areas with greater herbal cover and being able to colonise areas away from water (Palomo et al. 2007). Its range shrinks in areas where American Mink (Neogale vison) has been introduced (García-Díaz et al. 2013).
threats: Use of pesticides, poor water quality and loss of wetlands may be a problem in parts of the range (Cabral et al. 2005, Palomo et al. 2007). Tropical crop cultivation, decreased rainfall and increased drought can contribute to the degradation of its habitats (A. Hinckley pers. comm. 2022). Additionally, introduced predators, such as the American Mink, pose threats to this species.
population: The Iberian Water Shrew is considered to be generally abundant in favourable habitats (see Querejeta and Castersana 2018). Nonetheless, it may be at risk in some localities within, for example, Andalucia and Extremadura regions, where tropical crop cultivation as well as changes to the climate can influence habitat quality for this species (A. Hinckley pers. comm. 2022). Surveys undertaken in Málaga province in 2016 revealed a potential absence of this species where it had previously been recorded (A. Hinckley pers. comm. 2022). Detailed data are lacking, particularly given this species’ recent taxonomic revision whereby much of the known population data are only relevant to Miller's Water Shrew (N. milleri).
range: The Iberian Water Shrew (Neomys anomalus) is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In northern regions of the peninsula, it is widely distributed. It has also been recorded in isolated areas of southern Spain (Palomo et al. 2007).
useTrade: The species is not known to be utilised.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention, and it occurs in many protected areas such as the following national parks: Parque Nacional de Los Picos de Europa, Sierra de Guadarrama and Sierra Nevada.It is recommended that population trends are more widely monitored, as the species is likely vulnerable to the loss of aquatic habitats. This species would benefit from measures to prevent water pollution and the destruction or degradation of riparian vegetation (Palomo et al. 2007), as well as further research of distribution, abundance, and ecology.

rationale: This species has a wide, but fragmented, range, and occurs in numerous protected areas. It is presumed to be declining in some areas as a result of loss and degradation of its wetland habitat. However, data are scarce and there is currently no evidence to suggest a widespread decline that has exceeded the thresholds for the population decline criterion of the Red List (i.e. >30% in ten years or three generations). As such, this species is assessed as Least Concern, but populations should be closely monitored, and if significant declines are recorded, uplisting may be warranted.
habitat: It inhabits areas of vegetation next to slow-flowing or still eutrophic waters, such as marshes, swamps, lakes, rivers, and streams. As with other Neomys species, its diet likely primarily consists of soft-bodied invertebrates such as insect larvae, spiders and worms (Spitzenberger 1990, Palomo et al. 2007).
threats: The major threat to the species is habitat loss and/or degradation; in many parts of its range, wetlands are being destroyed, fragmented and degraded as a result of water extraction, canalisation of streams, agriculture, road building, and other human activities (see Bertolino et al. 2014, Kingsford et al. 2016). The use of pesticides in particular may be a problem in parts of the range (Cabral et al. 2005, Palomo et al. 2007).
population: It is suspected to be declining in line with rates of loss of its wetland habitat (Spitzenberger 1999, Spitzenberger pers. comm. 2006). In the Republic of Moldova, it was the second most common shrew species recorded in surveys in the 1960s, yet in annual surveys undertaken between 2003-2017, it was found to be typically the rarest species, with relative abundance declining from 30% to 2.3% (Nistreanu 2019). Numbers are thought to still be decreasing in the Republic of Moldova where it is listed as nationally endangered, as well as in the neighbouring countries of Romania and Ukraine (Akimov 2009, Nistreanu pers. comm. 2022). In the Crimean Peninsula, only 11 individuals were captured over 30 years of small mammal surveys and it is thought that the availability of suitable habitat has declined there (Evstafiev 2016). This species has likely disappeared from the Central Plateau region of Switzerland and is decreasing across the country (Capt 2022). It has also undergone a significant, long-term decline in Germany (Meinig et al. 2020). In northern areas of its range, e.g. Lithuania and further north, it is very rare but long-term trends are unknown (Balčiauskas pers. comm. 2022). Records are scarce in Iran (Yusefi et al. 2019). In some areas, its population may be stable, though it is difficult to interpret trends given natural population fluctuations and a lack of long-term data (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species has a patchy global distribution. It is found in parts of central and southern Europe from the northeast of Spain through to the middle of the River Don (European Russia), and to the south east in Türkiye and Iran, but its range is thought to be fragmented (Corbet 1978, Spitzenberger 1999). In recent decades, specimens have been discovered as far north as Lithuania and Estonia (Balčiauskas and Balčiauskienė 2012, Balčiauskas et al. 2016) possibly reflecting an increased study effort rather than recent range expansion. It is recorded from sea level to 1,850 m asl in Europe, and up to 2,100 m asl in Iran and Asia Minor (Spitzenberger 1999, S. Aulagnier pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: This species occurs in protected areas such as the Besaparski Ridove Special Protection Area in Southern Bulgaria (Nedyalkov and Koshev 2014). Nonetheless, it is recommended that population trends are more widely monitored, as the species is vulnerable to the loss of aquatic habitats and believed to be declining in multiple regions (Nistreanu 2019, Meinig et al. 2020, Capt et al. 2022). This species would also benefit from measures to prevent water pollution and the destruction or degradation of riparian vegetation (Palomo et al. 2007).

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC) EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This species is listed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 region because it has a relatively wide range and appears to be common in suitable habitats. There is no evidence of any severe decline at present.
habitat: The species is found in moist (e.g. riverside) habitats with dense vegetation cover (Lugon-Moulin 2004), alpine prairie (Chirichella et al. 2022) and mountain forests (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018). It feeds on earthworms, molluscs, beetles and other arthropods. It produces five to seven young per litter (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018).
threats: The most likely major threat stems from forest management, because this species is thought to require humid microhabitats which are lost by logging and are not present in young and degraded woodland. Additionally, climate change may shift timber lines to higher altitudes and consequently reduce and/or degrade the forest habitat, particularly in areas of Calabria. The species can also be the untargeted victim of trapping.
population: It is reported to be abundant between 1,400-2,500 m asl in Italy (Amori et al. 2008). Several small-scale assessments of small terrestrial mammals have further confirmed relatively high abundance: it was the most abundant shrew recorded in Maiella (central Italy; Kryštufek pers. comm. 2017), the Binn Valley (south Switzerland; Blant et al. 2020) and Val Poschiavo (south Switzerland; Müller et al. 2022).
