As of 2022 51 colonies were recorded in Slovakia, 40 of them are the focus of the LIFE SYSEL project, where the populations are expected to increase further in the following years. In Türkiye, the species is restricted to the lowlands of Thrace, where Kryštufek and Vohralík (2005) cites it from 12 localities, at low altitudes, without finding it abundant.In Hungary, historical data show that two-thirds of the colonies disappeared in the last fifty years, even though one tenth of these were especially large. Decrease of the estimated number of colonies was uneven during this period: there was a slight, gradual decline before 1995 but since then it has declined sharply. Besides, long term data indicate regional differences in population trends. The earliest structural change in the declining trend was observed parallel to the abandonment of mountain slope grasslands, but severe decrease was later documented at the lowland grasslands. Conservation status of the European Ground Squirrel changed from being considered as a pest to being protected in the last century (1982) and later to strictly protected (2012) due to the recognition of such definite decrease. Land use change, especially the abandonment of grazing, was the main cause of colony disappearance, and improved conservation efforts are necessary to stop and reverse these trends (Németh et al. 2018). Based on the results of the European Ground Squirrel Programme of the Hungarian Biodiversity Monitoring System, Hungarian populations of the species have shown significant density decrease since 2000. Density of individuals varied from 1.25 to 150 individuals per hectare but occasionally 250 individuals/ha were also recorded. Development of potential habitat maps based on GIS analysis, made it clear that not only present ground squirrel areas but potential distribution areas (where the ground squirrel is absent at the present) show significant fragmentation and are highly isolated. Although mosaic, fragmented habitat structure does not necessarily lead to the extinction of populations, maintaining habitat patches in at least the present quality and quantity is needed for the survival of the species, to ensure the connection between them (Váczi et al. 2019). Soft-release reintroductions and translocations have been carried out for the last 20 years. Methods used in translocations are based on validated experimental studies (Gedeon et al. 2011, 2012) to help increase longer term success of translocations. In order to have a strong evidence about their long term, positive effect on the trend and conservation status of the Hungarian population, we need further data but experience from the last 20 years has indicated that they may be able to slow down the loss of local populations. Based on these findings we can conclude that the status of the Hungarian population is in an alarming conservation status, but hopefully it can be sustained in the long-term with adequate conservation measures.In Ukraine the species became extinct from Zakarpatska region, but still survives in Chernivtsi and Vinnytsia regions with population estimates of ca 1,640 active burrows in 2022 (Rusin 2022).In Czechia occurrence and abundance of the European Ground Squirrel has moderately grown during the last two decades. There were 83 known localities of occurrence in 1990–2001, but by 2000-2001 only 26 colonies still existed (Cepáková and Hulová 2002). Since 2001, there has been regular monitoring of S. citellus. The occurrence of the species was recorded on 35 sites, and a total abundance was estimated to be 3,600 individuals in 2008 (Matějů et al. 2008). That[HZs2] year's Action plan for the European Ground Squirrel in Czechia was adopted by The Ministry of Environment (Matějů et al. 2010). In 2016, the European Ground Squirrel was known from 36 sites, and its total abundance was ca. 5,000 individuals. The European Ground Squirrel distribution was scattered throughout Czechia, with most populations occurring in south Moravia and central and north Bohemia. Olšová Vrata was the most northwestern site of European Ground Squirrel in its distribution area. Since 2016 ground squirrels have been successfully reintroduced at two sites, and populations at five localities were reinforced (Matějů and Brzobohatá unpublished data). European Ground Squirrels were recorded at 40 localities in Czechia in 2020. The overall abundance was estimated to be ca 8,000 individuals, and the total area of colonies was 920 ha. Density varies from about one individual per hectare in vineyards to more than 70 individuals/ha in some airfields (Matějů and Brzobohatá unpublished data). High density was usually connected to sites with an artificial food source. In 2021, the European Ground Squirrel was confirmed at 41 localities, but the overall estimated abundance decreased to ca 6,000 individuals. It is assumed that the main reasons for this decrease were cold and rainy spring weather and the number of summer storms accompanied by torrential rains (Matějů and Brzobohatá unpublished data). In 2022, the situation was very similar. The occurrence of ground squirrels was recorded at 40 localities with ca 6,000 individuals in total. Area of all ​​colonies covered less than 750 ha.In Serbia the population is disjunct, inhabiting fragments of steppe habitats in the north and mountain pastures in the southeast. Monitoring local population distribution resulted in mapping 130 northern and nine eastern local populations. There have been only two comprehensive population size surveys in the north part of the species range. One covered three local populations, two in Srem and one local population in southern Banat (from 2005 to 2015), and the other one in 20 local populations in the central Banat area (from 2013 to 2015). Population density varied from 1 - 112 individuals/ha in Srem, in southern Banat from 1 - 68 individuals/ha, and from 1 - 88 individuals/ha in central Banat, with an average density of 37.8, 34.3 and 17.2 individuals/ha, respectively (Ćosić N. 2015, Nikolić T. 2019, Nikolić et al. 2020). The estimated densities for the mountain population from southeast Serbia ranged from 7.6 individuals/ha at Besna kobila to 49 individuals/ha at Stara planina (author's unpublished data). The declining trend in active populations on mapped suitable habitats is denoted in central Banat. On the three-year scale, the number of active populations declined from 20 active populations in 2013 to 16 in 2015. The distribution range (regional) in the northern part has been constricted to 70% (Nikolić et al. 2019) and in the south-eastern, 90% (author's unpublished data) in comparison to the local population's historical distribution.In Bulgaria, the estimated extent of occurrence is approximately 110.000 km². The species has disappeared from the south-western part of the country and from some 10×10 km UTM grid squares in the north-western part. Reduction at the moment occurs as a reduction in the number of colonies, reduction of habitats and stepping stones (Y. Koshev – pers. records). In Bulgaria about 30% of colonies have disappeared, the reasons for this being the intensification of agriculture, the reduction of the number of grazing animals, often stimulated by European funds (Koshev 2022). In North Macedonia the species is found in an area of 884 ha on Mount Jakupica, where densities (0.8–5.5 individuals/ ha) are lower than those reported elsewhere for the species, and a total population of approximately 2,000 adults (Kryštufek et al. 2012). At least 15 scattered ground squirrel colonies are found in the lowlands of south-eastern North Macedonia (excluding Strumica area), all patchily distributed and embedded between fields and vineyards. These can be attributed to four distinct populations more or less isolated by geographic barriers (Haberl 2010).In Greece the species is distributed in three separate sub-populations in the northern country. The colonies are extremely small (mean area 6.4 ha) and have very low numbers of animals, with most localities containing less than 10 individuals each (Rammou et al. 2021). The mean population density is 7.4 individuals/ha. During the surveys from 2019–2020 (Rammou et al. 2021), colonies were mostly found in agricultural (cereal crops, alfalfa fields, olive groves) and artificial areas, with a low number of colonies found in natural, seminatural and wetland habitats. Surveys from 2019–2020 (Rammou et al. 2021) revealed a drastic decrease in both distribution area (by 62.4%) and colony numbers (by 74.6%). In Greece, populations of two subspecies (macedonicus and graolojenici) have been lost (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2006).
range: The European Ground Squirrel is endemic to central and south-eastern Europe, where it occurs at altitudes of 0 to 2,593 m. Its range is divided in two by the Carpathian mountains (Ružić 1978, Říčanová et al. 2013). The north-western portion extends through Czechia, Poland, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, northern Serbia, and western Romania, whilst the south-eastern portion extends from southern Serbia, North Macedonia and Greece through Bulgaria and southern Romania to Turkish Thrace, Moldova and Ukraine (Panteleyev 1998, Kryštufek 1999).
useTrade: The species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: The species is listed in the Resolution 6 of the Bern Convention and Annexes II and IV of the EU Habitats and Species Directive. It is currently a protected species in all countries where it occurs and included in the National Red Books of Ukraine, Moldova, Romania, and Greece. Occurs in several protected areas, however its conservation should always include pasture management. Lack of grazing on some protected areas resulted in population declines and extinctions. The EU Action Plan for the European Ground Squirrel was published (Janák et al. 2013), but national and regional action plans must be drafted. For example, the Action Plan for European Ground Squirrels in Czechia has been implemented since 2008 (updated in 2020 – Matějů and Matoušová 2020). The Action Plan for the European Ground Squirrel in Bulgaria was prepared, submitted to the Bulgarian government, and has been approved after six years of delay, in 2022 (Koshev 2022). Also, there was a regional plan in lower Austria to recover the population by maintaining extensive and high-quality habitat implemented through the Agro-ecological measures (AEM), which was successful until AEM subsidies were shifted for other purposes (ÖPUL-Maßnahme Ziesel 2015). Landscape-level conservation planning should be adapted across species distribution areas (Janák et al. 2013, Nikolić et al. 2019, Rammou et al. 2021). This spatial approach will assist in protecting and revitalising open grassland habitats and improving their connectivity. Habitats outside protected area networks or Natura 2000 habitats should become extensions to these conservation networks, or their land use conversion should be prohibited (1.2). The initial phase for landscape-level conservation is mapping of occupied or available habitats. A good example is those mapped in EU countries for the Natura 2000 programme, but also a habitat mapping campaign was successfully implemented in Serbia (Arok 2015, Ćosić 2018, Nikolić 2020). Furthermore, to ensure the survival of isolated populations while preserving 90% of genetic diversity and avoiding the harmful effects of inbreeding, it is necessary to ensure the MVP of 300 individuals over 50 years (Ćosić 2015). Also, one must consider maximal species dispersal capacity and individuals’ within-habitat movement (Spitzenberger 2002, Hoﬀmann et al. 2008, Kachamakova and Koshev 2018, Nikolić et al. 2019). To meet this requirement within the mapped habitat networks, the size of grassland habitats needs to be extended or the presence of transitional elements (preferably short vegetation) enabled (e.g. between occupied or suitable habitats) or habitat management improved (Nikolić 2019, Rammou et al. 2021). Habitat management should be based on habitat quality assessment, e.g. quantification of available resources, habitat productivity, complexity, and heterogeneity (Nikolić et al. 2020, Arok et al. 2021, Rammou et al. 2021). The results of the habitat assessment should then be used to make management decisions and, if needed, improve habitat conditions, or prepare unoccupied habitats for reintroduction. Several successful reintroductions have been conducted in: Czechia and Slovakia (Matějů et al. 2010 and 2012), Poland (Matějů et al. 2010 and 2012, Kończak et al. 2014), Hungary and Romania (LIFE13NAT/HU/000183) and Bulgaria (Koshev et al. 2019). Educating and raising the public's awareness of the functional role of European Ground Squirrels as ecosystem engineers or resources for predatory species is of great importance, as population loss also threatens the survival of several other animal species. In 2005, the species was reintroduced to Poland by the NGO PTOP Salamandra, and is still continuing. There are currently two stable wild populations in the country (Wojtaszym et al. 2015, A. Kepel unpublished 2023). In 2006 a project was initiated to reintroduce the species to Germany (H. Meinig pers. comm. 2006). Several reintroductions have also been made in Bulgaria at different altitudes, but with variable results (Koshev et al. 2019, Kachamakova et al. 2022). Research is needed to determine population status and trends, ecological requirements, potential threats, and appropriate conservation measures.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Critically Endangered (CR)EU 27 regional assessment: Endangered (EN)The global population decreased by 99% over the past 30 years. In the past decade, every generation lost approximately 30% in area of occupancy and number of subpopulations, amounting to a population decline of over 90%. The extent of occurrence has contracted and the formerly uniform range now consists of several small isolated communities. The rapid decline of habitats due to lack of grazing and ploughing of remaining colonies, together with climate change is putting the whole species at risk of extinction in the next 20-30 years. Therefore, the species is listed as Critically Endangered under criterion A2ac. In the EU region it occurs only in Poland. The population collapsed in Poland several times, but active conservation measures helped to stabilise its decline. Currently, the Polish population of Speckled Ground Squirrel is the largest and the strongest. Therefore, the species is assessed as Endangered in the EU 27 region, with a decline of 50% occurring in the past 10  years.
habitat: This species lives in dense colonies in pastures with low grass and it is often found close to water sources. For instance, all active populations in Moldova are found less than 100 meters from running water. It is often recorded also in urban graveyards, airfields, and road verges. In the past, this ground squirrel also lived in arable lands, but this seems to not be the case anymore. Overall, it has been observed that lack of grazing leads to quick degradation of the habitat and ultimately to population decline.The Speckled Ground Squirrel hibernates in winter and is active from February-March until July-November (S. Shokalo pers. comm. 2021). It feeds primarily on green grass and it is known to occasionally eat grains (primarily wild, rarely cultivated). In early summer, it also feeds various beetles (Melolontha spp) which can represent a significant portion of its diet (S. Shokalo, pers. comm. 2022). The species gives birth once a year to two to eight pups.
threats: This species is threatened by the loss and fragmentation of its habitat. The causes of habitat loss include the expansion of agriculture and forestry, urbanisation, reclamation of wasteland and industrial development (Glowacinski et al. 2001, Piskorski 2005, Z. Glowacinski pers. comm. 2006). Ploughing of terrains occupied by colonies and waste accumulation in the species' habitat have resulted in the extinction of several subpopulations in Belarus during 2010-2021 (S. Shokalo, pers. comm. 2021). Currently, all populations are declining and becoming more fragmented, which makes hybridisation less of a problem. The changing climate in parts of its range has caused a severe increase in mortality, especially due to particularly colder winters and decreased precipitation (Shekarova et al. 2008). Overall, climate change (i.e. droughts and regular catastrophic floods) has resulted in the extinction of many subpopulations in the past 10 years. The genetically richest populations are found in Odesa Region (Ukraine) and in Moldova, whereas populations from Central Russia are genetically depleted (Matrosova et al. 2016). Populations in Belarus (V. Matrosova, pers. comm. 2022) and Poland (Biedrzycka and Konopinski 2007) are also genetically poor.
population: The global population of this species declined by over 99% in the past 30 to 50 years. In Poland, the latest estimate counts approximately 9,000 individuals, where its largest colony in Swidnik airport collapsed between 2008-2009. The largest reported colonies are near Popowka and Susle Wzgorza, corresponding to 94% of the Polish overall population in 2015 (Ziolek et al. 2017). In Belarus, the species lives in several small colonies near the town of Nesvizh with a density of approximately 5,000 active burrows in 2021 (Shokalo, pers. comm. 2022). Since the start of regular monitoring (2019-2022), the Belarusian population has lost several subpopulations each year (S. Shokalo, pers. comm. 2022). In Ukraine, the species has undergone a severe decline, with over 99% of the population having gone extinct. Small isolated colonies are known in Western Ukraine (near the towns of Brody and Sokal), near Kharkiv (S. Viter, pers. comm. 2020). Monitoring of the colony close to the city of Mykolaiv has registered the extinction of several subpopulations with an estimated number of adult individuals counting less than 100 specimens in 2019. The largest colony near the city of Odesa (Sovignon) collapsed after the construction of residential buildings in the area after 2015. Several large colonies in Southern Bessarabia (Odesa region, Ukraine) collapsed during 2015-2019, with only tiny colonies remaining to this day. All of these colonies contain less than 100 mature individuals each, often a score or two. The largest colony in Ukraine - near the town of Ochakiv (Mykolauv Region)- had approximately 1,000 individuals in 2015, but the population later collapsed and the area of occupancy (AOO) of that colony was reduced by three times in 2019. In the Republic of Moldova, there are five to six populations with less than 100 individuals each. There, several colonies collapsed after catastrophic floods in 2017 and 2018 (V. Ajder, pers. comm. 2018). In Russia, the species has gone through a severe decline in the past 10 to 15 years with lots of colonies collapsing all over the Russian part of the range (O. Ermakov, pers. comm. 2022). It became extinct in Moscow, Belgorod, Rostov, Volgograd, Saratov, Orel, Tula, Penza Regions. A small and isolated colony still thrives in the Briansk Region. One of the largest Russian colonies exists in the Lipetsk City Graveyard.Since 2015 every year this species has lost at least of 30% of the global population, amounting to over a 90% decline within the past 10 years.
range: The Spotted Souslik is endemic to eastern Europe, where it is found in south-eastern Poland, small areas in Belarus, Ukraine, Moldova, and Russia eastwards to the river Volga. In Poland, the Souslik occurs on the western edge of its range and it is known from one relic enclave located between the Wieprz and Bug rivers in the region of Zamosc (Glowacinski et al. 2001, Piskorski 2005). It is a lowland species, occurring up to no more than 500 m (I. Zagorodnyuk pers. comm. 2006).
useTrade: In the past, this squirrel was hunted for pelts. It was also used as a food source during femines (e.g. femine in Ukraine in 1932-1933). In Russia, hunting continued until late 80th - early 90th centuries, but have ceased now (O. Ermakov, pers. comm. 2022). Both practices are unlikely to come back.
conservationActions: The Speckled Ground Squirrel is legally protected under Resolution 6 of the Bern Convention. In Poland, the souslik is strictly protected under national law, and five nature reserves have recently been created to protect the species. Several translocations have been conducted in Poland (Ziolek et al. 2017). In Ukraine, the species is protected by the Red Book of Ukraine (listed as Endangered since 2021). The species is also included in the Red Book in Belarus. In Russia, the species became protected at the national level and included in the federal Red Book in 2020 with the Vulnerable status becoming 1 of 7 rodent species that received nationwide protection in Russia. Some of the Regional Red Book assessments include Belgorod (CR), Voronezh (CR), Kursk (CR), Penza (VU), Rostov (DD), Samara (DD), Saratov (EN), Tatarstan (VU), Orel (CR) and Moscow (EW). Currently, there are no successful actions to stop the rapid decline of this squirrel. Susliks disappeared from some of the protected areas, hence simple protection of the site is not working for the species. Several attempts at reintroduction took place in Voronezh Region, Russia (Sapelnikov and Sapelnikova, pers. comm. 2019).

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Not RecordedAcross most of its range, this is an abundant and common species with no evidence of the population declining at a rate approaching the threshold for consideration as threatened under criterion A, for this reason it is listed Least Concern. However, small and isolated populations in the northern part of the range experience local population declines or even extinctions. The causes of these are not fully understood. The species has not been recorded in the EU 27 region.
habitat: This is a strictly subterranean species. It inhabits steppes with various soils, including chernozem, sands and calcipherous soils. It lives in crop fields, gardens, orchards, edges of forests, seashores, sides of roads and irrigation channels. It can be found within rural and sometimes urban settlements (e.g. in lawns and parks). It feeds on underground parts of dandelion, cow parsnip, chicory and tree seedlings (oak, mulberry, acacia), making hoards for winter, sometimes up to 10-14 kg. It often gathers human-cultivated plants, including potatoes, carrots etc. Breeding occurs once a year, with females giving birth in March to two to five young. During dispersal, juveniles emerge above ground and often fall prey to carnivorous mammals and birds. It can be a pest in the central part of its range.
threats: This species is persecuted by farmers and gardeners. Seventy percent of Ukrainian populations are within the areas affected by the military conflict which began in 2022. Trench construction and heavy shelling - among other activities - have negatively affected this species since the beginning of the conflict.
population: This is a common species with stable populations that do not experience periodical fluctuations. In historical times and in some parts of the range it became rare or even extinct, but elsewhere it extended its area of occurrence. Population density differs significantly in different parts of the range. Maximum densities are found in Central Black Earth Region (Russia) and Eastern Ukraine (Kharkiv, Luhansk, Dnipro Donetsk regions). On average, population density amounts to 3-10 individuals per hectare but it can reach up to 20. In the southern part of the range, the density can be lower as the arid climate of the steppes is less favourable. In the northern part of the range and in the Volga Region it occurs in small isolated populations and can considered rare. These populations are threatened by habitat loss (e.g. ploughing in major habitats). In the southern part of the range (Stavropol Region) in the 1950s, population and range declines occurred because of ploughing.
range: This species is distributed in steppes and forest-steppes in Ukraine and southern Russia between Dnieper and Volga Rivers, north to Orel-Kursk line, and south to Ciscaucasia (Gromov and Erbaeva 1995). In Crimea, it is most probably absent since the Pleistocene. During the Holocene the northern border of the range has moved significantly southward, leaving behind isolated relict populations, for example in Samarskaya Luka (Samara district, Russia). Cis-Caucasian populations may represent a different species, therefore a taxonomic reassessment is required (Arslan et al. 2016).
useTrade: This species is not utilised. There are records of gardeners feeding dogs with captured mole rats.
conservationActions: No conservation measures are currently in place, however this species occurs in several protected areas including Luhansk Nature reserve, Central-Chernozem Nature Reserve and others.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Critically Endangered (CR)EU 27 regional assessment: Critically Endangered (CR)This species is assessed globally as Critically Endangered under criterion A2c based on the availability of more precise population data. The species lost over 90% of its area of occupancy (AOO) (best estimates of 412 km2) which is suspected to have caused similar declines in the population size, and 70% of the global population is now concentrated in the Lower Dnieper Sands in Kherson Regions, which are currently under immediate threat of destruction due to ongoing military conflict in Ukraine.In the EU27 region a single location (with an AOO of less than 10 km2) is known from Romania, meeting criterion B2a. The construction works and expending housing results in the continuous decline of the quality of the habitat and further reduction in AOO. Therefore in the EU27, this species is also assessed as Critically Endangered, although under criterion B2ab(iii).
habitat: Nordmann's Birch Mouse inhabits various virgin steppe grasslands on various soil types, including sand, sandy loam, chernozem and castanozem. It avoids overgrazed habitats, preferring mid-tall grasses. It lives in steppes with Stipa spp., Artemisia spp., Cytisus spp. In the Black Sea Reserve (Kherson Region), it is most often found on psammophytic steppes dominated with sagebrush and feathergrass, while in the Yelanetskyi Steppe Reserve (Mykolaiv Region) it lives in typical steppes dominated by feathergrass and forbs. In the past was occasionally registered in the crop fields (winter cereals, including oats, buckwheat, ryes) but for the past 30 years is registered only in the steppes, avoiding agriculture.It is a winter hibernator, exiting winter hibernation in April, and going into hibernation in October-November. In warm winters in Crimea, it was rarely was reported in the winter time (Evstafiev 2020). Breeding season registered in May and in July. Possibly, younger animals take part in a second breeding. The species produces two to six pups in a litter. It feeds on various insects (grasshoppers, warms, moths), flowers, seeds of steppe plants and green leaves. It digs very primitive burrows, and often enters the burrows of other small mammals.An estimated 90% of the habitat of this species has been lost in the past 10 years as most steppe plots have been turned into croplands, tree plantations or solar power plants.
threats: Threats include the degradation of habitats, primarily due to the destruction of natural steppes and their transformation into arable lands. Renewable energy facilities pose a new threat for the species. Sandy steppes often turned into artificial tree plantations, which are not suitable for birch mice.The beginning of the military conflict in Ukraine in 2022 placed new unexpected threats on the species. Trenches have been constructed in the Lower Dnieper Sands, which hosts approximately 70% of the whole species population (M. Rusin, original data). Construction of these trenches and explosions from shelling and mining pose a huge threat to the survival of Nordmann's Birch Mice in the region. The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam during the conflict in 2023 resulted in the partial destruction by flooding of the largest population of the species.
population: Exact population censuses have never been done for any of the colonies. Relative abundance varies from 0.3 ind / 100 trap-nights up to 10 ind. / 100 trap-nights. The highest density was observed in the Solonoozernyi Department of the Black Sear Reserve (Khers Region, Ukraine). In all other areas populations are much smaller. No fluctuations between years has been observed. In the best populations, density remained stable.
range: The Nordmann’s Birch Mouse occurs in eastern Romania, southern Ukraine, and the West Belgorod region of Russia. In the past 10 years, it has been known to exist in a limited number of localities. In Romania, a single population was recorded near Iasi in 2014 (Cserkész et al. 2015). In Russia, a single population is known from the Belgorod Region from 2014 (Cserkész et al. 2016). Most of the range lies within Ukraine. It has been recently found in one locality from the Odesa Region, two localities from Mykolaiv Region, two localities from Dnipro Region, in Kherson Region four localities are recorded from Lower Dnieper Sands (M. Rusin: 2015-2020, O. Zinenko 2021 record from UkrBIN), one locality west of the Dnieper river and one locality on Syvash Lake. In Crimea, the species was recently registered in the Kerch peninsula in 2017 and in the Takhankut peninsula in 2017 (Evstafiev 2020). The species used to have a wider range, occurring up to Kyiv Region in the North and to Luhansk and Rostov Regions in the South-East. The status of Dobrogean populations, that were attributed to Nordmann's Birch Mouse, need both taxonomic and faunistic re-evaluation: trapping in all previously known old localities in Romania and Bulgaria (M. Rusin et al. 2016, unpublished data) failed to record any Sicista. No active population is known from the Republic of Moldova, though this is most likely due to the lack of knowledge. The status of the species in western Ukraine and in south-eastern Poland needs thorough taxonomic and faunistic studies.
useTrade: This species is not utilised.
conservationActions: It is included to the Red Book of Ukraine (Endangered as of 2021) and Romania. Populations are preserved in four protected areas of national importance: Black Sea Biosphere Reserve (Kherson, Ukraine), National Park Oleshkivski Sands (Kherson, Ukraine), Yelanetskyi Steppe Reserve (Mykolaiv, Ukraine), Belogorye Rserve (Belgorod, Russia). Several other protected areas of local importance host small populations in Ukraine, e.g. Sagi Sanctuary (Kherson Region, Ukraine), Tarutino Steppe Sanctuary (Odesa, Ukraine). In Romania, recent occurrence has only been verified from one locality, Valea lui David, Iasi, where the expanding city poses a risk to natural habitats; the survival of this population is likely ensured in a small part of a single protected area that hosts an exceptionally rich flora and fauna (Cserkész et al. 2015).Ex-situ conservation was planned to start in Ukraine by 2022, but this has been halted by the military conflict. Species reintroductions and habitat protection are recommended for this species, as well as further research into its population trends and threats faced.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC) Mus spicilegus is a widespread and abundant species. In recent decades it started to expand its northern and eastern distribution limits. Therefore it is listed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27, where it is abundant in Romania, Bulgaria and Hungary.
habitat: The Steppe Mouse occurs in a variety of open habitats with the highest densities in fields of soy and winter cereals. It is less frequent in sunflower, maize, and alfalfa plantations. Overall, it rarely occurs on pasturelands and avoids overgrazed areas. Often, it is found on roadsides and along channels. In natural grasslands, populations are more dispersed and never reach the density of populations inhabiting crop fields. It is often found at the edges of forests and near rural settlements. It feeds on grain and seeds, which it hoards in the winter in a soil-covered mound built above its nest chamber; a single mound may be up to 400 cm in diameter (although 100-200 cm is more typical) and contain up to 10 kg of grain (Macdonald and Barrett 1993, Sokolov et al. 1998). Groups of 4-14 mice cooperate to build these mounds (Sokolov et al. 1998).
threats: It is one of the most dominant species in arable lands throughout most of its range. Threats include the use of rodenticides and the shift to industrial farming. Mus spicilegus is treated as one of the major pests in Southern Ukraine and often persecuted by farmers with rodenticides or by destruction of mounds. It has been observed that larger fields with intensive agro-industrial practices have lower population densities of Mus spicilegus.
population: It remains common in suitable habitats but is suspected to be undergoing population decline in some areas. Densities of 1-20 mounds per hectare are typical, but densities of up to 60-100 mounds per hectare may be reached in particularly favourable locations. On average, each mound is inhabited by five to six individuals (Macholán 1999). In Slovakia, Ukraine and Russia the range of this species is expanding.
range: Mus spicilegus is endemic to Europe, occurring from Lake Neusiedl on the Austro-Hungarian border through Slovakia, Hungary, Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine, reaching as far as Rostov, Belgorod and Kursk regions of Russia. An isolated population occurs between Montenegro, Greece and Albania. This population has a fragmented range within a very narrow strip of habitat, and there are only three known localities (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2006).The Steppe Mouse occurs from sea level to over 300m asl. In recent decades, the species started to increase its extent of occurrence (EOO) in the northern and eastern directions. New populations have been found in Ivano-Frankivsk Region, (M. Rusin and M. Ghazali, 2022 observation on iNaturalist), in Zakarpatska Region (Barkaszi and Zagorodniuk 2018), in Khmelnytskyi Region (Vikyrchak 2020), reaching the closest vicinities of the Kyiv City (M. Rusin, iNaturalist observations), in Kharkiv Region (N. Brusentsova, pers. comm. 2022), and in Kursk region of Russia (A. Vlasov, pers. comm. 2021).
useTrade: This species is not utlised or traded.
conservationActions: It occurs in some protected areas within its range, including Black Sea Biosphere Reserve, Askania Nova Biosphere Reserve, Luhansk Nature Reserve, Tuzlivksi Lymany National Park and more. It is more abundant in crop fields than in natural habitats. Further agro-industrialisation of farming may lead to a rapid and unexpected decline (as happened previously to many other previously abundant cropland species, such as Cricetus cricetus. Constant monitoring is required.

rationale: East European Grey Vole is a common and widespread species, tolerant of a wide range of habitat types. No major threats are known, and consequently, it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species is typically found in open and structurally simple habitats with tall and dense herbs and grasses, frequently in humid depressions and on the shores of water bodies. In contrast to M. arvalis, M. rossiaemeridionalis is rare in agricultural land and mown fields (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022). M. rossiaemeridionalis is more common in lowland areas in Europe. In parts of eastern Ukraine, the species settles in parks and gardens and seeks shelter in haystacks and inside storage sheds where harvested crops are kept. The daily activity pattern of East European Grey Voles is polyphasic. They excavate extensive burrows with numerous entrances; tunnels are 20-25 cm below the surface, rarely deeper. These voles have a vegetarian diet and are pests to agriculture. The breeding season lasts from early April into October. The gestation period is 18-22 days and females have 2-10 (mean = 4.3-5.6, depending on the region). Females sexually mature at 45-60 days of age (mean 54 days; Krystufek 2017).
threats: No major threats are known to this species.
population: It is a relatively common species. Population densities fluctuate on an annual basis, and peak densities of as high as 200,000 burrow openings per hectare have been recorded in North Macedonia (Zima 1999).
range: Microtus rossiaemeridionalis has a broad distribution. In the European region, the range includes Albania, southern Serbia, North Macedonia, northern Greece, southeast Bulgaria, eastern Ukraine, Belarus, European Russia in the Russian Federation, European Türkiye, and isolated subpopulations in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022). Moreover, the species has been introduced to Svalbard Island (Norway, not mapped). Beyond the European region, the species is distributed in Kazakhstan, the Caucasus, Armenia, Iran, and the Anatolia region of Türkiye, and has been passively introduced in some areas of the Russian Far East (Malygin et al. 2020, Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).
useTrade: The species is not used or traded.
conservationActions: The species occurs in protected areas throughout its range. No specific conservation actions are needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened due to widespread heavy hunting pressure, combined with habitat loss and degradation. Increasing human population density, hunting intensity and deforestation make it unlikely that pressure on Cercopithecus nictitans will subside in the short term. It is suspected that the ongoing decline across the range will be in the order of 20–25% within three generations (ca 27 years), from 2003 projected to 2030. Therefore, the taxon almost qualifies as threatened under criterion A4cd.
habitat: The Putty-nosed Monkey is an arboreal species present in lowland and mid-elevation montane tropical moist forest, gallery forest and secondary forest; it is less commonly found in swamp forest. This species generally lives in groups of between 12 and 30 animals. It prefers the middle and upper strata of the forest canopy, and is uncommonly encountered below 10 m or on the ground (Gautier-Hion 2013).
threats: The Putty-nosed Monkey is threatened by bushmeat hunting and by habitat loss through deforestation for timber and agricultural land, especially in the west of its range.Hunting is an increasing threat throughout its range, as monkey meat is consumed in villages or traded to urban populations. Human population growth in the range states continues at roughly 2.7% annually and will not slow down for several decades (United Nations 2015, WorldPop 2016). Road access into once-remote forests—even around protected areas—has hugely increased over the last 20–30 years (Laporte et al. 2007), facilitating hunting and transportation of bushmeat to both local markets and distant urban centres (Abernethy et al. 2013, Ziegler et al. 2016).Although this taxon may be the most resistant of the arboreal monkeys to hunting pressure, it is less tolerant to forest disturbance (Oates 2011, Gautier-Hion 2013). In West Africa, and in much of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, the species is subject to habitat modification, as intact forest is converted to farmland and “farm bush” which can be seen clearly in Tyukavina et al. (2016). In the Cameroon (SE), CAR, DRC, Congo and Gabon portions of this taxon’s range, forest loss is relatively low (Hansen et al. 2013), due to historically lower human population densities and selective logging, as opposed to clear-cutting, practised in the region. However, forest loss in the most recent year available (2014) was higher than in all previous years (from 2001) in Cameroon, Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, DRC and Equatorial Guinea, and in Gabon, Guinea and Liberia this was true for 2013, followed by 2014 (World Resources Institute 2016). Deforestation will greatly increase in the future as industrial agriculture starts to expand, removing forests suitable for various forest-obligate species (Wich et al. 2014).
population: The status of Cercopithecus nictitans populations varies widely across its range. In West Africa, it is relatively rare. In Côte d’Ivoire, it is likely restricted to Taï National Park, where it has a density of 0.05 groups/km² (0.45 individuals/km²; Buzzard and Eckardt 2007). In Liberia, its population status is unknown. In southwestern Nigeria, encounter rates have declined significantly due mainly to forest conversion and excessive hunting. For example, in 2009 encounter rates of 1.18–3.12 groups/km were recorded, but in 2013, the encounter rate had decreased to 0.06–0.16 groups per km surveyed (Ikemeh 2009, 2013). In the Niger Delta, these monkeys were observed relatively frequently (although encounter rates were not recorded systematically; R.A. Ikemeh, pers. obs. 2009, 2013).On Bioko, the population has undergone steep declines – estimated to be an 80% reduction between 1986 and 2016, with approximately 136 groups remaining on the island, entirely restricted to the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve (D.T. Cronin, pers. obs. 2016).This taxon is more common in the central and eastern parts of its range, and some large and dense populations persist (Oates 2011, Gautier-Hion 2013, Cronin et al. 2015). At some sites, such as Korup National Park in Cameroon, these monkeys seem to be relatively resilient to heavy hunting pressure (Linder and Oates 2011), with density estimated at 1.1–2.6 groups/km² (Linder 2008). In protected areas, the C. n. nictitans subspecies has an estimated population density of 2–80 individuals/km², usually around 20 individuals/km² (Gautier-Hion 2013). Despite its relatively high abundance in the eastern part of its range, long-term heavy hunting has led to its absence or near absence in large areas of suitable habitat.Long-term heavy hunting has reduced population sizes. This, in combination with deforestation for timber and agricultural land, has led to absence or near absence in large areas of suitable habitat. Based on this, it is suspected that the species will undergo a reduction of 20–25% over the three generation period between 2003 and 2030.
range: Cercopithecus nictitans occurs as a disjunct population in Liberia and western Côte d'Ivoire, and then more continuously from the Osse River in western Nigeria south and east to the Congo River, across the Ubangui River as far east as Buta and Budjala (both in Democratic Republic of Congo) between the Congo River and Ubangui River. It is also found on the island of Bioko (Equatorial Guinea). Isolated of western population is thought to have resulted from competition with Cercopithecus diana.There are five subspecies: insolitus, ludio, martini, nictitans and stampflii.Cercopithecus n. insolitus is found in central-southern Nigeria, from the Niger Delta in the south to north of the Niger and Benue rivers. Its range extends westwards within much of the extent of the Nigerian lowland rainforest ecoregion.Cercopithecus n. ludio occurs in southeastern Nigeria and southwestern Cameroon in the area between the Cross and Sanaga rivers, as far as the Mbam River, east of which it is replaced by C. n. nictitans. Almost half their range lies north of the Cross River to the Mambila Plateau and the forested areas of Gashaka Gumti National Park in Nigeria, and corresponding areas in Cameroon, including Takamanda National Park.Cercopithecus n. martini is restricted to Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea, where its range is limited to approximately 280 km² in one protected area in the south—the Gran Caldera Scientific Reserve. Cercopithecus n. nictitans—is generally distributed through the moist forests south of the Sanaga river east to the Itimbiri River and down into the northern Congo Basin, along the right bank of the Congo River to the forest-savanna limits. Its range encompasses mainland Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and parts of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo and Republic of Congo. It may also be present in Angola (Cabinda). The Sanaga river is not a hard northern barrier; however, as in its northwestern extent, its range crosses the Sanaga River, extending northward east of the Mbam River into the Cameroon Highlands [where it meets the eastern limit of C. n. ludio in the vicinity of the Mambilla Plateau along the Nigeria-Cameroon Border] (Grubb et al. 2000, Oates 2011).Cercopithecus n. stampflii occurs in the disjunct western part of its range, distributed across northern Liberia and western Côte d’Ivoire. In Côte d’Ivoire, it is believed extirpated from nearly all its former range, except for Taï National Park. The current distribution of C. n. stampflii in Liberia is unknown; one specimen was recently recorded by Covey and McGraw (2014) in a bushmeat market along the Liberia-Côte d’Ivoire border, but it was not encountered by Abdulai et al. (2007) in a rapid survey of North Lorma, Gola and Grebo National Forests of western Liberia.
useTrade: Cercopithecus nictitans is hunted illegally throughout its range for both subsistence use and commercial trade to supply urban demand.
conservationActions: Cercopithecus nictitans is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. It is on the list of partially protected species in Nigeria, Congo and DRC, and on Class C in Cameroon and CAR (i.e., may be hunted with a permit). The hunting, sale or consumption of primates is forbidden in Equatorial Guinea by Presidential Decree. All primates are fully protected in Cross River State, Nigeria, under the Forestry Commission Law of 2010. It is not listed as a protected species in the legislation of either Gabon or Côte d'Ivoire.This species occurs in almost all the protected areas in its range, including the World Heritage sites of Dja (Cameroon), Lope (Gabon) and the Sangha Trinational (Congo-Cameroon-CAR). In southeastern Nigeria, the species is present in Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary, Cross River National Park and Mbe Mountains (all in Cross River State), and in Gashaka Gumti National Park in Taraba State. Due to its rarity, the western-most form, C. n. stampflii, occurs in very few protected areas; Taï National Park (Côte d'Ivoire) is a notable exception.

rationale: Azara's Capuchin (Sapajus cay) is assessed as Vulnerable (VU A2cd+3cd), based on past and future population decline over three generations (approximately 48 years for this species). While this species is widespread geographically, the species is suspected to be undergoing population declines due to high rates of habitat loss across its range (including losses of more than 30% in Brazil and over 58% in Paraguay). The threat of habitat loss is exacerbated by additional threats facing the species including hunting, poaching, and wildlife trafficking. Habitat requirement studies have indicated that this species is not more tolerant of habitat disturbance than other species of Sapajus (Smith 2021).Note that this species has also been assessed as Vulnerable (A4cd) at the national level within Brazil in 2019.
habitat: The genus is not restricted to primary habitats, but well recognized for its behavioral plasticity (Fragaszy et al. 1990, 2004) and the ability to survive in areas altered by man (Wallace 2008). However, Sapajus may still require relatively large areas of forest for their survival, as in the case of a group of tufted capuchin monitored by Spironelo (1988, 1991) in central Amazonia, which occupied a home range of 1,000 ha.Sapajus cay inhabits subtropical, humid, semi-deciduous, gallery forests and forested regions of the Pantanal, ranging into the Yungas, the dry deciduous forests of northern Bolivian Chaco and eastern Paraguay (not recorded in the Paraguayan Gran Chaco, Smith et al. 2021, Smith 2021, Stallings 1985, 1989, Wallace 2008; or the Ñeembucú Wetland Complex, Smith et al. 2021, Smith 2021). It inhabits Cerrado habitat and riparian and gallery forests in the valleys and hills of the Serra de Maracajú and the Serra de Bodoquena in Mato Grosso do Sul (Pinto 2006, Vieira 2006, Cazzadore 2007, Wallace 2008, Fernandes Jr. 2013, Fernandes Jr. et al. 2019).Capuchins are extractive and manipulative foragers. They are frugivores-insectivores, including a wide variety of fruits, seeds, arthropods, frogs, nestlings and even primates (Mico melanurus, Costa et al. 2020), birds (Peixoto-Couto et al. 2021) and small mammals in their diet (Milano and Moteiro Filho 2009), supplemented by stems and flower buds. In areas where crop plantations can be safely exploited, capuchins supplement their diets with pine seeds, corn and very occasionally soybeans (Smith et al. in Press, Smith 2021). Open fields (e.g. soybeans) are extremely different from the natural forested habitat of the species, hence are not exploited; probably perceived as risky habitat. Males and females disperse, and both sexes are organized in linear dominance hierarchies, the top ranking male being dominant over the top ranking female. Subordinate males and females are often peripheral (Vieira 2006, Pinto 2006, Cazzadore 2007, Fernandes Jr. 2013).Sapajus cay is an adaptable species that also occurs in degraded habitats, for example, one group survived for many decades in an urban area, in Segredo Stream State Park (189 ha) in Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (Pinto 2006, Kazzadore 2007, Rímoli et al. 2009). Two groups of Sapajus cay survive in Rancho Laguna Blanca, San Pedro, Paraguay, which is a 243 ha fragment of forest surrounded by soy field and human settlements. While the monkeys appear to have adapted to life in this small fragment, the long-term genetic consequences, including potential for gene flow from outside the fragment, are unknown (Smith 2021). While this species can adapt to degraded habitat, they do not use degraded forest evenly and appear to prefer more mature forest (Smith et al. 2018, Smith 2021). Hence, degraded forest do not maintain the same monkey density as mature forest, an important factor to consider when estimating the species status based on extent of occurrence.Movement Patterns: Sapajus cay is a predominantly arboreal, quadrupedal monkey that generally uses home ranges of 150-250 ha and travels >1,000 m per day (Vieira 2006, Fernandes Jr. 2013).Congregatory: Social groups (Vieira 2006, Pinto 2006, Cazzadore 2007, Rímoli et al. 2009, Fernandes Jr. 2013).
threats: In Paraguay, habitat loss is a major threat. Habitat loss has been mainly driven by the rapid and extensive advance of soy monocultures throughout eastern Paraguay (Da Ponte et al. 2017a, 2017b; Smith 2021). Today, the little remaining forest is threatened by the continued expansion of industrial agriculture, illegal settlements and increasing frequency and intensity of bushfires. In Paraguay, 58.39% (13,148 km²) of forest that had a 90% probability of capuchin presence (highly suitable habitat) was lost between 2000 and 2019, leaving only 9,368 km², in spite of the “Zero-Deforestation Law” being in place since 2004 (Smith 2021). In 2020 and 2021 this remaining forest suffered heavily from fires and illegal clearing. Paraguay is predicted to lose all its primary moist forest by 2028 (European Commission 2019).In Paraguay, this species is hunted for subsistence purposes in some parts of its range, but human population density is typically low in these areas. Forest loss is the main threat in eastern Paraguay (Stallings 1985, Smith 2021). Hunting by indigenous and rural people is also a threat, but it is unclear to what extent this is impacting the population in Paraguay today. As in other parts of its range, Sapajus cay is the most commonly kept primate pet in Paraguay.In Brazil, there are severe threats to the survival of the species. The main threats identified for the taxon are: fire, rural settlements, agriculture, livestock keeping, urban sprawl, vulnerability to epidemics, deforestation, increasing road and energy infrastructure, habitat isolation, habitat reduction, pollution, hunting and live capture for pet trade (Rímoli et al. 2015, 2018). For example, in Segredo Stream State Park (PEMS) in Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul, evidence for an inbreeding depression was observed, i.e. polydactyl individuals with six fingers on hands and feet occurred in some small fragments and habitat isolates (Pinto 2006, Cazzadore 2007) and individuals with facial malformations has been observed in San Pedro in Paraguay – though the underlying cause is unclear (Smith et al. 2021b). Currently, in Brazil, through the National Action Plan for the Conservation of Endangered Species of Ichthyofauna, Herpetofauna and Primates of the Cerrado and Pantanal (CERPAN, 2021), we seek to identify priority areas that favor connectivity between fragments in the area of occurrence.
population: The total remaining population size for this species is not known and it remains unclear whether the number of mature individuals is greater than 10,000 individuals (Rímoli et al. 2015). It is nevertheless suspected, however, that the species has undergone (and continues to experience) population decline of at least 30% (over the last three generations). If 'business-as-usual' continues, the population will continue to decline at the same rate (at least 30%) over the next three generations.In Brazil, for example, Sapajus cay is a species that occurs in the states of Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and Goiás. Here, it is suspected that the population decline is greater than 30% in the last three generations due to factors such as: habitat loss, fragmentation and disconnection; increase in the road network and energy infrastructure; urban sprawl; fires; hunting; vulnerability to epidemics; rural settlements and inbreeding; among other threats. The estimated reduction of at least 30% was based on information obtained from reporting forms on the genus Sapajus in the Amazon (that are used to monitor habitat areas of more than 1,000 ha; Spironelo 1988, 1991). Thus, the species has been classified as Vulnerable (VU) under the A4cd criterion at the national level within Brazil (Rímoli et al. 2018).In Argentina, the regions where the species is found have lost between 8.2% and 18% tree cover from 2001 to 2020 (Global Forest Watch, 2020). In Paraguay, the regions where the species is found have lost between 6.2% and 36% tree cover from 2001 to 2020 (Global Forest Watch, 2020). Paraguay is predicted to lose all its primary moist forest by 2028 (European Commission 2019).Stallings (1985) recorded a mean group size of seven individuals (n = 4 groups) in the Ybicui National Park, though much larger groups – between 18 and 33 individuals - have been recorded in Rancho Laguna Blanca and Área para Parque San Rafael (Tekoha Guasu) (Smith and Briggs 2015, Smith 2021). Groups averaging 22 (Vieira 2006) or 25 individuals (Fernandes Júnior 2013, Fernandes Júnior. et al. 2019) were also recorded.Population density in the Ybicui National Park was estimated as 4 groups/km² or 28 individuals/km² (Stallings 1985). At other sites population densities were estimated as 0.31 individuals/ha in the upper Rio Paraná region, MS (Aguiar et al. 2011), 0.15 individuals/ha in Terenos, MS (Vieira 2006), and 0.19 individuals/ha in Campo Grande, MS (Pinto 2006, Cazzadore 2007). In Rancho Laguna Blanca (243 ha) density was 15 individuals/km² or 0.77 groups/km² and in Área para Parque San Rafael (Tekoha Guasu) density was ~62 individuals/km² (and 2.62 groups/km²) (Smith 2021).
range: In Brazil, Sapajus cay occurs in the state of Mato Grosso, in the south (Cabrera 1957, Wallace 2008), east, west and south-west of Mato Grosso do Sul (Pinto 2006, Vieira 2006, Cazzadore 2007, Rímoli et al. 2009, Fernandes Jr. 2013), and in Goiás State (Calaça et al. 2018), where it is resident and native. It can also be found in the regions of Cassilândia (MS) and Itajá (GO) (Calaça et al. 2018) and the Comodoro region (MT) which represents the most western part of its distribution (Messias M. pers. comm.). The northern limit of the species’ range is the southern part of the Xingu Indigenous Park (Garapu Desk, Sete de Setembro River and Lake Ipavu) in Mato Grosso (Silva Jr. 2001). The eastern boundary seems to be the Araguaia River, while the southeastern limit is the Paraná River (Silva Jr. 2001) where it occurs on the islands and floodplains of the Paraná River in an Environmental Protection Area (Aguiar et al. 2011). Câmara and collaborators (2018) updated the geographic distribution of Sapajus cay in the south-central, southeastern and western portions of the state of Mato Grosso, Brazil, and here we extend the distribution of this species north to the Cabixi River, on the border with the state of Rondônia. Data were obtained from field surveys. The authors have observed individuals of S. cay in highly fragmented forests that were impacted by deforestation in the last 50 years, an alarming situation for the conservation of the region's fauna.This species is found in Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay (Cabrera 1957, Wallace 2008). It occurs throughout eastern Paraguay (excluding the Gran Chaco in the north and Ñeembucú Wetland Complex and Mesopotamian Grasslands in the southwest in Ñeembucú and Misiones departments), in south-east Bolivia, and in northern Argentina, including the provinces of Jujuy, Salta, Formosa and Chaco (Mantecon et al. 1984, Brown 1989).In Paraguay, S. cay occurs to the east of the Paraguay River (Hill 1960; Stallings 1985, 1989). The distribution extends southward to the eastern part of Paraguay (Stallings 1985, Brown and Colillas 1984), reaching into northwestern Argentina. Capuchin monkeys are not found in the Chaco region of the Provinces of Formosa and Chaco in northern Argentina. Thus, the distribution of S. cay forms a horseshoe shape, bordering the xerophytic Chaco of Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay (Brown and Rumiz 1986). In the west, the limits are defined by the Andes in Argentina and Bolivia, and in the east it is confined to eastern Paraguay, mostly within the remaining Upper Paraná Atlantic Forest. The species does not reach southwest Paraguay, particularly the department of Ñeembucú, and the humid Chaco environment appears to be a barrier to the species. It is unclear whether the population of this species in the area around Asunción, Central department, is natural or introduced; perhaps from escaped pets or released by the Asunción zoo (Smith et al. 2021). Probably, its southernmost limit in the east is defined by the Paraná River.More information to determine the exact occurrence of the species in the basins of the Araguaia and Paraná Rivers (Silva Jr. 2001) and the Mato Grosso do Sul State in Pantanal (Tomas et al. 2010, 2011; Garcia 2018) is needed.Given ongoing habitat degradation and loss across the region, it is suspected that there are ongoing reductions in this capuchin's extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO), and habitat quality. For example, in Argentina, the regions where the species is found have lost between 8.2% and 18% tree cover from 2001 to 2020 (Global Forest Watch 2020). In Paraguay, the regions where the species is found have lost between 6.2% and 36% tree cover from 2001 to 2020 (Global Forest Watch 2020). Paraguay is predicted to lose all its primary moist forest by 2028 (European Commission 2019).
useTrade: In Paraguay, hunting by indigenous and rural people is a threat, but it is unclear to what extent this is impacting the population today. As in other parts of its range, Sapajus cay is the most commonly kept primate pet in Paraguay.In Brazil, hunting and live capture for the pet trade are a threat.
conservationActions: This species occurs in the following protected areas (see areas listed below). Note however that many of these protected areas are being degraded by forest fires, illegal logging, and illegal settlements. In Paraguay, for example, 70% of the Cerro Cora National Park was burned in 2021.Argentina:El Rey National Park Province of Salta (44,162 ha) (Brown et al. 1986, Brown 1989)Calilegua National Park, Province of Jujuy (76,000 ha) (Brown et al. 1986, Brown 1989)Baritú National Park Province of Jujuy (72,000 ha) (Brown et al. 1986, Brown 1989)Bolivia:Kaa-Iya National Park (R. Wallace, pers. comm.).Brazil: Pantanal Matogrossense National Park (136,046 ha) (Wallace 2008)Serra da Bodoquena National Park (77,021 ha) (in range)Rio Negro State Park (7,000 ha) (in range)Segredo Stream State Park (189 ha) (Pinto 2006, Cazzadore 2006, Rímoli et al. 2009)SESC Pantanal Private Reserve (RPPN) (106,31 ha) (Brandão et al. 2011)Fazenda Acurizal Private Reserve (13,665 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Penha Private Reserve (RPPN) (13,409 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Boqueirão Private Reserve (RPPN) (173,60 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Singapura Private Reserve (RPPN) (456ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda América Private Reserve (RPPN) (401 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Trevo Private Reserve (RPPN) (27,75 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Floresta Negra Private reserve (RPPN) (971,06 ha) (Wallace 2008)Fazenda Nova Querência Private Reserve (50 ha in 8,500 ha of Gallery Forest) (Vieira 2006)Fazenda São Marcos (600 ha) (Fernandes Júnior 2013).Paraguay: Ybicui National Park (5,000 ha) (Stallings 1985)Cerro Cora National Park (5,500 ha) (Stallings 1985)Caaguazu National Park (6,000 ha) (Stallings 1985)Yakui Protected Forest (1,000 ha) (Stallings 1985)Nacunday Protected Forest (1,000 ha) (Stallings 1985)Bosque Mbaracayu Biosphere Reserve (~64,700ha) – privately owned reserve (Smith 2021)This species is listed on CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Plecturocebus vieirai is endemic from the top global deforestation frontier, the Amazonian arc of deforestation, in the States of Mato Grosso and Pará. Based on new occurrence data, and models of species occurrence and of future deforestation in Amazonia, this species already lost 56% of its area of habitat only 14% of the species area of habitat will remain in three generations due to agriculture and cattle ranching expansion (Costa-Araújo et al. in press). The State of Mato Grosso has lost 21% of its tree cover from 2001 to 2010 and the State of Pará has lost 14% of its tree cover in the same time period (Global Forest Watch 2022). Another threat to this species is human-driven climate change, which will impact populations inside protected areas (Costa-Araújo et al. in press). It is therefore assessed as Critically Endangered under Criterion A3c.
habitat: Plecturocebus vieirai inhabits mature, secondary and degraded Amazonia and Amazonia-Cerrado transition forests, but it does not occur in Cerrado vegetation (Costa-Araújo et al. in press). It is also present in areas near to igarapé with the presence of moriche palm (Mauritia flexuosa) (Gualda-Barros et al. 2012).
threats: The main threats identified for this taxon are agriculture and cattle ranching expansion, with consequent increase in human settlement and road constructions, as well as climate change, which is expected to cause population declines even inside protected areas. Construction of hydroelectric plants is also considered a threat to the species.
population: Based on the species mean group size and area of suitable habitat from Costa-Araújo et al. (in press), the total population of P. vieirai should be around 1,000,000 individuals. Based on new occurrence data, and models of species occurrence and of future deforestation in Amazonia, Costa-Araújo et al. (in press) found that 56% of the species area of habitat (AOH) was lost to date and only 14% of the AOH will remain in three titi monkey generations, a process that is expected to impact the species population at similar levels. Here, it is suspected that the population will decline at least 80% into the future on the basis of projected to habitat reduction for agriculture and cattle ranching expansion as well as human-driven climate change, which threatens populations inside protected areas.
range: The Vieira’s Titi Monkey is endemic of Brazil, in the States of Mato Grosso and Pará. The species occurs west of the Xingu River, south of the Iriri River, east of the Iriri and Teles Pires rivers, southward to the headwaters of the Xingu and Teles Pires rivers, until the border between Amazonia–Cerrado biomes, in northern Mato Grosso State and south-central Pará State (Costa-Araújo et al. in press).It is suspected that the extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO) and habitat quality are undergoing continuous decline across the species' range. The State of Mato Grosso has lost 21% of its tree cover from 2001 to 2010 and the State of Pará has lost 14% of its tree cover in the same time period (Global Forest Watch 2022).
conservationActions: A project "Assessment of the conservation status of the recently discovered Vieira's titi monkey (Plecturocebus vieirai 2012)" is in progress. The project aims to find new populations of Plecturocebus vieirai; to assess their conservation status and major threats to the species; to estimate population densities and locate urban populations of the species. The project is coordinated by Prof. Dr. Gustavo Rodrigues Canale (UFMT) and has the following funders: Primate Action Fund, Primate Conservation Incorporation. Although there is no specific monitoring for the species, since 2011 in the area of influence of Colíder Dam, there is an ongoing mammal monitoring program that is scheduled to end in 2015.

rationale: Mico schneideri was recently described by scientists, and currently there is no information on habitat availability and population sizes. Given high deforestation rates across its range, it is suspected that this marmoset's extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both undergoing ongoing decline. From 2001 to 2020, the Mato Grosso State lost 21% of its forest cover (Global Forest Watch 2022). Within the range of the species, the study by Boubli et al. (2019) is relevant, as it estimated historical forest loss for the range of Plecturocebus grovesi (which occurs throughout the range of and in syntopy with M. schneideri). This study estimated that 42% of habitat was lost from 1997 to 2017. In addition, the same paper modelled future habitat loss of 86% over a 24-year period into the future using a 'business-as-usual' scenario.If we assume that the forest loss rates from Boubli et al. (2019) are relevant here, and given the 5–6 year generation length of M. schneideri, we can estimate that the species has lost ca 32–38% of forest habitat in its range in over the past three generations. We can further project that M. schneideri will lose another 54–65% of its habitat in the next three generations (ca 15–18 years). This habitat loss and degradation (e.g., deforestation) is caused by intense and fast expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching in the Juruena-Teles Pires interfluve.Urgent conservation measures are needed to safeguard the future of this newly discovered primate.
habitat: There are no studies on specific habitat use and ecology of Mico schneideri to date.
threats: Mico schneideri population and habitat are threatened by agriculture, cattle ranching, mining and human settlement expansion. It is present in only one protected area.
population: Although there are no data on the population size of Mico schneideri, it is clear that the trend is of population decline due to habitat degradation and loss caused by expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching in the Amazonian arc of deforestation.On the basis of habitat degradation and loss rates, we infer that the species population has declined at least 32% to 38% in the past three generations (ca 15–18 years) and will decline between 54% to 65% in the next three generations.
range: Mico schneideri is endemic to the Amazonian forests within the arc of deforestation, Mato Grosso State, Brazil, and the species' range is limited by the Juruena River to the west and by the Teles Pires River to the east, proceeding north to their confluence. The southern portion of the species' range is less well-defined, but it extends to the headwaters of the Juruena and Teles Pires rivers, and no further south than the city of Lucas do Rio Verde (Costa-Araújo et al. 2021).Given high deforestation rates across its range, it is suspected that this marmoset's extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both undergoing ongoing decline. From 2001 to 2020, the Mato Grosso State lost 21% of its forest cover (Global Forest Watch 2022). Within the range of the species, the study by Boubli et al. (2019) is relevant, as it estimated historical forest loss for the range of Plecturocebus grovesi (which occurs throughout the range of and in syntopy with M. schneideri). This study estimated that 42% of habitat was lost from 1997 to 2017. In addition, the same paper modelled future habitat loss of 86% over a 24-year period into the future using a 'business-as-usual' scenario. If we assume that the forest loss rates from Boubli et al. (2019) are relevant here, and given the 15-18 year generation length of M. schneideri, we can estimate that the species has lost c. 32% to 38% of forest habitat in its range in over three generations into the past. We can further estimate that M. schneideri will lose another 54% and 65% of its habitat in the next three generations (c. 15-18 years). This habitat loss and degradation (e.g., deforestation) is caused by intense and fast expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching in the Juruena-Teles Pires interfluve.
useTrade: This species is sometimes captured for the pet trade.
conservationActions: Mico schneideri population and habitat are threatened by agriculture, cattle ranching, mining and human settlement expansion, and it is present in only one protected area. There is a conservation project underway, led by Dr. Rodrigo Costa-Araújo, focussing on developing a framework for the conservation of all Amazon marmosets and on awareness raising towards the implementation of such framework and behaviour change (@amazonmarmosets).

rationale: The African Savanna Elephant (Loxodonta africana) is assessed as Endangered A2bd. Analysis of estimates from 334 localities across their global range indicates a reduction of more than 50% of the continental population in the past three generations (75 years) that is understood to be continuing and likely irreversible. The continental trend is not, however, spatially uniform; some subpopulations are increasing or stable while others are declining significantly faster than the continental rate. Many local subpopulations have been extirpated.A generation length (GL) of 25 years is used; calculated in the standard format as the average age of mothers in the population (IUCN SPC 2019, p. 29). This figure is based on analysis of the life table of culled Savanna Elephant family groups in South Africa (Whyte 2001) and a 14-year study of Savanna Elephants in Kenya (Wittemyer et al. 2013) which generated a range of 24.1–25 years.Subcriterion A2 is applied because some of the major causes for population reduction, such as habitat loss due to human population expansion, have not ceased and are projected to increase in coming decades as well as unlikely to be reversible. The population reduction assessment for subcriterion A2 (considering three generations back) is inferred from published survey data using a modelling approach described in the Supplementary Information document. Density and distribution estimates for the African Savanna Elephant vary in methodology, completeness, regularity, date of first survey and confidence limits. Few credible estimates exist prior to the 1970s, and there is no credible estimate for the continental population more than two generations back. For this Red List assessment, an attempt was made to model the data three generations back to 1940 (see the attached Supplementary Information for description of data that is current as of and up to the end of 2015); however, given the sparseness of information available to inform the model, such modelling was of limited value. Therefore, rather than projecting declines well beyond the available data, we made the assumption that the continental African Savanna Elephant population of three generations back (1940) was equal to that of two generations back (i.e., 1965). Additional assumptions, necessary to fill gaps in the dataset, are detailed in the attached Supplementary Information document.Subcriterion A3 has not been applied, because although the major threats to the species are known, projecting the level of such threats 25 or more years into the future (i.e., three generations, up to a maximum of 100 years) would likely introduce high levels of uncertainty.An assessment of population reduction according to subcriterion A4 considering two generations back and one forward is in progress by this team of Assessors (Edwards et al. in prep.). Analysis of poaching and human influence in the recent past and anticipated in the future based upon available data of two representative indices (i.e., proportion of illegal killed elephants (PIKE) and the human footprint index) are being included as covariates in the projection.Criteria B, C and D are not relevant to the threatened status as the species currently occupies more than 20,000 km2 and there are more than 10,000 mature individuals. No quantitative analysis of the probability of extinction in the wild was conducted, and therefore criterion E does not apply.The species is categorized as EN A2bd given the modelled estimate of population reduction and its distribution. However, considering the uncertainty of the estimate as communicated in Table 1a in the Supplementary Information and data sparsity issues during the earliest time period as explained, a category of Vulnerable (VU) is plausible (see also section 3.2.5. of the Guidelines for Using the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria (IUCN SPC 2019)).Previous Assessments of African Elephant:This is the first assessment of the African Savanna Elephant (Loxodonta africana) as a species separate from the African Forest Elephant (L. cyclotis).The African Elephant, as a single species, was listed as Vulnerable (VU A2a) in the 2004 and 2008 updates of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, under the same IUCN Categories and Criteria used in this assessment (Version 3.1; IUCN 2001).Previously the African Elephant, as a single species, was listed as Endangered (EN A1b) under the IUCN Categories and Criteria Version 2.3 (IUCN 1994), in an assessment conducted in 1996 by the IUCN SSC African Elephant Specialist Group.
habitat: African Savanna Elephants are found over a wide latitudinal range between the northern tropics in Mali (16° North) to the southern temperate zone (34° South) in South Africa. They occupy a variety of habitats ranging from montane forest, miombo and mopane woodland, thicket, savanna and grasslands to arid deserts and a wide altitudinal range from mountain slopes to oceanic beaches.See also the list of habitats.African Savanna Elephants are capable of moving long distances and naturally do so in arid ecosystems and in response to climatic conditions (e.g., seasonality and drought). Depending on productivity, and water availability African Savanna Elephants demonstrate range residence, migratory, semi-migratory and near nomadic movement patterns in different regions of the continent. Home range sizes vary by several orders of magnitude primarily in relation to plant productivity and human activity in different ecosystems (Loarie et al. 2009, Wall et al. 2013). Thirty African Savanna Elephant subpopulations (eight of which number more than 1,000 individuals) span international boundaries, including the more than 200,000 elephants in the five-country Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (Lindsay et al. 2017, KAZA Secretariat 2018).Ecosystem Services:Ecosystem services provided by African Savanna Elephants vary and depend to a large extent on the ecosystem (forest, savanna, grassland or desert), specific conditions on the ground and the geographical context under consideration. In general, they play an important ecological role as bulk processors of plant material (Owen-Smith 1989). In savannas, African Savanna Elephants are manipulators of woody vegetation structure which in turn influences the tree to grass ratio with knock-on consequences for the fire regime and potentially species composition in the area (Dublin et al. 1990, Augustine and McNaughton 2004, Palmer et al. 2008, Holdo et al. 2009, Goheen et al. 2010, Pringle et al. 2016). Where they are associated with wetlands African Savanna Elephants can be important in maintaining channels and open water ways. Soil fertility can be maintained by the transport of nutrients by large herbivores from nutrient rich sources (e.g., eutrophic soils in flood plains and termite mounds) to dystrophic soils (e.g., upland miombo woodlands) (Cumming et al. 1997, Doughty et al. 2016, Malhi et al. 2016).The charismatic nature of African Savanna Elephants plays an important role in attracting tourism into national parks. They also hold important symbolic significance within the cultures of many African communities. African Savanna Elephants are one of the few iconic species that occur in the majority of African countries, and innumerable stories, songs, and cultural traditions revolve around them.
threats: Poaching of African Savanna Elephants for ivory is a major cause of individual death and population decline (Wittemyer et al. 2014, Thouless et al. 2016). After a sustained period of intense poaching between the late 1970s and 1989, many African Savanna Elephant populations (e.g., in Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, Uganda) experienced two to three decades of recovery. Some northern African Savanna Elephant populations, however, experienced persistent poaching pressure through the last three decades (Bouche et al. 2011, 2012). Data collected as a part of the CITES Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants programme (MIKE), indicate that poaching significantly intensified across the continent starting in 2008 and peaking in 2011 – an unsustainably high level of poaching has continued into current times in some areas of the continent (CITES 2018, 2019), and may be increasing in some of the historically less-affected southern African populations (CITES 2018, 2019). Rapid land use change by humans is driving the direct loss and fragmentation of habitat for African Savanna Elephants and is an increasing threat to populations across their range (Thouless et al. 2016, Mpakairi et al. 2019). Land conversion is a product of the ongoing expansion of the human population and associated agriculture and infrastructure development, which in turn are driven by economic and technological advances. A manifestation of this trend is the reported increase in human-elephant conflict (e.g., Pozo et al. 2018). Human population growth projections suggest land conversion will accelerate rapidly in the coming decades across Africa (see https://population.un.org/wpp/Publications/) which will likely increase this threat.
population: Over the past century, African Savanna Elephant subpopulations have declined across most of their range. The African Elephant Status Report 2016 estimated a continental population of 415,428 (+/- 95% C.I. 20,111) for both African Savanna and African Forest Elephants combined and reported a continental decline of approximately 111,000 elephants since 2006 (Thouless et al. 2016).
