The central-German subpopulation is also expanding, particularly in the southeast and north. In Austria an increasing number of records in the northeast (Lower Austria, along and north of the Danube river) indicate small, partly isolated populations that are slowly spreading. Immigration from neighbouring countries is very likely. Habitat for wildcats is abundant in Austria and its quality has also increased in recent years (Slotta-Bachmayr et al. 2016).Size:For Germany the population size was estimated at 5,000 to 10,000 individuals (National Report of the Article 17 Habitats Directive 2019).In France wildcats have extended their range (in both populations!) by ca 30 % in the last 30 years (Say et al. 2012).Assuming a conservative average population density of 0.1 wildcats per km², it is estimated that there are 25,600 wildcats only for the extant area of the Western-Central European metapopulation.Eastern-Central, Eastern and Southeastern EuropeThis is potentially the largest and most widespread metapopulation of the species. A rigorous review of the distribution as done for other metapopulations would probably show that the wildcat is less widespread than assumed, and that the fragmentation in south-east Europe is probably larger than shown in the current distribution map.Austria: There is an increasing number of records in the south of Austria (Carinthia), indicating a spreading population due to immigration from Italy and probably also from Slovenia (Slotta-Bachmayr et al. 2016).Albania: There is no reliable quantitative information on population size and trends of the wildcat population, but the species is considered fairly widespread (with exception of the more urbaniused coastal area), but with low population density in the mountainous and hilly areas of the country (Prigioni 1996, Trajçe et. al. 2008, Trajçe and Hoxha 2011). Experts estimate that there are <400 mature individuals with an unknown current population trend, but with a perceived decline of 30-40% since 1950.Bosnia and Herzegovina: There are no quantitative data on population size, but the species is widespread (Štrbac et. al. 2020). Experts estimate more than 2,000 individuals. The population trend is unknown.Bulgaria: The European Wildcat is considered widespread throughout the country (Spassov et. al. 1997). The population size was estimated by extrapolation from a limited amount of data as 1,610-4,375 individuals. The population trend is thought to be stable to decreasing, and the species has an Unfavourable - Inadequate (U1) population conservation status (Art. 17 Habitat Directive Report - Bulgaria). The population density in two mountains in Bulgaria (Vitosha and Pirin Mtn.) was estimated by camera traps to vary between 6 and 79 individuals per 100 km2 (Zlatanova 2014a, 2014b).Croatia: The European Wildcat is widespread throughout the country. The population size was estimated by extrapolation from limited data as 2,216-2,683 individuals. The population trend is unknown and the species has an Unknown (XX) population conservation status (Art. 17 Habitat Directive Report - Croatia).Czech Republic: The wildcat is restricted to some isolated pockets along the border with Germany and to the western Beskid Mountains, which are connected to the distribution in the Carpathians. However, records have increased in recent years in various regions.Greece: The species is widespread, inhabiting most of the forested mountainous areas and many wetlands, in continental Greece and on the island of Crete, with the exception of the Peloponnese. There are insufficient or no data available to assess population size. The population trend is unknown and the European Wildcat has an Unknown (XX) population conservation status (Art. 17 Habitat Directive Report - Greece).Hungary: According to the new distribution map, the wildcat occurs in many different parts of the country, though within a more closed distribution in the Northeast.Italy (north-east): According to the data compiled for the new distribution map, the wildcat is expanding westward from the region Friuli Venezia Giulia into the regions of Veneto and Trentino-South Tyrol.Moldova: The species occurs across the country, especially in the forested areas. There are no data on population size.Montenegro: The species is considered common and abundant in the country (Perović and Đurović 2013), but there are no quantitative data on population size or any population estimate. Also, the population trend is unknown.North Macedonia: The European Wildcat is widely distributed, but population size and trend are unknown.Poland: The species is restricted to the Polish part of the Carpathian Mountains in the south-east of the country.Romania: The species is widespread throughout the country. The population size is estimated at 8,005-9,150 individuals. The population trend is stable and the species has a Favourable (FV) population conservation status (Art. 17 Habitat Directive Report - Romania)Serbia and Kosovo: The species is distributed throughout both countries, with the exception of the north-east, but it is not considered abundant.Slovakia: The species is widespread across the country except for the western parts.Slovenia: The wildcat is widespread in the southern two-thirds of the country, especially in the Dinarics, but it also occurs in parts of the Slovenian Alps.Turkey (European part): The wildcat is widespread in this part of the country, except for the more densely populated and agricultural areas close to the Marmara Sea area. There are no data on population size.Ukraine: The wildcat is widespread in the Carpathians and, according to the data compiled for the new distribution map, the species extends to the east into the steppe region between rivers Dniester (Dnister) and Dnieper (Dnipro). There are no data on population size.Iberian PeninsulaPortugal: The European Wildcat is considered Vulnerable at the national level, on the basis of suspected declines reaching 30% over three generations in the past or future (Cabral et al. 2005).Spain: The species is considered Near Threatened at the national level (López-Martín et al.2007). A population size estimate is only available for the Andalusia region (South Spain, 88.000 km2), where 860 (794–926) adult individuals were estimated (Gil-Sánchez et al. 2020).The Iberian metapopulation of the European Wildcat is divided into two highly distinct biomes: i) the ‘Mediterranean Forests, Woodlands and Scrub’ biome, occupying ca. 2/3 of the Iberian land area; and ii) the ‘Temperate Broadleaf and Mixed Forests’ biome, occurring at the northern Iberian fringe (including the Pyrenees) and occupying ca. 1/3 of Iberia’s area. The ecological differences of the European Wildcat occurring in each of these biomes is striking, which is reflected in suspected different population trends.The European Wildcat populations occurring in the Mediterranean region are estimated to be declining, with an overall fragmented distribution and occurring at low population densities. Estimated European Wildcat population densities are as low as 6.9 ± 0.19 (Gil-Sánchez et al. 2020), 3.8 ± 1.7 (Ferreras et al.2021) or 3.2 ± 1.2 wildcats per 100 km2 (Matias et al. 2021). The estimated baseline probability of occupancy throughout Iberian protected areas is 11% (Monterroso et al. 2020). The only quantitative assessment of population trends, in Sierra Arana (Andalucía, Spain), indicates a 67% decrease in breeding females from 2004 to 2017 (J. M. Gil-Sánchez, pers. comm.). Although a general quantitative assessment of the extent of decline is not possible with the available data, both an observed decline and replacement by domestic cats in areas once occupied by wildcats (Sarmento et al. 2009, Sobrino et al. 2009) support a hypothesis of generalised population fragmentation and reduction due to the decreasing availability of rabbits as staple prey caused by rabbit haemorrhagic disease (Sobrino et al. 2009).Conversely, the population in the temperate region of Iberia appears to be stable (H. Ruiz and F. Urra, pers. comm.), and occurs at relatively high population densities in some places of 60-70 individuals per 100 km2 (H. Ruiz, pers. comm.) and 20-40 individuals per 100 km² (Sayol et al. 2018).Given that most of the Iberian land area is included in the Mediterranean biome, it is likely that the wildcat populations in this metapopulation have suffered from a population reduction during the period under analysis (2005-2020). The causes of reduction have not ceased and may not be understood (including density-dependent hybridisation effects, roadkills, diseases (especially diseases of the main prey), and competition with dominant competitors).Therefore, the wildcat population on the Iberian Peninsula can be considered to be severely fragmented. range: In Europe the distribution range of Felis silvestris silvestris is split into four continental metapopulations: (1) Western-Central Europe, (2) Apennine Peninsula and Sicily, and (3) Eastern-Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe (4) Iberian Peninsula. Furthermore, there are island populations in Scotland, Sicily (considered together with the Apennine metapopulation), and Crete. The continental metapopulations are in turn fragmented to a certain, partly unknown, degree.The situation on Crete is uncertain. Crete has been separated from the mainland since the middle Miocene (15,97–11,62 million years ago). Even at the peak of the Pleistocene glaciation there was no permanent land bridge between Crete and the mainland (Kuss 1977). The assumption is that the wildcat was introduced to Crete by humans.The distribution of Felis s. caucasica in Anatolia and the Caucasus is mainly based on generic expert guesses. The contemporary distribution reflects the re-colonisation of the continent from glacial refuges as much as the modern human-made fragmentation of the wildcat habitats (Piechocki 2001; see also Mattucci et al. 2015), posing some tricky questions with regard to the “correct” conservation units for the species. While human-made habitat fragmentation should be mitigated, regional phylogenetic adaptation over several thousand years should be conserved.Area for category “extant”: 1,423,300 km²Area for category “possibly extant”: 502,500 km²Area for category “possibly extinct”: 5,650 km² Western-Central EuropeThe western-central population’s range is mainly located in the Continental biogeographical region and a small percentage in the Atlantic region (European Commission DG Environment 2019). Recent records documented the species even in the Alpine biogeographical region. The largest contiguous distribution area includes central and north-eastern parts of France and south-western parts of Germany. This large population area also includes Luxembourg, Wallonia in Belgium, the province of Limburg in the Netherlands as well as the Swiss Jura. In the past 10 years wildcats have extended their range onto the Swiss Plateau and probably even the (Pre-) Alps. An isolated subpopulation survived in central Germany (see distribution map in Yamaguchi et al. 2015), but is increasingly merging with the south-western German distribution area as both population parts presently expand. The former isolated occurrence in the southern Massif Central in France (see distribution map in Yamaguchi et al. 2015) is now also connected with the main distribution area. The present distribution in France does not go as far south as shown in Yamaguchi et al. 2015). However, this does not indicate a range loss, but is due to improved data.Apennine Peninsula and SicilyWildcats are currently expanding their distribution range northward, following the mountain system of the central-north Apennines. The wildcat population is also expanding in Sicily, with verified records from the centre and from the west coast. However, records from newly recolonized areas have clearly shown that hybridisation with domestic cats is a continuing process (Gavagnin et al. 2018), and the same is occurring in some areas historically occupied by wildcats (Gaudiano et al. 2021 in prep.). These findings call for urgent conservation actions. The lack of standardization in research methodology makes it difficult to draw robust inferences about apparent expansion or demographic trends in Italy.Eastern-Central, Eastern and Southeastern EuropeThis metapopulation alone comprises 20 of the 34 range countries of the European Wildcat. However, data availability and quality vary significantly from country to country. According to the information available, the wildcat is relatively widespread, but is a neglected species in most range countries. Especially further surveys, including standardized monitoring regarding the distribution of the species, are needed for most regions. Even if for large parts of this metapopulation more data regarding a reduction or expansion of the distribution area are still missing, there is evidence of the species’ expansion towards the east in Ukraine into steppe-like habitats (Zagorodniuk et al. 2014). Similarly, wildcats are also expanding their range in the Italian Alps from east to west.Iberian PeninsulaThe wildcat population extends relatively continuously from the pre-Pyrenees westwards along the Cantabrian Mountain range towards the east of the Spanish autonomous community of Galicia. The westernmost distribution of wildcats in the temperate biome is mostly associated with forested areas around the Minho hydrographic basin towards the Peneda-Gerês National Park (Portugal), and extending from the Montesinho National Park (Portugal) northwards towards the Sanabria and Ancares mountains (Spain).A thorough inquiry among experts across Iberia has revealed that, in contrast to the former assessment (Yamaguchi et al. 2015), the distribution of the wildcat in the Mediterranean region of Spain and Portugal is considerably reduced, highly fragmented and split into apparently isolated populations. The relevant populations are concentrated in the main mountainous systems and in areas where the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) – as an important prey base - is most abundant. F. s. caucasica is distributed throughout maquis, deciduous and mixed-deciduous vegetation and around wetland habitats of western, north-western and northern Anatolia in Turkey and the southern and western slopes and lowlands of the Caucasus Mountains in Georgia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Russia. According to Kitchener et al. (2017) the status of the subspecies F. s. caucasica is unclear. In Anatolia, Caucasian wildcat populations occur continuously in the humid, relatively less fragmented, temperate mixed-deciduous forests of northern Anatolia, comprising the provinces of Balikesir, Bursa, Yalova, Sakarya, Düzce, Bilecik, Bolu, Zonguldak, Karabük, Bartin, Kastamonu, Sinop, Samsun, Ordu and the northern parts of Cankiri, Corum and Amasya. conservationActions: The European Wildcat is protected by several international treaties (EU Habitat Directives, Bern Convention, CITES) and accordingly by national legislation in the Range Countries. rationale: The Mainland Leopard Cat is widely reported and appears to be common across its large geographic range. Despite this, little is actually known concerning the species' global population size and status (i.e., declining, stable, increasing). Absolute abundance estimates available from only a handful of sites might not properly represent its population across its global range, however indicate good population in those surveyed sites. Thus, we believe the species warrants the treatment of Least Concern, given how widely reported the species is and how good the population size is in the surveyed sites.The habitat seems to be lost and/or modified in many regions (e.g. Hansen et al. 2013). However, an ability to adapt to different habitat types has helped its population to persist in those areas. There have been countries/regions too, for example Nepal which have experienced an increase in their forest cover (DFRS 2015). The Extent of Occurrence and the Area of Occupancy of the Mainland Leopard Cat are suspected to have remained more or less the same, and both are very much bigger than would be apt for categorisation as anything other than Least Concern.Although there have certainly been localized declines, there are no indications of an overall global population decline by the species at a rate sufficient for categorisation as anything other than Least Concern.
habitat: Mainland Leopard Cat inhabits a variety of habitats, from tropical rainforest to temperate broadleaf forest and marginally, coniferous forest, as well as shrub forest and successional grasslands (Thapa et al. 2013, Ghimirey et al. 2012, Shrivathsa et al. 2015, Coudrat et al. 2014). It also occurs in mountainous areas, lowland riparian habitats and agricultural wetlands (Kim et al. 2021). They are also known to adapt to a variety of habitats including monoculture like coffee, tea, rubber and palm plantations (Bali et al. 2007, Kumara et al. 2004, Tweedie 1978, Yu 2010, Nick Baker in litt. November 2021). Their adaptability to agricultural landscapes and plantations is often attributed to presence of rodents as prey in such habitats (Lim 1999). They are frequently reported along roads and human settlements. They have been recorded in the Himalayas as high as 4,474 m (Thapa et al.2013). Home range of leopard cat varies from 1.5 to 12.4 km2 (Chen et al. 2016).Mainland Leopard Cats prey primarily upon rodents like squirrels, rats and mice, ground birds and lizards. A total of 63 species of prey were found in their scats in Primorsky region of Russia with mammals and birds having highest frequency (89.3% and 30.6%) in their diet (Seryodkin and Burkovskiy 2019). They have been found to be mostly nocturnal and crepuscular (Can et al. 2019, Chua et al. 2016, Mukherjee et al. 2019, Petersen et al. 2019a).In the wild, birth dens have been found in hollow trees, amongst bushes, under overhanging rocks in small caves, under big roots, and between rocks. They are also excellent swimmers, and show an affinity towards water (Yu 2010). Available evidence from Thailand suggests Mainland Leopard Cat habitat use and activity patterns might be influenced by a combination of resource availability and inter-specific competition. Petersen et al. (2019a) found Leopard Cat habitat use within a forest fragment in north-eastern Thailand was positively associated with rodent biomass during a period of resource scarcity. However, no association was found between Leopard Cat habitat use and rodent biomass during a subsequent period of high rodent biomass.
threats: Potential threats to Mainland Leopard Cat vary across its geographic range, but overall, there is no evidence of any serious threats operating over large areas. Hunting and snaring occur in most parts of Mainland Leopard Cat’s range and is particularly intense in South-east Asia (Gray et al. 2018, Harrison et al. 2016, Willcox et al. 2014). But surveys in areas affected by heavy snaring show the Mainland Leopard Cat to be one of the most resilient species of small carnivores (Willcox et al. 2014). Hence there is little evidence to suggest that hunting and/or snaring is reducing Mainland Leopard Cat’s population at a global scale. The species is traded or hunted for meat in parts of north-east India (Selvan et al. 2013), in parts of Afghanistan (Karlstetter 2008), Bangladesh (S. Chaudhary pers. comm. 2021) and in South-east Asia (Willcox et al. 2014) but there is no evidence that this practice has dramatically reduced the species’ populations in those areas. A recent report shows that from North China to Sichuan, from Jiangxi to Yunnan, and areas like Guangxi and Guangdong showed a lower than expected number of wild Mainland Leopard Cat. The contributing reason behind the population decline in southern China is believed to be hunting for food and fur, however, more recently evidence shows illegal adoption, domestication, and hybrid breeding of Bengal Leopard Cat maybe other main factors (CFCA 2017). In recent years, the data indicate that the hunting pressure on the Chinese Mainland Leopard Cat populations has been dramatically reduced (Yu 2010). Additionally, China’s massive natural forest protection campaign since 1998 may also be very helpful for habitat recovery, which should be beneficial for the Leopard Cat (Yu 2010).Retaliatory killings in response to perceived poultry depredation are common though not at a rate to threaten its population either locally or globally. Misidentifications (as, for example mistaking the species as Leopard Panthera pardus or Snow Leopard Panthera uncia cub or Fishing Cat Prionailurus viverrinus) leading to lethal anthropogenic responses are common in countries like Bangladesh and Nepal. These perspectives instil fear, resulting in stern retaliatory anthropogenic responses however most of these responses are few and far between, with little impact in the global or even local scale.Deforestation is potentially an important driver of habitat deterioration and may be a localised threat to Mainland Leopard Cat survival in certain areas such as the eastern Afghanistan. Habitat loss or deterioration from other countries in its range has also been documented. Also, a recent study using ecological niche models suggests that the primary macroscale factors that negatively impact Leopard Cat are, climate change and human induced habitat degradation (Silva et al. 2020). However, its occurrence in areas without actual forests indicates that this is less of a threat than previously perceived. In Thailand, it is presumed to have higher mortality due to increased proximity to humans (Haines et al. 2004), but recent research in China shows much better adaptation by the species to human disturbance (Wu et al. 2018). The species’ overall tolerance to human disturbance allows for a much wider population of the species than would be the case if it inhabited in areas infrequented by humans. The species’ ability to disperse between the many isolated forest fragments in which it currently occurs is unknown, though available evidence suggests it may be limited in Taiwan (Chen et al. 2016). By contrast, in southern Korea, the species disperses freely across non-forest landscapes as shown by its strong colonisation of newly-reclaimed areas of formerly intertidal habitat converted to rice fields and brackish wetlands. In principle, inter-patch dispersal ability depends on the structure and composition of the surrounding matrix and overall landscape permeability, features that can be both site- and period-specific (Metzger and Décamps 1997). As such, the long-term viability of isolated populations living within many forest fragments is uncertain and probably variable.Free roaming dogs, Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) transmission from feral cats and reduced prey availability can also threaten the Mainland Leopard Cat in specific areas, such as for example the population on Tsushima island, Japan (Ministry of the Environment of the Government of Japan, no date). Protoparvovirus have also been found in Mainland Leopard Cat in China (Chen et al. 2019). Road kills in and around protected areas and forests is another visible potential issue for the Mainland Leopard Cat in some areas (Kim et al. 2019, Chen et al. 2016, Baskaran and Bhoominathan 2010, Izawa et al. 2009), though it is presumably not a prominent overall threat at the moment.
population: Information on the Mainland Leopard Cat’s population status is limited despite the widespread use of camera-traps across the species’ geographic range. Its population has not been estimated in most parts of its range and there is little information on the abundance of this species except for some very small and isolated areas or specific protected areas where its estimates are often the result of bycatch data. This reflects the species’ low interest to researchers.Despite the general paucity of information on the Mainland Leopard Cat population size and trends, the species is generally considered to be abundant and stable based on the following observations: (1) the Mainland Leopard Cat appears to be widely distributed throughout its historical geographic range and (2) it appears to tolerate human modified environments to a better degree than other sympatric cat species. However, this does not mean the species is invulnerable to habitat loss and degradation, as previous studies suggest the species is at least somewhat dependent on nearby forest cover and avoids large artificial open areas (e.g. non-woody agriculture) if vegetation cover is insufficient (e.g. Chen et al. 2016). Furthermore, any potentially detrimental effects of habitat loss and degradation will be exacerbated by illegal hunting, likely causing population declines in some regions. This is evident in parts of Southeast Asia where some Mainland Leopard Cat populations appear to have been negatively influenced due to ongoing wire-snaring crises (e.g. Coudrat et al. 2014a,b; Willcox et al. 2014).Published spatial capture-recapture derived density estimates for this species vary substantially (2.9-21.42 individuals / 100 km2) and are currently available from only a few locations, making generalizations about broader population abundance difficult at this time. These include six locations in India: Pakke Tiger Reserve: 2.9/100 km2 (Selvan et al.2014), Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple Tiger Reserve: 4.48/100 km2 (Srivathsa et al.2015), Bhadra Tiger Reserve: 10.45 / 100 km2 (Srivathsa et al.2015) and Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve: 17.52/100 km2 (Bashir et al.2013), one from Nepal: Banke National Park: 4.85/100 km2 (Dhakal 2018) and one location in Thailand: Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve: 17.7/100 km2 (Petersen et al.2019b). The highest density for the species (89.4±17.2 (SE) individuals/100 km2) has been recorded from Tekong Island, Singapore (an estimate of 21 adults; Chua et al. 2016).Mainland Leopard Cat population densities presumably vary by habitat type and level of human disturbance as those factors influence resource availability, foraging success, and the potential for inter-specific competition. Petersen et al.(2019b) found that Leopard Cat density varied by habitat type within a degraded forest fragment in north-eastern Thailand (Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve), being highest in semi-evergreen forest (21.42/100 km2), followed by mixed-acacia/eucalyptus plantation forest (7.9/100 km2). Detections were too few to estimate Leopard Cat density in the site’s third major forest type, dry dipterocarp forest. Spatial capture-recapture derived estimates of rodent biomass were highest in the semi-evergreen forest during the study period, followed by dry dipterocarp, and plantation forests (Petersen et al. 2019b). The potential for inter-specific competition between Leopard Cats and other sympatric small terrestrial carnivores was found to be greatest in the dry dipterocarp forest (Petersen et al. 2019a). Similarly, Srivathsa et al. (2015), using bycatch data from four camera-trap surveys targeting the Tiger (Panthera tigris) in the Western Ghats (India), found high Mainland Leopard Cat densities to be clustered around secondary, disturbed, or partly modified forests and human-use areas, and attributed the high leopard cat densities to presumably high rodent abundances in those same areas. Leopard Cat density estimates from core areas of larger, closer to intact forest landscapes, however, are lacking. Past studies from such areas have reported lower Mainland Leopard Cat photo-encounter rates than for some other sympatric felids (e.g. Petersen et al. 2020; with similar findings reported for the Sunda Leopard Cat (Prionailurus javanensis): McCarthy et al. 2015), suggesting the high Mainland Leopard Cat densities reported from smaller forest fragments and other disturbed locations should not be extrapolated to these less disturbed areas.Country-specific reliable population estimates for the species are not available though several educated guesses have been made across its range. Not more than 1,600 individuals are believed to inhabit the whole range on the territory of Russia (Yudin 2015) while only fewer than 2,500 and 100-150 individuals are believed to exist in Nepal and Pakistan respectively (Jnawali et al. 2011). A total of around 50 individuals were estimated from Singapore. For the islands Iriomote and Tsushima in Japan and for Taiwan, the population sizes of the Mainland Leopard Cat are supposed to be very small (Ross et al. 2015). Khan (2015) and Khan (2018) both labelled the species as uncommon in Bangladesh. Population size or trends are not known for any other country. In China, the population size of the MLC is about 230,000, and the population trend is stable (Jiang et al. 2021).
range: Mainland Leopard Cat is one of the most widely distributed cat species in the world with its distribution ranging from the Russian Far East in the north to Singapore in the south.Afghanistan: Afghanistan is the westernmost limit of the Mainland Leopard Cat’s global distribution range. The cat has been confirmed from Kunar, Nangarhar and Nuristan provinces (Habibi 2003, Stevens et al. 2011). One positive DNA sample also indicates its presence in Takhar province in north-east Afghanistan (Ostrowski et al. 2008).Bangladesh: The Mainland Leopard Cat is present in all major forest ecosystems of Bangladesh: Eastern mixed-evergreen forests of Sylhet and Chattogram Hill Tracts; central, north and north-western dipterocarp-dominated deciduous forests and in the Sundarbans mangrove forests in south-western corner of the country. It is a matter of discussion whether the species has the widest distribution (second to Jungle Cat Felis chaus) in the country as stated by Ahmed (2015). Based on Ahmed et al. useTrade: Mainland Leopard Cat’s involvement in illegal wildlife trade is not properly known from most parts of its range. However there have been many documented cases of this species in trade or hunted for meat in parts of north-east India, South-east Asia and China. The species is, for example, hunted as meat by indigenous tribes in Chattogram Hill Tracts (S. C. Rahman and S. Chakma pers. comm. 2020). According to Karlstetter (2008, pers. comm. with C. Miller), the Leopard Cat is the second most abundant of all cat species listed for Afghanistan at Kabul’s fur Market, and the same author reported pelts of Leopard Cat in Nuristan Province, although it was not specified whether they had been hunted specifically for fur trade or as retaliatory killing. A Kabul household consumption survey also confirmed that Leopard Cats continue to be hunted and their pelts traded (Jonson and Wingard 2010). Cross-border trade across Afghanistan and Pakistan has also been documented (Bader et al. 2013, Ostrowski et al. 2009). Even though hundreds of thousands were trapped for the fur trade in the 1980s, Leopard Cat still seems to be fairly common in the first decade of the 21st century. However, in China there was a decline in harvest of legal trapping which was an indication for over-hunting (Yu 2010). For many decades, some border town markets in Myanmar like Tachileik have sold various body parts, which are mostly pelts (Nijman et al. 2015). In addition, Leopard Cats were the second most common species found in wildlife trade markets of Tachileik and Mong La in Myanmar-Thailand border based on the total number of individual skins encountered (458 skins) while they were the most abundant considering number of individuals per survey (median 26 individuals/survey; Nijmann and Shepherd 2015). Body parts have also been seized in Nepal though the frequency of seizure is too little to indicate any serious threats to the Mainland Leopard Cat population in the country (Dangol 2015). Their fur and meat are especially popular in China and Japan, which played a major role in the decrease of the population in China in earlier decades. They are also popular in the pet trade industry, as they are often bred with domestic cats to create Bengal cats (Chan 2010). Illegal trade in this species using the internet is also known from Vietnam (Nguyen and Willemsen 2016).
conservationActions: Conservation measures tailored to the Mainland Leopard Cat are scarce, except the protected areas which provide safe refuge to the species, often under the umbrella of other keystone species. Generally, its population trend and status is not well known. In Afghanistan and Pakistan, the Leopard Cat is data deficient, hence the first concrete steps in these countries would be the systematic assessment of the species’ current range, abundance and threats. Its status in other countries of its geographic range is relatively more common though a comprehensive assessment in China regarding the illegal trade of the species would be a good step. In China, the species has been listed as Category II of National Key Protected Wild Animals (2021). The populations of the species in nature reserves are under protection, and it has been listed as Vulnerable in the China's Red List of Biodiversity (Jiang et al. 2021). Systematic monitoring of potential threats to the species is really the primary need, in case any of them should change into serious threats.Generally, the species is widely reported and presumably abundant in Nepal, India, Malaysia, Myanmar and Thailand. Thus, dedicated conservation measures targeting this species are rare in these countries. One of the important conservation initiatives for the Mainland Leopard Cat includes enlisting the species in the schedule I of National Park and Wildlife Conservation Act 1973 in Nepal. The species is also protected in Bangladesh, included in schedule I of the Wildlife (Conservation and Protection) Act 2012. Myanmar too has provided complete protection to the species according to the newly updated Conservation of Biodiversity and Protected Area Law (2018). In Japan the species has been declared a National Nature Monument in 1971 and an endangered species in 1994 and a conservation project plan has been initiated since 1995. The species is listed in the schedule I of the Forest and Nature Conservation Act of Bhutan 1995. Hence, hunting or trade of any sort is completely prohibited in the country.Since the species is not highly sought after by researchers it will be a great initiative if researchers from across its global range collaborate to produce a range-wide estimation of its habitat suitability including the already existing presence data of the species.

rationale: Originally, the Grey Wolf was the world's most widely distributed mammal, but its present distribution is more restricted. Their original Holarctic range (including the Indian subcontinent) has been reduced by about one-third by deliberate persecution due to depredation on livestock, fear of attacks on humans, and competition with humans for huntable species (which are also prey species of wolves, e.g. ungulates), all of which remain important drivers for wolf management in many regions of North America and some European countries. The Grey Wolf had been exterminated in much of Western Europe, in Mexico, and much of the USA by the mid of the 20th century. After being extinct in most of Western Europe for decades, wolves began returning in the late 20th century, mainly from populations that survived in Italy, Spain, and Eastern Europe, and by the 2020s the Grey Wolf had naturally recolonised much of continental Europe, marking a significant large carnivore recovery in modern Europe. In North America, since about 1970, legal protection, land-use changes, rural human population shifts to cities, and increasing prey populations have halted wolf population declines and fostered natural recolonisation in parts of its range and reintroduction in three areas of USA. Despite controversy, wolf reintroductions in the western USA have been successful with increased distribution following releases, but conflict with livestock and big game hunting continues to be an issue. In Asia, wolves continue to persist in diverse ecosystems from deserts to high altitudes at varying densities, with regionally harsh human persecution and insufficient research and conservation. Wolves are thought to be nearly extirpated in Southern and Eastern regions of China (Wang et al. 2016) and exist in small populations in the Indian subcontinent (Hennelly et al. 2025) and the Arabian Peninsula (Bonsen et al. 2024).Wolves thrive in wilderness and remote areas but they can also cope with anthropogenically dominated landscapes as found in Europe, Southern Asia, and elsewhere. Continued threats include competition with humans for livestock and game species, degradation and fragmentation of habitat, with resulting areas becoming unsuitable for long-term viability, politicisation of wolves, and exaggerated concern by the public regarding the threat and danger of wolves.Although the Grey Wolf still faces many threats, its relatively widespread range and stable population trend mean that the species, at global level, does not meet the criteria for the threatened categories. The global population is estimated to be in the order of 145,000–200,000 individuals, but note there is a high uncertainty in this estimate (North America ~80,000; Eurasia ~ 65,000; Poyarkov et al. 2022). Therefore, the Grey Wolf is globally assessed as Least Concern. However, at regional level, several wolf subspecies are threatened, such as the Arabian Wolf (C. l. arabs), the Mexican Wolf (C. l. baileyi), Himalayan Wolf (C. l. chanco), and the Indian Wolf (C. l. pallipes), but also to consider the European wolf population distributed over a discontinuous range.There are separate Red List assessments available for the European wolf populations and only the Scandinavian population is assessed as Vulnerable, all other European populations being not threatened (Boitani 2025). There are separate Red List assessments available also for the Indian and Himalayan Wolf, both are threatened and listed as Vulnerable based on low population size and decreasing population trends (Hennelly et al. 2025, Werhahn et al. 2024). The Mexican Wolf is listed as an Endangered Species under the U.S. Endangered Species Act.
habitat: Ranges in all northern habitats where there is suitable food (Mech 1970), densities being highest where prey biomass is high (Fuller 1989) and human tolerance allows. Food is extremely variable, but the majority comprises ungulates (e.g. Moose, Caribou, Red deer, Roe deer, Elk, Wild boar, Blue sheep, Tibetan and Nubian gazelles, Wild ass, Ibex). But wolves will also regularly eat smaller prey items (e.g. marmots, hares, rodents, birds), livestock, carrion, and garbage.
threats: The historical range of the Grey Wolf has been largely reduced primarily in developed areas of Europe, Asia, Mexico, and the USA by poisoning and deliberate persecution due to depredation on livestock. Since about 1970, legal protection, land-use changes, and rural human population shifts to cities have halted wolf population declines and fostered natural recolonization in parts of Western Europe and the USA, and reintroduction in the western USA and Mexico. Continued threats include competition with humans for livestock and large ungulate species, politicisation of wolves, poisoning and persecution of wolves due to livestock depredation, and perceived threats and concerns by the public about the threat and danger of wolves. Further, the fragmentation of habitat, with resulting areas becoming too small for wolf populations for long-term viability, potential of wolf-dog hybridization, disease transmission through feral dogs, and diminished wild prey populations are threats in parts of the range with high human density.
population: Because of the diversity in climate, topography, vegetation, human settlement and development of wolf range, wolf populations in various parts of the original range vary from extinct to relatively pristine. Wolf densities vary from about one/12 km² to one/120 km².Mech and Boitani (2004) provide details, for each range country, population status, approximate numbers, the percentage of former range occupied, main prey (where known), legal status, and cause of decline. For Europe, the wolf population presents a large meta-population with only few distinct and in part not connected subpopulations; the status and trends for each population is provided by the Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe (http://www.lcie.org/). The status and trends for wolf populations in the USA are provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and game agencies in several US states, including Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Oregon, Washington, California, Arizona, and New Mexico. In general, population increases in North America and Europe are likely to be off-set by localized declines in other parts of the range.
range: Originally, the Grey Wolf was the world's most widely distributed mammal, living throughout the northern hemisphere north of 15°N latitude in North America and 12°N in India. Wolves are recolonising Western Europe (Boitani 1995, Kaczensky et al. 2024), after near complete extinction in many parts due to human persecution (however wolves persisted on the Iberian and Italian Peninsula and in the Balkans), they have been reintroduced in Mexico, and have been reintroduced and are also naturally recolonising parts the western USA (Boyd et al. 2023). In Japan, wolves became extinct in the 20th century.Wolves occur primarily in wilderness and remote areas, especially in Canada, Alaska and northern USA, Europe, and Northern Asia from about 75°N to 12°N (Mech and Boitani 2004), but they are found also in human-dominated landscapes where there is sufficient prey base and human tolerance, i.e. human-caused mortality is low. Distribution is highly dynamic as wolf populations are currently increasing in range and numbers in north-central and western USA and much of Europe. Dispersing individuals can be found in almost any European country except the United Kingdom and Ireland.
useTrade: There is utilization of the species' fur in Canada, Alaska, Montana, Idaho, Minnesota and the former Soviet Union and Mongolia. Illegal hunting for fur and body parts does occur in some range states. Wolf body parts are illegally traded in various parts of Asia for medicinal and cultural purposes.
conservationActions: LegislationThe Grey Wolf Canis lupus is included in CITES Appendix II, except populations from Bhutan, India, Nepal and Pakistan, which are listed on Appendix I. In Europe, the species is protected under the Bern Convention (Appendix III) and Habitats Directive (Annex II and V), and there is legal protection in many European countries; however, there are national differences, and enforcement is variable and often non-existent. Endangered status in the USA varies by region and Distinct Population Segment (DPS) but is only delisted in the northern Rocky Mountains population segment, being a listed species everywhere else in the Continental USA (excludes Alaska). Presence in protected areasThe Grey Wolf occurs in many protected areas across its range. Occurrence in captivityThe species lives and breeds well in captivity and is common in many zoological gardens.Gaps in knowledgeMore research focusing on the ecological role of wolves, including ecosystem services and functioning, such as the wolves’ role in regulating forest generation, health of prey populations, biodiversity, and ecosystem resilience is needed. An important question about wolves involves the nature of their interaction with prey populations, such as when and how wolves regulate their prey population (Mech and Boitani 2003). Clarifying the role that wolves play in precipitating ecosystem effects, particularly trophic cascades in wilderness places (Mech and Boitani 2003, Ripple and Betscha 2004, Peterson et al. 2014) as well as in anthropogenically dominated landscapes like Europe and Southern Asia is of importance (Kuijper et al. 2024).More research to facilitate wolf human coexistence is of pressing importance, including the understanding of human attitudes towards wolves in relation to real and perceived damage caused by wolves, and advancing the effectiveness of non-lethal, ethical management tools. Research is needed into the social structure of the Grey Wolf and its behaviour and how both social structure and behaviour are affected by management actions, landscape fragmentation, and disturbance (Cassidy et al. 2023, Tallian et al. 2023). Scent-marking behaviour, pseudo pregnancy, and diseases are also of interest (Mech 1995).Further, questions remain around wolf genetics to understand their evolutionary and biogeographic history, relevant to conserve the species today, as well as for ensuring genetic viability of fragmented wolf populations. Of increasing interest is the issue of hybridisation with domestic dogs (and indeed other Canis spp.) in several parts of the range in Eurasia. Further research is needed to understand the factors that influence when hybridisation occurs, its consequence on wolf population dynamics, behaviour, and the long-term genetic integrity of wolf populations.

rationale: This species is relatively widespread within its range, though the population trends are not known. There are no significant threats to this species at present, but research is needed to quantify the impact of summer fires and agricultural intensification. On the smaller islands it may be more vulnerable to anthropogenic impacts. Overall, the species is assessed as Least Concern but should be reassessed if any decline is suspected.
habitat: The Sicilian Shrew is widespread in all island environments; at higher altitudes it is also active in winter. It is more frequent in mesophilic broadleaved woods than in thermophilic ones. Presence data suggest a preference for grasslands, arable land and open bushes and for gardens in urban and suburban areas. Regardless of the altitude and exposure, the most frequented biotopes have a thick and intricate layer of herbaceous and shrubby vegetation (Sarà 2008). The Sicilian Shrew preys upon arachnids, insects, annelids and molluscs, with a preference for spiders, crickets, larvae of ants and termites, actively sought both day and night. It also feeds on dead arthropods, small rodents and reptiles (Sarà 2008). Females give birth to three to nine young per litter, and individuals can reach an age of 12-18 months (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018).
threats: This shrew can suffer local persecutions aimed at rodent control (e.g. via the consumption of poison in agricultural and farmland areas), or predation by domestic cats in the most populated areas. Intensive agricultural practices and the use of biocides can be a limiting factor in some areas. The summer fires that destroy hundreds of hectares of habitat each year are likely a primary threat to this species, which recolonises habitats only 30-36 months after the fire (Sarà 2008).
population: It is widespread on Sicily (Maddalena et al. 1990). However, trapping results indicate that it occurs at much lower densities than other Crocidura species that inhabit Mediterranean islands (Vogel 1999). Its population trend is unknown. It may have gone extinct on Malta, but even if so, the date of that extinction is unknown. The exceptional melanic population of Ustica (8 km2) is perhaps under heightened risk of extinction; surveys undertaken in 2012 provided fewer records than the previous surveys undertaken in 1994-96 (Sarà and Vitturi 1996, M. Sarà pers. comm. 2022).
range: The Sicilian Shrew (Crocidura sicula) is endemic to Sicily, its surrounding islands and Malta: it is currently found on Sicily, Ustica, and the Egadi islands (Favignana, Levanzo, Marettimo). In the Maltese archipelago, it is present on Gozo, and possibly on Comino (two specimens were found in owl pellets, and one individual was recorded in a bucket on the north coast), but further investigation of its occupancy is required (Aloise et al. 2011, Sciberras et al. 2012). It may be extinct on the island of Malta where it is known only from subfossil remains (Vogel 1999). It is widespread in all Sicilian environments from sea level up to about 1,600 m (Sarà 2008).
useTrade: The species is not subject to trade or use.
conservationActions: It is protected under Appendix III of the Bern Convention. It is a species of interest in Italy, and therefore listed in Appendix IV of the EU Council Directive 92/43 / EEC ‘Habitat’. No specific conservation actions are recommended at this time, but research is needed to quantify abundance and population trends, and to measure potential impacts of agriculture and tourism (M. Sarà pers. comm. 2022). This is one of only three ancient endemic mammal species occurring on the Mediterranean islands (Gippoliti and Amori 2006), and for this reason, it is a valuable species to conserve.

rationale: This species is endemic to Crete where it is restricted to the central areas of the island. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 3,466 km², and it has been recorded from only three mountain tops (Lefka Ori, Mt. Psiloritis and Mt. Dikti), and the area of occupancy (AOO) is 52 km2. Since it is estimated that this species occurs at fewer than five locations, the population is fragmented, and it is suspected that population decline and range contractions are occurring as a result of out-competition by a non-native shrew, this species is assessed as Endangered under criteria B (B1ab(i,iii,v)+2ab(i,iii,v)).
habitat: It has been collected in open mountainous areas that are dry in summer and snow-covered in winter (Vogel 1999), mostly in humid settings with barberry shrubs (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018). It is possible it also occurs at lower altitudes, but if so, its habitat preferences there are unknown. The preferred habitat at high altitudes plateaus of various sizes, rather than cliffs and peaks (P. Lymberakis pers. comm. 2018).
threats: The introduction of Gueldenstädt's Shrew , and possibly the Pygmy White-toothed Shrew, during the Holocene may have forced it into a restricted range at comparatively higher altitudes as it was out-competed for habitat (Pieper 1990, Nowak 1999, van der Geer et al. 2013). Gueldenstädt's Shrew is abundant in coastal areas, but has also been found in the mountains at the same sites as Cretan Shrew (Vogel 1999). Climate change may affect the altitudinal distribution of the Cretan Shrew as habitats at lower elevations become less suitable (G. Mitsainas pers. comm. 2018).
population: This is a rare and little-known species which is only recorded from a small number of localities. Analysis of owl pellets has suggested that the Cretan Shrew is more than ten times rarer than its congener the Lesser Shrew (C. suaveolens) (Vogel 1999). The population trend has not been quantified but it is suspected to be decreasing. Based on available data, the population is considered to be fragmented, as there is likely to be no or very low genetic flow among the isolated populations on the three mountains (P. Lymberakis pers. comm. 2018).
range: The Cretan Shrew (Crocidura zimmermanni) is endemic to Crete (Greece) with the first evidence of its occurrence on the island dating from the Middle Pleistocene (Reumer 1986). It has been trapped in the central mountains (Lefka Ori, Mt. Psiloritis and Mt. Dikti) at altitudes of 1,150 to 1,400 m. However, owl pellets collected at 140 to 830 m contained remains of this species, indicating that it may also occur at lower altitudes (Vogel 1999). The extent of occurrence (EOO) is ca 3,400 km2 and the area of occupancy (AOO) is 52 km2.
useTrade: There is no record of this species being used or subject to trade.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention. It is also listed as endangered in the Red Data Book of Threatened Animals of Greece (Legakis and Maragou 2009). Research is required to determine its distribution and population trend, and to investigate potential threats (especially competition with Gueldenstädt's Shrew and potential effects of climate change) to identify appropriate conservation measures. A genetic study to understand genetic flow among populations on the three mountains is needed.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)The Mediterranean Mole (Talpa caeca) is endemic to Europe. The species has a wide range, a relatively large extent of occurrence of 567,446 km2, and is thought to be common in at least some areas. There is no evidence to suggest a decline reaching the thresholds of Red List criteria and it is therefore listed as Least Concern. However, given the lack of knowledge on this species’ general ecology and population status, additional research is needed.
habitat: It occurs in deciduous woodland, meadows and pastures in hilly or mountainous areas. It requires deep soil that is not too dry, which explains its sporadic distribution in karstic areas. Its diet is probably similar to that of the European Mole (Talpa europea) and Roman Mole (T. romana), which feed on soil-dwelling invertebrates, especially earthworms. It tends to be competitively displaced into marginal habitats by the larger European Mole in areas such as the Balkans (Kryštufek 1999). In Italy, it is similarly displaced by the Roman Mole (central-southern regions) and European Mole (northern regions) where the two species occur in sympatry (Loy et al. 2019). It is frequently found in areas with scarce soils with limited availability of feeding resources.
threats: Like other fossorial species, the Mediterranean Mole is potentially threatened by agriculture-associated habitat loss and/or fragmentation (Bertolino et al. 2015) and the use of chemicals such as pesticides. Threats to this species are, overall, poorly-known.
population: Its population status is unknown across the whole range, but it has a scattered distribution in the mountainous areas of Italy. It is possible that it is locally common in some areas. Its distribution is sporadic in karst limestone areas (Kryštufek 1999).
range: The Mediterranean Mole (Talpa caeca) is endemic to Europe, with a fragmented range in the western Alps (Switzerland, northwestern Italy, and southeastern France), the Apennines of Italy, and the Balkan Peninsula. It is known to occur as well in northern, central and southern regions of Italy (Loy et al. 2017), reaching at least as far north as the Simplon Pass and Bellinzone regions in Switzerland (Marchesi et al. 2000, Dubey et al. 2007) and, to the south, up to the Sila Mountains in the Calabria region (Aloise and Cagnin 2003). In the Balkan Peninsula, it is present from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Albania (particularly in the Albanian Alps, but records have also been collected towards southern Albania; Bego et al. 2008, Bego et al. 2018), and in a fragmented range of mainland Greece. The species occurs in mountain, submountain, and only occasionally, hilly areas, up to 2,500 m asl. The species has a large extent of occurrence of 567,446 km2; the area of occupancy has not been estimated, but based on GBIF data exceeds 500 km2.
useTrade: This species is not used or subject to trade.
conservationActions: It is not protected under international legislation, though occurs in protected areas across its range. On Italy’s National Red List, the Mediterranean Mole is listed as Data Deficient (Bertolino et al. 2015). Research is needed to investigate population variables, ecology, potential threats and actions.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)EU 27 regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)The species has a fairly wide but very fragmented distribution. In the core of its range the population appears to be stable, but declines are occurring in some isolated populations at the edges of the range. Overall, there is a slow population decline, but this is not at a rate high enough to trigger a threatened category. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is above the threshold for criterion B (>20,000 km²). There is some uncertainty surrounding the area of occupancy (AOO) and it is possible that it may meet the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion B (< 2,000 km²), and there is ongoing habitat loss and degradation. As such, this species is assessed as Near Threatened as it is close to qualifying as threatened under criterion B2 both globally and for the EU27 region.
habitat: This species tends to be found in open habitats (meadows, rocky areas with sparse vegetation, and banks of mountain streams) in mountainous areas, where it lives in cracks and crevices under rocks and in stone walls. At lower altitudes, it prefers cool, damp, shaded areas, such as densely-vegetated ravines and holes under mossy rocks, tree-roots and logs in forests (Spitzenberger 1990, 1999). In some parts of its range its habitat preferences differ: for example, in the Rhön Mountains (Hesse, Germany) it is restricted to forest streams with dense stands of Petasites, while in the Bavarian Alps, it persists in nitrogen-poor spruce stands bordering meadows (H. Meinig pers. comm. 2017). It mainly feeds on arthropods and molluscs (Spitzenberger 1990), with dietary analysis suggesting that prey items from the order Insecta and family Lumbricidae are most common (Klenovšek et al. 2013). Breeding occurs between May and October, with litters consisting of four to seven young (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018). The species coexists well with other Sorex species such as the Crowned Shrew (S. coronatus) in the Rhön Mountains, with the Eurasian Shrew (S. araneus) in the Bavarian Alps and Kleinwalsertal (H. Meinig pers. comm. 2017), and the Valais Shrew (S. antinorii) and Eurasian Pygmy Shrew (S. minutus) in the Italian Alps (S. Bertolino pers. comm. 2022).
threats: As a result of its relict distribution on mountain 'islands', isolated populations may be vulnerable to local extinction. Loss of alpine water courses due to water abstraction and hydroelectric power is a threat, just as loss of habitat due to intensification of winter tourism in the Alps. Human land use is a direct threat, both through habitat destruction and pollution (such as over-fertilisation of land, and illegal logging). Climate change may be a future indirect threat.
population: This species is difficult to detect unless using live-trapping methods (S. Bertolino pers. comm. 2017). In the Alps, the range appears large, but populations are fragmented and the species is often found in very low numbers (S. Bertolino pers. comm. 2017). Small, isolated populations at the edge of the species' range may be declining, and there have been subpopulation extinctions, for example, in the Pyrenees. Some subpopulations are fragmented due to areas of inaccessible habitat, for example in Hesse, Germany (H. Meinig pers. comm. 2017). The Alpine Shrew is considered to be in decline in Germany in general (Meinig et al. 2020). In the Harz, the northernmost population in Europe, it appears to have disappeared; the last record was in 1954 despite intensive studies to find the species there. There is little genetic differentiation between different populations and it is probable that range fragmentation was post-glacial (Starcova et al. 2016).
range: The Alpine Shrew (Sorex alpinus) is endemic to Europe, where it has an extremely fragmented range in the Alps, the Balkans, the Carpathians, the Tatra Mountains in Slovakia and a number of isolated mountains in Germany, Czech Republic and Poland (Spitzenberger 1999, Meinig 2004). It has been recorded twice in Ukraine in the previous decade (A. Mishta pers. comm. 2023). Records have confirmed its presence in the southern Carpathians in Romania (Nae 2010) and the Sudetes bordering Poland and Czech Republic (Bartmańska and Moska 2007, Anděra 2010). It previously occurred in the Pyrenees, where it is thought to have gone extinct in the early 20th century, and in the Harz (Spitzenberger 1999). Its vertical range is from 200 to 2,500 m (Spitzenberger 1999). The area of occupancy is difficult to calculate for this species, but it is estimated to be between 2,000-3,000 km².
useTrade: The species is not utilised or subject to trade.
conservationActions: The species is listed in Appendix III of the Bern Convention. A major part of the Alpine Shrew's range in the Carpathians is covered by the Carpathians Reserve (about 45,000 ha) and National Park (about 70,000 ha). There is a need for monitoring, particularly of isolated subpopulations. This species could benefit from habitat protection.

rationale: The Roman Mole (Talpa romana) is endemic to Europe, where it is widespread in central and southern Italy. Although intensive arable farming may be a problem in some areas, the population trend is not known to be declining to the extent that it would approach the thresholds for the criteria of the IUCN Red List (i.e. declining more than 30% in ten years or three generations). Therefore, it is evaluated as Least Concern.
habitat: The Roman Mole is a fossorial insectivore that feeds predominantly on earthworms and insect larvae. It is found in a variety of habitats including arable fields, olive groves, pastures, woods and urban grasslands (Niethammer 1990, Loy 1999, Beolchini and Loy 2004). It is solitary and territorial. The average home range of males is 2-3 km2 outside of the reproductive season, and up to 7 km2 during the reproductive season. Average home rage of females is 1-2 km2 (Loy et al 1994, Beolchini et al. 1996). It occurs in parapatry with the European Mole (T. europaea) and sympatry with the Mediterranean Mole (T. caeca) (Loy et al. 2017). Individuals of this species can be relatively large compared to other mole species, with recorded body weights of wild adults reaching 125g (Loy et al. 1994).
threats: Local population declines are suspected in areas where there is intensive arable farming (Loy 1999). The mole is widely persecuted as a pest, but this is not thought to be a serious threat to the species. The Italian National Red List indicates that the Roman Mole is threatened by the use of biocides and chemical products in agriculture (Bertolino et al. 2015), which is a common threat for bioturbator mammals (Beca et al. 2022). Climate change is likely impacting the species by extended and increased severity of summer drought, causing extended starvation (Loy et al. 2017).
population: The Roman Mole is widespread throughout its range (Loy 1999). This species may be more abundant on the east coast, but is overall less common nowadays than it was previously (A. Loy pers. comm. 2022). Data on abundance and trends are lacking.
range: The Roman Mole (Talpa romana) is endemic to Italy. Nowadays it is confined to the central and southern areas of the mainland, having last been recorded in Sicily in 1885 (Loy 1999). Reports of an isolated subpopulation in the Var region of southern France (Saint Girons 1973, Niethammer 1990) have not been confirmed (Niethammer 1990, Loy 1999, Wilson and Reeder 2005). It is found from sea level to approximately 2,000 m (Loy 1999).
useTrade: The species was hunted for fur. The practice is still ongoing, and the fur is used for the inner layer of gloves and raincoats.
conservationActions: It is not protected under national or international law, but occurs in protected areas within its range. No specific conservation measures are known. It is listed as Low Concern (LC) in the Italian Red List (Rondinini et al. 2013) but is thought to qualify as Near Threatened (NT) in the region of Umbria where it is missing from some mountain plane and subalpine habitats (Gaggi and Paci 2014). Further research into the population trends and threats faced by this species could be beneficial.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)This species is widespread and abundant with no serious threats affecting the global population at present. Hence, it is listed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 region.
habitat: It inhabits a variety of habitats with good soil moisture and dense vegetation at ground level, including woods, hedges, abandoned or unmown meadows, and marshes (Palomo et al. 2007) though appears to be most abundant in marginal habitats such as field margins and road verges (de Redon et al. 2015). It is scarce in intensively cultivated areas. It competes with the Eurasian Shrew (Sorex araneus), and the microhabitats used are different for each species where their ranges overlap (Hausser 1990, 1999). Its diet comprises terrestrial invertebrates, and occasionally vertebrates and plant matter. Breeding occurs from February to November, with typically fewer than four young produced per litter on average, which is unusually low for shrew species (Palomo et al. 2007).
threats: Threats include general habitat degradation and the indirect effects of pesticides and pollutants (accumulation of toxins through the species' diet) (Stone 1995, Palomo et al. 2007). Climate change in the future may threaten the range of this species (Morrison et al. 2018).
population: It is generally widespread and abundant in most areas of its range except the northern periphery (Mittermeier and Wilson 2018). In Paris, the Crowned Shrew was the most abundant species recorded in small mammal surveys (178 individuals recorded from 813 traps) (de Redon et al. 2015). However, at the edge of its range in Switzerland, intensive agriculture and pesticide use have caused the species to decline, such that now only relict populations remain in some areas (Palomo et al. 2007).
range: The Crowned Shrew (Sorex coronatus) is endemic to Europe, where it occurs from northern Spain, through France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxemburg, northern Switzerland, Germany, and the westernmost corner of Austria. It is also found on the island of Jersey (United Kingdom) (Hausser 1999). Its vertical range is from 0 to 2,200 m in Spain (Palomo et al. 2007).
useTrade: This species is not used nor subject to trade.
conservationActions: It is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention, and occurs in protected areas within its range. At the moment, no specific conservation measures are needed. Further research into the population trends of this species is recommended.

rationale: The Iberian Shrew, endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, occurs across a relatively wide area where it is found in a variety of habitats. The population size of this species has not been quantified, but it is not believed to be facing any significant threats at present and is not thought of as rare. Therefore, this species is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: It is found in Atlantic climates, where it inhabits a variety of woodland and scrub habitats, including native beech, oak, and pine forests, plantations of introduced Eucalyptus and Pinus pinaster, and damp areas with dense shrubby vegetation. It is also found in cultivated fields, stream- and river banks, scree slopes, and rocky areas near to pastures. It prefers humid locations and is restricted to areas where the annual rainfall exceeds 600 mm (García-Perea et al. 1997, Hausser 1999, Cabral et al. 2005, Palomo et al. 2007). In general terms, the areas occupied by the species are characterized by a mean annual temperature between 3 and 15 º C, with extremely cold winters (Araújo et al. 2011). Its diet consists mainly of invertebrates, including annelids, arachnids and molluscs (Palomo et al. 2007). In Portugal, breeding occurs in spring and summer, and gestation lasts 18-21 days (Mittermeir and Wilson 2018).
threats: It is not considered to be threatened in Spain or Portugal, though data are lacking (Palomo et al. 2007, Bencatel et al. 2019). It may be at risk of habitat destruction and pesticide use, as well as reductions in the abundance of invertebrate prey (Cabral et al. 2005).
population: The population size and trends for this species are not known. However, the species is quite common in the diet of nocturnal raptor species (Cabral et al. 2005) and mesocarnivores like foxes, wildcats, genets, and Beech Martens (Carvalho and Gomes 2004). In Portugal, it is thought to occur in almost all shrubby habitats (Palomo et al. 2007). According to Madureira and Ramalhinho (1984), most individuals do not survive their second year.
range: The Iberian Shrew (Sorex granarius) is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, where it is found along a strip of the northwest coast, central Portugal and central Spain (García-Perea et al. 1997, Bencatel et al. 2019). It occurs from the coast up to 2,000 m (Palomo et al. 2007).
useTrade: This species is not subject to trade and/or any use.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention. It occurs in protected areas within its range. Research is needed to evaluate its population status and trends (Cabral et al. 2005).

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)The Balkan Mole (Talpa stankovici) is endemic to the Balkans. The population has not been quantified, yet this species is considered relatively widespread, with an extent of occurrence of 145,333 km2, and likely locally abundant. It is not believed to be facing any significant threats at present. Therefore, this species is listed as Least Concern for both Europe and for the EU27 Member States.
habitat: The Balkan Mole is a fossorial insectivore which, like other species of Talpa, is likely to predominantly feed on earthworms. It occurs in broad sympatry with the Mediterranean Mole (T. caeca), but they are rarely encountered in the same locations (Bego et al. 2018). Co-occurrence with the European Mole (T. europaea) is unusual (N. Loukatou pers. comm. 2023). It is found in a variety of open habitats including sandy dunes, pastures, arable land, farmland, alpine meadows, road banks, and woodlands (Kryštufek 1999).
threats: No major threats are known. As with other mole species, this species could be at risk of agriculture-associated habitat loss and/or fragmentation (Bertolino et al. 2015) and the use of chemicals such as pesticides.
population: Its population status is not known, but it is reasonably widespread and may be locally abundant (Kryštufek 1999, Bego et al. 2018).
range: The Balkan Mole (Talpa stankovici) is endemic to the Balkans, where it is found in southern Montenegro, Albania, western North Macedonia, Greece (including the islands of Corfu and Kefalonia; Masetti 2012). In mainland Greece, at the southernmost part of its range, it occurs in the mountainous region of the Peloponnese (Tryfonopoulos et al. 2010). It is considered to be generally widespread, at least in regions south of the River Drin in Albania (Bego et al. 2018), and is found from sea level to 2,300 m (Kryštufek 1999).
useTrade: This species is not subject to trade or use.
conservationActions: The species receives no protection under European legislation, though does occur in some protected areas in North Macedonia (for example, National Park Galicica) and northern Greece. Research is needed to investigate the general ecology and population status of this species.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)The species is listed as Least Concern both globally and for the EU27 region because there is no evidence to suggest any significant decline at present. However, it should be noted that alpine prairie habitat quality may be declining, affected by climate change and reduction of livestock grazing. The status of this species should therefore be closely monitored as it could qualify for Near Threatened status in the future.
habitat: The Alpine Marmot occurs in families, usually composed of a dominant breeding pair, juveniles and subordinate individuals, which may help with the pups (Glad and Mallard 2022). Colonies inhabit burrow systems located over alpine prairies (Ferrari et al. 2022). It inhabits these alpine meadows and high-altitude pastures, typically on south-facing slopes from 1,6200-3,000 m (although it is occasionally found at lower altitudes). Over winter, it hibernates in winter burrows with other members of the family (Allainé and Theuriau 2004). It has a herbivorous diet, primarily composed of green parts of grasses, sedges, and herbs (Krapp 1978), also selecting mosses, lichens, cereal crops and sometimes insects and animal matter (Wilson et al. 2016).
threats: The Alpine Marmot was previously hunted for meat, fur, and fat (which was used for cosmetics and medicines). Hunting continues today but is primarily a leisure activity (Preleuthner 1999), though sometimes occurs for management purposes. In Slovenia and Austria, hunting levels are sustainable, but in Austria the populations living below the timberline are threatened by the loss of open habitats through the abandonment of high-altitude cattle grazing (Spitzenberger 2002, B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2006). All populations of the Alpine Marmot (both subspecies) are potentially threatened by the loss of open habitat generated by climate change and the reduction in grazing of livestock. Hybridisation with introduced M. m. marmota is a potential future threat to remaining pure-bred populations of M. m. latirostris in the High Tatras.
population: The subspecies M. m. marmota is abundant in at least parts of its core range in the Alps, although some subpopulations may be under threat (e.g. in the Jura and in Germany). Population density estimates are available from very local scales, for example, 3.9 marmots per hectaure in the Gran Paradiso National Park (Pellicioli and Ferarri 2013). It is known from three areas in Romania: Retezat, Fagaras and Rodna. In Retezat and Fagaras, the populations are stable; in Rodna, the population is very small and is threatened by poaching (Popescu and Murariu 2001, Botnariuc and Tatole 2005). Subspecies M. m. latirostris has a restricted range (it occurs at higher elevations in a small region of the High Tatras) and is considered to be rare and threatened (Preleuthner 1999). A general overview of population dynamics is lacking for this species.
range: The Alpine Marmot (Marmota marmota) is endemic to Europe. Its core range extends through the Alps of France, Italy, Switzerland, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. Isolated subpopulations are found in the Pyrenees, Massif Central, Jura, Vosges (all four resulting from recent introductions), Black Forest, Apennines, High Tatras, and Romanian Carpathians. A number of these isolated subpopulations (those in the Pyrenees, Massif Central, Jura, Vosges, Black Forest, and Apennines, and eastern Alps) are the result of introductions. The marmot has inhabited the Alps and High Tatras continuously since the end of the last Ice Age, and was reintroduced to the Romanian Carpathians (three attempts in 1973, the third attempt was successful). It occurs as two subspecies: M. m. marmota in the Alps (and most introduced subpopulations) and M. m. latirostris in the High Tatras. A hybrid population exists in the Low Tatras, the result of introductions of both subspecies. Likewise, populations in the Apennines are hybrids of both subspecies. Generally, this species inhabits sites between 1,600 to 3,000 m of elevation, but has been recorded up to 3,200 m asl (Ferrari et al. 2022).
useTrade: The Alpine Marmot was previously hunted for meat and fur. Hunting still occurs today as a sport.
conservationActions: The species occurs in a number of national parks within its range. It is listed under Appendix III of the Bern Convention. Subspecies latirostris requires strict protection in Slovakia and Poland. Quantitative monitoring over multiple years it is needed to assess the situation of the species in consideration of the relevant habitat loss it is experiencing. Following this analysis, conservation actions may be suggested. This species could benefit from habitat protection, as well as further research into population and habitat trends, and potential threats.

rationale: The Iberian Mole (Talpa occidentalis) is endemic to Portugal and Spain. It is listed as Least Concern as it is considered common in most areas of its range with a relatively large extent of occurrence of 511,670 km2. However, it has disappeared from some localities where land use practices have changed, and if such habitat changes continue, it could qualify for Near Threatened in the future. Consequently, conservation efforts should be put in place, ideally focusing on habitat management and the maintenance of traditional agricultural practices where possible.
habitat: It is a burrowing species found in a variety of habitats, especially those with higher water supply; it prefers deep soil that is not excessively stony, sandy, or waterlogged (Llorente et al. 2021). It is found in meadows, pastures, forests and developed land, as well as cultivated areas that use traditional methods of irrigation, such as poplar groves (Soriguer and Palomo 2001, García-López de Hierro et al. 2013). In central and southern parts of the Iberian Peninsula, it is generally restricted to upland and humid areas (Loy 1999, Román 2007) and makes use of habitats associated with human activities, such as traditionally irrigated areas or livestock grazing lands where prolonged retention of soil moisture can allow moles to maintain larger feeding areas during dry periods (Llorente et al. 2021). It occurs in higher numbers in areas with greater soil invertebrate density (García-López de Hierro et al. 2013) and where it is cooler, which may coincide with earthworm availability (Llorente et al. 2021).
threats: It is a pest species causing damage to pastures, so it is persecuted by farmers. Loss of meadows to afforestation (Román 2007) and changes in irrigation techniques likely pose serious threats to this species. In southern Spain, the Iberian Mole is less abundant where the irrigation techniques have become modernised, removing the need for ‘dry ridges’ in the irrigation system which moles would use as nesting areas (García-López de Hierro et al. 2013). Additionally, the abandonment of pasturelands due to changes in economic activities in mountainous regions has likely affected invertebrate prey density and diversity on such land, having negative implications for the Iberian Mole (Llorente et al. 2021). Climate-mediated changes to habitat suitability could also induce declines in this species (Hernández 2016).
population: The Iberian Mole is common in suitable habitats throughout most of its range (Loy 1999). In Portugal, it is fairly widespread and could be considered to consist of either a single subpopulation or three separate subpopulations divided by major barriers to dispersal (Bencatel et al. 2017). Conversely, in southern areas of Spain, it is confined to mountainous regions where it occurs in fragmented populations with few individuals. In local areas of the Sierras Subbéticas and Penibaetic mountain systems, it is believed to have disappeared (Soriguer and Palomo 2001).
range: The Iberian Mole (Talpa occidentalis) is endemic to Portugal and Spain (Loy 1999), largely concentrated in the northwest and absent from the northeast of the Iberian Peninsula (Soriguer and Palomo 2001) and Guadalquivir valley. Known records and distribution models suggest that there are two main range areas, in the northwestern half of the Iberian Peninsula and in the Betic Mountains, likely unconnected (Román 2007, Márcia Barbosa et al. 2013). It occurs from sea level to 2,800 m (Soriguer and Palomo 2001).
useTrade: The Iberian Mole is not used or subject to trade.
conservationActions: It occurs in a number of protected areas.
