Stable isotope analysis suggested a differential migration pattern, with different populations migrating separately, and showed evidence of long-distance movement in 23% ca. of 420 bats sampled across Europe 95 (Wright et al. 2020). The maximum known age is 21 years and 9 months for a male in the Caucasus (Gazaryan 2004).
threats: The main threat to this bat is disturbance to colonies, both in winter and summer roosts. Unsuitable physical protection of cave entrances (e.g. with improperly designed grilles) may lead to abandonment or decline in numbers.In 2002, mass mortality events were reported for subpopulations in France, Spain and Portugal, there are also historical records for such mortality in Italy. Hundreds of individuals were found dead in spring. Mortality up to 60% in one year was reported in France (Roué and Némoz 2002), and 40% mortality occurred in Spain during the same period including 1,000 dead individuals out of 6,000 in one colony. A number of sites were subsequently deserted. In 2013, a mass-mortality incident occurred in a Miniopterus schreibersii colony, causing the death of ~500 individuals in northeast Hungary (Bükk Mountains). Mortality events in Spain and Hungary were both associated with the Lloviu Virus (Kemenesi et al. 2018). Another event with ca. 200 casualties of uncertain origin were reported in 2018 from Georgia (EUROBATS 2018).Mortality at wind turbines was recorded in Spain, Portugal and France, but may occur everywhere within the range (Rodrigues et al. 2015).
population: The global population of Miniopterus schreibersiii is estimated to have declined by at least 30% throughout much of its range over the past three generation lengths (16.5 years: generation length = 5.5 years; Pacifici et al. 2013). Several colonies have disappeared from Slovakia (Uhrin et al. 1997), and Romania (Nagy and Postawa 2011) – in the latter country, half of the roosts have disappeared since the 1960s, the population has declined by 94.5% in the Dobrogea karst area (Pocora and Pocora 2011). The subpopulations in Serbia are estimated at 150,000 individuals without any conspicuous trend (Pejić et al. 2018). The species is almost extinct in Switzerland and only one small nursery is known in Austria (Presetnik and Podgorelec 2010), while in Murcia (Spain) the population has declined by 70% in the last decades (Lisón et al. 2011). However, no decline has been observed in large colonies in Croatia and Bulgaria (Aulagnier and Presetnik 2020). In the last two decades, mass mortality events have been repeatedly recorded in France, Spain, Portugal, and Italy, with colonies in France and Spain experiencing a 50-60% decline in one year, and more recently (2013 and 2016-17) in northeast Hungary. Another event with ca. 200 casualties of uncertain origin was reported in 2018 from Georgia (EUROBATS 2018). The reasons for such die-offs are unclear. The filovirus and herpesviruses isolated in the colonies were ruled out as possible causes (reviewed in Aulagnier and Presetnik 2020), but mortality in Spain and Hungary was associated with the Lloviu virus (Kemenesi et al. 2018). A baseline survey of main colonies in Anatolia brought a total of 18,251 Schreiber's Bent-winged Bats (Çoraman and Çelik 2012). No population estimate and trend are available for the North African range of the species.
range: Schreiber's Bent-winged Bat (Miniopterus schreibersii) occurs from southwestern Europe and north-western Africa through the Middle East to the Caucasus (Furman et al. 2010). In Europe, it is restricted to southern Europe, mostly in Mediterranean regions, including almost all major islands (Mallorca, Menorca, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicilia, Crete, Rhodes, Lesvos, Cyprus, etc); the ranges’ northern boundary crosses central France, the French and Swiss Jura Mountains, northern Italy, Slovenia, southeast Austria, Slovakia, and Romania (reviewed in Aulagnier and Presetnik 2020). It no longer occurs in southwestern Germany, western mainland Ukraine and southern Crimea (not shown on map). A single adult male was recently found in the Hranická Chasm, southeastern Czech Republic (Bartonička and Jedlička 2011), and several bats were also recorded in Slovakia near the Polish border (Ceľuch 2014). The two records available for Malta, possibly single vagrant bats (Aulagnier and Presetnik 2020), are not confirmed in recent times, and currently the species is not known to occur in the country (C.M. Mifsud pers. comm.). Beyond the European region, it is known from records in North Africa (Morocco (Aulagnier et al. 2017), Algeria, Tunisia, and Cyrenaica in Libya) where it occurs in sympatry with Miniopterus maghrebensis (Puechmaille et al. 2014). In the Middle East, it is mostly confined to the border of the Mediterranean and Black Sea. In the Caucasus, it has been found only in southern Russia (Gazaryan 2007) and Georgia, whereas M. pallidus occurs in Azerbaijan, Armenia and further eastwards (Bilgin et al. 2016).
useTrade: The species is used in traditional medicine in North Africa, but this has a very low impact.
conservationActions: In Europe, the species is protected by national legislation in most range states. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the Bonn Convention (Eurobats) and the Bern Convention in parts of the range where these apply. It is included in Annex II (and IV) of the EU Habitats and Species Directive and hence requires special measures for conservation including the designation of Special Areas for Conservation. There is some habitat protection through Natura 2000, and some roosts are already protected by national legislation. There have been a number of LIFE-funded projects for this species in France, Spain, Italy, Romania and Germany.Further conservation action is needed to protect key roost sites. Research is required to understand the cause of the mass mortality events and the drivers and impacts of other threats. Monitoring is required to understand populations trends and the distribution of this species, particular in relation to the ranges of former component taxa now recognised as valid species.

rationale: Stenonycteris lanosa is assessed as Least Concern due to its fragmented but widespread distribution across East and Central Africa. It is thought to have a reasonably large population that is stable in some regions as it is found in several protected areas. However, multiple threats such as continuing deforestation driven by agriculture, infrastructure development and extractive industries, and cave disturbance contribute to habitat loss and degradation throughout the species’ range and results in a small, but overall population decline for the species. These threats could lead to more significant population declines in the future without appropriate habitat conservation actions.
habitat: Stenonycteris lanosa is generally associated with montane tropical forests, but also occupies evergreen shrublands, wooded grasslands, and bamboo forests throughout East Africa across its elevational range of 500 to 4,000 meters asl (Kaipf et al. 2014, Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). The species may occasionally occupy some dry lowland rainforests and dry/wet miombo woodland, as well as deciduous bushland and Acacia thicket (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). The species’ habitat is currently declining largely due to deforestation, driven by the expansion of small-holder and, to a lesser extent, agro-industry cropland and pasture throughout East and Central Africa (Masolele et al. 2024). Additionally, cave disturbance from tourism, religious practices, and mining activities contribute to habitat loss/degradation, as these caves are the only suitable roost habitat for S. lanosa (Voigt and Kingston 2016, Masolele et al. 2024).Forest habitats are primarily used as foraging space for their diet, which consists of soft fruits, nectar, and possibly pollen based on the species’ delicate skull and a single reported observation of an individual feeding on the flowers of Lobelia giberroa (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Based on this information, S. lanosa is likely involved in ecosystem services such as pollination and seed dispersal throughout their range. In clusters reaching up to hundreds of individuals, the species prefers to roost in dark, damp caves and underground mines, which also likely serve as maternity roosts (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Females have one pup per litter, and S. lanosa appears to have an extended reproductive chronology based on pregnancy reports. Pregnant females were found in Ethiopia in the beginning of May and the middle of January, one lactating female was found in Malawi during late December, and pregnant females were reported in Tanzania during July (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019).
threats: The species is primarily threatened by deforestation, cave disturbance, climate change, and potential overhunting for bushmeat (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Deforestation is a major threat, largely due to expansion of small-scale cropland throughout various countries in East and Central Africa (Masolele et al. 2024). Illegal logging and wood harvesting also contribute to deforestation across the species’ range (Kelly and Pilgram 2023). Residential and commercial development presumably contribute to forest loss as well. This is an ongoing threat to the primary habitat which S. lanosa uses for foraging, as the species is presumed to depend on fruits and flowers within these forests for sustenance (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Cave disturbance is another major threat to S. lanosa, mainly in the form of tourism, religious activities, and mining practices (Voigt and Kingston 2016, Masolele et al. 2024). This is an ongoing threat which directly threatens the species’ roost sites, as S. lanosa is a cave-dwelling bat (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Climate change is also a threat to the species, mainly through increased wildfires which contribute to the loss of forest habitat throughout the species’ range (Bousfield et al. 2023). Overhunting is a potential threat to the species, however it is unknown whether it is ongoing or so extensive as to be considered an actual threat (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Hunting bats for bushmeat is known to occur in some regions in eastern Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, but more research is needed to determine if S. lanosa is affected (Voigt and Kingston 2016).
population: There are no data on the species’ population size, though S. lanosa is presumed to have a large population based on its distribution and tendency to roost in groups of hundreds of individuals (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019, P. Webala pers. obs. 2024). The species’ population trend is suspected to be declining due to continuing and increasing levels of deforestation due mostly to local expansion of small-scale cropland (Masolele et al. 2024), cave disturbance and development, and hunting of the bats. Based on species’ fragmented distribution, S. lanosa is thought to have at least 11 subpopulations (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Several locations are thought to be close enough in proximity to allow potential dispersal between them, but more research is needed to determine if this leads to fewer subpopulations than locations. There is no evidence that the species’ population is undergoing extreme fluctuations nor are the number of subpopulations declining or undergoing extreme fluctuations.
range: Stenonycteris lanosa has a moderately fragmented distribution resulting from extensive deforestation that further isolated its distribution in East Africa and Central Africa. It has been documented in isolated habitat fragments often associated with montane areas from central Ethiopia and the southern border of South Sudan to central Malawi and from coastal Tanzania to an isolated fragment in Uganda and Rwanda (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). Based on its presence in forest habitat in Rwanda which extends further south, the species may be extant in the forested region of Burundi immediately south of Nyungwe National Park in Rwanda (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019). The species has been confirmed in cave/forest surveys in Nyungwe National Park in Rwanda (Flanders et al. 2022), in the Mathews Forest, Menengai crater, Mt. Elgon Forest, Kakamega Forest, and South and North Forests in Kenya (Aggundey and Schlitter 1984, Namunyak Wildlife Conservancy 2010, P. Webala pers. obs. 2024), and at the Kafa Biosphere Reserve in Ethiopia (The Nature and Biodiversity Conservation Union 2017, Meheretu et al. 2022). The species is primarily, but not exclusively, a montane species, with an elevational range from 507 to 4,174 masl (Monadjem et al. 2024). The species’ extent of occurrence (EOO; minimum convex polygon around the species’ range) and area of occupancy (AOO; 4 km2 grid overlaid on the species’ range) is 1,608,667 km2 and 396,604 km2, respectively (Monadjem et al. 2024). Neither the EOO or AOO for this species are declining or experiencing extreme fluctuations. Given the species’ moderately fragmented range, the species is thought to be located in 10 to 20 locations that are threatened by deforestation, largely due to expansion of small-scale cropland in these areas (Masolele et al. 2024) and cave disturbance. There is no evidence of change in the number and/or size of these locations, and while the locations are fragmented it is unlikely that S. lanosa is detrimentally affected due to its dispersal capabilities (Wilson and Mittermeier 2019).
useTrade: The species is not known to be traded. However, it is possibly hunted as bushmeat as it is found in eastern Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo where people known to hunt fruit bats for their meat (Voigt and Kingston 2016).
conservationActions: There are no ongoing conservation efforts for S. lanosa, though the species is found in multiple protected areas throughout Central and East Africa, such as Nyungwe National Park, the Mathews Forest, and the Kafa Biosphere Reserve (Kaipf et al. 2014, Flanders et al. 2022, Meheretu et al. 2022, UNEP-WCMC 2024). The species has also been proposed as a potential flagship species for the bamboo forest of the Kafa Biosphere Reserve, though it is unclear as to whether this has led to any actual conservation efforts or monitoring for S. lanosa (Kaipf et al. 2014). Conservation efforts for S. lanosa should focus on protecting, managing, and restoring habitat space throughout the species’ range, especially tropical montane forests and cave systems. Additionally, efforts should be made to educate and spread awareness to both local communities and governments across the species’ range regarding the habitat and ecological significance of S. lanosa. Regular communication with these communities/governments should also take place in order to ensure that conservation actions are both effective and unobtrusive to local residents.There is much more research to be done on S. lanosa, particularly on population size and trends as these areas have essentially no data. The species’ distribution should also be updated, in particular regarding its potential presence in Burundi and the capability of the species to move over broader landscapes, connecting its severely fragmented range. Additionally, more research is needed to determine the reproductive chronology of S. lanosa, as well as its average reproductive age and generation length as these help predict population trends in response to disturbances/threats. More research should also be done on the composition of the species’ diet to identify which fruit/flowers on which the species relies most. Research on the movement patterns and dispersal capabilities of S. lanosa must be done as well, in order to help identify subpopulations and determine if the species’ distribution could be considered severely fragmented. Furthermore, research is needed on whether S. lanosa is being hunted, and, if so, where and to what extent. Some examples of research actions include monitoring and survey projects in order to gather more data on the species overall.

rationale: Endemic to Sulawesi, Indonesia, Haeromys minahassae is assessed as Near Threatened (approaching A2c) based on a population reduction that is likely to have approached 30% over a 10 year period, as inferred from rapid and extensive loss of lowland evergreen forest. Forest loss in Sulawesi is projected to continue, further reducing the area, extent and quality of habitat available for this species. This species would therefore benefit from further surveys to monitor its abundance, trends and distribution.
habitat: The species records are primarily from intact forests (Musser 1990). However, there is a record from Mt. Dako from disturbed forest adjacent to cocoa plantations, suggesting that the species may tolerate some level of habitat disturbance (Handika et al. 2021). The magnitude of forest disturbance that the species can withstand is unknown. Its arboreal habits may require the presence of large trees, though the species has also been recorded on the ground (Musser 2014). It is considered as a seed predator (Musser 1990). Its diet consists primarily of fruits, such as Herau Palm (Areca vestiaria) and figs (Ficus spp.) (Musser 1990).
threats: Although rats and mice are commonly hunted and consumed by Minahasan people of Sulawesi, due to its small body size, Haeromys minahassae is unlikely to be targeted. Generally, rodents with white tails are preferred (Latinne et al. 2020).This species is likely threatened to some extent by habitat loss. In areas of Central Sulawesi there has been a 24% loss in forest cover since 1990 which continues today (Rijal et al. 2019). This coincides with additional estimates of decline of forest cover of 6.89–11.04% in Central and North Sulawesi between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). The threat of deforestation for agriculture, logging and mining is considered is more severe in lowland areas, at elevations where this species occurs (see Margono et al. 2014).
population: There is little information on the population status of this species. It is rarely encountered and collected during surveys, partially due to its arboreal habits, diminutive size, and patchy distribution (Musser 1990), and also because most surveys do not involve the use of the appropriate techniques for capturing this species. Pressure from intensive forest loss over the past three decades is likely to have vastly reduced its population size, as for example, in areas of central Sulawesi there has been a 24% loss in forest cover since 1990 (Rijal et al. 2019).
range: Initially, Haeromys minahassae was only known from fragmented populations in the eastern tip of the northern peninsula and the northern part of the Sulawesi central core (Musser 1990, Musser 2014). Handika et al. (2021) reported new records of H. minahassae from Mt Dako and Mt Buliohuto, which are parts of poorly-surveyed areas in the west of the northern peninsula. A survey on Mt. Latimojong also indicated the existence of the species. Therefore, the species may have wider distribution than initially thought, and may occur throughout lowland forests in the northern peninsula and the central core of Sulawesi. There are no known records from the other peninsulas of the island. This species is known from 75 to 1,000 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Lore Lindu National Park and Mt. Dako Nature Reserve. It may occur in other such areas throughout its predicted distribution, such as Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park and Mt. Sojol Nature Reserve. Further survey work is needed to determine the geographic range and current population status of this species.

rationale: Surveys in Russia have indicated that the population has declined from at least 27,000 individuals in 2001 to 8,000–10,000 individuals in 2017. Based on these numbers, the decline by the year of assessment is estimated to have reached 83% over the previous 10 years. Whilst data are only available from the Russian extent of this species' range (which comprises the majority of its global range), it is likely that the data also reflect trends across the rest of its range in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, where populations are small and isolated. Threats include climate-driven changes in flood patterns, declining habitat quality, bycatch, water pollution and competition from introduced species, all of which remain present. Therefore, given the level of ongoing decline and threats faced by this species, it is assessed as Critically Endangered under criterion A2ac.
habitat: An aquatic species, it is found in oxbow lakes (with an area of 0.3 ha or more), and less frequently in ponds and rivers with slow flow, where it lives in holes in the banks. It does not inhabit all water bodies within its range; it has relatively strict habitat requirements and prefers water bodies 2–6 m in depth with rich water-marsh vegetation, bushes and primary forests along the banks, and with high macroinvertebrate abundance (Rutovskaya et al. 2020). In favourable years it is able to reproduce in any period of the year, but usually has two reproduction peaks at the end of spring and autumn with a brood of 1–6 young (more often 3–4) (Mishta and Merzlikin 2009). It is omnivorous, recorded feeding on water invertebrates and plant species (Kryštufek and Motokawa 2018).
threats: The widespread use of stationary fishing nets—prohibited by law in many regions—is a serious threat to the Russian Desman. The very low price and high durability of modern nets means that poachers often leave them in the water for days or even months, checking on them only occasionally and often abandoning them. Russian Desmans will die, on average, within 5–10 minutes of being trapped in a net (Rutovskaya et al. 2017). Another key threat is the use of illegal 'electric landing nets' (or electric rods), which use an electric current to stun fish (Yemets et al. 2020); these items, also used by poachers, have become widespread over recent decades. They are not believed to directly harm desmans as a general rule, but can deplete populations of fish and aquatic invertebrates that the Russian Desman depends upon.A further major threat to the Russian Desman is habitat loss and degradation. During the second half of the 20th century, water pollution, the creation of impoundments, drainage, clearance of riparian vegetation, and uncontrolled agricultural exploitation of flood plains became widespread and contributed to the decline in the species' population (M. Rutovskaya pers. comm. 2022). However, this process has abated somewhat in the last decade. Habitat and/or weather change as a result of climate change could be having a further marked impact on desman numbers, through modifying water flow regimes and water levels across suitable desman habitat. The absence of spring floods (which play an important role in the productivity of floodplain reservoirs, and in the success of desman breeding), and increasingly frequent and extremely destructive winter floods, as well as shallowing or drying up of floodplain reservoirs, is thought to have resulted in significant losses of individuals (Rutovskaya 2022).The introduced American Mink (Neovison vison) may prey on the Russian Desman. Competition for breeding sites with Muskrats (Ondatra zibethicus) may also be a threat. The introduced Chinese Sleeper (Perccottus glenii) competes for similar food resources as the desman and can reduce the availability of vegetation and invertebrates (Podshivalina et al. 2020).
population: At the beginning of the 1970s in the Soviet Union there were approximately 70,000 individuals, of which the majority occurred in Russia, with approximately 1,500 individuals in Kazakhstan and single records of occurrence in Ukraine and Belarus. Surveys in Russia indicate that the population there declined from 39,000 in 1985 to 27,000 by 2001 (see the Biodiversity Conservation Centre website http://www.biodiversity.ru/eng/programs/desman/results.html for further details). More recently, extensive burrow surveys undertaken during 2010–2016 have indicated a further decline: burrow density and the probable number of animals per burrow (which varies with month; Borodin 1963) were used to estimate relative abundance across 573 surveyed reservoirs, and then extrapolated to provide an estimate of 8,000–10,000 individuals remaining across Russia by 2017 (Rutovskaya et al. 2017). Assuming a linear ongoing decline, these estimates, when extrapolated, suggest that the population in 2023 will be around 3,600 individuals. This is consistent with recent population estimates of 4,000 or fewer (Rutovskaya 2022).The Russian Desman has disappeared completely from some localities in Russia: surveys from 2009–2011 of apparently suitable habitat failed to detect any individuals in the Medveditsa River or in its tributaries and floodplain lakes, with the last reliable record for that area in 2008 within a tributary of the Medveditsa River (Oparina et al. 2013). However, a small population is thought to have survived in the Khopersky Reserve. In the Volga River basin, up to 3,500 individuals are concentrated in the Oka-Klyazma river system in Okskiy (M.V. Rutovskaya pers. comm. 2022). In the Ryazan region along the Oka River, the number of individuals is estimated to be 1,500. A population of up to 550 individuals lives in the lower reaches of the Sura River, another tributary of the Volga. In other areas where the desman has been reliably recorded, the number of local populations is estimated to comprise less than 100 individuals (Rutovskaya et al. 2017) and numbers are generally low. For example, the Klyzama River was formerly inhabited by one of the larger populations with 465 individuals recorded in 2012, but recent surveys have reported the presence of just 35 desmans (Zimenko and Rutovskaya 2022).In Ukraine, currently the Russian Desman is very rare, potentially numbering a few hundred animals in one region (Mishta and Merzlikin 2009, Yemets et al. 2020). Its status in Kazakhstan is unknown. It is thought to now be locally extinct in Belarus, Lithuania and the Republic of Moldova.
range: The Russian Desman (Desmana moschata) occurs in Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan; previously, it was also present in Belarus, Lithuania (where it was introduced in the mid-1900s) (Balčiauskas 1996), and possibly the Republic of Moldova (see Genovesi et al. 2009), though its origins there are unclear. Its current range is very fragmented, and it has disappeared from many areas where it formerly occurred. At the beginning of the 20th century, the Russian Desman was common in the Dniepr, Don, Volga and Ural River basins. In Ukraine, historically it occurred in the basins of the Dnieper and the Don Rivers (Dniprovska and Siversko-Donetska populations), but currently only sporadically occurs in the floodplain of the Seym River (Dnieper River basin) and its tributaries approximately 200 km west of the border with Russia (Mishta and Merzlikin 2009, Yemets et al. 2019). In Kazakhstan, it is thought to occur in Kostanay, the Ural River and the Kushum Channel, but recent data are lacking (Institute for Zoology and Gene Pool of Animals of National Academy of Scientists of Republic of Kazakhstan 1996).
useTrade: This species now has no commercial or local use due to its low abundance. In the 19th and 20th centuries, it was caught extensively for fur and musk, which was used in perfumery. Desman trapping is now prohibited.
conservationActions: The Russian Desman is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention and is included in the Red Data Book in Ukraine (declining), Russia (under category 1: population decreased to critical numbers) and Kazakhstan (category 2: vulnerable). In Russia, it is protected in the buffer zone of Okskiy, Khopersky, Prisursky, and Ugra National Parks and several small protected areas. This species has been the subject of multiple reintroduction attempts. For example, a reintroduction of 51 individuals was undertaken in 2001–2002 in a tributary of the Volga river basin, but in 2017 the population was estimated to consist of only 6–10 individuals (Bakka et al. 2018). In 2002–2003, it was also reintroduced to the Desna basin within Bryansky Les Reserve, Orlovskoe Polissya National Park, and Kerzhensky Reserve, but these reintroduced populations also remain small (Rutovskaya et al. 2017). Attempts to breed this species in captivity have been ongoing since the mid-20th century, but have failed (Rutovskaya et al. 2017).Conservation measures recommended to stabilize and improve the condition of the Russian Desman throughout its range include: the establishment of breeding populations in captivity; termination of imports of netting materials into Russia; strengthening and expanding inspections of regionally protected areas; and identification of appropriate habitat management and restoration regimes (Zimenko and Rutovskaya 2022).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as it is widespread and relatively common on Sulawesi with a large extent of occurrence of 382,834 km2. It is present in several protected areas, and seems somewhat adaptable to human disturbance. There is no evidence of any severe decline at present, but trends should be monitored.
habitat: It is found in most forest formations on Sulawesi, from coastal lowland up to montane summits (Musser 1987, Musser and Carleton 2005), and has been recorded from secondary and slightly disturbed forest. It is terrestrial, and feeds on fruit, insects, and snails (Musser 1982).
threats: There are no major threats to this species, although it may be affected by extensive habitat loss (Supriatna et al. 2020), but seems able to survive in lightly degraded habitats as well as at higher elevations where the threat of deforestation is reduced. In a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi, this species was recorded (Laatung et al. 2021).
population: This is a widespread and common species (Durden 1986).
range: This species is found throughout Sulawesi (Musser and Carleton 2005) and has a relatively wide elevation range. For example, it has been recorded from at least 450 m asl in southeast Sulawesi and 600 m asl on Gunung Tompotika in central Sulawesi, to 2,794 m asl on Mount Bawakaraeng in south Sulawesi.
useTrade: This species is hunted for food.
conservationActions: It is present in Lore Lindu National Park, Morowali Nature Reserve, and probably several other protected areas. Research into the threat of hunting as well as population trends would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion A2cd given a population reduction that has likely reached 30% over the past ten years, based on a decline in the extent and quality of habitat and because of hunting levels. There has been rapid and extensive loss of lowland forest in the areas and at the elevations that this species appears to be restricted to, in addition to pressure from hunting to supply wild wet markets in North Sulawesi. Conservation and research measures focusing on quantifying population, distribution and threat impacts are needed.
habitat: This is a terrestrial and vermivorous species (i.e., it eats worms and worm-like invertebrates) that inhabits lowland tropical evergreen rainforest (Musser 1990). It is unlikely that it can survive in degraded habitats (K.C. Rowe and A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023).
threats: The major threat is likely to be habitat loss. Forest has been removed in north Sulawesi for logging, expanding agriculture, mining and human settlements. Deforestation across north Sulawesi between 2000 and 2017 was estimated at 6.9% (Supriatna et al. 2020) but, on a more local scale and at lower elevations, this figure is more likely to have exceeded 30% in the previous ten years (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023). In a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi, eight individuals of this species were recorded (Laatung et al. 2021). This species, and other white-tailed rats, are considered generally popular in the wildlife markets of Sulawesi (Latinne et al. 2020).
population: It is only known from collected specimens and observations in bushmeat markets (e.g., Laatung et al. 2021). Data on abundance and trends are lacking, but it is likely decreasing in line with local levels of forest loss (Supriatna et al. 2020, K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is endemic to the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it occurs in the north-east tip of the northern peninsula, from sea level (Musser and Carleton 2005). In a 2016 survey of Mt. Ambang it was recorded at 1,500 m asl (Handika et al. 2021). A 2019 survey recorded this species in the western edge of Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
useTrade: This species, as with the other species of white-tailed rat in Sulawesi, is hunted and is fairly commonly sold in markets (Latinne et al. 2020, Laatung et al. 2021). The extent and impacts of this hunting are unknown.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas, including Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park, Tangkoko Dua Saudara Nature Reserve and Gunung Ambang. Further work is necessary to better determine the distribution range and population status of this species, and to understand how it is impacted by bushmeat hunting.

rationale: Maxomys wattsi is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B1ab(iii) as the species has a small extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 5,157 km2, it is known from few locations, and the extent and quality of its habitat is undergoing a continuing decline associated with expanding agriculture and mining. Further research on its ecology, population and distribution would be beneficial.
habitat: It is found in upper and lower montane forest (Musser 1991).
threats: The major threat to this species is likely to be habitat loss due to expanding agriculture, nickel mining and logging activities, though the latter was more severe in the past (F. Fahri pers. comm. 2023). In Central Sulawesi, it is estimated that at least 11% of total forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: This species is known from individuals trapped on the forest slopes of Gunung Tambusisi in 1980 (Musser 1991) and Mt. Katapasa in 2017 (e.g., see Handika 2017). Nothing is known about its population trends, but it may be declining in line with habitat loss in the region.
range: This species is found on Gunung Tambusisi, central Sulawesi, from 1,430–1,830 m asl (Musser 1991, Musser and Carleton 2005), and 1,495 m asl on Mt. Katapasa (Handika 2017). Records previously reported from Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009) are considered to have been assigned incorrectly.
conservationActions: It has been recorded in Morowali Nature Reserve.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern because, although it is seldom recorded, it has a relatively wide distribution and large extent of occurrence of 215,926 km2, and is presumed not be declining at a rate fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. However, it is threatened by habitat loss and hunting, thus, population trends should be monitored.
habitat: It is a terrestrial species that appears to live in burrows, though trapping results suggest it may be primarily arboreal. It is present in tropical lowland evergreen forests to upper montane tropical moist forest. It has only been trapped in intact forest, it is not known if it can persist in modified habitats. It is a folivorous species. It has small litters, possibly with only a single young.
threats: Populations are generally more secure at higher elevations, however, lowland populations will be threatened by habitat loss resulting from human settlement, timber and firewood extraction, and conversion of land to agricultural use, mining and logging. The average level of deforestation across Sulawesi between 2000 and 2017 exceeded 10% (Supriatna et al. 2020). In a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats, Lenomys meyeri was recorded as hunted and traded in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021), though the population-level impacts of this are unknown. It might also be persecuted as a crop pest (Laatung et al. 2021), but such crop damage could be caused by a number of unidentified rodent species.
population: It is known from very few specimens. It may be difficult to trap as it is folivorous. However, it is possible that the species has a naturally low population density, and may be decreasing in line with rates of habitat loss on Sulawesi.
range: This species is endemic to Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it is found in northern and southwestern parts of the island (Musser and Carleton 2005). There are no specimens from the southeastern peninsula, but it may occur there. Modern specimens from the north to southwestern peninsula have been collected from the coastal plain near sea level to 1,159 m asl (Musser 2015). Small mammal surveys of Mt Ambang and Mt Dua Saudara in 2016 provided records of the species, however, surveys of Mt Dako in 2013 and Mt Buliohuto in 2014 failed to detect the species (Handika et al. 2021).
useTrade: This species is traded and consumed in North Sulawesi.
conservationActions: Its range might fall within protected areas, but records are lacking. Further surveys are needed to better determine both the distribution limits of this species, and whether it can persist in modified habitats.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern since it is widely distributed on Sulawesi, occurring both at low and high elevations and with a large extent of occurrence of 382,834 km2. It is not believed to be undergoing a decline at a rate fast enough to warrant listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in tropical evergreen lowland and montane rainforests (Musser and Carleton 2005); all specimens originate from forest, though the species probably does occur in areas of low-level disturbance. It is terrestrial, but can be found in the understory and canopy of trees scavenging for food (Musser 1982). One specimen was taken in a leaf-nest on the ground, and they have also been trapped in strangler figs (G. Musser pers. comm. 2008). It feeds only on fruit (Musser and Durden 2002).
threats: The major threat to the species is likely to be habitat loss due to agricultural expansion and logging. In the lowlands, much habitat has been converted for growing crops and mining concessions. This is the largest rat species present on Sulawesi, and, in some parts of the range, such as in the northeast, they are eaten (Laatung et al. 2021); however, this may be a localised threat.
population: It is known to be common in suitable habitat.
range: This species is endemic to Sulawesi, where it is found from sea level up to approximately 1,500 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005; Sulawesi Small Mammal Workshop pers. comm. 2023).
useTrade: It is hunted for food (Laatung et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas, including Lore Lindu National Park. Nonetheless, there is a need for population monitoring, as well as research into the extent and impact of hunting. Further phylogenetic studies are needed to determine whether Taeromys is monophyletic (Handika et al. 2021).

rationale: This species is only known from one locality. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 516 km2 as well as forest loss in Sulawesi, it could qualify as Endangered under criterion B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any ongoing, comprehensive surveys in the area. It is possible its EOO is considerably larger, which would potentially lead to a listing of Least Concern. Therefore, adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as an intermediate category, Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: The two specimens from Tanke Salokko were collected from montane forest. It is not known whether it could occur in modified habitats, but it seems reasonable to expect that it may be found in plantations adjacent to intact forest.
threats: It may be threatened by ongoing loss of habitat, although forest loss in this part of Sulawesi appears to be less severe than elsewhere. In South and Southeast Sulawesi, approximately 9-13% of forest cover was lost between 2000-2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Large areas of the southeastern peninsula were logged during 1990s and are now secondary regrowth or cacao plantations; formations above 1,500 m Asl are scarce and scattered between peaks separated by deep valleys (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
population: It is known only from three specimens, and was last collected in 1932 from Tanke Salokko. There is no recent information on population status.
range: This species is known only from the south eastern peninsula of Sulawesi, where it has been recorded at two localities: the type locality, Tanke Salokko at 1,500 m Asl (03°35'S, 121°15'E), and lowlands around Mowewe at 300 m Asl (03°57'S, 121°43'E) (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is quite likely to occur in areas between these two localities, and perhaps further to the north.
conservationActions: This species occurs within the proposed Mekongga National Park. There is a need for further survey work to determine the current population status of this species and to better understand its limits of distribution.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern given that it is fairly common, has a large extent of occurrence of 159,711 km2 and is not known to be undergoing any severe decline in abundance. However, it is likely to be under pressure from forest loss, so its distribution and population trends should be monitored.
habitat: This arboreal species is found in lowland tropical evergreen rain forest (Musser 1990, Musser and Carleton 2005). It has been collected from naturally disturbed riverside forest, and it appears to be forest dependent (G. Musser pers. comm. 2018). It is not known if it occurs in modified habitats.
threats: It is believed to be threatened by habitat degradation, resulting from deforestation for conversion of land to agricultural use and mining. Forest loss of over 23% has been recorded from Northern Sulawesi since 1990, while Central Sulawesi has had the largest declines on the island in terms of forest area (Rijal et al. 2019). Deforestation largely does not occur in areas with steep topography meaning remaining forest landscapes are clustered around hills and mountains. The development of road networks has been a major trigger of deforestation in the region (Rijal et al. 2019).
population: There is limited information on its population size. It appears to be a fairly common species. It is likely to be a forest-dependent species and therefore declining as a result of widespread deforestation. Population size and density is difficult to predict as it is thought to be a difficult species to trap without targeted effort, a recent study recorded only one individual, however this was attributed to the poor detectability chances of the methods used (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2018).
range: This species is found in central and northeastern Sulawesi (Indonesia), where it occurs from near sea level to 1,000 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is only known from a few areas, but it might be quite widespread outside of the known locations (Mortelliti et al. 2012). The most recent record of the species on Mt Balease at 900 m asl extends its range further south than previously mapped (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2018). The species was not detected during surveys of Mt Ambang and Mt Dua Saudara (Handika et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It has been recorded from the Lore Lindu National Park, and may be present in additional protected areas. Further studies are needed to determine both the full extent of the species range, and its tolerance to habitat disturbance.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as it has a moderate extent of occurrence of 17,083 km2, likely occurs in protected areas, is considered relatively common and is not thought to be undergoing a decline at a rate that would qualify it for a more threatened category.
habitat: It inhabits montane and upper-montane forest, and also occurs in forest at lower elevations.
threats: There are no major threats, but this species likely occurs in areas affected by forest removal for agriculture and logging. It may compete with introduced Rattus rattus.
population: This species is considered relatively common (K.C. Rowe and A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023), but data of population trends are lacking.
range: This species is known from southwestern Sulawesi, from the slopes of Gunung Lampobatang at 600–2,500 m asl, and also from adjacent coastal lowlands close to sea level (Musser and Carleton 2005). Its range extends northwards where it co-occurs with Rattus facetus.
conservationActions: It may occur in Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park. Greater understanding of this species' population trends, ecology and taxonomy would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is only known from two distinct locations and has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 4,169 km2, within which the extent and quality of its habitat is under decline. Therefore, it could qualify as Endangered under criterion B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any ongoing, comprehensive surveys to help clarify this. If its EOO is considerably larger, it could potentially qualify as Least Concern. Therefore, adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)) as the most appropriate category. Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This arboreal species appears restricted to montane rainforest, such as on the steep slopes of Gunung Nokilalaki, and has not been found in lowland forest (Musser 1981, Musser and Carleton 2005). It is not known whether it might survive in slightly degraded habitats.
threats: This species is likely under threat from habitat loss driven by logging or conversion for agriculture; between 2000–2017, Central Sulawesi lost approximately 11% of its forest cover (Supriatna et al. 2020). Although forest removal is more severe at lower elevations, this threat may increasingly encroach onto higher elevations.
population: It is potentially common on Gunung Nokilalaki, but could be decreasing in line with rates of habitat loss on Sulawesi.
range: The species is known to occur from 1,600–2,285 m asl on Gunung Nokilalaki, elsewhere in Lore Lindu National Park between 1,200 m and 2,099 m asl (Maryanto et al. 2009), and from a single specimen further south in the Mamasa Area (02°56' S, 119°22' E). It is likely to occur in other montane regions of central Sulawesi (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It has been recorded in Lore Lindu National Park. Further survey work is needed to determine whether it occurs more widely in central Sulawesi, and to understand the extent and impact of threats it faces.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large extent of occurrence of 191,997 km2, and presence in a range of habitats including secondary growth forest and gardens. It is also known to occur across a broad elevation range and within protected areas. It is not believed to be undergoing any extensive declines that would warrant listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This is primarily a lowland tropical evergreen rainforest species, but can reach higher montane forest in parts of its range (Musser and Carleton 2005, Musser 2014, Hasyim et al. 2017). It has mostly been recorded in secondary growth forest, but also scrubby areas close to relatively undisturbed forest, in village gardens (Musser 2014), and areas of agroforestry (M.R.T.J.P. Nurdin pers. comm. 2023). It is sympatric with other Bunomys species in parts of its range. Its diet consists of invertebrates, vertebrates, and fruit, but not fungi (Musser 2014).
threats: This species is threatened in lowland parts of its range by a general loss of forest habitat through logging, conversion to cultivated land and mining.
population: Although population densities are not known, it can be locally common in some areas of primary forest. The abundance of this species varies greatly and in some parts of its range it is generally uncommon.
range: This species is found throughout central Sulawesi (Indonesia) and the southeast and southwest peninsulas (Musser and Carleton 2005). The northernmost record is from Labuan Sore at the southern end of the northern peninsula (Musser 2014). It has also been recorded on the eastern peninsula, the two southern peninsulas, and on Pulau Buton off the coast of the southern margin of the southeastern peninsula (Musser 2014). It occurs in lowland areas from 30 m up to 1,600 m asl (Musser 2014), but has also been found at higher elevations; on Mt. Bawakaraeng on the southern peninsula it has been recorded between 1,300 m up to 2,200 m asl, though a gap in records occurs between 1,700 m and 1,899 m asl likely due to a fire at that altitude (Hasyim et al. 2017).
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Lore Lindu National Park in Sulawesi. Further research in general is needed for this species, but especially taxonomy as this may be a species complex. Conservation of suitable forested habitat, especially in the lowlands, is needed.

rationale: This species is currently only confirmed from one location, the island of Sangihe, where it has a small extent of occurrence of 696 km2. There has been a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat. It is therefore listed as Endangered under criteria B1ab(iii). This species is relatively understudied, and up-to-date population and distribution data are needed.
habitat: This species is commonly found in low elevation primary forests, where it has its highest population density, but it is also common in all cultivated areas (Riley 2002).
threats: Sangihe is heavily cultivated at low elevations. Its primary habitat is rapidly being transformed and, by the turn of the century, primary forest covered less than 1% of the island (Riley 2002). Today, gold mining activities pose a significant threat to Sangihe's forests, particularly around Gunung Sahendaruman in the south of the island (Berryman 2021).
population: Prosciurullus rosenbergii has been found more frequently on Sangihe than other small mammals. It occurs in higher densities in primary forest than secondary habitat (Riley 2002). Recent population data are lacking.
range: This species is endemic to Sangir Island (Sangihe) of Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser and Carleton 2005), though it may have also occurred historically on the nearby islands of Siau, Tahulandang, and Ruang (see Musser et al. 2010).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures currently in place. A Sangihe National Park has been proposed but, even so, would only overlap with a small extent of this species' range. Populations of this species should be monitored to record changes in abundance and distribution.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it is relatively widespread on Sulawesi with a large extent of occurrence of 382,834 km2. It is found across a broad altitudinal range and within several protected areas, and it is not believed to be undergoing extensive declines.
habitat: It has been collected in primary rainforest, although a few specimens have also been collected from slightly degraded forest. It is most common along ravines and rocky stream terraces in mesic shaded areas, such as the wet and shaded forests on Mt Bawakaraeng (Hasyim et al. 2017). It is strictly terrestrial and feeds primarily on small vertebrates (e.g., small frogs and lizards), fruit and earthworms (Musser 2014). Although it is commonly found in wet and shaded parts of the forest, it is also one of the few murids found in the drier steep hillside forest and ridgetops well away from streams (Musser 2014).
threats: The major threat is likely to be loss of habitat due to clearance for agriculture, mining and logging. No specimens have been collected from the lowlands of the south west peninsula, possibly because most of the original forest has been removed. This species is also hunted for bushmeat (Sheherazade pers. comm. 2023).
population: It is known to be abundant in some parts of its range, but uncommon elsewhere, for example, in the northeast of Sulawesi.
range: This species is endemic to the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia. It is found throughout the island and has an elevational range between 250 and 2,200 m asl (Musser 2014). However, no modern specimens of Bunomys chrysocomus have been collected from lowlands of the southwest peninsula, likely partly because most of the original forest has been removed and because the remaining tracts have not been adequately surveyed. The species did once occur in these deforested areas, because it has been found as subfossils (Musser and Carleton 2005). On Mt Bawakaraeng on the southern peninsula, it has been recorded between 1,500 m and 2,200 m asl (Hasyim et al. 2017), though these records could require further verification (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
useTrade: This species is known to be hunted for bushmeat (Sheherazade pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas, including Lore Lindu National Park and Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park.

rationale: Bunomys coelestis is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence is approximately 173 km2, and it is potentially restricted a single location on the mountain of Gunung Lompobatang where there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat driven by agriculture and logging. It may also be at risk of competition from introduced Rattus spp. as well as human disturbance.
habitat: It is found in primary montane forest formations (Musser and Carleton 2005), and has not been recorded outside of this habitat.
threats: The species has a very restricted distribution, and is threatened by conversion of forest to agricultural use (including for passion flower cultivation), and small-scale logging. It may also be threatened by competition from introduced Rattus spp. Tourism and camping activities have become popular on Gunung Lompobatang, disturbing areas where this species occurs.
population: Little is known about the population of this species, but it can be common where it occurs.
range: This species is restricted to the slopes of Gunung Lompobatang at the southwest tip of Sulawesi (Indonesia), at elevations between 1,800 and 2,500 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005). The species is likely to be restricted to montane rainforest formations on Gunung Lompobatang (Musser 2014).
conservationActions: The species occurs in the Gunung Lompobatang Protection Forest for watershed protection, but the forest has been degraded due to illegal logging and conversion to agricultural land. Further dedicated surveys to study the habitats and ecology of this species are needed. There is a need to protect any remaining suitable habitat.

rationale: This species is known from few localities and has a potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence of 5,752 km2. It may be under threat from forest removal, but the extent and impacts of this threat at higher elevations where this species occurs are unclear. As such, this species is assessed as Near Threatened as it fulfils some conditions of criterion B (B1a, approaching b(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: It has been collected in tropical upper montane rain forest (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is not known if the species can persist in modified habitats. It is scansorial, nocturnal, and feeds on earthworms (Musser and Carleton 2005).
threats: The threats to this species are not fully known, but it is potentially impacted by habitat loss as a result of logging and agricultural activities. In South and Central Sulawesi, approximately 9–11% of forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). There has been forest loss even within Lore Lindu National Park (Harris et al. 2014) and forest loss and degradation in National Parks more generally across Indonesia (Fuller et al. 2013). The extent of loss of montane habitat requires quantification.
population: This species is known from eight specimens recorded in 1975 (Musser 1982) and from 11 specimens recorded more recently (Achmadi et al. 2014).
range: This species is known from Mt. Nokilalaki in central Sulawesi (Indonesia), where it occurs from 1,982 to 2,287 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005), from Mt Gandang Dewata in the Quarles Range north of Mamasa, West Sulawesi Province, where it was recorded at elevations of 1,600 and 2,600 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2014), and from a specimen from Mt Rorekatimbo in Lore Lindu (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2016). It is possibly also present in nearby montane regions, but field surveys are needed to determine this. Fairly extensive surveys undertaken between 1,700–2,500 m asl of the Latimojong range failed to detect the species (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2016).
conservationActions: The species has been recorded from the Lore Lindu National Park. It is not known if the species occurs in any additional protected areas. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, ecology and threats to this poorly known species.

rationale: This species has a moderate extent of occurrence of 39,264 km2 and occurs in some protected areas and at high elevations where the risk of deforestation is currently reduced. There is no evidence to suggest that it is declining at a rate fast enough to warrant listing in a threatened category. This species is therefore assessed as Least Concern, though its population, and potential encroachment of threats into montane regions, should be monitored.
habitat: This terrestrial vermivore inhabits montane forest (Musser and Durden 2002).
threats: This species may be at risk from habitat loss in the future as loss of forest for agriculture and logging is increasingly encroaching on higher elevations. Lore Lindu National Park lost 11.8% of its forest between 2000 and 2010, with projections indicating that approximately 40% of the park will be deforested by 2050, even if the deforestation rate is cut by half (Harris et al. 2014). Lore Lindu National Park has been heavily impacted in the valleys around Mt. Nokilalaki, with climate change putting further pressures on high-elevation species (Harris et al. 2014).
population: There is no information available on population status.
range: This species is known from up to 2,535 m asl in Mt Latimojong, Mt Tokala and Mt Nokilalaki, in the central core of Sulawesi (Musser and Carleton 2005). More recently the range has been extended by records of 16 specimens on Mt Gandang Dewata between 2,200 m and 2,600 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2014) and Gunung Rorekatimbo in Lore Lindu National Park.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Lore Lindu National Park, and Latimojong is designated as Protection Forest. Further survey work is needed to determine whether this species occurs more widely throughout montane regions of central Sulawesi, as well as to monitor its population status.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because, whilst it is forest-dependent and is restricted to primary montane forest formations where it has a relatively small estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 36,678 km2, it is considered to be abundant where it is found and is present in at least one protected area. However, there is ongoing loss of forest across Sulawesi even within protected areas, so threats and impacts upon this species should be monitored.
habitat: This terrestrial species is known from tropical evergreen rainforest formations (Musser 2014). It has not been recorded outside of montane forested areas, however, no trapping has taken place outside of primary forest. Its diet consists of invertebrates, small vertebrates, some fruit and fungi (Musser 2014).
threats: Forest removal for agriculture and logging is a risk to this species over much of its range. There has been forest loss inside National Parks, including Lore Lindu, between 2000–2010 (Fuller et al. 2013), with studies suggesting that approximately 11% of forest was cleared since the early 2000s (Harris et al. 2014, Supriatna et al. 2020). Land use-change models predict that widespread deforestation of Lore Lindu NP may occur in the coming decades (34–40% of the park deforested by 2050), even if the deforestation rate is cut by half (Harris et al. 2014). Climate change may also affect high-elevation species in this region (Harris et al. 2014).
population: It is abundant in tropical evergreen montane forests (Musser 2014).
range: This species is endemic to tropical evergreen montane rainforest formations in the central core and southeast peninsula of Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser 2014). It may be found more widely than currently known on the southeastern peninsula (Musser 2014). It has been recorded between 1,285–2,287 m asl (Musser 2014).
conservationActions: It is common in montane forests (Musser 2014) and appears to be present in Lore Lindu National Park. Field surveys are needed to determine if the species can persist in modified habitats outside of forest.

rationale: Bunomys prolatus is assessed as Vulnerable as the species has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 5,243 km2, it is known from two locations, and the extent and quality of its habitat is undergoing a continuing decline associated with expanding agriculture and mining. Further research of its ecology, population and distribution would be beneficial.
habitat: It occurs in montane forest, in short and very mossy areas (Musser 1991).
threats: The major threat to this species is likely to be habitat loss due to expanding agriculture, nickel mining and logging activities, though the latter was more severe in the past (F. Fahri pers. comm. 2023). In Central Sulawesi, it is estimated that at least 11% of total forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: It was reported to be common (Musser 1991), although the type series collected is small. There is no information on current population status.
range: This species is known only from two locations on the eastern peninsula of Sulawesi (Indonesia): an area 1,830 m asl on Gunung Tambusisi (Musser and Carleton 2005) and 2,533 m asl on Mt Katopasa (Handika 2017). It is possible that it occurs in high elevation areas throughout the eastern peninsula.
conservationActions: It has been recorded in Morowali Nature Reserve. Further research of its population and threats would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large extent of occurrence of 382,834 km2, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at a rate fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. It exhibits some degree of tolerance to habitat disturbance. Nonetheless, threats of habitat loss and hunting should be quantified.
habitat: This terrestrial species is found in lowland and montane tropical moist forest (Musser 1982). It is tolerant of some habitat disturbance and can be found in secondary growth and scrub. It has been recorded from shade-grown coffee plantations. It is a frugivorous species. Ratus hoffmanni is found in all habitat types on Mt Bawakaraeng, namely: mixed garden, agroforestry, pine forest, secondary forest and primary forest (M.R.T.J.P Nurdin pers. comm. 2023). The highest number of individuals were found in secondary forest and primary forest (M.R.T.J.P Nurdin pers. comm. 2023).
threats: In the lowland parts of its range, it is threatened by habitat loss resulting from logging, mining and heavy conversion of land to open cultivated areas. It is presumably caught for food in the northern part of its range, but this seems unlikely to be a major threat. From South Sulawesi, specifically Mt Bawakaraeng, this species is still commonly found in secondary forests, agroforestry, and primary forest but at a certain altitudes where the habitat has been damaged it affects the number of individuals found, especially at 1,700 m asl (M.R.T.J.P. Nurdin pers. comm. 2023). Fires do occur on Mt. Bawakaraeng, however, these are not likely to pose a great threat for this species (M.R.T.J.P. Nurdin pers. comm. 2023).
population: It is a common species and populations are considered to be stable.
range: This species is found throughout the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia, with the exception of the upper slopes of Gunung Lampobatang at the end of the southwestern peninsula. It is also found on Malenge Island in the Togian Archipelago (Musser and Carleton 2005). Records previously reported from Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009) are considered to have been assigned incorrectly.
useTrade: It is presumably caught for food in the northern part of its range, but this seems unlikely to be a major threat
conservationActions: It is thought to be present in many protected areas. Some further studies are needed to determine how well the species can adapt to modified habitats.

rationale: This species is approaching threatened status under criterion B as it has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 3,843 km2 and is known from two locations. However, since it does not reach sufficient subcriteria (e.g., decline is unknown), it is listed as Near Threatened. There is a risk that the removal of forest for agriculture or logging could significantly encroach into this species' range at higher elevations in the future. Further research is needed to improve knowledge of its distributional limits and population trends, as it is currently only known from few specimens.
habitat: The species is considered to be terrestrial and nocturnal, having been found on the ground at night in montane forest (Musser 2014). Its diet is unknown (G. Musser pers. comm. 2017).
threats: Nothing is known about specific threats to this species, however, continued loss of forest habitat in on Sulawesi could be a risk; it is estimated that at least 10% of Sulawesi's forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). In the montane habitats where this species occurs, forest loss is likely less severe, though agricultural or logging activities may begin to encroach onto higher elevations (Supriatna et al. 2020). Research is needed to quantify this threat in mountainous areas.
population: This species is considered relatively abundant where it is found (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
range: The species is known from two locations: tropical lower montane forest at 2,500 and 2,600 m asl on Mt Gandang Dewata in the Quarles Range, which is part of the southern highlands of the west-central mountain block in Sulawesi (Musser 2014), and Mt. Latimojong (Winterhoff et al. 2020).
conservationActions: It occurs in Gandang Dewata National Park and Latimojong Protection Forest. Further research into its ecology and distribution is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern because it has a large extent of occurrence of 39,169 km2 and is not known to currently be undergoing any significant decline. However, it may be at risk of ongoing deforestation. As such, the population status of this species, and response to habitat loss, should be monitored.
habitat: This is a terrestrial and diurnal species (Musser et al. 2010). It is found in lower and upper intact montane rainforest where, for instance, there is suitable acorn production, but it is unlikely to occur in disturbed forest or plantations (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023). Its diet consists of invertebrates, fruits, and nuts (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: The threats to this species are poorly known, but it is probably negatively impacted by logging and deforestation for agriculture, particularly as it may rely heavily on tropical acorns (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
population: This species may be considered common where it occurs (Musser et al. 2010), but restricted to certain habitats.
range: This species can be found on mountains of central Sulawesi, Indonesia, at altitudes likely between 1,200 and 3,000 m asl (K. Rowe and N. Inayah pers. comm. 2023). It has been recorded from Gunung Gandang Dewata, Gunung Kanino, Gunung Nokilalaki, Pegunungan Takolekaju and Pegunungan Latimojong (Musser et al. 2010).
conservationActions: It is present in Lore Lindu National Park and Gandang Dewata National Park. Further studies are needed to understand the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, ecology, and threats to this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern because it has a large extent of occurrence of 40,866 km2, it is found in several nature reserves and in disturbed habitats, and it is not thought to be undergoing any significant decline. However, it is known from relatively low elevations, where levels of deforestation on Sulawesi are greatest. As such, the population status of this species, and response to ongoing habitat loss, should be monitored.
habitat: This species is known from primary forest as well as degraded, secondary forest and shrubland at elevations between 168 and 1,700 m asl (Musser et al. 2010, Thorington et al. 2012). This ground squirrel is altitudinally parapatric and found in less dense distributions compared to Hyosciurus heinrichi. However, further work needs to be carried out to understand the relationship between the distributions of Hyosciurus. This species forages in the leaf litter and its diet consists of arthropods and fruits, preferring figs and acorns (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss, predominantly as a result of expanding agriculture and logging activities. The average level of forest cover loss across Sulawesi between 2000 and 2017 was estimated to exceed 10% (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: Population abundance and trends are unknown.
range: This species is endemic to Sulawesi, Indonesia. Its distribution is considered poorly known overall, but it is known from lowland evergreen and lower montane rain forests in Gunung Ile-Ile in the northern peninsular and in the northeastern lowlands of central Sulawesi (Musser et al. 2010, Thorington et al. 2012). It has been recorded in the Dako region (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023) on the northern peninsula, but its range most likely extends beyond Gunung Ile-Ile into the western curve of the peninsula, from the Gorontalo region west to the base of the peninsula (Musser et al. 2010).
useTrade: There is no information regarding use and trade of this species.
conservationActions: The species' range broadly overlaps with Toli-toli Nature Reserve and Pinjan Tanjung Matop Nature Reserve. Further research is needed to quantify abundance, distribution and trends.

rationale: Rattus mollicomulus is assessed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is approximately 173 km2, and it is potentially restricted to a single location on the mountain of Gunung Lompobatang where there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat. Further research of its distribution, ecology and threats would be beneficial.
habitat: This species is restricted to upper montane tropical moist forest. It is not known if it can occur in modified habitats.
threats: The species has a very restricted distribution, and is threatened by conversion of forest to agricultural use (such as passion flower cultivation), and small-scale logging which may encroach into the mountain slopes. It may also be threatened by competition from introduced Rattus spp. Tourism and camping activities have become popular on Gunung Lampobatang, disturbing areas where this species could occur.
population: Little is known about the population of this species, but it can be common where it occurs.
range: This species is known only from the upper slopes of Gunung Lampobatang on Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser and Holden 1991, Musser and Carleton 2005; G. Musser pers. comm.). It has been collected between 1,100 and 2,000 m asl.
conservationActions: It is present in Gunung Lampobatang, a Protection Forest for watershed protection. Further research is needed to determine the full range of the species in the area of Gunung Lampobatang.

rationale: This species could be considered Vulnerable under criterion B as it is known from few localities and has a potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence of 9,651 km2. It may be under threat from forest removal encroaching onto higher-elevation areas, though the extent and impact of this threat are unclear, and evidence of decline at these elevations is lacking. As such, adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as Near Threatened (approaching B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This diurnal and terrestrial species is found in cool, wet, and mossy habitats within tropical upper montane rain forest (Musser and Carleton 2005). It feeds mostly on earthworms and fungus gnats (Durden and Musser 1992). It has not been recorded from modified habitats.
threats: Forest degradation is increasing at higher elevations due to improved logging roads (Margono et al. 2014), and one study found rapid deforestation occurring within the Lore Lindu National Park (Harris et al. 2014). Deforestation across Sulawesi between 2000 and 2017 (largely driven by agricultural land conversion and logging) exceeded 10% (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: This species has been recorded 35 times from Gunung Nokilalaki (Durden and Musser 1992) and more than once from Gunung Gandang Dewata and Gunung Rorekatimbo. It appears to be common within suitable habitat (G. Musser pers. comm.), but little else is known about its abundance or trends.
range: This species is known from the type locality of Rano Rano at 1,830 m asl (1°30' S, 120°28' E), and Gunung Nokilalaki between 1,950 and 2,286 m asl (1°16' S, 120°10' E), in central Sulawesi, Indonesia. More recently, it has been found at Gunung Gandang Dewata and Gunung Rorekatimbo between 2,200 and 2,600 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2014). It probably also occurs in upper montane forest on other mountains in the central core of the island (Musser and Carleton 2005).
conservationActions: It may be present in Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009). Further research is needed to clarify the distribution of this species and whether it can persist in modified or disturbed habitats.

rationale: Given this species' small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 166 km2, decline in extent and quality of habitat, and presence at a low number of locations, this species could meet the thresholds for Endangered under criteria B1ab(iii). However, the limited access to suitable elevations has restricted survey efforts in the area, and it is possible that this species is more widespread than is currently known. Nonetheless, it is unlikely that its EOO will be larger than 20,000 km2. Therefore, given the uncertainties surrounding its true EOO, but the knowledge of habitat decline, it is considered most appropriate to list this species as Vulnerable under criteria B1ab(iii).
habitat: The species inhabits streamside primary tropical lowland evergreen rainforest and is not known to occur on forested hillsides or ridgetops away from streams (Musser 2014). The species is terrestrial, nocturnal, and its diet predominantly consists of one species of ear fungus called karoko (Auricularia delicata) and, to a much lesser degree, invertebrates, vertebrates, and fruit (Musser 2014). Litters consist of 1–2 young (Musser 2014).
threats: The threats to this species are not known, however, continued loss of forest habitat for agriculture and logging are likely to be threats to the species. In lowland areas where this species occurs in Central Sulawesi, forest loss has likely exceeded 30% over the previous 10 years (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023). Additionally, given that it occupies streamside areas, it may be at risk of flooding events.
population: The species is likely to be uncommon (G. Musser pers. comm. 2017). It occurs in the same habitat types as Bunomys chrysocomus, however, it is infrequently trapped compared with this species (Musser 2014). No new specimens have been collected since 1974.
range: This species is endemic to the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia. All known specimens have come from three areas: the upper stretch of the Sungai Sadaunta (823–1,006 m asl), a tributary on the right side of the larger Sungai Miu; Tomado, near Danau Lindu (1,000 m asl); and Sungai Tokararu (1,150 m asl) in the watershed of Danau Lindu. These three locations are in the northern portion of the west-central mountain block of Central Sulawesi (Musser 2014). If the collection sites reliably reflect its elevational range, it should be found in tropical lowland evergreen rainforest habitats elsewhere in the west-central region and not in montane forest formations (Musser 2014).
conservationActions: The species is found in the upper stretch of Sungai Sadaunta, Tomado, Sungai Tokararu, which are all in Lore Lindu National Park (G. Musser pers. comm. 2017).

rationale: This species is listed as Near Threatened because it is approaching the thresholds of criterion B1 with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 17,118 km² and continued habitat decline within its range caused by logging and forest conversion to agriculture. Whilst these trends are within the threshold for Vulnerable B1b(iii), there is insufficient evidence to determine if the population has become fragmented (B1a) as a result of habitat loss, and population size and trends have not yet been established. However, the infrequency of recordings and loss of suitable habitat make it reasonable to assume that, based on current trends, populations this species could become severely fragmented in the near future, which would qualify the species for Vulnerable under criteria B1ab(iii). Further surveys are needed to determine the full geographic range of Prosciurillus topapuensis along with many aspects of its ecology.
habitat: This species is found in habitats ranging from tropical lowland evergreen rainforests in the lowlands and foothills to montane rainforest formations in the mountains (Musser et al. 2010). Prosciurillus topapuensis mainly inhabits tree crowns and woody vines in the high upper canopy of primary forests, but occasionally descends to the ground where the canopy is broken (Musser et al. 2010). It is most active during mornings and afternoons but may be active all day during overcast conditions. The diet of this species includes soft fruits (mostly figs) and arboreal insects (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss from human disturbance, agricultural conversion of land and deforestation (Whitten et al. 2012).
population: Its population size and trends remain unknown, however populations are expected to be fragmented and declining due to habitat loss within its known range (Whitten et al. 2012).
