range: The geographic range of Prosciurillus topapuensis extends over valleys, foothills and mountains in the western part of the central core of Sulawesi (Indonesia) extending from Lake Lindu in the north to the Latimojong mountains in the south, at elevations from 350 m asl in tropical lowland evergreen rainforest to 2,800 m asl in upper montane rainforest (Musser et al. 2010). The range overlaps those of the tree squirrels P. murinus, Rubrisciurus rubriventer, and both species of ground squirrels, Hyosciurus heinrichi and Hyosciurus ileile (Musser et al. 2010).
useTrade: Squirrel species have been recorded in Sulawesi markets, but species-level identification is lacking (Latinne et al. 2020), so it is not known whether Prosciurillus topapuensis is hunted.
conservationActions: Parts of its range overlap with national parks and protected areas, such as Lore Lindu National Park. Further surveys to improve knowledge of this species' ecology and population trends are needed.

rationale: This species is only known from one location. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 1,572 km2, it could qualify as Endangered under criterion B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any comprehensive surveys in the area. It is possible its EOO is considerably larger, which would potentially lead to a listing of Least Concern. Therefore, considering the decline in extent and quality of forest habitat where this species occurs, and adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)) as the most likely category. Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This species has been described within interspersed patches of primary and secondary forest at the beginning of tropical lower montane rainforest (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
threats: Large portions of the area where this species has been documented were logged during the 1990s, with areas of the mountain range now covered by secondary forest and other logged portions converted into cacao plantations (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
population: No information is available on population size or trends for this species.
range: Margaretamys christinae has been documented on the southern slopes of Osu (Gunung) Moserosero in Pegunung Mekongga, at 1,537m asl, but its distributional limits are unknown. The species is considered endemic to these high forests on Pegunung Mekongga (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
conservationActions: This species occurs within the proposed Mekongga National Park, but this park is only proposed at present. There is a need for further survey work to determine the current population status of this species and to better understand its limits of distribution.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion A2cd given a reduction that has likely reached 30% over the past ten years, based on both a decline in the extent and quality of habitat, and potential levels of exploitation. There has been rapid and extensive loss of lowland forest in the areas and at the elevations that this species appears to be restricted to, in addition to pressure from hunting to supply wild wet markets in North Sulawesi. Conservation and research measures focusing on quantifying population, distribution and threat impacts are needed.
habitat: Echiothrix is only recorded in the lowland rainforest on Sulawesi at elevations from sea level to 1,000 m asl (Carleton and Musser 2005, Handika et. al. 2020), and is unlikely to occur in disturbed habitats. The species is terrestrial and nocturnal. Echiothrix diets are composed mostly of earthworms, but they may eat some varieties of insects and centipedes (Musser and Durden 2014).
threats: The continuing degradation of Sulawesi rainforest due to logging, mining, and agricultural activities is a major threat for the species. In areas of central Sulawesi there has been a 24% loss in forest cover since 1990; deforestation is still continuing albeit at a slower rate due to there being less accessible forest extent to be cleared (Rijal et al. 2019). Forest cover has declined by 6.89–11.04% in Central and North Sulawesi between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020) and is more severe in lowland areas, at elevations where this species occurs (see Margono et al. 2014). At such elevations and on a local scale, this figure is more likely to have exceeded 30% in the previous ten years (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023). This species is also likely among white-tailed rats that are consumed by local Minahasan people and are traded in wild wet markets in the North Sulawesi (Latinne et al. 2020, Laatung et al. 2021).
population: The abundance of this species is not well known and it is rarely detected, however, pressure from intensive forest loss over the past three decades is likely to have vastly reduced its population size.
range: There are only two known species of Echiothrix. Echiothrix centrosa is a species restricted to the west of the northern peninsula and the northeastern part of the Sulawesi central core near the city of Palu and Lore Lindu National Park. Its sister species, E. leucura, is known from the east of the northern peninsula (Musser and Carleton 2005, Musser and Durden 2014). A lowland area of Gorontalo is commonly used as a geographic boundary for land vertebrates on Sulawesi (Evans et al. 2003, Musser 2014). Whether the two species co-occur in the contact zone in Gorontalo is uncertain. Within its known ranges, the species is only recorded in fragmented subpopulations in lowland rainforests from sea level to 1,000m asl (Musser and Durden 2014, Handika et al. 2020). The species may potentially occur in other suitable habitats across its known ranges. No other records have been found in the other parts of Sulawesi.
useTrade: This species, as with other species of white-tailed rats in Sulawesi, is hunted and sold in markets fairly commonly (Latinne et al. 2020, Laatung et al. 2021). The extent and impacts of this hunting are unknown.
conservationActions: Most of the known distribution of Echiothix centrosa is currently within Lore Lindu National Park. Further work is necessary to better determine the distribution range and population status of this species, and to understand how it is impacted by bushmeat hunting.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it has a moderate extent of occurrence of 23,945 km2, occurs in several protected areas and is considered to be relatively common in suitable habitats. Populations should be monitored given it is at risk of habitat loss and hunting.
habitat: It is a terrestrial species that has been recorded from primary lowland tropical moist forest and is also frequently caught in cacao agroforest systems (Clough et al. 2010). It is presumed to be a frugivorous species.
threats: It is threatened by habitat loss, likely resulting from logging, mining and the conversion of land for agricultural use. It is estimated that at least 10% of Sulawesi's forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Additionally, this species was recorded in a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021). It may hybridise with other Rattus species, though impacts are unknown.
population: This species is considered to be relatively abundant within suitable habitat (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is known only from northeastern Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it has been found from coastal areas (Musser and Carleton 2005) to 1,500 m asl (Handika et al. 2021). A 2019 survey recorded this species in the western edge of Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
useTrade: This species has been recorded as hunted and traded in markets in North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas, including Bongani Nani Wartabone National Park, Tangkoko Dua Saudara Nature Reserve and Gunung Ambang Nature Reserve. Further studies are needed to improve knowledge of its distribution, abundance and ecology.

rationale: The exact geographic range of Prosciurillus alstoni still requires resolution, as many montane areas have received little or no survey effort for small mammals. Whilst this species appears to have a fairly large distribution range on Sulawesi, it is a forest obligate and appears to be restricted to lower elevations, where habitat loss is most severe. It is likely that habitat loss within its range is approaching the 30% required to qualify for Vulnerable under criterion A2. Therefore, this species is assessed as Near Threatened.
habitat: Prosciurillus alstoni has only been encountered in primary tropical lowland evergreen rainforest, ranging in elevation from 30 m asl (Kuala Navusu and Pinedapa) to 1,200 m asl (Sungai Tolewonu). This species inhabits the upper canopy, moving through this high tree layer along pathways formed by interlaced branches and woody vines (Musser et al. 2010). P. alstoni’s diet comprises soft fruit and insects, with a preference for figs (Musser et al. 2010). P. alstoni is not sympatric with any other member of the P. leucomus group but its range does overlap ranges of P. murinus, Rubrisciurus rubriventer, and the ground squirrel, Hyosciurus ileile (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss from human disturbance, agricultural conversion of land and deforestation for mining and logging (Whitten et al. 2012). Primary forest cover loss in the lowlands of Sulawesi between 2000 and 2012 was estimated to be 7.1% (Margono et al. 2014). In Central and Southeast Sulawesi specifically, it is estimated that between 11–13% of tree cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: There is nothing known about the population of this species.
range: Prosciurillus alstoni is endemic to Sulawesi. Its geographic distribution ranges from the eastern part of the core of Sulawesi through its eastern and southeastern peninsulas, including Kabaena and Buton islands. P. alstoni may be restricted to lowland forests, since specimens have yet to be collected at elevations above 1,200 m asl (Musser et al. 2010). On the mainland of the southeastern peninsula, there are no records of specimens above 550 m asl (Musser et al. 2010).
useTrade: Squirrel species have been recorded in Sulawesi markets, but species-level identification is lacking (Latinne et al. 2020), so it is not known whether Prosciurillus alstoni is hunted.
conservationActions: Parts of this species range overlaps protected areas including the Rawa Aopa Watumohai National Park. Research on its population trends and abundance is needed.

rationale: This species is only known from a mountain range that has not been comprehensively surveyed for many decades. Based on the records available, its extent of occurrence is estimated to be 1,716 km2 which, combined with the fact that it is known from one location and may be under threat of habitat loss and hunting, would qualify this species for listing as Endangered under criterion B. However, its range and extent of occurrence could realistically be much larger, which would potentially lead to a listing of Least Concern. Therefore, adopting a precautionary approach, it is considered more appropriate to assess this species as Near Threatened (B1ab(iii)) based on the level of uncertainty surrounding its true distribution and impacts of threats. Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge about this species.
habitat: Prosciurillus abstrusus is one of the smallest-bodied of the species of tree squirrels endemic to Sulawesi (Musser et al. 2010). It is known only from montane forest habitats on Pegunungan Mekongga in the Southeastern Peninsula (the highest range on the southeastern peninsula of Sulawesi) (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is potentially threatened by hunting as well as habitat loss. Forest loss in Sulawesi was estimated to have exceed 10% between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020), largely driven by agriculture and logging, which may be increasing at higher elevations (Margono et al. 2014).
population: The abundance and population size of this species are not known, as it has not been recorded in surveys since the 1950s. It is potentially endemic to the Mengkoka Mts, but further research is required to confirm this.
range: This species is known only from the type locality in the Mengkoka Mts. in southeastern Sulawesi (Indonesia) from 1,500–2,000 m asl (Musser et al. 2010). It is known from the 30 original specimens collected in 1932 and by one additional specimen collected in the 1950s.
useTrade: Prosciurillus abstrusus is used as food by humans and represents a local livelihood.
conservationActions: This species is not known to occur in any actively protected area, though it is found in the proposed Mekongga National Park.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a wide distribution across Sulawesi, with a relatively large extent of occurrence of 262,554 km2, and it appears to be present across a wide elevational gradient wherever primary forest remains. It is thought to be relatively common in suitable habitats. Nonetheless, it may be under threat of habitat loss and hunting, and so populations should be monitored.
habitat: Prosciurillus murinus prefers primary forest from lowland tropical evergreen rain throughout the coasts and middle altitudes to tropical upper montane rain forests in high mountains (Musser et al. 2010). It is diurnal and arboreal and is commonly found in the understory of primary forest ranging from lowland evergreen rain forest habitats to montane landscapes (Musser et al. 2010). It feeds on soft fruits, seeds and insects (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by forest clearance due to small-scale agriculture, and at lower elevations due to forestry and mining operations. Primary forest loss across Sulawesi between 2000 and 2012 has been estimated to have been 7.1% in the lowlands and 2.7% in montane areas (Margono et al. 2014). It has been recorded as a species that is hunted in North Sulawesi (Lee et al. 2005).
population: The abundance and population size of this species are not known, but it is believed to be common (Musser et al. 2010). The records for this species are scattered across most of Sulawesi (Musser et al. 2010).
range: This species has been documented as occurring throughout mainland Sulawesi (Indonesia), with the exception of the eastern peninsula (Musser et al. 2010). It is also found on the small islands of Talisei and Lembeh, situated off the coast of the northeastern peninsula, and is likely to be found throughout Sulawesi where forest remains (Musser et al. 2010). It has been recorded at elevations from sea level up to 2,200 m asl (Musser et al. 2010). Prosciurillus murinus has also been observed on Sangihe Island in the Talaud Island group (Riley 2002), though, currently, its presence there is uncertain.
useTrade: It has been recorded as a species that is hunted in North Sulawesi (Lee et al. 2005).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas, such as Bogani Nani Wartabone National Park in northern Sulawesi. It would benefit from further surveys to improve knowledge of its population, distribution and potential threats.

rationale: This species is only known from few localities in the southern part of the central core of Sulawesi. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 2,271 km2, it could qualify as Endangered under criteria B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any ongoing, comprehensive surveys. It is possible its EOO is considerably larger, which would potentially lead to a listing of Least Concern. Therefore, considering the decline in extent and quality of forest habitat in Sulawesi, and adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as the intermediate category of Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: Specimens of Prosciurillus weberi were collected in areas once covered by tropical lowland evergreen rainforest. Otherwise, its ecological traits are undocumented and presently unknown. Its habits, however, are likely similar to other members of the P. leucomus group in that it occupies the upper canopy of primary forest and includes soft fruits, seeds and insects in its diet (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss for agriculture and logging (Whitten et al. 2012). Primary forest cover loss in the lowlands of Sulawesi between 2000 and 2012 was estimated to be 7.1% (Margono et al. 2014).
population: Nothing is known about population size or trends for this species
range: This squirrel is known from a few specimens collected in lowlands (up to 900 m asl) near Palopo and Masamba in the southern part of the central core of Sulawesi, Indonesia. Its actual distribution has yet to be resolved (Musser et al. 2010).
useTrade: Squirrel species have been recorded in Sulawesi markets, but species-level identification is lacking (Latinne et al. 2020), so it is not known whether Prosciurillus weberi is hunted.
conservationActions: No current conservation efforts are in place and it is not known if this species occurs within a protected area. Further research of its populations and ecology is needed.

rationale: This species is approaching threatened status under criterion B as it has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 5,391 km2 and is known from few locations. However, since it does not reach sufficient subcriteria (e.g., the timing and level of decline is unknown), it is listed as Near Threatened. There is a risk that the removal of forest habitat could significantly encroach into this species' range at higher elevations in the future, potentially qualifying it for threatened status. Further research is needed to improve knowledge of its distributional limits and population trends, as it is currently only known from few specimens.
habitat: This species has been recorded from tropical upper montane rain forest (Musser and Carleton 2005), slightly disturbed by human activities, close to a wooden hut (Musser and Durden 2002). It has more recently been found at lower elevations in the transitional tropical evergreen lowland-lower montane formations (Achmadi et al. 2014). It is not known if the species occurs in modified habitats, but it is presumed to be a primarily forest species. It is gracile, insectivorous, nocturnal, terrestrial, scansorial, and arboreal (Musser and Carleton 2005).
threats: This species is presumably threatened by deforestation, largely through small-scale firewood collection and clearance of land for subsistence cultivation. Loss of forest cover in Sulawesi is presumably less severe in upland and montane areas (Margono et al. 2014).
population: The population abundance is not known. It is known from a single specimen at the type locality, six captured in Gunung Gandang Dewata (Achmadi et al. 2014) and Mt Latimojong (K.C. Rowe and A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023). The species probably has a specialised ecology, which would account for the fact that regular surveys have not encountered it.
range: This species is known from the type locality of Gunung Tokala (02°13' S, 120°04' E) in central Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it was collected at 2,400 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has more recently been found at Gunung Gandang Dewata at elevations between 1,600 and 2,600 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2014). The species has not been recorded from intensively studied sites around Lore Lindu National Park in the east-central region, which suggest that it may be restricted to the southern highlands of the west-central mountain block in Sulawesi’s central core, but additional surveys are needed (Achamdi et al. 2014).
conservationActions: This species is present in Gandang Dewata National Park. Surveys are needed for this species, as no comprehensive trapping has taken place in the area of collection, and knowledge of its population, distribution and ecology is lacking.

rationale: This species is known from few locations with relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 16,949 km2. It may be at threat of habitat loss where it occurs. This species could therefore possibly qualify as Vulnerable under criterion B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and it might be present in additional locations. Further surveys could reveal a wider range. If its EOO is larger, this would potentially qualify this species for a listing outside of a threatened category. As such, considering the general decline in extent and quality of forest habitat in Sulawesi, and adopting a precautionary approach to select a category intermediate between Vulnerable and Least Concern, this species is assessed as Near Threatened (likely approaching B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This terrestrial insectivore has been found in tropical lowland evergreen rainforest (Musser and Carleton 2005) and in transitional habitat between lowland forest and primary lower montane forest (Achmadi et al. 2014). No further information on its ecology or habitats is known.
threats: The major threat is likely to be habitat loss and forest clearance due to expanding agriculture and logging, particularly at lower elevations. Surveys found much of the former rainforest habitat at the type locality had been converted to rice agriculture (L. Ruedas pers. comm.). In West Sulawesi, the extent of forest cover declined by 13.41% between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: There is no information on population status, and it is known only from specimens collected in the mid 1970s and 2011–2012 (Achmadi et al. 2014). Further survey work is needed to quantify occupancy, abundance and trends.
range: This species is known only from three localities: the mountain valley of Danau Lindu at 1,067 m asl; upper drainage of Sungai Miu in the Kulawi region at 823 m asl, Central Sulawesi (Musser and Carleton 2005); and from Gunung Gandang Dewata at 1,600 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2014).
useTrade: There is no use and trade information for this species.
conservationActions: This species has been found within Lore Lindu National Park and Gandang Dewata National Park, though biodiversity conservation in these areas has been limited. The type locality, Danau Lindu, is now an area heavily used by humans. Furthermore, there is urgent need for additional survey work (using, e.g., pit-fall traps) to determine the range and population status of this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern due its large extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 103,506 km2 and its presence within protected areas. However, it is a forest obligate species that is mainly found in primary forest (old growth), which is threatened by habitat loss due to logging and agricultural activity, thus population assessments to ascertain the extent of this threat should be a priority.
habitat: This species is restricted to forest, the majority of specimens collected from tropical evergreen rain forest between sea level to 1,000 m asl; the exception is Gunung Ile-Ile where it was found in montane evergreen forest at 1,700 m asl (Musser et al. 2010). These squirrels are diurnal and likely forage in the upper canopy for soft fruit and insects (Musser et al. 2010).
threats: This species is threatened by forest clearing due to small-scale agriculture, and at lower elevations due to forestry and mining operations. Between 2000 and 2012 in Indonesia there has been loss of lowland forests and an increasing loss of upland and montane primary forest as logging roads expand; nearly half of montane primary forest loss occurred within protected areas (Margono et al. 2014). In North Sulawesi, it is estimated that 108,334 ha of forest cover was lost between 2000 and 2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: This species likely occurs at low densities across its range. It is not encountered frequently, for example, surveys from the Binerean Cape in Northern Sulawesi detected the species very infrequently (Malir et al. 2017) and it is extremely difficult to study.
range: This species is restricted to the northern peninsula of Sulawesi (Indonesia) and the adjacent small island of Pulau Lembeh, and records have been found from sea-level up to 1,700 m asl (Musser et al. 2010). Bumbarujaba is the most southern collection site for Pprosciurillus leucomus, and it is not known how much farther south it may occur (Musser et al. 2010). More recent records have been obtained from Tanjung Binerean and Bolaang Mongondow Selatan, North Sulawesi (Malir et al. 2017).
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas.

rationale: This species is only known from one locality. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 490 km2, it could qualify as Endangered under criteria B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any ongoing, comprehensive surveys. If its EOO is considerably larger, it could potentially qualify as Least Concern. Therefore, adopting a precautionary approach, it is considered more appropriate to assess this species as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This species is found in montane forest, and is not likely to occur in degraded habitats.
threats: A major threat to this species is likely to be habitat loss. In South and Southeast Sulawesi, approximately 9–13% of forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Although the impacts of forest conversion for agriculture or logging are perhaps most severe at lower elevations, such threats have started to encroach on higher points in Sulawesi. In this region, habitat availability is reduced where cacao plantations have been created and primary/secondary mosaics have resulted from logging, and montane forest is scarce and scattered over peaks separated by deep valleys (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
population: This species is known only from the type series of three specimens collected in 1932 (Musser and Carleton 2005). Thus, there is no current population information available.
range: This species is known only from the type locality: Tanke Salokko in southeastern Sulawesi, Indonesia (03°35' S, 121°15' E, at 1,500 m asl) (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is possible that it might occur across a broader range, and at higher elevations, than current records suggest, though there has been a lack of surveys in the area (A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: Some of this species' range occurs within the proposed Mekongga National Park. There is a need for further survey work to determine the current population status of this species and to better understand its limits of distribution.

rationale: This species is only known from one location. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 516 km2, it could qualify as Endangered under criterion B1, but the limits of its distribution are not completely clear and there have not been any ongoing, comprehensive surveys in the area. It is possible that its EOO is considerably larger, which would potentially lead to a listing of Least Concern. Therefore, adopting a precautionary approach, it is considered more appropriate to assess this species as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)). Further surveys are needed to improve knowledge of its range, population and threats.
habitat: This species is recorded from montane rainforest. Based on habitat requirements of congeners, it is unlikely to occur in degraded habitats.
threats: A major threat to this species is likely to be habitat loss. In South and Southeast Sulawesi, approximately 9–13% of forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Although the impacts of forest conversion for agriculture or logging are perhaps most severe at lower elevations, such threats have started to encroach on higher points in Sulawesi. In this region, habitat availability is reduced where cacao plantations have been created and primary/secondary mosaics have resulted from logging, and montane forest is scarce and scattered over peaks separated by deep valleys (Mortelliti et al. 2012).
population: There is no population information available for this species.
range: This species is known from the type locality of Tanke Salokko, the highest point in the Mekongga Range, in southeastern Sulawesi (03°35' S, 121°15' E), between 1,500 and 2,000 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005). Records previously reported from Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009) are considered to have been assigned incorrectly. Thus, this species may be isolated on the Mekongga Range, but there has been a lack of surveys in the area (A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: Some of this species' range occurs within the proposed Mekongga National Park. There is a need for further survey work to determine the current population status of this species and to better understand its limits of distribution.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as it has a relatively large extent of occurrence of 213,055 km2, has been found across a broad elevation range and is not known to be undergoing a severe decline at present. However, it may be at risk of deforestation and hunting, thus, populations and threats should be monitored.
habitat: This terrestrial species is found in primary lowland tropical evergreen and montane forest, where it feeds on fruit, leaves, and insects (Musser 1982, Musser and Newcomb 1983). It is not known if it can be found outside of forest habitats.
threats: The habitat of this species at the lower elevations in its range is being deforested for timber, firewood and conversion to agricultural land. It may be trapped locally for food in the northeast of its range.
population: Detection rate is variable across its range, thus abundance is difficult to determine.
range: This species is found in northeastern Sulawesi, where it has been recorded from a few localities, from the central core of the island (Musser and Carleton 2005) to Mt Mekongga and Mt Latimojong. The elevational range is from 760 to 2,260 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005). A 2013 survey of Mt Dako and a 2014 survey of Mt Buliohuto produced new records for the species (Handika et al. 2021).
useTrade: It may be trapped locally for food in the northeast of its range.
conservationActions: It has been recorded from several protected areas such as Lore Lindu National Park.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as it is thought to be relatively widespread, with a large extent of occurrence of 371,336 km2, and is moderately common in suitable habitats below 800 m asl. However, it is at risk of habitat loss, thus populations should be monitored.
habitat: This arboreal species is found in lowland tropical evergreen rainforest (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is not likely to occur in secondary habitats, but it may be present in lightly disturbed forest patches. It has a very long tail relative to head and body length, unlike any other species in the genus, all of which are terrestrial and have relatively short tails (Musser and Newcomb 1983, Breed and Musser 1991).
threats: The major threat is likely to be habitat loss, particularly in lowland areas where this species occurs. It is estimated that at least 10% of Sulawesi's forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020), primarily driven by logging and agriculture. In the northeast, this species is likely to be found in bushmeat markets (Sulawesi Small Mammal Workshop pers. comm. 2023).
population: It is moderately common in primary forest, and is not difficult to trap, thus it is represented by many more specimens than other species of the genus (Musser and Carleton 2005).
range: This species is found throughout the lowlands of much of Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser and Carleton 2005). Subfossil specimens are known from the southwestern peninsula, suggesting that it occurs throughout Sulawesi in forest habitat. A 2013 survey of Mt Dako and a 2014 survey of Mt Buliohuto failed to record the species (Handika et al. 2021), however, previous surveys did find it in these areas (Musser 2014). It is found around sea level to 800 m asl (K.C. Rowe and A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023).
useTrade: In the northeast, this species is likely to be found in bushmeat markets (Sulawesi Small Mammal Workshop pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: It is likely present in several protected areas, such as Lore Lindu National Park. Research into its population trends and threat impacts would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is approaching threatened status under criterion B as it has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 8,894 km2 and is known from few locations. However, since it does not meet sufficient subcriteria (e.g., the timing and level of decline is unknown), it is listed as Near Threatened. There is a risk that the removal of forest habitat could significantly encroach into this species' range at higher elevations in the future, potentially qualifying it for threatened status. Further research is needed to improve knowledge of its distributional limits and population trends, as it is currently only known from few specimens.
habitat: This terrestrial species is found in primary montane tropical evergreen rainforest (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is not known if the species can persist in disturbed or modified habitats.
threats: This species may be threatened by deforestation for agriculture and logging, which has began to encroach on higher elevations (Harris et al. 2014). It is estimated that at least 10% of Sulawesi's forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: The abundance of this species is not well known, but it has not been detected within Lore Lindu National Park since the 1970s (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023), thus populations may have declined.
range: This poorly known species is known only from a few montane localities (Gunung Lehio, Gunung Kanino and Gunung Nokilalaki) in central Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser and Carleton 2005), from 1,280 to 2,287 m asl. It may range more widely in the central montane regions. This species was recorded in surveys of Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009), though such records are considered to potentially be misidentifications.
conservationActions: It is was previously known from Lore Lindu National Park but has not been detected there since the 1970s, as more current records (Maryanto et al. 2009) are likely to be misidentifications. Further field surveys are needed to learn more about the habitat, ecology, distribution range and threats to this poorly known species.

rationale: This species is only known from two localities. Based on its potentially restricted range and small extent of occurrence of 8,347 km2, as well as decline in extent and quality of forest habitat in that region and at elevations where this species occurs, it is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B. Further surveys are needed to monitor its population and threats.
habitat: It was collected in 1918 in primary lowland tropical evergreen rainforest, very little is known about its ecology but it may have specialised feeding habits (Musser and Carleton 2005; G. Musser pers. comm.). It is not known if the species can persist in modified habitats.
threats: A major threat to this species is likely to be habitat loss. On Sulawesi between 2000 and 2012 there was significant forest loss, but mainly in lowland and wetland areas (Margono et al. 2014) and primarily due to logging (Miettinen et al. 2011) or conversion for agriculture. In Central Sulawesi, between 2000–2017, it is estimated that at least 11% of forest cover was lost (Supriatna et al. 2020).
population: It is only known from three specimens and may be considered rare since local surveys have not recorded additional observations (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is endemic to Sulawesi, and known only from three specimens: two caught at the type locality in 1918 (Pinedapa, in central Sulawesi) and one caught in 2010 on Mt Balease (Rowe et al. 2019), as well as a few subfossil fragments collected in the southwest of the island (Musser 1984, Musser and Carleton 2005). It has been recorded from at least 900 m asl. Records previously reported in 2000–2001 from Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009) may have been assigned incorrectly.
conservationActions: Since the extent of its distribution is unknown, it is unclear whether it occurs in any protected areas. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, reproduction and ecology of this species.

rationale: Taeromys taerae is endemic to Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it has a relatively large extent of occurrence of 390,512 km2 and is considered potentially common and abundant in some areas. There is no evidence to suggest that it is declining at a rate fast enough to warrant listing in a threatened category. This species is therefore assessed as Least Concern, though its population, and response to threats such as habitat loss and hunting, should be monitored.
habitat: It inhabits intact montane forest and is not known to use degraded forest areas.
threats: It is likely to be affected by ongoing habitat loss. The loss of forest cover in North Sulawesi was estimated to reach 6.9% between 2000 to 2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Additionally, this species may be at risk of hunting; in a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi, this species was recorded (Laatung et al. 2021).
population: It is known from limited specimens, but is potentially common and abundant in some regions such as Mt Dako (K.C. Rowe. pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is found in the highlands of northeastern Sulawesi, where it is known from three nearby localities from 600–800 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005) as well as from surveys of Mt Dako at 1,600 m asl in 2013 and Mt Buliohuto in 2014 (Handika et al. 2021).
useTrade: This species was recorded in a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It occurs in Mt Dako Nature Reserve. There is a need for further survey work to determine the population status of this species and the extent of its distribution.

rationale: This species is approaching threatened status under criterion B as it has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 3,843 km2 and is known from two locations. However, since it does not reach sufficient sub-criteria (e.g., decline is unknown), it is listed as Near Threatened. There is a risk that the removal of forest for agricultural purposes could significantly encroach into this species' range and at higher elevations in the future. Further research is needed to improve knowledge of its distributional limits and population trends, as it is currently only known from few specimens.
habitat: It is currently only known from transitional lowland/montane and mature montane forest (Esselstyn et al. 2012). It is considered a vermivorous, ground-dwelling, nocturnal species (Esselstyn et al. 2012).
threats: Nothing is known about specific threats to this species, however, continued loss of forest habitat in general on Sulawesi could be a risk. Deforestation across Sulawesi between 2000 and 2017 (largely driven by agricultural land conversion and logging) exceeded 10% (Supriatna et al. 2020), though this threat is considered more severe at elevations lower than where this species is found.
population: No population information is available for this species as it is only known from three specimens collected in 2011 and 2016 (H. Handika pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is known from Mt. Gandang Dewata and Mt. Latimojong, Sulawesi, Indonesia, between 1,571 and 2,050 m asl (Esselstyn et al. 2012). It may occur in other mountains in the region, but data are limited (Esselstyn et al. 2012). The species is related to other shrew-rats that are restricted to the island of Sulawesi.
conservationActions: It occurs in Gandang Dewata National Park and Latimojong Protection Forest. Further research into its ecology and distribution is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as it has a large extent of occurrence of 73,310 km2, occurs across a relatively wide elevational range, can be found in at least one protected area and is not known to be undergoing any significant level of decline. Nonetheless, further research is needed to clarify its distribution and population trends.
habitat: This is a scansorial species found in montane primary evergreen forest (Musser and Carleton 2005).
threats: This species is likely under threat from habitat loss driven by logging or conversion for agriculture; between 2000–2017, approximately 11% of forest cover was lost across Sulawesi (Supriatna et al. 2020). Although forest removal is more severe at lower elevations, this threat could encroach onto higher elevations.
population: Although this species has a comparatively wide range, it is considered to be relatively uncommon compared to its sympatric congener Maxomys hellwaldii (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species has been recorded in numerous locations across Sulawesi, Indonesia: the type locality of Gunung Karua central Sulawesi (Rantekaroa, Quarles Mts. at 1,829 m asl); Gunung Balease in central Sulawesi (betwen 900–1,150 m asl); Gunung Tanke Salokko at 1,500 m asl in the southeast peninsula (Musser and Carleton 2005); Gunung Dako in the northern peninsula; Gandang Dewata in west Sulawesi, and Gunung Latimojong to the south.
conservationActions: It has been recorded in protected areas such as Gandang Dewata National Park. Further survey work is needed to determine the geographic range and population status of this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large extent of occurrence of 382,834 km2, potential presence in protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at a rate fast enough to qualify it for listing in a more threatened category. Nonetheless, research is needed to improve knowledge of its population trends, impacts of hunting, and taxonomy.
habitat: This terrestrial species occurs in tropical lowland evergreen rain forest (Musser 1991). It can be found in disturbed habitats close to forested areas. It has been recorded in oil palm plantations (Ikhsan et al. 2020).
threats: It is threatened to some degree by habitat loss and degradation, primarily driven by conversion for agriculture, human settlements, logging and mining. On average across Sulawesi, it is estimated that approximately 11% of total forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). This species is also at risk from hunting, and it was identified in a 2018 study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021).
population: It is considered an abundant species.
range: The species occurs throughout Sulawesi, Indonesia, from sea level to 1,006 m asl (Musser and Holden 1991).
useTrade: It is hunted and sold for food (Laatung et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It is possibly present in Lore Lindu National Park (Maryanto et al. 2009) and presumably is also present in a number of other protected areas. Further studies are needed of its taxonomy, as it may represent multiple species (K.C. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because it has a relatively large extent of occurrence of 30,954 km2 and is considered common in suitable habitats. Nonetheless, there has been a decline in habitat across its range, and this species would benefit from population monitoring and increased survey effort to study its distribution, trends and ecology.
habitat: This species has been recorded in montane tropical rainforest formations (Musser and Carleton 2005). It has only been collected in relatively undisturbed forest. It is generally considered to be a terrestrial species (G. Musser pers. comm.) and folivorous.
threats: Habitat decline in Sulawesi has been well documented, with approximately 11.04% of forest cover lost from Central Sulawesi (where this species is found) between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Much of the forest loss in this region is caused by expanding agriculture and logging activities.
population: It is relatively common within suitable habitats (K. Rowe and A. Achmadi pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is endemic to central Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it is known only from a few montane localities, including Mt Gandang Dewata, Mt Latimojong, Mt Rorekatimbo and Mt Torompupu. It has been recorded between 1,600 and 2,300 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005; K. Rowe pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Lore Lindu National Park and Gandang Dewata National Park. Further studies are needed to clarify the distribution and ecology of this species.

rationale: Saiga is assessed as Near Threatened because of extreme data uncertainty which makes an assessment as Endangered, Vulnerable, or Least Concern equally plausible. The previous assessment considered that Saiga crossed the threshold between Critically Endangered and Endangered in May 2015 and met Endangered under criterion A4 based on an observed, estimated, and projected decline of more than 50% over 11 years (three generations), commencing in May 2015, due to the risk of mass mortality events (MME) from outbreaks of disease, severe climate, and poaching for the illegal trade in horns. Under the 5-year rule, a reassessment was due in 2020.Numbers in Kazakhstan, which holds more than 98% of the global Saiga population, have recovered dramatically, increasing by about 1,100% between 2015 and 2022 and showing annual increases of up to 40%, necessitating a reappraisal. The total population size in Kazakhstan was estimated at 1,320,000 in May 2022, and there are a further ca. 20,000 in Russia and Mongolia.  Saiga are susceptible to a range of infectious diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease, brucellosis, and others, and their occurrence in large herds makes them liable to large-scale die-offs. Four major disease outbreaks since 2010 have caused mass mortality events (MME). The most severe outbreak caused the death of over 200,000 Saiga in one population in Kazakhstan over the course of three weeks in May 2015. The cause of this outbreak (and the suspected cause in the earlier two) has been shown to be haemorrhagic septicaemia possibly caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida. The most recent MME occurred in the Mongolian saiga population in early 2017, caused by peste de petits ruminants (PPR), when an estimated 54% of the population died.PPR is relatively new to the region, but is still spreading through Central Asia, posing a threat to all saiga populations. Pasteurella is endemic in Saiga, and the high lethal levels of mortality implicated in the Kazakhstan MMEs are believed to have been triggered by environmental conditions including abnormally high humidity and temperature. Warm and wet climatic conditions are expected to increase in frequency due to effects of recorded and predicted climate change. Given the Saiga’s inherent vulnerability to disease, likely exacerbated by climate-related and environmental stressors in the future, and the expanding interface between domestic livestock and Saiga across their global range which increases the risks of disease transfer, the risk of disease outbreaks causing significant mortality remains very high. The species is also threatened by climatic factors, poaching, and habitat degradation. Severe winter conditions known as dzhut or dzuud, consisting of heavy snowfall, sustained, very cold temperatures, and/or an ice crust preventing access to forage, are also known to cause high mortality in Saiga. Poaching for the international illegal trade in horns and local illegal trade in meat is a constant threat and requires the current stringent controls to be maintained. Local pressures include competition with livestock, overgrazing, steppe fires, drought, and damage to natural springs.The most severe recent MME killed around 80% of one population in Kazakhstan in 2015. Using an 11-year (three generation) window starting in 2020, a new disease outbreak on the same scale and resulting in the same level of mortality in the largest current population (801,000), would result in a reduction of the global population of 52%. A less lethal outbreak could cause a population reduction of 30–50%. These scenarios would justify a category of Endangered or Vulnerable, respectively, under criterion A4e. However, it is now clear that the rapid recent population increases resulted in full recovery of the affected population within a few years of the MME occurrence, and certainly in less than 11 years. If these population growth rates were to continue, Saiga would not meet the thresholds for either Endangered or Vulnerable for the full duration of the 3-generation window, in which case, Least Concern would apply. There are several caveats:1. Saiga population increases on this scale over almost a decade are unprecedented and may not be sustained for demographic or environmental reasons (e.g. a sequence of severe winter conditions or summer droughts). 2. The timing, location, severity, and frequency of MMEs is unpredictable and the possibility of a more lethal MME, simultaneous MMEs in more than one Saiga population, or consecutive MMEs within the same time-window cannot be discounted.3. An upsurge in poaching (e.g. due to relaxation of protection efforts, and/or an increase in the market price for Saiga horn) could exacerbate the effects of an MME, hinder recovery, or cause a substantial population reduction on its own.In view of the multiple unpredictable factors, and the potential interplay between them, the Endangered, Vulnerable, and Least Concern categories are all considered to be equally plausible, amounting to considerable and genuine data uncertainty. Saiga is therefore assessed as Near Threatened.
habitat: The Saiga is a nomadic herding species that inhabits open dry steppe grasslands and semi-arid deserts of Central Asia. Typical habitat consists of flat open areas covered with low-growing vegetation, allowing animals to run quickly; areas of broken terrain or dense cover are generally avoided, but animals may stray into these out of necessity or shelter in them during strong winds, they range from near or below sea level in the Caspian basin to ca 1,600 m in Mongolia (Heptner et al. 1961, Bekenov et al. 1998).Saiga are migratory, with most populations having widely separated summer (northern) and winter (southern) ranges. S. t. mongolica is not migratory. The NW Caspian population no longer migrates and the Ural population makes limited seasonal movements. The species lives in large herds, usually up to thousands of individuals. It has a high rate of reproduction and recruitment since females usually breed at 7-8 months and males in their second year (Heptner et al. 1961) and females often bear twins. In years with a favourable climate the population can increase by up to 60% in a single year (Chan et al. 1995). Very few animals in a population are more than 3.5 years old, indicating that the population is almost completely renewed after four years (Bekenov et al. 1998). Males defend a harem of 5-10 females and gestation lasts about 5 months (Heptner et al. 1961). Saiga are grazers and have been recorded feeding on a wide range of grasses and herbaceous plant species.For full details of the biology of the species see Heptner et al. (1961) and Sokolov and Zhirnov (1998).
threats: Saiga are susceptible to several diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease, brucellosis, and others, which can cause large numbers of deaths (Robinson 2018). There have been four recent mass-mortality events MME). In 2010, around two-thirds of a calving aggregation of 20,000 in the Ural population died of a peracute respiratory disease with bloat, and this was followed in 2011 by a smaller die-off of several hundreds of Saiga with similar clinical signs, immediately after calving, and grazing in the exact same location as the earlier MME, suggesting a site-specific cause. Pasteurellosis was implicated based on bacteriology, but very little pathology was undertaken and the clinical signs were more aligned with fog fever or bloat, caused by an excess of protein-rich grass (Kock et al. 2018, Robinson et al. 2019).In 2015, more than 200,000 Saiga died within three weeks in central Kazakhstan. The proximate cause of death, based on multiple strands of evidence, was confirmed as haemorrhagic septicaemia caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida type B (Kock et al. 2018, Robinson et al. 2019). Statistical modelling suggests that there was unusually high relative humidity and temperature in the days leading up to the outbreak; temperature and humidity anomalies were also observed in two previous similar events in the same region. The modelled influence of environmental covariates is consistent with known drivers of haemorrhagic septicemia. Given the Saiga population’s vulnerability to mass mortality and the likely exacerbation of climate-related and environmental stressors in the future, management of risks to population viability, such as poaching and viral livestock disease, is urgently needed, as well as robust ongoing veterinary surveillance (Kock et al. 2018).On 22nd December 2016 the first death of a Mongolian Saiga (S. t. mongolica) was reported by herders to the local authorities in Darvi soum (district) in the Khuisiin Gobi. Hundreds of live and dead Saiga were subsequently observed with a PPR-like signs. Samples were confirmed at the Mongolia State Central Veterinary Laboratory (SCVL) on 6th January 2017 to contain PPR virus and gene sequencing confirmed the virus to be highly similar to the virus recorded in sheep and goats. The Saiga infection developed rapidly into a full-blown epidemic and by the end of January; death and infection were reported across most of Mongolian Saiga range (Kock 2017). Based on carcass counts, over 54% of the population is estimated to have died. PPR is spreading through Central Asia, and infects a range of wild and domestic ungulate species, with the reservoir hosts being sheep and goats. Saigas appear to be uniquely susceptible to high levels of mortality from this disease (Pruvot et al. 2020). Saiga share many parasites with livestock, and in the past have been severely affected by some of these parasites (e.g. the Mongolian saiga gadfly that went extinct when saiga numbers were at their lowest levels in the 1920s). The presence of parasites generally does not cause mortality, but could interact with other factors such as climate change to reduce survival (Khanyari et al. 2022). Uncontrolled hunting for horns and meat caused the first major decline in saiga in the early 20th century. A surge in poaching for the horns of the males following the break-up of the former USSR in the late 1980s-early 1990s also led to a catastrophic fall in Saiga numbers. Selective hunting of males and subsequent distortion of the sex ratio further affected reproduction by heavily skewing the sex ratio (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). Evidence from Russia indicated that selective harvesting had left a skewed population containing few adult males, many females without young, and the population close to reproductive collapse (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). Extensive anti-poaching measures have been implemented, along with education programmes, training for customs and border officials, and action in end-user countries, resulting in a reduction in poaching and trade. This situation is entirely dependent on stringent enforcement and any relaxation of existing efforts can be expected to cause an upsurge in illegal killing and trade. Extreme climatic events pose a threat, both summer droughts and severe winters, especially a set of conditions known as dzuud or dzhut when heavy prolonged heavy snow cover, sustained very low temperatures, and/or an ice-crust preventing access to forage. During harsh winters, Saiga mortality in local populations can be up to 50%, followed by recovery in the next 2-3 years (Bekenov et al. 1998. The potential impacts of climate change on Saiga populations are poorly understood at present and modelling and vulnerability assessments are needed to better understand these.Loss or degradation of steppe habitats due to conversion for agriculture and overgrazing, as well as competition with livestock have affected some parts of the range. The Saiga population in eastern Kalmkyia, Russia, co-exists with very high numbers of sheep and goats (1,328,300 in 2019; Smelyansky et al. 2022/2023). Regular steppe fires pose an additional threat to the habitat in Kalmykia (Shinkarenko and Berdengalieva 2022/2023). although fires in moderation may promote flushes of vegetation on which Saiga preferentially graze.In Ural, the rapidly growing Saiga population is causing increasing concern about by local communities over damage to crops, competition for pasture and water, and concern about disease transmission. In Mongolia, livestock grazing pressure and competition with livestock are high, and habitat is reported as severely fragmented. The Saiga's main water sources are seasonally occupied by herders and their livestock, limiting access and causing damage. Linear infrastructure (railways, roads, pipelines, and a border fence) are impacting Saiga populations, particularly Ustyurt and Betpak-dala, and these negative impacts will increase with upcoming infrastructure projects, unless mitigation measures are implemented (CMS 2021).The unprecedented increase in the size of the Ural population in Kazakhstan (801,000 in May 2022) has led to complaints from farmers in the region of damage to crops. A conservation and management strategy for the Ural population has been developed in response (CMS 2023).The European population specifically is threatened by the current geopolitical isolation of Russia, such that international conservation support, funding and networking cannot include this population at the moment. For example, in 2022, the USFWS funded a portfolio of projects on saiga conservation along the trade supply chain, aiming to produce the evidence base underpinning transformative change towards sustainability. These projects go from on-the-ground actions in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Mongolia, to stockpile management in Thailand and consumer demand in Japan, Singapore and China. The European saiga population is not part of this portfolio as funding from most overseas sources  cannot be directed at conservation in Russia at the moment.Finally, the low levels of genetic diversity found in all Saiga populations (Rey-Iglesia et al. 2022) potentially reduce the capacity of the species to adapt to emerging diseases and environmental changes.
population: Historically, herds may have numbered in the millions, however counting methods were unreliable until the introduction of robust methods in several of the populations from the 2000s. Excessive hunting reduced Saiga numbers to an estimated total of ca. 1,000 by the early 20th century (Heptner et al. 1961) though the accuracy of this estimate is unclear. The species received legal protection in 1919 and soon began to recover. By 1960 Saiga numbers had reached an estimated 540,000 in Russia and 1,300,000 in Kazakhstan (Linnard 1963). Commercial harvests resumed in the 1950s and continued until 1990. There were still an estimated 1,250,000 Saiga in the mid-1970s.In Russia, the Saiga population steeply declined along with land reclamation of the Volga basin, but the species remained numerous. In the 1970s the population recovered to ca. 700,000-800,000 as a result of hunting regulations. In 1980 there were an estimated 380,000 individuals, in 1996 there were 196,000, but by the year 2000 just 26,000 (see Milner-Gulland et al. 2001 for annual survey results for 1980–2000).Saiga numbers fell catastrophically from 1989 on, when political and economic changes accompanying the break-up of the USSR led to weakening of nature protection systems and severe economic hardship, while at the same time, international borders were opened up, enhancing the opportunities for trading Saiga horn (Mallon 2016b and references therein). Poaching for horns surged and large numbers were killed locally for meat. The largest population of Saiga fell to 4% of its estimated 1990 size and other populations also suffered large reductions (Milner-Gulland et al. 2001). Evidence from Russia indicated that selective harvesting had left a skewed population containing few adult males, many females without young, and the population close to reproductive collapse (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). The full scale of the catastrophic decline was detailed by Arylov et al. (2004). Numbers in Kazakhstan fell to only 21,000 in 2003. The species was assessed as Critically Endangered in 2002. A wide range of conservation measures was implemented and Saiga numbers stabilized then increased (Milner-Gulland 2010). The largest population, in Betpakdala, Kazakhstan, grew by 76% annually during 2003 and 2010, demonstrating the resilience of the species. However, poaching and other factors reduced Saiga numbers in Russia and caused a 47% decrease in Ustyurt during 2009-2010. In May 2010 a disease outbreak killed ca 12,000 Saiga in the Ural population, a 31% loss. Nevertheless, numbers continued to grow overall and by spring 2015 there were >300,000 Saiga in Kazakhstan, plus a few thousand each in in Russia and Mongolia. Then in September 2015 a mass die-off occurred in Betpakdala, the largest population, with at least 200,000 dying in the course of three weeks, representing >80% of that population and >60% of the global population (Milner-Gulland 2015, Kock et al. 2018). The population in Kazakhstan has recovered dramatically, growing by about 1100% between 2015 and 2022, and showing annual increases up to 40%. The aerial census in May 2022 estimated a total of 1,320,000 Saiga in Kazakhstan (801,000 in Ural, 479,000 in Betpak-dala, 28,000 in Ustyurt) (Anon. 2022/2023). The size of the Ural population is now higher than at any time in recent memory.In Russia, a survey in 2020 by WWF-Russia using drones estimated 6,350 in the NW Caspian population (Safronova et al. 2022/2023). There are an estimated 4000 resident Saiga around Lake Bulukhta and in 2020 around 28,000-33,000 occurred seasonally in the Trans-Volga region (Smelyansky et al. 2022/23). A small population in eastern Kazakhstan not covered by the annual surveys may number around 2,000. Dash et al. (1977) estimated only 200 Mongolian Saiga. That population reached ca. 3,000 in 1998 and 5,200 in 2000, helped by favourable climatic conditions and active conservation measures. Numbers fell again between 2000 and 2002 as a result of severe winters and summer drought. The decline continued in 2002–2003, mainly because of poaching. Estimated numbers were 1,020 in 2003, and 750 in January 2004. However, numbers then increased steadily to ca. 11,000 in 2016, when an outbreak of peste de petits ruminants (PPR) killed around 54% of the population. This population has also now recovered. The annual survey by WWF-Mongolia in November 2022 estimated 13,925, a 38.2% increase on the previous year (Chimeddorj 2022/2023a).The global Saiga population in March 2023 is therefore estimated to number about 1,344,275 (ca 1,008,200 mature individuals). Numbers in all current populations are increasing, albeit at different rates and with different levels of uncertainty around the estimates (CMS 2021). Counts made using appropriate methods (aerial surveys with strip sampling in Kazakhstan, ground surveys with distance sampling in Mongolia) enable precision of the count to be estimated, and reduce, but do not eliminate, bias. Expert assessments, as carried out in Russia and Uzbekistan, are prone to unquantifiable levels of bias. For wide-ranging ungulates such as the Saiga, even well-conducted counts are likely to be underestimates, and the degree of underestimation increases as population gets smaller and more fragmented, because the animals are harder to detect. This means that population declines may appear worse, and increases faster, than they really are (McConville et al. 2008).
range: Saiga once inhabited the steppes and semi-desert regions of south-eastern Europe, across Central Asia to Mongolia and north-west China, but the original range has been greatly reduced. In the 18th century the range of the Saiga extended across the south-eastern steppes of Europe from the north-west side of the Caspian to the foothills of the Carpathians, at about 25 °E (Heptner et al. 1961). The European range covered the territories of modern-day Russia, Ukraine, Moldova, and probably the eastern part of Romania. Early reports of Saiga occurrence in Poland refer to the historic borders in the mid-1800s (Heptner et al. 1961) and the species has never been recorded within the current territory of Poland. The former European range has been greatly reduced. Saiga became extinct in Moldova and Ukraine in the 18th century, and by the 1920s-1930s the European range was restricted to the Kalmyk steppes (Heptner et al. 1961). Saiga disappeared from China in the middle of the 20th century (Cui et al. 2017). In 1958 the global range covered an estimated 2.5 million km² (Heptner et al. 1961).There are five main Saiga populations: one in Russia (North-West pre-Caspian), three predominantly in Kazakhstan (Ural, Ustiurt, Betpak-dala), and one in Mongolia. The principal Russian population occurs in the steppes north-west of the Caspian Sea in Kalmykia and adjoining parts of Astrakhan Region. Beginning in 2015, small numbers of Saiga began to be seen in Orenburg State Reserve, and also in the Saratov, Volgograd, and Astrakhan provinces, having dispersed from the expanding Ural population in Kazakhstan. In 2018-2021 numbers in these parts of Russia increased when the region was impacted by a series of droughts. This population is seasonal, from around April to September; very few remain in winter, except for a small sedentary population around Lake Bulukhta (Smelyansky et al. 2022/2023). However as the Ural population in Kazakhstan increases, dispersal may result in Saiga numbers in the Russian part of the range also increasing and more becoming permanently resident.The three Kazakhstan populations are located in Ural in the north-west (which is partially transboundary with Russia), Betpak-dala in central Kazakhstan, and Ustyurt in the south. Animals from the Ustyurt population migrate south in winter into Uzbekistan, in some years reaching Turkmenistan, returning in spring. These transboundary movements have declined in range and frequency and no Saiga have not been seen in Turkmenistan for several years. The number reaching Uzbekistan has also declined, further limited by construction of a border fence. There is a small outlying population east of the main Betpak-dala population, in the Semipalatinsk region.The nominate subspecies also formerly occurred in the Dzungarian Gobi of far south-western Mongolia and is assumed to have been a transboundary population with China, but became extinct in the 1960s. The Mongolian subspecies S. t. mongolica occurs in western Mongolia, north of the Altai mountains, which separate its range from the nominate subpopulations. Mongolian Saiga once occurred through the Great Lakes Basin from the north-west corner, east to approximately 101°E (Bannikov 1954), but both range and numbers became severely reduced. In the 1980s the range was small, and centred on Shargiin Gobi and Khuisiin Gobi with a small satellite population in Mankhan soum (district). The range expanded during the 1990s-2000s as a result of favourable climatic conditions and Saiga have now occupied Dorgon Tal, and Khomiin Tal (east of Khar Nuur), and moved north into Uvs aimag (province). The area of distribution in Khaliun and Sharga districts has also expanded. The Mankhan subpopulation has also extended its range but is still isolated from the core populations. The current northern limit is about 48030’N and eastern limit about 95030’E. Saiga are still absent from the eastern part of their historic range in the Lakes Valley (Biger Nuur, Boon Tsagaan Nuur, Orog Nuur).
useTrade: The horns of male Saiga are highly valued in Traditional Asian Medicine (Chan et al. 1995), while meat and hides have been used in saiga range states for centuries.  A legal harvest, predominately for meat, with fixed quotas operated from the 1950s to 1990. These harvests were formerly conducted on an industrial scale, using trucks , each with a team of up to 20 hunters. For example, west of the Volga River, 120,000–150,000 Saiga were harvested per year during 1957–1962 (Linnard 1963). A recent study in Singapore demonstrated high levels of use of saiga-containing products (19% of Chinese Singaporeans reported using it as their main medication for ‘heatiness’ in 2019; Doughty et al. 2019). Both China and Singapore have reported stockpiles of several tons of Saiga horn each. Meat is eaten locally and traded within the range. All aspects of sustainable use of Saiga are considered in a recent report (Milner-Gulland et al. 2020).
conservationActions: Saiga are protected in all range states but the level of enforcement varies. Anti-poaching efforts in Kazakhstan and other countries have been intensified over the last 10 years. Saiga are listed on the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) Appendix II and the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) Appendix II. The CMS Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) Concerning Conservation, Restoration and Sustainable Use of the Saiga Antelope came into effect in 2006 and has been signed by all five range states and ten Cooperating Organizations (local and international NGOs). The MoU has an associated Medium-Term International Work Programme (MTIWP) setting out a framework for conservation action by all partners. Technical coordination for the MOU is undertaken by the Saiga Conservation Alliance and Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan in close collaboration with the CMS Secretariat. The MTIWP is reviewed and updated periodically at technical workshops preceding CMS MoU range state meetings. In April 2019, a joint CMS-CITES technical workshop was held on Vilm Island, Germany, where a revised Medium Term International Work Programme for 2021-2025 was drafted and later approved by the range states.Since 2002 both CMS and CITES have worked in close cooperation, with Saiga as one of their joint target species. The CMS-CITES Joint Work Programme 2015-2020, adopted at the 42nd meeting of the CMS Standing Committee and the 65th  meeting of the CITES Standing Committee, outlines the current joint activities on Saiga. These focus on the implementation of the MTIWP, joint meetings and fundraising efforts (CMS 2021).At CITES COP18 in August 2019 the following decisions related to Saiga were adopted (Decisions 18.270-274). 1. To direct Range States, important consumer and trading countries to implement the CMS Medium-Term International Work Programme for the Saiga Antelope for 2016-2020 and for 2021-2025; 2. To encourage the range States to establish internal market controls for Saiga parts (including registration of stockpiles, labelling of parts and products, and registration of manufacturers and traders). 3. Subject to funding, the CITES Secretariat should consult with, and support, Range States and major consumer and trading states to manage their stockpiles and improve stockpile management. 4. CITES Parties also adopted a zero quota for wild specimens traded for commercial purposes, which entered into force on 16th November 2019 (CMS 2021).A conservation and management strategy for the Ural population has been developed in respone to concerns from farmers that the expanding population was damaging crops (CMS 2023).Population Monitoring In Kazakhstan a comprehensive monitoring programme covers nearly all of Saiga range. Since 2016, spring surveys of all three populations have been conducted using a standard methodology comprising aerial and ground surveys. Kazakhstan has also started implementing the SMART monitoring system for rangers. In Russia, aerial surveys using drones have been trialled. Ground-based monitoring by staff of the Chernye Zemli Biosphere Reserve and Stepnoi Sanctuary provides expert assessments, supplemented by opportunistic monitoring to give information on distribution and herd sizes outside these reserves. In Uzbekistan, a combination of participatory monitoring using motorbike transects and ground surveys gives a general impression of population change. In Mongolia, a comprehensive aerial survey was carried out in 2009/2010, and rangewide population monitoring using the distance sampling line transect approaches has been carried out annually since 2011, led by WWF-Mongolia. A Saiga ranger network carries out monthly monitoring and patrolling in core Saiga areas since 2015, and has been using SMART since July 2019 to improve effectiveness and support systematic data collection (CMS 2021).Protected areasThe distance between summer and winter ranges of some populations hinders full protected area coverage. In Russia, most Saiga are found in Chernye Zemli Biosphere Reserve (5,842 km²), established in 1990, and the adjoining Stepnoi Sanctuary (1,090 km²). Saiga are seasonally present in summer in Elton Nature Park (1,056 km²), Baskunchak Nature Park (395 km²), Orenberg reserve (382 km²), and Bogdinsko-Baskunchakskiy State Nature Reserve (185 km²).In Kazakhstan the Irgiz-Turgai Sanctuary (7,635 km²), Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve (4,897 km²), Korgalzhyn Reserve (5,431 km²), Naurzum Reserve (1,913 km²) and Barsalemess Reserve (1,608 km²)  have been established to protect Saiga populations. In May 2022 the Government of Kazakhstan gazetted the Bokeyorda State Nature Reserve (3,430 km²) and Ashiozek State Wildlife Sanctuary (3,145 km²) to protect the Ural population in West Kazakhstan province  (Smelyansky and Koshkina 2022/2023). In Uzbekistan the Saigachy Sanctuary was redesignated in 2015 to provide better coverage of Saiga range and now covers 8,481 km². The Mongolian Saiga has been legally protected since 1953 and occur in the following protected areas: Sharga-Mankhan Nature Reserve (3,962 km²), Khomyn Tal NP (4,111 km²), Khar-Us Nuur  NP (8,530 km²), Khyargas Lake NP (3,413 km²), Mongol Els NP (2,030 km²), Khar Azargiin Nuruu NR (1,926 km²), Bukhun Local protected Area (1,697 km²).  Since January 2021, three more Local Protected Areas have been designated, covering 2,581 km². A total of 56.1% of Mongolian saiga range is now protected by both State Protected Areas (29.4%) and Local Protected Areas (26.7%) (Chimeddorj 2022/2023b).Captive breedingSmall groups of Saiga have been kept in zoos in Europe and the USA but the species is difficult to maintain in captivity. Small rescue and captive breeding centres exist in Russia and Kazakhstan. A workshop to review options for Saiga captive breeding and reintroduction took place in Moscow in August 2017 (SCA, SDZG, IEEM 2017). At that time, there were c. 907 Saiga in eight captive or semi-captive facilities: 117 in four facilities in Russia; 20 at two facilities in Kazakhstan; 170 at the Wuwei Breeding Centre in Gansu, China; and c. 600 at the Askania Nova centre in Ukraine. There is no captive breeding currently in Uzbekistan. The population in Wuwei crashed to about 20 by early 2019. About 600 Saiga in Askania Nova, Ukraine, are kept in extensive semi-captive conditions and live animals have been sold in recent years to raise income to fund the centre. The status of these animals since the start of the conflict in 2022 is unknown (CMS 2021).Other projectsThe Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative in Kazakhstan is a collaboration between international and national NGOs and national and regional governmental bodies, which aims to provide an integrated approach to planning an implementation of sustainable land management, with the Saiga as its focal species. The initiative expanded its area of operations in 2016 to include the Ural and Ustyurt populations in addition to Betpakdala, and the project area now covers about 75 million ha. The Saiga Conservation Alliance (SCA) is a network of researchers and conservationists formed in 2016 to study and protect the saiga antelope. SCA maintains the online Saiga Resource Centre and publishes Saiga News one or twice a year (in English, Russian, Kazakh, Uzbek, Mongolian, and Chinese). It also provides small grants for research and awards for saiga protection and young conservationists.Saiga Day is an international initiative developed by SCA as a focus for rural communities to promote conservation of Saiga and its habitat. It takes take place each spring to mark the birth of the first Saiga calves of the year.The ‘Resurrection Island’ programme in Uzbekistan aims to lay the foundation for designating Resurrection Island in Uzbekistan as a Protected Area for Saiga and other species, while developing sustainable income streams for local enabling residents. It is a collaboration between the Uzbekistan government, industry, in-country NGOs, and the University of Oxford.In March 2023, the SCA hosted a ‘Saiga Inception’ meeting and ‘Conserving Wildlife in the Central Asian Steppes’ panel event in Oxford. These events brought together participants from different projects in the saiga antelope range, supported by the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s new 5-year “Catalysing Conservation Fund”, which focussed on generating evidence on Saiga product trade chains. The meeting aimed to facilitate collaboration among Saiga projects and address key aspects such as data availability, evidence gaps, theory of change, capacity needs, and opportunities for shared learning. The meeting brought together representatives from various organisations, including the CMS Central Asian Mammals Initiative, United States Fish and Wildlife Service, Oxford University, Zoological Society of London, Wildlife Conservation Society, Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, Flora and Fauna International, TRAFFIC, Frankfurt Zoological Society, The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, and other international and national stakeholders.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is not significantly threatened by hunting pressure and is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.It is, however, important to note that the subspecies Mallomys aroaensis ssp. hercules (on the Huon Peninsula) will probably qualify as threatened if it is made a distinct species.
