Combined with continual and heavy hunting, with the species being more sought after than other primate taxa for its use in over 100 traditional medicines, the species is considered to have lost 50% of its population. Future population declines are suspected on the basis that the threats facing this species continue.
range: This species is found in Mainland Southeast Asia east of the Mekong River in eastern Laos, southernmost China (southeastern Yunnan, historically north to Luchun), Northern Lao PDR as far west as Phôngsali, and Viet Nam north of the Hai Van Pass in Quang Nam Province (Blair et al. 2023). The western limit of distribution in Lao PDR is uncertain, but it appears to be absent in the extreme west of the Mekong plain.
useTrade: The species is hunted for the pet trade, for traditional medicine, photo props, food, and various other purposes (Thach et al. 2018). The intensity of the trade has increased over the years, which is reflected in the decrease in volumes of the trade due to impacts on the wild population as well as increase in market value of the depleted stocks. Traders in Japan report that this species is preferred over the less “fluffy” and longer snouted X. pygmaeus (Blair et al., 2023). Indeed, this species is more prevalent in videos on YouTube (Nekaris et al. 2016).
conservationActions: In Viet Nam this species is protected at the highest possible level (Appendix IB, Decree 32, 2006); in China, it is listed as Class 1 protected (involving potentially severe penalties). In Lao PDR, it is protected by the Wildlife and Aquatic Law (2007) that classifies lorises under the ‘prohibited’ category (Nekaris and Starr 2015). The species has been transferred from Appendix II to Appendix I of CITES (Nekaris and Nijman 2007). There is a need for close monitoring of harvesting rates of this species, not only in Viet Nam, but also in China and Lao PDR where the species may be extinct, or where rates of offtake could increase in the future. Pygmy Lorises are represented in at least 50 captive collections, where they are a ‘red light’ species’ due to high inbreeding and low breeding potential (Fuller et al. 2014). Work is currently underway to understand which species are held in zoological collections and it is essential to know whether or not the captive population consists of Northern or Southern species or hybrids. The species is reported in at several protected areas, but these reports need to be ground-sourced with systematic surveys (Nekaris et al. 2008).Researchers have attempted to bring attention to and mitigate the illegal online trade in Pygmy Lorises, which is particularly prevalent in Japan and Eastern Europe (Musing and Nekaris 2015). Ongoing campaigns combat the exploitation of Pygmy Lorises in illegal online videos (Nekaris et al. 2013, 2015).This species has been the subject of many releases of confiscated individuals in Viet Nam, both monitored and unmonitored, often being unsuccessful (Streicher 2004). The Endangered Primate Rescue Centre in Cuc Phuong National Park, Ninh Binh Province, Vietnam, has been releasing Pygmy Lorises to the wild for more than two decades, but as two species were not recognised, it is possible that wild hybrids now exist, and it is urgent to check the status of released individuals. New strategies for release have been developed, however, with the number of successful releases on the increase; a standardised best practice for release is beginning to be recognised (Kenyon et al. 2014).

rationale: Lagothrix lagotricha is considered Vulnerable (VU A4cd) based on a suspected population reduction of 30% or more over 45 years (three generations; 2018–2063). This decline is based on Global Forest Watch data that predict a 10–15% loss of forest habitat in the Brazilian state of Amazonas, the Peruvian department of Loreto, southeastern Colombia and the Ecuadorian departments of Napo, Orellano and Sucumbios during this period, and the fact that this large-bodied species is routinely hunted.
habitat: This species occurs in lowland primary terra firma forest, and occasionally also in secondary and disturbed/fragmented habitats. They enter flooded forests at certain times of the year to feed on fruits.Izawa (1975, 1976) and Nishimura and Izawa (1975) studied this species on the Río Peneya, a tributary of the Río Caquetá, Colombia. Nishimura and Izawa (1975) observed a group from 42–43 individuals (11 adult males, 15 adult females, 11 or 12 juveniles, and 6 dependant infants) at Puerto Japó, Río Peneya, using home ranges greater than 400 ha. At another site (Puerto Tokio) they saw six groups which they believed ranged in size from 25–70 animals. They estimated a home range of 1,100 ha for the Puerto Japón group. Defler (1989, 1995, 1996, 1999; Defler and Defler 1996) studied a group on the Río Apaporis, Colombia. It ranged over 760 ha, largely (90%) overlapping with three neighbouring groups. Nishimura (1990b) studied the ranging and social behavior of two groups at Puerto Tokio. Group A had 45 individuals and ranged over 450 ha, ands group B had 13 individuals and used a home range of 350 ha over about 10 months of his observations. Other studies of woolly monkeys have shown that their diet consists mainly of fruits, but includes also young leaves, petioles, and flowers (Ramirez 1988).Size:Adult male weight mean 9.0 kg (8.0–10.0 kg, n=3); adult female weight mean 5.75 kg (5.0–6.5 kg, n=6) (Ford and Davis 1992).
threats: This is a relatively wide-ranging species, susceptible to hunting pressure. It still occurs in a number of very remote regions. There is also some habitat loss due to agricultural expansion (including illegal crops).
population: This species is common, but naturally occurs at low densities. Nishimura and Izawa (1975) estimated a density of 5.5 individuals/km² on the Río Peneya, Colomibia. Defler (1989) recorded the same density on the Rio Apaporis.Global Forest Watch data suggest a 10–15% loss of forest habitat in the Brazilian state of Amazonas, the Peruvian department of Loreto, southeastern Colombia and the Ecuadorian departments of Napo, Orellano and Sucumbios during this period. This, in combination with the fact that this large-bodied species is routinely hunted, lead to a suspected population reduction of 30% or more over 45 years (three generations; 2018–2063).
range: In Colombia, Lagothrix lagotricha is known throughout the Amazon lowlands northeast to the Río Uva, a left bank affluent of the Río Guaviare in Vichada (Defler 2004). It extends east to the Río Orinoco and it may occur in Venezuela to the south of the Orinoco between the Ríos Orinoco and Cassiquiare (Linares 1998). Bodini and Pérez-Hernández (1987) reported that Lagothrix had never been collected in Venezuela, but that it should be found in the Territorio Federal Amazonas to the south of the Ventuari. It extends part way up the Rio Negro in Brazil—to the north at least as far the Ro Carauari. It does not occur in the eastern part of the Negro-Solimões interfluvium, but the exact boundaries of its occurrence there are not known. In Ecuador and Peru, it occurs north of the Rio Amazonas—Napo (L. poeppigii occurs to the south) (Tirira 2007). In Ecuador, the altitudinal range is 200 m to 1,400 m above sea level (Tirira 2007).
conservationActions: The species is present in a number of protected areas, including:BrazilJuami-Japurá Ecological Station (832,078 ha) (in range)ColombiaAmacayacu National Natural Park (293,000 ha) (INDERENA 1989, Defler 2004)La Paya National Natural (442,000 ha) (Polanco-Ochoa et al. 1999, Defler 2004 )Cahuinarí National Natural Park (575,500 ha) (Defler 2004)Serrania de Chiribiquete National Natural Park (1,280,000 ha) (in range) Nukak National Natural Reserve (855,000 ha) (in range)Ecuador Sumaco-Napo Galeras National Park (205,249 ha) (Tirira 2007)Cayambe-Coca Ecological Reserve (403,103 ha) (Tirira 2007)Cofán-Bermejo Ecological Reserve (55,451 ha) (Tirira 2007)Cuyabeno Ecological Reserve (Tirira 2007).This species is listed in Appendix II of CITES.

rationale: Following taxonomic revision, the Balkan Long-eared Bat (Plecotus kolombatovici) occurs from southeastern Europe to eastern Türkiye. The species' range is wide and the species uses a variety of habitats. The population trend has not been quantified, but it does not appear to be declining at a rate sufficient to qualify for a threatened category, and it is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: The species forages both in close and semi-open habitats in dry lowland and mountainous areas along the coast or river valleys, such as steppe, deciduous forest, olive groves, shrubland, clearings, meadows, farmland, and streams or other small water bodies. Foraging sites are located on average 1.5 km from the roost. Prey are generally caught on the wing and is mostly represented by lepidopterans (Razgour 2020). The foraging habitats and prey availability are impacted by the threats that impact habitat extent and quality., such as conversion for agriculture and urbanisation, and firesThe Balkan Long-eared Bat roosts in buildings as well as underground sites, rock crevices and trees, and in Crete and on other Greek islands, roosts in caves year-round (reviewed in Razgour 2020).
threats: Mediterranean coasts and islands are subject to strong human pressures, which are a major threat to this species, especially in terms of habitat loss or alteration due to urbanisation and recurrent wildfires. Pesticides are another potential threat, as is roost disturbance through activities such as recreational caving and potentially, cave tourism, but the latter is not thought to be significant at the global scale. The lack of knowledge about the species' ecology limits the implementation of effective monitoring and conservation measures.
population: Little is known about population size and trends in this species, although it is regarded as relatively common in the Balkans and in Cyprus. In Europe, the total population is estimated at fewer than 10,000 mature individuals, and it is suspected that the population might be declining. An overall suspected population decline caused by a range of factors (see Threats) likely exceeds 10% in the next three generations (generation length: five years; Pacifici et al. 2013).Summer colonies usually number 10-30 females, although a breeding colony of 120 females was found in a building in Croatia (F. Spitzenberger pers. comm. 2006). Winter clusters are smaller (10 individuals), and the species is often solitary at this time of year. It was thought that European and southwest Asian subpopulations were isolated from each other, but range extensions as a result of recent records indicate that they might not be as isolated as was previously thought.
range: The Balkan Long-eared Bat (P. kolombatovici) occurs from southeastern Europe to southern Türkiye and Cyprus. In Europe, it has a narrow distribution on the eastern Mediterranean coast and islands, especially on the coasts of the Adriatic Sea, Croatia, Albania, Greece (mainland Greece, Crete, Rhodes, Peloponnese, Ionian and Aegean Sea islands), southern Türkiye and Cyprus (Razgour 2020). Only one specimen was recently recorded for the Italian Peninsula, where the species’ presence might be overlooked, whereas a specimen from Pantelleria Island, between the eastern Libyan coast and Sicily, previously identified as P. kolombatovici from its morphology has not been genetically confirmed and long-eared bats on the island have been assigned to Plecotus gaisleri (Razgour 2020). The distribution continues east along the western and southern coasts of the Anatolia region of Türkiye. The species occurs from sea level to 1,665 m asl.The EOO is in excess of 1,200,000 km2. The AOO has not been estimated due to the absence of comprehensive locality records, and may be less than the threshold for a threatened category.In the other regions where the species had been previously recorded, its presence has been questioned and the P. kolombatovici subpopulations have been assigned to either Plecotus christii (Levant and northeast Africa) or Plecotus gaisleri (North Africa) by recent molecular and/or morphological assessments.
useTrade: The species is not utilised or traded.
conservationActions: The species is protected by national legislation in most range states. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the Bonn Convention (Eurobats) and the Bern Convention in those parts of the range where these apply. In the EU region, the species is included in Annex IV of EU Habitats and Species Directive, and there is some habitat protection through Natura 2000.Recommended actions include monitoring population trends and minimising or preventing disturbance to roost sites in Europe. Further taxonomic research is required, as well as research into the species' ecological requirements.

rationale: Global and European regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)EU 27 regional assessment: Near Threatened (NT)Myotis crypticus has a restricted distribution in Europe and, at least for Italy, a loss of > 30% of suitable habitat is suspected; as such, the species was assessed as VU under criterion A2c in the Italian Red List (Rondinini et al. 2022). It should be highlighted, however, that subpopulations from southern Italy and Sicily belong to a separate lineage whose taxonomic status awaits clarification. There is no information about the population size and trends for the remaining countries and M. crypticus is not mentioned even in the most recent releases of national Red Lists. Moreover, the actual species’ distribution is not yet fully understood, especially in the Balkans, where the occurrence of hybrids in the contact zone with M. nattereri further complicates the picture. However, a general decline is suspected mostly due to a loss of roosting sites and degradation of foraging habitat (forest and riparian vegetation), approaching, but not exceeding 30%, in three generations, on which bases the species is assessed as NT in Europe and in the EU27 Member States approaching VU under criterion A2c.
habitat: Since Myotis crypticus has been recognized as a distinct species within the “M. nattereri” complex only recently, its ecology is poorly known. However, since the Italian Natterer’s bats are all, in fact, M. crypticus (yet the southern populations might belong to a different subspecific taxonomic entity) the information collected in the Italian territory may be safely assigned to M. crypticus.The species hibernates in underground sites, and radiotracking has revealed that in the summer, nurseries roost in cavities of live trees, yet single individuals may also use rock crevices in that season (D. Russo unpublished). It forages in beech forests, Mediterranean woodlands, sweet chestnut plantations, as well as riparian vegetation, but it may also hunt near single trees in open habitats such as pastures or cultivations (D. Russo pers. obs.).Myotis crypticus feeds on a broad range of arthropods, especially Lepidoptera, Diptera and Araneae, and much of its prey is not volant at night and is therefore likely taken by gleaning. Although its diet is very similar to that of M. escalerai, the diets of the two species overlap less in syntopy, probably due to a shift in foraging strategy since the amount of prey that does not fly at night is smaller in M. escalerai (Novella-Fernandez et al. 2020).
threats: The species is put at risk by the loss, alteration, or disturbance of its underground roosts, as well as by the loss or fragmentation of unmanaged forests and suitable roost trees found there (Rondinini et al. 2013). At least at drinking sites, adverse reactions to artificial illumination are shown (Russo et al. 2017), and such reactions likely occur also at foraging sites or along commuting routes.
population: There is very scarce information on Myotis crypticus subpopulations, but it appears quite rare throughout its range. There are a few scattered records for the north of Portugal, where the species was first observed in 2018 (López Gallego et al. 2020) and might even be vagrant (F. Amorim pers. comm.). This species is widely distributed in southern France, but the northern limits of its range are undefined due to the absence of molecular surveys in some areas, and nothing is known about population trends (S. Aulagnier pers. comm.). In Italy, where it can be locally frequent, the species is suspected to have undergone a strong decline in the last decades. No information is available for the remaining countries that are part of the species’ range.A loss or degradation of important habitat (underground roosts, forests and riparian vegetation) is suspected to have led to a population decline approaching 30% in three generations.
range: Myotis crypticus is a European endemic species, where it is found in the mountains of the northern half of Iberia, mainly along the Pyrenees and 'Cordillera Cantábrica', in southern France, Italy, as well as in Switzerland, Austria, Slovenia, the Adriatic coast of Croatia, and Hungary (J. Juste pers. comm.). The situation in Croatia is complicated by the high genetic admixture with M. nattereri (D. Josić pers. comm.). Moreover, this distribution should be regarded as possibly incomplete since a comprehensive assessment of the species’ presence requires molecular identification, which has not yet been carried out comprehensively across the entire potential range. The specimens from southern Italy and Sicily belong to a separate lineage that could represent a distinct taxonomic entity deserving further investigation (Çoraman et al. 2019). The species is found from sea level up to 2,000, probably even more in the Pyrenees and Alps (J. Juste pers. comm.).The AOO and EOO have not been estimated because the available data are not considered representative of the range of the species, but based on the available locality records, they are expected to exceed the threshold for a threatened category.
useTrade: The species is not used or traded
conservationActions: Although not yet recognized in the official documents of all range countries (e.g., national red lists), Myotis crypticus is protected by national legislation like all other bat species. There are also international legal obligations for its protection through the EUROBATS Agreement since in October 2022 the species was added to the Annex to the Agreement under Resolution 9.2 adopted at Eurobats MoP9. Despite not yet being listed in Annex IV of 92/43/EEC Habitats Directive, it is protected under this Directive like all other bat species occurring in the EU territory.The survival of this species is highly dependent on the preservation of both its roosting sites and the surrounding forests and riparian vegetation. Further research is necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the species’ specific spatial and habitat needs. Additionally, it is important to confirm the occurrence of evolutionarily significant units (such as in southern Italy) within the general population that require unique conservation strategies tailored to their specific needs.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large population, active management, and because it is not declining at anything close to the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Most mountain goats occur in high altitude habitats, up to the limit of vegetation. Although they descend to sea level in coastal areas, they are primarily an alpine and sub-alpine species. Throughout the year, the animals usually stay above timberline, but they will migrate seasonally to higher or lower elevations within that range. Summertime movements to low-elevation mineral licks often take them several or more kilometers through forested areas. Their diet includes grasses, forbs, sedges, ferns, moss, lichen, twigs, and leaves from the low-growing shrubs and conifers of their high-altitude habitat. Their main predators are cougars, wolves and brown bears. The species lives in groups that can vary from a few to a hundred, and during the winter months groups generally coalesce to form large herds. The gestation length is approximately 180 days, with a single birth typically, although twins are common in introduced populations. The average age of primiparity varies from 2 to 5 years among populations. Male mortality is higher than female mortality and very few males live longer than 10 years. Very few females survive more than 16 years (Festa-Bianchet and Côté 2008).
threats: These animals are largely protected from threats due to the inaccessible nature of their habitat. The species is hunted, but regulations in both of its range states have stabilized past declines. Mountain goats are more sensitive to human disturbance than most other ungulates, and are particularly sensitive to harassment from aircraft. Increasing aircraft  use, particularly helicopters, for industrial and recreational purposes on mountain goat habitat is a major concern for their conservation.
population: In 2010, the total population in Canada was estimated at 43,700 to 70,200, distributed as follows: Alberta 2000; British Columbia 39,000-65,500; Northwest Territories 1,000 (earlier estimate); and Yukon 1,700. Recent total estimates in the United States are 37,000 to 47,000 individuals, with more than 13,000 animals in the contiguous states, and 24,000 to 33,500 in Alaska. (Myatt and Larkins 2010)Some historic ranges in southern part of distribution are now unoccupied.  These historic declines were likely due to overharvest, partly because managers initially did not realize that this species can only tolerate a very small amount of harvest in native populations.
range: This species is found in southeast Alaska (USA), south Yukon and southwest Northwest Territories (Canada) to north-central Oregon, central Idaho, and Montana (USA). It has been introduced to Kodiak, Chichagof, and Baranof Islands (Alaska), Olympic Peninsula (Washington), central Montana, Black Hills (South Dakota), and to Colorado, Utah and northeastern Nevada (USA) (Grubb 2005). In Canada, mountain goats inhabit all major mountain ranges from the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta, west to the Coastal Range of British Columbia, and north into the St. Elias, Coast, Cassiar, Logan and Selwyn Ranges of Yukon; and the Mackenzie Mountains of the Northwest Territories. In Alaska, the mountain goat is generally continuously distributed along the mountains extending up the west coast to Prince William Sound and the Kenai Peninsula. It also occurs in the southern Wrangell and Talkeetna Mountains and the northern Chugach Mountains. Goat populations have been established through transplants on Baranof and Kodiak Islands. In the contiguous states, it is found in a relatively continuous distribution across several large mountain ranges in Washington, Idaho and Montana. Mountain goats are also discontinuously distributed to the east and south of this area, where many herds have been established by transplanting animals, sometimes outside of known historic range.
useTrade: Hunting is now well managed in most jurisdictions. Changes in management regimes have stabilized past declines.
conservationActions: In Canada, mountain goat habitat, along with more than 3,500 goats, are protected in eight National Parks (Banff, Glacier, Jasper, Kootenay, Nahanni, Revelstoke, Waterton and Yoho), Kluane National Park Reserve, and in Kluane Wildlife Sanctuary. Numerous provincial parks and wildlife reserves throughout western and northern Canada provide additional varying levels of protection. Limited hunting by aboriginal people is permitted in some northern national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, and licensed hunting is permitted in many provincial parks. Outside protected areas, goats are legally hunted under strict controls issued by provincial or territorial government agencies. Harvests are set annually for each population. In British Columbia, for example, harvest rates vary between populations and range from 0.4 to 94% (BC Mountain Goat management Plan 2010) with about 600 goats shot by resident and non-residents each year. Aboriginal harvest is unknown. In Yukon, sport harvests are much lower, varying between three and 15 animals per year, with the aboriginal harvest estimated to be zero. Transplants have been used to re-introduce mountain goats into many areas of their former range. Habitat management continues to play a key role in its conservation, and developments are subject to environmental screening processes on public land. Conservation measures proposed for Canada: 1) Determine the species’ requirements for mature forests on steep slopes in coastal mountain ranges that are used as winter habitat in British Columbia (Hebert and Turnbull, 1977, Fox et al. 1989). Several coastal populations will be affected by current and future timber harvest operations. Ideally, much or most of this habitat should be preserved. 2) Obtain more accurate population inventories in all regions of Canada to allow more detailed management plans to be developed. 3) Encourage research on the possible effects of climate change on habitat trends, nutritional quality and snow cover. In the United States, primary conservation measures have included habitat protection, introductions and re-introductions, and harvest regulation. Eight state wildlife management departments have transplanted mountain goats from native ranges in Canada and the United States. Six of these states did not have native populations. Many transplanted populations were established with only 10 to 15 founder animals. Goats are harvested in nine states under conservative regulations of the wildlife departments which monitor populations. The mountain goat occurs in nine federal protected areas: Alaska: Glacier Bay, Kenai Fjords, and Wrangell - St. Elias National Parks; and Kenai National Wildlife Refuge; Montana: Glacier National Park; South Dakota: Mount Rushmore National Monument; Washington: North Cascades, and Mount Rainier National Parks. However, most herds are in national forests including many wilderness areas. One state, Colorado, uses two hunting licenses in an auction and a raffle to raise funds for these activities.

rationale: It is difficult to assign a conservation status to this species, given the limited available information on population size, extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO) and trends in these parameters. The limited monitoring data indicate ongoing decline in abundance; habitat is undergoing continuing decline in quality due to detrimental fire regimes, and this is likely to be exacerbated by spread of invasive grasses; predation by feral cats is likely to be the primary cause of decline (and its impact is amplified by fire) and is unlikely to be controlled in the near future. Although the survey data are meagre, the monitoring program at Kakadu National Park indicates a decline which exceeds 30% over successive 10-year periods from 2004 to 2013 and 2014 to 2023; hence the species qualifies for at least Vulnerable A2bce. Climate change will likely increase incidence and impacts of fire; and impacts of predation are unlikely to be controlled more effectively over the next 1-2 decades, so it qualifies also for Vulnerable A3bce+4bce. Its AOO is likely to be ca. 1,000 km2, and number of locations fewer than 10, and its habitat quality is undergoing continuing decline, and its population size is consequently also likely to be undergoing continuing decline, so it qualifies also as Vulnerable B2ab(iii,v).
habitat: The Kakadu pebble-mouse occurs mostly in hill slopes of savanna woodlands, in which the ground layer has extensive cover of gravel and small pebbles (Ford and Johnson 2007, Woinarski and Ford 2023). Animals build mounds of pebbles under which a burrow is located. Captive animals have produced seven litters of 22 young over a nine-month period (Woinarski and Ford 2023). There have been no detailed dietary studies, but it is likely to be predominantly granivorous. Habitat condition is influenced by fire; and the current regime is likely to be unfavourable. In Kakadu, about 60% of its habitat is burnt per year (Woinarski and Winderlich 2014). Such frequent fire is likely to increase the impacts of predation by feral cats as cats hunt selectively and more successfully in burnt areas (McGregor et al. 2015, 2016; Leahy et al. 2015). Introduced pasture grasses (especially gamba grass Andropogon gayanus) are spreading (for example, with their extent increasing from 14% to 21% of Litchfield National Park from 2014 to 2022: Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023), produce higher fuel loads and hence result in fires of greater intensity, which transform habitats (Setterfield et al. 2013).
threats: The Kakadu pebble-mouse has a relatively narrow habitat breadth and limited distribution. Frequent fires and invasive grasses are degrading its habitat (Setterfield et al. 2013, Russell-Smith et al. 2017, Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023), and likely leading to higher predation rates by feral cats (McGregor et al. 2015, 2016; Leahy et al. 2015). Ongoing trends for hotter days and more severe fire danger for this region (NESP Earth Systems and Climate Change Hub 2020) will likely lead to continuing increases in the impacts of fire.
population: There are no robust estimates of density or population size. Woinarski and Braithwaite (1990) reported results from a survey of 70 quadrats (each of 80 metres x 20 metres) in Kakadu National Park, sampled with 20 traps and 2 pitfall buckets over a 4-night period, with maximum abundance per quadrat of 11 captures.  Woinarski et al. (2014) suggested a population of 15,000 mature individuals but tagged this with a low reliability. Monitoring programs indicate ongoing decline, but the information base is sparse. For 136 monitoring sites at Kakadu National Park, the species was recorded by 10 individuals from 3 sites in 1995-96, 16 individuals from 5 sites in 2001-02, 4 individuals from 4 sites in 2006, and 0 individuals from sites sampled in 2011 (Woinarski et al. 2010, Russell-Smith et al. 2014, Einoder et al. 2023). Since 2015, this monitoring program has become less powerful for this species as the number of sites sampled sites has been reduced (Einoder et al. 2018, Southwell et al. 2019), and the species has not been recorded from Kakadu 'in recent years' (Luke Einoder pers. comm. 2024). Of 92 geo-coded and dated records in the Atlas of Living Australia, only four have been since 1999, however interpretation is constrained by inconsistent sampling intensity over time, and perhaps also to some lag-time in entering records to the national database.
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is known only from a relatively small area of the monsoonal tropics of the Northern Territory, extending from Litchfield National Park in the west to western Arnhem Land, and including Kakadu National Park.
conservationActions: It is present in Kakadu National Park and Litchfield National Park, but this reservation provides relatively little effective management control over the main threats (particularly predation by feral cats). There is some—but largely ineffective—control of fire; and fire regimes are deteriorating further due to spread of fire-promoting invasive pasture grasses (Russell-Smith et al. 2014), with these invasive grasses spreading even in some conservation reserves occupied by this species (Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023).This species is not listed as threatened under Australian environmental law.

rationale: The Pookila is listed as Vulnerable B2ab(i,ii,iii,iv,v)c(iv), because it has a small area of occupancy (AOO) of approximately 972 km2. Its geographic range is severely fragmented and there is a continuing decline in extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, habitat, number of locations and number of mature individuals. It is threatened by a number of factors, including introduced predators, habitat loss and fragmentation, and disease. It also undergoes marked fluctuations in abundance.
habitat: The Pookila is a small, nocturnal, native rodent and is an opportunistic omnivore, consuming seeds, stem and leaf tissues, roots, fungi, insects and other invertebrates (Cockburn 1980, Norton 1987, Wilson and Bradtke 1999, Fox and Fox 2006, DCCEEW 2024).During the day, Pookila mostly shelter in communal burrow systems. These vary in length and complexity, ranging from shallow surface nests to intricate tunnel systems (Kemper 1981).Radio-tracking studies indicate home ranges of 0.5 to 1.8 ha (Burns et al. 2023), with densities of up to 10–20 individuals ha-1 at peak abundance (Lock and Wilson 1999).Pookila occur in a range of heathlands and woodlands (with grassy or shrubby understorey) and vegetated sand dunes (DCCEEW 2024). Relationships with fire are complex and vary depending upon environments. Some studies have reported a preference for early successional vegetation (e.g., time since fire of 2–5 years) (Fox and McKay 1981), but subsequent studies have found a complex and inconstant relationship of time since fire due to the many variables associated with any fire event (e.g. scale, severity, rainfall post-fire (Burns and Phillips 2020). Soft sandy substrates, with deep top-soils are preferred (Abicair et al. 2020).There is evidence that populations of the Pookila are strongly impacted by rainfall. Subpopulations in New South Wales have been shown to increase the length of their breeding season, and thus reproductive output, during times of above average rainfall (Kemper 1976, 1980). Maximum population densities at Anglesea, Victoria were recorded following four years of above average rainfall and declined during below average rainfall and drought conditions (Lock 2005, Wilson et al. 2007) and there is evidence that population fluctuations at Gippsland sites are influenced by rainfall patterns (Wilson et al. 2005; Burns 2021). At Anglesea abundance was found to have a strong positive relationship to cumulative monthly residual rainfall exhibiting a 0–9 month lag time (Lock 2005). It is likely that the impact of rainfall is related to its influence on resource availability that can lead to variations in reproductive output such as births, recruitment, and adult survival.At Anglesea in Victoria, juveniles were captured from January to March (Wilson 1991) and the breeding season at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria was from December to May (Wilson et al. 2005), however, this varies annually and among sites (P. Burns, unpubl. data). In Tasmania, breeding is also seasonal and takes place from early November to late March and females are capable of producing at least two litters in a breeding season (Pye 1991).The longer breeding season of the Pookila in New South Wales means that females are capable of having up to six litters per season, while Victorian and Tasmanian subpopulations may have only 1–2 litters (Kemper 1990). The longer breeding season also means that first year females can breed, but this is not the case at Anglesea or in Tasmania (Norton 1987, Wilson 1991). A study in New South Wales found that mean litter size was 4.6 (range 2–6) (Kemper 1980).In a laboratory study, sexual maturity was earlier in females, at 13 weeks, than in males (20 weeks) (Kemper 1976). In the wild, females may live up to two years, occasionally three. Generation length is here assumed to be 1.5 years.
threats: The Pookila faces a complex series of threats across its range. Some of these compound and interact. Burns (2020) provided an account of threats to the species in its Victorian range:Habitat loss and fragmentation. Much of the habitat of this species has been cleared (mostly for residential development and agriculture), with some continuing clearing, and this clearing has directly reduced population size, but also fragmented populations, leading to likely losses of genetic heterogeneity within isolated populations and reduced ability to recolonise areas following local extirpations (such as by severe wildfire) (Wilson et al. 2017).Predation by cats and Red Fox is likely an ongoing threat, and may be exacerbated after fire because there is less cover/shelter from predators in recently burnt areas.Disease, such as toxoplasmosis (associated with cats), may be a threat although there is no direct evidence.The Pookila has a complex relationship with fire. It has previously been considered an early successional species (e.g., Fox and Fox 2006), but recent studies indicate that it can occur across a range of time-since-fire, up to at least 60 years (Burns 2020). Nonetheless fire regimes probably help shape habitat quality and resource availability.Introduced rodents Black Rat Rattus rattus may predate Pookila and House Mouse (Mus musculus) may compete with Pookila and both introduced species may spread disease. Although Pookila have been shown to be competitively superior to House Mouse (Cockburn 1980), recent data from Tasmania and Victoria indicate House Mouse may outcompete Pookila following drought (Burns, Lazenby, unpub. data).Weed invasion is recognised as a threat by DCCEEW (2024), including for example the encroachment to heathlands of the native coastal tea tree Leptospermum leavigatum at Wilson's Promontory (Burns 2020).Pookila may be susceptible to poison baits (carrots and oats: mostly targeting rabbits) containing 1080 or Pindone (Burns 2020). Some heathland and woodland habitats may also be susceptible to degradation caused by Phytophthora infection (DCCEEW 2024).Drought and climate change. Decline and extirpation of populations at Anglesea were associated with periods of lower than average rainfall (Wilson et al. 2007, 2017), and drought across remaining Victorian sites has been linked to population crashes (Burns 2021). Climate change may bring more such events.DCCEEW (2024) prioritised threats by their likelihood and consequences, with highest rankings for fire regimes that cause declines in biodiversity, climate change and predation by cats (all almost certain likelihood and major consequences).Many of the threats (e.g., cat predation, fox predation, fire, and Phytophthora) affecting this species are recognised nationally (under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999) as Key Threatening Processes.
population: There is no robust estimate of population size nor that of most subpopulations. Menkhorst et al. (2008) considered that there are probably fewer than 10,000 mature individuals, but the evidence base for this estimate is meagre. AOO is calculated as 984 km2. Using untested assumptions that density is 1 individual/ha, half of AOO is occupied, and there exist no unknown populations, total estimated number of individuals is 49,200. Given the short period to maturity, most of these would be mature. Abundance and population size varies seasonally (Kemper and Wilson 2008, Burns et al. 2019), between years associated with rainfall (Wilson et al. 2007, 2018; Burns 2021), and is influenced by fire history (Fox and McKay 1981, Burns and Phillips 2020). Detectability is influenced by survey methods and moon phase (Burns et al. 2019, Burns 2020). Density estimates at Anglesea were 10–20 individuals ha-1 during early 1995, with decline to 3–10 ha-1 in June 1995 (Wilson 1991, Lock and Wilson 1999, Lock 2005), with further declines leading to extirpation. The total population size is declining, with probable loss of all populations on the Tasmanian mainland by 2009 (Lazenby et al. 2018) and extirpation of seven of the 12 known subpopulations in Victoria since the 1970s (Burns 2020). The populations in Tasmania and Victoria are thought to comprise only about 5% of the species' total population (DCCEEW 2024). Recent (2021) records demonstrate an extant population on Flinders Island (DCCEEW 2024). Limited survey and monitoring in the New South Wales and Queensland parts of its range constrains assessment of overall population trajectory (DCCEEW 2024), but extensive and ongoing coastal development probably cause ongoing declines for this part of the range, although many of the known subpopulations are now in conservation reserves and protected from clearing.  Translocation sought to establish a new population in a fenced exclosure at Mulligan Flat in the Australian Capital Territory in 2013, but initially this did not expand (Abicair et al. 2020). Subsequent releases in 2019 tested whether 'mini safe havens' could increase reintroduction success, and showed some value, although did not necessarily secure establishment (Smith et al. 2023). Reintroductions to the Otway Ranges (Anglesea) between 2000 and 2003 failed. Nearly 50% of the species' range was burnt in wildfires in 2019–20 (Legge et al. 2022). There is considerable genetic distinction between populations in New South Wales and Queensland relative to those in Victoria, and these are considered and managed as separate Evolutionarily Significant Units (Burns et al. 2023, 2024).
range: The Pookila (or New Holland Mouse) is a small, nocturnal, terrestrial, burrowing rodent with a fragmented range mostly in coastal locations in southern Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania, including Flinders Island (Hocking and Driessen 2000, DCCEEW 2024). It has been found from sea level up to around 900 m asl (Menkhorst et al. 2008). Many subpopulations in Victoria and Tasmania have been extirpated in recent decades (Wilson et al. 2017, Lazenby et al. 2018, Burns 2020), and expansive coastal development has probably caused loss of subpopulations in New South Wales and Queensland. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 270,158 km2 and area of occupancy (AOO) is a minimum of 972 km2, based on all valid Atlas of Living Australia records since 2000, excluding records from mainland Tasmania given doubt about ongoing presence there (Lazenby et al. 2018). One record from near Narooma (NSW) was also excluded as likely misidentification (P. Burns pers. comm.). Note that these values are larger than given in TSSC (2010) [90,000 km2 and 420 km2, respectively]. The distribution of recent subfossils further suggests that the species has undergone a large range contraction since European settlement (Breed and Ford 2007, DCCEEW 2024).
useTrade: Pookila are not utilised.
conservationActions: A national Recovery Plan for this species was established in 2024 (DCCEEW 2024). A Recovery Team coordinates the implementation of this plan. The species is listed as threatened under Australian legislation, and in that of Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory, but not New South Wales.

rationale: The Heath Mouse has an estimated area of occupancy (AOO) of 328 km² and although known from numerous sites, the number of locations is considered to be between four and ten (best estimate of five). There is evidence from lack of success in recent targeted sampling of a continuing decline (of area of occupancy, population size, number of subpopulations) of the population in Western Australia, and more equivocal evidence of decline in Victoria. The impacts of historic clearing and fragmentation continue and introduced predators (cats and foxes) are ongoing threats across the entire range. The species is listed pursuant to the Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 as Endangered. It is listed in Victoria and South Australia as Endangered and in Western Australia as Vulnerable. The national listing advice (https://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/sprat.pl) depended on the number of locations being ≤5 (which is supported in this assessment), ‘severely fragmented’ (not supported in this assessment), ‘extreme fluctuations’ (not supported in this assessment as any fluctuations due to varying rainfall and/or fire are typically short term) and a continuing decline (supported in this assessment). Thus, the species is assessed here as Endangered B2ab(ii,iii,iv,v).
habitat: In Victoria, Heath Mice are most frequently found in species-rich dry heathland that has been burnt within the last 5–15 years, but they also occur in dry Stringybark Eucalyptus baxteri and E. arenacea open woodland and open forest with a heath understorey (Cockburn 1978, Menkhorst and Beardsell 1982, Meulman 1997). Heath Mice are able to exploit unproductive heathlands by colonising patches a few years after fire. However, where they occur in heathy woodland, they can inhabit much older vegetation, up to 50 years post-fire (Mitchell 2007, Menkhorst et al. 2008, Di Stefano et al. 2011). Recent surveys in Victoria found strongest habitat association with dense shrub cover rather than age-since-fire, and a negative association with fox abundance (Nalliah et al. 2022). In Western Australia, Heath Mice have been trapped mostly in species-rich heath but also in mixed scrub and mallee. They have not been located in heath of less than 10 years after fire and can attain high densities in 30-year old heath. Hale et al. (2016) found that, in the Grampian Ranges, Pseudomys shortridgei had high trap success in areas approximately 10 years post-fire before reducing in number until approximately 30 years post-fire. Breeding takes place in late spring and summer. Females first breed at about 12 months old, males at 18 months. Adults form pairs that remain together for the four-month breeding season, producing one or two litters of three young, a low reproductive rate for a murine rodent. Longevity is unknown. It is unlikely to exceed four years (Menkhorst et al. 2008), but may be less than four years in the wild. Generation length is assumed here to be ca two years. Diet comprises a diverse mix of forbs, seeds and monocots, with some invertebrates (Di Stefano et al. 2014).
threats: Threats to this species include: Predation by feral domestic cats (Felis catus; moderate, entire range): cats prey on native rodents; however, overall impact unknown (Dickman 1996, Abbott 2002); some evidence that cats increase in abundance and/or activity when foxes are controlled (Marlow et al. 2015).Inappropriate fire regimes (moderate, entire range): Heath Mouse abundance linked to age of vegetation since fire in Victoria where there is a consistent need to maintain a higher proportion of the habitat in older vegetation age classes (Hale et al. 2016); in Western Australia species has been located only in old vegetation (Menkhorst et al. 2008). There is an increasing threat of severe wildfire due to climate change.Habitat loss and fragmentation (severe to catastrophic, parts of range), mostly for agriculture. The species cannot survive outside natural bush; some subpopulations occur in small remnants; however, it also occurs in large areas of native vegetation.Predation by Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes; moderate, entire range): plausible, but impact not known; recent surveys have reported a negative association with fox abundance (Nalliah et al. 2022); impact likely to be less in dense vegetation.Habitat degradation due to Phytophthora (moderate, parts of range): listed as a threat by Watson et al. (2003) and Garkaklis (2021, 2022).Climate Change (moderate, part of range): a drying climate and increasing temperature extremes, especially in southwest of Western Australia and the Wimmera region of Victoria, are likely to affecting this species.Habitat degradation due to weed invasion (minor, small part of range): listed as a threat by Watson et al. (2003) and Garkaklis (2021, 2022).
population: There are no robust measures of overall population size. There once were ca 4,000 individuals in Lake Magenta Nature Reserve (Menkhorst and Morris 2008). It is common in limited habitat in Victoria (Menkhorst and Morris 2008), and by extrapolation it is inferred that there are probably 20,000 mature individuals in south-east Australia. In Western Australia, despite targeted survey, it is currently known only from a few sites within Lake Magenta Nature Reserve, Fitzgerald River National Park and near Ravensthorpe (S. Comer pers. comm. 2024). No population estimate for Western Australia is available, but numbers are presumed to be low. Long-term monitoring of small mammals in Grampians-Gariwerd National Park indicates relative stability in site occupancy with presence detected by cage or Elliott traps at between 42% and 66% of 36 sites monitored annually between 2014 and 2022 (with the highest number of positive sites in 2022) (Victorian Biodiversity Atlas Data extracted March 2024). Since 2014, the species has been recorded at only a few locations outside the Grampians-Gariwerd National Park but this likely reflects a lack of survey in Heath Mouse habitat in that region. For example, in 2016 Hill made a total of 57 captures at a single site in Drajurk State Forest but this number includes an unknown proportion of recaptures. However, there is evidence of a contraction in range in the north of the distribution: Hill (2004) surveyed for Heath Mouse in the Wimmera using hair funnels: sixteen historic sites were surveyed and no Heath Mice were recorded. Numbers fluctuate with rainfall and time since the last fire. Rainfall over the preceding 18 months is positively associated with trap success (Hale et al. 2016).
range: The Heath Mouse formerly was widespread in the southwest of Western Australia as indicated by subfossils north from near Shark Bay to the southern edge of the Nullarbor Plain (Menkhorst et al. 2008); extending into South Australia including Eyre Peninsula (McDowell 1997, McDowell and Medlin 2010), Yorke Peninsula (McDowell et al. 2012) and near Adelaide (Cooper et al. 2003). The first collection was near Pingelly in the Western Australian wheatbelt. Since 1987, it has been trapped in several localities in the southern parts of Western Australia: Reserve No. 31111, ca 6 km north of Burngup, near Lake Biddy, Dragon Rocks Nature Reserve, Lake Magenta Nature Reserve, Fitzgerald River National Park (Sanders et al. 2012), and the Ravensthorpe Range area (Sanders et al. 2012). In Western Australia, since 2011, despite surveys, there are only five records, two in 2016 and three in 2019, most from Lake Magenta Nature Reserve, near Ravensthorpe and the Fitzgerald River National Park, with one in Frank Hann National Park. Trapping in Lake Magenta Nature Reserve in March 2024 did not capture any individuals, but a few individuals have been recently detected via camera trapping. The paucity of recent records gives concern for its status in Western Australia, noting that climate change has led to a significant decline in rainfall and increasing temperatures within its known range, with drought over the past three years. In Victoria, the Heath Mouse occurs in the Grampians Range and at many localities to the south and west of that range, extending south to Lower Glenelg National Park and into southeastern South Australia (Menkhorst et al. 2008, Le Duff et al. 2009). Fossil and subfossil evidence suggests that it formerly occurred more widely in south-western Victoria and with greater abundance (Cockburn 1978, Watson et al. 2003). In South Australia, the species has been reported from the Lower Glenelg River Conservation Park, Dry Creek Native Forest Reserve and Honeysuckle Native Forest Reserve (Bachman and Hayward 2016). One individual was found on Kangaroo Island in 1967 (Kemper et al. 2010). Surveys there in 1990 (Robinson and Armstrong 1990) and in 2009 (Jones et al. 2010) did not locate Heath Mice, but it should be noted that the surveys were not directed specifically towards this species (Menkhorst and Morris 2008). Recent surveys targeting small mammals on Kangaroo Island have not detected it (e.g., Hohnen et al. 2019).
useTrade: Pseudomys shortridgei is not utilised.
conservationActions: The majority of land on which Heath Mice are known to occur is within conservation estate, which is managed by state conservation agencies, and where some threats are managed. However, their ability to manage fire regimes may be limited. A captive-breeding programme was previously established in Victoria, with individuals from this program used for translocation attempts (Watson et al. 2003). There is a proposal to reintroduce Pseudomys shortridgei to Dirk Hartog Island National Park, Shark Bay, where feral cats, sheep and goats have been eradicated. This will require captive breeding; however, capturing animals from Western Australia to establish a captive colony appears unlikely unless the current drought breaks and the species becomes more common. The Heath Mouse is listed as Endangered under Australian legislation and a conservation advice provides a general framework for its recovery (TSSC 2016).

rationale: Assessed as Least Concern considering its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. There has been habitat loss in the past, but the species appears to be stable at present. The species is protected under Western Australia law.
habitat: This is a nocturnal species found in areas of low heathland and shrubland on sandy soils. Females give birth to two to six young after a gestation period of 37 to 38 days (Morris and Cowen 2023). It is nocturnal and sociable, resting during the day in a burrow that may be 60 cm deep and extends horizontally for 3-4 m. It is predominantly herbivorous during winter but includes arthropods in its diet in summer when the water content of vegetation is insufficient for its needs (Morris and Cowen 2023).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. It has declined or disappeared in parts of its range through residential development of coastal areas and conversion of land to agricultural use (Morris and Cowen 2023). It may be threatened by predation from Cats Felis catus and Red Foxes Vulpes vulpes. Frequent or extensive fires within vegetation remnants is a possible threat.
population: The species is widespread in semi-arid south-western Western Australia and is relatively abundant in remnant vegetation in the Wheatbelt with its range extending into uncleared areas to the east. During the 1998 to 2000 biodiversity survey of the Western Australian agriculture zone (Burbidge et al. 2004), it was recorded on eight of the 252 quadrats sampled.
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is present in south-western Western Australia, including Bernier Island, Dorre Island, and Dirk Hartog Island (Morris and Cowen 2023). It has been recorded in the Carnarvon, Yalgoo, Geraldton Sandplains, Murchison, Swan Coastal Plain, Avon Wheatbelt, Coolgardie, Jarrah Forest, Mallee and Esperance Plains bioregions, with two records marginally within the Murchison bioregion. There is a 1975 record of a Pseudomys on Woody Island, Archipelago of the Recherche, which was identified in the field as this species (Goodsell et al. 1976), but the identification is uncertain. It has not been trapped there since (Burbidge et al. 2012).
conservationActions: It is present in a number of protected areas, including Dirk Hartog Island, Kalbarri, Alexander Morrison, Watheroo, Moore River, Stirling Range, Fitzgerald River and Cape Le Grand National Parks, and Bernier and Dorre Islands Nature Reserve. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy of this species.

rationale: The Northern Delicate Mouse is Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in many protected areas, and tolerance to some degree of habitat modification. Although population size and trends are not well resolved, it does not meet Criterion A for listing because if it is declining the rate of any such decline is likely to be much less than 30% over a 10-year period. It does not meet criterion B because its actual AOO and EOO exceed threshold values, is not severely fragmented, occurs at >5 locations and does not show extreme fluctuations. It does not meet criterion C because its population size is likely to substantially exceed 10,000 mature individuals. It does not meet criterion D because it does not have a very small or restricted population.
habitat: The Northern Delicate Mouse is a terrestrial nocturnal species, sheltering during the day in shallow but sometimes complex burrows (Diete et al. 2015). It occurs across a range of woodland and grassland environments, although typically at sites with sandy soils. It is mostly a granivore, but also eats fruits, grass stems and invertebrates (Braithwaite and Brady 1993). This species can occur in recently burnt and degraded sites (Braithwaite and Brady 1993). Individuals can breed repeatedly (with litters of 3-4 young) over a long breeding season from at least February to October (Taylor and Horner 1970, Taylor and Calaby 2004).
threats: More than most other co-occurring terrestrial small mammal species, it is tolerant of some habitat disturbance and modification (Legge et al. 2019). Feral cats Felis catus are known predators of this species (Woolley et al. 2019), but are unlikely to have serious population-level impacts, and it occurs on some islands without cats. Based on modelling, Roycroft et al. (2024) concluded that its distribution was likely to contract severely with ongoing climate change.
population: The Northern Delicate Mouse is common across much of its extensive distribution. However, there have been no estimates of population size. Using mark-recapture methods, Braithwaite and Brady (1985) estimated the number-known-to-be-alive at one 45 ha site in Kakadu, finding it showed substantial variation across seasons, with a peak of ca. 100 individuals (i.e., >2 individual/ha). Population trends are not well resolved. Although some local declines have been reported in Kakadu and Litchfield National Parks (Woinarski et al. 2004, 2010), it has not experienced the extensive marked recent population losses of many other mammals in northern Australia (Woinarski et al. 2011), and there have been some increases reported such as on the Tiwi Islands (Davies et al. 2018).
range: As redefined by Roycroft et al. (2024), the Northern Delicate Mouse is endemic to Australia. It occurs on mainland northern Australia from the north Kimberley in the west to the Gulf of Carpentaria hinterland (about the border of Northern Territory and Queensland) in the east. It also occurs on many islands including Bigge, Augustus, Sir Graham Moore (Niiwalarra) in Western Australia, and Melville, West, North, South-west, Vanderlin and Bathurst in the Northern Territory (Firth et al. 2006, Roycroft et al. 2024). Delicate mice on Groote Eylandt (Northern Territory) are referable to Eastern Delicate Mouse Psuedomys mimulus (Roycroft et al. 2024).
conservationActions: The Northern Delicate Mouse occurs in many protected areas (including  Kakadu, Litchfield, Mirrima and Limmen Gate National Parks) (Roycroft et al. 2024).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in protected areas and on at least 10 islands. Although it is undergoing a continuous decline, it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. The factors likely to be driving decline (changed fire regimes, predation by feral Cats, livestock grazing) are still operating across most of its range.
habitat: The Western Chestnut Mouse is found in grasslands, and eucalypt grassy woodlands on sandy volcanic and lateritic soils with a dense cover of tussock grass. In the north Kimberley and monsoonal Northern Territory, it is most abundant in riparian woodlands (Kitchener et al. 1981, Kerle and Burgman 1984), although other studies in the Kimberley found it occurred in similar abundance across a wider range of habitats (Legge et al. 2011a). In Purnululu, it was recorded most commonly on plains with sandy soils supporting woodlands with dense shrub or tussock grass understorey (Woinarski 1992). In a Northern Territory study, a preference for longer-unburnt areas was evident (e.g., Kerle and Burgman 1984), and in two Kimberley studies, it was reported far more abundantly in unburnt areas than in areas recently burnt by a high severity fire (Legge et al. 2008), and with decrease in fire prevalence over time (Legge et al. 2019). It was reported to be substantially more abundant in de-stocked areas than in comparable sites with livestock grazing (Legge et al. 2011a, 2019). It occurs across a wide rainfall gradient in the Kimberley (Start et al. 2012).It eats grasses and builds a grass-lined nest. In the monsoonal climate of the Alligator Rivers area of the Northern Territory, the Western Chestnut Mouse breeds in the latter part of the wet season and can extend its breeding activity through the dry season; it may reproduce virtually year-round, presumably when environmental conditions are favourable (Taylor and Calaby 2004). Females give birth to between three and five young (usually three), after a gestation period of around 22 to 24 days (Robinson et al. 2023).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. However, like other indigenous rodents in northern Australia, it is detrimentally affected by large and frequent fires (e.g., Legge et al. 2008) and, possibly, by predation by feral Cats Felis catus. In northern Australia, Cat predation may increase after fire as Cats are known to select areas recently burnt by intense fires, but only in habitats that typically support high abundance of small mammals (McGregor et al. 2014, 2016); it has frequently been recorded in the diet of feral Cats (Woolley et al. 2019). Grazing by introduced (including feral) herbivores may affect its habitat as it occurs mainly in dense vegetation, and it has been reported to be more abundant in ungrazed than comparable grazed sites (Legge et al. 2019).
population: The Western Chestnut Mouse is a widespread species, but now generally sparse. For example, in Kakadu and the Kimberley, its trap success rate is typically <0.1 individuals per 100 trap-nights (Braithwaite and Muller 1997, Start et al. 2007, Woinarski et al. 2010); however, one study in the Kimberley (Legge et al. 2008) reported trap success in unburnt habitat at 6.8 captures per 100 trap-nights. It is considered ‘reasonably abundant’ on Barrow Island (Morris 2000). There are no data on density or population size, but – given it occurrence across a very extensive area - it is inferred to be >10,000 mature individuals.von Takach et al. (2020) reported ongoing decline of this species in the Northern Territory, with losses most evident in lower rainfall areas. They found that Pseudomys nanus had suffered a 24.9% reduction decline in niche hypervolume, showing that its historical occurrence was largely predicted by rainfall, elevation and ruggedness, whereas its contemporary occurrence is much more related to vegetation cover. The decline in niche hypervolume was greater than the decline in Extent of Occurrence. Its ongoing decline is inferred from historical extirpations in southern and central Australia, more recent losses from the Pilbara mainland, and broad-scale losses, particularly in lower rainfall areas, in monsoonal Northern Territory (von Takash et al. 2020). However, there is no clear signal of change in abundance from recent monitoring at the most substantial monitoring sites in its range, Kakadu (Woinarski et al. 2010) and the Tiwi Islands (Davies et al. 2018).
range: This species is restricted to northern Australia ranging from Barrow, Sholl, Potter, Fortescue and South West Regnard Islands off the Pilbara coast and the Kimberley including Adolphus Island (Western Australia), eastwards through monsoonal Northern Territory, including Melville and Bathurst Islands and South West Island in the Sir Edward Pellew Group in the Gulf of Carpentaria (Burbidge and Abbott 2017, Woinarski et al. 2011, Robinson et al. 2023) to north-western Queensland. It once occurred on South West Island in the Sir Edward Pellew Group but may be locally extinct there. It was formerly far more widely distributed in north-eastern Western Australia south of the Kimberley and in southern Northern Territory. It has been extirpated on the Pilbara mainland, where there are subfossil records. It has been extirpated in south-west of Western Australia with several specimens collected from New Norcia in 1843 (Robinson et al. 2023). The species is still relatively common in parts of the Kimberley mainland and monsoonal Northern Territory.Start et al. (2012) trapped mammals across a rainfall gradient in the southern Kimberley recording Psuedomys nanus in all rainfall zones (800-900 to 500-600 mm mean annual rainfall). Its remains were abundant in subfossil sites in this area.
conservationActions: The Western Chestnut Mouse occurs in many protected areas. In Western Australia it occurs on Barrow, Sholl, Potter and South West Regnard Islands (Pilbara, all nature reserves), in the Kimberley it occurs in Prince Regent and Drysdale River National Parks, in the Uunguu and Dambimangari Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs), and in the Charnley River, Mornington and Tableland Wildlife Sanctuaries (Australian Wildlife Conservancy). In the Northern Territory it occurs on North and South West Islands (Sir Edward Pellew Islands), in Judburra/Gregory, Litchfield, Kakadu, and Nitmiluk National Parks, in Southern Tanami, Wardekken, Ganalanga-Mindibirrina and South-East Arnhem Land IPAs, and in the Wongalara Wildlife Sanctuary. All islands where it occurs in the Pilbara, Western Australia, are nature reserves and the Sir Edward Pellew Islands are within Yanuwa (Barni- Wardimantha Awara IPA. In Queensland it has been recorded in Boodjamulla (Lawn Hill) National Park.In some areas, recent programs of intensive management of fire, to maintain some longer-unburnt areas and to reduce the extent and frequency of higher severity fires (e.g., Legge et al. 2011b), are likely to provide some benefits to this species.

rationale: The Northern Hopping-mouse is assessed as Endangered under criteria B1ab(i,ii,iii,v)+B2(ab(i,ii.iii,v). Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 823 km2, its AOO is 256 km2; it now occurs at a single location; and it is undergoing a continuing decline in habitat quality and probably also in AOO, EOO and number of mature individuals. It is also close to meeting criterion C: the estimation of population size has not previously been robust, but more recent information derived from intensive studies that assess burrow density and home range size indicates that the current population is approximately 2,400 individuals. It is undergoing continuing decline, at a rate of plausibly 20% in 5 years, but this is inferred and therefore not yet robust enough to meet the criterion.  There is no robust estimate of extent of population decline, so criterion A cannot be applied, but current and future rates of decline are likely to be between 30 and 50%. It is now restricted to a single location and it is plausible that a single novel threat could rapidly dive the species towards extinction, so it also fits VU D2.
habitat: The Northern Hopping-mouse occurs in a range of vegetation types on sandy substrates (Woinarski et al. 2014, Diete et al. 2016). It is patchily distributed. It was previously thought to be most abundant in dunes and sand sheets, supporting coastal heathlands, shrublands, and tussock grasses (Woinarski et al. 1999, Woinarski and Flannery 2008) but recent work has found it more abundant in Eucalypt open forest and woodlands, particularly fringing sandstone plateaus (Diete et al. 2016). Coastal subpopulations have been detected in quaternary dune fields away from the coast. All confirmed populations are within ~700 m of the high tide line and inland populations are generally found on areas of alluvial sandy outwash within 700 m of sandstone margins (P. Barden Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers pers comm. September 2024). This species is difficult to trap in traditional aluminium box and wire cage traps (Woinarski 2005) but can be captured in deep pitfall traps (Diete et al. 2016). The gestation period is about seven weeks, and the females usually give birth to three young (Dixon and Huxley 1985, Diete et al. 2016).
threats: Feral cats, strip-mining (mainly manganese on Groote Eylandt but also bauxite in north-eastern Arnhem Land and Cape York Peninsula), and changes in fire regimes are threats, and these threats are probably compounding (Woinarski et al. 2014). Based on data held by the Anindilyakwa IPA, 10-20% of the currently known Groote Eylandt distribution is in close proximity (less than 500 m) or within active or granted mining and mining infrastructure areas proposed for mining in the next 5 to 10 years. All other remaining Northern Hopping-mouse areas on Groote Eylandt are covered by granted or under application mineral extraction licences. Northern Hopping-mouse populations are potentially at risk from mining due to direct clearing impacts and edge effects including dust, changes in vegetation cover, vegetation dieback due to dewatering or flooding, noise, light, vehicle movements, blast vibration, changes in hydrology and fire, and increased access for feral cats (Felis catus) (and increased density of cats in and around disturbed areas). Hard rock quarrying for road and other construction also presents a risk, as Northern Hopping-mouse populations often occur adjacent to preferred hard rock resource areas. The species appears to tolerate small scale, patchy burns; however, hot, large-scale fires are likely detrimental (Diete et al. 2016). Habitat degradation and structural changes to vegetation by introduced herbivores, combined with feral cats and altered fire regimes may have contributed to its decline and possible extirpation on the mainland (Dixon and Barden 2019). Feral cats are present on Groote Eylandt, but their impact on Northern Hopping-mouse is currently poorly resolved.
population: There are no reliable estimates of density or population size prior to 2014. Some early surveys using burrow densities were conducted before the potential for misidentification with burrows of other rodent species was fully understood (Diete et al. 2014, 2015), suggesting that old estimates using this technique are unreliable. Barden (2017) and Diete et al. (2016) estimated a population of 2,000 individuals based on the distribution of confirmed burrows and occupied areas with reference to radio tracking range polygons. Long term monitoring sites on Groote Eylandt (2020-2024) indicate approximately 0.8 burrows per hectare at key sites. Based on a maximum individual range polygon of 24 hectares (Diete et al. 2016), burrow data from extensive recent surveys indicates an occupation area of 3,050 hectares on Groote Eylandt. Allowing for a best-case scenario of 1-1.5 adults per burrow and assuming that all areas detected in the past decade remain occupied, a reasonable population estimate would be 2,440-3,660 breeding individuals. Actual numbers are likely to be considerably less than this in 2024, as there have been documented declines in numbers of active burrows at monitored sites between 2019 and 2024 and some sites have been found to support lower burrow densities. There have also been several catastrophic events that have impacted greater than 90% of Northern Hopping-mouse sites since 2022, including extensive hot fires in the 2022 mid to late dry season and extensive flooding, rainfall and extreme weather associated with a cyclone in early 2024. The species appears to have declined significantly in some areas, particularly coastal areas of Groote Eylandt, as intensive trapping and extensive searches for signs from 2012-2014 were only able to confirm the presence of the species in one coastal location in the south-east section of the island (Diete et al. 2016). Subsequent surveys using aerial helicopter burrow surveys, camera trapping and ground inspections have been conducted at all coastal areas on Groote Eylandt by the Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers and Territory Natural Resource Management. These surveys only detected this species from five discrete and restricted coastal sites on eastern Groote Eylandt (Dixon and Barden 2019, P. Bardon & K. Dixon unpublished data).
range: The Northern Hopping-mouse is endemic to Australia where it is now known only from Groote Eylandt (2,285 km2) in the Northern Territory. There has been an extensive program of surveys in recent years aimed at clarifying its distribution and status. Low level aerial helicopter survey transects (~4,800 km) targeting burrow clusters have covered broad areas of the Groote archipelago as well as targeting key habitats including sandy outwash areas adjacent to sandstone and coastal dune fields. Surveys in the north-eastern Northern Territory mainland and the Groote archipelago between 2014 and 2024 (Diete et al. 2016, Dixon and Barden 2019, Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers ongoing assessments, P. Barden & K. Dixon unpublished data) have provided improved information on the distribution and status of the species. Surveys between 2017 and 2024 included revisiting ~90% of former mainland record locations (all but two) combined with ~1,900 km low level aerial helicopter transects searching for burrow clusters, including coastal dune habitats between Nhulunbuy and the Queensland border (Dixon and Barden 2019). Mainland surveys included ground surveys for burrows and camera trapping at previous record sites and other potential locations (Dixon and Barden 2019). The type specimen was reportedly collected on the Cape York Peninsula, Queensland at some time prior to 1867. However, due to an absence of subsequent records, the provenance of this specimen was thought to be dubious (Winter and Allison 1980, Lee 1995, Woinarski and Flannery 2008). There are several recently discovered lines of evidence which now support the Cape York Peninsula collection locality. The specimen was acquired by the British Natural History Museum in a consignment with several other Cape York Peninsula endemic species (Barden 2022). Importantly, several previously unknown specimens of Northern Hopping-mouse have been recently discovered in museum collections that are likely to have come from Cape York Peninsula, including one with reasonably accurate collection locality details collected in the 1950s (Barden 2022). There are also historical records of Northern Hopping-mouse from the Northern Territory mainland, with the most recent specimen being from the Cadell River in 1973. However, there have been no confirmed specimen records for 50 years from the Northern Territory mainland and for 70 years (Cape York Peninsula), with all recent records coming from Groote Eylandt (Diete et al. 2016, Dixon and Barden 2019, Barden 2022). Surveys were conducted in 2018-19 at all except two mainland Northern Territory sites where the species was previously stated to occur (Woinarski et al. 1999), and no evidence of presence was found (Dixon and Barden 2019). Based on mainland surveys conducted to date (Dixon and Barden 2019), it is considered more likely than not that the species is no longer present on the Australian mainland, and therefore likely to be restricted to Groote Eylandt. Within the Groote Archipelago, surveys on all of the larger islands (Bickerton, Winchelsea, Connexion and the NE Island group) (Dixon and Barden 2019, P. Barden Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers pers. comm. September 2024) using aerial burrow surveys using helicopters, ground transect searches for burrows, broadscale and targeted camera trapping) indicates that the species is not present on islands other than Groote Eylandt. Surveys on Groote between 2012 and 2024 (greater than 120,000 camera trap nights across various projects, and other methods) indicate decline and local extinction at formerly occupied coastal dune areas. The species currently occupies limited specific habitats in the interior and eastern coast of the island (Paul Barden, Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers, pers. comm., September 2024; P. Barden & K. Dixon, unpublished data). A comparison of recent surveys with data collected between 1990 and 2010 indicate ongoing declines on Groote Eylandt, with populations identified during earlier assessments no longer present on the south-east coast, some areas of the southern interior along the Kings Crossing road, the Umbakumba area and northern Makbamanja Peninsula. Remaining populations occupy restricted areas (in the central western interior of Groote Eylandt and with a second disjunct range area on the eastern coast of the island (Paul Barden, Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers, pers. comm., September 2024; P. Barden and K. Dixon, unpublished data).
conservationActions: Groote Eylandt is managed as an Indigenous Protected Area, although large components of the IPA are subject to active ongoing mining and all other areas are covered by granted or under application mineral licences. There is ongoing research in the Groote archipelago investigating Northern Hopping-mouse distribution, population and trends, conservation genetics, general and fire ecology and survey methods (collaborative project with the Anindilyakwa Land Council, Territory Natural Resource Management, Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers and Charles Darwin University) with funding from the Commonwealth Government until June 2026.There is little amelioration of main threats. On Groote Eylandt, mining infrastructure development is expanding into areas that are occupied by or adjacent to Northern Hopping-mouse populations as a precursor to active mining at these locations. There is a Groote Archipelago Threatened Species Management Plan 2019-2028. The Northern Hopping-mouse is listed as Endangered under Australian national environmental legislation, and a Conservation Advice (TSSC 2021) provides general conservation guidelines. The Northern Hopping-mouse was listed as a ‘priority species’ in the Australian government’s Threatened Species Action Plan 2022-2032.

rationale: The Dusky Hopping-mouse has exhibited a historical decrease in abundance and distribution. However, abundance and distributional extent increased from 1995 to at least 2014 due to reduction in numbers of the invasive European Rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus and the introduced predators (cat Felis catus and red fox Vulpes vulpes) whose abundance was sustained by high rabbit numbers. Relatively high abundance of Dusky Hopping-mice appears to have persisted until at least 2021. Population size is likely to be substantially higher than 10,000 mature individuals in most years, but population numbers and area of occupancy (AOO) decline severely in drought, and the species may then occur in a limited number of drought refuge areas, before expanding its range again after substantial rainfall. Contraction in range and population decline in drought years may be sufficient to approach Vulnerable B2ac, with an AOO of possibly less than 2,000 km2, evidence of severe fragmentation and/or occurrence in less than 10 locations; but the evidence for this is tenuous. Nonetheless, adopting a precautionary approach, this species is assessed as Near Threatened, approaching Vulnerable B2ac(ii).
habitat: The Dusky Hopping-mouse is found primarily on longitudinal and irregular stabilised dune fields where perennial plant species such as Nitre Bush (Nitraria billardierei) and Sandhill Canegrass (Zygochloa paradoxa) persist. Moseby et al. (2006) studied the species at Pelican Waterhole, south-western Queensland, and Montecollina Bore in north east South Australia over an eight-year period. Whilst the population at Montecollina Bore exhibited large fluctuations in size, captures at Pelican Waterhole were lower but more consistent.
