Recaptures between sessions at Montecollina Bore peaked at 60% but no individuals were recaptured at Pelican Waterhole. The Dusky Hopping-mouse digs burrow systems on the stable crests and slopes of dunes and within sand hummocks, the depth varying with habitat but commonly being ca. 1 m deep with some up to 2 m deep. Animals live in groups of up to five individuals. At night they forage over a wide area, commonly 400 m per night and up to 1.5 km over three nights (Owens et al. 2008).Monitoring has shown that some subpopulations persist with low, yet stable numbers, while others vary in a boom-bust cycle in response to varying rainfall and resource availability (Owens et al. 2008).At at least some sites and in some seasons, the Dusky Hopping-mouse is one of the most frequent dietary items taken by cats (Feit et al. 2019). Letnic et al. (2009) showed that the Dusky Hopping-mouse was more abundant where Dingoes occurred and found that that generalised linear modelling showed that Dusky Hopping-mouse abundance was associated positively with Dingo activity and long-term annual rainfall, and negatively with Red Fox activity. Surveys in north-eastern South Australia in 2011 and 2012 found Dusky Hopping-mice to be occupying a wide range of landform types (rocky ranges, gibber plains, sand dunes, sand plains) but nearly always in association with at least small sandy areas. Sandy habitat is needed for the Dusky Hopping-mouse to build the burrow systems it requires to live communally and breed. Isolated sand dunes or rises were inhabited despite being separated by several kilometres of hard substrate indicating Dusky Hopping-mice are capable of dispersing over considerable distances and colonising small patches of suitable habitat (Southgate et al. 2012). Many subpopulations are found in habitats highly degraded by overgrazing by rabbits and livestock (Moseby et al. 1999, Owens et al. 2008). However, abundance and distributional extent of Dusky Hopping-mice increased following the effective control of rabbits using rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus from 1995. Litter size is between one and five. Both sexes reach maturity at 70 days (Aslin and Watts 1980). Longevity in the wild has been recorded as up to 13 months (Owens et al. 2008). In captivity other Notomys species live to 5.3 to 6.4 years of age (AnAge 2012). Generation length is here assumed to be 2 years.
threats: The major threats are habitat degradation and resource depletion by livestock and feral herbivores (moderate to severe, entire range): loss of burrowing and feeding habitat in areas degraded by rabbits and stock. However, the species can survive in at least some degraded areas (Owens et al. 2008). Range expansion/re-invasion over the period 1995-2014 occurred following reduced rabbit numbers after the introduction of Rabbit calicivirus (Pedler et al. 2016), with such increase due to reduced competition (food resources) from rabbits, increase in habitat suitability, and decrease in the abundance of predators formerly supported by the high abundance of rabbits.Predation by feral Domestic Cats (Felis catus; moderate to severe, across the entire range) and Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes) represents major threats: predation by cats was reported by Vernes et al. (2021a,b) and Feit et al. (2019), and hyper-predation has been linked to decline in rodents in low productivity landscapes (Smith and Quin 1996, TSSC 2008). Letnic et al. (2009) demonstrated that Dusky Hopping-mouse abundance was associated negatively with Red Fox activity, and some studies have demonstrated abundance is higher in areas with dingoes (and hence fewer foxes) than in areas where dingoes have been excluded or where dingo abundance is reduced by management (pastoral areas) (e.g., Letnic and Dworjanyn 2011, Sheldon et al. 2023). Conversely, Allen et al. (2018) found that variation in abundance of Dusky Hopping-mice was associated principally with broad habitat features and rainfall, rather than livestock grazing intensity or abundance of dingoes.There is likely to be competition from House Mice (Mus musculus; minor to moderate, across the entire range): the House Mouse is very common at times in sites where Dusky Hopping-mouse occurs (Moseby et al. 1999, TSSC 2008); although, the effects are not clear.Climate change (minor-moderate in short to medium term, entire range) could represent a major threat: if rainfall reduces or high rainfall events become less frequent and droughts more frequent, the species may decline or disappear.
population: At many sites, abundance varies with rainfall in a ‘boom and bust’ pattern. Watts and Aslin (1981) reported observations by Sturt suggesting that it was common near the Flinders Ranges in 1847. Moseby et al. (1999) inferred a total population of more than 10,000 individuals, but fewer than 2,500 individuals during drought. In 2011, trapping at Wooltana recorded the highest density of Dusky Hopping-mice (10 individuals/hectare) since trapping records began in South Australia in 1993; however, capture rate dropped to 0-0.5% when the sites were re-trapped in 2012 as the species began to contract under drier conditions. Track imprints were detected on 70% of 60 track-based monitoring plots sampled in 2011 and 43% of plots re-sampled in 2012 (Southgate et al. 2012). Across much of its range it is - at least in some seasons - abundant and one of the main prey items detected in predator samples (e.g., Lee et al. 2021, Sheldon et al. 2023). Abundance (along with distributional extent) increased substantially over the period 1995-2014 due to management that reduced rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) abundance (Pedler et al. 2016), with this high abundance persisting until at least 2021 (Indigo et al. 2021).
range: The Dusky Hopping-mouse occurs in arid South Australia (Watts and Aslin 1981, Moseby and Brandle 1999), south-western Queensland (Dickman et al. 2008a) and north-western New South Wales (Dickman et al. 2008b). There have been no records from the Northern Territory since 1939 (Woinarski et al. 2007). Burbidge et al. (2009), using modern, historical and subfossil data, recorded it in eight IBRA (Interim Bioregionalisation for Australia) bioregions, noting that it was extirpated in five and had declined or seriously declined in the remaining three. Ardeotis Biological Consultants (2007) extended the known range to the south and west. Recent records are from the Channel Country and Simpson Strzelecki Dunefield Bioregions in Queensland, South Australia and New South Wales. Trapping and track-based surveys in north-eastern South Australia in 2011-12 demonstrated a major reinvasion of the former range of this species in areas to the south and west of the Simpson-Strzelecki Desert Dunefields Bioregion following higher than average rainfall in 2010-12 (Southgate and Moseby 2011, Southgate et al. 2012), the known distribution being extended southward almost to the Barrier Highway and westward to the Flinders Ranges. A 2007 record from the Beverley mine lease, north of Lake Frome, extended its known range south-westward (Waudby and How 2008). A capture from the Broken Hill Complex Bioregion in an atypical habitat (bluebush shrubland) and new locality ca. 170 km south of the nearest New South Wales record may indicate a significant population eruption and subsequent migration into new areas following the widespread ephemeral and perennial plant production pulse that occurred after widespread heavy rainfall in 2010 (Val et al. 2012). Recent records from owl pellets at Pilungah Reserve in south-western Queensland were within 10 km of the Northern Territory border, suggesting it may still occur in the jurisdiction (Schoenefuss et al. 2024).
useTrade: The Dusky Hopping-mouse is not utilized.
conservationActions: The dusky hopping-mouse is listed as Vulnerable under Australian legislation. There is a conservation advice but no recovery plan for this species. This species is included in a broad-scale monitoring program across Australia's arid zone, with monitoring based on detection of tracks, burrows and other signs. Several hundred monitoring sites occur within its range, sufficient to detect changes in abundance (Indigo et al. 2021, Southwell et al. 2023). Some monitoring is also being carried out at trapping grids in north-eastern South Australia (Southgate et al. 2012).

rationale: Assessment of the conservation status of the Fawn Hopping-mouse is challenging because there is limited information on population size or trajectory, and it is difficult to evaluate the number of locations and subpopulations. In periods of low rainfall, when population size is lowest, it may approach Vulnerable B2ab(iii)c(iv), but the number of locations is poorly resolved. It may also approach Vulnerable C2b, however, 'continuing decline' is not established. It is therefore assessed as Near Threatened.
habitat: The Fawn Hopping-mouse is largely restricted to gibber plains and alluvial flats. A recent New South Wales record was in bluebush shrublands (Val et al. 2012). It spends the daytime in a burrow either in sand patches or in gibber or claypans. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, but also includes insects and green plant material. It utilises succulent, salt-adapted plants around the edges of claypans as a source of water (Breed 2008). Females become sexually mature at nearly 6 months; gestation period 38-43 days; litter size 1-5 (Watts and Aslin 1981). Generation length is here assumed to be 1.5 years (Pacifici et al. 2013).
threats: The major threat is predation by feral Domestic Cats (Felis catus; moderate, entire range), Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes; minor, entire range) and raptors (minor, entire range). Cats take rodents of this size and hyperpredation has been linked to decline in rodents in low productivity landscapes (Smith and Quin 1996); however, cats are relatively rare in Fawn Hopping-mouse habitat (Brandle et al. 2008) and the species has survived cat predation for a long time. Fox predation of small rodents occurs but the impact is unquantified. Construction of fences and other elevated structures provides perches for predatory birds (P. Canty pers. comm).Habitat degradation (including trampling of burrows) and resource depletion by livestock and feral herbivores (moderate, most of range) represent another threat: excessive trampling by domestic and feral ungulates can severely degrade the vegetated patches of sand in which this species burrows; this leads to de-stabilisation of these areas making them prone to wind and water erosion (Canty and Brandle 2008); higher stocking rates for sheep and cattle prior to 1950 may have been a significant factor in their historical decline; placement of artificial water points in areas of prime habitat may be a continuing threat to some populations, as this is done in order to increase extent of livestock grazing.Road construction  may also present a threat in some parts of this species' range: roads tend to traverse gibber pavement and road building material is harvested from gibbers (P. Canty pers. comm).
population: The Fawn Hopping-mouse is sparsely scattered in suitable habitat (Breed 2008). Abundance varies markedly between wet and dry periods (e.g., Morton et al. 1977, Canty and Brandle 2008), although Breed (2023) reported that it 'does not appear to undergo large fluctuations in density'. Brandle et al. (2008) used densities of 0.25-10 animals/km² estimated from the field records of Canty and Brandle (2008) and the extant potential area of occupancy of 18,000 km² to estimate minimum and maximum population size. The result was a range of 4,500-180,000 individuals depending on seasonal conditions.There is no robust evidence of recent population trajectories. If there is a continuing decline it is likely to be the result of local extinctions from isolated suitable habitat patches during prolonged dry periods.
range: The Fawn Hopping-mouse is now largely restricted to the Channel Country bioregion spanning from north-eastern South Australia to south-western Queensland, and immediately adjacent areas. Recent records have extended the known range in north-western New South Wales (including to the Broken Hill Complex bioregion) (Val et al. 2012), and in the northern edge of the Simpson Desert Queensland just east of the Northern Territory border (Schoenefuss et al. 2024).Formerly it was more widespread, including most of the Lake Eyre Basin, southern Northern Territory, and the eastern edge of the Nullarbor Plain. Subfossils are known from near Madura on the Nullarbor Plain of Western Australia, the Flinders Ranges of South Australia (Watts and Aslin 1981) and Mootwingee National Park, New South Wales (Ellis 1993). Burbidge et al. (2009), using subfossil, historical and modern data, recorded it in six IBRA (Interim Bioregionalisation for Australia) bioregions, and stated that it was extinct in three and declined or seriously declined in two. The overall decline of the species from its pre-European area of occupancy is more than 50% (Brandle et al. 2008).
useTrade: The fawn hopping-mouse is not utilized
conservationActions: There is no recovery plan and no specific management for this species. It occurs in some conservation reserves. It is not listed as threatened under Australian environmental law.

rationale: Assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. The species is protected under Australian and Western Australian law.
habitat: It is found in areas of rocky, hummock grassland with little or no soil and an overstorey of Acacia (Lee 1995, Ford and Johnson 2007). Animals live in small family groups in burrows below mounds of pebbles. The pebble mounds constructed by this species are distinctive. Mounds may contain many thousands of pebbles and may cover an area of 0.5-9.0 m2 and are used by successive generations (Start 2023). Gibson and McKenzie (2009) found that Pseudomys chapmani occupies a peculiarly specific category of rocky substrates (gentle pebbly hill-slopes) and percent nitrogen in the soil was the highest ranked variable for this species with a generally positive response (greater occurrences) to increasing levels. Females can produce several litters of four young annually (Start 2023).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. The reasons for its elimination from the southern portion of its former range are unclear, but may have been related to predation by Red Foxes Vulpes vulpes, with feral Cats Felis catus possibly having played a part (Start et al. 2000). Mining may be a very localised threat (Anstee et al. 1997), but this would not significantly affect the overall population size.
population: This species is sparsely distributed within abundant habitat (Start 2023). During the Pilbara Region biodiversity survey 2002-2007 (Gibson and McKenzie 2009) it was recorded on 29 of the 301 survey sites. There are no data on population size, but likely to be >10,000.
range: The species is now near-endemic to the Pilbara bioregion, with a small number of records close to that bioregion in the Carnarvon, Great Sandy Desert and Gascoyne bioregions. It was formerly more widespread, once being found in more coastal areas, as well as further to the south (Lee 1995). Start et al. (2000) found that it no longer occurred in 35% of its former extent of occurrence (340,000 km2), mainly in the Gascoyne and Murchison bioregions, where relictual pebble mounds remain (Dunlop and Pound 1981).
conservationActions: It has been recorded from Karijini, Rudall River, Millstream-Chichester Collier Range and Purungunya National Parks, Barlee Range Nature Reserve and Cane River Conservation Park. The species was previously listed as threatened in Western Australia until surveys found that it was more widespread (Start et al. 2000).

rationale: The Arnhem Rock-rat is assessed as Vulnerable because its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated to be 1,000 km² (the best estimate of a range of 240-5,560), and extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated at 14,004 km², it occurs at an estimated five locations, and its relative abundance and habitat quality are continuing to decline likely due to inappropriate fire regime and predation by feral cats (Felis catus). It may have declined by at least 30% over the last 10 years, however the data are too sparse to quantify this.
habitat: The Arnhem Rock-rat is a nocturnal terrestrial rodent. Its diet comprises mainly seeds, fruit and some other vegetable matter. The seeds eaten include those from many species of rainforest tree (Begg and Dunlop 1985). Large seeds may be cached, or at least moved to be eaten at relatively safe sites, resulting in distinctive piles of chewed hard seeds in rock fissures or under large overhangs (Begg and Dunlop 1980). On the basis of its known response to a single large fire, the Arnhem Rock-rat appears to be unusually fire-sensitive, with substantial decline for at least 1-2 years post-fire (Begg et al. 1981). The distribution of the Arnhem Rock-rat is entirely encompassed by the far more widely distributed (and appreciably smaller) Common Rock-rat Z. argurus. Within the broad area of overlap, the species may be locally spatially disjunct, and the Arnhem Rock-rat is much more associated with rainforest habitats (Begg 1981). Breeding may occur throughout the year, but the incidence of pregnant females peaks in March-May (Begg 1981). Litter size is small (two young reported from two litters: Watts and Aslin 1981). Generation length is derived from a mean of age at sexual maturity (5-6 months: Begg 1981) and longevity (probably 2-3 years).
threats: Woinarski et al. (2014) listed the main threats as inappropriate fire regime (fires that are too frequent and or of high intensity) and predation by feral cats (Felis catus). Notwithstanding some improvements in fire regimes over the last few decades in sandstone environments of Kakadu National Park and Wardekken Indigenous Protected Area, the current incidence of fire in sandstone rainforest habitats remains appreciably higher than thresholds set for conservation (Russell-Smith et al. 2017), with ongoing decline in the long-unburnt habitat favoured by this species. As a consequence, the mammal assemblage in the sandstone environments continues to decline (Einoder et al. 2023). With ongoing climate change, the fire regime is likely to become increasingly unfavourable (NESP Earth Systems and Climate Change Hub 2020).
population: There has been no robust estimate of the total population size or that of any subpopulations. The Arnhem Rock-rat may be locally common: Begg (1981) reported capturing about 350 different individuals over a 28-month study (1977-1979) at Little Nourlangie Rock (=Nawurlandja) (Kakadu), although those data cannot be used to assess density or population size at that site. Begg (1981) also reported that the relative abundance was highest in closed forest, of four habitats sampled.  Abundance has declined over the last 1-2 decades at sites subject to repeated sampling (Woinarski et al. 2007, 2010). For example, Ibbett et al. (2018) reported change in abundance at a well-sampled sandstone outlier (Nawurlandja) from 0.36 individuals per 100 trap-nights (from 10,800 trap-nights sampled) in 1977-79 to 0 (from 2400 trap-nights) in 2002.  A population size of 20,000 is estimated here, but this is without robust foundation.
range: The Arnhem Rock-rat (Zyzomys maini) is endemic to the Arnhem Land Plateau and nearby rocky outcrops, Northern Territory, Australia. Most of its range has been little sampled, but suitable monsoon rainforest patches probably occupy about less than 1,000 km² of the Arnhem massif (Russell-Smith et al. 1992).
useTrade: The Arnhem Rock-rat is not utilized.
conservationActions: Almost all of the distribution of this species is within Kakadu National Park and the adjacent Warddeken Indigenous Protected Area, in which fire management is a major objective. The Arnhem Rock-rat is listed as Vulnerable under Australian environmental law, with a Conservation Advice outlining management priorities. This species is included in a threatened species strategy for Kakadu National Park (Woinarski and Winderlich 2014).

rationale: Assessed as Least Concern in view of its moderately wide distribution, presumed large population and because if declining, the rate of decline is unlikely to be at a rate to qualify for listing in a threatened of near threatened category.There was a decline in rainforest patches in the past due to inappropriate fire regimes and feral cattle, but this decline is not continuing. Existing monitoring programs indicate population increase in areas where management imposes early dry season fires to limit damage to forest vegetation from high-intensity wildfire.
habitat: The species is most abundant in the high-rainfall country along the north-western Kimberley coastline. It is patchily distributed, preferring the most rugged areas of rock scree with massive boulders. It may be found in rainforest patches on sandstone, volcanic or lateritic scree but is mainly found in open sandstone country where a scatted cover of low trees growing above shrubs and hummock grass mantles precipitous slopes and boulder-strewn gullies, ledges and crevices along gorges or behind mangroves (McKenzie et al. 2023).
threats: The species was threatened by loss of habitat through inappropriate fire regimes (Radford et al. 2015, 2020; Ondei et al. 2017, 2020), in part caused by the opening up of forest patches to savanna grasses by cattle and other introduced herbivores (i.e. conversion of perennial grasses to annual grasses) (McKenzie et al. 2023). It may be predated by feral Cats Felis catus. However, its rugged habitat provides indestructible refuges and these threats are unlikely to be significant at the population level. Recent fire management has greatly reduced the impact of large, hot, late dry season fires and at least in some places the species is increasing.
population: There are insufficient data to estimate population size. The species is patchily distributed, but relatively abundant in suitable habitat. There is no evidence of significant population decline. Monitoring indicates that abundance increases in areas where management imposes early dry season fires to limit risks from high intensity wildfire (Radford et al. 2020).
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is almost restricted to the north-west Kimberley region of Western Australia (McKenzie et al. 2023). It has been recorded on 17 islands in the Buccaneer and Bonaparte Archipelagos (Gibson and McKenzie 2012, Burbidge and Abbott 2017). Outside the north-west Kimberley it has been recorded only near Kununurra, Western Australia, close to the type locality.
conservationActions: It is present in protected areas (e.g. Prince Regent National Park and Wunaamin Conservation Park) and in Indigenous Protected Areas. Monitoring of populations would be advisable given conspecific declines. Targeted fire management is required to reduce risks from destructive late dry season fires (Radford et al. 2015, 2020). Removal of cattle from sensitive areas of the species' habitat is needed (McKenzie et al. 2023). This species occurs on at least 17 offshore islands, most within Indigenous Protected Areas.

rationale: Colobus guereza is listed as Least Concern. Although this species is declining and locally threatened, it is widespread and common at many sites, especially in protected areas. There is no firm evidence for a significant range-wide population decline that warrants listing in a higher category of threat. Its status could change, however, as pressures on its habitat grow and if hunting of larger-bodied primates continues to intensify.
habitat: Colobus guereza is arboreal but will travel across the ground between patches of forest. It occupies a wide range of forest types including low, mid-altitude (=transition), and montane moist forest, ground water forest, secondary forest, riverine forest, swamp forest, and gallery forest. Often common in secondary or degraded forest (Fashing and Oates 2013, Groves and Ting 2013). More than any other African colobine, C. guereza does well in secondary forest and on forest edges (Struhsaker 1972, 1975, Oates 1977, 1996, Butynski 1984, Oates et al. 1990, Fashing and Oates 2013, Fashing 2022). For instance, moderate levels of logging in Kibale National Park resulted in an increase in abundance (Skorupa 1986, Johns and Skorupa 1987, Struhsaker 1997, 2010, Chapman et al. 2000). This may be partly due to dietary and behavioural flexibility and adaptability, and to the greater availability of fast-growing, high-protein/lower-fibre colonizing plants that occur in disturbed habitats (Onderdonk and Chapman 2000).Colobus guereza is largely folivorous in some regions, but feeds both on leaves and fruits in others (Fashing and Oates 2013). The leaf component of diet ranges from 51% (Budongo, western Uganda; Plumptre et al. 2006) to 87% (Kalinzu, southwestern Uganda; Matsuda et al. 2020) leaves. The diet in disturbed and fragmented forests is comprised of more fruit than in undisturbed forests (Tesfaye et al. 2021). In the Awi Zone, northern Ethiopia, C. g. guereza is most abundant in dry evergreen Afromontane forest at 1,859-2,557 m asl (Kifle and Bekele 2023). A total of 31 food plant species were recorded in Wof-Washa Natural Forest (Yazezew et al. 2023). The authors provide a list of the most consumed food items in both natural forest and in plantations. Plantation forest can provide effective buffer zones and corridors (Yazezew et al. 2023).Group size of C. guereza ranges from 2 to 23 individuals (Suzuki 1979, Fashing and Cords 2000), and group home ranges are 1.5-100 ha (Fashing and Oates 2013, Groves and Ting 2013).Adult male C. guereza emit a loud call (roar) daily, often around dawn. The roar appears to serve at least three roles: maintenance of intergroup spacing, predator alarm, and predator intimidation (Kingdon 1971, Marler 1972, Walek 1978, Oates and Trocco 1983, Poirier-Poulin and Teichroeb 2020). In favourable circumstances, the roar of C. guereza can be heard at >2 km (Butynski and De Jong 2022a).An overview of the natural history and conservation of C. guereza is provided in Fashing (2022) and Butynski and De Jong (2022a).
threats: Forest loss is the leading proximate threat for the majority of colobine taxa in Africa (Butynski and De Jong 2022a). Probably more than any other African colobine, however, C. guereza does well in secondary forest and on forest edge (Struhsaker 1972, 1975; Oates 1977; Butynski 1984; Fashing and Oates 2013). Colobus guereza is one of the few primate species which responds well to low to moderate levels of habitat disturbance. The species is, however, threatened in many parts of its range by habitat loss through timber extraction, through removal of natural forest for exotic tree plantations and agriculture, and from rapidly expanding human populations and climate change (von Hippel et al. 2000, Fashing and Oates 2013, Groves and Ting 2013, Fashing 2022, Kufa et al. 2022, Kifle and Bekele 2023).Bushmeat hunting is damaging populations of C. guereza in the western part of its range. It is also killed for its pelt, which is used in traditional ceremonies and as ornaments worn by various African peoples (including Kikuyu, Samburu, Chagga, Kuria and Luhya; Mwenja 2007, De Jong and Butynski 2010, Fashing and Oates 2013, Groves and Ting 2013, Butynski and De Jong 2022a). In the 19th and 20th centuries, the pelt featured in the international fur trade, and in the 1970s large numbers of skins were on sale to tourists in Kenya and Ethiopia (Oates 1977). Although the international trade in pelts has been largely stopped, use within Africa remains and hunting seems to have increased locally (Butynski and De Jong 2022a). It appears that C. guereza is increasingly involved in crop raiding and/or food-snatching as the monkeys adapt their ecology and diet to cope with human-modified habitats and increased sympatry with humans. For example, C. g. kikuyuensis often takes food from restaurant tables on Mount Kenya (Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs.). Colobus g. kikuyuensis crop-raids in Laikipia County and around the Aberdare Range, central Kenya (F. Jimmy pers. comm.). Understanding the importance of agroecosystems for Colobus guereza is becoming an increasingly important factor in planning for its conservation, and in improving the understanding and monitoring of zoonotic diseases.
population: Colobus guereza is a widespread species that is locally abundant. Densities range from 3 individuals/km² (Ituri Forest, DRC; Bocian 1997) to 800 individuals/km² (Murchison Falls, Uganda; Leskes and Acheson 1970 in Fashing and Oates 2013). Densities tend to be highest in patches of forest along lakes and rivers, intermediate in moist forests that have been subjected to low to moderate levels of human disturbance, and lowest in undisturbed moist forest (Fashing and Oates 2013). Where C. guereza occupies small, isolated, patches of forest, it is prone to decline and extinction.
range: Colobus guereza is endemic to equatorial Africa and has a large geographic range, by far the widest distribution of any African colobine (~2,750,000 km²); C. g. occidentalis alone accounts for 2,100,000 km² (Butynski and De Jong 2022a). This species ranges from eastern Nigeria and Cameroon, eastwards across the Oubangui River in the Central African Republic (CAR) to the northern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and then discontinuously eastwards to southern South Sudan, Uganda, the Kenyan and Ethiopian Highlands, and Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Meru, and Kahé District of Tanzania (Fashing and Oates 2013, Butynski and De Jong 2022a).Eight subspecies are recognised here:Colobus guereza occidentalis (Western Guereza) occurs from eastern Nigeria (Ngel Nyaki Forest Reserve on the western escarpment of the Mambilla Plateau) and the Yabassi District of Cameroon, southwards to northeastern Gabon, and eastwards across western and southern CAR through southern South Sudan and western Uganda to the Nile River, including the Otzi Mountains in northwestern Uganda (Oates 2011, Fashing and Oates 2013, De Jong and Butynski 2014, J. Hart pers. comm. 2016). Geographic range about 2,100,000 km², altitudinal range 170-2,500 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a).Colobus guereza guereza (Omo River Guereza) is endemic to Ethiopia. It occurs in the Ethiopian Highlands west of the Eastern Rift Valley, down into the lowland forests along the Awash River and Blue Nile Gorge (Fashing and Oates 2013, Zinner et al. 2019, Butynski and De Jong 2022a, 2022b). Overtaken by C. g. poliurus in the southern part of the range (presumably in Jimma Zone). Limits of its distribution, particularly in the southern extent of the range, poorly understood. Geographic range about 450,000 km², altitudinal range 400-3,350 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, 2022b).Colobus guereza poliurus (Greyish-white-tailed Guereza) occupies lowland forest along the Omo River and its tributaries in the West and South Omo Zones of southwestern Ethiopia. Isolated populations are present in southeastern South Sudan (De Beaux 1943, Napier 1985, Groves 2001, 2007, Butynski and De Jong 2022b). It occurs in Mago National Park and Omo National Park, perhaps as far north as Jimma, Kaffa Region (Carpaneto and Gippoliti 1990). Overtaken by C. g. guereza in the northern part of the range (presumably in Jimma Zone). Limits of its distribution are poorly understood. Geographic range about 70,000 km², altitudinal range 350-830 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022b).Colobus guereza gallarum (Djaffa Mountains Guereza) is endemic to the Ethiopian Highlands east of the Eastern Rift Valley (Fashing and Oates 2013, Zinner et al. 2019, Butynski and De Jong 2022a, 2022b). Geographic range about 24,000 km², altitudinal range 1,300-3,400 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, 2022b).Colobus guereza dodingae (Dodinga Hills Guereza) is endemic to the Imatong Mountains in southeastern South Sudan and Agoro Agu Forest Reserve, central northern Uganda. It is reported to occur in the hills in and around Kidepo Valley National Park, northeastern Uganda (De Jong and Butynski 2014, 2022b, De Jong and Butynski 2015). Geographic range about 6,100 km², altitudinal range 660-2,680 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, De Jong and Butynski 2023).Colobus guereza matschiei (Mau Forest Guereza) is endemic to southwestern Kenya, northwestern Tanzania, and extreme eastern Uganda. It occurs west of the Eastern Rift Valley (e.g., Mau Forest Complex, Kakamega Forest National Reserve, Cherangani Hills, and Loima Hills in Kenya, and Mount Elgon National Park on the Kenya-Uganda border), and in groundwater woodlands within the Eastern Rift Valley (including Lake Naivasha and Lake Nakuru National Park). It is also found along the Grumeti River in the western Serengeti, northwestern Tanzania (Butynski and de Jong 2012, Fashing and Oates 2013, De Jong and Butynski 2023). Reports of presence in the Ngorongoro Crater Highlands (e.g., Groves 2001) are unfounded (Butynski and De Jong 2012). Geographic range about 75,000 km², altitudinal range 630-3,010 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, De Jong and Butynski 2023).Colobus guereza percivali (Mount Uarges Guereza) is endemic to the Matthews Range and Ndoto Range of central Kenya (Mwenja 2007, De Jong and Butynski 2012, Fashing and Oates 2013). Geographic range about 4,200 km², altitudinal range 1,380-2,080 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, De Jong and Butynski 2023).Colobus guereza kikuyuensis (Mount Kenya Guereza) is endemic to the Kenya Central Highlands, including Ngong Escarpment, Mount Kenya, Aberdare Range, and small forest fragments in the Highlands, such as Ol Arabel Forest Reserve (Fashing and Oates 2013, De Jong and Butynski 2023). Geographic range about 15,400 km², altitudinal range 1,700-3,100 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022a, De Jong and Butynski 2023).Photographic maps of the above subspecies can be found on www.wildsolutions.nl
useTrade: Hunted for bushmeat and for its pelt. The pelt is used in traditional ceremonies and worn as an ornament. The international trade in Colobus pelts was substantial from about the 1850s until about the 1930s and continued into the 1970s (Oates 1977, Butynski and De Jong 2022a). The impact of the national and international Colobus pelt trade on populations is not known, but must have been considerable, probably causing the extirpation of many local populations (Oates 1977). Although the international trade in pelts has been largely stopped, local use within Africa continues and hunting seems recently to have increased in some locations (Butynski and De Jong 2022a). For example, hunting of C. g. percivali for its pelt in Kenya has recently increased (S. Kivai pers. comm.).
conservationActions: Colobus guereza is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. It occurs in many protected areas throughout its range and is common in many protected areas. Further taxonomic work is needed to assess the validity of the subspecies. For the long-term survival of C. guereza it is essential to determine the extent of the geographic distribution of all subspecies, investigate all threats and their impacts, establish and secure connectivity among forest fragments, and exclude livestock from forest fragments to avoid further forest degradation.

rationale: Cercopithecus pogonias is listed as Near Threatened because, although the species has a very large range, it is increasingly hunted for bushmeat and there is ongoing forest loss, especially at the northwestern and southwest edges of its range. It is likely that there has been a decline in the order of 20–25% over the past 27 years. This decline is expected to continue, and so this species almost qualifies as threatened under criterion A2cd.
habitat: Cercopithecus pogonias is found in primary lowland rainforest and submontane rainforest up to around 1,700 m (Bioko). These monkeys are mostly frugivorous: 60–87% of the diet is fruits and seeds; they also eat a smaller proportion of leaves, flowers and insects (Gautier-Hion 2013). Mean group size in an unhunted area of Lopé National Park in Gabon was 12.6, and biomass was 11 kg/km² (Tutin et al. 1997b). Mean group size in nearby Makandé was reported to be 14 individuals (Brugière 1998), but 12.2 (± 3.2) individuals in a subsequent study (Brugière 2005). The taxon is usually found with other monkey species (Gautier-Hion 2013) and prefers the upper strata of the forest above 20–25 m. Group size is 8–20 individuals.
threats: The major direct threats to C. pogonias are hunting and habitat degradation. Humans are the primary predator (Gautier-Hion 2013) and monkeys are eaten locally in villages or traded commercially for consumption in towns and cities. The indirect threats are increasing human populations, agricultural expansion and logging activities, which create easy access routes into previously remote forests. Human populations in the range states of this taxon are growing at roughly 2.7% annually and this rate will not slow down for several decades (UN 2015, World Bank 2017). Road access into once-remote forests—even around protected areas—has increased hugely during the last 20–30 years (Laporte et al. 2007), facilitating hunting and transport of bushmeat to both local markets and distant urban centres (Abernethy et al. 2013, Ziegler et al. 2016).The species is affected by habitat modification across parts of its range, especially in Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, DRC and Cabinda, as intact high forest, in which the species is most abundant, is converted to farmland and “farm bush” (see Tyukavina et al. 2016). Forest loss in the species range is much less evident in Gabon. Forest loss in the most recent year available (2014) was higher than in all previous years (from 2001) in Congo, DRC and Equatorial Guinea, and in Gabon this was true for 2013, followed by 2014 (WRI 2016). Deforestation will greatly increase in the future as industrial agriculture expands, removing the habitat of various forest-obligate species.
population: Data on Cercopithecus pogonias abundance are sparse. The species had the lowest biomass of all primates at Lopé in Gabon (Tutin et al. 1997a). Data from well-studied sites range from 9–11 kg/km² to 115 kg/km² and densities of 4–48 individuals/km² (Gautier-Hion 2013), with the lowest densities at the savanna-forest ecotone (Tutin et al. 1997a). The Bioko population is estimated at just 4,500 animals (in 369 km²), giving a rough population density of 12 individuals/km², so at the low end of the scale for the species (Cronin et al. 2015, Cronin, unpublished data 2016). Further details can be found in the subspecies accounts.
range: Cercopithecus pogonias has a large range, estimated to cover about 1,108,230 km² of moist tropical forest and forest-savanna mosaic. It is found in Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Equatorial Guinea (including the island of Bioko), Gabon and the Cabinda enclave of Angola. However, both the species and subspecies limits within this area remain poorly understood. Much more research is needed on the distribution and affinities of C. pogonias populations across this region. In particular, we know little about the populations found between the Sanaga River (Cameroon), the Ivindo River (Gabon) and the upstream tributaries of the Congo River in southeastern Cameroon. Gautier-Hion et al. (2013) describe this area as a putative hybrid zone but it is not clear which variants of C. pogonias inhabit this area, and if they are hybridizing. More research is needed.Hicks (2010) found that the species was abundant in Bili-Uéré, north of the Rubi River up to the border with CAR (Mbomu River). The northern limit of its distribution is probably the limit of high canopy forest to the north, between about 4° and 6° N, although some parts of the historic range are a little further north and are now degraded forest (if the species is still present). As far as is known, the eastern limit is at about 26° E. and then the right (north) bank of the Itimbiri River in DRC and the right (north) bank of the Congo River, down to the forest-savanna limits in Congo. It may overlap or abut with the distribution of Cercopithecus denti, but there is a lack of information from the possible overlap zone (Sarmiento and Kingdon 2013) and Hicks (2010) saw only C. denti in the bushmeat markets between the Uélé and Rubi Rivers (forest identifications could potentially have been confused with the very similar C. denti). To the southwest, it is possible that this species occurs all the way to the Congo estuary where suitable habitat remains and hunting pressure is low.Historically, this species was found in Cameroon (Takamanda National Park) at about 9.3° E; however, the most recent surveys in Takamanda (Ikfuingei and Kuchambi 2013) and Dimonika Reserve in Congo (Latour 2010) did not record it, so we must assume it is already extirpated or has become extremely rare in this region. Recent surveys across the Cross River region in Nigeria did not record C. pogonias (Imong et al. 2009), so the Cameroon-Nigeria border area is likely the present western limit.While we tentatively recognise three subspecies, their distributional limits are poorly studied and not well understood, thus complicating an understanding of their conservation status. According to Gautier-Hion et al. (1999) the nominate subspecies, C. p. pogonias, is restricted to Bioko, Equatorial Guinea, with an unnamed subspecies replacing C. p. pogonias on the mainland north of the Sanaga River. However, Groves (2001) reports C. p. pogonias as occurring from the Cross River across the Sanaga River to Río Muni (mainland Equatorial Guinea), and includes Bioko. In the current treatment, C. p. pogonias includes the animals on Bioko (ca 2,000 km²) and on mainland Africa in the moist forest region between Cross River State, Nigeria, and the Sanaga River in Cameroon, which would mark its southeastern distributional limit (Oates 2011)—a total area of over 50,000 km².According to Groves (2001), C. p. nigripes is found from Rio Muni, Gabon, and Republic of Congo, south to Cabinda, Angola. The western limit—where no river clearly demarcates its distribution—is the forest-savanna boundary in southern Congo.According to Groves (2001), C. p. grayi ranges from the middle River Sanaga in Cameroon east to the Central African Republic, the inland region of Congo, and, in DRC east of the River Oubangui to about the Itimbiri River, north of the River Congo.For more details on the different subspecies, see the separate subspecies assessments.
useTrade: This species is hunted illegally for local consumption and sale in urban markets.
conservationActions: Cercopithecus pogonias is listed on Appendix II of CITES, Class B of the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations, and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. Nationally, it is on the list of partially protected species in Nigeria (Federal Ministry of Nigeria 2004). Hunting, sale and consumption of primates in Equatorial Guinea were banned by Presidential Decree in October 2007 (Republic of Equatorial Guinea 2007), although no specific taxon is mentioned in that law. In DRC, C. pogonias is on the partially-protected list (may be hunted with a permit) (Enerunga 2006). In Congo, it is on Annex III of the current law (“all animals not on Annexes I or II”), meaning that it can be hunted for food, but only using traditional methods, and not for commerce, transport away from the site where it was hunted (in other words to a different village or other area), and trafficking products of the species on Annex III are strictly prohibited (MEFDD 2011). Similarly, they are on Class C (may be hunted with a permit) in Cameroon and CAR (Central African Republic 1984, MINFOF 2006).Hunting is banned in all national parks where C. pogonias occurs so, on paper at least, the species is protected in those areas. However, weak application of and poor compliance with the law outside protected areas (and inside some PAs) results in gun-hunting through most of its range. The taxon occurs in many protected areas including three World Heritage Sites: Lopé-Okanda (Gabon), the Sangha Trinational (Cameroon-CAR-Congo) and the Dja Biosphere Reserve (Cameroon).The species' strongholds (in terms of large areas of suitable habitat and abundance of individuals) are in the forests of Gabon, especially the protected areas, plus the Dzanga-Sangha complex in CAR, the protected areas of southeastern Cameroon, and the national parks of Conkouati-Douli, Nouabalé-Ndoki and Odzala in Congo. Outside protected areas, these monkeys are likely to be increasingly rare, especially in areas with medium-to-high human population density and active logging.

rationale: This species has a moderate extent of occurrence of 49,582 km2, is considered common in suitable habitats and occurs in protected areas, and there is no evidence of significant population decline. It is therefore assessed as Least Concern. However, this species is at risk of habitat loss, particularly at the lower elevations where it has been recorded, as well as hunting, and populations should be monitored. Taxonomic research is also needed.
habitat: This species inhabits tropical evergreen rainforest formations from lowlands to high elevations (Musser 2014). It is not known if it survives in degraded or disturbed habitats. It is likely to be terrestrial and nocturnal (Musser 2014).
threats: The major threat to this species is habitat loss due to logging, expanding agriculture and mining activities. It is estimated that at least 10% of Sulawesi's forest cover was lost between 2000–2017 (Supriatna et al. 2020). Additionally, hunting may be a threat; this species was recorded in a study of hunting and trading of white-tailed forest rats in Pinabetengan and Singsingon of North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021).
population: Based on early collections, this species is believed to have been common, and probably remains so where suitable habitat exists. It is at least likely to be common in areas such as Dako (Sulawesi Small Mammal Workshop pers. comm. 2023).
range: This species is known only from the northern peninsula of Sulawesi, Indonesia (Musser and Carleton 2005, Musser 2014). Most samples of this species come from elevations below 1,000 m asl, however its range extends to 1,982 m asl on Gunung Klabat (Musser 2014). Surveys from 2013 to 2016 found the species to be present on Mt Ambang, Mt Dua Saudara and Mt Dako, which extended its known distributed further west (Handika et al. 2021). The Mt Dako subpopulation could potentially be divergent enough to be considered a distinct species sister (Handika et al. in prep).
useTrade: This species has been identified in a study of rats traded for food in North Sulawesi (Laatung et al. 2021).
conservationActions: It is present in Bogani Nani Watarbone National Park and Mt. Dako Nature Preserve. Further research is needed to clarify its taxonomic status and to monitor populations and responses to threats.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, is tolerant of a broad range of habitats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at anything close to the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is diurnal and omnivorous, and alternatively arboreal and terrestrial. It resides in a range of habitats, including temperate coniferous, moist and dry deciduous, bamboo, and mixed forests, mangroves, scrub, rainforest, and around human habitations and developments, including cultivated areas, temples, and roadsides (Choudhury 2001; Srivastava and Mohnot 2001). In Pakistan this monkey remains in mountainous  regions with forest cover; it is typically associated with Himalayan moist temperate  forest (Roberts 1997). It is found at elevations up to 4,000 m (Molur et al. 2003).  Due to hunting in Lao PDR and Viet Nam the species does not occur in commensal situations there, and is restricted to forest areas where it is generally  associated with riverine environments over a range of altitudes (Timmins pers. comm.).  In  western and northern parts of its range it seems to occur in a wider array of environments. It is highly adaptable to man­ made habitat. Its generation time is 12 years (Molur et al. 2003). Most records are from under 2000m but they are also known to occur in 3200 m in Nepal and c.4000 m in Quinghai, China. They are commensally found in human habitation both in urban and rural landscapes. Primarily vegetarian, their diet is highly diverse and varies geographically. As in Sundarbans, they are known to fishing on mudflats. Other animal food includes crabs, shellfish, bird eggs, honeycombs, crayfish, crabs, and spiders. Plant materials include fruits, seeds, flowers, leaves, shoots, twigs, roots, twigs, shoots, buds, stems, gums and pith. Seasonal breeding with the mating activities peaking in autumn, winter and births in spring and summer. Gestation of 133-200 days at an average of 166 days. Mean annual birth rate in wild population 42.9-90.8%. In a study conducted on breeding energetic, high ranking or breeding males were found to be more spent and restless during copulation or breeding season and were seen to feed more and refurbish energy during birthing.(Higham et al, 2010). Interbirth intervals as studied Cayo Santiago macaques, of a data set of 50 years, ranged 300-2591 days and a median life span of 15 years. Average inter-interval for the age category 4 and 18 ranged 392 and 463 days (mean-425.6 days) but average increased to 541 days at 19 years (Hoffman et al. 2010) Diurnal. Forest dwelling population are more arboreal than their urban dwelling conspecifics. They are though known to spend 72% of their active time on the ground and just 28% on the trees. Home range of c.65ha as seen in 323 non-forest groups and of 198ha in 129 forest groups.
threats: This species is generally unthreatened, though its original habitat is increasingly being lost to development. While M. mulatta exists easily around humans, the increasing level of cohabitation has been associated with waning levels of human tolerance for the animals (Molur et al. 2003). Confiscation for laboratory testing is a mostly localized threat, but it is considerable in certain areas (A. Kumar pers. comm.). Capture and release of laboratory and “problem monkeys”  from rural and urban  areas into natural forests is a major  threat to wild macaques.In Lao PDR and Viet Nam the major threat to the species is hunting, although loss of forest in river valleys has also likely impacted the species (R. Timmins pers. comm.).  In Indochina hunting pressure is high, and thus tolerance to human disturbance is low. Introduction, through release of confiscated M. fasicularis, is at least a localized threat in parts of the species' Viet Namese range (R. Timmins pers. comm.).  Tolerance of the species varies locally, from heavily hunted and persecuted, to worshipped and fed.Main threat at present include habitat loss and habitat deterioration, human-primate conflict. Hunting for subsistence in eastern parts of India and trapping for pet trade in Afghanistan should also be considered as threats. Himachal Pradesh government in Indian undertook state wide sterilization program for these macaques but as to how successful they were from a conservation perspective is highly questionable.Opinion surveys conducted in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh report that 61% of the people coexisting with macaques find macaques to be damaging of crops and property, while 86 % want them relocated. (Imam and Ahmad 2013).Chauhan and Pirta (2010) argue that despite the relocation, macaques in Shimla continue to flourish unabated. They also point to the many threats in the region from man made hazards to garbage that seem to form a big part of the city dwelling macaques.Chauhan & Pirta (2010b) report of a macaque threatening behavior wherein the macaques in urban areas steal or grab valuable things off passers by and would not let go until threatened or given food in exchange. Such behaviors create a sense of panic and antagonism against these macaques in the minds of people, further complication conservation action.
population: This species is widely distributed in south, southeast and east Asia. Populations are sizable, but increasingly commensal with humans, resulting in some fragmentation of the distribution (Molur et al. 2003). It can be abundant in many places, including in cities. Hunting of this species in Lao PDR and Viet Nam has severely depressed populations in these countries although it still remains widespread. In Namdapha National Park, India, this species was found to have a group density of 0.44 groups/km2, with an average group size of 12.3 individuals (Chetry et al. 2003). The average group size in other parts of India is much higher (Siddiqui and Southwick 2004). Srivastava and Mohnot (2001) consider this species to be rare in the forests of north­eastern India. J.-Q, Lu (2007) reported c.2100 macaques in Taihangshan mountains, through direct surveys and review of previous reports of the other half of the park not surveyed. Population estimate of the macaques in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh yielded a total of 4051 individuals from various habitats. Average group size of 48 ranging between 15 and 155 (Imam & Ahmed 2013). In Shimla, density of Macaca mulatta was 37.02 individuals/km2. Mean group size of 16.65 (6-38), total individuals of 817 an group density of 2.22 groups/km2 (Chauhan and Pirta 2010).
range: From c.36°N (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, China) S to c.15°N (India, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam), in Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Hainan Islands. The isolated NE China population was extirpated in 1987. The species as a whole is found throughout most of southern Asia, in eastern Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, central and southern China (Anhui, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Hunan, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Tibet, and Yunnan, as well as the island  of  Hainan), northern and central India (in the states of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chattisgarh, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Jharkand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal), Lao PDR, Myanmar, Nepal, northern Pakistan, northern Thailand, and Viet Nam.  It occurs to the north of the Krishna River in central and eastern India and to the north of the lower Tapti River in western India, north intoAfghanistan, Nepal,Sikkim,  Bhutan, and northeast into China, where it extends to the  Yangtze and north of its  middle course to about 33°N,  110°E. It is absent north of the lower Yangtze, but there is an additional, possibly introduced population in northern China north of the lower Hwang He (Yellow River), formerly occurring as far as Beijing (Groves 2001).  There are introduced populations (mostly not mapped) in areas within this region as well as outside  it, for  instance south of the Krishna River in India; Kowloon and a  few small islands near Hong Kong; and to various other locations worldwide, including parts of Florida, USA and on Cayo Santiago island near Puerto Rico (M. Richardson pers. comm.). Kumar et al. 2011 reported of range extension by the Macaca mulatta southward, by 3500km2 displacing the Bonnet macaques, sometimes coexisting as mixed groups with the latter and some other time, just existing as separate species groups in sympatry.
useTrade: Hunted for food and live trapped for research purposes.
conservationActions: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. It is also listed in Schedule III in the Bangladesh Wildlife (Preservation) (Amendment) Act, 1974 and in Schedule I, Part I in the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act (amended up to 2002), on Category II of the Chinese Wildlife Protection Act (1989), and is protected with all other primates in the Nepalese National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 1973. Protection status varies widely throughout the species range. Rhesus macaques reside in a large number of protected areas throughout their range.

rationale: The species is listed as Near Threatened because of the smaller population size at islands, so it is suspected that migration does not occur frequently as to maintain high genetic diversity (Genoways 1988). In addition, severe weather (storms, hurricanes) and even volcanic eruptions, in addition to habitat changes may have fragmented these populations, although it occurs in a few protected areas. Current data almost meet "Vulnerable" under criterion B1a, with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of less than 15,504 km², although there is no evidence of continuing decline in populations.
habitat: Little is known of the ecology of this species, presumably it is the locally dominantly frugivorous as are other members of the genus (Jones and Genoways 1975). A male from Guadeloupe was the only specimen taken in a net set in a deep ravine that was located in "an area of extremely dense forest" (de la Torre and Schwartz 1966), a series from Dominica was taken in nets set across two streams described as "fairly placid and not torrential at the localities of the nets", both streams were in rainforests with no adjacent cultivated areas (de la Torre 1966). These studies reveal that Sturnira species could be relatively uncommon and unlike other frugivorous bats possibly needs native humid forests instead of tropical agriculture to flourish (Genoways 1988).
threats: Like other bat species in tropical islands, Sturnira angeli is subject to natural threats like hurricanes or volcanic eruptions (Genoways 1988; Pedersen et al. 2006, 2013). Change of land cover, and agriculture use are among the typical threats to its populations.
population: Studies at the Lesser Antilles reveal that Sturnira species could be relatively uncommon and unlike other frugivorous bats possibly needs native humid forests instead of tropical agriculture to flourish (Genoways 1988). Some isolated populations on islands are suspected to be at high risk because of events like hurricanes or volcanic eruptions; plus, species of this genus do not migrate well between islands (Genoways 1988).
range: This species is known from the islands of Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe and Montserrat, in the Lesser Antilles (de la Torre 1966, de la Torre and Schwartz 1966, Jones and Phillips 1976, Genoways 1988, Velazco and Patterson 2013). It has been recently split from the widespread and polyphyletic Sturnira lilium (sensu lato) based on phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequences.
conservationActions: Some protected areas (nature parks, nature reserves, national parks) exist on Martinique, Dominica, and Guadeloupe islands, but these are lacking at Montserrat.

rationale: The species is listed as Vulnerable under criterion D2, because it is only known to exist in one locality with a small area of occupancy (AOO) of approximately 16 km2. Whilst the forest is currently under protection, any change to the extent and/or quality of the habitat could result in the species rapidly becoming Critically Endangered or Extinct in a short time. Surveys are needed to improve knowledge of this little-documented species.
habitat: This species has been recorded in montane primary forest with dense stands of Entandrophragma sp., Parinari sp., Symphonia sp. and many climbers (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010).
threats: There are no direct current threats to this species. The only potential threats of concern would be any that affect the integrity of the reserve itself, as this is a greatly threatened forest island, in the heart of one of Africa's most densely populated regions (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010). However, the reserve is conserved by staff and community projects, involving the input of environmental clubs, local authorities and indigenous peoples (IUCN 2017), thus the species is not considered to be actively threatened.
population: Myosorex bururiensis may be a rare species (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010), but data are lacking and its population trends are unknown.
range: This species is endemic to the Bururi Forest Reserve in Burundi, and has been found at 1,880 m asl. It has been recorded from the Mumushwizi Valley, adjacent to the Mumushwizi Stream, and is currently only known from its type specimen (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010).
conservationActions: The sole known locality for this species falls inside the Bururi Forest Reserve. This reserve is protected via multiple staff and community projects, involving the input of environmental clubs, local authorities and indigenous peoples (IUCN 2017). Since this species is only known from its type specimen, research into its population and ecology is needed.

rationale: This species is relatively widespread with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of around 89,789 km2, and is found in a number of protected areas. There is no evidence to suggest a significant decline at present, though threats to the forest where it occurs, including logging and mining, could be of concern. Overall, it is assessed as Least Concern, but further research of its population and distribution is needed.
habitat: It lives in a variety of mid-elevation and montane habitats, including primary and secondary montane forests, mixed bamboo and hardwood forests, and shrublands (Kerbis Peterhans and Hutterer 2009).
threats: The integrity of Kibira National Park, the type locality for this species, is of concern, with illegal activities such as logging and burning of fuel wood, mining for minerals and harvesting of forest products noted (Kerbis Peterhans and Hutterer 2009). Socio-political conflict spanning more than a decade continues to stress the National Park (Kerbis Peterhans and Hutterer 2009). Threats to the other areas where this species is distributed are unclear.
population: Nothing is known about this species' abundance or populations.
range: This species is known from Burundi, southern Uganda, Rwanda and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kerbis Peterhans and Hutterer 2009, Field Museum 2024). It ranges from 1,170 to 2,350 m asl.
conservationActions: Many of the currently known localities fall primarily within protected areas, including Kibira National Park (Burundi), Bwindi-Impenetrable National Park, Mujuzi Forest Reserve, and Kasana-Kasambya Forest Reserve (Uganda). Further research into this species' ecology, population and distribution is needed.

rationale: The species is listed as Least Concern as whilst it has a reasonably restricted distribution and extent of occurrence of 36,805 km2, but is found in a number of different habitats and protected areas, and there are no known major threats.
habitat: It appears to live in a variety of habitats including disturbed hardwood forest, bamboo, mixed evergreen, and evergreen forests. The specimen from Binh Chau – Phuoc Buu Nature Reserve was collected in a small area of wetland surrounding a narrow brook and within Melaleuca forest (Jenkins et al. 2010), though since this specimen may represent a distinct species (Bannikova et al. 2011), wetland habitat is not categorised in this assessment.
threats: There are no known threats to the species.
population: This species is known from few specimens, and there is no information available on its abundance or populations.
range: This species potentially has a wide distribution across southern Viet Nam and northeastern Cambodia. It has been found in the Yok Don National Park, Ma Da Forests, Vinh Cuu Nature Reserve, Cat Tien National Park and Bu Gia Map Nature Reserve in Viet Nam, and the Virachey National Park, Cambodia, between 50 and 480 m asl (Jenkins et al. 2010, Bannikova et al. 2011, Abramov et al. 2013). These areas cover three ecoregions of dry forest types, as defined by Wickramanayake et al. (2002). It is suggested that the species might be widely distributed across lowland areas (Jenkins et al. 2010). Specimens from Binh Chau – Phuoc Buu Nature Reserve may represent a distinct species (Bannikova et al. 2011).
conservationActions: Most of its known localities fall inside national parks and nature reserves: Yok Don National Park, Cat Tien National Park, Vinh Cuu Nature Reserve and Bu Gia Map Nature Reserve (Viet Nam), and Virachey National Park, Cambodia.

rationale: This species is currently only known from the single location of Phu Quoc Island, Viet Nam. It was found in undisturbed forest, which has decreased in extent and quality on the island. This species has a low extent of occurrence (EOO) of 211 km2, which, combined with the potential threat of habitat loss and occurrence at one location, would mean that this species qualifies for listing in a threatened category (Endangered). However, it has been suggested that suitable habitats may be present in the nearby Cardamom Mountains in Cambodia, and further surveys in the region could reveal a wider EOO that might place the species outside of a threatened category (e.g., Near Threatened). Overall, given its potentially small distribution as well as uncertainties such as the unknown impacts of threats and true extent of its distribution, it is considered appropriate to assign this species a category intermediate of the possible options. This species is therefore assessed as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)). Research is urgently needed to clarify its range, population status and threats.
habitat: It has been found in undisturbed lowland tropical forest (dipterocarp forest), close to fallen trees (Abramov et al. 2008).
threats: Nothing is known about the specific threats to the species. Given that the species was found in forest habitat, forest loss and degradation could pose a risk. At least 29% of the island’s forest was lost between 2002–2023 (Global Forest Watch 2024), likely driven in part by illegal logging, agriculture and development (SGGP 2022).
population: Nothing is known about the abundance or population of the species.
range: This species is currently known from a northern areas of Phu Quoc Island, Kien Giang Province, Viet Nam and has been found at 30 m asl (Abramov et al. 2008). It is possible that the species is also present elsewhere in the Cardamom Mountain rainforest ecoregion (of southwestern Cambodia), within which Phu Quoc rainforests are included. However, this region has been little surveyed for small mammals (Abramov et al. 2008). Considering the full extent of Phu Quoc Island, the extent of occurrence (EOO) of this shrew could be a maximum of 812 km2, but if it does indeed include the Cardamom Mountain range, the EOO would likely exceed 30,000 km2.
conservationActions: The only known locality of this species is within Phu Quoc National Park, though deforestation and encroachment has occurred there (SGGP 2022). Surveys are urgently needed to clarify this species’ distribution, trends and response to threats.

rationale: This species is known from one high-elevation location where its extent of occurrence and area of occupancy are no greater than 321 km2. Since it has a highly restricted distribution, it almost qualifies as threatened under criteria B1a and B2a, but there is no evidence of extreme fluctuations, nor decline in extent or quality of habitat. As such, it is assessed as Near Threatened. Research is needed to clarify population trends and threats.
habitat: This medium-sized shrew has been found in montane broadleaf evergreen and elfin forests (Jenkins et al. 2007).
threats: Nothing is known about the threats to the species.
population: This species is currently only known from specimens collected in 2004 (Jenkins et al. 2007), and no information on the abundance and populations of the species is available.
range: This species is known only from Ngoc Linh Mountain, Kon Tum Province, Viet Nam, from specimens collected between 2,300 to 2,400 m asl (Jenkins et al. 2007). Surveys at lower elevations did not record its presence (Jenkins et al. 2007). It may be endemic to the Ngoc Linh area, therefore, its extent of occurrence and area of occupancy are likely no larger than 321 km2.
conservationActions: Ngoc Linh Mountain, where the species is known from, is included within the Ngoc Linh Nature Reserve (Abramov et al. 2006). Population, ecology and threat research would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because it has a reasonably large extent of occurrence (EOO) of 57,549 km2, it is found in many protected areas, and there are no known threats.
habitat: It lives in the closed, deciduous lowland forests of mountains, which are surrounded by plains (Kawada et al. 2012). The species has not been found in farms of grasslands around forest (Kawada et al. 2012). The species has been found near human settlement in Ba Vi and Xuan Son (A. Abramov pers. comm. 2024) and near human habitation in Tuyen Quang, Son La, and Quang Binh (H.T. Bui pers. comm. 2024). It has been found in both planted and regenerated forests, mainly in low-altitude areas with wet litter layers or soft soil (H.T. Bui pers. comm. 2024).
threats: There are no known threats to the species at this time (A. Abramov pers. comm. 2024). It may be affected by the conversion of lowland forests into agricultural or forestry land, along with the excessive use of pesticides and herbicides, however, the lack of hunting by people and the small population size of predators (such as civets and cats) probably means that this species appears to be unthreatened (H. Bui pers. comm. 2024).
population: It is likely to be common in suitable habitats.
range: Recently known only from Viet Nam. This species is distributed from Tuyen Quang province in the centre of northern Viet Nam to Quang Binh province in the south of the North Central region. In addition to these two provinces, specimens were also collected in the provinces of Phu Tho, Vinh Phuc, Hanoi, Ninh Binh, Son La, Thanh Hoa, and Nghe An. It is mainly known at low elevations between 200 to 450 m asl (Kawada et al. 2012, Bui et al. 2019, 2020). In Ba Vi National Park (west of Hanoi) the species was found at elevations between 300 and 1,000 m asl (Abramov et al. 2013b).
conservationActions: The species has been found inside the Na Hang Nature Reserve, the Pu Huong Nature Reserve, and the Tam Dao National Park (Kawada et al. 2012), and it has been recorded in Xuan Son and Ba Vi national parks (Abramov et al. 2013a). Based on collection at the Institute of Ecology and Biological Resources, this species was also recorded in Xuan Nha Special-use Forest (Son La Province), Cuc Phuong National Park (Ninh Binh Province), Xuan Lien Nature Reserve (Thanh Hoa Province), Pu Mat National Park (Nghe An Province), and Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park (Quang Binh Province) (H. Bui pers. comm. 2024).

rationale: This species is known from one or two locations that are swamps, with a very small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 39 km2, and is therefore also likely to have a small area of occupancy too. The species' associated habitats are threatened by human activities such as illegal logging and draining of swamp areas, though at present it is not known how severely these threats could affect the species and how much the habitat is afforded some level of protection as it falls within Kahuzi-Biega National Park. It therefore assessed as Near Threatened as it is close to being considered Vulnerable under criterion D2 due to the small number of locations and potential impact of threats, however, whether the threats could result in the taxon becoming Critically Endangered or Extinct is unclear. Further surveys may reveal that the species has a larger EOO than is currently known. Further research is also needed to clarify its taxonomic status.
habitat: It lives in Cyperus swamps and evergreen montane forests (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010). There may be seasonal movement between habitats.
threats: Its habitat is threatened by illegal logging, coltan mining and charcoal production (Gatambara et al. 2019), though the intensity of these threats at higher elevations, where this species occurs, is unknown. Its distribution depends on the swamp communities which may be susceptible to climate change and human activities such as draining (J. Kerbis Peterhans pers. comm. 2012).
population: Nothing is known about the population trends or abundance of the species.
range: This species is known from a low number of specimens collected in the montane region of Kahuzi-Biega National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo (Kerbis Peterhans et al. 2010; J. Kerbis Peterhans pers. comm. 2024). Its distribution is centred on two swamps: Musisi and Mugaba Swamp, but on occasion it has been found outside these swamps at 2,600–2,800 m asl, and even at the summit of Mt Kahuzi at 3,300 m asl (J. Kerbis Peterhans pers. comm. 2024).
conservationActions: The known range of this species falls within the Kahuzi-Biega National Park. Research of this species' taxonomy, ecology, population, distribution and threats is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern. It has been found in both primary and secondary forest types, and newer records have expanded its distribution and extent of occurrence (EOO), with its EOO now estimated to be 17,475 km2. Further surveys may continue to reveal a wider range. However, although there is no evidence to suggest any significant decline at present, the extent and impact of potential threats are unknown, the species is considered to be potentially rare, and further research is needed.
habitat: It has been recorded in lowland primary and secondary forest, including young regrowth forests (Mukinzi et al. 2009, African Mammalia 2019). No further information on its ecology is available.
threats: Nothing is known about the specific threats to this species. It may be at risk of habitat loss from deforestation (driven by agriculture and logging), with rates of loss varying from 0.10–0.23 between 2000–2010 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ickowitz et al. 2015), though impacts on Sylvisorex akaibei are unknown.
population: This species is potentially rare throughout its range. Of 1,265 shrew specimens collected in three forest areas around Kisangani from 2001–2006, only seven were identified as Sylvisorex akaibi (Mukinzi et al. 2009).
range: This species has been recorded from the right bank of the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 388 to 497 m asl (Mukinzi et al. 2009). Since being described in 2009, newer records have expanded its range eastwards to Reserve Forestier Masako near the Ugandan border (African Mammalia 2019), and it may be more widespread than is currently known.
conservationActions: It has been found in the Masako Forest Reserve, Yangambi Biosphere Reserve, and Reserve Forestier Masako (Mukinzi et al. 2009, African Mammalia 2019). Further research of its distribution, population, ecology and threats is needed.

rationale: Although this species has a small range with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of approximately 1,300 km2, it is widespread in the Mingan mountains and there is no reason to suspect that the species is declining or that the habitat for this species is under threat, hence it is listed as Least Concern.
habitat: It is found in a variety of tropical forest types, ranging from lowland dipterocarp forest to old-growth mossy forest (Balete et al. 2011). It appears to be tolerant of some disturbance, with the species found in second-growth montane forest (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016). It is nocturnal and terrestrial, consuming invertebrates and possibly seeds (Balete et al. 2011).
threats: The habitat is intact and there are no current threats to this species’ habitat on Mount Mingan (M.R. Duya pers. comm. 2024). However, large areas of forest in the Mingan Mountains below this species’ elevational distribution had been converted for agriculture and residential purposes. There has been widespread regeneration of second-growth forest on Luzon, because of economic improvement to the area over the last 15 years (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2016).
population: It is considered to be common throughout its range, and the most abundant species at higher elevations in its range (Balete et al. 2011).
range: This species is found in the Mingan Mountains on Luzon Island, Philippines, at elevations ranging from 733 to 1,675 m asl (Balete et al. 2011). It may also occur in the southern Sierra Madre range.
conservationActions: This species does not occur in any protected areas. There is ongoing action since 2015 to have Mt. Mingan declared as critical habitat (M.R. Duya pers. comm. 2024).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because whilst it has a limited distribution with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 18,739 km2, it is found across a broad elevational range, it is considered fairly common, and it occurs in a number of protected areas.
habitat: This species is mainly arboreal, occurring in lowland, montane, and mossy primary and secondary forest (Rickart et al. 1991, Heaney et al. 1998, Heaney et al. 2005). Specimens have also been taken from forest near sea level in Isabela Province (Danielsen et al. 1994) and on Catanduanes (Hollister 1913). There are no records from outside of forest (L. Heaney and D. Balete pers. comm. 2012). A study of Mt. Sto Tomas in 2010 only recorded a single observation of the species in slightly disturbed mossy forest, despite extensive trapping in pine forest and on agricultural land (Reginaldo and de Guia 2014). Between 2011 and 2012 the species was recorded in regenerating lowland forest in the northern Sierra Madre (Balete et al. 2020).
threats: There are no major threats to the species as the highlands, where a significant part of the species' range occurs, are not affected by deforestation. However, the lowland parts of its range have experienced severe deforestation (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2012), due to logging, slash-and-burn agriculture and mining (Perez et al. 2020).
population: This is a moderately common and widespread species (L. Heaney pers. comm. 2024).
range: This species is endemic to the Philippines where it is found only on Luzon and Catanduanes islands (Heaney et al. 1998). On Luzon it is widespread and occurs from near sea level up to 2,150 m (Heaney et al. 1998, Heaney et al. 2005).
conservationActions: The species is found in protected areas, for example, it is present in Caramoan National Park (Balete et al. 2013).

rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable B1ab(iii), because it has a relatively small estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 17,600 km2, where there is a continuing decline in the quantity and quality of its habitat due to threats such as iron mining on Mt Nimba. It is considered a rare species across its range. Research into its threats and population are needed.
habitat: It lives in a variety of habitats, having been found in low altitude and montane savannas, lowland and montane tropical forest, and cultivated plantations (Denys and Aniskine 2012).
threats: There is pressure on the forests of Mt Nimba from iron mining and related human activities (Denys and Aniskine 2012). Forests across West Africa are often small patches across the species' known range and threatened by human activities (C. Denys pers. comm. 2014).
population: Dendromus lachaisei is uncommon throughout its range.
