range: This species is known from several localities in Guinea, Liberia, and Côte d’Ivoire. As currently understood, its range stretches from southeastern Guinea in the Serendou District, across both the Guinean and Liberian sides of Mt Nimba, to central Côte d’Ivoire at Dabou and Adiopodoumé (Denys and Aniskine 2012). It ranges from 20 to 1,600 m asl (Denys and Aniskine 2012).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Mt Nimba Biosphere Reserve, which is still protected on the Guinean and Liberian sides. The Reserve’s status in Côte d’Ivoire is unknown.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because whilst it was only relatively recently described and is only known from a few localities, it has been recorded on both Java and Kalimatan, Borneo, including within two protected areas. Research into its distribution, ecology, and possible threats is needed.
habitat: It lives in primary lowland and montane forest (Maryanto and Sinaga 2008).
threats: Nothing is known about its threats.
population: There is nothing known about the population or population trend of this species.
range: This species is known from three localities in Kalimatan and Java, Indonesia, where it has been recorded at 400 and 1,100m Asl (Maryanto and Sinaga 2008).
useTrade: Nothing is known about use and trade information.
conservationActions: Two of the three known localities are inside national parks: Bukit Baka National Park, West Kalimantan, and Cibodas Gede Pangrango National Park, West Java (Maryanto and Sinaga 2008).

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, because, despite significant threats of logging of its habitat, it has a wide range and is found in numerous protected areas.
habitat: It lives in peat swamp forests, mixed dipterocarp lowland, and mixed dipterocarp/kerangas forests (Achmadi et al. 2012). The species is sympatric with Maxomys whiteheadi (Achmadi 2017).
threats: The majority of this species range is being affected by logging, which is occurring on both small and industrial scales.
population: Nothing is known about the population and abundance of this species.
range: This species is found in Malaysia and Indonesia on the Malaysian Peninsula, Borneo, and Sumatra, between 100 to 1,000 m asl (Achmadi et al. 2012, Achmadi 2017).
useTrade: It is used for non-consumptive, unspecified uses.
conservationActions: This species is known to occur in numerous protected areas in Malaysia: Kinabalu Park, Niah National Park, Lanjak Entimau Wildlife Sanctuary, Fraser’s Hill Forest Reserve, and Kubah National Park (Achmadi et al. 2012, Achmadi 2017).

rationale: The species is assessed as Least Concern. It has an extent of occurrence of 32,923 km2, is found in a nature reserve and is not known to be undergoing any significant declines. Research of its population, trends and threats is needed.
habitat: Individuals were found in abandoned farmland along the footpath of a rice field (Liu et al. 2012).
threats: Nothing is known about the specific threats faced by this species. The area where it is found has been considered for ecotourism (Yang and Li 2012).
population: Nothing is known about the population of this species.
range: This species is endemic to southern China. It is known from a number of specimens collected from five localities, including the type locality of Gongbu Nature Reserve, at elevations from 3,640 to 3,890 m asl (Liu et al. 2012).
conservationActions: This species is known from within Gongbu Nature Reserve, though specimens were collected from abandoned farmland, and it is not known to what extent the species uses natural habitats (and potentially more managed/protected habitats) within the reserve. It is listed as Near Threatened on the Red List of China’s Vertebrates (Jiang et al. 2016). Population, distribution, ecology and threat studies are needed.

rationale: This species has a small extent of occurrence of 14,216 km2, is known from two locations (Mechuka Valley and between Mechuka and Tato), and it may be at risk of habitat change driven by agriculture and development. It is also hunted, though the extent and impacts of this are unknown. Overall, this species is assessed as Near Threatened as it meets some conditions of criterion B (B1 and B1a), but it is not clear whether the species is undergoing any significant level of decline, nor whether its distribution could be wider than is currently known. Surveys are needed to clarify its population, distribution and response to threats.
habitat: It lives in temperate broadleaf and coniferous forests, and possibly some montane forest.
threats: This species may be experiencing declines due to hunting, construction (including of hydroelectric dams), an increased human population (especially relating to the influx of labourers for road and dam constructions), and shifting agriculture. These threats are likely to result in slow and significant declines in the future.
population: This is an uncommon species. There is no information available on its abundance or trends.
range: This species is known only from Arunachal Pradesh, India. It is known from two locations, Mechuka Valley (Choudhury 2007) and the mountains between Mechuka and Tato (Choudhury 2013). Both the sites are located in Shi Yomi district, formerly part of West Siang district. It is likely found from elevations of 1,500 to 2,500 m asl, including in the Siang (west of the river) and Subansiri river valleys that span India and China. It might occur in China (Choudhury 2009a).
useTrade: This species is hunted for its meat, although it is not specifically targeted. It is occasionally killed in festivals or ritual hunts. The skins may be preserved.
conservationActions: This species may occur in Mouling National Park, Arunachal Pradesh, India. Research into its population and distribution would be beneficial.

rationale: This species has a small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 19,438 km2, is known from a few localities in the Mishmi Hills area of Arunachal Pradesh, and it may be at risk of habitat change driven by agriculture and development. It is also hunted, though the extent and impacts of this are unknown. Overall, this species is assessed as Near Threatened as it very close to qualifying for a Vulnerable listing under criteria B1ab(iii), but it is not clear whether the species is undergoing any significant level of decline, nor whether its extent of occurrence could be smaller or larger than is currently estimated. Surveys are needed to clarify its population, distribution and response to threats.
habitat: It lives in broadleaf and coniferous subtropical and temperate montane forest (Choudhury 2009a).
threats: This species may be experiencing declines due to hunting, construction (including of roads and hydroelectric dams), an increased human population (including an influx of labourers), and shifting agriculture (A.U. Choudhury pers. comm. 2024). These threats are likely to result in slow and significant declines in the future.
population: The population trend for this species is unknown, although this species could potentially be common (A.U. Choudhury pers. comm. 2024).
range: This species is known from the Mishmi Hills area of Arunachal Pradesh in north-east India, bordering China, at elevations from 600 to 1,600 m asl (Choudhury 2009). In Mishmi Hills it has been recorded from a number of locations in Dibang Valley, Lower Dibang Valley and Anjaw districts (Choudhury 2009a). It has also been reported from areas higher than 2,000 m asl. Its distribution is likely to include the Siang (east only) and Lohit (west only) river valleys in China (Choudhury 2009b).
useTrade: This species is hunted for its meat, but is not specifically targeted by hunters. It is occasionally killed in festivals or ritual hunts (A.U. Choudhury pers. comm. 2024). The skins may be preserved.
conservationActions: This species’ range includes the Dibang and Mehao Widlife Sanctuaries (Choudhury 2009). Research into its population and distribution would be beneficial.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered under B1ab(iii), because the species is currently only known from a single location which is Gag Island, where it has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of just 56 km2. Whilst nothing is known about its population and there have been no studies since its description, Gag Island has recently become a site of a large surface nickel mine that covers approximately one third of the island, therefore it is inferred that this activity is reducing the quality and quantity of available forest habitat of the species. Surveys of neighbouring islands are a high priority, along with studies of the status of the species on Gag Island itself.
habitat: It presumably lives in ultrabasic, evergreen valley forests on the island (Maryanto et al. 2010).
threats: The Gag Island Project is a surface nickel mine that covers the central block of the island extending from the west coast to the east coast in a south easterly direction, covering approximately one third of the island (Minadat.org 2022).
population: There is no information regarding the population status of Rattus nikenii.
range: This species is known from Gag Island in West Papua, Indonesia, but could potentially be found on the other islands in the area (Maryanto et al. 2010).
useTrade: Use and trade information is unknown.
conservationActions: Although Gag Island has been declared a ‘protected forest’ under Indonesian law, the government made exemptions for nickel mining operations there. Urgent surveys of Gag Island and neighbouring islands are needed.

rationale: The Admiralty Rat has rarely been recorded and is only known from three specimens, fossil evidence and local anecdotes. The species was last recorded in 2016 on a camera trap, and significant surveys undertaken in 2021 failed to record any further evidence of its presence. It is considered probable that the Admiralty Rat was more common historically, and has been negatively impacted by invasive species, i.e., cats and rats, and habitat change. It is unlikely that there are now more than 250 individuals remaining, nor more than 50 individuals in any subpopulation. Furthermore, based on threats, records and survey models, an assessment of the likelihood that the species is now extinct estimated a probability of 0.76. Therefore, on the balance of evidence, this species is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) under criterion C2a(i).
habitat: It is highly likely to be terrestrial (Timm et al. 2016). The holotype was found in the vicinity of a small stream amongst a mosaic of Metroxylon (sago) palms (Arecaceae), mixed tapioca (Manihot esculenta, Euphorbiaceae) and vegetable gardens, and secondary regrowth. Records span a narrow elevational range from near sea level to 200 m asl (Timm et al. 2016). It is likely that Rattus detentus at one point occupied the full elevational range on Manus (Timm et al. 2016). It should be noted that the detections that have occurred to date are from locations that fringe the central forest of Manus (a complex mosaic of vegetable gardens, older forest, secondary regrowth, and now cut over forest), which itself has a very low human population density. This contrasts with eastern Manus Island, which is under more intensive cultivation, in which no sightings of R. detentus have been recorded (N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024).
threats: The main current threats to this species are likely to be cats, invasive rats (Rattus exulans and R. rattus), and habitat degradation (D. Fisher, N. Whitmore and A. Gazzard pers. comm. 2024). R. detentus is a large-bodied (~500g), terrestrial species. Cats and rats have likely caused the extinction of several other large-bodied, ground-dwelling, island-endemic rodents in Melanesia/the Pacific and the Caribbean. Recent camera-trapping and live-trapping surveys showed that rats and probably cats are distributed throughout the island, and hunters caught six cats in three months at Tulu and Lehewa in intact forest in the northern lowlands near one of the two specimen localities (D. Fisher pers. comm. 2024). Forestry has also been an ongoing threat. For example, in 2019–2022, an 8,000 ha logging operation in the southern portion of the central forest removed 44,000 cubic meters of timber (see Maxland (PNG) Ltd 2014; Davey 2020; Société Générale de Surveillance 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023). However, it is likely that habitat change wasn’t a major factor in the trajectory of the species pre-2019. To some extent, the species may be/may have been at risk of hunting. One specimen of R. detentus was snared by local villagers who were targeting bandicoots (Echymipera kalubu) and rats in secondary forest and gardens (Timm et al. 2016). Another villager interviewed in 2014 considered it too rare to be worth hunting. However, on Manus, unless there is a cultural prohibition, any animal captured opportunistically will typically be eaten (N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024).
population: This species apparently became rare before substantial habitat loss and degradation occurred in the 1990s, since several fauna collections and surveys between 1962 and 2014 failed to record it (D. Fisher and N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024). For instance, whilst many types of surveying methods were used in apparently suitable habitat on Mt. Sabomu and around the Yeri River in 2014, no individuals of Rattus detentus were captured (Aplin et al. 2015, Timm et al. 2016). The failure to find it at either site suggests that it was either absent or present only in very low numbers during the survey period (Timm et al. 2016). A number of local hunters in 2014 considered it too rare to be worth hunting, and targeted surveys and ethnographic questionnaires since 2014 have failed to find evidence of the species (D. Fisher and N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024). Formally, the species is known from three specimen records (2002 and two in 2012) and one camera trap survey in 2016 showing an Admiralty Rat approaching an artificial bird nest (Lamaris and Whitmore 2016). Significant surveys in 2021 failed to detect the species (University of Queensland 2022). It is now considered possible that the population has completely disappeared. Using a framework (Akçakaya et al. 2017) based on the threats model (Keith et al. 2017) and records and surveys model (Thompson et al. 2017), the average probability that the species is extinct is estimated to be 0.76 (D. Fisher, N. Whitmore and A. Gazzard pers. comm. 2024). In the past, R. detentus was evidently a more common species and was hunted, as most specimens (191) consist of subfossil remains <9,000 ybp at an archaeological site (Pamwak rock shelter, a prehistoric hunting camp) (D. Fisher and N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024).
range: The type locality for the Admiralty Rat (Rattus detentus) was near a small stream at the western end of Kawaliap Village, Manus Island, Admiralty Islands, Manus Province, Papua New Guinea (Timm et al. 2016). The species is currently only known to science as a living animal from its type locality at an elevation of 200 m asl, and from one other site by the village of Tulu No.1, Manus, at 34 m asl (Timm et al. 2016). It is also known from subfossil remains from the Pamwak archaeological site (Timm et al. 2016).  Field research by the Wildlife Conservation Society since 2013 on Manus has resulted only in one confirmed camera trap sighting at a location near the village of Lehewa on the north coast (Lamaris and Whitmore 2016). Proficient local hunters on the north coast report rarely encountering the animal (N. Whitmore and J. Lamaris pers. comm. 2024). Reliable records and circumstantial evidence have only been obtained between the villages of Tulu and Lehewa on the north coast, and an area encompassing Kawaliap, Pamwak rock shelter, and Mt Sabomu on the southern coast.
useTrade: The species may be/may have been at risk of hunting. One specimen of Rattus detentus was snared by local villagers who were targeting bandicoots (Echymipera kalubu) and rats in secondary forest and gardens (Timm et al. 2016). Another villager interviewed in 2014 considered it too rare to be worth hunting. However, on Manus, unless there is a cultural prohibition, any animal captured opportunistically will typically be eaten (N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024).
conservationActions: Although it is not likely that further survey work would identify any surviving populations, the possibility should not yet be entirely ruled out. Given that all capture events to date have been opportunistic, any ecological surveys on Manus have the potential to uncover evidence of vestigial populations, and therefore awareness of the species and vigilance from scientific teams should be encouraged. While the impact of recent logging events on this species is speculative, 6,350 ha of the central forest in 2022 was protected from commercial logging by conservation deeds enacted by local communities (facilitated by the Wildlife Conservation Society; N. Whitmore pers. comm. 2024). Furthermore, a number of forest communities on Manus continue to practice traditional (tambu) management which protects small parcels of forest (typically ranging 5–100 ha) from subsistence uses including both hunting and tree felling (J. Lamaris pers. comm. 2024).

rationale: The Red-tailed Phascogale suffered a major decline historically, however, that decline largely ceased more than 20 years ago. It was recorded in 142 localities from 1990 to 2011 (Short and Hide 2012), but re-trapping of some of these has failed to locate it. The number of mature individuals is unknown and fluctuates with rainfall, but is possibly less than 10,000. Although listed as Endangered in the past, new information shows that it occurs at many more localities than previously thought and suggests that it is not declining at a rate that would qualify it as threatened. It does not meet criterion B as extent of occurrence (EOO) exceeds 20,000 km2, and the number of locations is more than 10. It is assessed as Near Threatened approaching Vulnerable C2a(i), because the number of mature individuals is inferred as less than 10,000 and the largest subpopulation is inferred to be fewer than 1,000 individuals. The population trend is uncertain, as while four new subpopulations have been established through translocations it is likely that there is a continuing loss of small subpopulations in habitat remnants in the wheat belt of Western Australia. However, the continuing decline is unlikely to be more than 10% over 10 years. The increasing incidence and severity of drought in the near future may mean that such a rate of decline may occur. The Red-tailed Phascogale is listed as a Vulnerable species under Australian federal law, but not under Western Australian law, where it is listed as ‘Species of Special Conservation Interest’ consistent with Near Threatened.
habitat: The Red-tailed Phascogale’s preferred habitat includes communities of Wandoo (Eucalyptus wandoo), Rock Sheoak (Allocasuarina huegeliana), and Gastrolobium spp. (Bradley et al. 2008, Kitchener 1981). It is mainly nocturnal and largely arboreal and can leap up to two metres in the canopy, but also feeds extensively on the ground. Home range sizes are mean of 7 ha for females, 14 ha for males (Short and Hide 2015). Recorded nesting sites include hollow logs, tree hollows (Kitchener 1981, Bradley 1997), and the skirts and stumps of Grass Trees Xanthorrhoea spp. (Maxwell et al. 1996). It is an opportunistic feeder consuming a wide range of insects and spiders as well as small birds, mice (Pseudomys spp. and Mus musculus.) and dunnarts (Sminthopsis spp.) (Kitchener 1981, Stannard et al. 2010). Birds are consumed in higher numbers in spring than summer (Stannard et al. 2010). Diet choice is likely related to seasonal abundance of food items (Stannard et al. 2010) and lactational requirements (Stannard et al. 2015). The best habitat has numerous tree hollows for shelter and a semi-continuous canopy (Short et al. 2011) —this probably provides some protection against predation by feral Cats and Red Foxes. In the western desert it occurred in sand dune country and sheltered in hollows in Sand-dune Bloodwood Corymbia chippendalei (Burbidge et al. 1988).
threats: The historical decline of Red-tailed Phascogale was probably due to the presence of introduced predators, woodland clearance and fragmentation, and changed fire regimes (whereby frequent fire eliminated nest sites). The species now occurs in typically small protected areas (most <2.5 km2) (Short and Hide 2011) and remnant bushland on farms that are secure from habitat destruction and with generally well-managed fire regimes. Population and habitat are fragmented. Predation by feral Cats is considered to be a severe threat over the species' entire range but has not been quantified. Predation by the Red Fox is considered a minor threat because of the arboreal behaviour of phascogales. Too-frequent high-intensity fire remains a threat as it can lead to local extirpation in remnant vegetation. Drought can cause localised extinction, when coupled with habitat loss and fragmentation, due to the species semelparous life history (males die at the end of the breeding season and most females die after weaning their first litter) (Short and Hide 2012).
population: There has been no robust estimate of population size. Subpopulations fluctuate with rainfall (Friend and Scanlon 1996) and remnant, isolated subpopulations are apparently vulnerable to drought or wildfires that burn a whole remnant. Cowan et al. (2024) found that Red-tailed Phascogales were abundant at 2 WA wheatbelt nature reserves (>90% occupancy at camera sites in both reserves), and M. Cowan (pers. comm. 2024) also found them to be abundant at Dryandra Woodland National Park. At Mt Gibson (78 km2: Western Australia), translocations were established from Dryandra stock and a captive breeding program at the University of Western Sydney; animals were released into a large mainland island (predator-free fenced area) in 2017-2019. 165 individuals were translocated and site abundance within a 497-ha monitoring area within the fenced areas was estimated at 176 in April 2024 (Anderson et al. 2024). This is higher than estimates in previous years and suggests that the population is becoming established. The actual population size is likely to be larger than indicated by the site abundance estimate because red-tailed phascogales are regularly detected on camera across the northern half of the fenced area (~4,000 ha). This species has been difficult to monitor at Newhaven. The last confirmed detection was in June 2022 (Mihailou et al. 2023). Translocations to a predator-free fenced area (9,567 ha) at Mallee Cliffs National Park occurred in 2021-2023. A total of 114 founders were sourced from a captive breeding program at Adelaide Zoo, South Australia. The species has been difficult to monitor since release. In 2024, 15 individuals were captured of which only 2 were founders. Small captive populations are held at Alice Springs Desert Park in the Northern Territory and Cleland Wildlife Park in South Australia, and Adelaide Zoo in South Australia.
range: The Red-tailed Phascogale once had a wide distribution in arid and semi-arid Australia, including the MacDonnell Ranges near Alice Springs, near Adelaide, near the junction of the Murray and Darling Rivers in New South Wales (Short and Hide 2012) and parts of the western deserts (Burbidge et al. 1988). Subfossil remains known from arid areas of South Australia (Short and Hide 2012). Burbidge et al. (2009), using modern, historical and subfossil data, found that the Red-tailed Phascogale formerly occurred (at the onset of European colonisation in 1788) in 24 of Australia’s 85 bioregions and that it was extinct in 20 and declined or seriously declined in two. It appears now to be naturally confined to remnant vegetation in Western Australia’s southern wheatbelt, less than 1% of its former range, where annual mean rainfall is between 400 and 600 mm (Short and Hide 2012). It occurs in numerous protected areas. It has been successfully reintroduced for >5 years to Wadderin Sanctuary (4.3 km2) north of Narembeen (WA) in 2009 (Short and Hide 2015);an unfenced reserve near Kojonup in 2010 (Short and Hide 2015, de Visser et al. 2024) in Western Australia;Mount Gibson Wildlife Sanctuary (78 km2) in 2017 (Anderson et al. 2023).There have been recent translocations to:Newhaven Wildlife Sanctuary, Northern Territory (95 km2) in 2021 (Anderson et al. 2023);Secret Rocks, South Australia (SA), in 2022-23 (a 40 km2 fenced area that is free of the Feral Cat Felis catus and European Red Fox Vuples vulpes, where 35 animals were released; in 2024 this subpopulation was extant but in low numbers;Vulkathunha-Gammon Ranges National Park (SA) in March 2022 (an unfenced area subject to aerial Eradicat® baiting, animals were removed in August 2022, as the site was deemed to be not suitable habitat);Mallee Cliffs National Park, New South Wales (95 km2) in 2021-23 (Anderson et al. 2023, Short and Stone 2009);Gawler Ranges (South Australia) in 2024 (managed natural area where Red Foxes Vulpes vulpes and feral Cats Felis catus are controlled with aerial Eradicat® baiting, Felixer grooming traps, Cat trapping, and shooting; the aim being to keep Cats a low densities).Only Wadderin Sanctuary, Kojonup, and Mt Gibson Sanctuary are included in this assessment as translocations to the other sites were less than 5 years ago.
conservationActions: The Red-tailed Phascogale is currently found at >100 sites, many of which are within protected areas, with fairly low threat. Cowan et al. (2014) showed that detectability was significantly improved by using camera traps mounted on 4 cm wide by 0.8 m long wooden platforms attached to tree trunks by right-angle metal brackets approximately 1.6 m above ground level. They also demonstrated that the abundance of Phascogale calura at Tutanning Nature Reserve in the WA wheatbelt was not affected by the used of Eradicat® baits that were used to control Red Foxes and feral Cats. There are current and/or recent programs to reintroduce the species to central and eastern Australia, with mixed results to date. Reintroduced animals have been largely sourced from captive populations at Alice Springs Desert Park and Adelaide Zoo. Close monitoring of the Red-tailed Phascogale is important to detect and react early to any population declines.

rationale: Assessment of the conservation status of the Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale is challenging because there are few recent records and it is largely unrepresented in extensive biodiversity monitoring programs within its range (in part due to low detectability), rendering it difficult to evaluate population size and rate of decline. Although there is little robust monitoring data, decline is evident from marked reduction in records on the north Australian mainland. For example, the Atlas of Living Australia has zero records from the mainland since 2005, with the frequency of mainland records across preceding decades being: 1970-1979 (10 records); 1980-1989 (19 records); 1990-1999 (6 records); 2000-2010 (10 records); 2010-2019 (0 records); 2020-2024 (0 records). Although the rate of population decline cannot be estimated reliably; it is almost certainly greater than 30% over 10 years, and may be appreciably higher. Based on recent records, the area of occupancy (AOO) is 116 km2. This is likely to be an under-estimate given sparsity of sampling across range, and the actual value is considered here to be between 500 and 2,000 km2. It is known to persist in fewer than 10 locations, and it is likely to be undergoing continuing decline in habitat quality and number of mature individuals, so qualifies as Vulnerable B2ab(i,ii,iii,v). Population size is challenging to estimate, but is most likely less than 10,000 mature individuals and may be far fewer. The rate of decline is not resolved but is likely to be more than 10% over the last decade, so it could also qualify as Vulnerable C1, although the evidence is meagre.
habitat: The Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale is solitary, nocturnal, and arboreal. It nests within tree hollows during the day, and forages both on the ground and in trees mostly for invertebrates, but also some small vertebrates (Woinarski 2005). There is little information on the habitat requirements of this species. Most recent records are from tall open forest of Eucalyptus miniata-E. tetrodonta forests (Geyle et al. 2020; Rhind et al. 2023).
threats: Threats have not been well resolved, in part because there have been no detailed ecological studies on this species. It is likely that the current fire regime characterised by high frequency of fires (Russell-Smith et al. 2017) reduces habitat quality (including abundance of tree hollows, hollow logs and large trees) and hence is detrimental to this species. In some areas within its range, this regime is being exacerbated by ongoing expansion of invasive pasture grasses (Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023). Predation by feral cats (Felis catus) is a likely ongoing threat, and cats are abundant across at least part of its range (Davies et al. 2021); and frequent fire may cause increasing incidence or impact of such predation (McGregor et al. 2016). Cats have been implicated in the rapid and severe recent decline of other small mammals on Melville Island (Davies et al. 2021). In some parts of its mainland and Melville Island range, there has been extensive habitat clearing, mostly for horticulture and plantations (Firth et al. 2006). It is possible that the spread of invasive cane toads (Rhinella marina) across the phascogale’s entire mainland range over the last 2-3 decades may have caused major mortality and population loss, through poisoning during predation attempts, but there is no evidence for or against this possibility.
population: Historic accounts report that the Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale was common: for example, Dahl (1897) noted that ‘on the rivers Mary and Katherine it was frequently observed. In fact nearly everywhere inland it was very constant, and on a moonlight walk one would generally expect to see this animal’. However, this is no longer the case, and it has declined severely in range and abundance over recent decades (Woinarski et al. 2007, Rhind et al. 2023). Quantifying the extent of this decline is challenging. Although there were many reports of its former abundance in Kakadu National Park in the 1970s and 1980s (Calaby 1973, Woinarski and Fisher 2014), it had declined so severely by the time that an extensive biodiversity monitoring program was established in Kakadu National Park (late 1980s) that it was recorded in so few plots that rate of decline could no longer be assessed (Woinarski et al. 2004, 2010). In a baseline mammal monitoring program from 2000 to 2002 in its likely stronghold, Melville Island, it was reported with only two individuals from more than 25,000 trap-nights at 236 sampling sites (Firth et al. 2006), re-sampling in 2015 of 86 of those sites (using ~8,250 trap-nights) recorded only one individual (Davies et al. 2018a). To some extent, the sparsity of recent records is due to its low detectability using conventional trapping techniques. Davies et al. (2018b) used camera-trapping (48,627 trap-nights) on Melville Island (from 2013 to 2015) and reported nine detections, at a single site (Taracumbi). Geyle et al. (2020) used targeted sampling (50 baited camera traps placed in large trees and set over a 10-month period (2018-2019), at this same site on Melville Island) to improve detection, and reported 16 detections of this species. In eucalypt woodlands at Garig Gunak Barlu National Park (Cobourg Peninsula), Woolley et al. (2024) monitored 198 nest-boxes over three years (2015-2018) and detected no phascogales. However, in Kakadu, since 2021 Parks Australia has undertaken a targeted camera-trap survey, with cameras set at tree hollows in suitable forest, at 70 sites by 60 nights (i.e., 4200 trap-nights), but did not record any phascogales (Luke Einoder pers. comm., August 2024). The total global population of this species is estimated to be fewer than 10,000 mature individuals and it might be fewer than 2,500.
range: The Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale is endemic to the Top End of the Northern Territory, Australia, where it has been recorded from Melville Island, West Pellew Island, and tropical savannas of the Northern Territory mainland including near Gove, near Borroloola, Katherine area, Kakadu National Park, Garig Gunak Barlu National Park, and Litchfield National Park (Parker 1973, Woinarski 2005, Rhind et al. 2008). The population on West Pellew Island is probably extirpated (Ward et al. 2006, Woinarski et al. 2011) and over the last few decades it has suffered severe declines in distributional extent and population size on the Northern Territory mainland. It has not been reported from other large islands in the region with apparently suitable habitat (e.g., Bathurst Island, Groote Eylandt). Its continuing existence in Kakadu National Park, a former stronghold, is uncertain. The most recent records are of an individual seen in 2021, 20 km west of Jabiru (Steve Cutter, via Luke Einoder, pers. comm., August 2024) and one individual found dead in 2016 at Jim Jim ranger station (Luke Einoder, pers. comm., August 2024). With those exceptions, all recent (post 2010) records are from Melville Island, and its occurrence there is patchy (with recent records mostly from Jessie Creek, Goose Creek, and Taracumbi localities). EOO calculated in sRedList based on all records from the Atlas of Living Australia is 218,978 km2, declining to 46,678 km2 when only records since 2000 are included.
conservationActions: The Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale has been recorded from three protected areas: Litchfield, Garig Gunak Barlu, and Kakadu National Parks, although it may no longer persist at these. An Indigenous Protected Area was established for the Tiwi Islands (including parts of Melville) in 2024. The Northern Brush-tailed Phascogale is listed as Vulnerable under Australian national environmental legislation and there is an existing Conservation Advice (that provides broad conservation direction) for this species.

rationale: The Carpentarian Antechinus is assessed as Near Threatened because it is very close to meeting criteria for VU B2ab(iii): its area of occupancy (AOO) is estimated at 544 km2, the number of locations may not greatly exceed 10 and there is ongoing decline in habitat quality (due to fire and invasive grasses) and possibly in population size. Formerly a very poorly known species, recent research has helped clarify some aspects of its status.
habitat: The Carpentarian Antechinus is a nocturnal, generalist predator of invertebrates and small vertebrates. When food is plentiful, fat is stored in the tail. There is little information on dispersion, home range or movement patters, but one marked individual moved a straight-line distance of 2 km in 24 hours (Burnett et al. 2023). It occurs across a range of rugged rocky areas, across varied geologic types, but especially metamorphic (Lloyd et al. 2013, Barnes et al. 2024). The species has been recorded from a range of vegetation types, but always at rocky sites (Johnson and Kerle 1991, Woolley 2011, Ward 2012). Breeding is seasonal, with young born mostly in August and September (Woolley 2011). Litter size is up to 6 (Burnett et al. 2023).
threats: The magnitude of impacts of possible threats are not known. Some sites, especially in Queensland, are subject to mining. Increasing intensity and severity of wildfires may be a problem in some areas, in part fuelled by expansion of invasive Buffel Grass (Cenchrus ciliaris). Feral Cats (Felis catus) probably take some individuals, however the rugged nature of its habitat may reduce such predation impacts (Woinarski 2004, Burnett et al. 2023).
population: There are no reliable estimates of density, population size or trend. In extensive recent camera-trap sampling of suitable habitat mostly on the Queensland mainland, Barnes et al. (2024) detected it at a rate of 7.1% of trap-nights. Using box (Elliott) traps in surveys of the Pellew Islands, Woinarski et al. (2011) reported <1% trap success.
range: The Carpentarian Antechinus is endemic to Australia. It occurs on some islands (Vanderlin, North, Centre and South-west in the Sir Edward Pellew group) in the Gulf of Carpentaria (Woinarski et al. 2011). In the adjacent mainland, it occurs in rugged ranges through much of the Mount Isa Inlier bioregion (mostly in north-western Queensland), extending north-west to Pungalina – Seven Emu in the Northern Territory) (Sanders and Slater 2004; Baker and Griffiths 2005; Kanowski et al. 2010, 2011; Woolley 2011; Moran and Kanowski 2012; Lloyd et al. 2013; Barnes et al. 2024). There may be a marked disjunction between ranges in the Mount Isa Inlier and those further north-west in the Northern Territory (Barnes et al. 2024). Recent records provisionally attributable to this species, from remains in pellets of Eastern Barn Owls (Tyto delicatula), extend the known range further south in Queensland, into the Simpson Desert (Kutt et al. 2020, Schoenefuss et al. 2024). There are also three recent (2022) records from the Beetaloo Basin, to the west and inland of previous recent records from the Northern Territory (A. Kutt, 4/10/2024). The location of the original record from Alexandria Station in 1905 is considered unreliable or at least vague (Woinarski 2004, Johnson et al. 2008): a recent review considered it most likely that the actual location was the Mittiebah Range (Woolley 2011). However, recent sampling in this area failed to detect this species (Barnes et al. 2024).
conservationActions: The Carpentarian Antechinus is present in at least two protected areas (North Island, which is Barranyi National Park; and Pungalina - Seven Emu sanctuary). A recovery plan was developed for the 2004-2008 period (Woinarski 2004). Recommendations from this plan include: establishing a recovery team; communicating information about the species to stakeholders; targeting research in order to make informed decisions (e.g., towards total number and distribution, population trends, habitat suitability, and threatening processes); minimize the impacts of feral cats; and improve fire management. The Carpentarian Antechinus was formerly listed as Vulnerable under Australian environmental law, but was delisted in 2019.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in at least eight protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: This little-known species is generally found in areas of sandplain environments (raised in the surrounding landscape) shrubland – often with sparse mallee on sandy or gravely substrates, and on sandsheets on coastal limestone (McKenzie and Kitchener 2023). During a biological survey of the Western Australian wheatbelt, it was detected in 23 of the 252 quadrats trapped. These were largely those on sandy substrates, probably reflecting the species’ burrow requirements (Burbidge et al. 2004). It is an opportunistic feeder on arthropods. Mating occurs between April and July with young born in late winter. Juveniles are present in late spring and summer.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to White-tailed Dunnart. Much of its previous range has been cleared for agriculture, but it remains in many habitat remnants. Increased fire frequency on sand plains in combination with habitat fragmentation may continue to be an issue for this species.
population: It is a common species within its limited habitat (McKenzie and Kitchener 2023).
range: The White-tailed Dunnart is endemic to Australia, where it is found in south-western Western Australia.
conservationActions: The species is known from several large protected areas, including Lesueur, Alexander Morrison, and Badgingarra National Parks, and Bendering, North Karlgarin, Dragon Rocks, Lake Magenta and Jilbadji Nature Reserves. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.  It does not qualify for listing under criterion A because population decline, if any, is appreciably less than 30% over 10 years. It does not qualify under criterion B because EOO (182,587 km2) is much greater than threshold, it is not severely fragmented and does not exhibit extreme fluctuations. Although minimum AOO (244 km2) is under thresholds for EN or VU, this is likely to be a significant under-estimate due to limited sampling across the range, it is not severely fragmented and does not exhibit extreme fluctuations or a continuing decline. It does not qualify for listing under C because population size, although not known, is likely to exceed 10,000 individuals, population decline (if any) is likely to be <10% in 10 years, and there is no extreme fluctuation. It does not qualify under criterion D as population size is almost certainly > 1,000 mature individuals.
habitat: The species is found in areas of rugged rocky habitat.
threats: Mainland subpopulations have declined through predation by introduced Red Foxes (Pearson and Eldridge 2023). Foxes do not occur in some of the higher elevation areas of its current range; most of the fox threat is concentrated within the coastal section of the range. Feral Cats Felis catus have been recorded preying on a young P. rothschildi (Anderson et al. 2021, Lavery et al. 2021).
population: This species is locally common, although patchily distributed due to its preference for steep and rocky habitat. Mainland populations have declined, particularly from some of its southern range. The Dolphin Island subpopulation was almost extirpated by Red Fox Vulpes vulpes predation before fox control was implemented, and has since recovered. Subpopulations were lost from two offshore islands (East and West Intercourse Islands) during the 1960s due to fox predation.
range: This species is endemic to the state of Western Australia, Australia, where it is found in the Pilbara and Gascoyne bioregions including on Dolphin (330 ha), Rosemary (1,122 ha), Enderby (3,241 ha), East Lewis (993 ha) and West Lewis (1982 ha, introduced) Islands in the Dampier Archipelago. It also occurs in Murujuga National Park (Burrup Peninsula), which was an island until joined to the mainland by roads and a railway.
conservationActions: All the known island subpopulations are protected areas. This species also occurs in Murujuga and Karijini National Parks, Barlee Range Nature Reserve, and Meenthena Conservation Park. There is an ongoing fox control program on Dolphin Island and the adjacent mainland. Monitoring of this species' populations is needed.A recovery plan covering five species of rock-wallabies, including Rothschild’s Rock-wallaby, was prepared in 2013 (Pearson 2013).

rationale: The Scaly-tailed Possum is assessed as Near Threatened (nearly meets criterion B). There is routine monitoring at Charnley River–Artesian Range (AWC) and other management areas that shows the species is relatively common in parts of complex sandstone country of the north-west Kimberley.The has an area of occupancy (AOO) smaller than 2,000 km² and the population may be severely fragmented (individuals are found in small and relatively isolated subpopulations; in certain circumstances this is inferred from habitat information), and the number of locations is inferred to be fewer than ten. Its population trend is uncertain, but monitoring at Charnley River–Artesian Range and Bullo River (AWC) indicates population stability. The main threats to this species are inappropriate fire regimes (too frequent, extensive and hot) and predation by feral cats (Felis catus), although information on the effects of these threats is limited.
habitat: The Scaly-tailed Possum occurs in rugged sandstone habitat with adjacent open woodland or closed forest, often with rainforest or vine thicket elements (Humphries et al. 1984, Bradley et al. 1987, Hohnen et al. 2016). It forages mainly in trees but may venture into open areas to feed on flowers, fruits, seeds and leaves. In captivity it also eats nuts and insects. It is unclear whether the observed relationship with rocky and rainforest habitats reflects a true habitat preference, or is a result of recent reductions of habitat quality in the open savannas caused by current fire regimes, grazing by introduced herbivores, and the impacts of feral Cats. A phylogenetic study found that, unlike several saxicolous rock-wallaby species in the region, Wyulda showed no deep structure between eastern and western populations, suggesting recent colonisation or connectivity across the Kimberley (Potter et al. 2014). Historical records from the east Kimberley suggest that the species did once persist in much drier habitats (Alexander 1919), but probably in more mesic sites such as gorges.It shelters in rock piles, cliffs, under rock slabs and in underground crevices. Females give birth mainly in the dry season between March and August, although breeding may extend later in the dry season. A single juvenile is carried in the pouch for 150-200 days and is weaned after eight months. Females are sexually mature at two years (Humphreys et al. 1984, Runcie 1999, Burbidge and Webb 2008). At Artesian Range, the species is highly frugivorous (Hohnen et al. 2016). Males generally have larger home ranges than females, and male core home ranges rarely overlap with one another, suggesting some degree of territoriality. In contrast male home ranges often overlap with one or more females (Hohnen et al. 2016).
threats: Major threats are inappropriate fire regimes (too frequent, extensive and hot) and predation by feral Cats (Felis catus). Information on the effects of these threats is limited. The species often occurs in small rainforest patches, typically, but not only, restricted to deep gorges (Turpin 2015). Such complex, dissected rocky habitat provides shelter and protection from predation and fire and the rainforest areas provide food resources (Hohnen et al. 2016, Woolley et al. 2019). However, rainforest patches are highly restricted and vulnerable to degradation by cattle and fire (McKenzie et al. 1991). Repeat fire events or cattle grazing can degrade the margins of rainforest and influence patch size (McKenzie et al. 1991). In the drier areas of the southern Kimberley, rainforest patches only persist in perennially moist refugia, however they exhibit high rates of degradation by fire and cattle (McKenzie et al. 1991). Changes to the distribution or quality of rainforest habitat arising from fire or climate change are highly likely to influence the species distribution. Rainforest patches are small, isolated and embedded within a mosaic of mostly flammable eucalypt savanna woodlands (Kenneally 2018, Ondei et al. 2017, 2020). Fire induced rainforest contraction has been observed in parts of the Kimberley (e.g. Turpin 2015). Most rainforests and their associated faunal assemblages are not currently protected and many were found to be severely disturbed by fire and introduced feral cattle (Kenneally 2018). Large parts of the species range burn annually, and though complex rocky habitat provides protection, adjacent woodlands and forests are impacted (https://firenorth.org.au/nafi3/).
population: There is no robust estimate of population size. It is locally common at some sites in the north-west Kimberley and on Bigge Island, but is apparently uncommon in the east Kimberley. A 2003 survey demonstrated persistence in Prince Regent National Park and at Mitchell Plateau (Start et al. 2007). Surveys by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy have recorded Scaly-tailed Possums as locally common in the Artesian Range south of the Prince Regent River (Hohnen et al. 2016). It has been also been recorded at King George Falls, El Questro, Wunaamin (formerly King Leopold) Range (Turpin 2015), Bullo River Station (NT) and Bradshaw (NT). In 2024, occupancy in the Artesian Range was recorded at 75% of suitable sites surveyed by AWC (12 of 16 sites) (Sayers pers. comm. 2025).
range: The Scaly-tailed Possum was thought to be restricted to the Kimberley, Western Australia, but has recently been located at Bullo River Station and Bradshaw, near the western edge of the Northern Territory. Most records are from near-coastal, high-rainfall north-western Kimberley from Kalumburu south to Yampi Peninsula. The type specimen came from Violet Valley, near Warmun, east Kimberley in 1917. It was rediscovered in the east Kimberley at Emma Gorge, Cockburn Range, El Questro Station in June 2010 (Doody et al. 2012) and more recently at Wuggubun Gorge by the Kija Rangers in 2022. The East Kimberley subpopulations may be separated from those of the north-west Kimberley (Doody et al. 2012), but survey effort in areas between has been low. Potter et al. (2014) found significant but low genetic differentiation between the east and west Kimberley subpopulations. It occurs on Augustus (190 km²), Bigge (171 km²) and Boongaree (42 km²) Islands (Burbidge and McKenzie 1978, Gibson and McKenzie 2012) and probably on an unnamed island in Talbot Bay (2.6 km², Palmer et al. 2016) where distinctive scats were collected. A 1970 sight record from Broome reported by Ride (1970) was possibly a translocated animal as Broome is considered unlikely on habitat grounds. It is known to have disappeared from some sites, e.g., Lochman and Lochman (2003). The species is reasonably widespread in some parts of the Kimberley, such as at the Artesian Range (Hohnen et al. 2016). There has been too little survey effort to determine the number of locations at which it occurs, but this is likely to be less than 10. Rainforest patches, vine thickets and rocky complexity provide important habitat for the species (Turpin 2015, Hohnen et al. 2016, Sayers et al. 2024), which has a scattered and restricted occurrence across the species’ range (McKenzie et al. 1991).
conservationActions: National Parks and Conservation Parks within its range are managed by the Western Australian Parks and Wildlife Service, Department of Biodiversity Conservation and Attractions, in conjunction with Aboriginal Corporations. Aboriginal lands in the north-west Kimberley, most of which are Indigenous Protected Areas, are managed by the Wunambal Gaambera Aboriginal Corporation and the Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation. The Charnley River-Artesian Range Wildlife Sanctuary is managed by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy in partnership with the Wilinggin Aboriginal Corporation. Emma Gorge is within the El Questro pastoral lease. Bullo River Station is a pastoral lease with a conservation partnership with the Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Bradshaw Field Training Area is managed by the Department of Defence, with fire and feral animal management programs at Both Bullo River Station and Bradshaw.There is regional fire management in the western parts of its range, intensive management of fire in the Artesian Range, and regional fire management immediately to the east of the main distribution through the EcoFire Project. A research project on Scaly-tailed Possums at Artesian Range (Australian Wildlife Conservancy / University of Tasmania) described the ecology of the species, and the impacts of fire patterns and feral cats on their ecology and survival (Hohnen et al. 2016).

rationale: Yellow-footed Antechinus is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, presumed large population, and lack of any major threats.
habitat: The Yellow-footed Antechinus occurs in many habitat types, including tropical moist forest, dry sclerophyll forest, swampy habitat, mulga, woodlands, heathlands and suburban areas (e.g., in Brisbane) (Crowther 2023). In woodlands and heathlands of temperate south-eastern and south-western Australia, this species shelters selectively in the ‘skirts’ of grass-trees Xanthorrhoea spp. (Swinburn et al. 2007). Like others in the genus, it breeds once a year. It potentially has the largest litters of any antechinus species (12 teats (Crowther 2023)).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species, but it is preyed upon by feral cats Felis catus and Red Fox Vulpes vulpes (Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021). There is some evidence that the species survives fragmentation better than most small marsupials, and it is a habitat generalist (it tolerates drier regions and microhabitats than most species of antechinus do) (Crowther 2023).In temperate heathlands and woodlands of temperate Australia, habitat suitability for this species is strongly affected by root-rot fungus Phytophthora cinnamomi: for example, the abundance of mardo A. f. leucogaster was ten-fold greater in healthy forest than in comparable diseased forest (Armistead 2008).
population: This species is common, although sparsely distributed.
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it ranges through the east of the country from north-eastern Queensland to extreme south-eastern South Australia, and is also present as a disjunct population in south-western Western Australia. It is the most widespread of Antechinus species (Crowther 2023).
conservationActions: The Yellow-footed Antechinus occurs in many protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It does not meet Criterion A as even if it is declining it would not be at a rate of >30% over the past 10 years. It does not meet Criterion B as the EOO and AOO are greater than thresholds. It does not meet Criteria C or D as the population size is inferred to be >10, 000 mature individuals.
habitat: The species is found in Triodia hummock grassland and tussock grassland on sand plains and dunes (Woolley 2023). Hayes (2018) studied the Kaluta in Millstream-Chichester National Park and found that males were obligately semelparous (reproduce only once in their lifetime, after which they typically die) and that females were polyandrous, with litters sired by up to three males. In relation to fire, Hayes suggested that the frequency of fire is not as important for Kaluta persistence as is the occurrence of spinifex hummocks of sufficient size. In an extensive survey of Pilbara mammals, Kalutas were found more commonly at sandy sites (Gibson and McKenzie 2009). Diet is predominantly termites, as well as another small dasyurid species (Pseudantechinus sp.), spiders and centipedes (Hayes 2018).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species.
population: The Kaluta is widespread and abundant within its range. Density at a site near South Hedland was higher than 1.88/ha (Thompson and Thompson 2008). In a survey of 302 sample sites in the Pilbara, Kalutas were reported from 125 sites (Gibson and McKenzie 2009). The number of mature individuals is inferred to be >10,000.
range: The Kaluta is endemic to Australia, where it is distributed mainly in the Pilbara bioregion, and also in parts of the Carnarvon, Great Sandy Desert and the Little Sandy Desert bioregions of Western Australia.
conservationActions: The Kaluta is present in Karijini, Karlamilyi, Kennedy Range, and Murujuga National Parks, in Cane River, Giralia and Meentheena Conservation Parks, and on Potter Island, which is part of the Great Sandy Island Nature Reserve.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern as it is common, relatively widespread, and present in some protected areas, and there are no major threats to it. It does not meet Criterion A as even if it is declining it would not be at a rate of >30% over the past 10 years. It does not meet Criterion B as the EOO and AOO are greater than thresholds. It does not meet Criteria C or D as the population size is inferred to be >10, 000 mature individuals.
habitat: The Pilbara Ningaui is found in semi-arid spinifex grasslands on outwash plains close to rocky outcrops and ridges and along drainage lines (Dunlop et al. 2023). It is associated particularly with dense to mid-dense hummock grass (Dunlop and Sawle 1982). Females give birth to five or six young. Females can be found with pouch young from September to March. Juveniles become independent when weighing about 2 g and can be found from late December until early May. The species is short-lived, with few individuals surviving into a second breeding season (Dunlop and Sawle 1982, Dunlop et al. 2023). It is nocturnal, sheltering in hummock grass (Triodia spp.) by day. The Pilbara Ningaui is carnivorous, eating a variety of invertebrates and small skinks.
threats: There appears to be no major threats to this species. Extensive mining may destroy habitat and kill individuals at some sites. Feral cats are known to consume this species (Woolley et al. 2019).
population: The species is reasonably abundant in suitable habitat. Dunlop and Sawle (1982) reported it to be the most common mammal in a Pilbara study area, with 156 different individuals captured from 6,333 pit-trap-days. Gibson and McKenzie (2009) reported it to be the most prevalent small mammal species reported in a widespread survey of mammals of the Pilbara, with records from 179 of 301 sampled sites.
range: The Pilbara Ningaui is endemic to Australia, where it is found mainly in the Pilbara bioregion, but also in the Carnarvon, Gascoyne, Great Sandy Desert and Little Sandy Desert bioregions of Western Australia.
conservationActions: The Pilbara Ningaui is present in Karijini, Millstream-Chichester, Cape Range and Rudall River (now Karlamilyi) National Parks. The species is also found in the Meentheena and Cane River Conservation Parks.

rationale: Giles' Planigale is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Giles' Planigale is found in areas with deep cracking clay soils on the floodplains of creeks and rivers, on grassy plains and in interdune areas among sandhills (Blackett et al. 2008, Read 2023). It shelters mostly in cracks in the soil. This species is nocturnal and spends much of its time hunting within the clay cracks. The diet includes a wide range of invertebrate species and small vertebrates (Read 1987). It has a shifting home range (Read 1984a). Females give birth to one or two litters of six to eight young after a gestation period of 16 days (Read 2023). In the wild, breeding is seasonal, extending from mid-July to late January (Read 1984b).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. Giles' Planigale is detrimentally affected by habitat change, mostly for intensive horticulture, in parts of its range. Introduced Cats (Felis catus) and Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes) probably take some individuals (Murphy et al. 2019, Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021), but this species is smaller than preferred mammal prey size for these predators (Woolley et al. 2019), and the cracking clay soils in which it lives may provide secure shelter sites from some predators. Its high fecundity confers some resilience to impacts of predation. Climate change is likely to increase the frequency and intensity of droughts, which may cause future population reductions.
population: Giles’ Planigale is widely distributed but typically in low densities (Read 2023). This species is irruptive after rain and populations fluctuate seasonally and yearly (Read 2023), but there is no evidence that the total population size or distribution is subject to extreme fluctuations. There is no estimate of total population size or trends.
range: Giles' Planigale is endemic to Australia, where it occurs in the arid and semiarid portions of south-western Queensland and western New South Wales to eastern South Australia, extending to small portions of north-western Victoria and south-eastern Northern Territory.
conservationActions: It is found in many protected areas.

rationale: The Long-tailed Planigale is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large population, occurrence in many protected areas, lack of major threats, and because (if declining) it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Long-tailed Planigales are one of the smallest marsupials. They are found mainly on cracking clay grasslands. The diet includes a wide range of invertebrate species and small vertebrates. They shelter mostly in cracks in the soil.Females give birth to between four and eight young and adults may live to breed in more than one season (Fisher and Baker 2023).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to the Long-tailed Planigale. Intensification of pastoralism reduces the abundance of this species (Fisher 2001). Introduced Cats (Felis catus) and Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes) probably take some (Murphy et al. 2019, Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021), but this species is smaller than preferred mammal prey size for these predators (Woolley et al. 2019), and the cracking clay soils in which it lives may provide secure shelter sites from some predators.
population: The Long-tailed Planigale is abundant within its range. Populations decline with heavy livestock grazing pressure and intensive agriculture, such as in the south-eastern part of the species’ range (Fisher 2001, Fisher and Baker 2023). There is no estimate of density, total population size or trends.
range: The Long-tailed Planigale is endemic to Australia, where it has been recorded mainly across the northern part of the country. It also occurs in the north-eastern corner of South Australia.
conservationActions: Long-tailed Planigales occur in many protected areas.

rationale: The Common Planigale is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Common Planigales occur in a wide variety of habitats, including sclerophyll and temperate forest, grasslands, marshland, mangroves, and rocky areas. They also occur in gardens at the fringes of urban areas and in some agricultural areas. The diet includes a wide range of invertebrate species and small vertebrates.Females give birth to a litter of up to 10 young in the east and as many as 12 in the Top End (Burnett 2023).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. Predation by domestic Cats (Felis catus) occurs across its range (other than some islands), and by Red Fox in eastern Australia (Murphy et al. 2019, Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021), but this species is smaller than preferred mammal prey size for these predators (Woolley et al. 2019). The Cane Toad Rhinella marina has spread across almost all of the range of Common Planigale, and may have caused substantial mortality by poisoning, however planigales rapidly learn to avoid toads (Webb et al. 2008) or develop some tolerance to their venom (Llewelyn et al. 2010). Across much of its range in northern Australia, it may be exposed to increasing incidence of severe wildfire, which may degrade habitat quality, cause some direct mortality and expose it to higher risks of predation (Einoder et al. 2023).
population: Across much of its range it is an abundant species (Burnett 2023). However, there are no estimates of density or population size. A broad-based monitoring program in Kakadu National Park reported a 75% decline in abundance from 2001 to 2009, but the sample size for this species was small and the trend was not statistically significant (Woinarski et al. 2010).
range: The Common Planigale is endemic to Australia, where it is widely distributed in northern and eastern parts of the country It also occurs on at least 11 islands: Groote Eylandt (2,326 km2), Vanderlin Island (262 km2) (Woinarski et al. 2011), Croker (310 km2) and North Peron (1.7 km2) Islands (ALA) in the Northern Territory, and Russell (18 km2), Bribie (14.8 km2), North Stradbroke (269 km2), Great Keppel (13 km2), K’gari (formerly Fraser) (1,659 km2), and Bentinck (138 km2) Islands, Queensland (Abbott and Burbidge 1995; ALA), and Koolan Island (27 km2) in the Kimberley, Western Australia (Burbidge and Abbott 2017), although taxonomic review may re-classify some of these populations.
conservationActions: Common Planigales are present in many protected areas.

rationale: The Narrow-nosed Planigale is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in many protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The Narrow-nosed Planigale is found in open grassland, mallee scrub, and bankside vegetation in areas with cracking clay soils (Read 2023). It has a broader habitat tolerance than other planigales (Blackett et al. 2008). It shelters mostly in cracks in the soil. This species is nocturnal and spends much of its time hunting within the clay cracks. The diet includes a wide range of invertebrate species and small vertebrates (Read 1987). It has a shifting home range (Read 1984a).In captivity females give birth to two litters of an average of six young annually, but in the wild probably only a single litter is produced (Read 2023). In the wild, breeding is seasonal, extending from late July to mid-January (Read 1984b).
threats: There are no major threats to the species. There is a localized threat through habitat conversion to agriculture in parts of the range. Introduced Cats (Felis catus) and Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes) probably take some individuals (Murphy et al. 2019, Stobo-Wilson et al. 2021), but this species is smaller than preferred mammal prey size for these predators (Woolley et al. 2019), and the cracking clay soils in which it lives may provide secure shelter sites from some predators. Climate change is likely to increase the frequency and intensity of droughts, which may cause future population reductions.
population: The Narrow-nosed Planigale is a locally common species, although Read (2023) considered it ‘sparse’. The population fluctuates with rainfall, although fluctuations across the entire range are unlikely to meet the criteria for extreme fluctuations. There have been historic and perhaps ongoing declines in the eastern portion of range due to habitat conversion for agriculture. Read (2023) estimated that densities are ‘probably less than one individual per hectare’ but ‘with considerable year-to-year variation’. There are no estimates of population size and no monitoring program.
range: The Narrow-nosed Planigale is endemic to Australia, where it is distributed across much of the eastern interior of the country (Read 2023).
conservationActions: It is present in many protected areas.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. This species appears to be sparsely distributed within its range. There is no knowledge or inference of decline or major threats to the species, but more research is needed into both populations and threats.
habitat: Pseudantechinus ningbing is found in rocky habitats, including limestone and sandstone habitats. It is potentially a generalist insectivore. Breeding is thought to occur only once per year, with mating in June and young being born in July to early August. Both males and females may survive to breed in a second year.
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. Altered fire regimes could potentially affect it, though possibly less so in its rocky habitats. Fire is now better managed in much of the Kimberley.
population: This species is probably common (Woolley 2008).
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is distributed in the Kimberley region of northern Western Australia and in the north-western Northern Territory. It has been recorded from the Northern Kimberley, Central Kimberley, Dampierland, Victoria Bonaparte, Ord Victoria Plain and Pine Creek bioregions. It occurs on Augustus and Jungulu Islands off the Kimberley coast (Burbidge and Abbott 2017, Woolley 2023).
conservationActions: The species is known from several protected areas, including Prince Regent, Purnululu and Judbarra/Gregory National Parks and several Indigenous Protected Areas. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, lack of known major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It does not meet Criterion A as even if it is declining it would not be at a rate of >30% over the past 10 years. It does not meet Criterion B as the EOO and AOO are greater than thresholds and it does not meet Criteria C or D as the population size is inferred to be >10, 000 mature individuals.
habitat: It is found in a variety of vegetation types, but favours rocky areas (Woolley 2023). Little is known about the breeding habits of this species (Woolley 2023). Based on a captive colony, births may occur from late-July to early October.
threats: There appears to be no major threats to this species.
population: The abundance of this species is unknown, though it is probably widespread and common.
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is distributed in arid portions of western Western Australia. It has been recorded in the Pilbara, Gascoyne, Murchison, Little Sandy Desert, Geraldton Sandplains, Coolgardie and the extreme western edge of the Great Victoria Desert bioregions.
conservationActions: The species has been recorded from a number of protected areas (e.g., Barlee Range Nature Reserve, Meentheena Conservation Park, and Rudall River, Millstream-Chichester Range National Parks). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history of, and threats to this species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Little Long-tailed Dunnarts are found in arid and semi-arid woodlands, shrubland, heathland, and hummock grassland. It may be common in areas in early stages of regeneration after fire. Females generally give birth to a single litter of up to eight young (Pearson et al. 2023).
threats: The species is probably preyed upon by introduced Red Foxes Vulpes vulpes and Cats Felis catus, although populations generally seem to be secure (Pearson et al. 2023). Its Wheatbelt habitat has contracted in the last century due to land clearing. Little Long-tailed Dunnarts are not found in agricultural lands, but they do occur in intervening remnant areas with natural vegetation.
population: It is common in suitable habitat (Pearson et al. 2023). Populations may fluctuate with rainfall.
range: The Little Long-tailed Dunnart is endemic to Australia, where it is found in arid parts of south-western Western Australia and southern South Australia (Pearson et al. 2023).
conservationActions: This species is present in numerous protected areas (Pearson et al. 2023), including Dirk Hartog Island, Francois Peron, Kalbarri and Lesueur National Parks and Toolonga, Walyahmoning, Boyagin, Tutanning and Jilbadji Nature Reserves in Western Australia. In South Australia it has been recorded in Gawler Ranges National Park, Bascombe Well and Pinkawillinie Conservation Parks, Hiltaba Nature Reserve and Hambidge Wilderness Protection area.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: In the western parts of its distribution, it occurs in mixed woodland of wandoo Eucalyptus wandoo, Jarrah E. marginata and Marri (Corymbia calophylla on sandy loams. In the central and southern wheatbelt it occurs in open mallee-heath with Tall Sand Mallee Eucalyptus eremophila and Narrow-leaved Mallee E. foecunda on sandy loams and in open heath dominated by Shrubby She-oak Allocasuarina campestris. Throughout its range breeding occurs over spring to early summer. Pouch young are present in October and November and juveniles are present in February (Friend and McKenzie 2023).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to Gilbert's Dunnart. Salinity and rising water tables through land degradation is a threat to some areas of remnant habitat in the Western Australian wheatbelt.
population: Gilbert's Dunnart is a common species (Friend and McKenzie 2023). It was one of the most common species recorded during a 2000-2002 wheatbelt survey (Keighery et al. 2004).
range: Gilbert's Dunnart is endemic to Australia. It is now restricted to Western Australia, where it is found from the Darling Scarp near Perth and across the central and southern wheatbelt, with an outlying population on the Roe Plain (Friend and McKenzie 2023). Subfossil data show that it formerly occurred in far south-western South Australia.
conservationActions: The species has been recorded from several protected areas including Tuttanning, Boyagin, Dragon Rocks, Lake Magenta and Nuytsland Nature Reserves and Dryandra Woodland and Stirling Range National Parks. The species is protected under Western Australia law.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, lack of major threats, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found in rocky scree and plateau areas, generally with little vegetation or of spinifex hummock grassland, shrubs, and open woodland (Burbidge et al. 2023). It also occurs on rocky islands within major inland salt lakes of Western Australia. This species is nocturnal, and its diet includes a variety of invertebrates. Females in captivity give birth to up to five young in the months of August to December (Woolley and Valente 1986).
threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species. In parts of the range within the Northern Territory this species is affected by the spread of exotic buffel grass Cenchrus ciliaris, which increases frequency and intensity of fires (Marshall et al. 2012). This is also likely to be an issue in some areas in Western Australia. Predation pressure is likely to be mitigated by its preference for rugged, rocky habitats (Woolley et al. 2019). Some habitat loss may be attributable to mining.
population: It is a rare species that is patchily distributed, but at times it can be locally common (Burbidge et al. 2023). As the species favours often isolated, rugged, rocky areas, subpopulations appear fragmented, owing to the intermittent occurrence of suitable habitat. Migration potential between subpopulations is unknown. Due to its patchy occurrence and habitat specificity, the Long-tailed Dunnart can be difficult to detect.
range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is found in rocky areas of central Western Australia and central southern Northern Territory. In Western Australia it has been located in the Carnarvon, Gascoyne, Gibson Desert, Great Sandy Desert, Great Victoria Desert, Little Sandy Desert, Murchison, Pilbara and Yalgoo bioregions (McKenzie et al. 2023). In the Northern Territory it has been recorded in the Great Sandy Desert and MacDonnell Ranges bioregions.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix I of CITES. It is listed as Priority 4 by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions. It is present in a few protected areas (e.g., Gibson Desert Nature Reserve, West MacDonnell National Park, and Kennedy Range National Park).

rationale: Assessment is constrained by a limited information base, due to low detectability (this species is not readily trapped), probably low density across range, and very limited historical information (being first described in 1994). The rate of recent and ongoing decline may exceed the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion A, however the extent of decline is poorly resolved. A categorization of Near Threatened is preferred to Data Deficient because there is evidence of recent and ongoing decline and of habitat degradation due to the current fire regime and ongoing spread of invasive grasses. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) and likely area of occupancy (AOO) exceeds thresholds for eligibility under B. The population size is insufficiently determined, but is probably too large to allow for eligibility under C.
habitat: The Kakadu dunnart is a small nocturnal terrestrial marsupial. Most of the few records of the species have been from eucalypt woodlands on stony soils (Woinarski 1992, Van Dyck et al. 1994). Little is known of its ecology or life history. The diet includes a range of invertebrates, and probably small vertebrates.
threats: It is likely that habitat quality is decreasing due to the current regime of frequent and extensive fires (Russell-Smith et al. 2017). Predation by feral cats may also be a threat, with such predation likely to have increased impact in burnt areas (McGregor et al. 2015, 2016). Invasive pasture grasses, particularly gamba grass Andropogon gayanus are spreading in parts of its habitat, with considerable recent expansion in Litchfield National Park (Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023); and these grasses fuel fires of high severity, with recurrent such fires transforming ecosystems (Setterfield et al. 2013). The changing climate in this region is resulting in more days of extreme heat and causing increasing fire extent and intensity (NESP Earth Systems and Climate Change Hub 2020).
population: There has been no robust estimate of the total population size of the Kakadu dunnart, nor that of any of its subpopulations. It is considered ‘rare’ (Woinarski 2023). Of 136 plots (each 50 m x 50 m, sampled by 24 traps and 2 pitfall buckets, over a 3-night period) sampled in a wildlife monitoring program at Kakadu National Park in the period 2001-04 and re-sampled in the period 2007-10, the Kakadu dunnart was recorded in only two plots (Woinarski et al. 2010). It has not been recorded in Kakadu 'in recent years' (L. Einoder pers. comm. August 2024).Monitoring indicates some population decline, although the statistical power of this monitoring program is weak because this species has been reported from few monitoring sites (Woinarski et al. 2010, Russell-Smith et al. 2014, Einoder et al. 2023). Habitat quality is decreasing due to frequent fire and spread of invasive pasture grasses (Russell-Smith et al. 2017. Rossiter-Rachor et al. 2023).
