conservationActions: Dasypus septemcinctus is present in many protected areas.

rationale: Dasypus beniensis is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It should, however, be noted that part of its distribution lies in the Arc of Deforestation, where its habitat is rapidly declining.
habitat: Only exceeded in size by the Giant Armadillo (Priodontes maximus), D. beniensis has a head-body length of 51–58 cm and a tail length of 33–48 cm, and its carapace has 7–8 movable bands. It probably weighs around 8.5–10.5 kg, but it has been described as being the largest of the three species in the “Dasypus kappleri” complex, reaching up to 12 kg. Apart from its size, it can be distinguished from other armadillos of the genus Dasypus based on the enlarged projecting scales at the knee, a wide base of the tail, and non-uniform scutes on the pelvic shield (Feijó and Cordeiro-Estrela 2016). Morphologically similar to D. pastasae, both species have rough scales on the pelvic shield and flattened scales in the proximal rings of the tail. In addition, D. beniensis has diagnostic skull features that can only be observed in museum specimens but not in live animals (Feijó and Cordeiro-Estrela 2016). Dasypus beniensis is restricted to lowland tropical rainforest, and ecotones with savannas (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021). It has nocturnal habits, and is probably solitary and asocial. It is probably a generalist insectivore that feeds on arthropods and other invertebrates such as beetles, centipedes, millipedes and also earthworms (Noss et al. 2010). Two offspring are born per litter. Anecdotal evidence suggests that they are always of the same sex, but it remains to be studied whether they are the result of polyembryony, as occurs in other species of the genus Dasypus.
threats: The major threat to this forest-dependent armadillo is habitat loss, as most of its range is located in the arc of deforestation in the eastern portion of the Amazon forest where deforestation is widespread and has been rapidly increasing in the last decades. This species is unable to survive in converted savannas or open areas. Global demand for soy and beef has emerged as a primary driver of land-use change in tropical regions, contributing to the large-scale conversion of forests and savannas into croplands and pasture. In Bolivia, the uncontrolled agro-industrial expansion was accompanied by extensive forest fires from the years 2019 to 2024, which affected more than 10 million hectares (Aliaga- Rossel et al. 2021). Although their impact on Dasypus was not quantified, there are several anecdotal records of burned bodies. In the Brazilian Amazon, silviculture and agriculture have increased by 13.925% and 1.124%, respectively, in the last 35 years (MapBiomas 2022). In addition, D. beniensis seems dependent on large forested areas as it has not been recorded in small forest fragments (< 400 ha) (Stone et al. 2009) and its detectability was negatively associated with deforestation in areas near the Amazon-Cerrado ecotone in Mato Grosso state, Brazil (Massey 2021). Although no life history data are available for this species, a generation length of 4.76 years has been estimated based on data available for other similar-sized Dasypus species (Pacifici et al. 2013). Habitat loss within the Extent of Occurrence of the species in Brazil is about 5% over three generations.
population: There are virtually no details available on the population status of this species. A population density of eight individuals per square kilometre was estimated from the Kayapó of A’Ukre indigenous reserve in the Brazilian Pará state (Peres and Nascimento 2006). In a protected area in Pará, Brazil, D. beniensis was recorded at a rate of 0.1 per km walked (Rocha et al. 2021). These values are likely underestimated, and more studies are needed.
range: Dasypus beniensis can be found on the right bank of the lower Amazon and Madeira rivers in Brazil and the right bank of the Madre de Dios River in Bolivia. There are several records of the species along the northern border of Bolivia (in Madidi National Park), near Peru (Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021), suggesting that it likely also occurs in adjacent regions of Peru. Therefore, further studies are needed to confirm its presence in that area. Its southern limits are probably the dry forests and savannas of the Llanos de Moxos in Beni Bolivia and the Caatinga and Cerrado of Brazil.
useTrade: In Bolivia and Brazil, the species is utilized as a key protein source by Indigenous groups and rural communities, reflecting its cultural and subsistence value.
conservationActions: Dasypus beniensis is present in a number of protected areas. In Bolivia, it occurs in Madidi National Park and Noel Kempff Protected Area (Noss et al. 2010). In Brazil, it has been recorded in Kayapó of A’Ukre indigenous reserve (Peres and Nascimento 2006) and RPPN Cristalino (Rocha et al. 2021). The Red Book of Vertebrates of Bolivia lists the species as Near Threatened (NT), with deforestation identified as the main threat, compounded by its use as a source of animal protein through hunting (MMAyA 2009).

rationale: Dasypus pastasae is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Only exceeded in size by the Giant Armadillo (Priodontes maximus), the greater long-nosed armadillo has a head-body length of 49–58 cm and a tail length of 37–48 cm, and its carapace has 7–8 movable bands. Adult individuals weigh 6–10 kg. Dasypus pastasae seems to be the smallest of the species of the “D. kappleri” complex. Apart from its size, it can be distinguished from other armadillos of the genus Dasypus based on the enlarged projecting scales at the knee; a wide base of the tail; and a lighter skin color on the part of the head that is not covered by the cephalic shield (Trujillo and Superina 2013, Feijó and Cordeiro-Estrela 2016).Compared to D. kappleri, the scales on the pelvic shield of this species are non-uniform in size and have a rough texture, with the central scales being larger and standing up above the level of the smaller peripherals. Also, the posterior scales of the proximal rings on the tail are flattened (Feijó and Cordeiro-Estrela 2016).Dasypus pastasae is restricted to lowland tropical rainforest. In savanna areas, it is restricted to forest patches. It has nocturnal habits, and is probably solitary and asocial. Two offspring are born per litter. Anecdotal evidence suggests that they are always of the same sex, but it remains to be studied whether they are the result of polyembryony, as occurs in other species of the genus Dasypus.
threats: There are no major threats to this armadillo. Locally, the species is threatened by deforestation, and it is hunted in several countries (Tirira 2001, Aya-Cuero et al. 2021). It is unable to survive in savannas or open areas.
population: Limited information is available on the population status of this species. A study in Purus, Peru estimated a density of 0.11 individuals/km2 (Mena et al. 2016) and a camera-trap based study in the eastern plains of Colombia reported a low relative abundance (Aya-Cuero et al. 2021).
range: Dasypus pastasae can be found from the foothills of the eastern Andes in Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, and Venezuela south of the Orinoco River into the western Brazilian Amazon, between the Madeira and Branco Rivers. Its presence in northern Bolivia is very likely but pending confirmation. It has been recorded at elevations between 70 and 1,300 Asl.
useTrade: The species is used as a protein source.
conservationActions: Dasypus pastasae is present in a number of protected areas. An education and awareness program is being carried out by Fundación Omacha in the llanos of Colombia (Trujillo and Superina 2013, Superina et al. 2019, Superina and Trujillo 2023), and the species is included in an action plan for the armadillos of the Llanos of Colombia (Superina et al. 2014).

rationale: The Fishing Cat is widely distributed from southern Pakistan, northern India, southern Nepal and Bangladesh to Myanmar, southern Thailand and western Cambodia. However, its distribution is discontinuous as indicated by large gaps between known population units in the lower reaches of the Indus River and the Indian and Nepal Terai region, and between coastal areas along the Bay of Bengal and the Gulf of Thailand. No land corridor exists between continental and Sri Lankan populations. In all range countries, the Fishing Cat largely inhabits wetlands, riverine and mangrove forests, marshes, swamps and grasslands in the vicinity of waterbodies. Current human-dominated landscapes once featured these habitat types but are now fragmented due to severe land use changes in favour of aquaculture, agriculture, infrastructure and industrialisation since at least the late 1980s.Habitat loss and fragmentation of the Fishing Cat’s preferred habitat is aggravated by water pollution in aquaculture sites due to the use of chemicals and sewage reaching surrounding areas untreated. Killing of Fishing Cats is most pronounced in the Ganges Brahmaputra delta and northeastern Bangladesh, mostly in retaliation for perceived loss of small livestock and fish-stock. Linear infrastructure bisecting natural habitats has been entailing roadkills and mortally wounded Fishing Cats, especially in India and Sri Lanka. Several cases of Fishing Cat meat and body parts being consumed by ethnic groups have been reported in India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Thailand and Cambodia. There is also some evidence of Fishing Cats being caught, kept and traded as pets in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Thailand.The presently known and extrapolated sizes of population units suggest a global population of fewer than 8,000 mature individuals. Since Southeast Asia harbours the smallest population units of all, presently estimated at 200 individuals at most, this population faces a far greater extinction risk than populations in South Asia. We suspect a global population decline of 30% or more in the past three Fishing Cat generations during 2008–2023, as quality and extent of suitable grassland and wetland habitats declined during this period by more than 30% in several regions, where land use and land cover changes have been studied. We consider it highly likely that this decline will continue and accelerate in the future three generations during 2024–2038, concurrent with presumed future trends of severe and extensive habitat conversions and degradations in all range countries, especially in coastal areas. Effective and sustainable interventions are unlikely to be of sufficient magnitude to prevent such decline rates. We therefore categorize the Fishing Cat as Vulnerable under criteria A2cd+3cd+4cd.
habitat: In the Indus River basin, the Terai and Indian Dooars, camera trap records of the Fishing Cat have been obtained in mosaics of forests and dense grasslands covered by tall Imperata, Phragmites, Saccharum and Typha grasses (Nair 2012, Islam et al. 2016, Mishra et al. 2018, Jhala et al. 2020, Jhala et al. 2021, Guleria et al. 2022). In protected areas, it was also recorded in open riverine forest interspersed with grasses and herbs (Yadav et al. 2018), and in grassland patches close to streams, sandbanks, swamps, oxbow lakes and reservoirs (Taylor et al. 2016, Mishra et al. 2018, Yadav et al. 2020, Jhala et al. 2021, Jayasekara and Mahaulpatha 2022). In Indian Tiger Reserves, three individuals were recorded in dry deciduous forests at most 6 km away from streams (Sadhu and Reddy 2013, Talegaonkar et al. 2018, Dutta et al. 2021). Mangrove forests and remnant mangrove patches represent important habitats along coasts of the Bay of Bengal and the Gulf of Thailand (Sathiyaselvam et al. 2016, Das et al. 2017, Thaung et al. 2018, Chutipong et al. 2019, Naing and Platt 2019, Rana 2020, Shankar et al. 2020, Jhala et al. 2020, Jhala et al. 2021, Phosri et al. 2021). Outside protected areas, it has repeatedly been recorded near active and abandoned fishponds, in rice fields, oil palm and coconut plantations, abandoned unused land, marshland and on river banks (Cutter 2015, Dahal 2016, Taylor et al. 2016, Kantimahanti et al. 2019, Kolipaka et al. 2019, Naing and Platt 2019, Chakraborty et al. 2020a, b, Jhala et al. 2021, Mishra et al. 2021, Phosri et al. 2021). In the Indian state of Odisha, its presence in the Chilika Lagoon is higher in Phragmites dominated marshland than in more saline areas with sparse vegetation cover (Adhya et al. 2023). It has also been sighted in sugarcane fields during harvest seasons (Mishra 2022, Divyashree Rana pers. comm. 6 January 2023) and documented near commercial fish farms adjacent to tourist destination spots in West Bengal and Odisha (Samrat Chakraborty in litt. 21 August 2023, Adhya et al. 2024). In Sri Lanka, it also inhabits tea estates and dry rocky slopes in the vicinity of rivers, lakes and reservoirs (Kittle and Watson 2018), wetland environments in Colombo (Ratnayaka et al. 2022), both dry and wet zone forest patches, and intermediate savannah-type forests near waterbodies (Anjali Watson and Andrew Kittle, unpublished data).A genetic study by Rana (2020) using scat samples and microsatellite markers reveals a low diversity and strong genetic structure between Fishing Cat populations in India. This suggests several landscape level barriers due to the patchiness of wetland habitats and fragmentation owing to anthropogenic activities. The Terai population has comparatively high genetic diversity with a metapopulation structure (Rana 2020).The home ranges of three radio-collared female Fishing Cats in Chitwan National Park were estimated at 4–6 km², and that of a male at 16–22 km² (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002). The home range of a male individual in Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary was estimated at 18.46 km² (Nair 2012). In and around Khao Sam Roi Yot National Park, four females had home ranges of 2.3–5.3 km² in the dry season and of 3.0–4.4 km² in the wet season; the home range of a male varied from 8.9 km² in the dry season to 12.6 km² in the wet season (Cutter 2015). Camera trap records in the same study area indicate that female Fishing Cats moved 598–1,335 m, whereas males moved 1,373–2,285 m per day (Phosri et al. 2021). Home ranges of one male and two female Fishing Cats in the same area was estimated at 2.21–4.33 km² and 3.44–8.49 km², respectively, in the wet season of 2022 (Klakhaeng et al. 2023). Two females in urban areas of Colombo had home ranges of 3.06–3.39 km², and two males of 32.02–32.99 km² (Ratnayaka et al. 2022). Data of 11 radio-collared Fishing Cats in Nepal’s Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve indicate that males move in an area of about 18–58.4 km² and females in 1.2–34.7 km² both inside and outside the reserve (Rama Mishra in litt. 26 April 2024).Information on the reproduction of the Fishing Cat in the wild is limited to a few incidental observations. Mating of Fishing Cats was observed in late February to early March in the Indian Sundarbans (Sanyal and Roy 1985). Gestation period is 63–70 days (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002), and litters consist of one to three kittens (Sanyal and Roy 1985, Datye 1993, Cutter and Cutter 2009, Mishra et al. 2021, Divyashree Rana in litt. 21 August 2023). Kittens of less than 15 days old were observed in May and January (Sanyal and Roy 1985, Divyashree Rana in litt. 21 August 2023). Females followed by kittens of several weeks of age were observed in mid-March, early January and April to May (Datye 1993, Cutter and Cutter 2009, Malla et al. 2019). In the Bhitarkanika mangroves of Odisha, kittens are sighted in all seasons (Manas K Das, Range Officer, pers. comm. 7 September 2023), and newborn kittens were observed from November to June in the Chilika Lagoon (Tiasa Adhya in litt. 21 December 2023).The Fishing Cat was thought to be largely nocturnal (Mukherjee 1989, Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Sathiyaselvam et al. 2016). Several camera trap records obtained since 2011 show that it is also active during daylight hours (Nair 2012, Islam et al. 2016, Mishra et al. 2018, Shankar et al. 2020, Yadav et al. 2020, Jayasekara and Mahaulpatha 2022, Kantimahanti et al. 2022, Anjali Watson and Andrew Kittle, unpublished data).Faeces collected in Keoladeo National Park showed that Fishing Cats predominantly consumed fish all year round, followed by birds, insects and rodents (Haque and Vijayan 1993). Scat collected in Khao Sam Roi Yot National Park indicates that fish constituted 42% of the diet, followed by mammals and birds 24% each, reptiles 5% and crustaceans 2% (Cutter 2015). Scat collected in the same national park contained remains of 16 species including four fish, three rodent and three bird species; the diet varied slightly between summer, rainy and winter seasons, consisting of fish (46.9–54.5%), rodents (21.8–27.7%), birds (19.1–19.8%), insects (0–2.7%), snakes, crabs, snails and arthropods (Wongson et al. 2024). Fishing Cats were also observed hunting an Indian Pond Heron Ardeola grayii, a Dog-faced Water Snake Cerberus rynchops (Malla et al. 2018) and a Checkered Keelback Fowlea piscator (Kantimahanti et al. 2022). The first arboreal behaviour of Fishing Cats foraging on nests of colonial waterbirds 8 m above ground in the canopy of a tree was documented in 2022 (Sadik and Akash 2024). Scat collected in the Coringa mangroves contained remains of fish (36.6%), crabs (17.8%), rodents (16.8%), birds (14.8%), reptiles (11.4%), molluscs and insects (Malla et al. 2024).
threats: The major threat to the Fishing Cat across range countries appears to be the loss and fragmentation of forests, grasslands, wetlands, marshes and mangrove habitats due to the expansion of aquaculture, agriculture, infrastructure and industrialisation (see details in Supplementary Information). The expansion of commercial aquaculture in particular results in the pollution of the entire food chain due to microplastics and the use of chemicals and sewage reaching surrounding areas untreated (Chatterjee et al. 2024, Mitra et al. 2024). In most range countries, land use changes are aggravated by further conflict with humans for resources like space and small livestock. Such conflicts entail killing of Fishing Cats in retaliation for perceived livestock loss. With expanding linear infrastructure, roadkills are a potential major threat, especially in India and Sri Lanka.Poaching is a potential threat to the Fishing Cat in Cambodia (Thaung et al. 2018). Indiscriminate snaring of mammals in Cambodia and Viet Nam is a major and ongoing threat with a devastating impact on the region’s wildlife (Gray et al. 2021).Please see Supplementary Information for detailed threats by range country.
population: Camera trap surveys indicate that Fishing Cat population density in inland protected areas of the Indian Terai is 3–3.5 individuals/100 km2 (Nair 2012). Density is significantly higher in coastal areas, both within and outside protected areas ranging from 18–70 individuals/100 km2 (Sathiyaselvam et al. 2016, Phosri et al. 2021, Adhya et al. 2024). We therefore extrapolate these values to those inland and coastal areas, respectively, where population density estimates are lacking. In areas with fewer than three records in one Fishing Cat generation, we refrain from estimating population size due to the paucity of surveys and lack of data. These areas are predominantly situated in human-dominated landscapes, where the Fishing Cat's presence has become known through media reports about killed individuals (see e.g. Chowdhury et al. 2015, Chakraborty et al. 2022). Based on available and extrapolated estimates, we infer a total population size of 3,194–7,527 Fishing Cats. Most of the population resides in South Asia, with an estimated population size of 1,768–5,088 individuals in India and Bangladesh, and 1,392–2,187 individuals in Sri Lanka. Thailand and Cambodia combined retain an estimated population of 131–200 individuals at most. Please see Supplementary Information for details of estimated population densities and sizes in the range countries.
range: The Fishing Cat is widely but discontinuously distributed in South and Southeast Asia from southern Pakistan in the west to Cambodia in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills of the Terai and the Dooars in the north to Sri Lanka and Thailand in the south. However, currently known occurrence is highly localized with large gaps of more than 100 km between sites with authenticated presence records. Such gaps are most prevalent in the basins of the Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Ayeyarwady and Chao Phraya rivers, and along the coasts of the Bay of Bengal and the Gulf of Thailand. At present, its main range appears to be the Indian and Nepal Terai, and the lower reaches and delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra in India and Bangladesh. Its range extends along major river basins along the east coast of India and throughout much of Sri Lanka. Its range in Southeast Asia is limited to the southern Ayeyarwady Region of Myanmar, coastal areas of western peninsular Thailand and coastal Cambodia. In Viet Nam and Indonesia, it has not been recorded since the early 2000s.In most range countries, the Fishing Cat was recorded in new locations since the previous assessment of 2016. The majority of records were obtained during camera trapping surveys targeting the Tiger Panthera tigris in protected areas of the Terai, Dooars and Sundarban Mangroves, and the Leopard Panthera pardus in both protected and unprotected landscapes in Sri Lanka. Its distribution outside protected areas is still not well understood, and vast stretches with potentially suitable habitat in many human-dominated landscapes have not been surveyed to date. This paucity of surveys outside protected area networks clouds our understanding of the Fishing Cat’s biogeography, and how site-specific factors affect its distribution (Rana et al. 2022).The Fishing Cat occurs at sea level in parts of its range (Das et al. 2017, Thaung et al. 2018, Naing Lin and Platt 2019) to an elevation of 436 m in the Indian Terai (Guleria et al. 2022), which represents the highest reliable elevation record in this region to date. In Sri Lanka, it has been recorded up to 2,277 m in Horton Plains National Park (Anjali Watson and Andrew Kittle, unpublished data).Please see Supplementary Information for details of distribution by range country.
useTrade: Little is known about illegal use and trade of the Fishing Cat. In Pakistan, two captive individuals were confiscated and rescued in Karachi in 2015 (Bhatti 2015, Zubairi and Naidu 2016). Three live Fishing Cat kittens were offered for sale on a market in spring 2024, but it was not possible to figure out the location of this incident in Pakistan or abroad (Javed Mahar in litt. 17 May 2024). A few cases of ritual hunting of Fishing Cats for meat and skin have been reported in southern West Bengal (Mukherjee et al. 2012). Tribal people in Andhra Pradesh occasionally hunt Fishing Cats for meat (Kantimahanti et al. 2019). Indigenous hunters in Sri Lanka’s Central Province and in northeastern Bangladesh allegedly consume Fishing Cat meat and use their body parts for medicinal purposes (Thudugala 2016, Sultana et al. 2022). In the period 2016–2021, the Bangladesh Forest Department seized 24 live individuals from illegal trafficking that were destined as pets to India or West Asia (Uddin et al. 2023). A few local people in Thailand also admitted capturing Fishing Cats for sale as pets and eating their meat (Cutter 2015, Chutipong et al. 2019). In Cambodia, a dead Fishing Cat was recovered at a bushmeat stall near the Tonle Sap wetlands in 2018 (Herranz Muñoz and Vong 2022).
conservationActions: The Fishing Cat is listed in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, requiring permits for international trade (Acharjyo 1998). In Pakistan’s Sindh province, the Fishing Cat has been protected since 2020 under the First Schedule of the Sindh Wildlife Protection, Preservation, Conservation and Management Act 2020, rendering possession, hunting and trading of protected species illegal (Umar Farooq 2020). In India, it has been protected since 1972 under the highest protection level Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act (Acharjyo 1998) and in the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act (2022) (Ministry of Law and Justice 2022). In Nepal, it is not listed as protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 2029 (1973), but hunting wildlife without a license is prohibited (Nepal Law Commission 2018). In Bangladesh, it has been fully protected since 1973 under the Wild Life Preservation Order and since 2012 under the Wildlife (Conservation and Security) Act, 2012 (Sultana et al. 2022). In Myanmar, the Fishing Cat is completely protected under the Conservation of Biodiversity and Protected Areas Law of 2018 (Thu et al. 2024). It is strictly protected in Sri Lanka under the Fauna and Flora Protection (Amendment) Act of 2009 (Parliament of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka 2009). In Thailand, it is protected under the Wildlife Preservation and Protection Act of 2019, which prohibits intentional killing (Phosri et al. 2021). In Cambodia’s Natural Resource and Environmental Code, it is listed as common with minimal penalties for its trade and consumption (Gray et al. 2017).Sri Lanka was the first nation to legally protect all its mangrove forests in 2015 (Veettil et al. 2023). Mangrove restoration and plantation projects have been implemented in Pakistan (Gilani et al. 2021), India (Kubo et al. 2018, Parida and Kumar 2020, Samanta et al. 2021, Choubey 2024), Bangladesh (Uddin et al. 2022), Sri Lanka (UNCC 2023) and Cambodia (Veettil and Quang 2019). The Fishing Cat also benefits from establishment of wildlife corridors in the Indian Terai and the Central Highlands of Sri Lanka (Jhala et al. 2021, Resplendent Ceylon 2021, WWCT 2024).Local people have been sensitized to issues pertaining to the conservation and protection of the Fishing Cat in and around several survey areas in Sri Lanka, West Bengal, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh in India, in Nepal, Thailand and Cambodia (Thudugala 2016, Kolipaka et al. 2019, Malla et al. 2019,  Mishra et al. 2021, Phosri et al. 2021, Herranz Muñoz and Vong 2022, Kantimahanti et al. 2022, Adhya et al. 2024). In India, the Fishing Cat has been declared as the State Animal of West Bengal and as the flagship species of Odisha’s Chilika Lagoon; a blueprint designed to safeguard the Fishing Cat across the country provides a coherent scheme for essential district-level conservation actions (Rana et al. 2022). Educational material and outreach strategies need to be developed and implemented in human-dominated landscapes with a high conflict density like West Bengal and Bangladesh (Chakraborty et al. 2022, Sultana et al. 2022).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, as it occurs across a range of localities and elevations in Iran with an extent of occurrence of 285,546 km2. However, relatively little is known about this species' trends or ecology, and it may be threatened by climate and habitat change, so further research is needed.
habitat: This species likely occupies valleys, banks of irrigation channels and slopes, either in forested areas, or areas covered with scrub and clumps of grasses, in mountainous regions (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).
threats: Warming temperatures and aridification may shrink the quantity and quality of suitable habitat available for this species (A. Mahmoudi and B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2024). Additionally, land-use change for agriculture may pose further threat (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2024).
population: Very little is known about the population of this species, though declines in density are suspected (A. Mahmoudi pers. comm. 2024).
range: Previously, Microtus mystacinus was considered to include M. rossiaemeridionalis, with a wide range extending from Europe eastwards across Russia and Asia Minor. However, results from genetic studies support the taxonomic division of the species (Mahmoudi et al. 2017, Bikchurina et al. 2021), and M. mystacinus is now considered endemic to Iran (see also Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022), covering approximately 144,225 km2 (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022) in range area though with an overall estimated extent of occurrence of 285,546 km2. Specifically, the type locality of M. mystacinus is from the Lar River valley in northern Iran (Golenishchev et al. 2019). It is split across two fragments in this region and the surrounding areas: a northern fragment in Azarbayjan-e Sharghi, Zanjan, Gilan, Mazanderan, Tehran, Semnan, and Golestan, and a south-western fragment in the Zagros Mountains (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022). It has been recorded from between 200 m and 3,080 m asl (Kryštufek and Shenbrot 2022).
useTrade: This species is not known to be utilised.
conservationActions: This species appears to be present in a number of national parks, such as Lar, Golestan, Khojir and Soekhen Hesar National Parks (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2024). No specific conservation action is recommended at present, though further research of its trends and ecology is needed.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, because it has an extremely large extent of occurrence, is found across a number of forest habitats at a range of elevations, and within many protected areas. However, the species is dependent on primary forest and large trees for cavities to nest in, therefore it is likely to be declining across much of its range due to high rates of deforestation across southeast Asia, as well as threats such as hunting. It is recommended that further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, ecology, and threats to this poorly known species.
habitat: It is a mostly nocturnal and arboreal species. It occurs in temperate and subtropical dry deciduous forests. It has been found to occupy tree hollows of dense broadleaved forest patches and also in rock crevices (Molur et al. 2005). It appears to be limited to primary forest habitat. In the Yunnan Province of China, it is reported to inhabit the limestone forests between 700-800 m asl (pers. comm. M. Krishna 2025). In Thailand, it was observed in mixed deciduous and dry deciduous forest in Thailand (Robinson et al. 1995). The generation time is thought to be relatively long, and might be five or six years, with a litter size of one or two young. This species feeds on leaves and fruits and populations in the north and in higher altitudes are known to feed on oak leaves and needles of cedar and pine (Jackson 2012).
threats: Major threats to this species over most of its range include general habitat loss (often through logging operations and the conversion of land to agricultural use) and significant levels of hunting for food and sport (Mishra et al. 2006). In South Asia, it is threatened by shifting (jhum) cultivation, forest fires, monoculture plantations and hunting for sport and local consumption (Molur et al. 2005). Road kills of the species are recorded from Arunachal Pradesh, India (Mukherjee and Mhangore 2022).
population: The population abundance of this species is poorly known, however, it is believed to be significantly declining, or at least very rare, in some areas. In Taiwan, studies have shown that this species is found across the central mountain range but at low densities (Thorington et al. 2012). Also, several surveys in Southeast Asia have yielded very few sightings/captures of the species (M. Krishna pers. comm. 2025).
range: This poorly known species appears to have a wide, but patchy distribution, in northeastern South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia. In South Asia, it has been recorded from Nepal, India (Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and West Bengal) and possibly Bhutan (Molur et al. 2005). In China, it has been recorded from Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangxi, Hainan, Sichuan, and Guangdong (Smith and Xie 2008, Jackson 2012). It is present on the island of Taiwan (Smith and Xie 2008). In Southeast Asia, there are recorded from Myanmar, Thailand, Lao PDR, Viet Nam (Mt. Tay Con Linh II, Ha Giang Province—Lunde et al. 2003, Bac Me Nature Reserves—Tham et al. 2020) and possibly Cambodia, although there are no records from this country (Walmart pers. comm.). This species occurs at elevations of 800 to 2,400 m asl.
useTrade: Significant levels of hunting for local consumption and sport (Mishra et al. 2006, Molur et al. 2005).
conservationActions: It is listed in the Schedule II of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is known from the following protected areas in South Asia - Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary, Arunachal Pradesh and Nengpui Wildlife Sanctuary, Mizoram in India; Royal Chitwan National Park in Central Nepal. The species occurs in several protected areas in South and Southeast Asia. For instance, in Loas though species is widespread, this is reported in Khammouan Limestone National Protected Area, Khammouan Province (Sanamxay 2020) and in Western Thailand, it is reported in Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary (Rheddick 2024). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, ecology, and threats to this poorly known species. Populations of this species should be monitored to record changes in abundance and distribution.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, large extent of occurrence of 348,799 km², and lack of evidence of any decline at a rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Population and ecological studies are needed.
habitat: It has been collected in mid-montane primary and disturbed moss forest (Flannery 1995). The species has a small litter size. Other ecological information is unknown.
threats: The threats to this species are poorly known. General threats could include mining, logging, road development around Habbema, Mbuwa and Kenyam, and the associated impacts of pollution and habitat loss (F. Pattiselanno pers. comm. 2025). This species has also previously been considered "a favoured food item" (Flannery and Seri 1990), but up-to-date knowledge of this is lacking.
population: It can be locally abundant. Population studies of this species are lacking.
range: This poorly-known species is endemic to the mountains of the island of New Guinea (Irian Jaya - Indonesia and Papua New Guinea). It ranges from Lake Habbema (Papua Province, Indonesia) in the west to the Huon Gulf and to Mount Kemp in the southeast (Papua New Guinea) in the east. A 2013 survey of the Upper Ok Tedi found the species, which represented the first occurrence of the taxon on the southern side of the Hindenburg Range (Richards and Whitmore 2015). It has been recorded at elevations between 1,000 and 3,200 m asl.
useTrade: A 1990 paper indicated that this species was "a favoured food item" (Flannery and Seri 1990), but up-to-date knowledge of its 'use' is lacking.
conservationActions: It occurs in some protected areas (e.g., top end of the Lorentz National Park). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history, and threats to this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it has a relatively large extent of occurrence of 394,437 km2, is not known to be facing any severe threats and is considered to have a stable population.
habitat: This species occurs in mountainous forests (Smith and Xie 2008). Within the region of Sichuan and southern Gansu, it occurs in subalpine coniferous forest (Jackson and Schouten 2012). It is also found in mixed forest of spruce and red birch at 2,500-3,000 m asl (Liu et al. 2022).
threats: There are no known threats to the species, though it does have a small distribution area and small population size (Jiang et al. 2021).
population: The population is considered to be stable. The distribution area of Aeretes melanopterus melanopterus is small, however, naturalists report a high encounter rate in the Wuling Mountain National Nature Reserve in Hebei Province, where on average three individuals can be seen every night (Quan Li pers. comm. 2024). The distribution area of Aeretes melanopterus szechuanensis is large, but it is difficult to know encounter rates because it is similar in appearance to Petaurista xanthotis (Quan Li pers. comm. 2024).
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in Sichuan, Gansu, Hebei (Smith and Xie 2008), and Beijing (CSIS 2008). It exists as two isolated populations; Aeretes melanopterus melanopterus in Hebei and Beijing and Aeretes melanopterus szechuanensis in northeastern Sichuan and southern Gansu (Smith and Xie 2008) and Qiangshai (Specimen from Northeast Forestry University). Aeretes melanopterus szechuanensis has been recorded between 2,500-3,000 m asl (Liu et al. 2022) and Aeretes melanopterus melanopterus 1,200-1,600 m asl (Jian-Guo Hao and Fang-Zhou Lou pers. comm. 2024, photographers who have photographed this species in Hebei).
useTrade: The locals in the Aeretes melanopterus distribution do not hunt flying squirrels (Quan Li pers. comm. 2024).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It may be present in protected areas. It is often observed in the forest within the Jiuzhaigou National Park (Wright et al. 2013) and Wuling Mountain National Nature Reserve in Hebei Province (Jian-Guo Hao and Fang-Zhou Lou pers. comm. 2024). Further studies are needed into the abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Endangered A1ac (Wang and Xie 2004). China’s red list of biodiversity lists it as NT (Jiang et al. 2021).Taxonomic research is needed to determine whether the two sub-species are distinct enough to be considered separate species (Quan Li pers. comm. 2024).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU B1ab(iii)) because it is only found on the island of Hainan, China, where it has an estimated extent of occurrence of 13,807 km², and is considered to be a rare species. There has been a decline in the extent and quality of its forest habitat due to agricultural encroachment and disturbance in recent decades. Although the majority of its geographic range is now protected within Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, the species may continue to face threats in this landscape, and where it occurs in unprotected forests.
habitat: It is recorded from tropical rainforest and subtropical evergreen rainforest (Stone 1995). Little is known about the ecology of this species, including its dependence upon good-quality forest habitat (Stone 1995).
threats: The species is only recorded from forest habitats, and there has been a decline in the extent and quality of this habitat type on Hainan over recent decades due to agricultural encroachment and disturbance. The majority of its geographic range is now strictly protected within Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park. However, recent assessment suggests that suitable habitats within this national park may continue to face threats, including potential ongoing forest fragmentation, degradation and loss (Wang and Xie 2025). The species is also recorded from unprotected forests outside the national park, which are even more vulnerable to ongoing habitat degradation and loss (Qiao et al. 2025). The vulnerability of the species to predation by invasive predators, notably feral dogs and cats present in rural communities around the protected area, is also unknown. Species distribution modelling suggests that the species is likely to experience ongoing loss of suitable forest habitat on Hainan due to climate change impacts (Qiao et al. 2025).
population: This species has been characterised as very rare (Wang 1998), and few older records exist, representing several definite or possible records from Hainan’s remaining forest areas including Jiaxi, Jianfengling, and Wuzhishan (Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden 2003a, Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden 2003b). A camera-trap study in Wuzhishan that took place between February 2018 and April 2019 failed to detect the species (Li et al. 2019), but it has possibly been detected more recently in this landscape using infrared camera trapping. During the past 10 years, the species has been detected in Yinggeling, Jianfengling, Maorui, and Diaoluoshan; all of these sites are now designated as management areas within Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park. Individuals at Diaoluoshan and Yinggeling were caught using live trapping (Tu et al. 2023). More recently, the species has been recorded more widely across forested landscapes in Hainan, including 37 records reported from 2020–2025 by Qiao et al. (2025).
range: This species is endemic to the island of Hainan, China (Smith and Xie 2008). The species had been suggested to also occur in northern Viet Nam (Abramov et al. 2018), but this separate population has now been reassigned to a different species, Neohylomys vietnamensis (Bannikova et al. 2024).
conservationActions: This species has been recorded from several landscapes that were formerly managed as provincial or national nature reserves, but most of these sites are now managed and strictly protected within the recently-established Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park. Research is needed into the species’ population status, landscape distribution, biology and ecology, habitat status, and threats. In China, this species was previously regionally Red Listed as Endangered B1ab(i,ii,iii) (Wang and Xie 2004), and has now been regionally reassessed as Vulnerable B1+2a (Jiang et al. 2016).

rationale: Pteropus pelewensis is endemic to Oceania. This species is assessed as Vulnerable under criteria B2ab(i,ii,iii). The global population, comprising two subspecies, is fragmented into four subpopulations/locations including in Palau, Sonsorol and Fanna, Yap, and Ulithi Atoll, with an area of occupancy (AOO) of 1,500 km². Climate change-related threats to all subpopulations of P. pelewensis include increased severity of typhoons and droughts. The subpopulations at Ulithi Atoll and Sonsorol and Fanna are at greatest risk of loss from sea level rise caused by climate change and would directly result in a reduction in this bat's extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO), and habitat quality. Sea level rise also threatens other low-lying islands in the species’ range (i.e., Kayangel Atoll and some in Palau's main lagoon), which will be lost or greatly compromised, and will reduce mangrove forests. Another potentially significant threat to both subspecies comes from hunting, especially on Palau.
habitat: Both subspecies use a range of habitats including lowland forest, mangroves, and agroforest (Engbring 1985; Falanruw 1988a; Wiles et al. 1991, 1997). Pteropus p. pelewensis makes extensive use of volcanic, limestone, and swamp forests for both roosting and foraging, and to a lesser extent, mangroves, strand forest, and savannas. Mangrove forest use is likely seasonal with the bats heavily using this habitat when Sonneratia alba is in bloom (Wiles et al. 1997). Some habitat degradation and loss is currently happening across the species range due to development and agriculture with increasing losses projected in the near future due to planned airstrip expansion and climate change impacts (e.g., sea level rise).Feeding also regularly occurs in villages and farms. Pteropus p. yapensis roosts mainly in mangroves and secondary forests as there is little primary forest remaining on the four main islands of Yap (Falanruw 1988a). On the Ulithi Atoll, this subspecies resides in strand forest and agroforest (Wiles et al. 1991). Pteropus p. pelewensis is known to feed on the fruits of 54 plant species, the flowers of 28 species, and the leaves of one species (Wiles et al. 1997). The diet of P. p. yapensis includes the fruit, flowers, or leaves of 26 plants, but it likely contains several additional species as well (Falanruw 1988a, Wiles et al. 1991).Pteropus p. pelewensis generally roosts solitarily or in small groups away from human settlements. Colonies are uncommon and usually contain 30-200 animals (Wiles et al. 1997). This subspecies also has the unusual tendency to form regular colonies for only a few hours in the early morning. Most P. p. yapensis colonies hold fewer than 100 bats, but sizes reaching about 600 animals have also been recorded (Engbring 1985, Falanruw 1988a, Wiles et al. 1991).At dusk, P. p. pelewensis often makes short initial foraging flights of 1–2 km after emerging from their roosts but longer foraging flights of up to 10-12 km are also made (Wiles et al. 1997). Individuals are regularly seen flying between islands, sometimes as far as 10 km. This subspecies possibly moves seasonally within Palau in response to fruiting and flowering patterns (Wiles et al. 1997). Movement patterns of P. p. yapensis on the four main islands of Yap are undescribed, but individuals on the Ulithi Atoll have been observed flying between islets (Wiles et al. 1991).A single young is almost always produced, although Falanruw (1988a) noted twin fetuses in one of 30 pregnant females from the Yap subspecies. Pteropus p. yapensis reproduces throughout the year (Falanruw 1988a). Breeding seasonality in P. p. pelewensis is unclear, but young have been observed in January and April (Wiles et al. 1997), and it is likely that reproduction occurs throughout most of the year.For P. p. pelewensis, maximum head-body length reaches 215 mm in males and 206 mm in females, maximum forearm length reaches 131 mm in both males and females, and maximum body weight reaches 400 gr in males and 332 gr females (Wiles et al. 1997). For P. p. yapensis, maximum forearm length reaches 138 mm in both males and females (Falanruw 1988a).
threats: In the past, the major threat to both subspecies was over-exploitation, primarily for international commercial trade which ended in 1989 in Yap and in 1994 in Palau. Although significant levels of hunting for local use continue in Palau, P. p. pelewensis remained common and widespread throughout the archipelago until at least 2005 (Wiles et al. 1997, G.J. Wiles, unpublished data). Some hunting for local use also occurs in Yap and probably Ulithi, but it is not known how much of a threat this poses to P. p. yapensis. Hunting for commercial use (including export) is banned on Yap and Ulithi, but there is little or no enforcement of wildlife laws and some harvest of bats for local commercial use exists (M. Falanruw, pers. obs. 2025, B. Gorong, pers. comm. 2019). In 2017, there was sufficient hunting of the Yap subpopulation (for local use only) to cause resident conservationists to consider recommending hunting restrictions to benefit this subpopulation.Climate change is projected to bring several likely threats to P. pelewensis. These include 1) increased occurrence of especially intense typhoons that may produce direct mortality of bats and destroy or degrade habitats throughout the species’ range; 2) increased occurrence of severe droughts, which may add physiological stress to the species through changes in fruit and flower availability; and 3) sea level rise, which may permanently inundate low-lying the Ulithi and Kayangel atolls, and Sonsorol and Fanna, as well as damage or destroy much of the mangrove ecosystems present on the main islands of Palau and Yap. Sharp increases in the hunting of Pacific flying foxes can occur following major storms that severely reduce food and protective forest cover for bats (Esselstyn et al. 2006, Wiles and Brooke 2009).Palau, Sonsorol and Fanna, Yap, and Ulithi Atoll retain extensive forest cover (including agroforest) that has diminished little in recent decades (FAO 2015), thus wide-scale habitat loss is not considered a major threat to P. pelewensis. Forest loss due to development at critical roost sites does represent a significant threat. Satellite imagery indicates that the building of the Palau Compact Road around the largest island of Babeldaob, which was completed in 2007, did not result in significant forest loss on this island, as feared by Wiles et al. (1997). However, on Yap, selective cutting of large trees (e.g., Calophyllum inophyllum, which has fruit eaten by flying foxes and is a roost tree) is a concern by causing forest degradation (M. Falanruw, pers. comm. 2025).Climate change may exacerbate occasional drought conditions on these islands and lead to more wildfires in savannas, which burn into forest edges and result in a gradual decrease in forest cover. Expanding development, mainly for tourism, is another future concern for forests in Palau and Yap as Asian investors have sought and obtained long-term land leases in both island groups. The U.S. military also intends to expand its footprint in Palau and Yap, resulting in the clearing of some forest.
population: There is limited new information on the species’ overall abundance and trends since 2021 (Wiles and Waldien 2021). The species is thought to be organized into four subpopulations given its distribution in Palau, Sonsorol and Fanna, Yap, and Ulithi Atoll. Given the larger land area of Palau and observations that bats were common in many areas there in 2005, it is likely that most of this species’ overall population occurs in Palau. Pteropus pelewensis pelewensis was judged to be common and widespread throughout Palau in 2005, with a probable increasing trend despite extensive hunting pressure for subsistence use and minor commercial use within Palau (Wiles and Brooke 2009). Abundance and trend are more poorly known for P. p. yapensis, with no surveys made there since the mid-1980s (Engbring 1985, Wiles et al. 1991). This subspecies is suspected to be declining due to severe typhoons, droughts, deforestation and forest degradation, changes in seasonality of flowering and fruiting of food sources, unsustainable levels of subsistence hunting, and sea level rise. Although there is a lack of current population data, the species’ overall population is currently inferred to be stable as the larger subpopulation on Palau is thought to be stable and the suspected decline in Yap and on the atolls are thought to be minor. There is no evidence to suggest there is a decline in the number of subpopulations nor extreme fluctuations in its population, number of mature individuals, or subpopulations.In the 1940s, P. p. pelewensis was considered abundant in Palau (Marshall 1945, as reported in Wiles et al. 1997), but by the 1970s the main subpopulation was starting to decline (Owen 1977) due to commercial exploitation with thousands of bats being exported annually to markets in the Mariana Islands (Wiles et al. 1997). The subpopulation underwent a substantial decline by the late 1970s and early 1980s but then experienced some recovery by the mid-1980s in response to fewer bats being exported (Wiles et al. 1997). Two studies of the abundance of P. p. pelewensis were conducted using point counts in April-May 1991 (Wiles et al. 1997) and April-May 2005 (G. Wiles, unpublished data). Bats were found to be reasonably common in 1991. They were also common in many locations in 2005 and numbers appeared to have increased since 1991. Although neither study resulted in estimates of total numbers, they provided baseline encounter rates that should be used to determine future population trends. The subpopulation on Sonsorol and Fanna has never been surveyed, but brief observations in 1992 suggested the two islands probably held no more than a few hundred bats (Wiles et al. 1997).For P. p. yapensis, the subpopulation in Yap’s main islands was drastically reduced during the late 1970s through commercial hunting for export of animals to Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. The subpopulation was estimated to be about 1,000 bats in 1981 (Wiles and Payne 1986) and between 2,500-5,000 animals in 1984 following protection (Engbring 1985) and continued to increase even further by the early 1990s (G.J. Wiles pers. comm. 2019). The Ulithi subpopulation was estimated at 1,200 bats in 1986 (Wiles et al. 1991), corresponding to a high density of 280 animals/km². More recent survey data are not available for either subpopulation, but both are currently considered as being “viable” (M. Falanruw pers. comm. 2025). The Yap subpopulation has never recovered to the higher levels of abundance observed in the late 1960s and early 1970s before the onset of hunting for commercial export (M. Falanruw, pers. comm. 2025).
range: Pteropus pelewensis is endemic to Oceania and is known from the combined range of its two subspecies. This includes the main islands of Palau, nearby Kayangel Atoll, and the more distant islands of Sonsorol and Fanna (total land area of 497 km²) for P. p. pelewensis and the four main islands of Yap plus Ulithi Atoll (total land area of 104 km²) in the Federated States of Micronesia for P. p. yapensis. The species’ extent of occurrence (EOO) is 156,790 km², based on a minimum convex polygon around the islands within its range, and its area of occupancy (AOO) is 1,500 km², based on a 2x2 km grid over the islands within its range. The species is organized into four (4) locations and subpopulations as follows: 1) the main islands of Palau and Kayangel Atoll; 2) Sonsorol and Fanna located 269 km south of Palau’s main islands; 3) the four main islands of Yap; and 4) Ulithi Atoll located 160 km east of Yap. Its elevation range is from sea level to 213 m asl in Palau and to 178 m asl in Yap. The species’ habitat, EOO and AOO are projected to decline due to sea level rise, especially on the Ulithis Atoll, Kayangel Atoll, and Sonsoral and Fanna islands. There is no evidence to suggest there is a decline in the number of locations nor extreme fluctuations in its habitat, EOO, AOO, or number of locations where it is found.
useTrade: Both subspecies have experienced intense periods of overharvest for commercial trade in the past. From 1975 to 1994, an estimated 182,000 P. p. pelewensis were exported to Guam (151, 120 bats) and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (30,770 bats) for human consumption as a luxury food item (Wiles et al. 1997). Smaller numbers of P. p. yapensis totaling an estimated 25,538 individuals were also shipped to Guam (23,410 bats) and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (2,128 bats) between 1975 and 1989 (Stinson et al. 1992, Wiles 1992). Restrictions enacted under CITES in 1989 have been successful in stopping further commercial trade of the species (Wiles and Brooke 2009), although trade in P. p. pelewensis continued until 1994, when Palau dissolved its Trust Territory relationship with the United States (Wiles 1994, Wiles and Brooke 2009).Substantial hunting of P. p. pelewensis continues to occur for subsistence use and minor commercial use within Palau (Wiles et al. 1997, G.J. Wiles, pers. obs.). Subsistence harvest of P. p. yapensis historically occurred on the four main islands of Yap, with only residents of land-locked villages traditionally eating bats (Falanruw 1988a, 1988b). Reduced harvest levels for local use have continued since a 1981 ban on hunting for commercial purposes and export, with consumption apparently expanding in recent decades to include non-traditional users on special occasions (The Nature Conservancy 2017). The current extent of hunting on Yap is unknown. On the Ulithi Atoll, minor subsistence hunting of bats has been recorded (Wiles et al. 1991) and likely continues.
conservationActions: There are few species-specific conservation measures in place for the species. It is listed on Appendix I of CITES under the former species names of P. pelewensis and P. yapensis, requiring that the CITES listing be updated to reflect the current taxonomy and geographic limits of the species. Continued enforcement of the export ban on P. pelewensis has aided recovery of the species as subpopulations in both Palau and Yap increased following the ban (Wiles and Brooke 2009). Further, this subspecies occurs within several protected areas in Palau, including the large Rock Island Southern Lagoon Management Area (Olsen and Eberdong 2017). Although there is a general lack of terrestrial protected areas in Yap, this subspecies is protected within the Maa Mangrove Sanctuary (15 ha), which is a community sanctuary declared by Okaw and Kaday villages in Weloy municipality (B. Gorong, pers. comm). While these areas preserve habitat for bats, they do not offer protection from hunting. The species is also found in multiple Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) across its range but needs to be formally assessed under the global standard to determine if it will qualify as a KBA trigger species.Previously, several management tools that were identified for the conservation of the species, including designation of a seasonal hunting period, establishment of protected areas, establishment of regulations preventing hunting at bat roosts, and reactivation of traditional consumption practices (Wiles et al. 1997, The Nature Conservancy 2017). Enforcement of regulations of this type may be challenging in Palau and under Yap’s traditional form of governance, and these measures should be reevaluated for current relevance. In Yap and the Ulithi Atoll, P. p. yapensis was protected by domestic legislation banning hunting for non-traditional purposes beginning in 1981 (Falanruw 1988a,b), but some hunting for local commercial use persists because there is little or no enforcement of the law.To ensure adequate conservation measures are enacted, studies are needed for each subpopulation to determine status/abundance, trends, exploitation levels, connectivity across the species’ range, and ability to withstand habitat degradation. Community awareness programmes aimed at the conservation of flying foxes are desirable for all four subpopulations (Mickleburgh et al. 1992).

rationale: White-lipped Peccary is assessed Vulnerable under criteria A2bcde+3bcde due to an ongoing population reduction estimated to be 30% in the past three generations (18 years) due to habitat loss, illegal hunting, competition with livestock, and epidemics. White-lipped Peccary go through extreme population fluctuations. and the Peccary Specialist Group has documented these disappearances over decades of research, and this population dynamic is an important part of their red list category. Fragoso et al. (2022) reported 73 White-lipped Peccary disappearance events in 53 locations from 8 countries, including 63 in the Amazon. Ten disappearances were reported outside the Amazon in Southern Brazil and Argentina. Many of the disappearances (55%) were followed by re-appearances, but in 38% the populations are still absent. The disappearances averaged 7.6 years and ranged from 3 to 11 years except in the southern range where disappearances were 31 years in Rio Grande do Sul State (Brazil), and 16 years in Salta Province (Argentina). These events appear to be normal ecological population fluctuations of the White-lipped Peccary. Hypotheses for these disappearances include disease epidemics, starvation, and intensive or large-scale flooding. The high numbers of individuals in each group and the relatively high reproductive rate of White-lipped Peccary populations may lead to depletion of their food resources, increasing intraspecific competition and environmental stress, then leading to decreased immunological defences, and, when coupled with high population density, lead to an ideal scenario for the spread of pathogens and a crash in the population (Fragoso et al. 2022).This species has a wide distributional range, and its core population is in the Amazon region spanning 6.7 million km². These forests are largely remaining intact in central, western and northern Amazonia because around 60% are in protected areas, Indigenous territories, community-based reserves, and co-managed areas (Bodmer et al. 2023). However, white-lipped peccaries are disappearing from fragmented areas in the northern and southern parts of their range and in these regions have suffered range reduction in their historical distribution. This reduction has been more dramatic for Mesoamerican countries, where the White-lipped Peccary has been extirpated from El Salvador and has been greatly reduced in Costa Rica (89%), Mexico and Guatemala (87%) (Altrichter et al. 2012, Thorton et al. 2020).The relative vulnerability of white-lipped peccaries to local extinction in established conservation units in their northern and southern ranges means that extant conservation units in the different ecosystems outside of Amazonia are not necessarily adequate to ensure their survival, and even large, protected areas are not enough to guarantee the protection of viable populations. In other areas, within their northern and southern ranges, they are undergoing localized declines due to widespread and increasing deforestation and intense hunting pressure. According to Altrichter et al. (2012), within 48% of their current range, white-lipped peccaries have a reduced abundance and a low probability of long-term survival. However, the Amazonian region has the largest populations, and the extensive geographical area means that Amazonian populations have a greater probability of long-term survival than the northern and southern populations.
habitat: Approximately 60% of this species' distribution is in humid tropical forests. However, white-lipped peccaries are found in a wide diversity of habitats including wet and dry grasslands and woodlands, xerophytic areas like the Gran Chaco, tropical dry forests, and coastal mangroves (Wetzel and Lovett 1974, Mayer and Brandt 1982, Vaughan 1983, Sowls 1984, Altrichter and Boaglio 2004, Taber et al. 2008, Desbiez et al. 2009b). White-lipped peccaries tend to frequent areas close to water and may even visit coastal beaches to forage. In forest areas, they avoid open habitats such as savannas, and preferentially use forest corridors (Richard-Hansen et al. 2019, Jorge 2021). Peccaries are primarily frugivorous, but will eat other plant resources, invertebrates, fungi, and even occasional fish (Husson 1978, Kiltie 1981, Bodmer 1989, Fragoso 1994, Beck 2005, Desbiez et al. 2009a, Keuroghlian and Eaton 2008a, Fernandes et al. 2013). Beck (2006) determined that white-lipped peccaries fed on 144 plant species belonging to 36 families across their range. In some areas of the Brazilian Cerrado where forest reserves are surrounded by corn plantations, they will also feed on corn and soybeans (Jacomo 2002, Jacomo et al. 2013, Painkow et al. 2024). The species plays an important role as prey for large felines, ecosystem engineers, and in the function and structure of Neotropical forests as a major predator and disperser of seeds (Bodmer 1991, Painter 1998, Altrichter et al. 1999, Beck 2005, Keuroghlian and Eaton 2008a, Desbiez 2009a, Desbiez and Keuroghlian 2009, Keuroghlian et al. 2009, Cavalcanti and Geese 2010, Beck et al. 2010).A number of radiotelemetry-based home range size estimates are now available from a diversity of habitats across this species' distribution. White-lipped peccaries travel long distances, and long-term studies evaluating their home range indicate non-random seasonal movements (Fragoso 1994, 1998a; Keuroghlian et al. 2004, 2015; Keuroghlian and Eaton 2008; Jorge et al. 2019) or non-random but multiannual movements (Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009). They may also move long-distances of 10-100 km or more during population dispersal (Fragoso 2004, Fragoso et al. 2022). The main environmental factors that determine the movement and home range of the species are food availability, habitat and resource diversity, vegetation cover, and water sources (Altrichter et al. 2001; Keuroghlian and Eaton 2008; Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009, 2012; Camino 2016; Beck et al. 2017; Jorge et al. 2019). They are diurnal, typically more active early in the morning and late in the afternoon (Mayer and Wetzel 1987, Galleti et al. 2015), but they may forage and feed at night during full moon periods (Mendes-Pontes 2004).In Costa Rica, herds in tropical moist forest were found to have a mean annual home range size of 32-37.8 km² (100% Minimum Convex Polygon, MCP) (Carrillo et al. 2002). Fragoso (1998a, 2004) estimated home ranges from 21.8 to 200 km² (100% MCP) for groups monitored over three years in moist forest of Maraca Island in Roraima state, Brazil. Keuroghlian et al. (2004) estimated an annual herd home range of 29.51 km² (100% MCP) in a fragmented semideciduous Atlantic Forest in southern Brazil. Reyna-Hurtado et al. (2009b) found annual herd home ranges from 43.60 km² to 121.00 km² (100% MCP) in tropical semi-dry forest in the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve in Southern Mexico. Meyer et al. (2019) found herds White-lipped Peccaryto move from 27 to 51 km² in the Darien forests of Panama, while Richard-Hansen et al., (2019) found movements of two herds between 40 to 70 km². The largest home ranges of up to 253 km² have been observed in the Cerrado of Brazil (Jacomo 2004, Painkow-Neto 2024). All home range estimates presented are based on 100% or 95% minimum convex polygons for comparative purposes. Reyna-Hurtado et al. (2009), Carrillo et al. (2002), and Keuroghlian et al. (2004) observed a high level of spatial overlap between sub-herds, and the amount of overlap could vary depending on the season and resources available. In the Pantanal highlands, Jorge et al. (2019) demonstrated that area usage is related to fruit availability. The greater diversity and abundance of fruits during the rainy season led to increased area usage in the region, driven by changes in the spatiotemporal distribution of native fruits. The consensus is that white-lipped peccaries are clearly wide-ranging and require large areas for survival (Altrichter and Almeida 2002, Keuroghlian et al. 2004, Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009). Their movements respond in part to changes in the availability of fruit patches and water sources (Mendez 1970; Kiltie and Terborgh 1983; Sowls 1984; Bodmer 1990; Altrichter et al. 2001; Keuroghlian et al. 2004; Beck 2005; Keuroghlian and Eaton 2008a, 2008b, 2009b; Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009b; Camino 2016).Tayassuids, particularly white-lipped peccaries, are important ecosystem engineers. By disturbing the soil during foraging, they modify the understory and create water-rich environments. They also alter litter patterns and the composition of vegetation, which significantly impact other species (Silman et al. 2003, Keuroghlian and Eaton 2009). Frequently used sites, wallows, may experience soil compaction, enhancing water retention compared to natural puddles (Beck et al. 2010). Mud wallows, especially those frequented by large herds of white-lipped peccaries, are generally larger (~60 m²) than those used by smaller herds of collared peccaries (~10 m²). As a result, these wallows provide vital habitats for breeding and foraging for various anuran species, particularly during the dry season.White-lipped Peccary herds often exceed 100 individuals, though groups of as few as five to more than 200 individuals have also been observed (Kiltie and Terborgh 1983, Desbiez 2007, Donkin, 1985, Mayer and Brandt, 1987, Fragoso 2004, Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009). Reyna-Hurtado et al. (2016) found that large groups exist in areas with more water and far away from human villages. In certain seasons and some areas, large herds divide into smaller groups according to the distribution and abundance of food, although the more frequent reporting of smaller groups in some areas is probably correlated with increased hunting pressure (Ditt 2002). Group sizes in hunted areas adjacent to the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve in Mexico were smaller (Median = 16, SE = 1.84, n = 15) than those living inside the reserve, where no hunting is allowed (Median = 25, SE = 1.84 n = 9, Reyna-Hurtado 2009a). Keuroghlian et al. (2004) observed that a population of 150 white-lipped peccaries in a fragmented area of the Atlantic Forest periodically divided into 3-4 sub-herds with an average of 42 individuals each. They also observed a high frequency of switching of individuals among sub-herds and documented periodic sub-herd fusion and fission. Switching of individuals has also been observed in a long-term (10 years) radiotelemetry study in the Pantanal of Brazil (Keuroghlian 2003; Keuroghlian et al. 2004, 2015) and in Costa Rica (Sáenz and Carrillo 1999). Biondo et al. 2011 analysed two different populations 80 km apart in the Pantanal. They found a low degree of genetic differentiation between the locations analysed, and dispersal by both sexes (contrary to the predicted male-biased dispersal of most mammalian species). In addition, 30% of males and females were predicted to be dispersers, which can indicate high levels of gene flow between the two different herds. For this reason, the researchers stress the need for very large areas to maintain gene flow and genetic diversity between these distant but connected populations and suggest managing them as a unique population; this requires maintaining ecological corridors and natural links between herd populations (Biondo et al. 2011).In the Gran Chaco, white-lipped peccaries appear to be widely distributed across different habitats and ecotones, despite the presence of both other extant peccary species in this ecoregion. Small to medium-sized groups of white-lipped peccaries have been observed in and around Defensores del Chaco National Park in Paraguay, the country’s largest protected area. These xerophytic forests may be some of the driest habitats occupied by the species; here they appear to occur at low densities but are still frequently taken by jaguars (Giordano 2015). In the humid Paraguayan Chaco of President Hayes Department, they appear to be widely distributed and occur sympatrically with collared peccaries, Chacoan peccaries, and feral pigs (Giordano and Gimenez Baez, unpublished data). In the Palo Santo woodlands, Rio Pilcomayo Basin of Paraguay along the border with Argentina, fairly large herds (minimum of ~70-100 individuals) of white-lipped peccaries have consistently been recorded in the same private reserves for almost 9 years.The gestation period of the White-lipped Peccary is between 156 and 162 days in zoos (Roots 1966). The average litter size observed in pregnant females captured in the Peruvian Amazon ranged from 1.6 to 1.7 offspring (Gottdenker and Bodmer 1998, Mayor et al. 2009). Additionally, in the Peruvian Amazon, Mayor et al. (2009) estimated an annual reproductive production of 0.89 parturitions and 0.62 young per adult female, and no seasonal reproductive pattern was observed. A sex ratio of 1:1 was reported in pregnant females hunted in the Peruvian Amazon (Gottdenker and Bodmer 1998, Mayor et al. 2009) and in the Mexican dry forest (Reyna-Hurtado et al. 2009). However, other estimates in free-ranging individuals showed a sex ratio biased towards females in the Pantanal (ranging from 1.36:1 to 1.88:1, female-male ratio) (Biondo et al. 2011), and this was also seen in other biomes (Fragoso 1994, Painter 1998, Altrichter et al. 2001b, Jácomo 2004). The White-lipped Peccary is a highly precocial species and presents a high morphological preparation for the early autonomous functionality of newborns in terms of thermoregulation, nutrition, locomotion and sensory processing. Consequently, newborns possess a relatively high ability to detect and escape from predators, reducing their rate of predation (de Andrade et al. 2018, de Souza-Pereira et al. 2021). Generally, the young nurse for about six months and reach sexual maturity between one and two years of age (Schmidt 1990, March 1993). Using paternity and maternity testing, Leite et al. (2018) indicated that both males and females have offspring with multiple partners, demonstrating a promiscuous genetic mating system, a similar pattern observed in collared peccaries (Cooper et al. 2011).
threats: Threats to White-lipped Peccary populations are from habitat destruction, disease, overhunting, and climate change. Habitat destructionWidespread and continued deforestation is one of the main causes for the decline and extinction of many White-lipped Peccary populations, especially in their northern and southern ranges (Peccary Specialist Group 2022). White-lipped peccaries form large herds and consequently require extensive and contiguous areas of habitat to obtain sufficient resources throughout the year. In the northern and southern ranges, the progressive destruction of habitat for agriculture, cattle ranching, and timber extraction have already accounted for much of the species' habitat loss (Altrichter and Boaglio 2004, Altrichter et al. 2012) and is risking habitat connectivity for the peccaries in the Maya Forest (Falconi-Briones et al. 2024). As of 2005, large populations of white-lipped peccaries persisted only in 21% of their historic range (Altrichter et al. 2012) outside of Amazonia. Oshima et al. (2021) found that forest fragments smaller than 2,050 ha were the cutoff point for the presence of white-lipped peccaries. Additionally, their study revealed that by 2020, the range of White-Lipped Peccaries in Brazil had shrunk by approximately 60% from historical levels. Of the 40% of Brazil still suitable for White-Lipped Peccaries, only 12% is protected. In the Atlantic Forest, only half of the protected areas have suitable habitat, and even less in the Pantanal (44%), Cerrado (14%), and Caatinga (7%). Mapping areas with suitable climates and landscapes is crucial for informing conservation strategies aimed at slowing and potentially reversing the decline of White-lipped Peccary populations, thereby helping to protect ecosystem health in the Neotropics. Semper-Pascual et al. (2019) found that peccary occupancy declines in proportion to the reduction in forest cover. Forest cover can be completely lost, at least temporarily, due to large fires. Therefore, if fires occur repeatedly, peccary populations may be driven to local extinction much more quickly than through hunting.In the Atlantic forests, very few populations are within suitable habitat large enough to be exempt from extinction in the region (Oshima et al. 2021). Southeastern Brazil is densely populated, and native habitats have been extensively fragmented. In most cases with a similar scenario, recolonization of small, isolated fragments would be impossible without human intervention, because source populations are not available in the vicinity to replace populations that become locally extinct (Keuroghlian 2003). In some areas of the Cerrado biome, white-lipped peccaries feed extensively on corn in agro-industrial plantations. This leads to high population densities and creates conflict with farmers, leading to local extirpations from poisoning and shooting in some cases and continued conflict in others (Costa et al. 2023, Painkow-Neto 2024).In 2023, the IUCN and the Instituto Chico Mendes (ICMBio), the Federal Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, and the official assessor of species red listing for the Brazilian Ministry of Environment, held their second workshop. For the Brazilian Red List of Threatened Species, Tayassu pecari was classified as Vulnerable in Brazil (A4CD). In both the Cerrado and the Atlantic Forest, it was classified as Endangered, and it was the only ungulate that received a Critically Endangered category for the Atlantic Forest biome (Keuroghlian et al. 2023). The White-lipped Peccary was considered of Least Concern in the Amazon region of Brazil. In Ecuador, according to the published Red List (Tirira 2011), white-lipped peccaries are considered Endangered in the Amazon, and Critically Endangered in the Pacific Coast. In the Ecuadorian Amazon, white-lipped peccaries have been extirpated from large areas along the lower slopes of the Andes and are vulnerable in all parts of their geographic range. In the Coast, where large-scale deforestation occurred during the past century, G. Zapata-Ríos (pers.comm.) documented only a few small populations remaining in Cotacachi Cayapas Ecological Reserve and its buffer zone area. White-lipped peccaries are categorized as of Least Concern in the Peruvian Amazon, where large populations persist and hunting is managed in community and Indigenous areas (Bodmer et al. 2023). In December 2010, Mexico's National Ministry of the Environment also classified the species as Endangered (R. Reyna-Hurtado pers. comm.). In the Chaco of Paraguay, the alarming rates of deforestation and continued hunting are cause for alarm, and although no formal survey has taken place recently, the number of herds as well as the number of individuals in a herd are notably declining (J. Campos pers. comm.).In Argentina, the White-lipped Peccary was categorized as Endangered (de Bustos et al. 2019). In most of the areas of occurrence, the species has low population densities, although in optimal habitats such as protected areas, it can reach high densities (Paviolo et al. 2009, de Bustos pers. obs.). In the late 1990s in the Atlantic Forest, the species collapsed in large areas, including the Iguazú National Park and the Urugua-í Provincial Park. In 2010 and continuing to the present, the White-lipped Peccary began to be recorded again in the northern block of contiguous protected areas of Misiones. Similarly, in a sector of the Mountain Forests or Yungas, a significant population decline was observed starting in 2010, leading to the species disappearance in certain areas (Bardavid et al. 2019, Fragoso et al. 2022). However, the situation seems to be reversing (Reppucci et al. 2022). In the Humid Gran Chaco of Paraguay, white-lipped peccaries also now co-occur with feral pigs in habitats where the latter were recently introduced for sport hunting. It is unclear what competitive effects this introduction will have, if any, nor the potential role of feral pigs in the mediation of diseases like swine fever.DiseaseCyclical populations of White-lipped Peccary are well documented and this population dynamic coupled with large herd sizes makes them vulnerable to diseases. For example, in French Guiana, Richard-Hansen et al. (2014) documented a population crash between 2001 and 2012 and the subsequent recovery (Fragoso et al. 2022). The periodic and sometimes continuous White-lipped Peccary population crashes seem density-dependent and are most likely due to epizootic events (Fragoso et al. 2022). Although infectious diseases are probably involved in recurrent local episodes of disappearance of this species, their impact has not yet been adequately addressed (Menajovsky et al. 2023). Many species are threatened due to habitat fragmentation or overhunting, and the combination of these threats with infectious diseases increases the risk of local extinction. In situations of environmental stress, glucocorticoid levels increase, causing a negative impact on body condition and the immune response to pathogens. This is a particular cause of concern due to the increasingly fragmented distribution of White-lipped Peccary populations. Among the potentially fatal diseases for peccary populations, Aujeszky's disease virus, classical swine fever, Trypanosoma evansi, Leptospirosis, and Brucella spp. have already been reported in wild populations (Herrera et al. 2008, Freitas et al. 2010, Romero Solorio 2010, Menajovsky et al. 2023, Menajovsky et al. in press).
