Noting, however, that they are now extirpated from Hong Kong (Karthi Martelli pers. comm. 2022) and undergoing population control with the aim of extirpation in West Papua (Kemp and Burnett 2004).
useTrade: As mentioned above, a workshop with Long-tailed Macaque experts (see Valle 2024 and Table 1, Supplementary Information) found that biological resource use is a main threat to Long-tailed Macaque populations, though this threat differs in severity according to the location.  The capture of free-ranging M. fascicularis occurs for both trade of specimens and subsistence across its range. In some locations, M. fascicularis faces threats from subsistence hunting, such as in Myanmar (San and Hamada 2011). Long-tailed Macaques are the most highly traded species of primate and are heavily demanded for biomedical and toxicology research (Cowlishaw and Dunbar 2000; Eudey 2008; Foley and Shepherd 2011; Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; Gamalo and Ilham et al. 2023; Garber et al. 2024; Badihi et al. 2024). For many years now, large numbers of Long-tailed Macaques have been exported from Indonesia, Philippines, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, Myanmar, and Viet Nam; 163,780 individuals were traded from 2010 to 2019 in the legal international trade from these seven countries (Foley and Shepherd 2011; Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; Gamalo and Ilham 2023; CITES 2024). The trade is even larger when non-habitat countries are included, such as China and Mauritius. Badihi et al. (2024), Garber et al. (2024) and Gamalo and Ilham et al. (2023) provide overviews of the source, purposes, and volume of this trade. According to CITES, most trade concerns captive-bred individuals (90%), however, this does not include supplementation of breeding stock by wild individuals.  It is noted that there can be a lack of sufficient scrutiny of this trade by wildlife managers, in order to ensure that capturing from the wild population is managed sustainably, or where not sustainable, that it is ceased. One issue arising in relation to the M. fascicularis trade, is the capture of macaques from the wild, which are then brought into breeding facilities in the eastern nations of Southeast Asia – Cambodia, Lao PDR and Viet Nam, (Lee 2011, Hamada et al. 2011). These wild-captured macaques are subsequently traded as if they are captive born and bred, thereby masking the true level of impact on the wild population (Foley and Shepherd 2011). From 2010 to 2019, 450,000 live Long-tailed Macaques were traded legally internationally, accounting for approximately 90% of the legal global primate trade that is monitored through CITES (Hansen et al. 2022a, Badihi et al. 2024). As the illegal trade (trade without CITES export permits) and the trade within habitat-countries is not included in CITES trade numbers, the illegal trade and the in-country trade is in addition to the numbers quantified from CITES export/import records.The international trade of this species is coordinated by a few larger pharmaceutical companies with demand primarily coming from the USA, Japan, China and the EU, and most recently from Canada as well. China reduced exports greatly in 2019 (Warne et al. 2023, Kolby and Reaser 2024), which effectively changed the patterns of the international trade in Long-tailed Macaques, with habitat countries taking over as suppliers (Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; CITES Trade Database 2022). For example, there was a notable increase in the export of Long-tailed Macaques from Cambodia between 2019-2020, rising from 13,922 to 29,466 individuals in just one year (Warne et al. 2023). Should China continue to not export Long-tailed Macaques, we expect habitat countries to continue to attempt to meet the international demand, which threatens the wild populations of the species (Badihi et al. 2024, Garber et al. 2024).The international trade in Long-tailed Macaques is a multi-billion-dollar industry (Hansen et al. 2022a) with great fluctuations in price and export location (Gamalo and Ilham et al. 2023, Warne et al. 2023). According to CITES regulations, export countries must provide a Non-Detriment Finding report that contains information on the population sizes in the wild and in breeding centres to inform if the trade is sustainable or not. To date only Indonesia and China (a non-habitat country) have provided such a report (CITES 2024). It is pertinent for the conservation of the species that such reports are created, provided to CITES, and made publicly available.The species is also threatened by national trade for pets and entertainment (Hansen et al. 2021, SMACC 2021) as well as trade in body parts (Chavez and Nijman 2024). The species is traded in markets for pets and entertainment, and online through social media. Numerous recent studies have documented the scale of this trade:The Social Media Animal Cruelty Coalition (SMACC) found 3,348 media posts depicting one or more Long-tailed Macaques in non-exhaustive online searches between September 2021 and January 2024. As no breeding of Long-tailed Macaques for pet trade or entertainment exists, all are believed to be wild-caught and the trade is believed to be greater than the results so far (Nicola O´Brien pers. comm. 2024).During past CITES meetings, information documents regarding the threats to the Long-tailed Macaque have been submitted by a cluster of NGOs (see for example, SSN, 2024). In February 2025, the CITES Animals Committee recommended all CITES parties suspend trade in Long-tailed Macaques with Cambodia based on documents provided by the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Cambodian government. They also recommended that Viet Nam, the Philippines, and Cambodia remain under review of trade in Long-tailed Macaques reported as produced in captivity (CITES 2025). In 2025, another large report was released detailing illegalities in the trade in Long-tailed Macaques in and between numerous countries, albeit with anonymous authorship (Sandy River 2025).The increase in exploitation and wild capture during the pandemic is documented in a report about the unprotected macaques of Indonesia (MACC 2022). Prameswari et al. (2023) further supports this; from 2020–2022, both market and online trade saw an increase in Long-tailed Macaques offered for sale (with some fluctuation). More than 4,700 individual Long-tailed Macaques were offered for sale on Facebook in 2020 and 2021 in Indonesia alone (Prameswari et al. 2023). As no breeding centre claims to be selling Long-tailed Macaques privately within Indonesia, it is reasonable to assume that macaques offered for sale in these domestic/national markets are wild-caught. In total, 9,727 Long-tailed Macaques were detected for sale during the two years in Java and Sumatra, Indonesia.Nijman et al. (2017) focused on six animal markets in Java and Bali, Indonesia, and during 51 surveys 2012–2014) recorded 1,007 Long-tailed Macaques for sale. Morcatty et al. (2022) surveyed these six, and an additional seven, markets over the period 2016–2020 (179 surveys) and recorded 1,620 Long-tailed Macaques. This makes the Long-tailed Macaque the most common wild-caught mammal in these markets. Assuming that 60% of macaques are sold (or die) within a week, and with some 55 wildlife markets in Java and Bali (Nijman et al. 2017), this would suggest that 10,000–20,000 Long-tailed Macaques need to be extracted from the wild each year in order to meet the domestic demand for pets in this part of Indonesia alone.Chavez and Nijman (2024) surveyed wildlife trade shops in Bali, Indonesia, and 581 of the 754 primate skulls they recorded were from macaques, with traders indicating that most of these were Long-tailed Macaques. The trade of primate skulls in Bali was directed largely towards international tourists (Chavez and Nijman 2024).TRAFFIC (2023) has also documented the trade in the species.
conservationActions: In general, there are only a few sustainable efforts to maintain Long-tailed Macaque populations in Southeast Asia. There is only one national-level program run by governmental wildlife agencies for censusing Long-tailed Macaques, and that is in Singapore (Sha et al. 2009, Riley et al. 2013). Establishing wildlife management programs for Long-tailed Macaques is critical, and urgent efforts are needed to establish regular censusing of M. fascicularis, as well as designing and implementing evidence-based management and protection plans throughout Southeast Asia.It is also important to create coexistence programs for humans and Long-tailed Macaques led by local experts.In terms of protection already conferred to M. fascicularis, the species is included in Appendix II of CITES, and thus is monitored and requires permits for international trade of live specimens and its parts, as well as quotas for wild off-take. In Cambodia and the Philippines, it is a normally protected species. In Myanmar, it has recently been assessed to be vulnerable, but legally is still a normally protected species. It is a protected species on Appendix 2B of Decree 84/2021/ND-CP in Viet Nam. It is not listed as a protected species in Indonesia (MOEF 2018), but any harvest from the wild can only be done as part of a quota, which for at least the last decade has been at or close to zero. In Thailand, it is not specifically listed on the Wild Animal Preservation and Protection Act, B.E. 2535 from 1992, but it is given the normal protection of wildlife, which restricts hunting and capture in all protected areas and forest lands. In Singapore, all wildlife is restricted from being captured, held as pets, or traded without permission, according to the Wildlife Act. In Malaysia, it is protected according to the Wildlife Conservation Act of 2010. In India, it is listed on Schedule I, Part I, Indian Wildlife (Protection Act) of 1972, and is considered an endangered species due to its limited range. In Lao PDR, it is listed as a management species, not a protected one.

rationale: Relative to Neotropical cats and felids in general, the Güiña has a relatively small extent of occurrence (EOO = 246,431 km²) and a further restricted area of occupancy (AOO = 105,609 km²). However, it does not meet the threshold for a Threatened Category under Criterion B. Historically, most of the species’ area of occupancy has suffered from habitat loss and fragmentation due to logging, urban expansion, habitat conversion to pine plantations, forest fires, agricultural and livestock activities. There is evidence of genetic diversity loss from population bottlenecks due to these phenomena (Napolitano et al. 2015). Additionally, 6 distinctive geographic groups have been defined, from north to south, because of genetic characteristics, geographic distribution and differences in threats and habitat conversion dynamics (see online supporting information and Napolitano et al. 2014), however these are not isolated sub-populations. Current threats for Güiñas include habitat loss/fragmentation and degradation, road kills, retaliation hunting, domestic carnivore pathogens, as well as stochastic forest fires. There is evidence that whilst there may be opportunistic killings (i.e. via encounters and within chicken coups) habitat fragmentation and degradation may be a more important driver of population decline (e.g. Gálvez et al. 2018, 2021).For this assessment we draw on current information not available during the last assessment in relation to high resolution data on landcover/habitat extension and change between the years 2000–2022 (three generations). Also, several camera trap studies have provided occupancy estimates, species-habitat relationships, and relative abundance indexes (i.e. proxy from camera trap detection rates) that complement density estimates from a few telemetry studies throughout the species distribution and diverse ecological conditions. Our results most likely reflect improved information rather than true change.The species primary habitat is native forest cover (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Lucherini et al. 2000) but there is evidence that it can have high occupancy in secondary habitats such as forest plantations and agricultural mosaic landscapes, particularly in South-Central Chile (Gálvez et al. 2018, 2021a; Gúzman-Aguayo et al. 2023). During the last 3 generations, equivalent to the years 2000-2022, primary forest habitat (Chilean Sclerophylls forests and Temperate Rainforest) has had an overall reduction of 4% with a 0.2% annual rate of primary habitat loss. However, for the last three generations the suitable habitat area has remained relatively stable. A 4% reduction in primary habitat but increase in secondary habitat as a proxy to population trend does not meet any threshold for a Threatened Category under Criterion A1 or A2. Currently, there is no indication of a future decline in habitat for the species if we take the 2000–2022 period as the current tendency associated with current legislation regarding land use change and forest protection. Hence also under Criteria A3 and A4 it does not qualify for a Threatened Category. The population size of mature individuals, estimated from new and detailed information, provides a range between 26,383 and 101,294 individuals. Compared to the previous assessment (2014) we estimate an increase in the total population. This is most likely due to better information that allowed a more detailed analysis. Even though our lower limit estimate is within the range of the previous estimate (i.e. 5,980–92,092) there is uncertainty regarding the population trend. There are differences between geographic groups that may require specific conservation plans. Nonetheless, the total population size estimate of the species does not comply with the threshold for a threatened category under criterion C. For both the lower limit and upper limit, population size is well beyond the 10,000 mature individuals (MI) threshold. Although some geographic groups have <1,000 MI considering their lower limit, two of the six have over 10,000 MI.In consideration of the above evidence and criteria compliance, the species should be downlisted to Least Concern (LC). None of the values estimated in this assessment meet the Near Threatened (NT) category. It is likely that our population estimates do not represent an increase in population size from the last assessment but rather an improved estimate. Because threats and habitat degradation are still occurring it is important to update data for the next assessment to evaluate changes. Apart from threat reduction it is necessary to estimate density for some landcovers so that the next assessment does not rely on relative abundance (RAI) proxies from camera trapping detection rates. Although we used the most conservative values and prioritised density estimates from telemetry studies, the relationship between RAI and density should be a research priority to provide better population estimates, particularly for the Central, Northern and Argentinian groups.
habitat: Güiñas display facultative, differential home range size, dispersal range and spatial overlap in relation to landscape features (Napolitano 2012, Napolitano et al. 2015). In fragmented landscapes, home ranges are larger than in continuous native forest areas and thus, density is lower. Home range size of Güiñas in the highly modified, fragmented landscape of northern Chiloé Island was 1.3–22.4 km² (Sanderson et al. 2002), while in two protected areas in the Aysén Region (Laguna San Rafael and Queulat National Parks) was 0.3–2.2 km² (Dunstone et al. 2002). Maximum dispersal distances of Güiñas in fragmented landscapes was 13.9 km (mean=5.5±4.9) (Sanderson et al. 2002), while in protected areas was 1.83 km (mean=1.49±0.25) (Dunstone et al. 2002). Regarding spatial overlap, in fragmented landscapes of southern Chile, Güiñas displayed exclusive intrasexual home ranges (females can be found within the range of males; Sanderson et al. 2002). However, in continental agricultural areas there was low intersexual overlap (Schüttler et al. 2017). Within protected areas extensive overlap of home ranges and core areas was observed (Dunstone et al. 2002). Güiñas are agile hunters and mainly hunt on the ground. They feed primarily on small mammals, especially rodents, but also small marsupials, birds and reptiles are frequently taken (Correa and Roa 2005). They scavenge opportunistically on carrions (Freer 2004). They are mainly nocturnal with some daily activity depending on the level of habitat modification (Gálvez et al. 2021b).Vegetation cover is an important ecological requirement for Güiña, as it typically occurs in forest types with heavy understorey, probably used for dispersion, stalking prey and reproduction. In its northern range, the species is found associated with mediterranean Matorral composed of sclerophyll forest and thicket. In its southern range, the species is strongly associated with moist temperate mixed forests of the southern Andean and Coastal ranges, particularly the Valdivian and Araucaria forests of Chile, which are characterized by the presence of Southern Beech tree species (Nothofagus spp.) and bamboo (Chusquea culeou) in the understorey. In Argentina, the species has been recorded in moist montane forest Valdivian characteristics, but also in less moist northern Patagonian forests (Agostini et al. 2024), where in both forests there is a multi-layered structure with bamboo, numerous lianas and epiphytes (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Lucherini et al. 2000). It is clear that the species is able to use and survive within human modified landscapes always using vegetation cover areas, particularly in south-central Chile (Gálvez et al. 2018, Gálvez et al. 2021a), but less so in central Chile and in the northern extent of its distribution where it is mainly associated with remnants of sclerophyll forests (García et al. 2021, Beltrami et al. 2021).In southern Chile, where it is found in beech forest, Freer (2004) found that areas of dense shrubby understorey (thicket-forest) were preferred over primary forest. In the highly modified human agricultural landscapes of northern Chiloé Island, Güiñas exclusively use vegetation corridors (as small as 3 m wide) to move among forest fragments, avoiding open areas (pastures with vegetation <0.4-m high) (Sanderson et al. 2002). In continental Chile, Güiñas also depend on forest fragments in modified landscapes and make use of forest edges to move between fragments (Schüttler et al. 2017). The presence of these corridors is important to connect larger habitat areas, and is likely an important component of the species long-term persistence in human dominated landscapes (Sanderson et al. 2002, Acosta-Jamett et al. 2003, Acosta-Jamett and Simonetti 2007). Along with vegetation corridors, safe road crossing elements such as culverts, overpasses and underpasses are also important to favor Güiña connectivity in fragmented landscapes (Sanderson et al. 2002). However, more than a habitat specialist, the species can survive in human modified landscapes, particularly agricultural areas in south-central Chile, with low forest cover but with available forest fragments, bamboo understorey and low subdivision of land (i.e. urban sprawl) within their home range (Gálvez et al. 2018, Gálvez et al. 2021a, Fleschutz et al. 2016).  There is also evidence of presence within or near urban areas that maintain forest cover in South-Central Chile (Silva-Rodriguez et al. 2020).Güiñas are relatively tolerant to altered habitats, being found also in secondary forest, exotic pine and eucalyptus plantations (Acosta-Jamett and Simonetti 2004, Gúzman-Aguayo et al. 2023, Moreira-Arce et al. 2016, Ramírez-Álvarez et al. 2023). In central Chile, guiña activity was lower in exotic pine plantations compared to primary native forest, and plantations were only used when close to native primary forests or regeneration understorey (Acosta-Jamett and Simonetti 2004). However, Gúzman-Aguayo et al. (2023) recently found that species occupancy estimates were nearly 50% within forest plantations of Central Chile.Given current understanding of the species-habitat relationship we can define primary and secondary habitat for the species. Due to the importance of native forest, we define this landcover as the primary habitat throughout the species range. For those habitats in which the species survives but if particular conditions are met and where there may be reduced density of the species we will define as secondary habitat. For example, forest plantations with understory, agricultural mosaics with forest fragments and shrub type cover can all sustain populations of the species as it has been described above and are grouped as secondary habitat. This information can provide differentiated population estimates per land-cover and also allow a more detailed monitoring of the species in terms of habitat reduction or expansion. The impact on the Population given changes in primary habitat may be evaluated differently if secondary habitat is considered rather than discarded. Please see threat section for this analysis.To estimate primary and secondary habitat change we use the mapbiomas landcover database recently published and made publicly available that allows the estimation of different landcovers for Chile (https://chile.mapbiomas.org/) and Argentina (https://argentina.mapbiomas.org/). The database can provide estimates of landcover between the years 2000 and 2022 which is approximately the length of 3 generations for the species. We estimate change from the database within the EOO estimated for species (see geographic section). We group forest cover as the primary habitat and secondary habitat depending on the geographic group. For the Northern and Central group secondary habitat included shrub and forest plantation cover. For the Lake District and Chiloé Island we included forest plantations and agricultural mosaics as secondary habitat. For Aysen and the Argentinian groups only primary habitat was included based on existing evidence on use in these areas. Changes in primary and secondary habitat is used to provide evidence of threat from habitat loss in the different geographic groups. For more details, please see supporting online information.
threats: Current threats as important drivers of decline for Güiñas include habitat loss/fragmentation and degradation and stochastic forest fires. There is evidence that there may be opportunistic killings (i.e. vía encounters and within chicken coups), disease transmission, domestic dog predation and roadkill as a source of mortality that may be having an impact. These more direct sources remain to be evaluated as to the overall impact on the population.Historically the primary habitat (i.e. forest cover) in the Chilean Matorral ecosystem and temperate rainforest suffered important deforestation and landcover change (Lubert and Pliscoff 2017). There is evidence that the species suffered a bottleneck and subsequent loss of genetic diversity (Napolitano et al. 2014). In the northernmost part of its range, Güiñas inhabit the Chilean Matorral ecosystem, where more than half of the country’s total human population live and which has been dramatically reduced by habitat conversion to agricultural lands, leading to local extinctions and population fragmentation. Güiñas in the Northern-Central area have low genomic diversity, high homozygosity and low, recent declining Ne similar to what is reported in fragile populations such as the Iberian lynx (Lescroart et al. 2023). Güiñas occupy remnant sclerophyll forests in the coastal range mountains surrounding agricultural land in the northern distribution of the species (Beltrami et al. 2021, Napolitano et al. 2020). Central and Lake District populations have suffered from extensive and intensive habitat loss and fragmentation by land conversion to pine plantations and logging of the remnant temperate Valdivian rainforest (Willson et al. 2005, Echeverría et al. 2006, 2008). On Chiloé Island, native forests have been largely cleared and fragmented over large areas to support domestic fowl, grazing and farming, leaving only remnants of the original forest surrounded by a human-modified matrix (Armesto et al. 1998, Sanderson et al. 2002). In its southernmost range, human density is lower, there is a greater amount of forest cover and agricultural lands are more frequently surrounded by a concentration of protected areas. Similarly, in the Argentine portion of Güiñas range, the native forest is almost continuous, with a low degree of land-cover transformation, and nearly 75% of the area under protection (Monteverde et al. 2019).In the last assessment (i.e. 2014) an estimate of an annual forest loss rate of 4.5% per year for the period 1975–2000 in a particular area of the Chilean temperate rainforests (Echeverría et al. 2006) was used as evidence of forest loss. However, in this assessment and evaluating the entire EOO of the species, we found that the amount and rate of forest loss between the year 2000 and 2022 has substantially declined (i.e. 0.2% annual loss compared to 4.5% of previous assessment), even increasing forest cover in some of the geographic groups. In the mapbiomas data base we found that the overall % change in area had a net reduction of 4% in primary habitat for the period (i.e. 2000-2022) with an annual rate of primary habitat loss of 0.2%. The different groups had the following annual % of change in forest cover 1) -0.4% for the Northern group, 2) -1.6% for the Central group, 3) -0.3% for the Lake district group, 4) an increase of 0.4% for Chiloé group, 5) 0.1% for the Argentinian group and 6) 0.2% for the Aysen group. The groups with the largest decrease in total forest cover area during the period were the Northern group with a reduction of 9% and the Central group with a reduction in 35%. For the Chiloe Island, Argentinian and Aysen groups there was annual increase of primary habitat during the period.Forest fires may be the major driver in this loss of primary habitat discussed above and most likely represent highly negative stochastic events for the species. Particularly if we consider that the population estimates of the Central group and the Northern group with < 1,000 mature individuals (see population estimates). Fires have been increasing in a greater part of the distribution of the central and northern range of Güiñas. During 2017, central Chile had a megafire event in 92 locations totaling 529,794 hectares with high severity (De la Barrera et al. 2018). These fires reduced and degraded important habitat for the species such as shrub and forest plantations (Gúzman-Aguayo et al. 2023). In fact, probability of use-occupancy by the species is significantly reduced with increasing severity of wildfires (Osorio et al. 2021). Also, habitat, such as ravines with remnant native vegetation, in the northern distribution of the species are highly threatened by forest fires (Beltrami et al. 2021). Fires are expected to increase in frequency and severity in key areas of the species distribution (Castillo et al. 2020), particularly relevant for the L. guigna tigrillo Northern sub-species. In Argentina, between 2001 and 2017, 84% of the total loss of Patagonian forest area was due to fires, mostly concentrated in the Güiña’s distribution range in Neuquén, Río Negro and Chubut provinces (Mohr-Bell et. al.2019). It has been shown that the distribution range of Güiñas in both Chile and Argentina will decrease under climate change scenarios (Marquet et al. 2010, Cuyckens et al. 2015) where increased intensity of fire may be also an important consequence and detrimental to the primary habitat of the species.In contrast to primary habitat, secondary habitat has had a net increase of 20% in surface area between the years 2000 and 2022, mainly driven by an increase within the Central group (44% increase) and driven by an increase in forest plantations (Proyecto MapBiomas Chile). The fact that the species can survive in these modified landscapes of forest plantations of central Chile (Gúzman-Aguayo et al. 2023), opens the possibility that this may offset the reduction in primary habitat. However, this may need to be further assessed with meta-population dynamics in these forestry production landscapes, considering that these habitats have high turnover due to the harvesting of trees with clear cutting methods. In turn, within southern Chile agricultural mosaics may be highly important to safeguard the future of the species. Particularly, considering that the large population of the Lake District group is key for the survival of the species due to estimated numbers. In the Lake District group there is increasing support that the species can have high occupancy values in agricultural lands with very low forest cover, with existing array of forest fragments. However, in these landscapes there is an increasing threat from subdivision of land mainly driven by urban expansion or peri-urban sprawl rather than retribution killing of the species (Gálvez et al. 2018, 2021a). In fact, urban infrastructure has had a 33,2% increase between 2000 and 2022 (Proyecto MapBiomas Chile). In addition to increased fragmentation and human modification due to increased subdivision that may influence species persistence in agricultural landscapes (Gálvez et al. 2018, 2021a), evidence suggests that increased landscape fragmentation is associated with reduced genetic diversity in Güiñas (Napolitano et al. 2015) which could further hinder population viability in the long-term.Causes of direct mortality are also a threat to the species. Most people in rural landscapes of central and southern Chile have negative attitudes towards Güiñas, arguing livestock and poultry losses (Herrmann et al. 2013, Zorondo-Rodríguez et al. 2014), which could potentially end in retaliatory killings. 81.4% of 43 families interviewed in a rural area of southern Chile considered Güiñas “damaging" or "very damaging”, although there was only a single recent report of a Güiña killing 12 hens in a henhouse (Silva-Rodríguez et al. 2007). In a recent large scale socioecological study within agricultural landscapes of the Lake District geographic group it was documented that, from 233 people interviewed, encounters with Güiñas were rare, on average occurred 17 years ago, only 7% had lost poultry to the species in the last decade; even though the species occurred in >80% of the landscape from camera traps in those same places (Gálvez et al. 2018). In the same study it was estimated that 10% of respondents admitted to killing a Güiña in the last decade with specialized methods for sensitive questions (Gálvez et al. 2018, Gálvez et al. 2021c). However, on Chiloe Island, two out of seven radio-collared Güiñas were killed while raiding chicken coops (Sanderson et al. 2002). Retaliatory killings for poultry depredation accounted for 39.4% of the total 38 Güiña samples collected during a three-year study in Chiloé Island (Napolitano 2012, Napolitano et al. 2015). Direct persecution and attack by free-roaming dogs in human-dominated landscapes is also a threat for Güiñas. Dogs are an important conservation problem in Chile (Silva-Rodrígiez et al. 2023) and Güiñas have been reported to arrive injured by interactions with dogs at Wildlife Rescue Centers, and a high proportion of them die because of the severity of the injuries (Romero et al. 2019). For several species of mammals, including Güiñas, all animal interaction cases received in wildlife rescue centers were attacks by domestic dogs (Romero et al. 2019). It is also known that in these modified landscapes interspecific pathogen transmission from co-occurring domestic carnivores, cats and dogs, may also be a threat. Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) and Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) infection from domestic cat origin has been recorded in Güiñas inhabiting human perturbed landscapes across the species range (Mora et al. 2015, Sacristán et al. 2021) and also deadly Parvovirus infection from domestic dog origin (Ortega et al. 2021). Road kills also seem to be increasing as a death cause, especially in fragmented landscapes, where they accounted for 29% of the total 38 Güiña samples collected during a three-year study in Chiloé Island (Napolitano 2012, Napolitano et al. 2015). There needs to be roadkill data analysis across the distribution of the species to better understand this driver of mortality of individuals. It is not clear what the impact of direct mortality (i.e. retaliatory killings, diseases, attack by dogs and roadkill) for the populations.If population estimates show a decline in the future, but habitat area (primary and secondary) remains stable, it could be an early indication that these sources of mortality may be having relatively larger impacts. However, in general, the evidence presented above points towards habitat-based threats as a more important threat to the species survival than direct mortality, although these may be additive and must also be included in conservation action plans. The threats discussed above should guide conservation action for the species.
population: The total number of mature individuals inhabiting the distribution range was estimated. For each geographically limited group defined by Napolitano et al. (2014; see below), we identified suitable habitat land-cover categories based on recent field studies. From these same studies, we compiled occupancy estimates from hierarchical models for each land-cover category and geographic group (see supporting online information). Suitable habitat was then calculated by the sum of the surface area of each relevant land-cover. Occupancy estimates were used as a proxy to the proportion of each specific landcovers that is occupied or used by the species. Only for the Argentinian group a naïve estimate (i.e. not corrected for imperfect detection) was used as this was the best available information. To correct the total surface area of suitable habitat per geographic group we multiplied each land-cover by a corresponding value of occupancy from specific field studies. To be conservative we used lower limits of the occupancy estimates. This provided the best possible estimate of the effective surface area occupied by the species. From the sum of the effective surface areas for each geographic group we estimated the area of occupancy (AOO). For each geographic group, we also calculated the area of occupancy within each land-cover category identified as relevant for the species (here after as AOO-LandCover).The range for population size was estimated from published density estimates of telemetry studies and from Relative Abundance Index (RAI or detection rates) from camera traps multiplied by the AOO (i.e. AOO x density). Hence for each geographic group as a whole and per landcover, we estimated lower limits and upper values (i.e. most from average values), excluding maximum values as a conservative precautionary measure. We prioritized using density estimates from telemetry studies applied to those specific landcovers in similar geographic groups, meaning that we did not apply density for native forest from telemetry of the Aysen and Lake District groups to the Northern and Central groups. Currently there are no studies available with Spatially Explicit Capture and Recapture (SECR) density estimates with individual identification from camera traps or live trapping for the species (Gálvez et al. 2023) but reporting of detection rates as a RAI is common and available in some areas where density data from telemetry or SECR is non-existent.An important value used was density in primary habitat such as native forest. In the southern geographic groups (i.e. Lake district, Aysen, and Chiloé) we used values provided by Freer (2004) where only adult individuals were included in the estimates. We applied a correction factor of 0.37 to all estimates because in a recent review it was stated that density estimates may be overestimated by 63% in non-spatially explicit density estimates (Murphy et al. 2022). From Freer (2004) our lower limit was the median value of density, corrected for overestimation, of 0.32 ind/ km2 from five estimates (i.e. 0.06, 0.23, 0.32, 1.00, 1.22). For the upper limit, we used the highest value (i.e. 1.22 ind/ km2) of the estimates. This is a conservative approach for three reasons (i) the importance of native forest, (ii) the availability of several estimates and (iii) that we applied a correction factor for potential overestimation. For Agricultural landscapes, which are predominately in the Lake district and Chiloé group, we also used density from telemetry studies and corrected for the same factor as for native forests (i.e. 0.37). For our lower limit, we used estimates from Schüttler et al. (2017 /0.14 ind/km2).Proxies to density from RAI estimates from camera trapping were used for three landcovers of three geographic groups. For native forests in the Northern and Central groups we used values provided by Beltrami et al. (2021 / 0.23 RAI) and for Argentina values from Agostini et al. (2024 / 0.13 RAI). For forest plantations in the different geographic groups, we used values provided by Ramirez et al. (2023 / 0.032 RAI). A recent review by Palmer et al. (2018) shows that RAI can be a good proxy if the studies have a design with appropriate camera spacing, effort and if species are non-migratory. The studies mentioned above, that have provided proxies of density from RAI, have good survey effort (i.e. number, length and distancing) and the species is non-migratory, hence they could be a good approximation. Nevertheless, and to account for uncertainty, we have applied a correction factor of 60% of the estimated population to account for mature individuals in the detection rate, as a precautionary conservative measure. We are aware that the relationship between RAI and density is uncertain, and it should be a research priority for future assessments.Final population size range (i.e. lower and upper estimates) were obtained from the sum of AOO- LandCover x density (corrected telemetry density or RAI values). For detailed information and references please see the supporting online information that details habitat area for each land cover category, proportion of each landcover occupied by the species (AOO- LandCover), published RAI/telemetry density of the species per land-cover and geographic group.Based on the above analysis the range values of the population size per geographic group and in total are the following: Northern Group (31.5°-35° S; Administrative regions included: IV, V, RM, VI) population size: lower: 70 MI, upper: 373 MICentral Group (>35°-38.5° S, Administrative regions included: VII, VIII) population size: lower: 510 MI, upper: 3,359 MILake District Group (>38.5°-41.5° S; Administrative regions included: IX, X, XIV) population size: lower: 12,749 MI, average: 48,115 MIChiloé Island Group (39°-44° S; Administrative regions included: X) population size: lower: 1,831 MI, upper: 6,777 MIArgentinian Group (41.7°-43.5° S; Administrative regions included: Chubut, Neuguén, Río Negro) population size: lower: 63 MI, upper: 122 MIAysen (>44°-48.1° S; Administrative regions included: X) population size: lower: 11,160 MI, upper: 42,548 MITotal population estimate: lower: 26,383 MI, upper: 101,294 MIIt is worth noting that although the total population is driven by three groups with large numbers, there are three groups that show very low numbers. With their numbers, the Northern, Central and Argentinian groups have population size estimates that are very low (with the lower estimates meeting the threshold for Endangered (Northern, Central and Argentinian group) under Criterion D) and require urgent conservation attention. Furthermore, four out of six geographic groups have less than 10,000 mature individuals and the overall population size is driven mainly by two large groups; the Lake District and Aysén group. It is known that the species suffered genetic diversity reduction from a population bottleneck in the past (Napolitano et al. 2014), but it is also known that there is genetic connectivity between the Lake District group and the Central-Northern groups (Napolitano et al. 2014). As the former group contributes largely to the population size, the connectivity between this group and the northern distribution of the species becomes crucially important so that these populations may receive dispersing individuals.A recent whole-genome study of the Leopardus genus found that the northern subspecies of guigna (L. guigna tigrillo; Northern and Central geographic groups) has low genomic diversity (0.063%; Lescroart et al. 2023). The genome of the guiña contained a high fraction (11%) of long runs of homozygosity (ROHs), similar to what is reported in fragile populations of Iberian lynx (Lescroart et al. 2023). Consistent with its restricted range in Chile, the Güiña contains approximately twofold lower heterozygosity and higher ROH content than the Geoffroy's cat. The same pattern is found in other small carnivores with small ranges, low levels of genetic diversity and elevated ROH content in the genome, and contrasts with species such as the Geoffroy's cat which occupy a large geographic range and possesses a high level of genetic diversity (Lescroart et al. 2023). Analyzing effective population sizes (Ne) the study indicates that this Güiña population has been declining continuously since the Last Glacial Maximum (aprox. 20,000 years BP), in relation to anthropogenic deforestation and severe fragmentation of the Mediterranean forest in central Chile. Altogether, low heterozygosity, high ROH and recent decline in Ne are warning signs of an increasing vulnerability to issues mediated by low genetic diversity, such as inbreeding depression and a lack of adaptability to deal with a changing environment (Lescroart et al. 2023). Genetic diversity is associated with population size: high genetic diversity is related to large populations, while low genetic diversity to small populations. Therefore, low genetic diversity estimates suggest small population numbers in the Northern and Central groups, which coincide with our estimates.  Ecologically these areas at the northern limit of the distribution are most likely highly restrictive in terms of resources and connectivity.
range: The Güiña, the smallest felid in the Americas, also has the smallest distribution, being found primarily in central and southern Chile (30°-48°S) and marginally in adjoining areas of southwestern Argentina (39°-43°S west of 70°W) from sea level to 1962 meters above sea level. From the most updated records, its extent of occurrence is estimated at approximately 246,431 km². The species has been detected in north-central Chile (Coquimbo – O´Higgins Region; sympatric to Leopardus colocola) all the way to the Aysen Region in Southern Chile (>1,600 km in latitudinal length). On the eastern limit of the range, in Argentina, it is sympatric with Geoffroy's Cat (Leopardus geoffroyi; Lucherini et al. 2001, Agostini et al. 2024). It is also found on the large island of Chiloe off the coast of southern Chile (Sanderson et al. 2002). Recent records in the most northern part of the distribution show evidence of Güiña populations in remnant forests (i.e. left during glaciation and maintained by fog humidity) and of coastal areas in the Coquimbo region (Napolitano et al. 2020) which is a transitional sub-desert matorral type ecosystem. This population is possibly highly isolated from central and southern populations because this habitat type is represented by isolated forest remnants.Two subspecies are recognised based on morphological and genetic data: L. guigna tigrillo (from 31.5°-38°S in Chile) inhabits mediterranean matorral and sclerophyll woodlands and forests in northern and central Chile and has a lighter coat and larger body size. L. guigna guigna (from 38°-48° in Chile and 39°-43°S in Argentina west of 70°W) inhabits more-dense Valdivian temperate rainforest and north Patagonian forest in southern Chile and the Andean Patagonian forest in southwestern Argentina and is darker and smaller (Napolitano et al. 2014).
conservationActions: Included in CITES Appendix II and protected by national legislation in Argentina and Chile (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Using a broad approach for population distinctiveness based on genetic and ecological exchangeability (Crandall et al. 2000), two management units were proposed for the conservation of Güiñas, which correspond to the two identified subspecies (Napolitano et al. 2014). Within these management units six genetic groups are identified, displaying significant variation in patterns of genetic diversity, biogeographic history, available ecological habitats and conservation threats among them. Güiñas are recorded in 16 protected areas in Chile, but many are too small to support viable populations (Acosta-Jammett et al. 2003). In Argentina, it is known from three national parks: Lanin, Nahuel Huapi, Lago Puelo and Los Alerces (Monteverde et al. 2019), although densities may be low. The spatial extent of protected areas alone is not enough for the long-term viability of Güiña populations, thus incorporating private lands outside protected areas is crucial for Güiña conservation (Simonetti and Acosta-Jamett 2002, Acosta-Jamett et al. 2003, Haines et al. 2006, Gálvez et al. 2013). Conservation action should work to foster positive perceptions, attitudes and higher tolerance of landowners and rural people towards Güiñas which is currently quite negative (Gálvez et al. 2021c, Silva-Rodríguez et al. 2007, Herrmann et al. 2013). Future conservation challenges for Güiñas outside protected areas will hinge on fostering positive attitudes of landowners towards Güiñas, increasing local awareness and participation to reduce conflict in areas where they are considered poultry pests, improving chicken coops and highlighting the services provided by its role as controller of mice carriers of Hanta virus and exotic European Hares (Lepus europaeus; Silva-Rodriguez et al. 2007, Gálvez et al. 2013, Napolitano et al. 2014). These efforts may decrease direct mortality of individuals.In the Northern and Central groups, fire prevention, improved management of forest plantations to permit flow of individuals and maintenance of understory habitat structure, and further protection of native forest remnants will be key actions. Also, restoration of degraded areas, burned or otherwise could have an important impact on the population. Public policy oriented towards these targets will have benefits for biodiversity under scenarios of climate change (Marquet et al. 2019) and the Güiña. For example, initiatives from the wine and fruit industry to protect remnant Mediterranean sclerophyllous forests in surrounding hillsides (Gárcía et al. 2021; Márquez-García et al. 2018, 2019) will be important for the persistence of the small population in these geographic groups. Forest fire prevention in these areas is most likely good conservation investment. This is also true for the Argentinian group.In southern Chile, apart from protection of existing forests in the Coastal and Andean cordilleras, agricultural lands require specific policy-oriented interventions. An array of small fragments will permit the species persistence in these landscapes (Gálvez et al. 2018). Also, the mitigation of urban sprawl or the subdivision of land in agricultural areas without any clear public policy may be impacting the populations (Gálvez et al. 2018, 2021a). The outcome of current discussions regarding public policy of agricultural land subdivision may have a large impact on the species. Also, conservation efforts should focus on preserving vegetation corridors to facilitate connectivity between forest fragments or larger forested areas, along with providing safe road passages to decrease mortality by road kills (Dunstone et al. 2002, Sanderson et al. 2002, Gálvez et al. 2013). Vegetation corridors are essential to maintain viable Güiña populations for their long-term survival in increasingly fragmented landscapes. Further studies are required on the species ecology, demographics, natural history, and relative importance of threats (IUCN Cats Red List workshop 2007). We need improved estimates of density throughout the range to reduce uncertainty of population estimates. Regarding diseases, future studies should include elucidating the potential pathological effect and emerging disease risk Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) and Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) and parvovirus infections may have for Güiña populations. Finally, the importance of roadkill should be assessed and hotspots identified where speed reduction interventions may be implemented.Currently, the Güiña working group (https://guigna.org/) brings together academia, practitioners, NGO´s and professionals working for the national wildlife and forestry authorities in support and to conduct actions to reduce threats across the species range including education, roadkill mitigation, habitat protection among others.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern as it has an extent of occurrence of 63,386 km2, it appears to be a relatively common species in mountain forests in Viet Nam, and is known from several protected areas. Whilst the species is hunted for food and is likely to be affected by forest loss, there is not enough information at present to suggest there are any major declines in the population. Research into the threats to the species is recommended, as there is currently little information available on which to assess the species. There is a need for further taxonomic studies to revise the genus.
habitat: There is little information available for the ecology of this species, however it is a forest dependent species (Smith and Xie 2008, Dang et al. 2018, Chien et al. 2023). In the mid-mountain forest belt of the Hoang Lien Son range, it lives sympatrically with Dremomys ornatus, with which it is not ecologically separated, although it is usually less numerous (A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025).
threats: The species has a restricted distribution range and, similar to congeners, is likely to be harvested for bush meat. The species is dependent on forest, the loss of which is recorded across its distribution (Dang et al. 2018, Chien et al. 2023). It is hunted and consumed by locals (Balakirev et al. 2025, A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025). Further research into the threats is needed to inform the status of the species.
population: The abundance and population size of this species are not known, yet are expected to be low (M. Steiner pers. comm. 2025). In northern Vietnam, in the provinces of Lao Cai, Son La, and Yen Bai, it is a common species in the upper mountain forests. In some remote areas, it is even abundant.
range: This species has been recorded from the Hoang Lien Son Range in northern Viet Nam to south central Yunnan, China (Zhang et al. 1997). In Viet Nam it was captured in the forests of Sin Chai, near Sa Pa, above 2,300 m elevation (Duc et al. 2016), but also recorded at a lower elevation (1,400 m) near Sa Pa (Viet Nam) (M. Steiner pers. comm. 2025) and at Lay Chau at 1,000 m (A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025). The species is distributed throughout the mountain forest belt of the Hoang Lien Son Range, reaching east into Son La Province, Ta Hua Nature Reserve. It inhabits forests at altitudes of 2,000 m asl and above, and is occasionally found lower, where it coexists with the congener Dremomys ornatus (Balakirev et al. 2025). It is also found in Lay Chau Province in the Muong Te district (A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025) at significantly lower altitudes. To the north, it is distributed throughout the Ailaoshan Range in the counties of Dali, Chuxiong, Yuxi, Pu'er, and Honghe, where it is likely also can be found in lower altitudes. The northern edge of the range has not been precisely established.
useTrade: Because this species is less visually appealing in captivity than its congeneric counterpart, it is rarely kept as a pet and is not deliberately captured from the wild for use as a pet (A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025). There are no known cases of live exports from Vietnam. It is hunted and consumed by locals (Balakirev et al. 2025, A.E. Balakirev pers. comm. 2025).
conservationActions: It occurs in Hoang Lien and Ta Xua National Parks (Viet Nam). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history and threats to this species. The species is listed regionally in China as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2021).

rationale: Over the period since European colonisation of Australia (1788) to the 1930s, the Greater Stick-nest Rat was extirpated from a vast range on the Australian mainland, but fortunately it survived on two small inter-connected islands. Since the 1990s, a series of translocations to sites protected from introduced predators have increased the conservation security of the species. This likely resulted in increases in population size, area of occupancy (AOO), extent of occurrence (EOO) and number of locations in the previous assessment period (2004–14); however, notwithstanding subsequent translocations, this increase has not been sustained over the current assessment period (2014–24), although if establishment of the recently translocated subpopulations at Dirk Hartog Island (Western Australia) and Mallee Cliffs National Park (New South Wales) are successful, this is likely to lead to a future population and AOO increase. However, translocations have had mixed success, and trends over the period most relevant to this assessment are not well resolved. This is because there are inter-annual fluctuations at some sites, monitoring data are limited, some translocations that were considered to be established have subsequently failed, subpopulations at some translocation sites appear to be declining, it may be too early to confirm establishment at some locations, and longer-term trends for lower rainfall across southwestern Australia may lead to future declines. Focusing on the five currently established sites and locations, this species has an AOO of c. 52 km2. A continuing decline is not definitively projected, but it is possible that climate change – which is currently causing rainfall decline in the southwest of Western Australia – could drive the loss of subpopulations, and therefore EOO, AOO and the number of mature individuals. Thus, the Greater Stick-nest Rat is assessed at Near Threatened, as it is close to qualifying for EN B2ab(i,ii,iii,iv,v) when five locations are considered, and if the risks posed to this species intensify. However, should the recently-translocated subpopulations become successfully established, its number of locations, EOO and AOO will improve.
habitat: The Greater Stick-nest Rat is found in areas of perennial succulent and semi-succulent shrubland. Animals shelter in constructed stick nests, seabird burrows and amongst rocks (Lee 1995). Females give birth to between one and three young after a gestation period of 44 days (Robinson 2008). It typically lives in family groups of 5–20 individuals. Diet is strongly selective, favouring succulent vegetation (chenopods and other species with high water content).
threats: The major threat for Greater Stick-nest Rats is predation by feral cats (Felis catus) and Red Foxes (Vulpes vulpes). Both species have caused the extinction of medium-sized mammals on the Australian mainland and on Australian islands (Copley 1999, Burbidge and Manly 2002). All current populations are at sites without cats and/or foxes.Short et al. (2019) indicated that Black Rats (Rattus rattus) may be a threat, citing an instance of predation by Black Rats on a juvenile Stick-nest Rat. Translocated populations have also been shown to be highly susceptible to predation by native reptiles (snakes, monitors Varanus spp.) and birds.Island subpopulations of Greater Stick-nest Rat may be susceptible to disease (Adams and Fenwick 2004) and declining rainfall/increased temperatures due to climate change. Furthermore, failure to maintain mainland island and captive colonies may be an issue: there have been some problems with captive colonies, including obesity and cataracts, and a majority of translocations to mainland islands have failed. Reduction in genetic diversity may be a current and future problem, given the small source population (Short et al. 2019), although management seeks to move animals amongst some sites to help prevent inbreeding (White et al. 2020, Onley et al. 2023).Reintroduced populations may be highly vulnerable to climate change and increased drought and heat stress, as experienced in subpopulations at Arid Recovery and Mt Gibson. Some translocations may have failed due to insufficient area of suitable habitat.
population: The current population size is not well resolved. Population and abundance data for most subpopulations was compiled by Short et al. (2019). The likely current population is c. 2,800 to 3,600 individuals. Population trends have been inconstant due to translocations, followed by some failures, and are subject to inter-year variation driven by rainfall.Based largely on the review by Short et al. (2019), with some updated information (e.g., DBCA 2023) and expert advice, the following is a summary of the status of all subpopulations.Original (remnant) subpopulations:(1) East Franklin Island, South Australia (2.25 km2). Population estimated at c. 500 individuals in 1988 (Copley 1988), with subsequent fluctuations in abundance reported by Short et al. (2019). With low confidence, population size in 2014 was 500, and in 2024 was 500.(2) West Franklin Island, South Australia (2.47 km2). Connected at low tide to East Franklin. Population estimated at c. 500 individuals in 1988 (Copley 1988), with subsequent fluctuations in abundance reported by Short et al. (2019). With low confidence, population size in 2014 was 500, and in 2024 was 500.A 2011 visit to the Franklin Islands to source animals for release at Mt Gibson Sanctuary (WA) found stick-nest rats to be relatively common and easy to obtain for the translocation (Short et al. 2019). There are no data suggesting a significant decline since then, so the 2024 subpopulation size is c. 1,000.Translocations:(3) Reevesby Island, South Australia (3.44 km2). Translocations from 1990. Population estimated at 600–1,000 individuals in 2012 in Woinarski et al. (2014), with low confidence. Short et al. (2019) indicated that abundance may have declined subsequently; so, with low confidence, the population size in 2024 may be c. 500–1,000. (4) Salutation Island, Western Australia (1.63 km2). Translocations from 1990. Population estimated at <500 individuals in Short et al. (2019), prior to 2018, but they noted indications of decline subsequently; so, noting recent drought, population size in 2024 may be c. 50–100.(5) Yookamurra, South Australia (11.1 km2). Translocations from 1991. Failed by 2007.(6) Saint Peter Island, South Australia (40.3 km2). Translocations from 1993. Population estimated at 1,000 individuals in 2012 in Woinarski et al. (2014), with low confidence; so, population size in 2024 may be c. 1,000.(7) Venus Bay, South Australia (11.1 km2). Translocations from 1995. Failed by 1996.(8) Arid Recovery, South Australia (14 km2). Translocations from 1998. Population estimated at 350 individuals in 2017 in Short et al. (2019), subsequently failed.(9) Heirisson Prong, Shark Bay, Western Australia (12 km2). Translocations from 1999. Failed by 2014.(10) Faure Island, Shark Bay, Western Australia (58 km2). Translocations from 2006. Failed by 2008.(11) Scotia, New South Wales (40 km2). Translocations from 2006. Failed by 2014.(12) Mt Gibson, Western Australia (78 km2). Translocations established from Franklin Islands stock in 2011; and this population was released into a large mainland island (predator-free fenced area) in the Sanctuary (7,832 ha) in 2014. These individuals were supplemented with additional releases in 2015 and 2018–19, and established at two main locations on-site. Record low rainfall in 2023, coupled with continued drought conditions and extreme temperatures into 2024, and potentially suboptimal habitat, have impacted persistence at these sites and the subpopulation size now may be <10 individuals. As such the continued viability at Mt Gibson is yet to be determined.(13) Mallee Cliffs, New South Wales (40 km2). Translocations from 2020. Animals were translocated from a captive breeding program re-established at Monarto Safari Park 2019, founded from Franklin Islands. Greater Stick-nest Rats are persisting onsite, and the population appears to be establishing, but there is no estimate of subpopulation size. Plausibly could be established; population <100.(14) Dirk Hartog Island, Shark Bay, Western Australia (633 km2). Translocations from 2021. Plausibly now established; but occupying only a small proportion of the island to date, say 10–20 km2. No recent estimate of population size. Some recent indication of local establishment and possible expansion in area occupied (DBCA 2023).(15) Wild Deserts, Sturt National Park, New South Wales. 32 individuals, all captured from Reevesby Island, were translocated in May 2023, but 75% of these died within five days. The survivors were re-captured and moved to a captive breeding population (https://us7.campaign-archive.com/?u=bb499ea0b610866ef34d6c1a2andid=75dc9db5dd).
range: Subfossil data combined with information from early explorers and naturalists show that the distribution of Stick-nest Rats (Leporillus conditor and L. apicalis) formed arcs along the southeastern, southern and southwestern boundaries of the arid zone, from western Victoria to North West Cape. The Greater Stick-nest Rat (L. conditor) had a more restricted distribution along the arid zone boundary than did the Lesser Stick-nest Rat (L. apicalis). It did not occur in the Great Victoria Desert, and was probably absent from the northern parts of the Eastern Goldfields of Western Australia. There is little evidence of it much southwest of the arid zone boundary. However, unlike the Lesser Stick-nest Rat, it did occur all over the Nullarbor Plain (A. Baynes pers. comm. 2010).The Greater Stick-nest Rat became extinct on mainland Australia in the 1930s, remaining today only on East Franklin Island (2.25 km2) and West Franklin Island (2.47 km2), South Australia (Copley 1988, 1999). It has been translocated, for conservation purposes, to multiple sites. Translocations have failed in Yookamurra (11.1 km2), Venus Bay (11.1 km2), Arid Recovery (14 km2) (South Australia), Heirisson Prong (12 km2) and Faure Island (58 km2) (Shark Bay), and Scotia (40 km2) and Sturt National Park (New South Wales), although this latter site is a very recent attempt. Conversely, translocated populations remain established on Reevesby Island (3.4 km2) and Saint Peter Island (40.3 km2) (South Australia), and Salutation Island (1.63 km2) (Western Australia). Newer translocations (from 2011 onwards) have occurred at the following localities, where establishment is currently tenuous or too early to call: Mt Gibson (78 km2) (Western Australia), Mallee Cliffs (40 km2) (New South Wales), and Dirk Hartog Island (633 km2) (Shark Bay, Western Australia). Thus, the map accompanying this assessment shows the currently confirmed, established localities only: the Franklin Islands (remnant), and Reevesby, Saint Peter and Salutation Islands (introduced).The current area of occupancy (AOO) is c. 50–300 km2, with the three aforementioned translocation sites that are currently either tenuous or with translocations that are too early to know if they have been successful. If the two most recent translocations (Dirk Hartog Island and Mallee Cliffs) are excluded as required by the Red List Guidelines (since five years have not passed since the introduction), and Mt Gibson is also excluded as the survival of the subpopulation there is currently tenuous, there are five locations (all islands) and the AOO is c. 52 km2.
useTrade: The Greater Stick-nest Rat is not utilised.
conservationActions: Sustained conservation management actions over the last few decades have led to significant improvements in the conservation status of this species. It will continue to be dependent on ongoing management.When the first draft recovery plan for the Greater Stick-nest Rat was written in 1993, the species was listed nationally as Endangered. That recovery plan (Copley 1993, revised 1994 and 1995), had a stated objective of upgrading the conservation status to Vulnerable within five years. That objective was met through: maintaining the Franklin Island population(s), establishing an effective captive breeding program, increasing the number of wild populations from one to three (or more), substantially increasing the geographic spread of these populations within the species’ known former range, and increasing the number of mature individuals from c. 1,000 to c. 5,000 (or more), with each population consisting of at least 500 mature individuals (the equivalent of each of the two Franklin Islands). Current population size is estimated, with low confidence, to be 2,800.The ‘Review of the Recovery Plan for the Greater Stick-nest Rat, Leporillus conditor’ (Copley 1999b), noted that all five success criteria had been met and as a result of its recommendation the species status listing was downlisted from Endangered to Vulnerable. This is significant as it is one of few Australian mammal species to have changed status in a positive direction due to management and to have sustained that recovery. Since that time further subpopulations have been established, increasing overall extent of occurrence (EOO), area of occupancy (AOO), number of subpopulations, and population size; however, some translocations have failed (Short et al. 2018, 2019), including some that had persisted for 20+ years (Moseby et al. 2024).The Franklin Islands subpopulation was the source of animals for a captive-breeding programme, commenced in 1985, which in turn became the source for translocations to islands and mainland islands. Greater Stick-nest Rats were introduced to Reevesby Island, South Australia, in 1990, to Saint Peter Island, South Australia, in 1993-94 (Robinson 2008), to Salutation Island, Western Australia, in 1990 (Morris 2000). Later reintroductions to Mt Gibson Sanctuary, Mallee Cliffs (2020) and Dirk Hartog Island (2021) were a mix of wild-wild translocations from island stock and captive breeding programmes founded with animals from islands.The Franklin Islands are within the Nuyts Archipelago Wilderness Protected Area, and Saint Peter Island is part of the Nuyts Archipelago Conservation Park, both managed by the South Australian Department of Environment, Water and Natural Resources. Reevesby Island is part of the Sir Joseph Banks Group Conservation Park, also managed by the South Australian Department of Environment, Water and Natural Resources. Salutation Island is a nature reserve and Dirk Hartog Island is a national park, both managed by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions.Mount Gibson Sanctuary is managed by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Mallee Cliffs National Park is managed by the New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, and the reintroduction was carried out in partnership with the Australian Wildlife Conservancy.The Greater Stick-nest Rat is listed as Vulnerable under Australian legislation, and a conservation advice provides a general frame for conservation response (DEWHA 2008).Reintroductions to mainland sites have had limited success to date, in part because they have not been to prime chenopod habitat, have had competing herbivores and have not proven resilient to drought periods. Return of viable populations to the Australian mainland is a desirable conservation goal, but this is most likely to succeed at a large site with extensive high-quality habitat, in which introduced predators are excluded, impacts of native predators are constrained (e.g., through provision of artificial shelters, training of predator-naïve animals), potential competitors are effectively managed, underground refuges are available to escape extreme heat and some resources are provided in drought periods.

rationale: Colobus angolensis is listed as Vulnerable. Despite a very large geographic range, the species is threatened in most parts of its range by habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation caused mainly by collection of timber and fuelwood, conversion of forest to farmland, the expansion of human settlements and encroachment due to a fast growing human population (Bocian and Anderson 2013, McDonald et al. in prep).Hunting is also a major threat to C. angolensis, particularly in Central Africa. It is targeted for bushmeat because of its large size. Despite the existence of largely intact, suitable and protected habitat in the Domaine de Chasse de Swa-Kibula, southwestern DRC, C. a. angolensis became locally extinct before 1990 due to unsustainable hunting (Dino 2014). Although hunting may be a particularly high threat in the Congo Basin, a number of other populations have already been extirpated from suitable habitats elsewhere, suggesting unsustainable levels of hunting [i.e. Arabuko Sokoke Forest, Kenya (Anderson 2004), North Pare Mountains (Doggart et al. 2008), and Pande Game Reserve, Tanzania (Burgess and Clarke 2000, Doggart 2003)]. In the unprotected Udzungwa Scarp Nature Reserve in the Udzungwa Mountains, Tanzania, Rovero et al. (2012, 2015) documented declines to near local extinction of C. a. sharpei due to hunting in a span of less than 10 years.This taxon is suspected to have undergone a population decline exceeding 30% during the past 33 years (three generations), and is listed as Vulnerable using criterion A2cd. The threats that caused population reductions in the past are not reversible and have not been eliminated, nor will they be in the foreseeable future.
habitat: Colobus angolensis is a medium-sized, arboreal, folivorous primate. It lives in evergreen and semi-deciduous forest, including gallery forests, swamp forest, coastal forest, montane forest, and seasonally flooded forests. The species is rare in mangroves and bush-farm land (Bocian and Anderson 2007). They are generally found in small family groups (2–5 adults), but temporary aggregations of up to 300 animals have been reported in some subspecies. They feed primarily on leaves and seeds but also on fruit pulp, flowers and lichens (Bocian and Anderson 2013).
threats: Colobus angolensis is threatened in most parts of its range by habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation caused mainly by collection of timber and fuelwood, conversion of forest to farmland, the expansion of human settlements and encroachment due to a fast growing human population (Bocian and Anderson 2013, McDonald et al. in prep.). Tourism development is a threat in Kenya and Tanzania. Colobus angolensis is hunted for meat. Despite largely intact, suitable and protected habitat in the Domaine de Chasse de Swa-Kibula, southwestern DRC, C. a. angolensis became locally extinct before 1990 due to unsustainable hunting (Dino 2014). Although hunting may be a particularly high threat in the Congo Basin, a number of populations have already been extirpated from suitable habitats elsewhere, suggesting that unsustainable levels of hunting occurred [i.e. Arabuko Sokoke Forest, Kenya (Anderson 2004), North Pare Mountains (Doggart et al. 2008), and Pande Game Reserve, Tanzania (Burgess and Clarke 2000, Doggart 2003)]. In the unprotected Udzungwa Scarp Nature Reserve in the Udzungwa Mountains, Tanzania, Rovero et al. (2012, 2015) documented declines to near local extinction of C. a. sharpei due to hunting in a span of less than 10 years.Illegal hunting for pelts has also been reported in Kenya and Tanzania (Anderson et al. 2007, Rovero et al. 2012).The major threats for C. a. palliatus in residential areas on the southern Kenya coast are vehicle casualties and electrocution on power lines and transformers which, together, make up 60% of the animal welfare cases recorded by the NGO Colobus Conservation (Colobus Conservation unpubl. data 2017).
population: Colobus angolensis has a wide geographical range and can be locally abundant. Populations in the eastern part of the range are much more fragmented than populations across the Congo Basin. Densities vary widely (Bocian and Anderson 2013). In a comprehensive survey of the Kenyan range of the species, a total of 55 populations were located, with the Kenyan Colobus angolensis palliatus population estimated at 3,100–5,000 individuals (560–900 groups). In Shimba Hills National Park, southeastern Kenya, there are ca 15 individuals/km². At ca 2,400 individuals (Anderson et al. 2007), this is the largest population in Kenya. It exhibits at high density in Diani, a tourist suburban area with remnant forest and forest patches, where harassment is low. At least 10,000 C. a. sharpie are present in the Udzungwa Mountains, southern Tanzania (Rovero et al. 2009). Densities here are 0.8–5.0 groups km² (2.9–12.0 individuals km²) depending on threats and protection levels (Araldi et al. 2014). The Okapi Wildlife Reserve (central Ituri Forest, DRC) has a density of 16.7 individuals/km² (Bocian 1997).
range: Colobus angolensis ranges from northeast Angola north to the Congo-Ubangui river system, eastwards (with a disjunct range) to the montane and coastal forests of Tanzania and southeastern Kenya (Anderson et al. 2007, Bocian and Anderson 2013). It occurs from sea level to 2,415 m asl (Nyungwe, Rwanda) in East Africa (Anderson et al. 2007, Fashing et al. 2007).Eight subspecies are recognised, of which one is undescribed:Colobus angolensis angolensis (Sclater’s Angola Colobus) occurs in northeastern Angola, north to the great bend of the Congo River and southwards to perhaps extreme northwestern Zambia (Bocian and Anderson 2013). C. a. angolensis became locally extinct before 1990 in the Domaine de Chasse de Swa-Kibula in southwestern DRC (Dino 2014).Colobus angolensis cottoni (Powell-Cotton’s Angola Colobus) is endemic to DRC. It ranges from northeast of the Congo River, east to Lake Albert and north to the Uélé-Ubangui river system (it forms a hybrid zone with C. a. ruwenzorii in the southeast).Colobus angolensis ruwenzorii (Rwenzori Angola Colobus) occurs along both sides of the Western (Albertine) Rift, from the Semiliki Valley and the Rwenzori Mountains of extreme eastern DRC and extreme western Uganda, to Rwanda, Burundi and northwestern Tanzania. Colobus angolensis cordieri (Cordier’s Angola Colobus) is endemic to DRC between the Lowa River and Luama River from the Lualaba River in the western to near Lake Kivu in the east, where it forms a hybrid zone with C. a. ruwenzorii. Colobus angolensis prigoginei (Prigogine’s Angola Colobus) is endemic to Mount Kabobo, eastern DRC. Colobus angolensis palliatus (Peters’s Angola Colobus) is found in Kenya and Tanzania. It inhabits extreme southeastern Kenya in the north (Kwale County), the Eastern Arc Mountain blocks of East Usambara, Western Usambara, South Pare, Malundwe, Uluguru and Nguru. It is rare in Nguu. This subspecies is also found in the coastal forests of Tanzania north of the Rufiji River and riverine forest along the Rufiji River (Rogers 1981, Anderson et al. 2007). Colobus angolensis sharpei (Sharpe’s Angola Colobus) inhabits areas around Lake Rukwa in southwestern Tanzania to north Malawi and northeastern Zambia. This subspecies might occur in northern Mozambique (Groves and Ting 2013). Colobus angolensis ssp. nov. is presumably endemic to the Mahale Mountains, central western Tanzania (Nishida et al. 1981, Groves 2001, Grubb et al. 2003).
useTrade: Colobus angolensis is hunted for meat, often at unsustainable levels. Populations have been extirpated from the Domaine de Chasse de Swa-Kibula in DRC (Dino 2014), Arabuko Sokoke Forest in Kenya (Anderson 2004), North Pare Mountains and Pande Game Reserve in Tanzania (Burgess and Clarke 2000, Doggart 2003, Doggart et al. 2008), and the Udzungwa Scarp Nature Reserve in the Udzungwa Mountains, Tanzania (Rovero et al. 2012, 2015).Hunting for pelts has been reported in Kenya and Tanzania (Anderson et al. 2007, Rovero et al. 2012).
conservationActions: Colobus angolensis is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. Present in a number of protected areas across its range, including Lomami National Park, Salonga National Park, Virunga National Park and Okapi Wildlife Reserve (DRC), Rwenzori Mountains National Park (Uganda), Nyungwe National Park (Rwanda), Shimba Hills National Reserve (Kenya), and Udzungwa Mountains National Park and Mahale Mountains National Park (Tanzania).In the Eastern Arc Mountains of Tanzania the species is safe only where there is effective protection, such as in the Udzungwa Mountains National Park.Colobus Conservation based in Diani, Kenya (the only conservation organisation dedicated to a subspecies of Colobus), promotes the conservation, preservation and protection of C. a. palliatus (and sympatric primate species) and its associated coastal forest habitats.Colobus angolensis prigoginei is listed as Endangered due to its small range (Mount Kabobo, eastern DRC) and low densities (Plumptre et al. 2008). All other subspecies are listed as Vulnerable.

rationale: Although Theropithecus gelada has a large geographic range, its numbers are suspected to be declining. Major threats to Geladas include the conversion of their habitat into farmland, grazing land and human settlements, as well as the climate change impacts (Dunbar 1998, Beehner et al. 2007). However, in the absence of more detailed data regarding current geographic range and demographic trends, the species remains listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Geladas are associated with Afroalpine grasslands and adjacent rocky gorges and precipices (Bergman and Beehner 2013). This species feeds mainly on the flat margins of high grass plateaus, known locally as high Wurch or Puna grassland steppe, with Agrostis and Festuca grasses and giant Lobelia groves. Gelada bands consist of 30–289 animals, subdivided into 5–26 one-male units (Bergman and Beehner 2013, Abu et al. 2018). Bands keep within 2 km of the escarpment edges, where they retreat at night to sleep or if alarmed (Fashing & Nguyen 2016). Typical annual home-range size for Geladas is 9–12 km² (Hunter 2001, Moua 2015). Geladas are poor tree-climbers and are almost entirely terrestrial, partly a consequence of their unusual dietary specialization as a grazer (Dunbar 1983).Geladas feed primarily on the leaves of graminoids (grasses and sedges) and also forbs (Fashing et al. 2014, Abu et al. 2018, Jarvey et al. 2018). They also excavate and consume subterranean foods including roots, corms, tubers and rhizomes (Fashing et al. 2014, Abu et al. 2018, Jarvey et al. 2018), especially during the dry season when green vegetation is less abundant (Fashing et al. 2014, Jarvey et al. 2018). Invertebrates are eaten opportunistically (Fashing et al. 2010, 2014), and cereal crops may be taken where agriculture encroaches onto the Geladas' habitat (Abu et al. 2018, Jarvey et al. 2018).
threats: The overall range of the Gelada is being eroded by agricultural expansion resulting from rapid human population growth in the Ethiopian highlands. Conversion of Gelada habitat to farmland and livestock grazing is common (Bergman and Beehner 2013) and soil erosion is a serious problem throughout the region (Nyssen et al. 2015).
