Grazing pressure is intense, and competition from domestic livestock has forced the Gelada to remain on the less productive gorge slopes in some areas (e. g. eastern Arsi) (Abu et al. 2018). Gelada densities are considerably lower in heavily populated areas than in undisturbed habitats (R. Burke, pers. obs.). Geladas are also harassed, shot or hunted with dogs as crop pests (R. Burke, pers. obs.) and occasionally sold locally as pets (Bergman and Beehner 2013). In the past, Geladas were trapped for zoos though this practice no longer occurs. Also, in the past, adult male numbers were reduced as a result of selective shooting for their capes of hair, which were made into ceremonial costumes used by the Oromo people (Dunbar 1977). The extent of this practice today is unknown. There are also historic records of Gelada capes being made into fur hats for tourists (Dunbar 1977). Government-sanctioned trophy hunting of Geladas by tourists is currently allowed in controlled hunting areas, although the extent and impact of this practice are unknown. Parasitic swellings caused by tapeworms (Taenia serialis) are a major cause of death in some Gelada populations (Nguyen et al. 2015, Schneider-Crease et al. 2017). Climate change poses a long-term threat to Geladas, especially for populations inhabiting higher elevations, where agriculture has previously been impossible or uncommon (Dunbar 1998).
population: Geladas are widespread throughout much of their present range, although they are probably not as abundant as they were in the 1970s, when an aerial survey of the central Ethiopian Highlands yielded a population estimate of 440,000 individuals (Dunbar 1977). A concurrent alternative estimate based on known ground densities from a small proportion of the Gelada’s geographic range and the total area of gorge face on the plateau yielded a figure of 884,000 (Dunbar 1977). Detailed ground surveys at five sites yielded overall densities varying between 15 and 69 animals/km², although densities of animals within their home ranges typically reached 70–80/km² (Dunbar 1977). A recent estimate for what is believed to be the largest remaining population of Geladas, in and around Simien Mountains National Park, was ~4,300 individuals, down from ~10,000 individuals in the 1970s (Beehner et al. 2007, Bergman and Beehner 2013).While recent habitat conversion to farming and grazing lands has undoubtedly adversely affected the Afroalpine grassland habitats of Geladas (Fashing and Nguyen 2016), only further comprehensive surveys will reveal the extent to which Gelada populations across the highlands have changed since the 1970s.
range: Theropithecus gelada is restricted to Afroalpine grasslands adjacent to deep gorges and cliffs in the Provinces of Tigray, Begemdir (Gondar), Wollo, Shoa and Arsi at altitudes between 1,800 and 4,400 m asl (Jablonski 2005, Gippoliti 2010). The Blue Nile Gorge and the upper Wabe Shebelle Valley (east of the Bale Massif) mark the western and southeastern boundaries of the range, respectively.Two subspecies T. g. gelada and T. g. obscurus occur in Begemdir, Tigray, Wollo and Shoa Provinces, west of the Rift Valley, while a possible third undescribed subspecies, T. gelada ssp. nov., is found along the Wabi-Shebeli River in Arsi Province, east of the Rift Valley. T. g. gelada is found north of Lake Tana and west of the Takkazzé River, while T. g. obscurus is found south of Lake Tana and east of the Takkazzé River.
useTrade: Limited information is available on the extent of general use and trade in Geladas.Hunting of Geladas has been forbidden in Ethiopia’s protected areas since the 1960s. However, hunting of Geladas is permitted in designated controlled hunting areas, although the extent and impact of this practice are unknown. Furthermore, in Shoa, adult T. g. obscurus males have traditionally been hunted by Oromo men and their skins worn as headdresses and capes worn during ceremonies (Dunbar 1977, 1993). The extent and impacts of this practice today warrant investigation.Both the Orthodox Christian and Muslim faiths practiced widely in Ethiopia forbid the consumption of primates.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and as Class A under the African Convention.Approximately 4,300 Geladas inhabit Simien Mountains National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) in Begemdir, representing what is believed to be the largest remaining population (Beehner et al. 2007). Geladas are also formally protected in the recently established Borena Sayint National Park, South Wollo, and they receive local protection in several community conservation areas (e.g., Guassa, North Shoa and Abune Yosef, North Wollo).It is recommended that formal protection be given to the Wabi Shebelle and Robe Gorges which are occupied by the unique Geladas that occur east of the Rift Valley. There is also an urgent need for further research to resolve the intraspecific taxonomy of Geladas, determine the remaining population numbers and distributions of the different subspecies, and identify the most important locations for Gelada conservation.

rationale: The Canada Lynx (Lynx canadensis) is assessed as Least Concern because it has a widespread transcontinental distribution across the boreal forest of Canada and Alaska (US), where it is periodically abundant through 9–11 year population cycles (Poole 2003). Lynx are harvested for their fur in most Canadian provinces and territories as well as in Alaska, and this harvest has been ongoing for hundreds of years. Northerly lynx populations appear to be secure for the foreseeable future, although long-term and gradual changes in population trends cannot be reliably confirmed from available harvest data. Lynx distribution and abundance have declined in portions of their southern range in the boreal-mixed forest transition zone of southeastern Canada and the contiguous United States, resulting in northward range limit recession in the southeastern range (Koen et al. 2014a). Lynx distribution in the contiguous United States is less than in the early 1900’s (McKelvey et al. 2000, Thornton and Murray 2024), with confirmed population and range losses in Washington State, Montana/Idaho, Minnesota, and Maine. Lynx were listed as "Threatened" in the contiguous United States in 2000 (USFWS 2000), but this region represents <10% of the current geographical range of the species, and core populations occupy more northerly regions. In Nova Scotia, lynx occur in an isolated population on Cape Breton Island and are listed as "Endangered" (NSLRT 2006). Some southern lynx populations appear to be increasing, including in New Brunswick where they were recently downlisted to “Special Concern” (COSSARNB 2022), and in Maine and surrounding states (Vashon et al. 2012). However, these increases may be short-lived owing primarily to the maturation of regenerating forests in eastern North America, making them less suitable for snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus), the preferred prey of Canada Lynx. A reintroduced lynx population in Colorado appears to be well-established. Forest habitat loss and fragmentation are primarily responsible for lynx population decline across much of their southern range, and climate change likely contributes to habitat deterioration, including via decline in snowshoe hare numbers. In the next decades lynx and hare distribution and abundance likely will continue declining in the southern range, although some localized and short-term increases are predicted in regions of recent timber harvest. A federal plan for lynx recovery in the contiguous United States is in development (USFWS 2023). However, some long-term recovery goals may not be attainable given ongoing climate change and habitat loss (Thornton and Murray 2024, 2025). In the shorter term, lynx population sustainability in the contiguous United States may be dependent on connectivity with more northerly populations in Canada, meaning that establishment and protection of trans-boundary corridors should benefit southern populations (Thornton et al. 2018). At this time, Least Concern designation is appropriate for Canada Lynx because: 1) Although lynx harvest in their core range has declined since the 1970-1980 period, available harvest numbers and extensive field research results across the distribution exceed Data Deficient designation; 2) Harvest numbers for the northern range must be interpreted with care and do not clearly indicate a declining population trend or attenuating population cycle; and 3) Range loss and population decline in the southern distribution are unlikely to meet the conditions for Near Threatened status designation.
habitat: Canada Lynx are found primarily in boreal forests and mixed boreal-deciduous forests across North America, where their primary prey species, snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus), depends largely on forest patches comprised of successional growth in older multi-layered stands or younger regenerating stands following disturbance (Murray 2003). Across the lynx distribution, hares are the main component of lynx diet, making their habitat requirements closely associated with those of hares. There is no known occurrence of a viable Canada Lynx population in the absence of snowshoe hares, but lynx also require larger tracts of suitable forested habitat to sustain movements, breeding, and meta-population dynamics. Lynx home ranges vary widely across their geographical distribution, with range sizes 15-45 km2 being common in the north and >150 km2 being recorded in the south (Anderson and Lovallo 2003). Local snowshoe hare densities seem to have a strong influence on lynx home ranges, with sizes increasing dramatically when hare densities are <1.0 hare / ha (Mowat et al. 2000). The extent of lynx reliance on hares is lower in the southern range, where alternate prey like red squirrels (Tamiasciurus hudsonicus) and ground squirrels (Urocitellus columbianus) are more important (Roth et al. 2007, Hanson and Moen 2008, Maletzke et al. 2008, Fuller et al. 2007, Ivan and Shenk 2016, Squires and Ruggiero 2007, Szumski et al. 2023). Lynx reliance on hares varies according to cyclic phase (O’Donoghue et al. 1998, Burkstahler et al. 2016), with average hare consumption rates estimated at one hare every 1-2 days (Parker 1981, O’Donoghue et al. 1998, Ivan and Schenk 2016, Squires and Ruggiero 2007, Studd et al. 2021). Ungulates do not usually figure prominently in the lynx's diet, other than as carrion, although lynx preyed on caribou calves in Newfoundland after the hare population crashed (Bergerud 1983).
threats: In eastern Canada, including Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, eastern Quebec and southern Ontario, lynx numbers have declined during the last century (Poole 2003). These declines are manifest through northward recession of the southernmost lynx distribution (Koen et al. 2014a, Marrotte and Bowman 2021), although there is evidence of some recent range expansion in New Brunswick, Maine and other northeastern States (NBDNRED 2022, Vashon et al. 2012). However, these increases may be short-lived, owing to expected changes in forest succession and climate conditions, both which will reduce local snowshoe hare populations (USFWS 2017). There is no clear evidence of recent range shifts in the western portion of the Canada Lynx distribution, although substantive range loss was observed through the last century and is expected in the future (McKelvey et al. 2000, Thornton and Murray 2024). Projected losses are likely to be more severe in the southeastern range, although over the longer term some isolated areas in the southwestern mountainous range may remain suitable lynx habitat by providing sufficient forest structure and snow (Thornton and Murray 2024). Despite limited and inconsistent harvest controls during much of the last century, lynx-hare population cycles may be maintained in the northern range, with no discernible changes in distribution and abundance being detected (Mowat et al. 2000, Poole 2003). However, harvest statistics are recognized as weak indices of population abundance (Schmidt et al. 2015, Leclerc et al. 2016) and changes in trapping effort and regulations through time, combined with the prolonged duration of lynx population cycles, make it difficult to infer possible longer-term numerical change or cyclic attenuation. There are no other long-term datasets available for tracking broader population changes in Canada Lynx, but recent work from Alaska (Arnold et al. 2024, see also Ranta et al. 1997a,b) reveals that lynx population cycles travel in demographic waves that may challenge large-scale harvest management goals. Lynx population declines and range recession in the southern range are primarily related to forest loss and declining snow cover, with both changes directly impacting snowshoe hare populations and lynx habitat suitability (USFWS 2017). Interspecific competition from other carnivores including coyote (Canis latrans), bobcat (Lynx rufus) and fisher (Martes pennanti), whose populations have increased in recent decades, may also affect southern lynx through interference or exploitative competition (Buskirk et al. 2000, Bunnell et al. 2006, Bayne et al. 2008, Peers et al. 2013, but see Kolbe et al. 2007, Murray et al. 2008, King et al. 2021, Morin et al. 2020, Sirén et al. 2021a, Nakamoto et al. 2024). Notably, robust studies of interspecific competition involving Canada Lynx are absent from the literature (Murray et al. 2023) so the importance of interspecific competition in lynx population limitation is unclear. It is alleged that trapping may not be responsible for low lynx numbers at the southern range (USFWS 2000), but lynx harvest in southern Canada remains a concern in terms of incidental captures associated with trapping for other furbearers and limiting dispersalfrom core populations to the contiguous United States (Murray et al. 2008, Thornton et al. 2018). Further, a recent concern for southern lynx populations in British Columbia is related to hound hunting, which is not restricted to a select area (as trapping efforts are) but instead can span large regions (G. Mowat, pers. comm. 2024). This source of mortality may be impactful especially to lynx populations that occur in marginal or fragmented habitat. To date, hunting restrictions have not been enacted in British Columbia, although mandatory reporting is now required. Older multi-storied forests provide winter habitat for lynx and snowshoe hares (Koehler et al. 2008, Squires et al. 2010) and in the western US fire frequency has increased four-fold, with this disturbance expected to increase with warmer climate (Westerling et al. 2006). In the short-term, forest fires have removed substantial suitable habitat for lynx in parts of the western United States (Lyons et al. 2023). However, young dense conifer forest provide habitat for lynx and snowshoe hares, thus natural disturbance and logging practices that foster dense understoreys of conifers can benefit lynx and hares (Burdett 2008, Vashon et al. 2008, and Walpole et al. 2012). Climate change increases insect-related disturbance to boreal forests (Fleming et al. 2002, Logan et al. 2003), though lynx may make use of insect-disturbed forests and cope with insect outbreaks if horizontal cover and hare densities are maintained (Squires et al. 2020, 2022). Maintaining connectivity with the more abundant northern lynx population is considered essential for recovery of southern lynx populations (Ruediger et al. 2000, Nordstrom 2005, Walpole et al. 2012, Squires et al. 2013), especially with warmer climate (Hoving et al. 2005). Since listed as threatened in the contiguous United States, some lynx continue to be trapped incidentally in traps or snares set for other furbearers (DelGiudice et al. 2007, Vashon et al. 2012, NBDNRED 2022). Lynx are occasionally killed in vehicle collisions on roads with high/intermediate traffic speed and volume (Moen et al. 2008, Vashon et al. 2012). Both motorized and non-motorized recreation can result in lower lynx activity, reduced movement, or spatially avoidance of high recreation areas (Olson et al. 2018, Squires et al. 2019, Anderson et al. 2023). Given that recreation is increasing across most public lands in the US and Canada, these impacts may increase in the future. Although, hybridization with bobcats has been detected in Minnesota, Maine, and New Brunswick (Schwartz et al. 2003b, Homyack et al. 2008), hybridization in areas of distributional overlap between lynx and bobcats is surprisingly uncommon at a rangewide scale and does not appear to threaten southern lynx populations (Koen et al. 2014b).
population: It is not possible to obtain an accurate estimate of lynx population size across the entire distribution of the species. Over most of their geographic range in Canada and Alaska, lynx are trapped for fur and populations are managed accordingly, but harvest statistics are not a reliable source for population estimation (Poole 2003). Lynx populations in core northern areas can be periodically high in response to hare population cycles (Elton and Nicholson 1942, Mowat et al. 2000) and estimates range from 30-45 lynx/100 km2 to 2-3 lynx/100 km2 during the cyclic peak and low, respectively (O’Donoghue et al. 2022, Poole 1994, Slough and Mowat 1996). However, lynx population estimates vary widely depending on the estimator used and underlying assumptions (Doran-Myers et al. 2021). In the southern range, lynx densities tend to be lower (Parker et al. 1983, Banville 1986, Noiseux and Doucet 1987,  Kesterson  1988,  Fortin  and  Huot 1995) and across much of the contiguous US, lynx numbers are estimated below 5 lynx/100 km2 (Koehler  1990, Vashon et al. 2008a, Squires et al. 2012,  Anderson et al. 2023). Lynx in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are recognized as Special Concern and Regionally Endangered, respectively (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Poole 2003, NSLRT 2006, COSSARNB 2022). Northward recession of southern lynx range in Ontario is estimated at ~175 km during the past 50 years (Koen et al. 2014a), with some ebb and flow corresponding to the lynx population cycle and extrinsic conditions (Marrotte and Bowman 2021). In the contiguous US, lynx populations are smaller and protected from harvest, and in 2000 lynx were federally listed as threatened in 14 States (USFWS 2000). Lynx in the contiguous US occur as five recognized breeding populations (USFWS 2023): northern Maine/northeastern New Hampshire, northeastern Minnesota, northwestern Montana and northern Idaho, northcentral Washington, and a reintroduced population in southwestern Colorado. Lynx populations in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont are increasing (Vashon et al. 2012), but this increase may be temporary given anticipated changes in forest succession and climate change impacts on winter snow cover and snowshoe hare populations in the region (USFWS 2017). Declines in lynx numbers were recorded in Washington State following recent forest fires (Koehler et al. 2008) and population models suggest wildfires since 2013 have resulted in a 66-73% reduction in lynx carrying capacity in the region (Lyons et al. 2023). Studies in Washington (King et al. 2021) and Minnesota (Hostetter et al. 2020) find that lynx only occupy between 10-40% of designated critical habitat. Lynx are uncommon in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho and are functionally absent from Oregon, New York, Wisconsin, and Michigan (USFWS 2000). Lynx were reintroduced unsuccessfully in northern New York state in the late 1980s (Anderson and Lovallo 2003), and more recently, successfully, in Colorado where breeding has been documented (Devineau et al. 2010). A small reintroduction program in the Kettle Mountains, Washington State, is ongoing (USFWS 2023). In the northern parts of their range, lynx populations undergo dramatic 9-11 year fluctuations that correspond with cyclic population dynamics of their preferred prey, snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus). Southern lynx populations are possibly less reliant on hares (Roth et al. 2007, Szumski et al. 2023) and have more stationary population dynamics than their northern counterparts (McKelvey et al. 2000, Murray et al. 2008). Continental lynx populations are mostly panmictic (Row et al. 2012, Schwartz et al. 2002) except for possible differentiation south of the St Lawrence River (Prentice et al. 2019) and further differentiation in Newfoundland and Cape Breton Island (Prentice et al. 2019, 2017). Some evidence suggests fine-scale genetic differentiation in mid-continental lynx populations (Rueness et al. 2003) which may become aggravated with future loss of lynx habitat owing to climate change (Row et al. 2014). It appears that some southwestern lynx populations may be genetically differentiated from core populations (Schwartz et al. 2003a).
range: Canada lynx are mostly found in the boreal and mixed forest regions of North America, where they rely primarily on snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus) as prey (Krebs et al. 2001, Anderson and Lovallo 2003, Poole 2003). The geographic range of lynx across North America closely matches the snowshoe hare distribution, which overlaps the boreal forest distribution from mainland Alaska to Newfoundland and include most of the northern boreal region of Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Quebec. Lynx are found across most of the Canadian provinces but are absent from the west coast of British Columbia, the western prairies of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, southern Ontario and southern Quebec, eastern New Brunswick, and mainland Nova Scotia. Lynx are extirpated from Prince Edward Island. In southeastern Canada, lynx range has receded northward during the last century, and currently they occupy ~90-95% of their historic range in Canada (Poole 2003, Koen et al. 2014a). In the contiguous United States, lynx historically occurred in 24 states (McKelvey et al. 2000), possibly ranging as far south through the Rocky Mountains as New Mexico (Frey 2006). Currently, lynx occurrence in the contiguous US is considerably less than the historic (~1900) range (McKelvey et al. 2000, Thornton and Murray 2024), and is retracting (King et al. 2020). In 2000, lynx were listed as Threatened in 14 States: Colorado, Idaho, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, Utah, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. Subsequently, six "core" areas were identified where recent lynx reproduction is known, and currently there are five recognized breeding populations (northern Maine and New Hampshire, northeastern Minnesota, northwestern Montana and northeastern Idaho, the northern Cascade mountains of Washington State, and a reintroduced population in Colorado; USFWS 2017). The lynx population in the southern Rocky Mountains of Colorado was successfully established from translocated animals from Canada and Alaska. The continental lynx population is mostly panmictic across the boreal and southern mixed forests (Row et al. 2014). There is apparently no connectivity with the reintroduced Colorado population and the core lynx range, although lynx used to repopulate Colorado originate from across a range of locations across Canada and Alaska, and therefore genetic integrity of this population is mixed (Murray et al. 2008). Lynx populations south of the St-Lawrence River appear to be differentiated from the remainder of the continental population (Prentice et al. 2019). Newfoundland lynx are not connected to the continental mainland lynx population and the small Cape Breton Island lynx population is also isolated (Prentice et al. 2019, 2017). Nevertheless, given uncertainties related to lynx dispersal, connectivity, and genetic status across the distribution, and IUCN definitions of ‘Location’ (Criteria B and D), it is appropriate to consider the species as occurring across a single location. The Canada lynx distribution map is identical to that from the previous IUCN assessment because of the paucity and reliability of recent data related to range change. Using existing citizen science observations or research studies to develop a map would yield a weakly defensible product with bias due to low species detectability. Range change since the last assessment is probably <5% of the geographic range.
useTrade: Lynx are an important furbearer, with regulated trapping occurring in Alaska, Yukon, Northwest Territories, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Newfoundland, and Nunavut. Lynx trapping is closed in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the contiguous United States, although some lynx are captured incidentally in traps set for other species. The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) recognizes Lynx canadensis in Appendix II, meaning that their trade should be regulated to ensure sustainability. Exported lynx pelts require a CITES license, and illegal international trade of lynx pelts is negligible (Poole 2003). Lynx trapping seasons typically span November-March, which corresponds to the period when lynx fur is in its prime. Across Canada, lynx trapping is managed across provincial, and territorial jurisdictions, often through registered traplines and occasional bag limits. Wildlife Management Boards oversee furbearer harvest in areas with land claims settlements. Lynx trapping is a longstanding mainstay of the fur industry in North America, and through the 19th and early 20th century lynx and bobcat harvest records were combined (Obbard et al. 1987). During this time continental harvest ranged from 10,000-70,000 animals per year (Elton and Nicholson 1942, Mowat et al. 2000). Lynx harvest statistics for the past century have been categorized in 3 phases: ~1920-1950, spanning a decline in numbers apparently due to forest habitat loss and declining snowshoe hare abundance, ~1950-1980, involving harvest increase due to higher snowshoe hare numbers related to forest regrowth post-logging, high fur prices, and increased access to remote areas, and ~1980-present reflecting some increases in regulation and reduced trapping pressure (Poole 2003). In the 1980s, in response to concerns about declining numbers and possible over-harvest, Alaska and some Canadian provinces temporarily restricted lynx trapping seasons or established bag limits to better match harvest with lynx population levels and trends (Golden 1999, Mowat et al. 2000). It is understood that trapping can reduce lynx populations and historically, trapping may have impacted cyclic amplitude in harvest statistics (Poole 2003), but animals harvested during the peak/decline phase of the cycle may have naturally low survival due to the cyclic low density of snowshoe hares spanning several years and high risk of starvation during their cyclic nadir. Thus, some lynx trapping mortality likely is compensatory. Closing lynx trapping seasons during their cyclic low numbers may improve lynx harvest sustainability, but these measures have not been enacted consistently or at a meaningfully large scale because of spatial variability and asynchrony in lynx population cycles within jurisdictions (Arnold et al. 2024). During the last century reported lynx harvest numbers in Canada and Alaska ranged from 4588 (1949-50) to 58530 (1972-73) per year, and recent annual lynx harvest for the continent averaged 18891 (1980-89), 8360 (1990-99), 12714 (2000-2009), and 12351 (2010-2019) pelts per year (Novak 1987, ADF&G 2024, Statistics Canada 2024, FIC 2024). Although at a continental scale lynx harvest numbers have declined since the 1970’s-1980’s, some Canadian provinces (e.g., British Columbia) have not experienced notable changes in pelt numbers (G. Mowat, pers. comm. 2024).
conservationActions: Although Canada lynx are one of five North American furbearers included on CITES Appendix II, in order to monitor the international trade of their fur, there are no quotas or suspensions currently in place. In Canada, the national and provincial governments manage harvests by region (Government of U.S. 2007), using closed seasons, quotas, limited entry and long-term trapping concessions (Nowell and Jackson 1996). In the US, trapping takes place only in Alaska, and harvest quotas may be increased during periods of population increase and decreased during periods of cyclic decline (Government of U.S. 2007). However, for best success such dynamic harvest strategies require both numerical synchrony across large geographic regions, and robust understanding of regional population trends and future trajectories, including annual survival, recruitment and harvest rates. The lynx population in the contiguous US was listed as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2000, due to inadequate regulatory mechanisms to protect lynx or lynx habitat on Federal lands (USFWS 2000) requiring the US government to develop a recovery plan and identify critical habitat for lynx (Nordstrom 2005). A species status assessment was completed in 2017 (USFWS 2017), and a draft recovery plan was released at the end of 2023 (USFWS 2023). Currently, activities on federal lands are guided by the lynx conservation assessment and strategy (Interagency Lynx Biology Team 2013). In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, where lynx populations are known to be under pressure, recovery planning is initiated (NSLRT 2006, NBDNRED 2022) but currently (2025) without notable field implementation. Lynx are trapped incidentally in traps set for other furbearers like bobcat or coyote, including in jurisdictions where lynx trapping is closed for conservation purposes. In the contiguous United States, various measures have been recommended to trappers (e.g., avoid the use of hares or rabbits as bait) to reduce accidental taking of lynx in traps set for other furbearers (Golden and Krause 2003). In addition, several States have passed trapping regulations to further reduce accidental capture of lynx in traps set for other furbearers (Del Giudice et al. 2007, Vashon et al. 2012). In New Brunswick, a program is in place for recovery of carcasses of lynx caught incidentally in traps, and these are being used to track population demography (NBDNRED 2022). In some areas lynx may continue to be trapped either incidentally or illegally, but estimates of this harvest are not available. It is likely that not all carcasses from incidentally trapped lynx are surrendered through such programmes, and surrender rates likely represent an underestimate of the impact of trapping on lynx populations in regions where harvest is prohibited. In the contiguous US. critical habitat designations only apply to federal lands or private lands with federally funded or permitted activities. This designation gives the federal government authority to manage activities that affect the designated habitat. In 2009, the US Fish and Wildlife Service published a revised designation of critical habitat which significantly increased a 2006 designation of 4,768 square miles within the boundaries of Voyagers National Park in Minnesota, Glacier National Park in Montana, and North Cascades National Park in Washington (USFWS 2009). In total, 39,000 square miles of critical lynx habitat was designated in 2009 as follows: Maine: Approximately 15,284 km2 (9,497 square miles) in portions of Aroostook, Franklin, Penobscot, Piscataquis and Somerset Counties. Minnesota: Approximately 12,979 km2 (8,065 square miles) in portions of Cook, Koochiching, Lake, and St. Louis Counties, and Superior National Forest. Northern Rocky Mountains: Approximately 16,258 km2 (10,102 square miles) in portions of Boundary County in Idaho, and Flathead, Glacier, Granite, Lake, Lewis and Clark, Lincoln, Missoula, Pondera, Powell and Teton Counties in Montana. This area includes the Flathead Indian Reservation, National Forest lands and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) lands in the Garnet Resource Area. North Cascades: Approximately 1,836 square miles in portions of Chelan and Okanogan Counties which includes BLM lands in the Spokane District. Greater Yellowstone Area: Approximately 9,500 square miles in Gallatin, Park, Sweetgrass, Stillwater, and Carbon Counties in Montana, and Park, Teton, Fremont, Sublette, and Lincoln Counties in Wyoming. The Kettle range of Washington State was not included as critical habitat due to lack of recent evidence of reproduction, and the reintroduced population of Colorado and Utah in the southern Rockies was also not included due to lack of evidence that it is self-sustaining. A recovery outline for lynx in the contiguous US was released in 2005 and designated critical habitat was identified in 2006 and reevaluated 2007. Critical lynx habitat designation was revised in 2009 and 2014, and a complete species status assessment was released in 2017, with an addendum in 2023 (USFWS 2023).

rationale: Pteropus rufus is assessed as Vulnerable under criteria A2acd+B2ab(iii,iv,v) due to an estimated decline in the population size of 30–35% based on a rate of at least 40% roost abandonment over the last three generations (18 years; generation length = 6 years), with some regions experiencing roost desertion rates up to 70%. These rates of abandonment are coupled with site-specific annual adult mortality estimates approaching 50% in the most impacted areas, contributing to declines in population counts at monitored roost sites. In general, population declines appear to largely result from habitat degradation and forest loss, reflecting broader patterns across Madagascar (at least 25% decrease in Madagascar tree cover (4.85m ha) since 2000). In addition to habitat loss, this species is threatened by disturbance at roost sites and high levels of both legal (May-Sept, with proper permits) and illegal human hunting for consumption. The low reproductive rate of one offspring per year exacerbates the species’ vulnerability to these threats. The species’ area of occupancy (AOO) is 540 km² (based on known roosts) to 433,932 km² (based on the species’ range) and both the extent of occurrence (EOO) and AOO are suspected to be declining due to ongoing habitat loss, fragmentation, and human hunting pressures. There are an estimated 10–100 due to the connectivity among extant roosts, ongoing deforestation and other threats focused at roosts.
habitat: Malagasy Flying Fox roosts in both native and introduced tree species, typically in colonies ranging from 10 to 5,000 individuals, with a median of 400 (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Jenkins et al. 2007), though roosts up to 10,000 individuals have been reported (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). As intact forests are rare across this species’ range, roosts are more commonly found in degraded habitats, fragmented forests, small islands, mangroves, and occasionally in Eucalyptus plantations (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Jenkins et al. 2007), highlighting the species’ ability to survive in modified landscapes. Further, roost sites are often located near water bodies, which may help guide the bats during foraging (Jenkins et al. 2007). While roosting, this species is easily disturbed by people or cattle, and entire colonies will take flight when threatened (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Jenkins et al. 2007, Roberts et al. 2016). If disturbed repeatedly, the bats typically move to an alternative nearby roost site. Each colony typically occupies multiple roost sites spaced <10 km apart within a ~25 km average home range to avoid disturbance and respond to shifting food availability (Jenkins et al. 2007, Oleksy et al. 2015a).Although P. rufus can survive in heavily modified landscapes by feeding on a mix of native and introduced fruits and other plant parts (Bollen 2003, Raheriarisena 2005, Jenkins et al. 2007, Long and Racey 2007), they preferentially roost in native vegetation, such as forest fragments, within the modified landscape. These bats travel up to 30 km nightly between roosts and foraging areas, with an average flight speed of 9.13 m/s (±1.08 SD) and a top-recorded speed of 17.04 m/s (Oleksy et al. 2015a). During gestation, females travel significantly longer distances than males, possibly to meet their increased energy demands (Oleksy et al. 2015a).As frugivores, their diet consists mainly of fruits and pollen, though they also consume flowers, nectar, and leaves (Bollen 2003, Raheriarisena 2005, Jenkins et al. 2007, Long and Racey 2007). The species plays a critical role in seed dispersal. The seeds they ingest pass through their digestive tract often retain viability for over 20 hours. Studies show that seeds passing through their gut exhibit higher germination rates and greater survival compared to undigested seeds direct from the mother tree (Racey et al. 2009, Oleksy et al. 2017). This ecological role is particularly evident in species like Ficus polita and Ficus grevei in southeast Madagascar, where bat-dispersed seeds show significantly higher fitness. In southern Madagascar, pollen from introduced sisal forms an essential dietary component available to bats in all seasons of the year (Long and Racey 2007). The species is important for its ability to travel long distances and its capability as a seed disperser (Bollen and Elsacker 2002, Oleksy et al. 2015a), as well as its role as a pollinator for plants like the threatened baobab species, Adansonia grandidieri (Andriafidison 2016). It is believed to be an important species in fragmented forest ecosystems, where its seed dispersal and pollination capacities promote forest regeneration (Bollen and Elsacker 2002, Bollen et al. 2004, Oleksy et al. 2015a, Andriafidison 2016).As one of the largest bats in the world, P. rufus has a wingspan of 100–125 cm, weighs between 500–750 g, and has a relatively long gestation period of 5–6 months (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022, Andrianiaina et al. 2022). Females give birth to a single pup per season, which is weaned at approximately 4 months of age, coincident with the peak of fruit availability as they begin independent foraging (Andrianiaina et al. 2022). Due to this low reproductive rate, P. rufus is particularly vulnerable to population declines from environmental pressures, such as habitat loss and climate change (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Indeed, recent demographic assessments suggest that field-estimated adult survival rates in the eastern Central Highlands are unable to maintain replacement levels (Brook et al. 2019). Updated estimates of demographic parameters from a wider geographic region, including estimates of annual fecundity and juvenile survival, are critically needed (Brook et al. 2019).
threats: The main threats to P. rufus are habitat loss, hunting, and human disturbance (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Deforestation driven by agriculture, logging, and development continues to destroy or fragment the bats’ roosting habitats, primarily in coastal or fragmented forests (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Analyses suggest that Madagascar experienced a 25% decrease in tree cover (4.85 mha) from 2000 to 2021 (Suzzi-Simmons 2023), or to a 30% decrease (5.2 mha) from 2000 to 2024 (GFW 2024). Forest fragmentation isolates roosting sites, making them more vulnerable to disturbance and environmental changes (Racey et al. 2009). The conversion of forests into agricultural land results in the permanent loss of suitable trees used by roosting bats.Despite legal restrictions, P. rufus hunting remains widespread across Madagascar. The species is classified as a game species under Malagasy law and can be legally hunted between May 1 and September 1 (Randrianandrianina et al. 2010). However, only rare roosts located within protected areas receive some degree of protection (Racey et al. 2009, Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Hunting occurs at both roost sites and foraging sites, particularly when bats feed on village fruit trees (Jenkins and Racey 2008). In just 90 days of the year, 30 active hunters can kill over 9,000 P. rufus (Oleksy 2010). People in urban areas are more likely to consume P. rufus than those in rural areas, with 40% of urban dwellers eating P. rufus compared to 20% in rural areas (Jenkins et al. 2011). This hunting pressure contributes to the ongoing decline of the species’ population.Human disturbance also impacts roosting colonies. Roost sites near settlements are particularly vulnerable, and even minor disturbances can cause colonies to abandon their roosts, increasing energy expenditure and negatively affecting reproduction (Jenkins et al. 2007). These threats are most severe in degraded and fragmented coastal forests where the majority of roosts are located. Climate change poses an additional threat as stronger and more frequent storms have the potential to result in changes in the species’ diet (Reuter et al. 2016), disrupt food availability, and destabilize roosting habitats (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Racey et al. 2009, Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022).
population: Current data on the species’ population size are limited. From April 1999 to December 2000, the P. rufus total population was estimated to be around 300,000 individuals, based on counts of average colony sizes from a subset of roosts from across Madagascar (MacKinnon et al. 2003). Colony sizes varied widely, ranging from as few as 10 bats to as many as 5,000, with a median reported colony size of 400 individuals (MacKinnon et al. 2003). Roosts as large as 10,000 have been reported, though these larger roosts are increasingly rare (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Larger roosts tend to be conspicuous and noisy, with bats tightly clustered, which makes accurate abundance estimates challenging. During the 1999-2000 census, 154 historically recognized roost sites were visited, of which 17.5% were reported to have been abandoned in the past decade (MacKinnon et al. 2003). Of the extant roost sites identified during that census, 40% were reported abandoned by the following decade (Oleksy 2014, Oleksy et al. 2015a). In the Central Highlands, roost desertion rates as high as 70% have been reported (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022), and those remaining show low levels of adult annual survival and patterns of declining population counts over time (Brook et al. 2019). Surveys in the southeastern Anosy Region of Madagascar also indicate a trend of frequent roost abandonment (Roberts et al. 2016).It is unknown if the species’ populations are organized into multiple subpopulations. However, it is likely that subpopulations may develop with increasing habitat fragmentation and the continuing loss of roost sites that isolate portions of the species’ population. Population viability analyses of roost sites in the eastern portion of the Central Highlands estimated adult annual fecundity from field observations (at 0.866) and adult annual survival from age analysis of dentition (at 0.511 [0.313-0.719]) to identify demographic patterns of declining population trajectory for the species (Brook et al. 2019).There is an estimated decline in this species’ population size of 30–35% based on an observed rate of at least 40% roost abandonment over the last three generations (18 years; GL = 6 years) and ongoing threats including a 25% decrease in tree cover (4.85 mha) since 2000 (Suzzi-Simmons 2023) and associated loss of roost sites. In addition, this species is hunted throughout its range for human food, both legally during a specified hunting season from May 1–September 1 and illegally throughout the year (Jenkins and Racey 2008, Randrianandrianina et al. 2010, Oleksy et al. 2015b).
range: The Malagasy Flying Fox (Pteropus rufus) is endemic to Madagascar, where it is widely distributed across the island, ranging from the northern regions around Antsiranana to the southeastern Taolagnaro region, as well as on several coastal islands including Nosy Be, Nosy Komba, Nosy Tanikely, and Ile Sainte-Marie (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Rakotonandrasana and Goodman 2007, Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). This species primarily inhabits humid tropical to subtropical forests, including mangroves, occurring at elevations from sea level up to 1,200 meters; historically, roosts have been found between 100 and 1,400 meters, though higher elevation roosts in the Central Highlands have been deserted at faster rates in recent years (Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). Roost sites are most often located within 100 km of the coast, although a few have been recorded in the Central Highlands (MacKinnon et al. 2003).This bat's extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated between 417,808 and 577,104 km² encompassing the known roosts, while its area of occupancy (AOO) ranges from 540 km² up to 433,932 km². The AOO is calculated based on a 2x2 km² grid over the range, with the minimum AOO based on known roosts and the maximum AOO based on the species' entire range. Both EOO and AOO are suspected to be declining due to ongoing habitat loss, fragmentation, and human hunting pressure. There are an estimated 10–100 threat-based locations due to ongoing deforestation and hunting of the flying foxes that often work in tandem and are focused on the roost sites. While the roosts sites are connected through natural movement of the flying foxes, the threats and disturbance of deforestation and hunting near and at the roosts increases the movement of the bats among roosts sites. While there is increasing isolation of roost sites, the population is not currently considered severely fragmented as some connectivity among roost sites remains. There are no data to suggest extreme fluctuations in the number of locations, EOO, or AOO.
useTrade: Pteropus rufus is widely traded and hunted for human consumption in Madagascar, both for subsistence and commercial gain (Jenkins and Racey 2008, Golden 2009, Randrianandrianina et al. 2010, Jenkins et al. 2011, Razafimanahaka et al. 2012, Golden et al. 2014, Oleksy et al. 2015b); indeed at the commercial level, it is the principal bat species consumed across the country (Jenkins and Racey 2008). Hunting of P. rufus is legal with appropriate permits from May 1-September 1 (Randrianandrianina et al. 2010), though the species is hunted and persecuted illegally throughout the year. In some regions, such as western Madagascar, up to 60% of people consume P. rufus (Razafimanahaka et al. 2012), a pattern which persists today. Commercial sales occur in several regions and hunters have reported selling bats to local markets and restaurants (Oleksy et al. 2015b). Shipments of P. rufus are also sent from more remote locales within Madagascar to the capital for sale and consumption (Oleksy 2010). Although P. rufus is widely consumed locally and distributed in national trade, currently there is no evidence of international trade.
conservationActions: Pteropus rufus is only partially protected under Malagasy law, as it is classified as a game species and can be legally hunted with appropriate permits from May 1 – September 1 (Repoblikan’I Madagasikara 2006, Durbin 2007). It is listed in CITES Appendix II (CITES 2025), but this protection has little relevance as the species in not known to be traded outside of Madagascar (Racey et al. 2009). Some roosts are in protected areas, such as Parc National de Kirindy-Mité, Parc National de Masoala, and Berenty Private Reserve (MacKinnon et al. 2003, Long and Racey 2007, Andrianaivoarivelo et al. 2022). However, many protected areas lack active bat colonies (Goodman 1996). Local conservation efforts are underway, including protecting sacred forests and creating community agreements to safeguard bat populations (Jenkins et al. 2007). These community-driven initiatives have shown promise in some regions. However, hunting remains a significant challenge, undermining conservation efforts. To improve the situation, stronger enforcement of local and national hunting regulations, habitat restoration, and increased community education are necessary.More research is needed on P. rufus, particularly its population size, roost occupancy trends, annual survival rates, and reproductive success. Updated surveys to sites across the island are necessary to assess the current population status, especially in areas with heavy hunting pressure. Additional studies on foraging behavior, reproductive biology, seed dispersal effectiveness, and movement ecology would provide valuable insights to inform future conservation strategies. Research into the impacts of climate change and habitat fragmentation is also essential. Further work is needed to assess the sustainability of hunting at both local and regional scales (Racey et al. 2009), with the aim of developing a quantitative harvest management plan.

rationale: Rhinolophus hilli is endemic to Rwanda, where it is known only from Nyungwe National Park. This species is assessed as Endangered under criterion B1ab(i,ii,iii,v). Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is calculated at 1,654 km² based on a minimum convex polygon around Nyungwe National Park (its presumed range). It occurs as a single population within the park, which is inferred to be declining as there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to low-levels of agriculture. The loss of habitat also contributes to a suspected decline in both EOO and area of occupancy (AOO).
habitat: Rhinolophus hilli is an insectivorous bat species and the only records of this species are from the Albertine rift montane tropical moist forest in (Fahr et al. 2002). The day roost sites of the species are not known, but extensive cave surveys carried out in Nyungwe National Park, Rwanda in 2019 failed to locate any cave roosts, suggesting that tree cavities may be used as roosting sites. It is not known if the species can persist in areas of degraded forest.
threats: Fahr et al. (2002) indicates that while there is little information available on this seemingly limited range species, it is probably threatened by habitat destruction (presumably by logging operations and the conversion of land to agricultural use). Between 1984 and 2015 the forest area of Nyungwe National Park decreased by 15%. Fires, typically caused by illegal honey collection and poaching, consumed 13,000 ha of the park in 1997 (REMA 2015). There is continuing low-level deforestation due to agricultural encroachment in some parts of the park.
population: There is little information available on the population status of this species as it has rarely been captured and colonies of this species have yet to be found but are likely to be small (Fahr et al. 2002). It was confirmed as extant in 2019 with three new records documented in Nyungwe National Park. It is inferred to be organized in one population given the forest distribution within the region. The species population and number of mature individuals is suspected to be declining as there is a continuing loss in the extent and quality of its habitat. There is no evidence to suggest extreme fluctuations in the the species population.
range: This species is endemic to Rwanda and is known only from Nyungwe National Park; one location that is threatened by deforestation. Previously, it was known only from two sites that were approximately 8 km apart. In 2019, three new records for the species, from captures and acoustic surveys, were made in the same general area. It has an elevational range of between 1,750 and 2,512 m asl (Fahr et al. 2002). The species' extent of occurrence (EOO) is calculated at 1,654 km² based on a minimum convex polygon around Nyungwe National Park (its presumed range) and its area of occupancy (AOO) is calculated at 1,320 km² based on a 2x2 km grid overlaid on the national park. While its EOO and AOO are likely experiencing low level declines due to deforestation just within Nyungwe National Park, there is no evidence to suggest extreme fluctuations in its EOO or AOO.
useTrade: The species is not known to be used or traded
conservationActions: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for the species. However, it does receive the benefit of being located within the Nyungwe National Park, and given its range, would also qualify as a formal trigger species for the Nyungwe National Park Key Biodiversity Area as 100% of the species range and population is suspected to reside within the national park. Protection and restoration of forest habitat within and around Nyungwe National Park would benefit the species as would expanded community awareness programs. Additional research into the species' population size and trend, distribution, threats, ecology (e.g., roosting), and natural history would improve conservation actions for the species.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, and lack of major threats; it is tolerant to habitat disturbance and its population is increasing.
habitat: It is found in large blocks of hardwood or mixed forests, as well as in urban and suburban areas. Prefers mature deciduous and mixed forests with abundant supplies of mast (e.g., acorns, hickory nuts). A diversity of nut trees is needed to support high densities. It also uses city parks and floodplains. Seldom far from permanent open water. In southern Alabama, narrow bands of hardwoods along ephemeral streams were an important component of the habitat in even-aged pine and mixed pine-hardwood stands. It rests in tree cavity or leaf nest; leaf nests apparently are made primarily by dispersing juveniles 18-19 weeks old. It nests in tree cavities or in leaf nests, usually 25 feet or more above the ground. Most winter-spring litters are born in tree cavities, most spring-summer litters in leaf nests (Teaford 1986). Cavities suitable for nesting are dry, 15-25 cm in diameter, 40-50 cm deep, with an entrance hole about eight cm in diameter (Teaford 1986). Females may move young from tree cavity nest to leaf nest, possibly to escape fleas. In Illinois, most breeding occurs in December-February and May-June; slightly later in more northern latitudes (Koprowski 1994). One or two litters per year. First litter is produced mostly in February-March, sometimes as early as January in some areas; second litter, July or August. Gestation lasts 44 days. Litter size most often is 2-3. Young are tended by female. Weaning is completed at about 10-12 weeks (in spring and/or late summer-early autumn). Most breed as yearlings, sometimes sooner (as early as five months) or later. Reproductive output, including the percentage of adults that produce young and the number of litters per year, is positively correlated with mast abundance. Maximum reproductive longevity is about a decade.Home range averages 0.5-10 ha, with older males tending to have the largest ranges (Teaford 1986); usually home range is less than five hectares (Koprowski 1994). Not territorial, home range overlap is extensive; social system is characterized by a linear dominance hierarchy. Disperses up to a few kilometres from natal area upon approaching sexual maturity. Large-scale one-way emigrations have been observed, generally coinciding with high population density and mast crop failure. It is pray of many predators, but predation does not appear to limit populations (Teaford 1986). Mean annual mortality reported for adults is 42-57% (Koprowski 1994). Diet consists of seeds, fruits, nuts, fungi, occasional insects and small vertebrates (e.g., bird eggs). Scatterhoarder; buries nuts and acorn in autumn for later consumption (winter-spring). It is active during the day, particularly in the morning and late afternoon, though unimodal activity may occur in winter. May be inactive for a day or two during extremely cold, snowy weather.
threats: There are no major threats to this species.
population: This species is widespread and abundant.There are reported densities of 21/ha in urban parks. Population and range are increasing (J Koprowski pers. comm.).
range: This species is found in the eastern United States and adjacent southern Canada; southern Quebec to Manitoba, south to eastern Texas and Florida. Its range has been extended through introductions into Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, California, Oregon, Washington, and Montana (Teaford 1986, Koprowski 1994). It is also introduced in the British Isles, Italy, South Africa, and Australia (extirpated by 1973), but these introduced ranges are not included in the map here (Koprowski 1994).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in several protected areas (D. Tirira pers. comm).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered due to a suspected population reduction of at least 50% over the past ten years, based on ongoing declines in habitat quality. Out of 26 recorded localities, 14 are no longer classified as primary forest. These declines are primarily driven by agricultural expansion, urban development, and cattle ranching, which have resulted in extensive degradation and loss of suitable habitat across the species' range.
habitat: Xenomys nelsoni inhabits tropical deciduous and semi-deciduous forests. These forests are characterized by strong climatic seasonality and dense, closed canopies, which are critical to the species' arboreal and nocturnal lifestyle (Ceballos and Miranda 2000). This species is particularly associated with areas that have a high density of trees and woody vines, using these as arboreal runways and for shelter in holes and cavities within trunks and branches (Cervantes-Reza and Montaño-Sosa 2019).This species is active from shortly after dusk until midnight, predominantly foraging between 1 and 4 meters above the ground, although individuals have occasionally been found in ground traps (Schaldach 1960). It uses holes and cavities in the branches and trunks of trees as shelter, as well as bowers and clumps of foliage (Cervantes-Reza and Montaño-Sosa 2019). In the Chamela-Cuixmala region, around 65% of individuals were captured within trees, while the remainder were located at the tree base, highlighting its preference for arboreal habitats (Ceballos 2014).Reproduction occurs mainly from May through November, aligning with the rainy season. Females generally produce small litters, with an average of 1.6 offspring (Schaldach 1960). Pregnant females have been recorded with one or two embryos, captured during the late dry season and the beginning of the wet season (Schaldach 1960, Ceballos and Miranda 2000).
threats: The primary threats to X. nelsoni include significant habitat loss due to agricultural expansion, urban development, and cattle ranching (Ballesteros-Barrera et al. 2023). Moreover, it has been documented that 14 of the 26 recorded collection sites are no longer classified as primary forest, reflecting severe habitat degradation (Ballesteros-Barrera et al. 2023). The remaining forested areas in Colima, where the species was historically present, are now highly disturbed, placing the species' continued survival in these regions at serious risk (Cervantes-Reza and Montaño-Sosa 2019).
population: This species is known only from three localities (Ceballos et al. 2002). It is present in very low numbers. The only population study carried out was in the Chamela-Cuixmala Biosphere Reserve in Jalisco and revealed population densities were low, and varied from 0.3 to 1 individual per hectare in low tropical forests and adjacent medium tropical forests respectively. Destruction of dry tropical forests contributes to a population decline (Ceballos 2014). The Magdalena Wood Rat, Xenomys nelsoni, is characterized by a limited number of occurrences, with 69 records documented since 1892. Of these, approximately 65 individuals have been preserved across various scientific collections (Ballesteros-Barrera et al. 2023). The scarcity of these records, combined with the species' preference for intact tropical dry forests, suggests that X. nelsoni only exists in small, isolated populations (Ballesteros-Barrera et al. 2023).A population reduction of at least 50% is suspected over the past 10 years, inferred from the loss of primary forest at more than half of the species' known sites. Specifically, 14 of 26 recorded localities are no longer classified as primary forest (Ballesteros-Barrera et al. 2023).
range: This species is endemic to the tropical coastal lowlands (from sea level to 450 m asl) on Mexico’s Pacific coast, in Colima and southwest Jalisco, México (Musser and Carleton 2005, Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This species is currently known to occur within a single protected area, the Chamela-Cuixmala Biosphere Reserve. It is classified as Threatened under Mexican law (NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2010). An action plan for its conservation was proposed during the Mexican Small Mammal Assessment, Prioritization, and Conservation Planning Workshop (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018) and identified the following objectives and actions:Objective 1: Determine the status of the current populationMonitor the distribution and abundance - need to develop the detailed steps to be implemented for the monitoring protocolCharacterize the genetics of the populationObjective 2: Increase habitat protection coverage and connectivityEnlarge protected area network - develop detailed stepsExpand watershed management in the region - develop detailed steps (including restoration) for the required studies.Objective 3: Create assurance ex situ populationsInfrastructure, biosecurity, land purchasePermitsDevelop management protocolsEx situ management of the speciesObjective 4: Create public awareness and positive perception and attitudes Strengthen education actions at the local level

rationale: Heteromys nelsoni is restricted to cloud forests in the mountain range of the southern state of Chiapas, Mexico, and western Guatemala. It has a small extent of occurrence (EOO = 482 km²). The species currently is only known from three locations, all of which are experiencing significant and ongoing habitat loss from agricultural expansion, heavy logging, extensive cattle grazing, mining and extraction of firewood and timber for building houses. These threats are contributing to a continuous decline in its area of occupancy (AOO), EOO, and the overall area, extent, and quality of its habitat. Further reductions in available habitat are particularly concerning for Heteromys nelsoni, given its narrow altitudinal range within the cloud forest montane belt and this species could become Critically Endangered in the near future if its habitat availability and EOO continue to decline. For now, it is assessed as Endangered (EN B1ab(i,ii,iii)).
habitat: The biology and ecology of the species are poorly known. This species has a restricted, narrow altitudinal range. It is found on cold, wet slopes of cloud forest characterized by numerous epiphytes, mosses, and fallen trees (Rogers and Rogers 1992, Reid 1997, Wilson et al. 2016).
threats: This species is threatened primarily by habitat loss and degradation due to excessive logging, extensive cattle grazing, mining, extraction of firewood and timber for building houses, and agricultural expansion (Rios et al. 2016, Lorenzo et al. 2019a). Additional threats include stochastic events like storms and flooding (Cuarón and Vázquez 2018), and climate change, which may further reduce its limited distribution range (Rogers and Rogers 1992, Lorenzo et al. 2019b).
population: This rodent is considered rare and has a restricted distribution (Reid 1997, Wilson et al. 2016). Population sampling in Chiapas, Mexico, was conducted over two distinct periods (Lorenzo C. pers. comm. 2024). From 2008 to 2011, five field expeditions at Cerro El Mozotal involved 24 nights of sampling, totalling 5,220 trap nights, and yielded 38 captures, resulting in a capture index of 0.0072 individuals per trap night (Lorenzo C. pers. comm. 2024). In a subsequent monitoring period between 2017 and 2018, three expeditions were conducted at the species' type locality in Pinabeto, Chiapas (Lorenzo C. pers. comm. 2024). Over 17 nights of sampling, and 3,400 trap nights, only five individuals were recorded, yielding a reduced capture index of 0.0014 individuals per trap night (Lorenzo C. pers. comm. 2024). Additionally, sampling conducted in March 2010 over seven nights in San Marcos, Guatemala, at elevations ranging from 2,100 to 2,600 meters, failed to detect any individuals (Lorenzo C. pers. comm. 2024).
range: This species is restricted to cloud forests in the mountain range of the southern state of Chiapas, Mexico, and western Guatemala (Rios et al. 2016, Wilson et al. 2016). It has a narrow altitudinal range, occurring between 2,480 and 2,850 m asl (Lorenzo et al. 2019a). Only three locations are currently identified: two in southern Chiapas, Mexico, including Pinabeto, the type locality in the municipality of Motozintla, and Cerro Mozotal, which includes the municipalities of El Porvenir and Siltepec (Lorenzo et al. 2019a). The third location is on the southern slope of the Tajumulco volcano in western Guatemala. Although the Guatemalan population may have persisted beyond 2006, it is believed to have been severely impacted by Hurricane Stan (Cuarón and Vázquez 2018).
conservationActions: This species is classified as “Subject to special protection” by the Mexican Government (SEMARNAT 2010). In Guatemala, the population has been documented in a protected area at Tajumulco (Lorenzo et al. 2019a).

rationale: This species is endemic to the Ángel de la Guarda Island in the northern Gulf of California, México. It is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) under criterion D, as no individuals have been recorded since 1991 despite targeted surveys conducted in 2010 and 2015. The species is endemic to Ángel de la Guarda Island and previously occurred on the smaller islets of Mejía, Granito, and Estanque. It is now presumed to be extirpated from all but possibly one location. The continuing threats, including predation by feral cats and competition from the invasive house mouse (Mus musculus), are severe and ongoing, and are believed to have led to the near or complete extinction of the species.
habitat: This species inhabits xeric scrublands, including areas with hylophytes a few meters above sea level. It has been found in various microhabitats on islands: in rocky areas with vegetation, on open plains with chollas, and in dense bushes near the beach (Mellink and Luévano 2014). They are known to reproduce in the spring (Mellink and Luévano 2014). Their predators are owls, snakes, and domestic cats (Vázquez-Domínguez et al. 2004, Mellink and Luévano 2014).
threats: Primary threats to this species include competition with introduced rodents, particularly Mus musculus, predation by feral and domestic cats (Felis catus) (Vázquez-Domínguez et al. 2004), and vulnerabilities associated with its small population size and restricted distribution (Ríos and Álvarez-Castañeda 2011). Increased human activity is anticipated due to the Mexican government’s development plans for the Gulf of California as a major tourist destination, which could elevate the risk of additional non-native species introductions (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2006). Stable isotope analysis has indicated that Mus musculus consumes marine resources similar to those utilized by P. guardia, suggesting that the house mouse may have occupied the ecological niche left by the potentially extinct P. guardia (Blázquez et al. 2018). Additionally, predation by feral cats has likely been a significant factor in the decline of P. guardia, as evidenced by fecal analysis showing remains of native species, such as Chaetodipus spinatus guardiae, as well as seeds, insects, M. musculus, and other small animals (Blázquez et al. 2018).
population: Although this species apparently was common in the mid-1960s, population declines have been observed over the past three decades to the extent that no population is currently known to still be extant, and the species could in fact be extinct. On Ángel de la Guarda Island, it was last recorded in 1991 (Mellink et al. 2002); populations are thought to be extremely low on this island due to predation by feral cats, and the species may possibly have been extirpated (Vázquez-Domínguez et al. 2004). The most recent record of the subspecies in Angel de la Guarda Island is of two specimens collected in 1991 (Mellink and Luévano 2014), while surveys conducted in 2010 and 2015 failed to detect any individuals of P. guardia (Blázquez et al. 2018). No individuals have been recorded in several surveys on the Islands of Mejía and Granito (Álvarez-Castañeda and Ortega-Rubio 2003), and the subspecies seem to be Extinct or in danger of extinction from these islands (Mellink et al. 2002, Álvarez-Castañeda and Ortega-Rubio 2003). The species is said to be extirpated from Estanque Island (Vázquez-Domínguez et al. 2004).
range: This species is endemic to the Ángel de la Guarda Island in the northern Gulf of California, México (Peromyscus guardia guardia), and historically its islets: Mejía (P. g. mejiae), Granito (P. g. harbisoni), and Estanque (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). However, it is now extinct from Granito and Mejía Islands (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). On Ángel de la Guarda, it has only been recorded in the northern tip, the surrounding area of Puerto Refugio, and in the northeast in Los Cantiles (Mellink and Luévano 2014).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in a protected area (Comisión Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas 2024).  An action plan for its conservation was proposed during the Mexican Small Mammal Assessment, Prioritization, and Conservation Planning Workshop (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018) and identified the following objectives and actions:Objective 1: Determine the status of the populationsMonitor the distribution and abundance of populations - need to develop the detailed steps to be implemented for the monitoring protocol.Characterize the genetics of the populationObjective 2: Captive breeding and reintroductions to islands where the species is currently extinct fromEradicate House Mouse (Mus musculus) from Mejia and Granito.Confirm absence of cats (Felis catus) on Estanque Island.Reintroduction of P. guardia to Mejia, Granito, and Estanque.Find collaborating institution for the captive breeding program.Removing of individuals.Monitoring of genetic diversity.Objective 3: Monitor reintroduction successMonitor the distribution and abundance of populations - need to develop the detailed steps to be implemented for the monitoring protocol.Characterize the genetics of the populations.

rationale: Pteropus livingstonii is assessed as Endangered under criteria B1ab(i,ii,iii)+2ab(i,ii,iii) due to their limited extent of occurrence (EOO) of 1,602 km² and area of occupancy (AOO) of approximately 356 km². The species occurs in only two disjunct locations on Anjouan (total land area = 424 km²) and Mohéli (total land area = 290 km²) which are separated by ca 40 km, and both islands are small enough that a single severe weather event may impact all remaining habitat and the species’ population on either island negatively. There is a continuing decline in availability and quality of the remaining forest habitat due to continuing deforestation and agricultural activities, which in turn, leads to a continuing decrease in the size of the EOO and AOO.
habitat: The species occurs naturally in lowland and montane tropical rainforests on the islands of Anjouan and Mohéli (Smith and Leslie 2006). Their roost trees, mainly consisting of old-growth individuals of endemic or native tree species, are generally located between 500 and 1,100 m asl (Granek 2000, Ibouroi et al. 2018b). Roost sites are often situated on deep slopes, in the vicinity of rivers (Granek 2000, Ibouroi et al. 2018b). Larger colonies can be found at densely forested sites, as the bats are strongly associated with increased presence of endemic and native trees (Granek 2000, Ibouroi et al. 2018b). The bats heavily rely on native, old-growth forest trees for roosting and feeding (Granek 2002) which are targeted for timber by the local population (Shepherd et al. 2019). Deforestation continues to be a major threat to the species as it results in habitat loss. Since 2016 at least three long-term roost sites have been lost or abandoned due to disturbance through landscape change or weather events. The suitable habitat for this species is projected to continue declining if no further conservation measures are put into place.As long as large, native and endemic trees remain, this species seems to be able to survive in degraded forested habitat, with some feeding sites located in areas with extensive agricultural activities (Mandl et al. 2021). Pteropus livingstonii switches between roosts regularly but very little is known of their overall ecological requirements (Mandl et al. 2021). There seems to be clustered feeding sites throughout their range, but foraging behaviours and diet of the species are not well studied; preliminary data suggests a mixture of introduced and native fruit and flowers (Sewall et al. 2007).Life history traits are available based on information from a captive population at Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust in Jersey. Generation length can be estimated at 9.7 years based on data from captive individuals, closely related species, and taxonomically adjusted allometric equations (Sewall et al. 2007, Tidemann and Nelson 2011).
threats: The greatest threat to the species is habitat loss through deforestation to make room for small-holder farms and plantations, and shifting agriculture, as well as urban development, including housing and roads. The Comoros had some of the highest deforestation rates worldwide between 1990-2010, with an estimated 5–8% forest loss per year in that period (Hawlitschek et al. 2011, Boussougou and Brou 2015, Doulton et al. 2015, Olagunju 2015, Shepherd et al. 2019). Between 2010 and 2020 the Union of Comoros experienced a net loss of 1.24% of forest area per year (FAO 2020). On Anjouan, the remaining forest fragments are mainly located on inaccessible, steep slopes and are under high pressure from the local population. Deforestation is largely driven by a need for farmland and timber for construction (Shepherd et al. 2019, Ibouroi et al. 2021). Large, old-growth, native trees, that are of particular importance to P. livingstonii are preferentially targeted for furniture-building and construction, with over 1,200 trees logged annually in the south-west of Anjouan alone (Shepherd et al. 2019). When soil becomes infertile, the process is repeated, shifting agriculture into more forested areas. Widespread ylang-ylang distillation for the international perfume market has led to an increase in demand for fuelwood and space for plantations. Despite local protective measures, forested areas continue to be cleared and there may come a point when the bats’ ecological needs may no longer be met.Tropical storms impact the Comoros on average three times per year but the severity and the frequency of these storm in the Western Indian Ocean seem to be increasing due to climate change (Mavume et al. 2010, Mawren et al. 2022). Long-term effects of severe tropical storms on the bat population of Comoros are not understood, although comparative sites have shown increased mortality due to loss of critical resources (McConkey et al. 2004)—a scenario that is likely for Comoros, given the limited amount of forested area and the paucity of large, mature trees.
population: Regular population surveys since 2012 found a maximum of 1,200 to 1,500 P. livingstonii individuals on Anjouan and a maximum of 300 to 400 individuals on Mohéli (Daniel et al. 2017, Ibouroi et al. 2018b, Mandl et al. 2024). While the distance between the islands can be crossed by Pteropus (Breed et al. 2010), there is genetic evidence that the subpopulations do not interbreed, potentially forming two distinct populations (Ibouroi et al. 2018a). We estimate the number of mature individuals of the total population to be between 1,200 and 1,500, based on capture records and demographic studies on wild Pteropus populations, where ~20-30% of individuals in a population were considered immature (Fox et al. 2008). The species has been monitored at known roost sites between 1992 and 2006 by researchers and the NGO Action Comores (Reason and Trewhella 1994, Sewall et al. 2007), followed by ongoing bi-annual surveys implemented by the NGO Dahari since 2014 and in collaboration with the Mohéli Marine Park since 2019 (Mandl et al. 2024). Over the past decade, the P. livingstonii population on the Comoros has been stable (Mandl et al. 2024). The population may have been stable before, but irregular sampling effort provided inadequate information to draw conclusions over a longer time period. While the bat population does not undergo severe fluctuations, variations in population estimates over time stem from the discovery of new roost sites, seasonal differences (Ibouroi et al. 2018b), and previous weather events, such as cyclones in early 2019 and 2023 (Mandl et al. 2024).
range: Pteropus livingstonii is endemic to the Union of Comoros, occurring on the islands of Anjouan and Mohéli (Reason and Trewhella 1994, Goodman et al. 2010). The islands are approx. 40 km apart, a distance that many species of Pteropus can cross (Breed et al. 2010) and both islands are small enough (Anjouan: 424 km²; Mohéli: 290 km²) that a single severe weather event, such as a cyclone, can negatively impact the entire subpopulation on a single island. The bats inhabit forested areas between 200 and 1,100 m elevation above sea level: on Anjouan, which has a higher elevation profile, no important feeding or roosting sites are found below 450 m asl (Granek 2000, Daniel et al. 2017, Ibouroi et al. 2018b, Mandl et al. 2021). The species’ extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are based on habitat suitability modelling for P. livingstonii over the species’ elevation range of 200 to 1,100 m asl (Ibouroi et al. 2018b). A total area of suitable habitat for the species was 159.2 km² across both islands, consisting of two larger areas and several smaller disconnected patches. The EOO, calculated as a minimum convex polygon around the suitable habitat, is 1,602.7 km² which includes a considerable amount of non-inhabitable ocean area. The AOO, estimated by overlaying a 2x2 km grid over the suitable habitat and counting all occupied cells, is 316 km² across both islands.
useTrade: The species is not known to be used or traded.
conservationActions: Conservation actions in place: A detailed conservation plan for P. livingstonii, developed by the NGO Action Comores and a range of stakeholders, was published in 2007 (Sewall et al. 2007). It outlines necessary actions to preserve the species, including habitat protection and management, environmental education, population monitoring, ecological research, ex-situ breeding, and international collaborations. It was adopted by the government of the Union of the Comoros as the national conservation strategy for this species. Population monitoring was implemented by the NGO Action Comores in cooperation with Comorian communities between 1992 and 2006, establishing the basis for a long-term data set. Population and roost habitat surveys were continued by Engagement Communautaire pour le Developpement Durable (ECDD) of the Bristol Zoological Society and Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust between 2010 and 2012 and have since been undertaken bi-annually by the Comorian NGO Dahari and the Mohéli Marine Park.The majority of the important long-term roost sites, as well as the remaining natural forest habitat are located within the protected areas Mount Ntringui National Park on Anjouan and Mohéli National Park.The NGO Dahari has been implementing a Conservation Agreements scheme since 2015.
