Seven roost sites, including key sites as identified by the Conservation Action Plan, are currently protected through the scheme, with planning underway to expand further across the landscape, including important feeding sites and resources, on Anjouan.A successful ex-situ breeding colony has been established in the United Kingdom at the Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust since the 1990s. In 2023 another breeding colony was established at Northumberland Country Zoo, and additional breeding groups are planned for the future in at least one more zoo. These are meant as a genetic safety net for the species.A successful environmental education campaign, which raised local and international awareness of the species, and its threats was implemented by the NGO Action Comores until 2006. In addition, the campaign focused on training local personnel and increased participation in bat population surveys. The NGO Dahari continues to conduct awareness and outreach activities as part of their landscape conservation efforts.In the Union of the Comoros, the species is listed as an ‘integrally-protected species’ (Arrêté n°01/031/MPE/CAB, 14 May 2001), which prohibits the capture or detention of P. livingstonii individuals without a permit. This law also expressly prohibits the killing of flying fox individuals; transport, purchase, sale, export, or re-export of live or dead flying fox individuals or body parts; all disruption during the period of reproduction and raising of young; and the destruction of roosts. The species is also listed on Appendix II of CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora).Community-based ecotourism programs are available on Mohéli: guided tours including visits to a roost site are maintained by the local community (Ouallah Deux).Conservation actions needed:A new edition of the Conservation Action Plan is needed, incorporating the updated information on the species’ population, range and threats.Effective protection and restoration of important bat resources (such as roost sites and feeding trees) outside protected areas.Effective management of bat habitat within established protected areas.Replace the use of endemic trees for the construction and furniture trades. Alongside efforts to reduce tree cutting it will be important to work from the other end of the value chain and look at ways of replacing endemic species with imported timber or through planting appropriate non-native species.Improvement of agricultural practices towards more sustainable alternatives throughout Anjouan and Mohéli.Research implemented & needed:Since the 1990s ecological research has been conducted into a) taxonomy, b) habitat quality, c) population genetics, and d) population trends of this species, with further research into spatial and feeding ecology underway.Important research into habitat trends and projected habitat loss for the upcoming decades is needed to inform conservation priorities.

rationale: The Ampurta is listed Least Concern. Monitoring across much of the distribution of the species provides robust evidence of a large increase in abundance and distribution over the period 2015 to 2021 (Cullen et al. 2025), precluding it from listing under criteria A, B and C. Its population size is unknown, but is doubtless >1,000 mature individuals, and it does not have a restricted area of occupancy or number of locations, so it does not qualify for listing under criterion D. The Ampurta was de-listed (from Vulnerable) under Australian environmental legislation in 2018.
habitat: The Ampurta is a mostly nocturnal marsupial, with a diet comprising a broad range of invertebrates and small vertebrates and carrion (Masters 2008, Cullen et al. 2025). During the day it shelters in burrow systems, typically located at the base of grass clumps or bushes (Woolley 1990). It mostly occurs in sand dunes, with sparse vegetation (including the tall grass Zygochloa paradoxa), and in herblands and sparse grasslands bordering salt lakes (Masters 2008, Pavey et al. 2011). In an area of sympatry, the Spinifex Mulgara D. blythi occupied sand plain and gibber plain, and the Ampurta occupied sand ridges with tussock grasses (Woolley 2005, Pavey et al. 2011, Vega et al. 2025). Distributional modelling from all known records of ampurtas found that the likelihood of occurrence was negatively associated with elevation, and was also associated with some seasonal rainfall and other climatic parameters (Cullen et al. 2025). Modelling of monitoring data showed that Ampurta occurrence at plots was negatively related to both cat and rabbit abundance in the antecedent 12 months (Cullen et al. 2025). Reproduction is mostly seasonal, with births in winter and early spring (Wood Jones 1949, Masters 2023). Sexual maturity is reached in the first year (Wood Jones 1949).
threats: As with many mammals from arid and semi-arid Australia, this species is likely threatened by predation by and competition with feral Cats and Red Foxes, habitat degradation due to livestock and feral herbivores, and, possibly, inappropriate fire regimes (Finlayson 1961, Burbidge et al. 1988, Woinarski et al. 2015, Cullen et al. 2025).
population: There has been no robust assessment of population size, nor that of individual subpopulations. Woolley (2008) considered that it has ‘a presumed large population’. Pavey et al. (2011) captured only 23 individuals over a 39-month study on 20 monitoring plots and 49 survey sites across five habitat types in a 7,000 km2 area of the Simpson Desert region, and noted that predator impacts on population viability may be particularly pronounced when seasonal conditions lead to relatively small regional-scale population size. Between the 1930s and 1960s, Finlayson (1961) noted that mulgaras (including this species, in part) were ‘everywhere much reduced’ across large segments of central Australia; and on the basis of documentation of Aboriginal knowledge across central Australia in the decades leading to the 1980s, Burbidge et al. (1988) noted that ‘most people said it had disappeared. Some said it was still around and relatively common in certain areas, but these statements could have referred to what is now understood to be more than one species. Woolley (2008) considered that the population trend was ‘stable’. In at least the north of South Australia the distribution and (probably) population size of the species increased substantially over the period 1995-2015 in association with decline in European Rabbit numbers due to the spread of rabbit calicivirus, which had the effect of reducing the abundance of Red Foxes and feral Cats (Pedler et al. 2016).A fauna monitoring program (based on signs of burrows, tracks and spoors in 2-ha plots) was established in 2015 across an extensive area of South Australia. 110 of these plots were within the Ampurta’s range, with a further 44 plots added in 2019 and another 39 added in 2021 (to the east, mostly in far SW Queensland and far NW New South Wales) (Cullen et al. 2025). In addition, at four sites in this area, systematic vehicle-based spotlight surveys and live trapping was conducted three times per year from 2011 to 2021 (Cullen et al. 2025). These monitoring programs demonstrated that, notwithstanding a prolonged drought during part of the period of monitoring, Ampurtas increased their known range by >48,000 km2 since 2015. The total abundance of Ampurta spoor detected and the proportion of occupied plots increased across the period 2015-2021. In 2015, interpretation of evidence indicated that Ampurtas were common at 2% of sampled plots and moderately common at 21% of sampled plots. By 2021, Ampurtas were common at 26% of sampled plots and moderately common at 35% of sampled plots (Cullen et al. 2025). Over the period 2015 to 2021, the known extent of occurrence of Ampurtas increased from 189,878 km2 to 238,441 km2 (Cullen et al. 2025). Contextualizing this observed increase, Cullen et al. (2025) concluded that ‘The demonstrated 20.5 % increase in global extent of occurrence for Ampurta, achieved during severe drought, is one of the clearest recent examples of native mammalian re-expansion under climate extremes. This is a rare and hopeful conservation signal in an otherwise declining trend for arid-zone species’ As part of a reintroduction program at Wild Deserts (Sturt National Park, far NW NSW) a trial translocation of 19 Ampurtas within a predator exclosure was conducted in 2020 (West et al. 2023).
range: The Ampurta is endemic to Australia. It is known from the Simpson Desert, Sturt Stony Desert, Tirari Desert. Strzelecki Desert and throughout the southern Lake Eyre Basin (Letnic et al. 2016, Indigo et al. 2021, Newman-Martin et al. 2023, Vega et al. 2025). In at least the north of South Australia the distribution of the species increased substantially over the period 1995-2015 in association with decline in European Rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus numbers due to the spread of rabbit calicivirus, which had the effect of reducing the abundance of Red Foxes and feral Cats (Pedler et al. 2016). Geographic range has increased further over the period 2015-2021 (Cullen et al. 2025).
conservationActions: The Ampurta is present in some conservation reserves, where it is protected from some threats.

rationale: The Eastern Delicate Mouse is Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in many protected areas, and tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Although population size and trends are not well resolved, it does not meet Criterion A for listing because if declining the rate of any such decline is much less than 30% over a 10-year period. It does not meet criterion B because its actual AOO and EOO exceed threshold values, is not severely fragmented, occurs at >10 locations and does not show extreme fluctuations. It does not meet criterion C because its population size is likely to substantially exceed 10,000 mature individuals. It does not meet criterion D because it does not have a very small or restricted population.
habitat: It is generally found in sandy, well drained, sparsely grassed open areas (Flannery 1995). The species can survive in degraded, and heavily grazed, savanna woodland (Ford 2008). It is nocturnal and terrestrial. Its diet and reproductive characteristics are likely to be similar to the better-studied Pseudomys delicatulus, so is likely to be mostly granivorous, but including also fruits, grass stems and invertebrates. As with Pseudomys delicatulus, its litter size is likely to be 3-4, and individuals are likely to have multiple litters each year. In one study in north-eastern Queensland it (as Pseudomys delicatulus) occurred preferentially in recently burnt and ungrazed sampling plots (Kutt and Woinarski 2007).
threats: Feral Cats (Felis catus) are known predators (Woolley et al. 2019), but this predation is unlikely to have population-level impacts. Based on modelling, Roycroft et al. (2024) concluded that its distribution was likely to contract severely with ongoing climate change. Much of its range is subject to livestock production, and one study indicated a negative response to cattle grazing (Kutt and Woinarski 2007).
population: Although there are no estimates of density or population size, this is a common species across much of its extensive distribution.
range: The Eastern Delicate Mouse has an extensive distribution in eastern Australia. Records from southern Papua New Guinea (Morehead Station) are presumably Pseudomys mimulus, however no specimens were included in the genetic analyses and taxonomic review (Roycroft et al. 2024). The distribution also includes Groote Eylandt (Northern Territory) and adjacent Winchelsea Island (Roycroft et al. 2024). It also occurs on K’gari (Fraser Island) and Moa Island (Torres Strait).
conservationActions: The Eastern Delicate Mouse occurs in many protected areas including Groote Eylandt Indigenous Protected Area, White Mountain National Park, K’gari (Fraser Island), Dipperu National Park, and Pilliga Nature Reserve (Roycroft et al. 2024).

rationale: Pseudomys pilbarensis is evaluated as Least Concern because it is widespread, with an extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 494,178 km2, has a population size that is inferred to exceed 10,000 mature individuals, it is not severely fragmented and there is no evidence to indicate continuing decline.
habitat: In the Pilbara, the Western Delicate Mouse inhabits areas with mainly sandy soils where it can easily construct burrows, and avoids heavier soil types (Gibson and McKenzie 2009). In Purnululu National Park, Pseudomys pilbarensis was patchily common, especially on alluvial sands and deep sand plains, with relatively tall woodlands and dense cover of tussock grass or spinifex (Woinarski 1992).The Western Delicate Mouse is likely to have a similar diet to the better known Northern Delicate Mouse Pseudomys delicatulus: in Kakadu National Park, Northern Territory, the Delicate Mouse Pseudomys delicatulus is primarily herbivorous consuming grass seeds, leaves and stems, but will also eat fruits and insects (Braithwaite and Brady 1993).
threats: Introduced Red Foxes Vulpes vulpes and feral Cats Felis catus occur throughout the species’ range, but there are no data to suggest that predation is significant at the population level. European Rabbits Oryctolagus cuniculus occur only patchily in Pseudomys pilbarensis habitat and are unlikely to affect population size. Fire regimes have changed since First Nations people moved to settlements, now being reinstated in some areas (e.g. Legge et al. 2024), but there are no data to suggest that this is a significant factor affecting population size. Mining is a major industry in parts of its range, but the species’ total distribution is extensive.
population: There is no robust information on density or total population size, but it is almost certainly >10,000 mature individuals. The population size is likely to be stable; however, like other Australian arid zone rodents, population size will fluctuate with rainfall.
range: The species occurs in the Pilbara, Great Sandy Desert, Victoria River District and south-eastern Kimberley of Australia. This is a large distribution, with a total extent of occurrence of nearly 500,000 km2. Existing records suggest that the Western Delicate Mouse is widespread through this area, and that it is probably common where it occurs.
conservationActions: This species is known from several conservation reserves (e.g., Millstream-Chichester National Park, Purnululu). There are no critical management requirements.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened, because based on its current known range it has a small estimated extent of occurrence of 2,124 km², therefore it could qualify for Endangered under B1ab(iii) once more is known about the species, because there is currently almost nothing known about the population, ecology or threats. It is considered that it is likely to have a wider distribution than is currently understood and may persist in some modified habitats. Given the uncertainty of the data, it is considered that the species could fall into a number of categories between Endangered and Least Concern, so Near Threatened is deemed the most appropriate intermediate category at this point. Further surveys and research into the threats are needed.
habitat: The species was recorded in evergreen mixed forest at the elevations of 300–700 m asl in Cao Bang Province (Abramov et al. 2018). Local villagers in Nguyen Binh District, Cao Bang Province, said it could be found in slightly disturbed forests and in primary forests (Abramov et al. 2018). The species may survive well in disturbed forest (A. Abramov pers. comm. 2025).
threats: Very little is ecological information about the species and therefore the threats are not known.
population: There is little information about the population size and trends for this species, however, local villagers said that it is rather common in Nguyen Binh District, Cao Bang Province (Abramov et al. 2018, Bannikova et al. 2024).
range: This species is currently only known from northern Viet Nam, where it has been recorded in Cao Bang Province (Nguyen Binh District), Tuyen Quang Province (Na Hang District), and Bac Kan Province (Bannikova et al. 2024). In Cao Bang Province it was collected in evergreen mixed forest at elevations between 300–700 m asl, but not at higher elevations of 1,500–1,800 m asl (Abramov et al. 2018). It is likely that the species has a wider distribution than is currently known (A. Abramov pers. comm. 2025).
conservationActions: It has been recorded in and around the Phia Oac – Phia Den National Park in Cao Bang Province (Abramov et al. 2018).

rationale: All species in the genus Euroscaptor are poorly known due to their highly fossorial lifestyles. Euroscaptor ngoclinhensis is listed as Least Concern, because there is a lack of evidence for significant threats or decline, it is found in a number of protected areas, and has a relatively large extent of occurrence (64,824 km2). Research is needed to accurately assess population size, trends and potential threats. The systematics of the genus also require revision across its wide distribution range.
habitat: This species lives in mountainous forests (Zemlemerova et al. 2016). There is very little other information about the species’ ecology.
threats: There is no evidence of major threats to the species.
population: There is very little known about the population or population trends for this species.
range: The species is known from the north and central Annamite Range, Central Vietnam. This includes the provinces of Quang Tri (Bac Huong Hoa Nature Reserve), Hue City (Sao La Hue Nature Reserve), Da Nang City (Dong Giang Commune), Quang Ngai (Xop Commune, Ba Tô Commune, Kon Plong Commune, Ngoc Linh mountain), Gia Lai (Kon Chu Rang Nature Reserve, Kon Ka Kinh National Park), Dak Lak (Chu Yang Sin National Park), and Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park in Quang Tri Province (Zemlemerova et al. 2016, Bui et al. 2020, H.T. Bui pers. comm. 2025). The species occupies elevations of 500 – 1,750 m asl (Bui et al. 2020).
conservationActions: The locations occur in some protected areas, such as Ngoc Linh NR, Bac Huong Hoa NR, Sao La Hue NR, Kon Chu Rang NR, Kon Ka Kinh NP, Chu Yang Sin NP, and Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng NP.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, because whilst it has a relatively restricted distribution in the Cameron Highlands of Malaysia where it has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 19,894 km², it is found across both natural forest and human-modified habitats and there are currently no known major threats to the species or its habitats.
habitat: The species does not construct mole hills (Cranbrook 1966). Its diet includes earthworms, arthropods and small reptiles (such as the blind snake), and it will eat most subterranean animals it can find (Kawada et al. 2008). It is only known from the Kuala Terla Tea Estate, BOH Tea Estate, and some surrounding gardens, and in natural forest (Kawada et al. 2008). Its reproductive season is likely to fall in the period between January and March (Kawada et al. 2008).
threats: There is an increasing change in land-use due to urbanization in the Cameron Highlands leading to deforestation (How et al. 2021), which could threaten the habitat of the species.
population: There is nothing known about the population size or trends for this species.
range: The species has only been described from the Cameron Highlands, Pahang, Peninsular Malaysia, between elevations of 1,300 and 1,600 m (Kawada et al. 2008), though was described previously as occurring at elevations from 1,067 m to 2,012 m, reaching the summit of Mt. Brinchang (Medway 1983). It is only known from one location - Kuala Terla Tea Estate, BOH Tea Estate and some surrounding gardens (Kawada et al. 2008). There were no recent reports of collecting the mole from mountain forest of Cameron Highlands (Kawada et al. 2008), but possible range also includes these forest areas, as mentioned by Medway (1978). Further field survey in Peninsular Malaysia will possibly enlarge the distribution area of the Malaysian mole (Kawada et al. 2008).
conservationActions: The species has not been recorded in any protected areas. The Cameron Highlands are mostly protected, including Bukit Jerut Forest Reserve and Sungai Kial Forest Reserve. In the Malaysian Red List the species is listed as Least Concern (PERHILITAN 2017).

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution with an estimated extent of occurrence of 355,161 km2, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species inhabits forest habitat, and areas with loose sandy soil, especially near streams. It is not known whether or not it can adapt to anthropogenic habitats.
threats: The major threats to this species are not known. If it is dependent on forest, then threats are likely to include forest clearance for agriculture, plantations, logging and human settlement.
population: This species is locally abundant throughout its range.
range: The species ranges across the highlands of northern and western Thailand, probably extending to south-eastern Myanmar and north-western Laos.
conservationActions: Given its wide range, this species is likely to be present in a number of protected areas. Further studies are needed on the distribution, abundance, natural history and threats to this species.

rationale: This species has only been found on Mt. Mantalingahan, in the southwest of Palawan Island in the Philippines . It is assessed as Near Threatened because it could qualify for Endangered under B1ab(iii) with a small extent of occurrence of 377 km² and is only known from the single location, based on potential future threats. Whilst it appears reasonably common within its distribution and neither its habitat nor population currently are at serious risk of decline due to any known threats, habitat destruction could become a problem in the future.
habitat: Palawanosorex muscorum occurs in high-elevation forest that is cool, wet, and steep, where moderate to thick layers of moss and humus were present; this includes mature montane forest and heath montane forest, found from 1,550–1,950 m asl (Hutterer et al. 2018). These shrews were absent from habitat in warmer, less wet, and less steep lowland and lowland-montane transitional forest, where logging and agricultural clearings and trails were common (Hutterer et al. 2018). They are thought to feed on soil invertebrates, especially earthworms. Numbers of Palawanosorex muscorum were highest at 1,750 m asl. This is believed to represent ideal habitat, as there is bushy heath-like forests, high levels of leaf litter and humus, and an abundance of moss (Hutterer et al. 2018).
threats: Because the habitat of this species is cool, very wet, and steep, there is no immediate threat to this species (L. Heaney pers. comms. 2018). However, despite being a national park, areas of the mountain at lower elevations have undergone logging and clearing for agriculture, some currently and some historically (Hutterer et al. 2018). Mining and urbanisation are both major destructive pressures on the lowland rainforest on Palawan (Hirsch 2016).
population: There is no information available on the population size or trends for this species. Hutterer et al. (2018) trapped a total of 30 individuals during their study, and considered them to be fairly common within their habitat. Evidence was observed suggesting the species may also be present in other areas close by (Hutterer et al. 2018).
range: This species has only been found on Mt. Mantalingahan, in the southwest of Palawan Island in the Philippines (Hutterer et al. 2018). All specimens were found between 1,550–1,950 m asl, in cool, wet montane and mossy forest over ultrabasic soil (Hutterer et al. 2018). The same study found that the species was absent at study sites from 700 m to 1,300 m asl.
conservationActions: This species is located within Mt. Mantalingahan Protected Landscape, a national park with Mt. Mantalingahan at the centre. The entire area has a protected status. It has been submitted to the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status (Philippines National Commission for UNESCO 2015).

rationale: This species is listed as Endangered B1ab(i,iii), because it is only known from the two small islands of Bisa and Obi, Northern Moluccan Islands (Indonesia). It has a small extent of occurrence (EOO = 3,640 km²) and is estimated to occur in fewer than five locations. The species is likely to be declining due to loss of its habitats on the islands as a result of agriculture, selective logging, and mining.
habitat: Halmaheramys wallacei is a terrestrial mammal, found in secondary forest between 40 and 970 m asl (Fabre et al. 2018). It is believed to be present in all habitats throughout the islands (Fabre et al. 2018). It is most likely to be either herbivorous or frugivorous, as fruit remains were found in the stomach of one specimen (Fabre et al. 2018).
threats: Forests on Obi Island have undergone heavy selective logging in the previous 10–15 years (Fabre et al. 2018), and this is evident up to 1,100 m asl on Obi (Mittermeier et al. 2013). The mining industry and the potential expansion of the area mined presents a threat to other endemic species on Obi Island (Cottee-Jones et al. 2013), and this would likely also affect Halmaheramys wallacei (P. Fabre pers. comm. 2018). Coconut plantations, clove and nutmeg groves are extensive at lower elevations; a recent study found no primary lowland forest on Obi (Mittermeier et al. 2013).
population: The population size and trend are currently unknown, however, due to the small number of specimens found it is likely to be a small population (P. Fabre pers. comm. 2018).
range: The species has been found only on the Northern Moluccan Islands of Bisa and Obi, however, it is expected to occur on other small surrounding islands (Fabre et al. 2018). It is documented in the southwest of Obi at 870–970 m asl, and in the north of the island at 40 m asl, inland from Jikotamo (Fabre et al. 2018).  A specimen was also identified south of Madu Pob on Bisa Island (Flannery 1995).
conservationActions: It is not known from any protected areas, however, Pulau Obi Nature Reserve is located in the centre of Obi island, close to Jikotamo where one specimen was found (Fabre et al. 2018).

rationale: This species is only known from the small island of Hon Khoai in Viet Nam, where is has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of just 5–16 km² and an area of occupancy (AOO) of 4–16 km². Its primary forest habitat is being lost and degraded due to road construction and pollution. Based on these threats, the species is estimated to occur in one location. This species is assessed as Critically Endangered (CR B1ab(i,iii)+2ab(i,iii)).
habitat: Hon Khoai, where Callosciurus honkhoaiensis is found, has a dense tree cover of tropical primary forest (Nguyen et al. 2018).
threats: Habitat destruction from anthropogenic pressures such as the construction of roads and aquaculture has been recently recorded (Ngo et al. 2016).  The island is used as a base by local fishermen, polluting the immediate area (Ngo et al. 2016).
population: There is no information about the population size or trend, however, the population is likely to be small, because of the small size of the island. It is possible that subpopulations could be found on other neighbouring islands south of Viet Nam (Nguyen et al. 2018).
range: Callosciurus honkhoaiensis has only been found on the island of Hon Khoai, Ca Mau Province, off the southern tip of Viet Nam (Nguyen et al. 2018).
conservationActions: Preservation of the remaining forest on Hon Khoai Island is recommended to conserve the species (Nguyen et al. 2018).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, because whilst it has a relatively small current known extent of occurrence (EOO) of 649 km², the range is within the well-maintained Bu Gia Map National Park in Viet Nam and it is likely that its distribution extends into the neighbouring forest of Cambodia. There are no known major threats to this species.
habitat: The species was collected in old, mature, thick trunk bamboo thickets growing along a forest road (Abramov et al. 2011).
threats: The threats to this species are not known and Bu Gia Map National Park is relatively well protected (A. Abramov pers. comm. 2025).
population: Nothing is known about the population size or trend of this species.
range: This species is currently only known from the type locality in Bu Gia Map National Park, Binh Phuoc Province, Southern Viet Nam, where it was collected at 540 m asl (Abramov et al. 2017). It is considered likely to occur in the adjacent forest regions of Eastern Cambodia (Abramov et al. 2017).
conservationActions: This species is currently only known from the type locality in Bu Gia Map National Park, Binh Phuoc Province, Southern Viet Nam (Abramov et al. 2017).

rationale: This species is only known from a single specimen collected from the type locality in the Chingawa Forest of southwestern Ethiopia. It has not been recorded again despite trapping at the type locality and has not been recorded in other forest fragments in the region, therefore it is assumed that the species is rare. It has a very small extent of occurrence (EOO), estimated to be 99 km². The Chingawa Forest is unprotected and is threatened by various human activities, including intensive coffee cultivation which has increased in recent years. Based on this threat, the species is estimated to occur in one location. It is assessed as Critically Endangered (CR B1ab(iii)).
habitat: The single specimen of the species was found in very moist Afromontane forest where there was a notable abundance of tree ferns (Nicolas et al. 2021).
threats: This forest dwelling species is only found in Chingawa Forest, which is a small remnant of a tropical rainforest in southwestern Ethiopia threatened by human activities, especially intensive coffee cultivation (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
population: There is nothing known about the population size or trend for this species. It is likely to be a very rare species, because no additional specimens were recorded despite intensive trapping efforts at the type locality in 2007 and 2017 (Nicolas et al. 2021, J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species is known from a single specimen found in the Chingawa Forest, Ethiopia, where it was recorded at 2,340 m asl (Nicolas et al. 2021). Similar surveys of other humid Afromontane forest blocks in Southwest Ethiopia failed to detect the species, however these were at lower elevations (Nicolas et al. 2021). More recently, higher elevations (ca 2,200 m asl) in Beletta Forest and around Gecha were sampled and failed to detect the species (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
conservationActions: The Chingawa Forest is an unprotected area. Further studies are needed to understand the species' distribution, ecology, and threats. Formal protection of the area is a high priority for this species.

rationale: This mouse is endemic to Ethiopia, where it is known from the Bale Mountains (with most records from the Harenna forest) and the Chingawa forest. It is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B1ab(iii). The species has a fairly small extent of occurrence (EOO = 17,051 km²) and is only known from two locations in the Harenna and Chingawa forests. It is inferred to be experiencing a continuing decline in habitat quality as the Chingawa forest is unprotected and suffering losses of natural habitats due to agriculture, such as from increased coffee production.
habitat: It has been found in forest clearings and moorland areas between 1,950 and 3,730 m asl (Krásová et al. 2022). Animals were captured in the upper vegetation belt of Harenna forest, which is dominated by Hagenia abyssinica, Schefera abyssinica, S. volkensii, Aningeria adolf-friederici, and Hypericum revolutum (Krásová et al. 2022). It was also captured in the Erica arborea shrub on the southern slope of Sanetti Plateau (Krásová et al. 2022).
threats: The threats to this species are not known, however, Chingawa Forest is a small remnant of a tropical rainforest and associated habitats in southwestern Ethiopia are threatened by human activity, especially intensive coffee cultivation (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
population: There is nothing known about the population or trends of this species. The species does not seem exceptionally rare, because for example Yalden (1988) and Lavrenchenko et al. (1997) captured more than 10 individuals during relatively limited sampling effort (note in the papers it is under the name Mus triton). In 2012, in one night in the Harenna forest, two Mus harennensis were captured amongst 36 small mammals (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
range: The species is endemic to Ethiopia, where it has been found between 1,950 and 3,730 m asl in two regions: the Bale Mountains (with most records from the Harenna forest) and the Chingawa forest (Krásová et al. 2022). It may be found in other forested areas between these distant regions (Krásová et al. 2022), but despite intensive sampling in forests of south-western Ethiopia in the last decade it has not been captured (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
conservationActions: Harenna Forest is protected as part of the Bale Mountains National Park.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution with an extent of occurrence (EOO) of around 1,565,639 km2, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: It is found in dense evergreen forests in southern Africa. Animals have also been reported from drier bushveld or coastal forest (Taylor 1988, Skinner and Chimimba 2005). The species probably also lives in coastal forests of Mozambique (J. Bryja pers. comm. 2025).
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: This species is common in the localities where it is found.
range: The species is found in savanna woodland biomes in southern Africa from Pirie Forest (north-west of King William’s Town) in south-eastern Eastern Cape Province of South Africa north through KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo provinces into eastern Zimbabwe and Mozambique south of the Zambezi River (Musser and Carleton 2005). A more recent study has shown that this species has an even wider distribution, with the range including the Southern Rift Mountains of Mt. Gorongosa and Mt. Namuli in Mozambique, Mt. Mulanje in Malawi, and the Chimanimani Mountains on the Zimbabwe–Mozambique border, the Eastern Arc Mountains, and coastal forests of Tanzania (including Mafia Island) and southern Kenya (Bryja et al. 2025). Records of this species in South Africa outside Kwazulu-Natal need to be genetically re-analysed (Bryja et al. 2025).
conservationActions: There are no conservation measures in place; it is not known if the species is present in any protected areas. Further studies are needed into the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, reproduction and ecology of this species. Populations of this species should be monitored to record changes in abundance and distribution.

rationale: Euphractus sexcinctus is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, its tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category. However, due to the small quantity of patches of Amazon savanna, the growing human occupation and the advancement of large enterprises, the natural subpopulations of E. sexcinctus north of the Amazon River (northern region of Brazil) should be the focus of future monitoring.
habitat: This omnivorous species is found in open areas, savannas, shrubland, and dry, semi-deciduous forest. It can be found in secondary forests, and may also occur in primary Amazonian forest (Redford and Wetzel 1985). It adapts well to habitat modifications and has been observed in timber plantations, corn, soybean, and sugar cane plantations, pasturelands, and areas with subsistence agriculture (Dotta and Verdade 2011, Superina and Abba 2018). In fact, in some parts of its range it is more common and abundant in degraded habitat than in protected areas (Abba et al. 2019). In Paraguay it is largely associated with drier environments in the tropical Chaco and Cerrado zones (Smith and Ríos 2018).
threats: There are no major threats to this species. However, Euphractus sexcinctus is hunted extensively, mostly for local use as a protein source and for medicinal use. It is also a frequent victim of vehicle collisions (e.g. Santos et al. 2023, Alberici et al. 2024) and where it occurs in association with cattle, it may be persecuted because of the injury threat posed by burrow systems (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). In Bolivia, wildfires have been severe and widely extended since 2019, with unpublished government reports of several armadillo species burned, and some survivors killed by illegal hunters while escaping the fires (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021).
population: It is a common species (Redford and Wetzel 1985) and in some parts of its range, the subpopulations seem to be increasing.
range: Euphractus sexcinctus is present in a wide area of South America, from western Guiana, southern Suriname, and adjacent Brazil to Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina (Redford and Wetzel 1985, Superina and Abba 2018). It does not occur in Buenos Aires Province (Abba and Vizcaíno 2011, Abba et al. 2012, 2015). Studies in northern Brazil confirmed the occurrence of E. sexcinctus in Maranhão (Silva Júnior et al. 2001), Amapá (Silva Júnior and Nunes 2001), and parts of northern (Silva Junior et al. 2005a,b), northwestern (Oliveira et al. 2006), central (Lima et al. 2009), and eastern Pará (Andrade et al. 2006). Most of these records are located in the Cerrado and Amazon savanna. It occurs from sea level to at least 1,600 m asl.
useTrade: The species is hunted for food, though in some areas local beliefs related to its occasional carrion-feeding behaviour state that the species is unclean and should therefore not be eaten (Neris et al. 2002, Smith and Ríos 2018). In Bolivia it is widely hunted for subsistence by indigenous groups (Noss et al. 2010, Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021) It also has medicinal use (Ferreira et al. 2013) and is utilized to make handicrafts. The carapace is sometimes used as a plate (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024).
conservationActions: Euphractus sexcinctus is present in many protected areas.

rationale: Chaetophractus vellerosus is listed as Least Concern as, although susceptible to hunting and habitat loss and degradation in parts of its range, it is widespread and rates of offtake are not believed to be at a level that would warrant listing in a threatened category. However, there are two subpopulations that need attention: one in the east of Buenos Aires Province (Argentina), which is disjunct and subjected to habitat modification in its restricted range; and the other in Oruro department (Bolivia), which apparently is not disjunct and is intensely harvested and used to manufacture charangos (traditional music instruments), matracas or maracas (rattles), and handicrafts such as amulets and souvenirs, and also suffers the rapid destruction of its habitat (sand dunes above 4,000 m asl).Roughly 60% of the Bolivian range corresponds to the range of the high-altitude population previously known as C. nationi. Peredo (1999) reported more than 25 years ago that increasing difficulties in finding “quirquinchos” in the wild had led artisans from the region of Oruro and La Paz to start using C. vellerosus individuals (Tarifa and Romero-Muñoz 2009). Because Municipal Bylaw 31/99 in Oruro did not succeed in reducing the use of Chaetophractus carapaces in traditional dances, the Bolivian government made it illegal in 2015 to sell or possess a new matraca (Fobar 2019, Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021). In addition, illegal trade of specimens from Chile to Bolivia has been reported. This potential threat to the Chilean subpopulation should be closely monitored, as the Chilean subpopulation is not only threatened by the illegal trade with Bolivia but also by hunting for cultural reasons in the High Andes. However, as Bolivia still considers “C. nationi” as an endangered species, the efforts to reduce its threats are there. The cultural importance of this species, especially among High Andean communities, combined with weak enforcement, makes regulating quirquincho hunting a challenging issue to address (Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021). The genetic data published by Abba et al. (2015) indicate that Chaetophractus specimens from high-altitudes of Bolivia share a unique mitochondrial haplotype, which is also found in a C. vellerosus specimen from Argentina. This absence of genetic diversity observed in the 10 individuals sampled within the Oruro region suggests a local reduction of effective population size (Abba et al. 2015). There is therefore no doubt that the synonymized C. vellerosus would have to be listed in a threatened category—either Vulnerable or Endangered—within Bolivia and that conservation measures should be implemented as soon as possible to save the species from regional extinction (Abba et al. 2015).The subpopulation of the east of Buenos Aires Province (Argentina) is isolated and subjected to habitat modification in its restricted range. In fact, this subpopulation was categorized as Endangered at the national level (Abba et al. 2019) because of its high risk of extinction due to habitat loss and degradation by human activities (e.g., mining, agriculture, dogs, etc.; Abba et al. 2019, 2023).
habitat: The Screaming Hairy Armadillo Chaetophractus vellerosus is primarily found in xeric environments, in lowland and upland areas as well as high altitude grasslands with loose sandy soils and sand dunes. It also has been recorded from rangeland pasture and agricultural areas. In Buenos Aires province this armadillo lives on sandy-calcareous soils and prefers grasslands with low vegetation and high vegetation cover (Abba et al. 2011). This omnivorous animal constructs burrows and therefore is absent from rocky areas where burrows cannot be excavated (Greegor 1985; Abba et al. 2007, 2011, 2023; Abba and Cassini 2008; Pérez-Zubieta 2008, 2011). In Bolivia, Screaming Hairy Armadillos in the high Andeans use crop areas (potatoes) while searching for food, while sand dunes are vital for their survival because they use them for burrow construction and foraging (Pérez-Zubieta 2011).The estimated home range size is 3.4 ha in Catamarca, Argentina (Greegor 1980) and 1 to 5.3 ha in Buenos Aires province, Argentina (Glaz and Carlini 1999). Pagnutti et al. (2014) described seasonal differences in home range size in a closed population in Buenos Aires province, Argentina: in fall-winter, home range size was 0.23 ha and 0.27 ha in males and females, respectively, while it was 0.75 and 0.13 ha, respectively, during spring-summer. In this population, the spatial distribution of C. vellerosus was aggregated and possibly influenced by land use (Pagnutti et al. 2014).Densities of 0.58 animals/km2 have been observed in Kaa-Iya National Park, Bolivia (Cuéllar 2008). Peredo (1999) estimated a total population of 13,000 individuals in an area of 340 km2 in Bolivia and A.M. Abba (pers. comm. 2024) found around 0.6 individuals/ha in some parts of the east of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina.During the cold season, Screaming Hairy Armadillos are mainly active at noon and the early afternoon, while in warm seasons their activity period shifts to the afternoon and night (Greegor 1980, Abba et al. 2011). However, their activity seems to be diurnal throughout the year at high altitudes (Zúñiga and Araya 2014). The diet of C. vellerosus is mainly composed of beetles (larvae and adults), butterfly larvae, plant matter and small vertebrates (Greegor 1980; Soibelzon et al. 2007; Abba et al. 2011, 2019).Chaetophractus vellerosus is a seasonal breeder. Its reproductive season lasts from September to January in Buenos Aires province (Abba et al. 2011, Abba 2020) and November to January in Bolivia (Cuéllar 2008). One to two offspring per litter are born inside the burrow after a gestation period of 60 days. Offspring remain inside the burrow during the entire lactation and start emerging in January-February. Generation length of the subpopulation in eastern Buenos Aires Province has been estimated at 3.2 years (Abba 2020).
threats: Chaetophractus vellerosus is heavily hunted for its meat and carapace (including for charangos, a musical instrument, and matracas; Aguiar and Fonseca 2008, Romero-Muñoz and Pérez-Zubieta 2008) in Bolivia, in some parts of the Chaco region, and in Chile (Cuéllar and Noss 2003, Noss et al. 2008, Pasutti et al. 2020). It is also persecuted as an agricultural pest in some regions. In addition, some animals are killed by hunting dogs and by cars on roads. The isolated subpopulation on the coast of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, is negatively affected by mining activities (Abba 2008; Abba et al. 2011, 2019).Chaetophractus vellerosus also suffers from habitat loss from intense sand excavation for concrete production (Peredo 1999) and agricultural activities (Ríos and Rocha 2002). Animals living at high altitudes of Bolivia (previously considered to be C. nationi) are negatively affected by the intense use to make handicrafts. Twenty years ago, Cáceres (1995) estimated that 2,000 individuals were harvested each year for this purpose; this caused a dramatic reduction in the zone. The species has therefore been categorized as Endangered at the national level since 2009. Illegal trade from Chile to Bolivia as well as within Bolivia has been reported and seems to be related to the reduction of the subpopulation near Oruro and the resulting difficulties to obtain animals for handicraft production. Although the extent of this illegal trade has not been quantified, it is suspected to negatively affect the local population. The species can be legally traded in Paraguay with the corresponding permits. In 2010 in Paraguay the first permissions were granted establishing quotas for the harvesting of this species by for-profit companies for export abroad under the Proyecto de Conservación y Utilización de la Vida Silvestre (Project for the Conservation and Utilisation of Wildlife), and a value of 25,000Gs (US$3.40) was established as payment to landowners for each individual of this species captured on their land. Although exact numbers are not available, it cannot be ruled out that this has led to local extirpations of the species.
population: The population status of this species is not known, but is expected to be stable. Nonetheless, it is presumed that the high-altitude subpopulation in Bolivia, which was formerly classified as Chaetophractus nationi, is rapidly declining. Furthermore, field observations in Paraguay report a decrease in encounters over the last five years (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). Molecular analyses suggest that there is evidence of gene flow between C. vellerosus and the high-altitude subpopulation formerly classified as C. nationi (Abba et al. 2015). Despite subtle morphological differences in skull shape, high-altitude specimens are similar in size to specimens of the subspecies C. v. vellerosus, with which they also share mitochondrial haplotypes. They might thus be viewed as being part of this subspecies. Nevertheless, the reality of the subspecies definition within C. vellerosus requires more detailed phylogeographic and population genetics studies.The distance between the distribution areas of the high-altitude armadillos formerly classified as C. nationi and C. vellerosus is around 80 km (Abba et al. 2015), and there is no obvious geographic barrier that would prevent contact between individuals of the two subpopulations. Actually, this gap probably reflects the scarcity of field studies and the corresponding lack of geo-referenced localities from the potential area of contact. Small hairy armadillos have indeed been observed in this area (Abba et al. 2015). As a consequence, the high-altitude armadillos formerly identified as C. nationi cannot be considered a subpopulation under the IUCN definition (“Subpopulations are defined as geographically or otherwise distinct groups in the population between which there is little demographic or genetic exchange (typically one successful migrant individual or gamete per year or less”).
range: Chaetophractus vellerosus is generally known from the Chaco region of Bolivia (Cuéllar and Noss 2003, Noss et al. 2010), Paraguay and Argentina (Gardner 2005, Abba et al. 2012, Superina and Abba 2018). A disjunct population occurs in eastern Buenos Aires Province, Argentina (Crespo 1974; Carlini and Vizcaíno 1987; Abba et al. 2007, 2011, 2023; Abba and Cassini 2008). Recent studies have confirmed that C. nationi is an invalid species and a synonym of C. vellerosus (Abba et al. 2015, Gibb et al. 2016). Hence, the distribution of C. vellerosus now also includes the high altitudes of Chile (Arica y Parinacota, Antofagasta, Tarapacá), Bolivia (sand dunes in Oruro and Potosi) and Argentina. Its presence in Peru is uncertain. Pacheco et al. (2021) do not include it in their most recent list of the mammals of Peru, while Cossios (2018) reports that interviews with locals suggest that the species is present in southern Puno department. The species occurs at altitudes from sea level to 4,600 m asl.
useTrade: Chaetophractus vellerosus is hunted as a protein source throughout its range. In Bolivia the carapaces are also used to manufacture charangos (traditional music instruments) and the whole bodies are made into matracas or maracas (rattles), which are used in traditional dances—especially during the carnival in Oruro. These armadillos are also made into amulets and souvenirs (Pérez-Zubieta et al. 2009).  Although these practices are still used, the numbers of killed animals probably have reduced due to the strong campaigns in favour of the species, and the current population decrease in the Andean region. In Chile the Aymara and Quechua indigenous communities use the whole body as ornaments and for its believed protection that it gives, but they also still use it in cultural rituals as well as for food and medicine (Pasutti et al. 2020).
conservationActions: Chaetophractus vellerosus is present in a number of protected areas, including the Kaa-Iya National Park in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, in 13 protected areas of Argentina (https://sib.gob.ar/especies/chaetophractus-vellerosus), and in several protected areas in the Paraguayan Chaco (Smith and Ríos 2018). The high-altitude animals are present in the Sajama National Park, Bolivia, and in Lauca National Park, Las Vicuñas National Reserve and Volcán Isluga National Park in Chile (Pasutti 2017).The species is listed as Least Concern at the national level in Argentina (Abba et al. 2019) and Paraguay (Saldívar et al. 2017), and as Endangered in Bolivia for the Andean population (Perez-Zubieta et al. 2009). In Chile, where only the high-altitude armadillos occur, it is listed as Vulnerable under criterion B2ab(iii) (Pasutti and Superina 2019).The high-altitude armadillos, formerly known as C. nationi, were previously listed as globally Vulnerable (VU A2acd; IUCN 2014). They are still listed as C. nationi in Bolivia and Peru, where they are considered Endangered (Pérez-Zubieta et al. 2009, Cossios 2018), although its presence in Peru is uncertain.The subpopulation in eastern Buenos Aires province, Argentina, is categorized as Endangered at the national level (Abba et al. 2019).In spite of the taxonomic change, the species is still listed as C. nationi in CITES Appendix II (CITES 2023), which establishes a zero annual exportation quota for this species due to its traditional use (Peredo 1999).These animals are considered emblematic of the Bolivian highlands, particularly from the Oruro department (Cáceres 2004) where they are closely linked to the cultural heritage. In 2015, the Bolivian government made it illegal to sell or possess a new matraca. Therefore, old matracas were registered for all dancers in 2019 (Aliaga Rossel et al. 2021). The agreement seeks to prevent, catalogue, regulate, replace, and eliminate the use of wildlife specimens (Aliaga-Rossel et al. 2021). In April 2022, a national law (1424) declared the Andean Hairy Armadillo C. nationi as a Natural Heritage of the country, prioritizing the protection, conservation and defence of the species and its habitat.

rationale: Cabassous tatouay is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, its tolerance of a degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Cabassous tatouay inhabits tropical and subtropical lowland and submontane forests, and edge habitats (Redford and Eisenberg 1992), including occasionally agricultural areas (Mikich and Bernils 2004, Ubaid et al. 2010). It is broadly associated with the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado biomes and the transition to Pantanal and Caatinga (in the north) and Mesopotamian grasslands (in the south). Although recorded in open biomes, this species seems to prefer more humid areas as its presence in the Caatinga, Cerrado, and Uruguayan savannas is strongly associated with montane and xeromorphic forests (González and Lanfranco 2012, Queirolo 2016, Feijó and Anacleto 2021).Reproduction is unknown in the wild other than that a single young is born (González 2001). Matos et al. (2023) documented the growth and development of a neonate received at an animal rescue centre in Brazil. The species is highly fossorial and largely insectivorous, with food (especially ants and termites) detected by smell (Wetzel et al. 2008).
threats: There is extensive habitat loss in much of the range of this species, which is broadly associated with the threatened Cerrado and Atlantic Forest ecoregions. In addition, the species is hunted locally and there is potential for conflict with agriculturalists, foresters and bee-keepers. Regular burning of habitat (Mikich and Bérnils 2004) and vehicle collisions may be additional threats (Ribeiro et al. 2017, Abra et al. 2021, Massocato et al. 2022, González et al. 2024).
population: The population status of this species is unknown, and the tendency to report records of the species in the literature suggests that it is not commonly encountered. Nonetheless, these new records have expanded the distribution considerably in recent years, indicating that the species may be under-recorded because of its fossorial habits. Its home range has been estimated at 4.09 km² in the Brazilian Cerrado (Encarnação 1987).
range: This armadillo species is broadly associated with the Atlantic Forest, Pantanal and Cerrado regions of eastern and central Brazil (Feijó and Anacleto 2021, Desbiez et al. 2022, Rocha et al. 2022), northeastern Uruguay (Ameneiros et al. 2015, Queirolo 2016, Villalba-Macías et al. 2019), northeastern Argentina (Vizcaíno et al. 2006, Conil and Nigro 2012) and the eastern Oriental region of Paraguay (Smith and Ríos 2018, Smith et al. 2023). Records from Buenos Aires Province, Argentina are erroneous (Abba and Vizcaíno 2008). The species has also been recorded in montane evergreen forests (Brejos de Altitude) in northeastern Brazil (Feijó and Langguth 2013).
useTrade: This is a large armadillo that is occasionally hunted for food (Sanches 2001, Centrón et al. 2013), though local taboos as to the inedibility of the species are in place in some areas. The species has been recorded to raid commercial bee hives (Villalba-Macías et al. 2019), and its fossorial behaviour creates conflict in agricultural areas (Anacleto et al. 2015).
conservationActions: This species is present in many protected areas throughout its range (e.g., Bertrand and Soares 2018, Smith and Ríos 2018, Monteiro et al. 2019, SIB 2024). It is considered a conservation priority species in Uruguay (González et al. 2013) and is listed in CITES Appendix III (Uruguay).

rationale: Cabassous unicinctus is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, its occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category. It is, however, affected by habitat loss.
habitat: Cabassous unicinctus inhabits tropical lowland and submontane forests in the Amazon and the Orinoco region, as well as in the ecotone between forested areas and grasslands in the seasonally flooded Llanos (Aya-Cuero et al. 2019, Feijó and Anacleto 2021).
threats: The species is mainly affected by habitat loss due to deforestation for agro-industrial activities. It may be hunted throughout its range, but the species is not a target game species. Vehicle collisions have been reported, but seem to be relatively rare (Aya-Cuero et al. 2019).
population: The limited number of records (e.g. Aya-Cuero et al. 2019) suggests that this is a rare species.
range: This South American species is found east of the Andes from northern Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, through to Venezuela, Guyana, French Guiana and Suriname in the north, to the state of Mato Grosso do Sul (Brazil) and Bolivia in the south (Feijó and Anacleto 2021). It occurs at altitudes up to 1,200 m asl.
useTrade: The species is hunted for food.
conservationActions: The species is present in protected areas. An education and awareness program is being carried out by Fundación Omacha in the llanos of Colombia (Superina et al. 2019).

rationale: Tolypeutes matacus is listed as Near Threatened because this species is probably in significant decline (albeit at a rate of less than 30% over 12 years) because of widespread habitat loss through much of its range, and because of exploitation for food, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2cd.
habitat: This armadillo, which can roll into a ball when threatened, is found in areas of dry vegetation within the Chaco (Bolkovic et al. 1995). Although capable of digging its own burrows (Attias et al. 2015), it often uses abandoned burrows of other species or hides in dense vegetation. It has a slow reproductive rate; the females give birth to a single young per litter and per year. Its generation length has been estimated at four years; this estimate is based on an extrapolation from other armadillo species.
threats: Tolypeutes matacus is threatened by hunting for food. In Santiago del Estero, Argentina, it was found to constitute 55% of the wild fauna in the diet of local people. In the Argentine Chaco it made up 18.4% of the diet of local people and was consumed a mean of 16.5 days per year (+/-1.07) (Altrichter 2006). In Bolivia it is the second most hunted armadillo species by the Izoceño indigenous group, contributing 2% of their total diet.As it is less fossorial than other species and often active by day, it is easier to hunt than other armadillo species. It is also threatened by habitat destruction through conversion of suitable habitat to cultivated land; however, it is able to adapt to low levels of agricultural disturbance. This species is exported to zoos and, especially, for the pet trade, and there is a high mortality of individuals during this export process. It is sometimes killed on roads. The slow reproductive rate suggests that it may struggle to recover from steep population declines.
population: Few data are available about the abundance of Tolypeutes matacus. It was previously abundant in most xeric parts of the Paraguayan Chaco and Bolivia (Redford and Eisenberg 1992, Meritt 2008, Noss et al. 2010, Aguirre et al. 2019), but field workers in the area have reported a decline in recent years, at least in the Paraguayan subpopulations (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). More than 20 years ago, it was recorded at densities of 1.9 animals per km² in the Bolivian Chaco (Cuéllar 2002) and of 0.28 animals per km² in the Pantanal of Mato Grosso in Brazil (Schaller 1983). There are no population data of this armadillo in Argentina, but based on the higher number of presence records, higher genetic diversity (Ferreiro et al. 2023) and comments from locals, it is thought to have a higher abundance in the provinces of Chaco and Formosa. The wild population is decreasing, mainly due to intense hunting and habitat loss.Although no data exist on the longevity of wild individuals, generation length has been estimated at four years based on an extrapolation from other armadillo species.
range: Tolypeutes matacus is found from eastern Bolivia and southwestern Brazil, south through the Gran Chaco of Paraguay, to Argentina, with San Luis province being its southernmost limit (Feijó et al. 2015, Ferreiro et al. 2022). The species was once present in southern Buenos Aires Province (Yepes 1928) but recent surveys suggest that it is now extinct in this area (Abba and Vizcaíno 2008, 2011; Abba et al. 2012). The reason for its disappearance from Buenos Aires is unknown, but may be related to climate. It ranges from sea level up to 800 m asl (Argentina).
useTrade: This armadillo is heavily hunted for food and used as a pet species, especially by indigenous groups both within its range and in other countries. It is also used to make handicrafts. In Bolivia, overhunting and habitat destruction present a worrying threat to the species (Noss et al. 2010). In 2010, Paraguay established quotas for harvesting this species for export abroad under the Proyecto de Conservación y Utilización de la Vida Silvestre, and landowners received a payment for each individual captured on their land (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). However, captive breeding programmes in the USA have reduced the need to import wild-caught three-banded armadillos especially to zoos, which has reduced hunting pressure.
conservationActions: Tolypeutes matacus has been recorded from a number of protected areas but with no more than 12% of its suitable area under protection (Ferreiro 2022; A. Ferreiro pers. comm. 2024). There is a Population Management Plan in place for the captive populations in North American and European zoos.

rationale: The Mahali Mole-rat, Crypotmys mahali is listed as Least Concern because it is widely distributed throughout the assessment region, is reasonably common and adapt well to habitats modified by humans, such as agricultural areas and rural gardens.
habitat: Generally, the subterranean Cryptomys subspecies occur across a wide range of soil types from fine to medium grained clays and loams. They are often located within human- modified environments, such as lawns, golf courses and gardens (particularly in the presence of vegetable gardens). They specialise in bulbs, corms and tubers, especially those of Albuca, Lachenalia, Ornithogalum (Hyacinthaceae), Romulea, Micranthus, Homeria (Iridaceae) and Oxalis (Oxalidaceae) (Bennett 2013).Mahali’s Mole-rat, Cryptomys mahali, is found in more arid habitats when compared to Crypotmys pretoriae, and is typically located in clays and sandy soils in scrubland habitats. Colonies comprise of a single breeding pair and a number of non-breeders of both sexes. Mean colony size is 7.7, but colonies can attain a maximum size of 24. It is an aseasonal breeder producing 2 to 3 litters per annum with a mean litter size of 1.9 ±0.8. The mean body mass of males is 104±28 and females 76±12. The breeding period is from January to December. The mean biomass of the colony is 507g. Colony density is 1.5 colonies per hectare (Suess et al. 2024).Ecosystem and cultural services: Generally, Mole-rats are good ecosystem engineers, as they enrich the humus content of the soil, aerate the soil, assist with drainage systems and enhance plant species diversity (Hagenah and Bennett 2013). Additionally, they create refuges for other species to use to escape fire. Common Mole-rats also eat geophytes that contain cardiac glycosides (for example, Ornithogalum spp., Homeria spp., Morea spp.), which are toxic to livestock (Bennett 2013). They are eaten by a wide range of predators (Bennett 2013).
threats: No major threats have been identified for these species. However, they are occasionally persecuted as an agricultural pest and they are occasionally exterminated on golf courses.Climate change may threaten to reduce suitable habitat for these species in the future; however, it is currently not a threat to these species, especially because they can survive in transformed habitats. Further research is needed on climate change and Cryptomys species.
population: The population size of this genus varies depending on the subspecies. The Mahali Mole-rat has a density of 5.5 animals/hectare; the Natal Mole-rat 4.9/hectare, the Highveld Mole-rat 2.2/hectare and the Common Mole-rat 5/hectare (Suess et al. 2024, Spinks et al. 2000). However, it is widespread and abundant across the assessment region. Presumably the population is limited by soil requirements. In prime habitats the population density of Cryptomys hottentotus is known to surpass 150 individuals/km² (Spinks et al. unpubl. data, 2008). The populations are not predicted to be declining due to their broad distribution and their ability to survive successfully within transformed habitats.Regional population effects: Due to disjunctions in the distribution, dispersal is impossible for C. hottentotus and C. pretoriae. The dispersal of C. mahali and C. natalensis is currently unknown.
range: Mahali’s Mole-rat, Cryptomys mahali, is known from north of the Magaliesberg Ridge from near Patryshoek (Gauteng province) and Brits (North West) (Faulkes et al. 2004, Bennett, Hart, Finn, unpubl. data 2016). This species has also been identified in Van Zyls Rus (Northern Cape), Bloemhof (North West Province), and Bloemfontein (North West) (N.C. Bennett unpubl. data 2016). Further research is required in order to establish the precise limits of the species’ range.
useTrade: There is no information on the use of this species as bushmeat, although it may occur.
conservationActions: Cryptomys subspecies are located in numerous protected areas throughout the assessment region. For example, Bloemhof Nature Reserve, Kruger National Park and Nylesvley Nature Reserve, which are key protected areas for C. mahali, C. natalensis or nimrodi respectively. As a result, no specific interventions are necessary for these species. However, further research is necessary to delineate the population distribution, trends and abundance of these species.Recommendations for land managers and practitioners: Systematic surveys needed to gather information on population size, trends and distribution. Research priorities: Accurate species distribution mapping is necessary through molecular research museum record vetting. Encouraged citizen actions: Report sightings on virtual museum platforms (for example, iNaturalist and MammalMAP), especially outside protected areas. However, subspecific level identification will require molecular analyses.

rationale: The Highveld Mole-rat, Cryptomys pretoriae, is assessed as Least Concern, even though it has a restricted distribution to the grassland of Pretoria and Johannesburg suburbs. Currently, there are no major recognised threats that could result in significant population decline.
habitat: Generally, the subterranean Cryptomys occur across a wide range of soil types from fine to medium grained clays and loams. They are often located within human-modified environments, such as lawns, golf courses and gardens (particularly in the presence of vegetable gardens). They specialise in bulbs, corms and tubers, especially those of Albuca, Lachenalia, Ornithogalum (Hyacinthaceae), Romulea, Micranthus, Homeria (Iridaceae) and Oxalis (Oxalidaceae) (Bennett 2013). The Highveld Mole-rat, Cryptomys pretoriae, is found in an array of soils from clay and sandy through to loams. In contrast to Cryptomys hottentotus (which tends to avoid stony soils), this species will venture into stony soils. They are predominantly a grassland species, feeding on grass rhizomes and any associated geophytes in the area.  Again, this species is colonial, consisting of group sizes up to 15 individuals (Moolman et al. 1998). This species thrives in Highveld grasslands, but is also located within Burkhia scrubland. Similar to other Cryptomys species, they are able to survive in modified habitats and in particular gardens and golf courses but are also found on vacant plots and cultivated lands. The colony has a single breeding pair and subordinates of both sexes. Mean colony size 4.0, but 15 animals have been recorded. It is a seasonal breeder producing 1 or occasionally 2 litters per annum with a mean litter size of 1.3±0.5 pups. The mean body mass of males is 120±35g and females 98±20g. The breeding season is from July to November. The mean biomass of a colony is 410g. Colony density is 1.2 colonies per hectare (Suess et al. 2024). Ecosystem and cultural services: Generally, Mole-rats are good ecosystem engineers, as they enrich the humus content of the soil, aerate the soil, assist with drainage systems and enhance plant species diversity (Hagenah and Bennett 2013). Additionally, they create refuges for other species to use to escape fire. Common Mole-rats also eat geophytes that contain cardiac glycosides (for example, Ornithogalum spp., Homeria spp., Morea spp.), which are toxic to livestock (Bennett 2013). They are eaten by a wide range of predators (Bennett 2013).
threats: No major threats have been identified for these species. However, they are occasionally persecuted as an agricultural pest, and homeowners complain that Cryptomys pretoriae can become nuisances in their gardens (Power 2014), and they are occasionally exterminated on golf courses. Climate change may threaten to reduce suitable habitat for these species in the future; however, it is currently not a threat to these species, especially because they can survive in transformed habitats. Further research is needed on climate change and Cryptomys species.
population: The population size of this genus varies depending on the subspecies. The Highveld Mole-rat has a density of 2.2/hectare (Suess et al. 2024, Spinks et al. 2000). However, it is widespread and abundant across the assessment region. Presumably the population is limited by soil requirements. The populations are not predicted to be declining due to their broad distribution and their ability to survive successfully within transformed habitats.Regional population effects: Due to disjunctions in the distribution, dispersal is impossible for C. hottentotus and C. pretoriae. The dispersal of C. mahali and C. natalensis is currently unknown.
range: The Highveld Mole-rat, Cryptomys pretoriae, occurs in Gauteng (Bennett 2013). Its eastern limit is likely to be the Mpumalanga Drakensberg escarpment, which is the western limit of Cryptomys natalensis (Faulkes et al. 2004). For all Cryptomys species, further molecular research and vetting of museum records are required to more accurately delineate range distributions.
useTrade: It is not documented as being utilised but is likely to be used opportunistically as bushmeat.
conservationActions: Cryptomys species are located in numerous protected areas throughout the assessment region. However, further research is necessary to delineate the population distribution, trends and abundance of these species.Recommendations for land managers and practitioners:Systematic surveys needed to gather information on population size, trends and distribution.Research priorities:Accurate species distribution mapping is necessary through molecular research museum record vetting.Encouraged citizen actions:Report sightings on virtual museum platforms (for example, iNaturalist and MammalMAP), especially outside protected areas. However, subspecific level identification will require molecular analyses.

rationale: This species has a highly restricted range, confined to montane cloud forests in central Mexico. It has a small extent of occurrence (EOO = 75 km²) and it is restricted to a single location, which is facing significant and ongoing habitat loss driven by agricultural expansion, intensive urbanization, tourism activities, and cattle grazing. These threats are causing a continuous decline in EOO, and the overall area, extent, and quality of suitable habitat. This species is assessed as Critically Endangered under criteria B1ab(i,iii).
habitat: This species inhabits cloud forests, with a strong preference for trees such as Cleyera velutina, these forests offer a dense canopy and complex vertical structure that provides shelter and access to arboreal resources (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). The species primarily occupies the understory layer, though it has been observed across various forest strata, including the canopy (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). It favours trees in semi-flat areas, where the presence of specific epiphytes and fungi, such as Fabronia ciliaris and Everniastrum sp., is closely associated with its habitat use (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). These plants, along with moisture-retaining bryophytes, may contribute to its diet (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). Habromys schmidlyi exhibits small home ranges, with males averaging 0.83 ha and females 0.29 ha, and shows localized population structure, using a limited number of trees within its home range (Marines-Macías et al. 2018).
threats: Habromys schmidlyi is threatened primarily by habitat loss and deforestation of cloud forests, driven by agriculture, cattle ranching, and intensive urbanization (Contreras-Medina et al. 2024). Cloud forests now cover less than 0.5% of Mexico's land area. The Cerro del Huixteco State Park, one of only two known localities for the species, lacks a formal protection program, and its proximity to the tourist city of Taxco increases the risk of habitat disturbance (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). The natural fragmentation of this ecosystem, resulted from the emergence of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, makes it even more vulnerable to ongoing land-use changes and climate change. The species' populations are further threatened by their small effective population sizes, increasing their risk of extinction (Colunga-Salas et al. 2023, Contreras-Medina et al. 2024).
population: The population of this species is sparse and confined to isolated patches of cloud forest (León-Paniagua et al. 2007). In a study at the Taxco site, 42 individuals were captured, representing one of only two known populations (Marines-Macías et al. 2018). The species exhibits a low effective population size, with estimates of 20.8 for the Taxco population and 10.2 for the Zacualpan population (Colunga-Salas et al. 2023). In total, 48 individuals were sampled across both sites, with 29 from Taxco and 19 from Zacualpan (Colunga-Salas et al. 2020).
range: This species has a highly restricted range, confined to montane cloud forests in central Mexico, particularly within the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (Romo-Vazquez et al. 2005, León-Paniagua et al. 2007, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024, Contreras-Medina et al. 2024). Currently, Habromys schmidlyi is known from only two populations: one located in ‘Picacho de Oro y Plata’ State Park, Zacualpan, Estado de México, and the other in ‘Cerro del Huixteco’ State Park, within the Sierra de Taxco, Guerrero, Mexico (Marines-Macías et al. 2018).
conservationActions: The species inhabits Cerro del Huixteco State Park, but the area lacks a formal management program (Colunga‐Salas et al. 2020). An action plan for its conservation was proposed during the Mexican Small Mammal Assessment, Prioritization, and Conservation Planning Workshop (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018) and identified the following objectives and actions:Objective 1: Determine the status of the current populationMonitor the distribution and abundance - need to develop the detailed steps to be implemented for the monitoring protocolCharacterize the genetics of the populationObjective 2: Increase habitat protection coverage and connectivityEnlarge protected area network - develop detailed stepsPrevention of deforestationObjective 3: Create assurance ex situ populationsInfrastructure, biosecurity, land purchasePermitsDevelop management protocolsObjective 4: Create public awareness and positive perception and attitudes Strengthen education actions at the local level

rationale: Based on current knowledge, this species has a relatively small range and extent of occurrence (EOO) of 1,919 km², though based on a species distribution model, the EOO could approximately range up to 2,973 km². It may occur in a small number of locations (based on current knowledge 10 locations are estimated) and it is threatened by habitat loss driven by overgrazing and the conversion of land for growing crops. this birch mouse is therefore assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B1ab(iii). Further surveys would be needed to clarify its locations, threat impacts and population trends.
habitat: The species is known from areas with a mixed forest habitat and the subalpine zone from 1,500 to 2,380 m asl. It occurs in subalpine meadows with tall grass, extending above the upper forest line, and presumably reaches the lower part of the glacier belt (Sokolov et al. 1987, Shenbrot et al. 1995). The optimal habitat appears to be forb-rich meadows within the subalpine belt. For instance, in the type locality - the upper reaches of the Terek River, in the Kazbegi region of Georgia - Baskevich et al. (2024) captured birch mice on forb-dominated slopes in the subalpine zone at an elevation of 2,200 meters. Near Kobi, individuals were also trapped at approximately 2,000 meters in birch elfin woodlands interspersed with willow, dense undergrowth of Caucasian rhododendron (Rhododendron caucasicum), and a rich herbaceous layer, including bushes of fruiting blueberry and lingonberry (Vaccinium spp.; Zimina and Yasny 1977). In the Tseidon River valley of the North Ossetia Nature Reserve, S. kazbegica was captured at an elevation of 1,850 meters in an avalanche cone characterized by tall grass and pine vegetation. The species feeds on insects, fruits and seeds. Stomach content analysis of two wild-caught specimens from the Skazdon Gorge revealed that one individual’s diet was dominated by seeds, while the other contained primarily green plant material; insect remains were minimal. Like other members of the genus, S. kazbegica hibernates, with the hibernation period lasting at least six months annually. Little is known about the species' reproductive biology, though existing data suggest a potentially delayed onset of the breeding season in the studied populations. Litter sizes range from four to seven offspring. Birch mice are generally nocturnal and spend much of the day in shallow burrows.
threats: Overgrazing due to clearing of tall grasses is a major threat. Loss of tall grass from grass cutting for agriculture is also a threat in some areas. Habitat outside protected areas is projected to continue declining (Holden et al. 2017).
population: The species is locally common in the northern part of its range (in Russia) and maybe rare in Georgia.
