In the Tseidon River valley within the North Ossetian Nature Reserve, Baskevich et al. (2024) successfully captured 11 specimens of S. kazbegica, comprising 27.5% of all small mammals trapped. S. kazbegica was ranked as the second most abundant species, following wood mice (genus Sylvaemus).
range: This species is known only from the Kazbegi District and south Ossetia, Georgia (Sokolov et al. 1986, Sokolov et al. 1987, Bukhnikashvili 2004, Rusin et al. 2018), and in north Ossetia, Russia; however, further surveys could reveal that the range is significantly larger, and the results of species distribution models have implied that its distribution may extend to the east of its known localities along the southern slope of the Great Caucasus Ridge in Georgia (Shenbrot and Kryštufek 2021, G. Shenbrot pers. comm. 2025). The species has been karyotyped at two and genotyped in two other isolated localities (Pisano et al. 2015, Rusin et al. 2018). Two karyotypes or chromosomal races are known: 2n = 42, NF = 52 from the gorge in Suatisi, Kazbeg region of Georgia (Sokolov et al. 1986) and 2n = 40, NF = 50 from the Tsey gorge in North Ossetia, Russia (Sokolov and Baskevich 1992).
useTrade: Kazbeg Birch Mouse is not utilized.
conservationActions: Most documented occurrences of S. kazbegica are located within or in close proximity to protected areas, which play a critical role in the conservation of this rare and range-restricted species. In Russia, notable habitats include the North Ossetia Nature Reserve - established in 1967 and encompassing approximately 29,000 hectares - and the adjacent Alaniya National Park, which spans 54,926 hectares and was established in 1998. Both areas provide important refugia, offering suitable subalpine and montane habitats, as well as legal protection from development and intensive land use. In Georgia, S. kazbegica is known from within the Kazbegi National Park, which covers 144,600 hectares and was established in 1976. This protected area includes a diverse range of altitudinal zones, from forested valleys to alpine meadows, encompassing much of the species’ preferred habitat. The park’s management regime supports biodiversity conservation and limits activities that could degrade these sensitive ecosystems. Together, these reserves are sufficiently large to support viable populations of S. kazbegica, conserving both the species and the integrity of its mountainous habitat. Continued protection, along with ecological monitoring and habitat management, will be essential for the long-term survival of this poorly known rodent.

rationale: Procavia capensis is listed as Least Concern. This species has an extensive geographic range, is locally abundant, and present in many protected areas throughout its range. Although locally threatened by habitat destruction, hunting, fire, disease, and invasive predators, it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: Procavia capensis is predominantly diurnal and gregarious. This species lives in a wide range of habitats, from arid deserts to rainforest, but are typically associated with rocky outcrops (kopjes), cliffs or boulders with ample crevices, moderate vegetation cover, and connectivity across the landscape. This species is typically absent from regions which lack rocky refuges such as the Congo Basin rainforest, Kalahari sands, Mozambique-Maputaland coastal plains, Miombo woodlands, and lava deserts (e.g., northern Kenya). This species is an agile rock climber and occupies erosion gullies in the Karoo, South Africa, road culverts, and Aardvark Orycteropus afer holes (Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). Fairall et al. (1986) suggest that shelter is the factor limiting population growth. Procavia capensis occurs from sea level to at least 4,300 m asl on Mount Kenya (Coe 1962, Young and Evans 1993). Procavia capensis are generalist herbivores. Their diet consists of grasses, forbs, and shrubs, with a predilection for new shoots, buds, fruits, and berries (Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). Teklehaimanot (2015) identified more than 44 food plant species eaten by P. c. capillosa in Bale Mountains National Park, Ethiopia. Procavia capensis occur in colonies or family groups of up to 80 individuals. These consist largely of related adult females and a territorial male (Teklehaimanot and Balakrishnan 2018). Colony size depends mostly on the size of kopjes or rocky outcrops. Larger kopjes can support several colonies (Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). Sub-adult males disperse when mature while females disperse voluntarily. Dispersing individuals are highly vulnerable to predation (Hoeck et al. 1982). They often occur in association with Bush Hyrax Heterohyrax brucei (Hoeck 1975, Barry and Mundy 1988). A comprehensive review of the natural history of P. capensis is presented in Olds and Shoshani (1982) and in Hoeck and Bloomer (2013).
threats: Procavia capensis is locally threatened and may have been extirpated in some smaller localities (Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). The more serious threats across its range are driven by human activity. Main threats include habitat destruction, modification, and fragmentation mostly due to urban expansion, road construction, agricultural development, and fire. This species is highly dependent on the availability of rocky refuges with ample crevices, moderate vegetative cover (especially shrubs), and suitable microclimates for thermoregulation, as well as the connectivity of these habitats across the landscape. Other threats include disease, hunting (meat, skin), and vermin control because of conflict with humans, particularly due to crop damage (Rifai et al. 2000, Barry et al. 2008, Hoeck and Bloomer 2013, Visser and Wimberger 2014, Teklehaimanot and Balakrishnan 2018, Ben-Moshe and Iwamura 2020). Procavia capensis is hunted for its skin, meat, and traditional uses across much of its range. In Saudi Arabia it is poached for sport. This hunting appears to be heavy at some sites and is likely a major cause of its current restricted distribution in the country (T.M. Butynski pers. comm.). Procavia capensis is hunted in Jordan for consumption and considered a delicacy (Rifai et al. 2000). Due to its feeding on fruit trees and other cultivated plants, there is retaliation by farmers. In Israel, where it is protected by law and has few natural enemies, numbers have grown in cultivated areas and settlements, resulting in damage to crops and necessitating control measures (e.g., electric fences and culls; Mendelssohn and Yom-Tov 1999). Procavia capensis numbers have been ‘much reduced’ throughout their range in Egypt due to hunting and clearance of Acacia trees for charcoal (Hoath 2003). In South Africa, P. capensis it is locally hunted for bushmeat and vermin control which leads to local declines (Visser and Wimberger 2014). In Lesotho and Ethiopia, this species is hunted with dogs (Lynch 1994, Reda 2015), and with snares in South Africa (K. Wimberger pers. obs. 2007 in Visser and Wimberger 2014). These activities are, however, probably not, overall, greatly impacting this species (Visser and Wimberger 2014). Subpopulations have become locally extinct due to drought (Barry and Mundy 1998). Disease (sarcoptic mange) may have caused local extinctions in the KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa, in the late 1990s (Wimberger et al. 2009). Wildfires are a significant threat, leading to habitat degradation and population declines in the Bale Mountains, Ethiopia, (Reda 2015). Although cultivated areas and settlements locally facilitate higher densities of P. capensis, these areas are prone to an increase in human-wildlife conflict and zoonotic disease transmission. The latter is also a risk where P. capensis is hunted for bushmeat. Predation by invasive predators is a threat to P. capensis in places. For example, the spread of Middle Eastern Red Fox Vulpes vulpes arabica in Sinai, Egypt, has contributed to population declines (Coals and Gilbert 2015). This fox, first recorded in Sinai in the late 1990’s (Saleh and Basuony 1998), followed human settlement and became a common predator of P. capensis in St Katherine, Egypt (Gilbert and Zalat 2009). Coals and Gilbert (2015) note that local knowledge suggests a link between the expansion of V. v. arabica and the decline of P. capensis in South Sinai.
population: Procavia capensis is widespread and locally abundant in rocky areas. Populations are regulated by parasites, predation, intra-specific competition, reproduction, immigration, and dispersal (Hoeck et al. 1982). In some parts of their range (e.g. Matopo National Park, Zimbabwe, and Serengeti National Park, Tanzania), P. capensis is characterized by extreme local population fluctuations as a result of rainfall patterns (drought), presence of predators, and possibly disease outbreaks (Wimberger et al. 2009, Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). Procavia capensis densities range from 0.73 individuals per hectares in Matopo National Park, Zimbabwe, to 20-100 animals per km² on Mount Kenya, where they are considered among the most conspicuous mammals, (Young and Evans 1993). In Tanzania, South Africa, and Israel, P. capensis densities are positively correlated with human settlements (Fairall et al. 1985, Wiid and Butler 2014, Mbise 2015). These authors speculate that this is due to increased food availability and decreased numbers of predators.
range: Procavia capensis has a wide geographic range throughout sub-Saharan Africa, northeast Africa, and Arabia, in which it is discontinuously distributed. In Africa, P. capensis occurs from Senegal and south Mauritania through southern Algeria (isolated population), Libya and Egypt (east of the Nile River) to the Horn of Africa, East Africa, Central Africa (excluding the Congo Basin forests), and southern Africa. Within Arabia, P. capensis occurs in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen, Lebanon, Jordan, Syria, and Israel (Olds and Shoshani 1982, Harrison and Bates 1991, Rifai et al. 2000, Shoshani 2005, Hoeck and Bloomer 2013). Reports of occurrence in Turkey are in error as there is no evidence for its current or historical occurrence (Kryštufek and Vohralík 2001). Restricted and rare in southwest Syria (Aidek et al. 2025). The previous Red List assessment for P. capensis lists and maps Rwanda and Burundi as within the geographic range (Butynski et al. 2015). This now appears to be an error.
useTrade: Procavia capensis is hunted for its skin, meat, and traditional uses across much of its range. In South Africa it is hunted for vermin control (Visser and Wimberger 2014). In Saudi Arabia, it is poached for sport. This hunting appears to be heavy at some sites and is likely a major cause of its current restricted distribution in the country (T.M. Butynski pers. comm.). Procavia capensis is hunted in Jordan for its meat, which is considered a delicacy (Rifai et al. 2000).
conservationActions: Procavia capensis occurs in many large, well-protected areas across much of its range. Some forms of land use benefits P. capensis, including fruit orchards, human settlements, tourist facilities as they often have readily available foods and sometimes lack natural predators (Wiid and Butler 2015, Mbise et al. 2017, Ben-Moshe and Iwamura 2020). This can locally lead to increased population size or even over-population. In some parts of their range this species is a pest (Mendelssohn and Yom-Tov 1999, Wimberger et al. 2009, Wiid and Butler 2014). Although P. capensis is locally threatened throughout its geographic range and has been locally extirpated, there are no threats to its long-term survival.

rationale: Although this species is endemic to northwest South Africa, and has a relatively small distributional range, it is assessed as Least Concern because most of its habitat falls within protected areas, its current population is considered stable, it exists in rocky areas unlikely to be transformed and no current major threats have been identified. Calculated using the available natural habitat within its geographic range, the estimated area of occupancy is 20,725 km². While the extensive construction of solar and wind projects across the Northern Cape may become a threat to this species, the effects should be minimal since much of the distribution is in protected areas. However, outside these areas, extensive alternative energy projects may be problematic. Additionally, goat farming could have harmful and destructive effects on the habitat outside protected areas due to the grazing and browsing of goats amongst the rocks. Thus, all impacts should be carefully monitored. Additionally, extreme climate change may represent an emerging threat, especially due to its restricted range. Further field surveys, vetting of museum records and molecular research are necessary to resolve the distribution of this species and to quantify potential threats. This species should be reassessed once such data are available.
habitat: As a nocturnal and solitary species (Skinner and Chimimba 2005), the Barbour’s Rock Mouse is restricted to the arid regions of western South Africa, specifically within rocky areas of succulent shrubland. It is mainly granivorous (Coetzee 2013). There is limited research pertaining to its diet, reproduction and behaviour.Ecosystem and cultural services: This species is not known to provide any specific cultural services, but as a small rodent of the Succulent Karoo, it may be a valuable prey species for small predators and birds of prey and may also contribute to seed dispersal.
threats: There are no major threats that have been recognised for this species. However, overgrazing by nomadic livestock, in particular goats, may become a threat in parts of its range as they graze and browse the vegetation amongst the rocks (sensu Anderson and Hoffman 2007, Coetzee 2013). Additionally, alternative energy projects are expanding across much of the Northern Cape (van der Westhuizen 2013) and may pose a threat in the form of habitat fragmentation and/or alteration in areas outside of projected areas. Finally, climate change is predicted to affect resource availability and distribution in the region of the Succulent Karoo (Hoffman et al. 2009), which may have negative implications for this species.Climate Change: To quantify the potential threat of climate change on the species habitat, species distribution modelling under future climate projections were performed. From a conservation perspective, the models show a consistent reduction in habitat for P. barbouri ranging between 1%-3% by 2040 (Cowan 2025).
population: The population size or density of the species is unknown. Although the geographic range of this species is limited, they are not considered uncommon within their range. However, Coetzee (2013) considers them to be rare.Population Genetics: No population genetics studies have been undertaken on the species; however, it is possible the species exists as a metapopulation. While the population is listed as Least Concern, no measures of population density or overall size are known. A population genetic study across the species range would be highly informative at informing it structure and diversity.
range: Endemic to the arid northwestern region of South Africa (Monadjem et al. 2015), this species has been identified from the Namaqua National Park, Skilpad Nature Reserve and Goegap Nature Reserve in the region of Springbok (Northern Cape) (Coetzee 2013), southeastwards to the Tankwa Karoo National Park (Western and Northern Cape). It appears to be widely distributed in Namaqualand (Shortridge 1942, Coetzee 2013). In the lower Orange River basin, it is sympatric or parapatric with P. collinus and P. monticularis (Coetzee 2013). It ranges at altitudes between 100 m and 700 m asl. Further vetting of museum records is necessary to delimit distribution more accurately.
useTrade: This species does not appear to be utilised or traded in any form.
conservationActions: Barbour’s Rock Mouse is present within at least four protected areas within the assessment region, namely: Goegap Nature Reserve, Namaqua National Park, Skilpad Nature Reserve and the Tankwa Karoo National Park. Currently, no species-specific conservation interventions are necessary. However, further research is necessary to delineate the population dynamics, quantify current and potential threats, and investigate the general ecology and life history traits of this species.Recommendations for land managers and practitioners: Systematic surveys needed to gather information on population size, trend and distribution.Research priorities:Accurate distribution mapping and the identification of population size and trend estimates is necessary.  Potential threats to this species, as well as the implications and type of habitat loss and fragmentation impacting this species. For example, an analysis of the impact of alternative energy projects.Understanding the life history and ecology, paying particular attention to food and dispersal mechanisms. Research into the reproductive rate and breeding success of this species. Species contribution to ecosystem functioning.Vetting of museum records to delimit distribution more accurately.Encouraged citizen actions:Report sightings on virtual museum platforms (for example, iNaturalist and MammalMAP), especially outside protected areas. However, due to their morphological similarities, misidentification of this species with other Petromyscus species is common. rationale: This species has a wide distribution with a large extent of occurrence of 816,795 km2. It is naturally rare throughout its range, but is locally abundant in areas such as Bugeon-Gun. It is provisionally assessed as Least Concern, but data on its population trends and potential threats are lacking, and further research is needed.
habitat: Sicista caudata is known from only a few specimens, with limited ecological data available. In 2023, six individuals were collected in mixed forest at ~740 m in the Hengdaohezi region, Heilongjiang Province, China. The species occupies a range of habitats, including coniferous and broadleaf forests, ecotones, and tall-grass clearings. On northern Sakhalin Island, it avoids larch forests but prefers dark old-growth fir and spruce forests, shifting to mixed forests in the south. It is also found in disturbed areas such as reed grass stands, birch and bamboo groves, and river floodplains. In the Sikhote-Alin Mountains, it inhabits mixed forests at low elevations and coniferous taiga at higher altitudes. Generally, birch mice are mostly active at night. They spend much of the day in shallow burrows. Species of this genus undergo a hibernation period lasting at least six months each year. Feeds mostly on seeds. Litter size is 4-6 young.
threats: The threats to this species are unknown.
population: Fewer than 20 specimens have been reported to date (Liu et al. 2024), though additional unpublished captures have likely occurred in Russia, potentially providing more data (T. Cserkész pers. comm. 2025). However, population status and trends remain unknown. Sheremet'ev (2004) rarely trapped this species on both Russkiy Island and mainland southern Primorye. Peak abundance on the island was 1.3 individuals per 100 trap-days, with no captures in low-density years. In mainland areas, abundance can reach 5 individuals per 100 trap-days. The species is generally considered rare throughout its range (Holden et al. 2017) but is locally abundant in areas such as Bugeon-Gun (Won 1968).
range: This species is distributed in northeastern China (Heilongjiang and Jilin) as reviewed by Gao et al. (2024), the Ussuri region and from Sakhalin Island, Russkiy Island (Russia). It also inhabits the Korean Peninsula according to the review of Won and Smith (1999) but has been reported only from the northern peninsula: Gangjin Lake, Bugeon-Gun, Samjiyon-Gun in South Hamgyong and Yanggang (= northern part of Kangwon Province) provinces.
conservationActions: In China listed as Data Deficient, in Russia as Rare Species. Occurs in Changbaishan and Sikhote-Alin UNESCO-MAB Biosphere Reserves and some protected areas (eg. Kedrovaya Pad Nature Reserve, Botchinskii Nature Reserve).

rationale: Bearded Seals are a widely distributed, low-density, species that probably numbers in the low hundreds of thousands across its circumpolar Arctic range. No abundance-trend information is available for this species in any Arctic region. However, there is significant concern regarding climate change impacts on Bearded Seals because of dramatic declines in their sea ice habitats over the last three decades due to global warming and documentation of declines in breeding activity indicated by acoustic monitoring in areas that have experienced a shift from Arctic to Atlantic water masses in the Svalbard Archipelago. Bearded Seal mortality levels were high in recent unexplained mortality events (UME) in the Pacific Arctic that have been linked to sea ice losses, fortifying the concern that disease risks are increasing for this (and other) ice-associated seal species. Negative impacts of ocean acidification, toxic algae blooms and reduced fall-out of sea-ice algal production to benthic communities, which provide food for Bearded Seals, are additional concerns. Increasing ocean noise is also a concern for bearded seals that use acoustic communication over many kilometres to communicate, especially during the breeding season; noise can mask the seals signals to one another.Given the documented declines in sea ice in the Arctic and the expectation that these trends, and related negative effects on benthic community production, will continue in the coming decades, the Bearded Seal is assessed as Near Threatened under criteria A3ce on the basis of suspected future population declines over the next 40 years (three generation lengths; 40.2 years), which could approach 30%. Increasing risks of pathogens and potential competition from temperate species expanding northward add to the risk scenario. Whilst regional declines in vocalizations and sightings have been documented in the past 40 years in the Northeast Atlantic, the overall suspected decline is not thought to have reached the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion A2.The evaluation to list as NT is based on the precautionary principle because of major declines in their sea ice habitats (>50%), high death rates in recent disease episodes in the Pacific Arctic, possible declines in pregnancy rates and suspected declines in abundance in some areas based on acoustics data. These threats are tempered somewhat by the Bearded Seal’s current global population size, broad distribution, flexible feeding habitats and willingness to haul-out on shore, and pup and nurse on glacier ice, as well as their use of various ice types (first year land-fast ice, but also drift ice) for breeding, moulting and resting. Improved monitoring of population sizes and trends of Bearded Seals across their range is essential to improve assessment of the species’ status.
habitat: Bearded Seals are the largest northern phocid seal (Kovacs 2018). Adults are on average 2.3 m (standard) in length and weigh an average of 275 kg. Females are slightly longer and (seasonally) substantially heavier than males (Burns 1981, Andersen et al. 1999). In spring females can weigh in excess of 400 kg (Kovacs and Lydersen 2006, Cameron et al. 2010). Bearded Seals naturally occur at quite low densities, and they are typically solitary, although they do form small, loose aggregations at times, particularly if sea ice is limited during the spring (Bengtson et al. 2005, Kovacs 2018). Bearded Seals are strongly associated with sea ice and are principally benthic feeders; these two attributes explain their general distribution patterns in shallow coastal shelf seas (Citta et al. 2018, Hamilton et al. 2021, 2022). However, bearded seals do occupy offshore, deep water (3,000 m +) habitats in areas with high concentrations of drift-ice in the Arctic Ocean north of the Barents Sea (Llobet et al. 2023, KMK pers. obs.)In Svalbard, females reach sexual maturity at an age of five, while males are six years of age when they are sexually mature though they are likely some years older before they compete successfully to breed (Andersen et al. 1999). In Alaskan waters, sexual maturity is reached between 2.5–4 years in females (Quakenbush et al. 2011, Alaska Department of Fish and Game 2020) and males reach sexual maturity somewhat older, at 6–7 years (Burns 1981). Final body size in Bearded Seals is reached at approximately 9–10 years (McLaren 1958) with maximum longevity being 25–30 years (Cameron et al. 2010). Pups are born at an average length of 131 cm and an average weight of 37 kg (Burns 1981, Kovacs et al. 2020). Sex ratios are 1:1 at birth but are skewed toward females at older ages, perhaps due to higher mortality in males though this may be a hunt bias because struck and lost is lower in females because they are fatter and float when shot (Johnson et al. 1966, Quakenbush et al. 2011).Bearded Seal pups are born in drift ice areas or on small floes of annual ice that fracture away from shore-fast ice as it breaks up in late spring (Kovacs et al. 1996, Kovacs and Lydersen 2006). They also have been documented to use glacier ice pieces floating on the sea for birthing and nursing when forced to by the lack of availability of first-year sea ice (Lydersen et al. 2014, Kovacs et al. 2020). The large precocial pups swim within hours of birth (Lydersen et al. 1994, 1996). Peak birthing occurs between late March and mid-May, varying somewhat across the Bearded Seal’s range (Burns 1981, Kovacs 2018). Gjertz et al. (2000) estimated that pups in Svalbard are weaned when 18–24 days of age. Nursing might be somewhat shorter for the Pacific subspecies; Burns (1981) suggested that pups are weaned at 12–18 days of age (though longitudinal records for individuals are lacking for the Pacific subspecies). Prior to weaning, their aquatic skills develop to the degree that they spend about half their time in the water, diving for up to 5.5 minutes to depths of up to 84 m (Lydersen et al. 1994). Mothers spend over 80% of their time in the water while caring for a dependent pup (Lydersen and Kovacs 1999); about half that time is spent away from the neonate, presumably conducting foraging dives. Females haul-out to nurse their pups, on average three times a day. The small amounts of time mothers spend out of the water when pups are young is thought to be an adaptive response to Polar Bear (Ursus maritimus) predation; when only the pup is on the surface, it is less conspicuous to hunting bears (Krafft et al. 2000). Diving depths during the nursing period generally reflect local bathymetry (Gjertz et al. 2000, Krafft et al. 2000). Mating takes place toward the end of lactation, similar to other phocid seals.Following the spring nursing and mating periods, weaned pups disperse along coastlines in Svalbard, sometimes going offshore into ice-filled waters for periods of some days before returning to waters over the coastal shelf, and then settling into areas where they remain resident at least the rest of the first year of life (Hamilton et al. 2019a), and likely beyond this time. Diving skill develops over the first weeks of life, stabilizing to adult-like abilities by the time pups are about 50 days old, when pups spent 75% of their time diving and less than 10% of their time hauled out. However, pups lack the highly specialized behaviour patterns displayed by adults in terms of movement patterns. Similar short range coastal dispersion of pups has been documented in Alaska (Citta et al. 2018). Juvenile Bearded seals tracked in the Bering, Chukchi and Beaufort Seas occupied shallow coastal waters with intermediate concentrations and showed strong affiliation with sea ice edges (Breed et al. 2018, Cameron et al. 2018, Olnes et al. 2020). The strong affiliation with edges seems to have disappeared in a more recent study following reduction in overall sea ice availability in the Pacific Arctic and might have been an artifact of where intermediate ice concentrations were found in the past (Olnes et al. 2021).Bearded Seal males produce elaborate downward trilling vocalizations during the spring to display to females during their mating period. These “songs” dominate the Arctic soundscape in spring across the species range (e.g. Cleator et al. 1989, Ahonen et al. 2017, Heimrich et al. 2020, Moore et al. 2012, Llobet et al. 2023). Propagation models suggest that Bearded Seal vocalizations can travel up to 40 km, depending on ambient noise levels (Crance et al. 2022). Individual males use distinct songs and occupy the same territories over a series of consecutive years within constraints imposed by variable ice conditions, or they show a roaming strategy (Van Parijs et al. 2001, 2003, 2004). Males also exhibit aggressive behaviour to each other during breeding, including bubble-blowing and physical combat, so the mating system is presumably polygynous to some degree. Bearded Seals from different regions exhibit strong dialect differences in their songs and acoustic repertoires (Risch et al. 2007, Charrier et al. 2013) and males recognise songs from their region and respond differently to them compared to sounds from other regions (Charrier et al. 2013). Calling rates are linked to sea ice concentrations and earlier seasonal losses of sea ice cover in the Pacific region has been linked to earlier termination of spring calling (MacIntyre et al. 2015, Llobet et al. 2023). Bearded Seals have acute underwater hearing and an exceptionally broad frequency range, and they can extract species-specific signals from background noise well (Sills et al. 2020a). Loud noise exposure tests showed that Bearded Seals experience temporary threshold shifts when exposed to noise levels analogous to seismic air gun sounds (Sills et al. 2020b).In some Arctic regions Bearded Seals are reported to be very sedentary throughout the year, occupying relatively small coastal home ranges (e.g. Hamilton et al. 2018, 2021, Rosing-Asvid et al. 2012, 2015). In Svalbard pups settle into small home ranges after a dispersal phase following weaning; maximum straight-line displacement from the natal fjord was 150 km, and no tracked individuals left the archipelago (Hamilton et al. 2019a). However, In the Beaufort-Bering-Chukchi region as well as in Baffin Bay/Davis Strait between west Greenland and Canada Bearded Seals undergo seasonal movements linked with the advance and retreat of sea ice in the (Burns 1981, Frost et al. 2008, Cameron et al. 2010, Breed et al. 2018, Boye et al. 2020), although some individuals do remain in the northern reaches of their range throughout the year in both areas (Frouin-Mouy et al. 2017, Jimbo et al. 2019).Dive and movement behaviour suggest that Bearded Seals behave as a generalist species, with a lot of individual variation in foraging and movement patterns (Hamilton et al. 2018, Olnes et al. 2020) although adult animals in Svalbard appear to be highly specialized feeders at the level of the individual, remaining in small ranges and following set paths between resting and foraging areas over sequential seasons (Hamilton et al. 2018, 2019b). Additionally, Bearded Seals were found to have the smallest feeding niche-space among 10 marine mammal species studied in the Barents Region. This niche was described as benthic-benthopelagic and did not overlap with the other species (MacKenzie et al. 2022). Similar findings of a unique feeding niche are reported for Bearded Seals in the White Sea (Svetocheva and Svetochev 2015). Bearded Seals feed primarily on or near the bottom, although they do also take some pelagic prey, and most diving is to depths of less than 200 m though dive depths for both young-of-the-year and adults have been recorded down to 500 m (Gjertz et al. 2000, Rosing-Asvid et al. 2012, Hamilton et al. 2018). Bearded Seals use their elaborate, flexible whiskers to search for food items on and in soft bottom substrates and they have powerful suction abilities afforded by a unique bifurcated tongue and skull morphology that promotes suction abilities (Marshall et al. 2006, 2008, Summarell et al. 2015, Kienle and Berta 2016).The diet of Bearded Seals varies by age, location, and season (see Lowry et al. 1980). Polar Cod (Boreogadis saida), Sculpins, Spider Crab, and Shrimps (Sabinea sptemcarinatus and Sclerocrangon boreas) are the most frequent prey items in Svalbard (Hjelset et al. 1999). However, various Cod species and other demersal fish, and worms are also regular components of the diet. A wide variety of prey has been reported from the Pacific Arctic. Quakenbush et al. (2011) analyzed the frequency of occurrence of prey in 943 Bearded Seal stomachs collected from the Bering and Chukchi Seas during 1960–2009 and identified 213 different prey taxa. The most commonly eaten groups were Crabs, Shrimps, Clams, Snails, benthic and demersal fishes, and echiuroid worms. These authors found a significant increase in consumption of gadid fishes, principally Polar Cod (also known as Arctic cod in North America) and Saffron Cod (Eleginus gracilis), from the 1960s to the 2000s.Bearded Seals have an extended moulting period and animals can be found shedding hair from April to August, though there appears to be a peak in May/June for both subspecies (Burns 1981, Gjertz et al. 2000, Thometz et al. 2021). During the moult they spend much of their time hauled out and are reluctant to enter the water (Kovacs and Lydersen 2006). Bearded Seals use sea ice as a haulout platform on a year-round basis whenever it is available, preferring small and medium-sized floes and generally avoiding large floes (Simpkins et al. 2003). However, they will haul out on land in the summer in the absence of sea ice (e.g., Merkel et al. 2013, Olnes et al. 2020) and are known to use inland water bodies at least seasonally (Stewart and Lockhart 2005, Gryba et al. 2021). They are rarely found more than a body length from access to water, even if hauled out on land (Kovacs 2018).Natural predators of Bearded Seals include Polar Bears, Killer Whales (Orcinus orca), sleeper sharks (Somniosus spp.), and Walruses (Odobenus rosmarus) (Lowry and Fay 1984, Lowry et al. 1987, Kovacs and Lydersen 2006, Leclerc et al. 2012, Kovacs 2018). Killer whales are increasing in several Arctic locales, which is likely to influence predation rates on other marine mammals, including Bearded Seals (Ferguson et al. 2010, Stafford et al. 2019)
threats: Global climate warming is currently causing major reductions in the extent and duration of sea ice cover in the Arctic, creating a threat to all ice-associated marine mammals including Bearded Seals. Bearded Seals are dependent on sea ice for pupping, moulting, resting, and access to foraging areas (Laidre et al. 2008, 2015; Huntington et al. 2016, 2017; Kovacs 2011, 2012, 2018, 2021). Increasing disease risks with a warming climate is a major concern; Bearded Seals experienced significant mortality levels during recent UMEs (unexplained mortality events) in the Pacific Arctic (Vanwormer et al. 2019, Barratclough et al. 2023). The low historical exposure to diseases, and hence low immunity is likely to result in higher risk of epizootic events for Bearded Seals (Goertz et al. 2019). Increases in toxic algal blooms in the Arctic are a special concern for the benthically-feeding Bearded Seal in a climate change context, as are expected reductions in benthic production (Lefebvre et al. 2016, Grebmeier et al. 2018, Hendrix et al. 2021). Crawford et al. (2015) documented some new fish species in the diet of bearded seals in the North Pacific Arctic, but the small dietary changes were not associated with reduction in body condition, growth or age-at-maturity. Additionally, the proportion of pups in the hunt did not change between 1975-1984 and 2003-2012, suggesting that production and survival to weaning were unchanged with the sea ice reductions observed over their study period. Craine et al. (2021) also explored temporal changes in bearded seals pre- (1953–1968) and post- (1998–2014) sea ice declines. These authors found higher cortisol concentrations, more negative δ13C values and significantly lower pregnancy rates (though caution was suggested for the latter finding because the sample sizes in the period groupings was small) in the recent period compared to the earlier period. High cortisol values are usually interpreted as elevated stress levels and the change in carbon isotopes indicates a dietary shift toward more pelagic prey or more offshore prey or a greater dietary diversity.Declines in calling rates have been detected in areas where Atlantic Water intrusions are increasingly common (where Arctic Water prevailed some decades ago) in the Atlantic Arctic (Llobet et al. 2021) and sightings rates have declined in the southern parts of the Svalbard Archipelago (Bengtsson et al. 2021). Grebmeier (2012) suggested that the Alaskan Arctic ecosystem will shift to a more pelagic system, which is thought to already be underway (Huntington et al. 2020); such a shift will support new communities of secondary and tertiary consumers, potentially leading to a lack of suitable prey, increased competition, or dietary shifts for endemic species, such as bearded seals (Moore and Stabeno 2015, Moore et al. 2018, Huntington et al. 2020).Ongoing increases in shipping, development and industrialization of the Arctic (PAME 2019, 2021) is likely to threaten Bearded Seals in several ways. Increased anthropogenic noise is a specific concern for Bearded Seals, given that Bearded Seals will vocally compensate for increased ambient noise, up to a threshold, after which they cease calling (Fournet et al., 2021). This suggests a vulnerability to increased ambient noise and acoustic masking. If ambient noise levels in the Arctic continue to rise because of a lengthening in the open water season and increases in vessel traffic, and marine industrial activity, the resultant acoustic masking and/or the physical stress of altering their calling behaviour could have negative impacts on reproductive success (Halliday et al. 2020, Stafford 2021).Oil spills from offshore extraction and transportation could negatively affect Bearded Seals through direct contact with oil and damage to foraging areas and stocks of prey, particularly benthic invertebrates, that are vulnerable to oil contamination. Ice-breaking vessels can cause direct habitat destruction and elevated disturbance levels (Wilson et al. 2020). Other forms of pollution are not an acute threat to Bearded Seals because they are largely lower trophic feeders. But like all Arctic marine mammals, mercury, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS – that are not listed under the Stockholm Convention), current-use pesticides (CUPs), and organophosphate esters (OPEs) remain a concern to marine mammal health (Correa et al. 2015, AMAP 2020, 2021).Hunting by indigenous peoples continues throughout most of the species’ range. Reports from Alaska Native subsistence hunters do not give any indication that Bearded Seal numbers have declined (Quakenbush et al. 2011, 2019) and Nelson et al. (2019) assessed Alaskan harvests as being sustainable. Harvest monitoring should be more consistently undertaken and periodic assessments of sustainability are warranted for Bearded Seals given that some populations are locally resident, densities are naturally low, and population trends are unknown.
population: Population sizes are only estimated for some few regions (see Kovacs et al. 2021 for a summary) and abundance trends are not known at all for Bearded Seals. The natural low density of Bearded Seals and the fact that they spend very little of their time hauled out such that they are accessible for counting outside the peak moulting season (5%; Hamilton et al. 2018) makes it very challenging to determine the abundance of this species. Additionally, numbers on the surface are heavily influenced by wind and temperature conditions as well as seasonal patterns (Hamilton et al. 2018, Scherdin et al. 2022, London et al. 2024; see for more details) and perhaps also decadal oscillations (Chambellant et al. 2012). However, their distinctive spring breeding calls are easily monitored using passive acoustic listening/recording networks and such data suggests that this species remains widespread in the Arctic (Heimrich et al. 2021, Crance et al. 2022, Llobet et al. 2023, Dingwall et al. 2024).Bearded Seals have never been surveyed in Svalbard or western Russian waters. Expert opinion suggests that some 4,000–5,000 bearded seals occupy the White Sea (Svetochev and Svetocheva et al. 2012) and a population some 10 times this (40,000) live in the Kara Sea (Svetocheva et al. 2016), though no systematic surveys have been conducted in these areas. In other parts of the world, Bearded Seal abundance has been estimated, though most reports note that there are many regional gaps, and that the species is in fact data deficient. In northeast Greenland some survey effort has been undertaken in the Northeast Water Polynya area (NEW) for marine mammals, with some few Bearded Seals sighting (eight in winter and 14 in summer) in quite vast areas (circa 9,000 and 30,000 km2), so a population estimate was not possible based on these data (NAMMCO 2023), but it is likely that the population in this region is small. Heide-Jørgensen et al. (2013, 2016) produced several estimates for Bearded Seals in the North Water Polynya in West Greenland of some 6,000 animals. Chambellant et al. (2012) conducted surveys over 7 years in southern Hudson Bay and had very high interannual variance in density, with abundance estimates ranging from 279-1494. Fuirst et al. (2023) provide a thorough review of Bearded Seal estimates in Canadian waters, concluding that data coverage is too fragmentary to provide a comprehensive abundance estimate or trends, but regional populations range in size in Canadian waters from some hundreds to low thousands of animals.Population estimation of Bearded Seals has received considerable effort in the Pacific Arctic. A comprehensive review by Cameron et al. (2010) concluded that combined estimates for all regions in the Pacific Arctic summed to some 250,000 individuals, though the estimates were largely based on inadequate surveys. A lot of effort has gone into methods for surveying and estimating abundance of ice-seals in the broad Pacific Arctic region (Chernook et al. 2014, Conn et al. 2014, 2015, 2016; McClintock et al. 2015, Sigler et al. 2015). Recent estimates from Russian territories suggest 39,743 Bearded Seals occurred in the Sea of Okhotsk in 2013 (Chernook et al. 2014) and 42,000 occurred in the western Bering Sea during spring of 2012 and 2013 (Chernook et al. 2018). Conn et al. (2014) estimated there were 299,174 bearded seals in the eastern Bering Sea in 2012. In 2016, a comprehensive aerial survey of bearded seals over a substantial portion of their range produced a population estimate of 147,421 (CV = 0.13) for the Chukchi Sea and a small portion of the East Siberian Sea, an area of 846,250 km² (Boveng et al. 2024). A new genetics-based approach to population estimation, called close-kin mark-recapture, produced an estimate of 409,000 (CV = 0.35) Bearded Seals in the Bering, Chukchi, and Beaufort seas, combined (Quakenbush, in NAMMCO 2023, citing Taras et al. 2023). This region of shallow seas is undoubtedly a stronghold for Bearded Seals (Citta et al. 2018), with recent estimates totalling roughly 400,000–500,000 individuals.
range: The species has a patchy distribution throughout much of the Arctic and sub-Arctic and is found in West Greenland, Canada (Eastern Canadian Archipelago–Hudson Bay, south to Labrador), and in the Pacific Arctic throughout the shallow Beaufort-Bering-Chukchi region (including Alaskan coastal areas), as well as in the Sea of Okhotsk, extending westward across the coast of the Siberian seas, through the Laptev, Kara, and White sea as well as the coasts of Novaya Zemlya (in Russia) and westward across the Barents Region to South and East Greenland including the Svalbard and Frans Josef Land archipelagos (Kovacs 2018). Bearded seals also occur offshore in some deep-water areas (>2,000 m) in the Barents Region that have high concentrations of drift ice (Llobet et al. 2023, KMK pers. obs.).Bearded Seals have been reported as vagrants in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, northern Newfoundland, and in Massachusetts in the Northwest Atlantic (Gosselin and Boily 1994), as well as in Japan and China in the North Pacific (Naito 1979, Rice 1998). They are occasionally reported from the north coast of Iceland (Hauksson and Boganson 1995) and many vagrants have been reported within Europe, as far south as Portugal (van Bree 2000).
useTrade: Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have hunted Bearded Seals for subsistence use for thousands of years, a practice that continues today throughout the species’ range. Hundreds of Bearded Seals are hunted annually in Greenland (Garde 2013) and smaller hunts take place in northern Iceland and Svalbard (see NAMMCO marine mammal catch database). Harvests in many areas are not recorded. Historically, individual boats took large numbers (hundreds) of Bearded Seals as “by-catch” in Svalbard during the era of Polar Bear trapping and whaling, presumably depressing the population size regionally. But the virtual removal of Walruses from the archipelago probably enhanced the recovery of Bearded Seals and allowed them to reach higher than normal densities for this species around Svalbard (Weslawski et al. 2000). Bearded Seals are also harvested in the White Sea and elsewhere in Russia territories in the Atlantic Arctic, though the scale of this harvest is not known. Subsistence harvest levels are not closely monitored in Canada, but Cleator (1996) estimated that roughly 2,400 Bearded Seals were taken per year. Subsistence harvests of Bearded Seals in Alaska were estimated to average approximately 6,800/year during 1990-1998 (Allen and Angliss 2010) but have declined recently to circa 5,000 per year (Olnes et al. 2022). Nelson et al. (2019) assessed sustainability of Alaskan seal harvests and concluded that Bearded Seal harvests were within sustainable limits but noted that some stocks have not been surveyed recently (or ever) and that trend data are lacking (Muto et al. 2019). Coastal hunters in Chukotka take about 1,000–2,000 Bearded Seals annually (Cameron et al. 2010).The only commercial harvests for bearded seals took place in the North Pacific region, in the former Soviet Union times. Ship-based commercial harvests of Bearded Seals in the Bering, Chukchi, and Okhotsk Seas grew from 9,000 to 13,000 for the Bering and Okhotsk seas combined during 1957-1964 and were 8,000 to 10,000 per year from 1964-1967 (Reeves et al. 1992). Ship-based harvests were suspended from 1970 to 1975 but resumed thereafter (Kelly 1988). Trukhanova et al. (2017) estimated the harvest of Bearded Seals from logbooks of ships in the Sea of Okhotsk to be 34,858 individuals in 1976–1994. Sustainability of harvest have only been assessed in Alaska (Nelson et al. 2019); assessments are lacking for all other regions in the Bearded Seal’s range and there are no quotas set for any region.
conservationActions: Norway listed Bearded Seals on the national Red List in 2021 as Near Threatened because of the threats posed to the species through habitat deterioration due to global warming (Eldegard et al. 2021). However, licensed hunters can shoot Bearded Seals in Svalbard, outside protected areas and during open seasons, that are set in periods when Bearded Seals shot in the water are least likely to sink (Kovacs and Lydersen 2006). Bearded Seals are able to use glacier ice pieces that have calved into the sea as haul-out platforms, so tidal glacier fronts are increasingly important to them in areas where sea ice declines are marked and where tide-water glaciers are common (Lydersen et al. 2014). Such glacier fjords occur mainly in East Greenland, Svalbard and Frans Josef Land. These areas might represent important breeding refugia for some time to come, so should be considered for special conservation status.Boertmann and Bay (2018) evaluated Bearded Seals as being Least Concern in Greenland. Throughout Russia the Fisheries and Preservation of Aquatic Resources Law (Federal Law No. 338-FZ) provides for subsistence harvest of seals by aboriginal Russian peoples, including Bearded Seals. The Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada assessed this species in Canada as being a high priority conservation concern in need of assessment for extinction risk (COSEWIC 2024). In the USA Bearded Seals are listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act (Federal Registry 2012 - ESA 77 FR 76740) because of the threats from climate change (Cameron et al. 2010). This has resulted in a Designation of Critical Habitat for the Beringia Bearded Seal Population (Federal Register 2022). The Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1973 prohibits the taking of Bearded Seals except for Alaska Native subsistence hunts or for production of handicrafts. In Norway the Bearded seal is classified as Near Threatened because of the risks of climate change (artsdatabanken.no/rodlisteforarter/2021/835).The species is included on Annex V (animal and plant species of community interest whose taking in the wild and exploitation may be subject to management measures) of the EU Habitats Directive, and on Appendix III (protected fauna species) of the Bern Convention (Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats).Both the research community and Arctic indigenous knowledge holders have called for changing ice concentrations to be considered in the management and conservation of Bearded Seals (Gryba et al. 2021, Kovacs et al. 2021).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern. It has a moderate extent of occurrence of 21,075 km2 and is not known to be undergoing any severe decline. Research of its population trends and potential threats is needed.
habitat: It inhabits meadows, shrub areas and light larch mountain taiga in the south Altai Mountains. It has been caught in a variety of habitats such as high grass meadow with thickets of wild rose, barberry, and currant; among sparse park-like larch forests; and in spots of steppe overgrown with feather grass, fescue and the patches of white wormwood (Artemisia). It prefers areas with shrubs, where good shelter and a variety of food can be found. In 2016 near the city of Katon-Karagay, at the type locality of the species, three individuals were trapped along the edge of a 1.2-1.4 m high Spiraea-Caragana shrub belt at 1,275 m asl; two specimens obtained close to the type locality in a sparse larch-spruce forest with well-developed understory composed of Dactylis, Geranium, Aconitum, Filipendula and Spiraea sp. at 1,320 m asl. A single specimen was captured at Markakol Lake (Markakolsky State Nature Reserve, S Altai) at 1,550 m asl in tall herbaceous vegetation growing in a clearing of sparse Larix sibirica forest (Cserkész and Sramkó pers. comm. 2025). This species is active in dusk and is solitary. It hibernates during winter. It feed on invertebrates and seeds, and reproduces once a year.
threats: The threats to this species are unknown. Habitat loss may result in shrinking of the range.
population: No data available, but it is known not to be abundant. These mice can be common in optimal habitats in the southern Altai that are relatively undisturbed by human activity (Sludskiy et al. 1977, Holden et al. 2017). Presumably the population is neither declining nor extremely fluctuating.
range: Sicista pseudonapaea is known from Kazakhstan between the River Bukhtarma and Lake Markakol on the northern and southern slopes of the Narymsk Ridge in the middle mountain belt in the Altai Mountains between 1,000-2,200 m asl (Holden et al. 2017) and from a single sampling site (Baihaba) in China, Xinjiang (Zhang et al. 2013, Cserkész et al. 2019). The steppe zone defines the western distributional limit of the species, but the eastern boundary is unknown.
conservationActions: Species occurs in some protected areas (eg. Markakolsky State Nature Reserve and Katon-Karagay State National Nature Park). Further research on ecology, habitat status and conservation measures is required. Based on an assumption that populations are not declining, Holden et al. (2017) suggested a categorisation of Least Concern

rationale: Hooded Seals breed on drift ice in Eastern Canadian waters, in the Davis Strait and in the Greenland Sea northwest of Jan Mayen Island. Estimates of abundance for this species are usually created based on pup production surveys (in combination with demographic modelling, similar to harp seals). The Greenland Sea Hooded Seal stock has been reduced markedly from more than 1.2 million animals to less than 80,000 (ca 93% reduction), well below the critical limit set by International Council for Exploration of the Seas (ICES: ≤ 30% of the historical maximum). Modelling suggests that much of the decline took place between 1940 and the 1980s, due to overhunting. However, despite complete protection from commercial harvesting since 2007, the Greenland Sea stock is continuing to decline slowly (or possibly has stabilized at a new low level: population abundance models cannot differentiate between these two scenarios). In the Northwest Atlantic, hooded seals pup off the coast of Newfoundland (an area known as the Front), in the Gulf of St Lawrence and in the Davis Strait with the largest component being found off Newfoundland (90%). Pup production was thought to be increasing at the Front until the early 2000s, but the most recent surveys have demonstrated dramatic declines. Estimates between 2012 and 2017 were ca 35% of what they had been in 2005. Extensive reconnaissance in the Davis Strait conducted in 2024 failed to find any whelping hooded seals, but a small whelping patch (ca 600 pups) was found in 2025 (Charmain Hamilton, pers. comm.). The small Gulf of St Lawrence component of the Northwest Atlantic population has not been surveyed since 2005.Although it is difficult to determine the precise magnitude of declines on fine time scales in each of the Hooded Seal stocks, because of infrequent assessments in some, it is certain that the global Hooded Seals population has declined by more than 50% in the last three generations (1985–2024) because the largest stock (by far) has declined 60% since 2005. Given the direct measurements of declines in abundance (range-wide), a status of Endangered is warranted for Hooded Seals under criterion A2a. A future population decline has not been estimated but significant future declines are expected due to global warming, potentially also qualifying the species as Endangered under criteria A3c, due to extreme breeding habitat losses (in excess of 50%).
habitat: Hooded Seals are a markedly sexually dimorphic phocid seal species. Adult males average 2.5 m in length and weigh an average of 300 kg (Kovacs and Lavigne 1986), with large animals reaching over 400 kg (Kovacs et al. 1996). Adult females are smaller, averaging 2.2 m and 236 kg (ranging up to over 300 kg) (Kovacs and Lavigne 1992).Hooded Seals are a strongly ice-associated species that breeds and moults in loose herds on heavy drift ice (Lavigne and Kovacs 1986, 1998). They spend a lot of time in ice-filled waters outside the breeding season, but they also undertake extensive migrations within the North Atlantic, sometimes occupying pelagic areas without sea ice during the summer (Vacquié-Garcia et al. 2017, Hamilton et al. 2022). They are largely solitary outside the breeding and moulting seasons although food aggregations can result in small clusters during their pelagic phases (Storrie et al. 2018, Bengtsson et al. 2021).Hooded Seals give birth on drifting pack ice in late March and early April. They choose the heaviest available floes in quite dense ice areas (Kovacs 2018). Females are spaced out on the ice with several hundred meters between mother pup pairs. The breeding season for this polygynous (serially monogamous) species is very short, usually lasting about two to three weeks in total within a population (Kovacs 1990). Females, with their “blueback” pup are normally attended by a male. Males use their inflatable hood and septum to display to females and in contests with other males. If displays do not sort out who is remaining on site with a given female, males will fight violently. Mating takes place in the water once the female has weaned her pup. This species has the shortest lactation period for any mammal with most pups being weaned within four days (Bowen et al. 1985). During the nursing period pups grow extremely rapidly, gaining 7 kg per day and doubling their birth mass by the time of weaning (mean weaning mass 47 kg, Kovacs and Lavigne 1992). This amazing growth is achieved by drinking an average of 10.4 kg of milk daily, with very high efficiency of transfer of energy from maternal blubber through milk and into pup tissue with 73.2 ± 7.7% of the ingested energy as body tissue. (Lydersen et al. 1997). This species is likely on the edge of mammalian physiological limits, with pups running a slight “fever” they are growing so quickly (Lydersen et al. 1997).Hooded Seals are extreme divers. Although most dives are from 100–600 m deep and last 5–25 minutes, very deep dives to over 1,500 m and dives lasting almost an hour have been recorded for adult animals of both sexes (Folkow and Blix 1999, Folkow et al. 2010, Andersen et al. 2013b, Vacquie-Garcia et al. 2017). Age and sex classes show somewhat different foraging habitat preferences that result in somewhat different movement and diving patterns (Andersen et al. 2009, 2013a,b; Bajzak et al. 2009; Vacquie-Garcia et al. 2017). Hooded Seals feed on a wide variety of fish and invertebrates including Greenland Halibut, gadid fishes such as Atlantic Cod (Gadus morhua) and Polar Cod (Boreogadus saida), Redfishes (Sebastes spp.), Herring (Clupea harengus), Capelin (Mallotus villosus), Atlantic Argentine (Argentina silus), Squid (Gonatus fabricii), amphipods and shrimps (Pandalus borealis) (Haug et al. 2004, 2007, Tucker et al. 2009). A study of movement patterns over the last three decades for Hooded Seals in the Northwest Atlantic shows that their foraging areas have shifted northward, resulting in them remaining in similar oceanographic conditions throughout the decades (Vacquie-Garcia et al. 2024). This sort of range shifting is expected for highly mobile megafauna as a first response to climate change, but Arctic animals are limited in how far north they can shift and remain in productive areas (Gilg et al. 2012). Tracking set temperature and salinity values is likely the result of the preferences exhibited by their invertebrate and fish prey species. Animals from the Gulf and Front displayed somewhat different temperature preferences, which might provide some resilience at the species level. Greenland Sharks (Somniosus microcephalus), Polar Bears (Ursus maritimus) and Killer Whales (Orcinus orca) are known to prey on Hooded Seals (Leclerc et al. 2012, Foote et al. 2013, McKinney et al. 2013, Øigård et al. 2014, Kovacs 2018). Longevity is normally 25–30 years (Kovacs 2018). The generation length is estimated to be 12.8 years (Pacifici et al. 2013), giving a three-generation length period of 38.4 years.Ice conditions in the areas used for breeding and moulting have been deteriorating for decades. Sea ice losses have been extreme in the breeding areas used by the European population of Hooded Seals during the last three generations (57% thickness reduction, reduction in extent of ca 40%), and projections for the future suggest the declining trend will continue (Estathiou et al. 2022, Sumata et al. 2022). Sea ice conditions are also declining in the Northwest Atlantic, throughout the breeding range of hooded seals, with the Gulf of St Lawrence experiencing complete ice failures much more often in recent decades, putting hooded seals at risk of reproductive failure in this region already (Johnston et al. 2005, Stenson and Hammill 2014).
threats: Hooded Seals were subjected to intense commercial hunting in the 19th and 20th centuries. Harvests were often conducted in association with Harp Seal harvests and commercial fisheries for Greenland Sharks. Norway, the former Soviet Union, Canada, and Greenland, have all been involved in these commercial harvests. Following World War II, the hunt focused largely on pups because of their highly prized blue-back pelt, however, many adult females were taken when defending their pups (Sergeant 1976). Annual harvests of Hooded Seals continue in Canada (pups are protected) and Greenland; Greenlandic harvests are the largest (ICES 2019). The Davis Strait breeding population has likely been reduced by Greenlandic hunting on the west coast and currently the East Greenland subsistence catch likely in part from the Greenland Sea stock.Bycatch of low numbers of Hooded Seals in coastal net fisheries has been reported from the United States, from trawl fisheries off Norway and Newfoundland, and salmon drift nets used off Greenland (Reeves et al. 1992, Waring et al. 2005, Woodley and Lavigne 1991), but it is not thought to be a major cause of mortality. Competition for food with commercial fisheries and other predators has been suggested as a factor that may limit population growth or lead to declines (Reijnders et al. 1993). The Barents and Norwegian Sea Redfish stocks declined markedly in the 1990s which might have impacted food availability for Hooded Seals, and a large international fishery still targets Redfish (Sigurðsson et al. 2006). Currently, declining Polar Cod (Boreogadus saida) stocks are a concern for Hooded Seals in the Northeast Atlantic (Enoksen et al. 2017).Impacts of oil spills on Hooded Seals have not been reported but given the Hooded Seals ice breeding habit, there might be at risk of mortality from spills during the pupping season when newborn and newly weaned pups could be fouled (St. Aubin 1990). Hooded Seals are not known to have suffered fatalities during the mass die-off of Harbour Seals in European waters from phocine distemper virus in 1998 and 2002, but subsequent testing of a variety of Arctic seals revealed antibodies to the virus in 18–24% percent of the Hooded Seals sampled, indicating exposure and transmission of the virus (Harkönen et al. 2006). Hooded Seals in the Northeast Atlantic have high organohalogen contaminant burdens, which are thought to be high enough to cause thyroid disruption (Villanger et al. 2013).Climate change is the most serious threat to this ice-breeding species (Tynan and DeMaster 1997; Kovacs et al. 2011, 2012, 2021; Laidre et al. 2008, 2015). Sea ice losses have occurred throughout the species’ range over the last few decades (e.g. Stenson and Hammill 2014, Spreen et al. 2020), with complete ice failure in the southern parts of the range in the Northwest Atlantic being increasingly common (Johnston et al. 2005). Reduction in ice cover in the Greenland Sea has resulted in smaller floes and less stable ice conditions that likely impact survivorship of pups. Additionally, pupping areas have more open water, and they have shifted closer to Greenland. The occurrence of Hooded Seals has increased in the diet of both Polar Bears and Killer Whales in East Greenland concomitant with these sea ice changes (Foote et al. 2013, McKinney et al. 2013, Øigård et al. 2014). Polar Bear predation on Hooded Seals in East Greenland has increased 9.5% per decade since the mid-190s (McKinney et al. 2013). It is thought that this source of mortality is possibly becoming a driver of the declining population trend of Hooded Seals in the Greenland Sea (Øigård et al. 2014). Warming is occurring in the Arctic at 4x the average rate of other regions on the globe (Rantanen et al. 2022) and sea ice is continuing to decline. Ice-free summers are predicted in the coming decades (Kim et al. 2023). The whole Arctic marine system is undergoing dramatic changes (e.g. Kortsch et al. 2015; Grose et al. 2020; Deb and Bailey 2023)An indirect result of climate change is that prey abundance and distribution is undergoing significant change, with “borealization” of the community in the Barents Region that is likely having negative impacts on Hooded Seals (e.g. Beaugrand et al. 2009, Fossheim et al. 2015, Frainer et al. 2017, Christiansen 2017, Enoksen et al. 2017, Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2022). A recent dietary study on Greenland Sea Hooded Seals found that their diet is dominated by Polar Cod (Boreogadus saida) and despite Hooded Seals seeming to be able to do some prey shifting, Enoksen et al. (2017) concluded that Greenland Sea Hooded Seals show narrow niche breadth and specialization on Arctic fishes that are suffering negative impacts of climate change. However, they do display some flexibility in where they forage in the Northwest Atlantic stock, and their diet is quite varied (Tucket et al. 2009, Vacquié-Garcia et al. 2024). Increased fishing, disease risks, shipping, mining, ocean noise, oil exploration and extraction etc in areas previously ice covered, but now open, increase the general risk level for this species (St Aubin 1990, Pagnan 2000, Kovacs et al. 2021, PAME 2019). Ecological change within the system is seen as the likely cause of declines in Hooded Seal numbers (Frei et al. 2012, Biuw et al. 2022, also see Stenson et al. 2020, Hamilton et al. 2024).
population: Hooded Seals are managed as two groups: the Northwest Atlantic, with its three breeding areas, and the Northeast Atlantic stock, with a single breeding group in the Greenland Sea (ICES 2019, 2023). Hooded Seals in this latter stock have experienced a precipitous decline. Models suggest that a lot of the decline took place between 1940 and the 1980s (although unknown at that time). In 1997, pup production was estimated to be 24,000 (14,800–32,700) and the one-year-old+ population size was estimated to be 100,000–110,000. The combined total population number represented a 90%+ decline in population size from the estimated 1.2 million animals thought to have been in this stock prior to commercial harvests. In 2005, pup production was estimated to be 15,200 (CV = 0.25; Salberg et al. 2008). This decline was supported by an additional survey effort in 2007, which estimated a pup production of 16,140 (CV = 13.3%) (Øigård et al. 2010). In 2012, pup production was estimated to be 13,655 (CV = 13.9) (Øigard et al. 2014). A survey flown in 2018, had an estimate of 12,977 (CI = 9.87–17.07) pups (Biuw et al. 2019, ICES 2019). Surveys were conducted again in 2022 with a resulting pup production estimate of 13,509 (CV = 12.90%) i.e. no significant change from the previous estimate. Using the pup production values along with updated biological parameters for reproduction, a total population size of 76,832 (60,262–98,009) was estimated for 2022. There is considerable uncertainty in this number given model performance (ICES 2023). It is not known whether this population is continuing a slow decline, or whether it has stabilized at a new low level (ICES 2023). Because of the recent changes in the rate of decline it is not possible to determine a 3-generation decline % accurately, but its current size is ca 7% of what this population numbered 78 years ago (Haug et al. 2025). Northwest Atlantic Hooded Seals were depressed by overharvesting in the 1950s and 1960s (Sergeant 1974). Various management measures were put in place and Hooded Seal numbers increased through the 1990s, reaching a total population size of close to 600,000 animals by 2005; pup estimates from 2005 were 107,013 for the Front, 6,600 for the Gulf and 3,300 for the Davis Strait (Hammill and Stenson 2006, Stenson et al. 2006). Aerial surveys were flown in 2012 and 2017, and although designed to count harp seals, these surveys also captured most hooded seal whelping patches in these years. Hooded Seal pup production was estimated to be 41,129 (SE = 7,374) and 39,021 (SE = 18,334) pups in 2012 and 2017, respectively. This represented a decline of ≥60% compared to the pup production estimated on the Front in 2005. Extensive reconnaissance failed to locate whelping hooded seals in Davis Strait in 2024, and it was feared that this breeding area was extirpated (Hamilton et al. 2024). But in 2025 a small whelping patch was found in this area comprising ca 600 pups (considered a minimum estimate because coverage around this patch was not possible due to inclement weather; Charmain Hamilton, DFO Canada pers. comm.). This number is 18% of the 2005 pup production estimate for this breeding area. The Gulf breeding group has not been surveyed officially since 2005, but extensive reconnaissance of the Gulf in March 2017 found no hooded seals, though small numbers have been observed since this time (DFO unpubl. data, cited in Hamilton et al. 2024). Declines would be expected in this southernmost breeding area given that habitat conditions are known to have deteriorated markedly (Stenson and Hammill 2014). The decline rates of these smaller groups (Gulf and Davis Strait) will in any case have little impact on the total population numbers because the Front is by far the largest breeding group. The cause of the overall decline in all of the Northwest Atlantic breeding areas is unknown (harvests on the Front have been modest in recent decades and the Greenland Sea animals are protected from commercial harvest). But it is likely that negative impacts of ecosystem change on female fecundity and juvenile survival are the cause, as has been documented for harp seals in the Northwest Atlantic (Tinker et al. 2023, also see Frie et al. 2012). Investigation of the potential impacts of the Greenlandic harvests are warranted.
range: Hooded Seals are found throughout the North Atlantic, extending into drift ice areas within the Arctic Ocean (Kovacs 2018). Animals from the Greenland Sea stock reside in the Northeast Atlantic, ranging from mid-Norway in the south almost to the North Pole outside the breeding and moulting seasons (Folkow and Blix 1995, Folkow et al. 1996, Vacquié-Garcia et al. 2017, Hamilton et al. 2022). During breeding the whole adult population normally has concentrated in areas of drift-ice in the vicinity of the island of Jan Mayen and during moulting the whole 1+ population congregated to the north of the breeding area (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Recently, available ice at the time of breeding and moulting for this population is only present in areas close to the coast of East Greenland (Øigård et al. 2014).Northwest Atlantic Hooded seals breed in the Gulf of St Lawrence, on the Front (north of Newfoundland) and in the Davis Strait, where they aggregate in loose herds (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Following breeding these groups disperse to feed and then form aggregations once again on the heaviest available first-year drift ice in Southeast Greenland to undertake their annual moult. Following the moult, traditionally they leave the Greenlandic coast and spread through waters of Baffin Bay, Davis Strait and West Greenland (Andersen et al. 2009, 2013a). Little is known about the distribution patterns followed by animals from the Davis Strait, but it is assumed that their summering areas primarily are in waters west of Greenland and in the Eastern Canadian Archipelago, similar to the other Northwest Atlantic breeding groups. A new study on movement patterns suggests that Northwest Atlantic Hooded Seals are dispersing further to the north for summer feeding than they did in the past (Vacquié-Garcia et al. 2024).Some Hooded Seals wander widely (particularly young animals), and vagrants have been registered along European coastlines as far south as Portugal and the Canary Islands, which are likely animals from the Greenland Sea population. Vagrants have been registered in North America from New England south into the Caribbean; several Pacific occurrences have also been reported, as far south as California (Mignucci-Giannoni and Haddow 2002, Harris and Gupta 2006). During years with little sea ice strandings in the St Lawrence River area are common; this phenomenon seems to be increasing (Truchon et al. 2013). The North American observations of vagrant Hooded Seals likely stem from animals the breed in the Northwest Atlantic.
useTrade: Hooded Seals have been subjected to intense commercial hunting in the 19th and 20th centuries. Harvests were often conducted in association with Harp Seal harvests and commercial fisheries for Greenland Sharks. Norway, the Soviet Union (now Russia), Canada, and Greenland have all been involved in the commercial harvests of this species. Following World War II the hunt was primarily focused on pups because of their highly prized “blue-back” pelt, however, many adult females were taken while defending their pups until killing of mothers in the breeding areas was prohibited in the various areas (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988).In the past, tens of thousands of hooded seals were taken in individual years in Canadian waters, but various conservation measures were implemented over time in Canada to slow the hunt (see the Conservation section). In 2007, the allowable catch was set at 8,200, but since 2016 no quota has been announced. The hunt is “monitored” and market driven (hunt subsidies have been removed). This has resulted in Canadian catches being very low, some few tens of animals per year. See NAMMCO https://nammco.no/marine-mammal-catch-database for all Hooded Seal stock harvests 1992–present.Hooded Seals are harvested by indigenous people in Greenland at a current level of a few thousand animals per year. It is assumed that most of those animals are from the Northwest Atlantic breeding groups (Davis Strait, Gulf, and Front) given that most of the harvest takes place in West and Southeast Greenland (mainly around Tassilaqu). A small number are taken in Northeast Greenland; these are almost certainly from the endangered Greenland Sea stock. Pelts from hooded seals harvested in Greenland come into international trade, largely through Denmark. Hooded Seals have been harvested in the West Ice (Greenland Sea, north of Jan Mayen) for centuries. This hunt increased substantially after World War II, to levels that were clearly not sustainable. Regulatory measures were introduced in 1958 to reduce effort, and quotas were imposed in 1971 (Sergeant 1976; see Conservation below). Based on catch per unit effort analyses and mark-recapture pup production estimates it was assumed that the stock increased from the 1960s through to the 1990s at an unknown rate (Ulltang and Øien 1988). In hindsight this almost certainly was not the case. This stock is less than 10% of historical numbers and is now totally protected from commercial harvest.
conservationActions: The species is listed on Annex V (animal and plant species of community interest whose taking in the wild and exploitation may be subject to management measures) of the EU Habitats Directive (Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora - consolidated version 01/01/2007) and on Annex III (protected fauna species) of the Bern Convention (the Convention on the conservation of European wildlife and natural habitats).Numerous conservation measures, international management plans, harvest quotas and restrictions, as well as agreements and treaties, have been developed for the conservation of Hooded Seals dating back to the 1870s (Sergeant 1976). Hunting was banned in the Gulf of St Lawrence in 1964, and quotas were placed on the rest of the Canadian harvest beginning in 1974; blue-back harvesting became prohibited in 1987 in Canada (Ronald and Lavigne 2006). Total Allowable Catch (TAC) was 10,000 animals in Canadian waters prior to 2007 but was reduced to 8,200 because the stock was considered to be data deficient and increasing Greenlandic hunts had to be taken into account within the Canadian Atlantic Seal Management Strategy (Hammill and Stenson 2007, 2009). From 2016 onward no quotas were set in Canada, but subsidies had been removed, allowing the market to determine financial reward of the harvest; few Hooded Seals are harvested within this regime. In European waters, harvest quotas were implemented at Jan Mayen in 1971, and complete cessation of the commercial harvest was enacted in 2007 (2008 hunting season closure) for the Greenland Sea stock. The ICES/NAFO/NAMMCO Working Group on Harp and Hooded seals (WGHARP) models population numbers from surveys and provides advice for management. Based on surveys conducted in 2022 and new biological parameter data, zero quota was reiterated as being the recommended level for Greenland Sea Hooded Seals (ICES 2023).The EU ban on the import of seal products in 2009 markedly affected the market for Hooded Seal pelts, with the result that harvests decline. But this Regulation was amended in 2015 to allow for trade of hides from Indigenous harvests, opening the market for Greenland in particular (EU 2015).Hooded Seals were classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List in 2016 (Kovacs 2016). The European population is currently classified as Endangered on the Norwegian Red List (Eldegard et al. 2021). The European Red List for 2025 classifies hooded seals as regionally Vulnerable (Kovacs 2025), because the decline in the Greenland Sea population has recently slowed; this population might be stable at a new lower level (or still declining slowly - ICES 2023).Global assessment of population structure would help in the assessment process. More robust N1+ population estimates are needed for all stocks. Ongoing survey efforts are required to track impacts of climate change and population trends.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It inhabits treeless, grasslands and dry shrublands in temperate-cold arid Patagonia and restricted portions of the Monte ecoregions. This species is mainly terrestrial but can climb well, and dig into light substrates (Martin and Udrizar Sauthier 2011). The diet consists of insects, mice, small birds and probably fruits, depending on abundance and availability (Martin 2008, Martin and Udrizar Sauthier 2011, Geiser and Martin 2013, Zapata et al. 2013). Zapata et al. (2013) argued in favor of an opportunistic feeding behavior, characterized by the consumption of arthropods (87.2% frequency of occurrence), followed by birds and reptiles (10.6%), and a small proportion of fruits.
threats: There are no major threats to this species, although some subpopulations are threatened by livestock and agriculture, and their effects on soil destruction and desertification. Also, changes in land use might be affecting areas throughout its distribution.
population: Lestodelphys halli is known from a few skeletons of captured animals and several isolated fragments recovered from owl pellets in Argentina (Martin 2005, Martin 2008, Formoso et al. 2011). However, there is no information on the population dynamics of this species, and its interactions. The species is consumed by nocturnal and diurnal aerial predators (e.g., barn owl, black-chested buzzard eagle), and is presumed to be consumed by terrestrial predators (e.g., red fox, puma).
