range: The species is widely distributed in the extra-Andean Patagonia, with many records in Chubut, the central-northern part of Santa Cruz, and the western region of Río Negro; as well as some scattered localities in the central La Pampa, Neuquén, and Mendoza (Formoso et al. 2015). Its distribution has changed from the Pleistocene to the Recent period, shifting from the south-central Pampas region to the south-central Patagonia, apparently in association with climatic changes that occurred during this time period (Formoso et al. 2015). The species is found in xeric environments of the Patagonia and Monte phytogeographic provinces (sensu Olson et al. 2001).
useTrade: This species is not utilised.
conservationActions: Despite its wide distribution, the species has limited effective protection within Nahuel Huapi and Lihué Calel National Parks, the Petrified Forests National Monument, and some provincial reserves (e.g., Somuncurá Plateau). This is mainly due to the lack of protected areas in Patagonian Steppe and Monte environments, where most records are found.

rationale: This species is considered to be Near Threatened, and almost qualifies for a threatened category under criterion A2c due to ongoing population decline inferred from habitat destruction/reduction through logging and other human activities, which have led to an inferred decline in the order of 25% over 10 years. The species has a restricted distribution and more information of its area of occupancy is needed. Also, effects of the numerous threats on the species population throughout its range could lead to a more threatened category than currently suspected. This species is mostly found in a habitat type which is being heavily exploited/replaced.
habitat: This species lives in temperate rain forests, and was recently recorded (via camera traps) in eucaliptus (Eucaliptus globulus) plantations (Vasquez et al. 2023). It occurs at and is tolerant of a broad elevation range from sea level to 1,135 m asl, and is locally abundant. It is mostly terrestrial and nocturnal, foraging on the forest floor for insects, earthworms and other soil-inhabiting invertebrates, along with fungi (Meserve et al. 1988). Patterson et al. (1990) found a high correlation of abundance with bare soil, bryophytes and fallen logs with a diameter larger than 15 cm.
threats: Deforestation for logging is the main threat to this species. Also, habitat conversion for agriculture, and residential and commercial development, both commercial and housing, are a threat throughout most of the species' distribution. The effects of fire throughout the species' distribution are unknown, but suspected to be reducing its habitat.
population: This genus occurs at and is tolerant of a wide elevation range and is locally abundant (Patterson et al. 1990).
range: This species is restricted to south-central Chile, including Chiloé Island, and a single locality from Argentina (Puerto Blest) (Gardner 2008, Martin 2011). The species is known from less than 45 records distributed from -39.99º to -43.35º latitude, and occurs within the Valdivian Temperate Rainforest ecoregion (sensu Olson et al. 2001).
useTrade: The species is not utilized.
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas. More research is necessary to determine the area of occupancy and impact of numerous threats within the species' range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern because its extent of occurrence is estimated to be 40,252 km², it has a presumed large population, it occurs in at least one protected area, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category. Further research of its population would be beneficial.
habitat: This species occurs in broad-leaf forests and its edge habitat, and scrub (Smith and Xie 2008). Litter size is 2-3 (Yu and Lin 1999). It appears to have specific habitat requirements with dense shrub cover as an important variable (Wang et al. 2008). It is considered an important scatter-hoarder of seeds of species such as Castanopsis indica (Chou and Liao 2024).
threats: There are no major threats to this species at present. However, human land uses are expected to affect the dispersal of this species (Wang et al. 2008).
population: This species has a population density of 2-5 per hectare (Yu and Lin 1999). It is stated to be "common" throughout its range and its population may be stable (Denys et al. 2017).
range: This species is endemic to Taiwan, Province of China (Smith and Xie 2008). It is restricted to elevations below 2,000 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008), becoming common at 1,300 m asl (Yu 1993).
conservationActions: This species is present in Yushan National Park (Yu 1994), but it is not known if it occurs in any other protected areas. In China, this species has been regionally Red Listed as Least Concern (Wang and Xie 2004). Data on its population ecology are lacking.

rationale: Dama Gazelle (Nanger dama) is assessed as Critically Endangered under criterion C2a(i) because the wild population at sites where it is known to be currently present is estimated to be 48–75 mature individuals, well below the threshold of 250. All remaining subpopulations contain fewer than 50 mature individuals, and the population is still declining under the pressure from poaching, habitat degradation, livestock grazing, and climate change. On a highly precautionary basis, and assuming that no animals remain in Mali, the minimum estimate of mature individuals also falls just below the threshold for Critically Endangered under criterion D.
habitat: Dama Gazelles inhabit sparsely wooded savanna, Sahelian grasslands, sub-desert steppes, and mountain wadis with Acacia and Panicum vegetation (Scholte 2013). In the Atlantic Sahara it was found in areas without Acacia, but with dense shrub cover (Cuzin 2003). The rocky habitat in the Termit and Aïr mountains in Niger appears to be atypical. They were formerly seen occasionally in sandy desert (Dragesco-Joffe 1993). Dama Gazelle habitat in southern Morocco was investigated by Abaigar et al. (2020).
threats: The main causes of decline and continuing threats to this species are poaching, habitat loss and degradation, overgrazing by domestic livestock, and the expansion of livestock rearing facilitated in part by construction of bore wells that allow grazers to remain in a location all year-round (Scholte 2013, Al Ain Zoo, IUCN Antelope Specialist Group and Royal Zoological Society Scotland 2019, CMS 2024). Prolonged droughts have had a negative impact on pasture quality and some Dama Gazelles in Chad died during a period of unusually high temperatures in 2024.The main threats in Aïr-Ténéré NNR are poaching, gold panning, competition with livestock, and habitat degradation (ASG, RZSS, SAF 2024, DFCAP 2024).The lack of adequate resources to implement effective conservation action is a significant constraint across the range.
population: Numbers of Dama Gazelle have declined drastically since the 1950s and 1960s. The early 1970s population in Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve in Chad, one of the former strongholds of the species, was estimated at 10,000–12,000 individuals (Scholte 2013) but a catastrophic reduction in population size has taken place.At the end of 2013 there were six remnant populations, all fragmented, and estimated to total a maximum of 250 individuals (RZSS and IUCN Antelope Specialist Group 2014). The situation has deteriorated further. In May 2025, estimated numbers were 40–50 in Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve, Chad and 20–30 in Aïr-Ténéré National Nature Reserve, Niger. In Termit-Tin Toumma NNR, Niger, regular population monitoring has not been undertaken recently. Only two animals were observed on a field survey in 2024 and it is unlikely that the remnant population exceeds 20. In Chad, a 5-day aerial survey of the Manga region in November 2023 found no sign of the species and it is considered unlikely that no more than 10, if any, survive there. Recent information on the former tiny population in Ati is lacking and it may be extinct. There is no information from Mali since 2006 and it is unclear whether any Dama Gazelles remain.The total wild population is thus conservatively estimated at 62–110 wild dama gazelles, equating to 45–78 mature individuals. Even if small populations survive in Mali and Manga, it is highly unlikely that the number of mature individuals would exceed 100.GeneticsEstimates of the global population size and the number of mature individuals lie far below the recommended 5,000 Nc / 500 Ne thresholds for total and effective population size respectively. The ex-situ population also numbers below 5,000, hence its Ne is <500. Maternal haplotypes in the wild and the ex-situ populations have been identified (Senn et al. 2014, 2016). A study by Gooley et al. (2022) used genomic data on the US ‘addra’ population to highlight the importance and value of metapopulation management.
range: The former range of the Dama Gazelle extended across the Sahel from the Atlantic to the Nile, in and around some Saharan mountain massifs, and in semidesert and subdesert steppes on the northern side of the Sahara (Scholte 2013 and references therein; RZSS and IUCN Antelope Specialist Group 2014). Recent research has revealed 19th century records of Dama Gazelle in the south and southeast parts of the Lake Chad Basin, situated within far northern Cameroon (Schreiber 2021), which is consistent with their former occurrence in extreme northeast Nigeria (Rosevear 1933). A review of depictions in rock paintings, combined with some published reports by 19th century travellers, has also confirmed the historical occurrence of Dama Gazelle in Libya (Schreiber and Striedter 2022). The species was known in the far south of Tunisia but had become extinct by 1850 (Jebali 2004).The range has suffered a catastrophic reduction. Since the year 2000, Dama Gazelles have been recorded in only six sites: south Tamesna in eastern Mali; the Aïr massif and the Termit massif in Niger; Ouadi Rimé Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve, and the Manga and Ati regions in Chad (RZSS and IUCN Antelope Specialist Group 2014). There has been no information on the population in Mali since 2006. The last record of presence in Manga was in January 2020. In November 2023, a five-day aerial survey by Wings for Conservation and Sahara Conservation did not record any dama gazelles. The area is unprotected and there are believed to be few, if any, animals remaining. Recent information on the former tiny population in Ati is lacking and it may be extinct (Al Ain Zoo, IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group and Royal Zoological Society Scotland 2019, 2021; ASG, RZSS, SAF 2024).In mid-2025, three populations were confirmed as present, in Ouadi Rimé Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve (Chad), ;Aïr-Ténéré National Nature Reserve (NNR) and Termit-Tin Toumma NNR (both in Niger), with a possible remnant surviving in Manga (Chad) and the status of the former population in Tamesna (Mali) unknown. In Aïr-Ténéré NNR the Dama Gazelles are now restricted to Mount Takolokouzet and its adjoining area and in Termit-Tin Toumma NNR to the Termit massif. The rocky habitat at both sites probably represents a refuge from vehicle-based poaching.
useTrade: Dama Gazelles have traditionally been hunted for meat by local people but have also been subject to uncontrolled, vehicle-based, illegal hunting by outsiders. Dama Gazelle gallstones were also highly sought-after as a talisman, at least in the western part of the species' range (Cuzin 2003).
conservationActions: Legislation and international agreementsDama Gazelle is listed is listed on CITES Appendix I and on CMS Appendix I. It is included in the CMS Sahelo-Saharan Megafauna Initiative and the associated action plan (CMS 2024). The species is protected by law in all countries of occurrence.Protected and conserved areasThe three largest wild populations occur in protected areas: Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve (OROAFR), Chad (77,950 km²); Aïr & Ténéré National Nature Reserve ATTNNR), Niger (77,360 km²); Termit-Tin Toumma NNR (TTTNNR), Niger (90,507 km²).In ATTNNR Sahara Conservation supports surveillance and patrols, engagement of local communities, and ecological monitoring. So far, 17 officers have been trained and equipped, four community guards appointed, and seven health missions conducted, benefiting 1,121 people; 23 families were directly supported in goat farming as an alternative livelihood measure. Patrols have taken place in most months since January 2022 on Mount Takolokouzet where the Dama Gazelle population is concentrated.In TTNNR most conservation activities have been reduced by the withdrawal of support and financial sanctions imposed by the international community after the change in government in July 2023. Only some anti-poaching activities, community conservation and governance are maintained by the government and Sahara Conservation. In OROAFR the Dama Gazelle is integrated into the Scimitar-horned Oryx programme funded by Environment Agency - Abu Dhabi and the Government of Chad, and implemented on the ground by Sahara Conservation and its partners. The current Phase 3 of the programme extends until 2029, and some funding will be used to support Dama Gazelle conservation. A series of aerial surveys has been carried out by Wings for Conservation. High-definition photos were taken of all herds to analyse the sex and age structure of all groups seen. In December 2023, 64 Dama Gazelles were counted on the aerial survey comprising 23 females, 25 breeding age males and 16 individuals less than one year of age. Seven females are judged to be 1–2 years old and 16 are older. Estimates from sample ground counts during the same period are highly variable: recruitment was showing a slowly increasing trend, then as a result of exceptionally harsh conditions and high temperatures during the hot season (April–June) of 2024, high mortality rates were experienced by all ungulates, wild and domestic. These included the discovery of five wild Dama carcasses and three of the six Dama involved in the pilot release. The area is not fenced and there is a lot of suitable habitat, but the Dama are sensitive to human pressure. Staff are in the field every day, monitoring habitat use, seasonality, group sizes, and flight behaviour.PlanningA Dama Gazelle conservation planning workshop was held in 2013 in Edinburgh, Scotland, to develop a conservation review, including a long-term vision and a set of objectives and actions, and published in both English and French versions (RZSS and ASG 2014). In December 2018 a second conservation review and planning workshop took place in Al Ain, UAE, organized by Al Ain Zoo, the Royal Zoological Society Scotland and the IUCN Antelope Specialist Group. This workshop brought together all major Dama Gazelle stakeholders for the first time, including NGOs, representatives of current and former range countries, international experts, veterinarians, and ex-situ population managers and developed a conservation strategy for the species (Al Ain Zoo, IUCN Antelope Specialist Group and Royal Zoological Society Scotland 2019). In July 2021, an online review of progress was conducted to (i) review progress made after 2.5 years; (ii) highlight major developments since 2018; (iii) review, amend and update the actions as appropriate; add new required actions that had arisen since 2018; and (iv) outline the monitoring and evaluation plan for the strategy going forward (Al Ain Zoo, IUCN Antelope Specialist Group and Royal Zoological Society Scotland 2021). A third Dama Gazelle conservation planning workshop was held in Kerrville, Texas, on 17-19 September 2024, hosted by the Exotic Wildlife Association and the Second Ark Foundation. The aims of this workshop were to: (i) review progress made by the halfway (5-year) point in the conservation strategy; (ii) assess progress, amend and update the actions as appropriate and add new actions; (iii) increase contact and collaboration between the Texas rancher community and international Dama conservation practitioners (ASG, RZSS, SAF 2024). The 2019 Dama Gazelle Conservation Strategy Actions Table was also reviewed and updated in both 2021 and 2024.  A roadmap for the conservation of the Dama Gazelle in Aïr & Ténéré National Nature Reserve, Niger was published in 2024 (DFCAP 2024). Dama Gazelle is included in a revised national Action Plan for the Conservation and Restoration of Wild Ungulates in Morocco for 2023-2035, developed by the government agency (ANEF 2024).Several technical meetings have taken place online on to review progress with the captive breeding group at Ouadi Rime-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve, Chad (OROAFR) and recommend next steps on breeding and release.Field projectsFollowing a comprehensive analysis of the risks and benefits at the conservation planning workshop in Al Ain in December 2018, a decision was taken to attempt to capture a few of the remaining Dama Gazelles from the unprotected Manga population, which was known to contains unique genetic diversity, and to establish a captive breeding population in Chad. The capture operation was coordinated by Sahara Conservation and carried out by a multinational team from Chad’s Directorate for Wildlife Conservation and Protected Areas (DCFAP), the Environment Agency - Abu Dhabi, Zoological Society of London, Fossil Rim Wildlife Center, Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute, Gulf Breeze Zoo and Noé Conservation. Preliminary field surveys were undertaken in May and November 2019 to locate the gazelles and a capture mission was organized in January 2020. Three females were successfully captured and transported by air to the Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve (OROAFR), 350 km away. A male Dama was caught in OROAFR to form the first breeding group. Subsequently, two2 wild females that approached the breeding enclosure were encouraged to enter and join the breeding group (passive capture). Subsequently the Environment Agency Abu Dhabi transferred three groups of Dama Gazelles from their captive herd to the OROAFR breeding centre to further increase genetic diversity. Two groups of Dama Gazelles from the OROAFR breeding centre have been released into the reserve, the second in November 2025, as a genetic and demographic reinforcement.Ex situIn August 2025, the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS) listed 733 Dama Gazelles at 54 institutions worldwide. The final total may be higher because not all institutions are registered within ZIMS and not all institutions update their information regularly. In addition, there are almost 500 in North Africa and the Middle East and over 1,500 on Texas ranches (the last census dates from 2015). Almost all Dama Gazelles are managed separately as ‘mhorr’ (N. d. mhorr) or ‘addra’ (N. d. ruficollis). There is a small mixed population at Al Ain Zoo, UAE. There are about 160 ‘mhorr’ in Morocco and around 25 in Qatar. In the UAE there are 30 'addra' at the Environment Agency - Abu Dhabi’s breeding centre, 238 at Al Ain Zoo (117 'addra', 90 'mhorr' and 31 cross-bred), plus 68 (35 addra, 33 mhorr) in a collection managed by a private company. Dama Gazelles originating from the central part of its distribution, the putative range of N. d. dama, are not represented in captivity. The ‘mhorr’ breeding program began in 1971 with 4 founders (Abaigar 2018) and all “mhorr” in captivity are descended from these founders. All ex-situ 'addra’ are descended from 35 animals captured in Ouadi Haouach (Wadi Hawash) in northeastern Chad in 1967 (van den Brink 2018). All Dama Gazelles in Europe are included in the EAZA EEP (Ex-situ Progamme) which holds 312 animals in 31 institutions. A pedigree analysis of the captive population is >95% complete (Domínguez et al. 2024). In the USA, Dama Gazelles are held in zoos and on private ranches in Texas, almost all are ‘addra’. The American Zoo Association (AZA) Species Survival Plan (SSP) for ‘addra’ includes 201 animals (109 males and 92 females) in 15 AZA and a few private institutions. 98% of the pedigree is known. A captive population has been established at OROAFR in Chad. There were 32 Dama present at the end of December 2024, in two breeding groups. These animals originate from (i) the Manga region of Chad, (ii) the wild population in OROAFR, and (iii) the EAD herd in Abu Dhabi (so lineages are varied). Records indicating the identity and origin of all individuals are maintained. Six animals of 100% OROAFR origin were released into the reserve from the captive group on 23 January 2024. A management plan for the breeding population has been developed and a population viability assessment (PVA) is being carried out to identify optimal breeding and release strategies.In Morocco there are currently approximately 160 'mhorr' Dama Gazelles: R’Mila Royal Reserve (100), M’Cissi Reserve in eastern Morocco (26), Safia Reserve in the south (27), Rabat Zoo (unknown), and the private Al Maha Farm (unknown). Due to a lack of genetic differentiation found between the proposed Dama Gazelle subspecies, a diversity of phenotypes found in extant wild populations, and a likely lack of previous barriers to gene flow across Dama Gazelle range, a recommendation was agreed by all stakeholders at the December 2013 conservation workshop in Edinburgh to conduct a crossbreeding experiment between 'mhorr' and 'addra' gazelles. The objectives were to investigate: 1) whether the proposed subspecies were reproductively isolated; 2) the phenotypes of any mixed offspring, and 3) any implication of these on future management options. Al Ain Zoo in the United Arab Emirates agreed to undertake the experiment, which is ongoing, and currently 23 mixed dama are managed as a fully segregated group. Comprehensive breeding records have been kept.ReintroductionCaptive-bred Dama Gazelles have been released into fenced enclosures in Morocco, Senegal, and Tunisia for captive breeding or as part of long-term reintroduction programmes. None of these is yet considered a full reintroduction into the wild.In 2015, 24 Dama were released from Safia, Morocco, 10 of them with GPS collars. In the first week after release, feral dogs killed seven gazelles, poachers scattered the remaining group five months later, and eventually all the surviving gazelles moved out of monitoring range (Abaigar et al. 2019). In 2024, 10 dama were transferred to a breeding center in the lower Draa Valley as part of a planned reintroduction project.In Senegal, the Dama Gazelle populations released into fenced reserves since 1984 have suffered a sharp decline due to several factors, including management issues and predation of the young by jackals. In Guembeul Special Faunal Reserve, the residual population is four individuals in semi-captivity. In the Katané enclosure (12 km²) inside Ferlo Nord Faunal Reserve 20 individuals were held in 2012 but the latest sightings consist of only two individuals (ASG, RZSS, SPA 2024). Six Dama Gazelles from the captive breeding group in OROAFR were released in the reserve in January 2024 and a second group in November 2025. Further releases are envisaged.ResearchA book covering Dama Gazelle biology, ecology, recent history, conservation, ex-situ breeding and other topics has been published (Mungall 2018). In Morocco, EEZA (Experimental Station of Arid Zones) is carrying out comparative studies at the Safia and M’Cissi Reserves to evaluate the effects of different ecological and management conditions and social group composition using camera traps, direct observations and vegetation studies. A long-established observation and collaring study of ranched animals in Texas has been carried out to research movement patterns, group dynamics, and habitat use.Network and resourcesDama Gazelle conservation has featured regularly in presentations and side-events at the Sahel-Sahara Interest Group annual meetings. A Dama Gazelle email group has been established, and an updated central repository of Dama Gazelle resources can be found at: https://sites.google.com/site/damagazellenetwork/home. The IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group is collating new records. ASG and RZSS have produced a Dama identification card in French and Arabic which is available on request from the IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group: asgpo@marwell.org.uk. Observations and any other new information can be submitted to the same email address, or online at https://sites.google.com/site/damagazellenetwork/home

rationale: Harp Seals remain the most numerous northern phocid seal in the North Atlantic, numbering in the millions. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding population abundance and trends and some earlier high abundance estimates have recently been questioned. Despite these uncertainties, it is believed that all three Harp Seal populations are likely experiencing declines because of climate-change related increases in pup and juvenile mortality and decreasing fecundity rates. Ongoing ecosystems changes are thought to be lowering carrying capacity and density-dependent population changes are likely taking place.In 1999 pup production in the White Sea was estimated to be ca 300,000 pups. The White Sea population experienced a precipitous drop in pup production in 2003–2005 due to very poor ice conditions and high pup mortality because of industrial activities; pup production in 2013 was estimated to be 128,786. Population surveys were undertaken in the White Sea in both 2023 and 2024. Pup numbers remained close to the most recent prior estimate a decade before (ca 130,000). The estimated population size was 1.5 million. Modelling suggests that the overall population has been in decline for some decades and an increasing rate of decline is forecast for the coming decades.The Greenland Sea population had a slow population decrease from the 1940s to the 1990s, followed by an increase until about 2010, after which they are thought to have been in slow decline through to the present. Like the other populations, there is considerable uncertainty about abundance. Model estimates range between 2.2 M and 1.1 million – and new estimates are not directly comparable to those of the past complicating accurate trend calculations. Recent pup production estimates over the last decade are quite stable for this population (2012, 2018 and 2022, range - 89,590 to 92,769).The Northwest Atlantic Harp Seal population remains the largest. Recruitment in this population is thought to have been in decline since the 1990s (but hunting levels have dropped in recent decades from 400,000 in 2000 to ca 100,000 annually from 2010-present). Recent population abundance estimates are highly variable 7.6 million vs 4.6 million, but the scientifically accepted value for the previous survey period (2019) is 4.7 million. It is thought that there has been a decline in equilibrium abundance for this population. Documented increases in juvenile mortality (and more variance) as well as reduced female fecundity are thought to be the results of environmental change concomitant with global warming. The 2022 survey suggests a pup production of 614, 100 (CV 11%), which is the lowest values since 1994, and a decline in abundance to 4.4 million (3.65–5.35). The recent decline has occurred at a rate of 4.7 % per year. Adult mortality is dominated by the Greenlandic harvests, which now have an important impact on the Northwest Atlantic population dynamics.In summary, uncertainties in model outputs from previous decades make it impossible to calculate an accurate trend for the global Harp Seal population over the last three generations. However, it is clear that Harp Seal populations are in decline – slow decline in the case of the Greenland and White Sea populations, but quite rapid decline in the Northwest Atlantic population, which is largest. Breeding and resting habitat declines, which are significant, and the forecasts for further declines in sea ice in the coming decades are a cause for concern, as are Harp Seal population parameter such as increasing juvenile mortality and reduced pregnancy rates. In combination, these factors warrant a status of Near Threatened for Harp Seals globally under criteria A2c. Greenlandic hunts, which take a lot of adult animals might be a current population driver, which means that A2d might also be relevant for status classification at this time. It is suspected that in the last three generations and in the near-term future population decline may be close to, or exceed the threshold for Vulnerable under A3 and/or A4 (30%), so reassessment of this species should be scheduled within the decade. A new assessment should be undertaken as soon as there is a better understanding of current trends (rates of decline).
habitat: Harp Seals are medium-sized true seals. Adult males and females are similar in size; they are about 1.8 m long and weigh about 130 kg (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Females reach sexual maturity between four and eight years of age (e.g., Frie et al. 2003); this has varied considerably over the last century, largely as a consequence of population size variability that has been determined by harvest levels. Males reach physiological maturity around the same time as females but probably do not participate in breeding until they are somewhat older.Birthing takes place within drift-ice areas from late February to April in the respective breeding areas. There is some variation across the species’ range in the precise timing, but herds are highly synchronized (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Pups are born weighing about 10 kg and are nursed for 12 days, during which time they gain weight at about 2.2 kg per day (Kovacs and Lavigne 1985, Kovacs 1987, Kovacs et al. 1991, Lydersen and Kovacs 1996). Pups are referred to as “whitecoats” because they are born with an insulating coat of white lanugo. They are quite sedentary in the first weeks of life and few swim before they are weaned. Lactating females spend up to 85% of their time in the water, depending on the weather (Lydersen and Kovacs 1993). Mothers locate their pups in the drifting ice based on physical cues in the environment, with final identification of their pup by smell (Kovacs 1995). Pups are fed fat-rich milk six times per day throughout the lactation period, with fat increasing and water decreasing in the milk as lactation proceeds (Lydersen and Kovacs 1996). Female Harp Seals feed during lactation although at reduced levels compared when they are pregnant (Kovacs et al. 1991, Lydersen and Kovacs 1996). Towards the end of lactation, females come into oestrus and mate (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Weaned pups remain in the vicinity of the pupping patches for some weeks. Most pups remain on the ice during this period when their lanugo is being lost (Kovacs 1987), losing up to 50% of their body mass before entering the water and commencing to capture prey (Kovacs and Lavigne 1985). Having a stable ice platform during this post-lactation development period is likely quite important to future survival (Stenson et al. 2022). After the lanugo is shed, they have a short, stiff-haired, black and silver-grey pelage, and are known as “beaters” until they are about a year old. Pups disperse from the breeding patches when the ice melts, and do not return until they are breeding age (Grecian et al. 2022). Beaters transition into the “bedlamer” pelt over some years, which is heavily spotted; they have this colouration until close to sexual maturity. As they become mature, the black “harp” starts to form on their backs and the face becomes dark, and the spots are gradually lost. Males transition to the adult coat rapidly and fully, while in females the change is slower, with some individuals remaining spotted harps throughout life, never developing the fully black harp or face. Harp Seals are thought to have a promiscuous mating system, but little is in fact known about the breeding system (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). Gestation lasts about 11.5 months, including a three-to-four-month period of delayed implantation (Stewart et al. 1989). The maximum life span of a Harp Seal is approximately 40 years; most animals that reach sexual maturity live past 20 years. Both males and females are sexually active until the end of their lives, showing no signs of reproductive senescence (Ronald and Healey 1981).Harp Seals undergo an annual post-breeding moult, from early April to mid-May (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). They form large aggregations during moult north of the various breeding areas; the exact locations depend on ice availability. Harp Seals are highly migratory and disperse broadly outside the breeding and moulting times. Offshore areas such as the northern part of the Grand Banks (48-490N and 49-51oW) appear to be extremely important to wintering harp seals (Lacoste and Stenson 2000). But tracking data show that juvenile animals from the Northwest population travel north along the Labrador coastline in shelf waters or cross the Labrador Sea and spend time along the east or west coasts of Greenland (Grecian et al. 2022). The Greenland Sea and White Sea groups migrate northward following breeding and moulting and mix in the northern Barents Sea (Folkow et al. 2004). Harp seals in the Northeast Atlantic have distributional hot spots north of Svalbard, at ice edges in the Barents Sea and along the East Greenland shelf in the Fram Strait (Bengtsson et al. 2021, Hamilton et al. 2021). They spend the summer and fall in areas with drift ice, upon which they rest in groups ranging in size from 10s to thousands. High ice concentrations and relatively shallow depths seem to be preferred habitats (Grecian et al. 2022). All populations begin their return migration to their respective breeding areas in the late autumn/early winter. Despite mixing during the summer the two Northeast Atlantic populations return to their natal areas when they are breeding age. Young animals from the various populations generally stay at northern latitudes until they approach sexual maturity. Harp Seals pups and juveniles feed a lot on invertebrate prey, especially euphausiids (Thyanoessa spp.) and pelagic amphipods (Parathemisto spp.) (Nilssen et al. 2001). Adults in Greenlandic waters eat pelagic crustaceans, and fish such as Capelin (Mallotus villosus), Sandeel (Ammodytes sp.), Polar Cod (Boreogadus saida) and Arctic Cod (Arctogadus glacialis). Commercial species such as Atlantic Cod (Gadus morhua) appear to be of minor importance in the diet (Kapel 2000), largely because Harp Seals of all ages eat relatively small prey and tend to specialize somewhat on polar species (Lindstrom et al. 2013). In the Barents Sea, Harp Seals eat Amphipods, Shrimps and small fish including Polar Cod, Sculpin (Cottidae), Snailfish (Liparidae) and Capelin (Nilssen et al. 1995 a, b, Wathne et al. 2000, Lindstrom et al. 2013, Enoksen et al. 2017). During summer at the Barents Sea ice edge, invertebrate prey dominates the diet with Parathemisto libellula and Pandalus borealis being the most common species consumed (Lydersen et al. 1991). In the Northwest Atlantic harp seal diets are comprised predominantly of amphipods, Arctic Cod, Capelin, Herring (Clupea harengus), Sand Lance (Ammodytes americanus) and Redfish (Sebastes spp) (Tucker et al. 2009). Harp Seals are pelagic feeders and dive to modest depths for relatively short durations, but dive performance varies seasonally and regionally. During lactation diving is shallow and of short duration with dives usual being less than 40 m deep, although maximum dives to over 100 m are recorded for lactating females (Lydersen and Kovacs 1996). Animals satellite-tagged at Jan Mayen stay close to the edge of the pack ice during the spring moult, usually diving to less than 100 m, but by July tagged Seals in the Barents Sea dove to 400 m. Dive depths in the Barents Region are limited by local bathymetry. Overall, the deepest dives occur during the day in winter (Folkow et al. 2004).Natural predators of Harp Seals include Polar Bears, Killer Whales and Greenland Sharks (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). In Svalbard, 13% of Polar Bear prey was comprised of Harp Seals in the late 1990s and early 2000s (Derocher et al. 2002). Harps seals are more common in the archipelago now than they were in previous decades, so this % might be shifting (Bengtsson et al. 2021).
threats: Harp Seals have been harvested for thousands of years by native peoples of the North Atlantic, including coastal Northern Europeans historically when the species occurred in the Baltic (Stora and Ericson 2004, Bennike et al. 2008, Glykou et al. 2021). This southern most Harp Seal population was eradicated during the Medieval Warm Period some 1000 yr AD. It is thought that both warming and harvest levels played a role in this extirpation. Basque whalers began taking harp seals in more northerly waters in the 1500s. By the mid-1600s, French settlers began the hunt in the Gulf of St Lawrence, developing land-based netting techniques on the St Lawrence River in the 1700s. By the 1800s, schooner-based sealing developed, and the number of seals harvested rose dramatically in the Northwest Atlantic; from 1803-1816 the average annual was 117,000 animals. The peak of sealing in the Northwest Atlantic occurred between 1818 and 1862, when averages of 500,000 seals per year were harvested, reaching peaks of 640,000-740,000 in single years. During that time interval, it is estimated that 18.3 million harp seals, mostly whitecoats, were killed for oil. There was also early commercial harvesting in the Northeast Atlantic, though at somewhat lower levels. At Jan Mayen, the catch began falling in the late 1850s, likely due to overharvesting and population depression but from 1860 to 1900, an estimated 12.8 million seals were harvested from the West Ice (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988). The 20th century saw the advent of steel-hulled ships, and the hunt continued, though Harp Seals became more valued for their pelts than their oil. The size of all three Harp Seal populations has fluctuated through time, driven largely by the size of the commercial harvests (Sergeant 1976). In 1983, the European Economic Community imposed an import ban on seal products, because of public reactions to the white-coat pup harvest and the average annual commercial harvests fell precipitously. Indigenous groups lobbied the EU parliament successfully and in 2009 exemptions were made for subsistence harvest products. Greenlandic subsistence catches of Harp Seals in recent decades number 50,000-100,00 animals (https://nammco.no/catch-database). Norwegian catches for the Greenland Sea averaged 10,000 animals up to 2020, but recently catches have dropped to a few thousand animals.Capelin collapses in the Barents Region in the 1980s resulted in Harp Seals shifting their distribution southward and foraging along the coast of Norway, resulting in several major mortality events in shore-based net fisheries. Bycatch mortality from nets was estimated to be 56,647 (perhaps up to 100,000) in 1987, and 21,474 in 1988 though it is thought that mortalities might have exceeded 100,000 in each of these years (Haug et al. 1991). By-catch of Harp Seals in the Northwest Atlantic was also a big issue for some years when the lump-fish fishery took up to 45,000 animals annually, but this has dropped to under 2000 in recent years (Sjare et al. 2005, ICES 2023). These events demonstrated the potential risk that fisheries represent to Harp Seals. A major assessment of fisheries catches vs marine mammal consumption suggests that there is strong potential for direct competition between fisheries and pinnipeds (and other marine mammals) in the Greenland Sea, while competition in the Barents Sea is likely not currently an issue (Skern-Mauritzen et al. 2022).A major threat to Harp Seals is climate warming (Laidre et al. 2008, 2015; Kovacs et al. 2011, 2012, 2021) which is already impacting all populations through reductions in their drift ice breeding and resting habitats. The historical Baltic Sea Harp Seal population was extirpated when the region warmed during the Holocene, though hunting is also thought to have played a role in declining numbers (Stora and Ericson 2004, Bennike et al. 2008, Glykou et al. 2021, Bro Jørgensen et al. 2025). Warming over recent decades is having negative effects on Harp Seal breeding, moulting and resting habitats and likely also having negative indirect impacts on their prey populations as well. Recently there have been years with very high pup mortalities in the Northwest Atlantic because of low ice availability and generally low survivorship seem to be the new norm (Johnston et al. 2005; Bajzak et al. 2011; Stenson and Hammill 2014; Hammill et al. 2015, 2021; Stenson et al. 2016, 2020). In North America, years with high stranding numbers are correlated with environmental conditions, including warm temperatures and little sea ice (Haverkamp et al. 2022). Shifts have occurred in the location of whelping locations in the Greenland Sea and in the Northwest Atlantic during years when ice conditions have been extremely poor (Rosing-Asvid 2008; Stenson et al. 2016, 2020). When pupping occurs outside the traditional areas, the young may be exposed to ice that is less stable than in traditional breeding areas. In the Greenland Sea and in areas off Newfoundland, increased predation from polar bears, which travel great distances to seek out the pupping concentrations (Peacock et al. 2013), might become a significant survivorship issue. Other changes include shifts in abundance and distribution of many key prey species for Harp Seals which has negatively impacted body condition and reproductive rates at times in all populations (Øigård et al. 2013, Stenson et al. 2020). Large Atlantic cod stocks in the Northeast Atlantic are likely competing with Harp Seals for prey (Bogstad et al. 2015, Stenson et al. 2020) and the overall borealization and base-line nutrient shifts in the Barents Sea is likely to continue to negatively impact harp seal’s traditional Arctic fish and invertebrate prey populations (Fossheim et al. 2015, de la Vega et al. 2022).Given harp seals extremely social nature, disease is also a risk factor for them (Barratclough et al. 2023). Following the 1988 and 2002 phocine distemper outbreaks (mainly impacting Harbour (Phoca vitulina) and Grey (Halicoerus gyrpus) Seals), very high incidences of PDV antibodies were found in Harp Seals, suggesting extensive exposure in both the Northeast and Northwest Atlantic regions (reviewed in Härkonen et al. 2006).
population: Harp Seals number ca 7 million animals within their global range in the North Atlantic Arctic and Subarctic (see below). Although this makes them the most numerous pinniped species in the region, population numbers are currently significantly lower than historical levels. Numbers in the early 1800s for the three populations combined have been back calculated to range from 9–18 million (Sergeant 1976, Skaug et al. 2007, DFO 2011). Hunt management has been the largest driver of trends for the last hundred+ years, but environmental change is likely now a major factor, if not the principal driver of trends.All three Harp Seal populations have been assessed recently (ICES 2023, Sidorov et al. 2025, DFO 2025). Pup production surveys have been carried out in the Greenland Sea in 2012, 2018 and 2022. A total of 54,181 (95% CI: 36,078–72,284) pups were estimated to have been born in 2018 and 92,769 (CV 20.2) in 2022, returning to a level similar to the 2012 survey (89,590, CV 0 13.7%; ICES 2023). The estimated population size from the 2018 survey was 426,800 (95% CI 313,000–540,600; ICES 2019), significantly reduced from the 2013 estimate of 627,410 (95% CI ¼ 470 540–784 280; Øigård et al. 2014). Model fitting issues and uncertainty about the available reproductive data did not allow for a new estimate to be formulated with the most recent 2018 data, so the current size and trend for the Greenland Sea population is currently evaluated as unknown, although the Harp Seal working Group of ICES suggest that from 2010 through to the present this population has been experiencing a slow decline (ICES 2023). Model outcomes track the size of the Capelin stock (which are key prey) and also show some influence of Atlantic cod (a competitor for forage fish), but do not track pup production or other Harp Seal biological parameters well. The White Sea population was surveyed in both 2023 and 2024. During a survey in 1999 pup production in the White Sea was estimated to be circa 300,000 pups. The White Sea population experienced a precipitous drop in pup production in 2003–2005 due to very poor ice conditions and high pup mortality because of industrial activities; pup production in 2013 was estimated to be 128,786 (ICES 2019). Population surveys were undertaken in the White Sea in both 2023 and 2024 (Sidorov et al. 2025). Pup numbers remained close to the prior estimate a decade before (circa 130,000). The estimated population size was 1.5 million. Modelling suggests that the overall population has been in decline for some decades and an increasing rate of decline is forecast for the coming decades (ICES 2023).The Northwest Atlantic population was assessed in 2023 based on pup production surveys carried out in 2017 (ICES 2023). Pup production was estimated to be 746,500 (95% CI 572,000 - 922,500), which is the lowest since 1994, although not significantly different from the previous survey in 2012 (Stenson et al. 2022). Using new hierarchical Bayesian state-space models, the total Northwest Atlantic population was estimated to be 6.6 million in 1997 and 4,667,000 (3712000–5679000 in 2019 ICES 2023; it must be noted that other model estimates for 2019 produce much higher numbers (7.6 M; DFO 2020)). A survey undertaken in 2022 produced a pup production estimate of 614, 100 (CV 11%), creating a new low. The population estimate suggests an abundance of 4.4 million (3.65–5.35), and a decline rate of 4.7 % per year (DFL 2025). Reduced pregnancy rates and increased juvenile mortality are driving part of this trend (Tinker et al. 2023). But Greenlandic harvests (which mostly take adult Harp Seals) are thought to have important impact on Northwest Atlantic population dynamics; adult mortality is dominated by these hunts (DFO 2025).A small Harp Seal whelping patch was found near South Greenland in 2007 (Rosing-Asvid 2008). This is well outside the normal breeding range. The source of these animals and the inter-annual stability of this group is not known. Additionally, Stenson and Hammill (2014) suggested that there was some evidence of animals pupping further north generally, and in the 2017 survey there was evidence that Gulf animals pupped at the Front (Stenson et al. 2022). So there appears to be some flexibility for Harp Seals relocating under extremely bad ice conditions, although bad (thin) ice years in the Gulf have resulted in high mortality levels during storm events (Stenson and Hammill 2014, Stenson et al. 2020). Russian researchers also suggest the possibility that White Sea animals might be forced to breed further north in the Barents Sea (Sidorov et al. 2025).
range: Harp seals are widespread in the North Atlantic and adjacent Arctic seas. Their range extends from Hudson Bay and the Foxe Basin, Baffin Island, and the Davis Strait in the west, south to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence and Newfoundland in the western North Atlantic, east to Northern Norway, the White Sea and Kara Seas and northward through the Greenland and Barents Seas in the Northeast Atlantic region. The northern limit is at least to Franz Joseph Land (Russia) and Svalbard (Norway) and may extend to 85 degrees north depending on ice conditions (Lavigne and Kovacs 1988, Rice 1998, Lavigne 2018). In the Northeast Atlantic more harps seals are being seen in the fjords of Spitsbergen and north of Svalbard compared to previous decades, suggesting a shift of at least their summer foraging areas (Bengtsson et al. 2021). Harp seals often wander southward outside their core range and, in the eastern Atlantic, vagrants have reached the United Kingdom, the Faroe Islands, Denmark, Germany, France, and Spain (Heptner et al. 1996, Ronald and Healy 1981, Van Bree 1997, Bloch et al. 2000). In the Northwest Atlantic vagrants occur on Sable Island and along the northern east coast states, particularly in Maine and Massachusetts (Haverkamp et al. 2022) but they have been registered as far south as South Carolina (Hampton 2020).
useTrade: Harp Seals are hunted for meat, leather and fur. Some attempts have also been made to utilise oil in the nutraceutical trade.
conservationActions: Canada has sealing regulations pursuant to the 1993 Marine Mammal Regulations that have involved quotas, referred to as “Total Allowable Catches,” hunting licenses, and official observers of the commercial hunt (Sergeant 1976, Anon. 2005). In the Northeast Atlantic, quotas for Harp Seals are set by the Join Norwegian/Russian Commission, based on recommendations made by the International Council for Exploration of the Sea (see ICES 2019, 2023). White coated pups are protected in Canada and Norway; Russia banned hunting of white coated pups from 2009–2013 but the ban was removed in 2014. There are no quotas set for hunting of Harp Seals in Greenland, but average harvests are considered in the total allowable catch (TAC) calculations set within the management framework for the Northwest Atlantic Harp Seal population (see ICES 2023).The species is listed on Annex V (animal and plant species of community interest whose taking in the wild and exploitation may be subject to management measures) of the EU Habitats Directive (Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora - consolidated version 01/01/2007). Harp Seals are also listed on Annex III (protected fauna species) of the Bern Convention (the Convention on the conservation of European wildlife and natural habitats) – they are a highly migratory species. In the 2000`s changes in fashion, anti-hunt campaigns and market closure in some areas such as the EU led to reduced hunting. Commercial and subsistence harvests continue in Canada and Greenland but at low levels. In 2015 the EU amended its 2009 ban on the import of seal products, to allow for trade of hides from Indigenous harvests, opening the market for Greenland in particular (EU 2015).Harp Seals are listed on the European IUCN (regional) Red List as NT because of habitat deterioration (Kovacs 2025).Regular monitoring of population abundance and studies of the impacts of climate change are necessary given the risks posed to Harp Seals from global warming.  Arctic harvests should also be further assessed to ensure sustainability.

rationale: This species has a relatively wide distribution and large extent of occurrence of 207,989 km². It is found in multiple protected areas and not known to be undergoing any significant decline. However, data are lacking, and it is unclear whether the species faces any severe threats. At present, it is assessed as Least Concern, but further research is needed.
habitat: Very little is known about the habitat or ecology of this species. However, studies in Pakistan have reported this species from moist temperate forest (Batool et al. 2019) or around stream banks in dry and open hillsides (Manzoor et al. 2013). Another study reports to have found this species in Tham Khi Nok in a limestone cave surrounded by dry dipterocarp forest and patches of bamboo (Ellis 2012), though presence in Thailand is uncertain.
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: There appears to be no information available on the population trends of this species. It may be less common than other shrew species; in surveys of sites in Pakistan, Crocidura pullata has been the least common shrew species recorded (Shafique and Barkati 2010, Batool et al. 2019).
range: This little-known species has been reported from northern Kashmir in India and Pakistan and the Ladakh region of India (Jiang and Hoffmann 2001, Hutterer 2005). Its type locality sits at 2,134 m asl and altitudinal range is reported to reach up to 2,652 m asl (Burgin et al. 2018), with some records collected from sites at elevations below 1,500 m asl (Batool et al. 2019). It is stated to also occur in Thailand (Duff and Lawson 2004) based on specimen records labelled “Crocidura pullata vorax” from the 1990s, though its presence there remains unconfirmed and this species has often been confused with Crocidura russula, along with Crocidura rapax and Crocidura vorax (Burgin et al. 2018); it is therefore not mapped in Thailand in this assessment.
conservationActions: The species is known from some protected areas, such as Ayubia National Park, Pir Chanasi National Park, Chitral Gol National Park and Tushi Game Reserve in Pakistan (Shafique and Barkati 2010, Shabbir et al. 2013, Batool et al. 2019). Additional studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, general ecology and threats to this little-studied species.

rationale: This species is widespread, has a large extent of occurrence of 392,195 km2 and is present in protected areas. Although the population trend is unknown, there is no reason to suspect any significant decline. This species is therefore assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: It inhabits mountain forests, coniferous and broadleaf, alpine and subalpine belts. It is found in shrub area in piedmont steppes. The species is most abundant in forest-meadow and forest-steppe at lower and upper forest borders. It is active mostly at dusk. The species hibernates; the active period depends on altitude and can be 3 to 5 months. In the Issyk-kul region it is active from second half of May/beginning of June until the beginning of October. Individuals feed mainly on animals (insects, molluscs and earthworms) in spring and first half of summer (Zimina and Merkova 1960). Starting from June, seeds and berries dominate in the diet. It reproduces once per year (in the first half of July); litter size is 3-7 young.
threats: The specific threats to this species are unquantified. It is not clear to what extent it could be impacted by habitat loss, but forest steppes are considered to be among the most threatened of ecosystems, declining due to, e.g., agriculture and livestock grazing (Erdős et al. 2018).
population: It is locally abundant, but there are significant population fluctuations. The highest density was detected in the upper limit of forests in subalpine zones (Holden et al. 2017).
range: It is distributed from desert steppes in piedmonts to alpine belt in Tien Shan (except western ridges), possibly Tarbagatai.
conservationActions: It occurs in some protected areas (eg., Ile-Alatau State National Nature Park in Kazakhstan).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern as the species is common and widespread throughout much of mainland southeast Asia, where it is estimated to have an extent of occurrence of 4,034,622 km². It is found in a number of protected areas, and there are no major threats.
habitat: It inhabits grass, scrub, mangroves, cultivated fields and other human modified areas from sea level up to about 1,000 m. Studies in Viet Nam suggest that population sizes may fluctuate in relation to the availability of field crops (Smith et al. 2008).
threats: There are no major threats to the species.
population: This is a common and highly abundant species.
range: This species occurs in South East China (Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Jiangxi, Guizhou, Chongqing, east Sichuan, south Shaanxi, Hainan) and Taiwan, extending into central and southern Lao PDR, south and South West Cambodia, Thailand, and the Pescadores islands (Dang et al. 1994, Marshall 1977, Musser and Carleton 2005, Robinson et al. 1995, Smith et al. 2008). Wang (2003) recognized three subspecies in China: R. l. exiguus, Howell 1927, found in continental China; R. l. losea, (Swinhoe 1871), occurring in Taiwan; and R. l. sakeratensis, Gyldenstolpe 1917, from Hainan island. The populations in peninsular Thailand and Malaysia are included, until further revision of the genetics is undertaken.
conservationActions: It is present in several protected areas across its range.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because it has a restricted range with an extent of occurrence estimated to be 4,152 km². Whilst the population, ecology and threats to the species are not well known, the loss of its forest habitat as a result of the construction of hydropower stations in the region is likely to be causing declines in the extent and quality of the habitat and therefore declines in the species. The category of Near Threatened is used here until further information becomes available, as at present it is plausible that it could be in a range of categories from Vulnerable and Least Concern.
habitat: This is a poorly known species. It is found in fir forests and mixed coniferous-broadleaf forests (Yixian Li pers. comm. 2025). There are records of the species between 2,590 and 3,170 m asl (Anthony 1941). Its sympatric congener, Uropsilus soricipes, occurs at relatively lower elevations, suggesting potential strong interspecific competition (Yixian Li pers. comm. 2025).
threats: The threats to this species are not known, however, construction of numerous hydropower stations in Sichuan Province, China, may pose a threat to the survival of Uropsilus andersoni (Yixian Li pers. comm. 2025).
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species.
range: This species is endemic to China and occurs in the province of Sichuan where it is only known from Emei Shan and "adjacent small area of China where it is in limited geographic sympatry with Uropsilus gracilis and Uropsilus soricipes" (Smith and Xie 2008). Whilst there have been more recent records of the species, these have been within the current known range (Yixian Li pers. comm. 2025). There are records of the species between 2,590 and 3,170 m asl (Anthony 1941). Compared to sympatric and parapatric species with relatively broad distributions, such as Uropsilus soricipes and Uropsilus gracilis, Uropsilus andersoni has the smallest distribution range, which is restricted to high elevations.
conservationActions: This species occurs in Wawushan Nature Reserve (CSIS 2008), but it is not known if it is present in any additional protected areas. Mt. Emei was named a World Heritage Site in 1996 (UNESCO 2008). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, habitat status, natural history and threats to this species. In China it has been classified as Vulnerable (Jiang et al. 2021).

rationale: The Lion is assessed as Vulnerable under criterion A2c based on an estimated 34% decline in the species' range over three generations (approximately 21 years) and therefore a similar population reduction is suspected. Despite the Lion being well-studied, uncertainty remains a challenge in assessing this species (refer to the section on this topic under Population below for more detail). In recent years, considerable conservation effort has led to stable lion populations in some areas and even recovery in others (e.g., reintroductions into the Zambezi Delta in Mozambique, Akagera in Rwanda). However, over the last 21 years, declines in certain populations have also occurred (e.g., Limpopo National Park, Etosha National Park, and Niassa Special Reserve) with some becoming locally extinct (e.g., Quirimbus National Park in Mozambique, Yankari Game Reserve in Nigeria (P. Funston pers. comm. 2023) and Toro-Semuliki Wildlife Reserve in Uganda). The present assessment is guided by the best available data and methods. Uncertainty is a common problem in the assessment of long-lived species where trends are assessed over a time span that either includes historical periods where some survey techniques were not yet available, or future periods that are inherently unpredictable. A population of between 22,000 and 25,000 adult and subadult lions in Africa (African Lion Database, unpub. data 2025) and ~670 adult and subadult lions in India (Gujarat Forest Department 2020) was estimated in this assessment. Extant lion range in 2025 is estimated to be 1,566,675 km², only 6% of its historical range. This is an estimated 34% range decline since 2004 (three lion generations), where range was estimated to be 2,370,996 km² (Table 1 in the Supplementary Information). This decline, which is likely to continue, reflects a combination of recent known and inferred decline, as well as improved knowledge. Riggio et al. (2013) showed that declines in savanna habitat translate into declines in lion numbers. Lindsey et al. (2017) showed that lion densities vary substantially across their range, and that lions occur at levels below 50% of carrying capacity in two thirds of the sites they analysed. However, these sites were spread all over the African continent, and the range decline is also across the continent, so we have no reason to reject lion range decline as a direct proxy for lion population decline. This supporting evidence suggests that range declines equate to lion population declines, and that range is an appropriate measure for our assessment. Therefore, this suspected decline of 34% in population is justified. Lions are extant in 18 African Range States and possibly extant in four (Table 2 Supplementary Information). The most important driver of lion decline is habitat loss (Bauer et al. 2020). Prey base depletion is also a significant driver and is partly linked to habitat loss, but more importantly to poaching and the bushmeat trade (Becker et al. 2013). Human–lion conflict, which results in the indiscriminate killing of lions in defence of human life and livestock, is another major threat to the species (Sibanda et al. 2021). The trade in bones and other body parts for traditional medicine, both within Africa and in Asia (Williams et al. 2017, Mole and Newton 2020, Coals et al. 2022) is an emerging threat. Furthermore, although trophy hunting can contribute positively to lion conservation, improvements in management practices of this practice have been recommended (Edwards et al. 2014, Dickman et al. 2019), as when poorly regulated, it also contributes to population declines (Packer et al. 2009, Croes et al. 2011, Rosenblatt et al. 2014, Loveridge et al. 2023). Poorly regulated trophy hunting has been previously highlighted as a threat to lions, however, attempts have been made to mitigate through the implementation of science-based management practices. Populations that are trophy hunted should be effectively monitored to ensure that there are no negative population impacts. The impact of violent extremism in several parts of lion ranges in Africa (Lhoest et al. 2022) is likely to further drive the declining nature of lions in these regions. The increasing number of lions poached for their body parts in Mozambique (African Lion Database, unpub. data 2023; Mole and Newton 2020) is of concern, but this presently appears to be confined to this region (Coals et al. 2020), however, illegal trade is reported in at least six African countries (see CITES CoP 17 Prop. 4). Given the evidence of ongoing and increasing threats to lions across much of their fragmented range, we recommend that the Lion is a species under observation and its threat status is closely monitored, with a reassessment after a minimum three-year period or as soon as new information emerges. This decline in both population and range (as a proxy of area of occupancy), which is likely to continue, reflects a combination of recent known and inferred decline, as well as improved knowledge. This meets the requirements for listing as Vulnerable A2c.
habitat: The African Lion has a broad habitat tolerance, and is absent only from tropical rainforest and the interior of the Sahara Desert (Nowell and Jackson 1996). There are records of lions at elevations of more than 4,000 m in the Bale Mountains in Ethiopia and on Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania (West and Packer 2013). Although lions drink regularly when water is available, they can obtain their moisture requirements from prey and even plants (such as the Tsama Melon in the Kalahari Desert), and thus can survive in very arid environments.   Lions are the most social of the cats, with related females remaining together in prides, and related and unrelated males forming coalitions competing for tenure over prides. Prides can vary in size and up to 30 individuals have been observed in larger ecosystems, although the average pride size (including males and females) is four to six adults (Smuts 1976). In the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (South Africa/Botswana) it was found that the average pride size was 11.3 ± 1.1 individuals for prides in the park; similar in size to other areas (11.8 individuals in Kruger National Park, 12.5 in Etosha National Park (Funston 2011)). Lions tend to live at higher densities than most other felids, but with a wide variation from 1.5 adults per 100 km² in southern African semi-desert to 55/100 km² in parts of the Serengeti (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002). Pride ranges can vary widely even in the same region: e.g., from 266–4,532 km² in the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park of South Africa (Funston 2001). In the Kunene region in Namibia, the mean home range size of a pride of 18 male individuals was 4,344 km² (range 618–12,642 km²; Hanssen et al. 2022), while in Etosha the average home range size was 600 km² (range 150–2,075 km²; Stander, 1991). Across regions, lion home ranges can also vary significantly. For example, lion home ranges in Tarangire National Park in Tanzania can range between 52–616 km² (Laizer et al. 2014). In contrast, in more arid environments such as Etosha National Park, home ranges up to 2,075 km² have been recorded (Stander 1991). Mean home ranges for lions in Waza National Park were estimated to be 1,015 km² (Tumenta 2012). Medium- to large-sized ungulates (including antelopes, zebra, and wildebeest) make up large portions of lion’s prey base (Hayward and Kerley 2005), but lions will take almost any animal, from rodents to rhinos. Out of the five preferred prey species in Southern Africa (Hayward et al. 2007), three historically never occurred in West and Central Africa and giraffe are rare in that region, leaving only buffalo but even that species is notably smaller there. Instead, medium sized species such as Kob (Kobus kob) are the preferred prey in West and Central Africa (Bodendorfer et al. 2006, Bauer et al. 2008, Tumenta et al. 2013). Some lion populations have adapted to specialize in unique prey species within their own environments, such as Elephants (Loxodonta africana) in the Chobe (Power and Compion 2009) and in Hwange (Loveridge et al. 2006), and Cape Fur Seals (Artocephalus pusillus) on the Skeleton Coast in Namibia (Stander 2019). Lions will also scavenge, displacing other predators (such as the Spotted Hyaena, Crocuta crocuta, and Cheetah, Acinonyx jubatus) from their kills. In India, Asiatic lions prefer the most mesic and thick canopy forest vegetation available to them in the dry deciduous forests of Gir (Jhala et al. 2009). The Gir National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary is surrounded by cultivated areas and inhabited by the pastoralist Maldharis and their livestock (Meena et al. 2014). Domestic cattle have historically been a major part of the Asiatic lion's diet, although the Chital Deer (Axis axis) is the most common prey species. Mean pride size, measured by the number of adult females, tends to be smaller than for African lions: most Gir prides range between two and eleven adult females (Jhala et al. 2009).
threats: The main threats to lions include continued habitat loss and conversion of safe space. This has led to several subpopulations becoming small and isolated (Bauer et al. 2008, 2020). Other significant threats include indiscriminate killing (primarily due to retaliatory or pre-emptive killing to protect human life and livestock), and prey base depletion (Wolf and Ripple 2016). In recent years the targeted poaching for parts (Everatt et al. 2019, African Lion Database, unpub. data 2023) and violent extremism/warfare (Lhoest et al. 2022) have emerged as significant threats to the species. Furthermore, while trophy hunting has a net positive impact in some areas, it may, at times, contribute to local population declines in Botswana, Namibia, Tanzania, Zimbabwe (Packer et al. 2009, 2011, 2013), Cameroon (Croes et al. 2011) and Zambia (Rosenblatt et al. 2014). In general, there seem to be an increasing number of lions poached through snaring and targeted poaching in many areas across the species range (e.g., the Greater Kruger, Zambeze Delta, Niassa Reserve, Waza National Park, and WAP complex (African Lion Database unpublished data 2023)).A survey study by Nicholson (2024) found that the lack of/inconsistent funding for area operations, retaliatory or pre-emptive killing of lions, and human encroachment were the most severe local-level threats to the lions in East Africa. In southern Africa, the three most severe local threats were identified as the lack of/inconsistent funding for area operations, human encroachment, and development of infrastructure close to or within the area (Nicholson 2024). At a global level, climate change and a ban on lion trophy hunting were identified as the most severe threats to lions in Southern Africa. In East Africa, climate change and civil unrest/ local war (as it reduces effective management) were identified as the most severe threats to lions (Nicholson 2024). The study found that a loss of natural prey base (driven by poaching), targeted poaching for parts and small, isolated populations were perceived to be the most severe local-level threats to the species in West Africa. In Central Africa, the three perceived most severe local threats were a loss of natural prey base (driven by poaching), human encroachment, and retaliatory or pre-emptive killing of lions (Nicholson 2024). At a global level, civil unrest and local war were perceived as the most severe threat to lions in both West and Central Africa, as this threat reduces effective management (Nicholson 2024).Habitat loss and conversionContinued habitat loss and conversion in the subspecies’ range has led to several subpopulations becoming small and isolated (Bauer et al. 2020, Tumenta et al. 2013), such as Waza National Park in northern Cameroon and Niokolo-Koba National Park in Senegal. Continued land use change from natural habitat to agricultural use has also led to further habitat loss in Waza National Park and parts of the Bénoué Complex (Nicholson et al. 2023). Conflict The economic impact of stock raiding can be significant. Patterson et al. (2004) estimated that each lion costs ranchers in Kenya living alongside Tsavo East National Park US$290 per year in livestock losses. Likewise, annual losses of cattle to lions in areas adjacent to Waza National Park in Cameroon comprised only about 3.1% of all livestock losses but were estimated to represent more than 22% of financial losses, amounting to about US$370 per owner (Bauer 2003). Generally, economic losses caused by lions are among some of the highest reported in East Africa when compared to other wildlife species (Muriuki et al. 2017). Consequently, lions are persecuted intensely in livestock areas across Africa; their scavenging behaviour makes them particularly vulnerable to poisoned carcasses put out to eliminate predators. Little actual information exists on the number of lions killed as problem animals by local people, even though this is considered the primary threat to their survival outside protected areas. However, some case studies exist. For example, Hazzah et al. (2014) estimated that on average, 12.5 lions were killed per year between 2003 and 2008 by residents of Olgulului Group Range in Kenya. High number of lion killings have also been recorded in the Omo-Tama Complex over the past five years (Asfaw et al. In prep). Implementation of appropriate livestock management measures, coupled with problem animal control measures and mechanisms for compensating livestock losses, are some of the primary responses to resolving human-lion conflict (Hazzah et al. 2014). For example, Sibanda et al. (2021) studied lion conflict in three communal areas in northwestern Zimbabwe (~3,306 km²) and recorded 46 lions killed between 2008 and 2017. Following the implementation of livestock protection strategies, livestock losses generally decreased, and the number of lions killed per year declined by 41 % (Sibanda et al. 2021). Prey depletion Prey depletion is generally defined as the substantial decline in prey abundance, and its effect on the survival and reproduction of lions is still fairly under-studied (Vinks et al. 2021). Generally, prey depletion reduces an area’s carrying capacity, which therefore reduces lion density without necessarily reducing their survival rates (Vinks et al. 2021). Lion population density across the species’ range is known to track the biomass of principle lion prey species; large wild herbivores (Hayward et al. 2007, van Orsdol 1984). The latter are increasingly under threat from an unsustainable and increasingly commercialized bushmeat trade, leading to collapses in prey populations across large parts of savanna Africa (Lindsey et al. 2013). Regional lion population trends reported in this assessment, are closely mirrored by time series data on main lion prey species from 78 herbivore populations monitored between 1970 and 2005 in West, Eastern and Southern Africa; while herbivore population sizes increased by 24% in Southern Africa, they declined by 52% in Eastern Africa and by 85% in West (Ripple et al. 2015). It is likely that these declines have been even more dramatic since the publication of this study, although precise data is lacking. Bycatch in snares Wire snare poaching is widespread throughout much of the species’ range. Snares are generally set in an effort to capture species for bushmeat, although lions are not commonly targeted. However, lions are often captured in snares intended for other species (Becker et al. 2013, Everatt et al. 2015, Bauer et al. 2020). This threat has the potential to result in severe population declines of all large carnivores if not mitigated accordingly. For example, Becker et al. (2013) found that ~11.5% of the adult and subadult lion population and 20% of the adult (>4 years) males within the population were snared at some point (82% were treated and recovered). Use of lion bones and body parts and derivatives for traditional medicine While there has historically been some level of illegal trade and use of lion bones and body parts for traditional medicine, this threat has escalated in recent years and has emerged in several countries within the species range (Williams et al. 2017, Everatt et al. 2019, Coals et al. 2022). More information on this threat can be found under the Use and Trade section above. Trophy hunting Trophy hunting is carried out in several sub-Saharan African countries and is considered an important management tool for conserving wild land, providing financial resources for lion conservation for both governments and local communities (Holechek and Valdez 2018). However, there is concern that management regimes have not always been sufficient to deter unsustainable offtakes (Packer et al. 2006). A sustainable offtake level of one male lion per 2,000 km² has been recommended (Packer et al. 2011), but offtake has been higher in many areas, which suggests that it is potentially a threat (Lindsey et al. 2013b) to continued survival of lions in these areas. Trophy hunting can thus be a tool for conservation but also a threat, depending on how it is regulated and managed (Loveridge et al. 2007, 2023; Packer et al. 2011). Hunter et al. (2013) cautioned that regulatory measures which reduce the profitability of lion trophy hunting could have widespread negative impacts on wildlife-based land use, anti-poaching, and tolerance of lions outside protected areas. Violent extremism and warfare There are often unforeseen and dramatic consequences and severe environmental impacts resulting from violent extremism adjacent to protected areas (Bouley et al. 2018, Lhoest et al. 2022). Several protected areas (e.g., W-Arly-Pendjari complex, Niassa) within lion range are under pressure from rebel groups or violent extremist organisations. Unsafe areas result from such threats making conservation action and protected area management challenging. Protected areas which are occupied by such groups generally lack park management, see increased and unmanaged livestock invasion, suffer habitat loss due to increased crop planting and experience increased bushmeat poaching.This has resulted in local extinctions of lions in Comoé National Park (Côte d’Ivoire), where, following the civil war in 2002, the park was abandoned, resulting in all the intensification of existing threats, and causing the demise of many species (Aglissi et al. 2023). Several protected areas across the species range are increasingly threatened by rebel factions and violent extremist organizations. This threat needs to be particularly highlighted in the W-Arly-Pendjari complex (Burkina Faso, Niger and Benin). The W-Arly-Pendjari complex has the last remaining stronghold for lions in West and Central Africa. With the WAP being under severe threat from extremist groups in Niger and Burkina Faso, it places significant threat on this vital remaining population of lions. Supporting this claim is the fact that aerial survey reports in W Park in Burkina Faso, which is currently occupied by extremist groups, indicate that the area is devoid of any large mammalian wildlife (Ouindeyama et al. 2021, Lhoest et al. 2022). While lions may still occur throughout the complex, if the situation in the complex remains unchanged, this population may likely become significantly reduced, if not extinct altogether. Other We expect that climate change will likely have a negative impact on the species; however, the extent of this impact is largely unknown. The lack of sufficient funding to support protected areas with lions poses a significant challenge to their successful conservation (Lindsey et al. 2018). It has been estimated that protected areas with lions require between $1,000 to $2,000/km² annually to be managed effectively, yet receive, on average, $200/km² annually (Lindsey et al. 2018). Nearly all protected areas in Africa with lions are inadequately funded, with deficits totally $0.9 to $2.1 billion.
population: Abundance For this assessment, we do not aim to provide a new estimate of total lion numbers. Determining a population number for lions is incredibly challenging as most populations have yet to be surveyed and population numbers that may exist are based on guesses or extrapolations. In addition, some surveys are outdated. For this assessment, to determine a global population number, we used the latest population estimates published in the “Guidelines for the Conservation of Lions in Africa” (GCLA, Bauer et al. 2018), and where possible, updated those figures from the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group’s African Lion Database (ALD) where more recent surveys have been completed. Caution must be exercised when using these figures and inferring trends based on these data presented in the GCLA due to various data limitations. Considering the difficulty in interpreting lion numbers and the availability of an alternative, we decided not to base this assessment on total population numbers alone.
