habitat: This insectivorous species is known to occur in high-elevation forests, including those dominated by pine (Pinus spp.) and fir (Abies spp.), as well as in oak-dominated cloud forests (Goldman 1951). Within its habitat, it has occasionally been recorded in sympatry with Sorex stizodon (Carraway 2007). Cryptotis griseoventris exhibits morphological adaptations consistent with a fossorial lifestyle, including robust forelimbs and well-developed claws adapted for digging (Woodman and Stephens 2010).
threats: The primary threat to Cryptotis griseoventris is ongoing habitat loss driven by agricultural and cattle grazing expansion. Over the past 50 years, Chiapas has lost approximately 55% of its pine-oak forests, primarily due to coffee and maize cultivation and extensive cattle grazing (SEMAHN 2022). Climate change could further exacerbate these threats by intensifying droughts and altering forest composition, putting additional pressure on forest-dependent species like Cryptotis griseoventris (Guevara et al. 2014).
population: The species is known from only a limited number of specimens, with 10 collected historically between 1895 and 1956, and 12 more recent specimens collected in the early 1990s near the type locality (Guevara et al. 2014, 2024). Recent surveys indicate that Cryptotis griseoventris had the highest relative abundance among captured shrew species at sites in Chiapas, comprising 31.81% of captures with a trap success rate of 0.056 (Lorenzo et al. 2019).
range: This species is endemic to Chiapas, Mexico. It has been recorded in Los Altos de Chiapas in southern Chiapas (Woodman and Stephens 2009, Woodman 2010, Woodman 2011). It inhabits coniferous forests, including high-elevation pine-oak and cloud forests, at elevations above 2,100 m (Ramírez-Pulido et al. 2005, Carraway 2007, Lorenzo et al. 2019).
conservationActions: Currently, no specific conservation measures are known to be in place for Cryptotis griseoventris. It is found in small private protected areas (150 hectares) called Huitepec-Tzontehuitz and San José Educational Park, but otherwise it is not known from any other protected areas (Guevara et al. 2014, Lorenzo et al. 2019).

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because it almost meets criterion B (meets the Vulnerable threshold and conditions for criteria B2b(iii), but occurs in >10 locations). This species has an area of occupancy of 72–2,000 km² and is experiencing ongoing and substantial habitat decline due to deforestation for agriculture and urban development. Currently it is estimated to occur in around 13 locations, but a decrease in number of locations from continuing habitat loss could move this species to a threatened category. Additionally, more data on of the remaining number of individuals of this species may suggest a change to a threatened category under criterion C.
habitat: This species has been found in pine ridges (Engilis Jr. et al. 2012), secondary pine-oak and tropical deciduous forests (Lorenzo et al. 2019), and subtropical very wet forest (Kraker-Casteñada et al. 2018). It has also been found in human settlements and agricultural lands (Lorenzo et al. 2019). It uses ambulatory locomotion (not fossorial) to move through its environment (Woodman 2023). In Guatemala, it was rather closely restricted to a marshy habitat found bordering streams, where the vegetation consisted mainly of tall sedges and herbs (Murie 1935). There are records in natural history museums throughout the year (Guevara et al. 2024).
threats: Limited information is available on the direct threats to this species. Tree cover within its range declined by about 11% from 2014–2024 (database by Hansen et al. 2013), which likely limits available habitat for the species. Therefore, agriculture and urban development may negatively impact Cryptotis tropicalis (Lorenzo et al. 2019), though an individual was trapped in a coffee plantation, so the species may have some tolerance to disturbance (Woodman et al. 2012). Climate change is also a threat to this species (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2020).
population: Limited population information is available on this species as it is poorly studied. It has been observed from only a small number of specimens from a few scattered localities. The most recently recorded trappings of the species were a single individual in the southern lowlands of Guatemala (Kraker-Castañeda et al. 2018) and another single Guatemalan individual, trapped across 149 trap nights (Woodman et al. 2012). Interestingly, a cylindrical polychrome vase was found in the ruins at Uaxactun, north of Guatemala, with skeletal remains of 104 shrews as determined by counting the mandibles (Smith and Morley 1934, Murie 1935). Whether all these shrews come from the same region and at the same time or season, it is not possible to know, but it could be an indication of having been a common species in the past.
range: This species is found in Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras (Alvarez-Castañeda 2024, Carraway 2007), as well as El Salvador (Burgin and He 2018). It is generally a highland species, found in the physiographic subprovinces of the Sierras of Southern Chiapas and the Volcanoes of Central America (Lorenzo et al. 2019).
conservationActions: Cryptotis tropicalis has been listed as “Sujetas a Protección Especial” (Subject to Special Protection) by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010).There are records of this species from Reserva de la Biosfera El Triunfo (Mexico), Parque Nacional Laguna Lachuá (Guatemala), Parque Regional y Área Natural Recreativa Volcán de Suchitán (Guatemala) and outside of Reserva Natural Privada Dulce Nombre (Guatemala). Specimens collected in 1935 near the Chiquibul Forest Reserve in the Maya Mountains of Belize were identified as Cryptotis tropicalis (Engilis Jr. et al. 2012). The population size at each of these locations is unknown.

rationale: Pseudoromicia kityoi is assessed as Endangered under criterion B1ab(i.ii.iii,v)+2ab(i,ii,iii,v). There are only two specimens known from within 200 m from the edge of Mabira Forest Reserve, Mukono District of the Central Region, Uganda in a remnant patch of tropical rainforest. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 445 km² and its area of occupancy (AOO) is 336–404 km², based on its entire range, which is inferred to be the Mabira Forest Reserve. The species' is thought to occur in 2–5 threat-based locations due to the continuing decline of forest habitat within the reserve and the surrounding landscape. Conversion to agricultural lands and charcoal production are the primary threats to its habitat. Additionally, this bat's global distribution is likely suffering from habitat fragmentation. Due to the ongoing deforestation within the species' range, its population is suspected to be declining as its habitat, range, EOO, and AOO are continuing to decline.
habitat: The species is a small insectivorous bat known from medium-elevation tropical rainforest, and is assumed to share a similar ecology to other closely related species, the majority of which are forest dependent (Monadjem et al. 2021). It is inferred to be associated with the forested habitats of the Mabira Forest Reserve, which is declining in quality and extent due to ongoing illegal logging, charcoal production, and agricultural encroachment (Boffa et al. 2008, Jjagwe et al. 2021, Truscott 2023, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025). As the only two individuals of this species were caught at the edge of Mabira Forest in heavily degraded tropical forest, it is unclear the extent the species uses edge habitats or the more degraded lands around the Mabira Forest Reserve.
threats: This bat's ecology is poorly understood, and only two specimens are known, so threats to the species are unclear. Nevertheless, the global distribution of this species may be both fragmented and restricted in extent, as the majority of members of this genus are restricted to tropical rainforest habitats and the two known specimens were found in a remnant patch of rainforest. With the assumed association with forested habitats, the primary threats to the species centre on the degradation and loss of rainforest. The Mabira Forest Reserve is under pressure from government development for agricultural expansion as well as community use of the forest (Jjagwe et al. 2021, Truscott 2023, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025). There is ongoing firewood collection, charcoal production, illegal logging, and even encroachment for conversion to agricultural (small scale) and human settlement (Boffa et al. 2008, Jjagwe et al. 2021, Truscott 2023). Although a prior proposal for sugarcane plantation was stopped, large-scale agriculture remains a threat to the forest. Increased understanding of the species ecology will yield important insights into the threats to the species.
population: There are no data on this bat's population size or trend, as the species is known only from two specimens. It is assumed to occur in a single population given the current understanding of its distribution in the Mabira Forest Reserve and the highly degraded surrounding landscape. An overall population decline is suspected due to ongoing deforestation due to illegal logging, charcoal production, and agricultural encroachment in the forest reserve (Boffa et al. 2008, Jjagwe et al. 2021, Truscott 2023, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025).
range: Pseudoromicia kityoi is thought to be endemic to Uganda, as it is known from the area immediately around the Mabira Forest Reserve in Central Uganda (Monadjem et al. 2021). It was collected from two sites ca 200 m from the edge of Mabira Forest (1,130 m asl) which is ca 0.79 km northeast of Nagojje Station, Mukono District of the Central Region, Uganda (0.4451°N, 32.88876°E; Monadjem et al. 2021). Its range is inferred to encompass the Mabira Forest Reserve and the surrounding landscape, comprising 2–5 threat-based locations, within an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 445 km² (based on a minimum convex polygon around the species’ range) and an area of occupancy (AOO) of 336–404 km² (based on a 2x2 km grid overlain on the species’ range). The species is inferred to have an elevation range of 1,070 to 1,340 m asl, based on the minimum and maximum elevations within the Mabira Forest Reserve (Jjagwe et al. 2021, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025). Ongoing illegal logging, charcoal production, and agricultural encroachment into the forest are degrading and reducing the species' range. While the species’ EOO and AOO are suspected to be declining due to ongoing deforestation in the Mabira Forest Reserve (Jjagwe et al. 2021, Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025), there is no evidence to suggest a decline in the number of locations or extreme fluctuations in the species’ range, EOO, AOO, or number of locations.
useTrade: The species is not known to be used or traded.
conservationActions: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for the species, as it was only described in 2021. Its forested habitat does receive the benefit of some protection, as it is only known from the Mabira Forest Reserve and surrounding area (Monadjem et al. 2021). The Mabira Forest Reserve has three management zones (Jjagwe et al. 2021) with the greatest protection coming from the “strict nature reserve” and the greatest threat within the “production zone.” The species is not protected under national or international regulations and does not meet the criteria for inclusion on the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (UNEP-CMS 2025) or the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES 2025). However, it should qualify as a trigger species for the Mabira Forest Reserve Key Biodiversity Area (Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership 2025) and also as an Alliance for Zero Extinction species once the assessments are completed.There are ongoing initiatives with the communities to reduce the pressures on the forest through alternative livelihood projects (e.g., honey production from beehives) to reduce charcoal production (Truscott 2023). Expanded and new initiatives to reduce firewood collection, charcoal production, and agricultural expansion would benefit the species. Forest restoration is a priority to start to reverse the negative impacts of deforestation. Comprehensive research is needed into the species’ distribution, population status and trend, ecology, and threats. The species would benefit from community awareness programs as well as monitoring of its habitat. The explicit inclusion of the species in management documents for the Mabira Forest Reserve and a species recovery plan would also benefit it.

rationale: Although this species has a large distribution range, it remains restricted to areas of permanent fresh water, with sufficient shoreline cover and an abundant prey base. Thus, while the distribution range is large, the spatial size of their occupied habitats is much smaller and unknown, particularly due to the widespread habitat destruction and pollution reported for much of the African continent (Ponsonby et al. 2016). The impact of global climate change throughout Africa (Magadza 1994, Dixon et al. 2003, Hendrix and Glaser 2007) also has the potential of decreasing suitable habitat for otters and increasing human-otter conflict for increasingly scarce resources such as water, land, and fish. Both this decrease in suitable habitat and increase in human-otter conflict are currently occurring and will certainly increase over the next three generations (13 years). This reassessment is based on a perceived (in regions where studies have been conducted; Ray et al. 2005, Somers and Nel 2013) and assumed (in regions where no studies have been done) population decline over the last 18 years and beyond. In much of their range, populations of African Clawless Otters are faced with habitat loss or degradation, polluted waters, and/or degraded aquatic ecosystems due to the introduction of invasive alien species such as Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) and marginal agricultural practices. This habitat disturbance is exacerbated by poor sanitation infrastructure and growing industrial waste pollution. Moreover, the regional human populations are poverty-stricken, as a consequence, there is an ever-increasing pressure on all natural resources including water, vegetation, the otter prey base, as well as reducing suitable resting and denning sites vital to survival of the species. Thus, due to inferred cumulative effects of the threats, it is suspected that the African Clawless Otter population underwent a reduction in population by at least 20% in the past three generations (13 years based on Pacifici et al. 2013). Therefore, the species is assessed as Near Threatened (nearly meets criterion A2cde). Additionally, the exacerbation of these threats may lead to a suspected future population decline of at least 20% over the next three generations (nearly meets criterion A3), further supporting the Near Threatened assessment.
habitat: African Clawless Otters are predominantly aquatic and seldom found far from water. Freshwater is an essential habitat requirement, and they only occur in marine habitats where there is access to fresh water. In marine habitats, rocky shores are preferred (Van Niekerk et al. 1998). Elsewhere, they are found in diverse habitats, from impoundments, estuaries, and mangroves to desert conditions of the upper Doring River in the Western Cape (South Africa) and the Fish River in southern Namibia (Nel and Somers 2007, Somers and Nel 2013); they are also found in many seasonal or episodic rivers in the Karoo (South Africa), such as the Sak, Vis, Riet and Gamka Rivers, provided suitable-sized pools persist (Nel and Somers 2007, Somers and Nel 2013). They have been recorded up to 3,000 m in Ethiopia (Yalden et al. 1996). In Nigeria the African Clawless Otter is mainly restricted to brackish water streams (with mangrove vegetation along the banks) and, more occasionally, to transitional habitats between freshwater and brackish‐water environments (Angelici et al. 2005). African Clawless Otters have been found in towns and cities, and can occupy rivers with high pollution and eutrophication levels (Somers and Nel 2013). However, exposure to polluted waterways, dogs, traffic, and changes in the food web negatively impact the urban populations of the species (Okes and O’Rian 2017). The home range of the African Clawless Otters’ range length varied from 4.9 to 54.1 km and core length from 0.2 to 9.8 km. Total area of water used varied between 4.9 and 1062.5 ha, and core areas from 1.1 to 138.9 ha. As predicted using the resource dispersion hypothesis, total home-range length was correlated with mean reed bed (high food density patch) nearest neighbour distance. The pattern of home-range use by females was suggestive of territoriality. Male African Clawless Otters had overlapping home ranges, both with other males and with females (Somers and Nel 2004). The African Clawless Otters prefer hunting at depths of 0.5–1.5 m. This is despite having a higher hunting success, catching larger, more energy-rich prey (fish), and shortest time foraging per catch, at depths of 1.5–2.5 m. Some of the data presented support the optimal breathing hypothesis, which predicts that both surface and dive times should increase for dives of greater depths. However, diving efficiency does not decrease with increasing depth, and percentage time at the surface does not increase with increasing depth. These are contrary to the optimal breathing hypothesis (Somers 2000).
threats: The main threat to the species is the declining state of freshwater ecosystems in Africa. For instance, in South Africa the state of main river ecosystems is very poor: 84% of the ecosystems are threatened, with 54% Critically Endangered, 18% Endangered, and 12% Vulnerable (Nel et al. 2007). Otter habitat has been either drastically changed or lost, following bush clearing, deforestation, overgrazing, siltation, draining of wetlands or water extraction or denudation of riparian vegetation (Rowe-Rowe 1995, Nel and Somers 1998). In parts of their range, African Clawless Otters  are being killed for skins and other body parts (e.g., Cunningham and Zondi 1991, De Luca and Mpunga 2005), or because they are regarded as competitors for food, particularly in rural areas where fishing is an important source of income, or where they are believed to be responsible for poultry losses (Rowe-Rowe 1995), and damage to young maize plants (Reed-Smith pers. comm.). Fisheries managers of the Kairezi River Protected Area in Zimbabwe blamed trout declines on otter predation and competition with trout for food, even though scat analysis revealed that only 1% of otter faeces contained the remains of trout and their diets overlapped only 17% (Butler 1994, Butler and Marshall 1996). Occasionally, they are accidentally caught and drowned in gill nets and fish traps (Rowe-Rowe 1990).
population: African Clawless Otter populations are thought to be decreasing throughout most of their range based on assessed threats and decreasing reports of signs or sightings; however, there is a lack of research-based population status information over the last 15 years outside of South Africa. Density estimates from various studies in southern Africa are summarized by Somers and Nel (2013). In coastal habitats, Tsitsikamma Coastal N. P. in the Eastern Cape, and Betty’s Bay, Western Cape, South Africa, the density estimates are given as one individual per 1.9–2 km of coast (Van der Zee 1979, 1982; Arden-Clarke 1983, 1986; Verwoerd 1987). In freshwater habitats, the density estimates vary as one otter per 1.25–2.5 km² (Carugati 1995, Perrin and Carugati 2000), one otter per 3–4 km² (Rowe-Rowe 1992) and one otter per 8–10 km² of river (Butler and du Toit 1994). Somers (2001), using recovery of radioactive scats (n = 55), provided an estimate of 1.53 otters per km of river. Assuming there are two otters per km of river, the estimate for the total population in South Africa alone is around 21,500 animals (M. J. Somers pers. obs.).
range: The African Clawless Otter is the most widely distributed otter species in Africa, with a range stretching from Senegal and Mali throughout most of West Africa to Sudan and Ethiopia, and then southwards throughout East Africa to the Western Cape of South Africa. They are absent from the Congo basin, where they are replaced by the Congo Clawless Otter (Aonyx congicus), the two species being sympatric in Uganda and Rwanda (Somers and Nel 2013).
useTrade: This species is exploited for its meat and pelt (see under Threats).
conservationActions: African Clawless Otters are present in a number of protected areas across their range. The populations of Cameroon and Nigeria are listed on CITES Appendix I (as Aonyx capensis microdon). All other populations are included in CITES Appendix II. It is also listed as Endangered in Benin Red List (Neuenschwander et al. 2011).

rationale: The species occurs throughout most of tropical and sub-tropical sub-Saharan Africa, being restricted to areas of permanent fresh water, offering good shoreline cover and abundant prey base. Thus, while the distribution range is large, the spatial size of their occupied habitats is much smaller and faces continued loss particularly due to the widespread habitat destruction and pollution reported for much of the African continent (Ponsonby et al. 2016). The impact of global climate change throughout Africa (Magadza 1994, Dixon et al. 2003, Hendrix and Glaser 2007, Cianfrani et al. 2018) also has the potential of decreasing suitable habitat for otters and increasing human-otter conflict for increasingly scarce resources such as water, land, and fish. Both this decrease in suitable habitat and increase in human-otter conflict are currently occurring and will certainly increase over the next three generations. This reassessment is based on a perceived (in regions where studies have been conducted) (Akpona et al. 2011, Akpona et al. 2015, Dognimon et al. 2019, Reed-Smith in prep.) and assumed (in regions where no studies have been done) population decline over the last 16 years and beyond. In much of their range, populations of Spotted-necked Otters are faced with habitat loss or degradation, polluted waters, and/or degraded aquatic ecosystems due to the introduction of exotic species such as Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) and Nile Perch (Lates niloticus) and marginal agricultural practices. This habitat disturbance is exacerbated by poor sanitation infrastructure and growing industrial pollution. Additionally, the regional human populations are poverty-stricken, thereby, increasing pressure on all natural resources including water, vegetation, otters’ prey base, as well as reducing suitable resting and denning sites vital to the survival of the species. For all the above reasons and the lack of effective conservation measures, currently a continued decline in the overall Spotted-necked Otter population of at least 20% is suspected for the next three generations (23 years; Pacifici et al. 2013). Therefore, the species is listed as Near Threatened as it almost qualifies as threatened under criterion A3cde; this is a precautionary listing.
habitat: The Spotted-necked Otter inhabits freshwater habitats where water is unsilted, unpolluted, and rich in small to medium sized fishes (Reed-Smith 2010, d'Inzillo Carranza and Rowe-Rowe 2013). The species is comparatively common in Central and East Africa, where suitable habitat constitutes of large lakes and open waters, such as the Okavango Delta (Rowe-Rowe and Somers 1998). Elsewhere, it is found in streams, rivers and impoundments up to altitudes of 2,500m (Yalden et al. 1996). Wherever it occurs, the spotted-necked otter prefers shallow to deep waters (Larivière 2002). In a telemetry study conducted in Kwa-Zulu Natal, South Africa, the core areas of habitat included highland river and tributaries, natural oxbow lakes and some man-made lakes artificially stocked with alien trout (Perrin et al. 2000). Human presence negatively influences spotted-necked otter, but human presence alone cannot explain the absence of spotted-necked otters in an area, because other habitat features such as presence or absence of vegetation cover along the banks also determine the occurrence of otters (Dognimon et al. 2019). In Benin, West Africa the Spotted-necked Otter is frequently observed in the Ouémé valley especially along the River Hlan, possibly due to the abundance of fish (Akpona, 2004). In riparian and lacustrine habitats adequate vegetation in the form of long grass, reeds, dense bushes, overhanging trees and large boulder piles are essential to provide cover during periods of inactivity and for denning. Unlike African Clawless Otter, they do not occur in marine or estuarine waters (Angelici et al. 2004).Predominantly a piscivore, the Spotted-necked Otter, also occasionally feeds on crabs, frogs, insects and birds. In L. Muhazi (Rwanda) and L. Victoria (Tanzania) diet consists almost entirely of fish of the genus Haplochromis, followed by fish of the genus Tilapia (Procter 1963, Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990, Lejeune 1990). Kingdon (1977) in L. Bunyoni (Uganda/Rwanda) reported that the main prey before the introduction of Tilapia spp. was the Clawed Toad (Xenopus laevis), and the otter population at that time was thriving. In South Africa, where fish faunas of inland rivers are poor, the species appears to forage on almost equal amounts of fish, crabs and frogs, supplemented by small amounts of dragonfly (Odonata) larvae (Rowe-Rowe 1977a, Somers and Purves 1996, Perrin and Carugati 2000). In South Africa, the fish was consumed more during autumn and winter while crabs were consumed more during spring and summer (Rowe-Rowe 1977a, Perrin and Carugati 2000). This could be related to the effects of water temperature on the prey: during the cold season crabs retreat into inaccessible places and at the same time the efficiency of locomotion of fishes is reduced by cold water (Rowe-Rowe 1977a). In all studies to date, Spotted-necked Otters fed mainly on small fish, 80–90% being smaller than 100–150 mm fork length (Rowe-Rowe and Somers 1998). When preying on crabs, specimens with a carapace width <45 mm appear to be selected (Rowe-Rowe and Somers 1998) and Rowe-Rowe (1977) found that most crabs with a carapace width >50 mm were avoided. Somers and Purves (1996) in the Bushman R. also found fish of the genus Tilapia to be the main component of its diet, and they did not find remains of any other species of fish. Rowe-Rowe (1977) and Perrin and Carranza (2000) suggested that they hunt mainly by sight. However, in the lakes where both small fishes and Spotted-necked Otters are most abundant, the water is very turbid (Lejeune and Frank 1990, H. Kruuk pers. comm.), suggesting that senses additional to sight are used. Foraging occurs mainly within 2–10 m of the shore (Procter 1963, Lejeune 1989, Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990, Reed-Smith et al. 2014). Foraging dives generally have a duration of 16–25 sec in deep water (Lejeune 1989) and shorter (5–20 sec) in shallower water (Rowe-Rowe 1977). Surfacing periods between unsuccessful dives are brief (6–10 sec) as are those when small fish are caught and eaten in the water (11–16 sec) (Lejeune 1989). Larger prey is taken to the shore and eaten out of the water (Procter 1963, Rowe-Rowe 1977). Prey appears to be always captured in the mouth. Very small fish (<60 mm) are eaten from the head, but all larger fish and frogs are eaten tail first, with the heads sometimes being discarded (Rowe-Rowe 1977, Power and Slater-Jones 2010). Foraging is mostly solitary, except in lakes where the otters fish in large groups (Procter 1963, Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990, Reed-Smith et al. 2014).
threats: The Spotted-necked Otter is decreasing throughout its range, mainly as a result of the alteration or degradation of freshwater habitats and riparian vegetation. This rapid habitat loss is exacerbated by a growing, poor population engaged in unsustainable agricultural activity (Rowe-Rowe 1990, 1992, 1995; Kipkemboi et al. 2007) and unsustainable fishing practices (LVFO 2008, Yan 2017). These practices have led to bank and shoreline erosion, denuding the rivers of important vegetative cover used by the otters, increased human presence which is disruptive to otter denning, increased use of smaller mesh nets and poisoning to improve catches, and the change or depletion of the otters’ prey base (Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990). Pollution of waters with agricultural, livestock, and societal wastes also are threatening with evidence of the bioaccumulation of organochlorines and other biocontaminants recorded in Spotted-necked Otters (Mason and Rowe-Rowe 1992). The rate of otters becoming entangled in set and discarded fishing nets is impossible to determine. However, based on known entanglement of other species it has likely increased over the occasional drowning reported previously (Stuart 1985, Rowe-Rowe 1990). Otters are also killed for food or skins, as a perceived threat to poultry, or as a competitor for fish (Rowe-Rowe 1990, Akpona et al. 2011, Reed-Smith et al. 2010, Mgomo and Reed-Smith 2020). Introduction of alien fish species that out-compete the smaller indigenous fish was identified as a main threat for the Lake Victoria population (Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990). Increased commercial use of Africa’s fish resource as well as increasing dependence on fish as a source of protein for local populations is leading to an increase in conflicts between otters and fishermen (Akpona et al. 2015, Abdallah 2017, Ergete et al. 2018, Mgomo and Reed-Smith 2020. The Spotted-necked Otter is the most expensive species of small carnivore species sold in the animal-based medicine market in Benin (Djagoun and Gaubert 2009). Ammouso 2003 record that the hunting pressure on Hydrictis maculicollis for food and ritual practices is increasing because their capture does not require expensive investment in equipment. Habitat loss and increased conflict with people is impacting all populations. The increase in human numbers dependent on fish as a source of protein is particularly threatening in the large East African lakes which are historically important refugia for this species. It has been reported that the introduction of Nile Perch (Lates niloticus) into Lake Victoria and their impact on the diversity of the fish biomass in the lake is forcing a dietary shift for the otters (Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990). This shift in prey base has been observed (Reed-Smith 2010) but its full impact is unknown at this time particularly for areas outside of the protected national park where recent studies have occurred. The introduction of invasive alien species such as water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) is also degrading the water ecosystem. The impact of global climate change throughout Africa (Magadza 1994, Dixon et al. 2003, Hendrix and Glaser 2007, Cianfrani et al. 2018) also has the potential of decreasing suitable habitat for otters and increasing human/otter conflict for increasingly scarce resources such as water, land, and fish. UNECA projected in a 1999 study that portions of the Spotted-necked Otter’s current range would be experiencing fresh water stress and scarcity by 2025 with much of the rest of its range considered vulnerable to these hydrologic issues.
population: Like other otter species, abundance and density of Spotted-necked Otter appear to be dependent, in part, on the availability of fish; consequently, this species historically was common or fairly common in the fish-rich Central African lakes, but generally uncommon or rare in the rest of Africa where fish fauna tends to be poor (Rowe-Rowe 1990, 1995; d'Inzillo Carranza and Rowe-Rowe 2013). In an area that included a highland stream and man-made lakes in South Africa, Perrin et al. (2000) estimated one otter/1–2 km of stream, while in less suitable habitat Rowe-Rowe (1992) estimated one otter/6–11 km. In a more recent study (Kubheka et al. 2013) detected only 25% of the number of spraints located during two previous studies in an area of intense human disturbance but roughly the same number of spraints located in an undisturbed area during the latter 1993 study indicating a reduction in otter numbers in areas of increased human presence. In the Central and East African lakes, density was estimated at between one and two otters per kilometre of shoreline (Procter 1963, Kruuk and Goudswaard 1990, Lejeune and Frank 1990 cited in D’Inzilla-Carranza and Rowe-Rowe 2013). A more recent study (2006 – 2011) of Lake Victoria detected what could be a similar abundance on portions of the protected shoreline of Rubondo Island National Park, but local sources reported a perceived decline in, or absence of otters along other portions of the lake’s shorelines. Their abundance also appears to be dependent on suitable habitat (Reed-Smith 2010) which includes dense vegetative cover (Dognimon et al. 2019) and/or the presence of large, piled boulder shorelines. Early studies of this species inhabiting large East African lakes and South African riverine systems reported observations of group size ranging up to approximately 20 individuals (Rowe-Rowe and Somers 1998, Reed-Smith unpublished data). Recent studies in East Africa (Reed-Smith et al. 2010, Reed-Smith et al. in preparation, and unpublished data for Tanzania, Kenya, and Uganda) indicate population declines due to habitat loss, water course changes due to drought, increased human populations, and increased eradication of otters as perceived competitors as well as for consumption and traditional medicine. Based on informant interviews in East Africa (Reed-Smith et al. 2010 and unpublished data) as well as reports from other range countries, this species is seldom observed or not seen as often as it was 10 years ago and groups of more than five are rarely seen. Over the last six years, in areas of Lake Victoria where otters were routinely observed, informants now report rarely or never seeing them. From West Africa, recent studies have reported the presence of the Spotted-necked Otter to the south of Benin (Dognimon et al. 2019) based on field observation. Overfishing and destruction of the wetland habitat for agriculture are the main reasons of the declining population trend according to the local perception.  Although the species has been previously reported form the Northern Cape Province from the Vaal River (Stuart 1981, Skinner and Chimimba, 2005), Power and Slater-Jones (2010) reported a  range extension up to the Orange River, 1200 km downstream of the existing range, though they have mentioned that intensive surveys are required to determine their extensive occurrence in the Orange River. Unfortunately, beyond these personal accounts, there is a lack of data availability on the status and ecology of this species throughout most of their historic range for the last fifteen years and only marginally more for the last 30 years. An additional problem in assessing their status is that throughout most of their range there is often no distinction made by local people between Hydrictis maculicollis and Aonyx capensis or A. congicus which are sympatric species in some parts of their range countries.
range: Spotted-necked Otters are found in lakes and larger rivers throughout much of Africa south of 10°N latitude. They are common in Lake Victoria and across Zambia, but for some unexplained reason often are absent from what appear to be suitable habitats, such as the lakes and rivers, of East Africa and the Zambezi below Victoria Falls (Estes 1992). It is likely to be present throughout most of its historic range albeit, in reduced numbers due to habitat degradation, civil strife, polluted waterways, increasing human animosity towards this species, and use as a meat source (Reed-Smith 2010). However, due to the paucity of current information, their continued presence in Angola, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Chad, Côte d'Ivoire, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Guinea, Liberia, Mali, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Sudan is presumed. The species is believed to be extinct in Burundi, Ghana, Lesotho, and Togo (Reed-Smith et al. 2014). Current reports indicate the Spotted-necked Otter is present in reduced numbers in Benin, Botswana, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Rwanda, South Africa, United Republic of Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe (Reed-Smith et al. 2014, Akpona et al. 2015). The large lakes of Central and East Africa and possibly the larger river systems are important sites for the conservation of this species.
useTrade: The species is hunted for food, medicinal purposes, and pelt (De Luca et al. 2018, Reed-Smith et al. 2010, Mgomo and Reed-Smith 2020).
conservationActions: Currently there are only a few regionally based conservation actions in place for this species (e.g., African Otter Network and IUCN SSC-Otter Specialist Group projects, listed as Vulnerable in South Africa) and it is technically protected in all national parks. The species has also been listed as Vulnerable in the Benin Red List (Neuenschwander et al. 2011), informing about urgent conservation actions required on the species. They are present in several protected areas across their range but are little known and seldom seen by staff or visitors. Efforts should be made to educate range country park staff about all otter species and the role they play in a healthy ecosystem to increase awareness and protection for this species. This lack of knowledge by range country professionals can be mitigated by initiating an awareness campaign for all range country wildlife professionals. This campaign should be expanded to target human populations sharing their ecosystems with otters, particularly where traditional tales about otter behaviour are deleterious to the species future survival (e.g. otters rape women or raid young maize crops). Another significant conservation action is taking steps to create a network with field biologists working in ecosystems where otters are found. The creation of a user-friendly system to report otter sightings would significantly contribute to our knowledge of their current distribution and aid researchers in future assessments of status and population trends in Africa where they inhabit areas that are hard to reach, or dangerous to survey due to the presence of crocodiles, hippopotamus, etc. Networking with other researchers to create synergy between conservation efforts also would benefit preservation of important otter habitats and ecosystems. There is need for detailed studies on the distribution and current status of this species as well as conducting public relations campaigns to increase awareness of the presence of otters in Africa. It is listed in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Listed as Least Concern because, it is a widespread species that is fairly common, and very adaptable to anthropogenically disturbed habitats, including pasturelands and even rural gardens.
habitat: It occurs in a wide range of substrates from friable sandy loams to exfoliated schists and sandy soils; they tend to avoid stony soils. They are often located within human modified environments, such as lawns, golf courses and gardens (particularly in the presence of vegetable gardens). The species is subterranean, and social, with a colony size of around five animals (and up to 14) including a single reproductive pair. It has a litter size of two to six young and a generation time of about three years.
threats: There are no major threats to the species. However, they are occasionally persecuted as an agricultural pest, and homeowners complain that this species is a nuisance in their gardens (Power 2014).
population: The abundance of this species is not well-known. It is a widespread across the region. Presumably the species is limited by soil requirements. In prime habitats the population density of Cryptomys hottentotus is known to surpass 150 individuals per km2 (A.C. Spinks, J.U.M. Jarvis and N.C. Bennett, unpubl. data).
range: This species occurs throughout the Western Cape from the southwestern limits of Cape Town to the Gariep River, extending eastwards beyond Port Elizabeth in the Eastern Cape, and northwards into the Free State and the Northern Cape. It is expected to be the only Cryptomys species within its range; however, the exact northern and eastern limits of its distribution remain undefined, due to confusion with other species in this genus (Monadjem et al. 2015)
conservationActions: The species occurs in many protected areas throughout its range. Further taxonomic study of this species is needed to clarify the status of the various subspecies.

rationale: In 2017, this species was assessed as Critically Endangered, under the assumption that the population was still declining. However, the main cause of population decline was predation by feral cats, which were eradicated from the island by 2003 through trapping and hunting. Therefore, the 2017 assessment was an over-estimate of extinction risk for this species. It is now reassessed as Vulnerable (VU D2) because all individuals are in a single location, the 19.9 km² island of Montserrat off the coast of Baja California, Mexico and the risk of cats (or other invasives) being reintroduced to the island in future could rapidly push the species into Critically Endangered or even Extinct.
habitat: The biology of this species remains mostly unknown because trapping has not been very successful. A lactating female was captured in October 1994, so the species probably reproduces mostly in summer and autumn (Álvarez-Castañeda and Cortés-Calva 2002). Montserrat Island has hills and canyons, poor and often rocky soil, and is dominated by xeric scrubland (Álvarez-Castañeda and Cortés-Calva 2002, Ortiz-Ávila et al. 2020). The species’ range likely extends to all parts of the island, from 0–200 m (Yu et al. 2023). Other Peromyscus species have been reported consuming vegetation and arthropods (Zaragoza-Quintana et al. 2022), so this is probably similar for Peromyscus caniceps.
threats: This species was severely threatened by feral cats in its very restricted range, and predation by feral cats caused the extinction of Chaetodipus rudinorus fornicatus on the same island (Álvarez-Castañeda and Cortés-Calva 2002, Aguirre-Muñoz et al. 2011). Cats were removed from the island in 2001/2003, and surveys in 2008 confirmed their absence (Aguirre-Muñoz et al. 2008, Aguirre-Muñoz et al. 2011), but frequent visitation by humans may lead to future introductions of invasive species.
population: Most trapping efforts for this species were conducted prior to the eradication of feral cats. Only four individuals were trapped over 2,000 trap-nights between 1994 and 1997 (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 1998) and several individuals were trapped in various surveys from 1975–1998 (Álvarez-Castañeda and Cortés-Calva 2002). However, these trapping events occurred prior to cat eradication on the island in 2001 (Aguirre-Muñoz et al. 2008). It is now estimated that the species is abundant (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018), but more recent surveys are needed to fully understand current trends without invasive threats.
range: This species is endemic to Montserrat Island, an island off the coast of the Baja California Sur, Mexico in the Gulf of California with an area size of 19.9 km² (Mellink and Luévano 2014, Ortiz-Ávila et al. 2020, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
conservationActions: This species has been listed as “Sujetas a Protección Especial” (Subject to Special Protection) by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). While limited work has focused on specific conservation measures for this species, its entire range falls within the Bahía de Loreto National Park so its habitat has governmental protection (Centro Mexicano de Derecho Ambiental 1996). Ongoing monitoring and prevention of invasive species introductions would limit risk to this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU D2). It is only found in a single location, the 11.37 km² Isla Tortuga in Baja California Sur, Mexico. Plausible future threats such as the introduction of invasive rodents and cats could drive the taxon to Critically Endangered or Extinct in a very short time.
habitat: The species reportedly prefers rocky slopes and is more abundant in the southern end of the island, although it has been found in the upper parts of the island as well (Mellink and Luévano 2014). It inhabits xeric scrubland only, from sea level to the maximum elevation on the island. It is seen on both hillsides and the plateau, commonly around shrubs (Manrríquez 2024). It is known to reproduce during summer and early fall (Mellink and Luévano 2014). Peromyscus dickeyi is the primary source of prey for local rattlesnakes (Crotalus atrox tortugensis), potentially constituting over 80% of snake diet (Manrríquez 2024). It may also be eaten by other local snakes, including common kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula).
threats: Given its extremely restricted range, this species is threatened by stochastic threats such as El Niño/La Niña events, and the possibility of the introduction of exotic rodent species and/or feral cats to the island (Mellink and Luévano 2014).
population: A population survey for the species was conducted during both the wet and dry seasons at two sites on the island, using 200 traps/night in the dry season and 100 traps/night in the wet season (Manrríquez 2024). The dry season had a capture success rate of 18.5%, with 37 individuals trapped, but there was only one individual trapped during the wet season, indicating low general abundance and seasonal variability in active populations (Manrríquez 2024). Other Peromyscus species are known to undergo population fluctuations in response to climatic events such as El Niño (Ventura Rojas et al. 2024), so it is possible this island-restricted species does as well.
range: This species is endemic to and only found on Tortuga Island off the coast of Baja California Sur, Mexico in the Gulf of California (Cortés-Calva and Álvarez-Castañeda 2001, Mellink and Luévano 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
conservationActions: This species has been listed as “Sujetas a Protección Especial” (Subject to Special Protection) by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). The island is part of the Islands and Protected Areas of the Gulf of California, which is UNESCO World Heritage site (Global Volcanism Program 2025). The island also has little human presence as it is far from the coast and lacks areas for boats to anchor (Mellink and Luévano 2014). More research is needed to understand more about this species and how it would benefit from conservation efforts.

rationale: This species is classified as Least Concern due to its large extent of occurrence and assumed population size. However, it has been losing habitat due to agriculture and may lose more due to climate change, so this species may become threatened in the near future.
habitat: This species inhabits high-precipitation areas such as broadleaf evergreen forests, montane humid forests, and mid-elevation cloud forests along the coast (Pérez-Consuegra et al. 2023). It has also been found in shaded coffee fields (Reid 2009, Mendoza Sáenz and Horváth 2013). It is often trapped near fallen logs and around the roots of trees or by rocks. Pregnant females were found from March to August in Nicaragua; litter size is 2 to 4 young with a mean of 2.7 (Reid 2009).
threats: Much of this species' habitat within its known range may be gone (SMSG 2018). Peromyscus gymnotis is highly susceptible to habitat loss because it is dependent on high-precipitation forests and range expansion is limited by the coast (Pérez-Consuegra et al. 2023). From 2014 to 2024, this species' range lost 499 kha of tree cover (Global Forest Watch 2025). Much of its suitable habitat is being fragmented or replaced by coffee plantations, though it is still abundant in these areas (Mendoza Sáenz and Horváth 2013). Climate change is also projected to decrease available habitat by 30–50% by 2080; loss will move southeastward from Sierra Madre del Sur to Guatemala (Pérez-Consuegra et al. 2023).
population: There is little population information available for this species, though older reports listed that this species is common in suitable habitat (Reid 2009).
range: This species has been found in the Pacific coastal plain and adjacent foothills from south Chiapas, México, to south Nicaragua (Musser and Carleton 2005). Published maps show the species in Mexico, Nicaragua, Honduras, and El Salvador (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024), but some recent reports only describe its range to be from southern Chiapas to northwestern Guatemala (Hernández-Canchola et al. 2022, Pérez-Consuegra et al. 2023). It has been recorded from sea level to 1,700 m asl (Pérez-Consuegra et al. 2023).
conservationActions: This species is not listed under a protected status by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010), but is found in the Volcano Tacaná Biosphere Reserve in Chiapas, Mexico (Mendoza Sáenz and Horváth 2013). It also occurs in other protected areas throughout its range including in Mexico (La Pera, El Triunfo, El Recreo), Nicaragua (Volcán Mombacho, San Cristóbal Volcano, Laguna de Nejapa, Lagunas de Mecatepe and Río Manares natural reserve), and Guatemala (Tajumulco Volcano, Tecuamburro Volcano, Naciones Unidas, San Francisco de Asis, Finca el Porvenir, Jumaytepeque Volcano) (CONABIO 2024).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern due to its relatively wide range, limited significant threats, and likely large population size.
habitat: The primary habitat of Peromyscus hooperi is the grassland transition zone, a mixture of desert scrub and grassland vegetation (Schmidly et al. 1985, Álvarez-Castañeda 2002, 2024). Trapping success was higher on slopes than in arroyos, with more individuals captured in grassland transition vegetation (Álvarez-Castañeda 2002). This vegetation type separates the Chihuahuan desert scrub and montane chaparral, and includes Dasylirion, Nolina, Yucca, Agave, and Bouteloua species, interspersed with various grasses (Arellano 2014). In Durango, Peromyscus hooperi was significantly associated with Quercus depressipes, Quercus emoryi, Echinocereus pectinatus, Nolina sp., and Agave neomexicana, and with ground litter produced mainly by deciduous Quercus species (Villanueva-Hernández et al. 2017). However, the association with oaks in Durango is called into questions since the species is generally associated with a compact limestone layer with plants of the genus Yucca (Álvarez-Castañeda pers. comm. 2025).This species is nocturnal and feeds on small seeds, nuts, insects, and other small invertebrates (Arellano 2014). In wild populations, pregnant females have been collected from March to May, with an average of 3.5 embryos per female (Arellano 2014). In captivity, litter size averaged 2.9, with a gestation period of 33.5 days (range 30–40 days) while lactating, and the average age at first oestrus was 69 days (Álvarez-Castañeda 2002).
threats: This species is susceptible to changes in its environment due to its restricted distribution and habitat (Arellano 2014). Its survival is jeopardised by the fragile conditions of its habitat in central Coahuila as a result of overgrazing (Schmidly et al. 1985). Habitat shifts from native grasslands to crop zones have increased due to agricultural intensification, grain-fed cattle feedlots, and new land use policies in the Mexican states of Durango, Sinaloa, Chihuahua, Nuevo León, and particularly Coahuila, where Peromyscus hooperi is mostly distributed (Galván-Miyoshi et al. 2015, Bonilla-Moheno and Aide 2020, Castañeda-Rico et al. 2023).
population: Peromyscus hooperi is considered rare across its overall range (Álvarez-Castañeda 2002), but it has been reported as common in central Coahuila where it is restricted to its specific habitat. Because of its limited distribution, the population may be vulnerable to environmental changes (Arellano 2014). A total of 34 individuals were recently trapped over 1,176 trap-nights during the dry season in Durango (Villanueva-Hernández et al. 2017).
range: Peromyscus hooperi is endemic to Mexico and occurs in grassland–desert scrub transition of the semiarid mountains of central Coahuila to northernmost Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí (Musser and Carleton 2005, Arellano 2014). Individuals were recently trapped in Durango (Villanueva-Hernández et al. 2017), expanding the species’ range 300 km east-northeast from previous records (Schmidly et al. 1985, Álvarez-Castañeda 2002).
conservationActions: This species has been recorded from multiple state and federal protected areas including Parque Estatal Ruta Huichola, Reserva Natural Estatal Sierra de Zapalinamé, la Ruta Huichol por los Sitios Sagrados a Huiricuta, Semidesierto Zacatecano, and C.A.D.N.R. 004 Don Martín (CONABIO 2024). Peromyscus hooperi is not protected by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). This unique species requires additional research to understand more about its ecology, potential loss of specialized habitats, and conservation strategies (Castañeda-Rico et al. 2023).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered B1ab(iii) because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 2,944 km², it is only found in two locations, and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of habitat due to deforestation from agricultural activities and expanding human settlements.
habitat: This rodent inhabits montane rainforest and evergreen cloud forest. Both forest types have a dense, herbaceous understory and bamboo in common (Rickart and Robertson 1985). It is associated with steep, shady slopes and large trees (Rickart and Robertson 1985, Ruiz Velásquez 2019).This species likely reproduces throughout the year, though there is a seasonal peak in reproduction during the wet season. Litter size range is 1 to 3 (mean size 2.8 in wild animals; 1.8 in laboratory). The sex ratio (male : female) for 41 individuals born in captivity was 1.93:1; whereas that of 246 snap-trapped specimens from the Cerro Pelon region was 1.54:1. The length of gestation in the laboratory has been estimated at 1 month (Rickart and Robertson 1985). Mean adult weight is 58.9 g (Ramírez Bautista 2018).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation for small-holder agriculture and expanding human settlements. Tree cover loss has been recorded across the extent of its range. From 2014 to 2024, this species' range lost 9.08 kha of tree cover, which is about 5.35% of the total area in the year 2000 (Global Forest Watch 2025). Deforestation is controlled by environmental payment incentives, which improve management (SMSG 2018). This species may also be sensitive to climate change, with optimistic models showing impacts to 16.1% and 24.1% of its habitat in near-term (2015–2039) and long-term (2075–2099) scenarios, respectively. Pessimistic models predict that 21.6% of its range may be impacted in the short-term and 45.8% in the long-term (Ramírez Bautista 2018).
population: This species inhabits discontinuous mountain forest (Rickart and Robertson 1985). In mountain mesophilic forest, its observed population density ranged from 4.08 individuals/ha to 8.16 individuals/ha, with a maximum estimated population size of around 80 individuals (Ruiz Velásquez 2019). In traditional coffee polyculture, observed population density ranged from 4.08 individuals/ha to 6.12 individuals/ha. Eight males were caught in the forest and seven females were caught in the coffee plantation (Ruiz Velásquez 2019).
range: This species occurs in the Sierras de Zempoaltépec, Juárez, and Mazteca of north-central Oaxaca, México (Musser and Carleton 2005). It is endemic to Oaxaca and its range covers 0.4% of Mexico (Ramírez Bautista 2018, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).Specimens have been taken at Cerro Zempoaltepec (type locality; Álvarez-Castañeda and González-Escamilla 1997) and nearby Totontepec, and at localities between 900 and 2,800 m asl on the north slope of the Sierra de Juárez (Rickart and Robertson 1985).
conservationActions: In the Sierra de Juarez, there is a community-based forest management program that helps to protect its habitat (Chapela 2005). Deforestation may be controlled by conservation incentive payments and good forest management (SMSG 2018). Corona-Mendoza and Escalante (2021) identified priority regions for conservation across Mexico, nine of which are home to Peromyscus melanocarpus. This species is not protected by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable B1ab(i,iii) because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is around 16,747 km² and it is found in fewer than 10 locations, with the main threat from continuing habitat decline due to conversion, loss, and fragmentation of forests for coffee plantations and timber extraction.
habitat: Peromyscus ochraventer is mainly nocturnal and lives primarily on the ground, although it is also a skilled climber (Ceballos 2014). It constructs burrows between rocks and near fallen logs and is frequently found in rocky sites with little vegetation (Ceballos 2014). It is endemic to the Sierra Madre Oriental, where it inhabits temperate oak-pine and montane cloud forests (CONABIO 2010, Martínez de la Vega et al. 2016, Martínez de la Vega 2023).This species is a generalist feeder, consuming seeds, fleshy fruits, insects, and fungi (Ceballos 2014). Documented predators include rattlesnakes (Crotalus molossus and Crotalus lepidus), grey foxes, weasels, margays, and owls (Ceballos 2014). The mating season extends from late September to mid-February, with litters consisting of two to three young; in cloud forest habitat, reproduction coincides with the seasonal production of acorns (Ceballos 2014).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat destruction and fragmentation resulting from agricultural expansion, logging, land-use change, and the conversion of forest to coffee plantations (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005). Loss of tree canopy extends over the entire extent of the species’ range, as shown by data in the Hansen et al. (2013) database.
population: Peromyscus ochraventer can be locally abundant, at least within the El Cielo Biosphere Reserve and undisturbed cloud forest habitat (Castro-Arellano 2005). It is common where its habitat is well-preserved (Martínez de la Vega 2023). However, there are no precise population estimates (CONABIO 2010). The species is threatened by habitat loss and fragmentation due to timber extraction and forest conversion to coffee plantations, and it is likely that the majority of individuals persist in small and relatively isolated subpopulations within remaining habitat fragments (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005).
range: Peromyscus ochraventer is endemic to Mexico and occurs in moist forests east of the Sierra Madre Oriental, from the Rancho del Cielo area in Tamaulipas south to the vicinity of Platanito in San Luis Potosí, including submontane tropical areas (Baker 1963, Martínez de la Vega et al. 2016, Martínez de la Vega 2023, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). The species reaches its highest densities between 700 and 1,300 m asl in association with cloud forest (López-Ortega et al. 2003). However, it has been trapped at higher elevations and may reach up to 1,500 m asl (Castro-Arellano 2005).
conservationActions: Peromyscus ochraventer is known to occur in several protected areas, including El Cielo Biosphere Reserve in southern Tamaulipas (Castro-Arellano 2005, Ceballos 2014, CONABIO 2024). Increased monitoring and research are needed to determine the status of its populations within the state and to guide the development of appropriate conservation actions (Martínez de la Vega et al. 2016). This species is not listed as a protected status by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU B2ab(i,iii); D2) because it has an estimated area of occupancy of 60–2,000 km², it is found in around six locations, and it is experiencing ongoing loss in quality and extent of habitat due to deforestation, and mining.  future plausible threat that could result in the species rapidly moving to Critically Endangered is habitat loss due to the effects of climate change. It is perceived to be extremely rare.
habitat: This species is found in pine-oak vegetation, grasslands and xeric scrublands (Ceballos and Oliva 2005, Wilson et al. 2017). Details of its biology are scarce, but like other species of this genus it should be granivorous (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2020) and nocturnal (Wilson et al. 2017).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation and open-pit mining within its restricted range. As of 2000, about 20% of its habitat had been converted (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005) and tree cover within its range is still being reduced (Global Forest Watch 2025). Its range has no intact forest and it lost 2.25 k ha of tree cover from 2014 to 2024 (Global Forest Watch 2025). Under some climate change scenarios, 100% of this species range may be lost by 2070 (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2020). Assuming linear decline, this would amount to a loss of 20% over 10 years.
population: Limited population information is available for this species, with only a few specimens recorded across its range (CONABIO 2024, López González et al. 2023). It is perceived to be extremely rare (SMSG 2018).
range: This species lives in the Sierra Madre Occidental in a small area in the northern portion of the range (Ceballos and Oliva 2005). It is endemic to Mexico and is restricted to the western and central parts of Chihuahua and Durango. It is likely to be found in Sonora. It has been recorded in the state of Chihuahua (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This species is not yet protected under Mexican law (SEMARNAT 2010), but has been recorded in three federally protected areas: Janos, Campo Verde, and Papigochic (CONABIO 2024).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered B1ab(i,iii). It has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 2,664 km², is only found in two locations, and faces ongoing declines in the area, extent, and quality of its habitat due to deforestation driven by the replacement of native forests for pasture and agricultural lands.
habitat: Very little is known about the natural history and ecology of this species but it is very similar to other species of the genus; they are nocturnal and eat mostly seeds, fruits, plants, and invertebrates (Cruzado 2014). It is associated with vegetation from the central plateau, with many xerophilous elements (Álvarez-Castañeda, pers. comm 2024). Within its very restricted range, it is common in hilly areas associated with stony areas. The most frequent vegetation is scrubland with cacti, mainly Opuntia. The reproductive season is in spring and specimens were found with an average of 3.6 young (Álvarez-Castañeda, pers. comm. 2024).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat transformation for cattle ranching and transition to agricultural crops (Valderrama-Landeros et al. 2016). Forest cover loss in its range has been recorded over the past decade (Hansen et al. 2013), and it is likely that this decline will continue going forward. More research is needed to specifically quantify threats to this species.
population: Little is known about the population status for this species. It is common in hilly areas associated with stony areas.
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and is known only from the very small area of Los Reyes in northwest Michoacán (Ceballos 2005, Cruzado 2014). It was described from a specimen collected at La Palma (Elliot 1903).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures or actions currently in place for this species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because, although logging is probably a threat to the species, it has a large extent of occurrence, is common in suitable habitat, and presumably has a large population.
habitat: This is a montane species (López-González et al. 2014, León-Tapia et al. 2022) that is found primarily in pine-oak forests (Bradley et al. 2004, Cabrera et al. 2007, López-González et al. 2014, García-Mendoza et al. 2021), often with considerable slopes (Cabrera et al. 2007, García-Mendoza et al. 2021). It was mostly trapped beneath pine (Pinus), oak (Quercus), or pointleaf manzanita (Arctostaphylus pungens) trees in areas that may also contain juniper (Juniperus monosperma) or annuals like six-week threeawn (Aristida abscensionis) and spidergrass (Aristida ternipes). In all traplines, no other rodents besides Peromyscus schmidlyi were captured (Cabrera et al. 2007). However, this species was captured alongside undetermined Reithrodontomys in Sinaloa - Concordia - El Palmito, La Chara Pinta in 2016 (L.D. Arregoitia, pers. comm. 2025)This species is not generally found on the boulders or rocky, shallow soils on the western canyon rim of the Sierra Madre Occidental (López-González et al. 2013).Trapping at different types of year provides information on reproductive cycles. Eleven lactating females and a single juvenile were trapped in January 2020, females with embryos were trapped in June and July but no juveniles or lactating females were caught at this time, and 20 lactating females and 22 juveniles were trapped in August (García-Mendoza et al. 2021).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss due to logging. However, the risk to the overall survival of the species is slight, as there was only a 0.2% decrease in forest cover from 2015-2025 within its range (calculated from the database in Hansen et al. 2013).
population: This species is relatively common within suitable habitat, and is often the most abundant Peromyscus species where it occurs (López-González et al. 2013). García-Mendoza et al. (2021) trapped 89 individuals in January, 39 in June, 8 in July, and 105 in August, indicating some level of seasonal population fluctuations.
range: This Mexican endemic species is known from the Sierra Madre Occidental in the Madrean-North, Madrean-Central, and Madrean-South ecoregions (Cabrera et al. 2007, López-González et al. 2013, León-Tapia et al. 2022). It ranges from northern Chihuahua to northern Jalisco (López-González et al. 2013) and has been recorded in the Mexican states of Durango, Sinaloa, and Sonora (Bradley et al. 2004, Cabrera et al. 2007), as well as more recently in Jalisco, Zacatecas, and Nayarit (López-González et al. 2013, García-Mendoza et al. 2021).
conservationActions: This species does not have a protected status by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). Specimens have been recorded from several protected areas including Cuenca Alimentadora del Distrito Nacional de Riego 043 Estado de Nayarit, Área de Protección de Flora y Fauna Cerro Mohinora, Reserva Chara Pinta, and Reserva de la Biosfera la Michilia (CONABIO 2024).

rationale: The Jaguarundi is assessed as Near Threatened (A4bce) based on a suspected population size decline of over 20%, even likely in the range of 30% over a period of three generations, including past, present and future. This is due to a combination of loss and fragmentation of habitats, mostly due to agriculture, and the estimated unavailability of at least 20–30% of the remaining prime habitat in its extant range due to the very small size and isolation of fragments, as well as extensive fires (INPE 2023). Additionally, high occupancy areas by the species (Harmsen et al. 2024) were in habitats/biomes under high impact from habitat loss/fragmentation, like the tropical Andes, Mesoamerica, and Atlantic Forest. In addition, disease transmission and other impacts by domestic dogs and cats, retaliatory killing for poultry depredation, and roadkills eliminate a considerable number of Jaguarundis annually. An analysis of a series of 75 population assessments throughout the species range conducted for this assessment showed that the Jaguarundi is much less abundant than previously perceived by the scientific community. Known densities are typically ≤ 0.04 individuals/km² (de Oliveira et al. 2021, 2023a, see the Population section) and relative abundance mean (0.277/100 trap-days), median (0.137/100 trap-days), 25% and 75% interval (0.071–0.21 individuals/100 trap-days) are all below the rarity threshold of 0.3 individuals/100 trap-days of Neotropical mammals on camera (de Oliveira et al. 2018, 2023b). Beyond the inherently small population sizes, the limited data available on long-term population monitoring have revealed fluctuations, with some populations experiencing steep declines of nearly 40%. In certain cases, the species has vanished and reappeared three times within an eight-year monitoring period (de Oliveira et al. 2023a, Moura 2024, R.V. Marques pers. comm./unpl. data 2024, M.R. Luiz pers. comm./unpl. data 2024). This situation demands particular attention and ongoing surveillance, potentially indicating a widespread trend across its distribution range. Even in favourable habitats, the Jaguarundi usually ranks low (least abundant) within the felid guild of tropical America (Oliveira et al. 2010, Oliveira 2011). Therefore, the rampant habitat conversion to industrial agriculture/pasture of the Brazilian savannas of the Cerrado and semiarid Caatinga biomes, with a mean annual increase in deforestation of 15.6% between 2003 and 2023 (INPE 2023, Mapbiomas 2024), poses a serious threat to the species. Although there are no range-wide estimates, this scenario shows troublesome prospects. With density estimates being considerably low, relative abundance mostly at the rarity level, an area of extant range considerably smaller than its extensive extent of occurrence, the threat of diseases transmitted by domestic dogs and cats, and the negative impact of Ocelots (Caso 2013, de Oliveira et al. 2010, 2021a,b; de Oliveira 2011, Harmsen et al. 2024), it is likely that no conservation unit in isolation, not even the mega-reserves of the Amazon basin, could sustain long-term viable populations of Jaguarundis, as Amazonia comprises a suboptimal area for the species (de Oliveira et al. 2023b, Harmsen et al. 2024). Population decline for Brazil, which comprises most of the core and geographic range of the species, over three generations including the past, present and future, based on road kills and habitat loss data, is suspected to be >30% (Tirelli et al. 2023). In the Caatinga area, a decline in the past and future over three generations was estimated at 39.5%, likely caused by disease transmission from domestic carnivores (de Oliveira et al. 2022). Although refined calculations for the entire range are not available throughout the species range, Jaguarundis seem to linger between a possible Least Concern very close to Near Threatened as appointed on the previous assessment (Caso et al. 2015), to a de facto Near Threatened getting close to Vulnerable given its rarity, escalating ongoing threats, and higher-quality evidence presented. Therefore, the population status of the Jaguarundi should be regularly reviewed.
habitat: Jaguarundi occupies a broad range of both open and closed habitats, from the Monte desert, semi-arid thorn scrub, dry forests, restinga, swamp, and savanna woodland to primary rainforests (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Despite this broad range of habitats, the species tends to be more commonly associated with open shrubbery formations than with forest environments. The Jaguarundi is very rare across most rainforests of the Amazon Basin (Gonçalves 2023, de Oliveira et al. 2023, Harmsen et al. 2024), where the reported mean forest fragment size occupied is 7.9 km² (Michalski and Peres 2005). Interestingly, in open areas, it adheres to denser vegetative cover, similar to the savanna tiger-cat (de Oliveira et al. 2020, Marinho 2020), including secondary growth habitats. Jaguarundis are commonly associated with areas of dense shrub or undergrowth (Harmsen et al. 2024). Jaguarundis seem to have a preference for grasslands, savannas and shrublands (Harmsen et al. 2024), with occupancy analysis in the Brazilian drylands showing it selecting areas closer to water and being less associated with dense canopy cover (Dias et al. 2019b, Fox-Rosales et al. 2023), although it may occupy more forested areas during extreme drought events (Marinho 2020). In Eastern Amazonia’s deforestation arch, in secondary forest surrounded by mining, cattle ranching and agriculture a detailed analysis of its occurrence pattern showed that the determining facts for its occurrence were the forest border, with very limited use of the forest core and reforested areas, and no association whatsoever with anthropogenic areas (Ribeiro 2018). Although it can be found in disturbed areas, such as human-induced grasslands and in matrices with agriculture/palm oil plantations, they require the presence of natural denser vegetative formations (de Oliveira 1994, Caso 2013, Carvajal 2016, Mendes-Oliveira et al. 2017, Pardo et al. 2019, Moreno-Foglia et al. 2015, de Oliveira et al. 2023). This felid is perceived as more tolerant to human disturbance because of its use of open habitats. Meanwhile, in such disturbed areas, it still tends to be less abundant than other felids. In a mosaic of natural habitats with agriculture, density estimates were extremely low (de Oliveira et al. 2021a). A GPS-collared male in a natural area/agriculture matrix shed light on species movement, showing a very large home range of 200 km², using the matrix of forest/herbaceous-shrubbery environments, favouring the shrubbery “vassourais” and staying out of the agricultural areas (Peters et al. 2022). The home range patterns of Jaguarundis in southern Brazil conform to those of low densities (Kasper et al. 2016, Peters et al. 2022). The reported home range size varies greatly, from 1.4 km2 of a lactating female (likely an underestimation) to 200 km² of a GPS-collared male in a forest/shrub/agriculture matrix, larger than any other Neotropical small cat (Konecny 1989, Michalski et al. 2006, de Oliveira et al. 2010, Kasper et al. 2016). Mean home ranges were smaller in Mexican shrublands (16.2 km² males; 12.1 km² females) and larger in Central-American rainforests (20.1–100 km²) and subtropical forest/shrub/agriculture matrices (30.4–200 km²; Konecny 1989, de Oliveira et al. 2010, Caso 2013, Kasper et al. 2016, Peters et al. 2022). Jaguarundis are mostly diurnal and thus tend to be the most easily seen neotropical felid, which led to the false assumption that it was common. It has diurnal habits regardless of the habitat, Amazonian or Atlantic rainforests, savannas, semiarid formations, etc. This segregates it temporally with ocelot, margay, savanna tiger-cat, but not with other mesocarnivores like tayra and coatis. Additionally, high temporal overlap with domestic dogs has been detected (de Oliveira et al. 2010, Cruz et al. 2018, Dias et al. 2019, Fox-Rosales and de Oliveira 2022, 2023; Gonçalves 2023). Diet includes mostly small mammals, birds, and reptiles, with a mean prey mass of 380 g. However, larger-sized prey (>1 kg) is not unusual (de Oliveira and Cassaro 2005, de Oliveira et al. 2010). Dietary overlap with other felids varies from high to low and could even be high with other small carnivores such as tayra and lesser grisson (de Oliveira et al. 2010, Zuercher et al. 2022). This felid is not a dominant small cat species in most areas, even in open habitats. Additionally, Jaguarundi and other smaller tropical cats are also negatively affected by ocelots (the “ocelot effect”), and although large felids like pumas (Puma concolor) and jaguar (Panthera onca) can predate upon them, they do not affect their population (de Oliveira et al. 2010, 2021, Caso 2013, Carvajal 2016, Dias 2019). The Jaguarundi is a multicolored cat with varying shades of several color morphs, including brownish-black, grayish, and reddish-yellow, which can even be found in the same litter (Oliveira 1998). The color morphs in this small felid seem to follow Gloger’s rule, as darker forms tend to predominate in wetter areas compared to the paler forms, which inhabit drier biomes (da Silva et al. 2016). However, as much as a certain color predominates in an area, other colors are also always present (e.g. Moreno-Foglia et al. 2015, de Oliveira pers. comm. 2024).
threats: The main threats to Jaguarundis are the ever-increasing rates of habitat loss and fragmentation, notably for agriculture and pastures, especially in their most suitable shrub-woodland habitats. Brazil as a whole, the main range country for the species, has already lost 41% of its natural cover, and between 2020 and 2021, and between 2021 and 2022 deforestation increased by 14.2% and 25%, respectively (INPE 2022, WWF 2024). In addition, the most recent assessment of natural cover degradation showed alarming numbers: in the savannas 19.2–45.3% of the remaining natural cover is degraded, in the Caatinga dryland 16–54% and 13–73% in the Atlantic Forest domain, all highly fragmented (MapBiomas 2024). Additionally, the increasing frequency of fires poses a significant threat to Jaguarundis and Brazil's biodiversity alike. Fire incidents in the country escalated by 54% from 2013 to 2019, impacting an area of 1,902,854 km², or 54.56% of the remaining wilderness habitat in Brazil (INPE 2021). Analysis of each biome during this period shows varied increases in fire occurrences: the Amazon region experienced a 52% increase, affecting 463,061 km²; the Caatinga saw a 52% rise, covering 247,977 km²; the Cerrado had a 45% increase, encompassing 1,015,782 km²; the Atlantic Forest witnessed a 60% surge, impacting 106,351 km²; the Pampa experienced a 77% increase, involving 8,043 km²; and the Pantanal saw a dramatic 464% rise, covering 61,640 km² (INPE 2020). These numbers pose significant reduction in AOO and hence on population size. According to Instituto Centro de Vida, in 2024 the Pantanal has lost 19% of its area to the fires, and these burnt sites are expected to take at least 50 years to recover. The deforestation rates vary considerably across Central America. Low in Costa Rica, with high rates in Honduras and Nicaragua, reaching 95% loss in El Salvador. The primary causes of deforestation in this area include expansion of cattle ranching and agriculture. Additional significant factors contributing to forest loss are timber harvesting (both legal and illegal), infrastructure development, and urban growth. In certain nations, such as Honduras, Guatemala, and Nicaragua, the recent increase in drug trafficking has further exacerbated deforestation. Other factors leading to the destruction of forests include the growth of commercial palm oil plantations, the construction of new roads, human migration through the Darien Gap, and mining operations. The increasing frequency of forest fires also contributes to forest loss (Rainforest Foundation 2024 https://rainforestfoundation.org/our-work/where-we-work/central-america-and-mexico/). In South America, one of the areas appointed by modeling of higher importance for Jaguarundis was the already highly impacted and fragmented tropical and subtropical Andes, which expressed alarming rates of deforestation (ca. 5,000 km² of forest cover between 2001 and 2014), with Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina losing the greatest area, and the manner in which this occurs is complex (Aide et al. 2019).
