In particular, forests in the lower Andean belt (1,000–1,500 m) disappear faster than those in the highlands (2,000–4,500 m) because the former is more suitable for the establishment of pastures and croplands (Aide et al. 2019). In the elevation belts of importance for Jaguarundi populations (1,000–2,000 m), the area of forest loss is larger (3,608 km²) than that of the higher elevation belts (1,274 km²; Aide et al. 2019). Between 2005 and 2010, a review reported that a total of 20.57% (2,712 km²) of mountain cloud forests in the Tropical Andes were lost due to activities such as logging, cattle ranching, mining, and the establishment of illicit crops (Garavito et al. 2012). In short, the scenario that unfolds regarding the loss and fragmentation of habitats of the Jaguarundi is worrisome across all environments, ecosystems, and continents. This is particularly concerning for a species that generally occurs in small numbers throughout its range. Close to human settlements, where the Jaguarundi shares its habitat with domestic dogs and cats, it is threatened by direct attacks, prey competition and disease transmission. Disease transmission from domestic dogs and cats, seems to pose a serious threat (Doherty et al. 2017, Ellwanger and Chies 2019, Martins et al. 2024). Approximately 53% of wild-caught carnivores, including small neotropical felids, like Jaguarundis, tested positive for both canine distemper virus (CDV) and parvovirus in Emas National Park (Brazil; Furtado et al. 2016). Additionally, of a large number of domestic dogs found in Brazil’s second largest savanna protected area (Mirador State Park), 84.4% tested positive for CDV and 71.1% for leishmaniasis (Calixto-Campina 2022). Meanwhile, more than 90% of the dogs tested in the buffer zone of Furna Feia National Park in the Brazilian Caatinga were positive for tick-borne infections (Carmo et al. 2023). This indicates the widespread prevalence of fatal diseases in natural areas. Additionally, Jaguarundis with considerable sarcoptic mange infection have been detected on camera (de Oliveira et al. 2023a). There has been considerable density reduction detected after an increase in the number of dogs and cats on cameras, especially because their presence did not alter the behavior or occupation of small cats (Fox-Rosales and de Oliveira 2022, 2023). Jaguarundis are commonly killed in retaliation for killing poultry and by collision with vehicles mainly on primary roads (IUCN Cats Red List workshop 2007, Caso 2013, Peters et al. 2016, Pina and Magallanes 2020, Gil-Sánchez et al. 2021). There are reports of retaliatory killing for poultry depredation in Central America, Mexico, southern and northeastern Brazil, where animals are typically killed by shotguns, as well as in the Amazon, where 20 hens were reported to be killed in a single night (Peters et al. 2016, Gil-Sánchez et al. 2021). In the Brazilian northeast Jaguarundi is among the species with higher human-wildlife conflicts, not only for poultry depredation, but eventually also for sheep and goats (likely yearlings) and hence are highly persecuted (Mendonça et al. 2011, Alves et al. 2016). Killed felids are eaten which could increase the hunting pressure on the Jaguarundi (Mendonça et al. 2011, Barboza et al. 2016). There seems to be a higher mortality risk by road kills in landscapes with marginal conditions for their persistence and on roads with three to six lanes (Cerqueira et al. 2021). In an Amazon rainforest from Ecuador, Jaguarundi densities were negatively related to road proximity, probably as a response to daylight sound pollution produced by vehicle traffic and road kills (Gil-Sánchez et al. 2021). The number of Jaguarundis killed on paved roads in São Paulo state (36,500 km) in southeastern Brazil can vary between 5 and 553 individuals (Abra 2019). Projecting this to a broader scale, numbers of animals lost would be considerable. The species ranks #31 among the 450 most road-killed vertebrate in Brazil, being among the most road-killed felid from south to northeastern Brazil (Silva et al. 2014, Grillo et al. 2018, Sombra Jr 2018). The species is generally not exploited for commercial trade, although Jaguarundis are caught in traps set for commercially valuable species and may be subject to low-intensity hunting pressure around settled areas (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Meanwhile, a total of 14 Jaguarundis and one body part were confiscated by Peruvian government authorities between 2001 and 2020 (Mena et al. 2021).Lack of knowledge of the species, associated with misconceptions have also influenced negative perceptions of the species, which can produce lethal consequences and affect its conservation (Weston Flores et al. 2023). For example, in Mexico, it has been reported that rural individuals tend to misidentify the species as a melanistic leopard or jaguar, often referring to them as "panteras". Something similar happens in northeastern Brazil, with residents of rural areas often confusing the Jaguarundi with puma due to their reddish or light brownish colouration (P. Marinho pers. comm. 2024). This misidentification may further fuel misguided and exaggerated fear, likely leading to more intense persecution (Weston-Flores et al. 2023). In addition, the lack of outreach regarding the importance of the conservation of this small wild cat has also negatively impacted the funding available for the species, thus affecting conservation efforts towards mitigating its threats (Weston-Flores et al. 2023).
population: Contrary to earlier characterisations of the species as relatively common and abundant (Nowell and Jackson 1996), more recent research indicates that the Jaguarundi is an uncommon to rare low-density species (Marinho et al. 2018, Botts et al. 2020, de Oliveira et al. 2021a, 2023a; Fox-Rosales et al. 2023, Gálvez et al. 2023, Sánchez-Londoño et al. 2023). The myth of being a common species comes from the fact that Jaguarundis are diurnal and tend to favour open vegetative formations; thus, they are more easily seen (see the Habitat and Ecology section). Even though Jaguarundis are well known to tolerate habitat alteration and seem to benefit from open spaces, analysing a series of abundance estimates throughout its range revealed a distinctive scenario, showing that the Jaguarundi is much less abundant than previously perceived by the scientific community (e.g. Almeida et al. 2013). Densities are very low everywhere they have been sampled, and Jaguarundis are expected to be more commonly found at densities of 0.01–0.05/km² or lower, with median densities ≤0.04 individuals/km² (de Oliveira et al. 2021a – detailed methodology for density estimation can be found in de Oliveira et al. 2020), but they could eventually reach up to 0.2 individuals/km² in a few restricted high-density areas (Caso 2013). Jaguarundi’s density/numbers are negatively affected by those of the larger-sized ocelot - the “Ocelot effect” (de Oliveira et al. 2010, 2021a,b; Caso 2013). Relative abundance estimates (RAI) of 75 areas, from Mexico, Mesoamerica and South America, covering most of the species’ range conducted for this assessment showed mean of 0.277 individual detections/100 trap-days, median abundance of 0.137 ind. detections/100 trap-days, and 25% and 75% intervals of 0.071–0.21 ind. detections /100 trap-days (de Oliveira et al. 2023a,b, Marques 2023). All results were below the rarity threshold of 0.3 ind. detections/100 trap-days of neotropical mammals on camera (de Oliveira et al. 2018). At 30 sites where small felid population areas are being monitored in Brazil and Colombia, Jaguarundis were found in more areas than the other small felids (except for Ocelot), but at the same time showed the lowest abundance, with a mean value of 0.337 ind. detections/100 trap-days for 15 sites (de Oliveira et al. 2023a). This (non-by-catch data, i.e., studies targeting small felids) further highlights the fact that Jaguarundi usually ranks low within the felid guild (de Oliveira et al. 2010, de Oliveira 2011).Telemetry data showing predominantly large home ranges in most areas also corroborate that population sizes are intrinsically small (Konecny 1989, Peters et al.2020). Following the same trend, occupancy studies showed low occupancy average of 0.34 ± 0.22 (range 0.07–0.91; Gálvez et al. 2023). Recent monitoring has shown that populations in protected areas of mixed broadleaf araucaria forest and in the Atlantic rainforest of southern Brazil, as well as in a very large park in the northern Brazilian savannas and in the Brazilian semiarid Caatinga fluctuate, even with a sharp population decline (2011–2019) of 39.5% over a three-generation period, or even disappearing for three non-consecutive years over an eight-year period (de Oliveira et al. 2023a, Moura 2024, R.V. Marques pers. comm./unp.data 2023, M.R. Luiz pers. comm./unp. data 2024). It could be argued that these fluctuations could simply be a matter of low detection, not true fluctuation; however, the number of Jaguarundi records would otherwise attest to actual fluctuations. To date, these population fluctuations have unknown causes, but the sharp decline observed in the semiarid Caatinga was likely caused by disease transmission from domestic dogs and cats because it “coincided” with the increase in the number of dogs and cats on camera traps, and the simultaneous depiction of Jaguarundis with sarcoptic mange on camera. In turn, this requires special attention and continuous monitoring. In the Gurupi Biological Reserve in eastern Amazonia, the Jaguarundi population, although with very low abundance (0.045 ind./100 trap-days), showed a stable population with a slight tendency to decline and mean occupancy of 0.5 through 2016-2022 (Carvalho-Jr. et al. 2023). In the future, threats will persist and will likely further fragment and reduce the overall population. Jaguarundi is more commonly associated with open habitats, such as savannas, but can also eventually be found in disturbed habitats, such as pastures (Caso 2013). However, the Jaguarundi usually ranks low within the felid guild (de Oliveira et al. 2010,Oliveira 2011); therefore, the rampant habitat conversion to industrial agriculture of the Brazilian savannas of the Cerrado and semi-arid Caatinga biomes poses a serious threat to the species. The Jaguarundi is considered Near Threatened in Argentina (Diaz and Ojeda 2000), threatened in Mexico (SEMARNAT 2010), Vulnerable in Brazil (Tirelli et al. 2023), and Endangered in Costa Rica (SINAC 2017). Harmsen et al. (2024) provide a crude total global Jaguarundi estimate of 35,000 to 230,000 applying a 0.5 probability level of occupancy. For population estimation, we applied a methodology similar to that used for the Brazilian Red List Assessment. To avoid overestimation and compensate for areas of absence within area of occupancy, we used an average low-density estimate of 0.01/km², which is very close to the median density of the species and considerably above its lowest limit (de Oliveira et al. 2021a, 2023a). Additionally, population modelling for small felids in tropical America indicated that >90% of their area had low density (<0.05/km²; de Oliveira et al. 2021b). For mature individuals, we used the average proportion estimated for three sympatric species of small neotropical felids as a proxy, as there is very little information on this for felids (see Tirelli et al. 2023 for details). Considering the area of occupancy, estimated by modelling Jaguarundi records, of 4,453,406 km² (Harmsen et al. 2024), the low level average estimate density of 0.01 ind/km² (Oliveira 2011, de Oliveira et al. 2021a) to compensate for uninhabited places, and that 30% is the average adult:total population size ratio (Tirelli et al. 2023), the total and adult Jaguarundi population would be 44,534 and 13,360 individuals, respectively. For the state of Maranhão, Brazil, a refined assessment of area of occupancy and population size using density modelling for the Red List assessment predicted a suitable total area of 203,560 km². However, when a detailed analysis of satellite imagery was added to remove unsuitable patches or barren lands, the remaining area of occupancy dropped to 86,109 km², or only 42.3% of the originally assessed value, and the original population prediction went from 3,054 individuals to 1,292, that is, from Vulnerable to Endangered (de Oliveira, pers. com./unp. data 2024). Jaguarundis are under a tricky combination of low/very low abundance estimates, typically ranking low within the small felid guild, and are also negatively affected by Ocelot numbers. This is associated with high rates of habitat conversion and fragmentation, notably for the grain frontier. Current removal is concentrated in the northern savannas, Brazil’s new agricultural frontier, where agricultural lands increased by 87% between 2000 and 2014 (IBAMA 2015, NASA 2018). Furthermore, there is also the serious threat of disease transmission from domestic cats and dogs, which are widespread in both protected and unprotected areas throughout its range (Doherty et al. 2017, Ellwanger and Chies 2019, Calixto-Campina 2022, Martins et al. 2024). Additionally, the ratio of adult individuals to the total population of small neotropical cats is only 0.3% (see Tirelli et al. 2023 for details). This leads to very small population sizes that would require large areas for sustaining viable populations, which in isolation are unlikely to be met anywhere. Even in the mega-reserves of Amazonia, which pose as safe havens for most carnivorous species found there, but are considered as suboptimal area for Jaguarundis, there is no guarantee of a self-sustaining population in isolation scenarios, given the very low abundance and rarity of Jaguarundis (de Oliveira et al. 2023b, Harmsen et al. 2024). Given the species median density estimates, protected areas that could sustain longer-term Jaguarundi populations would likely need to be >31,000 km² (de Oliveira et al. 2021b) and not in rainforest areas. In Mexico, Jaguarundi populations are considered threatened and the subspecies H. y. cacomitli (Gulf Coast Jaguarundi) in northeast Mexico is the most threatened (SEMARNAT/CONANP, 2018). For Brazil, which encompasses the majority of the species' core and geographic range, a population decrease exceeding 30% was inferred over three generations, based on data from habitat destruction and roadkills (Tirelli et al. 2023). In the Caatinga region, a 39.5% decline was estimated for the past and future across three generations, likely due to disease transmission from domestic carnivores (de Oliveira et al. 2022). These findings led to the species being classified as Vulnerable (VU A4bcd) in Brazil (Tirelli et al. 2023).While precise calculations for the entire range are not available, a global decline of 20–30% is suspected over three generations, including past and future periods (2013 to 2031). This decline is attributed to various factors: habitat loss and fragmentation primarily due to agriculture, the estimated unavailability of 20-30% of remaining prime habitat in AOO due to small and isolated fragments, disease transmission and other impacts from domestic dogs and cats, retaliatory killings for poultry predation, and roadkills, which annually claim a significant number of Jaguarundis. Jaguarundi seem to linger between a possible Least Concern very close to Near Threatened as appointed on the previous assessment (Caso et al. 2015), to a de facto Near Threatened getting close to Vulnerable given its rarity, escalating ongoing threats, and higher-quality evidence presented. Thus, Jaguarundi qualifies as Near Threatened (A4bce), and its population status should be regularly reviewed as it might soon qualify as Vulnerable.
range: The Jaguarundi occurs from the eastern lowlands of Chipinque National Park in Nuevo Leon (Carvajal et al. 2004), Mexico (NE limit) and the western lowlands of Mexico, all the way to southernmost Brazil, Paraguay, and northernmost Uruguay and south through central Argentina with Rio Negro as its presumed natural limit at approximately 39ºS (Carvajal et al. 2004, Dotta et al. 2007, Vidal et al. 2017, F.D. Mazim pers. comm. 2023, F.B. Peters pers. comm. 2023). The updated distribution map of the species presented here only corrects the range with the availability of new information and does not reflect any proper expansion.In Peru, this species has been recorded in the mountain forests of the western Andean slopes and across rainforests in the eastern Andean slope, mainly in the Amazon foothills (García-Olaecha et al. 2019). The occupancy of the Jaguarundi was predicted to be low throughout much of the Amazonian lowlands (Harmsen et al. 2024). It is however not yet clear, if this area is suboptimal for the species or if there are other reasons for its low occupancy (Harmsen et al. 2024).Although, there has not been a survey in southern U.S. to look specifically for Jaguarundi presence, it may be extinct in south Texas, US (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002, Caso 2013, Lombardi et al. 2022).Recent evidence suggests that, between a timeframe spanning from 2000–2013 and 2014–2021, the geographic range of the Jaguarundi has retreated in the central part of Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay (Grattarola et al. 2023). The extent of reduction in its extent of occurrence (EOO) is unknown. The available habitat is expected to be significantly reduced compared to the EOO. Considering the extensive area requirements observed for radio-collared individuals within agricultural landscapes of the remaining habitats (see the Habitat and Ecology section), a significant portion will be insufficient to sustain viable Jaguarundi populations over the long term. These calculations were performed for Leopardus tigrinus in the Cerrado savannas but these also apply for the Jaguarundi as a savanna specialist. Of all the remaining potential available habitat, 300,000 km² of savanna fragments were all found to be too small and isolated to support the home range of a single individual (de Oliveira et al. 2024). Since the Jaguarundi's range is considerably larger than that of L. tigrinus, the anticipated inadequate reduction in available habitat is expected to be much greater, potentially affecting at least 20–30% of the prime Jaguarundi habitat, particularly in the open areas preferred by the species.While primarily found in lowland areas, the Jaguarundi can inhabit altitudes ranging from sea level to as high as 3,200 m (Cuervo et al. 1986). However, at higher altitudes, the species tends to be limited to the lower belt (1,000–1,499 m). The occupancy model of Harmsen et al. (2024) predicted high probability of Jaguarundi occurrence throughout Mesoamerica but low probability throughout much of Mexico (desert, temperate sierras, southern semi-arid highlands). However, in the Yucatan Peninsula the Jaguarundi seems to be relatively common (A. Caso pers. comm. 2024). High probability of Jaguarundi occurrence was also predicted for the northern Andes of Ecuador, Colombia and Venezuela, parts of the Guiana Highlands, Llanos of Colombia, the Cerrado, in the north-eastern semiarid Caatinga and the Atlantic Forests of Brazil and Paraguay, humid Chaco of Paraguay, central Bolivia and eastern Argentina). In the rest of South America the probability of occurrence of the Jaguarundi was predicted to be low, especially in the Amazon and coastal lowlands, moist forests of the Brazilian Shield and the Central Andes (Harmsen et al. 2024). The area of occupancy, based on modelling and not the IUCN methodology, was estimated at 4,453,406 km² (lowest probability threshold of 0.5) to 652,002 km² (probability threshold 0.8; Harmsen et al. 2024).
useTrade: Information on trade and use of Jaguarundis are mostly scattered and incidental. Government authorities in Peru confiscated 14 Jaguarundis and one body part between 2001 and 2020 (Mena et al. 2021). In Mexico, locals from the Sierrra Nanchititla forests were documented harvesting the skin of Jaguarundis for ornamental reasons (Monroy-Bilchis et al. 2008). In the Caribbean region of Colombia, the indigenous community Embera-Katios was documented consuming Jaguarundi meat during religious celebrations (Chacón-Pacheco and González-Maya 2013). There is no proper assessment on the exact number of Jaguarundis originated from the pet trade present at Brazil’s Fauna Rehabilitation Centers, where there seems to be a constant flow of a few animals. All of the above suggests that there is some trade and use of Jaguarundi, but these do not seem to pose a menace to the species’ population, yet.
conservationActions: Included in CITES Appendix II. Populations of Central and North America are in CITES Appendix I. The species is protected across most of its range. Hunting is prohibited in Argentina, Belize, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Costa Rica, British and French Guiana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Suriname, Uruguay, United States, Venezuela, and hunting is regulated in Peru (Nowell and Jackson 1996). However, for different reasons, including lack of resources, there seems to be a gap between policy and implementation in most countries where their populations are protected (Expert opinion 2023, Kamnitzer 2024). In most of its distribution, identifying, expanding, and conserving protected areas have been pinpointed as a conservation measure for the species in Mexico (SEMARNAT 2018, Lombardi et al. 2022, Weston-Flores et al. 2023a). Nonetheless, this might not be an effective conservation measure in all its range as there is evidence that populations in protected areas are expected to be very low, in some cases, likely because of the impact of higher ocelot densities (de Oliveira et al. 2021a,b). Given the inherently low abundance of this species, it is likely that there are very few protected areas that, if isolated, could hold viable populations. The mega-reserves of the Amazon, which typically function as safe areas for other carnivores, are very unlikely safe havens for Jaguarundis, if isolated (de Oliveira et al. 2023b, Kamnitzer 2024). This species is often perceived as unthreatened because of its visibility (diurnal) and the use of open habitats (de Oliveira et al. 2023b). Jaguarundi extirpation from the United States is highly likely and there is a Jaguarundi recovery plan that intends to re-introduce the species in Southern Texas (Lombardi et al. 2022). Different organizations in Costa Rica, Mexico and Brazil are working to mitigate conflict with rural farmers regarding poultry predation by working with local communities to coexist with small wild cats. For example, the Tropical Cats Conservation Initiative includes building and fixing henhouses to reduce poultry depredation as well as reimbursements for confirmed lost poultry, and subsequent retaliatory killing, on top of rehabilitation of animals apprehended by authorities for possible reintroduction (Sánchez-Lalinde et al. 2020, Ramírez Fernández et al. 2021, Mowbray 2023a, Weston-Flores et al. 2023a,b; Kamnitzer 2024). In deciduous dry forests in Mexico and El Salvador, and in semi-arid Brazilian Caatinga shrub-woodlands, independent NGOs and private landowners are implementing artificial water sources to enable access to water in dry seasons. This should help to mitigate the adverse effects on Jaguarundis and other wildlife from prolonged droughts associated with climate change (Ocelot Working Group 2023, Cañenguez 2024, Galvez et al. 2023, Mowbray 2023b, Weston-Flores et al. 2023b). In Mexico, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil, several projects are implemented to conserve small wild cats and reduce the threats posed by domestic dogs and cats. These initiatives include vaccination campaigns aimed at minimising the risk of disease transmission from pets. Additionally, many of these animals are being neutered to decrease their free-roaming populations and lessen the risk of attacks on small wild cats and their prey (Hurtado et al. 2023, Ocelot Working Group 2023, Galvez et al. 2023, Mowbray 2023c, Weston-Flores et al. 2023a, Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative 2024). Communication and capacity-building strategies, have also been developed, using educational materials and outreach tools, such as murals, games, comics, manuals, contests, and community workshops, to promote the mainstreaming and conservation of the Jaguarundi and other small cat species of the tropical Americas (Ramírez Fernández et al. 2021, Weston-Flores et al. 2023, Ocelot Working Group 2023, Weston-Flores et al. 2023b, Kamnitzer 2024). Most of these strategies target empowering children as Jaguarundi conservation champions, aiming to influence their parents on wild cat conservation issues (Marchini and Macdonald 2020). Aside from large-scale action taking, there is also widespread population monitoring at over 30 sites, counting only those in tropical South America (de Oliveira et al. 2023a, TCCI 2024). General conservation recommendations:Promote strategies to reduce habitat loss: Implement and support initiatives to prevent habitat destruction, notably in more open habitats like the Cerrado and Caatinga agricultural frontiers.Build collaboration networks: Strengthen networks across multidisciplinary stakeholders to share information and strategies for improved conservation impact.Address the potential impact of domestic dogs and cats: Promote conservation actions to minimise their presence in Jaguarundi habitats by encouraging responsible pet ownership in nearby communities. This could also involve anf facilitate neutering, vaccination, and other control strategies when necessary. These efforts should actively include NGOs, civil society, government institutions, and wild and domestic animal welfare organisations.Adopt and promote human-Jaguarundi conflict mitigation and coexistence strategies:  Develop and implement measures to reduce human-Jaguarundi conflict, involving relevant stakeholders and appropriate interventions to foster coexistence. The IUCN SSC Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence Guidelines are recommended as a planing framework for this purpose.Develop Jaguarundi-friendly infrastructure: Promote the creation of wildlife crossings and underpasses, and engage key decision-makers to support their implementation.Mitigate climate change impacts: Implement strategies to adapt or reduce impacts of climate change for the Jaguarundi where needed, such as providing water during droughts, while conducting risk assessments to prevent disease transmission or other unintended consequences.Enhance educational outreach: Expand education and outreach initiatives to emphasize the importance of Jaguarundi conservation.Facilitate funding for Jaguarundi conservation: Encourage funders and donors to provide resources for practical conservation measures, and to strenghen research on local populations.

rationale: This species is assessed Least Concern, as although it has a restricted distribution at high elevations and a small extent of occurrence (EOO) of 7,676 km², it occurs in protected areas, and therefore is not likely to decrease in area or population. There is a need for greater research into the threats to the species, which could result in the species being assessed as Near Threatened in the future.
habitat: This is a poorly known species. It occurs in open alpine meadows and may occur in high altitude fir forests (Smith and Xie 2008). The ecology of this species is unknown although it is likely to be similar to Uropsilus soricipes, in areas where they are sympatric.
threats: The threats to this species are not known.
population: There are currently no data regarding the population status of this species, but it is considered to have a relatively large population size (Y. Li pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species is endemic to China, occurring in the province of Yunnan, with collection records of the species now being shown to be further south than previously considered to areas such as Pianma Village and Yaojiaping in Lushui County, Yunnan Province, China (Y. Li pers. comm. 2025). Although there are no records of occurrence in Myanmar, it is likely that this species' distribution extends across the border. According to recent surveys and updates in molecular data, Uropsilus investigator is distributed at elevations of 2,000–4,000 m asl (Y. Li pers. comm. 2025).
conservationActions: This species occurs in the Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan Protected Reserve, and potentially Emawbum National Park in Myanmar. Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2016).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, in view of its large distribution with extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 768,611 km2, it is found in a number of protected areas, and there are no known major threats to the species.
habitat: This species inhabits broad-leaved forests, mixed coniferous and broad-leaved forests, rhododendron shrubs, alpine meadows with low shrubs, and alpine scree habitats from middle (~2,600 m asl) to high (~4,400 m asl) elevations (W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
threats: It is threatened by habitat degradation and loss resulting from logging and conversion to wasteland (Jiang et al. 2021). Considering their presence in meadow and shrub lands, livestock grazing may likewise pose a threat to this species (W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
population: This species has a wide distribution, but its population density is low (W. Song pers. comm. 2025). Different populations are separated by mountain-valley landscapes and anthropic infrastructures (W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species is endemic to China. It was originally known only from a restricted distribution within Gansu, with several additional specimens collected in southwest Gansu, adjacent Qinghai, and one undetailed from east Xizang (Smith and Xie 2008). The species has now been found in Shangri-la and Deqin of northwest Yunnan (Song et al. 2021); in Sichuan, Qinghai, and Shaanxi (Huang et al. 2022); and new specimens have been collected from Nyingchi in the southeastern Himalayan regions of the Tibet Autonomous Region (Zhu et al. 2024). It was previously recorded from elevations ranging 2,600-3,000 m asl (Smith and Xie 2008). New specimens in Yunnan and Nyingchi occurred between 3,800-4,400 m asl (Song et al. 2021, Zhu et al. 2024).
conservationActions: There are no known conservation measures in place for this species. It is known to present in protected areas such as the Taizi Mountain National Nature Reserve of Gansu, Baimaxueshan National Nature Reserve of Yunnan, Wanglang National Nature Reserve of Sichuan, and Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon National Nature Reserve of Xizang. Further studies are needed into the abundance, natural history and threats to this species. In China, it has been regionally Red Listed as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2021).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, in view of its large distribution with extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 758,380 km2, it is found in several protected areas, and there are no known major threats to the species.
habitat: This species generally favours cold, moist coniferous forests and alpine shrubs. The species has been found in thickets of shrubs dominated by brier (Rosa sp.) near rocky outcrops, in a willow forest on the roadside passing through a coniferous forest, in a mountain steppe in the valley of a small stream near Goin Ba and in a sparse juniper–spruce forest near the Lang Mu Monastery (Sheftel et al. 2018). It has also been found in forests and a magnolia (Magnolia officinalis) plantation (Xie et al. 2014). In the mountains from north-western Yunnan to south-eastern Xizang (Tibet), the species was recorded from fir-dominated forests and Rhododendron shrub lands (Song et al. 2021, W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
threats: It was assessed as “Near Threatened” in China by Jiang et al. (2021), but the primary threats were not explicitly identified. It may face similar threats of habitat degradation and loss to those affecting co occurring species in the same habitats (W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
population: The species' population could exhibit significant aggregations in particular habitats (undisturbed primary forests, shrubs, and meadows, characterized by cold, damp conditions) (W. Song pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species appears to be endemic to China, where it is distributed in Qinghai (south of the Kunlun mountains), Gansu, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Xizang (Smith and Xie 2008, Song et al. 2021). It has been found at altitudes between 2,800 and 3,000 m asl (Sheftel et al. 2018), while in Yunnan it was recorded between 3,800 and 4,400 m asl (Song et al. 2021).
conservationActions: The species has been recorded in  Lianhuashan National Nature Reserve (He et al. 2013, Sheftel et al. 2018, Bannikova et al. 2018) and Baimaxueshan National Nature Reserve (Song et al. 2021). Additional studies are needed into the taxonomy, distribution, abundance, general ecology and threats to this little-known species. The species has been classified regionally as Near Threatened in China (Jiang et al. 2021).

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern because it has a wide distribution with the extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 218,148 km², it is found in several protected areas, and there are no known major threats. Further research is needed to better understand population, ecology and threats to the species.
habitat: It seems to be distributed at middle to high elevations in moist broad-leaved forests, coniferous forests, and their mixed areas (Chen et al. 2017).
threats: Much of the species' distribution is in areas within protected areas, but in Yulong Snow Mountain, some of the distribution is unprotected and close to residential areas, where there is some grazing and logging, and the tourism industry is large, these may threaten the species (Z. Chen pers. comm. 2025).
population: The population of this species is relatively large in Yulong Snow Mountain, while populations are relatively small in other areas (Z. Chen pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species was previously only known from the type locality, Likiang Range, Sushancheng, Yunnan, China (Hutterer 2005). It has now also been found on Jinfo mountain, Chongqing (Han et al. 2024). One specimen from Fujian was also recognised as this species, and therefore the distribution may be larger than suspected (Chen et al. 2017). It occurs around 1,800 to 3,500 m asl (Qing et al. 2019, Smith and Xie 2008).
conservationActions: The species it may occur in the Lashihai Wetland or the Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan Protected Areas. Much of its distribution is within protected areas, for example Ailao Mountain National Nature Reserve in Yunnan and Jinfo Mountain National Nature Reserve in Chongqing, but in Yulong Snow Mountain some of the range in not protected (Z. Chen pers. comm. 2025). Further studies are needed into the distribution, abundance, natural history and threats to this species. It is classified regionally in China as Near Threatened (Jiang et al. 2016).

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered because the number of remaining mature individuals of this species is estimated to be approximately 42 and they all occur in one location.
habitat: Feeds mainly on grasses. Reproduction is year-round with litter sizes from one to two young which are born highly precocial. Home ranges were found to be 0.05-0.35 ha (Lacher 2016).
threats: People have free access to the island and protected area enforcement is not strict. The hunting of this rodent is presumed a threat.
population: Salvador and Fernandez (2008) studied the population dynamics of this species between March 2004 and June 2005 using monthly capture-mark-recapture sampling methods and radio telemetry. Over 5,530 trap-nights, there were 665 captures of 141 individuals. The minimum population was 24, and maximum population was 60. The population had a high and stable density, stable age structure with mostly adults, small home ranges, and high rates of survival. The total population is estimated at 42 (Lacher 2016).
range: This species in known from Serra do Tabuleiro State Park, on Moleques Island do Sul, in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil (Lacher 2016).
conservationActions: This rodent occurs in Serra do Tabuleiro State Park which may receive funds from the Global Environment Facility (GEF) for the conservation of biodiversity and ecosystem rehabilitation. C. intermedia habitat has been designated a Preservation Zone, and all entry is prohibited (Cherem et al., 1999). This park is unmanaged and the park status and entry prohibition are not enforced.

rationale: Since its previous assessment of Least Concern (in 2016), new information has become available regarding this species' geographic range, population size and status, and associated threats. This species is now assessed as Critically Endangered under criteria B1ab(i,ii,iii,v)+2ab(i,ii,iii,v); C2a(i,ii); D. Currently it is restricted to a single known locality in Callacami, Puno, with an estimated population of fewer than 50 mature individuals. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are both estimated at 4 km². This species faces ongoing declines in EOO, AOO, quality of habitat, number of locations, and number of mature individuals due to habitat loss and degradation from agricultural expansion and overgrazing by livestock. In addition, intense hunting for human consumption and traditional medicinal use continues to exert significant pressure on the remaining population.
habitat: The species inhabits high-Andean puna grasslands with clayey soils and flat terrain, often within grazed areas shared with cattle, sheep, and domestic camelids (Medina et al. 2024). Historically, it occupied open shrub-steppe habitats close to wetlands (bofedales) and rivers (Pearson 1951), but it has disappeared from most such areas within its range. The species constructs extensive burrow systems, which are also used by other fauna, including Galea musteloides (Medina et al. 2024).
threats: The primary threats to Ctenomys peruanus are habitat loss and degradation from the conversion of puna grasslands to agriculture and the deterioration of remaining habitat caused by intensive overgrazing by domestic livestock (Revollo-Cadima and Salazar-Bravo 2024). In addition to these pressures, the species is hunted for human consumption and traditional medicinal use, a practice that has been intense in the past and continues to affect the last remaining population (Medina et al. 2024). It is also persecuted as an agricultural pest, with individuals killed and burrow systems destroyed during land preparation (Medina et al. 2024).
population: The total number of mature individuals is estimated at fewer than 50 (Medina et al. 2024). Population densities previously estimated at 42 individuals per hectare (Pearson 1959) are now markedly lower (Medina et al. 2024).
range: This species is endemic to the high Andes of southern Peru. Historically recorded from four localities in Puno Department during the 1940s–1950s, and one site in 2011 (Sanborn and Pearson 1947; Pearson 1951, 1959). Recent surveys in 17 potential sites across Arequipa, Moquegua, Tacna, and Puno confirmed extirpation or nonexistence from all but one locality: Callacami, El Collao Province, Puno, at 4,075 m asl (Medina et al. 2024).
useTrade: The species is used locally for meat and in traditional medicinal practices (Medina et al. 2024). Although hunting is primarily opportunistic and not a principal source of livelihood, it provides an supplementary source of protein for some rural households (Medina et al. 2024).
conservationActions: There are currently no conservation measures in place for Ctenomys peruanus. None of the remaining habitat is within a formally protected area, and there are no specific management plans for the species.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern, given the extent of occurrence (EOO) of 39,904 km2, it is found in a number of protected areas, and there is no evidence of any major threats to the species or its habitat.
habitat: There are very few data on the species. The species is found in primary as well as regenerated forests (pers. comm. A. Abramov 2025). In Tam Dao, Euroscaptor kuznetsovi was recorded quite close to human settlements and in agricultural lands (pers. comm. A. Abramov 2025).
threats: There are some threats experienced by other Euroscaptor species in Viet Nam that overlap the same range as Euroscaptor kuznetsovi, such as habitat loss due to human activities such as increased urbanisation, mining and construction (Nguyen et al. 2024). There is no evidence of major threats to the species in China.
population: There are currently no population data available.
range: It is distributed in north-eastern Viet Nam, having been recorded from the Vinh Phuc Province (Tam Dao National Park), the Cao Bang Province (Nguyen Binh District), the Ha Giang Province (Khau Ca and Tay Con Linh) (Zemlemerova et al. 2016, Bui et al. 2020). It is found at elevations between 750 to 1,300 m asl. There is a record from Guangxi, in south-eastern China (Hoffmann and Lunde 2008) that probably belongs to this species as well (Zemlemerova et al. 2016).
conservationActions: There are some protected areas where the species has been recorded: in north-eastern Viet Nam, as well as the Tam Dao national park (Vinh Phuc Province), (Tam Dao National Park), Phia Oac – Phia Den National Park (Cao Bang Province), and Tay Con Linh Nature Reserve (Ha Giang Province) (pers. comm. A . Abramov 2025).

rationale: Crocidura wimmeri is assessed as Vulnerable under B2ab(iii). It occurs in six locations and has a small area of occupancy (AOO) which, based on currently known records, could be as low as 52 km2, but in any case, is considered unlikely to exceed 2,000 km2. There is ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat relating to agriculture, logging, urbanisation and mining. Surveys are needed to clarify its distribution and persistence in sites where it is known from older records, as well as to assess its population trends.
habitat: This species is known from wet, swampy forest near the coast in the type locality (Heim de Balsac and Aellen 1958) and from primary forest (Kadjo et al. 2013).
threats: It is believed that all suitable habitat for this species in the area of Adiopodoume (where the species has not been recorded for many decades) has now been cleared, presumably largely through the conversion of land to agricultural use as well as logging (Vogel et al. 2014). In other areas where it occurs, its habitat continues to be threatened by urbanisation, illegal logging, illegal mining, and legal mining operations (Boafo 2024, IUCN NL 2023, J. Decher pers. comm. 2024).
population: Little is known about the population of this species. During 5,014 small mammal trapping nights in Banco National Park, only 4 specimens of Crocidura wimmeri were caught (Kadjo et al. 2013). In the same area, between November 2020 to February 2021, surveys targeting this species recorded only 3 individuals out of a total 57 shrews captured (Laurent 2021). At its type locality (near Adiopodoume), 15 specimens were captured between 1971-1973, but, subsequently, C. wimmeri has not been recorded there since (Vogel et al. 2014). It is considered likely that C. wimmeri is a relatively rare species.
range: Crocidura wimmeri is known from very few records in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. In Côte d'Ivoire, it has been recorded in Parc National de Taï in the west (2001), Foro-Foro Savannah in the centre (1972) (Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University 2024), and the type locality near Adiopodoume and Banco National Park (Kadjo et al. 2013) as recently as 2021 (Laurent 2021), as well as in the nearby Azagny National Park (2009) (Nicolas et al. 2019) in the south. In southwestern Ghana, specimens have been identified via genetic analysis from Ankasa Game Reserve and Draw River Forest Reserve (Nicolas et al. 2019, J. Decher pers. comm. 2024), as well as recently further east in the Atewa Forest (see occurrence records at https://www.gbif.org/species/2435566; Lindsell et al. 2019). Specimens recorded from Cameroon and Gabon refer to Crocidura batesi (Brosset 1988, Hutterer 2005).
conservationActions: The species is currently known from Banco National Park (Kadjo et al. 2013), where a C. wimmeri-focussed awareness and education campaign has targeted local schools in recent years (Laurent 2021). There are no other direct conservation measures in place for this shrew. Research is needed to determine its trends, improve knowledge of its ecology, and also assess the impact of threats.

rationale: The Andean Cat has been categorised as Endangered under C2a(i) because the species population does not exceed 2,500 mature individuals, and there is an inferred continuing decline in the population, with less than 250 mature individuals in the largest subpopulation.A reduction in the population of the Andean Cat is inferred based on several lines of evidence: a. the decrease in reports of live animal sightings from local people; b. the increase of other threats that lead to the direct death of individuals, such as roadkills, retaliatory killings and dog attacks. In addition, a population decrease is suspected due to the rapidly increase in mining activities in most of the distribution range of this felid, especially the high Andes.Although formal population density estimates (using robust statistical methods) are only available for two sites (Reppucci et al. 2011, Huaranca et al. 2019), our conclusions are supported by a number of additional studies on the ecology and distribution of this felid and much anecdotal evidence collected over 20 years by a team of experts that is specifically dedicated to the investigation and conservation of the Andean Cat across its entire range, the Andean Cat Alliance. Furthermore, the low population number is fully congruent with the results of recent studies that found very low genetic and genomic diversity (Cossios et al. 2012, Lescroart et al. 2023).A further reason of concern for the conservation of this species is that most of the Andean Cat habitat is subject to major threats due to the expansion of the agricultural frontier, inadequate livestock management, and water extraction (Villaroel et al. 2014, Huaranca et al. 2022), as well as extensive water and soil transformation and contamination from a growing mining and petroleum industry (Walker et al. 2013, Chavez et al. 2023). While mining is already widely distributed on the Andean Cat's known distribution and is affecting the species both directly and indirectly, most of nearby unexploited areas are affected by requests or permits for mining exploration and exploitation. In addition, some areas, particularly in Bolivia and Peru, are subject to illegal mining. Besides this, the most suitable area (core area) for the Andean Cat population lying in the central part of its distribution, is located within the so called “lithium triangle”, and is now threatened by the growing lithium demand for batteries. Although the areas for lithium extraction are situated in salt flats, which are not the most suitable habitat for Andean Cats, possible impacts could arise from the growing demand of lithium in the surrounding areas, besides the increase of road construction and usage, urbanisation, chemical spillage, and contamination of surface and ground waters. Furthermore, models show that global climate change will be a great threat for Andean Cats throughout most of its range. The modification of the habitat due to changes in climatic patterns is causing the species to shift their range to higher altitudes, ultimately resulting in a decrease in the available habitat for the Andean Cat therefore reducing the size of its total geographic distribution (Bennett et al. 2017). Andean Cats require large home ranges to subsist (average size: 51.2 km2, N=4, Villalba et al. 2009, Tellaeche 2015), and the low density of the species reduces the chances of meetings between individuals of opposite genders in the mating season. The fast degradation of the regions surrounding the protected areas may turn those areas in unsuitable places for the species, acting as barriers for dispersal and mating. If corridors are not created urgently, the protected areas existing in Andean Cat habitat will be insufficient to ensure proper habitat connectivity.Considering the constant increase of the mentioned threats, the natural fragmentation of the habitat and the augmented fragmentation due to habitat loss and degradation, a continued decline of the population number is inferred.
habitat: The Andean Cat is found primarily in rocky and steep terrains, in arid and sparsely vegetated areas of the High Andes above the timberline, and in scrub and steppe habitats within the Andean foothills of Central Argentina and Chile. In general, climatic conditions are extreme, with very low winter temperatures, large daily thermal variations all year, and low precipitations that determine the presence of adapted plants such as bunchgrasses, cushion plants, and low shrubs with small or resinous leaves (Cabrera and Willink 1973). The High Andean peatlands are known as “bofedales” or “vegas” and are an important resource for wildlife and domestic animals, including the Andean Cat (Villalba et al. 2004, Lagos et al. 2020, Huaranca et al. 2022). At the local scale, in two studies in Argentina, Andean Cats were most likely to use areas with a high proportion of rocks (Tellaeche 2015, Palacios 2019), and elevated terrain ruggedness (Tellaeche 2015), closer to water (vegas or small creeks), and close to areas populated by their main prey (Palacios 2019). In the north of Chile, the more important variables to predict Andean Cat presence were temperature, distance to peatlands and topographic position (Lagos et al. 2020). According to the results of diet studies in Argentina, Bolivia and Chile, and compared with that of other sympatric carnivores, the Andean Cat occupies a narrower trophic niche with a wide overlap with the Pampas Cat (Walker et al. 2007, Marino et al. 2010). Rodents constitute the main prey item. Some studies identify Mountain Viscacha (Lagidium viscacia) as the more frequently consumed item (Napolitano 2008, Viscarra 2008), while in other areas, small rodents (mainly Phyllotis spp, Octodontomys gliroides, and Abrocoma cinerea) are more commonly consumed (Walker et al. 2007, Torrico 2009, Tellaeche 2010, Reppucci 2012). Among the Andean Cat prey items, the Mountain Viscacha stands out due to its significantly greater body mass, making a substantial contribution to the Andean Cat's biomass intake, despite the lower number of individuals consumed (Walker et al. 2007, Napolitano et al. 2008, Reppucci 2012).In Central Chile, the consumption of the exotic and invasive species European Hare (Lepus europaeus) has also been recorded by camera trap (C. Sepúlveda pers. comm. 2023). The Andean Cat is thought to be a solitary species, but may be seen in pairs or with a single kitten during the reproductive season. Estimation of reproduction dates are lacking, some kittens’ records on camera traps suggest a birth season from January to March (Segura in prep.) to February and July (Aravena et al. 2016). In Coquimbo´s Region, Central Chile, there are records of courtship vocalisations in October and January. In addition, in the month of August there was a record of a cub approximately four to six months old walking with her mother (C. Sepúlveda  pers. comm. 2023).  Data from several locations suggest that Andean cats deliver only one kitten per litter. A wide camera trap-based study showed that Andean Cats are mostly active during dusk and night, but compared with other sympatric species (Culpeo Fox, Pampas Cat and Puma), the Andean Cat was the most diurnal species (Lucherini et al. 2009). A similar result was found for the first radio-collared Andean Cat in southern Bolivia, where activity peaks were recorded between 18:00 and 23:00 hours (Villalba et al. 2009). Reppucci (2012) found activity peaks in the first half of the night and first half of the day (including a peak at noon) for the north of Argentina, while Huaranca et al. (2019) found peaks after dusk and after midnight with scarce activity during the day.Home range sizes of three Andean Cats through a telemetry study in Argentina ranged from 18.8 to 61.2 km2 for two females and 59 km2 for a single male monitored (Kernel 95%; Tellaeche 2015). Home ranges overlapped largely between the male and both females (between 52.8 and 100%). A single female Andean Cat that was radio-tracked between April and December 2004 in Bolivia, had a home range size of 65.5 km² (95% minimum convex polygon: Villalba et al. 2009). In an area with a high abundance of quality habitat for the species, it was found that Andean Cat home ranges exhibited extensive overlap between males and females and between sexes, as well as with the Pampas Cat (Tellaeche 2015).A very large overlap has been found in the ecological niche of Andean and Pampas Cats in the High Andes, which spans the diet, distribution, activity patterns, space and habitat use (Walker et al. 2007, Lucherini et al. 2009, Reppucci 2012, Tellaeche 2015). In all cases the niche breadth for the Andean Cat was narrower and more restricted (Reppucci 2012, Tellaeche 2018). It cannot be excluded that intraguild predation and competition is an additional factor reducing the Andean Cat population densities (Lucherini and Luengos Vidal 2003, Reppucci et al. 2011).
threats: The rapid increase in worldwide demand for metals and minerals, including lithium, and the rapid expansion of exploitation of shale oil and gas through hydraulic fracturing or fracking in northern Patagonia (Walker et al. 2013) are the most pressing threats to Andean Cat habitat. The impact of lithium exploration and mining in the core area of the distribution range of the Andean Cat has not been assessed yet but could have extremely negative impacts not only on the Andean Cat but also on other high Andean species. These activities not only change the disposition of the land and connectivity between patches, but more importantly they make an extensive use of water (Chavez et al. 2023) that is an important limiting factor on these arid ecosystems. In some areas, especially in the north of Chile extraction of underground and surface waters is seriously affecting suitable areas for the Andean Cat and its prey (Iriarte and Jaksic 2022, Iriarte et al. in prep.).The expansion of the agricultural frontier and inadequate livestock management are also impacting the high Andean peatlands. These peatlands are crucial for the presence of the Andean Cat (Marino et al. 2010, Lagos et al. 2020) and are at risk not only due to extensive use but also as a result of the effects of global climate change (Marino et al. 2010). These factors will have a negative impact on the Andean Cat throughout most of its range by a decrease in the geographic distribution size (Bennett et al. 2017).Poaching of Andean Cats is a complex phenomenon, and requires different interventions. Andean Cat killing by local people who consider them a predator of their small domestic livestock has been frequently reported particularly in some regions of Argentina, Chile and Peru (Lucherini and Merino 2008, Lucherini et al. 2016). In Argentina, high mortality rates due to hunting by local people have also been inferred both in the northwest (Tellaeche et al. unpublished data), and the northern Patagonia, where cats are being killed by herders in retaliation for predation by larger carnivores (Novaro et al. 2010; Rocío Palacios, unpublished data).Hunting also occurs for bad management of pets. Dog attacks on livestock and wildlife are quite common in the Andes and Patagonia and local herders perceive a marked increase in recent times (Rocío Palacios, unpublished data), and even some feral dog populations have been recorded (Juan Carlos Huaranca, unpublished data). A second effect of domestic dogs and cats on wildlife is their potential to transmit diseases and parasites between the domestic and wild settings. This threat has not been corroborated as the few tested Andean Cat individuals returned negative results for the most common diseases (Napolitano et al. 2019), but there is an urgency for more research on this topic, since domestic animals visibly sick with zoonotic diseases have been detected in or around Andean Cat habitat (Huaranca and Palacios, unpublished data).Since the first record of an Andean Cat road kill in 2018 several other vehicle-cat accidents (in most cases fatal for the cat) have been reported in different part of its distribution. This new threat has not been evaluated but it is important to keep monitoring it especially because of the increased extent of roads in the remote areas inhabited by Andean Cats related to mining exploration and exploitation.A final indirect threat, that is global and difficult to assess and address, is the increased migration of local people to cities. This creates opportunities for extractive industries to advance, unchallenged, over the land. Additionally, when people come back from cities, they bring with them a whole set of tools to perform retaliatory killing against carnivores, such as traps, guns or poison, to prevent or in response to predation on livestock. The lack of job opportunities and reduction in the sense of belonging, combined with needs that are largely created by global media, facilitate this situation that indirectly affects all high Andean wildlife.Although most of the threats have been identified at a general scale, including prime and secondary Andean Cat habitats, they cover a significant proportion of the species’ distribution. Nevertheless, a detailed assessment of the impact of the different threats on the species and its habitat is much needed.
population: Formal probabilistic estimates of population numbers for the Andean Cat have been conducted in only two sites that were selected because of the high quality of habitat available for the species (e.g., multiple Andean Cat records in the area, great abundance of prey, high terrain roughness, and rocky outcrops). In both cases spatially explicit capture recapture models (SECR, Royle et al. 2014) were applied to camera trap data. The first study obtained a density of 0.07 and 0.12 individuals/km2 in two consecutive years in northwestern Argentina (Reppucci et al. 2011) and the second study found a density of 0.064–0.069 individuals/km2 in central western Bolivia (Huaranca et al. 2019). A study in northern Chile reported a minimum density of 0.02 ind./km2 using genetic individual identification (Napolitano et al. 2008).To supplement the formal information available on Andean Cat abundance, we compiled information of camera trap surveys carried out in different locations. Using those surveys, we estimated a minimum density for each area in terms of number of individuals detected/sampled area. To reduce the possibilities of overestimation or sub-estimation, we only used data from surveys that met the following criteria: (i) surveyed area greater than 100 km2 (approximately two Andean Cat home ranges), (ii) camera density greater than 0.07 camera traps/km2 (to avoid gaps where an individual has no possibility of being detected), and (iii) sampling effort greater than 900 camera trap-days (Llerena-Reátegui et al. 2022). After these filters were applied, there were eight surveys to perform the estimations (see Supplementary Information), including formal density estimations. For one area where population density was estimated both formally and non-formally, the two procedures produced similar results once filters were applied (Reppucci et al. 2011).We grouped the surveys in three regions, since it is likely that abundance changes with latitude, being the more suitable habitats and higher densities in the centre of the species’ distribution (Brown 1984). The northern region ranges from central Peru to 21.5° of latitude South. The central region, considered the most suitable habitat for Andean Cats, ranges from 21.5° to 27.5° of latitude South. Finally, the southern region ranges from 27.5° of latitude South to the southernmost record in Argentina. The mean Andean Cat population densities for north, central and south regions were 0.048, 0.063 and 0.034 individuals/km2, respectively (see Supplementary Information). The mean density for all the published studies (Reppucci et al. 2011, Huaranca et al. 2019) and those compiled for this categorisation is 0.05 individuals/km2 (range: 0.012–0.120).The Andean Cat distribution is patchy and strongly associated with steep rocky environments and these habitat patches are surrounded by large areas that are unsuitable for the species. One study found a value of around 1.4% of a total area of approximately 65,000 km2 to be suitable for the Andean Cat in northern Patagonia (Palacios et al. 2019). A second study carried out in northern Chile over 13,711 km2 estimated that 6.7% of the area was suitable for the species (Lagos et al. 2020). This second study was carried out in an area where Andean Cat density was expected to be relatively high, so it might overestimate the representativeness of suitable habitat at greater scale.Considering the "Extant" area of 343,689.75 km2 (divided in 176,742.13 km2 in the north, 103,043.31 km2 in the centre and 63,904.32 km2 in the south; see Supplementary Information), for each region we used the mean population density found for that region and calculated the number of individuals for the 6.7% of the total area (being this the proportion of suitable habitat found by Lagos et al. (2020)). Although it is probable that the density for the remaining part of the area (93.3%) is close to 0, to avoid underestimating population numbers, we used the minimum density that we found in our compilation of surveys as explained above (0.01 individual/km2) for the rest of each area. It is necessary to remember that this local density estimation was obtained from good quality habitats, and therefore it likely overestimated the cat densities over much larger areas. As a result, we estimated the total population of Andean Cats at 4,354 individuals including adults and subadults. There is no information about population structure available, thus we used a default value of 50% for the proportion of mature individuals within the Andean Cat population (Nowell et al. 2007). This gave an estimate of only 2,177 mature individuals (see Supplementary Information).Given the naturally fragmented arrangement of the Andean Cat's habitat, a great patch or group of close patches would be necessary to sustain a population of 250 mature individuals. According to our estimations, the patch of suitable continuous habitat large enough to hold at least 250 mature individuals should measure a minimum of 2,083 km2 (considering the highest known density estimation). A patch that has or exceeds the size required to sustain a population of 250 mature individuals has not been identified anywhere in the Andean Cat range. Therefore, there is no subpopulation numbering 250 or more mature individuals.Given the uncertainty surrounding population estimates and the fact that they were obtained from areas that researchers identified as best habitat for the species, it is possible that we are overestimating population numbers (both at range and subpopulation level). The formal density estimates outlined above were obtained from two regions that are considered to have the most favourable conditions for Andean Cats (e.g., climate, habitat, topography and prey availability; Marino et al. 2011). Because of this, it is expected that Andean Cat densities in areas with less favourable conditions are much lower, as suggested by the additional studies reported here and that the ecological density might be even lower at landscape level. This hypothesis is supported by research done by Reppucci et al. (unpublished data) who extended their study site to the less suitable habitat surrounding the high-quality area and estimated that abundance decreased by 69%.The genetic diversity of the Andean Cat has been found to be very low in mitochondrial genes and nuclear microsatellites across its range (Napolitano et al. 2008, Cossios et al. 2012). A study sampled 56 individuals across Perú, Bolivia and Argentina and found only five mitochondrial haplotypes (Cossios et al. 2012). In the same study, Andean Cat microsatellite diversity (allelic richness) was also very low compared with the congeneric species, the Pampas Cat Leopardus colocolo, which inhabits the same geographic areas. Similarly, the number of alleles was three to five times lower in Andean Cats than in Ocelots Leopardus pardalis, Margays Leopardus wiedii and Northern Tiger Cats L. tigrinus from Brazil (Cossios et al. 2012). These initial results led to the determination that the Andean Cat had two distinct Evolutionary Significant Units” (ESUs). The geographical separation between the northern and southern ESU concurs with the third biogeographic barrier, the South American Arid Diagonal and the separation between the two northern management units coincides with the transition zone between the wet and dry Puna (Cossíos et al. 2012). A recent whole-genome study found that the Andean Cat has the lowest genomic diversity of the Leopardus genus, harbouring 10 times less genetic variation (heterozygosity) than the most diverse species evaluated (the Ocelot, Lescroart et al. 2023). Estimated heterozygosity was extremely low in the Andean Cat, comparable to the Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus). Also, the lowest effective population size (Ne) of the Leopardus genus was observed in the Andean Cat, which appears to have been steadily declining in population size since at least the Last Interglacial (LIG; 130–116 thousand years Before Present). This study suggests long-term small population size as the cause of the observed low diversity (Lescroart et al. 2023). Genetic diversity is associated with population size: high genetic diversity is related to large populations, while low genetic diversity to small populations. Therefore, low genetic diversity estimates complement camera trap low density estimates, and support that the Andean Cat has small population numbers across its range.
range: The Andean Cat was rarely recorded until the late 1990s, and its range was thought to be limited to southern Peru, southwest Bolivia, northwest Argentina, and northern Chile (Yensen and Seymour 2000). There were also few sightings (Scrocchi and Halloy 1986, Sanderson 1999) and museum specimens (Garcia-Perea 2002) of this species. However, the number of distribution records has grown significantly in the past 20 years, mainly because of the work of the Andean Cat Alliance (www.gatoandino.org), a group of expert researchers that works in the four countries where the species live.The Andean Cat has a patchy distribution due to a specialisation for naturally fragmented rocky habitats and most presence records are from the central Andes above 3,600 m in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile and Peru. However, it has also been found at lower elevations, as low as 1,800 m in the Andes of central-southern Argentina (Sorli et al. 2006) and 1,150 m in central Chile (Segura et al. 2021). More recent records of the Andean Cat in Argentina and Chile extend its distribution range to the south and outside the Andes, in proximity of the deciduous temperate forest of central Chile in Radal Siete Tazas (CONAF 2023) and of the Patagonian steppe and scrub habitats in Argentina, at elevations as low as 650 m (Martinez et al. 2008, Novaro et al. 2010).The known northern and southern distribution limits for the Andean Cat are respectively, in central Peru (9°54' S), and central Argentina (38°23' S; Cossios et al. 2007, Novaro et al. 2010), but the new information gathered by researchers confirms that throughout this range, the Andean Cat subpopulations are patchily distributed. The results of modelling the Andean Cat distribution, considering four bioclimatic variables (annual mean and mean diurnal range temperature, annual precipitation, and coldest season winter), showed the presence of three biogeographic barriers that affect the species’ distribution. These include: i) In the north of Peru, coinciding with the Huancabamba depression, known as the “Peruvian low,” which defines the northern boundary of its distribution range. ii) In the centre of Bolivia, with the “Andean knee,” an extremely arid transition zone between the wet and dry Puna. This area has no records of Andean Cats. iii) In the south, with the “Arid Diagonal” in Chile and Argentina, also a hyper-arid zone with very few records of Andean Cats (Marino et al. 2011). According to this model and despite the differences in elevation over the current geographic range, there are common climatic conditions that favour its presence, which are cold, dry and extreme diurnal variations in temperature (Marino et al. 2011).
useTrade: In Argentina, Bolivia, Chile and Perú, people of Aymara, and in some cases Quechua, origin have similar beliefs regarding the Andean Cat and Pampas Cat (both known as titi or osqollo). In some areas a common tradition is the use of a skin or a stuffed cat during ceremonies that people perform for marking their domestic livestock, mainly llamas or alpacas; the titi is considered a sacred animal related with abundance and fertility of the livestock or quality of crops (Giraldo-Jaramillo 2015). It is important to note that both the Andean Cat and Pampas Cat are part of these traditions and beliefs, and in general, are used indiscriminately. There are some local variations within and between countries and in some cases the Andean Cats (in some cases identified as a separate species but mostly together with Pampas Cats) are recognised as a special figure, with important influence in the cosmovision because of this felid’s relation with the mountainous areas, being considered the messenger with the local Apus, or mountain gods. The influence of western culture has resulted in a total or partial loss of the values of Andean cultures and the distortion of ancestral customs regarding the titi. Because of that, we do not believe the traditional use of the Andean Cat for ceremonies is currently affecting local populations, since its demand is reducing (Villalba et al. 2004). Beside this, the skins used for those ceremonies transfer through generations, so the real impact on Andean Cat subpopulations is expected to be low (Giraldo-Jaramillo 2015).
conservationActions: The Andean Cat Alliance (Alianza Gato Andino, or AGA) has worked to ensure the survival of the Andean Cat since 1999. AGA (www.gatoandino.org) is the only organisation exclusively dedicated to the protection of this species and has been leading all the past and current interdisciplinary and cross-border initiatives to protect this wildcat in its four range countries (Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina). Its rareness and strong association with the high Andean ecosystem make this felid an ideal flagship species for conservation of this habitat, which is considered one of earth's last wild places.AGA's activities are implemented throughout the four countries encompassing the distribution range of the Andean Cat, in the form of multinational programmes that have a sensible approach to the mitigation of the main threats that affect the species. With that in mind, the Alliance's work focuses on developing programs that diminish these threats globally, but are customised to each community they work with. These multinational conservation programs use flexible toolkits that adapt to the specific needs of each area and local community in order to find creative solutions that mitigate conservation threats. These programmes are also designed to work collaboratively, and the coordinators work together to have bigger impact programs can be summarised as follows:The CATcrafts Program provides alternative income sources, reducing hunting by changing the perception and attitude towards Andean Cats, and indirectly reducing population reduction rates and habitat loss to extractive industries. The Conflict Mitigation Program facilitates coexistence and reduces killing of Andean Cats and other carnivores by using non-invasive tools to reduce conflicts with pumas/foxes. The Pawsitive Actions Program aims to reduce killing of Andean Cats and disease transmission by domestic dogs, while also improving human health. The In the Field 24/7 program investigates to fill the gaps in our knowledge of the species, particularly their ecological and genetic characteristics through camera trapping monitoring and genetic analysis of non-invasive samples to assess connectivity among populations. Finally, the Education Program transverses all of the above creating content and strategies that can be applied to all schools and communities across the Andean Cat habitat. AGA members from each range country work collaboratively to coordinate conservation, education, and research programs (see https://gatoandino.org/programas/ for more information).One of the main and major threats for Andean Cat conservation is large scale mining activities, and actions at a political and institutional level are urgently needed in order to minimise the impacts of this threat. Desiccation and/or contamination of peatlands and habitat destruction derived from these extensive activities should be reduced, through the limiting of mining activities in core habitat areas for the Andean Cat on one hand while making mining more sustainable in the entire Andean ecosystem.An additional area where investigation and conservation efforts are recommended is the assessment and creation of awareness on the Ecological Services provided by Andean Cat subpopulations and, indirectly, the high Andes habitat they are primarily associated with, with emphasis on non-monetary and cultural values associated to native population cosmogony. The revitalisation of cultural traditions that involve the significant role the Andean Cat plays in Andean communities is necessary. These traditions encompass an inherent care and respect for both wildlife and the ecosystems in which communities reside, but they are being threatened by deculturisation and the influence of Western culture on Andean communities.

rationale: Leopards are widely distributed across Africa and Asia, but populations have become reduced and isolated and they are now extirpated from large portions of their historic range. Due to their wide geographic range, secretive nature and habitat tolerance, Leopards are difficult to categorize as a single species. Evidence suggests that Leopard populations have been dramatically reduced due to continued persecution from increased human populations (Thorn et al. 2013, Selvan et al. 2014, Abade et al. 2018, Bleyhl et al. 2021); habitat fragmentation (UN 2014); increased illegal wildlife trade (Datta et al. 2008, Rostro-Garcia et al. 2016); excessive harvesting for medicinal use and ceremonial use of skins, spiritual and cultural use of the body parts including skin, claws, teeth, tail, paws, skin and fat (Naude et al. 2020); prey base declines (Hatton et al. 2001, du Toit 2004, Fusari and Carpaneto 2006, Datta et al. 2008, Lindsey et al. 2014, Selvan et al. 2014); and poorly managed trophy hunting (Balme et al. 2009). Throughout North, East (specifically the Horn of Africa) and West Africa, Middle East, East and Southeast Asia, Leopards have suffered marked reductions and regional extirpations due to poaching for illegal wildlife trade, habitat loss and fragmentation, and prey loss. Human populations are increasing by 2.7 percent annually in sub-Saharan Africa according to the UN. Between 2022 and 2050, the fastest human population growth is projected to occur in Africa. The population in sub-Saharan Africa is projected to double by 2050 (https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/population). The rate of cropland expansion accelerated in Africa over the past two decades. There was a more than twofold increase from 2016–2019 compared to 2004–2007. Countries in West, Central, and East Africa all saw large increases in cultivated land. Most of those new croplands were carved out of natural habitats rather than pasture or abandoned farmland (https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/149624/crop-expansion-accelerates-in-africa). Deforestation in southeast Asia has increased for palm oil and rubber plantations (Sodhi et al. 2010, Miettinen et al. 2011). Intensive snaring for bushmeat in southeast Asia has substantially reduced Leopard prey and caused direct mortality (Rostro-Garcia et al. 2023). Since the last assessment in 2016, evidence of genetic inbreeding among isolated populations has presented an additional threat to population viability (Marchenkova et al. 2020, Cho et al. 2022, Yin et al. 2023). We estimate the current confirmed extant range of Leopards presented in this assessment (7,608,096 km², see map) is a reduction of 11% from the previous assessment from 2016 (8,515,935 km², Stein et al. 2016). Range losses in sub-Saharan Africa, Middle East, Southeast Asia and China counterbalance gains in India and Southwest Asia (Ostrowski et al. 2022). Only in Northeast China and Russian Far East the leopard’s breeding range increased during 20 years from 7,000 km² to 14,000 km² (Jiang et al. 2016, Vitkalova et al. 2023). Though our knowledge of the Leopard distribution is better today than in 2016, it is still limited at the national, regional and range-wide scales because reliable data on Leopard population trends are missing from large portions of their range. We suspect that suitable Leopard range has been reduced by >30% worldwide in the last three generations (22.3 years). We calculated generation length as 7.42 years (based on the formula presented in Pacifici et al. 2013 and data from wild Leopard populations presented in Balme et al. 2013).Leopard population density across the species’ range is known to track the biomass of principle Leopard prey species, small, medium-size and large wild herbivores (Marker and Dickman 2005, Hayward et al. 2007). Prey species are increasingly under threat from an unsustainable bushmeat trade, leading to collapses in prey populations across large parts of savanna Africa (Lindsey et al. 2013, Ripple et al. 2016, Rogan et al. 2017). A commercialized bushmeat trade has caused an estimated 59% average decline in Leopard prey populations across 78 protected areas in West, East and southern Africa between 1970 and 2005 (Craigie et al. 2010). In southern Africa, illegal bushmeat hunting removes up to 620,000 kg of wild ungulates annually from the Okavango Delta, Botswana (Rogan et al. 2017). Though ungulate populations have increased by 24% in southern Africa, potential prey numbers have declined by 52% in East Africa and 85% in West Africa (Craigie et al. 2010). Bushmeat poaching in Mozambique (Hatton et al. 2001, Fusari et al. 2006) and Zambia (Lindsey et al. 2014) has severely reduced Leopard prey (Becker et al. 2013) inside and outside of protected areas. Many wildlife areas are suffering from substantial ungulate decline, including Zambian Game Management Areas and National Parks, maintain large mammal populations at 93.7% and 74.1% below estimated carrying capacity, respectively (Lindsey et al. 2014).
