The IATTC has imposed annual bycatch limits on each purse seiner and has promulgated regulations regarding the safe release of dolphins impacted by the ETP tuna purse seine fishery (Bayliff 2001). In the eastern North Pacific, the U.S. driftnet fishery has been required to use acoustic warning devices (pingers) since 1996 to reduce cetacean bycatch.

rationale: This is a common species with no major threats and is assessed as Least Concern.
habitat: Rattus norvegicus is a highly adaptable synanthropic rodent that is found globally across most climatic regions, excluding the most extreme (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Russell and McClelland 2024) and elevations above 3,250 m asl (GBIF.org 2025). Given its strong association with humans, the species is virtually present in all lowland and coastal zones where human settlements are present (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Russell and McClelland 2024). The species is particularly widespread in temperate regions, where it occupies a wide range of environments. Rattus norvegicus can also be frequently found in natural or semi-natural environments such as along riverbanks, lake shores, marshes, estuaries, and secondary vegetation (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Russell and McClelland 2024). In tropical regions, by contrast, it tends to be more restricted to anthropized environments (Feng and Himsworth 2014, Panti-May et al. 2016). On oceanic islands, the species has invaded natural forests, shrublands, and wetlands in the absence of predators and/or competitors, and has caused significant ecological impacts on native fauna, such as seabirds, through predation (Russell and McClelland 2024). Rattus norvegicus is a ground-dwelling and fossorial rodent with an omnivorous and opportunistic diet, feeding on human waste, both plant and animal matter, and has been observed preying on a wide range of invertebrates and small vertebrates such as amphibians, reptiles, birds, hatchlings, eggs, and even fish (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Russell and McClelland 2024). Burrow systems are typically established in moist soil, often in proximity to water bodies, human waste streams, or food storage areas, and are used communally (Modlinska and Pisula 2020).
threats: There are no major threats to this species. Because of its invasive species and pest status, Rattus norvegicus is a target of control and eradication programs worldwide (Russell and McClelland 2024).
population: Rattus norvegicus is frequently abundant in suitable habitat categories, reaching high densities in anthropogenic environments and close to human-provided food resources (Desvars-Larrive et al. 2018, Russell and McClelland 2024).
range: Rattus norvegicus is considered to be native to temperate East Asia (Faurby et al. 2018), with its ancestral range probably located in eastern China and adjacent parts of northeastern Asia, including northeastern China, southeastern Siberia and Japan (Faurby et al. 2018, Munshi-South et al. 2024). However, the precise boundaries of its original distribution remain uncertain because the species has undergone a striking human mediated range expansion associated with human settlement and trade (Munshi-South et al. 2024). Genomic and zooarchaeological evidence indicates that this species likely dispersed out of East Asia during the late Holocene, first into southeast and western Asia and then, by the 18th century, into much of Europe, from where they subsequently spread to the Americas, Africa, Australasia and numerous oceanic islands, mainly via maritime trade (Munshi-South et al. 2024). Today, Rattus norvegicus is one of the most widespread terrestrial mammals, occurring on all continents except Antarctica. The global distribution of this strongly synanthropic species follows that of human settlements across both temperate and tropical latitudes (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Munshi-South et al. 2024).
useTrade: Rattus norvegicus is used in scientific research as a model organism across many life science fields (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Munshi-South et al. 2024). The domesticated form is also kept as a pet, particularly in Europe and North America (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Munshi-South et al. 2024). Its primary relevance to humans is as a highly problematic pest responsible for widespread damage to stored food, infrastructure, and electrical systems (Modlinska and Pisula 2020, Munshi-South et al. 2024). Furthermore, wild populations are vectors and reservoirs for numerous zoonotic diseases.
conservationActions: There are no conservation efforts in place and none are required.

rationale: Considering the possible extirpation of one subpopulation and reported declines in other fragmented subpopulations, it is plausible that this species has undergone a reduction in the region of 20–30% over the previous three generations (30 years). It is at risk of predation by invasive species, loss of forest habitat and hunting. In particular, the threat of hunting has intensified over recent years, having at least tripled in rural and coastal areas, including in protected areas. This species is therefore assessed as Near Threatened.
habitat: The species is forest dependent, occurring in both primary and secondary forest, close to rivers and humid zones. Its behaviour is completely arboreal, and it lives in the canopy using holes in tree trunks as refugia (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011). The species is a folivore (leaf eater), feeding on more than 30 species of plants, especially fruit trees (Borroto-Páez and Woods 2011). The species reproduces principally in the warm months, with about 2–3 births in the year. The gestation period is 90–120 days and litter size ranges from 1–3. The species is very difficult to breed in captivity (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011).
threats: Loss of forest habitat across its range, caused by conversion to agriculture, has reduced population size and driven population fragmentation (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012). Illegal hunting by local people can be intensive, and constitutes a significant threat (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012). Hunting pressure has increased by 3–4 times in rural and coastal areas since the Covid-19 pandemic (Borroto-Páez pers. comm. 2024). All populations are under threat from hunting, even in protected areas, and social media has aided the trade of this species. Hunting is conducted with dogs (which can be free-roaming), as well as through the use of fire in tree holes or caves to flush hutias out from refuges, which further damages hutia habitat.The arboreal nature of the species may mean that it is less vulnerable to dog predation, however dog scats containing the species were found in a short period walking in the western part of Cuba (Borroto-Páez, 2009). It may be vulnerable to competition and disease or parasite transmission from black rats (Borroto-Páez 2009) as both species can share refuges in the tree holes and caves. Feral cats may be a serious threat because they are known to predate this species on both Isla de la Juventud and mainland Cuba (Borroto-Páez and Ramos 2003, Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011, Borroto-Páez and Ramos 2012, Borroto-Páez and Mancina 2017).
population: This species has discontinuous populations (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011) and is declining. For example, reductions have been noted on the mainland in the Zapata Swamp, San Diego de los Baños, Guanes, and Cunagua (R. Borroto-Páez pers. comm. 2024). Subspecies Mysateles m. gundlachi is scarce, and M. m. meridionalis may already be extinct (R. Borroto-Páez pers. comm. 2024). Declines are predicted to continue as hunting pressure has increased by 3–4 times over recent years, particularly in rural and coastal areas.
range: This species occurs across mainland Cuba from Pinar del Rio Province in the West to Bolivia town in the East in Ciego de Avila Province (Borroto-Páez and Espinosa Romo 2011). On the Isle of Youth, the population of subspecies Mysateles m. gundlachi is scarce, and M. m. meridionalis is almost (or possibly already) extinct following declines (Borroto-Páez and Ramos 2003, Borroto-Páez 2011, Borroto-Páez and Ramos 2012, Borroto-Páez and Mancina 2017, R. Borroto-Páez pers. comm. 2024).
useTrade: The species is hunted for food. Hunting pressure has increased 3–4 times over recent years, partially driven by economic crisis and trade embargos in Cuba. Black markets and the use of social media has also increased. One hutia can be sold for 800 Cuban pesos by the hunter, but up to 1,000–1,200 Cuban pesos if sold by an intermediary party. Methods of hunting include the use of dogs and/or fire.
conservationActions: This species occurs in numerous protected areas in western and central parts of mainland Cuba (Borroto-Páez et al. 2012, Borroto-Páez and Mancina 2017). It would benefit from measures to deter hunting, and the control of invasive species.

rationale: This species is considered Vulnerable due to a suspected population reduction of at least 30% over the past 30 years (three generations) due to habitat destruction and illegal hunting.
habitat: The species is found in primary and secondary forest habitats, including in coffee, cacao, and fruit tree plantations (Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012). The species is found in either pairs or small family groups, high reproductive activities occur primarily in the first month of the year, with high percentages of pregnant in February and March, with one or two young. The sexual maturity is reached at 870 g in females and males (Borroto Páez et al. 2012).
threats: Current threats to the species come from habitat fragmentation and conversion for agriculture and mining, and invasive mammals (Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012). Available habitat decreased by 20% during a recent ten-year period (Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2012). The arboreal nature of this species means it could be less vulnerable to dog predation; however, harm by dogs has been observed, for example in the Alejandro de Humboldt National Park in eastern Cuba (Borroto-Paez, 2009). Destruction of nest sites in tree cavities by hunters to capture animals is a serious associated concern; in the core area and buffer zone of Alejandro de Humboldt National Park, it is estimated that 22.4% of nests have been partially or totally destroyed by hunters and the entrances of a further 24.8% of nests have been blocked or obstructed to facilitate capture, leading to substantial reduction in nest site availability (Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2011, Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2012).
population: Populations are extremely fragmented and its status varies across its range, with evidence of local abundance in some areas in recent decades (e.g., Guisa, Granma Province), but reduced abundance in most areas, such as Alejandro de Humboldt National Park (Borroto-Páez and Beque Quiala 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012).
range: This species is known from the far eastern provinces of Cuba: Holguín, Granma, Santiago de Cuba, and Guantánamo provinces (Silva Taboada et al. 2009, Borroto-Páez et al. 2005, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012).
useTrade: This species is hunted. It is not known whether it is traded at a national or international scale.
conservationActions: This species occurs in several protected areas (including in PN Pico Cristal, PN La Mensura-Piloto, PN Alejandro de Humboldt, PN Turquino, PN Desembarco del Granma, PN Sierra Maestra, PN Pico La Bayamesa, Cuchilla del Toa Biosphere Reserve and other protected areas with less categories (Borroto-Páez et al. 2012).

rationale: This species is assessed as Critically Endangered. It has a fragmented distribution comprising one native subpopulation and a tiny introduced subpopulation. It has an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 22 km² and area of occupancy (AOO) of around 5 km². The entire population within its small native range is considered to occur in only one location as it is all under threat from hunting, and it is experiencing a decline in area, extent and quality of habitat associated with a causeway construction and increased disturbance from local people and invasive mammals.
habitat: The species is found exclusively in Red Mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) where there is no firm ground (Borroto-Páez and Mancina 2011). It builds communal shelters in mangrove trees (Nowak 1999).
threats: The primary threat to this species is hunting; the species is accidentally captured in traps designed to catch the larger Desmarest's Hutia (Capromys pilorides) by fisherman who frequent the islands (Borroto-Páez et al. 2011). There is some level of competition with the introduced Black Rat (Rattus rattus), which is abundant in the area and shares refuges with Mesocapromys angelcabrerai (Borroto-Páez 2013); however, the extent of this threat is unknown. A recently built causeway from the mainland to the Cayos Salinas has damaged mangrove habitat and has enabled increased access for local people, who might also cause fires, and invasive predators and competitors. The increase in sea level and frequency of hurricanes has the potential to destroy mangrove forest habitat and could affect the species (Borroto-Páez et al. 2011).
population: The total population has around 750 individuals (based on a count of 190 refuges with each one estimated to have four individuals) and the population could be considered as stable in recent times. The population on the island Cayo la Loma, where six individuals were introduced in 2005, is estimated at 20 individuals (Borroto-Páez et al. 2011), however this area has not been surveyed recently and may no longer be present.
range: This species is endemic to Cuba. Despite previous reports, it has never been recorded on the Júcaro coast (Borroto-Páez et al. 2011). It is only found on some flooded mangrove keys named Cayo Salinas, within the group Cayos de Ana Maria, south of Ciego de Avila province (Camacho et al. 1994, Borroto-Páez et al. 2011, Borroto-Páez et al. 2012). It was introduced for conservation purposes to Cayo la Loma, a small protected key in the south of the keys in 2005 (Borroto-Páez et al. 2011).
useTrade: The species is accidentally captured in traps set for a larger animal and killed by hunters as think they are juveniles of the species Capromys pilorides.
conservationActions: The species occurs in the Wildlife Refuge Cayos de Ana María.

rationale: This species is listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct), as it has not been seen in nearly 40 years. It is known from only an extremely small remnant population of 43 animals collected in 1978 from one small cay, (Cayo Juan García). Later field surveys have not detected the species. If it is still extant, this hutia will have an extremely small extent of occurrence (EOO is less than 20 km²). In recent decades it has experienced declines in area, extent and quality of habitat, and number of mature individuals.
habitat: Very little is known about this species. It lived in coastal glass grass (Batis maritima) and in red mangrove (Frías et al. 1988, Berovides Alvarez and González 1991, Borroto-Páez 2011).
threats: It has been suggested that the reasons for the Little Earth Hutia's decline may have been hunting by humans, habitat loss from fires, and due to an infestation of Black rats (Frías et al. 1988, Berovides Alvarez and Gonzáles 1991, Borroto-Paez 2009). Information about habitat availability is conflicting, with Frías et al. (1988) suggesting that very little suitable habitat was left, whereas Meier (2004) reported that suitable habitat still was widely available. A military installation was previously located on these islands and it is believed that during this time hunting by military personnel was intensive. Fisherman use the island and many accidental fires have resulted from their cooking fires and mosquito control. There have also been reports of the presence of cats and dogs when the species was in the keys (Borroto-Páez, 2009, Borroto-Páez 2011), which would pose a threat.
population: Very little is known about populations of this species. Surveys in keys where the species was reported have not detected any evidence (Silva Taboada et al. 2009, Borroto-Páez 2011), however other keys of the Archipelago San Felipe were not surveyed.
range: This species has only been reported from one small cay, Cayo Juan García, which is within the Cayos de San Felipe (protected within Cayos de San Felipe National Park). Its presence has not been detected on the smaller neighbouring Cayo Real. It was last seen in 1978 when 43 animals were collected from the island. Later field surveys have not detected the species (Meier 2004).
conservationActions: It is not known whether this species is still extant; further surveys are required to confirm.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern, because it has a very large distribution with an extent of occurrence (EOO) estimated to be 852,002 km2 that includes a number of protected areas. There are no major threats to the species or its habitats.
habitat: Specimens have been collected in evergreen broadleaved forests from 802 to 2,800 m elevation (Chen et al. 2017, pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
threats: There are no known major threats to this species. The forest habitats on Mt. Tay Con Linh are being lost to Chinese cardamom (Lanxangia tsaoko) plantations, with preparations for new plantations occurring up the mountain (Saito et al. 2021). In China there are no major threats to the species or its habitats (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
population: Populations are relatively stable, with large populations in the Ailao and Wuliang Mountains in Yunnan but other areas are unknown (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
range: The species was described from Ailao Mountain and Wuliang Mountain, Yunnan, China, and Mt. Tay Con Linh II, northern Viet Nam (Chen et al. 2017). The Mekong River is likely the western boundary of the species’ distribution, separating Chodsigoa parca and Chodsigoa hoffmanni (Chen et al. 2017). Since then, it has also been recorded in China from Laojun Mountain in Sichuan, Jinfo Mountain and Shirugan Mountain in Chongqing, the Qixingguan District in Bijie city in Ghuizhou, and Xingshan county in Hubei (Fan et al. 2022, Liu et al. 2021, Lei et al. 2021, pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025). This species was collected from evergreen broadleaved forests from 802 to 2,600 m asl elevation (Chen et al. 2017, pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
conservationActions: The Tay Con Linh is a protected area in Viet Nam (Saito et al. 2021). Mount Wuliang and Mount Ailao in Yunnan, Mountain Laojun in Sichuan and Mountain Jinfo in Chongqing are national nature reserves (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).

rationale: Whilst there are only a few specimens known for this species, it is assessed as Least Concern due to its relatively high suspected extent of occurrence (EOO) of 234,787 km2, it likely occurs in some protected areas, and there are currently no known major threats to the species or its habitat.
habitat: The species lives above 2,000 m asl, because it is adapted to cool environments in high mountain ranges, probably in forests given the habitats of other Chodsigoa species in the same areas (Chen et al. 2017).
threats: There is nothing known about the threats to this species.
population: There no population data, however, fewer than 10 specimens are currently known to exist (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
range: The species is known from northern Myanmar and two localities in Yunnan, China (Chen et al. 2017), as well as Linzhi, Xizhang in Tibet (Zhang et al. 2021). All individuals have been captured at elevations above 2,000 m asl (Chen et al. 2017). It likely occurs throughout high mountain areas in northern Myanmar and western Yunnan (Chen et al. 2017).
conservationActions: There are some protected areas in northern Myanmar that could include some of the suspected range, also in western Yunnan and southeastern Xizang there are parts of its range in protected areas.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, and because it is unlikely to be declining at anything close to the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: The species lives in montane forests at elevations between 1,250 and 3,000 m asl (Chen et al. 2017, Lunde et al. 2003).
threats: There is nothing known about the threats to this species. Myanmar is in the middle of a civil war, although prior to this was starting a period of economic growth that was enabled by overexploitation and habitat loss (Rao et al. 2013). Northern Thailand, especially Chiang Mai, the province where most of the range in Thailand is located, is experiencing deforestation and a change in land-use (Akber and Shrestha 2013). There are no threats known in China (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
population: In Yunnan, such as Yongde Snow Mountain and Gaoligong Mountain, the population of this species is relatively large (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).
range: The species is found in Yunnan, China, northern Myanmar, northern Thailand, and one isolated area of northwestern Viet Nam. The Mekong River likely acts as the eastern boundary of its range (Chen et al. 2017). There is a large elevational range between 1,250 and 3,000 m, but most specimens have been collected between 2,400 and 2,600 m in broadleaf forests in western Yunnan (Chen et al. 2017).
conservationActions: It presumably occurs in several protected areas, because there are many protected areas in northern Thailand and parts of northern Myanmar and Yunnan are also protected. In Yunnan, China, many of its distribution areas are located within protected areas such as the Yongde Snow Mountain and Gaoligong Mountain National Nature Reserves, and there are no obvious factors threatening this species (pers. comm. Z. Chen 2025).

rationale: This species has a large range with an estimated extent of occurrence (EOO) of 37,058 km2, there have been no changes to distribution because the sandy habitats it occupies have little agricultural value and are therefore not likely to be threatened.
habitat: Inhabits loamy and sandy semi-deserts in NE cis-Caucasia. Prefers moderately moist areas with light soils in river valleys, lake basins and lowlands with luxuriant vegetation. Also occurs in semi-deserts with shrubs and reed, herb-grasses and herb-absinth steppes. Also found in anthropogenic landscapes such as orchards and fields, areas along road embankments,vegetable gardens, where it may be a pest (Omarov et al. 2009). Obligatory subterranean, feeds on subterranean plant parts. Active throughout the year. Generally monogamous. Heat occurs in December-January, females give birth to 2-3 young.
threats: There may be some habitat loss due to irrigation and subsequent soil salinization, overgrazing, and ploughing, however most of the sandy habitats it occupies have no agricultural value.
population: Data on population size are limited and somewhat contradictory. The total number in Ciscaucasia was estimated at about 20,000-25,000 animals in the 1960s (Pavlov et al. 1963). From the mid-1970s numbers declined at a high rate. In the 1980s, average density fell to 0.2-0.3 animals/1000 ha. According to some estimates, total numbers in Daghestan, where most of the population is located, fell to 1,000-1,200 animals during that period (Spasskaya and Gitinomagomedov 1980, Spasskaya 1982). The number in Daghestan was about 10,000 (Gineev et al. 1988). The fall in numbers and range fragmentation were caused by strong anthropogenic pressure that affected the entire range up to the end of the 1980s. In habitats with the least human pressure, numbers reached their upper limit despite the overall downward trend. Unfortunately, no data on population fluctuations in the 1990s are available. Also during the 1990s, the entire complex of human impacts, primarily overgrazing, decreased in the north-west Precaspian zone.
range: It occurs in Ciscaucasia and southernmost Kalmykia (Russia). Within the range it is distributed very patchily, as separate settlements that often occur in sandy areas.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: The species is listed in the Red Data Book of the Russian Federation in Cateory 3 (rare species). It occurs in reserves in Chechen Republic and Dagestan (Russia). Conservation proposed include: reductions in anthropogenic pressure in the largest concentration zones; establish protected areas around large colonies; long-term monitoring; and restoration of the species within its range using reintroduction techniques (Omarov et al. 2009).

rationale: Walia Ibex (Capra walie) is assessed as Critically Endangered (CR) under criterion C because the number of mature individuals is less than 250, with a projected continuing decline ≥ 25% within one generation (7 years) [criterion C1], and with an observed continuing decline and all mature individuals occurring in one subpopulation [criterion C2a(ii)].Under criterion B, the highest category the species qualifies for is Endangered (EN B1ab(i,ii,v)+2ab(i,ii,v)), as its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 353 km² and area of occupancy (AOO) is 196 km², it is restricted to a single location (the Simien Mountains National Park (SMNP) in northern Ethiopia), and there is continuing decline in EOO, AOO and the number of mature individuals.In response to the recent severe decline, the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority (EWCA), in collaboration with the African Wildlife Foundation (AWF), has initiated a number of actions including the recruitment of so-called Walia community ambassadors, charged with promoting Walia Ibex conservation, monitoring the species and its habitat, improving communication amongst stakeholders and enhancing trust between local people and national park staff. However, with the continuing political instability in Amhara, the regional state where SMNP is located, there is a distinct risk of further weakening of protection that could enhance poaching and habitat destruction. There also remains the risk of disease transmission from and hybridization with livestock, in particular domestic goats. These risks could drive the tiny Walia Ibex population to Extinct (EX).
habitat: Walia Ibex lives in mountainous habitats, montane forest, sub-afroalpine grasslands, afro-alpine and areas with low vegetation cover in the SMNP. The species is an outstanding rock-climber with strong and relatively short legs and hooves that hold the ground better than other ungulates. As infants need additional protection against predators, lactating Walia Ibex females prefer habitat ranges in steep inaccessible cliffs within the park (Nievergelt 1981). Walia Ibex prefers areas with little disturbances, occupying the steep inaccessible areas in the SMNP (Hurni and Ludi 2000). The species used to be widely distributed from Beyeda along the escarpment to Gich and Adi-Arkay (Nievergelt 2013). At the end of 1960s, for example, the main habitat ranges of Walia Ibex were in the central part of the Park, between Gich camp and Imetgogo. In the 1970s, the population had increased and its habitat gradually enlarged towards Sankaber and Chenek–Buahit areas. Walia Ibex habitat model indicates that most of its preferred habitats occur from Chenek-Buahit to Mesareria towards the eastern and southeastern parts of the park (Nievergelt 2013, Ejigu et al. 2013, Gebrmedehin et al. 2021).
threats: The SMNP has a fragile ecosystem that has faced problems, deeply rooted because of the pressure of local residents and their related activities, resulting in low protection efficiency of wildlife and ecosystems (EWCA 2019). Habitat destruction in SMNP by the local people affects the future survival of Walia Ibex (Hurni and Ludi 2000, Schwartz 2009). Livestock grazing inside the SMNP is the main threat to its wildlife in general and Walia Ibex in particular (Ejigu et al. 2013). Intensive anthropogenic disturbance near and within the park might be an important issue contributing to the decline of wildlife in general and threatening Walia Ibex in particular. Historically, local communities valued Walia Ibex for their social, cultural, ecological and economic role as a tourist attraction. During periods of relative stability, poaching was infrequent and communities reported any incident to Park rangers. During 2019-2023, however the annual number of visitors dropped from 32,000 to 4,300; the resulting decrease in income from tourism may have eroded the previously positive relationship between communities and Park authorities, leading to an increase in poaching. In interviews conducted in 2024, 70% of the responders attributed the drop of Walia Ibex to poaching, both for food and medicinal purposes. Instability as a result of the COVID-19 crisis, the 2021-2022 war on the northern edge of SMNP, and the following political unrest in Amhara the regional state where the Park is located, was seen as the fundamental cause (Scholte et al. 2025).It is assumed that in addition to human related problems, natural predators such as Leopard (Panthera pardus) and Spotted Hyaena (Crocuta crocuta) capable of killing Walia Ibex (Nievergelt 2013). Moreover, juveniles are at risk from different predators including African Wildcat (Felis lybica), Golden Jackal (Canis aureus) as well as larger birds of prey (Dunbar 1978, Nievergelt 2013).
population: The population of Walia Ibex numbered 150–250 individuals between 1966 and 1969 (Nievergelt 1981), increasing slowly until 1983 when there were possibly more than 500 individuals, decreasing again during the period of civil unrest from 1989–1991 (Wale 2016). Geberemedhin et al. (2009) and Grubb (2008) suggested that by 2004 the population had increased to around 500, from lower levels of 200–250 animals in 1994–1996. Ejigu et al. (2013) demonstrated a continuous increase in directly recorded numbers from 680 in 2009 to 790 in 2011 (mean population size from 2009 to 2011 was 752 individuals). In 2012, according to the SMNP annual count, the population of Walia Ibex was estimated at 800–850 individuals (Wale 2016). With the population trend of Ejigu et al. (2017) extrapolated, the 2020 population size might have been over 975 individuals. This projection was the basis of the 2020 assessment and was in line with the 2015 annual count of 865. However as mentioned in the 2020 assessment, the 2019 dry season count recorded only 619 Walia Ibex, with comparable numbers in 2020 and 2021, after which a dramatic decline to 361, 319 and 306 individuals has taken place in 2022, 2023 and 2024 respectively. These total numbers correspond to 185 adults and 63 subadults in 2023 and 194 adults and 51 subadults in 2024 (Scholte et al. 2025).In 2009–2011, Ejigu (2013) found more adult females than other age and sex classes, with females comprising 48.5% of the total population out of which adult females accounted for 38.3%. Males represented 31.4%, and adult males alone 19.4%. Yearlings and kids together constituted 19.2%. The ratio of total and adult only male to female ratio was 1:1.55 and 1:1.97 respectively. These figures changed only slightly in the 2015–2024 counts, with as averages, respectively 45.7 % females of which 36.4 adult females, and 39.3% males, of which 25.3 adult males. Yearlings and kids constituted 17.7%. The ratio of total and adult only male to female ratio was 1:1.15 and 1:1.53 respectively. These oscillations are likely to be based on somewhat different conditions, including observers, of the counts  (Scholte et al. 2025).The 2005–2015 increase in Walia Ibex population size was attributed to the park's expansion through re-demarcation and the expansion of habitat use by the species towards higher altitudes in the southern and southeastern part of the park, and strict conservation of Walia Ibex and its habitat in SMNP both by the local community and the government. The rapid decline that started in 2021 and continues till today (2025), has been attributed to poaching, both for food and medicinal purposes. Fundamental causes were seen as instability as a result of the COVID-19 crisis, the 2021–2022 Ethiopian northern war, and subsequent regional instability that lasts to today (Scholte et al. 2025).
range: The Simien Mountains National Park (SMNP) of Ethiopia is the southernmost limit of Capra species distribution in the world and is the only place where Walia Ibex occurs (Gebremedhin et al. 2009, Nievergelt 2013). Walia Ibex exists in highland massifs of Simien Mountains with altitudes ranging from 2,300 to 4,430 m asl within narrow and restricted habitats (Nievergelt 2013, Gebremedhin et al. 2021, Scholte et al. 2025). Its main distribution range is in steep, rocky and topographically heterogeneous slopes that are not more than 50 km from east to west along the escarpments and with restricted habitat range between the north and the south. Walia Ibex lives in mountainous habitats, montane forest, (sub-)afroalpine grasslands and areas with low vegetation cover. Its restricted distribution range in SMNP is a factor to its small total population (Yalden and Largen 1992, Hurni and Ludi 2000, Gebremedhin et al. 2021). Walia Ibex is an outstanding rock-climber with strong and relatively short legs and hooves that hold the ground well. As infants need additional protection against predators, lactating females prefer habitat ranges in steep and extremely inaccessible cliffs (Nievergelt 1981). The presence of livestock and other human activities in ibex habitat may have a negative effect on its relative abundance and distribution, causing Capra species to select poor habitats (Acevedo et al. 2007, Galvin and Haller 2008.). Large areas of otherwise suitable habitats in SMNP have been abandoned by Walia Ibex as they retreated to the most inaccessible and steepest parts of the National Park (Hurni and Ludi 2000, Ejigu et al. 2015).A century ago, the species used to be widely distributed from Walia Kend and Kidus Yared along the escarpment to Gich and Adi-Arkay (Maydon 1925). At the end of 1960s the main habitat ranges of Walia Ibex were in the central part of the National Park, between Gich camp and Imetgogo (Nievergelt 1981). In the 1970s, the population increased and the distribution was gradually enlarged towards Sankaber and Chenek–Buahit areas. Currently, when applied to the spatial context of quadrats within SMNP, the model indicated that preferred habitats of Walia Ibex occurred from Chenek-Buahit to Mesareria towards the eastern and southeastern parts of the park. Population censuses in 2009–2011 showed that ca 53% of Walia Ibex population occurred in this area of the park of ca 25 km² (Ejigu et al. 2013), increasing to ca 75% recently (Scholte et al. 2025). Applying the definitions of IUCN Red List Mapping Standards, the actual distribution range where the species is extant, is 77 km², in further 8 km² presence is uncertain because of unconfirmed reports of sighting by local people and in 57 km² the species is possibly extinct. The latter refers to areas west of the current extant range, where the species was not recorded in surveys during recent years, as well as the areas Walia Kend and Kidus Yared that were surveyed by Nievergelt (1981), and to the Ras Dejen cliffs mentioned as habitat by Hillman et al. (1977). From all these areas, no observations by local communities or others have been noted for over a decade.
useTrade: Since strict conservation measures are carried out by the Community and Government, currently this species is not legally used or traded.
conservationActions: Walia Ibex is the least known Capra species in the world (Festa-Bianchet 2009, Schwartz 2009). Walia Ibex has been considered one of the most threatened mammals in the world with, until the early 2000s, an alarming decline in number when only a small population was left in the SMNP (Nievergelt 2013). Genetic diversity in the Walia Ibex population is low, which may reduce their immunity to diseases and other environmental stochasticity (Gebremedhin et al. 2009). Socioeconomic aspects of the local community and their participation in conservation activities should be considered to bring changes in conducting sustainable conservation to the degraded Simien Mountains (Hurni and Ludi 2000). Enforcement of conservation policy by law, conservation strategies that could initiate community support and opportunities for the local community to share the available benefits should be designed for effective conservation strategy (EWCA 2019). In 1978, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO declared SMNP a World Heritage Site (Hurni and Ludi 2000; Debonnet et al. 2006; Anonymous 2006), based on its importance for biodiversity conservation and exceptional natural beauty (Debonnet et al. 2006). During its establishment, it was the smallest Park in the country, with an area of only 136 km² (Hurni and Ludi 2000). However, since then the area of the Park was extended gradually to include the main habitats of Walia Ibex. Currently, the park boundary also includes Limalimo, Ras Dejen, some areas in Telemit and Beyeda, with a total area of 412 km² (Anonymous 2009). Thus, conservation of Walia Ibex in SMNP would also benefit the conservation of the endemic Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis), Gelada (Theropithecus gelada) and other species.Over the past decades, conservation measures have been taken in the SMNP, including reduction of human and livestock impact in the park, the effective implementation of park regulations and establishment of a systematic monitoring program. Unfortunately, these measures have been jeopardized by a prolonged period of instability, starting with COVID-19, followed by the war in neighbouring Northern Ethiopia Region, and subsequent instability in Amhara regional state where Simien Mountains NP is located that continues till today (Oct. 2025) (Scholte et al. 2025). Moreover, a detailed ecological and biological study of the species and habitat assessment on the potential new areas for re-establishment of Walia Ibex is needed to ensure sustainable conservation of Walia Ibex in the SMNP and beyond (Gebremedhin et al. 2021).

rationale: Scotophilus heathii is assessed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution and presumed large population. It is distributed across a diverse range, including several protected areas, and is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in a variety of habitat types, including urban areas (G. Csorba pers. comm. 2025). It roosts in old forts, crevices and cracks in old buildings, undisturbed areas (including under roof tiles or corrugated sheets) in houses, among the leaves and crowns of palms, in hollows of trees and among leaves of banana trees either singly or in colonies of up to 100 individuals. It emerges late from roosts, is a relatively low flyer and flies at a steady speed. It has been reported to echolocate using characteristic ‘hockey-stick’ frequency modulated calls with a quasi-constant frequency component at the end, with a frequency of maximum energy ranging from 34–43 kHz (Győrössy et al. 2024, Srinivasulu et al. 2025). One or two young ones are born after a gestation period of 115 days (Bates and Harrison 1997).
threats: There are no known major threats to this widespread species. It may be locally threatened in some areas because of disturbance of roosting sites. In many areas of South India, green spaces (especially containing palm and banana trees) have been modified to make way for residential developments, resulting in the loss of suitable roosting sites (Srinivasulu, C., pers. obs. 2025). Specific threats to island populations of this species on Hainan, Sri Lanka, and Sulawesi are unknown.
population: There are no specific data on the species’ population size and trend. However, given its widespread distribution and its common occurrence across its range, the population is inferred to be large and stable. It is plausibly organized in numerous subpopulations. There is no evidence to suggest a decline in the number of subpopulations or extreme fluctuations in its population size or the number of locations.
range: This widespread species is found through much of South Asia, southern China and mainland Southeast Asia, from 0-1,500 m asl. In South Asia, it is presently known from Afghanistan (Nangarhar and Laghman provinces), Bangladesh (Sylhet division), India (Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, Orissa, Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal), Nepal (Central, Far Western, South Central, and mid-Western Nepal), Pakistan (North West Frontier Province and Punjab) and Sri Lanka (Central, North Central, Northern, North Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, Uva, and Western Provinces) (Myers et al. 2000; Khan 2001; Molur et al. 2002; Das 2003; Vanitharani  2006; Srinivasulu and Srinivasulu 2005, 2012; Benda and Gailser 2015). It ranges across southern China, including Hainan Island (Smith and Xie 2008). In Southeast Asia, the species ranges through Myanmar, northern Thailand, Lao PDR, Vietnam and northern Cambodia. The populations on Sulawesi (Indonesia) were thought to represent a distinct species Scotophilus celebensis Sody, 1928 but have been synonymized under S. heathii following Tu et al. (2021).
useTrade: This species is not known to be used or traded.
conservationActions: Across its range, this species has been recorded from some protected areas, but there are no direct species-specific conservation measures in place. Research needs include investigations on this species’ population size and trends, distribution, abundance, life history and ecology, and on the threats it faces.

rationale: The Juan Fernández Fur Seal does not meet any criteria for a threatened category within the IUCN Red List system. However, confirmed breeding is currently limited to just the three islands comprising the Juan Fernández Archipelago. The species hauls-out on the Desventuradas Islands but is not known to breed at this site. Thus, the terrestrial range includes a total of five islands (three with breeding colonies and two with only haul-out sites). These are the only landmasses ever reported to be inhabited by the species and no nearby alternative islands are available for potential colonization. Coastal sightings in Chile, Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador are considered extralimital records. It is a concern that over half of the population is concentrated on just one island— Alejandro Selkirk Island— making the species particularly vulnerable to local perturbations. Since the species’ rediscovery in 1960, population numbers have increased nearly a hundredfold and are now estimated to be in excess of 200,000 animals. This indicates a clear and encouraging positive trend in population growth. Given the increasing population trend, the approximate number of mature individuals, and the species’ current extent of occurrence, the Juan Fernández Fur Seal should remain classified as Least Concern based on the IUCN Red List criteria.
habitat: Juan Fernandez Fur Seals are sexually dimorphic, with males being much larger than females. Coloration of females is typically gray-brown to dark brown whereas males are mostly dark brown with the exception of the head crown and shoulders which are lighter gray with golden-tipped thick guard hairs on the back of the head, neck and shoulders (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018, Folkens and Reeves 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Adult males can reach 2.1 m in length and weight 140 kg, whereas adult females reach on average 1.5 m and weight between 45-50 kg (Torres 1987, Francis et al. 1998, Osman 2007). A distinctive characteristic of the species, present in both males and females, is a long muzzle with a slight downward curve at the tip (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018). Overall, there is a 50:50 female-to-male ratio across all three islands, consistent with patterns reported in other Fur Seal species (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022). However, this balance is not uniform if individual colonies are considered, breeding territories are primarily occupied by small groups of females, with only a few dominant males, while non-breeding areas across all islands have a greater presence of subordinate males and juveniles (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Harem composition today differs from early assessments. Torres et al. (1985), counted four females per territorial male in harems that occupied approximately 36m2 or 43m2 (Francis and Boness 1991). More recently, the density of animals has increased and the number of females per territorial male in the most dense areas such as “Loberia” on Selkirk Island has doubled to eight females per male (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Harem stability and female distribution is affected by how often females move to the water. This is driven by temperature, particularly during the summer. On sunny days females move to the water on average between 2-3 times per day (Francis and Boness 1991). This has led to males developing “male aquatic territoriality” with some males exclusively defending aquatic areas that are on average 2-10 m deep and four times larger than those on land (179 m2, Francis and Boness 1991).The reproductive cycle of Arctocephalus philippii follows an annual pattern, with females giving birth to a single pup each year. Most births take place between October and December, and the sexually active period extends from mid-November to late January (Francis et al. 1998, Ochoa-Acuña et al. 1999, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Lactation lasts at least seven months but is somewhat variable. Observations in the field suggest that pups are weaned sometime between their seventh and tenth month (Francis et al. 1998).Information on mortality within this species remains scarce. Early assessments estimated that pup mortality rates were 8.2% on Alejandro Selkirk Island and 4.5% on Robinson Crusoe Island, though the underlying causes were not specified (Torres 1987). More recent research conducted by Sepúlveda (1998) in the 1990s identified two primary factors contributing to pup deaths: trauma resulting from aggressive interactions among individuals (38%) and starvation (28%). Precise nursing/foraging movement patterns is not well known. But, approximately 11 days after giving birth, females embark on their first foraging trip (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018). Mean trip durations are the longest reported in any Fur Seal species. Mean trip duration has been reported to be 12.2 (Francis et al. 1998) or 28 days (Osman et al. 2007). Regardless which of these numbers is closest to being the norm, Juan Fernandez Fur Seal females also spend longer mean time periods ashore compared to other Fur Seals, averaging 5-8 days (Francis et al. 1998, Osman 2007). Due to the extended foraging cycles, pups experience long fasting periods. Milk delivered during the first month has a high fat (41%) and energy content (17.95 kj/g), the highest among otariid seals (Fur Seals and Sea Lions) (Ochoa-Acuña et al. 1999). Animals forage hundreds to thousands of kilometers from their breeding areas, feeding extensively in the waters of the Humboldt Current System in coastal Chile (Osman 2007). Females perform shallow dives (mean depth of 12.3m) with a median dive duration of 0.33 minute (range of 0.1-5.1 minutes, Osman 2007). Target prey consists mainly of cephalopods and myctophid fish (Ochoa-Acuna and Francis 1995, Díaz 2007) according to diet studies conducted on hard remains analyses (Díaz 2007, Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025).Breeding habitats vary among the islands. The largest breeding grounds for the species are located on the western side of Alejandro Selkirk Island, where approximately three kilometers of flat, accessible beaches provide ideal conditions for reproduction (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). These breeding areas extend toward the mountains, ranging from 50 to 300 meters inland. The rest of the island is dominated by rocks that limit habitability. Robinson Crusoe and Santa Clara Islands have limited beach-like habitats suitable for breeding, with most areas already at capacity. The majority of their coastlines consist of narrow, rocky, and highly exposed areas. Some breeding does occur in rocky areas, but such areas are not ideal breeding habitats (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025).
threats: There is abundant historical evidence of the exploitation that this species endured between the late 17th and late 19th century, which led to a severe population decline (Goldsworthy et al. 2000). It is estimated that nearly 4,000,000 Juan Fernandez Fur Seals were killed during this period (Hubbs and Norris 1971), highlighting the species’ vulnerability to overexploitation.Although the population has recovered and continues to increase, current numbers remain well below pre-sealing estimates. Breeding individuals are now restricted to a limited geographic range—specifically, the three islands of the Juan Fernández Archipelago. This restricted breeding distribution makes the species vulnerable to catastrophic events such as disease outbreaks, climate change, and impacts from industrial fisheries (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018, Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). For instance, ocean warming in the North Pacific could reduce marine productivity, disrupting the coastal food webs on which the species depends (Kovacs et al. 2012). As a result, climate change and rising ocean temperatures are considered direct threats to this and other Fur Seal species (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018).Another significant threat is interaction with industrial fisheries. The archipelago is currently a protected area where industrial fishing is prohibited near the colonies, but given the wide foraging range of the species and the extended time periods that females spend offshore, they are at risk of bycatch and other harmful interactions with pelagic fisheries operating beyond the protected areas (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Bycatch of Juan Fernandez Fur Seals has been reported in the drift net fishery for swordfish that operates in northern Chile (Zárate et al. 2021) where a total of 57 individuals were reported as bycatch between 2001 and 2020.At present, local fisheries and artisanal fishing communities do not pose a threat to the species and no negative interactions have been reported in the last decade (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022). However, there is a perception in the local community of the archipelago that the increasing Fur Seal population could lead to future conflicts both in terms of space use on land and potential overlap in targeted prey species between seals and fishermen (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, 2025). Entanglement in fishing gear has decreased significantly compared to earlier decades (Osman 2007), likely due to the removal of industrial fisheries from protected areas (Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Nevertheless, this remains a potential threat (Aurioles-Gamboa and Trillmich 2018).Pollution and heavy metal contamination are additional concerns. Studies have detected concentrations of mercury, cadmium, and lead in the livers and feces of Juan Fernandez Fur Seals (Sepúlveda et al. 1997, Toro-Valdivieso et al. 2023). In addition, microplastic fiber concentrations have been found in scats of Juan Fernandez Fur Seals (3.7 ± 4.7 fibers g−1 and 3.1 ± 3.3 fragments g−1). These values represent the highest concentrations of microplastic found to date in otariids distributed in continental coastal areas of Chile and Peru (Perez-Venegas et al. 2020). Their diet is suspected to be the primary source of cadmium/mercury accumulation (Toro-Valdivieso et al. 2023), and microplastics (Perez-Venegas et al. 2020), though further research and long-term monitoring are needed to identify the sources of these contaminants that are finding their way into the Fur Seals’ food.On the islands of the archipelago that are inhabited by humans—Robinson Crusoe and Alejandro Selkirk—a growing concern for the seals is the increasing number of domestic animals. Attacks on Juan Fernández Fur Seals by dogs have been reported, and 90.4% of respondents in a local survey regarding seal conservation support preventive measures such as responsible ownership (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Although a municipal ordinance regulates pet ownership in Chile, enforcement has proven insufficient to fully prevent interactions with wildlife (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Reports of interactions between domestic animals - dogs, cats, and cattle - and seal colonies date back to Osman and Pavés (2007), who warned of the risk of disease transmission and recommended fencing around all seal colonies near towns. While fencing has had limited success in excluding cattle from Alejandro Selkirk, it has been effective in protecting similar species elsewhere (Cassini et al. 2004).Finally, the ongoing global crisis caused by highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) has not yet been evaluated for Juan Fernandez Fur Seals. This virus has been the cause of mass mortality events observed in other pinnipeds of South America (South American sea lion, Otaria flavescens, Ulloa et al. 2023, Plaza et al. 2024, Szteren and Franco-Trecu 2024, de Lima et al. 2025) as well as deaths in southern elephant seals, Mirounga leonina, Campagna et al. 2023) and South American fur seals (Arctocephalus australis, Leguia et al. 2023, Tomás et al. 2024). The rapid evolution of this virus in Chile (Godoy et al. 2023) warrants consideration of H5N1 as a major threat for the Juan Fernandez Fur Seal, particularly because of the species endemic nature, restricted breeding distribution, and the current high population density.
population: Intense commercial sealing between the late 17th and late 18th centuries harvested millions of individuals, severely depleting the population (Hubbs and Norris 1971). By the end of the 18th century, fewer than 400 seals were thought to remain, and by 1900, the species was presumed extinct (King 1954). However, in 1960, a small remnant colony of approximately 200 individuals was rediscovered on Alejandro Selkirk Island (Bahamonde 1966). The first comprehensive population survey was conducted in 1970 reporting a total of 750 individuals (Aguayo-Lobo et al. 1971, Aguayo et al. 1979). By 2005, estimates indicated a substantial increase to approximately 32,278 individuals on land after only 35 years (Osman 2007). More recent field assessments in 2021/2022 confirmed a population expansion to approximately 183,500 individuals present on land (observed: Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). During 2021/2022, pup production was estimated to be circa 71,000 live pups, nearly seven times the number recorded by Osman (2007) only two decades earlier (2005 = 10,998). The total number of adult/subadult individuals (without including pups) observed on land within the archipelago, was 112,298 individuals (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Historically, population assessments for Juan Fernandez Fur Seals have used absolute counts (animals present in the archipelago, observed animals) rather than modelling total population size (i.e. which generally incorporate estimates of animals at sea). Using indexes from closely related species, estimatess of the total population using demographic models to account for individuals not present on the archipelago during surveys, suggests the overall population may now range between 280,000 and 300,000 individuals (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). There is currently no accurate estimation of the proportion of mature individuals in the population. But, it can be assumed that the total number of live pups observed on land roughly corresponds to the number of reproductive females in the population (present in the archipelago during surveys or not). Based on the 2021/2022 census (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025), which recorded approximately 71,000 live pups, it is reasonable to infer that at least 71,000 reproductive females exist. Second, assuming a 1:1 female-to-male ratio for the species (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025) a similar number of mature, males also likely exist. Consequently, the minimum estimated number of mature individuals across the entire population would be at least 142,000. This figure should be regarded strictly as a minimum estimate of mature individuals present in the population.Ten archipelago-wide surveys have been conducted in the last 55 years. All three metapopulations—Alejandro Selkirk, Robinson Crusoe, and Santa Clara—are increasing, although the overall rate of increase is slowing down (Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). The maximum observed population growth rates (Rmax) for Alejandro Selkirk (0.121), Robinson Crusoe (0.16), and Santa Clara (0.218) align with rates documented in other Fur Seal species (Wickens and York 1997, Hucke-Gaete et al. 2004).Different population growth trajectories across the islands may in part be attributed to available breeding habitat. Robinson Crusoe and Santa Clara exhibited near-exponential growth until 2017, reaching maximum recorded population sizes of 61,831 and 24,200 individuals, respectively. However, these sites have exhibited slowed growth in subsequent years, although numbers continue to increase at both of these islands. This trend is likely driven by spatial limitations, as available coastal habitat for breeding on these islands appears to have reached saturation. By contrast, Alejandro Selkirk Island has continued to expand without apparent constraints. The population there has nearly doubled (2021-22= 109,000 individuals) since the previous peak recorded in 2010 (61,909 individuals, Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). In contrast to Robinson Crusoe and Santa Clara, the western side of Alejandro Selkirk Island offers expansive sandy terrain that provides ample, protected breeding grounds (Osman 2007, Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025).
range: The Juan Fernandez Fur Seal is endemic to the Juan Fernández Archipelago, located approximately 700 km off the coast of Valparaíso, Chile. This archipelago consists of three primary islands where the species is known to breed: Robinson Crusoe (33.6414° S, 78.8461° W), Santa Clara (33.7074° S, 78.9444° W), and Alejandro Selkirk (33.7511° S, 80.7833° W). The population is distributed across the archipelago and although reproductive colonies are present on all three islands, Alejandro Selkirk Island sustains more than half of the total population (60%; Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025) followed by Robinson Crusoe (27%) and Santa Clara (13%; Borras-Chavez et al. 2022, Borras-Chavez et al. 2025). Notably, 45% of the total population occurs within just 3 km of coastline and an estimate area of 0.4 km2 (a sector called Loberia-El Tongo).  Across the Juan Fernández Archipelago there are a total of 27 breeding sites, and 14 non-breeding haul-out sites. Up until 2022, Robinson Crusoe hosted the highest number of breeding sites (18), alongside six non-breeding sites. Alejandro Selkirk Island has three breeding sites and eight non-breeding sites, whereas Santa Clara Island features six breeding sites but no non-breeding sites. Historical records, from the sealing era, suggest that breeding colonies likely also existed on two small islands located roughly 800 km north of Robinson Crusoe—the “Desventuradas Islands” (San Ambrosio and San Félix Island). However, recent surveys (i.e., within the current century) have not documented the presence of newborn individuals on these small islands, only aggregations of adult Fur Seals have been observed (Hubbs and Norris 1971, Torres 1987, Endémica NGO 2022, Personal Communication).Vagrant records were summarized by Aurioles-Gamboa (2015) including animals at: Punta San Juan, Peru (Majluf and Reyes 1989), Buenaventura Port, Colombia (Avila et al. 2014), and sighting records along the Chilean coast (King 1983, Osman 2007). Additionally, in June 2019, a Juan Fernandez Fur Seal was sighted in the Galapagos Islands at Playa de Oro, Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, San Cristóbal Island, Ecuador (Páez-Rosas et al. 2020, Alava et al. 2022).Little is known about the at-sea range of Juan Fernandez Fur Seals, but Osman et al. (2007) reported an average foraging trip length of 28 days with average distances travelled of 1,394 ± 877 km, which is extreme for a Fur Seal. Some females venture hundreds of kilometers, in extreme cases even 1000s of kilometers (mean distance 653 km) away from their breeding sites to forage (Francis et al. 1998). Tracking records document females foraging in deep oceanic waters over 550 km to the southwest and west of the Juan Fernandez Archipelago (Francis et al. 1998). Individuals reach the Chilean continental shelf near Concepción (1,850 km from the archipelago), while others travel even farther south, reaching Chiloé Island and the Corcovado Gulf, approximately 2,900 km from their breeding sites (Osman 2007).
useTrade: The Juan Fernandez Fur Seal was driven to near extintion during the 18th and 19th centuries (Hubbs and Norris 1971) and was in fact thought to be extinct in early 1900s (King 1954). The species has experience a remarkable recovery. It is still protected from hunting under chilean law, so trade is not a current issue of concern. Decree N° 225 (first published in 1995), prohibits the capture and hunting of any species of pinnipeds in Chile, including the Juan Fernandez Fur Seal. Furthermore, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) classified A. philippii under Appendix II; species that are not currently threatened but may face risks of rapid decline if exploitation is permitted.
conservationActions: Chilean Decree Number 225, first published in 1995, prohibits the capture and hunting of all pinniped species in Chile, including Juan Fernandez Fur Seals. In addition, the Law of Fisheries and Aquaculture (Law 18,892) regulates the bycatch of marine mammals in fisheries and aquaculture activities, which also contributes to the protection of this species.Regional initiatives aimed at protecting the Juan Fernández Archipelago also indirectly safeguard the Juan Fernández Fur Seal. In 2022, the archipelago was designated as an “Important Marine Mammal Area” by the IUCN (IUCN-IMMA), a recognition that prioritizes the conservation of the archipelago’s natural resources and, by extension, the Juan Fernández Fur Seal. Furthermore, the Marine Park called “Mar de Juan Fernández,” created in 2018, covers 262,000 km², including the waters surrounding the archipelago and a significant portion of Chile’s Exclusive Economic Zone. This marine park operates under a no-take policy, fully protecting the resources within its boundaries. Additionally, a Multiple-Use Marine Protected Area, established in 2016 and expanded in 2018, lies adjacent to the Mar de Juan Fernández Marine Park. Within this area, three out of the five smaller marine parks—Lobería Selkirk, El Arenal and Tierras Blancas—directly protect critical breeding and non-breeding sites of the Juan Fernández Fur Seal.

rationale: The Grey Seal currently occupies the same geographic distribution that it did in the late 19th century. Although some areas of the 19th century range were temporarily extirpated in the past, they have been recolonized over the past 40-50 years and Grey Seal abundance has increased in all regions in the past several decades. Total abundance globally is more than 600,000 and has not decreased since the last assessment. However, juvenile survival and pup production suggest that resource limitation has greatly slowed population growth in the Northwest Atlantic. Populations in the Baltic Sea, after decades of extremely low numbers, have increased rapidly in the past 20 years. Grey Seals do not meet IUCN criteria for any threatened category and they should remain classified as Least Concern globally.
habitat: Grey Seals are a large sexually dimorphic phocid. Northwest Atlantic Grey Seals are significantly larger than Northeast Atlantic animals. In the UK, adult males are on average 2 m long and weigh 233 kg, with a maximum of 310 kg. Adult females average 1.8 m and 155 kg. At birth, pups are 90-105 cm, with male pups averaging 15.8 kg and female pups averaging 14.8 kg in weight (Bonner 1981). Weaning weights average 40 kg for males and 35.8 -39.6 kg for females. In the Northwest Atlantic adult males are on average 2.1 m long and weigh 267 kg, with a maximum of 370 kg (Bowen unpublished data). Adult females average 1.9 m in length and weigh 186 kg with a maximum of 256 kg (Iverson et al.1993). Newborn pups average 16.6 kg or about 14% of maternal body mass (Mellish et al. 1999). In North America pups are heavier at birth than pups born in the UK and are 25% heavier at weaning, when male pups average 56.2 kg and females 51.6 kg, (measured for pups born on the ice near Amet Island - Haller et al. 1996). At Sable Island male pups weigh 56.6 and females weigh 54.5 kg at weaning (Bowen et al.2006). Baltic Grey Seal pups weigh about 12 kg at birth, but weaning mass differs between ice-born pups (48.3) and those born on land (37.4) (Jussi et al. 2008). Survival to the time of recruitment into the breeding population is positively related to pup size at weaning (Bowen et al. 2015).Lactation lasts 15-18 days on average, with ice breeders having slightly shorter lactation periods than land breeders; weaning is abrupt (Kovacs 1987, Haller et al. 1996, Bowen et al. 2006). Pre-weaning mortality of Grey Seal pups varies widely between colonies; it is usually between 5 and 20% but can be as high as 30% (Bowen et al. 2007, Hammill et al. 2014). Pup mortality rates are influenced by habitat quality, birth site, quality of maternal care, injuries resulting from male-male aggression and to a lesser extent predation by Greater and Lesser Black-backed Gulls (Larus marinus and L. fuscus) on weak, unprotected, pups, or pups born on the periphery of colonies (Baker and Baker 1988, Twiss et al. 2003).In the Baltic, pre-weaning mortality is low for pups born on ice, but varies between 5 and 30% on land, depending on pupping density (Jussi et al. 2008). The main predators in this region are White-tailed Eagles (Haliaeetus albicilla) and Greater Black-backed Gulls.In the UK, females give birth on land and show considerable site fidelity (Pomeroy et al. 1994), although this is not universally observed (Weitzman et al. 2017). Mothers typically stay with their pups until weaning (Boness and James 1979), but are rarely more than a few meters away from water at some UK colonies (Twiss et al. 1994). Reproductive performance of adult females varies with age and body mass. Females show evidence of reduced reproductive success, caused by senescence when they are 20 years of age and older (Bowen et al.2006).In the Gulf of St Lawrence, females that give birth on the ice spend about 72% of their time hauled out during lactation, nursing the pup every 2-3 hours. From the time of birth until weaning, females lose about 5.7 kg per day (Lydersen et al. 1994). Females in the UK lose an average of 65 kg over the lactation period (Fedak and Anderson 1982), whereas the somewhat larger females in the Northwest Atlantic lose an average of 75 kg (Haller et al. 1996, Mellish et al. 1999). Females come into estrus around the time of weaning (Boness et al. 1982). Females are at their lowest weight following the moulting period, averaging 126.2 kg in Canadian colonies; by the beginning of the next pupping period they again average 210 kg (Beck et al.2003a).Adult male Grey Seals come ashore about the time the first pups are born (Boness and James 1979, Bonner 1981). Their average age when first coming into the colony as breeders is 9-10 years at Sable Island (Manske et al. 2002). Males spend large amounts of time out of the water fasting during the breeding season. Some males go to sea for periods of 2-3 days while others remain hauled out for the entire breeding season (Lidgard et al. 2003). Males do not defend a fixed territory, but stay near a particular group of females (Lidgard et al. 2001). Breeding age males lose less weight per day than lactating females, but because they are ashore for an average of 36 days, up to an extreme of 57 days, they can experience considerable loss of mass (Anderson and Fedak 1985, Lidgard et al. 2005, Tinker et al. 1995).Pupping dates differ significantly between populations: peak dates in the Northwest Atlantic are in January; in the Northeast Atlantic peak dates vary between September and December in different areas. In the Baltic Sea peak pupping is in late February to early March, which coincides with the annual maximum ice coverage. Differences in pupping seasons may keep the subpopulations reproductively isolated (Bonner 1981). Pupping seasons may be plastic and sensitive to environmental changes. In the Northwest Atlantic, peak pupping advanced more than two weeks from early January to late December while the population was rapidly growing in the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, suggesting that pupping dates may move forward when resources are plentiful (Bowen et al. 2020). They now appear to be shifting later in the season once again, under strong intraspecific competition for resources (den Heyer et al. unpublished data). Pups are born on land in the Northeast Atlantic, and can be born on either ice or land in the Northwest Atlantic and in the Baltic (Bonner 1981, Baker et al. 1995). Pups are born with a woolly white lanugo that is moulted around the time of weaning. Pups stay on land from birth until the moult is finished (Noren et al. 2008), although some pups on small, exposed beaches often swim for short periods before moulting (Kovacs 1987). During the post weaning fast pups lose up to 25% of their body mass (Noren et al. 2008). In the United Kingdom, adult females moult from mid-January to mid-February, and males moult from mid-February through until early April. In Canada, the moult is later, with females moulting in May-June and males about a month later (Beck et al. 2003a). Peak moulting season for Baltic seals is the last week of May to the second week in June.Grey Seals are shallow, short-duration divers. Most adult diving is shallower than 120 m and less than 8 min (Beck et al. 2003b). Female’s dives are on average slightly longer (5.5 min.) than those of males (4.9 min.), although males tend to dive somewhat deeper (57 m compared to 49 m) (Beck et al. 2003b). On the Scotian Shelf in Canada, maximum dives recorded were 412 m for males, and 354 m for females (Beck et al. 2003b). Typically in the United Kingdom, dives are shorter averaging 4-10 min (max. 30 min.) and involve diving to shallow seabeds with most dives being less than 60 m, though dives to 200 m occur in some areas (Thompson et al. 1991).Grey Seals are not long-distance migrants. In Europe, tracking of individual seals has shown that they can feed up to several hundred kilometres offshore during short foraging trips lasting 2.3 days on average (McConnell et al. 1999). Individual Grey Seals, based at specific haulout sites, often make repeated trips to the same region offshore but will occasionally move to a new haulout and begin foraging in a new region. Movements of Grey Seals between haul-outs in the North Sea and the Shetland Isles, Outer Hebrides, and Faeroe Islands have been recorded. During foraging trips Grey Seals often target areas with fine gravel/coarse sandy sea-bed sediments, which are the preferred habitat of Sandeels (Ammodytes sp.), an important part of the Grey Seal’s diet. Satellite telemetry data from Canada show that Grey Seals perform much longer foraging trips (averaging 5-12 days) and often travel much larger distances than European Grey Seals (Breed et al. 2009). Foraging trip characteristics differ seasonally and by sex. Females typically fed closer to haulouts than males and spent more time foraging at these patches (Breed et al. 2009). Grey Seals in Canada also exhibit pronounced seasonal sex segregation in foraging distribution (Breed et al.2006). In the Baltic Sea, Grey Seals make short trips, spending roughly 75% of their time within 50 km of haulout sites (Sjøberg and Ball 2000).Grey Seals are generalist predators, consuming a wide range of prey species, although typically fewer than 10 species comprise most of the diet in a given area (Bowen and Siniff 1999). Grey Seal diet varies by season and location, though all Grey Seals tend to be demersal or benthic feeders (Bowen et al. 1993, Hall 2002). At times in Canada and the North Sea, the food consumed by Grey Seals can be over 50% Sandeels, although several dozen species are eaten (Bowen and Harrison 1994, Hammond et al.1994, Beck et al.2007). In Iceland, where 15 species make up the majority of the diet, the most common stomach contents by weight are Atlantic Cod (Gadus morhua) 24%, Sandeels 23%, Catfish (Wolf-fish Anarhichas lupus) 15%, and Saithe (Pollachius virens) 11% (Hauksson and Bogason 1997). At the Faroes, adults feed on Cod and Catfish, while subadults feed on Sandeels and Saithe (Mikkelsen et al. 2002). In the United Kingdom, Sandeels, Atlantic Cod (Gadus morhua) and Dover Sole (Solea solea) account for 56% of the diet by weight. Grey seals also eat other flatfish, including Dab (Limanda limanda), Flounder (Platichthys plessus) and Plaice (Pleuronectes platessa) (Prime and Hammond 1990). In the Outer Hebrides, gadids account for 40% or more of the diet (Ling, Molva molva), Atlantic Cod and Whiting (Merlangius merlangus)); Sandeels are less important in this area (Hammond et al. 1994). In Canada, the dominant prey species consumed by Seals differs by season, sex, and age-class; however, Sandeels and Redfish (Sebastes sp.) together accounted for between 40% and 91% of the diet in all seasons, for both sexes, and across age-classes (Bowen and Harrison 1994). Pollock (Pollachius virens), and flounders (Turbot Reinhardtius hippoglossoides; Witch Glyptocephalus cynoglossus; and Yellowtail Limanda ferruginea) account for more than 10% of the diet in some demographic groups within seasons (Beck et al. 2007). Atlantic Cod is also consumed and can be an important part of the diet in some areas and seasons (Hammill et al. 2014).
threats: Grey Seals have been important in subsistence harvests in coastal areas within their range throughout history. They have been hunted in the Baltic Sea for more than 10,000 years (Härkönen et al. 2005). Commercial harvesting has been ongoing in many areas for hundreds of years, and at times Grey Seals have been important to local economies (Mansfield 1988). Over-harvesting in the Baltic in the early 20th century led to a large decline; this population once numbered somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000, but was reduced to about 20,000 in the 1940s. A further decline to 1,500-2,000 seals was caused by high loads of PCB (Harding and Härkönen 1999).Government culls, bounties and licensed kills for protection of fishing gear have been put into effect in many countries and continue to be used to control Grey Seal numbers and reduce their impact on commercially important coastal fisheries (i.e., salmonid fisheries). Grey Seals feed on a number of commercial species, and by entering nets to depredate catches as well as damaging nets and traps they are in direct conflict with fisheries. They also are vectors for parasites that can impact on the economics of some fisheries (ICES 2005).Entanglement in commercial fishing nets causes by-catch mortality in most parts of the Grey Seals’ range (Woodley and Lavigne 1991, Nilssen et al. 2019), though the level is not well known (DFO 2023). In a broad review of seal bycatch mortality, Woodley and Lavigne (1991) suggested that 1-2% of UK Grey Seals less than one year old die in fishing gear. By-catch levels are approximately 300 per year in Swedish fisheries in the Baltic (ICES 2005). A Norwegian study from 1975-1998 reported the death of 259 seals, primarily animals less than a year old, which represented 7% of the tagged animals in the region (Bjørge et al. 2002). An additional 363 were reported as bycatch between 2006 and 2020 (Moan & Bjørge 2021). Photographic analysis of Grey Seals at haulout sites on Cape Cod, Massachusetts revealed 5-8% of Seals exhibited signs of entanglement (Sette et al. 2009). In the US commercial fisheries there was an average annual mortality of 853 Grey Seals reported for the period 2006-2010 (Waring et al. 2013). For the period 2008-2012, the total estimated human caused mortality (and serious injury to) Grey Seals was 4,533 per year of which about 1,000 were taken in US observed fisheries, about 400 in the Canadian hunt, 90 taken by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) in scientific collections, and about 3,000 were killings of nuisance animals in Canada (DFO 2011). Most mortality categories for Grey Seals in the Northwest Atlantic appear to have been stable in recent years in Canada (DFO 2023, Precoda and Orphanides 2024), but the largest fraction of the take (nuisance permits in Canada) are no longer permitted and are assumed to have dropped to zero. Grey Seals are known carriers of phocine distemper virus (PDV), in all populations (Ross et al. 1992, Duignan et al. 1995, Härkönen et al. 2006). However, they have suffered almost no mortality from the disease, in marked contrast to Harbour Seals (Phoca vitulina). Härkönen et al. (2006) report Grey Seal mortality of approximately 230 (equal to 1% of the Harbour Seal mortality) in the 1988 epizootic in Europe and the death of 30 Grey Seal pups in the Baltic were attributed to PDV. Because Grey Seals haulout with Harbour Seals in the Wadden Sea and are known to travel more widely than the more sedentary Harbour Seal, it is presumed that they had a role in the outbreak and spread of the 2002 epizootic of PDV (Härkönen et al. 2006).More recently, avian flu has become a concern for phocid seals worldwide, and surveillance monitoring and pathology testing of stranded animals has detected both low and high pathogenicity strains circulating in both the Northeast and Northwest Atlantic Grey Seal populations (Mirolo et al. 2023, Lair et al. 2024, Guilfoyle et al. 2025). These infections are causing potentially significant levels of mortality, but neither the level of mortality once infected nor the degree Grey Seals are susceptible to infection is currently understood.Grey Seals are exposed to agricultural pollutants through the food chain in their coastal ranges, some of which biomagnify. PCBs and DDT contaminant loads are extremely high in Baltic Grey Seals, despite the fact that tissue burdens have declined since the 1970s. Analysis of samples collected from 1996 to 1998 indicated that Grey Seals still had very heavy loads of contaminants when compared to other Seals outside the Baltic (ICES 2005). More recently these loads have been decreasing, but are still higher than Grey Seals elsewhere (Britt-Marie et al. 2021).Health effects on Grey Seals have been suggested to be linked to their high exposures to PCBs and DDT. Baltic Grey Seals have a relatively high rate of colonic ulcers associated with hookworm infestations, which are sometimes fatal. This condition is not found elsewhere (ICES 2005, Britt-Marie et al. 2021).
