Uterine stenosis and a host of other pathologies in other organs have been attributed to long-term exposure to environmental toxics, particularly in older Baltic Grey Seals. These are specifically linked to reproductive and population declines for this subspecies and are conditions not seen in other populations (Bergman et al. 2001). However, unlike organopollutants, no negative effects have been attributed to heavy metal contaminants in Baltic Grey Seals (Bergman et al. 2001, ICES 2005).Grey Seals live close to human population centres and shipping lanes and spend much of their time in the vicinity of favourite haulout locations. Spilled oil from vessel accidents and other sources have fouled Grey Seal sites since at least the 1940s (St. Aubin 1990). Despite numerous records of oiled animals and occasional reports of dead animals coated in oil, or animals having ingested oil, it has not been determined whether those mortalities are attributable to contact with oil (St. Aubin 1990). Grey Seals are generalist predators, and their populations have increased in recent decades during periods of declines of some commercial fish stocks that are important Grey Seal prey. The risks of over-fishing induced declines of fish stocks to Grey Seal populations that feed on these stocks is unclear. An ongoing threat is the potential for governments to impose large culls or other lethal control of Grey Seal populations to help rebuild fisheries stocks that are affected by, or simply perceived to be affected by, Grey Seals.
population: Available data on Grey Seal abundance indicate that the Northeast Atlantic population numbers approximately 180,000, most of which are found in UK territorial waters; with Grey Seals increasing in this region (SCOS 2021, Brasseur et al. 2021, ICES 2022). This Northeast Atlantic population also includes the Baltic Sea subpopulation, which was severely threatened in the late 20th century, but currently numbers approximately 50,000 and is increasing (ICES 2022, Carroll et al.2024). The Northwest Atlantic population numbers approximately 395,000 and is stable (Wood et al.2022, DFO 2023). The total worldwide population is 625,000 and contains circa 313,000 mature animals. The current global population trend is increasing. Note that the current global estimate is smaller than the previous IUCN Red List assessment (2016) had suggested, not because the global population has decreased, but because of a downward revision in the 2016 Canadian population estimate (DFO 2023).
range: Grey Seals have a cold temperate to sub-Arctic distribution in North Atlantic waters over the continental shelf (Hall 2002). There are three populations isolated both geographically and by the timing of reproduction (Bonner 1981); mtDNA and nuclear DNA differences are large between these three breeding areas, though the Baltic and Northeast Atlantic populations are much closer to one another than to the Northwest Atlantic population (Boskovic et al. 1996, McCarthy et al. 2025). In the western Atlantic, the population is centered on the eastern Scotian Shelf off northeastern North America, but Grey Seals there range from the Gulf of Maine to southern Labrador, including the Gulf of St Lawrence (Lesage and Hammill 2001). The northeast Atlantic population is concentrated around the UK and Ireland but is also found around Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and along the European mainland coast from the Kola Peninsula south to southern Norway, and from Denmark to Brittany in France. The Baltic Sea subpopulation is confined to the Baltic Sea (Bonner 1981, Hall 2002). Vagrants are known from as far south as New Jersey in the western Atlantic and Portugal in the eastern Atlantic (Rice 1998).
useTrade: Grey Seals have been important in subsistence harvests in coastal areas within their range throughout history. Currently Grey Seals are protected in the USA under the Marine Mammal Protection Act and in Canada under the Fisheries Act. Nevertheless, there is a management plan that permits commercial harvesting of Grey Seals in Canadian waters. Relatively few Seals are taken each year (DFO 2023). Grey Seal pups were taken in Orkney until the early 1980s, partly for commercial exploitation and partly as a population control measure. Large-scale culls of Grey Seals in the North Sea, Orkney, and Hebrides were carried out in the 1960s and 1970s as population control measures. In Norway, hunting quotas are set within the context of a Grey Seal management plan and bounties have also been paid to reduce numbers in areas where there are conflicts with fisheries (Nilssen and Haug 2007). Hunting of Grey Seals has been permitted in Iceland in the past (Hauksson 2007), but a general ban on seal hunting was introduced in 2019, with only limited exceptions for subsistence use. In the Faroe Islands, licenses to kill Grey Seals have been issued for the purpose of protecting marine fish farming in the past, but these were discontinued in 2020 (Mikkelsen and Hoydal 2021).
conservationActions: Numerous countries have invoked protective measures to limit Grey Seal harvests, culls, disturbance, and by-catch (Bonner 1981, ICES 2005, Mikkelsen and Hoydal 2021, DFO 2023). Pollutant loads in Baltic Grey Seals have declined following regulations banning the use and discharge of toxic pollutants such as DDT and PCBs beginning in the 1970s, and as a result of these and other conservation efforts the Baltic Sea population has grown rapidly in recent years to over 40,000 animals. Establishment of coastal marine reserves for Seals in Norway have been more effective in protecting Harbour Seals than Grey Seals because the latter are more likely to travel outside the areas closed to fisheries and become entangled in nets, particularly those set for Angler Fish (Lophius piscatorius - Bjørge et al. 2002). Recent declines in the Norwegian population have been attributed to bycatch in this fishery (Nilssen et al. 2019).

rationale: The Spotted Seal is an abundant species with no evidence of recent declines in the main part of its range and therefore is listed as Least Concern. However, given that this Arctic seal species breeds mostly on sea ice, and sea ice is declining due to global warming, a reassessment should occur in 5 years.
habitat: During the ice-free months of summer, in the Arctic seas (Bering, Chukchi, Beaufort), Spotted Seals range far to the north and throughout the region, but reduce their range substantially in winter and spring to areas of marginal sea ice at the southern ice edge of the Bering Sea (Citta et al. 2018, Olnes et al. 2023). Spotted Seals do not have robust claws and do not maintain breathing holes in solid ice, thus they require broken ice habitats where floes are separated by open water or brash ice (Burns 1970, Fay 1974). Similarly, in more southern seas (the Sea of Japan, the Yellow Sea, and the Sea of Okhotsk), their summer range is also larger than in winter, but for a different reason; after the breeding and moulting season, seals migrate to coastal waters with abundant food resources. Here, Spotted Seals winter only in the northern, ice-covered part of the range.During the summer, Spotted Seals feed offshore and nearshore, targeting salmon migrating into rivers for spawning, and regularly travel to the coast to haul out on land (Burns 1970, Burkanov 1990, Olnes et al. 2023). The numbers on some haul-out sites in Kamchatka, Russia, can exceed 10,000 individuals (V. Burkanov pers. comm.). As sea ice forms in winter, Spotted Seals in the Arctic seas move south to lighter and broken ice, but seals in the Sea of Japan and Yellow Sea move north to use sea ice as their primary platform for resting between feeding bouts (Burkanov 1990; Lowry et al. 1998, 2000; Olnes et al. 2023).The mean age of sexual maturity for female Spotted Seals during the 2000s is 3-4 years (Quakenbush 2020). Recent data on sexual maturity for males is not available, however, nearly all (i.e., 90%) were sexually mature by age 5 in the past (Tikhomirov 1966, Naito and Nishiwaki 1972, Fedoseev 2000, Boveng et al. 2009). Maximum longevity is at least 39 years (L. Quakenbush, unpubl. data).In the Bering Sea, Spotted Seals give birth to a single pup on sea ice within the southern margin of the pack ice in spring. In more southern parts of their range, particularly in the Bohai Sea, Peter the Great Bay, the second Kuril Strait, Utashud Island, and the east coast of Kamchatka, they give birth on shore (Trukhin 2005). Pups are born in a white natal coat (lanugo) that is shed at or before weaning, which occurs about four weeks after birth. Spotted Seals are monogamous (at least within a breeding season). Groups composed of a female with her pup and a male, called triads, are common during the breeding season. Mating occurs after pups are weaned (Quakenbush 1988). Pregnancy rates have been variable (78-98%) since the 1960s but have been greater than 95% since 2010 (Quakenbush et al. 2024).Spotted Seals primarily eat fish (e.g., Walleye Pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus), Arctic Cod (Boreogadus saida), Saffron Cod (Eleginus gracilis), Rockfish (Sebastes spp.), Herring (Clupea pallasii), Sand Lance (Ammodytes hexapterus), Smelt (Osmerus mordax), Capelin (Mallotus catervarius), Eelpout (Lycodes spp.), Salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.), Flatfishes (Family Pleuronectidae)), but also eat invertebrates including cephalopods (Squid and Octopus) and crustaceans (Shrimp and Crab) (Burkanov 1990, Quakenbush et al. 2009, Quakenbush 2020). Their known predators include Killer Whales, Walruses, Steller Sea Lions, Polar Bears, Brown Bears, Wolves, Arctic Foxes, Pacific Sleeper Sharks, Golden Eagles, Steller’s Sea Eagles, Ravens, and various Gulls (Quakenbush 1988).
threats: Intensive commercial fishing in the Japan, Okhotsk, and Bering seas poses a potential risk to Spotted Seals, whose prey species are targeted by commercial fisheries (Lowry and Frost 1985). Entanglement in commercial fisheries occurs occasionally in Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk, and the Bering Sea. However, in the U.S. Bering Sea few mortalities are documented (Muto et al. 2021). Small, controlled kills to limit damage to fisheries occur in Japan (Mizuno et al. 2001). In the Russian Far East, Spotted Seals sometimes damage fish and fishing gear and fishermen shoot small numbers in local areas to protect their catch and equipment (V. Burkanov, pers. comm.).Shipping through the Bering Sea is increasing and may cause disturbance to and adversely affect habitat used by Spotted Seals, especially shipping that occurs in spring during pupping, which may include ice breaking (Müller et al. 2023). Oil contamination related to shipping could impact Spotted Seals, especially if spills occurred during the pupping season, if food resources were negatively affected, or if the spill was an event that affected a large area (St. Aubin 1990, Frost et al. 1994). Warmer waters and less sea ice could affect the distribution and prevalence of marine parasites, however, a study of parasitic worms (helminths) in ice associated seals from samples collected during 2006-2015, including Spotted Seals, found no new species and no increases in the prevalence of endemic species in the Pacific Arctic (Walden et al. 2020). Trace elements and organochlorine contaminants were analyzed in Spotted Seals harvested in Alaska in the 2000s. Trace elements of concern (e.g., arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury) were within ranges that were similar or below concentrations measured previously (Olnes et al. 2025a). Organochlorine contaminants were found to be lower than those in seals in other parts of the Arctic and have been declining over time (Olnes et al. 2025b). Contaminant concerns may be greater for seals living in the western part of the range where they occur near large human population centers and industrial areas in China, Korea, and Japan.Declines in spring sea ice cover in the Bering Sea where most of the population uses pack ice at the southern limit of the ice extent for pupping (e.g., Tynan and DeMaster 1997), could result in lower survival of Spotted Seal pups. This threat is strongest in the southern parts of the range, the Yellow Sea and Sea of Japan, where ice extent and seasonal persistence have been greatly reduced (Boveng et al. 2009). The threat may be mitigated somewhat in the Bering Sea, where a long-term range shift northward is possible (Boveng et al. 2009). Disruption or alteration of the patterns of primary productivity and abundance of key prey species, either by sea ice loss or ocean acidification could also have detrimental effects on Spotted Seals, though the magnitude and even the direction of impacts are very uncertain (Boveng et al. 2009).
population: The global abundance of Spotted Seals has never been well quantified. Recent surveys suggest that the total number may exceed 550,000 individuals, with more than 460,000 in the Bering Sea (Conn et al. 2014) and 84,000 in the Sea of Okhotsk (Chernook et al. 2014). Although Spotted Seals are abundant in the Sea of Japan including in Peter the Great Bay, Russia, along the northwest coast of Hokkaido, Japan, and along the west coast of Sakhalin Island, Russia, there have been no surveys of this region since the 1960s when the estimate was 8,000–11,000 (Fedoseev et al. 1970).However, the population in Peter the Great Bay has increased over the last 25 years and is estimated to be 3,500 based on pup counts (Trukhin 2019, 2024). In contrast, the southernmost population in the Yellow Sea has declined to 700 (Han et al. 2010). Surveys have been too irregular and too imprecise to measure population trend, but data from the Alaska Native harvest indicates that the Spotted Seal population is not likely declining in the Bering Sea. Since the 1960s, body condition, pregnancy rate, and the proportion of pups surviving past weaning to be harvested are higher, and the age at maturity has not changed (Quakenbush et al. 2024). The perception of Alaska Native hunters in the Bering Sea during 2008–2018 is that the Spotted Seal population is stable or increasing (Olnes et al. 2022).
range: Spotted Seals are found west and north of the North Pacific Ocean in seasonally ice-covered waters in the Yellow Sea, Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk, Kuril Islands, and in the Bering, Chukchi, and Beaufort seas. Their northwest extent (70°N, 170°E) is Chaun Bay, Russia, in the western Chukchi Sea and their northeast extent (69.5°N, 135°W) is the Mackenzie River Delta, Canada, in the eastern Beaufort Sea (Shaughnessy and Fay 1977). In the southwest, they extend to the Yangtze River, China (31°N, 122°E), and in the southeast to Bristol Bay, Alaska (Rugh et al. 1997, Quakenbush 1988). Spotted seals rarely occur in water depths greater than 200 m (Lowry et al. 2000, Olnes et al. 2023), largely remaining on the continental shelf. Spotted Seals breed in eight concentrations within their distribution range (Shaughnessy and Fay 1977). There are no known breeding locations in the Chukchi or Beaufort seas. They breed mostly on sea ice, however, there are several sites along the Asian coast where Spotted Seals breed on small remote islands (e.g., in Peter the Great Bay, the Kuril Islands, and along the east coast of Kamchatka; Burkanov 1986, 1990; Trukhin and Katin 2001; Kostenko et al. 2004; Vertyankin and Nikulin 2004). During the ice-covered season, Spotted Seals occur primarily in the outer edge of the pack ice. During the ice-free season, Spotted Seals move north from the Bering Sea into the Chukchi and Beaufort seas and use coastal areas, including river mouths where they haul out on beaches, barrier islands, and sandbars (Burns 1970; Lowry et al. 1998, 2000; Citta et al. 2018; Olnes et al. 2023).
useTrade: Indigenous people harvest Spotted Seals for subsistence and cultural uses. Subsistence hunting of Spotted Seals has likely occurred since first contact with the species and they remain an important subsistence resource for coastal Alaska Natives in western Alaska where the estimated average harvest is ~5,000 per year (Nelson et al. 2019). Asian Natives also harvest Spotted Seals for personal use, but the number is unknown. From 1931 to 1994 the Soviet Union harvested several thousand Spotted Seals each year in the Okhotsk and Bering seas, mostly from large commercial vessels (Heptner 1996, Trukhanova et al. 2017). Large-scale commercial harvests of Spotted Seals no longer occur in Russia.
conservationActions: In the United States, the most recent status review for Spotted Seals was undertaken in 2009 (Boveng et al. 2009). The Spotted Seal is not considered to be a species of concern, however, it is generally protected from all but subsistence hunting by Alaska Natives under the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972, which also generally prohibits import and export of parts or products from all marine mammals.In the Russian Federation, large-scale commercial harvesting of Spotted Seals ended in 1994. Small scale commercial and subsistence harvests from small boats and land occurs along the Russian Far East coast, but the size of the harvest is unknown and probably relatively small (V. Burkanov pers. comm.).In China, Spotted Seals were elevated from Class II to Class I protection in 2021 due to population declines in the Bohai Sea caused by climate warming, marine traffic, and pollution (Wang 2023).In Korea, in the Yellow Sea, the Spotted Seal has been designated as a natural monument (No. 331) in accordance with the Cultural Heritage Protection Act, is considered an endangered species, and a protected marine species due to habitat destruction and illegal hunting (Kim et al. 2023).

rationale: This assessment is based on the global (Sliwa et al. 2016) and national Red List assessments for South Africa (Wilson et al. 2016) and Namibia (Küsters 2022). No national assessment exists for Botswana. The Black-footed Cat (Felis nigripes) is endemic to the arid regions of southern Africa, occurring in a patchy and restricted distribution across the western areas of its range. Historical data scarcity has led to inconsistencies in the literature, which in turn has affected conservation measures. The small size, rarity, and nocturnal behavior of Black-footed Cats have contributed to this lack of information. Additionally, this species is frequently misidentified as the Afro-Asiatic wildcat or the common genet (Genetta genetta). Black-footed Cats occur at low densities, making population size estimation challenging. The species’ stronghold is suspected to be in South Africa’s central Karoo region, where the highest number of distribution records and densities are reported. Other regions are likely to support medium to very low densities. Using population densities of 0.02 cats/km² and 0.01 cats/km², respectively (Sliwa et al. 2016), the total estimated population size is 8,840 of which 6,188 are mature individuals, applying a 70% mature population structure. Considering the extensive spatial (50 km) and temporal (25-year) buffers applied in the mapping process and population size estimation, the species’ densities are likely to vary substantially at finer spatial scales. High population densities of 0.03 cats/km² are very rarely used for subpopulation estimations, as the low to medium densities are more realistic across the entire range of the species. In 2016, the total population size estimate was 13,867 individuals, of which 9,707 were mature individuals. As both population estimates were calculated using slightly different methods, the figures cannot be compared directly with each other. Long-term data from monitored populations show a decline in the number of mature individuals, as evidenced by both field observations and surveys, as well as reduced capture rates of individuals for radio-collaring. Subpopulation sizes were calculated for each subpopulation (n=13) with densities of 0.01 or 0.02 cats/km², considering a 70% mature adult population. Subpopulation sizes vary from 63 to 918 mature individuals, with no subpopulation exceeding 1,000 mature individuals or densities above 3 cats per 100 km². Populations are defined as geographically isolated units separated by over 100 km (beyond the species’ dispersal ability) and limited by topographical or habitat barriers. The extent of genetic isolation is unknown. Population Trends and MonitoringLong-term monitoring by the Black-footed Cat Working Group indicates a consistent negative population trend from 1998 to 2025 (Sliwa 2004, Sliwa et al. 2010, 2019, 2024, 2025). At Benfontein Nature Reserve, a long-term study site on the border of the Northern Cape and the Free State Provinces, a continuing decline could be inferred from densities falling from 0.17 cats/km² in 1998–1999 (Sliwa 2004) to 0.08 cats/km² in 2005–2015 (Sliwa et al. 2016). There were fewer sightings of individuals in recent years during annual spotlight surveys for capture and collaring in high-density areas (Sliwa et al. 2024, 2025). Recent spotlighting surveys (June 2024, April 2025) revealed the lowest abundance recorded in more than 30 years (A. Sliwa pers. comm. 2025). In southern Namibia, unexpected high losses among 10 radio-collared individuals have been recorded, with 6 deaths and 4 disappearances (Küsters 2024, Sliwa et al. 2024). Conservation Status and ThreatsInferred and observed continuing declines have been demonstrated from long-term study areas, including near extinction in some monitored sites. These declines are driven by various factors, both linked to natural and human-related threats. The natural threats include the following:Predation and competition: predation by black-backed Jackals (Lupulella mesomelas) and Caracals (Caracal caracal), as well as competition by Caracals, compounded by increasing mesopredator densities (Sliwa et al. 2022, 2024; Minnie et al. 2016)Disease: renal failure linked to AA amyloidosis, which they are genetically susceptible to (Terio et al. 2008, Sliwa et al. 2022, Yuan et al. 2024), and emerging diseases from domestic cats and dogs (Lamberski et al. 2009).Natural mortality rates: mortality rates of adults can be high, with up to 50% of radio-collared cats dying annually (Sliwa et al. 2022, Wilson 2015). The human-related threats that can also be important and threaten the species’ survival are mostly the following factors:Persecution: non-targeted killings during predator culling and control efforts, including night hunts (i.e., shooting with a spot-light), gin/leg-hold and cage traps, poison, hunting dogs and free-roaming domestic dogs, are significant threats (Sliwa et al. 2016, Wilson 2015, Wilson et al. 2016, Küsters 2022, Küsters 2024, Sliwa et al. 2024). Blanket killing of all predators in small-livestock farms is also a key issue (Sliwa et al. 2024). However, it is important to note that farmers do not target to kill Black-footed Cats. Mortality often happens when farmers cannot distinguish the species from a larger predator such as the Afro-Asiatic Wildcat or Caracal, when traps are not set properly to target larger predators, and when traps are not checked regularly. Also, there is an increased threat for small carnivores being killed indiscriminately through organized illegal sport dog hunting, particularly in Mpumalanga and the Free State provinces (N. Avenant and G. Camacho pers. comm. 2025).Habitat Destruction: collateral killing, especially on farmland, of key species like springhare (Pedetes capensis) as well as Aardvarks (Orycteropus afer) and Aardwolves (Proteles cristata), which maintain essential den sites for Black-footed Cats, indirectly affects the species (Davidson et al. 2012).  Overgrazing, bush encroachment, eradication of termite mounds, conversion to agriculture, and climate change-related factors, such as drought and erratic rainfall, affect prey availability and habitat quality. Road collisions: vehicle-related mortality is also a concern in some areas (F. van den Berg and A. van der Westhuizen pers. comm. 2025).As a result of the above, the species is listed as Vulnerable (C2a(i)), with fewer than 10,000 mature individuals, no subpopulation exceeding 1,000 individuals and a globally continuous declining population. This is a 2nd attempt to define and estimate population sizes of Felis nigripes. The species faces numerous threats, including habitat degradation, disease, and direct persecution. The fragmented nature of its populations, small subpopulation sizes, and limited genetic exchange exacerbate its vulnerability. The estimated population size provided here must be interpreted cautiously due to uneven sampling, lack of extensive systematic field surveys, and variability in density data across the range of the species. Despite these uncertainties, documented declines necessitate a conservative approach, highlighting the urgent need for targeted conservation efforts
habitat: The Black-footed Cat is one of the world's smallest cats, with females weighing an average of 1.30 kg and males larger at 1.93 kg (Sliwa 2013). The congeneric and more common Southern African Wildcat (Felis lybica cafra (formerly F. silvestris)) is considerably larger (females: 3.9 kg, males: 5.1 kg; Sliwa et al. 2010). Unlike most cat species, these cats are predominantly ground dwellers and will not readily take to trees. They lead a solitary existence except when with kittens or during brief mating periods. Black-footed Cats are extremely secretive in nature. They are strictly crepuscular and nocturnal and are active throughout the night, even hunting at temperatures of -8˚ C (Olbricht and Sliwa 1997). During daylight, the cats make mostly use of dens. The species makes use of hollowed out abandoned termite mounds when available (especially for the kittens) but will utilise dens dug by other animals, predominately from Springhares, rarely Cape ground squirrels and Aardvark. It is a specialist of open, short grassland, dwarf shrub areas with an abundance of small rodents and ground-roosting birds. It inhabits dry, open savannah, grasslands and Karoo semi-desert with sparse shrub and tree cover and a mean annual rainfall of between 100 and 500 mm at altitudes up to 2,000 m above sea level. It is not found in the driest and sandiest parts of the Namib and Kalahari deserts (Sliwa 2013).Black-footed Cats mate during 2/3 of the year but with a distinct season from late winter (August) over the summer months up to March. Up to two litters a year may be produced, with one to four kittens (normally two) born after 63–68 day gestation inside a Springhare burrow or hollow termitarium (Olbricht and Sliwa 1997, Skinner and Chimimba 2005). Births are timed to coincide with rains and food availability. Kittens are likely independent at 5 months of age when having permanent dentition but may remain within the range of their mother for extended periods (Sliwa 2013). Whilst they are reported to live up to 16 years in captive situations, average life expectancy in the wild is about three to five years (Black-footed Cat Working Group unpubl. data), although two monitored mature individuals lived at least seven years (Sliwa et al. 2014).As with most cat species, Black-footed Cats are obligate carnivores. During a 6 year field study on Benfontein Nature Reserve in central South Africa, 1,725 prey items were observed consumed by 17 free-ranging habituated individuals (Sliwa 2006). Average prey size was 24.1 g. Eight males fed on significantly larger prey (27.9 g) than 9 females (20.8 g). Fifty-four prey species were classified by their average mass into eight different size classes, three for mammals, three for birds, one for amphibians/reptiles, and one for invertebrates. Small mammals (5–40 g) constituted the most important prey class (39%) of total prey biomass followed by larger mammals (>100 g, 17%) and small birds (<40 g, 16%). Together, mammals and birds comprised 72% and 26% of total prey biomass, respectively, whereas invertebrates and amphibians/reptiles combined constituted just 2% of total prey mass consumed. Heterothermic prey items were unavailable during winter, when more larger birds and mammals (> 100 g) were consumed. Small rodents like the large-eared mouse (Malacothrix typica), captured 595 times by both sexes, were particularly important during the reproductive season for females with kittens. Males showed less variation between prey size classes consumed among climatic seasons. This sex-specific difference in prey size consumption may help to reduce intra-specific competition (Sliwa 2006). In terms of interspecific competition, Sliwa et al. (2010) found that Black-footed Cats captured smaller prey on average than African Wildcats, although both captured approximately the same number (12–13) of prey animals per night.Of 17 radio-collared Black-footed Cats (7 males, 10 females) studied on Benfontein Nature Reserve, Northern Cape Province from 1997 to 1998, the home ranges of adult resident males averaged 16.1–20.7 km² while those of females were 8.6–10 km², where male home range overlapped with females’ by 60–67% (Sliwa 2004). Despite this overlap, all individuals hunted solitarily. Similarly, annual home range sizes of Black-footed Cats were 7.1 km² for an adult female, and 15.6 and 21.3 km² for two adult males in the same population from 2006 to 2008 (Kamler et al. 2015).Annual home range data for radio-collared adult females on Benfontein Nature Reserve from 2019 to 2023, were 7.1 km² (n=14, MCP 100%, range 3.2–17.6 km²) for adult females and 14.3 km² (n=14, MCP 100%, range 6.6–23.1 km²) for adult males, estimated from 9,364 location fixes (Sliwa et al. 2020, 2023).In southern Namibia, home range data (3,774 location fixes) collected from 2020-2023, showed annual home ranges of adult females were 13.2 km² (n=6, MCP 100%, range: 3.0–55 km²). One adult female shifted home ranges over an area of 81.3 (2020) and 82.8 km² (2021) (Küsters et al. 2022, Sliwa et al. 2023). The home ranges of adult male Black-footed Cats in southern Namibia were estimated from only four males over a period of 6 months, hence not a true reflection of range size, with an average of 7.25 km² (n=4, MCP 100%, range 2.5–18.8 km²; Sliwa et al. 2024, Küsters 2024) in this area.Home range data collected (2,955 location fixes) between 2014 to 2018 in the study site near De Aar in the Northern Cape, showed average overall home range sizes for resident males reached 66.0 km² (n=4, MCP 100%, range 52.7–95.2 km²) and for non-resident males home ranges ranged from 21.7–109.4 km² (n=3, MCP 100 %). Average overall home ranges for resident females were 20.1 km² (n=4, MCP 100%, range 15.4–26.8 km²), while non-resident and young females had ranges of 14.3 km² (n=2, MCP 100%, range 11.4–17.2 km²; Sliwa et al. 2019, Küsters in prep.).Since individual home range size is dependent on available prey resources, in more arid regions these home ranges can be considerably larger. Both sexes spray mark, particularly during the mating season when marking is deployed in proportion to intensity of use and may play a role in social spacing (Molteno et al. 1998, Sliwa et al. 2010).Adults travel an average of 8.42±2.09 km per night – further than the African Wildcat (5.1±3.4 km per night) despite their smaller size (Sliwa et al. 2010).
threats: Following 33 years of research effort by members of the Black-footed Cat Working Group, the threats to the species have become more apparent (Wilson et al. 2016). Threats include, but are not limited to predation by mesocarnivores, disease, habitat loss including loss of key refugia, and both direct and indirect anthropogenic mortality. These threats are currently unmanageable and predicted to worsen compounded by the negative synergies of small, fragmented populations, low genetic diversity, and climate change. Furthermore, the majority of the distribution occurs outside of formally protected areas and those where the species exists are suspected to be too small to adequately conserve a viable subpopulation. Thus, the conservation of the species currently relies on rural private and communal landowner stewards.Competition and predation by mesopredators Another threat concerns the impact of mesopredators, that may be increasing across South African rangelands (Avenant and du Plessis 2008, Drouilly et al. 2018, Drouilly and O’Riain 2019, Nattrass et al. 2020, Woodgate et al. 2023). In general, numbers of Black-footed Cats and other larger carnivores are negatively related due to competition and predation. Annually, the BFCWG loses about 30-50% of all radio-collared (adult) cats to larger predators (Sliwa et al. 2022, Lai et al. 2024). The most vulnerable individuals (kittens and subadults – below 1 kg body mass) are the more likely victims of predation, but these individuals are difficult to monitor (too small to fit a radio collar), thus the actual rate of loss is unknown. Similarly, during a study over 2006–2008 on Benfontein Nature Reserve, Northern Cape Province, two Black-footed Cats were killed by predation, at least one was from Black-backed Jackals (Kamler et al. 2015, Wilson 2015) and another by a Caracal (Wilson 2015). Thus, although Black-footed Cats can co-exist with Black-backed Jackals by using burrows during the day (see above for synergistic interaction) and also taking refuge in them at night during danger (A. Sliwa, pers. obs. 1998), and by partitioning activity and diets (Kamler et al. 2015), increasing Black-backed Jackal abundance caused by anthropogenic disturbance and food sources, and possibly the loss of apex predators, is likely to increase Black-footed Cat mortality. The BFCWG also has evidence of cats killed by traditional herding dogs and the increasing popularity of Anatolian shepherd dogs with sheep farmers is potentially a new emerging threat (Sliwa et al. 2014, Wilson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2020, Wilkes et al. 2023). Domestic dogs are used for unselective hunting for bushmeat and entertainment purpose with potential negative effects on threatened wildlife (D. Hayter pers. comm. 2025, DESTEA; N. Avenant pers. comm. 2025, National Museum). Free roaming dogs also cause conflict with farmers leading to baited poison along property boundaries (M. Schroeder pers. obs.), which may negatively affect scavenging Black-footed Cats.DiseaseAs a familiar disease, AA-amyloidosis was previously thought to be limited only to inbred captive populations, but both domestic and wild Black-footed Cats show a high prevalence for the disease (Olbricht and Sliwa 1987, Terio et al. 2008, Sliwa et al. 2022, Yuan et al. 2024). This is a disease characterised by fibrillar protein depositions in many organs as a result of chronic inflammatory processes usually culminating in renal failure. About 70% of the documented deaths of captive cats internationally are because of this disease. However, the presence of amyloid in a free-ranging subpopulation was detected by Terio et al. (2008) from a sample provided by the BFCWG. The BFCWG has continued submitting samples from deceased Black-footed Cats for necropsy from two South African study sites 300 km apart, and AA-Amyloidosis has been confirmed through histopathology in three samples and a further six deaths of cats that had displayed clinical signs of renal amyloidosis (Sliwa et al. 2022). This provides additional evidence for a species predilection and supports the existence of a possible familial type of amyloidosis in the species. Habitat fragmentation and subpopulation isolation can only exacerbate this disease at subpopulation levels, whilst at the same time, the disease is a major reason why currently global captive breeding programmes are not self-sustainable (A. Sliwa pers. comm. 2024). The species is known to have deleterious mutations associated with AA Amyloidosis, as wild subpopulations become genetically isolated, reduced genetic variability threatens population viability by increasing susceptibility to disease and reducing reproductive fitness (Yuan et al. 2024).An additional consequence of habitat fragmentation and population isolation is increased contact with other carnivores and the pathogens they carry. Because Black-footed Cats share their territory, prey base, and infectious disease susceptibility with many small carnivores, and even domestic dogs and cats, this provides numerous opportunities for disease transmission. Lamberski et al. (2009) found that Black-footed Cats showed no serologic evidence to FIV, FPV, FHC, FECV, Toxoplasmosis, Rabies virus and Avian Influenza, all common pathogens infecting domestic Cats. Serologic results for FeLV were uncertain. Domestic Cats in this study (rural and sub-rural areas, Northern Cape) showed high titres for FIV and FPV. Black-footed Cat samples (n=23) tested seropositive for CDV (22%), WNV (13%) and FCV (30%). These results highlight the potential for disease transmission between wildlife and cats and dogs. Emerging diseases in the inhabited ecosystems have potential cascading indirect effects on Black-footed Cat populations. Rabbit Haemorrhagic Disease (RHD) in hares (Lepus sp.), a prey species for Black-footed Cats (Sliwa 2006), is a highly infectious and lethal disease that causes significant declines in the abundance of rabbits and potentially wild hares. The disease emerged in southern Africa in 2022 (National Council of SPCAs 2023). It could lead to potential knock-on effects on mesopredators relying more on small livestock prey and leading to increasing lethal control by private landowners and with potential collateral effects on Black-footed Cats. Another disease that might be of concern to Black-footed Cats, although indirectly, is avian influenza. There has been an upsurge in this disease in South Africa in 2023 (Department of Agriculture, Land Reform, and Rural Development 2023). While it most severely affects domestic poultry, shorebirds, and waterfowl, it can easily be transmitted to other wild birds and can infect mammals, including felids as well as reduce the number of prey items available. Black-footed Cat populations could be at risk as much of their habitat in the Karoo includes ephemeral pans with high seasonal fluctuations of migratory shorebirds and waterfowl that could serve as disease reservoirs that impact prey populations and potentially increased risk of infecting Black-footed Cats. No research has been conducted on the topic yet, and the threat therefore remains hypothetical.Habitat Loss/DegradationHabitat degradation is reducing the availability and quality of suitable environments and prey for Black-footed Cats. This degradation is driven by overgrazing, bush encroachment, and structural changes to habitats, such as the removal of termite mounds and the conversion of land to agriculture. Climate change is expected to further compound these impacts, with increasing drought, unpredictable rainfall patterns, and other related effects further threatening both habitat and prey availability. A particularly serious long-term concern is the loss of key resources such as den sites and prey due to human disturbance. Black-footed Cats are unable to dig or maintain their own burrows and rely on structures created by other species, such as Springhares, Cape ground Squirrels (Xerus inauris), Aardwolves, and Aardvarks, with whom they share a commensal (inquilistic) relationship. The local decline or removal of these animals, whether through habitat degradation, overgrazing, or persecution, may critically reduce available shelter and refuge for the cats (B. Wilson unpubl. data., Olbricht and Sliwa 1987, Sliwa 2013). Springhares, in particular, are vital (Wilson 2015), as they provide den sites, yet they are often viewed as pests by farmers and are hunted for bushmeat by local communities (Butynski 1973, 2013, Erasmus and Hoffman 2020). Despite being listed as Least Concern, Springhares are vulnerable to localised extinction due to their long lifespan and low reproductive rate. With livestock farming and bushmeat hunting projected to increase in southern African savannas, caution is warranted (Lindsey et al. 2013). The continued survival of the Black-footed Cat may depend heavily on the protection of these key sympatric species and their shared habitats. Black-footed Cats were once thought to live mostly in panveld and short grass areas. However, they are now known to occupy a variety of open arid and semi-arid habitats. They prefer low, sparse vegetation and have even been found in fallow fields and heavily overgrazed areas (Wilson 2015). Their presence in open agricultural land suggests they may follow seasonal changes in rodent populations linked to planting and harvesting cycles. However, given the unpredictable nature of these events, and associated risks due to the proximity to humans and their domestic carnivores, the benefit to resident cats is uncertain. Also, there is no research as to how these human-dominated landscapes are used by Black-footed Cats and whether these specific records are because they are exposed and highly frequented by human observers (A. Sliwa pers. obs. 2025). Current and historic overgrazing from livestock farms results in desertification or bush encroachment. This not only reduces the habitat suitability for their normal prey, which might give some predators an advantage, but decreases the density of prey and the ecological index value as climax grass species (i.e., “decreasers”) are replaced with lower quality “increaser” species. This is further exacerbated by increased atmospheric CO2 as a result of climate change, which favours C3 tree growth over C4 grasses, aiding in densification of woody species (Bond and Midgley 2001). As an open habitat specialist, increased woody densification will therefore further negatively impact the Black-footed Cat through preferred habitat loss and fragmentation.Black-footed Cats are also vulnerable to natural disasters such as flooding of dens and den collapses (Sliwa et al. 2009, 2022). Climate change predicts increases in severe weather events such as more flash floods and droughts in Southern Africa (Binder et al. 2023). In addition, the impacts of climate change on the region are predicted to affect the ability of the natural resources to sustainably support livelihoods and may accelerate degradation and intensify eradication of predators and/or reliance on bushmeat. Finally, with less than 2% of the Karoo biome under formal protection and 95% of area under private ownership, the core range of Black-footed Cat habitat is under increasing pressure by the mining and renewable energy sectors, coupled with little conservation protection.Anthropogenic MortalityAcross the range, human-related mortalities continue to threaten the species’ survival. These include blanket predator control measures, especially through non-targeted shooting (during night hunts) and trapping, hunting with dogs for predator control, free-roaming domestic dogs (Wilson 2015, Sliwa et al. 2016, Wilson et al. 2016, Küsters 2022). Indiscriminate illegal bushmeat hunting and organized dog hunting are increasing in some areas, particularly in South Africa. In the southern and eastern Free State and Mpumalanga provinces, the expansion of informal settlements has been accompanied by a rise in dog hunts, which in turn increases the risk of Black-footed Cats being unintentionally killed (H. Grobbelaar pers. comm. 2024, N. Avenant pers. comm. 2025, G. Camacho pers. comm. 2025). Black-footed Cats are also lost through indirect persecution, such as accidental poisonings (for example locust spraying, predator control lures/baits) and general predator persecution throughout most of their range in South Africa (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Sliwa 2013, Terblanche 2020, Drouilly et al. 2023).Although the extent of road mortality on Black-footed Cat subpopulations is not known, we know that roadkill deaths are usually under-represented. Our records have nevertheless doubled since the previous assessment of 2016. Road deaths remain a concern as we do not understand their impact on dispersing individuals and metapopulation dynamics (Wilson et al. 2016). How they potentially increase localised extinction risks in different parts of the cat’s range is also unknown.
population: The Black-footed Cat is naturally rare compared to the other smaller cats of southern Africa (Sliwa 2013). Quantifying the presence and population abundance for the species is particularly difficult due to its secretive behaviour and small size (Sliwa et al. 2018). Black-footed Cats move quickly and do not habitually use game tracks or roads like larger carnivores, thus traditional methods such as camera traps are generally less effective (Sliwa et al. 2018). Since 2006, there has been extensive effort to establish the historical and current distribution of the species across its range (Wilson 2015), in South Africa (Wilson et al. 2016) and since 2012 in Namibia (Küsters 2013, 2022, 2024). In South Africa, Namibia and Botswana, there are 733 verifiable locality records which can be reliably mapped since 2000. As such, it is difficult to determine density, and thus a population estimate, for this species. High-density estimates come from two study sites in the Northern Cape Province of South Africa, a private nature reserve and on farmland (Sliwa 2004, Sliwa et al. 2010). For Benfontein nature reserve (private nature reserve), between 1998 and 1999, density (based on radio-collared individuals) was estimated at 0.17 cats/km² (Sliwa 2004), but only 0.08 cats/km² between 2005 and 2014. For Nuwejaarsfontein farm, density was estimated at 0.06 cats/km² from 2009–2014 (Sliwa et al. 2014). However, these two sites may represent already exceptionally high densities due to favourable climate and human management, and population densities in low-quality habitat are probably much lower (Sliwa 2013). Densities as low as 0.005 cats/km² were recorded in south-western Botswana, estimated from track counts (Keeping 2014), although tracks are not verified and not included in the distribution mapping and population estimation. Thus, we suspect that densities of 0.01–0.02 cats/km² represent more realistic densities across larger scales (B. Wilson and A. Sliwa unpubl. data). Highest densities are expected in the central part of South Africa, along a North-South axis with decreasing frequency of records either West or East of this region and northwards in the range. Distribution point data (records) were plotted in QGIS (version 3.34.6-Prizren), and a 50 km circular buffer generated around each record, i.e. the dispersal limit of the species is likely not more than 50 km (Wilson 2015). Extant ranges were mapped and when necessary, clipped in relation to suitable habitat extent, perennial rivers, mountains, big cities and any other barrier that affects the extent of occurrence. Using population density ranges of 0.01 (low) and 0.02 cats/ km² (medium), the extant ranges were calculated by multiplying the polygon area size with population estimates. The results were then multiplied by 0.70 to yield the number of mature individuals (MI; assuming a 70% mature population structure; Wilson 2015, Sliwa et al. 2016). This yielded a global population estimate of 6,188 MI. See Supporting Information for more details of mapping and population size estimation. Where this assessment focused on delineating populations based on verified sightings combined with landscape scale habitat features, the previous assessment (Sliwa et al. 2016) calculated density isopleths of locality records. We now think that the low-density estimate (0.01 cats/km) represents a more realistic measure of average density across the entire range in southern Africa.Population sizes in South Africa are estimated at 3,335 MI and subpopulation size estimates in South Africa range between 273 and 918 individuals. In the high-density areas in the Greater Karoo, the largest subpopulation is estimated at 918–2,753 MI, computed from low to medium population densities. Considering the extensive spatial (50 km) and temporal (25 year) buffers applied in the mapping process, the variability of densities at finer spatial scales, a more conservative population density of 0.01 cats/ km² was used, especially in large subpopulation ranges.In Namibia, the size of the population is estimated at 2,114 MI, computed at the medium density. Subpopulations size estimates in Namibia range between 63–914 MI, the largest subpopulation is expected in the south-central Kalahari. Similar total population size estimates were computed for the Red List of Terrestrial Carnivores of Namibia (Küsters 2022). However, only a few verified records (post-year 2000; n=6) exist for Botswana, within three subpopulations, yielding a total population estimate of 740 MI. Subpopulations size estimates in Botswana range between 130–423 individuals. Given that the majority of records are from the core range in central South Africa, subpopulation ranges could be defined with greater confidence.Thus, the global population estimate remains below 10,000 mature individuals and estimates yield no subpopulation with more than 1,000 mature individuals. However, this was a first attempt at defining subpopulations and was heavily reliant on expert opinion and spatial mapping of suitable habitats and reliable records.Recent significant declines (high mortality rates and low density) of Black-footed Cats in two intensive study areas monitored by the Black-footed Cat Working Group (BFCWG), in southern Namibia and in the Northern Cape Province, South Africa were observed in 2023-2024 (Küsters 2024, Sliwa et al. 2024) and continuing into 2025 in the latter (A. Sliwa pers. comm. 2025). Continuous declines were also observed from 2019 to 2024 (Sliwa et al. 2024, Küsters 2024). The decline is documented in annual survey activities by the BFCWG, with fewer overall sightings of Black-footed Cats in the study areas and lower average capture (to radio-collar) success since 2019. Populations in the central Upper Karoo areas indicate stable subpopulations, with regard to the amount of location records and ongoing awareness. However, it is difficult to demonstrate decline in a species that is so hard to census.Furthermore, to demonstrate the inferred continuing decline, density of radio-collared Black-footed Cats was 0.17 cats/km² (Sliwa 2004) during 1998 to 1999, and over a 10 year period (2005–2015), density decreased to only 0.08 cats/km², which is documented in field reports from Benfontein Nature Reserve, Northern Cape Province, South Africa (for example, Sliwa et al. 2014).Local subpopulations may also be low or even absent in areas where Black-backed Jackals and Caracals are abundant, due to interspecific competition, including intraguild predation (see Kamler et al. 2015), which may be especially true for adult female and juvenile cats. It is estimated that 29% of all radio-collared cats are killed by larger predators annually (Sliwa et al. 2022, Lai et al. 2024).
range: Black-footed Cats have the most restricted distribution of any of the African felid species (Nowell and Jackson 1996). The species is endemic to the arid grasslands, dwarf shrub, and savannah of the Karoo, Kalahari and Highveld in southern Africa. The majority of the range occurs within the boundaries of South Africa, thinning out northwards into Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe (Table 1 in the Supplementary Information). The species is found primarily in Namibia and South Africa, but also Botswana (where there are historical records but only limited recent ones). The species’ occurrence in western Zimbabwe and extreme southern Angola is not verified (Sliwa 2013), a status that persists as of 2025. It is considered extinct in Lesotho (Lynch 1994, Grab and Nash 2020, N. Avenant pers. comm. 2024).In South Africa, where the majority of research effort has taken place, compiled records suggested a wider range in virtually all directions, from previous literature (Wilson 2015, Wilson et al. 2016), however no further range expansion has been recorded since 2015. It is unlikely that true range extensions have occurred but was probably an artefact of reporting bias as a result of recently increased awareness and outreach in years before publication by researchers (Wilson 2015). Alternatively, this could also have been the result of fluctuations linked to small mammals, which are the main prey for Black-footed Cats. The largest extant subpopulation occurs in the Nama Karoo region in central South Africa. The region has relatively contiguous habitat with low human and livestock population densities, however populations may be highly variable due to low rainfall and extended periods of drought exacerbated by widespread persecution of predators including poison (Nattrass and Conradie 2018, Terblanche 2020, Slater et al. 2022, Drouilly et al. 2023). Densities likely decrease westerly with lower rainfall and the absence of Springhare and Ground Squirrel populations. The Karoo is divided laterally by the escarpment of the Greater Karoo plateau where gene flow is limited to the Baviaans Kloof pass. The lower Karoo region south of this plateau has a narrow lateral band of Black-footed Cat records with densities likely decreasing to the west, which is more arid and does not support Springhare or Ground Squirrel populations, and to the east with increasing rainfall and denser unsuitable thicket vegetation. However, recent camera trap and photographic records confirm the species occurs in suitable pockets of habitats. The Orange River and the extensive crop production along its boundaries likely limit gene flow to the northern Karoo. The Griqualand subpopulation region extends Northeast in the Free State Province where the Nama Karoo merges into the Savanna and endangered Grassland biomes, with the latter already extensively converted to agricultural production. On the Northeastern side of its range, occurrence records were confirmed 90 km west of the Kruger National Park in Mpumalanga Province and southward into the Drakensberg midlands of KwaZulu-Natal. This population appears sparce and fragmented in line with expectations from variable terrain and habitat.The range of Black-footed Cats in South Africa likely extends to the northern boundary at very low densities based on records south of Kalahari Gemsbok National Park bordering Namibia and Botswana and on private farms and reserves north of Johannesburg in the Savanna biome. South in the Fynbos biome it is possibly extinct with only one record in the past 20 years and previously based on only two specimen records collected near the town of Montagu. Fynbos is suspected to be an unsuitable/ not preferred habitat that is characteristically brushy with low prey densities. The Mediterranean climate lends the region to high human populations, and the historically suitable habitat was likely restricted to grassland valleys that have been converted to agricultural crops. Thus, the current southern extent of the species range in the Western Cape Province has been reduced. Similarly, the most western records in the Namaqualand region are based on only two sightings before the 21st century. A viable population in this region is unlikely, given the records are over 250 km to the nearest extant subpopulation. The occurrence of the species in Eswatini (M. Reilly pers. comm. 2024, and A. Monadjem pers. comm. 2014) and Lesotho (N. Avenant pers. comm. 2024) is considered highly unlikely, and no records exist to date.In Botswana, only six verified records were obtained since 2000, making population densities difficult to predict. Regular sightings by guides have been reported in the Makgadikgadi Pans National Park and given they historically occurred in the area (Stuart and Wilson 1988), the large salt pan landscape may host a uniquely small subpopulation. One sighting was reported in the Central Kalahari Game Reserve (G. Maude pers. comm. 2006), while there are large open grassland areas, the majority of the reserve is semi-arid shrub savanna and scrub, thus may only support very low Black-footed Cat densities that may extend west in the Ghanzi district, where two camera trap records were recently reported by Cheetah Conservation Botswana in 2023. Unverified recent and historical records exist in the Okavango Delta region, but the species’ ability to persist in wetland habitat has not been recorded elsewhere and validity of these records remains in question. The species likely occurs in very low densities in the southwest part of the country aside from the driest parts of the Kalahari (Sliwa 2013). A single specimen was brought to the Department of Wildlife and National Parks collected near the town of Tsabong near the South Africa border (K. Good pers. comm. 2011). Unverified records from the Kalahari Wildlife Landscape Connectivity Analysis conducted as part of the Kgalagadi-Ghanzi Drylands Ecosystem Project recorded only 35 Black-footed Cat track intersections, the lowest of any other recorded mammal species (423 cheetah Acinonyx jubatus for comparison). If these records are true, it would highlight the rarity of the species (Keeping 2014).In Namibia, Black-footed Cats were more commonly recorded in the southern regions, specifically in the Gamkab basin, in the Karas Region, from the Orange River around Noordoewer along the Great Escarpment in the west and eastwards to the Botswana border. This subpopulation is restricted northwards by the plateau near Keetmanshoop. Black-footed Cats may be possibly extinct east of Keetmanshoop as there are no historical or recent records, and historically high mortalities of all small carnivores (Joubert et al. 1982). An isolated camera trap record indicates that Black-footed Cats occur in the Tsau||Khaeb National Park (M. Le Merle pers. comm. 2024), not far from the Atlantic Ocean, however probably only in small patches of suitable habitat. They are absent from the true Namib Desert. Camera trap records from Neuhof Reserve (EIS 2023) and sightings on farms in the NamibRand area extend the known range into the eastern fringes of the Pro-Namib. In the south-central Kalahari Black-footed Cats occur from Mariental eastwards to the Botswana boundary and northwards to south of the mountainous terrain of the Khomas Highland (1,700 m) and east to the district of Gobabis in the Omaheke region. The Nossob and Auob rivers in the Kalahari may be important corridors for linking sub-populations locally and into southern Botswana (D. Joubert pers. comm. 2013, Küsters 2014). Further north, there seems to be a small pocket of suitable habitat in the central-western plains and restricted to areas that have been cleared of dense bush (M. Küsters pers. obs. 2025) in the Outjo district. The most northern population occurs in the central and eastern parts of the Etosha National Park, confined to the suitable habitat of dwarf shrubland habitat west and south of the Etosha pan (Küsters 2022). No records are documented from the Skeleton Coast National Park, except for an unverified sighting near Möwe Bay (EIS 2023) and one possible sighting in the Hoanib River floodplains (P. Stander pers. comm. 2018).Records of presence in national, state-owned protected areas in Namibia have only been confirmed in the Etosha National Park (Stander 1991, Küsters 2013), the Tsau //Khaeb (formerly Sperrgebiet) National Park and the Namib-Naukluft National Park. A few confirmed records occur in private nature reserves, but most distribution records in Namibia are from private farmland (commercial livestock and game farming). Overall, the distribution records are scarce and patchy, reflecting its status as a rare and under-reported species.Sightings of Black-footed Cats have been reported (not all verified) in formally protected areas in South Africa, notably in the Karoo National Park (Western Cape Province of South Africa), Camdeboo National Park, Addo Elephant National Park and Mountain Zebra National Park (Eastern Cape Province of South Africa), Lombard Nature Reserve (Northwest Province of South Africa), Meerkat National Park (Northern Cape Province of South Africa), Gariep Nature Reserve (F. van den Berg 2024), Tussen die Riviere Nature Reserve, Willem Pretorius Nature Reserve, Caledon Nature Reserve (A. van der Westhuizen pers. comm. 2025; Free State Province of South Africa) and in Makgadikgadi Pans National Park (Botswana). However, the lack of protected areas within the core range of Black-footed Cats is probably one of the reasons for the relatively low number of sightings in protected areas. Further field surveys are needed to determine the survival potential and sustainability of populations in larger protected areas.The extent of occurrence (EOO) in southern Africa is estimated to be 1,875,356 km², calculated as the minimum convex polygon covering all extant presence and subpopulations for the species. However, we suspect that Black-footed Cats do not occur continuously across the EOO, restricted by environmental conditions and threats (Sliwa 2013). The area of occupancy (AOO) in southern Africa is estimated to be 657,111 km². The current estimated AOO in South Africa is 407,581 km² (n=5 extant subpopulations), and 196,680 km² (n=5 extant subpopulations; one shared with South Africa) and 52,850 km² (n=3 extant subpopulations), in Namibia and Botswana respectively.
useTrade: The Black-footed Cat is accidentally killed in indiscriminate trapping, predator hunting (rifle and dogs) and poisoning events aimed at other damage-causing carnivores. They are most probably also killed during illegal dog hunts, a cultural activity among parts of the South African population, and a way to obtain bushmeat, resources for traditional medicine and other traditional use. These illegal sport hunts with pack dogs are being reported more frequently (N. Avenant pers. comm. 2025). However, as a protected species, in the instance that a Black-footed Cat is killed, the incident would never be reported for fear of prosecution (Wilson et al. 2016), so the impact of these activities is unknown. At least one specimen record reported to B. Wilson was of a Khoisan man in the Kalahari wearing a Black-footed Cat skin as part of a loincloth. The man indicated that he obtained the skin from a roadkill from the neighbouring Botswana area. Similarly, there are anecdotal reports of skins and mounts in households and in Nature Conservation offices in the Central Karoo and Free State (M. Drouilly pers. obs. 2014, M. Schroeder pers. obs. 2023, N. Avenant pers. obs. 2024 and 2025). We know that some of these came from roadkills, but others may stem from illegal killings, voluntary or not (such as the example where one flat skin was obtained from a shepherd close to Biesjiesfontein in the Victoria West area in 2012, likely killed by his hunting dogs; A. Sliwa pers. obs. 2012).Applications have been made for legal hunting permits in the Northern Cape and the Eastern Cape Provinces of South Africa but have never been granted. However, several South African taxidermists have acknowledged having mounted hunted animals (Wilson 2015), indicating that there is some interest in the hunting industry for the species. Only one legal hunting trophy export from South Africa to the US has been documented in 2004 (CITES https://trade.cites.org).In the 1970s, there was a demand for the species by overseas zoos and export permits were granted for cats to be caught and exported from the Eastern Cape Province. During further investigations, it was revealed that many of these cats actually came from the Victoria West/Britstown area in the then-Cape Province (now part of the Northern Cape Province; Olbricht and Sliwa 1997). Similarly in Namibia, Black-footed Cats were caught on farms in the Gobabis and Mariental districts in the late 1970s and sold to overseas zoological gardens and safari parks (Küsters unpubl. data, Küsters 2022). The exact numbers and sex of cats is unknown, but one farmer caught at least 10 cats in total during the 1980s for sale to European zoos through a local game capture operator (Anonymous pers. comm. 2012). In addition, several reports suggest that young and adult cats are found injured or are captured in the wild and subsequently kept as pets (Küsters 2013, 2014). These animals rarely survive, as they are not suitable pets and need specialised care and nutrition (Olbricht and Sliwa 1997). More recently, it has become an acknowledged fact that this species does not thrive in captivity and the demand for wild-caught individuals for zoos has diminished considerably (Sliwa and Schürer 2006). However, 10 live animals were legally traded to zoos and commercial purposes from South Africa since 2018 (CITES https://trade.cites.org). American Association of Zoos and Aquaria (AZA) accredited Zoos maintain and exchange animals between institutions. To increase genetic diversity in these captive populations, in-vitro fertilisation attempts have been made using oocytes of a captive female and semen collected from a wild-caught male during annual field research trips conducted by the Black-footed Cat Working Group (BFCWG, Herrick et al. 2010), but without generating a viable embryo.The extent to which the species is traded illegally as pets cannot be quantified, but given their small size and attractive appearance, demand would not be surprising and could pose a local threat to a wild population. In South Africa, some wild cat breeders have acknowledged ownership of Black-footed Cats, with prices between R30,000–40,000 (~2,000 USD) for purchase of a male within South Africa (https://www.karoocats.org/page/support-us). This is particularly concerning, as such a large financial reward creates a strong incentive to capture individuals from the wild, especially in South Africa’s rural sheep farming regions, where rising unemployment and poverty exacerbate the risk. Kittens are relatively easy to catch if located, and since Black-footed Cats generally do not thrive in captivity, it is likely that any individuals in trade would originate directly from wild populations.
conservationActions: Formally protected areas encompassing high quality Black-footed Cat habitat remains low, and large enough protected areas to maintain viable subpopulations are unlikely to be secured. It is unclear in how many protected areas Black-footed Cats occur due to a lack of systematic survey efforts within protected areas. However, the major protected areas in the Karoo biome – Karoo, Mountain Zebra, Camdeboo, Meerkat, and Addo Elephant national parks – may each protect a small but not self-sustaining population. Hunting of this species is banned in South Africa and Botswana (Nowell and Jackson 1996). The species is currently not protected in Namibia (Küsters 2022). Namibia recently assessed the species as Vulnerable, and it will be formally protected by legislation which is still under review in 2025 (Küsters 2022). Although the Black-footed Cat has been recorded at least marginally in all of the South African provinces, the effectiveness of local protection measures remains in question.Key interventions for the species include:Sustainable farmland management, especially of mesopredators, is essential. A holistic strategy should focus on targeting only target species or individuals causing damage, while avoiding the use of poison or other non-selective control methods. Maintaining balanced grazing pressure is also important to support healthy populations of small mammal prey. Tolerating apex predators can help regulate mesopredator numbers through natural top-down control. Together, these practices can lower unnaturally high mesopredator densities and create more suitable conditions for the Black-footed Cat on farmland. Ecologically responsible, adaptive sheep-farming practices should also be promoted. These may include synchronized lambing periods, lambing within electrified enclosures, night-time kraaling, use of trained livestock guarding dogs, and shepherd-based systems. Combinations of these methods should be tested and tailored to local conditions (Avenant and Morwe 2021, Du Plessis et al. 2015, 2018, Tambling et al. 2018, Bergman et al. 2020). The establishment of large conservancy areas to create viable Black-footed Cat subpopulations and facilitate ecological separation between Black-footed Cats and mesocarnivores (Kamler et al. 2015). The fragmentation of suitable habitats and potential isolation of subpopulations makes the formation or maintenance of dispersal corridors important in the prevention of inbreeding and prevalence of inherited diseases such as AA-amyloidosis. Despite their small size, individuals have very large home ranges, and to conserve subpopulations and create corridors, the emphasis should be on the establishment of large conservancy areas with suitable conditions for the species. This is particularly important in areas where the prospects of a formally protected area are unlikely.Conservancies and private lands with low mesopredator density or conflict can be targeted as possible sites for Black-footed Cat stewardship.Human activities that lead to habitat degradation and the loss of prey and burrowing species need to be addressed, particularly in the Karoo region, which is likely to be the remaining stronghold region for the species. This should also be achieved by creating awareness to the presence and needs of the species among landowners to reduce accidental persecution, whilst providing information about the special needs of Black-footed Cats that would enable them to be actively involved in the protection of the species.General farmer education and training, and public awareness raising campaigns for the cryptic species and encouragement of citizen scientists to submit distribution records through the promotion of citizen science platforms. This has been done previously by the BFCWG to establish a more accurate geographical distribution of the species (Wilson 2015). Further outreach and effective methods to incorporate indigenous knowledge with modern science would broaden participation in data deficient regions such as Botswana.Other interventions can involve applying stricter legal penalties to people involved in deliberate persecution of the species and illegally keeping or trading with the species, and clamping down on illegal hunting activities, for example the illegal bush meat and organised sport dog hunting. With less than 2% of the Karoo biome under formal protection, 95% private land, Black-footed Cat conservation in South Africa is reliant on private landowners. The development of outreach programmes for landowners and managers to promote custodianship and discourage indiscriminate lethal predator killing, which carries the risk to all non-target small carnivores, including the Black-footed Cat, should be supported. This should also include better staffing and policing through wildlife authorities. In addition, Black-footed Cats need to be promoted as flagship and indicator species of rangeland ecosystem in the Karoo. All these interventions could be listed and implemented through the development of a Regional Conservation Strategy and National Action Plans for the species.Recommendations for ex-situ managementA Biodiversity Management Plan, already developed in South Africa, could be updated and implemented, as an interim or pre-emptive conservation measure, which could be linked to the already existing international and national ex-situ management plans. Currently, there is no consistent and self-sustaining breeding and survival of Black-footed Cats in South African facilities and some only maintain their stocks by receiving rescued/confiscated individuals from the wild. We suggest the establishment of a national breeding studbook for Black-footed Cats, which would then allow a better overview on the stocks, which could in turn also feed into the international studbook, maintained by Lory Park Zoo, Midrand, South Africa since 2018 (previously Frankfurt Zoo and Wuppertal Zoo, Germany).  The keeping of captive Black-footed Cats via license from local wildlife authorities should carry the responsibility to register stocks with the studbook, providing accurate data annually as data sharing of many holders is still the exception. It is important to note that success in captive conditions is fraught by failure of individuals to thrive due to their highly specialized needs and the effects of inbreeding and/or AA-amyloidosis. Thus, ex-situ conservation efforts are not to be relied upon, but can serve multiple services in awareness raising, education, fund raising, research support for in-situ research and conservation. Translocation or reintroduction/restocking of individuals is not advised as it may disturb the social dynamics of an existing Black-footed cat population. A thorough survey on presence/absence of the species in the potential release area in advance is mandatory. The monitoring of the released cats to determine survival rates is necessary, as displaced individuals may suffer a high mortality rate and to ensure an adaptive process for the future of such practice.Research priorities: The Black-footed Cat has been extensively studied for more than 30 years in the Kimberley area, along the Free State-Northern Cape border, South Africa. The Black-footed Cat Working Group (BFCWG) focuses on the ecology, reproductive biology, geographical range, habitat preferences, health and conservation of the species. This provided information about the diet (Sliwa 2006, Sliwa et al. 2010), home range size and social organization (Sliwa 2004), and ecological relationships between the species and other sympatric carnivores (Kamler et al. 2015).  The BFCWG extended this study to include farms south of De Aar, in the Northern Cape Province of South Africa, in a different habitat type with different farming practices in place, a study run between 2009-2018. Most recently, a third intensive study ran between March 2020 and August 2023 on farmland close to Grünau, ||Karas Region, Namibia. However, there is little information for elsewhere within the Black-footed Cat range and the following are considered research priorities:1. rationale: Mexican Prairie Dog is endemic to Mexico and is assessed as Endangered (EN B2ab(i,ii,iii,iv,v)). Although it has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of just under 10,000 km², its habitat and distribution are fragmented resulting in an area of occupancy (AOO) of only 232 km². The population is severely fragmented and there is continuing decline in EOO, AOO, extent and quality of habitat, number of locations and subpopulations, and number of mature individuals. Declines are resulting from severe ongoing habitat loss and fragmentation from agriculture, ranching, and invasive vegetation, as well as from direct control by farmers and pollution from pesticide run-off.
habitat: Cynomys mexicanus is a keystone species that produces burrows that benefit its grassland ecosystem by increasing water infiltration capacity, oxygenation, and the incorporation of organic matter (Cano-Garcia et al. 2024). It is found in six large arid grassland valleys associated with gypsum soils and surrounded by arid scrub (Ceballos 2014). Its predators include coyotes, badgers, desert foxes, golden eagles, red-tailed hawks and rattlesnakes (Ceballos 2014), with coyotes as the most significant predator (Mellink and Madrigal 1993). The diet of this species includes different species of grasses, forbs, flowers, and seeds, but they will occasionally feed on cacti and yuccas (Ceballos 2014, Koprowski et al. 2016). In the spring, Cynomys mexicanus primarily feeds on young grasses, and later switches to primarily consuming forbs (Mellink and Madrigal 1993).This species lives in colonies made of several family groups, or coteries, consisting of several females, one or two unrelated males, and their offspring (Scott-Morales et al. 2005). The breeding season lasts from January through April (Mellink and Madrigal 1993, Loredo Sanchez 2020). Sexual maturity is reached after 1-2 years and litters consist of 2-10 pups that emerge in April after a lactation period of 23 days (Loredo Sanchez 2020).
threats: This species is at risk of extinction from habitat loss from expansion of agriculture and ranching throughout its restricted range (Scott-Morales et al. 2005, Ceballos 2014). It lost 51–77% of its habitat area between 1998 and 2023 (González-Uribe et al. 2024). Both grazing and agricultural activities have fragmented Cynomys mexicanus habitat, limiting species dispersal and increasing isolation between colonies (González-Uribe et al. 2024). Increasing proximity to roads also contributes to habitat loss and fragmentation (González Uribe and García Aranda 2024) and invasive plant species lead to habitat deterioration and decreased grassland health (Zaragoza-Quintana et al. 2022). Protected areas have been established in Nuevo Leon for this species, but still allow agricultural activities that negatively impact soil condition and habitat (Zaragoza-Quintana et al. 2022).In addition to habitat loss, agriculture also threatens Cynomys mexicanus through direct mortality and pesticide exposure. Due to erroneous belief that the species will compete with livestock, this species has been the target of intensive and widespread poisoning and other control efforts by farmers (Koprowski et al. 2016, SMSG 2018). This species is also heavily exposed to agricultural pesticides, which were found in all scat samples analysed. Recorded levels were high enough to cause reproductive problems and population stress and may be contributing to Cynomys mexicanus decline (Cano-García et al. 2023).Outbreaks of sylvatic plague can also cause rapid reductions to local populations (Koprowski et al. 2016).
population: The area of land occupied by Cynomys mexicanus is declining, with only around 232 km² of active colonies remaining as of 2023 (González-Uribe et al. 2024). Over 50% (50.7%) of these are in the state of Coahuila, 47.0% are in Nuevo León, and 2.3% are in San Luis Potosí (González-Uribe et al. 2024). Previously this species was extirpated from Zacatecas, but now translocated populations occupy an area of 45.15 ha (González-Uribe and García Aranda 2024). This species has a total of 60 colonies, with 26 in Coahuila, 25 in Nuevo León, and only six in San Luis Potosí (González-Uribe et al. 2024). Density ranges between 4 and 12.8 individuals per hectare (Pineda Perez 2018).
range: This Mexican endemic is found in grasslands near the nexus of the states of Coahuila, Nuevo León, San Luis Potosí, and Zacatecas (Cano-García et al. 2023, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It was previously extirpated from Zacatecas (Ceballos 2014) but has since been translocated to three sites within the state (González-Uribe et al. 2023). Its range is limited north and east by the Sierra Madre Oriental and to the south and west by arid hills and plains (Ceballos 2014). It only has 231.2 km² of active colonies, a 51–77% decrease since 1998 (González-Uribe et al. 2024).
useTrade: This species is listed in Appendix II of CITES.
conservationActions: This species is listed on Appendix II of CITES and at the highest risk category for extinction by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). The grasslands at the convergence of the Mexican states of Nuevo Leon, San Luis Potosi, and Zacatecas, known as El Tokio, has been designated as Grassland Priority Conservation Area (Baez-Gonzalez et al. 2018). 8,632 km² were allocated for the conservation of this species’ habitat (Loredo Sanchez 2020).In Nuevo Leon, three protected natural areas were created specifically to conserve this species: Llano de la Soledad, La Trinidad, and La Hediondilla.
