Together, these areas cover over 15,000 ha, allow for limited agricultural activity, and should utilize sustainable grazing to support Cynomys mexicanus populations (Zaragoza-Quintana et al. 2022). In addition, this species has been found in Mojonera Protected Natural Area (González-Uribe et al. 2023), as well as other federal and state protected lands (CONABIO 2024).Incorporating social participation in Cynomys mexicanus conservation is useful to its continued persistence. For example, implementing a management plan for invasive plant control and introducing native herbivores to regulate grasslands near burrow sites would benefit this species (Loredo Sanchez 2020). Limiting agricultural pesticide usage would also reduce impact to Cynomys mexicanus and other wildlife (Cano-García et al. 2023).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU B2ab(ii,iii)) because it has an area of occupancy of 1,012–2,000 km², the popualtion is severely fragmented, and there is an ongoing decline in its area of occupancy and area and quality of habitat. Declines are driven by land conversion for grazing and agriculture and the ongoing effects of climate change. While it does well in protected areas of pristine forest habitat, this species is intolerant of cultivation. Therefore, ongoing fragmentation from agricultural expansion may lead to this species becoming further threatened over time.
habitat: This species is mostly diurnal, though it is sometimes seen at dusk or during the night (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2012, Ríos-Solís et al. 2021, Rodas-Trejo et al. 2025). It is found in cloud forests (Ramírez Bautista 2018, Pérez-Gracida et al. 2023), as well as low deciduous forest and medium sub-evergreen forest (Reid 2009, Rodas-Trejo et al. 2025). It is a fairly large-bodied rodent, weighing several kilograms (Ramírez Bautista 2018, Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019).Dasyprocta mexicana is considered frugivorous or folivorous and eats fruit, soft seeds, and new growth of forest plants (Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019, Ríos-Solís et al. 2021). In Veracruz, fruits eaten include figs, hog plums (Spondias mombin), and Brosimum alicastrum. It may be seen alone or in pairs. Pairs occupy territories of 1 to 2 ha. One or two young are born during the dry season. Young are precocious and follow their mother soon after birth (Reid 2009).
threats: This species is threatened by habitat transformation and deforestation due to cattle ranching and agricultural expansion (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2011). Habitat impacts are particularly severe since this species prefers undisturbed forests. No individuals were seen in a restored pastureland in Veracruz, despite presence in a nearby cloud forest (Pérez-Gracida et al. 2023). Over 26% of its current range contains unsuitable habitats, and this will likely increase over time (Ramírez Bautista 2018). This species is highly vulnerable to climate change, with pessimistic models suggesting up to a 90% loss of habitat by 2075–2090 (Ramírez Bautista 2018).Dasyprocta mexicana is also impacted by hunting for food and as an agricultural pest throughout its distribution (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2011, Gilbert and Lacher 2016). Numbers in some areas have remained high despite illegal subsistence hunting (Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019).
population: Reid (2009) noted that this species is probably uncommon. Sánchez-Cordero et al. (2005) estimated 35% of the ecological niche of Dasyprocta mexicana was already lost in 2000. Threats continue to reduce populations, and records are predominantly from preserved lands. In preserved areas, Dasyprocta mexicana is often one of the most commonly sighted mammal species during camera trap surveys. In a study in Veracruz, it was the most commonly sighted species with 265 records, the next highest species only had 87 (Mezhua-Velázquez et al. 2022). It had the second highest number of reports of any mammal species at La Reserva de la Biosfera Selva El Ocote in Chiapas (Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019) and at La Reserva de la Biosfera de Los Tuxtlas in Veracruz, with 81 records over 1,110 camera trap days (Ríos-Solís et al. 2022). Another report from Los Tuxtlas reported this species as one of the top three most common mammals in the park (Zagal-García et al. 2022). It was also the third most numerous of 22 mammal species reported at Chimalapas forest, Oaxaca (n =81), despite local presence of subsistence hunting (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2012). It was sighted in both areas with high and low visitor frequency in Chiapas (Rodas-Trejo et al. 2025) and in a cloud forest but not a restored pastureland in Veracruz (Pérez-Gracida et al. 2023).
range: This species is endemic to southeastern Mexico (Rodas-Trejo et al. 2025) and is found in southern Veracruz, lowlands of northeastern Oaxaca, northwestern Chiapas, and western Tabasco (Gilbert and Lacher 2016, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It was introduced to western and eastern Cuba in the 1930s (Gilbert and Lacher 2016), but is only currently found on the western side of the island (Borroto-Páez 2009).
useTrade: This species is used for food and sport hunting, and has commercial value (Mezhua-Velázquez et al. 2022). It is hunted for food and as an agricultural pest throughout its distribution (Gilbert and Lacher 2016). It is also considered one of the primary sources of animal protein for those who inhabit the Selva Zoque area and unsustainable hunting has led to overexploitation (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2011). However, there is evidence that populations remain high even in areas with hunting (Lira-Torres and Briones-Salas 2012).
conservationActions: This species is not listed on any endangered species lists in Mexico (SEMARNAT 2010). Records are almost exclusively from in or around protected areas. These include Selva El Ocote Biosphere Reserve and El Zapotal Ecological Reserve in Chiapas (Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019, Rodas-Trejo et al. 2025) and Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve (Ríos-Solís et al. 2021) and some private reserves in Veracruz (Gallina and González-Romero 2018). This species would benefit from continued population studies to better inform sustainable management plans that mitigate impacts of hunting (Pozo-Montuy et al. 2019, Mezhua-Velázquez et al. 2022).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered B1ab(i,iii). Its extent of occurrence is 4,040 km² and it is only found in two locations. There is continuing decline in both extent of occurrence and habitat quality due to deforestation from expanding agriculture, grazing, and human settlements.
habitat: Habromys delicatulus is found exclusively in humid cloud forests at elevations above 2,000 m asl (Carleton et al. 2002, Contreras-Medina et al. 2022). The species occurs in the northernmost escarpments of the Cordillera Neovolcánica, where the landscape is characterised by steep ravines with large boulders that create a sheltered, moist microenvironment (Carleton et al. 2002). The general area is covered by dense oak forests (Quercus spp.), interspersed with small patches of oyamel fir (Abies sp.) (Carleton et al. 2002). The species' habitat within the ravine is a relict montane cloud forest, distinguished by tree species such as Ilex tolucana, Garrya aff. laurifolia, and Cornus aff. disciflora (Carleton et al. 2002). Habromys delicatulus is primarily arboreal (Carleton et al. 2002, Contreras-Medina et al. 2022), but many other aspects of its natural history and ecology remain poorly understood (Ceballos 2014).
threats: The Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt is affected by forest fragmentation and disturbance from increasing agriculture, grazing and urbanisation, which may be significant threats to this species (Rogers 2007, Contreras-Medina et al. 2022). Its micro-endemic status makes this species particularly susceptible to environmental changes and potentially extinction (Ceballos 2014). Both the species' inherent vulnerability to threats and its interactions with humans remain poorly understood (Ceballos 2014). Therefore, although its habitat may currently appear moderately favorable, its long-term stability is uncertain.Localized impacts from unsustainable tourism in Xilotepec may also be a problem for this species (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018).
population: Limited population information exists on this species as it is only known from a few specimens and is considered rare throughout its range (León-Paniagua et al. 2007). However, populations are inferred to be declining from habitat loss from deforestation and unsustainable tourism (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018).
range: This species is endemic to the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt and found at a mean elevation of 2,603 m asl (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022). While observations are scarce, it has been recorded at Cañada de Hermita, Dexcani Alto, Jilotepec, Estado de México (type locality; Carleton et al. 2002) and in Cerro Garnica, in the northeastern corner of Michoacán (Rogers et al. 2007, Ceballos 2014, González-Ruiz 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
conservationActions: There are currently no conservation measures in place for Habromys delicatulus and this species is not yet protected by the Mexican government (González-Ruiz et al. 2014). As one of Mexico’s more recently described mammal species, its biology and conservation status remain poorly understood (Ceballos 2014). However, due to its micro-endemic status and ongoing habitat fragmentation, this species should be prioritised in conservation efforts (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022).

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because it meets some of the criteria for Vulnerable under criterion B. Its area of occupancy (AOO) is 604–2,000 km² and it has been experiencing substantial loss of habitat quality and extent due to deforestation for agriculture and logging. It is unclear how many locations this species occupies, but it is likely more than 10.
habitat: This species is nocturnal and inhabits rocky walls of canyons, hollow logs, and roots and eats mostly fruits (Castro-Campillo et al. 2014). It has been recorded in cloud forests, pine forests, and pink-oak forests, often with groundcover of brushy vegetation (Rogers and Skoy 2011). Peromyscus furvus was trapped more frequently in the interior of forests, rather than on the edge (López-Barrera et al. 2007). This species sympatrically occurs with 1–3 other Peromyscus species (Rogers and Skoy 2011).Limited life history information is available on this species, but specimen collection records indicate that it may have a prolonged breeding season or breed throughout the year (Rogers and Skoy 2011).
threats: The majority of this species’ habitat has been affected by deforestation, which may be a significant threat (Rogers and Skoy 2011). Its range lost 75.7 k ha of tree cover from 2014 to 2024, about 4.3% of the total tree cover recorded in 2000 (Global Forest Watch 2025). Only 39.38% of this species habitat is untransformed (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005). Deforestation is likely caused by agricultural activities and logging (Navarro Cerrillo et al. 2019).There is also a potential risk of climate change and this species has been categorised as “high latent risk” due to its low adaptive capacity and high sensitivity to change (Ramírez‐Bautista et al. 2020). Under various climate change scenarios, up to 20% of its range will be exposed to climate impacts from 2015 to 2039 and up to 37.2% by 2075–2099 (Ramírez‐Bautista et al. 2020).
population: Limited population information is available on this species, though it appears there is substantial genetic variation between populations (Cruz-Gómez et al. 2021). Peromyscus furvus was the most frequently captured species in a cloud forest by López-Barrera et al. (2007).
range: Blackish Deer Mouse is endemic to Mexico, and it is found in the states of Hidalgo, Puebla, and Veracruz (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It is found in moderate- to high-elevation cloud forests along the eastern slopes of the Sierra Madre Oriental from southern Hidalgo to northern Oaxaca, Mexico (Rogers and Skoy 2011).
conservationActions: This species requires more research to understand more about its basic biology, population status, and threats. It has not been listed as a protected status by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010) despite the risk of deforestation within its range (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005). Peromyscus furvus has been recorded in multiple federal, state, and local protected lands (CONABIO 2024).

rationale: Catalina Deer Mouse is assessed as Critically Endangered B1ab(v). This species has a very restricted extent of occurrence (EOO) of 46 km², and is confined to a single location: the Santa Catalina Island in the southern Gulf of California (Sea of Cortez). It is experiencing a continuing decline in the number of mature individuals, primarily due to competition with two congeneric species: Peromyscus eremicus, introduced to the island by fishermen, and Peromyscus fraterculus, a species native to the Baja California Peninsula that is better adapted to arid environments.
habitat: Peromyscus slevini occurs in canyons and has been found in the bottom of a draw, where the soil was sandy (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2010, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). The island supports vegetation of the sarcocaulescent xerophilous scrub type. It is a triangular plain with sandy soil that becomes rocky toward the edges; its vegetation is sparse with few cacti (Ávila-Villegas 2005). The main plants on Santa Catalina Island include Bursera hindsiana, Bursera microphylla, Colubrina viridis, Encelia farinosa, Esenbeckia flava, Euphorbia polycarpa, and Ferocactus diguetii (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). Eight females captured in November were lactating and none were pregnant (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
threats: Peromyscus slevini is threatened by competition with two congeneric species: Peromyscus eremicus, introduced to Santa Catalina Island by fishermen (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024), and Peromyscus fraterculus, a species from the Baja California Peninsula that is better adapted to desert conditions (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2010). The probable invasion of Peromyscus fraterculus in the early 1990s led to its spread across the island and was immediately followed by a reduction in the Peromyscus slevini population (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2010). The decline has been further attributed to the combined effects of the introduction of mainland Peromyscus species and rising temperatures, which together are believed to be driving an ecological replacement of Peromyscus slevini by Peromyscus fraterculus (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2023). In addition, Peromyscus slevini constitutes the primary prey of the endemic Crotalus catalinensis, making up 71% of its diet, which may further influence population pressures (Arnaud 2015).
population: Historical accounts indicate that Peromyscus slevini was once abundant on Santa Catalina Island, with observations of individuals active even during daylight hours (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). However, trapping records from recent decades demonstrate a marked decline in population. No individuals were captured in 1993, followed by low capture rates in subsequent years, 15 specimens in 1995 and four in 1998, despite considerable trapping effort (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). This species is currently considered to be declining, with surveys reporting either extremely low or absent captures in recent decades (Cortés-Calva et al. 2016). The decline has been attributed to the accidental introduction of Peromyscus fraterculus, a congeneric species from the mainland that likely competes for resources and may be displacing the endemic species (Álvarez-Castañeda et al. 2023).
range: Peromyscus slevini is endemic to Santa Catalina Island, located in the Gulf of California off the eastern coast of the Baja California Peninsula, Mexico. It is the only native rodent species on the island and has not been recorded elsewhere (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
conservationActions: Peromyscus slevini is listed as Endangered under Mexican legislation (SEMARNAT 2010). Santa Catalina Island, the only known habitat of this species, is included within the Bahía de Loreto National Park and the Flora and Fauna Protection Area of the Gulf of California Islands, providing it with formal protection (Arnaud 2015). In response to the threat posed by feral cats to native species on the island, a targeted eradication program was initiated in 2001 by the Island Conservation and Ecology Group. This effort resulted in the successful removal of cats by 2004 (Ávila-Villegas 2005, Aguirre-Muñoz et al. 2008).An action plan for its conservation was proposed during the Mexican Small Mammal Assessment, Prioritization, and Conservation Planning Workshop (Small Mammal Specialist Group 2018) and identified the following objectives and actions:Objective 1: Determine the status of the populationsMonitor the distribution and abundance of populations - need to develop the detailed steps to be implemented for the monitoring protocol.Characterise the genetics of the population.Objective 2: Remove the invasive species of Peromyscus from the island Option 1. Remove Peromyscus sleveni, before then eradicating the invasive species, and replace with Peromyscus slevini from captive bred population.Option 2. Develop a size specific trap for the small invasive Peromyscus and trap individuals out while leaving Peromyscus slevini.Objective 3: Captive breeding for insuranceFind collaborating institution for captive breeding programRemoval of individualsMonitoring of genetic diversity

rationale: The African Golden Cat is a forest-dependent species restricted to equatorial Africa, where high deforestation is causing substantial reductions in its habitat quality. Data on the extent of African Golden Cat area of occupancy (AOO) loss is unavailable due to a lack of population monitoring. However, we can infer a population decline using data on forest/habitat loss (deforestation) and decrease in habitat quality (forest/habitat degradation primarily due to bushmeat hunting), and evidence of their effects on African Golden Cats.Tropical forests face growing loss and degradation from logging, urbanization, agriculture, and infrastructure. The African Golden Cat's forested habitat has been drastically reduced by approximately 17% in the Upper Guinean Forest between 2000 and 2019, with Côte d’Ivoire and Liberia accounting for 94% of the net area of forest lost (ca 15 times greater than deforestation in Sierra Leone and Guinea combined; Erazo-Mera et al. 2024). In addition, close to 9% of the tropical moist forest area of Central Africa has disappeared since 2000 and there is an increase in the annual disturbance rate of the forest from the years 2015–2020 compared to 2005–2015 (Eba’a Atyi et al. 2022). The African Golden Cat's forested habitat has also drastically reduced by approximately 93.0% in East Africa from 1900–2018. In Uganda alone, a deforestation rate of 17% in the tropical rainforest reserves was estimated for 1990–2020 (Nuwagira and Ikiriza 2022). In terms of degradation, an excess of 64% of forest habitat in the Congo Basin lies within 10 km of a road and is also predicted to be affected by higher hunting pressure (Blake et al. 2007). Development of roads has increased rapidly in the past 15 years (e.g. 35% increase in the Democratic Republic of Congo and >300% increase in the northern Republic of Congo since the year 2000; Laporte et al. 2007).Earlier landscape-scale surveys of the African Golden Cat in mainland Equatorial Guinea (Rio Muni) emphasize that prior range estimates based on forest cover may have significantly overestimated the remaining African Golden Cat range. Worryingly, the threats facing the African Golden Cat, particularly hunting, have not spared protected areas. Increased bushmeat hunting impacts African Golden Cats, either directly through increased mortality in snares (as either targeted or bycatch/incidental) or indirectly through increased mortality of their prey. Benítez-López et al. (2019) predicted large declines (>70%) of mammal populations in West Africa, by using datasets spanning 1980–2017. In Central Africa, a wide variety of terrestrial vertebrates are consumed as bushmeat, with ungulates, rodents and primates constituting the majority (Fa et al. 2005). Estimates for bushmeat harvested across the Congo Basin range from 1 million t Yr-1 (Wilkie and Carpenter 1999) to over 4.5 million t Yr-1 (Nasi et al. 2011). Such levels of harvesting are deemed unsustainable, and estimates suggest wildlife extraction is occurring at more than six times the sustainable rate (Bennett 2002). Another study showed that the mean proportion of animals sold in markets for bushmeat in tropical Africa increased from 34% of the total offtake in 1991 to 72% in 2020 (Ingram et al. 2025). Additional anecdotal evidence also shows a high level of African Golden Cat exploitation in some areas: for example, in only one year, 80 African Golden Cats were caught and killed in hunting snares at three protected areas in Uganda (Badru Mugerwa, unpublished data), and estimated abundance of African Golden Cats was nearly 50% lower in areas with hunting compared to areas with no hunting (Badru Mugerwa, unpublished data). In eastern Cameroon, 13 Golden Cats were captured at a rate of 6.6 animals per trap-night, giving an extrapolated estimate of 384 cats captured a year at a rate of 0.31 Golden Cats caught per km² (T. Davenport and G. Ngandjui, pers. comm.).We suspect that the cumulative loss of AOO (due to deforestation, reduction in habitat quality, and potential levels of exploitation of African Golden Cats and their prey), notably amounts to >30% over the past 15 years (i.e., three African Golden Cat generations; Pacifici et al. 2013) resulting, together with the potential levels of exploitation of the species, in a population size decline of the African Golden Cat of over 30%, qualifying it for the Vulnerable status under citerion A2cd. Additionally, the exacerbation of these threats due to human population growth, projected mining activities and forest clearance for oil palm plantations will likely cause further reduction in AOO for the African Golden Cat. We therefore predict that the AOO will be reduced by at least a further 30% in the next 15 years, lending additional support to the species’ listing as Vulnerable under criterion A3cd.
habitat: While the Neotropical and Indomalayan regions have several sympatric forest-dependent felid species, the African Golden Cat is the only forest obligate felid in Africa. This elusive predator is primarily associated with dense, moist equatorial forests, though at the margins of its distribution it extends into savanna landscapes along riverine forests. It also inhabits montane forests and even alpine moorlands in the eastern part of its range (Nowell and Jackson 1996, Ray and Butynski 2013).Comprehensive recent studies on the ecology of the African Golden Cat come from Bahaa-el-Din et al. (2015; 2016) and Mills et al. (2019a; 2019b), accruing from their PhD. dissertations conducted on the species in Gabon and Uganda respectively. Dietary studies based on scat analyses reveal a strong preference for small mammals (corrected frequency of occurrence provided thereafter). Studies of scats—from the Ituri forest of the Congo (Hart et al. 1996) and the Dzanga-Sangha Forest of the Central African Republic (Ray and Sunquist 2001)—found that rodents and squirrels were the main prey item (70% and 62% respectively), followed by small and medium-size duikers (antelopes; 25% and 33% respectively). Similar results were found in Gabon where rodents made up 70% of prey (represented by 16 species), with blue duikers Philantomba monticola making up another 12% (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015). Primates made up 5% of the prey items in Ituri and Dzanga-Sangha while they only made up 1.4% in Gabon, and there have been several observations by primate researchers of African Golden Cats hunting arboreal primates (Ray and Butynski 2013, Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015). Primates made up around 5% of prey in each study, with several direct observations confirming golden cats hunting arboreal primates (Ray and Butynski 2013, Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015), including red colobus (Piliocolobus tephrosceles) in Kibale National Park in Uganda (https://gizmodo.com/the-first-ever-footage-of-an-african-golden-cat-attacki-1682746897). The same general diet items were reported from Uganda’s Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, although with up to 60% of small ungulates (Kingdon 1977). In a recent study using metabarcoding to assess origin of scat and diet composition in Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park in the northern Republic of the Congo and its buffer zone (logged area), eight prey species were identified from 22 scats, with a majority of small ungulates (37.5%) and rodents (46.9%), occasionally supplemented with small primates (6.3%), small carnivores (6.3%), and birds (3.1%; Tossens et al. in review). Dietary overlap with sympatric leopards was low, with the only prey in common being Peters’ duiker (Cephalophus callipygus). Other prey items in general include birds, and pangolins, the latter frequently recorded in scats from Côte d’Ivoire’s Taï National Park (D. Jenny, pers. comm. in Nowell and Jackson 1996) and in some scats in the Republic of Congo (Ososky 1998 in Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015). In 2014, camera traps set up in the Gashaka Gumti National Park captured an African Golden Cat attacking a pangolin (see video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lPLLVPh3cNM).Despite being the only forest-dependent felid in Africa, the African Golden Cat occasionally becomes prey itself. Remains have been found in leopard diets, the only other felid sharing these forests. For instance, African Golden Cat remains appeared in five of 196 leopard scats collected in Gabon’s Lopé National Park (Henschel et al. 2005), and a carcass killed by a leopard was reported from the Ituri Forest (Hart et al. 1996). Leopards and golden cats were found to overlap in space use by an average of 52% in Gabon, with one site having as high as 92% overlap, based on the number of camera traps at which they were both recorded (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015).African Golden Cat temporal activity was found to be highly adaptable across a range of sites in Uganda and Gabon, ranging from cathemeral to nocturnal-crepuscular (Mugerwa et al. 2014, Bahaa-el-din et al. 2015). Although often reported to prey on livestock in adjacent local communities, a depredation assessment of the African Golden Cat in local communities adjacent Bwindi Impenetrable National Park using household pictorial surveys revealed that the species was responsible for only 5.94% of the depredation events, preying mostly on goats (Mugerwa et al. 2017). Poultry could also fall prey to African Golden Cats. African Golden Cats were placed in the low conflict category by Inskip and Zimmerman (2009), and Bahaa-el-din (2015) found them to be considered unproblematic by local communities in Gabon.
threats: The African Golden Cat is restricted to the tropical rainforests of equatorial Africa, a region under severe pressure from escalating human activities driven by rapid population growth, widespread poverty, urban expansion, economic development, and ongoing political instability (Lambin and Meyfroidt 2011; Tittensor et al. 2014; Harrison et al. 2015; Daskin and Pringle 2018; Braga-Pereira et al. 2020; Assede et al. 2021, 2023). Mining, road construction, agriculture expansion, hunting and intensive timber extraction are (and increasingly becoming) ubiquitous (Wilkie et al. 2000, Edwards et al. 2014, Tyukavina et al. 2018, Kleinschroth et al. 2019, Batumike et al. 2021, Giljum et al. 2022). Such developments offer financial gains in a region suffering severe poverty, but without care this has negative implications for African Golden Cat conservation (Edwards et al. 2014, Kleinschroth et al. 2019). Habitat loss and degradation, pollution and extraction of wildlife for consumption and trade have been the detrimental outcomes (Beaune et al. 2013, Potapov et al. 2017, Riddell et al. 2022). These anthropogenic pressures are likely causing extirpation of and declines in the African Golden Cat populations, as has been reported for other wildlife species. Yet these pressures are expected to increase with Africa’s human population and associated consumption, urbanisation and economic growth (Crist, Mora and Engelman 2017, Tilman et al. 2017, IPBES 2019, ).Africa’s human population alone is expected to increase from the current 1.34 billion to the UN medium variant projections of 2.08 billion by 2040 (Cilliers 2021). The annual human population growth in the countries of the African Golden Cat range is between 2.1–3.9% (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.GROW?locations=ZG&most_recent_value_desc=true).The anticipated increase in human population will undoubtedly increase human pressure on the African Golden Cat habitat. In West Africa, for instance, between 2000 and 2020, uncontrolled logging, charcoal production, and construction of a dense road network have led to decrease in forest cover by 1.44% per year; croplands have increased by 3.39% per year; forest conversions to rubber plantations have increased by 6.98% per year; and settlements/urbanisation have eroded forest cover by 7% per year (Ouattara et al. 2018, Kouassi et al. 2021, Yin et al. 2021). The outcome has been an estimated reduction of forest cover of approximately 17% in the Upper Guinean Forest between 2000 and 2019 (Erazo-Mera et al. 2024). Even in the absence of forest loss, as is the case inside protected areas, habitat degradation epitomised by unsustainable wildlife hunting, consumption and trade is likely driving African Golden Cats towards local extirpation (the empty forest syndrome).Nevertheless, the impact of the threats on the African Golden Cat populations across its putative tropical rainforest range have largely been based on anecdotal evidence lacking systematic primary (quantitative) assessments. Only a handful studies have been conducted at a few selected sites (Bahaa-el-Din et al. 2015, 2016; Mills et al. 2019a,b). As part of the African Golden Cat Conservation Alliance (AGCCA), initiatives are now in place to start to systematically assess the threats to the long-term survival of the African Golden Cat across the species range. For instance, work in Uganda has assessed the threat to the species due to retaliation in case of depredation of livestock and poultry by the African Golden Cat, unauthorised hunting (poaching) and habitat degradation. Household interviews showed that retaliatory killing following depredation by the African Golden Cat is a negligible threat to the species, with only 5.94% of the households reporting African Golden Cats responsible for depredation at Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (Mugerwa et al. 2017). Camera trap data from Bwindi Impenetrable National Park in Uganda showed that forest degradation was not a significant threat either. Differences in forest cover (measured as a proxy of habitat quality) at Bwindi did not elicit a significant influence on African Golden Cat abundance and habitat use (Mugerwa et al. 2017). A similar finding was reported in Gabon (Bahaa-el-Din et al. 2016). African Golden Cats may thus be resilient to habitat modifications and capable of thriving in disturbed forests such as those undergoing well-managed logging (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016), provided that the direct extractive hunting activities are kept to the minimum. Deforestation and bushmeat hunting are the main threats to the species.Both camera trap surveys and community interviews at three forested protected areas in Uganda (Bwindi, Kasyoha-Kitomi and Echuya forests) confirmed snare poaching as a serious threat to the African Golden Cat (Bitariho, Babaasa and Mugerwa 2016, Mugerwa 2018). The African Golden Cats at Bwindi exhibited significantly lower abundance and habitat use in areas with poaching than in areas without poaching (Mugerwa et al. 2017). Key informants’ interviews involving 84 hunters, 16 researchers, and 83 wildlife rangers from three protected areas in Uganda estimated that, in only one year (between February 2019 and February 2020), a total of 80 African Golden Cats perished because of snare poaching. Nine of those were directly hunted for skin and witchcraft and 71 were unintentionally killed in snares and traps as bycatch in what may be considered “collateral damage” (see case study here: https://www.speciesconservation.org/case-studies-projects/caracal/19655). Elsewhere, it was reported that snares killed four golden cats in two months over 20 km² in Gabon (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016), 13 golden cats in three months at four sites in Cameroon (Davenport pers. com, 2013), and a further 13 individuals in three months in Lobéké, Cameroon (Ray et al. 2005). Snares are non-selective, killing or maiming non-target species, including the African Golden Cat (Mugerwa et al. 2013, Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016, Simo et al. 2019, Mugerwa et al. 2020) and its prey. In fact, along a human disturbance gradient, hunting exhibited the strongest impact on the density of African Golden Cats in Gabon (Bahaa-el-Din et al. 2016). Camera trap images of African Golden Cats caught in snares continue to surface e.g. Simo et al. (2019), thanks to the increasing camera trap effort across the tropical forest belt of Africa.Snare poaching for bushmeat consumption and trade remains the most pervasive conservation threat causing direct mortality to the African Golden Cat in Africa (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016, Ripple et al. 2016, Simo et al. 2019, Mugerwa et al. 2020). In fact, hunting for bushmeat trade and consumption in Africa’s equatorial forest belt is a recognised crisis (Benítez-López et al. 2017, 2019), with >1 million tons of wildlife harvested in the Congo Basin per year (Wilkie and Carpenter 1999, Zvikonyaukwa et al. 2023) and mammal populations are predicted to strongly decline (>70%) in the forests of West Africa due to overhunting. Intensive hunting for bushmeat likely accounts for greater reduction in area of occupancy (AOO) for the African Golden Cat than habitat degradation but is more difficult to quantify. In an area of moderate bushmeat hunting, African Golden Cats were recorded at less than a quarter of the population densities that they are found at in pristine areas (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016). Systematic African Golden Cat field survey work in various land use types in Gabon found a >20% drop in population density in FSC-certified logging concessions, compared to pristine, primary forest, a near 40% drop in density in non-certified logging concessions, a >60% reduction in density in a forest-savannas mosaic, and a >75% decline in a site used for subsistence bushmeat hunting (Bahaa-el-Din et al. 2016). Even if African Golden Cats may be resilient to habitat modifications, such as FSC-certified logging concessions, their density will be impacted by loss of forest cover and hunting.Where more intense hunting occurs, such as in village hunting areas (e.g. Dibouka village in central Gabon; Henschel 2008) and national parks (e.g. Korup NP in southwest Cameroon), camera trap and bushmeat studies did not record the species despite the presence of suitable habitat contiguous with the main forest of the Congo Basin. Within 10–15 km of roads and settlements, large and medium bodied mammals experience sharp declines in population (Laurance et al. 2006, Blake et al. 2007, Henschel 2008, Kurpiers et al. 2016). In excess of 64% of forest habitat in the Congo Basin lies within 10 km of a road and is also predicted to be affected by higher hunting pressure (Blake et al. 2007). Earlier landscape-scale surveys of the African Golden Cat in mainland Equatorial Guinea (Rio Muni) emphasise that prior range estimates based on forest cover may have significantly overestimated the remaining African Golden Cat range. Its presence in the area was correlated with rugged, inaccessible terrain away from human disturbance (Martinez Marti 2011). In the same study, African Golden Cats were reported by locals to be easy to hunt and locally extirpated long before other medium-to-large mammal species (Martinez Marti 2011). African Golden Cat populations within these highly impacted areas are likely to be severely reduced or extirpated through direct mortality and loss of prey.The key drivers of hunting in Africa’s equatorial forest belt are multi-faceted, but poverty, stemming from limited employment opportunities, resulting in families struggling to access household income, animal protein or basic health care, remains a root driver in this region. Thus, important livelihood needs among people at the African Golden Cat habitat frontline encourage bushmeat poaching. If poaching is not locally curbed, we anticipate the species to be extirpated in several forests of its range as was the case for leopards (Panthera pardus), for example in Uganda forests (Butynski 1984, Mugerwa et al. 2013) and elsewhere. Evidence has shown that incentivising and engaging local communities strengthens interventions against poaching (Acharya et al. 2020, Ngorima et al. 2020). Therefore, successful anti-poaching initiatives should focus on improving the socio-economic status of local people, for instance, by increasing household income and providing an alternative source of meat (Lindsey et al. 2013). However, projects that combine local livelihoods with conservation are not new to Africa. Yet, poaching continues. This is partly because livelihood projects have not reached the right people in the community and are rarely tied to conservation (Harrison et al. 2015, Bitario et al. 2022). The threat of hunting on the African Golden Cat will intensify, as the human population within the species’ range shows the fastest annual growth rates in the world (+2.1–3.9%; https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.GROW?locations=ZG&most_recent_value_desc=true). The human population in main African Golden Cat range countries is projected to almost quadruple by 2100 (UN 2012; http://esa.un.org/wpp/). Further, the current “stampede of foreign investment” in exploitative activities (mining and logging) and associated infrastructure development, particularly within the tropical forest belt is of immediate concern (Edwards et al. 2014). In Central Africa, 42% of ecologically important areas would be directly impacted if there were complete development of mineral resources in the region (if ecological impacts extend within 10 km of mines; Edwards et al. 2014). China’s mineral investment alone has quadrupled in 10 years (Zhang 2011). In addition, it is predicted that the conversion of forests to oil palm plantations, which has caused extensive loss of forest habitat and biodiversity in Southeast Asia, will have similar impacts in Africa (particularly in West and Central Africa) as it expands over the coming years (Wich et al. 2014). The realisation of these investments includes habitat destruction and degradation, relocation of human populations into previously remote areas and massive-scale infrastructural development including road and railways, which in turn lead to the aforementioned surge in bushmeat hunting in these areas (Edwards et al. 2014).
population: The African Golden Cat is infrequently observed in the wild, directly or otherwise. It can be found at densities similar to small forest-dependent felids from other regions. A density of 16.23 individuals per 100 km² was recorded at a pristine site in Gabon (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016); 16.8 individuals per 100 km² at Bwindi, Uganda (M. Mugerwa, pers. comm. 2025); 23 individuals per 100 km² at Kibale, Uganda (D. Mills pers. comm. 2025); four individuals per 100 km² at Minziro, Tanzania (Greco and Rovero 2021). Densities are impacted by human disturbance, with estimates of 10.18 and 12.84 individuals per 100 km² in two logging concessions, and as low as 3.8 per 100 km² at a site with only moderate levels of bushmeat hunting in Gabon (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016). At Bwindi, the density estimates were nearly 50% fewer in areas with bushmeat hunting. In West Africa, in areas where leopards are present in high density, African Golden Cats seem to be less abundant (Drouilly et al. 2023), but more data are needed to verify this. So far, there is no information on population size trend over multiple years, even at the local level, which should be the priority of future research. Despite its wide extent of occurrence (EOO), sightings of the African Golden Cats are rare in many places of its known occurrence, requiring several camera trap nights to be detected in some areas. The African Golden Cat is even rarer in areas where hunting for bushmeat is widespread. For instance, African Golden Cats were not recorded in Dibouka village in central Gabon (Henschel 2008) and Korup National Park (NP) in southwest Cameroon (TEAM, http://www.teamnetwork.org), where hunting is prevalent. In an area of putatively suitable habitat in Equatorial Guinea, just 16% of the area was found to be occupied by African Golden Cats due to human disturbance (Martinez Marti 2011). Camera trap surveys in Mayombe National Park (Angola) for the African Golden Cat for 6,080 camera trap days produced no detection of the species despite several detections of other rare species, many of them first records for the country (E. Lutondo pers. comm.). Another study required 1,832 camera nights to get a first record of the African Golden Cat at Gatamaiyu Forest Reserve in Kenya (S. Omusula pers. comm.). Similar observations have been made at in Minziro Forest Reserve (Tanzania, E. Martin unpublished data), Echuya Forest Reserve (Uganda, Institute of Tropical Conservation unpublished data), Mgahinga Gorilla National Park (Uganda, B. Mugerwa unpublished data), Volcanoes National Park (Rwanda, Tropical Ecology Assessment and Monitoring unpublished data) and Kasyoha-Kitomi Forest Reserve (Uganda, Institute of Tropical Conservation unpublished data).
range: The African Golden Cat is endemic to the forests of Equatorial Africa. There are no confirmed records north of Guinea-Bissau. No records from Benin (Ray and Butynski 2013). This suggests a separation between Western (Togo, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Guinea Bissau) and Central African (Nigeria, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Republic of Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo, Angola and South Sudan) and East African (Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, and Kenya) populations (Nowell and Jackson 1996).In West Africa, the core of the African Golden Cat population is predicted to occur in Liberia, Sierra Leone and South-western Ivory Coast, as for other rare and Endangered forest-dwelling species such as the pygmy hippopotamus (Choeropsis liberiensis) and the zebra duiker (Cephalophus zebra). The same areas also record some of the highest levels of human modification of natural habitats, through deforestation, infrastructure development and hunting.In Central Africa, the African Golden Cat is predicted to be widespread, and perhaps the only remaining continuous population. Cameroon, Gabon, northern Republic of Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic have the highest predicted distribution of the African Golden Cat. These areas are potential strongholds for the species, and remain some of the less human modified landscapes, with minimal disrupted forest and probable high prey densities (Bahaa-el-din et al. 2016). However, the emerging logging industry, infrastructure development and hunting for bushmeat threatens the long-term survival of this only intact population.The East African population is fragmented, and the species population in this region is predicted to be low. Only the forests of the Albertine Rift region in Western Uganda have a higher predicted occurrence. In fact, the central Kenyan population is a recently confirmed population (Hartfield et al. 2019), so is the severely isolated population of the African Golden Cat at Minziro Forest Reserve in Tanzania (Tanzania’s only known record of the species; Greco and Rovero 2020). There are no recent records along the East African coast (stretching from Southern Somalia through Kenya up to the Eastern Arc Mountains in Tanzania).
useTrade: The African Golden Cat is often not a target species for bushmeat hunters, but it falls victim to snares used by bushmeat hunters (Simo et al. 2019) and can be eaten in some places when caught (Davenport et al. n.d. in Lobéké Forest area of southeastern Cameroon) and the skin used or sold. Skins are sometimes found for sale in markets, for example in Yaoundé and some local markets in Uganda where they are often sold alongside medicinal herbs and fetishes (T. Davenport pers. comm. in Ray and Butynski 2013, Simo et al. 2024). In Côte d’Ivoire, (Horion et al. 2025), African Golden Cat products were found in 9.7% of 93 visited stalls, mostly in the northern and western parts of the country. Skins may be used during circumcision rites or to wrap valuable objects, or as good luck charms for hunting success (Nowell and Jackson 1996). They are also used as ornaments in Cameroon (Simo et al. 2024). Around Budongo Central Forest Reserve and Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, the species, when caught in snares, is used in local traditional medicine and given to local chiefs as gifts to buy favor (B. Mugerwa pers. comm. 2023).
conservationActions: Included in CITES Appendix II. Hunting of this species is prohibited in Angola, Benin, Burkina Faso, Congo, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon, Kenya, Liberia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and the Democratic Republic of Congo, with hunting regulations in place Liberia and Togo (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Key protected areas for the species include Gola F.R. (Sierra Leone), Mount Nimba Strict N.R. (Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea), Sapo N.P. (Liberia), Taï and Comoé National Parks (Côte d'Ivoire), Gashaka Gumti N.P. (Nigeria), Dja Faunal Reserve (Cameroon), Lopé N.P. and Ivindo N.P. (Gabon), Odzala and Nouabale-Ndoki National Parks (Congo Republic) and Dzangha-Ndoki National Parks (CAR), Virunga N.P. (DR Congo), Bwindi Impenetrable National Parks (Uganda) (Butynski and Ray 2013).Although previous work was conducted on African Golden Cat in central Gabon, Kibale and Bwindi National Parks in Uganda, there is a need for further survey work to acquire additional reliable population density estimates in various forest types, including disturbed habitats, to help better determine the population status across the species’ range. Several additional species monitoring initiatives have been undertaken across various countries, notably Uganda (Bwindi), Tanzania (Minziro), Cameroon, Kenya, Angola, Côte d’Ivoire, etc., aimed at confirming the presence of the African Golden Cat using camera traps. These efforts have generated valuable insights used to update the species’ current distribution, but did not allow to estimate densities. A notable gap therefore persists in covering the species' entire distribution range and obtaining population densities in the sites where the species has been detected. To address this shortfall, initiatives such as the African Golden Cat Conservation Alliance (AGCCA), Panthera, ANI Foundation, etc. are working in different landscapes in partnership with local wildlife authorities to gather information on the species. The AGCCA in collaboration with Panthera and National Geographic Society gathers partners from across the African Golden Cat distribution range and is implementing a collective and standardised protocol for assessment and monitoring, aiming at determining presence/absence, identifying factors influencing African Golden Cat occupancy, and estimating potential density across the species range (M. Mugerwa per.comm. 2023).In addition, a continent-wide community-led conservation initiative to mitigate human threats, particularly bushmeat hunting and its lethal impacts on the African Golden Cat, spearheaded by the AGCCA, is already ongoing in multiple countries (M. Mugerwa per.comm. 2023). These include Togo, Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Republic of Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo, Angola, South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Tanzania and Kenya. These activities should be extended to Guinea Bissau, Burundi, Central African Republic, Nigeria and Senegal. The goal is to effectively address the direct causes of human-induced threats to the species and its habitat through local community engagement and the provision of various incentives, such as alternative income sources and animal protein options, while creating conservation awareness on the African Golden Cat and the role local communities can play for the species conservation. Examples of these initiatives include livestock husbandry, savings and credit cooperatives, school environmental education, mobile dental clinics, tree planting and village meetings.An ex-situ safety-net population would also bolster the long-term survival of the species. There is no zoological park that has African Golden Cats so far. The CTC and the Uganda Wildlife Education Center in Uganda are the only ex-situ facilities with African Golden Cats.

rationale: This species is endemic to the San Quintín Valley of northwestern Baja California, México. Previously it was thought to be possibly extinct because surveys did not find any records for several decades. However, four individuals were trapped in 2017 in San Quintín, on Mesa Agua Chiquita. Dipodomys gravipes is currently assessed as Critically Endangered C2a(i,ii); D because it very likely has a population size of fewer than 50 individuals, all within a single population. Expanding and extensive agriculture still pose a significant threat to this species due to the destruction of essential habitat, as this species is very specific to these deep agricultural soils. Only around 1.6% of its historical habitat remains and this is likely continuing to decline, resulting in further population decline. This species is not currently found in any protected areas and captive breeding should be considered to restore populations.
habitat: This species is nocturnal and constructs closed burrows connected by visible runways that are not under vegetation (Best and Lackey 1985, Tremor et al. 2019). It is found in flat coastal plains and floodplains with limited vegetation (Best and Lackey 1985, Tremor et al. 2019). Dipodomys gravipes is intolerant of ongoing cultivation (Best and Lackey 1985, Tremor et al. 2019).Reproduction has been documented throughout the year, with peak births in winter and spring, specifically in November, December, March, April, June, July, and August (Best and Lackey 1985).
threats: Threats include habitat destruction and agriculture, as well as intrinsic factors related to a restricted range. The species has been impacted severely by agricultural development since the mid-20th century, with dramatic population declines in the 1980s due to habitat conversion to roads and farmland (Best and Lackey 1985). Surveys in the early 1990s failed to locate the species, leading to concerns that it had become extinct (Mellink 1992, IUCN 2018). Though the species has been rediscovered, it appears that only 1.6% of its historical distribution remains optimal habitat, characterised by flat terrain, suitable vegetation, and climate (Cab-Sulub and Álvarez-Castañeda 2020). Many of these areas are confined to riverbanks surrounded by steep slopes, limiting the availability of suitable shelter. Additionally, 60% of climatically suitable habitat has been altered and is no longer viable for the species (Cab-Sulub and Álvarez-Castañeda 2020). Habitat loss remains a major threat to the species' survival (Cab-Sulub and Álvarez-Castañeda 2020, SMSG 2018).
population: Previously, Dipodomys gravipes was considered possibly extinct (SEMARNAT 2010, IUCN 2018), due to the lack of records since 1986. Surveys in the early 1990s failed to detect the species (Mellink 1992), as did surveys throughout the 2000s (SMSG 2018). After decades without confirmed records, the species was reported again in 2017, found in a small embankment surrounded by agricultural land near San Quintín, on Mesa Agua Chiquita (Tremor et al. 2019). Researchers trapped a total of four individuals (three female, one male), using 13 traps along visible runways and burrow entrances (Tremor et al. 2019). Morphometric and genetic analysis of eight specimens collected across 2,400 trap nights within the species’ range suggests the rediscovery of Dipodomys gravipes (Andrade-Sánchez et al. 2022), though more research is warranted. Cab-Sulub and Álvarez-Castañeda (2020) did not trap any Dipodomys gravipes across 2,460 trap nights at 30 sites within suitable habitats, but produced a habitat suitability map indicating that there is around 37.3 km² of ideal habitat remaining for the species.
range: Dipodomys gravipes is found in the San Quintín Valley of northwestern Baja California, México, along a narrow coastal plain between San Telmo and El Rosario (Best and Lackey 1985, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). The southern populations near El Rosario may be geographically isolated from those in the north (Best and Lackey 1985).
conservationActions: Although the species is protected under Mexican law (SEMARNAT 2010), its biology, ecology, and population dynamics remain poorly understood (Andrade-Sánchez et al. 2022). The rediscovery of Dipodomys gravipes after 32 years without records potentially suggests some level of resilience, but more research is warranted (Tremor et al. 2019). Significant knowledge gaps exist regarding its current distribution, habitat preferences, seasonal abundance patterns, reproductive cycles, and the influence of environmental variables (Andrade-Sánchez et al. 2022). Addressing these uncertainties is essential for assessing the species' long-term viability and implementing effective conservation actions. This species is not found in any protected areas (SMSG 2018). Captive breeding has been suggested as a conservation strategy (SMSG 2018).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered B1ab(ii,iii,v) because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 3,410 km², currently extant populations are known from only three locations, and it is experiencing ongoing declines. The quality and extent of its habitat is being reduced by agricultural conversion, and there is a decline in the number of mature individuals due to competition with Cratogeomys fumosus.
habitat: This species prefers deep, friable soil in high montane pine-spruce-alder forests and inhabits both undisturbed and cultivated regions on pine forest slopes (Hafner and Hafner 1982). Unlike in other geomyids, burrow entrances of Zygogeomys trichopus are covered by volcano-like mounds of earth with no opening. It is thought that the species may be entirely fossorial and forage below ground (Hafner and Hafner 1982). The main part of burrows are found more than 2 meters deep in the soil (Hafner and Barkley 1984).Limited information is available on the reproductive cycles of this species, but male testes were significantly smaller in March and August than they were in December. A pregnant female was also found in December (Hafner and Barkley 1984).
threats: Ongoing deforestation puts this species in danger of extinction (Hafner and Barkley 1984). Agricultural encroachment has led to the direct loss of forest habitat within the species’ range and has facilitated competition with a lower elevation gopher species, Cratogeomys fumosus (Hafner and Barkley 1984,  Fernández et al. 2014). Specifically, agricultural expansion led to the loss of the forest barrier separating the range of the two species, allowing the Cratogeomys fumosus to expand into higher elevations and compete with Zygogeomys trichopus (Hafner and Barkley 1984). Habitat loss and increasing competition caused a decline in the number of Zygogeomys trichopus and are likely responsible for the species no longer being found at its type locality (Hafner and Barkley 1984).This species is also considered a pest and is controlled by local farmers (SMSG 2018, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). The establishment of extensive avocado (Persea americana) orchards near known populations in recent decades may also impact this species, although the extent of this effect is unknown (Fernández et al. 2014). This species is also likely preyed upon by local predators, including coyotes (Canis latrans) and bobcats (Lynx rufus).
population: This species was once abundant and widespread, but now has a very limited and fragmented distribution (Fernández et al. 2014). It no longer exists at its type locality (Hafner and Barkley 1984). Populations are small (estimated to be fewer than 20 individuals per population), making specimen collection difficult and uncommon (Hafner and Barkley 1984). Existing populations have low genetic variability, likely from small population sizes and lack of gene flow between populations (Hafner and Barkley 1984).Ongoing decline of Zygogeomys trichopus is occurring from ongoing threats. For example, this species was recorded in the Barranca del Cupatitzio National Park by Orduña et al. (1993) but was not detected in more recent surveys, suggesting it may no longer exist in the area (Chávez-León and Zaragoza-Rivera 2009).
range: Zygogeomys trichopus is a microendemic species, restricted to the mountains of Michoacán, México within the western area of the Transmexican Volcanic Belt (Escalante et al. 2007, Fernández et al. 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It is currently known from only three localities, all within the state of Michoacán: the northwest slope of Cerro Tancítaro, the northwest slope of Cerro Patambán, and Cerro del Burro, approximately 10 km southeast of Pátzcuaro (Hafner and Barkley 1984, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). This species is no longer present at its type locality in Nahuatzen, Michoacán (Hafner and Barkley 1984). It occurs at elevations above 2,000 m asl (Hafner and Hafner 1982).
conservationActions: This species is protected under Mexican law as "en peligro de extinción" ("in danger of extinction") (SEMARNAT 2010). Studies of the continuing effects of agricultural encroachment and deforestation are critically needed to ensure the future of this endemic genus (Fernández et al. 2014). Records have been collected at Pico de Tancítaro (federal), and Estribito del Cerro Colorado and Cerro del Estribo Grande (state) (CONABIO 2024). In a 2004 study, this species was not observed in Parque Nacional Barranca del Cupatitzio, and its current presence in this location remains unknown (Chávez-León and Zaragoza-Rivera 2009).

rationale: The species is assessed as Endangered (EN B1ab(ii,iii,v)) because its extent of occurrence is 2,677 km², the population is severely fragmented, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, number of mature individuals, and area of occupancy due to timber extraction and clearing of habitat for agriculture. Climate change may exacerbate the impacts of habitat loss on this species.
habitat: The species is found in a variety of habitats, ranging from tropical, subtropical, prairies, woodlands, deserts, and temperate grasslands (Ochoa et al. 2012). It is particularly common near high-elevation pine forests and prefers arid grasslands with dense shrubs, where it digs burrows (Ochoa et al. 2012). It is more abundant in open habitats with low vegetation, where visibility is higher and predation risk may be reduced (García-Domínguez et al. 2014). It has also been recorded in shrubland and cropland, although these habitats support lower population densities (Best and Ceballos 1995, Castillo-Castillo and González-Romero 2010). There is no significant difference in range sizes for males and females (Castillo-Castillo and González-Romero 2010), but males tend to leave hibernation first (Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018).This species is active for approximately nine months of the year, from early March to November, with hibernation occurring from late October to March, interrupted by short feeding periods (Castillo-Castillo and González-Romero 2010). Reproduction occurs between May and August, with a gestation period of 30 days and an average litter size of four (Yensen and Sherman 2003). Observations of two pregnant females in July recorded litter sizes of six and seven embryos, suggesting a late breeding season or the possibility of two litters per year (Best and Ceballos 1995). Densities are highest during the breeding season and juveniles are most abundant in August (Montero-Bagatella and González-Romero 2014).Xerospermophilus perotensis is a diurnal, social, terrestrial, and primarily herbivorous rodent (Best and Ceballos 1995, Castillo-Castillo and González-Romero 2010). Its diet includes six main plant species, especially Scleropogon brevifolius, Verbena bipinnatifida, and Erigeron pubescens (Hernández-Hernández et al. 2018), but may consume at least 25 plant species and 4 animal materials (González-Romero et al. 2018). Squirrels likely increase protein consumption at certain times, such as during gestation and prior to hibernation (Hernández-Hernández et al. 2018). Predators of this species likely include long-tailed weasels (Mustela frenata) and domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) (Best and Ceballos 1995).
threats: Xerospermophilus perotensis is primarily threatened by extensive habitat fragmentation and destruction within its restricted range from timber extraction, agricultural expansion, urbanisation, and overgrazing by sheep and goats (Ochoa et al. 2012, Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005, Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018, García-Domínguez et al. 2014). Anthropogenic activities have resulted in the loss of approximately 70% of its original habitat (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005, Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018) and led to small and isolated populations with low genetic diversity (Montero-Bagatella and González-Romero 2014, Ochoa et al. 2012). Climate change is likely to exacerbate the scale and impacts of habitat loss, with multiple models showing decrease in suitable projected area by 2050 (García-Domínguez et al. 2014). Climate change may also disrupt hibernation patterns and affect other life history stages (García-Domínguez et al. 2014).Additionally, predation by feral dogs appears to be a threat (Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018, SMSG 2018) and a new road to Xalapa may be affecting the species (SMSG 2018).
population: Recent surveys have found few individuals, suggesting low population density (SMSG 2018). Current population trends indicate a significant decline for this species, with reductions in both population size and genetic diversity. The species is now only known from 16 localities, and population densities have decreased from 50 individuals per hectare in 2009 to 20 individuals per hectare in 2014 (Ochoa et al. 2012, González-Romero et al. 2025). This density is considered the minimum required for the development of land squirrel populations. During this period, few juveniles were recorded, which may indicate that the populations are not growing and that they have little chance of recovery. If this species continues decreasing in population and diversity, inbreeding may occur within populations and may compromise its ability to survive (Ochoa et al. 2012). Recent research has suggested that the species’ remaining populations are small and with low possibilities of development, despite persistence in fragmented and transformed habitats (González-Romero et al. 2025).Castillo-Castillo and González-Romero (2010) captured 213 individuals (130 males 83 females) over 3,240 trap-nights. Montero-Bagatella and González-Romero (2014) captured 85 individuals (29 female, 56 male) over the same number of trap-nights. Densities of Xerospermophilus perotensis are highest during the breeding season, reaching 24 individuals per hectare, and lowest in October during the onset of hibernation (Montero-Bagatella and González-Romero 2014).
range: This species is endemic to Mexico and only found in the oriental basin, located between the states of Puebla, Veracruz, and Tlaxcala. It is found from 2,200–2,700 m asl (Hall 1981). Its original range was 5,250 km², but this has since declined due to land conversion for agriculture and urbanisation (Ochoa et al. 2012).
conservationActions: This species is listed as endangered by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). A recently established State Natural Conservation Area in Veracruz may include a small portion of this species' range.Proposed conservation strategies include involving local communities through environmental education programs to prevent induced fires that destroy critical habitat, controlling feral dog populations to reduce predation, and installing fences to mitigate predation risks (Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018). Ex situ conservation and translocations may be useful to mitigate impacts from significant habitat loss and to maintain genetic diversity (Ochoa et al. 2012, Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018). Practical measures such as leaving strips of cropland unplowed and creating protected areas managed by both the state government and local livestock companies could support the persistence of native fauna (Montero-Bagatella et al. 2018, González-Romero et al. 2025). Increasing public awareness of the species' ecological benefits and conservation needs is recommended to foster empathy and support for conservation initiatives. Coordinating with environmental authorities and local communities to implement sustainable cattle and agricultural management practices, as well as establishing a network of small ecological reserves, could further mitigate habitat fragmentation and the impacts of climate change on this microendemic species (García-Domínguez et al. 2014).

rationale: This species is Endangered B1ab(iii). It has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 2,103 km², all individuals occur in a single location, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to ongoing deforestation for agriculture and grazing.
habitat: This species is restricted to humid cloud forests and other moist montane habitats within a very limited range in the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, Mexico (Ceballos 2014). It inhabits forests dominated by oak and/or pine, with dense undergrowth consisting of ferns, mosses, bromeliads, lichens, and other epiphytes (Ceballos 2014). It may also be found in areas of rainfed agriculture (Sosa Luría 2009), though it is generally associated with primary vegetation (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022). The species exhibits semi-arboreal habits but it is also commonly found on the ground (León-Paniagua et al. 2007, Ceballos 2014).
threats: This species is threatened by deforestation across its highly restricted range (Rogers et al. 2007, SMSG 2018). Montane cloud forests, its primary habitat, are among the most endangered and fragmented ecosystems, primarily due to land conversion for agriculture and grazing. These forests are also highly vulnerable to climate change and other anthropogenic disturbances (Toledo-Aceves et al. 2011). Montane cloud forests in Oaxaca are high risk habitats since they have highly restricted ecological conditions (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022).
population: Habromys ixtlani is better represented in collections than other species of Habromys (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022), but is still only known from a few localities and individuals (Carleton et al. 2002, Ceballos 2014). Population information is limited, but the species is suspected to be in decline due to habitat loss from deforestation (SMSG 2018).
range: This species is endemic to Oaxaca, Mexico, and is found near its type locality at Cerro Machín in the Sierra de Juárez (Carleton et al. 2002, León-Paniagua et al. 2007, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). Cerro Machín is located in the northern portion of the Sierra de Juárez, near the Sierra de Zempoaltepec, a geographically isolated region (Carleton et al. 2002). This species is found from 2,040-3,246 m asl (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022) and some models suggest that its range may include Cuicatlán and Mixe (Sosa Luría 2009). Habromys ixtlani has the most extensive distribution of the four Habromys species in Oaxaca, but it still has a limited range (Contreras-Medina et al. 2022). The species occurs on the same slope as Habromys chinanteco (Ceballos 2014).
conservationActions: This species is not protected by the Mexican government. None of its modelled range includes protected natural areas (ANPs), but its entire range is located within Priority Terrestrial Region No. 130: Northern Oaxaca-Mixe Mountains, 10% is within the San Juan Teponaxtla Conservation Area, and 90% is within State System of Natural Area Conservation (Sosa Luría 2009). It is found within a community protected area with actively managed forest; pockets of its range are protected, including state parks (SMSG 2018).

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened because its area of occupancy (AOO) is somewhere between 224 km² and 74,984 km² (but most likely around 2,000 km²) and it is experiencing ongoing decline in habitat extent and quality due to expanding agriculture and grazing. It is also negatively impacted by invasive species, fire, and climate change. It is found in two disjunct populations, but it is unclear exactly how many locations this species occupies. It therefore nearly qualifies for Vulnerable under criterion B2ab(iii).
habitat: Sciurus arizonensis is strongly associated with riparian woodlands and montane oak forests, where it depends on mature trees for food, nesting, and movement (Best and Riedel 1995, Cudworth and Koprowski 2010,  2013). Dense woodlands with thick shrub cover and high canopy provide protection from predators (Cudworth and Koprowski 2014), likely hawks and bobcats (Brown 1984). Records are mostly associated with riparian areas, especially broadleaf habitats (Frey et al. 2008). The majority of sightings in one study were along downed logs across rivers (Rorabaugh et al. 2023). Relative abundance is higher in forests composed of Fremont cottonwood and Goodding willow (Best and Riedel 1995, Rorabaugh et al. 2023). This species has also been associated with velvet mesquite, oaks, walnut, pecan, ponderosa pine, and Arizona sycamore (Cudworth and Koprowski 2013). Its lower elevational limits can extend into streams of chaparral and desert-like grasslands (Brown 1984).This diurnal species has a diverse diet including acorns, seeds, nuts, insect galls, tree bark, sap, and fungi (Cudworth and Koprowski 2010, 2013). It forages on both the ground and in the canopy and tends to prefer food from mast-producing trees, such as acorns (Quercus sp.), walnuts (Juglans sp.) and pine nuts (Pinus sp., Abies sp., and Pseudotsuga menziesii) (Wilson et al. 2016). It will also feed on flowers, juniper berries (Juniperus sp.), Netleaf Hackberry fruits (Celtis reticulata) hypogeous and epigeous fungi and opportunistically on insects (Wilson et al. 2016). It will occasionally scatter hoard large, storable seeds in the soil (Ceballos 2014, Wilson et al. 2016). Food availability is strongly influenced by annual rainfall fluctuations (Cudworth and Koprowski 2010). The Arizona walnut tree (Juglans major) is considered a key indicator of this species presence (Brown 1984). This species will "freeze" in the face of danger and may remain so for more than 45 minutes (Brown 1984).Sciurus arizonensis breeds from February to August, with at least one litter of 2–4 young produced in late spring or early summer (Wilson et al. 2016).  During mild years, females may be able to produce a second litter (Wilson et al. 2016). Females will nest in dreys composed of sticks, pine needles, and leaves in either the forest canopy or in cavities of large trees (Wilson et al. 2016). Male home ranges are extensive (113 ha) while females are much smaller (14 ha).
threats: The destruction of habitat by wildfires and anthropogenic pressures are major threats to this species (Ceballos 2014). It is experiencing ongoing habitat decline and fragmentation due to the expansion of agriculture and grazing (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011, Rorabaugh et al. 2023). It is severely restricted to riparian habitats, increasing susceptibility to habitat fragmentation and water changes (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011). Potential future damming of the Gila River would decrease riparian forest, and therefore habitat of Sciurus arizonensis in this region (Jones et al. 2021). Climate change may impact water availability, and therefore habitat suitability (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011).This species is not found in areas of high wildfire damage (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011, Wilson et al. 2016) and may be negatively impacted by fire (Jones et al. 2021). Fires can cause very rapid destruction to populations. Climate change may exacerbate negative impacts from fire, as well as increase the frequency and severity of flooding and other destructive events (Rorabaugh et al. 2023). This species is also competing with introduced Abert’s squirrel (Sciurus aberti) in parts of its range (Cudworth and Koprowski 2010).
population: Data are limited for this species (Cudworth and Koprowski 2014). It is likely not abundant in Sonora as there have been limited recent records (Caire 2019). Population density in the Huachuca Mountains, Arizona has been estimated as 1.31 individuals per hectare, with higher densities in riparian woodlands than in pine-oak woodlands (Cudworth and Koprowski 2010). Detection rates from a 4.5-year camera-trap survey at Rancho El Aribabi were low, suggesting a restricted local distribution (Rorabaugh et al. 2023). Populations of this species are thought to fluctuate from year to year; probably due to food supplies from mast-producing trees, which varies annually (Monson 1972).
range: This species is found in mountainous areas in the southwestern United States and in northwestern Mexico from around 1,120 to 2,700 m asl (Best and Riedel 1995, Thorington et al. 2012). It has been recorded in Arizona, southwestern New Mexico, and north-central Sonora (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It has three disjunct population segments: western and southern mountains of central Arizona high country (below Mogollon Rim), isolated mountain ranges in southern Arizona and New Mexico, and southern Arizona mountains extending into northern Sonora, Mexico. The Santa Catalina and Rincon population (previously known as S. a. catalinae) is a highly imperilled population.
conservationActions: This species is listed as endangered by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010) and has few recent records in the country (Caire 2019). It has been recorded in Bavispe Wildlife Protection Area, and in Rancho El Aribabi, a private conservation ranch in Sonora (Cudworth and Koprowski 2010, CONABIO 2024). In the United States, this species has been recorded in Ramsey Canyon Preserve, Miller Peak Wilderness, Patagonia Sonoita Creek Preserve, and Mount Wrightson Wilderness (CONABIO 2024).Protecting riparian habitats from damming and cattle intrusion would benefit this and other important species (Jones et al. 2021). Maintaining dense canopy cover, especially of trees like Arizona sycamore (Platanus wrightii) and Fremont cottonwood (Populus fremontii) that provide nesting sites, and ensuring continued riparian connectivity are essential for the protection of this species (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011). Interactions with introduced species and predators should be considered in the management of Sciurus arizonensis (Cudworth and Koprowski 2011, 2014).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU B2ab(iii)) because its area of occupancy is estimated to be around 780 km² due to its restricted habitat usage around streams, the population is severely fragmented, it occurs in six locations, and the extent and quality of its habitat are declining due to stream pollution from expanding human settlement and agriculture.
habitat: This nocturnal, amphibious species is found near the headwaters of cool, shady streams within cloud forests (Stirton 1944, Hooper 1968, Ceballos 2014) or near coffee plantations (Stirton 1944). It is found in areas with a constant flow of well oxygenated water.This species is primarily carnivorous, and its diet consists of snails, insects, frogs and fish (Ceballos 2014). In El Salvador, foods eaten include insects, birds, salamanders, mammals (possibly another Rheomys), and starchy pulp (Stirton 1944). One individual from Guatemala had eaten stonefly and mayfly larvae, beetles, and part of a catfish (Hooper 1968). A captive mouse readily consumed small fish and aquatic insect larvae (Reid 2009). More recent research is needed on this species’ ecology.
threats: A major threat to this species is its fragile environment (Ceballos 2014). Stream degradation and water quality degradation are major threats due to its reliance on stream habitats. Many of the streams within its habitat are near cultivation areas for coffee, bananas, corn, and other crops (Stirton 1944), which poses high risk to the species, mainly due to water pollution and habitat degradation. Landslides may also be a risk.
population: Little recent information on this species has been recorded, and only a few specimens are available (Martín-Regalado et al. 2016). This species is uncommon and local (Reid 2009) and has a small population size (Ceballos 2014).
range: This species occurs in the highlands of south México (Chiapas), Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras (Martín-Regalado et al. 2016, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It is found from 400 m to 2,700 m asl (Reid 2009). This species has been primarily trapped in El Salvador at Mount Cacaguatique, Finca San Carlos, and Los Esesmiles (Stirton 1944, Hooper 1968) as well as in México at El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve (Mena and Medellín 2017).
conservationActions: This species is listed as Subject to Special Protection by the Mexican government (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It has also been recorded in protected lands including El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve (Mena and Medellín 2017). It is possible the species may be found at Reserva de la Biósfera Volcán Tacaná (12,566 ha), but this needs to be confirmed (A. Cuarón pers. comm. 2026).In El Salvador, this species has been recorded in protected areas including El Imposible National Park, San Carlos Cacahuatique, and Trifinio-Fraternidad Biosphere Reserve (CONABIO 2024).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered (EN B2ab(iii)) because its area of occupancy is 32 km², it occurs in only five locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat. It has a restricted range because it is heavily reliant on forested riparian areas and has low adaptive capacity. Deforestation and water pollution within the range of Rheomys mexicanus are significant threats that remove essential habitat.
habitat: General ecology about this species is poorly understood, so additional research would be useful to better understand this semi-aquatic, endemic species. It is found in secondary oak forest, pine-oak forest, cloud forest, low deciduous and evergreen forests, and seasonally dry tropical forests (Ceballos 2014, Martín Regalado et al. 2016, Caviedes-Solis et al. 2017, Ramírez-Bautista et al. 2020). Its range may also extend into in cultivated grassland, low spiny forest, agricultural areas, and human settlements (Sosa Luría 2009). Importantly, it is reliant on aquatic systems, where it may be found diving to search for food at the base of small rocks (Sosa Luría 2009, Caviedes-Solis et al. 2017, León Tapia and Guevara 2025).
