It is restricted to forested riparian areas at the headwaters of streams, in particular it is restricted to small tributaries with closed tropical forest vegetation, and does not occur in larger rivers. It is found along the banks of small rivers and streams that have a continuous, clear flow of water and is highly susceptible to pollution. Rheomys mexicanus is nocturnal and carnivorous and mostly feeds on aquatic insects (Ceballos 2014). An adult male was found clogging a hosepipe used to collect water from the Rio Yavesia at 2,000 m in an area characterized by pine-oak forest (Santos-Moreno et al. 2003).
threats: This species is threatened by human activities within its range, specifically by continued deforestation and water pollution (Ceballos 2014, Martín Regalado et al. 2016). Any type of water pollution, including household pollution from washing clothes, is considered a threat to this species. Deforestation is occurring throughout the range of this species, except in steep riparian areas. This species may also undergo substantial impacts due to climate change, with up to 62% of its range affected by 2075–2099 (Ramírez-Bautista et al. 2020). Due to its low adaptive capacity and restricted range, this species is at high latent risk and will be highly vulnerable if pessimistic climate models are correct (Ramírez-Bautista et al. 2020).
population: This species is considered rare, and has only been recorded from five disparate localities within its range (Santos-Moreno et al. 2003, Ceballos 2014, Caviedes-Solis et al. 2017). More population surveys and improved trapping techniques are needed to better understand populations.
range: This species is endemic to Oaxaca, México (Ceballos 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It is only known from Guelatao, San Jose Lachiquiri, Union Hildalgo, and Tontatepec on the Pacific slope of Oaxaca (Santos-Moreno et al. 2003, Sosa Luría 2009, Ceballos 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024), and more recently from San Pablo Macuiltianguis (Caviedes-Solis et al. 2017).
conservationActions: This species is listed as Subject to Special Protection by the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010). It would benefit from the protection of water systems and decreasing pollution (Martín Regalado et al. 2016). This species has not been recorded in any protected areas, but niche modeling indicates habitat suitability in areas like the Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere Reserve (Sosa Luría 2009). More research is needed to understand ongoing population dynamics and interactions with its specialised habitat.

rationale: Cozumel Harvest Mouse (Reithrodontomys spectabilis) is assessed as Critically Endangered C2a(i) because it has an effective population size of 152 individuals and is estimated to exist in small subpopulations (10–49 individuals/subpopulation). It faces continuing decline from invasive species, habitat loss and fragmentation from development and tourism, and occasional and potential loss from hurricanes and flooding.
habitat: Reithrodontomys spectabilis occurs in dense, viney second growth and forest edge. It is currently found primarily near mangroves (A. Cuarón pers. comm. 2025). This species is semi-terrestrial, semi-arboreal, and lunar phobic (Fortes-Corona 2004, Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). It is negatively affected by edge effects caused by narrow (<3 m) openings in vegetation, showing lower abundance and activity near habitat edges (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). These edge effects are associated with age and reproductive condition: adults and reproductive individuals are more common near edges, while juveniles are found further away (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). This species produces a two-note whistling call at dusk (Reid 2009).
threats: Reithrodontomys spectabilis is severely threatened by introduced species, including predators such as boas (Boa imperator), feral dogs (Canis familiaris), and feral cats (Felis domesticus), as well as by competition with invasive rodents, particularly black rats (Rattus rattus) and house mice (Mus musculus) (Martínez-Morales and Cuarón 1999, Romero-Nájera et al. 2007, Reid 2009, Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009, Espíndola et al. 2014, Suárez-Atilano et al. 2019, Borja-Martínez and Vázquez-Domínguez 2024). Introduced margay (Leopardus wiedii), and perhaps ocelots (Leopardus pardalis), may be additional predators of this species (Cuarón et al. 2025).Habitat loss, fragmentation, and disturbance associated with tourism, urban expansion, and road development further threaten the species (Reid 2009, Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009, Espíndola et al. 2014, Borja-Martínez and Vázquez-Domínguez 2024). Road construction may intensify edge effects and increase mortality, and differential responses to edges suggest possible competitive exclusion by other native rodents (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). In addition, the species is vulnerable to natural disturbances such as hurricanes and flooding, which are frequent and intense on Cozumel Island. These events may exacerbate existing pressures, particularly given the species' small, fluctuating population and its interactions with invasive species (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009, Espíndola et al. 2014).
population: The species is reported as uncommon and difficult to observe, suggesting low population densities. It has declined since the 1990s and is now considered rare (Reid 2009, Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). It had an estimated density of 3.3 individuals per hectare (Fortes-Corona 2004). In one study, Reithrodontomys spectabilis was captured in only five of 16 plots, yielding 56 individuals; another endemic rodent (Oryzomys couesi cozumelae) had 756 captures (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). Another study trapped 90 individuals between September 2001 and January 2005; genetic structure suggested the presence of up to four subpopulations across the island (Espíndola et al. 2014). Despite being an island species with a small effective population size, this species maintains relatively high genetic diversity (Espíndola et al. 2014). Ongoing fieldwork is assessing current population status of the species, but it is said to be declining (A. Cuarón and E. Vázquez Domínguez, pers. comm. 2025). There are an estimated 152 individuals remaining, with 10–49 individuals in each of the four subpopulations (Espíndola et al. 2014, A. Cuarón and E. Vázquez Domínguez, pers. comm. 2025).
range: This species is restricted to Cozumel Island, Mexico (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024), a 486 km² island in the Caribbean Sea that is 17.5 km off the eastern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). It has been recorded at sites across the island and has at least four genetic groups (Espíndola et al. 2014).
conservationActions: Reithrodontomys spectabilis is classified as Threatened under Mexican law (SEMARNAT 2010). Significant progress has been made in habitat protection on Cozumel Island with the establishment of several protected areas, including the Refugio Estatal de Flora y Fauna de Laguna Colombia (1,114 ha; 1999), Reserva Estatal Selvas y Humedales de Cozumel (19,846.45 ha; 2011), Área de Protección de Flora y Fauna Isla de Cozumel (37,829 ha; 2012), and the designation of the entire island as the Cozumel Island Biosphere Reserve under UNESCO’s Man and Biosphere Program (134,624 ha total area; 46,886 ha of land; 87,738 ha of sea; 2016) (Cuarón et al. 2023). The species plan for Reithrodontomys spectabilis was discussed during the Small Mammal Specialist Group Workshop in 2018.The presence of invasive species remains the primary conservation challenge (Suárez-Atilano et al. 2019). Removal or control of introduced predators and competitors, particularly Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, Felis catus, and Boa imperator, is a conservation priority (Martínez-Morales and Cuarón 1999, Espíndola et al. 2014). Improving urban planning, especially to prevent further spread of invasive species from urban centers such as San Miguel, would also be highly beneficial (Borja-Martínez and Vázquez-Domínguez 2024). Continuous monitoring of populations is recommended to assess the effectiveness of existing protected areas and guide conservation strategies (Fuentes-Montemayor et al. 2009). Further studies on spatial ecology and population dynamics are needed, and potential conservation strategies may include captive breeding and reintroduction within protected areas (Espíndola et al. 2014).

rationale: This species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU B1ab(iii)) because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 10,043 km², it is only found in seven locations, and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat due to expanding agriculture and residential development.
habitat: This species occurs within the Transmexican Volcanic Belt, a region characterised by heterogeneous topography and a wide altitudinal range (Barrera-Moreno et al. 2011). It primarily lives in tropical deciduous forest, which represents 79% of its potential distribution area (Gámez et al. 2012). Hooper (1952) collected specimens from steep, rocky hillsides and with little cover. Associated vegetation included deciduous brush, tropical evergreen trees, smaller thorny trees, and sparse grasses (Hooper 1952). More recent trapping efforts indicate similar habitat preferences, with a specimen collected in a deciduous thorn forest with small, mostly leguminous shrubs, on plain ground near volcanic rocks (González-Ruiz et al. 2004). Reproduction may occur in the spring, as a specimen of Reithrodontomys hirsutus trapped in May contained four embryos (Hooper 1952).
threats: This species has a restricted range and occurs in tropical dry forest, which is heavily affected by habitat loss, fragmentation, and land use change from agricultural expansion and urban development (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005, Gámez et al. 2012). Across its range, native vegetation has been extensively lost due to the expanding cultivation of blue agave in monoculture. Urgent conservation is needed as deforestation threatens biodiversity in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (Barrera-Moreno et al. 2011).
population: Little is known about this infrequently captured species, with over 50 years elapsing between some records (González-Ruiz et al. 2004). As of 2004, there had only been 24 records of the species (González-Ruiz et al. 2004).
range: This Mexican endemic species is distributed from south-central Nayarit to Jalisco (Musser and Carleton 2005) and northeastern Colima (González-Ruiz et al. 2004, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It has been primarily found within tropical regions from 900 to 1,200 m asl (Musser and Carleton 2005), but may reach elevations of 2,000 m asl (Gámez et al. 2012).
conservationActions: Limited conservation information exists on this species. It has been recorded in both federal and protected areas (CONABIO 2024) but has not yet received protection from the Mexican government (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005, SEMARNAT 2010).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered because it has an area of occupancy (AOO) of 48-500 km², is only found in five locations, and it is experiencing ongoing decline in its extent of occurrence and quality of habitat due to expanding agriculture in the region.
habitat: Very little is known about the natural history of this species; its reproductive habits, diet and overall biology are unknown (Sánchez 2014). The only reported predator of this species are owls (Tyto alba), but it is possibly preyed upon by several carnivores (Bradshaw and Hayward 1960). This species was found in scrublands of mesquite, palo fierro, palo verde and grasses, and in cultivated fields with abundant wheat stubble in Sonora (Benson 1939, Hooper 1952). Individuals in Sinaloa were trapped in an open field alongside a brush fence, and in a mesquite and agave dominated field with short grasses (Russell and Alcorn 1957).
threats: Although this species is not included in the official list of endangered species in Mexico (SEMARNAT 2010), it can be considered fragile since it is an endemic species and it has a restricted distribution (Sánchez 2014). There is significant habitat transformation for agriculture within its range. There is only 52.61% untransformed habitat within this species’ range using data from 1970 to 2000 (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005).
population: Only a few specimens have been collected of this species (Caire 2019), including three from Sinaloa and 40 from Sonora (Arellano Arenas et al. 2010). Three separate attempts were made to capture this species at known localities, but all were unsuccessful, indicating that this species is very rare or possibly already extinct (Arellano Arenas et al. 2010).
range: This Mexican endemic is restricted to west-central Sonora and Sinaloa along the Pacific coast (Sánchez 2014, Álvarez-Castañeda 2024). It has been found in few localities in each state (Sánchez 2014), including the coastal plains of Sonora in the Bursera-Jatropha vegetation region, the western edge of the Olneya-Encelia, and the western parts of the Thorn Forest (Caire 2019). This is a lowland species that has been recorded up to 244 m asl (Hooper 1952).
conservationActions: This species does not have a protected status according to the Mexican government (SEMARNAT 2010), but has been recorded in two small protected areas: Abelardo Rodríguez Luján el Molinito and Islas del Golfo de California (CONABIO 2024). More research is needed on this species’ basic biology, life history, and necessary conservation measures.

rationale: This species is assessed as Near Threatened. It almost qualifies for a threatened category under criterion A2c due to a suspected ongoing population decline of 20% in the last ten years, based on habitat conversion (mainly deforestation) to agriculture and from logging activities over this time. Caenolestes caniventer is restricted to montane forest within its range, which is being exploited and increasingly fragmented and should be monitored. It is also close to meeting criterion B, as current information suggests its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 12,648 km², its area of occupancy (AOO) is 4 km², and it is undergoing continuing decline in habitat quality. Further information is needed on its full distribution, area of occupancy, and effects of the numerous threats on populations of this species, as it may be more threatened than currently suspected.
habitat: This species is known from primary and secondary subtropical montane forests (Albuja and Patterson 1996, Lunde and Pacheco 2003, Gardner 2008). It has also been found in wet grasslands and forest patches along small streams (Barkley and Whitaker 1984) and in secondary shrubby habitats dominated by bushes of the genera Chusquea (Graminae: Bambusoidea), Salvia (Labiateae), and Miconia (Melastomataceae), with poor ground cover and a sparse canopy (Barnett 1991). The diet of this species was found to be predominantly based on invertebrates, including lepidopteran larvae, centipedes, and arachnids, as well as small vertebrates (birds) and vegetation (Barkley and Whitaker 1984). Although scant, this data suggests the species is omnivorous, with a preference for invertebrates, but will opportunistically prey on vertebrates and fruits. Other information on the ecology of this species is unknown, but this species appears mostly terrestrial, being trapped under tree roots and along small streams near grasslands or wet areas, and is crepuscular or nocturnal (Osgood 1921, Tate 1931, Barkley and Whitaker 1984). It prefers cool, wet areas covered by thick vegetation.
threats: The major threat to this species is deforestation from logging activities. Also, and throughout its range in Ecuador, much of the land is being converted to agriculture, while in Peru the forest is being removed for timber sales.
population: No information is available on the population dynamics, density, and ecological interactions of this species. Few specimens of this species have been collected, possibly due to poor sampling, although it may be common in suitable habitats.
range: This species is found in southwestern Ecuador and northern Peru (Gardner 2008, Patterson 2015, González 2024). It occurs between 1,600 m asl (Anthony 1924) and 3,100 m asl (Bublitz 1987, Barnett 1991). Lunde and Pacheco (2003) gave the southern record as San Andres de Cutervo, Cajamarca, Peru, at 6° 13’ S, 78° 40’ W, and 2350 m asl. The Huancabamba depression in northern Peru does not appear to be a limit to its southern distribution (Lunde and Pacheco 2003). A recent revision on the diversity of Ecuadorean Caenolestes revealed cryptic diversity that needs to be described, which could change the current understanding of the species's distribution (Carrion-Olmedo and Brito 2025).
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: More information is needed on the distribution of this species, especially at its eastern limits, in relation to the closely occurring congeneric species Caenolestes condorensis and Caenolestes sangay and at its southern limits regarding the recently assessed cryptic diversity (Carrion-Olmedo and Brito 2025). Also, since this species occurs in areas where deforestation and agricultural activities are common, there is an urgent need to assess how these activities affect its populations. Caenolestes caniventer occurs in several protected areas, including Cajas National Park and the nearby Mazán Ecological Reserve, south-central Ecuador (Barnett 1999).

rationale: This species is assessed as Endangered under criterion B1ab(iii)+B2ab(iii), because it is known from fewer than five locations, has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 4,604 km², an area of occupancy (AOO) of 12 km², and a continuing decline is inferred in area, extent, and quality of habitat. It is plausible that this range-restricted species could become Critically Endangered or Extinct if its habitat suffers any kind of further disturbance (land conversion for agriculture and logging). Also, the number of mature individuals is estimated to be fewer than 1,000. Further research is necessary to define the species range.
habitat: The species inhabits cold and extremely humid environments (Albuja and Patterson 1996). At the type locality, the species was captured in a habitat represented by heath-like vegetation <1.5 m in height, dominated by spiny bromeliads (achupallas), and in a slope adjacent to a dense forest with shrubs 5–6 m tall (Albuja and Patterson 1996, Gardner 2008).
threats: Possible threats include land conversion for agriculture and logging.
population: This species is mainly known from the type series of three specimens (Albuja and Patterson 1996, Gardner 2008). Revisions on recently collected materials and museum specimens (Carrión-Olmedo and Brito 2025, González 2024) suggest the species extends further south and north. However, no information is available on the population ecology of this species.
range: This species is found only in one locality in the Cordillera del Cóndor, Provincia Morona-Santiago, Achupallas, 03°27'03'' S, 78°21'39'' W, 2,080 m asl, in southeastern Ecuador (Albuja and Patterson 1996). Very little information is available on its distribution, although it probably extends in the same cordillera into Perú (Albuja and Patterson 1996, Lunde and Pacheco 2003, Gardner 2008). Revisions on recently collected materials and museum specimens show the species is distributed further South along the Cordillera del Cóndor southwest to Zamora Chinchipe, Tapichalaca (Carrión-Olmedo and Brito 2025), and north to Paquisha Alto Emperador, Yantzaza (González 2024).
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: This species needs further research about its distribution and natural history; sampling is considered necessary in the upper part of the Cordillera del Condor to better determine the population status (Tirira 2021). New records South of its type locality (i.e., Tapichalaca at Zamora Chinchipe and Yacuri National Park at Loja) showed the species might be present in other nearby areas. Although little is known about this taxon, at least half of the known localities come from strict conservation areas (Gonzalez, 2024). The known range of the species is within a previously proposed Cordillera del Condor Transboundary Protected Area between Ecuador and Perú, but this has not been completed yet. If present in the Peruvian slope of the Cordillera, it would be protected under the Santiago-Comaina Reserve Zone. This region was under some conflict in the mid-1990s but is now settled.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its wide distribution, presumed occurrence in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining at the rate required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
habitat: It is found only in terra firme forest (Patton et al. 2000), from sea level to 300 m asl (Patton pers. comm.). It is found around fallen logs in lowland evergreen rainforest (Eisenberg and Redford 1999, Emmons and Feer 1997). Activity is predominantly terrestrial and crepuscular.
threats: There are no major threats to this species at this time.
population: Loss of habitat will most probably have caused a decline in the population. The species is apparently rare (Emmons and Feer 1997).
range: The species is known from southwestern and southeastern Amazonia (south of the Amazon river), from near the base of the Andes in Peru and Bolivia to eastern Pará, Brazil (Pavan and Voss 2016).
useTrade: This species is not utilised.
conservationActions: It is presumed to occur in several protected areas throughout its range.

rationale: This species is listed as Least Concern because of its broad distribution, presumed large population, occurrence in a number of protected areas, tolerance to some degree of habitat modification, and because it is unlikely to be declining at nearly the rate required to qualify for listing it in a threatened category.
habitat: This species is found in a variety of habitats, including lowland and montane forest, grasslands, and savanna (de la Sancha et al. 2007, Cáceres et al. 2011a, Gettinger et al. 2011). This species could be found in moderately disturbed and fragmented habitats (Anderson 1982, Cáceres et al. 2010). It is terrestrial (Cáceres et al. 2011b), but it could be partially fossorial given its external characteristics, like its longer claws in its forelimbs (Lemo and Cáceres, unpubl. data). Captive records revealed an adult specimen biting small flies quickly in the air (N.C. Cáceres, pers. observ.). No or very few information is available on habits, behavior, diet, or reproduction (Anderson 1997).
threats: There are no major threats to this species. However, local habitat destruction and fragmentation might be reducing the size of some subpopulations.
population: This species is estimated to be widespread with locally low to moderate densities.
range: This species is known from Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and northern Argentina (Pine and Handley 2008). It is found from lowlands up to 1,500 m asl.
useTrade: This species is not used.
conservationActions: This species is found in many protected areas.

rationale: Ctenomys terraplen is assessed as Vulnerable B1ab(iii)B2ab(iii). It has an extremely restricted distribution, both spatially and geographically, to open patches within the Valdivian Temperate Rainforest ecoregion in northwestern Chubut province, Argentina. Its estimated area of occupancy (AOO) is very small (26 km²) and the extent of occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 2,021 km². it is thought to occur in only seven locations, where the habitat is declining in quantity and quality due to a number of threats, including from livestock grazing, urban expansion, wildfires, and land conversion for cattle grazing.
habitat: Ctenomys terraplen is an endemic species of Chubut province, occurring between the localities of Esquel and Corcovado. Its distribution is restricted to open patches within the Andean Patagonian forest (Brook 2025, Brook et al. 2025).
threats: Ctenomys terraplen is distributed in open patches within forested environments, which are frequently grazed by livestock, and is therefore affected by competition for food. In addition, it occurs in the peri-urban area of the town of Corcovado, where it is impacted by urban expansion (Brook 2025, Brook et al. 2025). The expansion of the town of Corcovado might pose a threat to its conservation, along with the degradation of forest patches by wood extraction, wildfires, and land conversion for cattle grazing. The direct effects of habitat loss caused by fires pose a plausible threat to this species populations, mainly due to the obvious habitat conversion and the posterior colonisation of suitable habitats by exotic pine trees.
population: There are no studies that have assessed the population trend of the species; however, Ctenomys terraplen is estimated to have stable populations, as it is commonly recorded throughout its distribution. Populations have remained stable at the same sites over the last eight years (Brook 2025). The species genetic variability is 0.5%, based on nine studied specimens with nine haplotypes (Brook et al. 2025). A pregnant female was captured in November, and juveniles were captured in February (Brook 2025).
range: Ctenomys terraplen has a distribution restricted to open patches within the eastern extension of the Valdivian Temperate Forest ecoregion, between the localities of Esquel and Corcovado, Chubut province, Argentina (Brook 2025, Brook et al. 2025).
useTrade: As with other species of the genus Ctenomys, this species is viewed negatively by farmers and cattle ranchers due to the soil disturbance caused by the excavation of the burrow systems in which it lives.
conservationActions: There are no actions towards the conservation of this species, despite its restricted distribution. The species is not found in any protected area throughout its distribution.

rationale: Ctenomys plebiscitum is assessed as Endangered (EN B1ab(i,ii,iii)+2ab(i,ii,iii)). It has a very restricted distribution within the urban areas surrounding the city of Esquel (Chubut, Argentina), where it has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 403 km² and an area of occupancy (AOO) estimated at 76 km². It is found in fewer than five locations, where its area of occupancy and extent of occurrence are declining due to its habitat being threatened by livestock grazing, urban expansion, and wildfires.
habitat: The species lives in open areas with sparse shrubs and high grass soil coverage (i.e. it is rarely found in bare soil). Occasionally, the species can be found within patches of open forest and overgrazed areas, and is usually associated with typical Patagonian wetlands called "mallines". Although most of its life history is poorly known, females with 4 to 6 embryos in different stages of development were found between October and November, and lactating females were captured in November and December. Young individuals were observed during December.
threats: Species of the genus Ctenomys are viewed negatively by livestock producers because of soil disturbance caused by the excavation of burrow systems and by fruit and horticultural producers because they consume crops. In some cases, they cause damage to irrigation canals or systems, as well as to electrical installations. However, there is no direct persecution (i.e., trapping/hunting) by farmers. Ctenomys plebiscitum is distributed mainly in grasslands used for livestock grazing and is affected by competition for food. In addition, it occurs in the peri-urban area of the city of Esquel, where it is impacted by recent urban expansion through new housing developments. Furthermore, the city itself separates the known populations of the species. The area has suffered major wildfires recently, many of which occurred in areas where the species has been recorded (e.g., Laguna Larga; Brook et al. 2025). In areas close to the city, attacks by domestic dogs have been reported (Brook pers. obs.).
population: Although there are no studies on the population trends of Ctenomys plebiscitum, the species is common throughout its limited range, and populations have been recorded in the same sites for the last 8 years (Brook 2025). However, threats to the habitats might be causing the continuing decline of some populations within the species range. Genetic variability of cytochrome b mitochondrial gene is 0.5% (Brook et al. 2025), which also supports the monophyly of the species (Brook et al. 2022).
range: Ctenomys plebiscitum is an endemic species, restricted to the area surrounding Esquel city, northwestern Chubut province, Argentina. The species lives in the ecotone between the Valdivian Temperate Forests and the Patagonian Steppe ecoregions (Brook et al. 2022, 2025). Currently, the species is divided into two populations by the city of Esquel: a southern population located in the Nahuel Pan mountain range and the Nahuel Pan valley, and a northern population associated with the Esquel mountain range and the Percy river valley. This urban barrier has resulted in population fragmentation and reduced connectivity, which may further increase the species’ vulnerability. The species' range is restricted to an area between 42.825349° to 43.013501° South and 71.560866° to 71.223415° West, from 800 to 2,000 m asl (Brook 2025, Brook et al. 2026).
useTrade: The species is currently not used, but might have been consumed by local Americans (northern Tehuelche tribes) in the past.
conservationActions: The species occurs in a local protected area (Reserva Natural Urbana Laguna La Zeta) under municipal management.

rationale: The African Forest Elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) is assessed as Critically Endangered A2bd. Analysis of estimates from 181 localities across the species range indicates a reduction of more than 80% of the continental population in the past three generations (93 years) that is understood to be continuing and likely irreversible. The continental trend is not, however, spatially uniform. Some subpopulations are stable; others are declining significantly faster than the continental rate. Several subpopulations have been extirpated, mostly in West Africa. A generation length (GL) of 31 years is used; calculated in the standard format as the average age of mothers in the population (IUCN SPC 2019 p. 29, 2024 p. 26). This figure is based on findings from demographic studies on GL for African Forest Elephants on the basis of a 23-year study in Central African Republic (Turkalo et al. 2018). Subcriterion A2 is applied because some of the major causes for population reduction such as habitat loss due to human population expansion have not ceased, are projected to increase in coming decades, and are unlikely to be reversible. The population reduction assessment for subcriterion A2 (considering three generations back) is inferred from published survey data. Density and distribution estimates for the African Forest Elephant across its continental range vary in methodology, completeness, regularity, date of first survey and certainty. Few credible site-specific estimates exist prior to the 1980s. For this assessment, an attempt was made to model the data three generations back to 1929 (see Supplementary Information for description of data that is current as of and up to the end of 2023); however, given the sparseness of information available to inform the model, such modelling was not informative. Therefore, rather than projecting declines well beyond the extent of the survey data used in the assessment, we made the assumption that the continental population of three generations back (1929) is equal to that of just over one generation back (1984). Additional assumptions, necessary to fill gaps in the dataset, are detailed in the attached Supplementary Information document. Subcriteria A3 and A4 have not been applied, because although the major threats to the species are known, projecting the level of such threats 31 to 93 years into the future (i.e., one to three generations, up to a maximum of 100 years) would likely introduce high levels of uncertainty. Criteria B, C, and D are not relevant to the threatened status, as the species currently occupies more than 20,000 km2 and there are more than 10,000 mature individuals. No quantitative analysis of the probability of extinction in the wild was conducted, and therefore criterion E does not apply. Previous Assessments of African Forest Elephant: This is the first reassessment of the African Forest Elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) as a species separate from the African Savanna Elephant (L. africana). The African Forest Elephant, as a single species, was listed as Critically Endangered (CR A2abd) in the 2021 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (Gobush et al. 2021), under the same IUCN Categories and Criteria used in this assessment (Version 3.1; second edition, IUCN 2012). In the 2008 Assessment, African elephants were considered as a single species and listed as Vulnerable (VU A2a); the Central African region, which consists mainly of Forest Elephant range plus Savanna Elephant range in Cameroon, Chad, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, was considered Data Deficient.
habitat: African Forest Elephants are primarily found across the Guineao-Congolian tropical and subtropical moist forests of western and central Africa, stretching from remnant habitat in the northwest in Guinea and Sierra Leone (10° North, 12° West) to the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and the western edge of Uganda (4° South, 29° East). They occupy a variety of forest habitats including lowland forest on terra firma, swamp forests, the lower reaches of Afro-montane forests, and forest-savanna mosaics. In addition, African Forest Elephants occupy semi-arid areas adjacent to the large forest blocks; this includes Sudanian savannas in the north and possibly wet miombo woodlands in the south. They have a wide altitudinal range from the Atlantic coastal forests to about 2,000 metres in the Albertine Rift and around Mount Cameroon. African Forest Elephants are not considered to be migratory. However, they are capable of moving long distances and may do so regularly, usually depending on fruiting events and a requirement for mineral salts (Wall et al. 2021, Blake and Maisels 2023). African Forest Elephants also demonstrate range residence and regular movement patterns with home ranges varying between less than 10 km2 to more than 2,000 km2 and an annual median range within forests of 64.6 km2 (Blake et al. 2008, Schuttler et al. 2012, Wall et al. 2021). Their movements are largely predicted by human pressure such as roads and villages rather than by vegetation type (Blake et al. 2008, Molina-Vacas et al. 2019, Wall et al. 2021). Twenty African Forest Elephant subpopulations (six of which number more than 1,000 individuals) span international boundaries (Maisels et al., 2025), including more than 25,000 African Forest Elephants in the three-country TRIDOM landscape where a trans-frontier management agreement is formalised between Cameroon, Congo, and Gabon (Lindsay et al. 2017). Such management agreements also exist for the WAP complex in Burkina-Faso, Benin, and Niger, and for the Sangha Tri-National Landscape in Cameroon, Congo, and the Central African Republic. Ecosystem Services: Specific ecosystem services provided by both species of African elephants vary and depend to a large extent on the ecosystem (forest, savanna, grassland or desert), specific conditions on the ground and geographical context under consideration. In general, they play an important ecological role as bulk processors of plant material (Owen-Smith 1989). African Forest Elephants are highly frugivorous and are instrumental in dispersing many tree species (Blake et al. 2009, Terborgh et al. 2016). They are obligate seed dispersers for some tree species (Blake et al. 2009, Campos-Arceiz and Blake 2011, Beaune et al. 2013) and particularly the seeds of large trees, which tend to have high carbon content (Stephenson et al. 2014). The loss of the largest herbivores has repercussions on carbon storage in Amazonia (Doughty et al. 2015) and the same may occur in Africa. African Forest Elephants create and maintain forest clearings in mineral-rich soil on which a wide variety of African forest fauna depend; they distribute the limited micronutrients available in "bais" to outlying areas (Turkalo and Fay 1995, 2001; Turkalo et al. 2013; Cromsigt et al. 2018). Finally, they play an important role in the phytosociology of African forests, affecting tree species composition, tree species diversity, and forest structure (Keany et al. 2024, Terborgh et al. 2025).
threats: Poaching for ivory is currently the principal cause of death of African Forest Elephants (Wittemyer et al. 2014, Thouless et al. 2016, Maisels et al. 2025) with persistent poaching pressure at many sites evident from their first surveys in the 1970s to the present day (Douglas-Hamilton 1989, Barnes et al. 1993, Maisels et al. 2025). Data collected as a part of the CITES Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants programme (MIKE), indicate that poaching significantly intensified across the continent starting in 2008, peaking in 2011 and then decreasing during the years thereafter; however, no increase or decrease is apparent in the data from 2020 to 2024 (CITES 2025a). The continental PIKE (proportion of illegally killed elephants) estimate for 2024 has 95 per cent confidence interval ranging from 0.31 to 0.42. In two regions that contain the vast majority of forest elephants and their range, West and Central Africa, indicators of poaching remain at levels that appear unsustainable (i.e., PIKE = 0.50 and 0.48 respectively for 2024) (CITES 2025a). Rapid land use change, driving the direct loss and fragmentation of habitat, is an increasing threat to African elephants across their range. Land conversion is a product of the ongoing expansion of the human population and associated agriculture and infrastructure development, which in turn are driven by economic and technological advances. A specific manifestation of this trend is the reported increase in human-elephant conflict (e.g., Ngama et al. 2016). Human population growth projections suggest land conversion will accelerate rapidly in the coming decades across Africa (see https://population.un.org/wpp/) which will likely increase this threat.
population: Over the past century, African Forest Elephant numbers have declined across most of their range. The African Elephant Forest Status Report 2025 (based on data reported through 2023) estimated a continental population of 135,690 (95% C.I. 99,343–172,297). Population guesses for sites that have not been systematically surveyed add another 7,728–10,990 forest elephants yielding a total of 145,050 individuals. As this was the first status report devoted to African Forest Elephant as a species (and did not include African Savanna Elephant), no comparison to a previous continental population estimate is available. Importantly, DNA capture-recapture was used in 2021 to estimate the number of African Forest Elephants in Gabon (Laguardia et al. 2021). This method, indicated a larger population estimate than the earlier 2013 estimate (Maisels et al. 2013); however, it is not statistically significant due to the large uncertainty associated with each of the estimates. For this reason, it is not indicative of an actual population increase (i.e., due to more births and immigration and/or fewer deaths and emigration). The first Red List assessment of the species reported an estimated 86% decline over the last three generations (i.e., 1922–2015) based on a density model fit with data for years 1974 to 2015 (Gobush et al. 2021).
range: African Forest Elephants are believed to once have occurred across the entire area of tropical and subtropical moist forest in western and central Africa, plus additional forested and semi-arid areas adjacent to these (Mauny 1957, Roth and Douglas-Hamilton 1991, Milner-Gulland and Beddington 1993, Gobush et al. 2025). The species is currently found in these habitats in 22 countries (see range map). Their range, estimated to cover 907,830 km2, is decreasing; it is especially highly fragmented in western Africa where today, four countries have fewer than 100 elephants each and only two have more than 1,000 (Bouche et al. 2011, Maisels et al. 2025). The majority of the remaining population (85%) is found in Gabon and Congo (Laguardia et al. 2021, Maisels et al. 2025). As a result, Central Africa holds the vast majority of all forest elephants today (95%) yet current range in the region is estimated to be just 25% of the former range (Maisels et al. 2013). In West Africa, range loss is believed to be much worse (Gobush et al. 2025). Recent observations in mainland Angola and South Sudan indicate African Forest Elephant presence though no systematic survey data are available. African Forest Elephants are considered nationally extirpated in the Gambia.
useTrade: Ivory: Use of African elephant ivory is entrenched in numerous cultures across the globe, primarily for ornamental and decorative items. Historically, demand for African elephant ivory has been high in Europe, the USA and Asia. For example, beginning in the 1920s, Japanese carvers turned to African elephant ivory as Asian supplies diminished through the 1970s when Japan accounted for about 40% of the global ivory market with a particular preference in Japan for African Forest Elephant ivory due to its hardness, suitable for hankos and the large plectrums for shamisen (Martin 1986; Nishihara 2003, 2012).In 1989, the Convention on International Trade of Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) banned the international commercial trade of ivory in response to a steep decline in African elephants across a substantial portion of their range. Thereafter, two CITES-sanctioned sales of national ivory stockpiles occurred in 2002 and 2008 with Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa selling ivory to China and Japan. At the same time, a nine-year moratorium (ending in 2017) on any new ivory sale proposals from the four African countries followed (www.cites.org). In the 2000s, Chinese demand for ivory greatly surpassed that of Japan where demand for ivory appeared to substantially decline (CITES 2014). As a consequence, prices rose steeply in China and in Africa (Wittemyer et al. 2011, 2014). Debates about the benefits and consequences of the sale of national ivory stockpiles are highly polarised with limited consensus (Stiles 2004, 't Sas-Rolfes et al. 2014, Bennett 2015, Biggs et al. 2017).Analysis of ivory seizure data indicates illegally trafficked ivory has increased substantially since 2006 (Underwood et al. 2013; Milliken 2016; CITES 2018, 2019). Undercover investigations and DNA forensics point to the laundering of illegal ivory in legal domestic ivory markets and seizure analyses indicate that the majority of illegally trafficked ivory is destined for Asia, especially China, Viet Nam and Thailand (Lui 2015, CITES 2016, 2018 and 2019, Krishnasamy 2016). As a result of this and other concerns, China closed its legal domestic ivory market in 2017, Hong Kong SAR took steps to do the same by 2021 (https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/201706/02/P2017060100655.htm), and Thailand tightened its domestic Asian elephant ivory trade regulations in 2015 (http://www.mfa.go.th/main/en/media-center/14/52929-Thailand-Submits-First-Progress-Report-on-Implemen.html). Ivory price fluctuations in mainland China and Viet Nam are evident since China's market closure, a drop since the peak in 2014, but with some increase around the time of the worldwide Covid pandemic (Vigne and Martin 2017, Meijer et al. 2018, https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2021-09-09-worrying-signs-for-elephant-conservation-data-shows-2020-rise-in-black-market-ivory-prices/).Furthermore, large scale ivory seizures continued to be made, albeit less frequently than during the years of peak poaching. These multi-ton hauls of illegal ivory are a hallmark of transnational organised crime (TOC) (Wasser et al. 2022; Stiles 2024a, 2024b). Global ivory seizures totalled 18.2 tons for 2023 (the most recent year with data available) and included a 7-ton seizure made in Viet Nam coming from Angola (an African Forest Elephant range country) demonstrating that such TOC remains a serious issue (CITES 2025). Significant illegal ivory markets, including online, remain in several Southeast Asian countries, such as Lao PDR, Myanmar and Viet Nam that involve trafficked ivory from African Forest Elephant range countries (https://cites.org/eng/prog/etis; TRAFFIC 2017, 2020, 2023, 2024; Vigne and Martin 2018a, 2018b; https://reports.eia-international.org/out-of-africa/, https://eia-international.org/global-environmental-crime-tracker Accessed 20 March 2025). Non-consumptive Tourism: African Forest Elephants potentially have a significant tourism draw for wildlife watching and photographic tourism along with other iconic species that share their habitat, such as western lowland gorillas and chimpanzees. National parks in Gabon, Republic of Congo and Benin - among others - are actively developing tourism opportunities despite the species' cryptic nature and often closed canopy habitat. Unlike the African Savanna Elephant, tourism does not contribute substantially to the conservation of African Forest Elephants in central Africa (Naidoo et al. 2016) and little documentation of its success in west Africa exists. Also, African Forest Elephants are an important symbol within the cultures of many African communities. African elephants (both species) are among the few iconic animals that occur in the majority of African countries, and innumerable stories, songs, and cultural traditions revolve around them (van der Water et al. 2022). Trophy Hunting: Trophy hunting for African Forest Elephant appears to be very rare. Cameroon and Gabon have been the only range countries to submit quotas to CITES for trophies or tusks with purpose code "hunting trophy" and source "wild" in the last 20 years (Gabon last submitted a quota in 2008) (https://cites.org/eng/resources/quotas/). In the last five years, there is evidence that only Cameroon has exported trophies or tusks under codes "hunting trophy" and "wild", numbering four tusks to Panama (https://trade.cites.org/en/cites_trade/). However, Cameroon has both species of African elephant; therefore, it is not possible to discern if these are African Forest Elephant specimens or not. Other Trade: There have been limited reports of African Forest Elephant poaching for body parts other than ivory, such as tails, bone, skin and hair (e.g., www.enca.com/africa/tusks-and-elephant-tails-seized-in-ivory-coast-ngo). The bushmeat trade is thriving in parts of west and central Africa and likely includes a considerable volume of African Forest Elephant meat as indicated in hunter interviews (Stiles 2011, Abernethy et al. 2013). No live trade of African Forest Elephants is known to occur.
conservationActions: The African Forest Elephant was listed in CITES Appendix I in 1989 when all African elephants were considered a single species. Subsequently, the populations of Botswana (1997), Namibia (1997), South Africa (2000) and Zimbabwe (1997) were transferred to Appendix II, with a specific annotation 'A10' limiting trade in specimens to certain conditions (https://cites.org/eng/app/appendices.php). CITES updated the taxonomy and nomenclature of African Elephants in 2025 with the effect that African Forest Elephants are listed under a genus-level as Loxodonta spp. on Appendix I. The standard nomenclature reference adopted for the species is Wilson and Reeder 2005 with a supplement on distribution consisting of Kuhner et al. 2025 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-CoP20-Com-I-Rec-12.pdf). The African Elephant Action Plan (AEAP) (developed and adopted by African elephant range countries) was adopted by CITES in March 2010 and updated in 2023 to include, inter alia, acknowledgement of the two species of African elephants (CITES 2023). The AEAP is a sanctioned statement by all range countries regarding the most important and immediate activities that require implementation and funding if Africa's elephants are to be conserved. The AEAP's goal is "To secure and restore, where possible, sustainable elephant populations throughout their present and potential range in Africa recognizing their potential to provide ecological, socio, cultural and economic benefits." The African Elephant Fund was established to support the implementation of the African Elephant Action Plan and is administered by the UN Environmental Programme. A number of CITES-initiated instruments were created to monitor and combat illegal trade in ivory. The CITES MIKE programme was established in 2002, has 69 designated sites across the range of both African Elephants; this includes 29 sites in 15 range countries of the African Forest Elephant (https://cites.org/eng/prog/mike, Accessed 15 March 2025). Angola, Guinea Bissau, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, and Uganda do not have MIKE sites for their African Forest Elephant populations; South Sudan is not a Party to CITES (and does not participate in the MIKE programme). The MIKE programme provides the most detailed and reliable data available on continental poaching pressure (https://cites.org/eng/prog/mike/index.php/portal). However, metrics used by the MIKE programme that depend on carcass finds are less robust in closed canopy forest habitat because detection of carcasses is difficult and decomposition in humid environments is relatively rapid. The Elephant Trade Information System (ETIS) established in 1996, is managed by TRAFFIC as a comprehensive information system for tracking illegal trade in ivory and other elephant products (CITES 2016, 2019, 2025). At a national level the implementation of National Ivory Action Plans (NIAPs) are a practical tool designed to track significant and timely action to combat the illegal trade in ivory; the process is thoroughly reviewed in CITES 2025a. Currently 12 African, Middle Eastern and Asian countries, as identified by ETIS analyses, are required to produce and implement a NIAP (https://cites.org/eng/niaps, Accessed 12 January 2026). Seven countries in the NIAP process are range countries of the African Forest Elephant. At a national level African Forest Elephants are subject to varying degrees of legal protection in the 22 range countries, with most granting them the highest possible protection status. However, up to 70% of the animals may live outside protected areas (Maisels et al. 2013) and are vulnerable to poaching, as the degree of protection (by anti-poaching agents) and road access are both important predictors of their density (Blake et al. 2008, Yackulic et al. 2011, Maisels et al. 2013). Conservation measures usually include habitat management and protection through legislation, policy and law enforcement. Successful anti-poaching and management has resulted in the maintenance of numbers of African Forest Elephants in some localities. In other instances where protection efforts have failed, African Forest Elephant numbers have been reduced by 70% or more in a decade (ANPN, WCS, and WWF 2013; Nzooh Dongmo et al. 2016; Poulsen et al. 2017).

rationale: Although systematic surveys are lacking, available evidence suggests that the Tibetan Fox remains widespread in the steppes, alpine meadows, and semi-deserts of the Tibetan Plateau, and is also present in the Mustang and Humla Regions of Nepal, and in Ladakh, India. There are no major threats to the species at present, although poisoning of pikas (a major prey item) in much of the Tibetan plateau poses a concern. Nonetheless, there is no evidence that the species is currently undergoing a decline that would warrant listing in a Near Threatened category.
habitat: The species is found in upland plains and hills from about 2,500–5,200 m (Clark et al. 2008); however, the preponderance of Tibetan Fox habitat is >3,000 m, and the majority of that > 4,000 m. Most of its habitat consists of sparse grasslands devoid of trees and shrubs (Wang et al. 2007, although see also Gong and Hu 2003), particularly where Black-lipped Pikas are abundant. It appears that Tibetan Foxes are closely tied to the presence of pikas, their primary prey species (Liu et al. 2010, Zheng et al 2023) and may in fact be an obligate predator (Harris et al. 2014). Tibetan Foxes appear particularly adept at capturing pikas (including, at times, following brown bears (Ursus arctos) excavating pika burrows in order to capture pikas that escape; Harris et al. 2008), and are rarely encountered where pikas are absent. They also feed on carrion, insects, galliform birds, and other small mammals (Zheng 1985, Zheng et al. 2023). Tibetan Foxes spend considerable time resting in small burrows, hollows and rock crevasses (Wang et al. 2003). They are most active at dawn and dusk (Wang et al. 2022), although they can be seen at any time of the day (Wang et al. 2004).
threats: There are no major threats to the species at present. Ongoing government-sponsored programmes involving poisoning of pikas, the main prey, takes place across much of the Tibetan plateau and poses the main threat; secondary poisoning of Tibetan Foxes may occur, although does not appear to be common. However, reductions or complete elimination of their major prey would certainly be damaging to Tibetan Fox populations. If such pika reduction programmes continue or increase, the status of the Tibetan Fox would require reassessment. Domestic dogs can kill Tibetan Foxes, and may be a major source of mortality in some areas (Wang et al. 2007).
population: In general, Tibetan Fox occur at low densities. Fox abundance depends primarily on prey availability. In northwest Tibet, in a remote region of desert steppe with little prey, only five foxes were seen in 1,848 km of driving. In southwest Qinghai in a benign environment with much prey, 15 foxes were tallied in 367 km (Schaller 1998). In Serxu county, northwest Sichuan Province, an area abundant with Black-lipped Pika (Ochotona curzoniae), eight Tibetan Foxes were sighted along 11 km of country road during a night count in 2001 (Anonymous 2000), and 27 sightings (at least 12 individuals) were recorded along line transects in the same area in August 2003 (Wang Xiaoming and Wang Zhenghuan pers. obs.). More recent studies with marked animals (Liu et al. 2007) have suggested that Tibetan Foxes can achieve relatively high densities where preferred prey is abundant and human hunting pressure low. Densities of 2-4/km² may occur. A very coarse and unreliable estimation of population density of Tibetan Foxes in the Tibetan Autonomous Region was provided by Piao (1989), which extrapolated to an estimate of 37,000. No systematic surveys of Tibetan Fox abundance have been conducted.
range: Widespread in the steppes, alpine meadows, and semi-deserts of the Tibetan Plateau from the Ladakh area of India, east across China including parts of Xinjiang, Gansu, Qinghai, and Sichuan provinces and all of the Tibet Autonomous Region, and into northwestern Yunnan (Gong and Hu 2003, Wang 2003, Namgail and Bagchi 2005, Clark et al. 2008, Wozencraft 2008, Jnawali et al. 2011). Also present in Nepal north of the Himalaya, known specifically from the Mustang and Humla areas (Schaller and Ginsberg 2004, Werhahn et al. 2016) as well as extreme northern Uttarakhand, India (Pal et al. 2021). There are no confirmed records for Bhutan.
useTrade: Hunting and snaring occurs for the pelt (which is used to make hats), but is not common because the coarse pelts of Tibetan Foxes are of minor value.
conservationActions: The species is not listed on the CITES Appendices. Tibetan Fox is legally protected in several large Chinese reserves, including Arjin Shan (45,000 km²), Xianza (40,000 km²), Chang Tang (ca. 334,000 km²), Kekexili (ca. 45,000 km²), and Sanjiangyuan (ca. 152,000 km²) (Schaller and Ginsberg 2004). However, actual protection remains minimal. The species is likely to occur in other protected areas throughout the species' range. The species is not known to be held in any formal conservation breeding programme, although some animals may be held in a few zoos. Li et al. (2015) reported that pastoralists around the Qinghai Lake area held generally negative opinions toward foxes (although not nearly as negative as opinions about wolves or bears), although they did not distinguish between Tibetan and red foxes, and there is little evidence to suggest depredation on livestock by Tibetan foxes is common. Despite recent studies that have helped further understanding of the species' biology and niche overlap with the red fox (V. vulpes; Tsukada et al. 2014, Wang et al. 2022), very little remains known of their natural history.

rationale: Historical unregulated exploitation of Antarctic Fur Seals reduced the global population from millions to commercial extinction. However, despite evidence of severe bottlenecks, high levels of genetic variability were retained at different locations via the persistence of small, isolated populations. When sealing ceased, high reproductive success and locally abundant food supplies resulted in a fast recovery, particularly in the South Atlantic region of the Southern Ocean. At South Georgia, which currently holds 90+% of the global population, breeding range expansion likely reached a maximum in 2007/2009, when a survey-based assessment suggested an abundance of 3.5 million fur seals. However, this peak has been followed by declines, which are ongoing at South Georgia, Bouvetøya and especially the South Shetland Islands.There has been considerable uncertainty regarding global numbers for Antarctic Fur Seals in recent decades, and some speculative, unverified numbers have been in circulation. However, a recent quantitative re-evaluation of all the subpopulations shows that the annual change for the global (mature) population over the last three generations (26 years, based on a mean generation length of 8.63 (SD=0.26)), is -3.19% [95% CI: -4.015; -2.347]. The global population has dropped from an estimated 2,187,424 (SD=153,141) mature seals in 1999 to 943,756 (SD=89,727) in 2025, which corresponds to a reduction of -0.57 [-0.64; -0.48] (with a 90% probability of reduction being equal to or greater than 50%).The ongoing population declines are thought to be a response to environmental changes, particularly at South Georgia and the Scotia Sea. Climate change driven increases in temperature and cascading ecosystem-wide repercussions are thought to be limiting the amount of available Antarctic Krill (Euphausia superba). This is unlikely to be a reversible trend, unless effective mitigation of greenhouse warming occurs soon. Other factors that are potentially exacerbating the decline include competition for prey by recovering whale populations, increasing levels of commercial fishing for krill, emerging pollutants (Aznar-Alemany et al. 2019) including plastics and especially, outbreaks of new epizootic diseases causing extensive mortality, such as H5N1-H5 Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). However, the quantitative impact assessment of these threats is difficult, if not impossible due to insufficient data, and therefore assigning causality remains a challenge. Given that the causes of the 50%+ population reduction are unlikely to be reversible, have not ceased, and are to a degree not yet fully understood, the Antarctic Fur Seals should be classified as Endangered according to criterion A2. This assessment reports a nongenuine change from the 2016 assessment, arising from new data availability.
habitat: The Antarctic Fur Seal is a small otariid, with newborn pups having a standard length of between 58 and 66 cm, and males being marginally heavier at birth (4.9–6.6 kg) than females (4.8–5.9 kg). They are highly sexually dimorphic as adults, with males being almost 1.5 times longer (170–200 cm) and four times heavier (90–197 kg) than females (117–140 cm and 20–51 kg, respectively) (Bonner 1968, Payne 1979).Female mean age at first breeding is 3–4 years (range 2–7) (Payne 1977, McCann and Doidge 1987), although full adult size is typically not attained until ages 6–7 (Lunn et al. 1994), and longevity is around 20–21 years. They breed annually after a gestation of 8–9 months which follows a diapause period of 3–4 months, before blastocyst implantation, which closely links a pup birth with the next pup's conception (Boyd 1996). They give birth mostly to a single pup, but twins (of single and multiple paternity) are reported at least at South Georgia and South Shetlands Islands (Hoffman and Forcada 2009, Bonin et al. 2012). Adoption or foster nursing of unrelated pups and milk stealing are frequently observed at high-density sites, particularly when mothers struggle to find food at sea and return late to attend the pups (Lunn 1992).Fecundity increases rapidly from age two, peaks at 0.80 at age eight, and remains high (0.68–0.77) until ages 11–13, with a possible onset of a senescent decline thereafter (Forcada 2021, Forcada et al. 2023b). Weaning success normally improves with age (Doidge and Croxall 1989), although it is individually variable, in part due to heterozygosity (Forcada and Hoffman 2014). Fecundity also depends on individual foraging efficiency and provisioning rates (McDonald et al. 2009, Jeanniard-du-Dot et al. 2017). Early pup survival primarily depends on food availability (Reid and Forcada 2005, Forcada et al. 2023b), although in dense colonies, trauma inflicted by adults is a source of mortality (Doidge et al. 1984). At the South Shetland Islands, predation by Leopard Seals can be a major cause of mortality among pups (Boveng et al. 1998, Krause et al. 2022).Females usually breed annually but defer breeding in times of low food availability (Lunn et al. 1994). At South Georgia, variation in fecundity and survival is linked to climate fluctuations. Severe anomalies from the Southern Annular Mode and El Niño-Southern Oscillation can reduce adult survival by as much as 15–20% (Forcada et al. 2008, Forcada et al. 2023b). Biometric traits including birth mass, size and age at first breeding, and adult size in females are phenotypically plastic and linked to environmental conditions; directional selection due to environmental change might also play a role (Forcada and Hoffman 2014). Warming temperatures at Bird Island, South Georgia, have resulted in females maturing later, at larger size.Males reach sexual maturity at ages 3–4, although they only start competing for breeding territories at ages 7–11; between ages seven and nine they reach maximum body size (Payne 1979, McCann and Doidge 1987). Survival rate after age seven is below 0.7, which is lower than the average survival for adult females (0.87–0.93) (Forcada et al. 2023b). Successful males can hold territories for several years, up to ages 17–18, and their probability of return as territorial males depends on individual heterozygosity (Hoffman et al. 2003), density of territorial individuals at breeding beaches (Bonin et al. 2016), and previous breeding experience (Arnould and Duck 1997). At Bird island, the average male hold territories in one or two seasons over a lifetime (Forcada et al. 2023b), although rare cases of an individual male holding a territory for seven or eight consecutive years have been observed. During territory tenure, males mainly fast, but sometimes they go to the sea for short foraging trips, and attempt to recover their territories upon return (McCann 1980).Based on the most recent sex-specific life tables, the cohort-method (Coale 1972) generation length estimate is 8.21 (SD=0.28) for females and 9.90 (SD=0.58) for males. Using mean absolute abundance estimates for mature females and mature males between 2007 and 2009, when the population of South Georgia was estimated to be at its maximum, the mean generation length weighted by the abundance of mature seals of each sex is 8.63 (SD=0.26) (Forcada 2025b).Adult males arrive at the breeding colonies in late October, 2–3 weeks before the arrival of pregnant females. While breeding territories are being established, females start arriving and pupping, in mid to late November, and pupping continues until late December or early January. The pupping season peaks with high synchrony across subpopulations (Duck 1990, Goebel et al. 2003, Forcada et al. 2005, Hofmeyr et al. 2007). Births occur 1–2 days after females arrive at the colony and pups are initially nursed for 6–7 days. Females come into oestrous during this time on shore, mate and then depart on their first foraging trip of the nursing season (Doidge et al. 1986). Alternate foraging trips and pup attendance bouts on land continue for the duration of lactation (mean 117 days). The duration of foraging trips and attendance periods varies according to food availability, with approximately 4–5 days at sea followed by 2–3 days on land being a norm (Costa et al. 1989, Boyd 1999, Guinet et al. 2000, Kirkman et al. 2003, Biuw et al. 2009). Most pups wean by the end of March.Pups moult their natal coat at about 1–2 months of age. After this first moult, the black pelage of pups turns into the adult grizzled dark brown colour, with paler shading below. One in approximately 600 (1–2‰) pups is born with a hypopigmented (blond) colouration in the guard hairs and paler underfur and skin, due to a mutation in the melanocortin 1 receptor (MCR1) which regulates pigment production. Blond seals are homozygous for the serine alleles through simple Mendelian inheritance; dark colouration is dominant (Peters et al. 2016). Data from Bird Island show no differences in inbreeding levels between blond and wild-type individuals, suggesting no selective disadvantage for blonds, including active territorial males (Forcada 2021). Other colour morphs, including brindled (Forcada and Staniland 2018) and other variations (Acevedo et al. 2009) have also been reported at the South Shetland Islands and Marion Island (de Bruyn et al. 2007), but not in East Antarctica. The proximity with South Georgia, where blond seals are more common, would suggest a limited contribution of gene flow towards the East Antarctic colonies (Hoffman et al. 2018). Moult in Antarctic Fur Seal adults can be incomplete or partial (Bonner 1968). Females moult in February and March while they are still suckling their pups, and they can continue foraging at sea during this time.Central place foraging and income breeding determine foraging activity, which is generally associated with oceanographic conditions, prey distribution and availability, and distance from the colony (McCafferty et al. 1998, Guinet et al. 2001, Lea et al. 2006, Staniland and Robinson 2008, Biuw et al. 2009). Together with very high sexual dimorphism, it leads to sexual segregation in foraging strategies and diet (Staniland and Robinson 2008). As income breeders, nursing females can only spend a maximum of 10–12 days foraging at sea before returning to their pups on land, which limits their foraging range. At South Georgia, females dive to shallow depths (≤40 m), exploiting diurnally migrating prey such as Antarctic Krill and lantern fish (Myctophidae) within the mixed surface layer, predominately at night (McCafferty et al. 1998). They travel to the shelf break and beyond, to deeper oceanic waters. Males dive mostly on the continental shelf, but in deeper areas than females, and benthic dives are frequent for them. Maximum dive durations and depths are around 5 min and 210 m in females, and 10 min and 350 m in males (Forcada and Staniland 2018).At South Georgia, when Antarctic Krill is locally very abundant, females make short foraging trips and fewer dives and spend more time ashore, feeding almost exclusively on krill; frequent and shallow dives in daytime indicate that the krill is close to the surface and accessible during the day. In poor krill years, deeper and longer daytime dives are associated with a higher proportion of fish in the diet. Females increase the time spent foraging when less krill is available (Boyd et al. 1994, McCafferty et al. 1998). Maternal mass and pup traits, such as pup mass and energy demands, affect energy allocation (Costa et al. 1989, Arnould et al. 2001, Hiruki-Raring et al. 2012) and therefore determine maternal attendance and diving behaviour. Larger females usually give birth to larger pups and invest more in pups during the perinatal and moult stages (McDonald et al. 2012b).Foraging trip durations in females tends to increase as the pup-rearing period progresses to meet increased lactation demands (Arnould et al. 2001, McDonald et al. 2009, McDonald et al. 2012b). Some seals travel to more distant oceanic waters, where more energy-dense prey is found (Staniland et al. 2007). High individual variation in foraging trip characteristics during breeding appears to be a response to prey variability (Staniland and Pond 2004, McDonald et al. 2012a), and to climate (Lea et al. 2006). In winter, Antarctic Fur Seals disperse broadly, though some show fidelity to foraging sites when prey are available near colony sites (Arthur et al. 2015).At the Kerguelen Islands, female yearlings show total segregation in diet and foraging distribution (based on isotopic niche) from breeding females until age two, whereas juvenile males show a progressive change in niche throughout their development until age five, and have a different diet than bulls (Kernaleguen et al. 2016). At Bird Island, South Georgia, stable isotope analysis (Jones et al. 2020) shows high sexual segregation in foraging habitats, with males spending more time foraging south of the Polar Front in maritime Antarctica than females and generally spending more time south as they age.In the South Atlantic sector, the main prey of Antarctic Fur Seals is Antarctic Krill (Doidge and Croxall 1985, Reid and Arnould 1996, Kirkman et al. 2000, Hofmeyr et al. 2010, Polito and Goebel 2010). At South Georgia, krill accounts for 75–88% of the fur seal diet. They do eat some Mackerel Icefish (Champsocephalus gunnari), notothenids, and myctophid fishes (North et al. 1983, North 1996). In poor krill years, notothenids and myctophids predominate in the diet. Krill is also the main prey in the South Shetland Islands, particularly during the breeding season. Other prey includes myctophid fish, squid, and penguins. In non-breeding males, krill are also important, followed by myctophid fish, Antarctic Silverfish (Pleuragramma antarcticum), and notothenids (Daneri and Carlini 1999, Daneri et al. 2005). Squid are also eaten and male fur seals eat penguins in some areas, although infrequently. At Heard Island, Macquarie Island, the Crozet Islands and the Prince Edward Islands where krill is less abundant, primary prey are cephalopods, myctophid fish and notothenids (Guinet et al. 2002, Robinson et al. 2002, Cherel et al. 2007, Makhado et al. 2008, Casper et al. 2010, Reisinger et al. 2010).
threats: Global warming poses a significant threat to Antarctic Fur Seals and their ecosystems via impacts on food availability, habitat deterioration, life history and population dynamic impacts (Forcada et al. 2005, Forcada et al. 2008, Schwarz et al. 2013, Forcada and Hoffman 2014, Forcada et al. 2023b, Krause et al. 2024, Ouled-Cheikh et al. 2024). Global warming impacts Antarctic Krill habitats, sea ice contraction, and rising ocean temperatures, with cascading effects on krill distribution, physiology and behaviour (Hill et al. 2013, Atkinson et al. 2019, McBride et al. 2021, Kawaguchi et al. 2024). Large colonies of Antarctic Fur Seals in the South Atlantic sector are highly dependent on large and predictable aggregations of Antarctic Krill (Bonner 1968, Daneri and Coria 1992, Daneri 1996, Croxall et al. 1999, Kirkman et al. 2000).In Antarctica, sea ice density is positively related to krill density (Hiruki-Raring et al. 2012), and krill biomass (Reid et al. 1999, Osman et al. 2004) has a direct impact on Antarctic Fur Seal life history and vital rates (Croxall et al. 1988, Croxall et al. 1999, Forcada et al. 2008, Forcada and Hoffman 2014, Forcada et al. 2023b). Poor krill recruitment, linked to climate warming and low sea ice concentrations are the main causes of the ongoing reductions.At South Georgia, krill biomass is not self-sustaining, it depends on advection and transport from the Antarctic Peninsula and the Weddell Sea, and special conditions for enhanced individual krill growth (Murphy et al. 2007b, Murphy et al. 2017). This leads to variable densities, with years of abundant or poor krill supply for predators (Croxall et al. 1999, Murphy et al. 2007a). Frequent breeding deferral and increased adult and especially juvenile mortality of Antarctic Fur Seals are correlated with coupled climate and sea surface temperature cycles that affect krill (Forcada et al. 2008, Forcada and Hoffman 2014, Forcada et al. 2023b). Within the last two decades, there has been a selection for low pup mass at birth. Only the largest and most heterozygous pups have high survival and recruitment probability, which has reduced the population (Forcada and Hoffman 2014). Recently, sustained krill shortages at South Georgia have: 1) dropped first year survival from 0.45 to 0.15; 2) increased the age of the breeding population; and 3) concomitantly increased generation time (Forcada et al. 2023b). Increasing trends in age of breeding females and duration of their foraging trips and effort, which is typically associated with the lack of krill and sufficiently abundant alternative prey (Boyd 1999, McCafferty et al. 1998, Polito and Goebel 2010, Krause et al. 2022), have also been observed at the South Shetland Islands (Krause et al. 2022).Apart from predation by Killer Whales (Orcinus orca), which is currently unquantified and probably underreported for Antarctic Fur Seals, Leopard Seal predation is a main cause of concern at colonies from the South Shetland Islands (Boveng et al. 1998, Vera et al. 2006, Krause et al. 2024). Numbers of seasonally resident Leopard Seals appear to have increased at Fur Seal colonies (Boveng et al. 1998, Krause et al. 2022), reducing their size through predation on pups (Krause et al. 2020). As the size of populations decline, low colony numbers and demographic stochasticity, along with climate change impacts on the food supply may exacerbate predation impacts through top-down control (Boveng et al. 1998, Vera et al. 2006).Antarctic Krill is also essential to recovering populations of large whales, which are potentially their main consumers (Zerbini et al. 2019, Calderan et al. 2020, Jackson et al. 2020, Baines et al. 2021, Biuw et al. 2024, Savoca et al. 2024). Antarctic Fur Seals recovered from sealing in a transformed environment in which whales and fin-fish had been depressed by overexploitation (Laws 1977, Gulland 1983, Miller 1991). However, some of the whale populations have reached near pre-exploitation levels (Zerbini et al. 2019) and have become direct competitors for krill with Antarctic Fur Seals and other krill predators (Atkinson et al. 2019).Antarctic Krill are targeted by a growing multinational fishery (Cappell et al. 2022, CCAMLR 2024), which operates in areas within the distribution range of the Antarctic Fur Seal. Regionally, the fishery operates near important breeding aggregations of krill-dependent predators, including fur seals, seabirds and whales, with impacts that are difficult to quantify and manage (Lowther et al. 2020, Watters et al. 2020, McBride et al. 2021). Where Antarctic Fur Seals and fisheries use the same areas and potentially target the same krill (e.g., Bamford et al. 2021, Owen et al. 2024), intensive krill harvesting by the fishery can deplete the krill biomass required by the fur seals (Lowther et al. 2020, Watters et al. 2020, Cappell et al. 2022). Moreover, the allocation of krill extraction targets does not directly take climate change effects on krill into consideration currently, despite being identified as a potential risk to krill-dependent predators in a fishery management context (Reiss et al. 2017).Incidental mortality of Antarctic Fur Seals and other marine vertebrates in the mid-water trawls used by the Antarctic Krill fishery were identified as a threat by The Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) (Hooper et al. 2005). Even though the impact is thought to be relatively low (CCAMLR 2005), fishing vessels are required to use pinniped excluding devices on all trawlers, and international fishery observers are required to report entangled marine mammals during fishing operations. However, there are limited assessments of the effectiveness of these conservation measures (Krause et al. 2024).Not many studies have addressed pathogens of human origin in Antarctic seals but increasing temperatures and anthropogenic activity represent increasing risks to Antarctic wildlife. Antibodies against herpes viruses have been found in Antarctic Fur Seals (Tryland et al. 2012). Brucellosis has been detected in a limited number of Antarctic Fur Seals at the South Shetland Islands (Blank et al. 2001) suggesting the presence of the infection, but with unknown prevalence. Positive tests for antibodies of Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular protozoan parasite, were found in Antarctic Fur Seal samples from South Shetland Islands (Rengifo-Herrera et al. 2012). Campylobacter insulaenigrae and C. lari have been found in fur seal faecal swabs at Deception Island but the source of infection, the prevalence in seals, and whether it is the result of microbial pollution associated with human activity is unknown (García-Peña et al. 2010). Similarly, enteropathogenic Escherichia coli was found in two out of 33 fur seal pups at Cape Shirreff, in colonies close to human research stations, but the origin of the bacteria is unknown (Hernandez et al. 2007).A Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) virus of the H5 subtype, first reported in wild mammals and birds in South America in 2022, spread rapidly throughout the continent with repercussions for a variety of pinnipeds (Kuiken et al. 2025). It first reached South Georgia and the Falkland Islands in 2024, causing mortality of seabirds, and Southern Elephant Seals (Mirounga leonina) and Antarctic Fur Seals (Banyard et al. 2024, Bennison et al. 2024). Antarctic Fur Seal mortality at South Georgia continued in 2025, but practicalities of sampling all possibly affected locations precludes any estimate of total associated mortality. Warmer climate conditions are likely to increase disease risk for Antarctic Fur Seals from viruses and other vectors (Gulland et al. 2022, Sanderson and Alexander 2020) because the high density of animals within Antarctic Fur Seal colonies provides optimum conditions for outbreaks with severe conservation implications. Stopping the spread of the viruses in wildlife is nearly impossible; but proposed conservation actions include: 1) targeted surveillance of populations for HPAI H5 virus, including presence in previously affected locations; 2) assess and evaluate epidemiology as much as possible, including vectors, targeted species, and locations; 3) assess spread and impact of disease and mortality; 4) inform wildlife managers and agencies to enact or adapt conservation plans; and 5) reach out to policymakers to help mitigate/prevent HPAI outbreaks (Kuiken et al. 2025).Entanglement in plastic debris is a persistent problem for Antarctic Fur Seals, especially juvenile males.
