Entangled animals are commonly reported at South Georgia (Bonner and McCann 1982, Croxall et al. 1990, Arnould and Croxall 1995, Waluda and Staniland 2013), and elsewhere including Heard and Macquarie Islands (Slip and Burton 1991), Livingston Island (Hucke-Gaete et al. 1997), Marion Island (Hofmeyr and Bester 2002), and Bouvetøya (Hofmeyr et al. 2006). The most common entanglements occur when juvenile seals put their heads through materials that move down onto the neck/chest and get stuck. As the neck grows, the skin breaks, and bands penetrate deep in the blubber layer causing severe injuries and infection. At Bird Island, South Georgia, these "collar bands" include polypropylene straps, synthetic strings, fishing trawl net, plastic sheets or bags, vegetable bags, elastic strips, twine, cloth strips, hard-hat liners, leather strips, synthetic rope with up to 30% of these entanglements causing physical injuries (Croxall et al. 1990). Population consequences are considered insignificant (Arnould and Croxall 1995, Waluda and Staniland 2013), but from an animal welfare perspective collar bands can be horrific. There are treaties such as The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships in 1973, as modified by the Protocol of 1978 (MARPOL 73/78) and monitoring of impacts of marine debris which in the Subantarctic and Antarctic is overseen by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) that attempt to reduce debris. Tighter regulation on marine debris by CCAMLR and strong enforcement in the South Georgia fisheries by the local government, for example, have led to a significant reduction in the incidences of entanglement at South Georgia. However, the presence of widespread marine debris and especially plastics has been increasing throughout the Antarctic Fur Seal's range (Waluda et al. 2020, Bargagli and Rota 2023). Microplastics (Bargagli and Rota 2023), which have been investigated in different Antarctic pinnipeds, are also a concern (Garcia-Garin et al. 2020, Cebuhar et al. 2024, Santillán et al. 2025). The consensus is that the prevalence of microplastics is currently low. However, microplastic levels are globally increasing, posing potential risks to human health and the environment and by extension marine wildlife. Continued monitoring of their prevalence is necessary.Trace metals, particularly mercury and cadmium (Malcolm et al. 1994, Cipro et al. 2017, Toro-Valdivieso et al. 2023), are present in Antarctic Fur Seals breeding at South Georgia and the South Shetland Islands, with concentrations thought to be in the toxic range. Similarly, persistent organic pollutants, including PCBs and DDTs, have been found in seals from the South Shetland Islands (Brault et al. 2013, Cipro et al. 2012), and also brominated flame retardants (Schiavone et al. 2009) such as polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs). These compounds are mostly used in household appliances, office electronics, textiles, and furniture far from the Antarctic, which suggests long-range transport and propagation across the marine environment. While detected levels are currently low, they persist in the environment, biomagnify in the food webs, and their toxicity may affect hormonal regulation as well as hepatic, neuronal, and thyroid activities. Emerging compounds such as dechloranes may cross the blood-brain barrier and are found in fur seals of the South Shetland Islands (Aznar-Alemany et al. 2019). Similarly, concentrations of perfluorochemicals (PFCs), which are also emerging anthropogenic global pollutants, have been found in juvenile Antarctic Fur Seals from the South Shetland islands, although in marginal levels far below those that cause toxicity in laboratory species (Schiavone et al. 2009). Greater knowledge of the origin, presence, and persistence of these chemicals across subpopulations of Antarctic Fur Seals is required to assess actual risks.
population: Commercial harvests during the 18th and 19th centuries took the Antarctic Fur Seal to the brink of extinction (Bonner 1968, Payne 1977). However, when sealing ceased, high reproductive success and locally abundant food supplies resulted in a fast recovery particularly in the South Atlantic region of the Southern Ocean (Laws 1973, Payne 1977, Bengtson et al. 1990, Hucke-Gaete et al. 2004, Hofmeyr et al. 2005). The species does show evidence of severe bottlenecks, but despite this, high levels of genetic variability have been retained via the persistence of small, isolated populations that survived the sealing periods (Hoffman et al. 2011, Paijmans et al. 2020). Pre-bottleneck population estimates are unavailable, although genetic analysis indicate that the effective pre-bottleneck population size at equilibrium could have ranged between 770,000 to 2.41 million females (Hoffman et al. 2011), encompassing the current population levels (see Table S1 in the Supplementary Information).A complete re-evaluation of the species' population status has been carried out for this assessment because considerable misinformation has made its way into assessments, government documents and even the scientific literature (e.g., SCAR 2006, Hofmeyr 2016, Foley and Lynch 2019, Convey and Hughes 2023). For the purpose of documentation and reproducibility, details of the reassessment can be found at the Github and Zenodo repositories (Forcada 2025a,b). Population abundance, annual change and reduction (where relevant) are presented by population/subpopulation in Table S1 in the Supplementary Information. For East Antarctica, these data are also presented by breeding location. The South Sandwich Islands are considered separately, given that the genetic identity of animals in this area has yet to be established. Based on the latest data, the global population has declined over a period of three generations (25.9 years based on a mean generation length of 8.63 (SD=0.26)), from 2,187,424 (SD=153,141) mature seals in 1999 to 943,756 (SD=89,727) mature seals in 2025. This represents a mean annual decline of -3.19% [SD=0.43; 95 CI: -4.015; -2.347], and an estimated reduction of -0.57 [SD=0.05; CI: -0.64; -0.48], with a 90% probability of reduction being equal to or greater than 50%.For the subpopulation at South Georgia, the quantitative assessment was based on comprehensive helicopter-based survey data obtained in 2007/9 (Forcada et al. 2023a) and recent data obtained via RPAS (Remotely Piloted Aerial Systems) surveys to reassess the population at representative locations, in 2021/22. This allowed for a population projection for South Georgia over the assessment period, which was augmented assuming an estimated mean annual change 0.98 (SD=0.01) from 1996 to 2006 (Forcada et al. 2008) to create a 3-generation assessment (Forcada 2025b). This produced a mean annual rate of decline of -3.93% [CI: -2.73; -5.13], and an estimated reduction over three generations of -0.57 [-0.65; -0.48], with a 92% probability of the reduction being greater than or equal to 50% .The recolonisation of South Georgia after sealing probably reached a peak by 2009, due to a maximum occupancy of suitable breeding habitat (Forcada et al. 2023b), although by then Bird Island was already declining slowly due to increasing environmental pressures (Forcada et al. 2008). This was exacerbated by a major population collapse in the winter of 2009 (Forcada and Hoffman 2014), but at the time it was unclear if this had affected South Georgia in its entirety. The new survey data consistently supports a decline across South Georgia and using an updated adjustment factor to account for immature and pre-territorial individuals, the total population in 2022 was estimated to be 1,983,687 [95% CI: 1,606,408–2,411,876], approximately 1.5 million seals fewer than in 2007/2009.At the South Orkney Islands, the numbers of Antarctic Fur Seals increased rapidly in the mid-1980s and peaked in the 1990s (Dunn et al. 2025), paralleling the recovery of the breeding population of South Georgia. Pup counts at the main study locations of Signy and Laurie Islands have however been zero since the mid-2010s (Carlini et al. 2006, Waluda et al. 2010), suggesting that pupping at the South Orkney Islands continues to be marginal. Surveys of Gosling, Monroe, Powell, and Michelsen Islands have not been updated since the 1970s (Laws 1981). The new analysis shows that the numbers of Antarctic Fur Seals at Signy Island have declined markedly (Forcada 2025b), see also Dunn et al. (2025). The large decline observed at Signy Island in recent decades reflects the similarly large decline of South Georgia.Data from surveys of the South Sandwich Islands Archipelago, conducted in January and February 1997, and completed during February of 1998 (Convey et al. 1999), provide the best baseline for total pup counts at this difficult to access location. Most of the pups in 1997/1998 were found on Zavodovski Island (n=500), Visokoi Island (n=900), and the Candlemas Islands (n=346), in the northwest of the archipelago. In December 2023, a survey of Zavodovski Island (only) was completed, with an estimated RPAS count of 1,265 pups. If this site is representative of the archipelago, the regional population size in 2025 would be 3,782 (SD=124; up from 2,535 in 1997/98), suggesting a population increase. However, complete population assessments of the South Sandwich Islands are needed for accurate assessments.Bouvetøya has been monitored through pup production estimates at Nyrøysa on several occasions (Hofmeyr et al. 2005). It was thought to be declining in the mid-2000s (Hofmeyr 2016). In 1999 15,448 (SD=370) pups were counted, corresponding to a mature population size of 22,832 (SD=1,141) individuals, using the new pup count-to-mature population adjustment (Forcada 2025b). A pup production estimate of 8,080 (SD=310) during the austral summer of 2015 is the most recent data available, as research teams have not returned to the island since that year (Andrew Lowther pers. comm.). This corresponds to a mature population size of 11,990 (SD=610), and an annual rate of change of -3.98% [CI:3.44; 4.52] between 1999 and 2015. Assuming a similar rate of decline until the assessment year (2025), the reduction over three generations would be -0.65 [-0.70; -0.60]. The reasons for the declines remain unknown but are likely linked to loss of breeding habitat because landslides are reducing the available coastal colony site.The South Shetland Islands have experienced one of the most precipitous declines for the species in the recent decades (Krause et al. 2022, Krause et al. 2024). The causes of the decline are mixed. In recent years they are thought to be linked largely to Leopard Seal (Hydrurga leptonyx) predation on the pre-weaning pups (Schwarz et al. 2013, Krause et al. 2020). This hypothesis is justifiable on the basis that pup counts at main study colonies where predation is observed have fallen since 2015 (Boveng et al. 1998). However, there are other effects that might also be contributing to the declines, such as climate-driven pressures on female survival and fecundity (Schwarz et al. 2013). This is corroborated by a linear annual increase in the foraging effort of nursing mothers (Krause et al. 2022), which is typically environmentally driven (Boyd 1998). The South Shetland Islands subpopulation has been considered a genetic reservoir (Krause et al. 2024) for the species, but is now at risk of genetic mixing with other subpopulations, given the ongoing southward expansion of males and females (Larsen et al. 2025) from South Georgia, as the habitat changes (Ouled-Cheikh et al. 2024). The mature population size at the South Shetlands in 1999 was estimated to be 14,531 (SD=556). With the mature population size estimated as 1,336 (SD=44) in 2025, based on the latest pup data (Krause et al. 2025), the annual rate of change was -8.77% (SD=0.07), and the estimated reduction over three generations was -0.908 [-0.911; -0.904], with maximum probability of being higher than 80%, and equal or higher than 90%. For the East Antarctica population, including the estimates for all its breeding locations except McDonald Islands, where there have been no surveys within the 3-generation assessment period, the results support a stable trend, with the caveat that there are also data gaps for Macquarie Island, Heard Island, part of Kerguelen Islands, and Prince Edward Islands, which have not been surveyed recently. The overall assessment indicates a 3-generation change of 10,474 (SD=410) mature seals in 1999 to 20,514 (SD=710) in 2025, with a mean exponential growth of 2.62% (SD=0.09). This population now comprises approximately 2.19% (SD=0.22) of the global mature population. For breeding locations within this group, the closest available pup count to 1999 for Marion Island was obtained in 2000. It was 343 (Wege et al. 2016), which is equivalent to an estimated mature population 470 (SD=36). The latest pup production estimate, for 2025, is 3,172 (SD=156), which corresponds to a mature population of 4,704 (SD=278), suggesting an estimated annual increase of 9.30% [95% CI: 8.88–9.72]. The most recent data for Prince Edward Island are from 2001, when a pup count of 404 was reported (Bester et al. 2003). This would correspond to an estimated mature population of 599 [95% CL: 563–639]. The main breeding location at the Crozet Islands is on Possession Island, which has been surveyed repeatedly (Guinet et al. 2025). The pup count was 234 in 2000, which corresponds to a mature population of 347 (SD=11), and a back-projected mature population of 337 (SD=15), three generations ago. The latest pup count of 540 was produced in 2024, corresponding to a mature population size of 786 (SD=26). The projected population in 2025 is thus 813 (SD=27), assuming the same estimated annual growth of 3.47% obtained for the observed period.There are several breeding locations in the Kerguelen Islands, but only the Courbet Peninsula has been counted regularly (Guinet et al. 2025). The closest assessment to 1999 was in 2000, when 1,600 pups were counted. There is another rounded pup count of 3,600 pups in 2000 at Nuageuses Islands, where the numbers are likely to have remained stable (Christophe Guinet pers. comm.); but there are no more recent counts. Assuming that the population at Nuageuses Islands has remained stable, the pup count of 3,600 was added to both of the pup counts obtained at Courbet Peninsula to facilitate the assessment of the entire East Antarctica subpopulation. The mature population three generations ago would then be equivalent to 7,616 (SD=267), and with the latest pup count at Courbet Peninsula of 4,793, the population size in 2025 would be 12,698 (SD=415). The resulting estimated annual increase is 2.02%.Due to its remoteness and difficult access, the Heard Island and McDonald Islands group have been visited only rarely and few pup counts have been undertaken. In March 1980, "up to 100 pups and 200 other" (Johnstone 1982) were counted at the McDonald Islands. No more recent data are available for this assessment, so these islands are not considered numerically in the assessment of East Antarctica herein. In contrast, Heard Island has been visited on several occasions, the most relevant counts being undertaken in 2001, when 1,012 pups were counted, and most recently in 2004, with a count of 1,278 pups (Simon Goldsworthy pers. comm.). This would correspond to a mature population of 1,501 (SD=49) in 2001, and 1,895 (SD=62) in 2004, with a possible population in 1999 of 1,296 (SD=90). For the observed period, the annual increase was 8.09%. However, these data alone cannot warrant a new assessment, so the same approach as MacDonald and Kerguelen Islands was used in this assessment, keeping the last value (in this case for 2004) stable until 2025. New survey data are required to properly assess this location.At Macquarie Island, in the southwestern Pacific Ocean, there are three species of fur seals breeding, Antarctic (Arctocephalus gazella), Subantarctic (A. tropicalis) and New Zealand Fur Seals (A. forsteri) (although there are no New Zealand Fur Seal females). All three species hybridise, and best attempts at discriminating pups to species level depends on genetic rather than phenotypic identification, which tends to overestimate A. gazella (Goldsworthy et al. 2009). Based on early counts, the number of A. gazella pups was approximately 100–105 in 1999, which would be equivalent to a mature population of 156 (SD=498), and of 280 (SD=9) in 2012, when long-term studies were terminated. Annual change between these estimates would be 4.65%. As with previous data deficient populations, the assumption of stability after the last count was used to evaluate its contribution to the East Antarctica subpopulation.
range: Antarctic Fur Seals have a wide circumpolar distribution in Subantarctic and Antarctic waters, both north and south of the Antarctic Convergence (Bonner 1968, Forcada and Staniland 2018; see distribution map and Figure S1 in the Supplementary Information). Most of the global population (98%) is in the Southwest Atlantic region of the Southern Ocean, and the species is largely confined to the South Georgia Archipelago, with ca 96% of the global population located in this area.There are at least four distinct genetic groups or subpopulations of Antarctic Fur Seals (Humble et al. 2018, Paijmans et al. 2020), three of which reside in the South Atlantic region of the Southern Ocean, including South Georgia, Bouvetøya (Bakken 1991, Hofmeyr et al. 2005), and the South Shetland Islands (Bengtson et al. 1990, Goebel et al. 2003). Other breeding locations, currently part of a single genetic group referred to as the East Antarctica population, are distributed in Subantarctic islands of the southern Indian and southwestern Pacific Oceans. These include, from West to East, Marion Island and Prince Edward Islands (Bester et al. 2003, Hofmeyr et al. 2006, Wege et al. 2016), the Crozet Islands Archipelago (Guinet et al. 1994), the Kerguelen Islands Archipelago (Guinet et al. 2000, Lea et al. 2008), Heard Island and McDonald Islands (Page et al. 2003), and Macquarie Island (Goldsworthy et al. 2009).In the Scotia Sea, in the Southwest Atlantic region, there are also small numbers of animals breeding in the South Orkney and South Sandwich Islands Archipelagos (Holdgate and Baker 1979, Laws 1981). The genetic identity of the South Sandwich Islands seals has not been assessed, but the South Orkney Island group has a population almost exclusively composed of non-resident juvenile and adult males (in post-breeding temporary migration), largely from South Georgia (Laws 1973, Kightley and Caldwell 1982, Boyd et al. 1998, Jones et al. 2021), although some seasonal transients to the South Orkneys come from the South Shetland Islands (Lowther et al. 2020, Ouled-Cheikh et al. 2024).Males from South Georgia and the South Shetland Islands typically migrate along the Weddell Sea and west Antarctic Peninsula, as far South as the Bellingshausen Sea (Boyd et al. 1998, Jones et al. 2021, March et al. 2021). There are also incidental records of pups on the Antarctic Peninsula, e.g., near Palmer Station (64.7743°S, 64.0538°W; Parmelee et al. 1977, Larsen et al. 2025), but these records of births can be considered extralimital. At the long-term study locations of Signy Island and Laurie Island, in the South Orkney Islands, only some few pups have been recorded since 2010 (Carlini et al. 2006, Waluda et al. 2010), suggesting that breeding in the South Orkneys continues to be marginal. In contrast, the number of pups at the South Sandwich Islands might be increasing (Holdgate 1963, Convey et al. 1999), but recent data are lacking so the trend cannot be fully determined.During the breeding season (late mid-November to early April), the foraging range of breeding females is restricted by their need to provision their land-based offspring (central-place foraging); thus their foraging trips are restricted to ca 100 km from their pupping locations (Boyd 1998, Guinet et al. 2001, Lea and Dubroca 2003, Staniland and Boyd 2003, Goebel et al. 2008, Lea et al. 2008). The males stay close to the breeding archipelagos, but many leave these areas when breeding is finished (Shaughnessy and Burton 1986, Boyd et al. 1998, Staniland and Robinson 2008, Jones et al. 2021, March et al. 2021). Densities of Antarctic Fur Seals at sea in summer are correlated with bathymetry and distance to the continental shelf break, and locations near the Polar Front (Hunt et al. 1992, Lea et al. 2003, Lea and Dubroca 2003, Staniland et al. 2012, Santora 2013), which are related to prey availability, notably Antarctic Krill density, across a wide range of spatial scales (Hunt et al. 1992). After the breeding season, adult females from South Georgia forage over much greater ranges, and may travel as far south as the pack ice edge, but mostly they go to the northwest, around the Falkland Islands and the Patagonian Shelf, up to Río de la Plata, Argentina, and Uruguay, and southern Brazil (see Forcada 2021). The winter distribution of females breeding at Cape Shirreff, South Shetlands, includes the southern coast of Chile, near the shelf break and pelagic waters further west of this region (Arthur et al. 2016). Movements between islands also occur, mainly from high-density breeding areas to areas of lower density (Lowther et al. 2020, March et al. 2021, Ouled-Cheikh et al. 2024). By proximity, most of the individuals found in South America, including northern Peru (Forcada 2021), are likely vagrants from the Southwest Atlantic region, especially South Georgia and the South Shetland Islands. Vagrants from other breeding sites have been recorded in Australia (Shaughnessy et al. 2014), Tristan da Cunha (Bester et al. 2014) and at Gough Island (Wilson et al. 2006, Bester and Reisinger 2010).
useTrade: Antarctic Fur Seals were commercially exploited for their fur throughout the species' range in the 18th and 19th centuries, and into the early in the 20th century. They have not been exploited since that time. Large-scale sealing began in the southern hemisphere in 1775; peaked at South Georgia in 1800–1801, when 17 British and American vessels took 112,000 skins, including a single ship with a recorded catch of 57,000 seals for that season. Near extirpation was recorded by James Weddell by 1821, who estimated a total capture of 1.2 million seals (Weddell 1825, Bonner 1968). At South Georgia, the last seal found was killed in 1915. In the South Shetland Islands, seal catches began as soon as they were discovered in 1819, and the species was nearly exterminated from this archipelago in just three seasons. James Weddell calculated that 320,000 were taken during 1821 and 1822. At Bouvetøya, the last fur seals were taken in 1927 (Hofmeyr 2016), and at other breeding locations in East Antarctica exploitation mostly occurred in the 19th century, as sealers continued their discovery expeditions. This led to the local extinction of breeding populations, including Crozet Islands, Kerguelen Islands, and possibly Heard Island (Hofmeyr et al. 1997, Page et al. 2003), sometimes in less than 20 years. At Macquarie Island, intense harvesting exterminated the population by 1820, with at least 199,444 fur seal skins taken from the island (Goldsworthy et al. 2009).
conservationActions: After the Antarctic Treaty entered into force (1961) and the Agreed Measures for the Conservation of Antarctic Fauna and Flora were approved (1964), the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings Committee (ATCM) afforded the status of Specially Protected Species (SPS) to the genus Arctocephalus within the Antarctic Treaty area (SCAR 2006); in practice, it was only protection for Arctocephalus gazella. In 1972, the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Parties developed the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals (CCAS; https://documents.ats.aq/keydocs/vol_1/vol1_13_CCAS_CCAS_e.pdf), following concerns over vulnerability to commercial overexploitation, and to reduce perturbations in the Antarctic marine ecosystem. Protection entered into force in 1978, although no sealing was taking place at the time. The CCAS was practically superseded by The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, signed in Madrid (Spain) on 4 October 1991 and entering into force in 1998. In its Annex II, commercial exploitation of seals is explicitly prohibited.In 1999, the ATCM asked the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR) to provide a recommendation about the continued listing of Antarctic Fur Seals as SPS (Resolution 2, 1999). On the basis of populations and trends of the species at the time, fur seals were not considered threatened or endangered under the IUCN Red List Criteria and were thus considered not to be in need of special protection (SCAR 2006). Following this, the ATCM removed fur seals from the list of SPS through Measure 4, although without a specific action plan for monitoring and reassessment (Jabour 2008).Currently, protection is provided to Antarctic Fur Seals under CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), which lists the Antarctic Fur Seal in Appendix II. Additional protection is provided by designated areas of special protection including marine protected areas (MPAs). South of 60°S, the species is protected under the Antarctic Treaty system in Antarctic Specially Protected Areas, such as ASPA 149 for the colonies at the South Shetland Islands (Krause et al. 2024). Special protection is also afforded via marine protected areas, such as the South Orkney Islands Southern Shelf Marine Protected Area (SOISS MPA), which was established by CCAMLR in 2009 (CCAMLR 2009).North of 60°S, Antarctic Fur Seals are protected by the nations which govern the sites at which they breed. A major level of protection is granted by the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands Marine Protected Area (SGSSI-MPA) (GSGSSI 2025), which is one of the world's largest MPAs (1.24 million km²), although no take zones where all fishing activity is prohibited only cover 470,000 km². Fishing is prohibited in the summer months (November-March; "krill season"), in these zones, but the rest of the year fishing is possible and a significant part of the Antarctic Fur Seal population, notably juveniles and breeding females, spend the winter there.Other critical MPAs for the conservation of Antarctic Fur Seals are the Bouvet Island Nature Reserve (Norway), Prince Edward Islands MPA (South Africa), Crozet Islands MPA (France), Kerguelen Islands MPA (France), Heard Island and McDonald Islands Marine Reserve, the Macquarie Island Marine Park (Australia) and the Ross Sea Region MPA. More recently there have been efforts to establish new protected areas the Antarctic Peninsula (including North of South Orkney Islands) MPA, the Weddell Sea MPAs 1 and 2, and an East Antarctica MPA. These areas, particularly where the Antarctic sea ice is contracting fastest are critical for the conservation of Antarctic Krill and all the dependent predators including Antarctic Fur Seals (Lui 2024).In summary, priority conservation actions for the Antarctic Fur Seal include a) assessment of current threats and of suspected threats where there is circumstantial or growing evidence of impacts, b) effective protection of the species habitat (i.e., through creation of proposed Marine Protected Areas in critical parts of the distribution range), c) continued population, demographic, and habitat monitoring to assess change d) genetic and population assessment of the South Sandwich Islands breeding colonies, e) increasing public awareness of ongoing declines and dissipation of perception bias on the prevailing views on the status of the species, f) monitoring and mitigating direct negative interactions with fisheries, g) evaluating the competitive exclusion from Antarctic Krill by recovering whale populations, while taking other predator populations needs into account, h) assessing competitive exclusion of prey by fisheries, i) monitoring emergence of new pathogens and their consequences for mortality, spread and epidemiology, and j) monitoring of pollution, including plastics and chemical compounds.

rationale: The California Sea Lion does not meet the thresholds for any threatened category when assessed at the global population level: there is no evidence of a population reduction over three generations (or 10 years); the species' geographic range is broad and not severely fragmented; the global number of mature individuals and the number of locations (rookeries) are large; and Population Viability Analysis does not indicate a high risk of extinction for the species. Accordingly, the California Sea Lion should remain classified as Least Concern.However, there are relevant conservation concerns for this species. Rookeries in the Gulf of California have experienced a reduction in total abundance exceeding 50% since the early 1980s, with only the Los Islotes rookery exhibiting a positive growth trend. Burgoin-Diaz (2025) applied the five IUCN Red List criteria to the 13 Gulf of California rookeries using historical counts (1968, 1977–1981, 1991–1997, 2000–2010, and 2010–2023). Rookeries were grouped following the regionalization proposed by Pelayo-González et al. (2021a), incorporating population growth trends and inter-rookery distances. This assessment confirmed that Gulf of California qualifies for threatened categories ranging from Vulnerable to Endangered, depending on the specific region assessed.Although recent information is limited for rookeries along the Pacific coast of the Baja California Peninsula, available evidence indicates that some rookeries are sensitive to shifts in prey availability associated with extreme climatic events, such as the 2014 marine heatwave (“the Blob”) and the 2015 El Niño. Similar responses have been documented in the US population, where these events were associated with high mortality of pups and immature individuals; however, rookeries in Mexico appear to be recovering more slowly following such episodes.The US population, which comprises most individuals globally, has begun to recover after recent declines associated with warm-water events. However, these events are expected to become more frequent and intense under future climate scenarios (Lowry et al. 2021), potentially increasing the vulnerability of regional subpopulations and individual rookeries of California Sea Lions.In summary, the California Sea Lion is maintained in the Least Concern category despite multiple lines of evidence indicating that several rookeries in Mexico—particularly in the Gulf of California—are experiencing sustained declines and face an increased risk of local extinction. For this region, special conservation attention is warranted because, in addition to experiencing population declines, rookeries are small and genetically isolated from the rest of the rookeries along the Pacific coast of Baja California and the United States, making them especially vulnerable (González-Suárez et al. 2009, Schramm et al. 2009). In the case of the Gulf of California rookeries, mortality associated with entanglement, illegal catches, and diseases seems to have a disproportionate effect on population dynamics (Acevedo-Whitehouse et al. 2003, Kovacs et al. 2012, Avalos-Téllez et al. 2016, Pelayo-González et al. 2021a, Gallo Reynoso 2019).
habitat: The California Sea Lion is a sexually dimorphic species; adult males weigh three to four times more, and are up to 1.2 times longer, than females (King 1964). Male California Sea Lions measure up to 255 cm in length and can weigh up to 523 kg (Wright et al. 2010). Females measure up to 200 cm and weigh an average of 110 kg (Peterson and Bartholomew 1967). By two weeks of age, male pups are larger and heavier (75.7 cm, 9.01 kg) than their female counterparts (72.3 cm, 7.6 kg; Le Boeuf et al. 1983). Pups are born with a thick brownish-black lanugo that is generally molted between the first and second month and is replaced by a darker coat. Nursing may last from one to two years (Newsome et al. 2006, Rosas-Hernández et al. 2024). Lactation duration might have a latitudinal trend, with longer lactation at southern rookeries such as Los Islotes and Isla Santa Margarita Island compared to northern sites in the Gulf of California (Rosas-Hernández et al. 2024, Villanueva-Iñiguez 2025). Furthermore, lactation duration and maternal attendance patterns vary with environmental conditions, rookery density, and local topography, reflecting substantial behavioral plasticity in maternal care (Pelayo-González et al. 2024). Both sexes usually reach maturity by four to five years of age. Females produce one pup each year, with a gestation period of approximately 11 months. A long-term mark-resighting study (1980–2006) recorded a maximum observed lifespan of 19 years for males and 25 years for females (Hernández-Camacho et al. 2008a). Mean birth rates vary among age classes: for five-year olds the rate is 0.59; for six- to 10-year-olds it is 0.79 (Melin 2002, Hernández-Camacho et al. 2008b); 10- to 12-year-olds exhibit the highest rate (0.80), but the rate gradually decreases for individuals 13 years old to 0.06 in 22- to 25 years olds (Hernández-Camacho et al. 2008b).Pupping and breeding take place from May through July. Pupping starts earlier in the Gulf of California (May 8) than off the coast of California (May 20); the duration of the breeding season is also longer in the Gulf (13 weeks) than off the coast of California (9.5 weeks; García-Aguilar and Aurioles-Gamboa 2003a). However, recent observations reveal that the breeding season can be less synchronous and more environmentally modulated than previously described. Evidence from Santa Margarita Island and Los Islotes indicates births occurring after the expected breeding season, with pups estimated to have been born in August–November and confirmed observations of pregnant females in late autumn (Pelayo-González et al. 2022). These findings suggest that embryonic diapause may be prolonged in some females under suboptimal environmental conditions, producing delayed parturitions and a more extended reproductive phenology (Villanueva-Iñiguez 2025).Males are highly polygynous and defend territories both on land and in shallow waters near the shore for periods of up to 45 days. A study on the plasticity of male territorial behavior in response to varying environmental conditions showed that males inhabiting high-temperature environments (air temperatures 30°C, e.g., the Gulf of California) defend territories adjacent to the coast while immersed in the water (Bohorquez-Herrera et al. 2014). Females remain on shore with their newborn pups for approximately seven days before departing for the first of many foraging trips that usually last two to three days, followed by another one to two days of caring for their pups at the rookery (Melin et al. 2020, García-Aguilar and Aurioles-Gamboa 2003b).Following the breeding season, large numbers of adult and subadult males and juveniles migrate north from the major rookeries in southern California and Baja California and winter from central California to Washington (Fry 1939, Mate 1975, Odell 1975). Smaller numbers of animals migrate to British Columbia (Wright et al. 2010) and southeast Alaska, reaching the northern Gulf of Alaska, the Alaska Peninsula, and the eastern Aleutian Islands (Maniscalco et al. 2004). Other animals remain in the Gulf of California year-round and do not undertake long migrations; numerous adults and subadult males are observed every year at rookeries and haul-out areas around the southern tip of the Baja California Peninsula (Aurioles-Gamboa et al. 1983).Environmental conditions exert a strong influence on sea lion physiology, reproduction, and survival. In the Gulf of California, a three-decade increase in sea surface temperature explained up to 92% of the population’s long-term decline, with a 65% reduction from 1991 to 2019 (Adame et al. 2020; Pelayo-González et al. 2021a). Population size is maximized at moderate warm anomalies (+0.17 to +0.40°C) but declines steeply under warming beyond this threshold. Elevated SST reduces primary productivity and alters prey composition, forcing females to undertake longer foraging trips, decreasing pup body condition and survival. Central Gulf rookeries show reduced birth rates when SST anomalies surpass +1°C, while southern rookeries recover more rapidly due to higher prey diversity and local oceanographic conditions. During warm years, females from Los Islotes spent more time foraging, pups exhibit reduced body condition, and maternal investment declines despite overall rookery resilience. These differences reflect local oceanographic heterogeneity, prey availability, and the capacity of some rookeries to exploit diverse foraging habitats (Adame et al. 2020; Pelayo-González et al. 2021a).California Sea Lions mostly live in waters on the continental shelf and slope, but they also use coastal areas like bays, harbors, lagoons, and river mouths. These coastal ecosystems strongly influence the foraging behavior of California Sea Lions, which exploit a wide range of prey (Rosas-Hernández et al. 2019). Recent dietary analyses at Los Islotes show that California sea lions consume an exceptionally diverse prey assemblage, with ~105 taxa documented between 2015 and 2022, including 79 fish species, several cephalopods, and numerous mesopelagic fishes (Mejía-Guarnizo et al. 2025). Metabarcoding sea lion stomach contents revealed more than 20 additional genera, including deep-water cephalopods such as Ancistrocheirus, demonstrating that trophic breadth had been previously underestimated (Mejía-Guarnizo et al. 2025). Diet composition varies annually rather than seasonally, shifting among demersal, pelagic, and mesopelagic prey in relation to fluctuations in sea surface temperature (Mejía-Guarnizo et al. 2025). This high feeding plasticity, in which a few dominant prey taxa change from year to year, likely contributes to the sustained demographic stability of the Los Islotes rookery within a warming Gulf of California (Mejía-Guarnizo et al. 2025).Despite their broad dietary niche, California Sea Lions typically focus on four to five prey species at a given site, generally exploiting locally or seasonally abundant resources (Lowry et al. 1990; García-Rodriguez and Aurioles-Gamboa 2004). Their main prey in California are Pacific sardines (Sardinops sagax), Northern anchovies (Engraulis mordax), Pacific hake (Merlucius productus), Jack mackerel (Trachurus symmetricus), Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus), various species of the genus Sebastes, Red octopus (Octopus rubescens), and Market squid (Loligo opalescens; Antonelis et al. 1984, Lowry and Carretta 1999, Lowry 1991, Lowry et al. 1990). On the Pacific coast of Baja California, sea lions consume many of these same prey species, as well as North Pacific argentine (Argentina sialis) and Jumbo squid (Dosidicus gigas; Aurioles-Gamboa and Camacho-Rios 2007). Long-term dietary analyses across the Gulf of California (1980–2020) document at least 88 dominant prey taxa, including 60 benthic fishes, 21 schooling pelagic fishes, 7 lanternfish species, 15 squids, and numerous mesopelagic taxa (Pozas-Franco et al. 2025). At Los Islotes, diet studies report ≥105 prey species, with frequent consumption of mesopelagic fishes (e.g. Benthosema panamense, Triphoturus mexicanus, and Lampanyctus spp.) as well as serranids, scorpaenids, and cutlassfishes. Annual shifts in dominant prey indicate a plastic specialist strategy, where only a few prey species dominate each year, but key species change through time. Central Gulf rookeries often rely heavily on a single benthic species in some years (e.g. Trichiurus lepturus), while others exhibit a broader dietary breadth. Dietary energy density in the Gulf of California is comparable to that of the Channel Islands but exhibits greater interannual variability. During the 2014–2016 marine heatwave, diet composition shifted markedly: contributions of schooling fishes declined from 27% to 16%, squid from 7% to 1%, and benthic prey increased from 36% to 56%, reducing mean dietary energy density (Pozas-Franco et al. 2025). Nearly half of prey species identified during this warm period had not been recorded previously, indicating a major ecological shift in prey communities.Diving behavior of lactating adult females is well documented and varies seasonally and regionally (Weise and Costa 2007, Weise et al. 2010). At San Miguel Island, California, during the breeding (warm) season, 96% of dives occur between 8 and 75 m, with 92% lasting less than four minutes. During the non-breeding (cold) season, 77% of dives fall within the same depth range, and 81% last four minutes or less. In both seasons, most dives (84.5% during breeding and 81.2% during non-breeding) take place within 150 km of the rookery (Melin et al. 2000). In the Gulf of California, lactating females generally dive deeper. Mean dive depth during this period is 81.7 ± 32 m, with an average duration of 3.5 ± 0.9 min. During the cold season, dives become shallower and shorter, averaging 48.9 ± 18.5 m in depth and 1.7 ± 0.6 min in duration. Seasonal foraging distances also vary, ranging from 72.7 ± 21.8 km during the breeding season to 101.2 ± 18.5 km during the cold season (Villegas-Amtmann et al. 2011).Foraging ranges and strategies differ among rookeries and with varying oceanographic conditions. During warm periods at Santa Margarita Island, reproductive output and population abundance decrease due to diminished productivity, which restricts prey availability (Pelayo-González et al. 2021b). In contrast, females at Los Islotes show flexible foraging behavior and eat a wide range of prey, including mesopelagic fishes, which may help the population survive changes in the environment.Extreme heat events substantially modify the foraging ecology and life-history traits of California Sea Lions, with responses that vary by age and sex. Satellite telemetry and stable isotope studies indicate that during climatic anomalies such as El Niño, adult females increase foraging effort by traveling farther from breeding colonies, expanding their foraging ranges, and extending the duration and depth of foraging trips (Weise et al. 2006, Orr et al. 2011, Cruz-Vallejo et al. 2024). Concurrently, lactation patterns are altered relative to cooler conditions and regional marine productivity, with adjustments in the length of maternal investment (Melin et al. 2008, Rosas-Hernández et al. 2024). Adult males normally foraging almost exclusively over the continental shelf expanded their foraging range, spending more time at sea and traveling up to 450 km offshore (Weise et al. 2006). In contrast, juveniles show more limited behavioral plasticity and generally remain closer to haul-out sites, likely due to physiological constraints (McHuron et al. 2018).Trace element concentrations in tissues (e.g., Cd, Hg, Pb, Zn, Se) vary in relation to large-scale climatic events and oceanographic conditions, reflecting changes in prey composition, trophic transfer, and contaminant exposure pathways (Symon et al. 2025). Recovery of the population in southern California over recent decades has been associated with sex-specific shifts in isotopic niches, with males showing expansion in trophic diversity and geographic range, while females have maintained more stable and localized foraging strategies (Valenzuela-Toro et al. 2023).Predators of California Sea Lions include killer whales (Orcinus orca), sharks, coyotes (Canis latrans), and feral dogs (Anderson et al. 2008, Williams et al. 2004). Before their recent eradication from California’s Channel Islands, bald eagles (Haliaaetus leucocephalus) were known to take young pups (Collins et al. 2005).
threats: Due to their coastal distribution, abundance, and feeding habits, California Sea Lions interact with several fisheries, including those for Pacific salmon (DeMaster et al. 1985; Aurioles-Gamboa et al. 2003; Weise and Harvey 2005; 2008), causing economic losses for sport and commercial fishermen and a high incidence of sea lion entanglement (Stewart and Yochem 1987; Harcourt et al. 1994; Zavala and Mellink 1997, 2000; Aurioles-Gamboa et al. 2003). Also, conflicts with fisheries, poaching and entanglement in marine debris contribute to California Sea Lion mortality (Stewart and Yochem 1987, Howorth 1994, Harcourt et al. 1994, Zavala and Mellink 1997, Aurioles-Gamboa et al. 2003). Prey availability is greatly reduced during El Niño events and large numbers of pups born during these periods die of starvation, as do weaker animals of all age classes (Francis and Heath 1991, Shirasago-German et al. 2015). Extended warm-water anomalies have increasingly produced nutritional stress, reduced milk production, weakened immune responses, impaired pup growth, and increased physiological stress, leading to elevated vulnerability of all age classes (Rojas-Castellanos, 2025). Historical evidence shows that strong warm events have produced population-level declines, such as those documented during the 1982–83 El Niño across the west coast of the US and Baja California Peninsula. While previous assessments suggested limited ENSO influence in the Gulf of California (Aurioles and Le Boeuf 1991, Szteren et al. 2006), recent regional studies show that sustained warming affects maternal condition, shifts reproductive timing, increases late-term abortions, and extends pupping seasons, thereby increasing neonatal vulnerability (Pelayo-González et al. 2022).California Sea Lions accumulate pollutants through the food chain, and large amounts of DDT and PCBs discharged in the past continue to accumulate in coastal marine food chains that include this species (DeLong et al. 1973, Le Boeuf et al. 2002). Exposure to pollutants remains pervasive; pups from Los Islotes exhibit detectable maternal transfer of mercury and selenium, with interannual increases in both elements and negative correlations with body weight and body condition in some years. Element analysis also reveals variation in essential and non-essential metals influenced by year, maternal foraging ecology, and pup morphology, indicating that changing oceanographic conditions and anthropogenic inputs alter elemental exposure pathways (Symon et al. 2023; 2025). Although most pups fall below pinniped toxicological thresholds for Hg, a substantial fraction exceeds human-health thresholds, and annual increases in mercury suggest heightened environmental exposure that should be monitored (Symon et al. 2023; 2025).Warm years are associated with decreased pup body condition, alterations in gut microbiota, elevated dehydration risk, and reduced early survival. California Sea Lions occasionally die of paralytic shellfish poisoning caused by domoic acid, a biotoxin produced by diatom blooms that enters the food web through planktivorous fish, such as Northern anchovy and Sardines (Scholin et al. 2000, Silvagni et al. 2005). Similarly, harmful algal blooms, particularly Pseudo-nitzschia, have produced domoic acid exposure and mortality (Scholin et al. 2000, Silvagni et al. 2005). Disease continues to be a major concern, as leptospirosis outbreaks coincide with climatic anomalies and generate significant morbidity and strandings (Vedros et al. 1971, Lloyd-Smith et al. 2007). Contact with feral and domestic dogs and other terrestrial animals may expose the species to additional diseases like brucellosis, which can cause miscarriages (Goldstein et al. 2009, Avalos-Tellez et al. 2014).Human disturbance has intensified in the Bahía de La Paz, in the southern Gulf of California. Within the bay, new haul-out rookeries at San Rafaelito, Tijeretas, San Francisquito and Las Ánimas have increased unregulated human–pinniped contact (Rojas-Castellanos 2025). At San Rafaelito, vessels frequently approach within 8–20 m and swimmers come within 10–20 m, at resting sites that cause individuals, especially juveniles and subadult males, to enter the water more often or abandon preferred haul-outs (Rojas-Castellanos 2025). Although short-term monitoring detected no significant increase in aggression, sustained disturbance may elevate energetic costs, reduce resting opportunities and affect social stability (Rojas-Castellanos 2025). At Los Islotes, territorial males have previously engaged in aggressive interactions with swimmers, leading to temporary closures of tourism zones during the breeding season (Rojas-Castellanos 2025). These human-driven pressures occur simultaneously with environmental threats, including reduced prey availability, lower productivity and anomalous thermal conditions that diminish pup condition, reproductive success and survival, particularly in smaller or environmentally sensitive rookeries in the Gulf of California (Galindo-Romo 2024). Environmental variability also influences maternal foraging behavior, diving effort and energy transfer to pups, making rookeries affected by tourism more vulnerable under warm-water regimes (Galindo-Romo 2024).
population: Exploitation during the 19th and 20th centuries did reduce the California Sea Lion population, but not as much as some other pinniped species (Gerber and Hilborn 2001). Since the 1970s, the global abundance of California sea lions has increased. However, significant reductions have occurred within specific areas and subpopulations, and some rookeries may be extirpated (Hernández-Camacho et al. 2021, Pelayo-González et al. 2021a). Five geographic populations or subpopulations have been identified, considering only rookeries, based on mitochondrial DNA: 1) temperate Pacific, from California to northern Baja California; 2) tropical Pacific, along the west coast of the Baja California peninsula; 3) southern Gulf of California; 4) central Gulf of California; and 5) northern Gulf of California (Schramm et al. 2009). Using both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, the population structure in Mexico suggests a pattern of isolation by distance resulting in at least three management units: the Pacific coast of Baja California, the southern Gulf of California, and the north-central Gulf of California (González-Suárez et al. 2009). The species does not show signs of a reduction in genetic variability (González-Suárez et al. 2009, Schramm et al. 2009, González-Suárez et al. 2010). Due to the species' wide geographic distribution and the large number of rookeries, systematic counts of all rookeries are not undertaken. Additionally, total population counts are challenging because not all age- and sex-classes are on shore at the same time. Therefore, correction factors are applied to account for animals that are not seen during surveys (due to substrate or visibility) and for at-sea animals. Some studies have used the number of newborn pups as an index of population size because pups remain on land during the reproductive season. This provides a reference point for estimating the other age classes (Berkson and DeMaster 1985, Lowry and Maravilla-Chavez 2005, Milanés-Salinas 2012).At the global scale, the California Sea Lion population has increased over the last three generations (43.6 years; Pacifici et al. 2013); however, the trend has not been uniform through time, nor across rookeries or regions. Additionally, changes have occurred in the relative proportion of California Sea Lions among populations (Szteren et al. 2006, Ward et al. 2010, Pelayo-González et al. 2021a). Le Boeuf et al. (1983) estimated that during the 1971-1981 reproductive seasons, the worldwide population was roughly 145,000 animals, primarily located in Mexico: 46% along the Pacific coast of Baja California (tropical Pacific subpopulation), 16% in the Gulf of California (southern, central and northern Gulf subpopulations), 35% in the United States (temperate Pacific subpopulation), and 3% in Canada. By the early 2000s, Lowry and Maravilla-Chavez (2005) estimated a population of 334,000-359,000 individuals using pup counts from rookeries in the California Channel Islands in the United States and on the western coast of Baja California peninsula in Mexico, as well as counts from rookeries in the Gulf of California (1980-1990) reported by Aurioles-Gamboa and Zavala-González (1994). The geographic distribution had shifted to circa 67–69% of the population occurring in the United States, 22–24% along the Pacific coast of the Baja California Peninsula, and about 9% in the Gulf of California.Data from the early 2000s show pronounced regional differences in population size and trends. California Sea Lions on the Channel Islands, Año Nuevo Island, and the Farallon Islands reached a peak of 67,396 pups and an estimated 306,220 individuals in 2012, consistent with the sustained population increase observed since the early 1970s. Following this peak, both the number of pups and total abundance declined, reaching a low of 36,039 pups and 121,243 total individuals in 2016 (Laake et al. 2018, Lowry et al. 2021). Similar to previous years (e.g., 1993, 1998, 2003, 2010), this decline was associated with changes in the abundance and distribution of prey, linked to warm-water events (McClatchie et al. 2016). In this case, the effects of the 2014 marine heatwave (“the Blob”) and the 2015 El Niño acted in combination, resulting in reduced birth rates and increased mortality of pups, juveniles, and adult females during a period that became known as an Unusual Mortality Event (Lowry et al. 2017a, b; Lowry et al. 2021). Pup counts increased to 53,646 in 2019; no estimate of total population size is available for that year (Lowry et al. 2021). Rookery sizes in Mexico have declined during the last 3 generations. Milanés-Salinas (2012) estimated that the population along the west coast of Baja California was 52,846–54,482 during the 2010 breeding season. This represents a decline of 14 % relative to the estimate of 63,020 individuals reported by Le Boeuf et al. (1983) for the period between 1979 and 1981. In the same period (2010), the population in the Gulf of California was estimated to be 16,705–22,117 individuals (Hernández-Camacho, unpublished data). There are no counts from the last decade for rookeries in the Gulf of California; therefore, it is not possible to estimate the current population size for this region. However, it is thought that the overall population in the Gulf of California is in decline, despite some rookeries—such as Rocas Consag, San Esteban, San Jorge, and Los Islotes—being stable or increasing (Szteren et al. 2006, Hernández-Camacho et al. 2021).Based on pup counts conducted between 1995 and 2018, Pelayo-González et al. (2021a) estimated population growth rates and total abundance for 2018 by grouping rookeries into three regions according to genetic information, population growth trends, and diet (González-Suárez et al. 2009, Schramm et al. 2009, Ward et al. 2010, Szteren and Aurioles-Gamboa 2011). Rookeries were grouped as follows: Lobos Island in the northern region; Granito, Los Cantiles, Los Machos, El Partido, and El Rasito in the central region; and Los Islotes in the southern region. Populations in the northern and central regions declined at annual rates of −4% and −1%, respectively, whereas the southern region increased at a rate of 3%. The estimated population size for these seven rookeries in 2018 was 6,185 individuals and 2,021 pups. Considering the same rookeries, totals of 6,128 individuals and 2,459 pups were recorded during 2023–2025 (Hernández-Camacho and Ávalos-Téllez, unpublished data). The population size of these seven Gulf of California rookeries in 2023 was similar to 2018. However, numbers dropped in 2024, except at Los Islotes. Over three generations, the population size of these seven rookeries was 10,676 individuals in 1981, indicating an approximate 57% reduction over the past 44 years (1981–2015/2023; Hernández-Camacho and Ávalos-Téllez, unpublished data).The rookeries not included in the analysis by Pelayo-González et al. (2021a) were Rocas Consag, San Jorge, San Esteban, San Pedro Mártir, San Pedro Nolasco, and Farallón de San Ignacio. Between 1995 and 2015, these rookeries exhibited a negative overall population trend, except for Rocas Consag, San Jorge, and San Esteban, which remained relatively stable (Gallo-Reynoso et al. 2015, Gallo-Reynoso 2019).Adame et al. (2020) reconstructed the historical trends of the 13 California Sea Lion rookeries in the Gulf of California based on available counts from 1978 to 2019. They estimated that the total population size across these rookeries reached 43,834 individuals (range: 27,892–47,682) in 1991 and declined to 15,291 individuals (range: 11,861–20,316) by 2019, representing a 65.2% reduction.The San Benito Archipelago rookery remained relatively stable during the 2012–2014 period, with an estimated population size ranging from 7,136 to 8,859 individuals and 2,902 to 3,944 pups (without correction factors; Elorriaga-Verplancken et al. 2015). In 2015, abundance declined sharply to 3,426 individuals, likely reflecting changes in prey availability associated with the combined effects of the 2014 marine heatwave (“the Blob”) and the 2015 El Niño event (Elorriaga-Verplancken et al. 2016). Abundance estimates for the 2012–2014 period were slightly lower than the 10,548 individuals reported for the 1981 breeding season (Le Boeuf et al. 1983). In contrast, the Santa Margarita Island rookery declined at an annual rate of –4 % between 1979 and 2015. Population size was estimated at 1,334 individuals in 2015, representing an approximate 75% reduction over a 36-year period relative to the first available estimate from 1979 (5,298 individuals; Pelayo-González et al. 2021b).
range: California Sea Lion rookeries are found on islands ranging from Los Islotes in Baja California Sur, in Mexico in the south, north to the Channel Islands in southern California, in the United States. Pups have been reported from Año Nuevo Island and the Farallon Islands in central California (Keith et al. 1984). In addition to rookeries, this species also occupies haul-out sites, mainly during the fall and winter when adult and sub-adult males move north to Oregon (USA) and British Columbia (Canada; Fry 1939, Mate 1975, Odell 1975). In the southern part of their range, haul-out areas are known to occur on islets off the coast of Mazatlán and the Tres Marias Island north of Puerto Vallarta, Mexico; however, this area has not been surveyed for decades. This species’ overall range extends north through the Gulf of Alaska as far as the Aleutian Islands (Maniscalco et al. 2004) and south around the end of the Baja California Peninsula to the Gulf of California. Between 2005 and 2013, several California Sea Lion sightings were reported as far south as Punta San Pedrillo, Costa Rica (Lenin Oviedo pers. comm.). Recently, in 2023 and 2025, two verified occurrences of California sea lions have been recorded at coastal locations in Guatemala (iNaturalist). A California Sea Lion male was sighted off the coast of the Yam Islands in the Sea of Okhotsk (Russia) in 2007, 2008 and 2011. On each occasion, the animal was seen with a group of Steller sea lions. Females, which were only very rarely found north of Point Conception, California in the early 1980s, are now routinely found in northern California, where former rookeries have been reoccupied. Based on estimates of sex biases in gene flow, females disperse less frequently (1:6.75x) than their male counterparts (González-Suárez et al. 2009).
useTrade: California Sea Lions were historically important to indigenous people living in coastal areas and on islands used by sea Lions for rookeries (Arellano-Peralta and Medrano-Gonzalez 2015). Huge middens in southern California and on the Channel Islands with large numbers of California Sea Lions and other pinniped bones attest to the past importance of marine mammals for subsistence prior to the arrival of Europeans on the west coast of North America (Porcasi et al. 2000, Braje and DeLong 2009). In Mexico, use of California Sea Lions is characterized by four historical phases: pre-Hispanic, colonial, independent, and post-revolutionary. During the pre-Hispanic period, maritime Indigenous groups used the species for meat, shelter materials, clothing, and tool manufacture. The Concaac (Seri) hunted Sea Lions in the Gulf of California by striking the head and nasal region with stones and used both meat and skins for multiple purposes. The Híac ed O’odham (Sand Papago) similarly hunted Sea Lions in the Puerto Peñasco region using stones and processed the skins to manufacture sandals and straps (Felger and Moser 1985, Zavala-González and Mellink 2000).During the colonial and independence periods (1534–1911), harvest was largely incidental to the exploitation of other marine mammals and was conducted primarily by foreign operators, though harvests were increasingly regulated through permits and concessions (Sierra and Sierra-Zepeda 1977, Zavala-González and Mellink 2000).Exploitation intensified from the late 18th through the 19th centuries in Baja California and the Gulf of California, targeting oil, hides, and by-products, facilitated by industrial technologies during the Porfiriato. Harvests were progressively restricted through phases of open hunting (1930–1940), partial prohibitions (1956–1969), and a comprehensive moratorium that was put in force in 1982 (Cass 1985, Gerber and Hillborn 2001, Arellano-Peralta and Medrano-González 2015).
conservationActions: Legal protection of the California Sea Lion was established in the mid-20th century and consolidated through the US Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972. In Mexico, all rookeries occur within federally designated Natural Protected Areas, and the Comisión Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas (National Commission on Protected Natural Areas; CONANP) has conducted annual population counts and health monitoring in the Gulf of California for many decades. Despite this legal and management framework, most rookeries in the Gulf of California have experienced long-term population declines. In contrast, Los Islotes, located within the Marine Zone of the Archipiélago de Espíritu Santo National Park, is the only colony in Mexico that has shown sustained population growth for more than four decades. This protected area has received IUCN Green List certification on two occasions, reflecting effective governance, management and conservation outcomes (https://iucngreenlist.org/es/sites/marine-zone-of-espiritu-santo-archipelago-national-park/).A coordinated national conservation program has been suggested for Mexico, which would provide a structured framework for priority actions, including enhanced surveillance at rookeries, regulation of tourism during the breeding season, reduction of fisheries-related mortality through gear modification, continued health monitoring, and systematic assessment of population status, diet, reproductive output and environmental conditions. (Pelayo-González et al. 2021a). However, this programme has not yet been implemented.

rationale: Climate change, in particular sea ice losses and potential negative effects on krill in the Southern Ocean, is likely to negatively impact Crabeater Seals in the future. However, at this time, its widespread occurrence and very large population size dictate that the Crabeater Seal should remain listed as Least Concern.
habitat: Despite their relatively large size compared to Arctic pack-ice seals, Crabeater Seals are the second smallest species among Antarctic phocids. Adult individuals can reach lengths of up to 2.6 metres and weigh approximately 200–300 kg. Although some studies have reported reverse sexual dimorphisms in certain regions (McDonald et al. 2008), others have found no significant difference in body size between sexes during the breeding season (Shaughnessy and Southwell 2019). Neonates are estimated to weigh 20–35 kg and measure at least 1.1 m in length. Pups reach 77–130 kg at weaning (Shaughnessy et al. 2019). The mean age of sexual maturity in females ranges from 2.5 to 4.2 years, with this variation potentially linked to regional differences in food availability (Bengtson and Laws 1985). Although the sex ratio at birth is approximately 1:1, post-weaning survival is higher in females, resulting in a female-biased adult population in which 63% of individuals older than 20 years are female (Bengtson and Laws 1985).Crabeater Seals do not form breeding colonies. Instead, adult females haul out individually on ice floes to give birth and are typically joined shortly thereafter by a male (Siniff et al. 1979, Adam 2005). Adult males attend female-pup pairs and remain with the female until she enters oestrus, which occurs one to two weeks after the pup has been weaned. Although mating has not been directly observed, it is presumed to occur in the water. Pupping takes place from September through December (Southwell et al. 2003). Neonates are born with a soft, woolly lanugo coat that is greyish-brown in colour and has been described as a light “milk coffee” brown, with darker pigmentation on the flippers. Adult females fast throughout the lactation period, weaning their pup after an average of three weeks (Southwell 2004, Adam 2005), at which point the pups begin moulting into a subadult pelage that resembles that of adults. Adults and subadults undergo their annual moult in January and February, during which time a large proportion of individuals are thought to be hauled out on the ice.Mortality in Crabeater Seals during the first year of life is high, potentially reaching 80%. A significant proportion of this mortality is attributed to predation by Leopard Seals (Hydrurga leptonyx) (Laws 1977, Bengston and Laws 1985). Studies have shown that up to 78% of individuals surviving their first year of life bear injuries and scars consistent with Leopard Seal attacks (Laws 1977, Siniff and Bengston 1977). These include long linear wounds and sets of parallel scars, which are often conspicuous against the pale, relatively unmarked pelage of young Crabeater Seals. The frequency of such attacks appears to decline substantially after seals reach one year of age (Laws 1977).Recent studies have shown that Crabeater Seals are capable of diving to depths of up to 600 metres and remaining submerged for as long as 24 minutes. However, most foraging dives occur within the upper 50 meters of the water column and are of shorter duration (Burns et al. 2004, 2008). Foraging takes place primarily at night, and instrumented individuals have been recorded diving almost continuously for periods of up to 16 hours. Dives conducted at dawn and dusk tend to be deeper than those at night, suggesting that their feeding behaviour is influenced by the diel vertical migration of Antarctic Krill (Euphausia superba), their preferred prey. Overall, Crabeater Seals exhibit a general pattern of foraging from dusk until dawn and hauling out during the middle of the day.Crabeater Seals are best known for their uniquely shaped post-canine teeth, an evolutionary adaptation for efficiently capturing their primary prey, Antarctic Krill. Each post-canine tooth bears multiple accessory cusps that interlock, forming a complex sieve-like structure that they use to filter krill from seawater (King 19961). Additionally, a bony ridge on each mandible occupies the gap between the last upper post-canine tooth and the back of the jaw, helping to prevent prey loss during feeding.Antarctic Krill make up over 90% of the Crabeater Seal’s diet, with the remainder consisting of fish and squid. However, their dietary composition can exhibit a degree of plasticity. In response to low sea ice and reduced krill availability, Crabeater Seals are capable of increasing their consumption of fish, which may exceed 25% of their diet when krill is scarce (Hückstädt et al. 2012). Data from the western Antarctic Peninsula confirmed that Crabeater Seals increased their consumption of fish during the recent record-breaking low sea-ice conditions observed, increasing from 20% in 2022 to 26% in 2023 (Anna Pearson pers. comm.).Crabeater Seals are commonly observed alone or in small groups of up to a few individuals, either on the ice or in the water. However, substantially larger aggregations comprising up to 1,000 hauled-out individuals have been documented. At sea, they may travel in groups of several hundred, swimming in coordinated formations and surfacing to breathe and dive almost synchronously (Gales et al. 2004).
threats: Crabeater Seals are thought to be the most abundant seal species globally and are among the most numerous large mammals on Earth.Mass mortality events involving Crabeater Seals have been reported periodically. For example, in 1955, approximately 3,000 individuals died near a research station on the Antarctic Peninsula after becoming trapped 5–25 km from open water. The mortality occurred over a two- to three-month period. Post-mortem examinations revealed that seals were not emaciated; numerous foetal abortions were observed. A disease outbreak was suspected, but not confirmed. In the 1980s, antibodies to Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) were detected in Crabeater Seals from this region (Bengtson and Boveng 1991).More recently, a potential Unusual Mortality Event (UME) was documented in November 2024, involving 37 adult and subadult Crabeater Seals found within 500 m of each other (Jessica Farrer pers. comm.). The carcasses appeared to have been deceased for some time, as they were frozen, partially snow-covered, and showed signs of some scavenger activity. Starvation was considered unlikely, as the seals were in good body condition. However, the cause of death was not determined because the carcasses were not sampled or examined. This UME coincided with the arrival of the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in Subantarctic islands and on the Antarctic continent, where the virus has been confirmed in several avian species. Although cases of HPAI-associated mortality have been reported in Southern Elephant Seals (Mirounga leonina) and Antarctic Fur Seals (Arctocephalus gazella), and Walruses (Odobenus rosmarus), there is limited monitoring of ice-associated seals. Consequently, the presence of HPAI in Crabeater Seals cannot currently be confirmed or ruled out.Several short-lived episodes of commercial harvesting of Crabeater Seals were ultimately discontinued due to a lack of economic viability. While there are currently no direct anthropogenic threats across most of the species' range, large-scale commercial exploitation of Antarctic Krill, the primary component of the Crabeater Seal’s diet, could pose a significant threat if it becomes widespread. Although there are no reports of fisheries interactions, at least one mortality of a Crabeater Seal has been reported for the Antarctic Toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni) fishery in the Ross Sea (CCAMLR 2023).The effects of global climate change on Antarctic seals remain largely unknown. However, Learmonth et al. (2006) suggested that Crabeater Seal populations may decline with increasing temperatures if Antarctic sea ice is significantly reduced. Loss of sufficient areas of pack ice, used for pupping, resting, predator avoidance, and access to preferred foraging grounds, could result in population decreases.Furthermore, Crabeater Seals' high dietary specialisation on Antarctic krill makes them particularly vulnerable to reductions in sea ice, which is critical for the survival of juvenile krill and ultimately determines the biomass available to higher trophic-level predators. Habitat preference models based on movement and diving data project a southward shift in the distribution of Crabeater Seals, consistent with observed and predicted shifts in Antarctic krill distribution (Hückstädt et al. 2020). Such a shift could result in spatial mismatches between suitable haul-out sites and foraging grounds, potentially increasing energetic costs as individuals may need to travel to greater distances to access prey.It remains unclear whether Crabeater Seals can shift from their highly specialised, krill-based diet to a more generalist foraging strategy in response to the rapid loss of sea ice. Stable isotope analyses of individuals from the Antarctic Peninsula have shown an increased incorporation of fish in their diets during years of reduced sea ice extent (Huckstadt et al. 2012). Similarly, evidence from the 2022-2023 period indicates that the contribution of fish to the Crabeater Seal diet increased during these record-breaking low sea ice years (Anna Pearson pers. comm.). The broader impacts of large-scale sea ice loss on the Antarctic continent, ongoing climate warming, and sea-level rise – particularly regarding changes to ocean circulation, ecosystem productivity and the implications for Antarctic marine predators such as seals – remain poorly understood.Seasonal tourism in the Antarctic and Subantarctic regions has increased steadily over the past three decades and bounced back quickly after the COVID-19 pandemic, to reach record numbers during the last austral summer season (Convey 2024). However, the potential effects of increased vessel noise, disturbance from ship traffic, and close human approach, either via small boat or land-based excursions, on the behaviour, distribution, foraging activity, and health of Crabeater Seals remain poorly understood. Additionally, there is a minor but non-negligible risk of physical harm to seals from vessel collisions or crushing injuries due to the passage of large ships through sea ice.
population: The Crabeater Seal is widespread in Antarctic waters. As with other Antarctic seals that inhabit the pack ice, population assessments are logistically challenging, costly, and therefore infrequently conducted. Published global population estimates vary widely, ranging from approximately two million individuals (Scheffer 1958) to as many as 50-75 million (Ericson et al. 1971). However, these early estimates were based on limited sampling and are considered highly speculative.The most recent available global estimates were derived over three decades ago from a multinational effort conducted under the Antarctic Pack Ice Seals (APIS) programme during the late 1980s and early 1990s. This survey yielded a population estimate of approximately 9.5 million individuals within the areas surveyed; however, this figure may be inflated due to likely overestimates in the region between 26°W and 7°W (Southwell et al. 2012). However, given that substantial regions of the Antarctic pack ice were not included in the survey, the total global population is likely to be considerably higher. Regional efforts using traditional methodologies (i.e., ship-based surveys) are still ongoing (e.g., Bester et al. 2019, 2021), and over the past decade, the use of satellite imagery has emerged as a promising tool for obtaining continent-wide estimates of Crabeater Seal and other pack-ice seal populations (LaRue et al. 2022).
range: The distribution of Crabeater Seals is closely linked to seasonal fluctuations in Antarctic pack ice. These seals are commonly found near the Antarctic coast, extending as far south as McMurdo Sound during late summer ice break-up (Nachtsheim et al. 2017, Hückstãdt et al. 2020). Their highest concentrations occur in seasonally shifting pack ice areas encircling the Antarctic continent. Crabeater Seals have been recorded as far north as the southern coasts of New Zealand, Australia, Africa, and South America as vagrants. Occasionally, Crabeater Seals travel far inland. Alive Crabeater Seal has been observed 113 km from open water at an elevation of 920 m above sea level, and mummified individuals have been found well away from the coastline in regions such as the dry valleys near McMurdo Sound, James Ross and Seymour Islands in the Antarctic Peninsula, and various other inland locations (Kooyman 1981, Rice 1998, Negrete et al. 2015).
useTrade: Several brief episodes of commercial harvesting of Crabeater Seals ended when they were determined to be economically unsuccessful.
conservationActions: The Crabeater Seal is not listed as endangered or threatened. They are protected from hunting by the Antarctic Treaty and the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals, and any future commercial harvest would have to be regulated through those international agreements (Reijnders et al. 1993).

rationale: This species is classified as Near Threatened. It has an area of occupancy (AOO) estimated to be 484 km² and faces ongoing declines in the area, extent, and quality of its habitat due to urbanization and agricultural expansion. Two localities with previously high densities are no likely longer viable due to city expansion and collapse of a hillside. This species nearly meets the qualifications for VU B2b(iii), but data does not exist to support severe fragmentation or low location number.
habitat: The Jalapan Pine Vole is a habitat generalist that occurs in cloud and wet oak-pine forests (Ramírez-Pulido et al. 1991, Cervantez et al. 1997). Typical habitat has been described as marshy meadows, grassy swales, grasslands in forest openings, and edges of fruit orchards (Ramirez-Pulido et al. 1991, Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018). It has also been documented in rocky hillsides, rock piles, rock walls, cornfields, cattle pastures, sugarcane plantations, herbaceous secondary growth vegetation resulting from agricultural practices, and along stream and creek banks within pine-oak forests (Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018). It also appears to prefer edges and open areas in fragmented forest habitats (Ruán et al. 2008). Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis (2018) state that there are currently no details on the adaptation of the species to anthropogenic change. This species feeds mainly on roots and the bases of stems of annual plants and possibly some grasses (Hall and Dalquest 1963). It is considered to be a generalist herbivore (López-Wilchis and Torres-Flores 2005, 2007). These voles live in habitats similar to their northern congeners but have a much reduced litter size. They breed year round, with females producing litters of 1–4 offspring (Ramírez-Pulido et al. 1991).
threats: This species occurs in small populations, has a restricted geographic distribution, and has experienced the destruction and fragmentation of its primary habitat due to urbanisation, agriculture and deforestation (Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018). It has been estimated that 45.7% of its former habitat has been lost (Sánchez-Cordero et al. 2005). The majority of the specimens in collections came from localities in Veracruz; but using a combination of GIS and recent distributional records, revealed that suitable habitat for this species now is restricted to only small areas situated in the main mountain ranges in the central part of the state (Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018). Its status is unknown elsewhere in its range (Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018).
population: Microtus quasiater is an uncommon species with a limited geographic distribution and small populations (Torres-Flores and López-Wilchis 2018). A study conducted by Ramírez-Pulido et al. 1991 reported only 1–26 specimens across 34 localities in suitable habitat. López-Wilchis and Torres-Flores (2005, 2007) conducted extensive surveys with Sherman live traps (300–500 per night) in 19 of the 34 localities reported by Ramírez-Pulido et al. 1991 and in eight other localities, no specimens were captured.
